summary: A vigorous woody climber of China's Yangtze valley forests, brought to New Zealand in 1904 by schoolteacher Isabel Fraser and rebranded 'kiwifruit' in 1959 for export. iNaturalist treats it as a variety of Actinidia chinensis.
nativeRange: Central and south-west China (Shaanxi, Sichuan, Hubei, Henan); cultivated in New Zealand, Italy, Chile and elsewhere
abilities: Dioecious: separate male and female vines; one male pollinates up to about eight females
Flowers produce no nectar, so bees visit only for pollen
Contains actinidin, a protease that tenderises meat and stops gelatin from setting
Twining stems can climb 9 m or more
edibilityNote: Fruit and fuzzy skin are edible. Kiwi allergy is relatively common and can be severe, especially in children; actinidin may make the mouth sore.

uses.use: Fruit to clear heat and quench thirst; root in folk remedies
Two kiwifruit a day shown in trials to ease chronic constipation; EU-authorised claim for normal bowel function (green kiwi)

medicinal.cautions: Common food allergen; cross-reacts with latex, birch pollen and other fruits.

fruit.description: Oval berry 5–8 cm with thin brown skin covered in stiff hairs; bright emerald-green flesh with a pale core ringed by tiny black seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, flattened, oval, black to dark-brown seeds about 1.5–2 mm, arranged in a ring around the white core; over 1,000 per fruit
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks, surface-sow at 20–25 °C; 2–4 weeks. Half of seedlings will be male; fruiting takes 4–7 years

grow.sun: Full sun, with shelter from strong wind
grow.water: High; regular deep watering in summer
grow.propagation: Grafting or cuttings of named female cultivars (e.g. 'Hayward') and male pollinisers
steps: Plant at least one male vine (e.g. 'Tomuri') for every 6–8 female vines (e.g. 'Hayward'), 4–5 m apart.
Build a strong T-bar trellis or pergola about 1.8 m high before planting — mature vines are very heavy.
Train one trunk to the wire, then two permanent arms (cordons) along it; fruiting canes hang from these.
Prune hard in winter, cutting fruited canes back and tying in new canes; summer-prune to control vigour. Protect spring shoots from late frost.
Pick firm in autumn when seeds are black and sugars reach about 6.5 °Brix; ripen in a bag with an apple at room temperature.

lore: The botanist E. H. Wilson collected it in Hubei in 1900, and Isabel Fraser carried seeds home to Whanganui, New Zealand, from a mission school in Yichang in 1904. In 1959 New Zealand exporter Turners & Growers renamed it 'kiwifruit', after the national bird, partly to avoid US tariffs on 'melons' and 'berries'.
funFact: Almost all green kiwifruit sold worldwide is the single cultivar 'Hayward', bred by Hayward Wright in Auckland in the 1920s.

photos.attribution: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez (Lmbuga) (CC BY-SA 3.0), Wikimedia Commons

wiki.extract: Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa, also known as Actinidia deliciosa, green kiwifruit or the fuzzy kiwifruit, is a fruiting vine native to central Southern China, growing naturally at altitudes between 800 and 1,400 metres. The vine was the first commercially available cultivated variety of kiwifruit, and is the source of many of the green varieties of kiwifruit, including the most popular cultivar globally, Hayward, as well as the Chinese cultivars Qinmei, Guichang and Miliang No. 1.

plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a medicinal plant, identified as Yang Tao (羊桃).
plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts the plant 'Yang Tao' (羊桃), featured in Li Shizhen's monumental work, the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica). The illustration serves as a visual guide for identifying the plant, showing its climbing stems, leaves, and root system, which were crucial for practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine.

summary: A plant disguised as a pebble. Each Lithops is just a pair of fat, fused leaves sunk in the ground, with only patterned 'windows' at the top showing. Light enters through these windows and lights up the inside of the leaf, letting it photosynthesise while staying mostly buried.
nativeRange: Grasslands and rocky outcrops of northern South Africa (Gauteng, North West, Free State, Limpopo, Northern Cape) and edges of Botswana
abilities: Camouflages as stones, with colours that match the local rock
Lets light into the leaf through translucent 'windows' on top while the rest of the body stays below ground
Each year grows a new pair of leaves inside the old, which then shrivels and is absorbed
Its seed capsules open only when wet, so raindrops splash seeds out
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

fruit.description: Small capsules that open when wet and close as they dry.

seed.description: Dust-like brown seeds
seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix, keep humid at 15–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.sun: Full sun to very bright light
grow.water: Very low; water in summer and autumn growth, none while old leaves are being absorbed
grow.soil: Mostly mineral grit (pumice, sand) with a little compost
steps: Surface-sow seed on fine grit and cover to hold humidity
Gradually reduce humidity as seedlings grow
Water during summer–autumn growth; stop while new leaves are emerging
Overwatering is the main cause of death: the old leaves split and rot

lore: Named after Thomas Leslie, an amateur botanist who collected it near Pietersburg (now Polokwane) in 1912. Afrikaans farmers called Lithops 'beeskloutjies' because their split shape looks like a cow's hoof print.
funFact: Lithops are so well hidden that many species were found only when the plants were flowering.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts 'Lens Palustris' (water lentil) in its natural environment, shown here as a pond beneath a large stone bridge. The inclusion of a human figure and a detailed landscape is characteristic of the narrative style found in early modern botanical texts, which sought to place plants within their ecological and human contexts.

plates.long: This engraving from Scheuchzer's 'Geestelyke natuurkunde' (1728) illustrates various plant fossils, then known as 'lithophytes'. It reflects the 18th-century scientific effort to document the natural world, often interpreting fossils as evidence of the biblical Deluge.

plates.long: This large-scale woodcut depicts a branch of the 'Pinus Domestica' (Stone Pine), meticulously detailing its long, slender needles and robust cones. Such illustrations were vital in early modern herbals, like those of Pietro Andrea Mattioli, for the accurate identification of plants used in medicine and commerce.

plates.author: Unknown

plates.long: A botanical woodcut depicts several tall plants with oval seed heads growing behind a low, rectangular stone wall. In the foreground, a stylized green patch of earth or water sits before the masonry. The image illustrates the entry for Politricon, or maidenhair fern, used in historical medicine.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut illustrates a section on stones, possibly 'Elochites' as mentioned in the accompanying text. It depicts a cluster of vibrant flowers alongside a rectangular stone, reflecting the early modern practice of categorizing natural specimens by their perceived relationships or properties.

summary: A goosefoot domesticated around Lake Titicaca about 5,000–7,000 years ago, quinoa is not a grass but a 'pseudocereal' related to spinach and beet. It grows at nearly 4,000 m on salty, frosty altiplano soils and its seeds are a complete protein.
nativeRange: Andes of Bolivia and Peru (Lake Titicaca basin), also lowland Chile; now grown in many countries
abilities: Tolerates soil salinity close to that of seawater in some varieties
Survives frost, drought and intense UV at high altitude
Leaves have bladder-like hairs that store salt away from tissues
Seed coats are covered in bitter saponins that deter birds and insects
edibilityNote: Seeds must be rinsed or scrubbed to remove bitter saponins, which irritate the gut. Leaves contain oxalates; eat cooked and in moderation.

uses.use: Seed and leaf poultices for bruises, fractures and inflammation; saponin-rich wash water as soap

compounds: complete protein (all essential amino acids, rich in lysine)
medicinal.cautions: Rinse well to remove saponins; leaves high in oxalate.

fruit.season: Late summer to autumn (5–6 months after sowing)
fruit.description: Large dense seedheads 15–70 cm on stems 1–2 m tall, ripening red, purple, orange, yellow or cream.

seed.description: Small, flattened disc-shaped seeds 1.5–2.5 mm, white, cream, red or black, with a visible pale ring (the embryo) around the edge, coated in a powdery bitter saponin layer
seed.germination: Very fast: sow shallow (1 cm) in cool soil at 5–20 °C; sprouts in 1–4 days, even in a dish of water

grow.zones: Annual; best in regions where summer days stay below about 32 °C
grow.soil: Well-drained, tolerates poor, sandy and saline soils, pH 6–8.5
steps: Sow in spring when soil reaches about 7–10 °C, 1 cm deep, in rows 40–50 cm apart; thin to 15–20 cm.
Weed carefully in early weeks — seedlings look like the weed lamb's quarters, its close relative.
Water lightly; heavy watering and humid heat (over 32 °C) at flowering cause pollen sterility.
Harvest when leaves drop and seeds can be rubbed out of the head with a fingernail, before autumn rain.
Dry heads fully, rub over a screen, winnow, and wash seeds repeatedly in water until no foam forms.

lore: The Inca called quinoa 'chisiya mama', mother of all grains, and the emperor is said to have sown the first seeds of each season with a golden tool. Spanish colonists discouraged its cultivation because of its role in Andean rituals.
funFact: The United Nations declared 2013 the International Year of Quinoa.

wiki.extract: Quinoa is a flowering plant in the amaranth family. It is a herbaceous annual plant grown as a crop primarily for its edible seeds; the seeds are high in protein, dietary fiber, B vitamins and dietary minerals especially potassium and magnesium in amounts greater than in many grains. Quinoa is not a grass but rather a pseudocereal botanically related to spinach and amaranth, and originated in the Andean region of northwestern South America. It was first used to feed livestock 5,200–7,000 years ago, and for human consumption 3,000–4,000 years ago in the Lake Titicaca basin of Bolivia and Peru.

plates.long: This engraving from Joseph Pitton de Tournefort's 1719 work 'Institutiones rei herbariae' depicts the reproductive and structural components of four plant genera. Tournefort's systematic approach to plant classification, which emphasized the structure of flowers and fruits, was a critical precursor to the modern botanical taxonomy later refined by Carl Linnaeus.

summary: A bulb so long domesticated that most varieties no longer set seed, propagated clove by clove for over five thousand years. Its sharp smell forms only when the cells are crushed, as a chemical defence.
nativeRange: Derived from wild Allium in Central Asia (Tian Shan region); known only in cultivation
abilities: Crushing mixes alliin with the enzyme alliinase to make allicin, a pungent antimicrobial defence compound
Most cultivars are sterile, making tiny bulbils in the flower head instead of seed
Needs a winter chill to divide into cloves
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. Toxic to dogs and cats, causing anaemia. Garlic stored in oil at room temperature can grow botulism bacteria.

uses.use: Lashuna as a rasayana for heart, joints, cough and worms; the Bower Manuscript opens with its praise
Thum used for chest complaints, as an antidote to poisons, and as an aphrodisiac
Dasuan to kill parasites, treat dysentery and reduce swellings
Raw cloves and syrups for colds, infections and 'thinning the blood'

medicinal.cautions: Meta-analyses show modest falls in blood pressure and cholesterol. High intake increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants and before surgery, and lowers blood levels of some HIV drugs such as saquinavir. Raw garlic on the skin can cause chemical burns.

seed.description: Most cultivars do not produce true seed; flower heads carry bulbils
seed.dispersal: Human propagation of cloves and bulbils
seed.germination: Plant cloves instead

steps: Plant cloves pointed end up, 5 cm deep and 15 cm apart, in autumn
Mulch over winter and weed in spring
Snap off flower scapes of hardneck types to grow larger bulbs
Lift when the lower third of the leaves have browned; cure in an airy place for 2–3 weeks

lore: Herodotus wrote that an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded the radishes, onions and garlic given to the builders. The Bower Manuscript, a Sanskrit medical collection of the late 5th or early 6th century CE found near Kucha, opens with a treatise on garlic that tells the legend of its origin.
funFact: Medieval Europeans called garlic 'the poor man's treacle', from theriac, the costly universal antidote.

wiki.extract: Garlic is a species of bulbous flowering plants in the genus Allium. Its close relatives include the onion, shallot, leek, chives, Welsh onion, and Chinese onion. Garlic is native to Central Asia, northeastern Iran and the foothills of Himalayas. It has naturalized in many other parts of the world, including Mediterranean Europe and China. There are two subspecies and hundreds of varieties of garlic.

plates.title: Notable Commentaries on the History of Plants
plates.author: Leonhart Fuchs
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of Allium sativum (garlic)
plates.long: A botanical illustration of a garlic plant, identified as Allium hortense and Gartenknoblouch. The woodcut shows the underground bulb with fibrous roots and long, slender leaves rising vertically. This image represents the standard Renaissance method for documenting medicinal flora.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica) depicts the garlic plant (Allium sativum), known in Chinese as suan or hu. The drawing clearly shows the bulbous root, long leaves, and a developing flower stalk, serving as a vital visual aid for identifying medicinal herbs in 16th-century China.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts Victorialis longa, known today as Allium victorialis or Victory Onion. Produced for Carolus Clusius's seminal work on the flora of Pannonia, it represents the Renaissance shift toward empirical botanical study, meticulously documenting the plant's anatomy from its fibrous bulb to its flowering head.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts a leek (Allium porrum), identified by the Latin 'Porrum' and German 'Lauch'. It is part of the 'Herbarius latinus', one of the most influential early printed herbals, which provided both botanical descriptions and medicinal uses for various plants in the late 15th century.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1486 'Herbarius latinus' depicts a garlic plant (Allium), identified by the German synonym 'knoblach' below. Such illustrations were essential in early printed herbals for the identification of medicinal plants, representing a transition from manuscript traditions to the standardized dissemination of botanical knowledge.

plates.long: This page features two woodcut illustrations of garlic varieties: garden garlic (Allium hortense) and wild garlic (Sylvestre). These images served as essential visual aids for identifying medicinal plants in Dioscorides' influential pharmacopeia, 'De medicinali materia'.

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of Allium sive Moly montanum II
plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts 'Allium sive Moly montanum II', a species of wild onion or garlic. It is a characteristic example of the scientific accuracy sought by Carolus Clusius in his 1583 study of Pannonian flora, illustrating the plant's entire structure from its fibrous roots and bulb to its distinctive flowering head.

plates.long: This finely detailed engraving depicts three flowering bulbous plants: a tulip (Tulipa), a fritillary (Fritillaria), and wild garlic (Allium ursinum). Each specimen is rendered with scientific precision, showing the complete anatomy from the fibrous roots and bulb to the delicate petals and foliage. Such illustrations were central to the 'florilegium' tradition of the 17th century, which celebrate

plates.author: Macer Floridus (Odo of Meung)
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of garlic bulbs within a double-line border.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts garlic (Allium sativum), a plant long valued for its culinary and medicinal properties. Featured in an early herbal, the illustration serves as a practical guide for identification, showing both the whole bulb and individual cloves. Such images were essential in early modern medicine for documenting the 'materia medica' used by physicians and apothecaries.

gerard.title: Of Garlick
gerard.names: It is called in Latine Allium: in Greeke σκοροδον: the apothecaries keepe the Latine name: the Germanes call it Knoblauch; the low Dutch Look: the Spaniards Aios, Alho: the Italians Aglio: the French Ail or Aux: the Bohemians Czesnek: the English Garlicke and poore mens Treacle.
gerard.place: Garlick is seldome sowen of seede, but planted in gardens of the small cloues in Nouember and December, and sometimes in Februarie and March.
gerard.temperature: Garlick is very sharpe, hot, and drie, as Galen saith, in the fourth degree, and exulcerateth the skin by raising of blisters.
gerard.vertues: Being eaten it heateth the bodie extremely, attenuateth and maketh thin, thicke and grosse humors; cutteth such as are tough and clammie, digesteth and consumeth them, also openeth obstructions, is an enimie to all colde poisons, and to the bitings of venemous beasts: and therefore Galen nameth it Theriaca rusticorum, or the husbandmans Treacle. It yeeldeth to the body no nourishment at all, it engendreth naughtie and sharpe blood. Therefore such as are of a hot complexion must especially abstaine from it. But if it be boiled in water vntill such time as it hath lost his sharpnes, it is the lesse forcible, and retaineth no longer his euill iuice, iuice, as Galen writeth. It taketh away the roughnes of the throte, it helpeth an old cough, it prouoketh vrine, it breaketh the stone, and consumeth winde, it is a remedie for the dropsie proceeding of a colde cause. It killeth wormes in the belly, and driueth them foorth. The milke also wherein it hath been sodden, is giuen to yoong children with good successe against the wormes.

summary: A sprawling tree from north-east Brazil whose kidney-shaped nut hangs beneath a juicy, swollen 'cashew apple'. The nut's shell holds a caustic oil related to poison ivy's urushiol, so every cashew sold must be roasted or steamed before shelling.
nativeRange: North-eastern Brazil; spread by the Portuguese to India and Africa in the 16th century; grown throughout the tropics
abilities: The true fruit is the nut; the 'apple' is a swollen flower stalk (hypocarp)
Shell oil (CNSL) is rich in anacardic acid and cardol, which blister skin
Thrives on poor sandy soils and resists drought
The Pirangi cashew tree in Brazil covers roughly 7,500–8,400 m², spreading from a single trunk
edibleParts: kernel (after roasting/steaming to remove shell oil)
cashew apple (fresh, juiced, fermented into feni)
edibilityNote: Raw cashew nuts in the shell are not safe: the shell oil causes severe burns and dermatitis, and roasting fumes irritate the lungs. 'Raw' cashews in shops have already been steamed. Cashew is a common, sometimes severe, tree-nut allergen.

uses.use: Bark tea for diarrhoea; cashew-apple juice for coughs and as a tonic
Shell oil applied to warts and corns

medicinal.cautions: Shell oil is caustic; tree-nut allergy; cross-reactivity with mango and pistachio.

fruit.season: Dry season (e.g. February–May in India and West Africa)
fruit.description: A pear-shaped, glossy red or yellow cashew apple 5–10 cm, juicy and astringent; from its tip hangs a single grey-green, kidney-shaped nut 3 cm long.

seed.description: The kernel is pale ivory, curved, kidney-shaped, about 2.5–3 cm, inside a hard grey-brown double shell filled with dark caustic oil
seed.dispersal: Bats and birds carry the apple and drop the nut
seed.germination: Sow whole nuts (in shell) fresh, 3–5 cm deep, stalk-end up, at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Wear gloves

grow.water: Low–moderate; a dry season is needed for flowering
grow.soil: Deep sandy or lateritic soils, well-drained, pH 4.5–6.5
grow.propagation: Seed (nut), or softwood grafting of high-yielding clones
grow.timeToHarvest: 3 years from graft; 3–5 years from seed
steps: Sow nuts directly where the tree will grow (it dislikes transplanting), or plant a grafted dwarf clone.
Space 7–10 m apart in full sun; keep weeds down around young plants.
Water young trees during the first dry seasons only; mature trees need no irrigation.
Prune low branches and dead wood after harvest.
Collect fallen fruit, twist the nut from the apple, and sun-dry the nuts; roast or steam them in shells (outdoors, with gloves) before cracking.

lore: The French monk André Thevet drew the cashew in 1558, and Portuguese traders introduced it to Goa, where cashew-apple juice is distilled into the spirit feni. The Pirangi tree near Natal, Brazil, planted around 1888, is billed as the world's largest cashew.
funFact: Cashews are almost never sold in their shells, because the shell is lined with a caustic resin related to poison ivy's urushiol.

wiki.extract: Cashew is the common name of a tropical evergreen tree Anacardium occidentale, in the family Anacardiaceae. It is the source of the cashew nut and the cashew apple. The tree can grow as tall as 14 meters.

plates.title: Tractado de las Drogas y Medicinas de las Indias Orientales
plates.author: Cristóvão da Costa
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a cashew plant (Anacardium occidentale) showing leaves, flowers, and fruit.
plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts the cashew plant, known here as 'Caius', illustrating its distinctive fruit and nut. It is a plate from Cristóvão da Costa's 1578 treatise on the drugs and medicines of the East Indies, representing an early European effort to scientifically document tropical botany.

plates.desc: A detailed botanical illustration of a cashew branch (Anacardium occidentale) showing leaves, flowers, and fruit.
plates.long: A botanical study of a cashew branch featuring large green leaves and clusters of small pink flowers. The illustration depicts several fleshy cashew apples in shades of red and yellow, each with a kidney-shaped nut attached to its base. It captures the unique relationship between the accessory fruit and the true seed of the Anacardium occidentale.

plates.title: Flora Sinensis (Chinese-Latin Natural History)
plates.author: Michał Boym
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of a cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale) with detailed views of its fruit and leaves, accompanied by Chinese characters and Latin transliterations.
plates.long: This detailed engraving from Michał Boym's 1656 'Flora Sinensis' illustrates the cashew tree, providing one of the earliest European scientific records of the species in Asia. The plate uniquely combines Western botanical observation with Chinese nomenclature, featuring both the tree's overall form and close-up views of the cashew apple and nut.

plates.title: De Indiae utriusque re naturali et medica
plates.author: Willem Piso
plates.desc: Botanical engravings of cashew nuts (Anacardium occidentale) showing different perspectives and cross-sections.
plates.long: These detailed engravings illustrate the cashew nut (Anacardium occidentale), a fruit native to northeastern Brazil. Featured in a 17th-century natural history treatise, these scientific renderings document the unique morphology of the nut and its fleshy receptacle for European audiences, reflecting the era's expansion of botanical knowledge.

plates.title: The Natural History of Carolina Florida and Bahama Islands Vol. 2
plates.author: Mark Catesby
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of a cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale) showing leaves, flowers, and fruit.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), showcasing its distinctive fruit structure where the nut grows outside the fleshy 'apple.' Mark Catesby's work was pioneering in documenting the flora and fauna of the Americas, combining scientific accuracy with artistic elegance.

plates.title: Mark Catesby — Piscium, serpentum, insectorum (pt. 2) (1777)
plates.author: Mark Catesby
plates.desc: Detailed botanical illustration of a cashew plant (Anacardium occidentale) showing leaves, flowers, and fruit.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's 'Piscium, serpentum, insectorum' depicts the cashew plant (Anacardium occidentale). The illustration meticulously details the plant's anatomy, including its broad leaves, delicate pink flowers, and the distinctive fleshy 'apple' (hypocarp) with the kidney-shaped nut (drupe) attached below.

plates.title: Berthe Hoola van Nooten — Fleurs, fruits et feuillages choisis de la flore et de la pomone de Java (1863)
plates.author: Berthe Hoola van Nooten
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), showing a branch with leaves, ripe cashew apples, and nuts, along with detailed floral dissections at the bottom.
plates.long: This exquisite chromolithograph by Berthe Hoola van Nooten depicts the cashew tree, Anacardium occidentale, native to the tropics. The composition combines a lush, life-sized rendering of the fruit-bearing branch with precise, monochromatic botanical dissections, reflecting the 19th-century scientific endeavor to document the biodiversity of Java.

plates.title: A key to physic, and the occult sciences
plates.author: Sibly, Ebenezer
plates.desc: Hand-colored botanical engraving of a cashew nut tree branch.
plates.long: A botanical illustration shows a branch of a cashew tree with large oval leaves and clusters of small pink flowers at the top. Several large, pear-shaped reddish fruits called cashew apples hang from the branch, each with a single kidney-shaped nut attached to its base. The plate identifies the plant as 'The Cashew Nutt Tree' and includes the names of the artist Dodd and the engraver Pass.

plates.title: Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium
plates.author: Maria Sibylla Merian
plates.desc: Botanical and entomological study of a cashew plant with insects
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 masterpiece depicts the life cycle of a butterfly on a cashew plant (Anacardium occidentale). Merian was a pioneer in observing and documenting insect metamorphosis in their natural habitats in Suriname, blending rigorous scientific observation with exquisite artistic composition.

plates.desc: Botanical engraving of tropical fruit trees including cashew (Cajus), jackfruit (Iaquas), and ginger (Gember).
plates.long: A botanical engraving shows several species of tropical plants and their fruits in a landscape setting. Labeled specimens include a cashew tree (Cajus), a jackfruit tree (Iaquas), and ginger plants (Gember) in the foreground. The illustration depicts the natural growth habits and fruit structures of these East Indian species.

summary: Domesticated in South Asia over 4,000 years ago, the mango is the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines. A long-lived evergreen that can exceed 30 m, it bears hundreds of fruit a year and some trees are known to fruit for over 300 years.
nativeRange: Indo-Burma region: north-east India, Bangladesh, Myanmar; cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Polyembryonic varieties produce several seedlings from one seed, most of them genetic clones of the mother tree
Flowers in huge panicles of up to several thousand tiny blossoms, pollinated mainly by flies
Deep taproot lets mature trees survive long dry seasons
Sap contains urushiol-like resorcinols, related to the irritant in poison ivy
edibleParts: young leaves (cooked, in parts of Southeast Asia)
edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is safe. Skin and sap contain urushiol-related compounds that cause contact dermatitis around the mouth in sensitive people, especially those allergic to poison ivy or cashew. Burning mango wood releases irritant smoke.

uses.use: Bark, leaves and seed kernel used as astringents for diarrhoea and bleeding; unripe fruit drink (aam panna) against heatstroke
Stem-bark extract (Vimang) developed as an antioxidant supplement

medicinal.cautions: Sap and peel can cause dermatitis; cross-reactivity with cashew, pistachio and poison ivy.

fruit.season: Spring to summer (March–August in South Asia)
fruit.description: Oval to kidney-shaped drupe 5–25 cm long, green ripening to yellow, orange or red-blushed; juicy, fragrant orange flesh around a large fibrous stone.

seed.description: Single large flattened oval seed enclosed in a hard, fibrous, hairy whitish husk (the stone); the kernel inside is kidney-shaped, cream to pale brown, 4–7 cm long
seed.dispersal: Large mammals (bats, monkeys, elephants) and humans; seeds are recalcitrant and die if dried
seed.germination: Sow fresh within days of eating; remove husk and plant kernel 2–3 cm deep, hump up; sprouts in 2–4 weeks at 25–30 °C

grow.water: Moderate; a dry season before flowering improves fruit set
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained; tolerates sandy and lateritic soils, pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Veneer or cleft grafting onto seedling rootstock; polyembryonic seed comes true
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 6–10 years from seed; fruit ripens 100–150 days after flowering
steps: Choose a grafted tree of a variety suited to your climate (e.g. 'Kent' or 'Nam Doc Mai' for humid areas resistant to anthracnose).
Plant in the warmest, sunniest spot available, at least 8 m from buildings; do not amend the planting hole heavily.
Water regularly for the first two years, then reduce watering in the 2–3 months before flowering to induce bloom.
Prune after harvest to keep the canopy open and low (3–4 m) for easier picking and less fungal disease.
Pick when the shoulders fill out and the flesh near the stem yields slightly; ripen at room temperature.

lore: Mughal emperor Akbar planted the Lakhi Bagh, an orchard of 100,000 mango trees near Darbhanga, and the Buddha is said to have rested in a mango grove gifted by the courtesan Amrapali. In Hindu tradition mango leaves are strung over doorways (toran) at festivals and weddings.
funFact: Mango, cashew and pistachio are botanical cousins — and all three are relatives of poison ivy.

wiki.extract: Mangifera indica, commonly known as the mango tree after its fruit, is an evergreen species of flowering plant in the family Anacardiaceae. It is a large fruit tree, capable of growing to a height and width of 30 m (100 ft). There are two distinct genetic populations in modern mangoes – the "Indian type" and the "Southeast Asian type".

plates.title: Berthe Hoola van Nooten — Fleurs, fruits et feuillages choisis de la flore et de la pomone de Java (1863)
plates.author: Berthe Hoola van Nooten
plates.desc: Botanical chromolithograph of Mangifera indica (Mango) showing fruit, leaves, flower, and seed.
plates.long: A botanical study of the mango tree, Mangifera indica, featuring a branch with dark green leaves and two large ripening fruits. Above the main branch, two smaller figures illustrate a single white flower and the fibrous texture of the internal seed. The plate was painted from nature in Batavia and printed as a chromolithograph in Brussels.

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a mango plant (Mangas) showing leaves, flowers, a cross-section of the fruit, and a seed.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the mango tree (Mangas), detailing its lanceolate leaves, clusters of small flowers, and the internal structure of its fruit and seed. Published in Cristóvão da Costa's 1578 treatise, it represents an early European scientific effort to document and categorize the medicinal and economic plants of the East Indies.

It provides a detailed visual guide to the plant's morphology, including its leaves and fruit, which was essential for practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine to correctly identify and utilize the species for its medicinal properti

plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a mango tree (Anluole).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the mango tree, referred to in the text as 'Anluole'. It is featured in the 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica), the most comprehensive medical book ever written in the history of traditional Chinese medicine. Such illustrations were vital for the accurate identification of plants used for their therapeutic properties.

plates.author: 吳其濬
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut illustration of a mango branch with leaves and fruit.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a mango branch, labeled as 'Shuiguo' (檨果), from the 1848 botanical compendium Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao. The work is renowned for its scientific accuracy and detailed line drawings, which served as a primary reference for plant identification in 19th-century China.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a mango branch with fruits and leaves.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Anluoguo' (mango), characterized by its large, rounded fruit and elongated leaves. It is an illustration from Wu Qijun's 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' (1848), a monumental work in Chinese botany that combined traditional herbal knowledge with meticulous observational drawings.

summary: A tough desert tree of Central Asia, related to cashew and mango, whose nut shells split open as they ripen — the 'smiling nut' of Iran and 'happy nut' of China. Wild stands in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan are declining and assessed Near Threatened.
nativeRange: Central Asia: north-east Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Kyrgyzstan; cultivated in Iran, Turkey, the US, Syria and the Mediterranean
abilities: Survives summer heat above 40 °C and winter cold below −20 °C
Tolerates saline irrigation water better than most nut crops
Dioecious and wind-pollinated: one male tree serves about 8–10 females
Bears in alternate heavy and light years
edibleParts: kernel (raw, roasted, in sweets like baklava)
edibilityNote: Kernels are safe; pistachio is a tree-nut allergen and cross-reacts with cashew. Poorly stored or damaged nuts can carry aflatoxin, and bulk-stored nuts can self-heat and ignite.

uses.use: Nuts as a tonic for the heart, liver and brain; resin of related species (mastic) for the stomach
Pistachio intake associated in trials with improved blood lipids

medicinal.cautions: Tree-nut allergy (cashew cross-reactivity); aflatoxin risk in damaged nuts.

fruit.description: Oval drupe 2–2.5 cm in grape-like clusters, with a thin rosy-pink to red-tinged hull over a cream, hard shell that splits along its seam when ripe.

seed.description: Elongated, green to yellow-green kernel 1.5–2 cm with a thin purplish-red papery skin, inside a smooth beige shell that gapes open
seed.germination: Remove shell, soak 24 hours, cold-stratify 4–6 weeks, sow at 20–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.water: Low; deep, infrequent irrigation improves yield
grow.soil: Deep, very well-drained sandy loam; tolerates alkaline and saline soils, pH 7–8
grow.propagation: Budding female cultivars ('Kerman', 'Ahmad Aghaei') and males ('Peters') onto P. atlantica, P. integerrima or UCB-1 rootstock
steps: Check that you have long, hot, dry summers (pistachios need heat to ripen) and at least 800 chill hours in winter.
Plant one male tree for every 8–10 females, upwind, in deep, perfectly drained soil.
Water deeply but rarely; mature trees need little water but crop better with irrigation.
Train to an open vase in the first years, then prune lightly in winter.
Shake ripe nuts from the tree when hulls slip easily from the shells, hull and dry within 24 hours to prevent staining and mould.

lore: Pistachios were found at the Neolithic site of Jarmo in Iraq, about 6750 BCE, and legend says the Queen of Sheba reserved them for herself and her court. Iran's Rafsanjan region has been a famed pistachio centre for centuries.
funFact: Large stockpiles of pistachios can self-heat and even spontaneously combust, so shippers treat them as a fire risk in cargo holds.

wiki.extract: The pistachio is a small to medium-sized tree of the cashew family. The tree produces seeds that are widely consumed as food. Pistachios can be used as an ingredient in desserts, chocolate, candy, ice cream, and as a paste or butter. As a tree nut, pistachios are considered a priority allergen that may induce allergic reactions in susceptible people.

plates.long: This woodcut from Carolus Clusius's 1601 botanical treatise depicts the Terebinth tree (Pistacia terebinthus). It accurately illustrates the plant's pinnate leaves and the distinctive horn-shaped galls often found on its branches, which were of significant interest to early modern naturalists for their medicinal properties.

The clear, linear style of the woodcut was essential for identifying species in an era before photography.

otherNames: Tsuta-urushi ツタウルシ (Japanese, for East Asian forms)
summary: A vine, shrub or ground cover whose oily resin, urushiol, causes an itchy, blistering rash in most people. Urushiol stays active on clothes, tools and pet fur for a long time. To wildlife it is a valuable plant: dozens of bird species eat its pale berries in winter.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean; related forms in East Asia
abilities: Produces urushiol, which triggers allergic contact dermatitis in most people
Grows as a ground cover, shrub or high-climbing vine with hairy aerial roots
Feeds songbirds, woodpeckers and wild turkeys with fat-rich winter berries
Grows faster and makes more potent urushiol under higher CO₂, experiments show
edibilityNote: All parts contain urushiol: leaves, stems, roots and berries, in all seasons, even dead plants. Touching causes an itchy red rash with blisters 12–72 hours later. Burning it releases urushiol in smoke, which can cause severe lung and eye inflammation. Eating any part is dangerous. Lookalikes: Virginia creeper (five leaflets), boxelder seedlings, fragrant sumac and young raspberry or blackberry; 'leaves of three, let it be' is a good guide. Wash skin with soap and cool water soon after contact.

fruit.description: Clusters of small, waxy, greyish-white berries.

seed.description: Ribbed stone inside the berry
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Captain John Smith described it at Jamestown in 1609, comparing it to English ivy and recording that it caused 'redness, itchiness, and lastly blisters'. Urushiol is named after urushi, the lacquer from the related Asian lacquer tree.
funFact: In a Duke University experiment, poison ivy grown at elevated CO₂ grew bigger and made a more allergenic form of urushiol.

wiki.extract: Toxicodendron radicans, commonly known as eastern poison ivy or poison ivy, is a species of allergenic flowering plant. It has numerous subtaxons and forms both vines and shrubs. Despite its common name, it is not a true ivy, but rather a member of the cashew and sumac family, Anacardiaceae. It is different from western poison ivy, Toxicodendron rydbergii, and resembles a number of species.

otherNames: Hassomin (Algonquian, origin of the genus name)
summary: The largest edible fruit native to the United States, a temperate member of the tropical custard-apple family. Its maroon flowers smell faintly of rotting meat to attract carrion flies and beetles, and its fruit tastes of banana, mango and custard.
nativeRange: Eastern United States and southern Ontario, from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast
abilities: Forms clonal thickets (patches) by root suckers
Leaves and bark contain acetogenins that deter most herbivores and insects
Pawpaws and their Asimina relatives are the only host plants for zebra swallowtail caterpillars, which store their toxins for defence
Flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles drawn to a fermenting, yeasty scent
edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is eaten fresh or frozen. Skin and seeds contain annonaceous acetogenins and should not be eaten; seeds are toxic if chewed. Some people get stomach upset or skin rashes from handling the fruit.

uses.tradition: Cherokee and other Indigenous American medicine
uses.use: Seeds and bark preparations used to treat lice and as an emetic
Twig extract acetogenins (asimicin) studied for pesticidal and anticancer activity in the lab

medicinal.cautions: Annonacin is a neurotoxin linked to atypical parkinsonism in heavy consumers of related Annona fruit; avoid seeds, skin and concentrated extracts.

fruit.description: Oblong, slightly kidney-shaped berry 5–16 cm, green ripening to yellowish with dark flecks, often in clusters; soft, custardy, pale-yellow to orange flesh.

seed.description: Large, flattened, bean-like seeds 2–3 cm long, glossy dark brown, in two rows of 10–14 inside the fruit
seed.dispersal: Raccoons, opossums, foxes, bears and formerly megafauna
seed.germination: Never let seeds dry; cold-stratify moist for 90–120 days, then sow 2–3 cm deep in deep pots at 25 °C. Shoots emerge slowly (6–10 weeks) after a long taproot forms

grow.sun: Shade when young (first 1–2 years); full sun for best fruiting
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, moist but well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–7)
grow.propagation: Seed (after cold stratification), or grafting named cultivars ('Shenandoah', 'Susquehanna', 'Sunflower')
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from graft; 5–8 years from seed
steps: Plant at least two genetically different trees (two grafted cultivars or seedlings), as pawpaws are self-incompatible.
Use container-grown plants — the long taproot resents digging — and shade them with a tube or cloth for the first summer.
Keep soil moist and mulched; feed lightly with compost.
If fruit set is poor, hand-pollinate with a small brush, or hang rotting meat or fish nearby to attract flies (a traditional trick).
Pick when fruit gives gently like a ripe peach and smells fruity; eat within 2–3 days or freeze the pulp.

lore: In 1541 the de Soto expedition found Native Americans growing and eating what was probably pawpaw east of the Mississippi, and Lewis and Clark relied on pawpaws when food ran short in 1806. A popular but undocumented story makes chilled pawpaw George Washington's favourite dessert.
funFact: Pawpaw is the largest fruit native to North America, sometimes reaching 0.5 kg.

wiki.extract: Asimina triloba, the American papaw, pawpaw, paw paw, or paw-paw, among many regional names, is a species of small deciduous tree. It has large leaves and produces a large, yellowish-green to brown fruit.

summary: A creeping herb of damp tropical ground with kidney-shaped leaves, eaten as salad and juice from Sri Lanka to Vietnam. Its triterpenes are used in wound-healing and scar creams.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa (including Madagascar), Australia and the western Pacific
abilities: Asiaticoside and madecassoside stimulate collagen synthesis in wound and scar models
Spreads quickly by runners, rooting at each node to form a ground carpet
Thrives in waterlogged and semi-shaded ground
edibilityNote: Eaten raw in Sri Lankan gotu kola sambol, as Thai bai bua bok juice and as Vietnamese rau má drink. Wash well and avoid plants from polluted water.

uses.use: Mandukaparni as a medhya rasayana for memory and as a remedy for skin disease and wounds
Jixuecao clears heat and damp, for jaundice, heatstroke, bruising and swellings
Used in Madagascar and elsewhere for leprosy sores, wounds and skin complaints
Titrated extract for chronic venous insufficiency; topical creams (e.g. Madécassol) for wounds and scars

medicinal.cautions: Rare liver injury has been reported with oral products. May cause drowsiness and add to sedatives. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Small, flattened, ribbed fruit splitting into two mericarps.

seed.description: Small flattened mericarps
seed.dispersal: Water and soil; mostly spreads by runners
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; runners are easier

steps: Plant rooted runner sections in moist, rich soil
Keep constantly damp and lightly shaded
Harvest outer leaves with stalks regularly
Grow in a container or contained bed to stop it spreading

lore: Jixuecao is listed in the Shennong Bencao Jing, and mandukaparni in the Charaka Samhita. The French pharmaceutical name Madécassol comes from 'Madécasse', the old French word for Madagascar, an early supply source.
funFact: Despite looking like a tiny lily pad, gotu kola belongs to the carrot family, Apiaceae.

wiki.extract: Centella asiatica, commonly known as Indian pennywort, Asiatic pennywort, spadeleaf, coinwort or gotu kola, is a herbaceous, perennial plant in the flowering plant family Apiaceae. It is native to tropical regions of Africa, Asia, Australia, and islands in the western Pacific Ocean. It is consumed as a culinary vegetable and is used in traditional medicine.

summary: Often called the most toxic plant in North America. Water hemlock's thick, chambered roots contain cicutoxin, which triggers violent seizures within as little as 15 minutes. A piece of root the size of a walnut can kill a 550 kg cow, and people have died after eating only small amounts.
nativeRange: Most of North America, from Canada to Mexico
abilities: Makes cicutoxin, which blocks GABA-A receptors in the brain and causes uncontrolled seizures
Stores most toxin in thickened, chambered roots that ooze yellowish oily liquid when cut
Grows in wet ground where it can be confused with edible wetland plants
Is toxic enough to kill cattle that eat a few roots exposed by ploughing or flooding
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, most of all the roots and stem base, especially in spring. Symptoms within 15–60 minutes: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, frothing at the mouth, then violent seizures, irregular heartbeat and death from respiratory failure; survivors may have lasting muscle and memory problems. Lookalikes: water parsnip (Sium suave), wild parsnip, wild carrot, angelica, cow parsnip and edible wetland roots. Key sign: chambered (hollow with cross-walls) root crown and leaf veins ending in the notches between teeth rather than at the tips.

fruit.description: Small round ribbed fruits in loose umbels.

seed.description: Small corky-ribbed mericarps
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Colonial writers and Indigenous traditions alike recorded water hemlock as a deadly poison, and it was a long-feared killer of cattle on the American frontier, where roots exposed by spring floods or ploughing were eaten by stock.
funFact: Children have been poisoned by using the hollow stems as peashooters or whistles.

summary: The poison that killed Socrates. Poison hemlock looks like a tall, lacy wild carrot or parsley, but every part contains coniine and related alkaloids that paralyse muscles from the legs upward, ending in respiratory failure while the mind stays clear.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; invasive in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Makes piperidine alkaloids (coniine, γ-coniceine) that block nicotinic receptors at the nerve–muscle junction
Grows as a biennial to 2–3 m tall, forming dense stands along ditches
Gives off a musty, mouse-like smell when crushed, from its alkaloids
Coniine was the first alkaloid ever synthesised in a lab (by Albert Ladenburg, 1886)
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, especially seeds and roots; leaves are most toxic in spring before flowering. Symptoms begin 30 minutes to a few hours after eating: burning mouth, salivation, dilated pupils, tremors, then ascending muscle paralysis, slowing heart and death from respiratory failure. Lookalikes: wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace (hairy stem, no purple blotches, carrot smell), parsley, chervil, fennel, cow parsley and wild parsnip. Key signs of hemlock: smooth hollow stem with purple-red blotches and a mousy smell. Even handling can irritate; wash after contact.

uses.use: Applied externally for tumours and swellings and as a sedative; used in Athens as a method of execution

medicinal.cautions: Deadly; no safe home use.

fruit.description: Small, grey-brown ribbed fruits with wavy ridges, in umbels.

seed.description: Ridged mericarps, ~2–3 mm
seed.germination: Not for cultivation; controlled as a noxious weed in many places

lore: Plato's Phaedo describes Socrates' death in 399 BCE after drinking hemlock, the numbness creeping upward from his feet. Hemlock was named among the ingredients of the witches' brew in Macbeth: 'Root of hemlock digg'd i' the dark'.
funFact: Migrating quail that eat hemlock seeds have reportedly poisoned people who ate the birds, a syndrome called coturnism.

summary: A monster of a plant up to about 5 m tall, with umbrella flower heads up to a metre across, introduced to Europe and North America as a Victorian ornamental. Its sap makes skin dangerously sensitive to sunlight, causing burns and blisters that can scar for years.
nativeRange: Western Greater Caucasus; invasive across Europe, Canada and the northern United States
abilities: Its sap contains furanocoumarins that bind DNA when struck by UV light, causing phytophotodermatitis
Grows to about 5 m tall with umbels up to a metre across
Produces thousands of seeds per plant (often around 20,000), which spread along rivers
Lives several years as a leafy rosette, then flowers once and dies
edibilityNote: The sap in all parts, especially stems and leaves, contains furanocoumarins (e.g. bergapten, psoralens). On skin followed by sunlight, it causes burns and blisters within 24–48 hours, leaving dark patches and sensitivity for months or years; sap in eyes can cause temporary or lasting blindness. Do not eat any part. Lookalikes: native cow parsnip (Heracleum maximum or H. sphondylium), angelica, wild parsnip and poison hemlock. If exposed, wash immediately and keep out of sunlight for 48 hours.

fruit.description: Flat, oval, ribbed fruits with brown oil channels.

seed.description: Flat oval mericarps
seed.dispersal: Wind and water, often along rivers
seed.germination: Do not plant: it is a legally controlled invasive species in many countries

lore: Seeds from the Caucasus were listed at Kew Gardens in 1817 and it was planted in Victorian gardens as a spectacle. Genesis recorded 'The Return of the Giant Hogweed' (1971), a mock-epic about the plant taking revenge on Britain.
funFact: It is named after Paolo Mantegazza, a 19th-century Italian physician, physiologist and anthropologist.

summary: A tough little pink-and-white bedding plant from Madagascar that yields vinblastine and vincristine. These cancer drugs helped turn childhood leukaemia from almost always fatal to usually curable.
nativeRange: Endemic to Madagascar; naturalised throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Makes more than 130 terpenoid indole alkaloids, including vinblastine and vincristine, which block cell division
Flowers almost continuously in warm climates
Tolerates drought, heat, salt spray and poor sandy soil
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous. Ingestion can cause low blood pressure, nerve damage and suppression of blood-cell production. Toxic to pets.

uses.use: Decoctions for diabetes, fevers, menstrual problems and as a bitter tonic
Leaf tea taken for diabetes, which led to its scientific investigation
Sadabahar leaves chewed or brewed for diabetes and wounds
Vinblastine (Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular cancer) and vincristine (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and other cancers) as chemotherapy

medicinal.cautions: The isolated drugs are hospital chemotherapy with serious toxicity; injecting vincristine into the spine by mistake is fatal. Do not use the plant to treat diabetes or cancer: it is poisonous and its blood-sugar effect is unproven.

fruit.description: Pair of narrow, cylindrical follicles, 2–4 cm, splitting along one side.

seed.description: Small, black, grooved seeds
seed.dispersal: Gravity and ants; self-sows in warm gardens
seed.germination: Cover (needs darkness); 1–3 weeks at 24–28 °C

grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained; dislikes cold wet soil
steps: Sow in warm conditions, lightly covered
Plant out after nights stay above 15 °C
Water only when dry; overwatering causes root rot
Keep away from pets and children

lore: In the 1950s Robert Noble and Charles Beer at the University of Western Ontario tested leaves sent from Jamaica as a diabetes remedy. They found no effect on blood sugar but a sharp fall in white blood cells, and isolated vinblastine. Eli Lilly separately developed vincristine.
funFact: The leaves hold only traces of vinblastine (about 1 g from 500 kg of dried leaves is often quoted), which is why chemists have long worked on making it from its more plentiful precursors, catharanthine and vindoline.

wiki.extract: Catharanthus roseus, commonly known as bright eyes, Cape periwinkle, graveyard plant, Madagascar periwinkle, old maid, pink periwinkle, rose periwinkle, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the family Apocynaceae. It is native and endemic to Madagascar, but is grown elsewhere as an ornamental and medicinal plant, and now has a pantropical distribution. It is a source of the drugs vincristine and vinblastine, used to treat cancer. It was formerly included in the genus Vinca as Vinca rosea.

summary: A beautiful, tough flowering shrub planted on highways and in gardens throughout warm climates, and one of the most poisonous common garden plants. Every part contains cardiac glycosides that disrupt the heart's rhythm. It was the first plant to bloom in Hiroshima after the 1945 bombing.
nativeRange: Mediterranean region and North Africa through the Middle East to South Asia and southern China
abilities: Tolerates drought, salt spray, heat, poor soil and city pollution
Makes potent cardiac glycosides (oleandrin) in all its tissues
Grows along seasonal riverbeds, surviving floods and long dry seasons
Its flowers offer no nectar; it is pollinated by insects that it 'deceives'
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous: leaves, flowers, stems, seeds, roots and sap, fresh or dried. The cardiac glycosides oleandrin and neriine cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, slow or irregular heartbeat, high blood potassium and can cause fatal cardiac arrest. Smoke from burning it, using stems as skewers, and honey from oleander-rich areas have all caused poisoning. Deadly to dogs, cats, horses and livestock. Treatment may include digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Not to be confused with yellow oleander (Cascabela thevetia), also deadly.

uses.use: Root and leaf (karavira), after purification, applied externally for skin diseases
Leaf preparations used externally for ringworm and swelling

medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal if taken internally; 'oleandrin' supplements and extracts are dangerous and unproven.

fruit.description: Long, narrow paired pods that split to release silky-haired seeds.

seed.description: Brown seeds with a tuft of hairs
seed.germination: Usually propagated by cuttings; seed germinates readily in warmth

steps: Wear gloves when pruning; the sap irritates skin
Root cuttings in water or moist sand in summer
Plant in full sun away from where children and pets play
Never burn the prunings or use stems as skewers

lore: Oleander is painted in the garden frescoes of Pompeii, and Pliny the Elder warned that it was poisonous to animals. Oleander is the official flower of Hiroshima because it was the first to bloom after the atomic bombing.
funFact: Despite its poison, oleander is the main food of the oleander caterpillar (larva of the polka-dot wasp moth, Syntomeida epilais), which stores the plant's toxins for its own defence.

wiki.extract: Nerium oleander, the oleander, is a shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean region east to southern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal east to India and Myanmar; the Flora of China also cites it as native in Yunnan in China. It is the only species currently classified in the genus Nerium, belonging to subfamily Apocynoideae of the dogbane family Apocynaceae. It is also cultivated widely in temperate and subtropical areas as an introduced ornamental and landscaping plant.

summary: A small shrub of Asian monsoon forests whose twisting roots gave medicine reserpine. It was one of the first drugs for high blood pressure and for psychosis, and its effects helped launch modern psychopharmacology.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka to Myanmar, Thailand, southern China, Malaysia and Indonesia
abilities: Roots contain over 50 indole alkaloids, including reserpine and ajmaline
Reserpine depletes the brain and nerves of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin
White-pink flowers on red stalks are followed by glossy purple-black drupes
edibilityNote: Not a food. The root is a potent drug; self-medication is dangerous.

uses.use: Sarpagandha root for insomnia, anxiety, insanity (unmada), high blood pressure, and snake and insect bites
Asrol (root) as a sedative for hypertension, insomnia and mania
Reserpine for hypertension and formerly for psychosis; ajmaline as an antiarrhythmic and diagnostic for Brugada syndrome

medicinal.cautions: Reserpine can cause severe depression, including suicidal thoughts, as well as nasal congestion, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, stomach ulcers and parkinsonism. It interacts with MAOIs, digoxin and anaesthetics. Use only under medical supervision. Wild populations are over-collected (CITES Appendix II).

fruit.description: Small, paired, shiny purple-black drupes on red stalks.

seed.description: Single seed within a hard endocarp
seed.germination: Low and erratic (often under 50%); fresh seed sown in shade, 2–6 weeks

steps: Sow fresh seed in a shaded nursery bed at the start of the monsoon
Transplant at 2 months, 30–45 cm apart
Pinch flowers for better root growth unless saving seed
Dig roots in winter of the second year

lore: The genus honours the 16th-century German physician and botanist Leonhard Rauwolf. In 1949 the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil reported its blood-pressure-lowering effect in the British Heart Journal, and in 1952 chemists at Ciba isolated reserpine.
funFact: Reserpine caused depression in some patients by draining the brain of monoamines, which helped inspire the 'monoamine hypothesis' of depression.

wiki.extract: Rauvolfia serpentina, the Indian snakeroot, devil pepper, serpentine wood, Sarpagandha or Chandrika, is a species of flower in the milkweed family Apocynaceae. It is native to the Indian subcontinent and East Asia.

The illustration meticulously captures the plant's morphology, including its characteristic leaves, delicate flower clusters, and root system, serving as a vital scientific record of Malabar's biodiversity in the 17th century.

summary: The largest unbranched inflorescence in the plant world, rising up to about 3 m from a corm that can weigh more than 150 kg. When it blooms it heats its central spike and pumps out a stench of rotting flesh to draw carrion beetles and flies through the Sumatran forest.
nativeRange: Equatorial rainforest of western Sumatra, Indonesia
abilities: Heats its spadix (thermogenesis) to near human body temperature, helping the scent spread
Releases sulfur compounds such as dimethyl trisulfide that smell like a carcass
Stores energy in a giant corm; a record corm at Edinburgh weighed 153.9 kg in 2010
Between blooms it grows a single huge leaf that can reach about 6 m, like a small tree
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Like many aroids its tissues contain calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth if eaten raw.

fruit.description: Hundreds of olive-sized berries ripen from yellow to red.

seed.description: One or two seeds per berry
seed.dispersal: Birds such as hornbills eat the berries
seed.germination: Sow fresh (seeds don't store) in warm, humid mix

grow.water: High while in leaf; reduce during dormancy
grow.propagation: Fresh seed, or leaf cuttings in specialist collections
steps: Sow fresh seed immediately in warm, humid conditions
Pot the corm into progressively larger containers as it grows
Keep humid and warm (24–30 °C) year-round
Let the leaf die back naturally and rest the corm before regrowth

lore: Italian botanist Odoardo Beccari sent seeds to Europe after finding it in 1878, and it first bloomed in cultivation at Kew in 1889. David Attenborough coined 'titan arum' for his BBC series The Private Life of Plants, finding the Latin name too rude for television.
funFact: The Latin name means 'giant misshapen phallus'.

wiki.extract: Amorphophallus titanum, the titan arum, is a flowering plant in the family Araceae. It has a large unbranched inflorescence, a tall single leaf branched like a tree, and a heavy tuber which enables the plant to produce the inflorescence. A. titanum is endemic to rainforests on the Indonesian island of Sumatra.

summary: A slow-growing forest herb whose forked, human-shaped root has been the most prized tonic of East Asian medicine for two thousand years. Wild roots have been dug almost to extinction, and old specimens fetch extraordinary prices.
nativeRange: Mixed and broadleaf forests of north-eastern China, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East; now almost entirely cultivated
abilities: Makes ginsenosides, triterpene saponins studied for effects on fatigue, immunity and blood sugar
Can live for decades, adding one stem scar to the root neck each year
Seeds have a double dormancy and take about 18–22 months to germinate
Needs deep forest shade; leaves scorch in full sun
edibilityNote: Eaten in Korean dishes such as samgyetang (ginseng chicken soup) and taken as tea or extract. Large or long-term doses can cause insomnia, raised blood pressure and nervousness.

uses.use: Renshen strongly tonifies yuan qi; used for exhaustion, shortness of breath, collapse and as a superior longevity herb
Steamed red ginseng (hongsam) used as a daily restorative and for fatigue and immunity
Extracts trialled for fatigue, cognition, erectile dysfunction and blood sugar control

medicinal.cautions: May reduce warfarin's effect, lower blood sugar and interact with MAOIs and stimulants. Can cause insomnia, headache and high blood pressure. Not recommended in pregnancy. Buy cultivated roots; the wild plant is critically endangered.

fruit.description: Bright red, two-seeded berries in a single round cluster above the leaves.

seed.description: Cream-white, flattened, wrinkled seeds
seed.germination: Needs warm then cold stratification over 18–22 months; usually sold pre-stratified

grow.soil: Loose, humus-rich forest loam, slightly acidic
steps: Plant stratified seed 2 cm deep in autumn under a hardwood canopy or 70–80% shade cloth
Mulch with leaf litter and keep weeds down
Watch for slugs and fungal rots in wet years
Dig carefully in autumn of year 4–6, keeping the fine root hairs intact

lore: The Shennong Bencao Jing (c. 1st–2nd century CE) ranks ginseng among the 'superior' herbs that nourish life. In 1716 the Jesuit Joseph-François Lafitau found its relative, American ginseng, near Montreal after reading a colleague's description of the Chinese plant, and started a transpacific root trade.
funFact: Panax comes from the Greek panakeia, 'all-healing', the same root as panacea.

wiki.extract: Panax ginseng, ginseng, also known as Asian ginseng, Chinese ginseng or Korean ginseng, is a species of plant whose root is the original source of ginseng. It is a perennial plant that grows in the mountains of East Asia. It is mainly cultivated in China, Korea, Russia, and Japan.

The illustration clearly shows the plant's distinctive leaves and berries, as well as its fleshy root, which is famously noted for its human-like form, reflecting its name 'ren shen' or 'man root.'

plates.long: This detailed engraving illustrates the legendary mandrake root, depicted both as a botanical specimen and in its folkloric 'artificial' forms as hairy humanoid figures. Published in Picard's 'Superstitions anciennes et modernes', it serves as a visual record of how natural history and myth were intertwined in the early modern imagination.

The engraving features anatomical details of roots and flowers alongside full-plant depictions, reflecting the era's rigorous approach to documenting global natural history. The plate is dedi

plates.author: [Picard, Bernhard]
plates.desc: Engraving of mandrakes and ginseng, featuring anthropomorphic 'artificial' mandrake roots.
plates.long: This engraving from Bernard Picard's 1733 work on superstitions illustrates the folklore surrounding the mandrake root. It depicts 'artificial mandrakes'—roots carved or manipulated to resemble human figures—alongside a botanical representation of the plant and a ginseng root, highlighting the intersection of early modern botany and popular belief.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Christoph Jakob Trew's 'Uitgezochte planten' (1771) depicts the Ginseng plant (Araliastrum). The illustration meticulously details the plant's trifoliate leaves, small white flowers, red berries, and its famous bifurcated root, which was highly valued in traditional medicine for its supposed life-extending properties.

plates.long: This intricate engraving provides a comprehensive botanical study of the ginseng plant, a highly valued medicinal herb from East Asia. The illustration meticulously details the plant's morphology, from its distinctive root structure to its delicate floral umbels, and includes a microscopic view of a flowerlet, reflecting the scientific advancements of the era.

summary: A tree known only from fossils until 1994, when ranger David Noble abseiled into a gorge in Wollemi National Park near Sydney and found a living grove. Fewer than 100 mature trees survive in the wild, in a location kept secret.
nativeRange: A few sandstone gorges in Wollemi National Park, New South Wales, Australia
abilities: Belongs to an ancient lineage of the Araucariaceae; pollen like it (Dilwynites) goes back about 90 million years
Grows multiple trunks from its base (coppicing), helping it survive rockfall and fire
Sheds whole branches rather than individual leaves
Has bubbly, chocolate-brown bark often compared to the cereal Coco Pops
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

fruit.description: Green spherical female cones at branch tips; male cones lower down.

seed.description: Small, papery-winged seeds
seed.germination: Sow fresh at 18–25 °C; germination can be patchy

grow.propagation: Cuttings (most plants sold are clones from the 2005 release program)
steps: Buy a nursery-raised plant
Plant in sheltered, well-drained soil or a large pot
Water regularly while young and avoid waterlogging
Never visit the wild site: footsteps carry the deadly Phytophthora cinnamomi root rot

lore: Its 1994 discovery was compared to finding a living dinosaur. In January 2020, during the Black Summer fires, firefighters were winched in by helicopter and set up irrigation and water drops that saved the wild grove.
funFact: Nursery plants were sold worldwide from 2005, partly to remove the incentive for collectors to raid the secret wild grove.

wiki.extract: Wollemia nobilis is a species of coniferous tree in the family Araucariaceae. It is the single known species in the monotypic genus Wollemia. The species represents one of only three living genera in the family, alongside Araucaria and Agathis, which was discovered in 1994 in a temperate rainforest wilderness area of the Wollemi National Park in New South Wales. It was growing in a remote series of narrow, steep-sided, sandstone gorges 150 km (93 mi) north-west of Sydney. The genus is named after the National Park.

summary: The 'tree of life' of tropical coasts, providing food, drink, oil, fibre, thatch and timber. Its buoyant, waterproof fruit can drift on ocean currents for months and still germinate on a distant beach.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific; domesticated separately in the Pacific and South Asia; now pantropical on coasts
abilities: Fruit floats and survives seawater for over 100 days, colonising islands
Tolerates salt spray, sandy soil and brackish groundwater
Coconut water inside a young nut is sterile and has been used as an emergency IV fluid
A single palm can yield 50–100 nuts a year for 60–80 years
edibleParts: meat (fresh, dried as copra, pressed for milk and oil)
edibilityNote: All these parts are widely eaten. Coconut oil is very high in saturated fat. Falling nuts are a real hazard — don't stand under laden palms.

uses.use: Coconut water for heat, thirst and urinary complaints; oil for hair and skin
Young coconut water as a rehydrating drink for illness
Coconut water used as emergency intravenous fluid in the Pacific

medicinal.cautions: Rare tree-nut-type allergy. Coconut oil raises LDL cholesterol.

fruit.description: Large ovoid drupe 20–30 cm with a smooth green, yellow or orange skin, a thick fibrous husk (coir) and a hard brown shell with three 'eyes', holding white meat and clear water.

seed.description: The 'coconut' of the market is the seed inside its hard, hairy brown endocarp, round, 10–15 cm across, with three dark germination pores at one end; inside is a layer of white endosperm (meat) and liquid endosperm (water)
seed.germination: Lay a whole mature husked nut on its side, half-buried in moist sandy soil in warm shade; shoots in 3–6 months

grow.timeToHarvest: Dwarf varieties 3–4 years; tall varieties 6–10 years
steps: Choose a fully mature nut that sloshes when shaken; soak for 2–3 days, then half-bury it on its side in sandy soil.
When the shoot is 30–60 cm and roots emerge, transplant into a large hole in full sun, keeping the nut at soil level.
Water regularly for the first two years and mulch with old husks, which hold moisture.
Feed with potassium-rich fertiliser; remove dead fronds and old nuts safely.
Harvest green nuts at 6–7 months for water, or let them ripen and fall at about 12 months for mature meat.

lore: In Hindu ritual a coconut is broken before the deity as an offering, symbolising the breaking of the ego, and Tamil and Malayali tradition calls it the 'kalpavriksha', the wish-fulfilling tree. Marco Polo described the 'nux indica' in the 13th century.
funFact: The word 'coco' comes from Portuguese for a grinning face or goblin, after the three dark eyes on the shell.

wiki.extract: The coconut is a member of the palm family (Arecaceae) and the only living species of the genus Cocos. The term "coconut" can denote the whole coconut palm tree or the large hard fruit. Originally native to the Southeast Asia, New Guinea, and the Southwestern Pacific, they are ubiquitous in coastal tropical regions.

Produced for the landmark botanical work 'Hortus Malabaricus' (1678–1693), the plate features inscriptions in Latin, Malayalam, Arabic, and Konkani, reflecting the cross-cultural scientific collaboration of the era. The work of artist Ant

The plate illustrates various stages of the fruit's development, including its outer husk, internal shell, and the process of germination, reflecting the rigorous scientific documentation of tropical flora in the 17th century.

summary: One of the oldest cultivated fruit trees, grown in Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf for over 6,000 years. The date palm made oasis life possible across the Sahara and Arabia — its fruit a storable staple, its fronds and fibre a building material.
nativeRange: Probably the Persian Gulf region and south-west Asia; cultivated across North Africa, the Middle East, Pakistan and arid zones worldwide
abilities: Tolerates extreme heat (over 50 °C) and saline groundwater, provided roots reach water
Dioecious: separate male and female trees, traditionally hand-pollinated by climbing farmers
A 2,000-year-old seed from Masada germinated in 2005, among the oldest seeds ever germinated
A single female tree can produce 70–150 kg of fruit a year
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh at the khalal (crunchy), rutab (soft) and tamr (dried) stages. Harvesting palm heart kills the tree.

uses.use: Ajwa dates eaten in the morning as protection; dates traditionally break the Ramadan fast
Dates as a strengthening food for the weak and during convalescence
Eaten in late pregnancy; some trials suggest it eases labour

medicinal.cautions: Very high in sugar; caution in diabetes.

fruit.description: Oblong fruit 3–7 cm long in heavy hanging clusters; green ripening to yellow or red, then brown and wrinkled when dried; sticky, sweet, honey-to-caramel flesh.

seed.description: Hard, elongated cylindrical seed, grey-brown, 2–3 cm long, with a deep groove along one side and a small dot-like germ pore on the back
seed.dispersal: Animals and humans; long viability in dry conditions
seed.germination: Soak 2–3 days, sow in warm moist sand at 25–35 °C; sprouts in 2–8 weeks. Half of seedlings will be male and fruit is variable

grow.water: Roots need deep water; leaves need dry heat. Low humidity at fruiting
grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained; tolerates salinity and alkalinity
grow.propagation: Offshoots (suckers) taken from the base of named female cultivars such as 'Medjool' or 'Deglet Noor'; tissue culture
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–7 years from offshoot; fruit ripens 150–200 days after pollination
steps: Detach an offshoot weighing 10–25 kg with roots from a female palm, or buy a tissue-cultured plant of a named variety.
Plant in full sun in deep sand, keeping the soil level at the offshoot's widest point; tie the fronds up to shade the heart while it roots.
Water deeply and often in the first year; mature palms need deep, infrequent irrigation.
In spring, place strands of male flowers inside opened female flower clusters (or dust with male pollen).
Thin bunches and bag them against birds and rain; harvest at the rutab or tamr stage.

lore: Mesopotamian tablets record date cultivation and hand-pollination as early as the 3rd millennium BCE, and Hammurabi's code fixed a fine for cutting down a tree in another man's orchard. The date palm is the most-mentioned fruit tree in the Qur'an, where Maryam is told to shake its trunk for ripe dates.
funFact: 'Methuselah', a palm sprouted in 2005 from a roughly 2,000-year-old seed found at Masada, has since fathered dates by pollinating 'Hannah', a female palm raised from another ancient seed.

wiki.extract: Phoenix dactylifera, commonly known as the date palm, is a flowering-plant species in the palm family Arecaceae, native to the region from the Gulf States and Iraq to Pakistan and India. It is cultivated for its edible sweet fruit called dates. The species is widely cultivated across northern Africa, the Middle East, Australia, South and Southeast Asia, the coastal Mediterranean basin, and Southern California. It is naturalised in many tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. P. dactylifera is the type species of genus Phoenix, which contains 12–19 species of wild date palms.

summary: An umbrella-shaped tree found only on the island of Socotra, whose bark bleeds a deep red resin, the 'dragon's blood' traded across the ancient world. Its dense, upturned crown catches mist and shades its own roots in a harsh, dry climate.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Socotra archipelago, Yemen
abilities: Its umbrella crown condenses mist and funnels water down the branches while shading the soil
Exudes a red resin (dragon's blood) when the bark is cut
Survives on fog and monsoon moisture on dry limestone plateaus
Shades seedlings of other species, creating micro-habitats on bare ground
edibilityNote: Not a food; resin is used medicinally and as a dye. Livestock graze seedlings.

uses.use: Resin applied to wounds and burns and taken for diarrhoea and fevers
Resin as an astringent for wounds and eye problems

medicinal.cautions: Commercial 'dragon's blood' often comes from other species (Daemonorops, Croton); identity varies.

fruit.description: Small orange-red berries eaten by birds.

seed.description: Round seeds 1–3 per berry
seed.germination: Sow fresh in warm, free-draining mix; germination slow

steps: Sow fresh seed in gritty mix at 25 °C
Grow on in bright light, letting it dry between waterings
Keep frost-free; overwatering causes rot
Be patient: it may take decades to branch

lore: Socotra's resin is thought to be the 'cinnabar' of Pliny and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. A Socotri legend says the trees first grew from the blood of two brothers who fought to the death.
funFact: It branches only when its growing tip stops, usually after flowering, so the forks of its umbrella crown record the tree's flowering history.

wiki.extract: Dracaena cinnabari, the Socotra dragon tree, or dragon blood tree, is a dragon tree native to the Socotra archipelago, part of Yemen, located in the Arabian Sea. It is named after the blood-like color of the red sap that the trees produce. It is also the national tree of Yemen.

plates.title: The Great Herbary with all the figures of the herbs
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of the Sanguis draconis (Dragon's blood) plant.
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts the 'Sanguis draconis' or Dragon's blood tree, valued in the 16th century for its medicinal resin. The illustration is characteristic of early botanical works, focusing on identifying features like leaf shape and flower clusters to assist practitioners in identifying the source of potent remedies.

It originates from the Bencao Gangmu, the most comprehensive medical text of the Ming Dynasty, compiled by Li Shizhen to systematically categorize thousands of medicinal substances.

summary: The shaggy, twisted tree-yucca of the Mojave Desert, which depends completely on one moth. The yucca moth deliberately packs pollen into the flower and lays its eggs there, and its larvae eat some, but not all, of the seeds. Climate warming is shrinking the areas where it can live.
nativeRange: Western Mojave Desert, California and Nevada (eastern populations often treated as Yucca jaegeriana)
abilities: Is pollinated only by the yucca moth Tegeticula synthetica, which gathers pollen and stuffs it into the flower on purpose
Sprouts clones from roots and rhizomes, especially after damage
Branches only after flowering or when the growing tip is damaged
Provides nest sites and food for desert birds, lizards and woodrats
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples of the Mojave roasted the buds and ate the seeds. Like other yuccas it contains saponins, which are bitter and can upset the stomach.

fruit.description: Green, egg-shaped capsules that dry and release flat black seeds.

seed.description: Flat, black seeds
seed.germination: Sow fresh, warm, in sandy mix; germination is quick but seedlings are slow

steps: Sow seed in deep pots of sandy mix
Keep warm and barely moist
Plant out young in full sun on free-draining ground
Do not move wild plants: Joshua trees are protected in California

lore: Mormon settlers crossing the Mojave in the 1850s are said to have named it after the biblical Joshua, raising his hands to heaven. The Cahuilla used its leaf fibres for baskets and sandals and its roots for red dye.
funFact: Studies predict that under high-warming scenarios Joshua Tree National Park could lose most of its suitable Joshua tree habitat by 2100.
