summary: A stemless succulent whose plump leaves hold a cool, clear gel under a yellow, bitter latex, two quite different medicines in one leaf. It is grown on every continent but no longer known in the wild.
nativeRange: Probably originated in the Arabian Peninsula; known only in cultivation. Naturalised in arid regions worldwide
abilities: Uses CAM photosynthesis, opening its pores only at night to save water
Leaf gel is mostly water bound in polysaccharides such as acemannan
Yellow latex under the skin contains aloin, a strong purgative
Survives months of drought by drawing on water stored in its leaves
edibilityNote: The clear inner gel is eaten and drunk, for example in Asian aloe drinks, once the yellow latex has been rinsed off completely. The latex (aloin) is a harsh laxative and can cause cramping, diarrhoea and potassium loss.

uses.use: Ghritakumari gel for burns, skin disease, liver disorders and as a female tonic (kumari asava)
Dried latex (sibr/musabbar) as a purgative and in pills for liver and skin complaints
Luhui (dried latex) used to purge heat and for constipation and worms
Topical gel for minor burns, psoriasis and radiation skin reactions

medicinal.cautions: Topical gel for burns has modest, mixed support. In 2002 the US FDA removed aloe latex from over-the-counter laxatives for lack of safety data, and whole-leaf extract caused intestinal tumours in rats. Oral latex can cause severe diarrhoea, low potassium and kidney injury, and should be avoided in pregnancy and with digoxin or diuretics.

fruit.description: Dry three-valved capsule; seldom sets seed in cultivation.

seed.description: Flat, black, winged seeds (rarely produced)
seed.germination: Warm (above 21 °C), on gritty mix; 1–4 weeks

steps: Pot offsets in cactus mix and wait a week before watering
Water deeply only when the soil is dry; much less in winter
Cut outer leaves at the base and stand upright to drain the yellow latex
Bring indoors below about 5 °C

lore: Dioscorides described aloe for wounds and purging in the 1st century CE, and dried aloe latex was traded from the Red Sea to India and China. In Arabic, sabr means both 'aloe' and 'patience'.
funFact: Barbados was long a leading exporter of dried aloe latex, sold as 'Barbados aloes', which is why the plant was once called Aloe barbadensis.

gerard.place: This plant groweth very plentifully in India, & in Arabia, Cœlosyria, & Egypt: from whence the iuice put into skins is brought into Europe. It groweth also, as Dioscorides writeth, in Asia on the sea coasts, and in Andros, but not verie fit for iuice to be drawne out.
gerard.time: The herbe is alwaies greene, and likewise sendeth foorth braunches, though it remaine out of the earth, especially if the roote be couered with lome, & now & then watered: for so being hanged on the feelings and vpper posts of dining roomes, it doth …

summary: A feathery-leaved perennial of meadows and roadsides found across most of the Northern Hemisphere, named for Achilles, who by legend used it to stop his soldiers' bleeding. Its flat-topped white flower clusters are visited by hundreds of insect species.
nativeRange: Circumboreal: Europe, temperate Asia and North America (where both native and introduced forms occur)
abilities: Contains achilleine and tannins traditionally used to slow bleeding from small wounds
Feathery, finely divided leaves ("millefolium" = thousand-leaved) reduce water loss in dry sites
Spreads by rhizomes to form drought-tolerant mats, used in lawns and erosion control
Flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) feed a broad range of hoverflies, small bees and parasitoid wasps that control garden pests
Grows from sea level to above 3,500 m in the Rockies and Himalaya
edibilityNote: Young leaves are bitter and used in small amounts as a herb; historically used to bitter beer. Contains thujone in some chemotypes. Avoid in pregnancy. Can be confused with poisonous Apiaceae such as poison hemlock by beginners; check the leaves carefully.

uses.use: Crushed leaves on cuts and nosebleeds; tea for colds, fever and digestive complaints
Used by many nations, including the Cherokee, Ojibwe and Navajo, as a poultice for wounds and as a tea for fevers, colds and toothache
Biranjasif given as a diaphoretic and for digestive and menstrual complaints
Related Achillea species used externally for wounds, swelling and snakebite

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy and contact dermatitis. Traditionally used to bring on menstruation, so avoid in pregnancy. May increase sensitivity to sunlight.

fruit.description: Tiny, flattened, silvery-grey; not eaten.

seed.description: Flat, oblong, grey seeds without a pappus
seed.dispersal: Wind, animals and soil movement; also spreads by rhizomes
seed.germination: Needs light; surface-sow, 10–14 days at 18–24 °C

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; thrives in poor, dry ground
grow.propagation: Seed or division in spring or autumn
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers the second summer from seed, or the first from divisions
steps: Surface-sow in spring or plant divisions about 30 cm apart
Water until established, then leave dry; rich soil makes it floppy
Cut flowering stems when the clusters are fully open and hang to dry
Divide every few years to control spreading

lore: Pliny the Elder records that Achilles used the plant on wounds, which gave the genus its name. In China, dried yarrow stalks were the traditional tool for casting I Ching hexagrams.
funFact: The classical I Ching divination used 50 yarrow stalks, sorted by hand over and over to build each six-line hexagram.

wiki.extract: Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. Growing to 1 metre tall, it is characterized by small whitish flowers, a tall stem of fernlike leaves, and a pungent odor.

The fine engraving technique allows for a high degree of anatomical accuracy, serving both aesthetic and scientific purposes in the study of medicinal plants during the Scientific Revolution.

summary: A pretty woodland wildflower that killed thousands of American settlers indirectly. Cattle grazing it pass its toxin, tremetol, into their milk, and people who drank the milk developed 'milk sickness', which killed Abraham Lincoln's mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, in 1818.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America
abilities: Makes tremetol (a mixture including tremetone), a toxin that builds up in the milk and meat of grazing animals
Flowers in late summer and autumn, feeding bees, butterflies and moths when few flowers remain
Grows well in shade where most toxic forage plants do not
Spreads by seed and short rhizomes into woodland colonies
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are toxic to livestock (horses, cattle, sheep, goats), causing 'trembles'. People are poisoned indirectly by drinking milk or eating meat from poisoned animals: weakness, vomiting, tremors, severe constipation, acetone-smelling breath, and in serious cases death. Modern milk pooled from many farms is not a risk. Lookalikes: boneset (Eupatorium perfoliatum) and other white-flowered Eupatorium species.

uses.use: Root tea used for diarrhoea, kidney stones and fevers, and the root as a snakebite poultice (as the name suggests)

medicinal.cautions: Toxic; not for internal use.

fruit.description: Tiny black achenes with white hairs.

seed.description: Small black achene with a white pappus
seed.germination: Cold-stratify; self-sows freely

steps: Sow in autumn or cold-stratify seed
Plant in shade where it can naturalise
Keep out of any pasture used by livestock
Deadhead to limit self-seeding

lore: Milk sickness devastated frontier settlements in Ohio, Indiana and Illinois in the early 1800s; Dr. Anna Pierce Hobbs Bixby of Illinois is credited, in local tradition, with identifying the plant in the 1830s with help from a Shawnee woman. The cause wasn't accepted by science until the 1920s.
funFact: Milk sickness cases have mostly vanished since farms began pooling milk from many herds.

wiki.extract: Ageratina altissima, also known as white snakeroot, richweed, or white sanicle, is a poisonous perennial herb in the family Asteraceae, native to eastern and central North America. An older binomial name for this species is Eupatorium rugosum, but the genus Eupatorium has undergone taxonomic revision by botanists, and some species once included in it have been moved to other genera.

otherNames: Zhōng yà kǔ hāo 中亚苦蒿 (Chinese)
summary: A silvery, intensely bitter perennial that gave its name to absinthe and vermouth. Its thujone was blamed for 'absinthism', and that fear got absinthe banned across much of Europe and the US in the early 20th century.
nativeRange: Temperate Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; naturalised in North America
abilities: Absinthin is among the most bitter substances known in plants and stimulates bitter receptors that drive digestive secretions
Thujone blocks GABA-A receptors and can cause seizures at high doses
Releases compounds from its leaves and roots that suppress nearby plants (allelopathy)
Silky grey hairs reflect sunlight and reduce water loss
edibilityNote: Used only in tiny regulated amounts as a bitter flavouring in absinthe, vermouth and bitters. The essential oil and large doses are toxic, and the herb is not a food.

uses.use: Bitter tea or wine for poor appetite, indigestion, gallbladder complaints and intestinal worms
Afsanteen as a liver and stomach tonic, a deobstruent and for fevers and worms
EMA traditional-use monograph for loss of appetite and mild dyspepsia; a small trial in Crohn's disease

medicinal.cautions: Thujone is a convulsant: avoid the essential oil, long-term use, pregnancy, breastfeeding and epilepsy. Drinking wormwood oil has caused seizures, muscle breakdown and kidney failure. Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute brown achenes without a pappus.

seed.description: Tiny, oblong, pale-brown seeds
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–2 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.timeToHarvest: Leafy tops from year 2, at flowering
steps: Surface-sow under cover or root cuttings in spring
Plant away from vegetables, as its exudates inhibit neighbours
Cut flowering tops in midsummer and hang to dry
Cut back in spring to keep it compact

lore: Absinthe was banned in Switzerland (1910), the United States (1912) and France (1915). Modern analyses of pre-ban bottles found thujone levels too low to explain 'absinthism'; the high alcohol content is the more likely culprit. 'Wormwood' in English Bibles (Revelation 8:11) stands for bitterness.
funFact: The word 'vermouth' comes from the German Wermut, wormwood, the herb that gave the original fortified wines their bitterness.

wiki.extract: Artemisia absinthium, otherwise known as common wormwood, is a species of Artemisia native to North Africa and temperate regions of Eurasia, and widely naturalized in Canada and the northern United States. It is grown as an ornamental plant and is used as an ingredient in the spirit absinthe and some other alcoholic beverages.

The illustration emphasizes the plant's diagnostic features, including its distinctive lobed leaves and seed heads, serving as a visual guide for medieval pharmacists and physicians.

summary: A tall, sweet-smelling annual weed whose leaf glands make artemisinin, the basis of the world's front-line malaria drugs. Its rediscovery came from a 4th-century Chinese recipe and won Tu Youyou the 2015 Nobel Prize.
nativeRange: Temperate Asia, especially China; naturalised in Europe, North America and elsewhere
abilities: Glandular hairs on leaves and flowers make artemisinin, an endoperoxide that kills malaria parasites
Grows from seed to over 2 m tall in a single season
Produces enormous numbers of tiny wind-pollinated flowers
edibilityNote: Not a food. Bitter; used medicinally as tea or extract.

uses.use: Qinghao clears summer heat and 'deficiency heat' and treats intermittent fevers (malaria); Ge Hong's 4th-century recipe soaks the herb in cold water and drinks the juice
Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate, artemether, dihydroartemisinin) in artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), the WHO-recommended treatment for malaria

medicinal.cautions: The purified drugs are strongly proven, but the WHO advises against using the dried leaf or tea to treat or prevent malaria: dosing is unreliable and it may encourage resistance. Malaria needs prompt medical treatment. Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute, smooth, brown achenes.

seed.description: Dust-like seeds
seed.germination: Needs light; surface-sow, 5–10 days at 20 °C

steps: Surface-sow under cover in spring
Plant out 60–100 cm apart after frost
Harvest leaves at early bud stage, when artemisinin peaks
Dry in shade

lore: Ge Hong's Zhouhou Beiji Fang (Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, c. 340 CE) told readers to soak a handful of qinghao in water and drink the juice for fevers. In 1971 Tu Youyou of China's secret malaria programme, Project 523, read the line and switched to a low-temperature extraction, which preserved the active compound.
funFact: Artemisinin is also made by engineered yeast. Sanofi launched semi-synthetic artemisinin production in 2013, but it struggled to compete on price with farm-grown plants.

wiki.extract: Artemisia annua, also known as sweet wormwood, sweet annie, sweet sagewort, annual mugwort or annual wormwood, is a common type of wormwood native to temperate Asia, but naturalized in many countries including scattered parts of North America.

The image provides a clear visual guide to the plant's morphology, including its serrated leaves and fibrous root system, which was essential for pharmacological identification and standardization in the 16th century.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the plant Artemisia annua, known in Chinese as Huanghuahao, a species of great importance in traditional medicine. It is featured in Wu Qijun's 1848 work 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' (Illustrated Investigation of Plant Names and Realities), which is renowned for its high standard of botanical accuracy and artistic quality in its woodblock prints.

otherNames: Nagadamani (Sanskrit, as applied in some Ayurvedic texts)
summary: A tall, silver-backed roadside perennial named for Artemis, goddess of women and childbirth. It is the first of the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs, and in late summer one of Europe's worst hay-fever plants.
nativeRange: Temperate Europe, Asia and North Africa; invasive in eastern North America
abilities: Silvery, felted leaf undersides reflect heat and carry aromatic oil glands
Spreads by rhizomes and can regrow from small root fragments, making it hard to eradicate
Releases huge amounts of wind-borne pollen; the allergen Art v 1 is a leading cause of late-summer hay fever
Its aromatic compounds repel insects; sprigs were laid in shoes and linen
edibilityNote: Used as a bitter flavouring for fatty meats and goose and, historically, in gruit ale before hops. It contains thujone, so avoid large amounts and avoid it entirely in pregnancy. Can cross-react in people with celery or spice allergies.

uses.use: Bitter tea for poor appetite, indigestion and irregular or painful menstruation; laid in shoes against travel-weariness
Mugwort leaf (ai ye, mainly the related A. argyi) is dried into moxa and burned over acupuncture points (moxibustion)
Leaves used for worms, fevers and menstrual complaints

medicinal.cautions: Avoid in pregnancy, as it was traditionally used to provoke menstruation and abortion. Thujone toxicity is possible at high doses. Pollen and food allergy (the 'mugwort–celery–spice syndrome'). Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Minute brown achenes without a pappus.

seed.description: Tiny, oblong, brown seeds
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–2 weeks at 15–25 °C

grow.soil: Any; thrives on disturbed, nitrogen-rich ground
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from year 1, just before flowering
steps: Grow in a sunk container or a contained bed, as it is invasive in North America
Surface-sow or plant divisions in spring
Cut leafy tops just as the flower buds form
Hang to dry and strip the leaves

lore: The Old English Nine Herbs Charm in the 10th-century Lacnunga manuscript names Mucgwyrt first, calling it 'the oldest of plants'. Pliny wrote that a traveller carrying artemisia would not feel weary.
funFact: On St John's Eve, medieval Europeans wore mugwort garlands ('St John's girdle') and threw them into the midsummer bonfire to burn away bad luck.

wiki.extract: Artemisia vulgaris, commonly known as mugwort, common mugwort, or wormwood, is a species of flowering plant in the daisy family Asteraceae. It is one of several species in the genus Artemisia commonly known as mugwort, although Artemisia vulgaris is the species most often called mugwort. Mugworts have been used medicinally and as culinary herbs.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the mugwort plant (Artemisia vulgaris), identified by the German heading 'Beifuß'. The illustration meticulously details the plant's morphology, including its characteristic lobed leaves, flowering spikes, and root system, serving as a vital reference for early modern herbalists and physicians.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts Artemisia (mugwort), a plant valued in medieval medicine for its warming and drying properties. It is a characteristic illustration from the Herbarius latinus, an influential early printed herbal used for identifying medicinal plants and understanding their therapeutic properties according to medieval medical traditions.

summary: A cheerful orange-and-gold daisy of cottage gardens whose resinous petals colour soups and soothe skin. It is not the Tagetes 'marigold' of Indian garlands, though the two are often confused.
nativeRange: Known only in cultivation; probably derived from Mediterranean Calendula species. Grown worldwide
abilities: Petals contain carotenoids (lutein, lycopene) that dye food and fabric yellow-orange
Triterpenoid faradiol esters show anti-inflammatory activity on skin
One plant bears several very different seed shapes (heterocarpy), spreading its bets on dispersal
Flowers open in sunshine and close in dull weather
edibilityNote: Petals colour rice, cheese and butter and garnish salads. Do not confuse it with Tagetes marigolds or the poisonous marsh marigold (Caltha). People allergic to Asteraceae may react.

uses.use: Ointments and infused oils for cuts, burns, nappy rash and sore nipples; petal tea for digestion and menstrual pain
Flowers used as a resolvent for swellings and for liver and menstrual complaints
Topical creams studied for radiation dermatitis, leg ulcers and episiotomy healing; EMA traditional-use monograph for minor skin inflammation

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy and contact dermatitis. Trials for radiation dermatitis are conflicting. Avoid medicinal oral doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Curved, hooked and ridged achenes of several shapes on the same head.

seed.description: C-shaped, knobbly, beige-brown seeds of several forms
seed.dispersal: Hooked forms catch on fur; others fall or blow
seed.germination: Easy; 5–14 days at 15–21 °C; cover with 1 cm soil (needs darkness)

steps: Sow directly 1 cm deep in spring or autumn
Thin to 25–30 cm
Pick flowers every few days to keep new ones coming
Dry petals in shade for tea, oils or colouring

lore: Nicholas Culpeper's Complete Herbal (1653) prized marigold flowers for 'comforting the heart'. Medieval cooks used the petals as a cheap stand-in for saffron.
funFact: Its name comes from the Latin calendae, the first day of the month, because in mild climates it seemed to be in flower at the start of every month.

wiki.extract: Calendula officinalis, Mary's gold, common marigold, the pot marigold, Scotch marigold, or ruddles, is a flowering plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is probably native to southern Europe, but its long history of cultivation makes its precise origin unknown, and it is widely naturalised. The florets are edible and the plant has historically been used as medicine.

plates.long: A naturalistic woodcut of a Marigold (Ringelblüm) from Otto Brunfels' landmark herbal. Illustrated by Hans Weiditz, this image represents a shift toward empirical observation in science, capturing the plant's specific morphology including its root structure and leaf arrangement with unprecedented accuracy for the 16th century.

The illustration is celebrated for its 'ad vivum' (from life) approach, capturing the plant's morphology from the fibrous roots to the characteristic composite flower heads. Fuchs's work set a new standard for botanical accuracy, moving away from stylized medieval depictions toward modern s

plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of the Jin Zhan Cao (Calendula officinalis) plant, showing flowers, leaves, and roots.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the Jin Zhan Cao (Calendula officinalis), or pot marigold, as presented in Li Shizhen's 1596 masterpiece, 'Bencao Gangmu'. The illustration serves as a critical diagnostic tool, detailing the plant's morphology for practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine. It represents the high standard of botanical observation and woodblock printing achieved during the Ming Dynasty.

The central specimen, Tanacetum, is particularly notable for its highly dissected, feathery foliage and numerous flower heads. As a masterpiece of early modern florilegia, this work repre

plates.desc: A detailed botanical and entomological study featuring a flowering Marigold (Calendula) plant with various insects including caterpillars, a moth, a ladybug, a damselfly, and a pupa.
plates.long: A vibrant hand-colored engraving from Maria Sibylla Merian's seminal work on the metamorphosis of insects. The illustration depicts a Marigold plant as a host to a diverse array of insects at various stages of development, reflecting Merian's pioneering approach to ecological observation and scientific illustration.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Calendula plant with a central stem, serrated green leaves, and small yellow circular flowers. The illustration includes a stylized root system at the base to aid in identification for medicinal harvesting.

Such illustrations were essential in Hieronymus Brunschwig's 'Liber de arte distillandi' to ensure the correct identification of botanical specimens for medicinal distillation.

The accompanying text details the plant's medicinal use in treating heart conditions and soothing toothaches. Such illustrations represent the transition from medieval herbalism to early modern botanical science, where woodblock prints standardized the id

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Calendula plant, commonly known as a marigold, showing its entire structure from roots to flowers. It is featured in Hieronymus Bock's influential herbal, which was noted for its detailed and accurate botanical descriptions and illustrations based on direct observation rather than traditional copying.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut illustrates a Calendula plant, or marigold, as featured in Rembert Dodoens' influential 1568 work on flowers. The image provides a comprehensive view of the plant's anatomy, including its distinctive rayed flowers and fibrous root system, reflecting the growing Renaissance interest in accurate botanical documentation for both scientific and aesthetic purposes.

summary: A prairie daisy with drooping magenta petals around a spiny copper cone, now one of the best-selling herbal medicines in the world. The genus name comes from the Greek echinos, hedgehog, after that prickly cone.
nativeRange: Eastern and central United States: open woods and prairies from Ohio and Michigan south to Louisiana and Georgia
abilities: Roots contain alkamides that cause a tingling numbness on the tongue
Long-lasting flowers feed bees and butterflies, and seed heads feed goldfinches into winter
Deep taproots and fibrous roots let it survive prairie droughts and fires
edibilityNote: Used as tea, tincture or extract rather than as food.

uses.use: Plains nations used Echinacea, mainly E. angustifolia and E. pallida, for toothache, sore throat, snakebite and wounds; E. purpurea itself was less used
Popularised from the 1880s by Eclectic physicians and the Lloyd Brothers for infections and 'bad blood'
Aerial-part and root extracts taken to prevent or shorten colds; pressed juice approved in Germany

medicinal.cautions: Trials are inconsistent: some show a small effect on preventing colds, few show it shortens them. Asteraceae allergy, including rare anaphylaxis, and rashes in children. Theoretically unsuitable with autoimmune disease or immunosuppressant drugs.

fruit.description: Four-angled, tan achenes in the spiny cone; eaten by birds, not people.

seed.description: Angular, tan, crowned with tiny teeth
seed.dispersal: Falls near the parent; birds scatter some
seed.germination: Improved by 4–6 weeks' cold moist stratification; 10–20 days at 20 °C

grow.soil: Well-drained loam; tolerates clay and drought
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in year 1–2; roots at 3–4 years
steps: Sow outdoors in autumn or stratify seed in the fridge before spring sowing
Plant 45 cm apart in sun
Leave seed heads standing for birds over winter
Divide clumps every 4 years

lore: In the 1880s the Nebraska patent-medicine maker H. C. F. Meyer sold 'Meyer's Blood Purifier' made from Echinacea. In the 1930s the German firm Madaus mistakenly imported E. purpurea seed instead of E. angustifolia, and so built Europe's echinacea industry on this species.
funFact: Linnaeus first classed it as a Rudbeckia, a black-eyed Susan. It was moved to its own genus, Echinacea, by Conrad Moench in 1794.

wiki.extract: Echinacea purpurea, the eastern purple coneflower, purple coneflower, hedgehog coneflower, or Echinacea, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to parts of eastern North America and present to some extent in the wild in much of the eastern, southeastern and midwestern United States, as well as in the Canadian Province of Ontario. It is most common in the Ozarks, the Mississippi Valley, and the Ohio Valley. Its habitats include dry open woods, prairies, and barrens.

plates.long: A slender, dark-scaled snake with yellow-green lateral stripes and a speckled pattern is positioned horizontally across the frame. Behind it, a flowering plant features a prominent brown conical center and drooping purple petals. The plate is labeled 'Caecilia Maculata' and 'Chrysanthemum', representing an early scientific study of North American flora and fauna.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's seminal work depicts a 'Caecilia Maculata' (now known as the Eastern Glass Lizard) alongside a flowering plant. Catesby was a pioneer in illustrating North American flora and fauna in their natural associations, a revolutionary approach for the time that influenced generations of naturalists.

summary: A small, apple-scented annual daisy whose hollow, domed flower heads have been steeped into one of the world's most-drunk herbal teas for over two thousand years. Its essential oil turns an inky blue when distilled, thanks to chamazulene formed from the flower's matricin.
nativeRange: Southern & Eastern Europe and Western Asia; naturalised across temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Produces apigenin and α-bisabolol, compounds studied for calming and anti-inflammatory effects
Yields a deep-blue essential oil: matricin in the flowers converts to chamazulene during steam distillation
Colonises compacted, poor and slightly saline soils such as field margins and roadsides
Completes its life cycle from seed to flower in about two months
edibilityNote: Dried flower heads are brewed as tea. People allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums or other Asteraceae may react, occasionally severely.

uses.use: Tea for sleeplessness, nervous stomach, colic and menstrual cramps; compresses and rinses for inflamed skin and gums
Bābūnaj used as a resolvent and anti-inflammatory, in oils for joint pain and in decoctions for digestive complaints
Babuna flowers given for indigestion, flatulence and restlessness in children
Oral extracts trialled for generalised anxiety disorder; topical preparations approved in Germany for skin and mucosal inflammation

medicinal.cautions: Asteraceae allergy (including anaphylaxis in rare cases). May add to the effect of sedatives and has been reported to interact with warfarin. Avoid large medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Tiny, dry, pale and ribbed, without a pappus; not eaten.

seed.description: Minute pale-brown, ribbed seeds
seed.dispersal: Falls near the parent; carried by water, soil and machinery; self-sows freely
seed.germination: Needs light; surface-sow and keep moist, 7–14 days at 15–20 °C

grow.propagation: Seed, sown in spring or autumn
steps: Scatter seed on the surface of raked soil and press in lightly without covering
Keep moist until seedlings appear, then thin to about 20 cm
Pick flower heads on a dry morning when the white petals are flat or just turning back
Dry on screens out of direct sun and store airtight

lore: Dioscorides described it as anthemis in De Materia Medica (1st century CE), and bābūnaj became a fixture of medieval Arabic and Unani pharmacy. In Beatrix Potter's The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902), Peter's mother doses him with chamomile tea.
funFact: You can tell true German chamomile from the lookalike scentless mayweed by slicing the flower head: chamomile's cone-shaped receptacle is hollow.

wiki.extract: Matricaria chamomilla, commonly known as chamomile, German chamomile, Hungarian chamomile (kamilla), wild chamomile, blue chamomile, or scented mayweed, is an annual plant of the composite family Asteraceae. Commonly, the name M. recutita is applied to the herbal product chamomile, although other species are also used as chamomile. The plant is commonly used to make a tea.

plates.title: Hortus Eystettensis
plates.author: Basilius Besler
plates.desc: Detailed botanical engraving of two Matricaria (feverfew) varieties, showing double and single flower forms.
plates.long: This plate features two varieties of Matricaria, commonly known as feverfew, likely from a 17th-century herbal. The left side illustrates a 'double-flowered' variety (Matricaria flore pleno), while the right shows the 'single-flowered' version (Matricaria flore simplici), demonstrating the era's commitment to precise botanical observation and the classification of cultivars.

plates.title: Latin Herbal with German Synonyms

summary: A handsome, fiercely spiny thistle whose glossy leaves are marbled with white veins, said in legend to be drops of the Virgin Mary's milk. Its seeds yield silymarin, which is used as an antidote for death-cap mushroom poisoning.
nativeRange: Mediterranean, North Africa and South-West Asia; invasive in California, Australia and South America
abilities: Seeds contain silymarin, a flavonolignan complex that protects liver cells in lab studies
Intravenous silibinin can block uptake of death-cap toxins (amatoxins) by the liver
Grows quickly into dense, spiny thickets that grazing animals avoid
Can accumulate nitrates to levels toxic to cattle and sheep
edibilityNote: Young parts are eaten like artichoke or cardoon once the spines are removed. Plants on heavily fertilised ground can hold nitrates harmful to livestock.

uses.use: Seeds for liver and gallbladder complaints, jaundice and to increase breast milk
Seeds used for liver disorders and as a diuretic
Intravenous silibinin (Legalon SIL) used in Europe for Amanita mushroom poisoning; oral silymarin trialled for alcoholic and fatty liver disease

medicinal.cautions: Clinical trials in chronic liver disease are mixed and mostly show no clear benefit. Mild digestive upset is common, and Asteraceae allergy is possible. May lower blood sugar. Mushroom poisoning is an emergency for hospital treatment only.

fruit.description: Shiny, mottled black-brown achene with a deciduous white pappus.

seed.description: Glossy, mottled, oval seeds
seed.germination: Easy; 10–20 days at 15–20 °C

grow.timeToHarvest: Seeds about 4 months after spring sowing
steps: Check whether it is a listed weed locally before planting
Sow 1 cm deep in spring, 60 cm apart
Bag flower heads with paper as they dry so the seeds are not lost
Wear thick gloves to harvest and clean the seed

lore: Dioscorides recommended thistle seeds for snakebite, and medieval Europeans dedicated the plant to the Virgin Mary, giving it the name Carduus Mariae. Culpeper wrote that it was good against 'the jaundice' and liver obstructions.
funFact: Silymarin is not one compound but a mixture of at least seven flavonolignans plus the flavonoid taxifolin. Silibinin, the main one, is the form given by drip for mushroom poisoning.

wiki.extract: Silybum marianum is a species of thistle. It has various common names including milk thistle, blessed milkthistle, Marian thistle, Mary thistle, Saint Mary's thistle, Mediterranean milk thistle, variegated thistle and Scotch thistle. This species is an annual or biennial plant of the family Asteraceae. This fairly typical thistle has red to purple flowers and shiny pale green leaves with white veins. Once native from Southern Europe through Asia, it has spread throughout the world.

summary: A bitter, strongly scented little daisy whose name is a corruption of 'febrifuge'. Today it is best known as a herbal migraine preventative.
nativeRange: Balkan Peninsula, Anatolia and the Caucasus; naturalised widely in Europe, the Americas and Australasia
abilities: Leaves contain parthenolide, a sesquiterpene lactone that blocks NF-κB inflammatory signalling in lab studies
Pungent camphor-scented foliage repels many insects
Self-seeds freely into wall crevices and paving
edibilityNote: Very bitter; chewing fresh leaves causes mouth ulcers in some people.

uses.use: Leaves eaten in bread or as tea for headache, fevers, arthritis and to bring on menstruation
Dried leaf or CO2 extract to prevent migraine attacks; EMA traditional-use monograph
Infusions used in Mexico and Central America for colic, stomach ache and menstrual pain

medicinal.cautions: Trials for migraine prevention are mixed; a Cochrane review found any benefit small and uncertain. Causes mouth ulcers and digestive upset, and stopping suddenly may cause rebound headaches ('post-feverfew syndrome'). Avoid in pregnancy because it stimulates the uterus, and with anticoagulants or Asteraceae allergy.

fruit.description: Tiny ribbed achenes with a short crown.

seed.description: Minute ribbed seeds
seed.germination: Needs light; 10–15 days at 15–20 °C

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from 3–4 months; flowers first summer
steps: Surface-sow in spring
Plant 30 cm apart in sun
Pick leaves as needed and dry for capsules or tea
Deadhead to limit self-seeding

lore: Dioscorides recommended parthenion, a name later linked to the Parthenon. The modern migraine interest began in the 1970s with Welsh patients' reports and led to a 1985 trial at the London Migraine Clinic published in the BMJ.
funFact: 'Feverfew' comes from the Latin febrifugia, 'fever-chaser', although the plant does little to lower fevers.

summary: The world's most familiar weed. Each flower head is a cluster of up to 200 florets, and most of its seeds are clones made without pollination. Every part is edible and its bitter roots and leaves have long been used as a liver and kidney remedy.
nativeRange: Eurasia; now naturalised on every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Sets seed asexually (apomixis): most seeds are genetic copies of the parent
Its pappus parachute creates a stable 'separated vortex ring' of air, a kind of flight unknown before 2018
Deep taproot regrows from fragments and draws up minerals
Flowers from early spring, an important early nectar and pollen source
edibilityNote: All parts are edible; young leaves are less bitter. Avoid plants from sprayed lawns or roadsides. People allergic to Asteraceae or latex may react.

uses.use: Leaf as a diuretic ('pissenlit'); root as a bitter tonic for liver, gallbladder and digestion
Pugongying clears heat and toxins, for breast abscess, boils, sore throat and urinary infections
Adopted after European introduction by several nations, such as the Ojibwe and Iroquois, as a spring green and for heartburn and kidney complaints

medicinal.cautions: Only one small pilot trial supports the diuretic effect. Can interact with lithium, diuretics and some antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin. Avoid with gallbladder obstruction. Asteraceae and latex allergy.

fruit.description: Ribbed achenes on a slender beak topped with a parachute, forming the 'clock'.

seed.description: Olive-brown spiny achene with white pappus
seed.germination: Needs light; 7–21 days at 15–25 °C

grow.soil: Any; deeper soil gives larger roots
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves 6–8 weeks; roots in autumn of year 1–2
steps: Scatter seed on the surface in spring
Blanch leaves under a pot for a week for milder salad greens
Pick flowers for wine or fritters at midday when fully open
Dig roots in autumn, roast and grind for 'coffee'

lore: The genus name came into medieval Latin from the Arabic and Persian tarakhshaqūq, a plant discussed by Arabic physicians around the 10th–11th centuries. The English name comes from the French dent de lion, 'lion's tooth', after the jagged leaves.
funFact: In 2018 Edinburgh researchers showed that a dandelion seed's bristly parachute is about 90% empty space, yet it traps a stable bubble of swirling air that keeps it aloft.

wiki.extract: Taraxacum officinale, the dandelion or common dandelion, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae. The common dandelion is well-known for its yellow flower heads that turn into round balls of many silver-tufted fruit, which disperse in the wind. These balls are sometimes called "clocks" or "blowballs".

gerard.title: Of Dandelion
gerard.names: These plants belong to the Succories, among which Theophrastus in his 7. booke nameth ἀφάκη, Leonardus Fuchsius thinketh that Dandelion is Hedypnois Plinij, of which he writeth in his 20. booke 8. chapter, affirming it to be a wilde kinde of broade leafed Succorie, and that Dandelion is Taraxacon: but Taraxacon as Auicen teacheth in his 692. Chapter is Garden Endiue, as Serapio, Serapio mentioneth in his 143.
gerard.place: They are found often in medows neere vnto water ditches, as also in gardens and in high waies much troden.
gerard.time: They flower most times in the yeere, especially if the winter be not extreame colde.
gerard.vertues: Dandelion is like in temperature to Succorie, that is to saie to wilde Endiue. It is colde, but it drieth more, and doth withall clense and open by reason of the bitternes which it hath ioined with it: and therefore it is good for those things for which Succorie is.

summary: The pioneer of the north. Silver birch is among the first trees to recolonise burned, cleared or glacier-scoured ground, and its white bark, rich in betulin, reflects sunlight. People have tapped its sap, written on its bark and built canoes and boxes from it for thousands of years.
nativeRange: Most of Europe to Siberia and northern Kazakhstan, south to Turkey and Iran
abilities: Disperses millions of light winged seeds, so it is quick to colonise open ground
Its bark is rich in betulin, a white triterpene that reflects light and repels water
Pushes large volumes of sugary sap up in spring before leafing out
Prepares soil for later trees by cycling nutrients through fast-rotting leaves
edibilityNote: Sap is drunk fresh in spring across Eastern Europe and Scandinavia. Birch pollen is a major cause of hay fever, and people with birch allergy often react to raw apples, hazelnuts and cherries.

uses.use: Leaf tea as a diuretic for urinary tract irrigation (approved by German Commission E)
Birch tar (dyogot) applied to skin conditions; birch twigs used in the banya

medicinal.cautions: Not for people with oedema from heart or kidney failure. Birch tar contains irritants. Birch pollen allergy is common.

fruit.description: Cylindrical catkins break up into tiny winged seeds and three-lobed scales.

seed.description: Tiny two-winged nutlets
seed.germination: Surface-sow; needs light. Brief cold stratification improves germination.

grow.timeToHarvest: Sap from trees ~20 cm diameter, about 15–20 years
steps: Surface-sow seed in late winter and keep moist and bright
Plant out small: birches transplant poorly when larger
To tap sap, drill a small hole in early spring before bud-break and collect for a few days only
Plug the tap hole afterwards to protect the tree

lore: Medieval citizens of Novgorod scratched letters onto birch bark; more than 1,000 such 'beresty' documents have been dug up since 1951. Ötzi the Iceman carried birch-bark containers and birch-tar adhesive. It is the national tree of Finland and Russia.
funFact: Birch tar is the oldest known synthetic material; Neanderthals were making it as a glue more than 200,000 years ago.

wiki.extract: Betula pendula, the silver birch, is a species of tree in the flowering plant family, Betulaceae. The trees can reach a height of 30 m, and have white bark that sheds regularly. It is native to Europe, Morocco, temperate Asia, Canada, and Alaska, although in southern Europe and Morocco it is only found at higher elevations. Its range extends into Siberia, China, and southwest Asia in the mountains of northern Turkey, the Caucasus, and northern Iran.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a birch tree (Betula), characterized by its slender trunk and drooping branches. It is part of Rembert Dodoens' influential herbal, which provided accurate visual and textual descriptions of plants for medicinal and scientific study during the Renaissance.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the Birch tree (Betula), emphasizing the serrated edges of its leaves and the hanging catkins. It reflects the systematic approach of Panckow's 'Herbarium Portatile' in cataloging both local and foreign species.

summary: A big, bristly riverside perennial whose roots were once packed around broken limbs to set like plaster. It works well on bruises and sprains, but contains alkaloids that harm the liver when taken by mouth.
nativeRange: Europe to Western Asia; naturalised in North America and elsewhere
abilities: Leaves and roots contain allantoin, which promotes cell proliferation in wound healing
Thick, mucilaginous roots once set hard enough to splint fractures
Deep roots draw up potassium, making its leaves a prized garden fertiliser
Bell flowers are a staple of bumblebees; short-tongued bees 'rob' nectar by biting holes in them
edibilityNote: Formerly eaten as a vegetable and tea, but all parts, especially the roots, contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that cause liver damage. Before flowering its leaves can be mistaken for deadly foxglove.

uses.use: Root and leaf poultices for fractures, sprains, bruises and wounds; formerly teas for coughs and ulcers
Alkaloid-reduced root creams for ankle sprains, back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with positive trials

medicinal.cautions: Never take by mouth: its pyrrolizidine alkaloids can cause veno-occlusive liver disease, and in 2001 the FDA advised removing oral comfrey products from the US market. Use topically on unbroken skin only, for a limited time, preferably as alkaloid-reduced products. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

fruit.description: Shiny dark nutlets with an oil-rich attachment that ants carry off.

seed.description: Glossy black nutlets
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; root cuttings are easier

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from year 1; cut 3–4 times a season
steps: Plant root sections 5 cm deep where it can stay; any root fragment left behind will regrow
Keep moist the first season
Cut leaves for compost or liquid fertiliser before flowering
Label clearly and keep away from edible greens and foxgloves

lore: The name Symphytum comes from the Greek symphyo, 'to grow together', and 'comfrey' from the Latin confervere, 'to boil together' or heal. Its old English name knitbone records its traditional use on fractures.
funFact: Organic gardeners grow sterile 'Bocking 14', a Russian comfrey (S. × uplandicum) bred by Lawrence Hills, as a fertiliser plant that cannot seed itself about.

wiki.extract: Symphytum officinale is a perennial flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae. Along with 34 other species of Symphytum, it is known as comfrey. Internal or long-term topical use of comfrey is discouraged due to its strong potential to cause liver toxicity.

The illustration emphasizes the plant's diagnostic features, including its distinctive drooping bell-shaped flowers and thick, fleshy root, which were essential for identification in early pharmaceutical practice.

Created by Hans Weiditz for Otto Brunfels' 'Herbarum vivae eicones', it represents a landmark in botanical illustration for its unprecedented realism, capturing the plant's specific morphology from a live specimen rather than copying stylized medieval models.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the Comfrey plant (Symphytum officinale), identified in the text as 'Wael-wortel'. The illustration captures the plant's distinctive broad leaves and thick, branching root system, which was highly valued in early modern medicine for its perceived ability to heal wounds and knit broken bones.

Malpighi was a pioneer in microscopic anatomy, and this illustration highlights the complex internal vascular structures he observed, marking a significant step in the scientific understanding of plant biology.

The illustration shows a thick, curved yellowish root system supporting a green stem with multiple branches and clusters of oval leaves. This image served as a visual guide for identifying medicinal herbs in the late 15th century.

Featured in Otto Brunfels' 1532 herbal, it exemplifies the new Renaissance standard of botanical accuracy, based on direct observation of living specimens rather than traditional manuscript copies.

The illustration meticulously details the plant's broad leaves, bell-shaped flowers, and substantial root, serving as a practical guide for identification in this 1532 Dutch herbal.

summary: A spiny terrestrial bromeliad from South America whose 'fruit' is a fusion of 100–200 individual berries around a central stalk. Its CAM photosynthesis lets it open its pores only at night, making it extraordinarily water-efficient.
nativeRange: Southern Brazil and Paraguay (Paraná–Paraguay basin); domesticated by Indigenous South Americans and spread pantropically
abilities: CAM photosynthesis: takes in CO₂ at night to save water
Fruit forms from up to 200 fused flowers, each 'eye' a separate berry
Hummingbirds pollinate wild plants; cultivated plants are self-incompatible, so fruit is seedless
Leaves yield piña fibre, woven into fine sheer cloth in the Philippines
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, cooked, juiced, fermented as tepache)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten. Bromelain makes the mouth tingle or sore when large amounts are eaten raw. Very unripe fruit is irritating and purgative.

uses.use: Fruit applied to wounds and taken for digestive troubles
Bromelain-based enzyme (NexoBrid) approved in Europe and the US for removing burn eschar

medicinal.cautions: Bromelain may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants; pineapple allergy and latex cross-reactivity occur.

fruit.season: Year-round in the tropics; can be forced
fruit.description: Oval fruit 15–30 cm, covered in hexagonal scales ('eyes'), green ripening to golden-orange, topped with a crown of spiny leaves; juicy yellow flesh around a fibrous core.

seed.description: Usually absent in cultivated fruit; when cross-pollinated, small hard seeds appear just under the skin — dark brown to black, 3–5 mm, angular-oval
seed.germination: Seed rarely used; crowns, slips and suckers root easily

grow.zones: USDA 10–12 (11–12 outdoors year-round; also grown in pots indoors)
grow.propagation: Crowns, slips (shoots below the fruit) or suckers
grow.timeToHarvest: 18–24 months from a crown; 12–18 months from suckers
steps: Twist the leafy crown off a ripe pineapple, strip the bottom 3 cm of leaves and let it dry for 2–3 days.
Plant it 5 cm deep in sandy, acidic mix in full sun; water lightly, also into the leaf cup.
Feed lightly every 2 months; keep frost-free and above 15 °C.
To force flowering on a mature plant (12+ months), enclose it in a bag with a ripe apple for a few days, as the ethylene triggers blooming.
Harvest when the fruit smells sweet at the base and the eyes flatten and turn golden; the plant then produces suckers for the next crop.

lore: Columbus encountered the pineapple on Guadeloupe in 1493, and it became an emblem of luxury in 17th–18th century Europe, where wealthy hosts rented pineapples as table centrepieces. The Dunmore Pineapple in Scotland is a 1761 garden folly shaped like the fruit.
funFact: Pineapple's bromelain digests proteins so well that fresh pineapple stops gelatin from setting.

plates.long: This exquisite botanical study depicts a pineapple plant, a prized exotic specimen cultivated in the Amsterdam Hortus Medicus in 1687. The work exemplifies the meticulous observational style of the Moninckx Atlas, capturing the plant's structural details with scientific precision and artistic elegance.

The plate illustrates a pineapple plant serving as a host for the life cycle of various insects, demonstrating Merian's pioneering work in documenting the relationship between flora and fauna in South America.

plates.long: This woodcut from Jean de Léry's 1578 account of Brazil depicts a Tupinambá family. The man is shown with traditional weaponry and a lip plug (tembetá), while the woman carries an infant in a woven sling, illustrating early European observations of indigenous South American life and flora, such as the pineapple in the foreground.

The scene includes palm trees, a monkey consuming the fruit, and a distant figure, reflecting the European fascination with the exotic flora and fauna of the East during the 17th century.

This plate illustrates Merian's groundbreaking ecological approach, showing insects in direct relationship with their host plants, a revolutionary concept in 18th-century natural history.

Merian was a pioneer in documenting the metamorphosis of insects in relation to their host plants, a revolutionary approach in the early 18th century. plates.long: This engraving from Kircher's 'China Illustrata' (1667) showcases the 17th-century European fascination with exotic nature. It depicts a variety of plants, including a banana tree (labeled Ficus Indica) and a pineapple, alongside a monkey, representing the diverse biological discoveries reported by Jesuit missionaries in the East.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts an Ananas comosus (pineapple), a fruit that was a symbol of wealth and exoticism in 18th-century Europe. Produced for Christoph Jakob Trew's 'Uitgezochte planten,' the illustration showcases the meticulous detail and scientific accuracy characteristic of the era's finest botanical publications.

The illustration captures the intricate geometric patterns of the fruit's skin and its distinctive spiky foliage, serving as an early scientific record of tropical flora for a European audience.

summary: A small, papery-barked tree that clings to sun-scorched limestone in Dhofar and Somalia. For thousands of years its milky resin was the backbone of the incense trade, and caravans carried it to temples from Rome to China.
nativeRange: Dhofar (southern Oman), Hadramawt (eastern Yemen) and northern Somalia
abilities: Bleeds a milky resin rich in boswellic acids, which inhibit the inflammatory enzyme 5-lipoxygenase in lab studies
Grips sheer rock with a swollen, cushion-like base
Survives in hyper-arid country by drawing on summer monsoon fog (khareef)
edibilityNote: Small pieces of high-grade resin are chewed as gum in Oman and soaked in drinking water, but it is not a food.

uses.use: Resin chewed or soaked in water for digestion, coughs and memory; smoke to purify homes and after childbirth
Kundur for memory and the brain, for coughs, diarrhoea and to heal wounds
Ruxiang to invigorate blood and relieve pain, often paired with myrrh (moyao)
Boswellia extracts (mostly the Indian B. serrata) trialled for osteoarthritis and inflammatory bowel disease

medicinal.cautions: Most clinical trials used Indian frankincense (B. serrata), not this species. It can cause stomach upset, reflux and skin rash. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Overtapping and grazing are reducing wild populations, so buy sustainably sourced resin.

fruit.description: Small three- to five-valved capsule.

seed.description: Small, winged seeds
seed.germination: Low; warm (25–30 °C), sharply drained gritty mix, 2–4 weeks

grow.timeToHarvest: Resin from trees about 8–10 years old
steps: Sow fresh seed in pure grit and pumice
Keep warm and barely moist
Grow in containers in a greenhouse outside desert climates
Never overwater; it is easily killed by wet roots

lore: The Land of Frankincense in Dhofar, including the ancient port of Sumhuram (Khor Rori) and the wadi Dawkah tree groves, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. Pliny claimed southern Arabia was the richest land on earth because of the incense trade.
funFact: Its name lubān (and Greek libanos) comes from a Semitic root meaning 'white' or 'milk', after the pale resin.

wiki.extract: Boswellia sacra, also known as Boswellia carteri and others, and commonly called the frankincense tree or the olibanum tree, is a tree in the genus Boswellia, in the Burseraceae family, from which frankincense, a resinous dried sap, is harvested. The olibanum tree is a plant native to the countries of Oman and Yemen, in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, and to Somalia and Ethiopia, in the Horn of Africa. In 2012, it was replanted in Israel in the Middle East, 1,500 years after dying out there.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts the frankincense tree, known in traditional Chinese medicine as Xunlu Ruxiang. It is featured in Li Shizhen's monumental work, the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), providing a visual reference for the source of this valuable aromatic resin used in various medical treatments.

summary: A small, thorny, gnarled desert tree of the Horn of Africa and Arabia whose bitter, aromatic resin was worth its weight in gold in antiquity. It was burned in temples, used in embalming and brought as a gift to the infant Jesus.
nativeRange: Somalia, Ethiopia, Djibouti and northern Kenya, and the southern Arabian Peninsula (Yemen, Oman, Saudi Arabia)
abilities: Bleeds a reddish oleo-gum-resin when wounded that seals the cut and deters insects and microbes
Furanosesquiterpenes in the resin have measurable antimicrobial and pain-relieving activity
Thrives in thin, stony soil on very little rain, leafing only briefly after rains
edibilityNote: Resin is used medicinally in small amounts, as incense and as a flavouring, not as food.

uses.use: Resin for wounds, stomach complaints and mouth ulcers, and burned to fumigate homes
Mur makki for wounds, chest complaints, menstrual problems and as a mouthwash
Moyao to invigorate blood and relieve pain from trauma and swelling, often with frankincense (ruxiang)
Tincture for mouth and gum inflammation; EMA traditional-use monograph

medicinal.cautions: May stimulate the uterus, so avoid in pregnancy. Can lower blood sugar and has been reported to reduce warfarin's effect. Can cause contact dermatitis. A myrrh-based drug for schistosomiasis (Mirazid) performed poorly in controlled trials.

fruit.description: Small, ovoid, pointed drupe about 7 mm long.

seed.description: Single seed within a hard stone
seed.germination: Slow and low; cuttings are more reliable

grow.soil: Stony, sandy, sharply drained, often alkaline
grow.timeToHarvest: Resin from mature trees (several years old)
steps: Root thick cuttings in dry, gritty mix in hot weather
Keep almost dry, especially when leafless
Protect from frost
Traditionally, resin is tapped by making small cuts in the bark and collecting the hardened tears weeks later

lore: Around 1470 BCE Queen Hatshepsut sent an expedition to the Land of Punt that brought back live myrrh and incense trees, as shown in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. The Gospel of Matthew (2:11) names myrrh among the Magi's gifts.
funFact: Hatshepsut's Punt expedition is often called the first recorded attempt to transplant living trees from one country to another.

wiki.extract: Commiphora myrrha, called myrrh, Somali myrrh, herabol myrrh, common myrrh, is a tree in the family Burseraceae. It is one of the primary trees used in the production of myrrh, a resin made from dried tree sap. The Commiphora myrrha tree is indigenous to Somalia, in the Somali regions of Ethiopia and Kenya, Djibouti, Eritrea and parts of the Arabian Peninsula.

summary: The giant cactus of the Sonoran Desert, which can grow taller than 12 m, live for around 150–200 years and weigh several tonnes when full of water. It may take 50–100 years to grow its first arm. Its pleats swell like an accordion after rain.
nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, south-eastern California and Sonora, Mexico
abilities: Expands its pleated stem to store hundreds of litres of water after rain
Opens night-blooming flowers pollinated by lesser long-nosed bats, then birds and bees by day
Its hollows, carved by Gila woodpeckers and gilded flickers, house owls, martins and other birds
Feeds desert animals in early summer, when its fruit ripens and little else is available
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten fresh, dried, or boiled into syrup and jam. Harvesting from wild plants on protected land requires permission.

fruit.description: Green fruits split to reveal red pulp packed with tiny black seeds.

seed.description: Tiny glossy black seeds
seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix, warm and humid; seedlings need shade

steps: Surface-sow seed under a clear cover and keep warm and lightly moist
Shade seedlings, as wild ones grow under 'nurse' trees like palo verde
Water sparingly; protect from frost
Buy only nursery-grown plants: removing wild saguaros is illegal in Arizona

lore: For the Tohono O'odham the saguaro harvest (bahidaj) in early summer begins the new year, and fermented saguaro wine is used in a rain ceremony to call the monsoon. The saguaro blossom is Arizona's state flower.
funFact: Saguaro seedlings may grow only a few centimetres in their first decade.

wiki.extract: The saguaro is a tree-like cactus species in the monotypic genus Carnegiea that can grow to be over 12 meters tall. It is native to the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, the Mexican state of Sonora, and the Whipple Mountains and Imperial County areas of California. Saguaro typically grow at elevations ranging from sea level to 4,500 feet (1,400 m), although they may be found at up to 5,000 feet (1,500 m). The saguaro blossom is the state wildflower of Arizona. Its scientific name is given in honor of Andrew Carnegie. In 1933, Saguaro National Park, near Tucson, Arizona, was designated to help protect this species and its habitat.

summary: A small spineless cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert that produces mescaline, used in ceremony by Indigenous peoples for at least 5,700 years. It grows very slowly, taking years to reach harvest size, and overharvesting and land clearing have made it vulnerable.
nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert and Tamaulipan thornscrub of southern Texas and north-central Mexico
abilities: Synthesises mescaline and dozens of related phenethylamine and isoquinoline alkaloids
Has no spines; relies on bitter alkaloids and camouflage under shrubs
Regrows new 'buttons' from its carrot-like root after the crown is cut, if cut correctly
Grows extremely slowly, often 10+ years to flowering size in the wild
edibilityNote: Not a food. The crown is intensely bitter and typically causes nausea and vomiting, along with powerful hallucinations from mescaline, raised heart rate and blood pressure. Dangerous for people with heart conditions or psychosis; illegal in most places except for protected religious use.

uses.tradition: Indigenous Mexican and Native American medicine
uses.use: Used for pain, fever, wounds and in healing ceremonies
Sacramental use in all-night prayer meetings

medicinal.cautions: Hallucinogenic; can trigger psychosis and dangerous behaviour; interacts with MAOIs and other drugs.

fruit.description: Small, pink, club-shaped fruit with black seeds.

seed.description: Small black seeds
seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix under cover; very slow growth

lore: Peyote buttons found in Shumla Caves, Texas, have been radiocarbon-dated to about 5,700 years ago. The Wixárika (Huichol) make an annual pilgrimage to Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí to gather hikuri, and US federal law (AIRFA amendments, 1994) protects its sacramental use by Native American Church members.
funFact: Mescaline, isolated from peyote by Arthur Heffter in 1897, was the first psychedelic compound ever isolated.

wiki.extract: Peyote, also known as Lophophora williamsii, is a small, spineless cactus which contains psychoactive alkaloids, particularly mescaline. Peyote is a Spanish word derived from the Nahuatl peyōtl, meaning "caterpillar cocoon", from a root peyōni, "to glisten".

summary: A large, paddle-jointed cactus domesticated in central Mexico, cultivated for its sweet fruit (tunas) and tender young pads (nopales). It also hosts the cochineal insect, source of the brilliant carmine red that dyed European royalty's robes and still colours food.
nativeRange: Domesticated in central Mexico; naturalised throughout the Mediterranean, North and East Africa, the Middle East, India and Australia
abilities: CAM photosynthesis lets it fix carbon at night, using up to 5 times less water than grain crops
Any pad that touches soil can root into a new plant
Hosts cochineal scale insects, whose carminic acid gives carmine dye
Prickly pears became notorious weeds in Australia (mainly O. stricta), famously cleared by the Cactoblastis moth; O. ficus-indica itself is invasive in South Africa
edibilityNote: Fruit and young pads are eaten. Remove the tiny barbed hair-like spines (glochids) carefully — they lodge in skin and mouth. Eating very many seeds can cause intestinal blockage.

uses.use: Nopal pads eaten to lower blood sugar in diabetes, with small clinical studies showing reduced post-meal glucose
Flowers as a tea for kidney stones and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: May add to the effect of diabetes medication; glochids cause skin irritation.

fruit.description: Barrel- or egg-shaped berry 5–10 cm, green, yellow, orange, red or purple, studded with tufts of tiny spines; juicy, sweet, melon-like flesh of the same colour, full of seeds.

seed.description: Hard, flattened, round to kidney-shaped seeds 3–5 mm, beige to light brown, with a thick woody coat; 100–300 per fruit
seed.germination: Slow; scarify and sow at 25–30 °C in gritty mix; 2–8 weeks. Pads are the usual propagation

grow.soil: Sandy, rocky, very well-drained; tolerates poor and alkaline soils
steps: Cut a healthy pad with tongs or thick gloves and let the cut end dry for 1–2 weeks until calloused.
Plant it upright, one-third buried, in dry, gritty soil in full sun; do not water for the first 2–3 weeks.
Water occasionally in the first summer; established plants need almost none.
Harvest young pads (nopalitos) in spring when 15–20 cm long, and scrape off spines before cooking.
Pick fruit with tongs when fully coloured, roll it in sand or burn off the glochids, then slice off the ends and peel.

lore: The Aztec founding legend says their wandering people would build their city where they saw an eagle perched on a nopal cactus — the image on Mexico's flag and the origin of Tenochtitlan. In Israel 'sabra', the prickly pear, is the nickname for native-born Israelis: prickly outside, sweet inside.
funFact: Carmine from cochineal insects on prickly pear was Spain's second most valuable export from the Americas after silver.

wiki.extract: Opuntia ficus-indica, the Indian fig opuntia, fig opuntia, or prickly pear, is a species of cactus that has long been a domesticated crop plant grown in agricultural economies throughout arid and semiarid parts of the world. O. ficus-indica is the most widespread and most commercially important cactus. It is grown primarily as a fruit crop, and also for the vegetable nopales and other uses. Cacti are good crops for dry areas because they efficiently convert water into biomass. O. ficus-indica is the most widespread of the long-domesticated cactuses. Opuntia species hybridize easily, but the wild origin of O. ficus-indica is likely to have been in central Mexico, where its closest genetic relatives are found.

summary: One of humanity's oldest crops, grown for rope and cloth, edible seeds, oil, medicine and its mind-altering resin. The flowers' resin glands make THC and CBD, compounds that act on the body's own endocannabinoid system.
nativeRange: Central and South Asia (possibly East Asia); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Produces long, strong bast fibres used for rope, sails, paper and cloth
Makes resin in glandular trichomes rich in cannabinoids (THC, CBD) and terpenes
Many varieties switch to flowering when nights lengthen
Grows extremely fast, reaching 2–5 m in one season
edibilityNote: Hemp seeds and oil contain little or no THC and are widely eaten. Flowers and resin are psychoactive; edibles can cause severe intoxication, especially in children and pets (dogs are very sensitive). Legal status varies by country.

uses.use: Purified bhang (vijaya) for pain, digestion and sleep
Seeds (huo ma ren) as a laxative
Purified CBD (Epidiolex) approved for certain epilepsies; THC drugs (dronabinol, nabilone) for chemotherapy nausea and appetite loss

medicinal.cautions: THC can cause anxiety, psychosis in vulnerable people, impaired driving and dependence; heavy use is linked to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. CBD interacts with drugs such as clobazam and blood thinners. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Small, smooth, grey-brown seeds enclosed in a bract.

seed.description: Hard, oval, mottled achenes
seed.germination: Sow 1 cm deep at 20–25 °C; 3–7 days

steps: Check local laws: growing is restricted or licensed in many places
Sow after the last frost in fertile soil
For fibre, sow densely; for seed, sow widely spaced
Harvest fibre stems at early flowering; harvest seed when most seeds are brown

lore: Hemp cloth and cord are known from Neolithic China, and Herodotus (5th century BCE) described Scythians throwing hemp seeds on hot stones and howling with joy in the vapour. Braziers from a ~2,500-year-old cemetery at Jirzankal in the Pamirs contain residues of high-THC cannabis.
funFact: The English word 'canvas' comes from cannabis, via Old French and Latin.

wiki.extract: Cannabis sativa is an annual herbaceous flowering plant. The species was first classified by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. The specific epithet sativa means 'cultivated'. Indigenous to Eastern Asia, the plant is now of cosmopolitan distribution due to widespread cultivation. It has been cultivated throughout recorded history and used as a source of industrial fiber, seed oil, food, and medicine. It is also used as a recreational drug and for religious and spiritual purposes.

summary: A tall, damp-meadow perennial with sweetly scented pink-white flowers above roots that smell powerfully of old socks. Those roots have been Europe's classic sleep remedy since Galen's day, and cats find them irresistible.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia; naturalised in North America
abilities: Roots produce valerenic acid and valepotriates, which act on GABA-A receptors in lab studies
Root odour comes from isovaleric acid, which forms as the roots dry
Attracts cats, which roll on the roots much as they do on catnip
Fragrant flower heads draw hoverflies, bees and butterflies
edibilityNote: Root is used as tea, tincture or capsules, not as food.

uses.use: Root tea for insomnia, nervous tension, palpitations and cramps; Galen prescribed 'phu' for insomnia
Root extracts approved in Germany and by the EMA (traditional use) for mild nervous tension and sleep disorders
Related valerians (asaroon, sumbul-ut-teeb) used as nervines; V. officinalis root used similarly in Persian pharmacy

medicinal.cautions: Sleep trials are inconsistent and effects modest at best. Can cause drowsiness, headache and morning grogginess, and adds to alcohol and sedative drugs, so do not drive after taking it. Rare cases of liver injury. Not advised in pregnancy or for young children.

fruit.description: Small one-seeded fruit crowned with a parachute of plumes.

seed.description: Oblong, ribbed seed with a feathery pappus
seed.germination: Needs light; 2–3 weeks at 18–20 °C; viability falls after a year

steps: Surface-sow fresh seed in spring
Plant 45–60 cm apart in moist soil
Remove flower stems in year 2 to send energy into the roots
Lift roots in autumn, wash quickly and dry at under 40 °C

lore: Dioscorides and Galen called it phu, a word thought to echo disgust at its smell. It is reported to have been used in Britain during the World Wars for nervous strain, including the stress of air raids.
funFact: Cats react to valerian root because of actinidine, a compound related to the nepetalactone in catnip.

wiki.extract: Valerian is an herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to Europe and southwestern Asia. It is the type species of the genus Valeriana.

The illustration is part of 'Den groten herbarius,' a seminal Dutch herbal that combined traditional knowledge with detailed botanical imagery to aid in identification.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts 'Phu Magnum' (Great Valerian) from Leonhart Fuchs's landmark 1542 herbal. Fuchs revolutionized botanical illustration by insisting on drawings made from life, capturing the plant's entire lifecycle from the fibrous root to the delicate terminal flowers. This work set a new standard for scientific accuracy in the transition from medieval herbals to modern botany.

summary: A fast-growing, short-lived, soft-stemmed tree that can fruit within a year of sowing. Native to Mesoamerica, it is now grown across the tropics, and its milky latex is the source of papain, an enzyme used to tenderise meat.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico and Central America; cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Grows from seed to fruiting tree 2–3 m tall in 6–12 months
Plants can be male, female or hermaphrodite, and some switch sex with temperature
Latex rich in papain digests proteins and protects the plant from insects
A genetically engineered virus-resistant papaya saved Hawaii's papaya industry from ringspot virus in the 1990s
edibleParts: green fruit (cooked or shredded in som tam salad)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Unripe fruit and latex are high in papain and can irritate skin and the mouth; latex is traditionally avoided in pregnancy because it may stimulate uterine contractions.

uses.use: Leaf juice taken during dengue fever, with small trials suggesting raised platelet counts
Ripe fruit for digestion and constipation; seeds against intestinal worms
Green papaya poultice and latex on wounds and burns

medicinal.cautions: Unripe fruit and latex avoided in pregnancy. Latex allergy cross-reactivity. Seeds in large amounts may be harmful.

fruit.description: Oblong to pear-shaped berry 10–45 cm, green ripening yellow-orange; soft, sweet, musky orange-to-red flesh around a hollow cavity lined with seeds.

seed.description: Round, wrinkled, black seeds about 5 mm across, each wrapped in a clear, gelatinous sac (sarcotesta); hundreds per fruit, peppery-tasting
seed.germination: Wash off the jelly sac, sow 1 cm deep in warm (25–32 °C) free-draining mix; sprouts in 1–3 weeks

grow.soil: Light, very well-drained, rich in organic matter, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed (choose seed from hermaphrodite fruit, e.g. 'Solo' types)
steps: Sow several seeds per pot of a hermaphrodite variety like 'Solo' or 'Red Lady' so most plants will fruit.
Plant out 2–3 m apart into a warm, sunny, wind-sheltered spot on a raised mound, as roots rot easily.
Feed every month with balanced fertiliser and mulch; water deeply in dry weather.
Once flowers appear, remove male-only plants (long-stalked flower clusters), keeping one per 10–20 if you grow dioecious types.
Harvest when the skin starts to turn yellow and ripen at room temperature; replace trees after 3–4 years as they grow tall.

lore: Christopher Columbus is said to have called the papaya 'the fruit of the angels'. Spanish and Portuguese sailors spread it across the tropics in the 16th century, reaching the Philippines and India by the 1600s.
funFact: Chymopapain from papaya latex was once injected to dissolve slipped spinal discs, and papain is still sold as meat tenderiser.

summary: A deciduous tree of Asian forests whose wrinkled, tannin-rich fruit is the 'king of medicines' in Tibetan tradition. The Medicine Buddha is shown holding a sprig of it, and it is one of the three fruits of Ayurveda's Triphala.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent to Myanmar, Thailand, Indochina and south-western China
abilities: Fruit is rich in hydrolysable tannins such as chebulagic and chebulinic acid
Tannins have long been used to tan leather and, with iron, to make black dyes and inks
Laxative when ripe, astringent when unripe, an unusual dual action that Ayurveda exploits
edibleParts: fruit (as medicine: powdered, chewed or preserved)
edibilityNote: Eaten mostly as medicine. Very astringent, and laxative in larger amounts.

uses.use: Haritaki as a rasayana and gentle laxative; one of the three fruits of Triphala; for constipation, cough and wounds
A-ru-ra, the 'king of medicines', said to treat all three humours and found in a great many formulas
Halela siyah/zard in Itrifal compounds for constipation, piles, brain and digestion
Hezi as an astringent for chronic diarrhoea, dysentery and chronic cough with hoarse voice

medicinal.cautions: Can cause diarrhoea and dehydration, so avoid with acute diarrhoea or exhaustion. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy. May interact with diabetes drugs.

fruit.description: Ovoid, ridged drupe 2–4 cm, yellow-green ripening brown-black and wrinkled when dried; very astringent.

seed.dispersal: Mammals such as deer and monkeys
seed.germination: Slow; crack or soak the stone; 1–3 months

grow.soil: Well-drained, including poor and stony soil
steps: Soak stones for 2–3 days, then sow in deep pots
Plant out in the rains in full sun
Protect saplings from frost and browsing
Gather fallen fruit and sun-dry

lore: The Medicine Buddha (Bhaiṣajyaguru) is traditionally painted holding a myrobalan sprig in his right hand. Medieval Arab and European pharmacies imported 'chebulic myrobalans' from India, and they were a costly drug in Renaissance Europe.
funFact: Black myrobalan (dried unripe fruit) and chebulic myrobalan (mature fruit) were sold in old apothecaries as separate drugs, though they come from the same tree.

summary: A trailing morning-glory relative from tropical America with sweet, starchy storage roots. Sweet potatoes reached Polynesia centuries before Columbus — widely taken as evidence of pre-Columbian contact between Polynesians and South Americans.
nativeRange: Tropical Central and northern South America; grown throughout the tropics and warm-temperate regions
abilities: Natural GM crop: its genome carries genes inserted by Agrobacterium thousands of years ago
Vines root at nodes, so a single plant can cover several square metres
Orange-fleshed types are very rich in β-carotene, used in Africa to fight vitamin A deficiency
Produces food in poor soils and survives typhoons that flatten grain crops
edibleParts: leaves and shoot tips (cooked, widely eaten in Africa and Asia)
edibilityNote: Roots and leaves are eaten cooked. Roots attacked by weevils or mould can contain toxic furanoterpenoids (e.g. ipomeamarone); cut away bitter, blemished parts.

uses.use: Roots to strengthen the spleen and ease constipation
White-skinned sweet potato ('caiapo') extract taken for diabetes, with small trials
Orange-fleshed sweet potato promoted to prevent vitamin A deficiency (World Food Prize 2016)

medicinal.cautions: Discard damaged, bitter roots. High oxalate in leaves.

fruit.description: Small, round, dry capsule about 5–8 mm, holding 1–4 seeds; flowers are lavender-to-white morning-glory trumpets.

seed.description: Hard, angular to rounded, dark-brown to black seeds about 3–4 mm, with a very tough coat
seed.dispersal: Gravity; vegetatively by humans; possibly ocean drift and birds
seed.germination: Breeding only: scarify (nick or acid) and sow at 25–30 °C. Gardeners use slips

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop (USDA 4–11 with 90–150 frost-free days); perennial in tropics
grow.soil: Loose, sandy loam, well-drained, pH 5.5–6.5; avoid rich nitrogen soils (all leaves, few roots)
steps: Grow slips by half-submerging a sweet potato in water or burying it in damp sand in a warm place; snap off sprouts at 15–20 cm and root them in water.
After frost, when soil is above 18 °C, plant slips 30–40 cm apart in raised ridges, burying them to the top leaves.
Water until established; avoid heavy nitrogen feeding.
Lift vines periodically so they don't root everywhere, and pick some tips for cooking.
Dig carefully before frost, when roots are a good size; cure in a warm (around 30 °C), humid place for 7–10 days to sweeten and heal skins, then store at 13–15 °C.

lore: Kūmara reached Polynesia by about 1000–1100 CE, and Māori grew it in New Zealand with elaborate rituals to the god Rongo. In Japan, the Edo scholar Aoki Konyō promoted the sweet potato as famine insurance in the 1730s, earning the nickname 'Kansho Sensei' (Master Sweet Potato).
funFact: The Polynesian word 'kūmara' closely resembles the Quechua 'kumar' — often cited as a clue that Polynesians reached South America, though linguists still debate the link.

wiki.extract: The sweet potato or sweetpotato is a dicotyledonous plant in the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae. Its sizeable, starchy, sweet-tasting, tuberous roots are used as a root vegetable, which is a staple food in parts of the world. Cultivars of the sweet potato have been bred to bear tubers with flesh and skin of various colors. Moreover, the young shoots and leaves are eaten as greens with nutritional composition comparable to spinach. The sweet potato and the potato are only distantly related, both being in the order Solanales. Although darker sweet potatoes are often known as yams in parts of North America, they are even more distant from actual yams, which are monocots in the order Dioscoreales.
