summary: The tallest living thing known. Hyperion, found in Redwood National Park in 2006, measured about 116 m, taller than a 35-storey building. Redwoods drink fog through their leaves, sprout new trunks from burls, and grow whole hanging gardens in their crowns.
nativeRange: A narrow fog belt along the Pacific coast from south-western Oregon to Big Sur, California
abilities: Absorbs fog water directly through its foliage, which matters in rainless California summers
Resprouts from basal burls and root crowns after fire or felling, forming 'fairy rings' of clones
Builds canopy soils that support ferns, huckleberries and even other trees high above the ground
Has a hexaploid genome, with six sets of chromosomes, unusual among conifers
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Not considered significantly toxic.

fruit.description: Olive-sized cones 1.5–3 cm long that release tiny seeds.

seed.description: Tiny two-winged brown seeds, mostly of low viability
seed.dispersal: Wind; most regeneration is clonal sprouting
seed.germination: No pretreatment needed; sow on moist mix, germination often under 10%

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental or timber; cones from 5–15 years
steps: Sow fresh seed in spring on moist, sterile mix (expect low germination)
Keep seedlings humid and sheltered from drying wind
Plant out in deep soil and water through dry summers for the first years
Give it space: it can add 1 m or more a year in good conditions

lore: Old-growth logging after the 1849 Gold Rush removed about 95% of the original redwood forest; the Save the Redwoods League, founded in 1918, began buying groves back. The Yurok and Tolowa used fallen redwood for plank houses and dugout canoes.
funFact: Hyperion's exact location is kept quiet, and since 2022 visitors who go off-trail to find it risk a fine of up to $5,000 and up to six months in jail.

wiki.extract: Sequoia sempervirens, the coast redwood, is the sole living species of the genus Sequoia in the cypress family, Cupressaceae. Other common names include coastal redwood and California redwood. It is a coniferous, long-lived, monoecious tree that has reached ages of about 2,000 years. The species has produced the tallest living trees on Earth, reaching up to 116.22 m (381.3 ft) in height and up to 8.9 m (29 ft) in diameter at breast height. These trees are also among the longest-living trees on Earth.

summary: The most massive single-stem tree on Earth. General Sherman, in Sequoia National Park, holds roughly 1,487 cubic metres of wood, and the oldest sequoias counted by rings passed 3,000 years. Its bark, up to about 90 cm thick at the base and nearly resin-free, lets it shrug off the low fires its cones depend on.
nativeRange: About 70 scattered groves on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, California, at 1,400–2,000 m
abilities: Grows fibrous, tannin-rich bark up to about 90 cm thick that insulates the cambium from surface fires
Keeps cones closed and green on the tree for up to 20 years; heat from fire, Douglas squirrels and a cone-boring beetle release the seeds
Seedlings need bare mineral soil and open sky, conditions that low-intensity fire creates
Reaches the largest trunk volume of any tree: General Sherman is about 83.8 m tall and 11 m across at the base
edibilityNote: No part is eaten. Not known to be significantly toxic.

fruit.season: Matures over two seasons; may persist green for many years
fruit.description: Egg-sized cones 4–7 cm long, holding about 200 seeds each.

seed.description: Flat, winged, straw-coloured seeds
seed.dispersal: Wind, after cones are dried by fire or chewed open by squirrels and beetles
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks; sow on the surface of bare, moist mineral soil

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; cones begin at around 10–20 years
steps: Stratify seed in moist sand in the fridge for 4–8 weeks
Surface-sow in a free-draining mix and keep evenly moist and bright
Pot on yearly and plant out at 1–3 years where it has room to become enormous
Avoid planting near buildings: roots spread widely and the crown becomes massive

lore: Specimens were stripped and shipped east for exhibition in the 1850s, and the outcry over the felled 'Discovery Tree' helped lead Lincoln to sign the 1864 Yosemite Grant, an early act of American wilderness protection. Fires in 2020–2021 killed an estimated 13–19% of all large sequoias.
funFact: Despite its fire-proof reputation, the 2020 Castle Fire alone killed an estimated 7,500–10,600 large sequoias, about a tenth of the world's mature population.

wiki.extract: Sequoiadendron giganteum is a species of coniferous tree, classified in the family Cupressaceae in the subfamily Sequoioideae. Giant sequoia specimens are the largest trees on Earth. They are native to the groves on the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountain range of California but have been introduced, planted, and grown around the world.

summary: A plant that counts. Its hinged leaf-traps snap shut in about a tenth of a second, but only after two touches of the trigger hairs within about 20 seconds, and it starts making digestive enzymes only after more touches. In the wild it grows only in a small area of the Carolinas.
nativeRange: Coastal plain wetlands within roughly 120 km of Wilmington, North and South Carolina
abilities: Snaps its trap in about 100 milliseconds using stored elastic energy that flips the leaf's curvature
Counts trigger-hair touches: two to close, five or so to start full digestion
Sends electrical action potentials through the leaf, much like a nerve
Gets nitrogen and phosphorus from prey, which lets it grow in very poor, boggy soils
Depends on regular fire to keep competing plants from shading it
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Not significantly toxic.

fruit.description: Small capsules on a tall stalk, held well above the traps so pollinators are not caught.

seed.description: Shiny black pear-shaped seeds
seed.germination: Surface-sow on damp peat-sand; 2–4 weeks in light and warmth

grow.water: Constantly moist with rainwater or distilled water only
grow.soil: Unfertilised sphagnum peat with sand or perlite
steps: Pot in pure peat and perlite (no fertiliser, no potting compost)
Stand the pot in a tray of rainwater in full sun
Never use tap water with dissolved minerals and never fertilise the soil
Give a cool winter dormancy (around 0–10 °C) for 3–4 months

lore: Governor Arthur Dobbs of North Carolina described it in 1759, and Charles Darwin called it 'one of the most wonderful plants in the world' in Insectivorous Plants (1875). Since 2014, poaching wild flytraps in North Carolina has been a felony.
funFact: Small insects that can wriggle out between the 'teeth' are released on purpose; the trap does not seal for prey too small to be worth digesting.

wiki.extract: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States. Although various modern hybrids have been created in cultivation, D. muscipula is the only species of the monotypic genus Dionaea. It is closely related to the waterwheel plant and the cosmopolitan sundews (Drosera), all of which belong to the family Droseraceae. Dionaea catches its prey—chiefly insects and arachnids—with a "jaw"-like clamping structure, which is formed by the terminal portion of each of the plant's leaves; when an insect makes contact with the open leaves, vibrations from the prey's movements ultimately trigger the "jaws" to shut via tiny hairs on their inner surfaces. Additionally, when an insect or spider touches one of these hairs, the trap prepares to close, only fully enclosing the prey if a second hair is contacted within (approximately) twenty seconds of the first contact. Triggers may occur as quickly as 1⁄10 of a second from initial contact.

summary: A small bog plant whose leaves are covered in red tentacles, each tipped with a drop of sticky 'dew'. Insects that land get stuck, the tentacles slowly bend over them, and the leaf digests them. Darwin spent years experimenting on it.
nativeRange: Circumboreal: Europe, northern Asia, North America, Greenland
abilities: Its glandular tentacles secrete sticky mucilage that traps insects
Bends tentacles, and sometimes the whole leaf, around struggling prey over minutes to hours
Secretes digestive enzymes and absorbs nitrogen from prey
Survives harsh winters as a tight bud (hibernaculum)
edibilityNote: Not a food. Historically used to flavour liqueur and curdle milk.

uses.use: Herb tea or tincture for dry and spasmodic coughs and whooping cough
Remedy for coughs (homeopathic preparations contain essentially no plant material)

medicinal.cautions: Wild collection is restricted in many countries; most commercial Drosera is other species. Naphthoquinones irritate skin.

fruit.description: Tiny capsules on a slender stalk well above the leaves.

seed.description: Minute spindle-shaped seeds
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks; surface-sow on damp peat in light

steps: Sow stratified seed on damp peat or live sphagnum
Keep in a tray of rainwater in full sun
Give a cold winter rest outdoors or in a fridge
Don't fertilise; let it catch its own insects

lore: Darwin wrote in 1860 that he cared more for Drosera than for the origin of all the species in the world, and his Insectivorous Plants (1875) begins with it. Italian rosolio liqueur gets its name from the sundew (ros solis, 'dew of the sun').
funFact: A sundew leaf can tell a real insect from a raindrop or grain of sand and responds far more strongly to nitrogen-containing objects.

wiki.extract: Drosera rotundifolia, the round-leaved sundew, roundleaf sundew, or common sundew, is a species of carnivorous flowering plant that grows in bogs, marshes and fens. One of the most widespread sundew species, it has a circumboreal distribution, being found in almost all of Europe, all of Siberia, large parts of North America, Korea and Japan but is also found as far south as eastern China, the Philippines, and into the Southern Hemisphere in New Guinea.

summary: A relative of ebony, cultivated in China for over 2,000 years for its glowing orange fruit that hangs on bare branches into winter. Astringent varieties are inedibly puckering until soft-ripe; non-astringent types like 'Fuyu' can be eaten crisp like an apple.
nativeRange: China; long cultivated in Japan and Korea, now grown in warm-temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Soluble tannins in unripe astringent fruit bind proteins in the mouth, causing a dry pucker
Fruit can set without pollination (parthenocarpy), giving seedless fruit
Fruit hangs on leafless branches well into winter
Unripe juice (kakishibu) is fermented into a waterproofing dye for paper and cloth
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, or dried as hoshigaki / shìbǐng)
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Eating lots of unripe astringent persimmons, especially on an empty stomach, can form hard stomach masses (diospyrobezoars) that may need surgery.

uses.use: Dried calyx (shì dì) used for hiccups; dried fruit for cough
Persimmon-leaf tea, rich in vitamin C, as a tonic

medicinal.cautions: Bezoar risk from large amounts of unripe fruit, especially after stomach surgery.

fruit.description: Round to acorn-shaped berry 5–9 cm, glossy orange to red-orange, with a persistent four-lobed green calyx; flesh orange, jelly-soft when ripe or crisp in non-astringent types.

seed.description: Flattened, oblong, dark-brown seeds 1.5–2 cm long, smooth and hard; 0–8 per fruit, often none
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow 2 cm deep at 20–25 °C; slow and taprooted, 3–8 weeks

grow.water: Moderate; even moisture reduces fruit drop
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5; tolerates clay if drained
grow.propagation: Grafting onto D. kaki, D. lotus or D. virginiana seedling rootstocks
steps: Choose a variety: non-astringent ('Fuyu', 'Jiro') to eat crisp, or astringent ('Hachiya') to eat soft or dry.
Plant a grafted tree in full sun, sheltered from strong wind, which damages brittle branches.
Water regularly in the first years and during fruit swell; feed lightly, as excess nitrogen causes fruit drop.
Prune lightly in winter to thin crowded branches; thin heavy crops to prevent limb breakage.
Cut fruit with a short stalk; ripen astringent types until jelly-soft, or peel and hang them to dry as hoshigaki.

lore: Persimmon trees that survived the atomic bombing of Nagasaki have been propagated as 'Kaki Tree Project' saplings planted in schools worldwide. In Korea, dried persimmon (gotgam) is offered at ancestral rites during Chuseok.
funFact: Diospyros means 'fruit of the gods' (or 'grain of Zeus') in Greek.

wiki.extract: Diospyros kaki, the Oriental persimmon, Chinese persimmon, Japanese persimmon, kaki persimmon, or Fuyu persimmon, is the most widely cultivated species of the genus Diospyros. Although its first botanical description was not published until 1780, D. kaki cultivation in China dates back more than 2000 years.

The illustration uniquely integrates Chinese characters (柿餅樹 - Shìbǐng shù) alongside Latin text, documenting the Jesuit author's efforts to bridge Eastern and Western scientific knowledge during the early modern period.

The plate includes a cross-section of the fruit and detailed views of its floral components, exemplifying the rigorous scientific documentation of exotic plants during the early modern period. Such images played a vital

It served as a vital visual reference for identifying the plant, which was documented by Li Shizhen for its various medicinal properties in traditional Chinese practice.

summary: A leafless, broom-like gymnosperm of the steppes whose green jointed stems contain ephedrine. For two thousand years it has been a Chinese remedy for colds and asthma; in the 20th century it became a decongestant drug, and later a deadly diet supplement.
nativeRange: Northern China, Mongolia and adjacent Russia
abilities: Makes ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, which mimic adrenaline, open the airways and raise heart rate and blood pressure
Leaves are reduced to tiny scales; the green stems do the photosynthesis
A gymnosperm related to conifers, with fleshy red seed cones instead of flowers and fruit
Spreading roots bind sandy steppe soils
edibilityNote: Not a food. The stems are potent stimulants.

uses.use: Mahuang to release the exterior and induce sweating in wind-cold colds, calm wheezing and promote urination; core herb of Mahuang Tang
Ephedra in formulas such as kakkonto for early colds and stiffness
Ephedrine for low blood pressure during anaesthesia; pseudoephedrine as a nasal decongestant

medicinal.cautions: Can cause high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, seizures and sudden death. The US FDA banned ephedra dietary supplements in 2004 after many adverse events and deaths. Dangerous with heart disease, thyroid disease, MAOIs and other stimulants. Pseudoephedrine sales are restricted because it is a methamphetamine precursor.

fruit.type: Fleshy seed cone (not a true fruit)
fruit.description: Red, berry-like cone of fleshy bracts around 1–2 seeds.

seed.description: Dark brown, ovoid seeds
seed.dispersal: Birds and small mammals eat the fleshy cones
seed.germination: 1–3 weeks at 15–20 °C in sandy mix

steps: Grow only where legal; possession is restricted in some countries
Sow in a gritty, sandy mix in spring
Plant in full sun in a dry bed
Water rarely; it rots in wet soil

lore: The Shennong Bencao Jing lists mahuang for coughs and fevers, and Zhang Zhongjing's Shanghan Lun (c. 200 CE) built a whole family of formulas around it. In 1885 the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi isolated ephedrine, and in the 1920s Chen and Schmidt introduced it to Western medicine.
funFact: Ephedra is not a flowering plant: it belongs to the Gnetophytes, an odd group of gymnosperms related to conifers.

wiki.extract: Ephedra sinica is a species of Ephedra in the plant family Ephedraceae. Native to Mongolia, northern China, and Russia, it is a shrub found on arid highland slopes, dry river beds, steppes, fields or mountain sides.

summary: A deciduous shrub of eastern North American bogs and woods, domesticated only in the early 20th century. It needs strongly acidic soil and is pollinated best by bumblebees, which 'buzz' its bell-shaped flowers to shake out pollen.
nativeRange: Eastern North America from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to Texas; cultivated widely in temperate regions
abilities: Partners with ericoid mycorrhizal fungi that unlock nitrogen in acidic, nutrient-poor soil
Bell-shaped flowers release pollen best by sonication (buzz pollination)
Brilliant red autumn foliage
Blue colour comes from anthocyanins under a waxy bloom that scatters light
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe and widely eaten.

uses.use: Berries dried as winter food; root and leaf tea used in childbirth and as a blood purifier
Blueberry anthocyanins studied for memory and vascular health, with some positive small trials

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood sugar.

fruit.description: Round berries 1–2 cm, dark blue with a pale waxy bloom and a five-pointed crown at the tip; sweet-tart, pale-green flesh.

seed.description: Tiny, soft, flattened brown seeds about 1 mm, 20–100 per berry, barely noticeable when eaten
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist sphagnum or peat at 20 °C (light helps); 1–2 months. Rarely used outside breeding

grow.water: Moderate–high; shallow roots need constant moisture
grow.soil: Strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), loose, peaty, well-drained; add sulphur or plant in ericaceous compost
grow.propagation: Softwood or hardwood cuttings of named cultivars
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from planting; full crops at 5–6 years
steps: Test soil pH; if above 5.5, lower it with elemental sulphur months ahead or plant in a raised bed or large pot of ericaceous compost.
Plant two or more varieties (e.g. 'Bluecrop', 'Duke', 'Elliott') 1.5 m apart for better cross-pollination and bigger berries.
Mulch 10 cm deep with pine needles or bark and water with rainwater where tap water is hard.
Remove flowers in the first year; from year four, prune in late winter by cutting a few of the oldest canes to the ground.
Net against birds and pick berries a few days after they turn fully blue, when they fall off easily.

lore: Botanist Frederick Coville and New Jersey farmer Elizabeth White domesticated the highbush blueberry from wild bushes in the Pine Barrens between 1908 and 1916. Many Algonquian peoples dried the berries and mixed them into pemmican.
funFact: Elizabeth White paid local pickers to find the best wild bushes — one, found by Rube Leek, became the parent of early cultivars like 'Rubel'.

Merian was a pioneer in ecology, being one of the first to document the relationship between insects and their specific host plants through direct observation and meticulous illustration.

summary: The sacred leaf of the Andes, chewed for thousands of years to ease hunger, fatigue and altitude. Its leaves contain about 0.5–1% cocaine, which in the leaf form is mild, but became a powerful drug of addiction once it was extracted in 1860.
nativeRange: Eastern slopes of the Andes in Peru and Bolivia; cultivated in Colombia and elsewhere
abilities: Makes cocaine and related alkaloids in its leaves, which deter insect herbivores
Grows on steep, terraced Andean slopes and can be harvested several times a year
Its leaf is nutritious, with significant calcium and iron
edibilityNote: Leaves are chewed with an alkaline ash (llipta) or brewed as mate de coca, legal in Peru and Bolivia but illegal in many countries. Extracted cocaine is highly addictive and can cause heart attack, stroke and death. Leaf use causes positive drug tests.

uses.use: Leaves chewed or drunk as tea for altitude sickness, hunger, fatigue and stomach pain
Cocaine hydrochloride used as a topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor in nose and throat procedures

medicinal.cautions: Cocaine is addictive and cardiotoxic. Leaf products are controlled in most countries outside the Andes.

fruit.description: Small red drupes about 1 cm long.

seed.description: Single seed per drupe
seed.germination: Sow fresh; germinates in a few weeks

lore: Coca appears in Moche ceramics showing chewers with bulging cheeks, and under the Inca its use was reserved largely for nobility and ritual. Albert Niemann isolated cocaine in 1860, and in 1884 Carl Koller showed it could numb the eye for surgery, the first local anaesthetic.
funFact: Coca-Cola originally contained coca extract; the company still uses de-cocainised coca leaf flavouring, processed by a single licensed US facility.

otherNames: Manzanilla de la muerte ('little apple of death', Spanish)
summary: Often called the most dangerous tree in the world. Its small green apple-like fruits burn the mouth and throat, its milky sap blisters skin, and sheltering under it during rain can cause burns as sap is washed off the leaves. It still does important work holding Caribbean beaches together.
nativeRange: Southern Florida, the Caribbean, the Bahamas, Central America and northern South America
abilities: Its latex contains phorbol esters that cause severe blistering of skin and eyes
Stabilises sandy beaches and dunes with dense roots and windbreak crowns
Tolerates salt spray, storms and nutrient-poor sand
Fruits float, spreading the tree along coasts by sea
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic. Eating the sweet-smelling fruit causes intense burning, blistering and swelling of the mouth and throat, vomiting and bloody diarrhoea; historical accounts describe deaths, though modern documented fatalities are rare. Sap causes blistering dermatitis and can cause temporary blindness; rain dripping from the leaves and smoke from burning wood are also harmful. Lookalike: crab apples or guava. Trees are often marked with red bands or warning signs.

fruit.description: Small green to yellowish fruits like crab apples, with a pleasant smell.

seed.description: Hard stone with several seeds
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: The Spanish called it 'manzanilla de la muerte', and Caribbean peoples reportedly used its sap on arrows; legend says Juan Ponce de León died in 1521 after being wounded by such an arrow in Florida.
funFact: Some animals are unaffected: the black spiny-tailed iguana (Ctenosaura similis) eats the fruit and even lives among the branches.

summary: A tree armoured with dark conical spikes whose pumpkin-shaped seed capsules explode with a sound like a gunshot. Recorded seed speeds reach about 70 m/s, throwing seeds tens of metres. Its milky sap is caustic and has been used as fish poison and arrow poison.
nativeRange: Tropical Americas, from Central America and the Caribbean to the Amazon; invasive in parts of tropical Africa
abilities: Its drying capsules build tension and burst apart, launching seeds at around 60–70 m/s
Throws seeds up to about 45 m from the tree
Protects its trunk with dense, sharp conical spines
Grows fast into a canopy tree up to 40–60 m
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic. The milky sap (latex) causes blistering skin burns and can cause serious eye damage. Seeds cause violent vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea if eaten; they contain the toxic protein hurin. Children are sometimes poisoned after eating the seeds, which resemble small nuts.

fruit.description: Segmented capsules like small pumpkins, up to 8 cm across, that dry and explode.

seed.description: Flat, round, coin-like seeds
seed.germination: Sow fresh in warm soil; handle with gloves

lore: Before blotting paper, the unripe capsules were cut and filled with fine sand used to blot ink, the origin of the name 'sandbox'. Carib peoples reportedly used the sap to poison arrows and stun fish.
funFact: The species name crepitans means 'crackling' in Latin, for the gunshot crack of its exploding capsules.

wiki.extract: Hura crepitans, known by the common names sandbox tree, possumwood, monkey no-climb, assacu, and jabillo, is a species of evergreen tree in the family Euphorbiaceae, native to tropical regions of North and South America including the Amazon rainforest. It is naturalized in parts of Africa with sufficient rainfall. It is also present in parts of Tanzania, where it is considered an invasive species. Because its fruit explodes when ripe, it has also received the colloquial nickname "dynamite tree".

summary: A woody shrub from the southern Amazon whose starchy roots feed over half a billion people, mainly in Africa. Every part contains cyanogenic glucosides, and Indigenous Amazonians developed elaborate grating, pressing and fermenting methods to make it safe — techniques later adopted across Africa and Asia.
nativeRange: Southern Amazon basin of Brazil (Rondônia/Mato Grosso); grown throughout the tropics
abilities: Survives drought, poor acidic soils and erratic rainfall where grains fail
Roots can be left in the ground for up to two years and harvested when needed
Contains linamarin and lotaustralin, which release hydrogen cyanide when cells are damaged
Grown easily from stem cuttings
edibleParts: roots (peeled, soaked, fermented, cooked — as fufu, gari, farinha, tapioca)
young leaves (pounded and long-boiled, e.g. pondu, saka-saka)
edibilityNote: Never eat raw. Roots and leaves release cyanide; 'sweet' varieties need peeling and thorough cooking, while 'bitter' varieties must be grated, soaked or fermented, pressed and cooked. Poorly processed cassava causes acute poisoning and the paralytic disease konzo.

uses.use: Leaf poultices applied to wounds and sores
Tapioca porridge as a gentle food for diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Cyanogenic: inadequately processed roots and leaves are poisonous; chronic exposure linked to konzo and tropical ataxic neuropathy.

fruit.description: Rounded, six-winged green capsule about 1.5 cm that dries and splits explosively, throwing out three seeds.

seed.description: Oval, smooth, mottled grey-brown seeds about 1 cm long, with a pale fleshy appendage (caruncle) at one end
seed.dispersal: Explosive capsules; ants carry seeds by the caruncle
seed.germination: Seed used mainly in breeding; needs warmth (30–35 °C). Farmers plant stem cuttings

grow.zones: Tropical only (USDA 10–12); annual in warm subtropics
grow.soil: Light, sandy or loamy, well-drained; tolerates poor acidic soils (pH 4.5–7)
grow.propagation: Stem cuttings 20–30 cm long from mature, disease-free stems
steps: Cut 20–30 cm lengths with 5–8 nodes from mature, virus-free stems (check for mosaic disease).
Plant at the start of rains, 1 m apart, either upright, angled or flat with two-thirds buried and buds pointing up.
Weed for the first three months, after which the canopy shades out weeds.
Harvest by lifting the stem and pulling roots; process within 1–2 days as roots spoil quickly.
Peel, then soak, grate, ferment, press and cook as appropriate to the variety before eating — never eat raw.

lore: The Tupi and Arawak peoples grew cassava long before European contact, inventing the woven tipiti press to squeeze out its poisonous juice. Portuguese traders carried it from Brazil to the Congo basin in the 16th century, where it became central to Central African cuisine.
funFact: The 'pearls' in bubble tea are made from tapioca, the purified starch of cassava roots.

wiki.extract: Manihot esculenta, commonly called cassava, manioc, or yuca, is a woody shrub of the spurge family, Euphorbiaceae, native to South America, from Brazil, Paraguay and parts of the Andes. Although a perennial plant, cassava is extensively cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions as an annual crop for its edible starchy tuberous root. Cassava is predominantly consumed in boiled form, but substantial quantities are processed to extract cassava starch, called tapioca, which is used for food, animal feed, and industrial purposes. The Brazilian farofa, and the related garri of West Africa, is an edible coarse flour obtained by grating cassava roots, pressing moisture off the obtained grated pulp, and finally drying and roasting it.

summary: A fast-growing, dramatic plant whose mottled seeds hold both castor oil and ricin, one of the most toxic natural proteins. Pressing separates them: the oil is a safe, ancient laxative and industrial lubricant, while ricin stays in the seed cake.
nativeRange: Probably north-eastern Africa (Ethiopia) and the Middle East; naturalised throughout the tropics and warm temperate regions
abilities: Produces ricin, a protein that disables ribosomes and stops cells making proteins
Stores up to ~50% oil in its seeds, mostly ricinoleic acid, an unusual hydroxy fatty acid
Launches seeds from explosive capsules, then ants carry them off by their fatty caruncle
Grows several metres in a single season
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly if chewed or crushed: ricin causes symptoms after a delay of several hours, including severe vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, dehydration, low blood pressure and failure of the liver, kidneys and spleen; a few well-chewed seeds can kill a child. Swallowed whole seeds may pass through intact. Commercial castor oil is ricin-free. Seeds are used in jewellery and are attractive to children; also highly toxic to dogs.

uses.use: Castor oil as a laxative and in ointments
Castor oil (eranda taila) as a purgative and for joint pain (vata disorders)
Castor oil is an approved stimulant laxative; ricinoleic acid also used in drug formulations

medicinal.cautions: Castor oil can cause cramps and diarrhoea and can trigger uterine contractions; avoid in pregnancy unless medically supervised. Never ingest seeds.

fruit.description: Three-lobed, spiny green-to-red capsules that split explosively.

seed.description: Glossy seeds mottled brown, black and white, with a pale caruncle
seed.germination: Soak overnight and sow in warmth (with gloves); 1–3 weeks

steps: Wear gloves and keep seeds away from children and pets
Soak seed overnight and sow indoors in warmth
Plant out after frost in rich soil
Remove flower spikes before seeds form if children or animals visit

lore: Castor seeds have been found in Egyptian tombs from about 4000 BCE, and Herodotus described Egyptians using 'kiki' oil in lamps. In 1978 Bulgarian dissident Georgi Markov was killed in London by a tiny ricin pellet fired, it is believed, from a modified umbrella.
funFact: 'Ricinus' is Latin for 'tick', because the seeds look like a swollen tick.

wiki.extract: Ricinus communis, the castor bean or castor oil plant, is a species of perennial flowering plant in the spurge family, Euphorbiaceae. It is the sole species in the monotypic genus, Ricinus, and subtribe, Ricininae.

plates.long: A vibrant hand-colored engraving from Maria Sibylla Merian's 'Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium', depicting the life cycle of insects on a Castor oil plant. This plate illustrates Merian's groundbreaking approach to entomology, showing insects in direct association with their botanical hosts, a revolutionary concept in the early 18th century.

Merian was a pioneer in entomology, being one of the first to document the metamorphosis of insects in relation to their host plants through direct observation in the field.

Such illustrations were vital for the classification and study of tropical flora in the 18th century, bridging the gap between European science and the natural world of the East Indies.

Published in Leonhart Fuchs's landmark 1542 herbal, the illustration is celebrated for its naturalism and scientific accuracy, prioritizing clear observation over the stylized depictions common in earlier medieval texts.

The illustration meticulously details the plant's characteristic large, lobed leaves and prickly fruit clusters, serving as a vital scientific record in an early modern herbal. Such images were essential for physicians and apothecaries to accurately identify plants used for medicinal purposes.

The woodcut depicts the entire specimen including its fibrous root system, segmented stalk, large palmate leaves, and spiny seed capsules at the crown. It is labeled with the Latin name 'RICINVS' and the German name 'Wunderbaum'.

The work is celebrated for its naturalistic approach, capturing the specific textures of the palmate leaves and the prickly seed capsules, reflecting the burgeoning scientific interest in botany during the early 17th century.

summary: A climbing legume whose glossy scarlet seeds with black eyes are strung into rosaries, necklaces and toys, and contain abrin, a toxin even more potent than ricin. The hard coat usually protects a swallowed whole seed, but a single chewed or crushed seed can be fatal.
nativeRange: Tropical Asia and probably tropical Africa and Australia; naturalised widely, invasive in Florida and the Caribbean
abilities: Makes abrin, a protein that disables ribosomes, as ricin does
Its hard, waterproof seed coat lets seeds survive for years
Its leaves contain glycyrrhizin and are sweet, like liquorice
Fixes nitrogen and climbs over other vegetation
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly if chewed, crushed or broken (drilling seeds for jewellery has poisoned craftspeople). After a delay of hours to days: severe vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, dehydration, seizures and failure of liver, kidneys and other organs. Whole seeds swallowed intact often pass harmlessly. Leaves are chewed as a sweetener in India, but the plant should not be eaten; keep seed jewellery away from children.

uses.use: Seeds used only after 'purification' (shodhana) by boiling in milk, and roots and leaves for coughs and sore throats
Leaf tea for coughs and colds

medicinal.cautions: Seeds can be fatal; traditional detoxification is not reliable for home use.

fruit.description: Short pods that curl open to show red-and-black seeds.

seed.description: Glossy scarlet seed with a black spot at the hilum
seed.dispersal: Birds attracted by the bright seeds (which offer no food reward)
seed.germination: Not recommended: invasive and toxic

lore: In India the seeds served goldsmiths as a unit of weight, the ratti (about 0.12 g), and the Sanskrit name gunja appears in Ayurvedic texts that prescribe elaborate purification before any use.
funFact: In 2012 the Eden Project in Cornwall withdrew bracelets from its shop after it emerged they were strung with rosary pea seeds.

wiki.extract: Abrus precatorius, commonly known as jequirity bean or rosary pea, is a herbaceous flowering plant in the bean family Fabaceae. It is a slender, perennial climber with long, pinnate-leafleted leaves that twines around trees, shrubs, and hedges.

plates.author: Prospero Alpini
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of the Abrus plant (Abrus precatorius), showing its characteristic pinnate leaves and climbing habit.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the Abrus plant, commonly known as the Rosary Pea, as observed by Prospero Alpini during his time in Egypt. Published in 1592, this image represents an early effort to scientifically document non-European flora, combining artistic detail with botanical accuracy.

This botanical illustration from Willem Piso's 1658 work depicts the climbing habit, pinnate leaves, and characteristic seed pods of the plant, which was studied for its medicinal properties in the East and West Indies.

These depictions from Carolus Clusius's 1576 work represent early efforts to systematically document and categorize global flora during the Age of Discovery, providing some of the first European records of non-native species.

The image clearly shows the plant's characteristic pinnate leaves and seed pods, serving as a vital visual reference for identifying medicinal herbs in 16th-century China.

The illustration meticulously details the plant's twining stem, pointed leaves, and elongated seed pods, serving as a vital record for early modern botanical and medical study.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut depicting two specimens of 'Phaseolus Indicus' (Indian bean). This illustration reflects the 16th-century interest in documenting exotic flora brought to Europe from the East Indies, showcasing the characteristic dark and light coloration of the seeds.

plates.long: This woodcut displays four distinct seeds, illustrating the morphological differences between Indian bean varieties. It serves as a scientific record of botanical specimens collected during early global exploration, emphasizing the diversity of the Phaseolus genus.

summary: A small, hairy-leaved legume domesticated in south-east Turkey about 10,000 years ago and the base of hummus, falafel, chana masala and besan flour. India grows about 70% of the world's crop.
nativeRange: South-eastern Turkey (wild ancestor Cicer reticulatum); grown across South Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, Ethiopia, Australia and the Americas
abilities: Leaf hairs secrete malic and oxalic acid, deterring insects (dew on leaves is sour)
Deep taproot lets it mature on stored soil moisture after rains end
Fixes nitrogen through root nodules
Two main types: small, dark, angular 'desi' and large, cream 'kabuli'
edibleParts: seeds (cooked, roasted, ground into besan/gram flour)
edibilityNote: Dry seeds must be soaked and cooked. Raw dry chickpeas are indigestible and contain antinutrients.

uses.use: Chickpea broth as a diuretic and for kidney stones
Besan paste (with turmeric) as a skin cleanser (ubtan)
Chickpeas as a diuretic and to promote menstruation

medicinal.cautions: Legume allergy (cross-reaction with peanut and lentil reported).

fruit.season: Spring to early summer (winter crop in India)
fruit.description: Short, inflated, hairy pods 2–3 cm, like small balloons, usually holding 1–2 seeds.

seed.description: Round to angular seeds with a pointed beak like a ram's head: kabuli types cream-beige, smooth, 8–12 mm; desi types smaller, wrinkled, brown, green or black, 5–8 mm
seed.germination: Sow 4–8 cm deep in soil above about 10 °C; emerges in 7–14 days

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop (spring in temperate areas, winter in subtropics)
grow.water: Low; grows on residual soil moisture
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or clay loam, pH 6–8; intolerant of waterlogging
steps: Sow seed 4–8 cm deep after the last hard frost (or in autumn in mild-winter areas), 8–10 cm apart in rows 30–45 cm apart.
Do not fertilise with nitrogen; inoculate seed with Mesorhizobium ciceri if chickpeas haven't grown there before.
Water sparingly — damp conditions encourage Ascochyta blight.
Pick some green pods to eat fresh, or wait until plants turn yellow-brown and pods rattle.
Pull or cut plants, dry, thresh and store seed dry; soak overnight before cooking.

lore: The Roman orator Cicero's family name is said to come from 'cicer', chickpea, perhaps after a wart on an ancestor's nose. Roasted chickpeas were sold as street food in ancient Rome and are still the 'leblebi' of Turkey.
funFact: During coffee shortages in Europe, roasted ground chickpeas were brewed as a coffee substitute.

wiki.extract: The chickpea or chick pea is an annual legume of the family Fabaceae, subfamily Faboideae, cultivated for its edible seeds. Its different types are variously known as gram, Bengal gram, chana (চানা), garbanzo, garbanzo bean, or Egyptian pea. It is one of the earliest cultivated legumes, the oldest archaeological evidence of which was found in Syria.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a chickpea plant (Cicer arietinum), illustrating its characteristic pinnate leaves and inflated seed pods. Hieronymus Bock's herbal was notable for its accurate, life-like botanical illustrations, which marked a shift towards empirical observation in early modern science.

Such illustrations were crucial for the identification of medicinal and culinary plants in early modern herbals.

summary: Domesticated in north-east China from wild Glycine soja around 9,000–5,000 years ago, soybean is now one of the world's most important protein and oil crops, mostly fed to livestock. Its seeds are about 36–40% protein and 18–20% oil.
nativeRange: North-east and central China; grown worldwide, especially in Brazil, the United States, Argentina and India
abilities: Root nodules host Bradyrhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air
Flowering is triggered by shortening day length (photoperiod sensitive)
Seeds contain isoflavones that mimic oestrogen weakly
Raw beans contain trypsin inhibitors that block protein digestion until cooked
edibleParts: seeds (cooked, as tofu, soy milk, miso, tempeh, natto, soy sauce)
edibilityNote: Beans must be cooked or fermented; raw soybeans contain trypsin inhibitors and lectins that cause digestive upset. Soy is one of the major food allergens.

uses.use: Fermented black soybean (dàn dòu chǐ) for colds and restlessness
Soy protein modestly lowers LDL cholesterol; isoflavones studied for menopausal hot flushes

medicinal.cautions: Soy allergy. Large doses of isoflavone supplements are not advised with hormone-sensitive cancers without medical advice; may affect thyroid medication absorption.

fruit.description: Hairy, slightly curved pods 3–8 cm in clusters, green maturing to tan or brown, each with 2–4 seeds.

seed.description: Round to oval beans 5–11 mm, smooth, most commonly pale yellow-cream with a small dark or light hilum (scar), but also green, brown, black or mottled
seed.dispersal: Pods split on drying (wild forms more strongly)
seed.germination: Sow 2.5–4 cm deep in warm soil (above 15 °C); emerges in 5–10 days. Inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium where soy is new

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; choose maturity group for your latitude
grow.water: Moderate; most critical at flowering and pod fill
steps: After the last frost, when soil is warm, dust seed with soybean inoculant and sow 3 cm deep, 5–8 cm apart, in rows 40–75 cm apart.
Keep weed-free for the first 6 weeks; no nitrogen fertiliser is needed once nodules form.
Water during flowering and pod fill if dry.
For edamame, pick when pods are plump and bright green; boil in salted water.
For dry beans, harvest when pods are brown and rattle, before they split; thresh and dry to below 13% moisture.

lore: Chinese tradition counts soy among the 'five sacred grains', and tofu is credited (doubtfully) to Liu An, prince of Huainan, in the 2nd century BCE. Benjamin Franklin sent soybeans from London to America in 1770.
funFact: Henry Ford had a car body built from soybean-based plastic in 1941 and wore a suit made of soy fibre.

wiki.extract: The soybean, soy bean, or soya bean is a species of legume native to East Asia, widely grown for its edible bean. Soy is a staple crop, the world's most grown legume, and an important animal feed.

plates.desc: Botanical illustration of a soybean plant (Glycine max) showing its leaves, flowers, and pods, with various types of beans labeled below.
plates.long: This detailed woodcut from the 1848 botanical compendium 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' depicts the white soybean (Glycine max). The illustration captures the plant's morphology, including its characteristic trifoliate leaves and seed pods, alongside several labeled varieties of dried beans, serving as both a scientific record and a practical guide for agriculture during the late Qing Dynasty.

plates.title: Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao (Vol. 1)

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts the soybean plant (Glycine max), a fundamental crop in East Asian agriculture. The image provides a detailed view of the plant's morphology, including its trifoliate leaves, seed pods, and root system, alongside various types of harvested beans. It is a prime example of the descriptive accuracy found in Wu Qijun's seminal 1848 botanical work, 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao'

The illustration highlights the plant's structure, including its distinctive pods, serving as a visual guide for identification and medicinal use.

otherNames: Gāncǎo 甘草 (Chinese, applied to G. uralensis and G. glabra)
summary: A legume whose long yellow roots contain glycyrrhizin, a compound 30–50 times sweeter than sugar. It is so widely used in medicine that Chinese tradition calls it 'the great harmoniser' of formulas, but too much raises blood pressure dangerously.
nativeRange: Mediterranean and North Africa through Western & Central Asia to Xinjiang and northern India
abilities: Glycyrrhizin is about 30–50 times sweeter than sucrose
Blocks the enzyme 11β-HSD2, causing the body to hold on to salt and lose potassium
Fixes nitrogen through root-nodule bacteria
Deep runners let it survive saline, arid floodplains
edibilityNote: Root and extract flavour sweets, beer, tobacco and drinks. Regular large amounts of true liquorice can cause high blood pressure, low potassium, heart rhythm problems and, rarely, death.

uses.use: Yashtimadhu as a soothing demulcent for cough, sore throat, ulcers and as a rasayana for voice and skin
Gancao tonifies spleen qi, moistens the lungs, eases spasms and harmonises other herbs; it appears in a large share of classical formulas
Asl-us-sus for cough, chest complaints, ulcers and as a flavouring corrective in compounds
Deglycyrrhizinated liquorice (DGL) for dyspepsia; carbenoxolone, a glycyrrhetinic-acid derivative, was formerly prescribed for ulcers

medicinal.cautions: Can cause pseudohyperaldosteronism, with hypertension, oedema, low potassium and arrhythmia. Dangerous with heart or kidney disease and with diuretics, digoxin or corticosteroids. Avoid in pregnancy, as heavy intake is linked to preterm birth and effects on the child. A man in Massachusetts died in 2020 after eating a bag and a half of black liquorice daily for weeks.

fruit.description: Flat, reddish-brown pod, 1.5–3 cm, with 2–6 seeds.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, hard-coated seeds
seed.dispersal: Gravity, water; spreads mainly by runners
seed.germination: Scarify or soak in hot water; 1–3 weeks at 20–25 °C

steps: Plant 15 cm runner sections with buds in spring, 45 cm apart
Give deep, loose soil so the roots can run
Leave undisturbed for three years
Dig in autumn, keeping runners to replant

lore: Theophrastus wrote of a sweet 'Scythian root' that let warriors go days without water. Liquorice was grown around Pontefract in Yorkshire from the medieval period, home of the Pontefract cake sweets.
funFact: Glycyrrhiza comes from the Greek for 'sweet root', and the word 'liquorice' is a corruption of it.

summary: The source of indigo, the dye of blue jeans and once one of the world's most valuable trade goods. The leaves are green; the blue appears only when they are fermented in water and the liquid is beaten with air, turning the colourless indican into insoluble blue indigotin.
nativeRange: Uncertain due to ancient cultivation; probably tropical Asia or Africa; grown across the tropics
abilities: Stores indican, a colourless glycoside, which turns into blue indigo when fermented and exposed to air
Fixes nitrogen in root nodules, so it was used as a soil-improving crop
Regrows after cutting, allowing several leaf harvests a year
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Some Indigofera species (e.g. Indigofera spicata) are poisonous to livestock; I. tinctoria should not be eaten.

uses.use: Leaves (nili) in hair oils for hair growth and greying, and for liver and skin complaints
Indigo pigment (qing dai, mostly from other plants) for skin and inflammatory conditions

medicinal.cautions: Internal use is not well studied; avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Thin, straight brown pods with small seeds.

seed.description: Small, squarish seeds
seed.germination: Soak or scratch seed; sow in warmth, 1–2 weeks

steps: Scarify and soak seed, then sow in warm soil
Grow in full sun with moderate water
Cut leafy stems just before flowering
Steep leaves in water for 12–24 hours, add lime, then beat in air until it turns blue

lore: The Greeks called the dye 'indikon', 'from India'. The Bengal Indigo Revolt of 1859 and the play Nil Darpan (1860) protested forced indigo growing, and Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, at Champaran in 1917, defended indigo farmers.
funFact: Adolf von Baeyer worked out indigo's structure and synthesis by 1883, and BASF's synthetic indigo from 1897 destroyed the plant indigo trade within a few decades.

summary: A plant that folds its leaves within seconds when touched. Electrical signals travel through the stem, and motor cells in swellings at the leaf bases suddenly lose water and collapse. Experiments suggest it can 'learn' to ignore harmless repeated disturbances.
nativeRange: Tropical Central and South America; now a pantropical weed
abilities: Folds leaflets within seconds of touch, heat or shaking (seismonasty) using pulvinus motor cells
Sends electrical action potentials along its stem to coordinate leaf collapse
Folds its leaves at night on an internal circadian clock
In a 2014 experiment, stopped folding in response to repeated harmless drops and kept this 'memory' for weeks
Fixes nitrogen through root nodules
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Contains the amino acid mimosine, toxic to livestock in quantity (hair loss, poor growth). Stems carry small prickles.

uses.use: Roots and leaves (lajjalu) for bleeding piles, diarrhoea and wound healing

uses.tradition: Traditional medicine in the Philippines and Africa
uses.use: Leaf poultices for wounds and swellings

medicinal.cautions: Mimosine is toxic in large amounts; avoid in pregnancy. Invasive weed in many countries.

lore: In 1729 French astronomer Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan kept a sensitive plant in total darkness and found its leaves still opened and closed daily, the first experiment showing an internal biological clock.
funFact: Monica Gagliano's 2014 experiment found habituated plants still 'remembered' to ignore harmless drops up to 28 days later.

wiki.extract: Mimosa pudica is a creeping annual or perennial flowering plant of the pea/legume family Fabaceae. It is often grown for its curiosity value: the sensitive compound leaves quickly fold inward and droop when touched or shaken and re-open a few minutes later. For this reason, this species is commonly cited as an example of rapid plant movement. Like a number of other plant species, it undergoes changes in leaf orientation termed "sleep" or nyctinastic movement. The foliage closes during darkness and reopens in light. This was first studied by French scientist Jean-Jacques d'Ortous. In the UK it has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

summary: A small yellow-flowered desert shrub whose leaves and pods are among the world's most used laxatives. It was introduced to medicine by medieval Arab physicians and still sold in pharmacies everywhere.
nativeRange: North-east Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Somalia), the Arabian Peninsula and across to Pakistan and India
abilities: Contains sennosides, inactive 'prodrugs' that gut bacteria convert into rhein anthrone in the colon
Survives extreme heat and drought in desert wadis
Flat pods carry the seeds on the wind
edibilityNote: Not a food. Leaves and pods are used only as a laxative medicine.

uses.use: Sana makki as a purgative of black bile and phlegm, in compounds for skin disease, joint pain and melancholy
Leaves as a purgative (virechana) and for constipation
Fanxieye (introduced from abroad) to purge heat accumulation and relieve constipation
Standardised sennoside tablets as an over-the-counter stimulant laxative and for bowel preparation

medicinal.cautions: For short-term use only (about 1–2 weeks). Causes cramps and diarrhoea. Prolonged use or abuse causes potassium loss, dependence and melanosis coli, and low potassium can be dangerous with digoxin or diuretics. Do not use with bowel obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease, unexplained abdominal pain or in young children.

lore: Medieval Arab physicians brought senna into medicine; the word comes from Arabic sanā. 'Alexandrian senna' was named after the Egyptian port it was shipped from, and 'Tinnevelly senna' after the district in Tamil Nadu where it was later grown.
funFact: Senna leaf does nothing until it reaches the colon, where gut bacteria break the sennosides into the active laxative compound.

wiki.extract: Senna alexandrina is an ornamental plant in the genus Senna. It is used in herbalism. It grows natively in upper Egypt, especially in the Nubian region, and near Khartoum (Sudan), where it is cultivated commercially. It is also grown elsewhere, notably in India and Somalia.

summary: A long-lived, drought-hardy legume tree from tropical Africa whose brown pods hold a sticky, sweet-sour pulp essential to South Indian, Thai, Mexican and Middle Eastern cooking. Its very name comes from the Arabic 'tamar hindi', Indian date.
nativeRange: Tropical Africa (Sudan and the Sahel to East Africa and Madagascar); naturalised and cultivated throughout the tropics, especially India
abilities: Pulp is among the most acidic fruit pulps known, rich in tartaric acid, yet also very sugary
Withstands long droughts, strong winds and cyclones
Leaflets fold together at night
Trees can live and fruit for over 200 years
edibleParts: pod pulp (fresh, dried, as paste or drinks)
edibilityNote: Pulp, leaves and flowers are eaten. Seeds must be roasted or boiled and peeled before eating.

uses.use: Ripe pulp as a mild laxative and digestive
Pulp drinks for fever and to treat sunstroke
Tamarind sherbet as a cooling remedy for bilious complaints

medicinal.cautions: Laxative in quantity; may increase absorption of aspirin and ibuprofen.

fruit.description: Curved, bean-like pod 5–15 cm with a brittle cinnamon-brown shell; inside, sticky brown sweet-sour pulp laced with fibres around 3–10 seeds.

seed.description: Hard, glossy, dark reddish-brown to chocolate seeds, flattened and irregularly squarish-rhomboid, about 1–1.5 cm
seed.germination: Nick or soak in hot water overnight, sow 2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–2 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 10–12 (mature trees tolerate brief light frost)
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained; tolerates poor, sandy and slightly saline soils, pH 5–8
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting / air layering of sweet varieties
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 7–10 years from seed
steps: Soak seeds overnight in warm water and sow in deep pots, or buy a grafted 'sweet tamarind' tree.
Plant out in full sun with plenty of space (it can reach 20 m and spread widely).
Water regularly for the first two years, then only during prolonged drought.
Prune young trees to shape a strong framework; little pruning is needed later.
Harvest pods when the shell is brittle and brown; shell them, remove strings and seeds, and press the pulp into blocks for storage.

lore: Tamarind reached India so long ago that it appears in Sanskrit texts as 'amlika', and Arab traders named it 'Indian date'. In Myanmar and India, folklore warns not to sleep beneath a tamarind tree, said to harbour spirits.
funFact: Tamarind is one of the listed ingredients that gives Worcestershire sauce its tangy depth.

summary: A clover-like legume whose bitter-sweet seeds smell of maple syrup and whose leaves are a staple green in Indian cooking. Its name means 'Greek hay', because Romans grew it as fodder.
nativeRange: Eastern Mediterranean and Western Asia; ancient crop, now grown widely (India is the largest producer)
abilities: Seeds contain sotolon, a compound so potent its maple aroma passes into sweat and urine
Seed gum (galactomannan) swells in water and slows sugar absorption
Fixes nitrogen through root-nodule bacteria
Seeds contain diosgenin, once a raw material for synthesising steroid hormones
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. People allergic to peanuts or chickpeas may react to it.

uses.use: Methika for poor appetite, diabetes (prameha), joint pain and to increase breast milk
Hulba as a demulcent for cough and chest, and in poultices to ripen boils
Hulba drink after childbirth and for stomach complaints; Yemeni hilbeh paste as a digestive
Huluba to warm the kidneys and dispel cold, for hernia pain and cold in the legs

medicinal.cautions: Small trials show modest falls in blood sugar. May cause low blood sugar with diabetes drugs, and may interact with warfarin. Stimulates the uterus, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Causes a maple odour in sweat and urine, and in breastfed babies this has been mistaken for maple syrup urine disease. Can cause bloating.

seed.description: Hard, rhomboid, yellow-brown seeds with a deep diagonal groove
seed.germination: Quick; 3–5 days at 20–30 °C

steps: Sow seed 1 cm deep in cool weather
Cut leaves for greens when 10–15 cm tall
For seed, let pods dry yellow on the plant
Thresh and store seeds dry

lore: Columella and Cato wrote of fenugreek as cattle fodder. Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis (c. 800) included it among plants to grow on his estates.
funFact: A mysterious maple-syrup smell that drifted over Manhattan several times from 2005 was traced in 2009 to a New Jersey factory processing fenugreek seed.

summary: One of the Neolithic 'founder crops' of the Fertile Crescent, gathered and grown for over 9,000 years. Its flat, lens-shaped seed literally gave its name to the optical lens. iNaturalist now places it in Vicia.
nativeRange: Fertile Crescent (Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Israel); domesticated from wild Vicia orientalis; grown widely in South Asia, the Middle East, Canada and Australia
abilities: Fixes nitrogen through root nodules with Rhizobium leguminosarum
Grows on minimal water in cool seasons
Cooks quickly without soaking, unlike most dry pulses
Seeds contain about 25% protein
edibleParts: seeds (cooked whole or split as dal, soups)
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten cooked. Raw lentils contain lectins; always cook.

uses.use: Lentil decoctions and poultices for skin sores and digestive complaints
Pulses including lentils lower post-meal blood sugar and LDL cholesterol in trials

medicinal.cautions: Raw lentils contain lectins; flatulence common.

fruit.description: Short, flat, oblong pods 1–2 cm, holding 1–2 seeds, on a slender bushy plant 30–50 cm tall.

seed.description: Flat, round, biconvex, lens-shaped seeds 3–8 mm across; seed coat green, brown, grey, tan, black or speckled, with orange, red, yellow or green interior when split
seed.dispersal: Humans (pods of domesticated forms do not split readily)
seed.germination: Sow 2–5 cm deep into cool soil (from 5 °C); emerges in 7–10 days

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop; spring sowing in cold regions, winter crop in subtropics (e.g. India's rabi season)
steps: Sow in early spring (or autumn in mild regions) 2–4 cm deep, about 2–5 cm apart in rows 20–30 cm apart; inoculate seed if lentils are new to the soil.
Keep weeds down early, as lentil seedlings compete poorly.
Water only if very dry; too much water encourages disease.
Harvest when lower pods turn brown and rattle; pull whole plants and dry them on a sheet.
Thresh by trampling or beating, winnow, and store dried seeds in airtight jars.

lore: In Genesis, Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. Lentils have been found in Egyptian tombs, and in Italy they are eaten on New Year's Eve for prosperity, their shape recalling coins.
funFact: The word 'lens' comes from the Latin for lentil, because early convex glass lenses were the same shape as the seed.

summary: A huge, long-lived tree of southern Europe and Asia Minor whose starchy nuts were the 'bread tree' staple of mountain villages from Corsica to Galicia. Individual trees live for over 2,000 years, their trunks twisting into spirals.
nativeRange: South-eastern Europe and Asia Minor; spread by the Greeks and Romans across Mediterranean and western Europe
abilities: The 'Hundred Horse Chestnut' on Mount Etna is estimated at 2,000–4,000 years old
Resprouts vigorously when coppiced, providing durable poles for centuries
Spiny burrs protect the nuts from most animals
Timber is rich in tannins, making it naturally rot-resistant
edibleParts: nuts (roasted, boiled, dried and milled into flour, candied as marrons glacés)
edibilityNote: Nuts are eaten cooked; the bitter inner skin (pellicle) is removed. Do not confuse with horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), whose shiny conkers are toxic — sweet chestnut burrs are densely needle-spined and contain 2–3 flat-sided nuts with a tufted tip.

uses.use: Leaf infusion for whooping cough and other coughs
Sweet chestnut flower essence for despair (no pharmacological evidence)

medicinal.cautions: Do not confuse with toxic horse chestnut.

fruit.description: A green, densely spiny burr 5–10 cm that splits into four, holding usually three glossy brown nuts.

seed.description: Glossy, reddish-brown nuts 2–4 cm, rounded on one side and flat on the other, with a pale scar at the base and a tuft of hairs at the pointed tip; creamy-white starchy kernel under a bitter brown skin
seed.dispersal: Jays, squirrels, wild boar and mice cache the nuts
seed.germination: Sow fresh nuts in autumn, or stratify cold and moist for 60–90 days; plant 3–5 cm deep. Never let them dry out

grow.soil: Acidic, light, well-drained sandy loam (pH 4.5–6.5); does poorly on chalk or heavy clay
grow.propagation: Seed; grafting of named cultivars and hybrids (e.g. 'Marron de Lyon', 'Bouche de Bétizac')
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from a grafted tree; 8–12 from seed
steps: Plant two or more varieties for cross-pollination, as most chestnuts are self-sterile, on acidic, free-draining ground.
Water young trees well in their first two summers and guard them against deer and rabbits.
Prune to a strong central leader in early years; older trees need little pruning (or coppice on a 12–20 year cycle for poles).
Watch for chestnut blight and gall wasp in affected regions, and buy resistant stock.
Gather nuts from the ground daily as burrs drop; score each nut before roasting so it doesn't explode, or dry and mill for flour.

lore: Xenophon described Greek soldiers eating chestnuts in Asia Minor around 400 BCE, and in Corsica and the Cévennes chestnut flour ('farina di castagne') sustained villages so fully that the tree was called 'l'arbre à pain', the bread tree.
funFact: The 'Hundred Horse Chestnut' on Mount Etna got its name from a legend that it sheltered a queen and her hundred knights from a storm.

summary: The tree that shades out nearly everything else. Beech casts such deep shade that it came to dominate huge areas of Europe after the last Ice Age, forming cathedral-like forests with almost no undergrowth. The word 'book' comes from it.
nativeRange: Western, central and southern Europe, from southern Scandinavia to Sicily and the Balkans
abilities: Casts some of the deepest shade of any European tree, suppressing competitors
Its seedlings tolerate deep shade for decades, waiting for a gap to open
Masts heavily every few years, flooding the forest with beechnuts
Forms extensive root networks with ectomycorrhizal fungi such as chanterelles and ceps
edibilityNote: Beechnuts are edible in small amounts and better roasted; eating many raw causes stomach upset, from mildly toxic compounds (historically called "fagin"). Beechnuts are toxic to horses.

fruit.description: Bristly husks that split into four to release two triangular nuts.

seed.description: Three-sided brown nut (beech mast)
seed.dispersal: Gravity, plus jays, rodents and formerly pigs
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 8–12 weeks; sow in spring

steps: Collect nuts as they fall and stratify over winter
Sow in spring in pots or a seedbed
Keep young plants lightly shaded and moist
Plant as a tree or keep clipped as a hedge, which holds brown leaves all winter

lore: Germanic peoples carved runes on beech tablets, and the Old English 'bōc' and German 'Buche/Buch' link beech and book. The 'Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe' became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007 and later grew to cover 18 countries.
funFact: Beech holds dead leaves through winter when kept as a young tree or hedge (marcescence), which is why beech hedges stay brown and dense in winter.

summary: A living city. A 2019 study found that English oak supports more than 2,300 species in Britain, including hundreds that live on nothing else. Individual trees can live for more than 1,000 years, and oak has been a sacred tree in Europe since before history.
nativeRange: Most of Europe to the Caucasus and northern Turkey
abilities: Supports more invertebrates, lichens and fungi than any other native British tree
Masts: produces huge acorn crops in some years and few in others, which outpaces seed-eaters
Relies on jays to plant acorns, sometimes kilometres away
Lives for more than 1,000 years, often hollowing out in old age and surviving as a shell
Reacts to gall wasps by growing galls rich in tannin, used for iron-gall ink
edibilityNote: Raw acorns are bitter with tannins and cause stomach upset; they must be leached repeatedly in water before being ground into flour. Acorns and leaves poison cattle and horses in quantity.

uses.use: Bark decoction as an astringent for diarrhoea, sore throats and skin inflammation
Oak bark approved for external use on inflamed skin and for acute diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: High-tannin preparations can irritate the stomach and reduce absorption of other medicines; avoid on large damaged skin areas.

fruit.description: Acorns held in scaly cups on long stalks (peduncles).

seed.description: Acorn; seed must not dry out
seed.dispersal: Jays, squirrels and mice that bury and forget acorns
seed.germination: Sow fresh in autumn; root emerges the same winter, shoot in spring

steps: Collect acorns as they fall and float-test them (discard floaters)
Sow at once in deep pots or straight into the ground
Protect from mice and squirrels with mesh
Plant out within 1–2 years before the taproot gets long

lore: Pliny the Elder described Gaulish druids cutting mistletoe from oaks with a golden sickle, and Charles II hid in the 'Royal Oak' at Boscobel in 1651. Oak was the timber of the Royal Navy and of Europe's cathedrals.
funFact: Magna Carta, Leonardo's notebooks and Bach's manuscripts were written in iron-gall ink, made from tannin-rich oak galls and iron salts.

wiki.extract: Quercus robur, pedunculate oak, European oak, or English oak, is a species of flowering plant in the beech and oak family, Fagaceae. It is a large tree, native to Europe and western Asia, and is widely cultivated in other temperate regions. It grows on soils of near neutral acidity in the lowlands and is notable for its value to natural ecosystems, supporting a diversity of herbivorous insects, acorn eating mammals and birds, and fungi.

otherNames: Umckaloabo (trade name, from Zulu, roughly 'heavy cough')
summary: A low, silvery-leaved grassland pelargonium with tiny, almost black-purple flowers and a thick red tuber. A Victorian Englishman's 'tuberculosis cure' from that tuber became Germany's best-selling herbal cold remedy.
nativeRange: Highveld grasslands of South Africa and Lesotho
abilities: Tuber contains highly oxygenated coumarins such as umckalin and prodelphinidins with antimicrobial and immune-modulating activity
Thick tubers survive frost, drought and grassland fires and resprout
Flowers almost year-round in mild climates
edibilityNote: Not a food. The tuber is used as decoction or extract.

uses.tradition: Southern African traditional medicine (Sesotho, Zulu, Xhosa)
uses.use: Tuber decoction for coughs, chest infections, diarrhoea and dysentery, and for colic in calves
Root extract EPs 7630 for acute bronchitis, sinusitis and the common cold

medicinal.cautions: A Cochrane review rated the evidence that it eases bronchitis and sinusitis symptoms as low quality, and nearly all trials came from the manufacturer; the EU registers it only on the basis of traditional use. Rare cases of liver injury and allergic reactions have been reported. May theoretically increase bleeding with anticoagulants. The EU monograph restricts it to ages 6 and over; avoid in pregnancy. Wild harvesting is under pressure, so choose cultivated sources.

fruit.description: Beaked fruit splitting into five one-seeded segments with spirally twisting tails.

seed.description: Small seeds with a feathery, corkscrew tail
seed.dispersal: Wind; the tail twists with humidity and drills the seed into soil
seed.germination: 1–3 weeks at 18–22 °C

steps: Sow seed in gritty compost in spring
Plant out in full sun with sharp drainage, or grow in pots
Water in summer and keep drier in winter
Lift tubers in autumn of year 2–3, replanting the crowns

lore: In 1897 Englishman Charles Henry Stevens travelled to South Africa for his tuberculosis. He said a Basotho healer cured him with the root, and in Britain he sold it as 'Stevens' Consumption Cure'.
funFact: Its seed tail twists and untwists with changes in humidity, working the seed into the ground like a corkscrew.

wiki.extract: Pelargonium sidoides is a plant native to South Africa, Eswatini, and Lesotho. Its common names include African geranium and South African geranium.

summary: The last survivor of an order of trees that goes back more than 290 million years, often called a living fossil. Its fan-shaped leaves look much like Jurassic fossils, and several trees near the Hiroshima hypocentre survived the 1945 bombing and still leaf out every spring.
nativeRange: Possibly wild populations in Zhejiang and Guizhou/Chongqing, China; planted worldwide
abilities: Has motile, swimming sperm with thousands of flagella, discovered in 1896 by Sakugoro Hirase
Tolerates air pollution, compacted soil and road salt, making it a favourite street tree
Has very few insect pests or diseases
Lives for well over 1,000 years; some temple trees in China are estimated at 3,000+ years
edibilityNote: Only the cooked kernel is eaten, and only a few at a time. Kernels contain ginkgotoxin (4′-O-methylpyridoxine), which can cause vomiting and seizures, especially in children who eat many; raw kernels are riskier. The smelly fleshy seed coat holds ginkgolic acids that cause poison-ivy-like dermatitis, so wear gloves.

uses.use: Seeds for cough, asthma and urinary frequency
Standardised leaf extract (e.g. EGb 761) studied for dementia, memory and circulation

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extract may raise bleeding risk with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs and before surgery. Seeds can cause poisoning and seizures; the seed coat causes contact dermatitis.

fruit.description: Apricot-like seeds on female trees with a yellow outer coat that smells of rancid butter (butyric acid).

seed.description: Hard, cream-coloured inner shell around a green kernel, inside a fleshy outer coat
seed.dispersal: Falls; probably once carried by animals that are now extinct
seed.germination: Clean the flesh off with gloves, cold-stratify 1–3 months, sow 2–3 cm deep

grow.propagation: Seed, cuttings, grafting (male clones for streets)
grow.timeToHarvest: Female trees bear seed after 20–35 years
steps: Clean the seed with gloves and stratify it in damp sand in the fridge
Sow in deep pots, since it makes a long taproot
Grow in full sun; growth is slow for the first few years
Plant grafted male clones if you don't want the smelly seeds

lore: Monks kept ginkgo alive for centuries in temple gardens in China, Korea and Japan; Engelbert Kaempfer described it for Europe after visiting Japan in the 1690s. Goethe sent a pressed leaf with his 1815 poem 'Ginkgo biloba', using its split leaf as an image of one being that is also two.
funFact: The odd spelling 'Ginkgo' was long blamed on a misprint by Engelbert Kaempfer; later research suggests it reflects how his Nagasaki interpreter pronounced 'ginkyō'.

wiki.extract: Ginkgo biloba, commonly known as ginkgo, also known as the maidenhair tree, and often misspelled "gingko" is a species of gymnosperm tree native to East Asia. It is the last living species in the order Ginkgoales, which first appeared over 290 million years ago. Fossils similar to the living species, belonging to the genus Ginkgo, extend back to the Middle Jurassic epoch about 170 million years ago. The tree was cultivated early in human history, remains commonly planted, and is widely regarded as a living fossil.

summary: A golden-flowered meadow perennial that blooms around midsummer, St John's Day. Its leaves are pricked with translucent oil glands and its flowers bleed red. It works as an antidepressant, but also speeds up the liver's clearance of many prescription drugs.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; invasive in North America, Australia and elsewhere
abilities: Extracts containing hyperforin and hypericin outperform placebo for mild to moderate depression in clinical trials
Translucent leaf glands make the leaves look perforated when held to the light
Flowers stain the fingers and oils red with hypericin
Hypericin is photodynamic: grazing animals that eat it can suffer severe sunburn (hypericism)
Spreads aggressively by seed and runners; a major rangeland weed outside its native range
edibilityNote: Not a food. Toxic to livestock, which become photosensitised. In people it is taken only as standardised medicine.

uses.use: Red flower oil for wounds, burns and nerve pain; tea for melancholy and bedwetting
Hufariqun used as a diuretic, wound-healer and for sciatica
Standardised extracts prescribed in Germany for mild to moderate depression

medicinal.cautions: Systematic reviews find it better than placebo and similar to standard antidepressants for mild to moderate depression. It strongly induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which can make oral contraceptives, warfarin, ciclosporin, HIV drugs, digoxin, some chemotherapy and many other drugs fail. Do not combine with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs, as serotonin syndrome can result. Causes photosensitivity. Seek medical advice before using it for depression.

fruit.description: Three-chambered dry capsule with many seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, cylindrical, dark brown, finely pitted
seed.dispersal: Wind, water, animals and machinery; long-lived seed bank
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–3 weeks at 20 °C

steps: Check local rules first: it is a declared noxious weed in many US states, Australia and elsewhere
Surface-sow in spring
Harvest the top third of flowering stems at peak bloom
Macerate fresh flowers in olive oil in sun for 'red oil', or dry quickly for tea

lore: Medieval Europeans hung it over doors on St John's Eve (23 June) to repel evil spirits, and it was known as fuga daemonum, 'devil's flight'. Dioscorides and Pliny recommended hyperikon for sciatica and burns.
funFact: In the 1940s California released Chrysolina leaf beetles against Klamath weed, as St John's wort was called there. It became one of the first great successes of biological weed control.

wiki.extract: Hypericum perforatum, commonly known as St. John's wort, is a flowering plant in the family Hypericaceae. It is a hairless, perennial herb with woody roots, yellow flowers marked by black glands, and leaves that appear perforated due to translucent glands, producing thousands of seeds per plant.

gerard.title: Of Saint Iohns woort
gerard.names: S. Iohns woort is called in Greeke ὑπερικόν: in Latine Hypericum: in shops Perforata: of diuers Fuga Demonum: in Dutch San Iohans kraut: in Italian Hyperico: in Spanish Caraconzillo: in French Mille pertuys: in English S. Iohns woort, or S. Iohns grasse.
gerard.place: They grow very plentifully in the pastures in euery countrie.
gerard.time: They flower and flourish for the most part in Iuly and August.
gerard.temperature: S. Iohns woort, as Galen teacheth, is hot and drie, being of substance thinne.
gerard.vertues: S. Iohns woort, with his flowers and seede boiled and drunken, prouoketh vrine, and is right good against the stone in the bladder, and stoppeth the laske. The leaues stamped are good to be laide vpon burnings, scaldings, and all wounds; and also for rotten and filthie vlcers. The leaues, flowers, and seedes stamped, and put into a glasse with oile oliue, and set in the hot sunne for certaine weekes together, and then strained from those herbes, and the like quantitie of new put in, and sunned in like maner, doth make an oile of the colour of blood, which is a most pretious remedy for deep wounds, & those that are thorow the bodie, for sinewes that are prickt, or any wound made with a venomed weapon. I am accustomed to make a compound oile hereof, the making of which yee shall receiue at my hands, bicause that I knowe in the world there is not a better, no not naturall Balsam it selfe; for I dare vndertake to cure any such wound, as absolutely in each respect, if not sooner and better, as any man whatsoeuer shall or may with naturall Balsam.

summary: An autumn-flowering crocus whose three crimson stigmas, picked by hand, are the world's most expensive spice. It is a sterile triploid that has not set seed in thousands of years and survives only because people replant its corms.
nativeRange: Known only in cultivation; arose from the wild Crocus cartwrightianus in Bronze Age Greece. Grown mainly in Iran, Kashmir, Spain, Greece and Morocco
abilities: Stigmas contain crocin, a water-soluble carotenoid that dyes intensely golden
Safranal, formed from picrocrocin as the stigmas dry, gives saffron its hay-like aroma
Sterile triploid: every plant is a clone, multiplied only by daughter corms
Flowers in autumn, before its leaves fully emerge
edibilityNote: Safe in culinary amounts (a few threads). Doses of about 5 g or more are toxic, and around 12–20 g has been reported as potentially lethal. Do not confuse it with the deadly autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale), which looks similar but has six stamens and no long red stigmas.

uses.use: Zafran as an exhilarant (mufarrih) for melancholy, a heart tonic and an aphrodisiac
Kunkuma for skin complexion, menstrual complaints, cough and as a rejuvenating tonic in milk
Zanghonghua ('Tibetan red flower', also fanhonghua) to invigorate blood, cool the blood and calm the spirit, for amenorrhoea, postpartum pain and low mood
Small trials of 30 mg/day extract for mild to moderate depression, with positive results

medicinal.cautions: Depression trials are small and mostly from one region. High doses stimulate the uterus, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. Large doses are toxic. Saffron is widely adulterated with safflower, turmeric or dyed fibres.

seed.description: Sterile; does not produce viable seed
seed.germination: Not grown from seed

steps: Plant corms 10 cm deep and 10 cm apart in late summer
Water lightly in autumn if dry
Pick flowers in the morning as they open and pluck out the three red stigmas
Dry stigmas gently and store airtight in the dark; lift and divide crowded corms every 3–4 years

lore: The 'Saffron Gatherers' frescoes at Akrotiri on Thera (c. 1600 BCE) show women gathering crocus stigmas and a monkey presenting saffron to a goddess. Iran today grows the great majority of the world's saffron.
funFact: About 150,000 flowers are needed for one kilogram of dried saffron.

wiki.extract: Crocus sativus, commonly known as saffron crocus or autumn crocus, is a species of flowering plant in the iris family Iridaceae. A cormous autumn-flowering cultivated perennial, unknown in the wild, it is best known for the culinary use of its floral stigmas as the spice saffron. Human cultivation of saffron crocus and the trade and use of saffron have endured for more than 3,500 years and span different cultures, continents, and civilizations.

plates.long: This plate from Basilius Besler's 'Hortus Eystettensis' showcases the diversity of the Prince-Bishop of Eichstätt's garden. It features meticulously rendered specimens of Crocus, Iris, and Lily, highlighting the intricate details of their bulbs and root systems which were of great interest to early modern botanists.

plates.author: Leonhart Fuchs
