plates.long: This woodcut from Leonhart Fuchs's 1542 herbal depicts the Saffron crocus, labeled in Latin and German as 'Croci Flores' and 'Saffranblümen'. The illustration is notable for its scientific accuracy, showing the plant's life cycle stages including the distinctive corm, linear leaves, and the three-parted stigma used to produce the precious spice.

plates.title: Discourses on the Six Books of Dioscorides

plates.title: The Flowering Garden: Autumn

plates.long: An exquisite copperplate engraving from Crispijn van de Passe's 'Hortus Floridus' (1616), depicting the Crocus (Saffron) plant. The illustration showcases the plant's lifecycle from bulb to bloom and includes a small field mouse, a characteristic touch of the artist that brings a sense of life and scale to the botanical study.

plates.title: Hortus Eystettensis
plates.author: Basilius Besler
plates.desc: A detailed botanical engraving from the Hortus Eystettensis featuring four plant specimens: Aristolochia Vulgaris (Birthwort), Laureola (Spurge Laurel), Cornus (Dogwood), and Crocus Vernus (Spring Crocus).
plates.long: This plate is from Basilius Besler's monumental 'Hortus Eystettensis', a landmark florilegium that documented the plants in the garden of the Prince-Bishop of Eichstätt. The engraving depicts four distinct species—Aristolochia, Laureola, Cornus, and Crocus—with scientific precision and artistic elegance, representing the pinnacle of botanical art in the early modern period.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a crocus plant, meticulously detailing its bulbous root, linear leaves, and delicate blossom. It reflects the 16th-century shift towards empirical observation in the natural sciences, as championed by the pioneering botanist Carolus Clusius.

plates.long: A scientific illustration of a crocus variety, specifically noted for its 'double flower' (flore duplici). Such detailed woodcuts were essential for early modern herbalists and botanists to accurately identify and categorize plant species across Europe.

The image is hand-colored, a common practice in early printed herbals to aid in plant identification.

gerard.title: Of Saffron
gerard.names: Saffron is called in Greeke κρόκος: in Latin Crocus: in Mauritania Zaffaran: in Spanifh Açafron: in Englifh Saffron: in the Arabicke toong Zahafaran. Some that are difposed to dissemble and ieft with their friends and to make them merrie with pretie Poeticall figmentes, haue giuen it the name of a Damfell, whereof Ouid maketh mention, which to recite were impertinent to our hiftorie.
gerard.place: Common, or the beft knowne Saffron groweth plentifully in Cambridgefhire, Saffron Walden and other places thereabout, as corne in the fieldes.
gerard.time: Saffron beginneth to flower in September, and prefently after fpring vp the leaues, and remaine greene all the winter long.
gerard.temperature: Saffron is a little aftringent or binding, but his hot qualitie doth fo ouer rule in it, that in the whol essence it is in the number of thofe herbes which are hot in the fecond degree, and drie in the firft: therfore it alfo hath a certaine force to concoct, which is furthered by the fmall aftricti…
gerard.vertues: A Auicen affirmeth that it caufeth headach, and is hurtfull to the braine, which it cannot doe by taking it now and then, but by too much vfing of it: for too much vfing of it cutteth off fleepe, through want whereof the head and fences are out of frame. But the moderate vfe of it is good for the head, and maketh the fences more quicke and liuely, fhaketh off heauie and drowfie fleepe, and maketh a man merrie. B Alfo Saffron ftrengtheneth the hart, concocteth crude or rawe humors of the cheft, openeth the lungs, and remooueth obftructions or ftoppings. C It is alfo fuch a fpeciall remedie for thofe that haue confumption of the lungs, and are, as we tearm it, at deaths doore, & almoft paft breathing, that it bringeth breath againe, & prolongeth life for certaine daies, if ten or twentie graines at the moft be giuen, with new or fweete wine. For we haue found by often experience that being taken in that fort, it prefently, and in a moment remooueth away difficultie of breathing, which moft dangerously and fuddenly happeneth.

summary: A majestic, long-lived nut tree from the mountains of Central Asia, prized for its oily nuts, its fine dark timber and the brown dye in its husks. Its roots and leaves release juglone, a chemical that suppresses many plants growing beneath it.
nativeRange: Mountains of Central Asia, Iran, the Caucasus, the Himalaya and south-west China; cultivated across temperate Eurasia and the Americas
abilities: Leaves, husks and roots contain juglone, an allelopathic compound that can inhibit some nearby plants, though less strongly than black walnut
Wild walnut–fruit forests of Kyrgyzstan's Arslanbob are among the largest natural walnut forests on Earth
Wind-pollinated; male and female flowers on the same tree often mature at different times
Green husks stain skin and cloth dark brown
edibleParts: nut kernel (fresh, dried, pressed for oil)
green immature nuts (pickled, or in nocino liqueur)
edibilityNote: Kernels are safe; walnut is a common tree-nut allergen. Mouldy nuts may contain mycotoxins. Husk sap stains and can irritate skin.

uses.use: Walnut kernel (hé táo rén) to tonify kidneys and lungs, ease cough and moisten the bowels
Leaf decoction (Commission E) for mild skin inflammation and excess sweating
The brain-like kernel was thought to strengthen the head and brain

medicinal.cautions: Tree-nut allergy. Husks and leaves contain juglone and can irritate skin; horse laminitis is linked mainly to bedding made from black walnut (J. nigra) shavings.

fruit.description: Round fruit 4–6 cm with a smooth, green, aromatic husk that blackens and splits, releasing a wrinkled, two-halved woody shell.

seed.description: Brain-like, wrinkled, two-lobed kernel, cream-coloured inside with a thin papery light-brown skin, about 3–4 cm across, held inside a ridged tan woody shell
seed.dispersal: Rodents, crows and jays cache and forget nuts
seed.germination: Cold-stratify in moist sand 90–120 days (or sow outdoors in autumn) 5 cm deep; protect from squirrels

grow.water: Moderate; deep watering in dry summers
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–6 years from a grafted tree; 8–12 from seed
steps: Choose a late-leafing variety where spring frosts occur, and plant where its 15–20 m canopy and juglone will not affect vegetable beds.
Plant in winter in deep soil; walnuts form long taproots and resent transplanting.
Water young trees deeply in dry spells and keep grass away from the trunk.
Prune only in late summer (bleeding sap in spring weakens the tree), removing low and crossing branches.
Gather nuts as they fall, remove husks promptly (wear gloves), and dry in shade until the kernel snaps crisply.

lore: The Romans called the walnut 'Jovis glans', acorn of Jupiter, which gave the genus name Juglans. Walnuts travelled from Persia to Greece and Rome, and Carpathian, Kashmiri and Xinjiang walnuts remain famed regional strains.
funFact: The English word 'walnut' means 'foreign nut', from Old English wealh-hnutu.

wiki.extract: Juglans regia, known by various common names including the common walnut, English walnut, or Persian walnut amongst other names, is a species of walnut. It is native to Eurasia in at least southwest and central Asia and southeast Europe, but its exact natural area is obscure due to its long history of cultivation.

summary: A silver-leaved Mediterranean mountain shrub whose purple spikes have perfumed linen, baths and soap since Roman times. Despite its common name it is not English, and its finest oil comes from the high Provençal plateaus.
nativeRange: Mountains of the western Mediterranean: Spain, southern France, Andorra and Italy
abilities: Essential oil is dominated by linalool and linalyl acetate, studied for anxiety-reducing effects
Thrives on dry, stony, alkaline soil where few crops will grow
Silvery hairs reflect sunlight and reduce water loss
One of the most visited garden plants for bumblebees and honeybees
edibilityNote: Flowers flavour shortbread, honey and herbes de Provence in small amounts. The essential oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity.

uses.use: Flower tea, pillows and oil for sleeplessness, headaches, nervous indigestion and insect bites
Lavender species (khuzama, ustukhuddus) used as nervines to 'cleanse the brain', for headache and epilepsy
Oral lavender-oil capsules (Silexan) trialled with positive results for generalised anxiety; aromatherapy for sleep

medicinal.cautions: Essential oil can cause contact dermatitis and is poisonous if swallowed undiluted. Oral capsules can cause belching and nausea. Topical lavender and tea-tree products have been linked to breast enlargement in boys, though this is debated. May add to sedatives.

fruit.description: Four tiny dark nutlets inside each dried calyx.

seed.description: Small, oval, glossy dark brown
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; 3–4 weeks cold stratification helps; 2–4 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.soil: Poor, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline
grow.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings (true to type) or seed
steps: Root 8–10 cm summer cuttings in gritty compost
Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; wet winter soil kills it
Harvest stems as the first flowers open
Trim back after flowering, but never cut into old bare wood

lore: Hildegard of Bingen (12th century) wrote that lavender kept away lice and cleared the vision. The perfumer-chemist René-Maurice Gattefossé popularised the word aromathérapie with his 1937 book of that name, partly after treating a laboratory burn with lavender oil.
funFact: Lavender oil is not one product: oil from L. angustifolia is low in camphor, while hybrid lavandin (L. × intermedia) gives much more oil with a harsher, camphoraceous smell.

gerard.title: Of Lauander spike
gerard.names: Lauander spike is called in Latine Lauandula, and Spica: in Spanish Spigo, and Languda. The first is the male, and the seconde the female. It is thought of some to be that sweete herbe Casia, whereof Virgil maketh mention in the seconde Eclog of his Bucolicks. > Tum Casia atque alijs intexens suauibus herbis, > Mollia luteola pingit vacinia Caltha.
gerard.place: In Spaine, and Languedocke in France, most of the mountaines and desert fieldes, are as it were couered ouer with Lauander. In these cold countries they are planted in gardens.
gerard.time: They flower and flourish in Iune and Iuly.
gerard.temperature: Lauander is hot and drie, and that in the third degree, and is of a thin substance, consisting o many airie and spirituall partes. Therefore it is good to be giuen any way against the diseases of th head, and especially those which haue their originall or beginning not of abundance of humor but chie…
gerard.vertues: The distilled water of Lauander smelt vnto, or the temples and forehead bathed therewith, is refreshing to them that haue the Catalepsie, a light Migram, and to them that haue the fallin sicknes, & that vse to swoune much. But when there is abundance of humors, especially mixed wit blood, it is not then to be vsed safely, neither is the composition to be taken, which is made of disti led wine: in which such kinde of herbes, flowers, or seedes, and certaine spices are infused and steeped, though most men do rashly and at aduenture giue them without making any difference at all. For by vsing such hot things that fill and stuffe the head, both the disease is made greater, and the sicke man also brought into danger, especially when letting of blood, or purging haue not gone before.

summary: A natural hybrid of water mint and spearmint, almost sterile and spread around the world entirely by runners. Its menthol tricks nerve endings into feeling cold.
nativeRange: Arose as a hybrid in Europe; cultivated and naturalised worldwide
abilities: Menthol activates TRPM8, the body's cold receptor, causing a cooling sensation without any change in temperature
Relaxes smooth muscle in the gut, which underlies its use for irritable bowel syndrome
Spreads rapidly by underground and overground runners
Rarely sets viable seed; almost every peppermint plant is a clone
edibilityNote: Leaves are used in teas, sweets and food. Concentrated oil is toxic in large amounts, and menthol products should not be applied near the faces of infants, where they can cause breathing problems.

uses.use: Tea for indigestion, nausea, colic and colds; oil rubbed on temples for headache
Pudina and its distilled water (araq-e-pudina) for indigestion, flatulence and vomiting
Bohe (mainly Mentha haplocalyx) disperses wind-heat in colds, sore throat and headache
Enteric-coated peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome; topical menthol for tension headache

medicinal.cautions: Can worsen heartburn and reflux by relaxing the oesophageal sphincter. The oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity. Keep menthol away from infants' faces. Enteric-coated capsules can interact with antacids.

fruit.description: Usually aborted; viable nutlets very rare.

seed.description: Seeds are rarely viable; 'peppermint seed' sold commercially usually grows into other mints
seed.germination: Propagate from cuttings instead

grow.propagation: Runner or stem cuttings (roots in water within days)
steps: Root a stem cutting in water, or plant a runner
Grow in a sunk container to stop it spreading
Cut stems just before flowering for the strongest oil
Replant every 3–4 years as clumps weaken

lore: The naturalist John Ray first described 'pepper-mint' in 1696 from a plant found in Hertfordshire. Commercial growing began at Mitcham, Surrey, in the mid-18th century.
funFact: Peppermint's chromosome counts are irregular (from 66 to 120 have been recorded), a legacy of its hybrid origin from water mint and spearmint, which is why it almost never sets viable seed.

wiki.extract: Peppermint is a hybrid species of mint, a cross between watermint and spearmint. Indigenous to Europe and the Middle East, the plant is now widely spread and cultivated in many regions of the world. It is occasionally found in the wild with its parent species.

It is featured in Li Shizhen's 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica), a monumental work that revolutionized the study of natural history and pharmacology in the 16th century.

summary: A clove-scented basil that grows in a raised shrine (tulsi vrindavan) in the courtyard of countless Hindu homes, where it is worshipped as the goddess Tulsi. It is also the peppery basil of Thai street food.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia and northern Australia
abilities: Leaves are rich in eugenol, the clove-scented compound that deters many insects
Flowers almost year-round in the tropics and feeds bees and other small pollinators
Contains ursolic and rosmarinic acids, studied for anti-inflammatory activity
edibilityNote: Leaves are used fresh in Thai cooking (pad kraphao) and in teas. Medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.

uses.use: Leaf tea and juice for cough, colds, fever and stress; used as a rasayana and to support breathing
Thulasi leaves given for respiratory infections and as a general tonic
Leaf infusions in Thailand for stomach ache, colic and colds
Small trials of extracts for stress, blood sugar and lipids

medicinal.cautions: Clinical trials are few, small and of mixed quality. May lower blood sugar and slow clotting. Animal studies suggest reduced fertility, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy or when trying to conceive. Methyl eugenol in the essential oil is a concern at high doses.

fruit.season: Most of the year in the tropics
fruit.description: Tiny dry nutlets held in the persistent calyx.

seed.description: Small brown-black seeds that turn mucilaginous when wet
seed.germination: Needs warmth (above 20 °C) and light; 7–14 days

steps: Sow on the surface of warm compost and keep moist
Plant out after frost into full sun
Pinch out tips to keep it bushy
Harvest leaves often; let some flower for bees and seed

lore: In the Puranas Tulsi is the consort of Vishnu, and the annual Tulsi Vivah festival ritually marries the plant to Vishnu as the shaligram stone or to Krishna. Vaishnava devotees wear prayer beads (kanthi mala) carved from tulsi stems.
funFact: Much medical literature still calls holy basil Ocimum sanctum. But Linnaeus had already named it O. tenuiflorum in 1753, fourteen years earlier, so that name takes priority.

wiki.extract: Ocimum tenuiflorum, commonly known as tulasi, tulsi, or holy basil, is an aromatic perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae. It is widely cultivated throughout the Southeast Asian tropics. It is native to tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, Australia and the western Pacific. This plant has escaped from cultivation and has naturalized in many tropical regions of the Americas. It is an agricultural and environmental weed.

summary: A woody, grey-green Mediterranean sub-shrub whose very name, from the Latin salvere, means 'to be well'. Medieval doctors put it in nearly every remedy.
nativeRange: Northern and eastern Mediterranean, especially the Balkans and Adriatic coast; cultivated worldwide
abilities: Contains carnosic acid and rosmarinic acid, strong antioxidants
Leaf oil is rich in thujone, which repels insects and is toxic at high doses
Felted grey hairs shade the leaves and cut water loss in summer drought
Its hinged stamens act as a lever, dabbing pollen onto the backs of visiting bees
edibilityNote: Leaves are a culinary herb. The essential oil and very large amounts of the herb contain enough thujone to cause seizures.

uses.use: Gargles for sore throat and gum inflammation; tea to reduce sweating, for indigestion and to dry up breast milk
Maramiya tea taken after meals for stomach ache, colds and menstrual cramps
EMA-recognised for excessive sweating and mouth inflammation; small trials for menopausal hot flushes and memory

medicinal.cautions: Thujone is a convulsant, so avoid the essential oil, long-term high doses, pregnancy, breastfeeding and epilepsy. Culinary use is safe.

fruit.description: Four round dark nutlets in the calyx.

seed.description: Round, dark brown seeds
seed.germination: Easy; 10–21 days at 15–20 °C

grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves lightly in year 1; fully from year 2
steps: Sow or root cuttings in spring
Plant in sun in free-draining soil
Prune lightly after flowering to stop it getting leggy
Replace plants every 4–5 years as they become woody

lore: The medieval health manual of the School of Salerno asked: 'Cur moriatur homo cui salvia crescit in horto?' ('Why should a man die who grows sage in his garden?'). Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis (c. 800) ordered it grown on imperial estates.
funFact: Salvia is the largest genus in the mint family, with roughly 1,000 species, and since 2017 it has included rosemary.

wiki.extract: Salvia officinalis, common sage or sage, is a perennial, evergreen subshrub, with woody stems, grayish leaves, and blue to purplish flowers. It is a member of the mint family (Lamiaceae) and native to the Mediterranean region, though it has been naturalized in many places throughout the world. It has a long history of culinary use, and in modern times it has been used as an ornamental garden plant. The common name "sage" is also used for closely related species and cultivars.

otherNames: Iklīl al-jabal إكليل الجبل (Arabic, 'crown of the mountain')
summary: An aromatic evergreen shrub of sea cliffs and garrigue, the herb of remembrance at weddings and funerals. Botanists moved it out of Rosmarinus and into the sage genus in 2017 after DNA studies.
nativeRange: Mediterranean basin, from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey
abilities: Carnosic acid and carnosol make it one of the most effective natural food antioxidants
Needle-like, rolled leaves with hairy undersides survive drought and salt spray
Flowers in late winter and early spring, an important early source of nectar for bees
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are a culinary herb. The undiluted essential oil is toxic if swallowed and can trigger seizures.

uses.use: Tea and wine infusions for memory, headache, poor circulation and indigestion; spirits rubbed on aching joints and the scalp
Iklil-ul-jabal used as a nervine and brain tonic, carminative and for rheumatic pain
Azir leaf infusions for digestive complaints, diabetes and as a general tonic
EMA traditional-use monograph for dyspepsia and as a bath additive for muscle and joint pain

medicinal.cautions: Only a few small clinical trials exist, so the evidence is weak. The essential oil can provoke seizures in high doses, so avoid it with epilepsy and in pregnancy. Medicinal doses may interact with anticoagulants and diuretics.

fruit.description: Four small brown nutlets.

seed.description: Small, oval, light-brown seeds
seed.germination: Low and slow; 2–4 weeks at 18–22 °C. Cuttings are far easier

steps: Root 10 cm cuttings in gritty compost in late summer
Plant in the hottest, best-drained spot available
Water only in prolonged drought
Trim after flowering, never into bare wood

lore: In Hamlet, Ophelia says 'There's rosemary, that's for remembrance'. In medieval and Tudor England sprigs were carried at both weddings and funerals. 'Hungary water', a rosemary-based spirit, was one of Europe's first alcohol-based perfumes.
funFact: Rosemary extract is approved in the EU as a food antioxidant under the code E 392.

wiki.extract: Salvia rosmarinus, synonym Rosmarinus officinalis, commonly known as rosemary, is a shrub with fragrant, evergreen, needle-like leaves and purple or sometimes white, pink, or blue flowers. It is a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae. The species is native to the Mediterranean region. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.

summary: A tree in the mint family that became the world's most famous ship timber. Teak's oily, silica-rich wood shrugs off water, rot and termites, so it was used for warships, temples and deck planks for centuries. The great natural teak forests of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand are now largely gone.
nativeRange: India, Myanmar, Laos and Thailand; long naturalised in Java; plantations across the tropics
abilities: Makes heartwood with natural oils and tectoquinone that repel termites and fungi
Its wood barely shrinks or swells with moisture, so it was ideal for ship decks
Drops its huge leaves in the dry season and survives fire
Its leaves are among the largest of any tree, up to about 50 cm long, and yield a red dye
edibilityNote: Not a food. Leaves are used to wrap food in parts of India and Java. Teak sawdust can cause dermatitis and asthma.

uses.use: Bark and wood (shaka) as astringent; leaf preparations for skin disease and bleeding
Young leaves used as a red dye and for skin problems

medicinal.cautions: Teak dust is a skin and respiratory sensitiser for woodworkers.

fruit.description: Hard, four-chambered stone inside a papery, balloon-like calyx.

seed.description: Very hard, woody fruit stone with up to four seeds
seed.germination: Alternately soak and sun-dry fruits for 1–2 weeks to break dormancy; germination is erratic

steps: Soak fruits overnight and sun-dry by day for 1–2 weeks
Sow in nursery beds; transplant 'stumps' (pruned seedlings) at the start of the rains
Weed well: teak is intolerant of competition
Thin plantings over time to produce straight trunks

lore: Britain's Royal Navy and the East India Company built ships from Malabar and Burmese teak, and the timber trade shaped colonial forestry in British India.
funFact: Teak is in the mint family, Lamiaceae, the same family as basil and lavender.

wiki.extract: Teak is a tropical hardwood tree species in the family Lamiaceae. It is a large, deciduous tree that occurs in mixed hardwood forests. Tectona grandis has small, fragrant white flowers arranged in dense clusters (panicles) at the end of the branches. These flowers contain both types of reproductive organs. The large, papery leaves of teak trees are often hairy on the lower surface. Teak wood has a leather-like smell when it is freshly milled and is particularly valued for its durability and water resistance. The teak wood is used for boat building, exterior construction, veneer, furniture, carving, turnings, and various small projects.

otherNames: Ṣaʿtar / Zaʿtar (Arabic, used loosely for thyme-like herbs)
summary: A tiny-leaved, low woody shrub of sun-baked Mediterranean hills whose oil, thymol, was among the first antiseptics of modern medicine. Wild populations come in distinct 'chemotypes' that smell quite different.
nativeRange: Western Mediterranean: Spain, southern France, Italy
abilities: Thymol and carvacrol in its oil kill many bacteria and fungi
Forms distinct chemotypes (thymol, carvacrol, linalool, geraniol and others) that sort out by local soil and frost
Survives summer drought by shedding some leaves and thriving in shallow, stony soil
Small flowers are heavily worked by honeybees; thyme honey is a prized Mediterranean speciality
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are a classic culinary herb. The essential oil is irritating and toxic in quantity.

uses.use: Tea and syrup for coughs, whooping cough and bronchitis; antiseptic washes for wounds
Satar (various thyme species) for coughs, digestive complaints and intestinal worms
Thyme extract, often combined with ivy or primrose, approved in Germany for coughs from bronchitis; thymol in mouthwashes

medicinal.cautions: Trials of thyme combination products for acute bronchitis are positive. The essential oil irritates skin and mucous membranes and should not be swallowed. People allergic to other Lamiaceae may react. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Four minute, dark nutlets in the calyx.

seed.description: Tiny, round, dark brown
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–3 weeks at 18–20 °C

grow.soil: Poor, stony, alkaline, very well drained
steps: Surface-sow under cover in spring, or root tip cuttings
Plant in full sun in gritty soil
Shear after flowering to keep plants compact
Renew every 3–4 years

lore: Thymol was first isolated by the German apothecary Caspar Neumann in 1719. When the First World War cut off German supplies, thymol ran short just as it was urgently needed for dressing soldiers' wounds, and new production started in Britain and India.
funFact: Thymol is used by beekeepers to treat honeybee colonies against the parasitic varroa mite.

gerard.title: Of garden Time
gerard.names: The first may be called harde Time, or common garden Time: the seconde broade leafed Time: the thirde Time of Candie; our English women call it Muske Time: the last may be called Dodder Time.
gerard.place: These kindes of Time growe plentifully in England euery where, except that with broad leaues, and Time of Candie, which I haue in my garden.
gerard.time: They flourish from Maie vnto September.
gerard.temperature: These kindes of Time are hot and drie in the thirde degree.
gerard.vertues: Time boiled in water and honie and drunken, is good against the cough and shortnesse of the breath; it prouoketh vrine, expelleth the secondine or afterbirth, and the dead childe; and dissolueth clotted or congealed bloud in the bodie. The same drunke with vineger and salt, purgeth flegme: and boiled in Meade or Metheglin, clenseth the brest, lungs, reines, and matrix, and killeth wormes. Made into powder and taken in the waight of three drams with Meade or honied vineger, called Oximell, Oximell, and a little salt, purgeth by stoole tough and clammie flegme, sharpe cholericke humours, and all corruption of blood. The same taken in like sort, is good against the Ischiatica, the paine in the side and brest, against the winde in the side and bellie, and is profitable also for such as are fearefull, melancholike, and troubled in minde. It is good to be giuen unto those that haue the falling sicknesse to smell unto.

summary: A small evergreen laurel of Sri Lanka whose inner bark, peeled and rolled into fragile quills, is 'true cinnamon'. Its trade was so lucrative that Arab middlemen spun tales of cinnamon guarded by giant birds to hide its origin. The wild species is assessed as Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Sri Lanka and the southern Western Ghats of India; cultivated in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, the Seychelles and elsewhere
abilities: Inner bark curls naturally into quills as it dries
Coppiced stools regrow new shoots for harvest every 2 years for decades
Contains far less coumarin than cassia cinnamon (C. cassia)
Young leaves flush bright red before turning green
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Concentrated essential oil irritates skin and mucous membranes; cassia (often sold as cinnamon) is high in coumarin, which can harm the liver in large regular doses.

uses.use: Tvak (bark) for colds, indigestion and to balance kapha
Cinnamon bark (ròu guì, mainly cassia) to warm the body and kidneys
Used in embalming and kyphi incense

medicinal.cautions: Cinnamon oil is a strong irritant and sensitiser; supplements may lower blood sugar.

fruit.season: Ripens about 6 months after flowering (often June–August)
fruit.description: Small, oval, dark-purple to black drupe 1–1.5 cm, sitting in a cup-like persistent calyx.

seed.description: A single oval, smooth seed 8–10 mm, pale brown to dark brown, inside the thin black flesh
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: clean and sow fresh, 1 cm deep, in warm shade at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks

grow.soil: Sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the famous Negombo cinnamon grows on white sand
grow.propagation: Seed or semi-hardwood cuttings; air layering
grow.timeToHarvest: First cut 2–3 years after planting; then every 1–2 years
steps: Sow fresh seed or root cuttings and plant out in sandy, well-drained soil 1–1.5 m apart.
After 2–3 years, coppice the plant to 10–15 cm above the ground to make it sprout many straight shoots.
Cut shoots 1.5–2.5 cm thick in the rainy season, when the bark peels easily.
Scrape off the outer bark, rub the stem with a brass rod to loosen the inner bark, slit and peel it in long strips.
Nest smaller strips inside larger ones to form quills; dry in shade for 4–5 days, then in sun.

lore: Herodotus reported that Arabians gathered cinnamon from the nests of giant birds, and Nero is said to have burned a year's supply of Rome's cinnamon at the funeral of his wife Poppaea. Portuguese and then Dutch control of Ceylon's cinnamon was fought over for two centuries.
funFact: The Dutch burned stocks of cinnamon in Amsterdam to keep prices high, and cultivated it on plantations only from the 1760s.

wiki.extract: Cinnamomum verum, also known as true cinnamon or Ceylon cinnamon, is a small evergreen tree belonging to the family Lauraceae, native to Sri Lanka. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this name has also been used for C. cassia (cassia) as well.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's seminal work on the flora and fauna of the Americas depicts a branch of the Wild Cinnamon tree (Canella winterana) alongside a coiled ribbon snake. Catesby was a pioneer in illustrating species within their natural ecological contexts, a revolutionary approach for 18th-century natural history that influenced later naturalists like Audubon.

summary: A laurel-family tree from Mesoamerica whose oily fruit evolved, many think, to be swallowed whole by giant ground sloths and gomphotheres. Its flowers switch sex on a daily schedule to avoid self-pollination.
nativeRange: South-central Mexico to Guatemala and Central America; cultivated in tropical and Mediterranean climates worldwide
abilities: Synchronous dichogamy: 'A' and 'B' varieties open as female and male at opposite times of day
Fruit does not ripen on the tree; it softens only after picking
Flesh can be 15–30% oil, unusually high for a fruit
Leaves, bark and seed contain persin, a toxin dangerous to birds, horses and livestock
edibleParts: leaves (dried, as a flavouring in Mexican cooking — Mexican race only)
edibilityNote: The flesh is safe for people. Persin in leaves, skin, seed and bark is toxic to birds, rabbits, horses, goats and other livestock; the seed is not a food.

uses.use: Leaves and seed used in remedies for diarrhoea and as an aphrodisiac; recorded in the Florentine Codex
Avocado–soybean unsaponifiables (ASU) prescribed for osteoarthritis

medicinal.cautions: Leaves, skin and seed toxic to many animals. People with latex allergy may react (latex-fruit syndrome).

fruit.season: Varies by variety; often year-round in suitable climates
fruit.description: Pear-shaped to round fruit 7–20 cm, skin green to purple-black, smooth or pebbly ('Hass'); buttery pale-green to yellow flesh around one large seed.

seed.description: Large, round to egg-shaped seed 4–6 cm, with a thin papery brown seed coat over a hard cream-to-pinkish interior that browns when cut
seed.dispersal: Formerly megafauna; now humans and rodents
seed.germination: Clean seed, plant broad end down with the top exposed in moist mix (or suspend over water); roots in 2–6 weeks at 20–25 °C. Seedlings take 7–15 years to fruit and are unlike the parent

grow.zones: USDA 9b–11 (Mexican types to about −5 °C; West Indian to 0 °C)
grow.water: Moderate; regular deep watering, very sensitive to waterlogging
grow.soil: Very well-drained sandy loam, pH 5–7; avoid heavy clay (root rot)
grow.propagation: Grafting named cultivars onto seedling or clonal rootstocks
steps: Buy a grafted tree; for best pollination, plant one 'A' type (e.g. 'Hass') and one 'B' type (e.g. 'Fuerte' or 'Bacon') near each other.
Plant on a raised mound in full sun with superb drainage; mulch thickly with wood chips but keep mulch off the trunk.
Water deeply but let the topsoil dry between waterings; protect young trees from frost and sunburn (whitewash the trunk).
Prune lightly to control height; avocados drop many fruitlets naturally.
Pick mature fruit (test one) and ripen indoors for 3–10 days; fruit can be 'stored' on the tree for months.

lore: The Nahuatl word āhuacatl also meant 'testicle', likely for the fruit's shape. The 'Hass' avocado, now about 80% of world trade, traces to a single seedling tree in the garden of postman Rudolph Hass in La Habra Heights, California, patented in 1935.
funFact: Every 'Hass' avocado in the world is a clone of one tree, which died in 2002.

wiki.extract: The avocado, alligator pear or avocado pear is an evergreen tree in the laurel family (Lauraceae). It is native to the Americas, with archaeological evidence of early human avocado use dating back thousands of years across various regions of Central and South America. It was prized for its large and unusually oily fruit. The native range of avocado extends from Mexico to Peru, encompassing much of Central America and parts of northern and western South America.

summary: One of humanity's first crops, giving both linen and linseed oil. Its bast fibres are among the strongest plant fibres, and dyed wild flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old. The seeds are rich in omega-3 fatty acids and fibre.
nativeRange: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent from wild Linum bienne; cultivated worldwide
abilities: Produces long, strong bast fibres used for linen, rope and fine paper
Its seeds are rich in α-linolenic acid (an omega-3) and lignans
Its oil dries to a tough film, the basis of oil paints, putty and linoleum
Its seed coat makes mucilage when wet, which swells to many times its volume
edibilityNote: Seeds are widely eaten. They contain cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin); normal amounts are safe, but very large quantities of raw or unripe seed should be avoided. Drink plenty of water with ground seed, since it swells. Linseed oil sold for wood finishing is not food-grade.

uses.use: Whole or cracked seed as a bulk laxative; poultices for skin inflammation
Seeds (atasi) for cough, constipation and skin conditions
Ground flaxseed studied for lowering blood pressure and cholesterol

medicinal.cautions: Can block the gut if taken without enough water; may slow absorption of other medicines; caution with bowel obstruction.

fruit.description: Round capsules with ten shiny seeds.

seed.description: Flat, glossy brown or golden seeds
seed.dispersal: Capsules mostly stay closed on modern cultivars; harvested by people
seed.germination: Sow 1–2 cm deep in cool spring soil; 5–10 days

grow.timeToHarvest: Fibre at ~90 days; seed at ~100–120 days
steps: Broadcast seed thickly in early spring
Keep weeded in the first weeks
For fibre, pull whole plants when lower stems yellow, and rett them in dew or water
For seed, harvest when capsules are brown and rattle

lore: Ancient Egyptians wrapped mummies in linen and called it 'woven moonlight'. Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia yielded dyed wild flax fibres around 30,000 years old, among the oldest known fibres used by people.
funFact: The species name usitatissimum means 'most useful' in Latin.

wiki.extract: Flax, also known as common flax or line, is a flowering plant, Linum usitatissimum, in the family Linaceae. It is cultivated as a food and fiber crop in regions of the world with temperate climates.

gerard.title: Of Garden Flaxe
gerard.names: It is called both in Greeke and Latine Linon, Linum: in high Dutch Flachs: in Italian and Spanish Lino: in French Du lin: in lowe Dutch Vlas: in English Flaxe and Lyne.
gerard.place: It prospereth best in a fat and fruitfull soile, in moist and not drie places; for it requireth as Columella saith a very fat grounde, and somewhat moist. Some, saith Palladius, do sowe it thicke in a leane grounde, and by that meanes the flaxe groweth fine: Pliny saith that it is to be sowen in grauellie places, especially in one forrowe: Nec magis festinare aliud: and that it burneth the ground …
gerard.time: Flaxe is sowen in the spring, it flowreth in Iune and Iuly. After it is cutte downe (as Plinie in his 19. booke first chapter saith) the stalks are put into the water subiect to the heate of the sunne, and some waight laide on them to be steeped ther…
gerard.vertues: Galen in his first booke of the faculties of nourishments saith, that diuers vse the seede hereof parched as a sustenance with Garum, no otherwise then made salt. They also vse it mixed with honie; some likewise put it among bread, but it is hurtfull to the stomacke, and is hard of digestion, and yeeldeth to the bodie but little nourishment: but touching the qualities which maketh the belly soluble, neither wil I praise or dispraise it; yet that hath it some force to prouoke vrine, is more apparant when it is parched: but then it also staieth the belly more. The same author in his bookes of the faculties of simple medicines saith, that Lineseede being eaten is windie although it be parched, so full is it of superfluous moisture: and it is also after a sort hot in the first degree, and in a meane betweene moist and drie.

summary: A tree whose disc-shaped seeds contain strychnine, one of the most notorious poisons in history. Strychnine blocks inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord, so muscles convulse uncontrollably while the victim stays fully conscious.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
abilities: Makes strychnine and brucine, mostly in its seeds (about 1–1.5% strychnine)
Produces orange, apple-sized fruits whose pulp birds such as hornbills eat while discarding the seeds
Its alkaloids are so bitter that strychnine can be tasted at extremely low dilutions
Grows in dry and moist forests across the Indian subcontinent
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly; bark, leaves and root also contain strychnine and brucine. Within 15–60 minutes: anxiety, muscle twitching, then violent convulsions triggered by any noise or touch, arching of the back (opisthotonus), a fixed grin (risus sardonicus) and death from respiratory failure or exhaustion, while the person stays conscious. The fruit pulp is sometimes described as edible but is risky and not recommended.

uses.use: Seeds (kupilu) used only after purification in cow's urine, milk or ghee, in tiny doses for nerve and digestive disorders
Processed seeds (ma qian zi) for pain and paralysis
Strychnine used as a 'tonic' and stimulant

medicinal.cautions: Deadly; poisonings from traditional preparations are still reported. No safe home use.

fruit.description: Smooth, hard-shelled orange fruit with white jelly-like pulp and several seeds.

seed.description: Flat, grey, velvety discs
seed.dispersal: Birds and monkeys eating the pulp
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou isolated strychnine in 1818. At the 1904 St Louis Olympics, marathon winner Thomas Hicks was given strychnine and brandy by his trainers during the race and nearly collapsed.
funFact: Strychnine's complex structure took until 1946 to work out (Robert Robinson), and R. B. Woodward first synthesised it in 1954.

wiki.extract: Strychnos nux-vomica, the strychnine tree, also known as nux vomica, poison fruit, semen strychnos, and quaker buttons, is a deciduous tree native to India and to southeast Asia. It is a medium-sized tree in the family Loganiaceae that grows in open habitats. Its leaves are ovate and 5–9 centimetres (2–3.5 in) in size. It is known for being the natural source of the extremely poisonous compound strychnine.

summary: A thorny, drought-hardy shrub or small tree whose leathery fruit holds hundreds of jewel-like seeds. Cultivated from Iran to the Mediterranean since the Bronze Age, it has symbolised fertility, abundance and resurrection in nearly every culture that grew it.
nativeRange: Iran to northern India (Caucasus, Persia, Afghanistan, Himalayan foothills); cultivated across the Mediterranean and arid subtropics
abilities: Tolerates drought, heat, alkaline and moderately saline soils
Fruit keeps for months on the shelf thanks to its tannin-rich leathery rind
Brilliant scarlet, trumpet-shaped flowers attract sunbirds and hummingbirds
Rind yields a yellow-brown dye used for Persian carpets and leather
edibilityNote: Arils and juice are eaten. Root and stem bark contain toxic alkaloids (pelletierines) and should not be consumed.

uses.use: Rind decoction for diarrhoea and dysentery; fruit as a heart tonic
Sour and sweet pomegranate juices prescribed to balance hot and cold temperaments
Root bark used to expel tapeworms

medicinal.cautions: Bark and root alkaloids are toxic. Juice may interact with some drugs metabolised by CYP enzymes (e.g. warfarin).

fruit.description: Round fruit 6–12 cm topped with a crown-like calyx; leathery red to yellow-pink rind enclosing white membranes and 200–1,400 juicy translucent arils, ruby to pale pink.

seed.description: Each seed is wrapped in a juicy, glassy red to pink aril; the seed itself is angular, cream to pale-yellow, woody, about 5–8 mm long
seed.germination: Clean off the aril, sow fresh 0.5 cm deep at 20–25 °C; sprouts in 2–6 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 7–11 (some Russian and Central Asian varieties to 6)
grow.water: Low–moderate; even watering at fruit set reduces splitting
grow.soil: Well-drained; tolerates poor, alkaline and loamy soils, pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings (25 cm, winter) root readily; seed for rootstock or novelty
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from cutting; fruit ripens 5–7 months after flowering
steps: Take 25 cm hardwood cuttings of a good variety (e.g. 'Wonderful', 'Bhagwa') in winter and root them in a pot or directly in the ground.
Plant in the hottest, sunniest place, training to a single trunk or a few stems; remove suckers from the base.
Water regularly in the first year, then deeply but infrequently; keep watering steady once fruit sets to avoid cracking.
Prune lightly in late winter, as fruit forms on short spurs on 2–3-year-old wood.
Harvest when the rind colours fully and the fruit sounds metallic when tapped; cut, don't pull.

lore: In Greek myth Persephone ate pomegranate seeds in the underworld, binding her there for part of each year and explaining the seasons. Pomegranates were embroidered on the hem of the Hebrew High Priest's robe and appear in the Qur'an as a fruit of paradise.
funFact: The city of Granada in Spain shares its name with the fruit, and the grenade was named after the pomegranate for its seed-like shrapnel.

wiki.extract: The pomegranate is a fruit-bearing, deciduous shrub in the family Lythraceae, subfamily Punicoideae, that grows to between 1.5–5 metres (5–16 ft) tall. Rich in symbolic and mythological associations in many cultures, it originated in the region spanning the Caucasus and the Iranian plateau — including modern-day Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Pomegranate was first domesticated by ancient Iranians in the Iranian plateau and nearby regions about 5,000 years ago. It is extensively cultivated for its fruit.

Merian's work was revolutionary for its time, as she was one of the first naturalists to observe and illustrate insects in direct relation to their host plants in the wild.

summary: A woody Amazonian liana at the heart of ayahuasca, the visionary brew of many Amazonian peoples. Its harmala alkaloids block the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which lets DMT from leaves such as chacruna (Psychotria viridis) act when drunk.
nativeRange: Amazon basin and adjacent tropical South America (Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia)
abilities: Makes β-carboline alkaloids (harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine) that inhibit monoamine oxidase A
Climbs high into the rainforest canopy as a thick, twisting liana
Its MAO inhibition allows DMT to be orally active, a combination Indigenous peoples discovered without any chemistry
edibilityNote: Not a food. The brew causes vomiting and diarrhoea (regarded as 'purging' in ritual) and intense visions. Dangerous with SSRIs, other antidepressants, stimulants and certain foods because MAO inhibition can cause serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis; deaths have occurred, often with mixed brews or drug interactions.

uses.use: Healing, divination and spiritual guidance in ceremonies led by curanderos

uses.tradition: Brazilian ayahuasca religions (Santo Daime, União do Vegetal)
uses.use: Sacramental use
Small trials of ayahuasca for treatment-resistant depression

medicinal.cautions: MAO inhibitor: serious interactions with antidepressants, stimulants and tyramine-rich foods; not for people with psychosis, heart disease or in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Winged fruits typical of the Malpighia family.

seed.description: Winged samara
seed.germination: Usually propagated by stem cuttings rather than seed

lore: English botanist Richard Spruce collected the vine among the Tukanoan peoples of the Rio Negro in 1851. In 2006 the US Supreme Court (Gonzales v. O Centro Espírita Beneficente União do Vegetal) upheld a church's right to use hoasca tea.
funFact: Harmine was once called 'telepathine' in the 1920s because of the visions reported by those who drank ayahuasca.

wiki.extract: Banisteriopsis caapi, also known as caapi, soul vine, yagé (yage), or ayahuasca, is a South American liana of the family Malpighiaceae. It is commonly used as an ingredient of ayahuasca, a decoction with a long history of its entheogenic use and holds status as a "plant teacher" among the Indigenous peoples of the Amazon rainforest.

summary: A colossal, swollen-trunked tree of the African savanna that stores thousands of litres of water in its spongy wood and lives for over 2,000 years. Its velvety pods hold a dry, tangy, vitamin-C-rich powdery pulp eaten across the continent.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal to Sudan, Ethiopia and south to South Africa; also the Arabian Peninsula; introduced in India, Madagascar and the Caribbean
abilities: Trunks store water and swell in the wet season; elephants gouge them for moisture
The oldest dated individual, Panke in Zimbabwe, was about 2,500 years old when it died in 2011
Large white flowers open at night and are pollinated by fruit bats
Bark regrows after stripping, so it can be harvested for fibre repeatedly
edibleParts: young leaves (fresh or dried as 'lalo' or 'kuka' soup thickener)
edibilityNote: Pulp, leaves and roasted seeds are widely eaten. Raw seeds contain antinutrients and are usually roasted or fermented.

uses.use: Fruit pulp mixed with water for diarrhoea and fever; leaves for kidney and bladder ailments
Bark decoction used as a substitute for quinine against fever

medicinal.cautions: Seed oil contains cyclopropenoid fatty acids; usually refined before use.

fruit.season: Dry season (pods ripen months after the wet-season flowering)
fruit.description: Hanging, oval to oblong pod 15–25 cm with a hard, velvety greenish-grey to brown shell; inside, chalky cream-white pulp in dry chunks around seeds and reddish fibres.

seed.description: Hard, kidney-shaped, dark brown to black seeds about 1–1.5 cm, embedded in powdery white pulp
seed.dispersal: Baboons, elephants and other mammals; also water
seed.germination: Very hard coat: soak in hot water or nick, then soak 24 hours; sow at 25–30 °C; 1–4 weeks

grow.soil: Sandy or rocky, very well-drained, pH 6–8
grow.timeToHarvest: 8–23 years from seed; grafted trees in as little as 4–5 years
steps: Scarify seeds, soak, and sow in deep pots to accommodate the taproot.
Plant out in full sun in deep, free-draining soil, with lots of space — trunks can reach 10 m across.
Water young trees only in the dry season; protect from goats and cattle.
Harvest young leaves for cooking regularly without harming the tree; in bonsai or pots, keep dry in winter.
Gather fallen ripe pods, crack the shell and sieve the dry pulp to separate seeds and fibres.

lore: In many African traditions the baobab was planted upside down by a god, its roots in the air, and in Senegal griots were once buried inside hollow baobab trunks. Hollow baobabs have served as stores, shelters and even a prison near Derby in Western Australia (the related boab).
funFact: Between 2005 and 2017, nine of the 13 oldest known African baobabs died or lost their oldest parts, a collapse scientists suspect is linked to climate change.

wiki.extract: Adansonia digitata, the African baobab, is the most widespread tree species of the genus Adansonia, the baobabs, and is native to the African continent and the southern Arabian Peninsula. These are long-lived pachycauls; radiocarbon dating has shown at least one individual to be 1,275 years old. They are typically found in dry, hot savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, where they dominate the landscape and reveal the presence of a watercourse from afar. They have traditionally been valued as sources of food, water, health remedies or places of shelter and are a key food source for many animals. They are steeped in legend and superstition. In recent years, many of the largest, oldest trees have died, for unknown reasons. Other common names for the baobab include monkey-bread tree, upside-down tree, and cream of tartar tree.

Published in Prospero Alpini's 'De plantis Aegypti liber' in 1592, it represents one of the earliest European scientific depictions of this iconic African tree.

summary: A velvety, pale-pink mallow of salt marshes whose roots are so full of slime that they soothe sore throats. The original marshmallow sweet was made from them.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; especially coastal salt marshes and damp ground
abilities: Roots are rich in mucilage, which coats and soothes mucous membranes
Tolerates brackish, salt-influenced soils
Velvety hairs cover the whole plant
edibilityNote: All parts are edible; roots were boiled and fried, and leaves eaten as a pot herb. Wild populations are scarce in some countries, so use cultivated plants.

uses.use: Cold root infusion and syrup for dry cough, sore throat and gastritis; poultices for inflamed skin
Khatmi root and seed as a demulcent for cough, urinary burning and in softening poultices
EMA traditional-use monograph for dry cough and mouth/throat irritation

medicinal.cautions: The mucilage may slow the absorption of other medicines, so take them an hour apart. May lower blood sugar.

fruit.description: Flat ring of nutlets like a small round cheese.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, brown seeds
seed.germination: Benefits from cold stratification; 2–3 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.soil: Moist, rich; tolerates heavy and slightly saline soil
steps: Sow in spring after chilling the seed in the fridge for 3–4 weeks
Plant 60 cm apart in moist soil
Harvest leaves before flowering
Dig roots in autumn of year 2, peel and dry

lore: Theophrastus and Dioscorides recommended althaia, from the Greek althein, 'to heal'. In 19th-century France, confectioners whipped the root mucilage with sugar and egg white into pâte de guimauve; gelatine later replaced the root.
funFact: Today's marshmallows contain no marshmallow: gelatine replaced the root in the late 19th century.

wiki.extract: Althaea officinalis, the marsh mallow or marshmallow, is a species of flowering plant indigenous to Europe, Western Asia and North Africa, which is used in herbalism and as an ornamental plant.

summary: A towering Southeast Asian rainforest tree famous for spiky fruit with a smell banned on many trains and hotels, yet a custardy flesh revered as the 'king of fruits'. Its flowers open at dusk and are pollinated mainly by fruit bats.
nativeRange: Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula; cultivated across Southeast Asia
abilities: Pollinated chiefly by nectar bats such as the cave nectar bat (Eonycteris spelaea)
Odour comes from dozens of volatile sulphur compounds and esters
Trees grow 25–50 m tall in the wild
Ripe fruit falls from the tree on its own — it is gathered from the ground
edibilityNote: Flesh and cooked seeds are eaten; raw seeds are not. Traditional belief, with some lab support, warns against combining durian with alcohol, as it may inhibit alcohol breakdown.

uses.use: Leaf and root decoctions given for fever and jaundice
Considered a 'heating' food, balanced by eating 'cooling' mangosteen

medicinal.cautions: Avoid with alcohol. High in sugar and calories.

fruit.season: Varies; main seasons June–August in Malaysia and Thailand
fruit.description: Oval to round fruit 15–30 cm and 1–3 kg, covered in hard pyramidal thorns, green to brown; splits into five sections with creamy yellow, custard-like arils that smell strongly of onion, cheese and fruit.

seed.description: Glossy, chestnut-brown, oval to kidney-shaped seeds 2–4 cm long, enclosed in the soft aril; 1–7 per section
seed.dispersal: Orangutans, elephants, tigers, bears and other large mammals
seed.germination: Recalcitrant — sow fresh within days, 1–2 cm deep, at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–3 weeks

grow.sun: Full sun when mature; shade for young plants
grow.water: High, with a short dry spell to trigger flowering
grow.propagation: Grafting (cleft, approach) of named cultivars such as 'Musang King' or 'Monthong' onto seedling rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 4–6 years from graft; 8–15 years from seed
steps: Buy a grafted tree of a named clone; plant 8–10 m apart in deep soil with excellent drainage, as durian is prone to Phytophthora root rot.
Shade young trees for the first 1–2 years and keep the soil mulched and moist.
Feed regularly with compost and balanced fertiliser; plant other durian clones nearby for better cross-pollination.
Prune to a single leader with well-spaced lateral branches for fruit to hang on.
Collect fruit as it falls (or tie fruit to branches with nets), and eat within 2–3 days.

lore: Naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating durian was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East'. Singapore's Esplanade concert hall is nicknamed 'the Durian' for its spiky roof.
funFact: Durian is banned on Singapore's metro trains, where signs show it alongside smoking and flammable goods.

The scene illustrates the European fascination with the exotic flora and customs of the East, blending botanical observation with ethnographic curiosity through the depiction of local dress and a distant pagoda.

Engraved by Johannes Baptista van Doetechum, these images were crucial in shaping the European imagination of the 'Orient' and served as a practical guide for Dutch merchants and explorers.

summary: The source of about 90% of the world's cotton. Each fibre is a single seed-coat cell that can grow to about 3 cm long. Domesticated in Mesoamerica thousands of years ago, it became the crop at the centre of the Industrial Revolution and the transatlantic slave economy.
nativeRange: Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean (wild forms on coasts); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Grows single-celled seed hairs up to about 3 cm long, the cotton fibre
Is an allotetraploid that combines two ancient genomes, one from Africa/Asia and one from the Americas, which merged 1–2 million years ago
Defends itself with gossypol-filled glands visible as black dots on leaves and seeds
Feeds ants and other insects with extrafloral nectaries on leaves and bracts
edibilityNote: Refined cottonseed oil is widely eaten. Raw seeds contain gossypol, which is toxic, can damage the liver and reduce fertility, and is especially harmful to pigs, poultry and young animals. A low-gossypol cotton variety (TAM 66274) was cleared by US regulators in 2018–2019 for food use.

uses.tradition: Traditional medicine in the American South
uses.use: Root bark used to bring on menstruation or abortion, including by enslaved women
Gossypol tested in thousands of men as a male contraceptive; abandoned due to permanent infertility and low potassium

medicinal.cautions: Gossypol is toxic; root bark preparations may cause miscarriage.

fruit.description: Green bolls that split into three to five sections to release fluffy white lint around seeds.

seed.description: Dark seeds covered in long lint and short fuzz
seed.dispersal: Wind and water for wild forms; humans for crops
seed.germination: Sow 2–3 cm deep in soil above 18 °C; 1–2 weeks

grow.zones: Annual in USDA 7–11; perennial in frost-free areas
steps: Sow after soil warms in late spring
Thin to 15–30 cm apart in full sun
Water through flowering and boll set
Pick lint from open bolls in dry weather

lore: Cotton textiles in Mexico's Tehuacán Valley date back thousands of years, and the Aztecs collected cotton cloth as tribute. Eli Whitney's 1793 cotton gin made upland cotton hugely profitable, fuelling the expansion of slavery in the American South.
funFact: A cotton seed sprouted on the far side of the Moon aboard China's Chang'e 4 lander in 2019, the first plant to grow there, though it died soon after.

wiki.extract: Gossypium hirsutum, also known as upland cotton or Mexican cotton, is the most widely planted species of cotton in the world. Globally, about 90% of all cotton production is of cultivars derived from this species. In the United States, the world's largest exporter of cotton, it constitutes approximately 95% of all cotton production. It is native from Mexico to Ecuador and northeast Brazil, the Leeward Antilles in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

summary: A small understorey tree of the Amazon whose seeds become chocolate. Its tiny flowers sprout directly from the trunk and are pollinated almost entirely by minute midges, and Mesoamerican peoples prized its beans so highly they used them as money.
nativeRange: Upper Amazon basin (Ecuador, Peru, Colombia, Brazil); domesticated in Mesoamerica and South America; grown across the humid tropics
abilities: Cauliflorous: flowers and pods grow straight from the trunk and old branches
Pollinated by biting midges (Forcipomyia) only a few millimetres long
Thrives in deep shade beneath taller rainforest trees
Seeds contain theobromine, a stimulant toxic to dogs
edibleParts: seeds (fermented, dried and roasted for cocoa and chocolate)
edibilityNote: Beans and the sweet white pulp are safe for people. Theobromine makes chocolate dangerous to dogs, cats and horses.

uses.use: Cacao drinks mixed with herbs for fatigue, fever and digestive complaints, recorded in the Florentine Codex
Cocoa flavanols studied for improving blood-vessel function and lowering blood pressure

medicinal.cautions: Toxic to dogs and cats. Stimulant effects can cause palpitations or migraine in sensitive people.

fruit.description: Ridged, rugby-ball-shaped pod 15–30 cm long, green or red maturing to yellow, orange or purple, with a thick husk around 20–60 seeds in sweet-tart white pulp.

seed.description: Almond-shaped, flattened oval beans 2–3 cm long, purple to ivory-white inside (white in rare criollo types), coated in slippery white pulp
seed.dispersal: Monkeys, squirrels and bats crack pods to eat the pulp and discard seeds
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow within a week of opening the pod, 1 cm deep, at 25–30 °C in humid shade; sprouts in 1–2 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade (30–50%); young plants need shade
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting / rooted cuttings of selected clones
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years to first pods; pods ripen 5–6 months after pollination
steps: Sow fresh seed in deep bags under shade, or buy grafted plants of a productive, disease-tolerant clone.
Plant out under temporary shade (banana, plantain) and permanent shade trees (e.g. Gliricidia, Inga) about 3 m apart.
Mulch heavily with leaf litter, which also breeds the pollinating midges; keep soil moist.
Prune to a single trunk with a 'jorquette' of 3–5 main branches and remove diseased pods promptly against black pod and frosty pod rot.
Cut ripe pods with a knife, scoop beans and pulp, ferment in covered heaps or boxes for 5–7 days, then sun-dry before roasting.

lore: Residues on pottery at Santa Ana-La Florida in Ecuador show cacao was used about 5,300 years ago, and the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II is said to have drunk chocolate from golden cups. Linnaeus named the genus Theobroma, 'food of the gods'.
funFact: In the Aztec market, a turkey hen cost about 100 cacao beans and a tomato one bean — and counterfeiters filled empty bean husks with mud.

wiki.extract: Theobroma cacao is a small evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family. Its seeds—cocoa beans when dried and fermented—are used to make chocolate liquor, cocoa powder, cocoa butter and chocolate. Although the tree is native to the tropics of the Americas, the largest producer of cocoa beans in 2022 was Côte d'Ivoire.

summary: A fast-growing, drought-hardy evergreen of the Indian subcontinent, known in Sanskrit as sarva roga nivarini, 'healer of all ailments'. Its seeds yield azadirachtin, one of the most powerful natural insect deterrents known.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and drier parts of mainland Southeast Asia; widely planted across Africa, the Middle East, Australia and the Americas
abilities: Seeds contain azadirachtin, which stops many insects feeding and disrupts their moulting, at very low doses
Survives on as little as 400–1,200 mm of rain a year and puts down a deep taproot
Grows quickly on degraded, stony and alkaline soils; widely planted to hold back the Sahel
Stays in leaf through the dry season and casts dense shade
edibilityNote: Tender leaves and flowers are eaten in small amounts in South Asian dishes, such as Bengali neem-begun and the Ugadi pachadi of South India. Neem seed oil is toxic if swallowed and has caused fatal encephalopathy and liver failure in infants. Never give neem oil by mouth.

uses.use: Bitter leaves and bark for skin diseases, fever, intestinal worms and blood purification; twigs used as a chewing stick (datun) for teeth
Leaves and bark used as a blood purifier and antiseptic for boils, eczema and wounds
Dogonyaro leaf and bark decoctions widely used against fever and malaria
Leaf paste and oil applied for skin infections, smallpox and chickenpox care

medicinal.cautions: Seed oil is poisonous by mouth, especially to children, and can cause vomiting, seizures, metabolic acidosis and death. Leaf extracts have antifertility effects in animals, so avoid during pregnancy or when trying to conceive. Not proven to treat malaria.

fruit.season: Early to mid summer (June–August in India)
fruit.description: Olive-like, 1.5–2 cm, ripening yellow with thin sweetish pulp around one hard seed.

seed.description: Single oily kernel inside a hard shell
seed.dispersal: Birds and bats eat the fruit
seed.germination: Fresh seed only, as viability falls within weeks; 1–3 weeks at 25–35 °C

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; tolerates poor, stony and alkaline ground; dislikes waterlogging
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves within a year; fruit from 3–5 years
steps: Sow freshly cleaned seed within days of collection
Transplant seedlings at 3–4 months into a sunny, frost-free site
Water through the first dry season only
Prune to shape, as it tolerates heavy lopping

lore: Neem is worshipped in many Indian villages as an embodiment of the goddess Shitala or Mariamman, and its leaves are hung over doorways at Gudi Padwa and Ugadi. The Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita both prescribe nimba for skin disease.
funFact: In 2000 the European Patent Office revoked a patent on a neem-based fungicide, finding that its use had long been known in India. The case became a landmark in fights over 'biopiracy'.

wiki.extract: Azadirachta indica, commonly known as neem, margosa, nimtree or Indian lilac, is a tree in the Mahogany family Meliaceae. It is one of the two species in the genus Azadirachta. It is native to the Indian subcontinent and to parts of Southeast Asia, but is naturalized and grown around the world in tropical and subtropical areas. Its fruits and seeds are the source of neem oil. Nim is a Hindustani noun derived from Sanskrit nimba (निंब).

The illustration serves as a visual companion to the Dutch text, which describes the tree's physical characteristics and its cultivation in local pleasure gardens. Such woodcuts were

summary: The 'true' mahogany of fine furniture, whose deep-red, stable wood made it one of the most valuable timbers of the Americas. Heavy logging ran ahead of the law, and it was listed on CITES Appendix II in 2003. Its fruit capsules point skyward and split open to release winged seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin (Bolivia, Brazil, Peru)
abilities: Produces dense, stable, rot-resistant red-brown heartwood
Its upright capsules split into five valves and release winged seeds that spin away on the wind
Grows into a forest giant over 40 m tall with buttressed trunks
Regenerates best after large disturbances such as floods, fires or hurricanes
edibilityNote: Not a food. Seeds are very bitter and used only medicinally; high doses have been linked to liver injury.

uses.use: Seeds taken for diabetes and high blood pressure
Bark decoctions for fever and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Seed preparations have caused liver toxicity in case reports; they may add to the effect of diabetes drugs.

fruit.description: Upright, pear-shaped brown capsules 12–20 cm long that split from the base.

seed.description: Flat seeds with a long brown wing
seed.germination: Sow fresh (short viability); 2–4 weeks in warmth

steps: Sow fresh seed with the wing pointing up, barely covered
Keep in partial shade in the nursery
Plant out in mixed stands: monocultures are attacked by the mahogany shoot borer (Hypsipyla)
Prune to a single leader

lore: Mahogany furniture became a status symbol in 18th-century Britain, and Chippendale's designs relied on Caribbean and Central American mahogany cut and shipped largely by enslaved and forced labour. Illegal logging of mogno in the Brazilian Amazon was a major conservation scandal of the 1990s.
funFact: In Malaysia the seed is called 'sky fruit' because its capsules point straight up at the sky.

wiki.extract: Swietenia macrophylla, commonly known as mahogany, Honduran mahogany, Honduras mahogany, or big-leaf mahogany is a species of plant in the Meliaceae family. It is one of three species in genus Swietenia that yield genuine mahogany timber, the others being Swietenia mahagoni and Swietenia humilis. It is native to South America, Mexico and Central America, but naturalized in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia and Hawaii, and cultivated in plantations and wind-breaks elsewhere.

summary: A heart-leaved climbing vine that drapes trees across India, sending down thread-like aerial roots. Its Sanskrit name Amrita, 'nectar of immortality', reflects its toughness, and its popularity as an immune booster during COVID-19 brought both fame and safety warnings.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar
abilities: Cut stem pieces can survive for long periods and resprout, even when hung up to dry
Sends long, thread-like aerial roots down from the canopy to the ground
Stems contain clerodane diterpenes, alkaloids such as berberine and magnoflorine, and polysaccharides studied as immune modulators
edibilityNote: Not a food. The stem is used as medicine (juice, decoction, starch 'guduchi satva').

uses.use: Guduchi as a rasayana for chronic fevers, gout, skin disease, jaundice and diabetes; the starch (satva) for burning sensations
Gilo for fevers, jaundice and as a blood purifier
Seendhil for fevers, diabetes and as a general tonic

medicinal.cautions: In 2020–21, Indian hepatologists reported cases of serious autoimmune-like liver injury after giloy use. India's AYUSH ministry suggested the culprit was the related Tinospora crispa, but investigators linked the injury to T. cordifolia itself, which is now among the most reported causes of herb-induced liver injury in India. May lower blood sugar and stimulate the immune system, so take care with diabetes, autoimmune disease or immunosuppressant drugs. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Pea-sized, glossy red drupes in clusters.

seed.description: Curved, single seed in each drupe
seed.germination: Erratic; stem cuttings are far more reliable

steps: Plant 20–30 cm stem cuttings at the start of the rains
Give a tree, fence or trellis to climb (traditionally neem, considered best)
Water until established
Cut mature stems thicker than a finger, leaving the plant to regrow

lore: Hindu legend tells that guduchi sprang from drops of amrita that fell to earth when Indra revived the fallen monkeys of Rama's army. Ayurvedic texts hold guduchi grown on a neem tree to be the most potent.
funFact: A cut length of giloy stem left to hang on a fence can still put out fresh shoots and aerial roots, which is why it is called 'the one that never dies'.

wiki.extract: Tinospora cordifolia, guruchi, guduchi, amrita, or the heart-leaved moonseed, is a herbaceous vine of the family Menispermaceae native to South and Southeast Asia. It has been used in Ayurveda in an attempt to treat various disorders.

summary: A Pacific staple domesticated from wild breadnut in New Guinea and carried by Polynesian voyagers across the ocean. Roasted, its starchy fruit tastes like fresh bread or potato, and one tree can feed a family for decades.
nativeRange: Domesticated from Artocarpus camansi in New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago; spread by humans across Oceania; now pantropical
abilities: Seedless Polynesian varieties survive only by human propagation from root cuttings
A mature tree can produce 150–200 fruit a season
Fruit can be fermented in pits and kept for months or years as emergency food
Latex used as caulking for canoes and as birdlime
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten cooked at the mature-starchy stage, or soft and sweet when fully ripe. Sticky latex is irritating.

uses.use: Latex applied to skin injuries, and diluted for diarrhoea
Yellowing leaf tea for high blood pressure

medicinal.cautions: Latex can irritate skin and eyes.

fruit.season: Main and secondary seasons; often almost year-round in the tropics
fruit.description: Round to oval fruit 10–30 cm and 1–5 kg, bright green with a patterned skin of hexagonal facets, turning yellow-brown; cream-white starchy flesh.

seed.description: Seedless in most Polynesian cultivars; seeded types hold brown, rounded to angular seeds about 1.5–2.5 cm, with a thin papery coat
seed.dispersal: Humans (root cuttings); bats for seeded forms
seed.germination: Seeds are recalcitrant and short-lived; most cultivars are propagated from root suckers

grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained; tolerates coral sands and slight salinity in some varieties
grow.propagation: Root cuttings or suckers; air layering; tissue culture
steps: Dig a 2–3 cm-thick section of surface root, cut into 20–25 cm lengths and lay in moist sand in shade until shoots appear (2–5 months).
Plant out in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot 10–12 m from other trees when shoots are 50–60 cm.
Mulch thickly and water during dry spells; protect from strong wind.
Prune to keep the tree under about 6 m for easy picking.
Harvest when small drops of latex appear on the skin; cook within 1–2 days, as fruit spoils quickly.

lore: William Bligh's 1789 voyage on HMS Bounty to carry breadfruit from Tahiti to the Caribbean as cheap food for enslaved people ended in the famous mutiny; he succeeded on a second voyage in 1793. In Hawaiian tradition the god Kū became a breadfruit tree to save his starving family.
funFact: Breadfruit was carried by Polynesian navigators across more than 10,000 km of open ocean as living root cuttings.

wiki.extract: Breadfruit is a species of flowering tree in the mulberry and jackfruit family Moraceae. Its name is derived from the texture of the moderately ripe fruit when cooked, similar to freshly baked bread and having a potato-like flavor.

summary: Jackfruit bears the largest tree-borne fruit in the world, up to 50 kg and nearly a metre long, hanging straight from the trunk. It is the national fruit of Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, eaten ripe as a sweet fruit and green as a meaty vegetable.
nativeRange: Western Ghats of south-west India; cultivated throughout South and Southeast Asia, East Africa, Brazil and the Caribbean
abilities: Produces the largest fruit borne by any tree, up to about 50 kg
Cauliflorous: fruit grows on the trunk and main limbs, which can bear the weight
A single tree can yield 100–200 fruit a year
Heartwood yields a saffron-yellow dye used for Buddhist monks' robes
edibleParts: unripe fruit (cooked as a vegetable or meat substitute)
edibilityNote: All main parts are eaten. Sticky white latex in the rind and core is not poisonous but is very gluey; oil hands and knives before cutting. Raw seeds contain trypsin inhibitors and should be cooked.

uses.use: Ripe fruit as a cooling, nourishing tonic; leaf ash applied to ulcers
Leaf decoction used for diabetes, with small studies on blood-sugar effects

medicinal.cautions: Latex allergy cross-reactions; birch-pollen allergy cross-reactivity reported.

fruit.description: Huge oblong fruit 30–90 cm, green to yellow-brown, covered in blunt hexagonal spines; inside, dozens of golden, sweet, fibrous bulbs among stringy 'rags', smelling of banana and pineapple.

seed.description: Smooth, light-brown, oval to kidney-shaped seeds 2–4 cm long, each inside a fleshy bulb and covered by a thin white membrane; up to several hundred per fruit
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh within a month, 2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–6 weeks. Taproot dislikes transplanting

grow.water: Moderate–high; tolerates a dry season but not waterlogging
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam or sandy soil, pH 5–7.5
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from graft; 4–8 years from seed
steps: Plant a grafted tree or sow fresh seed directly where it will grow (8–10 m from buildings).
Water well for the first two years and mulch heavily; feed young trees with compost every few months.
Prune early to keep the tree low (4–6 m) and open, so fruit forms within reach on the trunk.
Thin to one or two fruit per cluster; tie heavy fruit with cloth slings if branches are weak.
Harvest when the spines flatten slightly, the fruit sounds hollow when tapped and it gives off a sweet smell; for vegetable use, pick young and green.

lore: Pliny the Elder, drawing on reports from Alexander's campaigns, described a huge Indian fruit eaten by sages that some identify as jackfruit (others as the banana), and it figures in the ancient Tamil 'mukkani' (three fruits) of mango, banana and jackfruit. Its wood is prized for temple furniture and veena lutes in South India.
funFact: The heaviest jackfruit on record, verified by Guinness World Records, weighed 42.72 kg and was grown in Hawaii in 2003.

wiki.extract: The jackfruit or jakfruit is a fruit tree in the mulberry family of Moraceae. Native to India, the species was first described under the name Artocarpus heterophyllus in Encyclopédie Méthodique, Botanique in 1789 by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, based on a specimen collected by botanist Philibert Commerson.

summary: A tree that becomes a forest. Banyans drop aerial roots from their branches that thicken into new trunks, so one individual can spread across more than a hectare. India's national tree, it has shaded village councils, markets and teachers for millennia.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent; planted across the tropics
abilities: Turns hanging aerial roots into pillar trunks, letting a single tree expand indefinitely
Often starts life as an epiphyte from a bird-dropped seed, then strangles and replaces its host
Thimmamma Marrimanu in Andhra Pradesh covers about 1.9 hectares from a single tree
Fruits year-round in many places, feeding birds, bats and monkeys when little else is fruiting
Relies on a single fig-wasp species, Eupristina masoni, for pollination
edibilityNote: Ripe figs are edible but bland and often contain fig wasps. The milky latex irritates skin and eyes.

uses.use: Bark and aerial roots (vata) used as astringents for diarrhoea and in preparations for diabetes
Latex applied to cracked heels, sores and toothache

medicinal.cautions: Latex is a skin and eye irritant and can cause allergy in people sensitive to Ficus or latex.

fruit.description: Paired, cherry-sized figs that ripen scarlet, borne in leaf axils.

seed.description: Tiny achenes inside the fig
seed.dispersal: Birds, bats and monkeys; seeds often germinate in tree crowns or walls
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist mix, warm and bright; 2–4 weeks

steps: Root a semi-ripe cutting or air-layer a branch in warm, humid conditions
Plant far from buildings, drains and walls
Guide young aerial roots into the ground (in pipes of soil if needed) to form pillars
Indoors it can be kept as a pot plant or bonsai

lore: The banyan is the tree of the Hindu fast Vat Purnima, when married women tie threads around it in memory of Savitri, who won back her husband's life from Yama. The English word comes from 'banias', the Hindu merchants Portuguese and English traders saw trading under its shade.
funFact: The Great Banyan in Howrah's botanic garden lost its main trunk to fungal rot in 1925 yet still stands as a ring of more than 3,000 aerial-root trunks.

wiki.extract: Ficus benghalensis, Ficus indica, or Ficus audrey commonly known as banyan, banyan fig, audrey fig and Indian banyan, is a tree native to the Indian subcontinent. The countries where it originated include Sri Lanka, Nepal, Pakistan, India, and East Himalaya. Specimens in India are among the largest trees in the world by canopy coverage. It is also known as a "strangler fig" because like many other trees in the genus Ficus it starts out as epiphyte, that is, leaning on another tree that it ends up enveloping.
