summary: The fig may be the first plant humans domesticated: parthenocarpic figs found at Gilgal in the Jordan Valley date to about 11,400 years ago, before wheat. Its 'fruit' is actually an inverted flower cluster, a syconium, with hundreds of tiny flowers lining the inside.
nativeRange: South-west Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; widely cultivated in warm-temperate regions
abilities: Wild figs depend on a tiny wasp, Blastophaga psenes, which breeds inside the fig and pollinates it
Common figs (e.g. 'Brown Turkey') set fruit without pollination
Roots seek water aggressively and can crack walls and pipes
Thrives in poor, rocky, dry soil and grows out of cliff faces and ruins
edibleParts: leaves (as wrappers; used to infuse flavour)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe. The milky latex of leaves and stems contains furanocoumarins that cause blistering burns when skin is exposed to sunlight (phytophotodermatitis).

uses.use: Dried figs as a laxative and for coughs and chest complaints
A poultice of figs laid on King Hezekiah's boil (2 Kings 20:7)
Fresh latex dabbed on warts

medicinal.cautions: Latex causes phytophotodermatitis and is a strong irritant; avoid latex in eyes. May contain natural rubber allergens.

fruit.season: Early summer (breba crop) and late summer to autumn (main crop)
fruit.description: Pear-shaped, 3–8 cm, skin green, purple or nearly black; inside, soft honey-sweet pink to red flesh packed with tiny crunchy achenes.

seed.description: Tiny, round to lens-shaped, yellow-tan 'seeds' (actually achenes), about 1–1.5 mm, hundreds per fig; in unpollinated common figs they are hollow and sterile
seed.germination: Only fertile (wasp-pollinated) seed sprouts; surface-sow on moist mix at 20–25 °C, 1–3 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 7–11 (to 6 with winter protection; dies back but resprouts)
grow.sun: Full sun, ideally against a warm wall
grow.water: Low–moderate once established; even moisture while fruit swells prevents splitting
grow.soil: Any well-drained soil, including poor, rocky, or chalky; pH 6–8
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings 20–30 cm taken in winter root very easily; also air layering and suckers
steps: Choose a self-fertile common fig variety (e.g. 'Brown Turkey', 'Chicago Hardy' for cold areas).
Plant against a sunny south- or west-facing wall; in rich soil, restrict roots in a box or large pot to encourage fruiting rather than leaves.
Water through dry summers once fruits form; avoid heavy nitrogen feeding.
In cold regions, wrap or mulch heavily in winter; prune in late winter to remove crowded and frost-damaged shoots.
Pick when figs droop on their stalks, soften and a drop of nectar appears at the eye; wear gloves against latex.

lore: In Genesis, Adam and Eve sew fig leaves to cover themselves, and Romulus and Remus were said to have been suckled by the she-wolf beneath the Ficus Ruminalis in Rome. The Buddha's Bodhi tree is a related fig, Ficus religiosa.
funFact: Gilgal figs, about 11,400 years old, came from a seedless mutant that could only survive by people planting cuttings — evidence of deliberate cultivation.

wiki.extract: The fig is the edible fruit of Ficus carica, a species of tree or shrub in the flowering plant family Moraceae, native to the Mediterranean region, and to western and southern Asia. It has been cultivated since ancient times and is now widely grown throughout the world. Ficus carica is the type species of the genus Ficus, which comprises over 800 tropical and subtropical plant species.

plates.title: Christoph Jakob Trew — Uitgezochte planten (1771)
plates.author: Christoph Jakob Trew
plates.desc: Hand-colored botanical engraving of a Ficus branch with large ovate leaves and small reddish fruits, including anatomical details of the fruit at the bottom.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a species of fig (Ficus), characterized by its large, smooth-edged leaves and small, reddish fruits. Produced for Christoph Jakob Trew's 'Uitgezochte planten' (1771), it exemplifies the precision and artistry of 18th-century botanical science, providing both a lifelike representation and detailed anatomical views of the plant's reproductive structures.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a botanical specimen, identified as Ficus lupi or Arbutus unedo.
plates.long: A botanical woodcut depicts a plant with a curved, thick root and a cluster of green leaves bearing five round, orange-yellow fruits. The text identifies it as 'Ficus lupi' or 'Comarus', likely referring to the strawberry tree (Arbutus unedo).

summary: The tree under which Siddhartha Gautama is said to have attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. Its heart-shaped leaves end in a long 'drip tip' that sheds rain, and they tremble in the slightest breeze. A cutting planted in Sri Lanka in 288 BCE is still alive.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and Indochina; planted at temples across Asia
abilities: Leaves taper into a long drip tip that channels rain off the leaf
Germinates on walls, temples and other trees and pries masonry apart with its roots
Pollinated only by its own fig wasp, Platyscapa quadraticeps
Lives for many centuries; the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi has a documented history of more than 2,300 years
edibleParts: young leaves and shoots (cooked, famine food)
edibilityNote: Small figs are eaten but usually contain fig wasps. The latex is an irritant.

uses.use: Bark decoction for skin problems, wounds and diarrhoea; fruit for asthma
Bark and latex for inflammation and gum problems

medicinal.cautions: Latex can irritate skin and eyes and cause allergy.

fruit.description: Pea-sized paired figs that ripen dark purple.

seed.description: Minute achenes within the fig
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist mix in warmth and light

steps: Root a cutting or air-layer in warm, humid conditions
Pot on in free-draining mix in bright light
Plant away from walls and foundations, which its roots crack
In cool climates grow as a large houseplant or bonsai

lore: Emperor Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta is said to have carried a cutting of the Bodh Gaya tree to Anuradhapura, where King Devanampiya Tissa planted it in 288 BCE; it is often called the oldest human-planted tree with a recorded planting date. Hindus circle the peepal and tie threads around it; it is the ashvattha of the Bhagavad Gita (15.1), the cosmic tree with roots above and branches below.
funFact: The tree at Bodh Gaya today is traditionally said to descend from the one in Sri Lanka, so the Sri Lankan tree is in effect the 'parent' of its own ancestor's replacement.

wiki.extract: Ficus religiosa or sacred fig is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to the fig and mulberry family Moraceae. It is also known as the bodhi tree, bo tree, peepul tree, peepal tree, pipala tree or ashvattha tree. The sacred fig is considered to have religious significance in four major religions that originated on the Indian subcontinent: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism. Hindu and Jain ascetics consider the species to be sacred and often meditate under it. Gautama Buddha is believed to have attained enlightenment under a tree of this species. The sacred fig is the state tree of the Indian states of Odisha, Bihar and Haryana.

As a landmark in Chinese botanical literature, this work combined traditional knowledge with meticulous observation, represented here through fine woodblock printing. The image captures both the botanical details o

plates.title: Hindu Mythology, Vedic and Puranic
plates.author: W.J. Wilkins
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of Pipal leaves on a branch.
plates.long: This engraving depicts leaves from the Pipal tree (Ficus religiosa), a species of great sacred significance in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The illustration captures the characteristic heart-shaped leaves with their long, tapering tips, often associated with the tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment and a symbol of eternal life in Vedic texts.

plates.title: Garden of Malabar, Vol. 1
plates.author: Hendrik van Rheede
plates.desc: Botanical engraving of a branch with leaves and small fruits, identified as 'Arealu'.
plates.long: This detailed engraving from Hendrik van Rheede’s monumental 'Hortus Indicus Malabaricus' depicts a branch of the Arealu (Sacred Fig, Ficus religiosa). The plate is notable for its scientific precision and the inclusion of the plant's name in Latin, Malayalam, Arabic, and Brahmi scripts, reflecting the collaborative effort between European and local Indian scholars.

summary: The tree that built the Silk Road: its leaves are the only food of the domestic silkworm, and China guarded sericulture as a state secret for millennia. Its catkins also fling pollen at over half the speed of sound, one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.
nativeRange: Northern and central China; cultivated and naturalised across Asia, Europe and the Americas
abilities: Stamens spring open like catapults in under 25 microseconds, flinging pollen at more than half the speed of sound
Leaves are the sole natural food of the silkworm Bombyx mori
Fruit colour varies from white to pink to near-black despite the name 'white'
Tolerates drought, pollution and poor soil; often invasive
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe; unripe fruit and the milky sap can cause stomach upset and mild hallucinogenic effects have been claimed for unripe fruit.

uses.use: Leaf (sāng yè) for colds and sore eyes, root bark (sāng bái pí) for cough, fruit (sāng shèn) as a blood tonic
Leaf extract containing 1-deoxynojirimycin studied for lowering post-meal blood sugar

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extract may lower blood sugar; caution with diabetes medication. Pollen is allergenic.

fruit.description: Blackberry-like cluster 1–2.5 cm long, white, pink, purple or black; very sweet and mild, staining if dark.

seed.description: Minute, pale-brown, lens-shaped seeds about 2 mm, one inside each tiny drupelet
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks, then surface-sow lightly covered at 20–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings in winter, softwood cuttings in summer, grafting; seed
steps: Take 20–30 cm hardwood cuttings from a good fruiting tree in winter and root them in moist soil, or buy a named variety (fruitless male clones are sold for shade — avoid those if you want fruit).
Plant away from paths and parking, as dark fruit stains everything.
Water young trees in dry spells; established trees need little care.
Prune in winter to shape; for silkworm leaf production, pollard annually.
Shake ripe fruit onto a sheet spread beneath the tree; eat or freeze promptly.

lore: Chinese legend credits Empress Leizu with discovering silk around 2700 BCE when a cocoon fell into her tea beneath a mulberry tree. In 552 CE two monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople in hollow canes, breaking China's monopoly.
funFact: The white mulberry's pollen-launching stamens move at roughly half the speed of sound — among the fastest motions known in plants.

wiki.extract: Morus alba, known as white mulberry, common mulberry and silkworm mulberry, is a fast-growing, small to medium-sized mulberry tree which grows to 10–20 m (33–66 ft) tall. It is native to China and is widely cultivated and naturalized elsewhere. The species is widely cultivated to feed the silkworms employed in the commercial production of silk. It is also notable for the rapid release of its pollen, which is launched at greater than half the speed of sound.

The use of vibrant green and brown pigments applied by hand highlights the spe

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts a mulberry plant, meticulously illustrating its serrated leaves and characteristic berry-like fruit clusters. Found within a medical treatise, such botanical illustrations served as vital visual aids for physicians and apothecaries to accurately identify plants used in the preparation of remedies.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the mulberry tree, a vital plant in Chinese history for its role in silk production (sericulture). The detailed rendering of the leaves and fruit served as a practical guide for cultivation in the late imperial period.

The fruit is depicted in varying shades of yellow and reddish-brown to indicate different stages of ripeness. plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts a mulberry plant (Morus), identifiable by its distinctively shaped leaves and dark berries. It appears in a late 15th-century herbal, where it would have served as a visual guide for identifying plants used in medicinal preparations.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a mulberry plant, illustrating the serrated leaves and berry clusters characteristic of the species. It appears in the 'Hortus sanitatis', one of the most important early printed herbals, which served as a comprehensive encyclopedia of the natural world and its medicinal uses.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a mulberry tree (Morus), illustrating its characteristic leaves and root structure. It appears in a 1552 edition of Dioscorides' seminal work on pharmacology, serving as a visual aid for identifying medicinal plants.

Such illustrations were essential in early modern herbals, like this commentary on Dioscorides, to aid in the accurate identification of medicinal plants for pharmacological use.

summary: A fast-growing, drought-hardy tree from the Himalayan foothills whose leaves, pods and flowers feed millions across the tropics. Its crushed seeds can clear muddy water.
nativeRange: Sub-Himalayan foothills of north-western India, Pakistan and Nepal; planted throughout the tropics
abilities: Can grow several metres in its first year from seed or cuttings
Seed proteins carry a positive charge that clumps suspended particles and bacteria, clarifying water
Leaves are rich in protein, vitamin A precursors, calcium and iron
Survives long dry seasons by shedding leaves and storing water in a swollen root
edibilityNote: Leaves, pods and flowers are widely eaten cooked. Root and root bark contain toxic alkaloids such as spirochin, and the root's horseradish taste has led to poisonings. Avoid root and bark, especially in pregnancy.

uses.use: Shigru bark, leaves and seeds for swellings, joint pain, worms, abscesses and as a pungent digestive
Sahajna and ben-seed oil applied for rheumatism and gout, and taken for liver and spleen enlargement
Zogale leaves used for malnutrition, fevers, diabetes and to increase breast milk
Malunggay leaves eaten in soup by nursing mothers in the Philippines to boost milk supply

medicinal.cautions: Most evidence comes from animal and small human studies. Root and bark are toxic and can cause miscarriage. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure, and may interact with thyroid, diabetes and blood-pressure drugs.

fruit.description: Long, ribbed, three-sided pod, 20–50 cm, eaten green as a vegetable ('drumstick').

seed.description: Round, dark-brown oily seeds with three papery wings
seed.germination: Fast; 5–12 days at 25–35 °C; no pre-treatment needed

grow.soil: Sandy or loamy, well-drained; hates waterlogging
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves from 2–3 months; pods from 6–12 months
steps: Sow seeds 2 cm deep in warm, well-drained soil
Plant out in full sun, protected from frost
Cut back the leader at 1–1.5 m to encourage a bushy, easy-to-pick tree
Harvest leaves continuously and pods while they snap cleanly

lore: The Sushruta and Charaka Samhitas list shigru among useful pungent herbs. Ben oil, pressed from the seeds, was traded to Europe where watchmakers prized it for lubricating fine mechanisms because it does not go rancid quickly.
funFact: In some trials a few crushed moringa seeds per litre cut the cloudiness of river water by over 90%.

wiki.extract: Moringa oleifera is a short-lived, fast-growing, drought-resistant tree of the family Moringaceae, native to northern India and used extensively in South and Southeast Asia. Common names include moringa, drumstick tree, horseradish tree, ben tree, or malunggay.

plates.author: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx
plates.desc: Detailed botanical illustration of a Moringa tree (Moringa oleifera) with compound leaves and white flowers.
plates.long: This plate from the Moninckx Atlas (1686) depicts the Moringa tree, identified in the text as 'Mouringo'. The illustration meticulously captures the plant's slender trunk, bipinnate leaves, and delicate white blossoms, serving as both a work of art and a scientific record of exotic flora studied in the Amsterdam Hortus Medicus.

plates.desc: Detailed botanical engraving of the Muringu plant (Moringa oleifera), showing its compound leaves, flowers, and seed pods.
plates.long: This intricate engraving from the 'Hortus Indicus Malabaricus' (1683) illustrates the Muringu tree, or Moringa oleifera, native to the Indian subcontinent. The plate provides a comprehensive view of the plant's morphology, including its delicate flowers and distinctive long pods, reflecting the era's burgeoning interest in global natural history and scientific classification.

plates.title: Herbarium Portatile, Oder Behendes Kräuter- und Gewächs-Buch: Darinn nicht allein 1363. so wol Einheimische als Außländndische Kräuter mit Lateinisch und Deutscher Benennung abgebildet, sondern auch die meisten, so in der Medicin gebräuchlich, kürtzlich erkläret werden

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut illustration of Glans unguentaria (1344)
plates.long: This illustration depicts the Glans unguentaria, or 'oil nut,' showing both the elongated pods and the seeds contained within. Such images were essential for the accurate preparation of medicinal oils and ointments in the 17th century.

summary: The banana plant is not a tree but the world's largest herb: its 'trunk' is a pseudostem of tightly rolled leaf sheaths. Wild Musa acuminata has fruit packed with hard seeds; the seedless sterile triploids we eat, like the 'Cavendish', are propagated only as clones.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia and Malesia to northern Australia; cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Pseudostem can grow to about 3–7 m in under a year, then dies after fruiting while suckers replace it
Cultivated triploids set fruit without pollination (parthenocarpy)
Wild forms are pollinated at night by bats and by day by sunbirds
Fruit curves upward as it grows, turning toward light (negative geotropism)
edibleParts: leaves used as food wrappers and plates
edibilityNote: Fruit, flower and stem core are all eaten. Wild seeded bananas have large hard seeds that must be spat out.

uses.use: Unripe banana and banana-stem juice used for diarrhoea and urinary stones
BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) for recovery from gastroenteritis
Sap applied to wounds and burns

medicinal.cautions: Latex-fruit syndrome: people with latex allergy may react to banana.

fruit.description: Elongated curved berry 10–30 cm, borne in 'hands' on a hanging bunch; green ripening to yellow, flesh cream and starchy-sweet. Cultivated forms show only tiny black specks where seeds aborted.

seed.description: In wild plants: hard, angular, black or dark-brown seeds about 4–6 mm, densely packed in the flesh. Cultivated dessert bananas show only rows of tiny brown-black specks of aborted ovules
seed.dispersal: Bats, birds and primates (wild); vegetatively by suckers (cultivated)
seed.germination: Wild seed: scarify and soak, sow warm (25–30 °C); erratic, 2 weeks to several months

grow.sun: Full sun; shelter from wind which shreds leaves
grow.soil: Rich, deep, well-drained loam high in organic matter, pH 5.5–7
grow.propagation: Suckers (sword suckers with narrow leaves are best), corms, or tissue-cultured plantlets
grow.timeToHarvest: 9–15 months from planting to bunch; fruit ready ~3 months after flowering
steps: Plant a sword sucker or tissue-culture plant in a hole enriched with compost, in a warm sheltered spot.
Feed heavily (bananas are hungry for potassium and nitrogen) and water deeply; mulch with chopped old leaves.
Keep one main stem plus one follower sucker per clump; cut away extra suckers.
After the last hand forms, snap off the male bud; harvest the bunch when fruits are plump and the first one yellows.
Cut down the spent pseudostem after harvest and chop it into mulch around the clump.

lore: Alexander the Great's soldiers reportedly saw sages resting under banana plants in the Indus valley, giving rise to Linnaeus's name Musa sapientum, 'fruit of the wise'. Bananas were among the first crops of New Guinea, where cultivation at Kuk Swamp dates back about 7,000 years.
funFact: Almost all export bananas are one clone, 'Cavendish', which replaced 'Gros Michel' after Panama disease wiped it out in the 1950s.

wiki.extract: Musa acuminata is a species of banana native to Southern Asia, its range comprising the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Many of the modern edible dessert bananas are derived from this species, although some are hybrids with Musa balbisiana. First cultivated by humans around 8000 BCE, it is one of the earlier examples of domesticated plants.

plates.long: This vibrant engraving from Jan Huyghen van Linschoten's 'Itinerario' illustrates the exotic flora of the East Indies, specifically focusing on coconut palms and banana trees. Below the main plant, five numbered diagrams illustrate the internal structures of the flower, including the stamens and perianth. The work was painted from nature by Berthe Hoola van Nooten in Batavia.

plates.title: Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium
plates.author: Maria Sibylla Merian

plates.long: A vibrant hand-colored engraving from Maria Sibylla Merian's 'Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium' (1705). The plate illustrates the life cycle of a moth in direct relation to its host plant, the banana (Musa), representing a pioneering approach to ecological study. Merian's work was revolutionary for its time, documenting the flora and fauna of Suriname with unprecedented scientific accuracy a

plates.title: Maria Sibylla Merian — Dissertatio de generatione et metamorphosibus insectorum Surinamensium (1719)
plates.author: Maria Sibylla Merian
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving depicting a banana plant with its flower and fruit, accompanied by a moth and its caterpillar.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving by Maria Sibylla Merian depicts the life cycle of a moth alongside a banana plant (Musa). Merian was a pioneer in ecology, being one of the first to illustrate insects together with their host plants, showing the stages of metamorphosis from caterpillar to adult moth. Her work in Suriname at the turn of the 18th century remains a landmark in both art and natural history

plates.title: Kircher: China Illustrata (1667)
plates.author: Athanasius Kircher
plates.desc: Detailed engraving of exotic flora and fauna, including a banana plant (Ficus Indica), a pineapple, and a monkey in a tropical landscape.
plates.long: This engraving from Kircher's 'China Illustrata' (1667) showcases the 17th-century European fascination with exotic nature. It depicts a variety of plants, including a banana tree (labeled Ficus Indica) and a pineapple, alongside a monkey, representing the diverse biological discoveries reported by Jesuit missionaries in the East.

plates.title: Sacred Physics
plates.author: Scheuchzer, Johan Jacob
plates.desc: Detailed botanical engraving of a banana plant and a melon variety.
plates.long: An intricate botanical plate from Johann Jacob Scheuchzer's Physica Sacra, engraved by Johann August Corvinus. It depicts a banana plant (Musa) and a variety of melon, showcasing the era's commitment to documenting the natural world as a reflection of divine creation.

plates.title: The Embassy of the Dutch East India Company to the Tartar Cham
plates.author: Johan Nieuhof
plates.desc: A detailed landscape engraving of tropical flora including pineapple and banana plants.
plates.long: A large-scale engraving depicts tropical plants in a coastal landscape, featuring a prominent pineapple plant labeled 'ANANAS' and a banana tree labeled 'MUSA'. In the background, palm trees and a distant mountain rise above a body of water where several birds are gathered. The scene illustrates the exotic flora encountered during the Dutch East India Company's travels.

plates.title: Sacred Physics
plates.author: Scheuchzer, Johan Jacob
plates.desc: Detailed botanical engraving of a banana plant and various cucurbits.
plates.long: This intricate engraving from Scheuchzer's 'Geestelyke natuurkunde' (Physica Sacra) depicts a banana plant (Musa) and various cucurbits including Dudaim Melo and Luffa. The work represents a pinnacle of 18th-century scientific illustration, where natural history was documented to illustrate the wonders of divine creation.

plates.title: Garden of Malabar, Vol. 1
plates.author: Hendrik van Rheede
plates.desc: Detailed botanical engraving of banana plants (Musa species) showing different growth stages, leaves, and fruit clusters.
plates.long: This detailed engraving from Hendrik van Rheede's 'Hortus Indicus Malabaricus' depicts the banana plant (Bala) in various stages of development. The work is a masterpiece of early modern botanical science, notable for its accuracy and its inclusion of plant names in Latin, Malayalam, Arabic, and Devanagari scripts, acknowledging the indigenous knowledge used in its compilation.

plates.title: Mosaic History of the Hebrew Church
plates.author: Goeree, Willem
plates.desc: A hand-colored botanical engraving of a banana plant (Musa), identified in the caption as 'Dudaïm' (mandrakes) found by Reuben. The plate shows the mature plant with broad leaves and a drooping flower bud, alongside details of the fruit and a smaller sapling.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Willem Goeree's 1700 history of the Hebrew church illustrates the 'Dudaïm' or mandrakes mentioned in Genesis 30:14. Interestingly, the artist has depicted a banana plant (Musa) to represent the biblical mandrake, reflecting the early modern attempt to identify exotic flora within a scriptural context. The plate provides a detailed botanical study, including the pla

summary: An evergreen tree endemic to the tiny Banda Islands of Indonesia that yields two spices: nutmeg, the seed, and mace, its scarlet lace-like aril. The Dutch East India Company massacred and enslaved the Bandanese in 1621 to seize the monopoly.
nativeRange: Banda Islands, Maluku, Indonesia; cultivated in Indonesia, Grenada, India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Produces two different spices from one fruit — the seed (nutmeg) and the aril (mace)
Dioecious: about half of seedlings are male and fruitless
Myristicin and elemicin in the seed are psychoactive and toxic in large doses
Trees can fruit for 60 years or more
edibleParts: fruit flesh (candied, jams, Indonesian manisan pala)
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice in culinary amounts. Eating about 5 g or more (one or two whole nuts) can cause nutmeg poisoning: nausea, palpitations, hallucinations and delirium lasting a day or more.

uses.use: Jaiphal in small amounts for diarrhoea, insomnia and as a digestive
Nutmeg for stomach complaints and as an aphrodisiac
Carried in pomanders against plague

medicinal.cautions: Toxic and psychoactive in doses above about 5 g; dangerous in pregnancy and for children.

fruit.description: Pale-yellow, apricot-like fruit 5–8 cm that splits in two when ripe, revealing a glossy brown seed wrapped in a crimson, net-like aril.

seed.description: Egg-shaped, hard brown seed 2–3 cm with a dark, glossy, ridged shell; inside, the kernel (nutmeg) is grey-brown with cream marbling; when fresh it is wrapped in bright scarlet branching mace
seed.dispersal: Fruit pigeons (Ducula) swallow the seeds with their aril
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh, in shell, 2 cm deep in shade at 25–30 °C; slow, 4–8 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade when young; sun when mature
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained volcanic or loamy soil, pH 6–7
grow.propagation: Seed (then select females), or grafting/approach-grafting female scions
grow.timeToHarvest: 5–8 years from seed; full crops after 15–20 years
steps: Sow fresh seeds in shaded nursery beds; plant out at 1–2 years, or plant grafted female trees to avoid fruitless males.
Space trees about 9 m apart under light shade (e.g. bananas or coconuts), with one male per 10 females.
Mulch thickly and keep moist; protect from strong winds.
Collect fruit when it splits open; separate the mace from the seed by hand.
Dry mace flat in the sun for a few days; dry seeds in the shell for 6–8 weeks until the kernel rattles, then crack and store.

lore: Under the 1667 Treaty of Breda, England and the Netherlands each kept what they had seized: the Dutch kept Run, a tiny nutmeg island in the Bandas, and the English kept New Amsterdam — Manhattan. Nutmeg remains so central to Grenada that it appears on the national flag.
funFact: Grenada's flag shows a nutmeg pod — the only national flag with a spice on it.

wiki.extract: Myristica fragrans, commonly known as the nutmeg tree, is an evergreen species indigenous to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia. This aromatic tree is economically significant as the primary source of two distinct spices: nutmeg, derived from its seed, and mace, obtained from the seed's aril.

summary: A tough, small tropical American tree with peeling coppery bark and intensely fragrant fruit, often far richer in vitamin C than an orange. It thrives so well that it has become an invasive weed on many tropical islands.
nativeRange: Tropical America from Mexico to northern South America; naturalised throughout the tropics
abilities: Fruits within 2–4 years from seed and can crop twice a year
Tolerates drought, poor soils and periodic flooding
Spreads rapidly via bird- and pig-dispersed seed, invading Pacific islands such as the Galápagos
Peeling, mottled coppery bark sheds in thin flakes
edibilityNote: Fruit, skin and seeds are eaten. Seeds are hard; eating many can cause constipation.

uses.use: Guava-leaf tea for diarrhoea and stomach ache
Leaf chewed or used as mouthwash for toothache and mouth ulcers
Guava-leaf polyphenol tea (approved FOSHU) for moderating post-meal blood sugar

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood sugar.

fruit.season: Varies; often two crops a year (summer and winter)
fruit.description: Round to pear-shaped berry 4–12 cm, green to yellow skin; white, pink or red flesh, musky-sweet, with a central pulp full of seeds.

seed.description: Many small, hard, kidney-shaped to angular seeds, cream to pale-yellow, 3–5 mm, embedded in the central pulp
seed.germination: Soak 2 weeks or boil briefly to soften the coat, sow at 25–30 °C; 2–8 weeks

grow.water: Moderate; tolerates drought but fruits better with regular water
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 years from seed, 1–2 years from layers
steps: Plant an air-layered or grafted plant of a good variety ('Allahabad Safeda', 'Ruby Supreme') in full sun.
Water regularly while establishing; mulch and feed every few months with balanced fertiliser.
Prune after each crop to keep the tree 2–3 m tall and open; fruit forms on new growth.
Bag young fruit with paper or mesh in areas with fruit flies.
Pick when the skin turns from dark to light green or yellow and the fruit smells strongly; ripen at room temperature.

lore: Spanish chronicler Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo described guavas in the Caribbean in 1526, and the Portuguese carried them to India, where Allahabad guavas became famous. Guava paste eaten with cheese ('Romeo y Julieta') is a classic in Brazil and the Caribbean.
funFact: Guava fruit can hold about four times the vitamin C of an orange by weight — roughly 228 mg per 100 g.

wiki.extract: Psidium guajava, the common guava, yellow guava, lemon guava, or apple guava is an evergreen shrub or small tree native to South America. It is pollinated by insects. When cultivated, it is pollinated mainly by the common honey bee, Apis mellifera.

As one of the first European books dedicated to Chinese natural history, this work represents a crucial moment of scientific and cultural exchange between the East and West, facilitated by Jesuit missionaries.

summary: Cloves are the unopened flower buds of an evergreen myrtle from the North Moluccas, the original 'Spice Islands'. Cloves were found in a kitchen at Terqa, Syria, dated to about 1720 BCE — evidence of a spice trade spanning 8,000 km nearly 4,000 years ago.
nativeRange: North Maluku, Indonesia (Ternate, Tidore, Moti, Makian, Bacan); cultivated in Indonesia, Zanzibar and Pemba, Madagascar and Sri Lanka
abilities: Buds contain up to 15–20% essential oil, mostly eugenol
Eugenol is a natural anaesthetic and antiseptic
Trees can crop for over a century
Afo, a clove tree on Ternate, is reputed to be over 350 years old
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Undiluted clove oil can burn the mouth and gums, and swallowed oil has caused serious liver damage and seizures in young children.

uses.use: Lavanga for toothache, bad breath, cough and indigestion
Eugenol mixed with zinc oxide as a temporary filling and dressing for dry socket
Officials held cloves in their mouths to sweeten their breath before addressing the emperor

medicinal.cautions: Undiluted oil is caustic; oil is dangerous to children if swallowed; eugenol may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.

fruit.season: Buds harvested twice a year in many regions; fruits rarely allowed to form
fruit.description: If left, buds open into fluffy crimson-stamened flowers and then purple-red oval berries ('mother of cloves') about 2.5 cm long.

seed.description: The dried spice is a nail-shaped bud 1–2 cm long, reddish-brown, with a ball-like head of petals. The true seed is one oblong, soft, pale-brown seed about 1.5 cm inside the purple berry
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow fresh ripe berries in shade at 25–30 °C; 2–5 weeks

grow.sun: Partial shade when young; sun when mature
grow.water: High (1,500–2,500 mm), with a short dry season for flowering
grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam or volcanic soil, pH 5–6.5
grow.timeToHarvest: 5–7 years to first buds; peak at 15–20 years
steps: Sow fresh seeds from ripe berries in a shaded nursery; transplant at 1–2 years.
Plant out about 6–8 m apart with temporary shade such as bananas; protect from wind.
Mulch and water regularly in the first years; weed around the base.
Pick bud clusters by hand when the buds turn from green to pink but before they open.
Separate buds from stems and sun-dry for 4–5 days until dark brown and they snap cleanly.

lore: Magellan's 1519–22 expedition sailed largely to reach the clove islands of Maluku, and the one surviving ship, Victoria, returned with 26 tonnes of cloves. Omani Sultan Said bin Sultan made Zanzibar the world's leading clove producer in the 19th century, using enslaved labour.
funFact: The word 'clove' comes from Latin clavus, 'nail', after the bud's shape — the same image behind the Chinese name 'nail spice'.

wiki.extract: Cloves are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum. They are native to the Maluku Islands, or Moluccas, in Indonesia, and are commonly used as a spice, flavoring, or fragrance in consumer products, such as toothpaste, soaps, or cosmetics. Freshly harvested cloves are available throughout the year owing to different harvest seasons across various countries.

summary: The flower that rises clean from the mud, central to Hinduism and Buddhism. Its leaves are so water-repellent that droplets roll off carrying dirt with them (the 'lotus effect'), its flowers warm themselves, and a seed about 1,300 years old has been sprouted.
nativeRange: South and East Asia to northern Australia; ancient introductions elsewhere
abilities: Its leaf surface is covered in wax nano-bumps that make it superhydrophobic and self-cleaning
Warms its flowers to around 30–35 °C for days, even on cool nights
Produces seeds that can stay alive for centuries; one from a dry lakebed in north-east China germinated after about 1,300 years
Pipes air down to its rhizomes through hollow channels in its stalks
edibilityNote: All main parts are eaten. Cook the rhizome before eating, since raw aquatic plants can carry parasites such as Fasciolopsis; remove the bitter green embryo of seeds if desired.

uses.use: Seeds (lian zi) to calm the heart; leaves (he ye) for summer heat; the seed embryo (lian zi xin) as a cooling bitter
Flowers and rhizome (kamala) for bleeding, diarrhoea and skin conditions

medicinal.cautions: Leaf and embryo preparations may lower blood pressure and blood sugar; caution with medication.

fruit.description: A flat-topped, shower-head seed pod with each nut set in its own hole.

seed.description: Hard, acorn-like nut
seed.dispersal: Water, after the pod tips over
seed.germination: File through the hard coat at the non-pointed end and soak in warm water; sprouts in days

grow.soil: Heavy loam or clay at the pond bottom
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in 1–2 years from seed; rhizomes after one season
steps: Nick the seed coat and soak in warm water, changing it daily
Pot the sprouted seed into heavy loam in a wide, hole-free container
Submerge in still, sunny water and raise depth as leaves grow
Give at least 6 hours of sun and warm water to flower

lore: In Hindu iconography Lakshmi and Brahma sit on lotuses, and Buddhist art shows the Buddha on a lotus throne; 'Om mani padme hum' means 'the jewel in the lotus'. Zhou Dunyi's 11th-century essay 'On the Love of the Lotus' praised it for rising unstained from mud.
funFact: Self-cleaning paints and fabrics are modelled on the lotus leaf's microstructure; 'lotus effect' is a registered trademark.

wiki.extract: Nelumbo nucifera, also known as Padma or Kamala, sacred lotus, pink lotus, Indian lotus, or simply lotus, is one of two extant species of aquatic plant in the family Nelumbonaceae. It is sometimes colloquially called water lily, though this more often refers to members of the family Nymphaeaceae. The lotus belongs in the order Proteales.

The bottom frame shows a banana tree (E), an Egyptian-style bust with a banana-leaf headdress (F), and a branch of a Persea tree with fruit (G).

It notably includes a figure wearing an Egyptian-style headdress made of banana leaves, reflecting the 18th-century interest in connecting natural history with ancient cultural traditions and mythologies.

Such illustrations were crucial for the scientific documentation of Southeast Asian flora in the 18th century, combining artistic precision with botanical accuracy to aid in identification and study.

Pietro Andrea Mattioli's commentaries on Dioscorides were renowned for their high-quality, accurate botanical illustrations, which played a crucial role in the standardization of plant identification in early modern medicine.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Faba Aegyptia' or Egyptian Bean, likely Nelumbo nucifera (the sacred lotus). The illustration captures the plant's distinctive large, peltate leaves and its characteristic seed pod, which was noted by ancient authors like Dioscorides for its medicinal properties.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts the 'Faba Aegyptia' (Egyptian bean), illustrating its large peltate leaves, flowers, seed pod, and tuberous rhizome. Such illustrations were crucial for the identification of medicinal plants in early modern herbals, bridging classical knowledge with direct observation of nature.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut illustration of 'Phaseolus v. sive Aegyptiacus' (Egyptian bean) from Carolus Clusius's 1576 botanical treatise. The print meticulously depicts the plant's root system, branching stems, trifoliate leaves, and developing flowers, showcasing the era's advancement in scientific observation and recording.

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a Phaseolus plant (Egyptian bean), showing its climbing habit, leaves, flowers, seed pods, and individual seeds.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Phaseolus plant, identified in the text as an Egyptian variety. Carolus Clusius was a pioneering botanist, and this illustration from his 1576 work demonstrates the increasing focus on accurate scientific observation and recording of plant species in the early modern period.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica
plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of a lotus plant showing flower, seed pod, leaves, and rhizome.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1596 edition of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica) depicts the lotus plant (Nelumbo nucifera). It clearly delineates the flower, seed pod, leaves, and the segmented rhizome, all of which have significant medicinal uses in traditional Chinese practice. The illustration serves as a vital visual aid for identifying the plant in its entirety.

summary: Maker of the largest pitchers of any carnivorous plant, up to about 40 cm tall and holding litres of fluid. It catches insects, but also gets nitrogen from tree shrews that sit on the rim to lick nectar from the lid and leave their droppings in the pitcher.
nativeRange: Endemic to Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon, Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, about 1,500–2,650 m
biomes: Montane ultramafic grassland and forest edges
abilities: Forms urn-shaped pitchers big enough to hold several litres of fluid
Feeds mountain tree shrews (Tupaia montana) with lid nectar, and the pitcher fits a tree shrew's body exactly
Its slippery rim (peristome) sends insects into digestive fluid
Grows on serpentine (ultramafic) soils rich in metals and poor in nutrients
Occasionally traps frogs, lizards or rats
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Protected species.

fruit.description: Narrow capsules on a tall raceme, plants are male or female.

seed.description: Thread-like winged seeds
seed.germination: Surface-sow fresh on milled sphagnum, high humidity, cool nights

grow.soil: Open mix of sphagnum, bark, perlite and pumice
grow.propagation: Tissue culture or seed (wild collection is illegal)
steps: Buy legal tissue-cultured plants (it is on CITES Appendix I)
Keep days around 20–25 °C and nights about 10–15 °C
Give 70–90% humidity and rainwater only
Don't fertilise the medium; an occasional insect in a pitcher is enough

lore: Hugh Low collected it on Kinabalu in 1858 and Joseph Hooker named it in 1859 for James Brooke, the 'White Rajah' of Sarawak. Victorian nurseries such as Veitch sent collectors to Borneo for these plants.
funFact: The opening of the pitcher matches a tree shrew's body length, so the animal sits where its droppings fall straight into it.

wiki.extract: Nepenthes rajah is a carnivorous pitcher plant species of the family Nepenthaceae. It is endemic to Mount Kinabalu and neighbouring Mount Tambuyukon in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo. Nepenthes rajah grows exclusively on serpentine substrates, particularly in areas of seeping ground water where the soil is loose and permanently moist. The species has an altitudinal range of 1,500–2,650 m (4,920–8,690 ft) above sea level and is thus considered a highland or sub-alpine plant. Due to its localised distribution, N. rajah is classified as an endangered species by the IUCN and listed on CITES Appendix I.

summary: A water lily whose leaves reach up to about 3 m across, ribbed underneath like the girders of a bridge. Its flowers open white and fragrant on the first night, shut beetles inside, and reopen pink the next night to release them covered in pollen.
nativeRange: Amazon basin: Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Guyana
abilities: Grows floating leaves up to about 3 m across with upturned rims
Its spiny underside ribs trap air and spread load, so a leaf can bear a small child if weight is spread
Heats its first-night flower and releases a pineapple-like scent to attract Cyclocephala scarab beetles
Changes sex in two nights: female and white on night one, male and pink on night two
edibilityNote: Starchy seeds are roasted or ground into flour locally. Stalks and leaf undersides are covered in sharp spines.

fruit.description: Prickly fruit that develops underwater and releases pea-sized seeds.

seed.description: Round, hard seeds
seed.germination: Store in water (they die if dried); germinate at about 30 °C

grow.zones: Tropical only (USDA 11–12) or heated glasshouse pool
grow.soil: Rich, heavy loam in a large container
steps: Keep seed in water until sowing
Germinate in shallow water at about 30 °C
Move to a large, very fertile container in a big warm pool
Fertilise heavily: a single plant needs a lot of feeding

lore: John Lindley named the genus after the young Queen Victoria in 1837 from specimens Robert Schomburgk sent from British Guiana; Joseph Paxton at Chatsworth first brought it to flower in November 1849. Paxton said the ribbed leaf inspired the iron-and-glass structure of the Crystal Palace for the Great Exhibition of 1851.
funFact: Paxton had his daughter Annie stand on a leaf (on a tray to spread her weight), an image that made the plant famous.

wiki.extract: Victoria amazonica is a species of flowering plant, the second largest in the water lily family Nymphaeaceae. It is called Vitória-Régia or Iaupê-Jaçanã in Brazil and Atun Sisac in Inca (Quechua). Its native region is tropical South America, specifically Guyana and the Amazon Basin.

summary: The defining tree of the Mediterranean, domesticated in the Levant around 7,000 years ago. Gnarled olive trees can live for well over 1,000 years, resprouting from their base after fire, frost or felling.
nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin and Near East (cultivated form); wild subspecies across Africa, Arabia and South Asia
abilities: Silvery leaves with scaly hairs reduce water loss, letting trees fruit on as little as 200–400 mm of rain
Resprouts from a burl (lignotuber) after the trunk is killed
Individual trees in Crete, Lebanon and Sardinia are estimated at 2,000–3,000 years old
Wind-pollinated; pollen is a major springtime allergen in the Mediterranean
edibilityNote: Raw olives are inedibly bitter because of oleuropein; they must be cured in brine, lye, water or dry salt before eating.

uses.use: Olive leaf tea for fever and high blood pressure
Olive oil eaten and applied to the body, called 'from a blessed tree'
Extra-virgin olive oil central to the Mediterranean diet; EU-authorised claim for polyphenols protecting blood lipids

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extracts may lower blood pressure and blood sugar; caution with antihypertensive and diabetes medication.

fruit.season: Autumn to winter (green olives October, black November–January)
fruit.description: Oval drupe 1–4 cm, green ripening through violet to black; oily, bitter flesh around a hard stone.

seed.description: A hard, pointed oval stone, pale brown and finely ridged, 1–2 cm long, enclosing a single slender cream-coloured seed
seed.dispersal: Birds (especially starlings and thrushes) and mammals
seed.germination: Slow and erratic: crack or clip the stone, cold-stratify 1–2 months, then sow warm; 1–3 months

grow.soil: Well-drained, even poor, stony or chalky; dislikes waterlogging, pH 6.5–8.5
grow.propagation: Semi-hardwood cuttings under mist, or grafting onto seedling or wild rootstock
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years for first crop; full production at 10–15 years
steps: Choose a cultivar suited to your climate and use (e.g. 'Arbequina' self-fertile for oil, 'Manzanilla' for table olives).
Plant in spring in a sunny, frost-sheltered spot with excellent drainage; on clay, plant on a mound.
Water weekly for the first summer, then only during long droughts; most olives fruit better with some summer water stress.
Prune in late winter to an open vase shape to let light into the canopy, since fruit forms on last year's growth.
Pick by hand or rake onto nets; cure table olives in brine (changed weekly) for 1–3 months, or press within 24 hours for oil.

lore: Athena won Athens from Poseidon by giving the city an olive tree, and olive wreaths crowned victors at the ancient Olympic Games. In Genesis the dove returns to Noah's ark with an olive leaf, the origin of the olive branch as a sign of peace.
funFact: Olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane in Jerusalem have been radiocarbon-dated to the 12th century, and their roots may be far older.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts an olive tree (Olijfboom), a plant highly valued in the 16th century for its medicinal and culinary properties. It is a characteristic example of the botanical illustrations found in 'Den groten herbarius', which served as a visual guide for identifying plants used in traditional medicine.

summary: A climbing orchid from Mexican and Central American forests and the source of real vanilla, the second most expensive spice after saffron. Outside its homeland every flower must be hand-pollinated, a method invented in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico, Central America and northern South America; cultivated in Madagascar, Réunion, Indonesia, Uganda, Papua New Guinea and India
abilities: Climbs trees with aerial roots that cling to bark
Each flower opens for only a few hours on a single morning
A thin flap (rostellum) separates male and female parts, preventing self-pollination without help
Green pods have no flavour; vanillin develops only after weeks of curing
edibilityNote: Cured pods and extract are safe. The sap of fresh stems and green pods can cause skin irritation ('vanillism') in plantation workers.

uses.use: Vanilla mixed into remedies and amulets and taken with cacao as a tonic
Listed as a stimulant, digestive and aphrodisiac

medicinal.cautions: Contact dermatitis from fresh sap.

fruit.description: Slender, fleshy green pod 15–25 cm long that, when cured, turns supple, glossy, deep chocolate-brown and intensely aromatic, sometimes frosted with vanillin crystals.

seed.description: Tens of thousands of minute, round, glossy black seeds about 0.3 mm — the 'vanilla specks' in ice cream
seed.dispersal: Probably bees and other animals in the wild; seeds lack food reserves
seed.germination: Needs symbiotic fungi or sterile lab culture; practically impossible at home. Cultivation is by cuttings

grow.water: High humidity; regular water, with a 2–3 month drier spell to trigger flowering
grow.soil: Loose, humus-rich mulch over well-drained soil (it roots mostly in leaf litter)
grow.propagation: Stem cuttings 1–2 m long with 6–12 nodes
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years to first flowers; pods 8–9 months after pollination
steps: Plant a 1–2 m cutting at the base of a living support tree (e.g. Gliricidia, Jatropha) or a post, laying 2–3 leafless nodes on the soil and covering them with mulch.
Tie the vine to its support and keep it shaded and humid; mulch thickly with leaves.
Loop the vine back down when it reaches 1.5–2 m so flowers form within reach.
Each morning in the flowering season, hand-pollinate open flowers: lift the rostellum with a toothpick and press the anther onto the stigma.
Pick pods when the tip yellows; cure by scalding in 65 °C water, 'sweating' wrapped in blankets, then sunning by day and wrapping at night for weeks before slow drying.

lore: The Totonac people of Veracruz say vanilla sprang from the blood of a princess, Xanat, and her lover. Edmond Albius's thumb-and-stick technique (1841) made Réunion and Madagascar the centre of world vanilla, but he died in poverty.
funFact: Less than 1% of the vanilla flavour sold worldwide comes from real vanilla; the rest is synthetic vanillin.

wiki.extract: Vanilla planifolia is a species of vanilla orchid native to Mexico, Central America, Colombia, and Brazil. It is one of the primary sources for vanilla flavouring, due to its high vanillin content. Common names include flat-leaved vanilla and West Indian vanilla, though it is often simply referred to as vanilla. It was first scientifically named in 1808.

plates.author: Francisco Hernández
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of the Tlilxochitl (Vanilla) plant
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the Tlilxochitl plant, known today as vanilla, as documented by Francisco Hernández during his scientific expedition to Mexico. It illustrates the plant's characteristic climbing habit and elongated seed pods, which were highly valued for their aromatic and medicinal properties in both Aztec and early colonial medicine.

plates.long: This botanical woodcut depicts the Tlilxochitl plant, known today as vanilla. The illustration shows the plant's characteristic climbing habit, elliptical leaves, and the elongated seed pod or bean.

summary: A grey-leaved annual poppy whose unripe seed capsules bleed a latex that has given humanity its strongest painkillers, and some of its worst addictions. Its seeds, by contrast, are harmless enough to scatter on bread.
nativeRange: Probably derived from wild Papaver setigerum in the western Mediterranean; cultivated since the Neolithic and naturalised widely
abilities: Latex contains morphine and codeine, which act on the body's opioid receptors
Makes over 40 benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, including thebaine (precursor of many semi-synthetic opioids), papaverine and noscapine
Seed capsules release seed through a ring of pores, like a pepper pot, when shaken by wind
edibilityNote: Ripe seeds are a common food and contain almost no alkaloid. Unwashed seeds can carry morphine from the capsule, enough to cause positive drug tests, and 'poppy seed tea' has caused fatal overdoses. Latex, green capsules and straw are poisonous.

uses.use: Afyun in small amounts in sedative, anti-diarrhoeal and cough compounds; seeds (khashkhash) as a cooling nutritive
Ahiphena (introduced in the medieval period) for diarrhoea, pain and insomnia, after purification procedures
Poppy husk (yingsuqiao) to stop chronic cough and diarrhoea
Source of morphine and codeine and the raw material for semi-synthetic opioids; papaverine as a smooth-muscle relaxant

medicinal.cautions: Opioids cause dependence and addiction, and overdose depresses breathing and can kill. Cultivation and extraction are legally controlled in most countries. Never prepare home extracts from capsules or seed washings, as their strength varies wildly.

fruit.description: Smooth, rounded capsule up to 5 cm, crowned by a flat stigmatic disc, releasing seed through pores.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped, finely netted seeds, blue-black, white or brown
seed.dispersal: Shaken from capsule pores; long-lived soil seed bank
seed.germination: Sow on the surface in cool soil; 7–14 days at 10–15 °C

steps: Check national law: growing opium poppy is restricted or illegal in many places
Broadcast seed thinly in autumn or early spring
Thin to 15–20 cm, as poppies resent transplanting
For ornamental seed, cut capsules once dry and rattling

lore: Seeds and capsules have been found at the Neolithic lake village of La Marmotta near Rome (c. 5600 BCE). Between 1804 and 1817 the German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner isolated and described morphine, which he named morphium after Morpheus, the god of dreams. Britain's opium trade triggered the Opium Wars with China (1839–42, 1856–60).
funFact: Morphine was the first alkaloid ever isolated from a plant, launching the chemistry of drugs taken from plants.

wiki.extract: Papaver somniferum, commonly known as the opium poppy or breadseed poppy, is a species of flowering plant in the family Papaveraceae. It is the species of plant from which both opium and poppy seeds are derived and is also a valuable ornamental plant grown in gardens. Its native range is the western Mediterranean region, but has since been obscured by widespread introduction and cultivation since ancient times to the present day. It is now naturalised across much of the world with temperate climates.

gerard.title: Of garden Poppie
gerard.names: Poppie is called of the Græcians μήκων: of the Latines Papaver: the shoppes keepe the Latine name: it is called in high Dutch Magfamen: in lowe Dutch Heul and Mancop: in English Poppie, and Cheesebowles: in French Pavot, and Oliette Gallobelgis. The garden Poppie which hath blacke seedes, is surnamed of Dioscorides ἀγριον, or wilde, and is as he saith, called ῥοιάς, bicause Opium is gathered from it: of Plinie and of the Latines Papaver nigrum: and of most of our age of the red colour of the flo…
gerard.place: These kindes of Poppies are sowen in gardens, which do afterwarde come of the fallings of the seede.
gerard.time: They flower most commonly in Iune. The seede is perfected in Iuly and August.
gerard.temperature: All the Poppies are colde, as Galen testifieth in his booke of the faculties of simple medicines.
gerard.vertues: The seede, as Galen saith in his booke of the faculties of nourishments, is good to season breade with; but the white is better then the blacke. Hee also addeth that the same is colde and causeth sleepe, and yeeldeth no commendable nourishment to the bodie; it is often vsed in comfits, or serued at the table with other iunketting dishes. The oile which is pressed out of it is pleasant and delightfull to be eaten, and is taken with bread or any other waies in meate, without any fence of cooling. A greater force is in the knobs or heads which do specially preuaile to mooue sleepe, and to stay and represse distillations or rheumes, and come neere in force to Opium, but more gentle. Opium, or the harde iuice of Poppie heads is strongest of all: Meconium (which is the iuice of the heads and leaues) is weaker. Both of them any waies taken either inwardly, or outwardly applied to the heade, prouoke sleepe. Opium somewhat too plentifully taken doth also bring death, as Plinie truelie writeth.

summary: A vigorous tendril-climbing vine from South America with elaborate fringed flowers that Spanish missionaries read as symbols of Christ's Passion. Its wrinkled purple or yellow fruit holds fragrant, tangy pulp around crunchy black seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina; cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: Flowers last a single day and are pollinated mainly by carpenter bees (Xylocopa)
Climbs fast with coiling tendrils, covering a fence in a season
Yellow form (flavicarpa) is largely self-incompatible and needs cross-pollination
Leaves and unripe fruit contain cyanogenic glycosides
edibilityNote: Ripe pulp and seeds are safe. Leaves, stems and very unripe fruit contain cyanogenic glycosides and should not be eaten.

uses.use: Leaf tea ('maracujá') as a calming sedative
Leaves and flowers as a remedy for sleeplessness and nerves

medicinal.cautions: Leaves are cyanogenic; sedative leaf preparations may add to sedative drugs.

fruit.season: Summer to autumn; often two crops in the tropics
fruit.description: Round to egg-shaped berry 4–8 cm, smooth skin turning deep purple or yellow and wrinkling when ripe; hollow inside, filled with juicy golden pulp sacs around seeds.

seed.description: Flat, oval, black seeds 5–6 mm, with a finely pitted surface, each enclosed in a juicy yellow-orange aril
seed.germination: Clean off pulp, soak 1–2 days, sow 0.5 cm deep at 20–30 °C; 2–4 weeks

grow.soil: Light, well-drained, rich in organic matter, pH 6–7.5
grow.propagation: Seed, cuttings, or grafting onto disease-resistant yellow rootstock
steps: Sow seed or plant a grafted vine next to a sturdy trellis, fence or pergola at least 2 m tall.
Train the main stem up to the top wire, then let side shoots hang down — fruit forms on new growth.
Water deeply and feed every 1–2 months in the growing season with a balanced fertiliser; mulch roots.
Prune lightly after harvest to remove old, tangled growth; hand-pollinate yellow forms in the afternoon if carpenter bees are scarce.
Gather fruit as it falls or when it colours fully; let it wrinkle for a few days for the sweetest pulp.

lore: In the 17th century Jesuit missionaries saw the corona as the crown of thorns, the five anthers as Christ's wounds and the three styles as the nails, calling it 'flos passionis' — the root of the genus name Passiflora. Brazil is today the world's largest producer.
funFact: The name has nothing to do with romance — it refers to the Passion (suffering) of Christ.

wiki.extract: Passiflora edulis, commonly known as passion fruit, is a vine species of passion flower native to southern Brazil, through Paraguay, and northern Argentina. The fruit is a pepo, a type of botanical berry, round to oval, either yellow or dark purple at maturity, with a soft to firm, juicy interior filled with numerous seeds.

The passion fruit is shown with its characteristic tendrils and serrated leaves, while the Amozotl features upright stalks with small clustered flowers or seeds.

The delicate rendering of the vine's tendrils and the complex geometry of the flower petals reflects the era's fascination with documenting exotic flora with scientific precision and artistic elegance.

plates.long: This exquisite botanical study from the Moninckx Atlas depicts a species of passion flower, identified by its characteristic slender, smooth leaves and delicate yellow blossoms. Such illustrations were commissioned by the Amsterdam Botanical Garden to document the rare and exotic plants arriving from global trade routes, serving as both scientific record and artistic achievement.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a passion flower, known in Chinese as 'Xifanlian', showing its distinctive radial corona and lobed leaves. It is an illustration from Wu Qijun's 1848 masterpiece 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao', which is celebrated for its accurate and detailed depictions of flora based on direct observation.

summary: A trailing Kalahari herb with pink trumpet flowers and a fearsome woody fruit armed with hooked arms that clamp onto animals' feet. Its secondary tubers are a major European pain remedy and an important income for San and other Kalahari harvesters.
nativeRange: Kalahari sands of Namibia, Botswana and South Africa, extending to southern Angola and Zimbabwe
abilities: Storage tubers survive the dry season and send up new stems after rain
Woody fruits with grapple hooks lodge in hooves and fur, spreading the seed widely
Tubers contain iridoid glycosides (harpagoside) with anti-inflammatory activity
edibilityNote: Not a food. The bitter dried tubers are used as tea or extract.

uses.tradition: Southern African traditional medicine (San, Khoikhoi, Tswana)
uses.use: Tuber for pain, fevers, digestive complaints and in childbirth; ointments for sores and boils
Standardised extracts for low back pain, osteoarthritis and loss of appetite; EMA traditional-use monograph

medicinal.cautions: Some trials show benefit in low back pain and osteoarthritis, but quality is limited. Causes digestive upset, and should be avoided with stomach ulcers and gallstones. May interact with warfarin, diabetes and heart-rhythm drugs. Avoid in pregnancy. Buy sustainably harvested products.

fruit.description: Hard, flattened capsule 7–20 cm across, with long arms ending in sharp hooks.

seed.description: Dark, rough, oblong seeds inside the woody fruit
seed.dispersal: Fruits hook onto the feet and fur of animals
seed.germination: Deeply dormant; erratic; needs warmth and rain

steps: Sow in deep containers of pure sand in warmth
Water in summer only and keep dry in winter
Harvest only secondary (side) tubers, leaving the central taproot
Slice and sun-dry quickly

lore: In the early 1900s G. H. Mehnert, a German settler in Namibia, learned of its use from local healers and introduced it to Europe. Today it is harvested from the wild in Namibia under community-based permit schemes.
funFact: The genus name means 'grappling-hook plant' in Greek. Its fruits can lame antelope and sheep by clamping onto their feet or mouths.

wiki.extract: Harpagophytum, also called grapple plant, wood spider, and most commonly devil's claw, is a genus of plants in the sesame family, native to southern Africa. Plants of the genus owe their common name "devil's claw" to the peculiar appearance of their hooked fruit. Several species of North American plants in the genus Proboscidea and certain species of Pisonia, however, are also known by this name. Devil's claw's tuberous roots are used in folk medicine to reduce pain.

otherNames: Makham pom มะขามป้อม (Thai)
summary: A feathery-leaved deciduous tree whose translucent green fruits are among the richest natural sources of vitamin C. Amla is one of the three fruits of the Ayurvedic formula Triphala and the base of the tonic jam chyawanprash.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka to southern China and Malaysia
abilities: Fruit is rich in vitamin C, protected from breakdown by abundant tannins
Ellagitannins and gallic acid give strong antioxidant and astringent activity
Leaves are tiny and arranged in two rows, so the shoots look like pinnate leaves
Tolerates poor, dry and somewhat saline soils
edibilityNote: Very sour and astringent raw. Widely eaten as pickles, murabba (preserve), juice and powder.

uses.use: Amalaki as a supreme rasayana for longevity, digestion, eyes, hair and skin; one of the three fruits in Triphala and the base of chyawanprash
Amla as a cold, astringent tonic for the heart, brain, stomach and hair; in Itrifal compounds
Yuganzi to clear heat, cool the blood and soothe the throat; skyu ru ra in Tibetan medicine
Small trials of extracts for cholesterol, blood sugar and dyspepsia

medicinal.cautions: Trials are small. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs. Large amounts can upset the stomach.

fruit.description: Round, pale yellow-green, 2–3 cm, with six faint vertical segments; translucent, sour and astringent, around a six-sided stone.

seed.description: Six small seeds inside a hard, three-chambered stone
seed.dispersal: Animals eat the fruit; deer and monkeys
seed.germination: Soak 24 h; 2–4 weeks at 25–30 °C

grow.soil: Any well-drained soil; tolerates poor and alkaline soil
steps: Plant grafted saplings at the start of the rains, 8–10 m apart
Water through the first dry seasons
Plant two cultivars together for better fruit set
Harvest fruit when it turns translucent and pale in winter

lore: Hindus worship the amla tree on Amla Navami in the month of Kartika, when families eat meals beneath it. Chyawanprash is named after the sage Chyavana, who by legend regained his youth through it.
funFact: Its Chinese name yuganzi means 'lingering sweetness', because water drunk after eating the sour fruit tastes sweet.

It showcases the meticulous detail of early modern botanical engravings and includes the plant's name in Latin, Malayalam, Arabic, and Devanagari, highlighting the cross-cultural knowledge exchange involved in the book's creation.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the Myrobalani Emblici, showcasing the fruit's characteristic form and seeds. Such illustrations were vital for the accurate identification and preparation of herbal remedies in the early modern period.

summary: A tree that built empires. Its fragrant, rot-resistant wood went into Phoenician ships, Egyptian tombs and, the Bible says, Solomon's Temple. Ancient demand stripped the Lebanon mountains, so only scattered groves now survive, and the tree stands on the Lebanese flag.
nativeRange: Mountains of Lebanon, western Syria and southern Turkey (Taurus), 1,300–3,000 m
abilities: Grows broad, tiered horizontal branches in old age
Produces aromatic wood rich in sesquiterpenes that resists insects and decay
Lives for well over 1,000 years in favourable sites
Withstands cold, snowy mountain winters and dry Mediterranean summers
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Essential oil is not for internal use.

uses.use: Cedar oil and resin used in embalming (the botanical source of some 'cedar' oils is debated)
Resin and oil applied to skin infections and as an insect repellent

medicinal.cautions: Essential oils can irritate skin and are toxic if swallowed in quantity.

fruit.description: Barrel-shaped cones 8–12 cm that break apart on the tree to release seeds.

seed.description: Resinous seeds with a large wing
seed.germination: Short cold stratification (2–4 weeks); sow in spring

steps: Soak seed overnight and stratify briefly
Sow in deep pots in spring
Plant out young (it dislikes root disturbance) in a spacious, sunny spot
Water through the first summers; after that it is drought-tolerant

lore: In the Epic of Gilgamesh the hero kills Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, to take its trees. The Cedars of God grove at Bsharri, Lebanon, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1998 with the Qadisha Valley.
funFact: The Palermo Stone records pharaoh Sneferu (c. 2600 BCE) bringing 40 ships filled with cedar wood, usually read as a shipment from Byblos on the Lebanese coast.

wiki.extract: Cedrus libani, commonly known as cedar of Lebanon, Lebanon cedar, or Lebanese cedar, is a species of large conifer in the pine family, Pinaceae, and is native to the mountains of the Eastern Mediterranean basin. Known for its longevity, height, and durable wood, it has held profound significance for millennia. The tree features in ancient Mesopotamian literature. It is the national emblem of Lebanon and is widely used as an ornamental tree in parks and gardens. Historically, the ancient Phoenicians used Cedar wood for shipbuilding and traded Cedar trees with Ancient Egypt, Ancient Greece, Anatolians, Iberians, Punics, Sicilians, Romans and Ancient Iraq.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Christoph Jakob Trew's 'Uitgezochte planten' (1771) meticulously depicts a cedar tree (Cedrus). The plate combines a representation of the mature tree with detailed anatomical studies of its reproductive structures, exemplifying the fusion of scientific accuracy and artistic skill in Enlightenment-era natural history.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the Cedar of Lebanon (Cedrus libani), highlighting its distinctive layered branching and upright cones. The fine line work captures the texture of the bark and the intricate structure of the foliage.

summary: Among the oldest individual non-clonal organisms on Earth. The tree called Methuselah, in California's White Mountains, germinated more than 4,800 years ago, before the Great Pyramid was finished. Bristlecones survive by growing incredibly slowly and letting most of their bark die back.
nativeRange: High mountains of eastern California, Nevada and Utah, mostly 2,600–3,500 m
abilities: Lives more than 4,800 years on dry, alkaline dolomite where few competitors grow
Practises 'sectored architecture': when roots die, only the matching strip of bark dies, so the tree survives on a narrow living ribbon
Produces dense, resinous wood that resists rot, insects and fungi, so dead wood can lie on the ground for thousands of years
Keeps needles for up to 40 years or more, saving energy on dry ground
edibilityNote: Pine seeds are small and not a traditional food; not considered toxic.

fruit.description: Dark purple cones 6–10 cm long with a fragile bristle on each scale.

seed.description: Small seeds with a detachable wing
seed.dispersal: Wind, and caching by Clark's nutcrackers
seed.germination: Cold-stratify ~60 days; sow in gritty mineral mix

steps: Cold-stratify seed for about two months
Sow in a gritty, low-nutrient mix
Grow on in full sun with minimal fertilizer
Plant in poor, well-drained ground; rich soil and wet roots kill it

lore: Edmund Schulman's ring-counts in the 1950s revealed the trees' age, and bristlecone chronologies stretching back more than 8,000 years were used to calibrate radiocarbon dating. In 1964 a researcher cut down the tree later named Prometheus, at about 4,900 years old, with Forest Service permission.
funFact: Because bristlecone ring-widths record past climate, the trees helped show that early radiocarbon dates were off by centuries.

wiki.extract: Pinus longaeva is a long-living species of bristlecone pine tree found in the higher mountains of California, Nevada, and Utah. In 1987, the bristlecone pine was designated one of Nevada's state trees.

plates.long: This page features two detailed woodcuts of pine species, Pinus Sylvestris (Scotch Pine) and Pinus Maritima (Maritime Pine), illustrating their distinct needle patterns and cone structures. summary: A pepper-family shrub from Vanuatu whose root drink brings calm and sociability without clouding the mind like alcohol. It is the ceremonial drink of the Pacific, and every plant is a sterile clone carried from island to island by voyagers.
nativeRange: Domesticated in northern Vanuatu from wild Piper wichmannii; spread by people across Melanesia, Polynesia and Micronesia
abilities: Roots contain kavalactones, which act on GABA-A receptors and sodium channels, relaxing muscles and easing anxiety
Cultivated kava is sterile and propagated entirely from stem cuttings by people
Kava chemistry differs between cultivars, which Pacific growers classify by effect
edibleParts: root and rhizome (as a cold-water drink)
edibilityNote: Traditionally drunk as a water extract of fresh or dried root. Use only peeled root and rhizome of 'noble' cultivars; leaves, stems and 'tudei' (two-day) cultivars are linked to more side effects. Do not combine with alcohol or drive.

uses.use: Drunk ceremonially and socially; also for urinary complaints, headaches, insomnia and to calm nerves
In Vanuatu and Fiji, for relaxation, sleep and pain, and in ritual to honour guests and chiefs
Standardised extracts trialled for generalised anxiety disorder, with mixed but partly positive results

medicinal.cautions: Reports of severe liver injury led to bans in several European countries from 2002; Germany's ban was overturned in court in 2014. Risk seems linked to extract type and plant parts. Heavy use causes a scaly skin rash (kava dermopathy). Avoid with liver disease, alcohol, sedatives, Parkinson's disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding.

seed.description: Cultivated kava does not set viable seed
seed.germination: Not grown from seed

grow.soil: Loose, rich, well-drained volcanic or forest loam
steps: Lay node-bearing stem sections on moist soil, half-buried, under light shade
Keep warm (above 20 °C) and humid; it cannot tolerate frost or drought
Mulch and weed for several years
Dig the whole root mass at 3–5 years, keeping stems to replant

lore: At the Tongan royal kava ceremony (taumafa kava), seating and the order of serving show each chief's rank, and it is an essential part of a king's coronation. Captain Cook's naturalists, including Georg Forster, described the drink in 1777.
funFact: Because cultivated kava cannot set seed, every kava plant across the Pacific descends from cuttings carried by people, some over thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

wiki.extract: Kava or kava kava is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands. The name kava is from Tongan and Marquesan, meaning 'bitter'. Kava can refer to either the plant or a psychoactive beverage made from its root. The beverage is a traditional ceremonial and recreational drink from Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. Nakamals and kava bars exist in many countries. Traditional kava is made by grinding fresh or dried kava root, mixing it with water or coconut milk, and straining it into a communal bowl. Outside the South Pacific, kava is typically prepared by soaking dried root powder in water and straining it. It is consumed socially for its psychoactive effects, comparable to those produced by alcohol but without significant cognitive impairment or addiction risk. Kava also produces a numbing sensation in the mouth.

summary: A woody climbing vine from the Western Ghats of Kerala whose dried berries are the world's most traded spice. Black, white, green and red peppercorns all come from the same plant, harvested and processed differently.
nativeRange: Western Ghats, south-west India (Malabar Coast); cultivated in Vietnam, Indonesia, Brazil, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia
abilities: Climbs by roots at each node that grip tree bark
Pungency comes from piperine, which also increases absorption of curcumin and some drugs
Spikes of tiny flowers are self- and rain-pollinated
Vines produce for 20–30 years
edibleParts: dried berries (black, white, green, red peppercorns)
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice. Large amounts irritate the gut, and inhaled powder causes sneezing.

uses.use: One of the 'trikatu' (three pungents, with long pepper and ginger) to kindle digestive fire and clear mucus
Pepper for colds, coughs and as a digestive
Piperine added to curcumin supplements to raise bioavailability

medicinal.cautions: Piperine can raise blood levels of some drugs (e.g. phenytoin, propranolol) by inhibiting their metabolism.

fruit.season: Harvested 6–8 months after flowering, usually in the dry season
fruit.description: Long hanging spikes 7–15 cm carrying 50–150 small round drupes, green ripening to red.

seed.description: Each peppercorn is a single-seeded drupe about 4–6 mm; black pepper is the wrinkled, dried unripe fruit; white pepper is the smooth, cream-grey seed with the outer skin removed
seed.germination: Sow fresh ripe red berries (pulp removed) 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C in shade; slow and erratic, 3–6 weeks. Cuttings preferred

grow.water: High (2,000–3,000 mm rain), with good drainage
grow.propagation: Runner-shoot or stem cuttings of 2–3 nodes
steps: Root 2–3-node cuttings from runner shoots in shaded, moist potting mix.
Plant beside a living support tree (e.g. Erythrina, Gliricidia, coconut, areca) or a rough post 3–4 m tall, in partial shade.
Tie the vine to its support as it climbs; mulch heavily and feed with compost.
Keep soil moist but never waterlogged — wet roots invite foot rot (Phytophthora).
Pick whole spikes when 1–2 berries turn red; dry in the sun for 5–7 days until black and wrinkled, or soak ripe berries and rub off skins for white pepper.

lore: Peppercorns were stuffed in the nostrils of Ramesses II's mummy (died 1213 BCE). Alaric the Visigoth demanded 3,000 pounds of pepper as part of the ransom of Rome in 408 CE, and Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival in Calicut was driven by the pepper trade.
funFact: In medieval Europe pepper was so valuable it was used to pay rent — the origin of the term 'peppercorn rent'.

wiki.extract: Black pepper is a flowering vine in the family Piperaceae, cultivated for its fruit, which is usually dried and used as a spice and seasoning. The fruit is a drupe (stonefruit) which is about 5 mm in diameter, dark red, and contains a stone which encloses a single pepper seed. Peppercorns and the ground pepper derived from them may be described simply as pepper, or more precisely as black pepper, green pepper, or white pepper.
