summary: A small, creeping, succulent-leaved marsh herb found in wetlands across the tropics. Ayurveda prizes it as a medhya rasayana, a tonic for memory and learning, and it is one of the better-studied herbal 'nootropics'.
nativeRange: Pantropical and warm-temperate wetlands of Asia, Africa, Australia and the Americas (including the southern USA)
abilities: Contains bacosides, saponins studied for effects on memory and the survival of nerve cells
Grows submerged or emerged, rooting at every node
Tolerates brackish water
Takes up heavy metals from polluted water, which makes clean sourcing important
edibilityNote: Eaten as a bitter herb in parts of South and Southeast Asia. Collect only from clean water, as it accumulates heavy metals.

uses.use: Medhya rasayana for memory, learning, anxiety and epilepsy; given as juice, ghee (brahmi ghrita) or powder
Nirbrahmi for fever, nervous disorders and as a brain tonic
Standardised extracts trialled for memory in healthy adults and the elderly, with small benefits in some trials

compounds: bacoside A (bacoside A3, bacopaside II, bacopasaponin C)
medicinal.cautions: Effects on memory are modest and take 8–12 weeks to appear. Common side effects are nausea, cramps and diarrhoea. May slow the heart and interact with thyroid drugs and sedatives. Choose products tested for heavy metals. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.season: Most of the year in the tropics
fruit.description: Small ovoid capsule with many tiny seeds.

seed.description: Minute seeds
seed.germination: Rarely grown from seed; cuttings root within days

grow.water: Very high: bog, pond edge or submerged
steps: Push stem cuttings into wet mud or a pot standing in water
Keep warm (above 15 °C) and constantly wet
Snip shoot tips regularly to keep it bushy
Use clean water only

lore: The Charaka Samhita lists brahmi among the medhya (intellect-promoting) rasayanas. Scholars still debate whether some classical references to 'brahmi' meant this plant or Centella asiatica.
funFact: Bacopa is a common aquarium plant, and the very same species is sold in health shops as a memory tonic.

summary: A towering biennial of woodland clearings whose spotted purple bells are built for bumblebees, and whose leaves gave medicine one of its most important heart drugs. Every part is poisonous; the gap between a healing dose and a deadly one is very small.
nativeRange: Western and south-western Europe and north-western Africa; naturalised in North America, New Zealand and elsewhere
abilities: Makes cardiac glycosides such as digitoxin that strengthen and slow the heartbeat
Spotted flower tubes act as landing guides for bumblebees, its main pollinators
A single plant sheds vast numbers of dust-like seeds that persist for years in the soil
Springs up quickly after woodland is felled or burned
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous. Before flowering its leaf rosettes have been mistaken for comfrey or borage, with fatal results. Children and pets are at risk.

uses.use: Leaf preparations for dropsy (oedema), recorded by William Withering from a Shropshire family remedy
Source of digitoxin, used for heart failure and atrial fibrillation; the related D. lanata yields digoxin

medicinal.cautions: Deadly poisonous. Symptoms include vomiting, yellow-green vision, dangerous heart rhythms and death. The isolated glycosides are prescription drugs with a narrow safety margin. Never self-medicate with the plant.

fruit.description: Egg-shaped dry capsule splitting in two to release seed; poisonous.

seed.description: Minute reddish-brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Shaken from capsules by wind; persistent soil seed bank
seed.germination: Needs light; surface-sow, 2–3 weeks at 15–20 °C

grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in its second year (ornamental only)
steps: Surface-sow in late spring or summer
Plant rosettes out in autumn, away from children's play areas and edible beds
Let it flower the next summer and self-seed
Wear gloves when handling

lore: In 1785 William Withering, a Birmingham physician, published An Account of the Foxglove, describing ten years of careful dose trials for dropsy. It is a founding text of clinical pharmacology.
funFact: The name Digitalis comes from Leonhart Fuchs, who in 1542 Latinised the German Fingerhut, 'thimble', as digitalis.

wiki.extract: Digitalis purpurea, the foxglove or common foxglove, is a toxic species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae, native to and widespread throughout most of temperate Europe. It has also naturalized in parts of North America, as well as some other temperate regions. The plant is a popular garden subject, with many cultivars available. It is the original source of the heart medicine digoxin. This biennial plant grows as a rosette of leaves in the first year after sowing, before flowering and then dying in the second year. It generally produces enough seeds so that new plants will continue to grow in a garden setting.

otherNames: White man's footprint (English, from Indigenous American usage)
summary: A flat-rosetted weed of paths and farmyards so tough it thrives where it is trodden on daily. European colonists spread it around the world on their boots, and it has been one of folk medicine's standard wound leaves for at least a thousand years.
nativeRange: Europe and northern & central Asia; now cosmopolitan
abilities: Flat rosette and tough, ribbed leaves survive heavy trampling
Seeds turn sticky with mucilage when wet and hitch rides on feet, hooves and tyres
Leaves contain aucubin and acteoside, studied for anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects
A single plant can produce many thousands of long-lived seeds
edibilityNote: Young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked, but older leaves are stringy. Avoid plants from sprayed or polluted ground.

uses.use: Chewed or crushed leaf on stings, bites, cuts and burns; tea for coughs and diarrhoea
Adopted by many nations after European contact as a poultice for wounds, snakebite and boils
Bartang seeds and leaves as a cooling demulcent for dysentery and coughs
Plantago herb and seed (cheqiancao, cheqianzi) to drain damp, for urinary difficulty and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Generally safe. The pollen is allergenic. In 1997 supplements labelled 'plantain' were found to be contaminated with Digitalis, so buy only from reputable sources.

fruit.description: Small capsule whose top pops off like a lid, on dense spikes.

seed.description: Small, angular brown seeds that become sticky when wet
seed.dispersal: Sticky seeds carried on feet, animals and vehicles
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–3 weeks at 15–25 °C

steps: Scatter seed on the surface in spring
Leave in a lawn or path edge where it is wanted
Pick young leaves for food or poultices
Remove seed spikes if you want to stop it spreading

lore: The Old English Nine Herbs Charm calls it Wegbrade, 'way-broad', the 'mother of herbs' that withstands carts and riders. Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha (1855) records the Indigenous name 'White-Man's Foot'.
funFact: The name Plantago comes from the Latin planta, 'sole of the foot', after its flat leaves lying on the ground like footprints.

gerard.title: Of Land Plantaine
gerard.names: Plantaine is called in Latine Plantago, and in Greeke ἀρνόγλωσσος, and Arnoglossa, that is to say, Lambes toong. The Apothecaries keepe the Latine name: in Italian Piantagine, and Piantagine: in Spanish Lhantem: the Germaines Wegrich: in Low Dutch Weechbree: in English Plantaine and Weybred: in French Plantain.
gerard.place: The greater Plantaines do grow almost euery where. The lesser Plantaines are found on the sea coastes, and banks of great riuers, which are somtimes washed with brackish water.
gerard.time: They are to be seene from Aprill vnto September.
gerard.temperature: Plantaine, as Galen saith, is of a mixt temperature: for it hath in it a certaine waterie coldnesse with a little harshnesse, earthie, drie, and cold. Therefore they are cold and drie in the second degree. To be briefe, they are drie without biting, and cold without benumming.
gerard.vertues: Plantaine is good for vlcers that are of hard curation, for fluxes, issues, rewmes and rottennesse, and for the bloodie flixe. It staieth bleeding, it healeth vp hollow sores, and concauate vlcers as well olde as new. Of all the Plantaines the greatest is the best, and excelleth the rest in facultie and vertue. The iuice or decoction of Plantaine drunken, stoppeth the bloodie flixe and all other fluxes of the belly, stoppeth the pissing of blood, spitting of blood, with all other issues of blood in man or woman, and the desire to vomite. Plantaine leaues stamped and made into a Tansie, with the yelks of egges, staieth the inordinate fluxe of the termes, although it haue continued many yeeres. The roote of Plantaine with the seede boiled in white wine and drunke, openeth the conduites or passages of the liuer and kidneies, cure the iaundies, and vlcerations of the kidneies and bladder. The iuice dropped into the eies, doth coole the heate or inflammation thereof.

otherNames: Luǎn yè chēqián 卵叶车前 (Chinese)
summary: A small, woolly desert plantain whose seed husks swell to many times their volume in water, forming a soft gel. The husk is the world's most widely used bulk-forming fibre supplement and laxative.
nativeRange: Canary Islands and the Mediterranean, North Africa and West Asia to Pakistan and north-western India; cultivated mainly in Gujarat and Rajasthan
abilities: Seed husk mucilage (an arabinoxylan) absorbs many times its weight in water
Gel softens stool, slows sugar absorption and binds bile acids, lowering LDL cholesterol
Completes its life cycle in about four months of the cool dry season
edibilityNote: Husk is taken stirred into plenty of water or used in gluten-free baking. Always take it with enough fluid.

uses.use: Isapghol as a cooling demulcent for dysentery, diarrhoea, constipation and urinary burning
Husk for constipation, diarrhoea and to soothe the gut (introduced via Persian medicine)
Bulk-forming laxative; for irritable bowel syndrome and as a cholesterol-lowering fibre (FDA heart-health claim, 1998)

medicinal.cautions: Take with at least a full glass of water: dry husk can swell and choke or block the oesophagus or bowel. Do not use with bowel obstruction or difficulty swallowing. Take other medicines 1–2 hours apart. Inhaled dust has caused asthma and anaphylaxis in healthcare and factory workers.

fruit.description: Small capsule on dense spikes with two boat-shaped seeds.

seed.description: Boat-shaped, pinkish-grey seeds coated in a translucent husk
seed.dispersal: Seeds turn sticky when wet and cling to animals
seed.germination: 4–7 days at 20–25 °C

grow.zones: Annual; cool-season crop in warm climates (USDA 8–11)
grow.water: Low; dry weather at ripening is essential
steps: Sow broadcast in the cool season on fine, well-drained soil
Irrigate lightly and only as needed
Harvest when spikes turn reddish-brown, in dry weather (rain at ripening makes seeds swell and shatter)
Thresh and mill to separate the husk

lore: Persian physicians named it asp-ghol, 'horse's ear', after the shape of the seed. It entered Indian practice through Unani medicine under the Mughals, and India now grows most of the world's supply.
funFact: Stirred into water, psyllium husk sets into a thick gel within minutes, which is why bakers use it as a binder in gluten-free bread.

summary: The grain that feeds more than half of humanity, domesticated from wild Oryza rufipogon in the Yangtze valley about 9,000 years ago. Rice can grow in standing water because hollow channels in its stems pipe air down to its roots.
nativeRange: Domesticated in the Yangtze valley of China (japonica) and later hybridised in South Asia (indica); grown in tropical and warm-temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Aerenchyma tissue carries oxygen from leaves to roots in flooded soil
Some varieties carry the Sub1 gene, letting them survive two weeks fully underwater
Paddy fields support fish, frogs and ducks in traditional integrated systems
The International Rice Genebank in the Philippines holds over 130,000 rice accessions
edibleParts: fermented into wine, vinegar and sake
edibilityNote: Cooked grain is safe. Rice can accumulate inorganic arsenic from soil and water; rinsing and cooking in excess water reduces it. Cooked rice left warm can grow Bacillus cereus.

uses.use: Rice congee as a gentle food to strengthen digestion; red yeast rice (fermented with Monascus) for blood circulation
Rice-based oral rehydration solutions for diarrhoea
Navara rice used in Kerala's 'Njavarakizhi' massage therapy

medicinal.cautions: Arsenic in rice products, especially for infants. Red yeast rice contains lovastatin and shares statin side effects.

fruit.season: Late summer to autumn in temperate zones; multiple crops a year in the tropics
fruit.description: Drooping panicle of 50–500 spikelets, each enclosing a single grain in a tough, ridged, straw-coloured husk (hull).

seed.description: Paddy grain is oblong, 5–10 mm, enclosed in a golden, ridged, sometimes awned hull; dehulled brown rice is smooth, slim to round and tan, red or black, with a white starchy interior
seed.dispersal: Humans; wild relatives shatter and float on water
seed.germination: Soak 24 hours, keep moist and warm (25–35 °C); sprouts in 2–4 days

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; needs 3–6 frost-free months above about 20 °C
grow.water: Very high (paddy) or high rainfall (upland rice)
grow.soil: Heavy clay or silt that holds water; pH 5–7
grow.propagation: Seed, direct-sown or transplanted as seedlings
steps: Soak seed for a day and sow thickly in a moist nursery bed or trays.
After 3–4 weeks, transplant seedlings in clumps of 2–3, about 20 cm apart, into a levelled, puddled (muddy) bed or tub.
Keep 5–10 cm of standing water over the soil through growth to suppress weeds; drain briefly mid-season to strengthen roots.
Drain the field 2–3 weeks before harvest, when panicles droop and grains turn golden.
Cut, dry the sheaves, thresh, then dry grain to about 14% moisture before hulling.

lore: In Japan, the emperor ritually plants and harvests rice in the palace paddies, and Shinto's Inari is the god of rice. The Ifugao rice terraces of the Philippines, a UNESCO World Heritage site, are popularly said to be 2,000 years old, though radiocarbon studies suggest many were built in the last 400 years or so.
funFact: The 1966 'miracle rice' IR8 from the International Rice Research Institute roughly doubled yields across Asia and averted predicted famines.

wiki.extract: Oryza sativa, having the common name Asian cultivated rice, is the much more common of the two rice species cultivated as a cereal, the other species being O. glaberrima, African rice. It was first domesticated in the Yangtze River basin in China 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.

gerard.title: Of Rice
gerard.names: The Grecians call it $\text{ὄρυζα}$, or as Theophrastus faith $\text{ὄρυζον}$: the Latines keepe the Greeke worde Oryza: in French it is called Riz: in the Germaine toong Rifz, and Rys: in Englifh Rife.
gerard.place: It groweth in the territories of the Bactrians, in Babilon, in Sufium, & in the lower part of Syria. It groweth in thefe daies, not onely in thefe countries before named, but alfo in the fortunate Ilands, and in Spaine, from whence it is brought vnto vs, purged and prepared, as we fee after the maner of French barly. It profpereth beft in fenny and waterifh places.
gerard.time: It is fowen in the fpring in India, as Eratosthenes witneffeth, when it is moiftened with fommer flowers.
gerard.vertues: Galen faith, that all men vfe to ftaie the belly with this graine, being boiled after the fame maner that Chondrus is. In England we vfe to make with milke and Rife, a certaine food, or pottage which doth both meanely binde the belly, and alfo nourifh. Many other good kinds of foode is made with this graine, as thofe that are skilfull in cookerie can tell.

summary: A grass that grows into a forest. Moso shoots can push up close to a metre a day and reach full height of 20 m or more in a couple of months. It is China's most important timber bamboo, used for scaffolding, flooring, textiles and the spring shoots of East Asian cooking.
nativeRange: Central and southern China and Taiwan; long cultivated in Japan
abilities: New culms can grow close to 1 m in a day at peak growth
A culm reaches full height in one season and then hardens for several years
Spreads by vigorous running rhizomes, forming huge connected groves
Flowers only at long intervals; a Japanese stand flowered 67 years after sowing, then died
edibilityNote: Shoots must be peeled and boiled before eating: raw shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides (taxiphyllin) that release cyanide.

fruit.description: Grass-like grains produced only in rare flowering events.

seed.description: Grain-like caryopsis
seed.germination: Sow fresh at 20–25 °C; viability drops within months

grow.timeToHarvest: Shoots in spring after 3–5 years; timber culms at 4–6 years
steps: Plant a rhizome division in spring in deep, rich soil
Install a rhizome barrier at least 60 cm deep, since running bamboo invades
Water and mulch heavily
Harvest shoots as they emerge in spring and boil them before eating

lore: Chinese literati such as Su Shi praised bamboo, and moso is part of the story of Meng Zong, one of the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, who wept in a winter grove until bamboo shoots sprang up for his sick mother; the Japanese name 'mōsōchiku' honours him.
funFact: A moso grove is often a single connected plant, with every culm linked by an underground rhizome network.

wiki.extract: Phyllostachys edulis, the mōsō bamboo, or tortoise-shell bamboo, or mao zhu, , is a temperate species of giant timber bamboo native to China and Taiwan and naturalised elsewhere, including Japan where it is widely distributed from south of Hokkaido to Kagoshima. The edulis part of the Latin name refers to its edible shoots. This bamboo can reach heights of up to 28 m (92 ft). This particular species of bamboo is the most common species used in the bamboo textile industry of China and other countries, for the production of rayon. Moso is less cold-hardy than many Phyllostachy, surviving at a reduced height down to −15 °C (5 °F).

plates.title: Description of China, Korea, and Tibet
plates.author: Du Halde
plates.desc: A comprehensive botanical plate illustrating various Chinese plants including Rhubarb, Ginseng, Cotton, Varnish Tree, Tea Shrub, Fu lin, Lichi, Jaca, Betel, and Bamboo.
plates.long: This detailed botanical plate from Du Halde's 'Description of China' (1738) showcases the diverse flora of the region, including economically and medicinally significant plants like Ginseng, Tea, and Rhubarb. The engraving features anatomical details of roots and flowers alongside full-plant depictions, reflecting the era's rigorous approach to documenting global natural history. The plate is dedi

plates.title: Itinerary: Voyage to the East or Portuguese Indies
plates.author: Jan Huyghen van Linschoten
plates.desc: A hand-colored engraving depicting three types of exotic flora from the East Indies: Bamboo (Bambus), the Banyan tree (Arbore de Rays ofte Wortelboom), and the Durian tree (Durioens).
plates.long: This plate from Jan Huyghen van Linschoten’s 'Itinerario' (1596) provides a scientific and visual record of Southeast Asian flora, including bamboo, the sprawling Banyan tree, and the spiky Durian fruit. Engraved by Johannes Baptista van Doetechum, these images were crucial in shaping the European imagination of the 'Orient' and served as a practical guide for Dutch merchants and explorers.

plates.title: 本草綱目圖3卷. [3]
plates.author: Li Shizhen
plates.desc: A 2x2 grid of woodcut illustrations depicting botanical specimens like bamboo and a tree, alongside a water buffalo.
plates.long: A collection of woodblock illustrations featuring bamboo, a tree, and a water buffalo. These images served as visual aids for identifying medicinal sources in the Bencao Gangmu, the most comprehensive medical book in the history of traditional Chinese medicine.

plates.title: The Embassy of the Dutch East India Company to the Tartar Cham
plates.author: Johan Nieuhof
plates.desc: A detailed copperplate engraving showing two types of tropical plants: rattan (Rottingh) and bamboo (Bamboes).
plates.long: This engraving depicts rattan palms on the left and bamboo stalks on the right, both labeled in Dutch. In the background, a landscape features a body of water and a distant city with a prominent pagoda. The image illustrates the botanical species described in the text as being native to the East Indies.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui (Vol. 69)
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a bamboo stalk with fresh sheaths.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1609 encyclopedia 'Sancai Tuhui' depicts a bamboo stalk, specifically focusing on 'xiantuo' or fresh bamboo sheaths. The work reflects the Ming dynasty's commitment to documenting the natural world through detailed and standardized visual representations. Such illustrations served as both scientific records and artistic models for scholars and artists of the peri

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui (Vol. 69)
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of bamboo branches with calligraphic inscriptions.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts bamboo branches, a classic subject in Chinese art representing resilience and integrity. The image captures the dynamic movement of 'wind-blown branches' (風枝) and 'sturdy stalks' (幹挺然), showcasing the high level of woodblock printing craftsmanship during the Ming dynasty which aimed to replicate the fluid lines of ink painting.

plates.title: Illustrated Compendium of Materia Medica (Vol. 19)
plates.author: 吳其濬
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine, identified as Yuzhizi (Akebia), twining around a bamboo stalk.
plates.long: This woodcut from Wu Qijun's 1848 work, 'Illustrated Investigation of the Names and Realities of Plants,' depicts the Yuzhizi (Akebia) vine. The illustration captures the plant's characteristic climbing habit as it wraps around a bamboo pole, providing a clear visual reference for identification in traditional Chinese medicine.

plates.title: 竹譜·卷五~卷七 (vol 2)
plates.author: 李衎
plates.desc: Woodblock print of a bamboo stalk with nodes and branches.
plates.long: A detailed woodblock print depicts a bamboo culm with several nodes and internodes. Thin, segmented branches extend from each node, and solid black shading on the right side of the main stalk indicates depth. This illustration is part of the Siku Quanshu edition of the Bamboo Manual.

plates.title: 竹譜·卷五~卷七 (vol 2)
plates.author: 李衎
plates.desc: A woodblock print illustration of bamboo stalks and leaves.
plates.long: A thick bamboo culm rises diagonally across the frame, accompanied by thinner branches and clusters of pointed leaves. This woodblock print follows the aesthetic of traditional Chinese ink wash painting manuals, emphasizing the structural elegance of the plant. The composition uses varying line weights to suggest depth and texture in the bamboo stalks.

plates.title: 竹譜·卷八~卷十 (vol 3)
plates.author: 李衎
plates.desc: Woodblock illustration of a bamboo branch with spotted leaves.
plates.long: A woodblock print depicts a segmented bamboo stalk with five large leaves. The leaves are filled with a dense pattern of white dots on a black ground, representing the 'cinnabar-spotted bamboo' variety. This stylistic choice illustrates a specific botanical type described in the accompanying text as having spots like sesame seeds.

summary: A giant perennial grass domesticated in New Guinea about 8,000 years ago whose stems store sucrose at up to 20% of their weight. Its spread shaped world history — from Indian sugar crystallisation in the Gupta era to the Atlantic slave trade and Caribbean plantations.
nativeRange: New Guinea (derived from Saccharum robustum); modern canes are hybrids with S. spontaneum; grown throughout the tropics and subtropics
abilities: C4 photosynthesis makes it one of the most efficient converters of sunlight into biomass
Stems store sucrose at up to about 20% of fresh weight
Grows 3–6 m tall and regrows from the stubble ('ratoon') for several harvests
Crushed fibre (bagasse) fuels the mills that process it
edibleParts: stem juice (fresh, boiled into jaggery, panela, sugar, molasses, fermented to rum)
edibilityNote: Juice and chewed stems are safe. Refined sugar in excess is linked to tooth decay, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

uses.use: Fresh cane juice and jaggery (guḍa) as a cooling tonic and for jaundice; jaggery as the sweet base of many remedies
Policosanol from cane wax developed as a cholesterol-lowering drug (later trials outside Cuba were negative)

medicinal.cautions: Sugar overconsumption; stem edges and leaves are sharp.

fruit.season: Flowers in the short days of late autumn–winter in the tropics (rarely sets seed)
fruit.description: A large, silky, silvery-plumed panicle (arrow) up to 1 m long; most commercial canes rarely set seed.

seed.description: Minute, brown, oblong grains about 1–1.5 mm, enclosed in fluffy hairy spikelets; produced mostly in breeding stations
seed.germination: Breeding only: surface-sow fuzz at 30 °C under high humidity; farmers plant stem cuttings ('setts')

grow.timeToHarvest: 10–18 months; ratoon crops each year after
steps: Cut mature, healthy canes into setts of 2–3 nodes (buds).
Lay setts horizontally in furrows 10–15 cm deep, 1–1.5 m apart, buds to the sides, and cover with 5 cm of soil.
Keep moist and feed with nitrogen and potassium; earth up soil around the base as shoots grow to prevent lodging.
Harvest when the cane is mature (sweet tasting at the top as well as the base, 10–18 months), cutting close to the ground.
Crush canes to extract juice — drink fresh or boil down slowly into jaggery or syrup. New shoots (ratoons) regrow for 3–5 years.

lore: Alexander's admiral Nearchus reported Indian 'reeds that make honey without bees' in 325 BCE, and the word 'sugar' comes from Sanskrit 'śarkarā' via Persian and Arabic. Columbus carried cane to Hispaniola on his second voyage in 1493.
funFact: Sugarcane is the world's largest crop by harvested weight, about 1.9 billion tonnes a year.

wiki.extract: Saccharum officinarum is a large, strong-growing species of grass in the sugarcane genus. Its stout stalks are rich in sucrose, a disaccharide sugar which accumulates in the stalk internodes. It originated in New Guinea, and is now cultivated in tropical and subtropical countries worldwide for the production of sugar, ethanol and other products. It is one of the most productive and most intensively cultivated kinds of sugarcane.

plates.title: De medicinali materia libri sex
plates.author: Dioscorides
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of Arundo Saccharata (sugarcane) within a frame
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates Arundo Saccharata, or sugarcane. It features a detailed view of the segmented stalk and root system, alongside a separate detail of the stem, reflecting the scientific observation characteristic of 16th-century botanical texts.

The illustration serves as an early scientific record of the plant's morphology, emphasizing the structural characteristics essential for identification. Such botanical prints were pivotal i

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica
plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of sugarcane (甘蔗) showing stalks, leaves, and roots.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts sugarcane (甘蔗, gānzhè) from the 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica), a monumental work on Chinese medicine by Li Shizhen. The drawing clearly shows the segmented stalks, tufted leaves, and fibrous roots, serving as a visual guide for identification in traditional pharmacology.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a sugarcane plant (Saccharum officinarum), meticulously detailing its segmented stalk, long tapering leaves, and root system. It appears in a 17th-century botanical treatise, reflecting the era's growing scientific interest in New World flora and its economic potential.

plates.title: De Indiae utriusque re naturali et medica

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a sugarcane plant, identified in the accompanying Latin text as 'Viba & Tacomaree.' The illustration meticulously details the plant's segmented stalk, fibrous roots, and long, blade-like leaves, serving as an early scientific record of tropical flora. Such images were essential for European naturalists seeking to document and understand the botanical diversity of the Americas

It comes from Wu Qijun's 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' (Illustrated Investigation of the Names and Realities of Plants), a monumental work of 19th-century Chinese botany known for its accurate and detailed depictions of flora.

The image reflects the Ming Dynasty's interest in documenting the natural world and agricultural products. The clear, bold lines are characteristic of the woodblock printing techniques of the period.

gerard.title: Of Sugar Cane
gerard.names: The Latines haue called this plant Arundo Saccharina, with this additament Indica: bicause it was first known, or brought from India. Of some it is called Calamus Saccharatus: in English Sugar Cane: in Dutch Suijckerriet.
gerard.place: The sugar Cane groweth in many parts of Europe at this day, as Spaine, Portugale, Olbia and in Prouence. It groweth also in Barbarie, generally almost euery where in the Canarie Ilands, and in those of Madera, in the east & west Indies, and manie other places.
gerard.time: This Cane is planted at any time of the yeere in those hot countries where it doth naturally growe, by reason they feare no frostes to hurt the yoong shootes at their first planting.
gerard.vertues: The Sugar or iuice of this Reede is of a temperate qualitie: it drieth and clenseth the stomacke, maketh smooth the roughnesse of the breast and lungs, cleereth the voice, and putteth away hoarsnes, the cough, and all sowrenes and bitternes, as Isaac saith in Dictis. The use. Of the iuice of this Reede is made the most pleasant and profitable sweete, called Sugar, whereof is made infinite confections, confectures, sirupes, and such like, as also preseruing and conseruing of sundrie fruits, herbes and flowres; as Roses, Violets, Rosemary, flowres, and such like, which still retaine with them the name of Sugar, as Sugar Roset, Sugar Violet, &c. The which to write of would require a peculiar volume, and not pertinent vnto this historie, for that it is not my purpose to make of my booke a confectionarie, a Sugar bakers furnace, a gentlewomans preseruing pan, nor yet an apothecaries shop or dispensatorie, but onely to touch the chiefest matter that I purposed to handle in the beginning; that is, the nature, properties, and descriptions of plants.

summary: A heat- and drought-hardy grain domesticated in the eastern Sahel of Sudan around 5,000–6,000 years ago, and the fifth most important cereal in the world. It feeds hundreds of millions across Africa and India, and its stalks give sugar syrup, broom straw and fodder.
nativeRange: North-east Africa (Sudan, Ethiopia and the eastern Sahel); grown in semi-arid regions worldwide
abilities: C4 photosynthesis and a waxy leaf bloom let it yield where maize fails in heat and drought
Can go dormant in drought and resume growing when rain returns
Roots exude sorgoleone, a compound that suppresses nearby weeds
Young plants and regrowth contain dhurrin, which releases cyanide
edibleParts: grain (flour for roti, injera-style flatbreads, porridge, couscous; brewed into beer)
edibilityNote: Grain is safe and gluten-free. Young leaves, shoots and frost- or drought-stressed regrowth contain dhurrin, which can poison grazing livestock with cyanide.

uses.use: Red leaf-sheath extract (from dye sorghum) as a blood tonic for anaemia
Jowar as a light, cooling grain for digestive and urinary complaints

medicinal.cautions: Forage is cyanogenic to livestock, especially young or stressed regrowth.

fruit.season: End of the rainy season / late summer–autumn
fruit.description: Compact or open panicle (head) at the top of a stalk 1–4 m tall, bearing hundreds of round grains.

seed.description: Round to slightly oval grains 3–5 mm, white, cream, yellow, red, brown or near-black, often partly enclosed in papery glumes
seed.germination: Sow 2–4 cm deep once soil exceeds about 15 °C; emerges in 4–10 days

grow.soil: Tolerates poor, sandy, clay or slightly saline soils, pH 5.5–8.5
steps: Sow in warm soil after the rains start or after frost, 2–4 cm deep, 15–20 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart.
Thin seedlings and weed in the first month; little care is needed afterwards.
Water only in prolonged drought; avoid grazing animals on young or stressed plants.
Protect ripening heads from birds with netting or paper bags.
Cut heads when the grain is hard and can't be dented with a fingernail, dry them, then thresh by beating.

lore: Sorghum grains impressed into pottery at Kassala in Sudan are among the earliest evidence of its domestication. In China, sorghum is distilled into baijiu spirits such as Moutai, and the novel and film 'Red Sorghum' made its fields an icon of rural China.
funFact: Sorghum stalks can also be pressed for sweet juice: 'sorghum molasses' was a staple sweetener in the 19th-century American South.

wiki.extract: Sorghum bicolor, commonly called sorghum and also known as broomcorn, great millet, Indian millet, Guinea corn, jowar, or milo, is a species in the grass genus Sorghum. It is typically an annual, but some cultivars are perennial. It grows in clumps that may reach over 4 metres (13 ft) high. The grain is 2 to 4 millimetres in diameter.

plates.title: Notable Commentaries on the History of Plants
plates.author: Leonhart Fuchs
plates.desc: Full-page botanical woodcut of Sorghum bicolor, identified as 'SORGI' and 'Welscher Hirß'.
plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts Sorghum bicolor, known in the 16th century as 'Sorgi' or 'Welscher Hirß'. It is a prime example of the revolutionary botanical illustrations in Leonhart Fuchs's 1542 herbal, which prioritized direct observation from nature over medieval tradition. The image captures the plant's entire structure, from its fibrous root system to the dense seed head and elongated leaves.

plates.title: De medicinali materia libri sex
plates.author: Dioscorides
plates.desc: Two botanical woodcuts depicting Sorghum (Sorgi) and Millet (Milium) plants.
plates.long: These two detailed woodcuts illustrate Sorghum and Millet, cereal grains described in Dioscorides' influential herbal. Produced in 1552, these images represent the Renaissance shift toward empirical observation in natural history, providing readers with accurate visual references for identifying medicinal and dietary plants.

plates.title: Notable Commentaries on the History of Plants
plates.author: Leonhart Fuchs
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a Sorghum plant (Sorgi).
plates.long: A full-page botanical illustration shows a Sorghum plant, labeled as Sorgi and Welscher Hirß. The image depicts the fibrous root system, numerous long blade-like leaves, and a dense seed head at the top of the central stalk.

plates.title: On Medical Materials in Six Books
plates.author: Dioscorides
plates.desc: Botanical woodcuts of Sorgi (Sorghum) and Milium (Millet)
plates.long: This page features two detailed woodcuts illustrating Sorgi (Sorghum) and Milium (Millet). These botanical depictions were essential for identifying plants used in medicine and agriculture during the 16th century, as documented in Dioscorides' influential work.

plates.long: A large-scale botanical woodcut depicting 'Milium Indicum', commonly known as Indian millet or sorghum. This illustration is part of Pietro Andrea Mattioli's influential commentaries on the medical works of Dioscorides, showcasing the Renaissance commitment to empirical observation in natural history. The print captures the plant's entire structure, including its distinctive seed heads and root sy

plates.title: A New Herbal, or History of Plants
plates.author: Rembert Dodoens (trans. Henry Lyte)
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of 'Indian Panick' (sorghum), showing a robust plant with broad leaves and a dense seed head.
plates.long: Depicting 'Indian Panick' or sorghum, this woodcut highlights the plant's dense, upright seed head and broad foliage. It reflects the expanding botanical knowledge of the period as explorers and naturalists documented crops from different regions.

plates.title: Six Groups of the History of Plants
plates.author: Rembert Dodoens
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a sorghum plant, showing its roots, stalks, leaves, and seed heads.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates 'Melica sive Sorghum,' commonly known today as sorghum. The image meticulously details the plant's robust root system, jointed stalks, and distinctive panicles of seeds, reflecting the growing interest in natural history and accurate botanical documentation during the 16th century.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica: Illustrated Volume Middle of Middle

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a sorghum plant (Shushu).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a sorghum plant, known in Chinese as 'Shushu', as featured in the 1596 edition of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica). Compiled by Li Shizhen, this work is a cornerstone of traditional Chinese medicine, and its illustrations were crucial for the accurate identification of natural substances used in healing.

plates.title: Hortus Eystettensis
plates.author: Basilius Besler
plates.desc: Botanical engraving of two sorghum plants, identified as 'Sorgum fructu rubro' (red-fruited) and 'Sorgo fructu albo' (white-fruited).
plates.long: This detailed engraving from Basilius Besler's monumental 'Hortus Eystettensis' (1613/1640) depicts two varieties of sorghum, distinguished by their fruit color. The work is celebrated for its scientific accuracy and artistic elegance, capturing the intricate textures of the seed heads and the graceful, rhythmic curves of the leaves and roots.

plates.title: Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao (Vol. 1)
plates.author: 吳其濬
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a cereal plant, likely a type of millet or sorghum, showing its long leaves and branching seed heads.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration is from Wu Qijun's 1848 masterpiece, 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' (Illustrated Investigation of Plant Names and Realities). It depicts a cereal plant with remarkable clarity, showcasing the artist's ability to capture botanical details through traditional woodblock printing. This work is considered one of the most important and accurate botanical records of the Qing Dynasty.

gerard.title: Of Turkie Millet
gerard.names: It is called of the Insubers, Melegua, and Melega: in Latine Melica: in Hetruria Saggina: in other places of Italy Sorgho: in Portingale Milium saburrum: in English Turkie Mill or Turkie Hirsse.
gerard.place: It ioieth in a fat and moist ground: it groweth in Italy, Spaine, and other hot regions.
gerard.time: This is one of the sommer graines: it is ripe in Autumne.
gerard.vertues: The seed of Turkie Mill is like vnto Panicke in taste and temperature: the countrie people sometimes make bread heerof, but it is brittle and of little nourishment, and for the most part it serueth to fatten hens and pigeons with.

summary: Bread wheat is a hexaploid hybrid of three wild grasses, formed when cultivated emmer crossed with goatgrass near the Caspian about 9,000 years ago. Grown on more land than any other crop, it supplies about a fifth of all calories humans eat.
nativeRange: Of cultivated origin in the Fertile Crescent and south-west of the Caspian (Transcaucasia/northern Iran); grown on every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Hexaploid: carries three complete genomes (A, B and D) from three ancestral species
Gluten proteins form an elastic network that traps gas, letting dough rise
Domestic wheat lost the 'shattering' trait, so ripe grain stays on the ear until harvested
Winter wheat needs cold vernalisation before it will flower
edibilityNote: Grain is a staple. Gluten triggers coeliac disease in about 1% of people; wheat is also a common allergen. Grain infected with ergot fungus is toxic.

uses.use: Wheat porridges for convalescents and bran poultices
Wheat bran as a bulk-forming laxative with good trial evidence for constipation

medicinal.cautions: Coeliac disease, wheat allergy and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity.

fruit.season: Early to midsummer (winter wheat); late summer (spring wheat)
fruit.description: Dense ear (spike) of 30–60 grains arranged in spikelets, golden when ripe, awned or awnless.

seed.description: Oval to egg-shaped grain 5–7 mm, with a deep crease along one side and a tuft of fine hairs at the tip; red-brown, amber or white, hard and glassy or soft and floury
seed.germination: Sow 2.5–4 cm deep at 4–25 °C; emerges in 5–10 days. Winter varieties need weeks of cold to flower

grow.zones: Annual crop: winter wheat in USDA 3–8; spring wheat in short-summer regions
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or clay loam, pH 6–7.5
grow.timeToHarvest: Winter wheat 8–10 months; spring wheat 90–120 days
steps: Prepare a fine, firm seedbed; sow winter wheat in autumn or spring wheat as early as the soil can be worked, about 2.5–4 cm deep in rows 15–20 cm apart (or broadcast and rake in).
Keep weeds down in the first weeks; a small plot can be hoed between rows.
Feed with nitrogen (compost or fertiliser) in early spring as the plants begin to stretch.
Harvest when the straw is golden and a grain dented with a thumbnail is hard; cut and bundle stems into sheaves to dry for a week.
Thresh by beating sheaves in a sack or on a tarp, then winnow in a breeze to blow away the chaff.

lore: Wheat was one of the 'founder crops' of Neolithic agriculture at sites like Abu Hureyra and Göbekli Tepe's region, and Egyptian tombs held bread loaves for the afterlife. In the Lord's Prayer and the Eucharist, wheaten bread became the central Christian symbol of sustenance.
funFact: The bread-wheat genome is about five times larger than the human genome.

wiki.extract: Common wheat, also known as bread wheat, is a cultivated wheat species. It originated around 8,000 years ago, from the hybridization of an already existing domesticated variety of wheat and the wild goatgrass in the South Caucasus or southwestern Caspian area. About 95% of wheat produced worldwide is this species; it is the most widely grown of all crops and the cereal with the highest monetary yield.

plates.title: On the Names of Plants
plates.author: Hieronymus Bock (Tragus)
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a wheat plant (Triticum aestivum) showing stalks, grain heads, and roots.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts Triticum aestivum, or common wheat, from a 16th-century botanical treatise. The illustration meticulously details the plant's morphology, including the bearded spikes, slender stalks, and root system, reflecting the era's growing emphasis on empirical observation in natural history.

gerard.title: Of Corne
gerard.names: Wheate is called of the Grecians πυρὸς: of the Latines Triticum. Triticum doth generally signifie any kind of corne, which is threshed forth of the eares, & made cleane by fanning, or such ordinary meanes. The Germaines call it Weitsen: in low Dutch Tarwe: in Italian Grano: the Spaniards Trigo: the French men Bled, ou Fourment: in England we call the first white Wheate, and Flaxen Wheate.
gerard.place: Wheate groweth almost in all the countries of the world that are inhabited and manured, and requireth a fruitfull and fat soile, and rather sunnie and drie, than waterie grounds and shadowy: for in a drie ground as Columella reporteth, it groweth harder, and better compact: in a moist & darke soile, it degenerateth somtime to be of another kinde.
gerard.time: They are most commonly sowen in the fall of the leafe or Autumne: sometime in the spring. It is sowen in Autumne or the fall of the leafe, and oftentimes in the spring, and for that cause hath been called Trimestre or three months graine, it bringeth…
gerard.temperature: The kindes of Wheate according to their naturall qualities, are hot and moist in the first degree, and drie in the middle of the second. Wheate saith Galen is very much vsed of men, and with greatest profit.
gerard.vertues: Rawe Wheate saith Dioscorides, being eaten, breedeth woormes in the belly: being chewed and applied doth cure the biting of madde dogs. The flower of Wheate being boiled with hony and water, or with oyle and water, taketh away all inflammations or hot swellings. The bran of Wheate boiled in strong vineger, clenseth away scurffe and dry scales, and dissolueth the beginning of all hot swellings, if it be laid vnto them. And boiled with the decoction of Rue, it slaketh the swellings in womens brests. The graines of white Wheat, as Pliny writeth in his 22. booke, & 7. chap. being dried browne, but not burnt, & the powder thereof mixed with white wine, is good for watering eies, if it be laid therto. The dried powder of red Wheate, boiled with vineger, helpeth the shrinking of sinews. The meale of Wheate, mingled with the iuice of Henbane, and plaisterwise applied, appeaseth inflammations, as Ignis sacer, or S. Anthonies fire, and such like: staying the fluxe of humors from the ioints, which the Grecians call Rheumismata.

summary: Bred about 9,000 years ago in Mexico's Balsas River valley from teosinte, a wild grass with tiny, rock-hard seeds. Maize is now the world's most-produced grain by weight and cannot survive without people, since its kernels never fall free of the cob.
nativeRange: Domesticated in south-western Mexico (Balsas valley) from Zea mays subsp. parviglumis; grown worldwide
abilities: C4 photosynthesis makes it one of the most productive crops in heat and strong light
Each silk is a pollen tube channel leading to one kernel
Kernels remain locked on the cob, so maize depends entirely on humans to sow it
Grown in the 'Three Sisters' polyculture: beans climb maize stalks and squash shades the soil
edibilityNote: Safe when cooked. A diet dependent on untreated maize causes pellagra (niacin deficiency); nixtamalisation with lime, as practised in Mesoamerica, prevents it. Mouldy maize may carry aflatoxins.

uses.use: Corn silk (yù mǐ xū) as a diuretic for oedema and urinary complaints
Corn-silk tea and atole (maize gruel) for the sick and nursing mothers

medicinal.cautions: Pellagra risk where maize is the main food and is not nixtamalised.

fruit.description: Female inflorescence (ear) 15–30 cm wrapped in green husks with silky threads, bearing 8–24 rows of kernels on a central cob.

seed.description: Wedge- to tooth-shaped kernels 8–12 mm, smooth and glossy; yellow, white, red, blue-purple or multicoloured; dent types show a dimple on top, flint types are round and hard
seed.germination: Sow 3–5 cm deep once soil exceeds 10–12 °C; emerges in 5–10 days

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; frost-free season of 70–120+ days
grow.water: Moderate–high, especially at tasselling and silking
steps: After the last frost, sow seeds 3–5 cm deep, 25–30 cm apart, in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row — maize is wind-pollinated.
Feed generously (it is a heavy nitrogen feeder) and keep weeds down while young; or interplant with climbing beans and squash in the Three Sisters pattern.
Water deeply when tassels and silks appear; drought then leaves gaps on the cob.
Pick sweetcorn about three weeks after silking, when silks are brown and a pierced kernel gives milky juice.
For dry grain or popcorn, leave cobs on the plant until husks are papery, then dry further indoors and shell.

lore: In the K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh, the gods finally made true humans out of maize dough after failed attempts with mud and wood. The Aztec honoured maize deities such as Centeotl and Chicomecōātl.
funFact: Maize cobs about 6,250 years old from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca are tiny — one is only about 2.5 cm long.

wiki.extract: Maize, also known as corn, is a tall stout grass that produces cereal grain. The leafy stalk of the plant gives rise to male inflorescences or tassels which produce pollen, and female inflorescences called ears. The ears yield grain, known as kernels or seeds. In modern commercial varieties, these are usually yellow or white; other varieties can be of many colors. Maize was domesticated by indigenous peoples in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte. Native Americans planted it alongside beans and squashes in the Three Sisters polyculture.

gerard.title: Of Turkie corne
gerard.names: Turky wheat is called of some Frumentum Turcicum, and Milium Indicum. Strabo, Eratosthenes, Onesicritus, Plinie and others, haue contended about the name heereof, which I minde not to rehearse, considering how vaine and friuolous it is: but leauing it vntill such time as some one Oedipus or other shall bewraie any other name thereof that hath been described, or known of the old writers.
gerard.place: These kinds of Graine were first brought into Spaine, and then into other prouinces of Europe, out of Asia which is in the Turkes Dominions, as also out of America and the Ilands adioyning from the east and west Indies, and Virginia or Norembega, where they vse to sowe or set it, and to make bread of it, where it groweth much higher than in other countries.
gerard.time: It is sowen in these countries in March and Aprill, and the fruite is ripe in September.
gerard.vertues: Turky wheate doth nourish far lesse than either Wheate, Rie, Barly or Otes. The bread which is made thereof is meanly white, without bran: it is hard and drie as bisket is, and hath in it no clammines at all: for which cause it is of hard digestion, and yeeldeth to the body little or no nourishment, it slowly descendeth and bindeth the belly, as that doth which is made of Mill or Panick. We haue as yet no certaine proofe or experience concerning the vertues of this kinde of Corne, although the barbarous Indians which know no better, are constrained to make a vertue of necessitie, and think it a good food; whereas we may easily iudge that it nourisheth but little, and is of hard and euill digestion, a more conuenient foode for swine than for men.

summary: One of the largest single flowers on Earth, up to about a metre across and weighing up to roughly 11 kg. Rafflesia has no leaves, stems or roots: it lives as threads inside a jungle vine and appears only when a cabbage-like bud bursts through the bark and opens into a flower that smells of rotting meat.
nativeRange: Rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Is a holoparasite with no leaves, stem, roots or chlorophyll, living as cell strands inside Tetrastigma vines
Produces flowers up to about 1 m across, the largest single flowers known
Mimics a carcass in colour, texture and smell to attract carrion flies as pollinators
Has lost its chloroplast genome, and has taken up many genes from its host by horizontal gene transfer
edibilityNote: Not eaten as food. Buds are harvested in some areas for traditional medicine, which threatens wild populations.

fruit.description: Round, rough fruit with oily pulp and thousands of tiny seeds.

seed.description: Minute seeds with oily pulp
seed.dispersal: Probably small mammals such as tree shrews, and ants
seed.germination: Only on Tetrastigma host vines; how infection happens is poorly understood

lore: A guide working for Joseph Arnold and Stamford Raffles found it in Sumatra in 1818; Arnold died shortly afterward and the plant was named after both men. It is one of Indonesia's three national flowers.
funFact: Each flower lasts only about five to seven days, after a bud that took roughly nine months to a year to develop.

summary: A stately garden perennial with hooded blue-violet flowers, and one of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Aconitine can enter through the skin and causes tingling and numbness, vomiting, and deadly heart rhythms. Greek myth said it grew from the saliva of Cerberus.
nativeRange: Mountains of western and central Europe
abilities: Makes aconitine, which locks sodium channels open in nerves and heart muscle
Its hooded flowers can be opened only by long-tongued bumblebees
Stores toxin-rich tuberous roots that replace themselves each year
Alkaloids can be absorbed through broken skin when handled
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, especially roots and seeds. Within minutes to an hour: tingling and numbness of the mouth and face spreading to limbs, nausea, vomiting, sweating, weakness, then dangerous ventricular arrhythmias and death. Roots have been mistaken for horseradish or other roots, and leaves for wild greens. Wear gloves when handling; gardeners have been poisoned through the skin. No antidote; treatment is supportive.

uses.use: Tincture of aconite as a pain reliever and fever remedy (now abandoned)
Processed roots of Aconitum carmichaelii (fuzi) used for 'cold' conditions; processing reduces toxicity

medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal, even in herbal products; poisoning from improperly processed aconite herbs is still reported in Asia.

fruit.description: Clusters of three to five dry pods that split along one side.

seed.description: Small, wrinkled, dark seeds
seed.germination: Needs cold stratification; slow

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; flowers in 2–3 years from seed
steps: Always wear gloves when planting, dividing or cutting
Plant tubers in moist, rich soil in partial shade
Keep away from vegetable beds and places children or pets play
Label clearly; never plant near horseradish or other edible roots

lore: Ovid's Metamorphoses tells how aconite sprang from the foam of Cerberus when Hercules dragged him from the underworld. The name 'wolfsbane' comes from its use in baits and arrow poisons for wolves.
funFact: The 'monk's hood' is a sepal, not a petal; the true petals are reduced to two hidden, nectar-holding spurs inside it.

wiki.extract: Aconitum napellus, monkshood, aconite, Venus' chariot or wolfsbane, is a species of highly toxic flowering plants in the genus Aconitum of the family Ranunculaceae, native and endemic to western and central Europe. A perennial plant, it is herbaceous and grows to 1 m tall, with hairless stems and leaves. The leaves are rounded, 5–10 cm (2.0–3.9 in) diameter, palmately divided into five to seven deeply lobed segments. The flowers are dark purple to bluish-purple, narrow oblong helmet-shaped, 1–2 cm (0.39–0.79 in) tall. Plants native to Asia and North America formerly listed as A. napellus are now regarded as separate species. The plant is extremely poisonous in both ingestion and body contact. It is the most poisonous plant in all of Europe.

summary: A woodland wildflower of eastern North America whose knotty yellow rhizome stains everything gold with berberine. Overharvesting for herbal supplements has made it a threatened species.
nativeRange: Rich deciduous forests of eastern North America, from southern Ontario to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Arkansas
abilities: Rhizome contains berberine and hydrastine, alkaloids active against many bacteria and fungi
Strongly inhibits the liver enzymes CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 in people, altering drug levels
Spreads slowly by rhizomes into clonal colonies on the forest floor
edibilityNote: Not a food. The rhizome is a bitter, potent medicine; large amounts are toxic.

uses.use: Cherokee, Iroquois and other nations used the root for eye and skin infections, sores and digestive complaints, and as a yellow dye and insect repellent
Popularised in the 19th century for catarrh, mucous membrane infections, eye washes and digestive tonics
Root products sold for colds, sore throats and digestive upset, often combined with echinacea

medicinal.cautions: Goldenseal products have little clinical evidence; berberine alone is better studied. It strongly inhibits drug metabolism and can raise levels of many medicines, including metformin and some statins, antidepressants and anticoagulants. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and in newborns, as berberine can worsen jaundice. Choose cultivated sources only.

fruit.description: Single bright red, raspberry-like cluster of fleshy berries above two leaves; not eaten.

seed.description: Small, glossy black seeds
seed.germination: Sow fresh; needs warm then cold stratification, germinating the following spring or later

grow.propagation: Rhizome division (most reliable), root cuttings or fresh seed
steps: Plant rhizome pieces with a bud 5 cm deep in autumn under hardwood shade or shade cloth
Mulch with leaf litter
Keep weeds and slugs down for several years
Harvest in autumn after the tops die back, replanting small pieces

lore: In 1997 goldenseal was listed in CITES Appendix II because of wild overharvest. The belief that it masks drugs in urine tests comes from John Uri Lloyd's 1900 novel Stringtown on the Pike, in which it fools a chemist.
funFact: Goldenseal does not hide drugs in urine tests; the myth comes from a plot device in a novel by John Uri Lloyd, who was a pharmacist and goldenseal promoter.

wiki.extract: Goldenseal, also called orangeroot or yellow puccoon, is a perennial herb in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae, native to North America. It may be distinguished by its thick, yellow knotted rootstock. The stem is purplish and hairy above ground and yellow below ground where it connects to the yellow rhizome. Goldenseal reproduces both clonally through the rhizome and sexually, with clonal division more frequent than asexual reproduction. It takes between 4 and 5 years for a plant to reach sexual maturity, i.e. the point at which it produces flowers. Plants in the first stage, when the seed erupts and cotyledons emerge, can remain in this state one or more years. The second vegetative stage occurs during years two and three and is characterized by the development of a single leaf and absence of a well developed stem. Finally, the third stage is reproductive, at which point flowering and fruiting occurs. This last stage takes between 4 and 5 years to develop.

summary: A delicate, pale-blue-flowered annual of the buttercup family whose small, pungent black seeds are sprinkled on naan and pastries. A hadith calls them a cure for every disease except death.
nativeRange: Probably South-West Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; ancient crop, wild origin uncertain
abilities: Seeds contain thymoquinone, studied for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and blood-sugar-lowering effects
Inflated capsule of fused follicles protects the seeds
Completes its life cycle in about four months
edibilityNote: Seeds are a common spice in South Asian, Middle Eastern and Turkish breads and pickles. The oil applied to skin can cause contact dermatitis.

uses.use: Black seed and its oil taken daily as a general tonic, based on the hadith of its blessing
Shoneez / kalonji for asthma, cough, flatulence, worms, skin disease and as a diuretic
Upakunchika for digestion, fever, menstrual and lactation complaints
Small trials of seed or oil for blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and asthma

medicinal.cautions: Trials are mostly small and short. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure and add to the effect of related drugs. Possible bleeding risk with anticoagulants. Large doses are traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Cases of kidney injury and contact dermatitis have been reported.

fruit.description: Inflated capsule of 3–7 fused follicles, each with many seeds.

seed.description: Matte black, angular, trigonous seeds
seed.germination: 7–14 days at 15–20 °C; sow 1 cm deep (darkness aids germination)

steps: Sow directly in spring (or autumn in mild climates), as it dislikes transplanting
Thin to 15–20 cm
Cut stems when the capsules turn brown and dry
Dry in paper bags and shake out the seeds

lore: Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad saying that black seed is a cure for every disease except death. Dioscorides called it melanthion and recommended it for headache and catarrh.
funFact: Despite the name 'black cumin', Nigella is no relation of cumin: it belongs to the buttercup family, and its garden cousin is love-in-a-mist.

summary: A thorny, zigzag-branched small tree cultivated in northern China for over 4,000 years. Its fruit, eaten crisp like an apple or dried into chewy 'red dates', is a cornerstone of Chinese cooking and medicine.
nativeRange: Northern China (probably the middle Yellow River valley); cultivated across East, Central and West Asia, the Mediterranean and North America
abilities: Survives extreme heat, cold to about −28 °C, drought and alkaline or saline soil
Leafs out late in spring, so it escapes frost damage to flowers
Paired spines, one straight and one hooked, guard each node in wild forms
Spreads by root suckers into thickets
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe and widely eaten. Seeds are used only medicinally.

uses.use: Dried fruit (dà zǎo) to tonify qi and blood and harmonise herbal formulas; seed (suān zǎo rén, from the sour jujube) for insomnia and anxiety
Unnab fruit decoction for coughs, sore throat and as a blood purifier

medicinal.cautions: Seed preparations are sedative and may add to sedative medicines.

fruit.description: Oval to round drupe 2–5 cm, glossy green ripening to mahogany-red; crisp, sweet, apple-like white flesh that wrinkles and turns date-like when dried, around a single stone.

seed.description: Hard, elongated, pointed-oval stone 1–2 cm, reddish-brown and roughly ridged, holding one or two small flat brown seeds
seed.germination: Crack or scarify the stone, cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow at 20–25 °C; erratic. Named varieties are grafted

grow.sun: Full sun; needs summer heat to fruit well
grow.soil: Any well-drained soil, including alkaline, saline or poor, pH 5.5–8.5
grow.propagation: Grafting named cultivars ('Li', 'Lang', 'Sugar Cane') onto seedling or sour-jujube rootstock; root suckers
steps: Plant a grafted tree in the hottest, sunniest spot available; most varieties set fruit alone, but two varieties improve the crop.
Water for the first year, then rely on rain except in severe drought.
Remove suckers from the rootstock below the graft regularly.
Prune lightly in winter to thin crowding; fruit grows on short, deciduous branchlets each year.
Pick crisp when half to fully red for fresh eating, or leave on the tree until wrinkled to dry.

lore: The jujube is one of China's traditional 'five fruits', and jujubes and chestnuts were a bride's ritual gift in the classical rites; red dates are still scattered on wedding beds to wish couples early children — 'zǎo' sounds like 'early'. Ziziphus is also the 'lote tree' (sidr) of the Qur'an, though that is mainly Z. spina-christi.
funFact: China grows about 90% of the world's jujubes, and some trees in Shanxi are said to be over 1,000 years old.

wiki.extract: Jujube, jujuba, Chinese jujube, red date or Chinese date is a species in the genus Ziziphus in the buckthorn family Rhamnaceae. It is often confused with the closely related Indian jujube, Z. mauritiana. The jujube tolerates a diverse range of climates, from temperate to tropical. Its origin is thought to be in eastern Asia, but it has been widely dispersed through cultivation, and is today cultivated in gardens as a shrub as well as in agriculture as a food crop. Its fruit is eaten freshly harvested as well as dried and candied.

summary: A tree that walks into the sea on stilts. Red mangroves arch prop roots into salty mud, keep most of the salt out at the root surface, and drop seedlings that have already germinated on the tree and can float for months. Their roots shelter young fish and buffer coasts from storms.
nativeRange: Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts: Florida, Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Central and South America, West Africa; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Is viviparous: seeds germinate on the tree and drop as pencil-like propagules up to about 30 cm long
Its propagules float and stay viable for months, colonising new coasts
Its roots filter out most salt from seawater
Breathes through lenticels on prop roots that stand above the anoxic mud
Builds coastlines by trapping sediment and buffers storm surge
edibilityNote: Propagules have been eaten as famine food after processing, but they are astringent and bitter; generally not eaten.

uses.tradition: Caribbean and Latin American folk medicine
uses.use: Bark decoction as an astringent for diarrhoea, sore throat and wounds

medicinal.cautions: High-tannin preparations can irritate the gut.

fruit.season: Much of the year, peaking in summer
fruit.description: Brown leathery fruit from which a long green propagule grows while still on the tree.

seed.description: Germinates on the tree into a long, cigar-shaped propagule
seed.germination: Already germinated; plant the propagule upright in tidal mud

lore: The word 'mangle' came into Spanish from the Taíno of the Caribbean. Tannin from red mangrove bark was used across the tropics to tan leather and preserve fishing nets and sails, giving them a red-brown colour.
funFact: Mangrove propagules can drift for months and still root, which is how Rhizophora reached both sides of the Atlantic.

wiki.extract: Rhizophora mangle, also known as the red mangrove, is a salt-tolerant, small-to-medium sized evergreen tree restricted to coastal, estuarine ecosystems along the southern portions of North America, the Caribbean as well as Central America and tropical West Africa. Its viviparous "seeds", in actuality called propagules, become fully mature plants before dropping off the parent tree. These are dispersed by water until eventually embedding in the shallows.

summary: A small, crooked tree whose hard, golden, perfumed fruit is almost inedible raw but turns rosy-pink and fragrant when slowly cooked. The quince was the 'golden apple' of much ancient Greek myth, and its jelly-like paste gave the world the word 'marmalade'.
nativeRange: The Caucasus, northern Iran, Turkmenistan and adjacent West Asia; cultivated across Europe, West and Central Asia and South America
abilities: Fruit flesh turns from white to deep pink-red when cooked long, as tannins convert to anthocyanin-like pigments
Self-fertile; large single flowers appear after the leaves, escaping most frosts
Used worldwide as a dwarfing rootstock for pears
Seed coat produces a thick mucilage when soaked
edibleParts: fruit (cooked into paste, jelly, stews; raw in mild varieties)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe, mostly cooked. Seeds contain amygdalin and should not be crushed or eaten; whole soaked seeds are used only for their outer mucilage.

uses.use: Bihidana (quince-seed mucilage) for sore throats, coughs and dry skin
Quince syrup for nausea, vomiting and reflux; small trials report benefit in GERD

medicinal.cautions: Do not crush or eat seeds (cyanogenic).

fruit.description: Large pear- or apple-shaped pome 7–12 cm, covered in grey down when young, ripening to golden yellow and intensely fragrant; hard, astringent, gritty cream flesh.

seed.description: Many dark-brown, glossy, wedge-shaped seeds about 6–8 mm, packed in the five core chambers and coated in a gel that swells when wet
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days, sow in spring; usually propagated vegetatively

grow.water: Moderate; tolerates damp soil better than apples
grow.soil: Deep, moist, well-drained loam, pH 6–7; becomes chlorotic on chalk
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings, layering, budding onto quince rootstock
steps: Plant a named variety (e.g. 'Vranja', 'Meech's Prolific', 'Isfahan') in full sun in moist but well-drained soil.
Water during dry summers; a single tree is enough as quinces are self-fertile.
Prune lightly in winter just to thin crowded and crossing branches — fruit forms at the tips of shoots, so avoid hard tip pruning.
Watch for fireblight and leaf blight; remove infected shoots promptly.
Pick in mid-to-late autumn when fully yellow and fragrant, before hard frost; store separately as their scent taints other fruit.

lore: Plutarch records that Solon's laws had Athenian brides eat a quince before entering the bridal chamber, and many scholars think the golden apples of the Hesperides were quinces. Portuguese 'marmelada', quince paste, gave English its word marmalade.
funFact: A ripe quince left in a room will perfume it for weeks — medieval Europeans kept them in linen chests.

wiki.extract: The quince is the sole member of the genus Cydonia in the Malinae subtribe of the Rosaceae family. It is a deciduous tree that bears hard, aromatic bright golden-yellow pome fruit, similar in appearance to a pear. Ripe quince fruits are hard, tart, and astringent. They are eaten raw or processed into jam, quince cheese, or alcoholic drinks.

It features both macroscopic cross-sections and a remarkable magnified view of the cellular tissue, demonstrating the early modern shift towards empirical observation and the use of the microscope to understand biological life.

summary: The garden strawberry is an 18th-century accident: a hybrid of a Chilean and a North American wild strawberry that crossed in a French garden around 1750. The red flesh is a swollen receptacle — the true fruits are the tiny 'seeds' on the outside.
nativeRange: Hybrid of cultivated origin (Brittany, France, c. 1750) from F. chiloensis (Chile) and F. virginiana (North America); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Octoploid: carries eight sets of chromosomes
Spreads by runners (stolons) that root to form new clone plants
Each 'seed' on the surface is a separate achene, a true fruit
Day-neutral varieties fruit continuously regardless of day length
edibilityNote: Fruit and leaves are safe. Strawberries are a common trigger of allergy-like reactions in children.

uses.use: Leaf tea (mainly from wild strawberry) as a mild astringent for diarrhoea
Fruit to cool fevers and cleanse the teeth

medicinal.cautions: Can trigger hives and oral allergy in sensitive people.

fruit.season: Late spring to early summer; everbearers into autumn
fruit.description: Heart- to cone-shaped red fruit 2–5 cm, juicy and sweet, the swollen receptacle dotted with 200 or so tiny achenes.

seed.description: Tiny yellow to reddish-brown achenes, about 1 mm, egg-shaped, set in shallow pits on the outside of the berry
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 2–4 weeks, surface-sow (needs light) at 18–22 °C; 1–6 weeks. Seedlings differ from the parent except for seed-bred F1 varieties

grow.water: Moderate; keep evenly moist, especially as fruit swells
grow.soil: Rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5); raised beds ideal
grow.propagation: Rooted runners; certified virus-free plants; some varieties by seed
grow.timeToHarvest: 60–90 days from spring planting (everbearers) or the following spring (June-bearers)
steps: Buy certified disease-free plants and set them 30–45 cm apart in late summer or early spring, with the crown exactly at soil level.
Mulch with straw (hence the name) to keep fruit clean and the soil moist.
Remove flowers in the first spring on June-bearers to build strong plants; water at soil level to avoid grey mould.
Net against birds; pick fully red berries in the morning, with the cap on.
After harvest, trim old leaves, root a few runners into pots for new plants, and replace beds every 3–4 years.

lore: French spy and engineer Amédée-François Frézier brought Chilean strawberry plants to France in 1714; crossed with North American plants in Brittany, they produced the modern berry, named 'ananassa' for its supposed pineapple scent. Wimbledon has served strawberries and cream since 1877.
funFact: Botanically, a strawberry is not a berry — but a banana is.

wiki.extract: The garden strawberry is a widely grown hybrid plant cultivated worldwide for its fruit. The genus Fragaria, the strawberries, is in the rose family, Rosaceae. The fruit is appreciated for its aroma, bright red colour, juicy texture, and sweetness. It is eaten either fresh or in prepared foods such as jam, ice cream, and chocolates. Artificial strawberry flavourings and aromas are widely used in commercial products. Botanically, the strawberry is not a berry, but an aggregate accessory fruit. Each apparent 'seed' on the outside of the strawberry is actually an achene, a botanical fruit with a seed inside it.

This illustration, created by the artist Hans Weiditz, exemplifies the shift toward modern scientific observation by depicting the plant exactly as it appeared in nature, including its runners and complex root structure.

summary: The domestic apple descends mainly from the wild apple forests of the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, carried west and east along the Silk Road. Apples do not come true from seed, so every named variety — from 'Gala' to 'Bramley' — is a clone propagated by grafting, some for centuries.
nativeRange: Domesticated from Malus sieversii of Central Asia (Tian Shan), with genes from M. sylvestris; cultivated throughout temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Self-incompatible: most varieties need pollen from a different variety to set fruit
Seeds are genetically shuffled, so almost every pip grows into a new, unique apple
Requires winter chilling (often 500–1,000 hours below 7 °C) to break dormancy and flower well
Fruit stores for months in cool conditions as cells slowly respire sugars
edibleParts: fruit (raw, cooked, juiced, fermented to cider)
edibilityNote: Flesh and skin are wholesome. Seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide when chewed; a few swallowed whole are harmless, but large quantities of crushed seeds should be avoided.

uses.use: Grated raw apple (rich in pectin) given for diarrhoea; stewed apple for convalescents
Apple preparations (e.g. murabba-e-seb) used as a heart and brain tonic

medicinal.cautions: Seeds contain amygdalin (cyanogenic). Apple allergy (cross-reacting with birch pollen) causes oral itching in some people.

fruit.season: Late summer to late autumn (Northern Hemisphere)
fruit.description: Round to conical fruit 5–10 cm across, skin green, yellow or red, crisp white to cream flesh around a papery five-chambered core; the swollen fleshy part develops from the floral receptacle, not the ovary.

seed.description: Glossy dark-brown to almost black teardrop-shaped pips, flattened, about 7–10 mm long, typically 1–2 in each of the five core chambers
seed.dispersal: Animals (deer, bears, birds, horses) eat the fruit and pass the seeds
seed.germination: Needs 60–90 days of moist cold stratification at 1–5 °C; seedlings will not resemble the parent

grow.zones: USDA 3–8 (varies by cultivar; some low-chill types to 9–10)
grow.water: Moderate; regular water while fruit swells
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7; avoid waterlogged ground
grow.propagation: Grafting or budding of named cultivars onto rootstocks (e.g. M9 dwarf, MM106 semi-vigorous); seed only for breeding or rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 years on dwarfing rootstock; 5–8 years on vigorous stock
steps: Buy a grafted tree of a variety suited to your chill hours, and plant a second compatible variety (or a crab apple) nearby for cross-pollination.
Plant bare-root in winter with the graft union 5–10 cm above soil; stake dwarf rootstocks permanently.
Water deeply weekly in the first two summers and mulch a 1 m circle to suppress grass.
Prune in winter to an open-centre or central-leader shape, removing crossing, diseased and inward-growing wood; thin fruitlets to one per cluster in early summer.
Pick when the fruit lifts and twists off easily and pips have turned brown.

lore: In Norse myth the goddess Iðunn kept apples that preserved the youth of the gods, and in Greek myth Eris's golden apple 'for the fairest' sparked the Trojan War. Johnny Appleseed (John Chapman) planted seedling nurseries across the American frontier in the early 1800s, mostly for cider.
funFact: An apple grown from a seed is almost never like its parent — the 'Granny Smith' itself arose as a chance seedling in Australia in 1868.

wiki.extract: An apple is the round, edible fruit of an apple tree. Fruit trees of the orchard or domestic apple, the most widely grown in the genus, are cultivated worldwide. The tree originated in Central Asia, where its wild ancestor, Malus sieversii, is still found. Apples have been grown for thousands of years in Eurasia before they were introduced to the American continent by European colonists. Apples have cultural significance in many mythologies and religions.

summary: A peach relative from West and Central Asia grown not for its leathery flesh but for its seed. Wild almonds are lethally bitter with amygdalin; a single mutation for sweetness, selected thousands of years ago, made almonds one of the first domesticated nut trees.
nativeRange: Western and Central Asia (Iran, Turkey, the Levant to Central Asia); cultivated in Mediterranean climates worldwide
abilities: One of the first fruit trees to bloom each year, covering hillsides in pink-white blossom in late winter
Bitter almonds contain enough amygdalin that a few dozen can kill an adult
Most cultivars are self-incompatible, so orchards depend on bees; California hires over a million beehives each February
Drought-tolerant once established
edibleParts: kernel of sweet almonds (raw, roasted, as milk, flour, marzipan)
green immature fruit (eaten whole in spring in the Middle East)
edibilityNote: Sweet almonds are safe. Bitter almonds (and wild almonds) release hydrogen cyanide; eating even small numbers raw can be fatal to children. Almond is a common tree-nut allergen.

uses.use: Soaked almonds and badam rogan (almond oil) as a brain and nerve tonic
Regular almond intake modestly lowers LDL cholesterol in trials

medicinal.cautions: Bitter almonds and bitter almond oil are poisonous; tree-nut allergy.

fruit.description: Oval, flattened, grey-green velvety drupe 3–6 cm with a thin leathery hull that dries and splits open to reveal the pitted shell.

seed.description: Teardrop-shaped, flattened kernel 2–3 cm with a cinnamon-brown, finely wrinkled skin and creamy white interior, inside a pale, pitted, tan shell
seed.germination: Cold-stratify in the shell 4–6 weeks, sow 5 cm deep; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Seedlings may produce bitter nuts

grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–8; intolerant of waterlogging
grow.propagation: Budding onto almond, peach or peach–almond hybrid rootstock
steps: Plant a self-fertile variety (e.g. 'Independence', 'Tuono', 'All-in-One') or two compatible varieties, in a frost-free, sunny site — blossom opens in late winter.
Plant bare-root in winter on well-drained ground; water deeply every 1–2 weeks in the first summer.
Prune to an open vase in the first three winters; later prune only lightly in summer to reduce disease.
Encourage bees with nearby flowers; protect blossom from late frost with fleece where practical.
Harvest when hulls split open: shake onto tarps, remove hulls and dry nuts in the sun for a week before storing.

lore: Aaron's rod miraculously budded and bore almonds in the Book of Numbers, and the Temple menorah's cups were shaped like almond blossoms. Almonds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and the 'almond-eyed' ideal of beauty appears in Persian poetry.
funFact: California grows around 80% of the world's almonds, and pollinating them each February takes more than half of all US commercial honeybee colonies.

wiki.extract: The almond is a species of tree from the genus Prunus. Along with the peach, it is classified in the subgenus Amygdalus, distinguished from the other subgenera by corrugations on the woody shell (endocarp) surrounding the seed.
