summary: Named 'Armenian plum' by the Romans, the apricot actually originated in Central Asia and northern China. It is one of the first trees to bloom in spring, and in Hunza and Ladakh dried apricots and their kernel oil have long been winter staples.
nativeRange: Central Asia (Tian Shan, Dzungaria) and northern China; cultivated in Mediterranean and continental climates worldwide
abilities: Flowers very early, before the leaves, so blossom is often lost to late frost
Most cultivars are self-fertile
Tolerates hot dry summers and very cold continental winters in Central Asian types
Kernels contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide
edibleParts: sweet kernels of selected varieties (in moderation)
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. Bitter apricot kernels are rich in amygdalin and have caused cyanide poisoning — a few bitter kernels can be dangerous to a child. Do not eat bitter kernels raw.

uses.use: Bitter apricot kernel (kǔ xìng rén) in small, prescribed doses for cough and wheezing
Dried apricots as a mild laxative and nutritive

medicinal.cautions: Bitter kernels are cyanogenic and poisonous; 'laetrile' from kernels is not an effective cancer treatment and has caused poisonings.

fruit.description: Round drupe 3–5 cm with a shallow groove, velvety yellow-orange skin often blushed red; sweet, slightly tart, firm orange flesh around a smooth flattened stone.

seed.description: Smooth, flattened oval stone 2–3 cm, light brown with a ridged edge; inside is a single almond-like kernel with a brown skin, sweet or bitter depending on variety
seed.germination: Cold-stratify the stone 60–90 days at 2–5 °C, sow in spring 3 cm deep; seedlings are variable but often fruit acceptably

grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8)
grow.propagation: Budding onto apricot, peach or plum rootstock; seed
steps: Choose a late-flowering variety if your area has spring frosts, and plant in a sunny but not frost-pocketed site.
Plant bare-root in winter; fan-train against a warm wall in cool climates.
Water deeply in dry spells during fruit growth; avoid wet soil around the trunk.
Prune in summer (after harvest) to reduce the risk of silver leaf and canker; thin fruit to 8–10 cm apart.
Pick when fully coloured and slightly soft; halve and sun-dry or dehydrate for keeping.

lore: Apricots reached Greece and Rome via Armenia, hence 'armeniaca', and Arab gardeners spread them through Spain. The Hunza people of Pakistan's Karakoram are famed for their apricot orchards, drying the fruit on rooftops each summer.
funFact: The word 'apricot' comes from Latin praecoquum, 'early-ripening', via Arabic al-barqūq and Spanish albaricoque.

wiki.extract: Prunus armeniaca is the most commonly cultivated apricot species. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation. Genetic studies indicate Central Asia is the center of origin. It is extensively cultivated in many countries and has escaped into the wild in many places. The specific epithet armeniaca refers to the country of Armenia.

summary: A tall, glossy-barked European and West Asian tree whose wild form, the gean or mazzard, gave rise to all sweet cherries. Its spring blossom is a key early nectar source for bees, and birds spread its stones widely — hence 'avium', of the birds.
nativeRange: Europe, Anatolia, the Caucasus and north-west Africa; cultivated in temperate regions worldwide
abilities: Extrafloral nectaries on the leaf stalks attract ants that defend the tree
Bark peels in horizontal shining bands with conspicuous lenticels
Most varieties are self-incompatible and need a compatible pollinator variety
Wood is a fine-grained, reddish cabinet timber
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. Crushed stones, leaves and bark contain cyanogenic glycosides; swallowed whole stones pass harmlessly, but crushed kernels in quantity are dangerous. Leaves are toxic to livestock.

uses.use: Cherry-stalk tea as a diuretic
Cherry stalks for kidney stones and fluid retention

medicinal.cautions: Kernels, leaves and bark are cyanogenic.

fruit.description: Round to heart-shaped drupe 1.5–3 cm on a long stalk, glossy deep red to almost black, or yellow-red in 'Rainier' types; sweet, juicy flesh around a smooth stone.

seed.description: A smooth, round to slightly oval, cream to pale-tan stone 7–10 mm, with a faint ridge; it holds one almond-like kernel
seed.germination: Needs 90–120 days moist cold stratification at 1–5 °C (or sow outdoors in autumn); sprouts in spring

grow.water: Moderate; avoid heavy watering near harvest (causes splitting)
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 6–7.5; dislikes wet clay
grow.propagation: Budding or grafting onto rootstocks such as 'Colt' or 'Gisela 5' (dwarfing)
steps: Choose a self-fertile variety (e.g. 'Stella', 'Lapins') or plant two compatible varieties; use a dwarfing rootstock for easy netting.
Plant bare-root in winter in a sunny spot with good air drainage to avoid spring frost on blossom.
Water deeply in dry spells during fruit growth but ease off in the last week before harvest.
Prune only in summer, after fruiting, to reduce the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker.
Net the tree as fruit colours, and pick cherries with stalks attached when fully coloured and sweet.

lore: Pliny says the Roman general Lucullus brought cherries to Rome from Kerasous (Giresun) on the Black Sea in 74 BCE, though wild cherries grew in Europe long before. Cherry stones are common finds at Bronze Age sites across Europe.
funFact: The Greek town name Kerasous may have given us the very word 'cherry', via Latin cerasum.

summary: Despite its name ('Persian plum'), the peach was domesticated in China's Yangtze valley about 7,500 years ago and reached Europe via Persia. Nectarines are the same species, differing by a single gene for smooth skin.
nativeRange: Northwest and central China; cultivated worldwide in temperate and subtropical climates
abilities: Self-fertile, unlike many relatives: a single tree sets fruit
Nectarines arise from a recessive mutation that removes the fuzz
Fruits on one-year-old wood, so it needs hard annual pruning
Kernels contain amygdalin, which yields cyanide
edibleParts: flowers (in salads and tea, small amounts)
edibilityNote: Flesh is safe. The kernel inside the stone, and the leaves and bark, contain cyanogenic glycosides and should not be eaten in quantity.

uses.use: Peach kernel (táo rén) used to 'invigorate blood' and relieve constipation, in prescribed doses
Leaf tea as a sedative and for coughs

medicinal.cautions: Kernels, leaves and bark are cyanogenic; peach-skin lipid-transfer protein is a common cause of serious fruit allergy in the Mediterranean.

fruit.description: Round drupe 5–9 cm with a groove along one side; velvety (or smooth in nectarines) yellow skin blushed red; juicy white or yellow flesh around a deeply pitted stone, 'clingstone' or 'freestone'.

seed.description: Hard, deeply furrowed and pitted, oval stone 2–3.5 cm, reddish-brown, with a pointed tip; holds a single almond-shaped, brown-skinned kernel
seed.germination: Remove kernel or crack the stone, cold-stratify 60–90 days at 2–5 °C, sow in spring; seedlings often give decent fruit

grow.water: Moderate; regular in dry spells while fruit swells
grow.propagation: Budding onto peach seedling or 'St Julien A' rootstock; seed
steps: Choose a variety matched to your chill hours (e.g. 'Redhaven' for cold areas, 'Florida Prince' for low-chill areas), with resistance to peach leaf curl if possible.
Plant in the sunniest, warmest spot, ideally a fan trained against a south-facing wall in cool climates.
Prune to an open vase each year in late winter or just after bud-break, removing a third of old wood, as fruit grows only on last year's shoots.
Thin fruitlets to 15–20 cm apart when marble-sized for bigger, sweeter peaches.
In wet climates, cover with a rain shelter from late winter to spring to prevent leaf curl; pick when the fruit gives slightly near the stalk.

lore: In Chinese myth the Queen Mother of the West grows peaches of immortality that ripen once every 3,000 years, and the Monkey King steals them in Journey to the West. The 'Peach Blossom Spring' of the poet Tao Yuanming (421 CE) is China's archetypal hidden paradise.
funFact: Peach stones about 2.6 million years old have been found fossilised in Kunming, China, showing wild peaches existed long before humans.

summary: A small Andean cloud-forest tree whose bitter bark gave the world quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria. That trade shaped empires, and Britain and the Netherlands smuggled seeds out of South America to found plantations in India and Java.
nativeRange: Montane forests of the Andes in southern Ecuador and northern Peru
abilities: Bark contains quinine and quinidine, alkaloids toxic to malaria parasites and active on heart rhythm
Grows in the misty mid-elevation Andes, roughly 1,600–2,700 m
Winged seeds are carried by wind across mountain slopes
edibilityNote: Bark is not food. The small amount of quinine in tonic water is safe for most people, but bark preparations and quinine overdose are dangerous.

uses.use: Bark for fevers and chills; whether it was used before the Spanish arrived is debated by historians
'Jesuits' powder' for intermittent fevers (malaria) from the 1630s; the decisive drug against malaria for three centuries
Quinine for severe or resistant malaria (now largely replaced by artesunate); quinidine as an antiarrhythmic

medicinal.cautions: Quinine causes cinchonism: ringing ears, hearing loss, headache, nausea and blurred vision. It can trigger dangerous drops in platelets, haemolysis (especially with G6PD deficiency), low blood sugar and heart arrhythmia, and overdose can be fatal. The US FDA warns against using quinine for leg cramps.

fruit.description: Small oblong dry capsule splitting from the base.

seed.description: Flat seeds with a papery wing
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist, shaded, acidic medium; 2–4 weeks at 20–25 °C

grow.sun: Part shade when young; sun later
steps: Sow on the surface of sterile, acidic compost in high humidity
Grow seedlings under shade cloth and mist frequently
Plant out on cool, misty, frost-free slopes
Bark was traditionally stripped in sections or the trees were coppiced

lore: Linnaeus named the genus in 1742 after the Countess of Chinchón, who legend said was cured of fever in Lima around 1638, a story historians now doubt. He also misspelled her title. A cinchona tree appears on the national coat of arms of Peru.
funFact: Quinine glows bright blue under ultraviolet light, which is why a gin and tonic fluoresces under a blacklight.

wiki.extract: Cinchona officinalis is a South American tree in the family Rubiaceae. It is native to wet montane forests in Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, between 1600–2700 meters above sea level. It is the national tree of Peru.

The illustration meticulously depicts the characteristic thorny climbing stems and the large, irregular tuberous roots which were the primary part used in early modern pharmacology.

The plant is set against a landscape containing a multi-tiered pagoda, mountains, and small boats on a river. This composition combines scientific observation with an exoticized view of the Chinese environment.

It is featured in Wu Qijun's seminal 1848 work, Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao, which is celebrated for its scientific accuracy and detailed renderings of flora. The image clearly shows the plant's distinctive leaf venation and clusters of small berries, serving as a vital reference for traditional Chinese medicine and botan

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the leaf of the 'palo de la China' (Smilax china), a plant highly valued in the 16th century for its medicinal properties. Featured in Cristóvão da Costa's seminal work on Eastern drugs, it represents the early modern effort to scientifically document and categorize global flora.

It is part of the 'Sancai Tuhui', a comprehensive Ming dynasty encyclopedia that aimed to categorize all knowledge of the 'three realms' of heaven, earth, and humanity.

The image captures the plant's thorny stems, delicate leaves, and full blossoms emerging from a rocky outcrop, reflecting the traditional Chinese style of botanical representation which often integrates plants with natural elements like stones.

The inclusion of a hand-drawn manicule in the margin highli

summary: An evergreen shrub of Ethiopia's highland forests whose roasted seeds make about 60% of the world's coffee. A natural hybrid of two wild species, it is unusual in its genus for being self-fertile, and wild populations are Endangered by deforestation and climate change.
nativeRange: South-western Ethiopia, the Boma Plateau of South Sudan and Mount Marsabit in Kenya; cultivated in tropical highlands worldwide
abilities: Allotetraploid hybrid of Coffea canephora and Coffea eugenioides
Self-pollinating, unlike almost all other Coffea species
Caffeine in seeds and leaves deters insects and inhibits competing seedlings
Jasmine-scented white flowers open all at once after the first rains
edibleParts: leaves (brewed as tea in Ethiopia and Sumatra)
edibilityNote: Beans, cherry husk and leaves are used for drinks. Caffeine overdose from concentrated products can be dangerous.

uses.use: Coffee drunk to stay awake during night prayers in the 15th century
Caffeine is an approved drug, used with analgesics for headache and for apnoea in premature infants
Coffee leaves and husks brewed with butter or salt as a tonic

medicinal.cautions: Caffeine can cause insomnia, anxiety and palpitations; limit in pregnancy. Unfiltered coffee raises LDL cholesterol via cafestol.

fruit.season: Varies by region; 6–9 months after flowering
fruit.description: Oval cherry 1–1.5 cm, green ripening to bright red or yellow, with thin sweet pulp around two seeds back to back.

seed.description: Pale greenish-grey to bluish 'green beans', oval, about 1 cm long, flat on one face with a central S-shaped groove, domed on the other; covered by a papery parchment and a silver skin. A single round seed ('peaberry') forms in some cherries
seed.dispersal: Birds and mammals eat the cherries
seed.germination: Remove pulp, sow fresh seed in parchment 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C in shade; slow, 6–10 weeks

grow.zones: USDA 10–12; best in frost-free tropical highlands (900–2,000 m)
grow.sun: Partial shade; tolerates sun with ample water
grow.water: Moderate–high, with a short dry season to trigger flowering
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), rich volcanic or forest loam
grow.propagation: Seed (comes reasonably true because self-pollinating); cuttings of selected lines
steps: Sow fresh seed of a named variety (e.g. 'Typica', 'Bourbon', or rust-resistant 'Castillo') in shaded nursery bags.
Transplant at 6–12 months, 2–2.5 m apart, under light shade trees that also protect against wind.
Mulch, feed with compost, and water during dry spells, while allowing a short dry spell before the main rains to induce mass flowering.
Prune to control height (1.5–2 m) and remove old unproductive stems periodically; watch for coffee leaf rust.
Hand-pick only fully red cherries; process by washing and fermenting or by sun-drying whole cherries.

lore: Ethiopian legend credits the goatherd Kaldi with noticing his goats dancing after eating coffee cherries. Coffee houses spread from Yemen to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul by the 16th century, and Ottoman authorities repeatedly tried to ban them as places of sedition.
funFact: The Typica coffee of much of the Caribbean and Latin America traces to a few plants: one given to Louis XIV in 1714 was the source of seedlings Gabriel de Clieu carried to Martinique around 1720, sharing his water ration with it on the voyage.

wiki.extract: Coffea arabica, also known as the Arabica coffee, is a species of flowering plant in the coffee and madder family Rubiaceae. It is believed to be the first species of coffee to have been cultivated and is the dominant cultivar, representing about 60% of global production. Coffee produced from the less acidic, more bitter, and more highly caffeinated robusta bean makes up most of the remaining coffee production. The natural populations of Coffea arabica are restricted to the forests of South Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Yemen.

plates.long: A hand-colored botanical engraving depicts a branch of a coffee tree with large green leaves, white flowers, and reddish-purple cherries. Below the main branch, a series of labeled diagrams show the internal structure of the fruit and seeds, including the coffee beans. The plate is titled 'The Coffee Tree' and includes the names of the artist and engraver.

summary: The sweet orange is an ancient hybrid of pomelo and mandarin that arose in southern China; iNaturalist now groups it with bitter and other oranges under Citrus × aurantium. It is the world's most-grown citrus, its highly scented blossom (orange blossom, neroli) as valued as its fruit.
nativeRange: Hybrid origin in southern China and north-east India; cultivated throughout the tropics, subtropics and Mediterranean
abilities: Many seeds are polyembryonic and produce clones of the mother tree via nucellar embryos
Peel is studded with oil glands full of limonene, which repels many insects
Fruit can hang ripe on the tree for months without spoiling, 'storing' itself
Blossom nectar yields a prized single-flower honey
edibilityNote: Fruit, juice, peel and blossom water are widely eaten. Essential oil is concentrated and not for internal use.

uses.use: Dried citrus peel (chén pí, mainly of mandarin) to regulate qi, aid digestion and resolve phlegm
Oranges and lemons as a cure for scurvy, shown in James Lind's 1747 trial
Orange-blossom water as a calming tonic

medicinal.cautions: Peel oil is phototoxic on skin in sunlight. Bitter-orange types (same species in iNaturalist) contain synephrine, a stimulant to avoid with heart conditions.

fruit.season: Winter to spring (Northern Hemisphere); 'Valencia' into summer
fruit.description: Round fruit 6–10 cm, with an oil-dotted orange rind, a white spongy pith (albedo) and 10–13 juicy segments filled with tiny juice vesicles.

seed.description: Pale cream to whitish, ovoid to wedge-shaped seeds with a pointed end and wrinkled surface, about 8–12 mm long; seedless navel and 'Valencia' types have few or none
seed.germination: Sow fresh, never dried, 1 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Often several shoots per seed

grow.water: Moderate; deep regular watering, never waterlogged
grow.propagation: Budding onto rootstocks such as trifoliate orange or 'Carrizo' citrange; seed for rootstocks
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–4 years from a budded tree; fruit takes 7–12 months from flower to ripe
steps: Buy a budded tree on a rootstock suited to your soil and cold (trifoliate for cold, 'Swingle' for sandy soils).
Plant with the bud union well above soil in full sun, sheltered from cold wind; in pots use a fast-draining citrus mix.
Water deeply when the top 5 cm of soil is dry; feed with a citrus fertiliser containing iron, zinc and manganese in spring and summer.
Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the graft; prune only to shape and remove dead wood.
Taste-test before picking — colour is not a reliable sign of ripeness, and fruit stores well on the tree.

lore: Portuguese traders brought improved sweet oranges from Asia in the 16th century, which is why the fruit is called 'portokali' in Greek and 'burtuqāl' in Arabic. The Versailles orangery built for Louis XIV still houses over 1,000 potted citrus and other trees, wheeled outside each summer.
funFact: In tropical climates without cool nights, ripe oranges stay green outside — the orange colour develops only when temperatures drop.

wiki.extract: The bitter orange, sour orange, Seville orange, bigarade orange, or marmalade orange is the hybrid citrus tree species Citrus × aurantium, and its fruit. It is native to Southeast Asia and has been spread by humans to many parts of the world. It is a cross between the pomelo, Citrus maxima, and the wild type mandarin orange, Citrus reticulata. The bitter orange is used to make essential oil, used in foods, drinks, and pharmaceuticals. The Seville orange is prized for making British orange marmalade.

summary: The lemon is a hybrid of citron and bitter orange that arose in north-east India or Burma and travelled west with Arab traders. Unlike most citrus, it flowers and fruits almost year-round, carrying blossom and ripe fruit at once.
nativeRange: Hybrid origin in north-east India, northern Myanmar or south China; cultivated in the subtropics and Mediterranean worldwide
abilities: Flowers repeatedly through the year ('everbearing') in mild climates
Juice is about 5–6% citric acid, with a pH near 2.2
Peel oil glands release limonene and citral, deterring insects
Thorny shoots protect young growth from browsing
edibleParts: zest and peel (fresh, candied, preserved in salt)
edibilityNote: Juice and peel are widely used. The acid erodes tooth enamel with frequent neat use.

uses.use: Lemon juice issued to sailors against scurvy from 1795
Nimbu with warm water and salt as a digestive and for nausea
Hot lemon and honey for colds and sore throats

medicinal.cautions: Peel oil is phototoxic on skin exposed to sun. Acid can aggravate reflux and erode teeth.

fruit.description: Oval fruit 7–12 cm with a nipple-like tip; bright yellow, oil-dotted rind and pale-yellow, very sour segments.

seed.description: Smooth, pale cream to whitish, pointed-oval seeds about 8–10 mm long, slightly flattened
seed.germination: Sow fresh 1 cm deep at 22–28 °C; sprouts in 2–3 weeks. Seedlings take 5–10 years to fruit

grow.water: Moderate; keep evenly moist, never soggy
grow.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy soil, pH 5.5–7
grow.propagation: Budding or grafting onto rootstock; lemons also root from semi-hardwood cuttings
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–3 years from a grafted tree; fruit 6–9 months from flower
steps: Choose a variety for your climate: 'Eureka' or 'Lisbon' for warm zones, 'Meyer' for pots and cooler areas.
Plant in full sun in very well-drained soil; in pots, use a 40–50 cm container with gritty mix and move indoors below 0 °C.
Water when the top few cm dry out and feed monthly in the growing season with a citrus fertiliser.
Pinch out water shoots and rootstock suckers; prune lightly after the main harvest.
Pick when fully yellow and slightly glossy; lemons store on the tree for weeks.

lore: Arab agronomists such as Ibn al-Awwam described lemon cultivation in Andalusia in the 12th century, and Genoese ships carried lemons across the Mediterranean. Preserved lemons remain a cornerstone of Moroccan cuisine.
funFact: A 1747 experiment by naval surgeon James Lind, giving scurvy-stricken sailors oranges and lemons, is often called one of the first controlled clinical trials.

wiki.extract: The lemon is a species of small evergreen tree in the Citrus genus of the flowering plant family Rutaceae. A true lemon is a hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange. Its origins are uncertain, but some evidence suggests lemons originated during the 1st millennium BC in what is now northeastern India. Some other citrus fruits are called lemon.

plates.desc: A botanical and entomological study showing a lemon branch with fruit, flowers, and leaves, populated by two black butterflies with pink spots, a caterpillar, and a pupa.
plates.long: This plate from Maria Sibylla Merian's 'Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium' illustrates the life cycle of a butterfly on a lemon branch. Merian's work was groundbreaking for its time, as she was among the first to observe and record the metamorphosis of insects in their natural habitats, specifically documenting their host plants.

As a pioneer of plant anatomy, Grew's work represents some of the earliest systematic attempts to document the microscopic and macroscopic organization of plant tissues.

Published in the 1532 Dutch herbal 'Den groten herbarius', such illustrations were essential for the accurate identification of plants used in early modern medicine and pharmacology, bridging the gap between traditional folk knowledge and emerging botanical science.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts Melissophyllum (Lemon Balm) from Leonhart Fuchs's landmark 1542 herbal, 'De Historia Stirpium'. Fuchs revolutionized botanical science by insisting on accurate, life-like illustrations based on direct observation of plants, including their roots and flowers, to aid in correct identification for medicinal use.

summary: One aspen grove in Utah, called Pando, is a single male clone with about 47,000 trunks on one root system, covering some 43 hectares and weighing around 6,000 tonnes. It is often called the heaviest known organism. Aspen leaves flutter in the faintest breeze on flattened stalks.
nativeRange: Across Canada and Alaska, south through the Rocky Mountains to northern Mexico
abilities: Spreads by root suckers into vast clones; Pando is one genetic individual of about 47,000 stems
Its flattened leaf stalks make leaves tremble in the slightest wind
Photosynthesises through its pale green-white bark, even in winter
Re-sprouts quickly after fire, acting as a natural firebreak and pioneer
Is the most widely distributed tree in North America
edibilityNote: Inner bark was eaten in spring by Indigenous peoples and in hard times. Bark contains salicin and related compounds, so people with aspirin allergy should avoid it.

uses.use: Bark tea for fever, pain and coughs; the bark's white powder used as sunscreen

medicinal.cautions: Salicylates: avoid with aspirin allergy, anticoagulants, and in children with viral illness.

fruit.description: Catkins of small capsules that release cottony seeds.

seed.description: Minute seeds with cottony hairs
seed.germination: Sow immediately on moist soil; viability lasts only days to weeks

grow.propagation: Root cuttings or suckers; fresh seed
grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; individual stems live about 100–150 years
steps: Take root cuttings or dig a sucker in early spring
Plant in full sun with space to spread
Expect suckers; mow or cut them where unwanted
Protect young stems from deer and elk browsing

lore: Pando was identified as one clone in the 1970s, and genetic testing in 2008 confirmed it. A 2024 genetic study estimated Pando may be between about 16,000 and 80,000 years old, though this is uncertain.
funFact: Pando is not regenerating well, because mule deer and elk eat nearly all young shoots; fenced areas are being used to help it.

wiki.extract: Populus tremuloides is a deciduous tree native to cooler areas of North America, one of several species referred to by the common name aspen. It is commonly called quaking aspen, trembling aspen, American aspen, mountain or golden aspen, trembling poplar, white poplar, and popple, as well as others. The trees have tall trunks, up to 25 metres tall, with smooth pale bark, scarred with black. The glossy green leaves, dull beneath, become golden to yellow, rarely red, in autumn. The species often propagates through its roots to form large clonal groves originating from a shared root system. These roots are not rhizomes, as new growth develops from adventitious buds on the parent root system.

summary: A tall riverside tree whose leaves flash silver in the wind and whose bark held the salicylates that led chemists to aspirin. Its catkins are among the first spring food for bees.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western & Central Asia; widely planted and naturalised elsewhere
abilities: Bark contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylic acid, a pain-relieving and anti-inflammatory compound
Roots readily from cut stems; a branch pushed into wet ground can become a tree
Binds riverbanks with dense roots and tolerates long floods
Catkins, opening with the leaves in spring, give early pollen and nectar to bees
edibilityNote: Bark is used as a medicinal tea or extract, not as food. People allergic to aspirin should avoid it.

uses.use: Bark decoction for fevers ('agues'), rheumatism and pain
Leaves and bark of bed used for fevers, inflammation and as a cooling astringent
Standardised bark extracts for low back pain and osteoarthritis

medicinal.cautions: Avoid with aspirin or salicylate allergy, asthma triggered by aspirin, anticoagulant therapy, stomach ulcers, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Not for children with viral illness because of the theoretical risk of Reye's syndrome.

fruit.description: Small capsules on female catkins, splitting to release cottony seeds.

seed.description: Tiny seeds wrapped in silky white hairs
seed.germination: Short-lived (days); must land on wet bare mud to germinate within 24–48 h

steps: Push 30–50 cm dormant cuttings into moist soil in late winter
Keep well watered the first summer
Plant at least 15 m from drains and buildings, as the roots are aggressive
Coppice or pollard every few years for bark and withies

lore: In 1763 the Rev. Edward Stone reported to the Royal Society that powdered willow bark cured agues in 50 patients. Salicylic acid chemistry later led Felix Hoffmann at Bayer to acetylsalicylic acid, sold as Aspirin from 1899.
funFact: Cricket bats are made from a variety of this tree, the cricket-bat willow, Salix alba var. caerulea.

summary: The source of maple syrup and the blaze of New England autumns. On spring days after freezing nights, pressure changes inside the wood push sugary sap out of any wound, and about 40 litres of sap boil down to one litre of syrup.
nativeRange: Eastern Canada and north-eastern and central United States
abilities: Flows sap during freeze–thaw cycles, when gas pressure in the wood fibres pushes sap from wounds
Lifts water from deep soil at night and releases it into dry topsoil (hydraulic lift), which helps nearby plants
Turns brilliant red, orange and yellow in autumn as chlorophyll breaks down and anthocyanins form
Tolerates deep shade as a sapling, waiting decades for a canopy gap
edibilityNote: Sap is boiled into syrup and sugar. Not toxic to people, but wilted leaves of the related red maple (Acer rubrum) poison horses.

fruit.description: Paired winged seeds ('helicopters') joined at a U-shaped angle.

seed.description: Round seed at the base of a papery wing
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days; sow in spring

grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained; dislikes road salt
grow.timeToHarvest: Tap for syrup at about 25 cm diameter (30–40 years)
steps: Stratify seed over winter in moist sand
Sow in spring; protect seedlings from deer
Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil away from salted roads
Tap in late winter when days are above freezing and nights below; boil the sap down to 66% sugar

lore: Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee and other nations made maple sugar long before Europeans arrived, holding sugar camps each spring; the Haudenosaunee honour the sap run with a Maple Ceremony of thanksgiving. A stylised maple leaf has been on Canada's flag since 1965.
funFact: The 2012 'Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist' saw about 3,000 tonnes of syrup, worth around C$18 million, stolen from a Quebec strategic reserve.

summary: A West African evergreen, now Jamaica's national fruit, whose creamy arils are delicious — but only when the pod has opened naturally on the tree. Unripe ackee contains hypoglycin A, which causes 'Jamaican vomiting sickness' and can kill.
nativeRange: West Africa from Senegal to Gabon; introduced to Jamaica in the 18th century and grown across the Caribbean and Central America
biomes: Tropical dry forest and savanna woodland
abilities: Pods split open by themselves when ripe, revealing three arils and black seeds
Unripe arils and seeds contain hypoglycin A, which blocks fat metabolism and causes severe hypoglycaemia
Hypoglycin falls to safe levels in the arils only once the fruit opens naturally
Crushed pods and bark lather in water and were used as soap and fish poison
edibleParts: aril of naturally opened ripe fruit (boiled)
edibilityNote: Only the cream-yellow arils of fruit that has split open on the tree are eaten, after removing every seed and the pink-red membrane and boiling (discarding the water). Unripe or forced-open fruit, seeds and the membrane are poisonous and have caused many deaths.

uses.use: Leaf and bark preparations used for fever, headache and as eye drops
Leaf decoction for colds

medicinal.cautions: Unripe fruit and seeds are deadly; never force open pods.

fruit.season: Two crops: January–March and June–August in Jamaica
fruit.description: Pear-shaped, three-lobed capsule 7–10 cm, ripening from green to bright red-orange and splitting open to show three cream-yellow, brain-like arils, each capped by a glossy black seed.

seed.description: Shiny, jet-black, round to slightly oval seeds about 2–3 cm, one sitting atop each cream aril
seed.germination: Sow fresh 2–3 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 2–4 weeks. Seeds are poisonous — handle with care

grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, fertile; tolerates limestone soils
grow.propagation: Seed, or grafting/air layering for earlier fruiting
grow.timeToHarvest: 3–5 years from graft; 5–7 years from seed
steps: Sow fresh seed or plant a grafted tree in full sun, 10 m from buildings.
Water during dry spells in the first years and mulch generously.
Prune to shape and keep fruit within reach.
Never pick closed pods: wait until each pod has split open wide on the tree.
Remove the arils, discard every seed and all of the pink membrane, then boil 10–15 minutes and discard the water before cooking (e.g. with saltfish).

lore: The tree likely came to Jamaica aboard a slave ship from West Africa before 1778; it was named after Captain William Bligh, who took specimens to Kew in 1793. Ackee and saltfish is Jamaica's national dish.
funFact: The genus is named after Captain Bligh of the Bounty, who carried ackee from Jamaica to Kew Gardens.

wiki.extract: The ackee, also known as ackee apple, is a fruit of the Sapindaceae (soapberry) family, as are the lychee and the longan. It is native to tropical West Africa. The scientific name honours Captain William Bligh who took the fruit from Jamaica to the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, England, in 1793. The English common name is derived from the West African Akan-language name akye fufo.

summary: A handsome evergreen of southern China whose fruit was so treasured that Tang dynasty relay riders galloped them over 1,000 km to the court. Under a rough red skin lies translucent, perfumed white flesh.
nativeRange: Guangdong, Fujian and Hainan, southern China, and northern Vietnam; cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions
abilities: Needs a cool, dry winter period to flower reliably
Fruit does not ripen further after picking
Flowers are a major honey source in South China
Unripe fruit contains hypoglycin A and MCPG, which lower blood sugar
edibilityNote: Ripe flesh is safe. Unripe lychees contain hypoglycin A and MCPG; eating many on an empty stomach has caused severe hypoglycaemia and deaths among undernourished children in Muzaffarpur, India, and in Vietnam. Seeds are not eaten.

uses.use: Seed (lì zhī hé) to relieve hernia and testicular pain; fruit considered warming

medicinal.cautions: Do not let malnourished children eat many lychees on an empty stomach; seeds are toxic.

fruit.season: Late spring to summer (May–July in the Northern Hemisphere)
fruit.description: Round to heart-shaped fruit 3–4 cm, rough pinkish-red bumpy skin that peels easily; juicy, translucent white aril with a rose-like scent.

seed.description: Glossy, smooth, deep mahogany-brown seed, oval, 1.5–2.5 cm; 'chicken-tongue' varieties have shrivelled seeds only a few mm long
seed.germination: Recalcitrant: sow within a few days, 1–2 cm deep at 25–30 °C; sprouts in 1–3 weeks; seedlings take 8–12 years to fruit

grow.water: Moderate–high in summer; drier in late autumn–winter to induce flowering
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), rich in organic matter
grow.propagation: Air layering (marcotting) — the traditional method; grafting
steps: Buy an air-layered tree of a reliable variety (e.g. 'Mauritius', 'Brewster', 'Kwai Mai Pink').
Plant in a sunny, wind-sheltered spot, and mix in soil from under an existing lychee if possible, as it carries helpful mycorrhizal fungi.
Water regularly in the growing season, then withhold water and fertiliser for 2–3 months in autumn/winter so the tree flowers.
Net trees against birds and bats as fruit colours.
Cut whole clusters with a bit of stem when fruit is fully red and sweet; refrigerate, as skins brown within days.

lore: The Tang emperor Xuanzong had fresh lychees rushed by relay horse to his consort Yang Guifei, a luxury the poet Du Mu lamented. Cai Xiang's 'Lizhi Pu' (1059 CE) is often called the world's first monograph on a fruit tree.
funFact: Cai Xiang's 11th-century 'Treatise on Lychees' lists 32 named varieties.

summary: A biennial that spends its first year as a rosette of leaves as soft as felt, then sends up a 2 m spike of sulphur-yellow flowers. Its dried stalks, dipped in tallow, were once burned as torches.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Asia; naturalised and invasive in North America, Australia and elsewhere
abilities: Dense branched hairs shield the leaves from sun, drought and grazing
Seeds stay viable in soil for many decades
Colonises bare, burned or disturbed ground quickly
A single plant can bear over 100,000 seeds
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are used for tea only, and the irritating hairs must be strained out through fine cloth. Seeds contain saponins and have been used as fish poison; do not eat them.

uses.use: Flower and leaf tea for coughs, bronchitis and sore throat; flower oil dropped into the ear for earache
Adopted after introduction by nations including the Navajo, Cherokee and Iroquois, who smoked or brewed the leaves for coughs and asthma

medicinal.cautions: Strain teas carefully, as the hairs irritate the throat. Do not put oil in the ear if the eardrum may be perforated. The seeds are toxic.

fruit.description: Woolly, egg-shaped two-valved capsule with many seeds.

seed.description: Tiny, pitted, brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Shaken out by wind and passing animals; long-lived seed bank
seed.germination: Needs light; 1–3 weeks at 15–20 °C

steps: Check local status first, as it is invasive in some regions
Surface-sow in spring or autumn
Harvest leaves from first-year rosettes and flowers daily in year 2
Cut spikes before seed sets to prevent spread

lore: Dried mullein stalks dipped in tallow were burned as torches ('hag's tapers'), and the woolly leaves were used as lamp wicks and as linings for shoes. Dioscorides recommended phlomos for coughs and eye complaints.
funFact: In W. J. Beal's buried-seed experiment, begun in Michigan in 1879, seeds of the related moth mullein still germinated after 120 years.

summary: A desert spikemoss that can dry out until it looks dead, curl into a tight brown ball, and turn green again within hours of being watered. It can lose about 95% of its water and survive for years like this. It belongs to the lycophytes, a lineage more than 400 million years old.
nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico and south-western United States (Texas, New Mexico, Arizona)
abilities: Survives losing about 95% of its water content (desiccation tolerance)
Curls its stems inward as it dries, protecting the living centre from sun
Accumulates trehalose and other sugars that protect its cells while dry
Uncurls and resumes photosynthesis within hours of rehydrating
edibilityNote: Not a food; used only as a tea in folk medicine.

uses.use: Tea (doradilla) for kidney stones, urinary complaints and as a diuretic

medicinal.cautions: Little safety data; avoid in pregnancy.

seed.description: Reproduces by spores (no seeds): large megaspores and tiny microspores
seed.dispersal: Wind and water; also tumbles when uprooted
seed.germination: Usually grown from divisions rather than spores

steps: Set the dry ball on a dish of gravel with a little water
Let it open and green up, then move it onto gritty soil
Allow it to dry out between waterings; constant wet causes rot
It can be dried and revived repeatedly, but each cycle stresses it

lore: Sold in Mexican and US markets for luck and prosperity, often under the name 'rose of Jericho', a name that belongs to the Middle Eastern Anastatica hierochuntica. In Mexican tradition it is placed in water on Fridays to bring good fortune.
funFact: It is not a moss and not a fern, but a lycophyte, related to the giant club-mosses whose remains formed much of the world's coal.

wiki.extract: Selaginella lepidophylla, also known as a resurrection plant and sometimes as the rose of Jericho is a species of desert plant in the spikemoss family (Selaginellaceae). It is native to the Chihuahuan Desert of the United States and Mexico. S. lepidophylla is renowned for its ability to survive almost complete desiccation. Resurrection plants are vascular rooted plants capable of surviving extreme desiccation, then resuming normal metabolic activity upon rehydration. The plant's hydro-responsive movements are governed by stem moisture content, tissue properties and a graded distribution of lignified cells affecting concentric stem stiffness and spiraling. During dry weather in its native habitat, its stems curl into a tight ball, uncurling only when exposed to moisture.

summary: A shade-loving perennial of chalky woods whose glossy, sweet black berries can kill a child. Its alkaloid atropine is an essential medicine, still used to restart slow hearts and to counter nerve agents.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia (to Iran); naturalised locally elsewhere
abilities: Makes tropane alkaloids (hyoscyamine, atropine, scopolamine) that block acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors
Dilates the pupils, relaxes gut and airway muscle and speeds the heart
Some rabbits and other animals carry an enzyme, atropinesterase, that lets them eat it safely
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, including the sweet-tasting berries, and a few berries can kill a child. Symptoms include dry mouth, flushing, dilated pupils, racing heart, delirium, hallucinations and coma.

uses.use: Leaf plasters for pain and as an antispasmodic; famously misused as a poison and in 'witches' ointments'
Atropine for slow heart rate, organophosphate and nerve-agent poisoning, before anaesthesia and to dilate pupils; scopolamine for motion sickness

medicinal.cautions: Deadly poisonous, and rubbing the eyes after handling the plant can dilate the pupils. Atropine is a prescription drug on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Never self-medicate. Treat suspected poisoning as an emergency.

fruit.description: Glossy black cherry-sized berry, 1–1.5 cm, sitting in a five-pointed green star of sepals; sweet and deadly.

seed.description: Many small, kidney-shaped, pitted brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Birds, which are less affected by the toxins
seed.germination: Slow and erratic; needs cold stratification

grow.propagation: Seed (stratified) or root division; grown only in licensed physic gardens
grow.timeToHarvest: Leaves at flowering, years 2–4 (pharmaceutical crops only)
steps: Not recommended for home gardens, especially with children or pets
In physic gardens grow behind barriers with clear labels
Wear gloves; wash hands after handling
Remove berries before they ripen in public plantings

lore: Renaissance Italian women are said to have used belladonna drops to make their pupils large and alluring. Linnaeus named the genus after Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life.
funFact: Scottish chronicle tradition, retold by the 16th-century historian George Buchanan, says the Scots drugged an invading Danish army in the 11th century with drink laced with a sleep-inducing nightshade, often identified as belladonna. It is probably legend.

wiki.extract: Atropa bella-donna, commonly known as deadly nightshade or belladonna, is a toxic perennial herbaceous plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, which also includes tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant. It is native to Europe and Western Asia, including Turkey, its distribution extending from England in the west to western Ukraine and the Iranian province of Gilan in the east. It is also naturalised or introduced in some parts of Canada, North Africa and the United States.

gerard.title: Of sleeping Nightshade
gerard.names: It is called of Dioscorides στρύχνος ὑπνωτικος : of Theophrastus στρύχνος μανικὸς : of the Latines Solanum somniferum somniferum or sleeping Nightshade; and Solanum lethale, or deadly Nightshade; and Solanum manicum, raging Nightshade; of some Apollinaris minor vlticana, & Herba Opfago: in English Dwale or sleeping Nightshade: the Venetians and Italians call it Bella dona: the Germaines Dollwurtz: the lowe Dutch Dulle bessen: in French Morelle mortelle: it commeth very neere vnto Theophrastus hi…
gerard.place: It groweth in vntilled places neere vnto high waies and the sea marshes and such like places. It groweth very plentifully in Hollande in Lincolneshire, and in the Ile of Elie at a place called Walsoken, neere vnto Wisbitch. I founde it growing without the gate of Highgate neere vnto a pound or pinfold on the left hād.
gerard.time: This flourisheth al the sommer and spring, beareth his seede and flower in Iuly and August.
gerard.temperature: It is colde euen in the fourth degree.
gerard.vertues: This kinde of Nightshade causeth sleepe, troubleth the minde, bringeth madnes if a fewe of the berries be inwardly taken, but if mo be giuen they also kill and bring present death. Theophrastus in his 6. booke doth likewise write of Mandrake in this maner; Mandrake causeth sleepe, and if also much of it be taken it bringeth death. The greene leaues of deadly Nightshade may with great aduise be vsed in such cases at Pettimorrell: but if you will follow my counsell, deale not with the fame in any case, and banish it from your gardens and the vse of it also, being a plant so furious and deadly: for it bringeth such as haue eaten thereof into a dead sleepe wherein many haue died, as hath beene often seene and prooued by experience both in England and else where. But to giue you an example hereof it shall not be amisse: It came to passe that three boies of Wisbich in the Ile of Ely, did eate of the pleasant and beautifull fruite hereof, two whereof died in lesse then 8. howers after they had eaten of them.

summary: A shrub with huge, nodding white trumpets that perfume the night air, popular in gardens worldwide. It is no longer known in the wild: every Brugmansia species is listed as Extinct in the Wild, possibly because the animal that spread its seeds vanished. All parts carry scopolamine and related alkaloids.
nativeRange: Atlantic Forest of south-eastern Brazil (now known only in cultivation and as escapes)
abilities: Produces scopolamine, hyoscyamine and atropine in all tissues
Releases strong evening scent to attract night-flying moths
Grows flowers up to about 30 cm long
Survives today only through human cultivation
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous, especially seeds and leaves. Eating any part, or tea from flowers, causes an anticholinergic delirium: dilated pupils, blurred vision, fast heart, hot dry skin, confusion, terrifying hallucinations, amnesia and sometimes death. Rubbing an eye after handling flowers can cause one dilated pupil for hours to days. Teenagers using it as a 'legal high' are often hospitalised. Similar-looking Datura is equally toxic.

fruit.description: Smooth, spindle-shaped green fruits, rarely produced in cultivation.

seed.description: Corky, angular brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Unknown in the wild; possibly extinct animal dispersers
seed.germination: Usually grown from cuttings

grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in the first or second year
steps: Wear gloves and wash hands after handling
Root cuttings in water or moist mix in warmth
Feed and water heavily while growing
Keep away from children and pets; bring indoors before frost

lore: Brugmansia species have long been used by Andean and Amazonian shamans as powerful and dangerous visionary plants. Long classified in Datura, angel's trumpets were split out by Christiaan Persoon in 1805 as Brugmansia, named after Dutch naturalist Sebald Justinus Brugmans.
funFact: Brugmansia flowers hang down, whereas Datura flowers point up; this is the easiest way to tell them apart.

wiki.extract: Brugmansia suaveolens, Brazil's white angel trumpet, also known as angel's tears and snowy angel's trumpet, is a species of flowering plant in the nightshade family Solanaceae, native to south eastern Brazil, but thought to be extinct in the wild. Like several other species of Brugmansia, it exists as an introduced species in areas outside its native range. It is a tender shrub or small tree with large semi-evergreen leaves and fragrant yellow or white trumpet-shaped flowers.

summary: The species behind bell peppers, jalapeños, cayenne, paprika and most chillies, domesticated in Mexico over 6,000 years ago. Its fiery capsaicin deters mammals while birds, which lack the pain receptor it triggers, eat the fruit and spread its seeds.
nativeRange: Southern North America to northern South America, domesticated in central-east Mexico; grown worldwide
abilities: Capsaicin binds the TRPV1 heat-pain receptor in mammals but not in birds
Capsaicin also protects seeds from Fusarium fungal attack
Heat is concentrated in the pale placental tissue, not the seeds themselves
Spread from the Americas to India, China and Africa within a century of 1492
edibleParts: leaves (cooked, in Filipino tinola and Korean dishes)
edibilityNote: Fruit is safe; very hot types can burn skin, eyes and the gut. Wash hands after cutting chillies.

uses.use: Chilli used for toothache, cough and to treat infections, recorded in the Florentine Codex
High-strength capsaicin patches (Qutenza) are approved for nerve pain after shingles; low-dose creams for arthritis pain

medicinal.cautions: Irritant to skin, eyes and mucous membranes; may aggravate reflux and haemorrhoids.

fruit.description: Hollow berry ranging from pea-sized wild chiltepins to 15 cm bell peppers; green ripening to red, yellow, orange, purple or brown; seeds attached to a pale central placenta.

seed.description: Flat, kidney- to disc-shaped, cream to pale-yellow seeds about 3–5 mm, smooth, clustered on the placenta
seed.germination: Sow 0.5 cm deep at 25–30 °C (bottom heat helps); sprouts in 7–21 days

grow.zones: Annual in temperate zones; short-lived perennial in USDA 10–12
grow.water: Moderate; let the surface dry slightly between waterings
grow.timeToHarvest: 60–90 days from transplanting (longer for very hot types)
steps: Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost on a warm mat; chillies need warmth to germinate.
Transplant after night temperatures stay above 12 °C, 40–50 cm apart; pots of 10+ litres work well.
Water evenly, mulch and feed with a potassium-rich fertiliser once flowers appear; pinch the first flowers on small plants to build size.
Stake heavy-cropping plants; slight dryness near ripening increases heat.
Snip fruit with scissors when green or fully coloured; dry on strings (ristras) or freeze. Overwinter plants indoors to crop earlier next year.

lore: Columbus called chillies 'pimiento', mistaking them for relatives of black pepper, and Portuguese traders carried them to Goa, Bengal and Africa within decades. Today India is the world's largest producer, and the chilli is inseparable from Sichuan, Thai and Korean food.
funFact: Wild chiltepin, the ancestral chilli, is the official native spice of Texas.

wiki.extract: Capsicum annuum is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades), native to the northern regions of South America and to southwestern North America. The plant produces berries of many colors including red, green, and yellow, often with pungent taste. It is one of the oldest cultivated crops, with domestication dating back to around 6,000 years ago in regions of Mexico. The genus Capsicum has over 30 species but Capsicum annuum is the primary species in its genus, as it has been widely cultivated for human consumption for a substantial amount of time and has spread across the world. This species has many uses in culinary and ornamental applications.

gerard.title: Of Ginnie or Indian Pepper
gerard.names: Actuarius calleth it in Greeke κεψικὸν, in Latin Capficum: & it is thought to be that which Auicenne nameth Zinziber caninum, or dogs Ginger: and Pliny Siliquaftrum, which is more like in tafte to pepper then is Panax, and it is therefore called Piperitis, as hee hath written in his 19. booke 12. chapter: Panax (faith he) hath the tafte of pepper and Siliquaftrum, for which caufe it is called Piperitis.
gerard.place: These plants are brought from forren countries, as Ginnie, India, and those parts, into Spaine and Italy: from whence wee haue receiued seede for our English gardens, where they come to fruite bearing: but the cod doth not come to that bright red colour which naturally it is possessed with, which hath hapned by reason of these vnkindely yeeres that are past: but we expect better when God shall sen…
gerard.time: The feedes hereof muft be fowen in a bed of hot horfedung, as muske Melons are, and remooued into a pot when it hath gotten three or fower leaues, that it may the more conueniently be carried from place to place to receiue the heate of the funne: and…
gerard.temperature: Ginnie pepper is extreme hot and drie euen in the fourth degree: that is to faie, farre hotter and drier then Auicen fheweth dogs ginger to be.
gerard.vertues: Ginnie pepper hath the tafte of pepper, but not the power or vertue, notwithftanding in Spaine and fundrie parts of the Indies they do vfe to dreffe their meate therewith, as we do with Calecute pepper: but (faith my author) it hath in it a malitious qualitie, whereby it is an enimie to the liuer & other of the entrails; Auicen writeth that it killeth dogs. It is faide to die or colour like faffron, and being receiued in fuch fort as faffron is vfually taken, it warmeth the ftomacke, and helpeth greatly the digeftion of meates. It diffolueth the fwellings about the throte called the Kings Euill, as kernels and cold fwellings; and taketh away fpots and lentiles from the face, being applied therto with honie.

summary: A rank, weedy nightshade with large white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods, packed with tropane alkaloids that cause terrifying delirium. It takes its English name from Jamestown, where soldiers who ate it in 1676 reportedly behaved like fools for eleven days.
nativeRange: Probably North and Central America; now a cosmopolitan weed
abilities: Makes scopolamine, hyoscyamine and atropine, which block acetylcholine receptors
Opens fragrant flowers at dusk for hawkmoth pollinators
Produces seed that stays alive in soil for decades
Thrives in disturbed, fertile ground and contaminates grain and vegetable crops
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially seeds. The anticholinergic syndrome ('blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone') includes dilated pupils, blurred vision, flushed hot dry skin, fast heart, urinary retention, hallucinations and delirium, seizures and sometimes death. Poisoning has happened through seeds contaminating buckwheat, soy or millet, leaves mistaken for other greens, and deliberate use as a hallucinogen. Physostigmine is used as an antidote under medical care.

uses.use: Purified dhatura used for asthma, pain and skin disease
Leaves smoked in 'asthma cigarettes' for bronchospasm

medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal; dose varies hugely between plants. Purified atropine and scopolamine are approved drugs, but the plant itself is not safe to use.

fruit.description: Walnut-sized green capsules covered in spines that split into four to release many seeds.

seed.description: Kidney-shaped dark seeds
seed.dispersal: Falls from the capsule; carried in contaminated grain
seed.germination: Not recommended for cultivation

lore: Robert Beverley's History and Present State of Virginia (1705) describes soldiers at Jamestown who ate the plant in salad and spent days in a foolish delirium. In Hindu tradition dhatura flowers and fruits are offered to Shiva.
funFact: Seeds of Datura can lie in the soil for over 30 years, waiting for the ground to be disturbed.

wiki.extract: Datura stramonium, known by the common names thornapple, jimsonweed or stink blade, is a poisonous flowering plant in the Daturae tribe of the nightshade family Solanaceae. Its likely origin was in Central America, and it has been introduced in many world regions. It is an aggressive invasive weed in temperate climates and tropical climates across the world. D. stramonium has frequently been employed in traditional medicine to treat a variety of ailments. It has also been used as a hallucinogen, taken entheogenically to cause intense, sacred or occult visions. It is unlikely to become a major drug of abuse owing to effects upon both mind and body frequently perceived as being highly unpleasant, giving rise to a state of profound and long-lasting disorientation or delirium with a potentially fatal outcome. It contains tropane alkaloids which are responsible for the psychoactive effects, and may be severely toxic.

gerard.title: Of Thorne apples
gerard.names: The first of these Thorne apples may be called in Latine Stramonia, & Pomum or Malum spinosum: of some Corona regia & Melospinus: the Grecians of our time name it παλαίοκυλον, or rather βαρυοκύκυλον, as though they should saie a nut stuffing and causing drowfinesse and troublesome sleepe: the Italians Paracoculi: it seemeth to Valerius Cordus to be Hyoscyamus Peruvianus, or Henbane of Peru: Cardanus doubteth whether it should be inserted among the Nightshades as a kind thereof: of Serapio & othe…
gerard.place: This plant is rare and strange as yet in Englande, I haue receiued seedes thereof from Iohn Robin of Paris, an excellent Herbarist; which did growe and beare flowers, but perished before the fruite came to ripenesse. The Thorne apple last described was brought in seede from Constantinople, by the right honorable the Lorde Edwarde Zouch and giuen vnto me, and beareth fruite and ripe seede.
gerard.time: The first is to be sowen in a bed of horsedung, as we do Cucumbers and Muske Melons. The other may be sowen in March or Aprill as other seedes are.
gerard.temperature: The whole plant is colde in the fourth degree, and of a drowsie and numming qualitie, not inferiour to Mandrake.
gerard.vertues: The iuice of Thorne apples boiled with hogges grease to the forme of an vnguent or salue, cureth all inflammations whatsoeuer, all maner of burnings or scaldings, as wel of fire, water, boiling lead, gunpowder, as that which comes by lightning, and that in very short time, as my selfe haue found by my daily practise to my great credite and profite. The first experience came from Colchester, where mistresse L'Obel, a marchants wife there, being most greeuously burned with lightning, and not finding ease or cure in any other thing, by this founde helpe when all hope was past, by the report of master William Ramme, publike notarie of the saide towne was perfectly cured. The leaues stamped small and boiled with oile oliue vntill the herbes be as it were burnt, then strained and set to the fire againe with some waxe, rosin, and a little turpentine, & made into a salue, doth most speedily cure olde vlcers, newe and fresh wounds, vlcers vpon the glandulous part of the yarde, and other sores of hard curation.

summary: A sprawling Andean nightshade, domesticated in Mexico, that Europeans long feared as poisonous before it conquered Italian and then world cuisine. Its pea-sized wild ancestor still grows in coastal Ecuador and Peru.
nativeRange: Wild ancestor (Solanum pimpinellifolium) in coastal Ecuador and Peru; domesticated in Mesoamerica; grown worldwide
abilities: Flowers are buzz-pollinated: bumblebees vibrate them to release pollen
Glandular hairs on stems release the distinctive 'tomato' smell and trap small insects
Fruit ripening is triggered by the plant hormone ethylene
Stems lying on soil sprout roots along their length
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is safe. Leaves and stems contain tomatine and other glycoalkaloids and are mildly toxic, especially to pets; green fruit has small amounts that are usually harmless when cooked.

uses.use: Fruit and leaves applied to skin infections and sore throats
Lycopene from cooked tomatoes studied for prostate and cardiovascular health, with mixed results

medicinal.cautions: Leaves and stems are toxic to pets; tomatoes can worsen reflux.

fruit.description: Juicy berry 1–15 cm, round, oval, plum- or heart-shaped; red, yellow, orange, pink, green-striped or near-black; fleshy walls around gel-filled seed chambers.

seed.description: Flat, round to kidney-shaped, pale tan to buff seeds about 3 mm across, covered in fine silky hairs and coated in jelly in the fruit
seed.dispersal: Birds, tortoises (in the Galápagos) and mammals
seed.germination: Sow 0.5 cm deep at 20–28 °C; sprouts in 5–10 days. Ferment saved seed in its jelly for 2–3 days, then rinse and dry

grow.zones: Annual warm-season crop; frost-tender perennial in USDA 10–12
grow.water: Moderate, steady; irregular watering causes splitting and blossom-end rot
grow.propagation: Seed; side-shoot cuttings root in water
steps: Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; pot on seedlings when they have true leaves.
After frost, harden off and plant deeply — bury the stem up to the first leaves, as it will root along its length.
Stake or cage plants; on cordon (indeterminate) varieties, pinch out side shoots in leaf axils.
Water deeply at the base and mulch to keep moisture even; feed with a high-potassium fertiliser once fruit sets.
Pick when fully coloured; at season's end, ripen green fruit indoors in a bag with a banana.

lore: The Italian herbalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli called it 'pomi d'oro' (golden apples) in 1544, and Europeans grew it as an ornamental for decades fearing it was poisonous. The Spanish town of Buñol throws well over 100 tonnes of tomatoes each August at La Tomatina.
funFact: In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled (Nix v. Hedden) that the tomato is legally a vegetable, though botanically a fruit.

wiki.extract: The tomato is a plant whose fruit is an edible berry that is eaten as a vegetable. The tomato is a member of the nightshade family that includes tobacco, potato, and chili peppers. It originated from western South America, and may have been domesticated there, in Mexico, or in Central America. The Spanish introduced tomatoes to Eurasia in the Columbian exchange in the 16th century.

gerard.title: Of apples of Loue
gerard.names: The apple of Loue is called in Latine Pomum Aureum, Poma Amoris, and Lycopersium, of some Glaucium: in English apples of Loue, and golden apples: in French Pommes d'amours: howbeit there be other golden apples whereof the poets do fable growing in the gardens of the daughters of Hesperus, which a dragon was appointed to keepe, who, as they fable, was killed by Hercules.
gerard.place: Apples of Loue do growe in Spaine, Italie, and such hot countries, from whence my selfe haue receiued seedes for my garden, where they do increase and prosper.
gerard.time: It is sowen in the beginning of Aprill in a bed of hot horse dung after the maner of muske Melons and such like colde fruits.
gerard.temperature: The golden Apple with the whole herbe it selfe is colde, yet not fully so colde as Mandrake, after the opinion of Dodonaeus: but in my iudgement it is very colde, yea perhaps in the highest degree of coldnesse: my reason is, bicause I haue in the hottest time of sommer cut away the superfluous braun…
gerard.vertues: In Spaine and those hot regions they vse to eate the apples prepared and boiled with pepper, salt, and oile: but they yeelde very little nourishment to the bodie, and the same naught and corrupt. Likewise they do eate the apples with oile, vineger and pepper mixed together for sauce to their meate, euen as we in these cold countries do mustarde.

summary: Domesticated around Lake Titicaca 7,000–10,000 years ago, the potato is the world's leading non-grain staple. Andean farmers still grow thousands of varieties, and freeze-dry them into chuño that keeps for years.
nativeRange: Andes of southern Peru and north-west Bolivia; also Chilean lowlands; grown worldwide
abilities: Stores energy in underground stem tubers that can each sprout a new plant
Over 4,000 varieties are known in the Andes
Tubers turn green and produce toxic glycoalkaloids when exposed to light
Cold storage converts starch to sugar, which is why chilled potatoes taste sweet
edibilityNote: Tubers are eaten cooked. Leaves, stems, berries, sprouts and green-skinned or sprouting tubers contain solanine and chaconine, which cause vomiting and neurological symptoms; cut away all green parts and sprouts.

uses.use: Raw grated potato poultices on burns, bruises and swollen eyes
Slices applied to the temples for headache and fever

medicinal.cautions: Green tubers, sprouts and all aerial parts are toxic.

fruit.description: Small, green, tomato-like berry 1–4 cm, poisonous, holding up to 300 seeds.

seed.description: 'True potato seed' is tiny, flat, kidney-shaped, cream to pale-yellow, about 1.5–2 mm; growers instead plant 'seed potatoes' — small whole tubers or chunks with eyes
seed.dispersal: Tubers spread vegetatively; berries by animals
seed.germination: True seed: sow on the surface at 15–20 °C; 1–2 weeks. Seed potatoes: chit (pre-sprout) in light for 4–6 weeks

grow.zones: Annual cool-season crop; grown in USDA 3–10 by adjusting planting time
grow.water: Moderate–high, steady, especially while tubers form
grow.soil: Loose, deep, slightly acidic (pH 5–6.5), well-drained; acidity reduces scab
grow.timeToHarvest: Early 'new' potatoes 60–90 days; main crop 100–140 days
steps: Set certified seed potatoes in egg cartons in a bright, cool room 4–6 weeks before planting to grow short, sturdy sprouts.
Plant 10–15 cm deep, 30 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart, once soil reaches about 7 °C and frost risk is passing.
'Earth up' by drawing soil over stems as they grow, leaving only the top leaves showing — this keeps tubers covered and prevents greening.
Water regularly once flowers appear; watch for late blight (brown leaf patches in warm, wet weather) and remove infected foliage.
Dig new potatoes when plants flower; for storage, cut down foliage when it yellows, wait two weeks, then lift and cure tubers in the dark.

lore: Spanish conquistadors brought tubers to Europe around 1570. Ireland's dependence on a few varieties led to the Great Famine of 1845–52, when late blight killed about a million people.
funFact: In 1995 the potato became the first vegetable grown in space, aboard the shuttle Columbia.

wiki.extract: The potato is a starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas that is consumed as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of the plant Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family Solanaceae.

This plate exemplifies Merian's revolutionary approach to natural history, documenting ecological relationships between plants and insects in their native Surinamese habitat.

summary: A grey-velvety nightshade-family shrub of dry country, whose horse-scented roots are Ayurveda's best-known rasayana (rejuvenating tonic). Its small orange-red berries hide inside papery lanterns, like those of its cousin the Chinese lantern.
nativeRange: Dry regions from the Mediterranean and North & East Africa through the Middle East to India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Makes withanolides, steroidal lactones such as withaferin A that are studied for anti-inflammatory and anti-stress activity
Tolerates drought, heat and poor alkaline soils, needing very little water
Encloses its berries in an inflated papery calyx that protects them as they ripen
edibilityNote: Roots are taken as a powder or extract, not eaten as food. Like many Solanaceae, leaves and unripe berries contain potentially toxic compounds.

uses.use: Rasayana tonic for debility, ageing, insomnia, stress and low libido; given in milk (ashwagandha ksheerapaka)
Asgandh used as a nervine and aphrodisiac tonic and applied to painful swellings
Leaves and roots used in parts of East and Southern Africa as poultices for wounds and for fever
Root extracts trialled for stress, anxiety and sleep, with small positive studies

medicinal.cautions: Liver injury has been reported with supplements, and Denmark banned ashwagandha products in 2023. May raise thyroid hormone levels and add to sedatives. Avoid in pregnancy, as it was traditionally used to cause abortion, and take care with autoimmune disease or immunosuppressants. Trials are mostly small and short.

fruit.description: Orange-red berry about 6 mm wide, enclosed in a papery husk; not eaten.

seed.description: Flat, kidney-shaped, yellowish seeds
seed.germination: 8–14 days at 20–30 °C; sow shallowly

grow.soil: Sandy or stony, well-drained, slightly alkaline
steps: Sow seed shallowly in warm soil in late spring or at the start of the rains
Thin seedlings to 30–60 cm and water sparingly
Harvest roots when the berries ripen and the leaves begin to dry
Wash, cut and sun-dry the roots

lore: The Charaka Samhita (c. 1st–2nd century CE) lists ashwagandha among the strengthening herbs. Its Sanskrit name, 'smell of horse', is said to describe both the root's odour and the strength it was believed to give.
funFact: Linnaeus first placed the plant in the genus Physalis, alongside tomatillos and Cape gooseberries, because of the lantern-like husk around its berry.

wiki.extract: Withania somnifera, known commonly as ashwagandha, is an evergreen shrub in the Solanaceae family that is native to the Middle East and North Africa, other African regions, southern Europe, Indian subcontinent, and Southeast Asia. Several other species in the genus Withania are morphologically similar. Other common names include Indian ginseng and winter cherry.

summary: A moss that builds landscapes and stores carbon. Sphagnum holds many times its own weight in water in dead, empty cells, acidifies its surroundings, and decays so slowly that its remains pile up as peat. Peatlands cover about 3% of Earth's land but store more carbon than all the world's forests combined.
nativeRange: Widespread in temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with records from other continents
abilities: Holds up to around 20 times its dry weight in water in large, dead hyaline cells
Acidifies its environment by exchanging hydrogen ions for mineral cations
Builds peat that preserves organic matter for thousands of years, including bog bodies such as Tollund Man
Fires its spores out of a pressurised capsule, forming a tiny vortex ring that carries them upward
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

uses.use: Dried sphagnum used as absorbent, mildly antiseptic wound dressings by the million

uses.tradition: Northern Indigenous and European folk practice
uses.use: Used as nappy lining and menstrual padding

medicinal.cautions: Sphagnum can carry the fungus Sporothrix, which causes 'rose gardener's disease' through skin cuts; wear gloves.

seed.description: Spores in a round capsule on a short stalk
seed.germination: Mostly spreads from fragments; place live strands on wet peat

grow.timeToHarvest: Covers a tray in a few months
steps: Spread chopped live strands on wet peat in a tray
Keep wet with rainwater and humid
Give bright light to keep it compact and colourful
Use it as a living top-dressing for carnivorous plants

lore: Bog acids and sphagnan in Sphagnum peat preserved Iron Age bodies such as Tollund Man (found in Denmark in 1950) in astonishing detail. Peat cut from sphagnum bogs fuelled homes in Ireland, Scotland and the Netherlands for centuries.
funFact: High-speed video shows Sphagnum capsules launching spores at about 3.6 m/s, with the spores lifted 10–20 cm by a self-made vortex ring.

wiki.extract: Sphagnum palustre, the prairie sphagnum or blunt-leaved bogmoss, is a species of peat moss from the genus Sphagnum, in the family Sphagnaceae. Like other mosses of this type it can soak up water up to the 30-fold amount of its own dry weight thanks to its elastic spiral fibers. S. palustre is rather frequent and is spread almost all over the world. It mainly grows in wet forests and—compared to other specimens of this genus—rarely grows in moors.

summary: Europe's ancient churchyard tree, some individuals possibly 2,000 years old or more, and one of its most poisonous. Its needles and seeds contain taxine alkaloids that can stop the heart, yet its needles are also the starting material for the cancer drug docetaxel.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa (Atlas Mountains), western Asia to northern Iran
abilities: Lives for many centuries; the Fortingall Yew in Scotland is estimated at 2,000–3,000 years
Regrows from old wood and can send down internal roots inside its hollow trunk
Tolerates deep shade and heavy pruning, which makes it ideal for hedges and topiary
Its elastic heartwood and springy sapwood made the best longbows
edibilityNote: Everything except the red fleshy aril is deadly; the seed inside the aril is toxic if chewed, so arils should not be eaten. Needles (fresh or dried) contain taxine B, causing dizziness, dry mouth, dilated pupils, vomiting, slow or irregular heartbeat and sudden cardiac arrest, sometimes within hours. Clippings are deadly to horses and cattle. Lookalikes: other dark conifers; children may eat the sweet red berries.

uses.use: 10-deacetylbaccatin III from yew needles is used to semi-synthesise docetaxel and paclitaxel, chemotherapy drugs for breast, lung and prostate cancers
Leaves used for respiratory complaints

medicinal.cautions: Raw plant material is deadly; taxane drugs are given only under specialist care.

fruit.description: Bright red, juicy cups with a single dark seed visible at the opening.

seed.description: Hard, dark seed in a red aril
seed.dispersal: Thrushes and other birds eat the arils and pass the seed
seed.germination: Needs warm then cold stratification; often takes two years

steps: Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer
Plant in well-drained soil; yew dies in waterlogged ground
Clip annually for hedges or topiary
Never let livestock or horses near clippings

lore: The Clacton spear, about 400,000 years old and among the oldest known wooden artefacts, is made of yew, and Ötzi the Iceman carried a yew longbow. In Britain yews were planted in churchyards, and Shakespeare's Macbeth includes 'slips of yew' in the witches' cauldron.
funFact: Paclitaxel (Taxol) was first found in the bark of the Pacific yew in the 1960s; making it from European yew needles meant trees no longer had to be stripped of bark.

wiki.extract: Taxus baccata is a species of coniferous tree in the family Taxaceae. It is the tree originally known as yew, though to distinguish it from related species it is sometimes called common yew, European yew, or, in North America, English yew. It is a woodland tree in its native range, which spans much of Europe and parts of West Asia, the Caucasus and Northwest Africa. All parts of the plant except the fleshy aril are poisonous, with toxins that can be absorbed through inhalation, ingestion, and transpiration through the skin.

summary: A slow-growing understorey conifer of Pacific Northwest old-growth forests. Loggers once burned it as trash, until its bark yielded paclitaxel (Taxol), one of the most important cancer drugs ever found.
nativeRange: Pacific Northwest of North America, from south-east Alaska to northern California, inland to Idaho and Montana
abilities: Bark contains paclitaxel, which freezes the microtubules that dividing cells need
Tolerates deep shade beneath Douglas fir and western hemlock
Wood is extremely dense, springy and rot-resistant
Foliage and seeds contain taxine alkaloids that can stop the heart
edibilityNote: Foliage, bark and seeds are deadly poisonous (taxines). The red fleshy aril is the only non-toxic part, but the seed inside is lethal if chewed. Highly toxic to horses and cattle.

uses.use: Several nations used bark or needle preparations as medicines for various ailments and topically, and prized the wood for bows, paddles, digging sticks and tools
Paclitaxel (Taxol) for ovarian, breast and lung cancer and Kaposi sarcoma; also coats some coronary stents

medicinal.cautions: The plant is deadly: taxines cause dangerously slow and irregular heartbeat and death, sometimes without warning. Paclitaxel itself is hospital chemotherapy with serious side effects. Never prepare remedies from yew.

fruit.type: Aril (fleshy seed cup; not a true fruit)
fruit.description: Bright red, juicy cup around a single dark seed; the seed is deadly.

seed.description: Olive-brown, ovoid seed partly enclosed in a red aril
seed.dispersal: Birds swallow the arils and pass the seeds intact
seed.germination: Deeply dormant; warm then cold stratification over 1–2 years

steps: Root semi-ripe cuttings in autumn under mist, or sow seed outdoors to stratify naturally
Plant in a cool, shady, sheltered spot
Keep away from livestock and play areas
Clippings are poisonous; dispose of them carefully

lore: In 1962 USDA botanist Arthur Barclay collected Pacific yew bark in Washington for a National Cancer Institute screening programme. Monroe Wall and Mansukh Wani isolated paclitaxel in 1966 and published its structure in 1971, and the clamour for bark led to the US Pacific Yew Act of 1992.
funFact: At first the bark of several mature trees was needed to treat a single patient. The drug is now made semi-synthetically from European yew needles or by plant-cell culture.
