summary: An evergreen camellia whose young leaves give every true tea — white, green, oolong, black and pu-erh differ only in processing. Left unpruned it becomes a tree; some Assam-type trees in Yunnan are claimed to exceed 1,000 years old.
nativeRange: South-west China (Yunnan) and adjacent northern Myanmar, Laos and north-east India; cultivated in Asia, East Africa and South America
abilities: Accumulates fluoride and aluminium from acid soils in its leaves
Contains L-theanine, an amino acid almost unique to tea, which smooths caffeine's effect
Can be repeatedly plucked: the bush regrows a fresh 'flush' every few weeks
Trees can live for many centuries
edibleParts: leaves (fermented and eaten as lahpet in Myanmar)
edibilityNote: Leaves are brewed or pickled. Very strong tea in excess can cause stomach upset and reduce iron absorption.

uses.use: Green tea to clear heat, refresh the mind and aid digestion; described in Lu Yu's Classic of Tea (c. 760 CE)
Eisai's 'Kissa Yōjōki' (1211) promoted tea for long life and wakefulness in meditation
Green-tea catechin ointment (sinecatechins) is a US FDA-approved drug for genital warts

medicinal.cautions: Caffeine; high-dose green-tea extract supplements have caused liver injury. Reduces absorption of non-haem iron.

fruit.description: Woody, round to three-lobed capsule 2–3 cm, green turning brown, splitting to release 1–3 seeds.

seed.description: Round to hemispherical, hard, smooth dark-brown seeds 1–1.5 cm across, oily inside
seed.dispersal: Gravity; rolled and cached by rodents
seed.germination: Short-lived: soak fresh seed 24 hours, discard floaters, sow 2–3 cm deep at 20–25 °C; 1–3 months

grow.sun: Partial shade to full sun in cooler areas
grow.water: Moderate–high; at least 1,200 mm rain or regular irrigation
grow.propagation: Single-leaf cuttings of selected clones, or seed
steps: Plant a rooted cutting in acidic, free-draining soil; in alkaline areas grow in a large pot of ericaceous compost.
Mulch with pine bark or leaf litter and water with rainwater if tap water is hard.
Prune back to about 75–100 cm in the second and third years to make a flat-topped, bushy 'plucking table'.
Pluck 'two leaves and a bud' from new flushes in spring and summer.
For green tea, steam or pan-fire leaves within hours, roll, and dry; for black tea, wither, roll to bruise, let oxidise 1–3 hours, then dry.

lore: Chinese legend says the emperor Shennong discovered tea in 2737 BCE when leaves blew into his boiling water. In 1848–51 the Scottish botanist Robert Fortune smuggled tea plants and seeds out of China for the East India Company, helping found the tea gardens of Darjeeling.
funFact: Almost every word for tea worldwide descends from either 'te' (via Dutch traders in Fujian, by sea) or 'cha' (by land along the Silk Road).

wiki.extract: Camellia sinensis, commonly known as tea plant, tea shrub, and tea tree, is a species of evergreen shrub in the flowering plant family Theaceae. Originally native to the highlands of the Hengduan–Purvanchal region between southwestern China, northern Myanmar and northeastern India, the leaves, buds and stems of C. sinensis are harvested by humans to produce tea, leading to its artificial introduction and cultivation as valuable cash crops in many other parts of the world, with China, India and Kenya being the three largest tea-producing countries.

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of a tea plant (Camellia sinensis), showing its leaves, branches, and small flowers.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Frutex The', or tea plant, as described by Jacobus Bontius. It is a significant early European botanical representation of the plant, detailing its serrated leaves and delicate flowers, reflecting the growing interest in Asian flora during the 17th century.

plates.long: This meticulous botanical engraving depicts the tea plant (*Camellia sinensis*), identified by the Chinese character '茶' at the top center. The plate illustrates various stages of the plant's growth, including its serrated leaves, multi-petaled flowers, and the development of its distinctive three-lobed seed capsules, shown in detail at the bottom. Such illustrations were crucial for European scie

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tea plant (Camellia sinensis) with a mountain landscape in the background.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a tea plant, labeled 'Cha' (茶), within a landscape setting. It is part of the 'Nōgyō Zensho', the most influential agricultural manual of the Edo period, which aimed to standardize and disseminate farming knowledge across Japan.

plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tea plant (Camellia sinensis) showing its leaves, flowers, and branching structure.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), identified by the characters 'Ming Cha' (茗茶) at the top of the page. It is featured in Li Shizhen's 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica), a monumental 16th-century work on Chinese pharmacology, where it serves as a visual guide for identifying the plant's medicinal and dietary properties.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a tea plant (Camellia sinensis), characterized by its serrated leaves and delicate blossoms. It is part of Wu Qijun's 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao' (1848), a monumental 19th-century Chinese botanical encyclopedia renowned for its extensive and accurate depictions of flora, bridging traditional herbal medicine and modern botanical science.

plates.long: A detailed copperplate engraving showing a tea plant (labeled 'Thee') with its leaves and flowers on the left side. The right side depicts a mountainous Chinese landscape featuring a pagoda, a walled city, and figures engaged in labor and travel. This illustration reflects the 17th-century European interest in Chinese botany and geography.

plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts the tea plant, identified as 'Cia' or 'Te Herba', within a stylized Chinese landscape. It reflects the 17th-century European fascination with exotic flora and the botanical knowledge transmitted through Jesuit missions, illustrating both the plant's morphology and its cultural environment.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a tea tree (Camellia sinensis), labeled as '茶樹' (Chashu). It is an entry from the Sancai Tuhui, a comprehensive Ming dynasty encyclopedia published in 1609, illustrating the plant's morphology for educational and reference purposes. Such illustrations were crucial for the dissemination of agricultural and botanical knowledge in early modern China.

summary: Australia's most painful plant, a nettle relative whose heart-shaped leaves are covered in hollow, silica-tipped hairs. A sting can cause excruciating pain that flares for days or weeks, and in some cases months. In 2020 researchers found the cause: tiny peptide toxins they named gympietides.
nativeRange: Rainforests of north-eastern Queensland, Australia; also eastern Indonesia (Moluccas) and Papua New Guinea
abilities: Covers its leaves, stems and fruit with silica-tipped hollow hairs that inject toxin like hypodermic needles
Makes gympietides, peptide toxins that act on pain-sensing sodium channels, similar to spider and cone snail toxins
Is a pioneer that quickly fills rainforest gaps after storms or clearing
Its hairs stay able to sting in dried herbarium specimens for decades
edibilityNote: Every surface of the plant stings. Contact causes intense burning pain, swelling and redness, with flare-ups from touch, cold or water for weeks; severe stings have caused collapse. The pink-purple fruits are eaten by animals but stinging hairs make them dangerous for people. Remove hairs with wax strips or adhesive tape, not by rubbing; seek medical help for large stings.

fruit.description: Mulberry-like clusters of pink to purple fruits, also covered in hairs.

seed.description: Small achenes on fleshy stalks
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: The name gympie-gympie comes from the language of the Gubbi Gubbi (Kabi Kabi) people of south-eastern Queensland, and early settler accounts reportedly tell of horses driven mad by the stinger. Australian ecologist Marina Hurley, who studied the plant, described being stung as like being 'burnt with hot acid and electrocuted at the same time'.
funFact: Despite its stings, Dendrocnide leaves are eaten by red-legged pademelons and certain beetles, which seem unaffected.

wiki.extract: Dendrocnide moroides, commonly known in Australia as the stinging tree, stinging bush, or gympie-gympie, and also sometimes referred to as the suicide plant, is a plant in the nettle family Urticaceae found in rainforest areas of Queensland and New South Wales in Australia. It is notorious for its extremely painful and long-lasting sting. The common name gympie-gympie comes from the language of the indigenous Gubbi Gubbi people of south-eastern Queensland.

plates.long: Depicted here is the hazelnut bush, rendered with characteristic woodcut line work to emphasize the texture of the leaves and the clusters of nuts. This image served as a visual reference for practitioners seeking to identify the plant for its various medicinal applications.

otherNames: Yì zhū qiánmá 异株荨麻 (Chinese)
summary: A plant armed with thousands of tiny glass-tipped syringes that inject an irritant cocktail into the skin. It is also nutritious, a source of fine linen-like fibre, and food for some of Europe's most familiar butterflies.
nativeRange: Europe, temperate Asia and western North Africa; with native subspecies in North America
abilities: Stinging hairs have silica tips that snap off and inject histamine, acetylcholine, serotonin and oxalic and tartaric acids
Grows thickly wherever soil is rich in phosphate and nitrogen, marking old settlements for centuries
Stem fibres are long and strong enough to spin and weave into cloth
Caterpillar food for peacock, small tortoiseshell, red admiral and comma butterflies
edibleParts: young leaves and tops (cooked or dried)
edibilityNote: Young tops are cooked as soup, pesto or tea; heat or drying destroys the sting. Use gloves when picking. Eat young growth before flowering; older leaves become gritty with cystoliths.

uses.use: Nettle tea as a spring tonic and diuretic; 'urtication', beating aching joints with fresh nettles, for rheumatism
Anjura seeds and leaves for cough, kidney stones and as a diuretic
Native nettles were used by many nations, including Pacific Northwest peoples, for fibre, as food, and by urtication for arthritis
Root extracts for urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia; leaf for arthritis and allergic rhinitis

medicinal.cautions: Diuretic effects may interact with lithium, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs. Mild digestive upset. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy. The sting can cause severe reactions in rare cases.

fruit.description: Minute flattened achenes on drooping female catkins (plants are mostly single-sexed).

seed.description: Tiny oval greenish-brown seeds
seed.dispersal: Wind, water and animals; long-lived seed bank
seed.germination: Needs light; 10–14 days at 15–20 °C

grow.soil: Rich, moist, high in nitrogen and phosphate
steps: Plant a rhizome piece in a corner or a sunk container
Cut back hard several times a year to keep a supply of young tops
Harvest with gloves before flowering
Leave a patch uncut over summer for butterfly caterpillars

lore: In Hans Christian Andersen's The Wild Swans (1838), the heroine weaves nettle shirts to break a spell on her brothers. During the First World War, Germany made uniform cloth from nettle fibre when cotton was blockaded.
funFact: A Bronze Age burial cloth from Lusehøj in Denmark, about 2,800 years old, turned out to be nettle fibre, and its chemistry suggests the nettles grew in Austria.

wiki.extract: Urtica dioica, often known as common nettle, burn nettle, stinging nettle, nettle leaf, or just a nettle or stinger, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Urticaceae. Originally native to Europe, much of temperate Asia and western North Africa, it is now found worldwide.

plates.desc: A detailed natural history illustration of a stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) featuring the life cycle of the European Peacock butterfly (Aglais io), including caterpillars, pupae, and adults, along with a fly and a wasp.
plates.long: This plate from Maria Sibylla Merian's seminal work on caterpillars illustrates the life cycle of the Peacock butterfly on its host plant, the stinging nettle. Merian was a pioneer in observing and documenting the ecological relationships between insects and plants, including the role of parasitoids like the wasp and fly shown here.

Illustrated by Hans Weiditz, this image represents a shift toward empirical observation in science, depicting the plant with all its natural imperfections and specific botanical features rather than as a stylized icon. The German caption 'Beyter Nesselen' identifies the specimen for contemporary

plates.long: A detailed botanical woodcut of a nettle plant (Urtica), showcasing the naturalistic style of Hans Weiditz. summary: A fast-growing hedgerow shrub with plates of creamy, muscat-scented flowers in early summer and drooping clusters of purple-black berries in autumn. It has been called the medicine chest of the countryside.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia; naturalised elsewhere
abilities: Berries are rich in anthocyanins, which inhibit influenza viruses in laboratory studies
Thrives on nitrogen-rich ground around rabbit warrens, farmyards and middens
Soft white pith is easily pushed out of stems, leaving hollow tubes
Fruit is a major autumn food for thrushes, blackcaps and warblers fattening up for migration
edibilityNote: Flowers and fully ripe, cooked berries are used in cordials, wine, syrups and jams. Raw or unripe berries, seeds, leaves, stems, bark and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides and can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Remove all stalks.

uses.use: Hot elderflower tea to bring on sweating in colds and fevers; berry syrup for coughs and flu; bark as a purgative
Khaman flowers and leaves used as a diaphoretic and diuretic and in poultices for swellings
Standardised berry extracts studied for shortening influenza and colds; EMA traditional-use monograph for elderflower in colds

medicinal.cautions: A handful of small trials suggest it shortens flu and colds; the evidence is limited. Raw plant parts are poisonous, so cook berries and avoid leaves, bark and seeds. May interact with diuretics and immunosuppressants.

fruit.description: Small purple-black drupes, 5–6 mm, in drooping flat clusters; each with 3–5 seeds.

seed.description: Small, wrinkled, light-brown pyrenes
seed.germination: Slow; needs warm then cold stratification, often 2 seasons

grow.soil: Fertile, moist; tolerates chalk and clay
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings in winter (easiest) or seed
steps: Push 25 cm hardwood cuttings into the ground in winter
Water through the first summer
Pick flower heads on a dry sunny morning, leaving some for berries
Prune out old stems each winter to keep it productive

lore: John Evelyn wrote in Sylva (1664) that if the virtues of elder were fully known, no Englishman would ail anything. Scandinavian and English folklore held that an Elder Mother lived in the tree and that wood should not be cut without asking her leave.
funFact: The name Sambucus is thought to come from the sambuca, an ancient instrument, because elder's hollow stems were made into pipes and whistles.

wiki.extract: Sambucus nigra is a temperate species of tree or shrub in the family Viburnaceae native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East. Common names include elder, common elder, black elder, European elder, and also elderberry for the fruit, and elderflower for the flowers. It grows in a variety of conditions including both wet and dry fertile soils, primarily in sunny locations. The plant is widely grown as an ornamental shrub or small tree.

plates.title: Notable Commentaries on the History of Plants
plates.author: Leonhart Fuchs
plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of an elderberry plant (Sambucus nigra).
plates.long: A full-page botanical illustration of an elderberry plant, identified by the Latin text 'SAMBVCVS' and German 'Holder'. The woodcut depicts the entire specimen including the gnarled root system, serrated pinnate leaves, and flat-topped flower clusters known as corymbs. It represents the scientific style of the 16th-century herbalists who prioritized clear, diagnostic outlines over shading.

summary: The Eurasian grape was domesticated in the South Caucasus and Near East around 8,000 years ago, where the oldest known wine residues were found in Georgian pottery. Thousands of cultivars, from 'Cabernet Sauvignon' to 'Thompson Seedless', are clones propagated by cuttings.
nativeRange: Wild subspecies sylvestris from Western Europe to the Caucasus and Central Asia; cultivated worldwide in temperate and Mediterranean climates
abilities: Climbs using coiling tendrils that wrap around supports within hours of touching them
Domestication turned a dioecious wild vine into self-pollinating hermaphrodite cultivars
Fruit skin hosts wild yeasts that can ferment crushed grapes into wine unaided
Can live and fruit for centuries; a vine in Maribor, Slovenia, is over 400 years old
edibleParts: fruit (fresh, dried as raisins, juiced, fermented)
edibilityNote: Fruit and leaves are eaten widely. Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and can cause kidney failure.

uses.use: Drākṣā (raisins) as a cooling laxative and in tonics such as Drākṣārishta
Red vine leaf extract for chronic venous insufficiency (heavy, swollen legs)
Raisins (munaqqa) for coughs and as a nutritive

medicinal.cautions: Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and cats. Alcohol from wine carries its own risks.

fruit.description: Round to oval berries 1–3 cm in tight bunches; skin green, golden, red, purple or blue-black with a waxy bloom; juicy translucent flesh.

seed.description: Pear- or teardrop-shaped pips with a short beak, light to dark brown, 4–7 mm long, with a hard woody coat; usually 1–4 per berry (absent or vestigial in seedless types)
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 2–3 months at 2–4 °C, then sow at 20–25 °C; 2–8 weeks. Offspring differ from the parent

grow.zones: USDA 6–10 (vinifera); hybrids and American species to 4
grow.water: Low–moderate; mild water stress after fruit set improves flavour
grow.soil: Deep, well-drained, even stony or poor; pH 5.5–7.5
grow.propagation: Hardwood cuttings of 3–4 buds taken in winter; grafting onto phylloxera-resistant rootstock where the pest is present
grow.timeToHarvest: First crop in year 2–3; full crop by year 4–5
steps: Select a variety for your heat and season length; where phylloxera or nematodes occur, buy vines grafted onto resistant American rootstock.
Plant in winter or early spring beside a sturdy trellis, wire fence or pergola, 1.5–2.5 m apart.
In year one, let one strong shoot grow and tie it up as the trunk; remove others.
Each winter, prune hard — leave 2-bud spurs (spur pruning) or 1–2 long canes (cane pruning), since fruit forms on new shoots from last year's wood.
Thin leaves around bunches for airflow, net against birds, and pick when berries taste sweet and seeds have turned brown.

lore: Clay jars at Gadachrili Gora in Georgia hold wine residues from about 6000 BCE, and wine was central to the rites of Dionysus and the Christian Eucharist. Persian poets such as Omar Khayyam and Hafez made the vine and its wine a symbol of mystical intoxication.
funFact: Nearly every European wine vine today grows on American rootstock, after the aphid-like phylloxera devastated Europe's vineyards in the 1860s–1890s.

wiki.extract: Vitis vinifera, the common grape vine, is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran. As of 2012, there were between 5,000 and 10,000 varieties of Vitis vinifera grapes though only a few are of commercial significance for wine and table grape production.

At the base of the vine, a narrative scene shows a man collapsed on the ground, presumably from the effects of wine, while three companions observe him. summary: A plant that grows just two leaves in its whole life, which can be more than a thousand years. The leaves keep growing from the base like conveyor belts while the tips fray in the Namib wind. It is the only species in its family, a gymnosperm lineage that branched off over 100 million years ago.
nativeRange: Namib Desert of western Namibia and south-western Angola
abilities: Grows only two strap-shaped leaves, which lengthen continuously from a basal meristem for its whole life
Large plants are estimated by radiocarbon at 1,000–2,000 years old
Survives where rain may not fall for years, drawing on fog and a deep taproot
Its genome carries signs of an ancient duplication and stress-tolerance adaptations linked to its longevity
edibilityNote: The core was reportedly eaten raw or roasted in hard times by local peoples, but it is protected and should not be harvested.

fruit.type: Cones (male and female on separate plants)
fruit.season: Mostly spring and summer after rare rain
fruit.description: Female plants bear blue-green to salmon cones; male cones are smaller and salmon-coloured.

seed.description: Papery-winged seeds
seed.dispersal: Wind; establishment only after unusual rains
seed.germination: Sow fresh on sandy mix at 25–30 °C; fungal rot is the main killer

grow.water: Low but regular in deep pots
steps: Dust fresh seed with fungicide and sow in a very deep pot of sterile sand
Keep at 25–30 °C and lightly moist until germination (1–3 weeks)
Never transplant: the taproot hates disturbance
Give strong sun and water deeply but infrequently

lore: Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch found it in southern Angola in 1859 and reportedly knelt and stared, afraid it would vanish if he touched it; Joseph Hooker described it in 1863. It appears on Namibia's national coat of arms.
funFact: Each plant has only two true leaves; the many 'leaves' you see are those two, split lengthwise by wind into ribbons.

wiki.extract: Welwitschia is a monotypic genus of gnetophytes containing only the species Welwitschia mirabilis. It is named after the Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch, who documented the plant in the 1850s. In common use, it is sometimes referred to as the tree tumbo or onyanga. It is native to Angola and Namibia, where it grows in the extreme conditions of the Namib desert, tolerating high heat and low precipitation. Welwitschia is the only living genus of the family Welwitschiaceae and order Welwitschiales, and is one of three extant genera of gnetophytes, alongside Gnetum and Ephedra.

summary: A ginger relative whose orange rhizomes colour curries, robes and wedding rituals across South Asia. Cultivated turmeric is a sterile hybrid that survives only because people have replanted its rhizomes for thousands of years.
nativeRange: Domesticated in South Asia, probably India; not known in a truly wild state. Cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Rhizomes contain curcuminoids, intensely yellow pigments that dye cloth and food
Curcumin is one of the most-studied plant compounds for anti-inflammatory activity
Triploid and seed-sterile; it is propagated entirely by people replanting rhizome pieces
Survives the dry season dormant underground and resprouts with the monsoon
edibleParts: leaves (used to wrap and steam food)
edibilityNote: Safe as a culinary spice. Concentrated curcumin supplements, especially those with added piperine, have been linked to rare cases of liver injury. Ground turmeric has been found adulterated with lead chromate in some markets.

uses.use: Haridra used as a blood purifier, for wounds, skin disease, cough and diabetes (prameha); applied as a paste to skin
Zard chob used externally for swelling and wounds and internally for jaundice and liver complaints
Jianghuang said to move blood and qi, for pain in the chest, abdomen and shoulders
Rhizome drinks such as Indonesian jamu kunyit asam for menstrual pain and general wellbeing

medicinal.cautions: Curcumin is poorly absorbed, and trials are mixed apart from modest effects in knee osteoarthritis. High-dose supplements may raise bleeding risk with anticoagulants, aggravate gallstones and, rarely, injure the liver. Buy from tested sources because of lead adulteration.

seed.description: Cultivated turmeric is triploid and practically never sets viable seed
seed.germination: Not grown from seed

grow.zones: USDA 8–12 (rhizomes lifted or protected where winters freeze)
grow.water: High during growth; dry when dormant
grow.timeToHarvest: 8–10 months, when leaves yellow and die back
steps: Plant rhizome pieces 5 cm deep in warm soil (above 20 °C) at the start of the wet season
Mulch heavily and keep evenly moist while leafing
Harvest when the foliage dies back; keep some rhizomes for replanting
Boil, sun-dry and grind the rest for spice

lore: Turmeric paste is applied to the bride and groom at the Hindu haldi ceremony before a wedding. The saffron-yellow robes of Theravada Buddhist monks were traditionally dyed with turmeric or jackfruit heartwood.
funFact: A 2019 Stanford-led study found that some turmeric in Bangladesh had been brightened with lead chromate, a toxic industrial pigment. It was traced as a likely source of lead in people's blood.

wiki.extract: Turmeric, or Curcuma longa, is a flowering plant in the ginger family Zingiberaceae. It is a perennial, rhizomatous, herbaceous plant native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia that requires temperatures between 20 and 30 °C and high annual rainfall to thrive. Plants are gathered each year for their rhizomes, some for propagation in the following season and some for consumption or dyeing.

summary: A tall rainforest herb of the ginger family whose small green pods hold the 'queen of spices'. It flavours Arabic coffee, chai and Scandinavian buns, and is the third most expensive spice by weight after saffron and vanilla.
nativeRange: Moist evergreen forests of the Western Ghats in southern India (and Sri Lanka)
abilities: Seeds hold an essential oil rich in 1,8-cineole and α-terpinyl acetate
Flowering stems creep along the ground, so pods form at the base of the plant
Grows in the deep shade of the forest understorey
edibilityNote: Safe as a spice.

uses.use: Ela for indigestion, nausea, bad breath, cough and to balance the heaviness of other foods and medicines
Qaqula / heel khurd as a carminative, heart and stomach tonic, and to stop vomiting
Cardamom-spiced coffee and chewed seeds for digestion and freshening breath

medicinal.cautions: Safe in food amounts. Medicinal amounts are traditionally avoided with gallstones, as they may trigger colic.

fruit.description: Pale green, three-sided oval pod, 1–2 cm, holding 15–20 sticky black seeds.

seed.description: Angular, wrinkled, dark-brown seeds
seed.germination: Fresh seed; 3–6 weeks at 25 °C in shade

steps: Plant divisions under 50–70% shade in rich soil
Keep moist and humid all year
Pick pods just before full ripeness, every few weeks
Dry pods slowly to keep their green colour

lore: Cardamom-scented qahwa is a symbol of hospitality across the Arabian Peninsula. Guatemala became the world's largest exporter after a German coffee planter introduced the plant there around 1914.
funFact: Most of the world's green cardamom now comes not from India but from Guatemala, where hardly any is eaten locally.

wiki.extract: Elettaria cardamomum, commonly known as green cardamom or true cardamom, is a herbaceous, perennial plant in the ginger family, native to southern India. It is the most common of the species whose seeds are used as a spice called cardamom that has a strong aroma used in both savory and sweet cooking. It is cultivated widely in tropical regions and reportedly naturalized in Réunion, Indochina, and Costa Rica.

summary: A reed-like tropical herb whose knobbly, pungent rhizome was one of the first spices traded from Asia to the Roman world. It is not known in the wild, and has been carried around the world by people.
nativeRange: Domesticated in Island Southeast Asia or southern China; unknown in the wild. Cultivated throughout the tropics
abilities: Gingerols in the fresh rhizome turn into hotter shogaols when dried or cooked
Acts against nausea, probably through serotonin (5-HT3) receptors in the gut
Rarely sets seed; spread worldwide entirely by rhizome cuttings
edibilityNote: Widely eaten. Large doses can cause heartburn.

uses.use: Shunthi to kindle digestive fire (agni), for nausea, colds, joint pain and as a carrier in many formulas
Fresh ginger (shengjiang) to induce sweating in colds and stop vomiting; dried ginger (ganjiang) to warm the interior
Zanjabil as a digestive and carminative, for phlegm, and as an aphrodisiac
Powdered rhizome for pregnancy nausea, motion sickness and post-operative and chemotherapy nausea

medicinal.cautions: Reasonable trial support for pregnancy nausea, much weaker for other uses. High doses may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants, worsen gallstones and cause heartburn. In pregnancy keep to the doses used in trials, about 1 g a day.

seed.description: Seed is very rarely produced in cultivation
seed.germination: Not grown from seed

grow.timeToHarvest: Young ginger at 4–5 months; mature at 8–10 months
steps: Soak a fresh organic rhizome overnight and cut into pieces each with a bud
Plant 5 cm deep in warm compost, buds up
Keep warm (above 20 °C) and moist in dappled shade
Harvest when leaves yellow, or dig 'baby ginger' earlier

lore: The Analects record that Confucius 'was never without ginger when he ate'. Zanjabil is named in the Qur'an (76:17) as a flavouring of the drink of paradise.
funFact: Ginger's name has travelled through Sanskrit śṛṅgavera ('horn-shaped'), Greek zingiberis and Latin zingiber to English.

wiki.extract: Ginger is a flowering plant whose rhizome, ginger root or ginger, is widely used as a spice and a folk medicine. It is an herbaceous perennial that grows annual pseudostems about one meter tall, bearing narrow leaf blades. The inflorescences bear flowers having pale yellow petals with purple edges, and arise directly from the rhizome on separate shoots.

gerard.title: Of Ginger
gerard.names: Ginger is called in Latine Zinziber.
gerard.place: Ginger groweth in Spaine, Barbarie, in the Canarie Ilands, and the Acores. Our men which sacked Domingo in the Indies, digged it vp there in sundry places wilde.
gerard.time: Ginger flourisheth in the hot time of sommer, and loseth his leaues in winter.
gerard.temperature: Ginger heateth and drieth in the third degree.
gerard.vertues: Ginger, as Dioscorides reporteth, is right good with meate in sauces, or otherwise in conditures: for it is of an heating and digesting qualitie, it gently looseth the bellie, and is profitable for the stomacke, and effectually opposeth it selfe against all darknes of the sight, answering the qualities and effects of Pepper. It is to be considered, that greene canded or condited Ginger is hot and moist in qualitie, prouoking venerie: and being dried, it heateth and drieth in the third degree.

otherNames: Ji tui gu 鸡腿菇 (Chinese, 'chicken-leg mushroom')
summary: A tall, shaggy white cylinder that pushes up through lawns and roadsides, sometimes even through asphalt. Within hours of picking it digests itself from the bottom up into black ink. It has also been found to trap and digest nematode worms.
nativeRange: Cosmopolitan in temperate regions; Europe, Asia, North America, and introduced elsewhere
abilities: Autodigests (deliquesces) its gills into black, spore-laden ink as the spores mature
Immobilises and digests nematodes using spiny cell structures and a toxin (first reported in 2004)
Can push through hard ground and thin tarmac by growth pressure
Accumulates heavy metals and arsenic from polluted soil
edibleParts: young white caps (cooked soon after picking)
edibilityNote: Good edible when young and white, cooked within a few hours of picking. Lookalikes: the common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria), which contains coprine and causes a severe alcohol reaction (flushing, palpitations, vomiting) if alcohol is drunk with the meal or up to about three days afterwards; and white Amanita and Lepiota species, which have white gills, a volva or ring and white spore prints. Shaggy ink cap gills turn pink then black, and its spore print is black. Avoid collecting it on roadsides or polluted ground.

seed.description: Spore print black; spores ellipsoid, smooth, with a germ pore, about 10–15 × 6–8.5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores shed as the gills liquefy from the cap edge upward

grow.soil: Composted manure, straw-based compost or rich lawn soil
steps: Mix spawn into pasteurised composted manure or straw compost in a tray or outdoor bed
Incubate at about 22–26 °C until colonised
Cover with a 2–3 cm 'casing' layer of moist soil
Fruit at 15–20 °C with high humidity; harvest while caps are tight and white

lore: Ink caps (this and the common ink cap) were once boiled down for writing and drawing ink, as their name suggests. Commercial cultivation as 'ji tui gu' in China expanded from the 1980s.
funFact: Self-digestion is the point: the gills liquefy from the bottom edge up so that each newly exposed layer of spores can drop freely.

wiki.extract: Coprinus comatus, commonly known as the shaggy ink cap, lawyer's wig, or shaggy mane, is a species of fungus. The young fruit bodies first appear as white cylinders emerging from the ground, then the bell-shaped caps open out. The white caps are covered with scales, the origin of its common names. The gills beneath the cap are white, then pink, then turn black. This mushroom is unusual because it will turn black and dissolve itself in a matter of hours after being picked or depositing spores.

summary: The red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy tales. It is a mycorrhizal partner of birch, pine and spruce, and it carries the psychoactive, poisonous compounds ibotenic acid and muscimol.
nativeRange: Temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere; introduced with pine plantations to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America
abilities: Forms ectomycorrhizal partnerships with birch, pine, spruce and fir, trading soil nutrients for tree sugars
Produces ibotenic acid, which converts to the more potent muscimol when dried
Its white 'warts' are fragments of the universal veil that wrapped the young button
Spread around the Southern Hemisphere on the roots of plantation pines
edibilityNote: Poisonous. Ibotenic acid and muscimol cause vomiting, confusion, delirium, muscle twitching and deep sleep. Deaths are rare but have been recorded. Some regions eat it after prolonged parboiling, but this is risky and not recommended. Young white buttons can be confused with deadly Amanita species and with puffballs.

seed.description: Spores (not seeds): spore print white; spores broadly ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, about 9–13 × 6.5–9 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores shed from the free white gills

lore: Siberian peoples such as the Koryak used it ritually. R. Gordon Wasson's 1968 book 'Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality' proposed it as the Soma of the Rig Veda. The name 'fly agaric' comes from the old European practice of crumbling it into milk to stupefy flies.
funFact: Muscimol passes into urine largely unchanged. Accounts from Siberia describe people drinking the urine of someone who had eaten the mushroom to get the effect a second time.

wiki.extract: Amanita muscaria, commonly known as the fly agaric or fly amanita or simply red toadstool, is a basidiomycete fungus of the genus Amanita. Its name may come from its historical use to kill flies or from the effects it causes. It is a distinctive, large, white-gilled mushroom typically featuring a bright red cap covered with white warts. The complex genetic diversity of A. muscaria suggests that it is a species complex. It is a widely distributed mushroom native to temperate and boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere, now also naturalised in the Southern Hemisphere, forming symbiotic relationships with various trees and spreading invasively in some regions.

summary: A pure-white, deadly Amanita of the North American Pacific coast. It contains the same amatoxins as the death cap. It fruits in late winter and spring under coast live oak, when foragers are out looking for other white mushrooms.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America, from Washington through California to Baja California
abilities: Contains amatoxins and phallotoxins that cause delayed liver and kidney failure
Forms mycorrhizae mainly with coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia), and also with other oaks and pines
Fruits in the cool wet season (January–April), unusually early for an Amanita
edibilityNote: Deadly. It is all white with a sac-like volva, and its buttons can be mistaken for edible puffballs, meadow mushrooms (Agaricus), young Amanita velosa (springtime amanita) and white Lepiota. Always dig up the whole base and cut buttons vertically. A seriously poisoned person may feel better for a while before organ failure begins.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, amyloid, about 9–14 × 7–10 µm

lore: It was formally described by Charles Horton Peck in 1909 from California specimens. It has caused several serious poisonings in California.
funFact: A drop of potassium hydroxide (KOH) stains its flesh yellow, a reaction it shares with other destroying angels.

wiki.extract: Amanita ocreata, commonly known as one of the many destroying angels, or more precisely the western North American destroying angel, is a deadly poisonous basidiomycete fungus, one of many in the genus Amanita. The large fruiting bodies generally appear in spring; the cap may be white or ochre and often develops a brownish centre, while the stipe, ring, gill and volva are all white. A. ocreata resembles several edible species commonly consumed by humans, increasing the risk of accidental poisoning. Mature fruiting bodies can be confused with the edible A. velosa, A. lanei or Volvopluteus gloiocephalus, while immature specimens may be difficult to distinguish from edible Agaricus mushrooms or puffballs.

summary: The world's deadliest mushroom, responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings. Half a cap can kill an adult. It has an olive-green cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring and a sac-like volva at the base, and is reported to taste pleasant.
nativeRange: Europe; introduced to North America (notably California and the Pacific Northwest), Australia, southern Africa and South America
abilities: Produces amatoxins (chiefly α-amanitin), which block RNA polymerase II and destroy liver cells
Its toxins survive cooking, drying and freezing
Symptoms are delayed 6–12 hours and are followed by a deceptive 'honeymoon' remission before liver failure
Has spread to new continents as a mycorrhizal hitchhiker on imported oak and chestnut roots
edibilityNote: Deadly. No part is safe, and cooking does not destroy the amatoxins. Victims have mistaken it for edible paddy-straw mushrooms (Volvariella volvacea), Asian Amanita species, field mushrooms (Agaricus), green Russula and young puffballs. Suspected ingestion is a medical emergency, even if the person feels well.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores globose to subglobose, smooth, amyloid, about 8–10.5 × 7–9 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores; also spread as mycorrhizae on transplanted tree roots

lore: Ancient historians wrote that the Roman emperor Claudius died in 54 CE after Agrippina served him poisoned mushrooms. A death cap is often suggested as the culprit, though this is speculation. Voltaire wrote that a dish of mushrooms killed the Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI in 1740 and so changed the course of Europe.
funFact: The deadly amanitin is so specific in blocking gene transcription that molecular biologists use it as a laboratory tool.

wiki.extract: Amanita phalloides, commonly known as the death cap, is a deadly poisonous basidiomycete fungus and mushroom, one of many in the genus Amanita. Originating in Europe but later introduced to other parts of the world since the late twentieth century, A. phalloides forms ectomycorrhizae with various broadleaved trees. In some cases, the death cap has been introduced to new regions with the cultivation of non-native species of oak, chestnut, and pine. The large fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn; the caps are generally greenish in colour with a white stipe and gills. The cap colour is variable, including white forms, and is thus not a reliable identifier.

summary: The blue-green mould whose accidental growth on a Staphylococcus plate at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1928 led Alexander Fleming to penicillin. DNA work in 2011 showed both Fleming's isolate and the high-yield industrial strain belong to P. rubens, not P. notatum or P. chrysogenum as long thought.
nativeRange: Cosmopolitan in soil, indoor air, damp buildings and decaying food
abilities: Secretes penicillin, a β-lactam that blocks bacterial cell-wall construction
Its brush-shaped conidiophores ('penicillus' = little paintbrush) release dry chains of airborne spores
A common indoor mould on damp walls, bread and fruit
Industrial strains descended from a 1943 isolate from a mouldy cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois, produce thousands of times more penicillin than Fleming's original
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Mouldy food should be discarded. Related food moulds (P. roqueforti, P. camemberti) are used deliberately in cheese. Spores can trigger allergies and asthma.

uses.use: Source of penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, which transformed the treatment of bacterial infections

medicinal.cautions: Penicillin allergy (rashes to anaphylaxis) affects a small percentage of people. Bacterial resistance results from overuse. The mould itself is an allergen, not a medicine.

seed.description: Conidia (asexual spores) blue-green en masse, globose to subglobose, smooth, about 2.5–3.5 µm, in dry chains from brush-like conidiophores
seed.dispersal: Airborne conidia, abundant in indoor and outdoor air

lore: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain turned Fleming's observation into a drug at Oxford in 1940–41, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize. Mass production in the US in time for D-Day in 1944 saved many thousands of wounded soldiers.
funFact: Mary Hunt, a lab assistant nicknamed 'Mouldy Mary', found the super-producing strain on a rotting cantaloupe in a Peoria market.

photos.attribution: Houbraken, J., Frisvad, J.C. & Samson, R.A (CC BY-SA 4.0), Wikimedia Commons

wiki.extract: Penicillium rubens is a species of fungus in the genus Penicillium and was the first species known to produce the antibiotic penicillin. It was first described by Philibert Melchior Joseph Ehi Biourge in 1923. In 1928, Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London discovered that the fungus produced an antibiotic that killed bacteria, and named the unknown compound penicillin. For the discovery and development of penicillin, Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Ernst Boris Chain and Howard Florey.

summary: A rubbery, ear-shaped brown jelly fungus, mostly on elder in Europe. It dries hard and revives when soaked. The closely related Asian wood ears (A. heimuer, A. cornea) are among the most-eaten mushrooms on Earth.
nativeRange: Europe, on elder (Sambucus) and other hardwoods; East Asian 'mu'er' is now treated as A. heimuer
abilities: Survives drying completely and revives within minutes of rain
Decays dead branches, especially of elder
Contains compounds that inhibit platelet clumping
edibilityNote: Edible and widely eaten cooked, but soak dried wood ear for only a few hours, in the fridge. Wood ear soaked for days at room temperature has caused fatal bongkrekic-acid poisoning from bacterial contamination (Burkholderia gladioli), with deaths reported in China. It thins the blood mildly. There are no deadly lookalikes; other jelly fungi such as witches' butter and Exidia are not dangerous.

uses.use: Mu'er taken to 'move blood' and nourish the lungs and stomach
Boiled in milk for sore throats; used as eye poultices (recorded in early modern herbals)

medicinal.cautions: May increase bleeding with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs, and before surgery. Risk of bongkrekic acid poisoning from over-soaked mushrooms.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores sausage-shaped (allantoid), smooth, about 15–23 × 4–8 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores from the smooth inner surface

grow.water: High humidity; tolerates drying between rains
grow.soil: Hardwood logs (elder, oak, beech) or supplemented sawdust bags
grow.timeToHarvest: Sawdust bags about 2 months; logs 6–12 months
steps: Inoculate fresh hardwood logs with plug spawn, or sterilised sawdust bags with spawn
Incubate at about 22–28 °C until colonised
Cut slits in bags (or water logs) and keep humidity high at about 18–28 °C
Pick ears when fully expanded, then dry them for storage

lore: Its name comes from the medieval legend that Judas Iscariot hanged himself from an elder tree, whose ears grew from it after. 'Judas's ear' was garbled to 'Jew's ear' in English. Chinese texts describe growing mu'er on logs from at least the Tang dynasty (7th century CE).
funFact: Dried wood ear can expand to several times its size within an hour of soaking.

wiki.extract: Auricularia auricula-judae, commonly known as wood ear, jelly ear or historically as Jew's ear, is a species of fungus in the order Auriculariales. Basidiocarps are brown, gelatinous, and have a noticeably ear-like shape. They grow on wood, especially elder. The specific epithet is derived from the belief that Judas Iscariot hanged himself from an elder tree.

plates.author: Carolus Clusius
plates.desc: Woodcut of a fungus growing on a piece of wood, identified as Jew's ear fungus.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates a fungus growing on a tree trunk, identified as 'Auricula Judae' or Jew's ear. It highlights the observational accuracy of 17th-century botanical illustration, showing the fungus's characteristic ear-like shape and its relationship to its host substrate.

summary: A stout, bun-capped mushroom with a sponge of pores instead of gills and a fat, net-patterned stem. It is one of the most traded wild mushrooms in the world and gives Italian cooking its deep, nutty dried porcini flavour.
nativeRange: Temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere; introduced with pines and oaks to southern Africa, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Ectomycorrhizal with pine, spruce, fir, oak, beech, chestnut and birch
Pores start white and turn yellow-olive as spores mature, without bruising blue
Can produce fruiting bodies weighing over 3 kg
Accumulates selenium and, in polluted areas, radiocaesium from the soil
edibilityNote: Choice edible. Lookalikes: the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus), with pinkish pores and a dark net, is not dangerous but ruins a dish; Satan's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) and other red-pored, blue-staining boletes cause severe gastric poisoning. Rule of thumb: avoid boletes with red or orange pores or flesh that quickly turns blue. Never eat raw in quantity.

seed.description: Spore print olive-brown; spores spindle-shaped (fusiform), smooth, about 12–17 × 4–5.5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores released from the pore tubes

lore: Italians call it porcino ('piglet'). The Latin name 'edulis' (edible) was given by Pierre Bulliard in 1782. Dried porcini have been traded across the Alps for centuries.
funFact: Despite intense effort, nobody has cultivated porcini commercially. Every porcino sold is wild-picked.

wiki.extract: Boletus edulis is a basidiomycete fungus, and the type species of the genus Boletus. It is prized as an edible mushroom.

The plate illustrates the mushroom at different stages of growth and includes a vertical cross-section to show its internal structure, reflecting the scientific precision of late 18th-century natural history documentation.

The larger specimen is tilted to reveal the greenish-yellow pore surface beneath the brown cap and a thick, bulbous stem. A smaller mushroom stands behind it, and a green oval to the left provides a detail of the spore or pore color.

summary: An egg-yolk-yellow, apricot-scented woodland mushroom and one of the most prized wild edibles in Europe. Instead of true gills it has blunt, forking ridges that run down the stem, a key identification feature.
nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia; North American 'cibarius' records mostly belong to related species (e.g. C. californicus, C. formosus, C. flavus)
abilities: Ectomycorrhizal with beech, oak, birch, pine and spruce; it has never been reliably cultivated
Its false gills are blunt, forked ridges, not true blade-like gills
Highly resistant to insect larvae, so it rarely turns maggoty
Can keep fruiting from the same spot for decades
edibilityNote: Excellent cooked. Dangerous lookalikes: the jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus olearius in Europe, O. illudens in North America), which has true, sharp gills, grows in clusters on wood and causes severe vomiting; the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca), which has thin, true forked gills; and orange webcaps (Cortinarius species, including deadly C. orellanus and C. rubellus) with rusty spore prints. Check for blunt ridges, solid pale flesh and a pale spore print.

seed.description: Spore print pale yellow to pinkish-cream; spores ellipsoid, smooth, about 8–11 × 4.5–6 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores shed from the ridged underside

lore: Pickled and dried chanterelles have long been a winter staple in Baltic and Slavic households. Lithuania and Poland still export them by the tonne, and a large share of Europe's girolles comes from Eastern European foragers.
funFact: DNA studies since 2011 have shown that North America's 'golden chanterelles' are several separate species; true Cantharellus cibarius is essentially a European mushroom.

Such plates were essential for the emergin

plates.long: This plate from Paulet's 'Iconographie des Champignons' illustrates the Chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius), known in French as 'Girole'. The detailed engraving captures the characteristic funnel shape and ridged gills of this prized edible fungus, serving as both a scientific record and a work of botanical art.

summary: A pale grey, finely branched lichen that carpets huge areas of tundra and boreal forest floor. It is the main winter food of reindeer and caribou, which smell it beneath the snow. It grows only a few millimetres a year, so overgrazed carpets take decades to recover.
nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic and boreal regions; also high mountains further south
abilities: Can make up most of the winter diet of reindeer and caribou
Grows only about 3–5 mm a year
Produces atranorin and fumarprotocetraric acid; its lichen acids make it hard for most animals to digest
Survives freezing and drying, reviving when moistened
edibilityNote: Famine food for people, eaten only after soaking in water or wood-ash lye and boiling to remove bitter lichen acids. Raw lichen causes stomach upset. Lichens accumulate radioactive fallout and heavy metals; reindeer herders in Scandinavia were affected by Chernobyl caesium in 1986 through lichen.

uses.tradition: Indigenous Arctic and Subarctic peoples (e.g. Cree, Dene)
uses.use: Decoctions taken for colds, fevers and joint pain
Boiled for coughs and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Lichen acids irritate the gut when raw. Lichens concentrate heavy metals and radionuclides.

seed.description: Mainly reproduces by fragments; rarely produces brown apothecia with colourless, one-celled ascospores
seed.dispersal: Fragments broken off by trampling animals, wind and water

lore: Sámi reindeer herding has followed the lichen pastures for centuries. Indigenous Arctic peoples ate the half-digested lichen from caribou stomachs. After Chernobyl in 1986, radioactive caesium in lichen-fed reindeer forced Sweden and Norway to cull herds.
funFact: Despite the name 'reindeer moss', it is not a moss but a fungus partnered with green algae.

wiki.extract: Cladonia rangiferina, also known as reindeer cup lichen, reindeer lichen or grey reindeer lichen, is a light-coloured fruticose, cup lichen species in the family Cladoniaceae. It grows in both hot and cold climates in well-drained, open environments. Found primarily in areas of alpine tundra, it is extremely cold-hardy.

plates.author: François Le Vaillant
plates.desc: A male Cuvier's Bee-eater perched on a lichen-covered branch.
plates.long: A male Cuvier's Bee-eater is shown in profile, perched on a textured, lichen-covered branch. The bird features a long, curved black beak, a white throat, and distinctive green and blue plumage with long, bifurcated tail feathers. This scientific illustration is a hand-colored engraving from the early nineteenth century.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts the 'Colibri à tête noire' (Black-headed Hummingbird), showcasing its distinctive long tail feathers and iridescent plumage. It is a plate from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 1802 masterpiece 'Histoire naturelle des colibris', which was celebrated for its innovative use of metallic inks and gold leaf to capture the unique brilliance of these birds.

plates.author: François Le Vaillant
plates.desc: A detailed natural history engraving of a male Promerops promerup bird perched on a lichen-covered tree stump, featuring iridescent blue and green plumage and a long curved beak.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a male Promerops promerup, showcasing the iridescent plumage and specialized curved beak characteristic of the species. Produced for François Le Vaillant's 'Histoire naturelle des promerops et des guêpiers' (1807), it represents the peak of early 19th-century French ornithological publication, combining scientific observation with artistic precision.

plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of Usnea (tree moss or lichen)
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1486 'Herbarius latinus' depicts Usnea, commonly known as tree moss or lichen. In the late medieval period, such herbals were essential medical texts, and Usnea was documented for its astringent and cooling properties in treating various ailments.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a plant identified in the text as Lichen, likely referring to Lungwort (Pulmonaria). The illustration emphasizes the plant's distinctive leaf patterns, which were historically believed to indicate its medicinal use for lung ailments according to the Doctrine of Signatures.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates 'Lichen Marinus', characterized by its unique chain of rounded, leaf-like segments. It serves as an early taxonomic record of marine flora, demonstrating the precision of Renaissance-era botanical woodcuts.

As an early example of botanical printing, the image was designed to be functional for identification, while the hand-applied green pigment reflects the transition from manuscript traditions to printed books.

summary: A parasite of rye and other grasses that replaces grain with a hard, purple-black, horn-like sclerotium full of alkaloids. Contaminated bread caused mass poisoning in medieval Europe. The same alkaloids gave medicine drugs for childbirth and migraine, and gave chemistry LSD.
nativeRange: Worldwide in temperate grasses and cereals; especially rye in Europe
abilities: Infects grass flowers and replaces the ovary with a sclerotium (the 'ergot')
Exudes sticky, sugary 'honeydew' full of conidia that insects carry to new flowers
Produces ergot alkaloids (ergotamine, ergometrine, lysergic acid derivatives) that constrict blood vessels and act on serotonin and dopamine receptors
Sclerotia overwinter in soil and sprout tiny drumstick-like stromata in spring
edibilityNote: Deadly. Ergotism takes two forms: gangrenous (burning limbs that blacken and drop off) and convulsive (seizures, hallucinations). Grain is screened to remove sclerotia, and modern regulations set limits for ergot in flour.

uses.use: 'Pulvis parturiens' given to speed labour; later used against haemorrhage after birth
Ergometrine/methylergometrine for postpartum haemorrhage; ergotamine and dihydroergotamine for migraine

medicinal.cautions: Raw ergot is lethal; only standardised pharmaceutical drugs are safe. Ergot drugs are dangerous with HIV protease inhibitors, macrolide antibiotics and triptans, and in pregnancy outside obstetric use.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds) thread-like (filiform), about 50–76 × 0.6–0.7 µm, from flask-shaped perithecia in purple stromata; asexual conidia in sugary honeydew
seed.dispersal: Ascospores shot into the air in spring; conidia spread by insects attracted to honeydew and by rain splash

lore: Medieval Europe called ergotism 'St Anthony's Fire', and the Antonite monks ran hospitals for victims. Albert Hofmann first synthesised LSD from ergot's lysergic acid at Sandoz in 1938. In 1976, Linnda Caporael proposed (controversially) that ergotism lay behind the Salem witch trials.
funFact: One of the last major outbreaks was in Pont-Saint-Esprit, France, in 1951, though its cause is still debated.

wiki.extract: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. C. purpurea most commonly affects outcrossing species such as rye, as well as triticale, wheat and barley. It affects oats only rarely.

otherNames: Chong cao hua 虫草花 (Chinese, 'cordyceps flower')
Bei chong cao 北冬虫夏草 (Chinese)
summary: Bright orange clubs that rise from moth and butterfly pupae buried in soil, which the fungus has killed and filled with mycelium. Unlike its Himalayan cousin it can be grown on grain, and it is sold in Asian markets as dried 'cordyceps flower' for soup.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Europe, Asia and North America
abilities: Infects lepidopteran larvae and pupae, replaces their tissues with mycelium and then fruits from the corpse
Produces cordycepin (3′-deoxyadenosine), an adenosine mimic studied as an anticancer and antiviral compound
Needs light to make its orange carotenoid pigments
Its thread-like ascospores break into many short part-spores
edibilityNote: The cultivated orange fruiting bodies are eaten in Chinese and Korean soups and teas. Do not confuse with other insect fungi, or with orange club and coral fungi of unknown edibility, when foraging. Most people should buy cultivated product.

uses.use: A cheaper substitute for Ophiocordyceps sinensis (yartsa gunbu) as a lung and kidney tonic
Tea for fatigue and stamina

medicinal.cautions: Human trial evidence is limited. Cordycepin affects purine metabolism. Avoid with immunosuppressants, anticoagulants or during pregnancy. Supplement quality varies widely.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds) long and thread-like, multiseptate, breaking into short cylindrical part-spores about 3–6 × 1 µm; no conventional spore print
seed.dispersal: Ascospores ejected from flask-shaped perithecia in the club's orange head; asexual conidia also infect insects

grow.sun: Bright indirect light, 12 hours daily (needed for orange colour)
grow.soil: Brown rice or other grain with nutrient broth; commercially also silkworm pupae
grow.propagation: Liquid culture; strains degenerate quickly, so start from fresh culture
steps: Fill jars with brown rice and a nutrient broth (e.g. potato-dextrose with a little peptone) and sterilise
Inoculate with liquid culture and incubate in the dark at about 18–22 °C for 1–2 weeks
Once colonised and yellowing, give 12 hours of light daily and cool nights (about 16–20 °C)
Harvest the orange clubs at about 5–8 cm, then dry at low heat

lore: Since the 1980s, Chinese growers have mass-produced it as 'chong cao hua', a substitute for wild Himalayan caterpillar fungus, which costs more than its weight in gold. It gave the 'cordyceps' of popular culture an easy-to-grow stand-in.
funFact: Cordycepin was first isolated from Cordyceps militaris in 1950, one of the earliest nucleoside antibiotics discovered.

wiki.extract: Cordyceps militaris, commonly known as the caterpillar fungus, is a species of fungus in the family Cordycipitaceae, and the type species of the genus Cordyceps, which consists of hundreds of species. The species was originally described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753 as Clavaria militaris. Cordyceps militaris parasitizes insects and is used in traditional Chinese medicine.

plates.title: Illustrations of Fungi which Grow in Bavaria and the Palatinate around Ratisbon, Vols 1–2

summary: A modest orange-brown mushroom of conifer bogs and mossy forest. It contains orellanine, which destroys the kidneys days or even weeks after a meal, by which time the cause may not be suspected.
nativeRange: Northern Europe (especially Scandinavia and Scotland) and parts of North America and Asia, with conifers
abilities: Contains orellanine, a bipyridine toxin that accumulates in the kidneys and causes kidney failure
Orellanine glows blue-white under UV light, which helps forensic identification
Forms ectomycorrhizae with spruce and pine
Its cobweb-like veil (cortina) leaves rusty threads on the stem
edibilityNote: Deadly. Symptoms begin 2–20 days after eating, starting with thirst, nausea and back pain, followed by kidney failure. Many survivors need lifelong dialysis or a kidney transplant. Cooking does not destroy orellanine. Victims have mistaken it for ceps (Boletus edulis, which has pores, not gills), chanterelles (Cantharellus, with blunt ridges and a pale spore print), and hallucinogenic Psilocybe. Webcaps have rusty-brown spore prints and true gills.

seed.description: Spore print rusty brown; spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, warty, about 9–12 × 6.5–8.5 µm

lore: In 2008, Nicholas Evans, author of 'The Horse Whisperer', and three relatives were poisoned in Scotland after mistaking deadly webcaps for ceps. Three of them suffered kidney failure, and Evans received a kidney transplant from his daughter in 2011. The danger of orellanine came to light after a 1952 mass poisoning by the related Cortinarius orellanus in Konin, Poland, which affected 102 people and killed 11; Stanisław Grzymala isolated the toxin in 1962.
funFact: Orellanine's chemical structure was not worked out until 1979, almost three decades after the Konin poisoning revealed the danger.

wiki.extract: Cortinarius rubellus, commonly known as the deadly webcap, is a species of fungus in the family Cortinariaceae, native to high-latitude temperate to subalpine forests of Eurasia and North America. Within the genus it belongs to a group known as the Orellani, all of which are highly toxic. Eating them results in kidney failure, which is often irreversible. The mushroom is generally tan to brown all over, with a conical to convex cap 2.5 to 8 centimetres in diameter, adnate gills and a 5.5 to 11 cm tall stipe.

summary: A brain-like, red-brown spring mushroom of sandy conifer woods. It contains gyromitrin, which the body converts to monomethylhydrazine, a component of rocket fuel. Despite this, Finland sells it with mandatory warnings and parboiling instructions as a traditional delicacy.
nativeRange: Europe and North America, mainly in conifer forest on sandy soil
abilities: Contains gyromitrin, which breaks down to the toxin monomethylhydrazine (MMH)
Fumes from boiling can poison the cook
Fruits in early spring, at the same time as true morels
MMH is carcinogenic in animal studies, even in small repeated doses
edibilityNote: Deadly when raw and dangerous even when prepared. Gyromitrin causes vomiting and diarrhoea, then liver damage, seizures and death. Finnish practice of boiling twice in fresh water with good ventilation reduces but does not reliably remove the toxin, and cumulative and carcinogenic risks remain. Do not eat. It is commonly mistaken for true morels (Morchella), which have a regular honeycomb of pits and are hollow throughout; the false morel has a brain-like, wrinkled cap and a chambered or cotton-filled interior.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds) ellipsoid, smooth, with two oil droplets, about 17–22 × 7–10 µm, 8 per ascus; spore print whitish
seed.dispersal: Ascospores forcibly discharged from the cap surface

lore: In Finland, korvasieni is sold fresh with warning labels and instructions for parboiling. It has also been eaten in parts of Sweden, the Pyrenees and Michigan. Many other European countries ban its sale.
funFact: Monomethylhydrazine, its breakdown product, was used as rocket fuel in the Space Shuttle's manoeuvring thrusters.

wiki.extract: Gyromitra esculenta is an ascomycete fungus from the genus Gyromitra. The fruiting body, or mushroom, is an irregular brain-shaped cap, dark brown in colour, that can reach 10 centimetres high and 15 cm (6 in) wide, perched on a stout white stipe up to 6 cm high. It is widely distributed across Europe and North America, normally fruiting in sandy soils under coniferous trees in spring and early summer.

summary: Overlapping shelves of brilliant sulphur-yellow and orange on oak, willow and cherry, visible from far across a wood. When young it has a texture so like chicken breast that it is a common meat substitute.
nativeRange: Europe and eastern North America in the strict sense; related species replace it in western North America and elsewhere
abilities: Causes brown cubical heart rot in living trees, digesting cellulose and leaving lignin
Can produce brackets totalling over 20 kg from a single tree
Has no gills; it releases spores from tiny pores on the sulphur-yellow underside
edibleParts: tender outer edges of young brackets (thoroughly cooked)
edibilityNote: Popular edible but must be well cooked. A minority of people get vomiting, dizziness or swollen lips, even from cooked mushrooms. Avoid specimens growing on yew (Taxus), eucalyptus, locust or conifers, which some foragers report as more likely to cause illness. There is no deadly bracket lookalike, but the toxic jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus), which has gills and grows in clusters, is sometimes confused with it at a distance. Old brackets are tough and sour.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, about 5–7 × 3.5–5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores; also spreads by thick-walled asexual chlamydospores

lore: German foresters call it 'Schwefelporling' (sulphur polypore). It is feared in old orchards because its brown rot leaves trunks hollow and brittle.
funFact: Rotted heartwood left by this fungus breaks into neat cubes, the classic sign of brown rot.

wiki.extract: Laetiporus sulphureus is a species of bracket fungus. Its common names include sulphur polypore, sulphur shelf, and chicken-of-the-woods. Its fruit bodies grow as striking golden-yellow shelf-like structures on tree trunks and branches. Old fruitbodies fade to pale beige or pale grey. The undersurface of the fruit body is made up of tubelike pores rather than gills.

The illustration showcases the characteristic overlapping, fan-shaped caps and vibrant yellow-orange coloration of this wood-decay fungus. summary: A frilly grey-brown rosette of overlapping fronds at the base of old oaks, sometimes weighing over 20 kg. In Japan it was said to be so valuable that finders danced for joy, hence 'maitake', the dancing mushroom.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Japan, China, Europe and eastern North America
abilities: A parasite and decomposer of oak roots and heartwood (white rot), returning to the same tree for years
Grows from an underground tuber-like sclerotium
Rich in β-glucans, including the 'D-fraction' studied for immune effects
edibilityNote: Choice edible when cooked. Lookalikes are not deadly: black-staining polypore (Meripilus sumstinei/giganteus, edible but tougher and bruises black) and Berkeley's polypore (Bondarzewia berkeleyi, edible but bitter). Beginners should check that the underside has pores, not gills. Some people react to large servings, and it may lower blood sugar.

uses.use: Eaten as a tonic and to support digestion
Maitake D-fraction extracts trialled for immune modulation in cancer patients

medicinal.cautions: May lower blood sugar and blood pressure; take care with diabetes or blood-pressure medicines and with warfarin. Human trials are small and early-phase.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores broadly ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, about 5–7 × 3.5–5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores from tiny pores beneath the fronds

grow.soil: Supplemented oak sawdust, or short oak logs buried in shaded soil
grow.timeToHarvest: Indoor blocks 3–4 months; buried logs fruit from the second autumn
steps: Inoculate sterilised oak sawdust with bran, or short pasteurised oak logs
Incubate at about 20–24 °C for 6–10 weeks until a firm, browning skin forms
Chill to about 10–15 °C with high humidity and fresh air to trigger primordia
Harvest the rosette when the edges of the fronds are still soft

lore: Japanese mountain foragers in Tōhoku traditionally kept their maitake spots secret, even from family, until death. Commercial cultivation in Japan began in the 1980s.
funFact: A single maitake can return to the same oak each autumn for decades.

wiki.extract: Grifola frondosa, also known as hen-of-the-woods, sheep's head, ram's head, or maitake  in Japanese, is a polypore mushroom that grows at the base of trees, particularly old growth oaks or maples. It is native to China, Europe, and North America.

summary: A snow-white cascade of soft icicle-like spines that grows from wounds in old hardwoods. It is a gourmet mushroom with crab-like texture and is studied for compounds that stimulate nerve growth factor in the lab.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Europe, Asia and North America; rare and legally protected in parts of Europe (e.g. the UK)
abilities: Decays the heartwood of living and dead beech, oak and other hardwoods (white rot)
Produces hericenones (fruiting body) and erinacines (mycelium), which promote nerve growth factor in cell and animal studies
Its spores form on the outer surfaces of the hanging spines, which can be 1–5 cm long
edibleParts: whole fruiting body (cooked, while still white)
edibilityNote: Good edible when young and white; it turns sour and yellow with age. It has no known dangerous lookalikes. Related species such as coral tooth (H. coralloides) and bear's head (H. americanum) are also edible. Wild specimens are rare in Europe and protected in Britain, so eat cultivated ones. Some people develop skin rashes or breathing allergies.

uses.use: Taken for stomach and digestive complaints and as a general tonic
Small trials of the dried mushroom for mild cognitive impairment

medicinal.cautions: Clinical trials are few and small. Allergic reactions, including skin rash and breathing difficulty, have been reported. Possible effect on blood sugar and clotting; take care with anticoagulants or diabetes medicines.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores subglobose, smooth to faintly roughened, amyloid, about 5–6.5 × 4–5.5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores shed from the hanging spines

grow.soil: Supplemented hardwood sawdust (e.g. oak sawdust with 10–20% wheat bran) or hardwood logs
grow.timeToHarvest: About 4–6 weeks from inoculating a sawdust block
steps: Sterilise bags of moist hardwood sawdust with bran, then inoculate with spawn once cool
Incubate in darkness at 21–24 °C for 2–3 weeks until fully white
Cut a small X in the bag and move to fruiting conditions: 15–21 °C, 85–95% humidity, fresh air and indirect light
Harvest when the spines are about 0.5–1 cm long and still white, before they yellow

lore: In China, monkey-head mushroom (hou tou gu) has long been prized as a 'mountain delicacy' of banquet cuisine. The Japanese name 'yamabushitake' compares the shaggy mushroom to the pom-pom robes of yamabushi mountain ascetics.
funFact: Vegetarian chefs in China and Japan have long shredded lion's mane as a convincing stand-in for crab meat.

wiki.extract: Hericium erinaceus, commonly known as lion's mane, yamabushitake, bearded tooth fungus, or bearded hedgehog, is a species of tooth fungus. It tends to grow in a single clump with dangling spines longer than 1 centimetre. It can be mistaken for other Hericium species that grow in the same areas.

The plate shows the fungus in its young state (marked 'A') and its mature, shaggy form (marked 'B'), highlighting the distinctive cascading spines that grow from the scars of old oak trees. Bulliard's work was instrumental in the early systemati

summary: What looks like a lump of burnt charcoal on a birch trunk is actually a sterile mass of fungus and wood, the conk. Its golden-orange interior has been brewed as tea across Siberia and northern Europe for centuries.
nativeRange: Boreal and cool-temperate Northern Hemisphere, mainly on birch: Russia, Scandinavia, Baltic, Korea, Japan, Canada, northern USA
abilities: Infects living birch through wounds and decays its heartwood for decades (white rot)
The black crust is rich in melanin; the interior concentrates betulin and betulinic acid from birch bark
Fruits only once, as a thin pore layer under the bark after the host tree dies
edibleParts: sterile conk (ground, as decoction or tea)
edibilityNote: Not a food. The conk is simmered as tea. It is extremely high in oxalate, and heavy daily use has caused kidney failure (oxalate nephropathy). Don't confuse it with burnt wood or with black Phellinus brackets. Harvest only from birch.

uses.tradition: Russian and Siberian folk medicine (incl. Khanty)
uses.use: Tea for stomach ailments, tuberculosis and as a general tonic
Wartime coffee substitute and health drink
Befungin, a chaga extract, was approved in the USSR for gastritis

medicinal.cautions: Very high oxalate content; documented kidney damage with regular use. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and lower blood sugar. No good human trials. Over-harvesting is depleting wild populations.

seed.description: Spores are produced only by a short-lived pore layer under the bark of dead trees. Spore print white to pale yellowish; spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, about 8–10 × 5–7.5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores, which enter living birch through wounds

lore: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's novel 'Cancer Ward' (1966) has a doctor who believes Russian peasants avoid cancer by drinking chaga. The book helped spread chaga's fame worldwide.
funFact: The word 'chaga' comes into Russian from Komi (tšak), a Uralic language of the Kama basin, where it simply means mushroom.

wiki.extract: Inonotus obliquus, commonly called chaga, is a fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae. It is parasitic on birch and other trees. The sterile conk is irregularly formed and resembles burnt charcoal. It is not the fruiting body of the fungus, but a sclerotium or mass of mycelium, mostly black because of a substantial amount of melanin. It is commonly marketed as a dietary supplement for various health benefits but lacks sufficient scientific evidence for safety or effectiveness, and quality can vary due to inconsistent processing and labeling.

plates.title: Coloured Figures of English Fungi or Mushrooms
plates.author: James Sowerby
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of Boletus radiatus (now Inonotus radiatus), showing multiple specimens from different angles, including the upper surface with concentric zones and the lower pore surface.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from James Sowerby's 'Coloured Figures of English Fungi or Mushrooms' (1797) depicts Boletus radiatus, known today as the alder bracket (Inonotus radiatus). The plate meticulously illustrates the fungus's characteristic concentric growth rings and its porous underside, serving as a vital record for 18th-century mycological study.

summary: A golden-capped, dung-loving mushroom that bruises blue. It is the world's most widely grown psilocybin mushroom. Psilocybin, the compound it carries, is in late-stage clinical trials for depression, and it is illegal to possess in most countries.
nativeRange: Pantropical and subtropical; grows on cattle dung in the Americas, Southeast Asia, India and Australia
abilities: Produces psilocybin, which the body converts to psilocin, a serotonin 5-HT2A receptor agonist
Bruises blue-black from oxidised and polymerised psilocin
Grows on the dung of cattle and water buffalo, which spread its spores
Its spores survive passage through a cow's gut
edibilityNote: Not a food. It causes strong hallucinations, anxiety and panic, raised heart rate and impaired judgement, which can lead to dangerous accidents. It is controlled by law in most countries. Foragers have died after mistaking deadly amatoxin-containing Galerina marginata or Pholiotina rugosa (P. filaris) for Psilocybe; non-psychoactive Panaeolus and Agrocybe also grow on dung.

uses.use: Psilocybe mushrooms (traditionally other species, e.g. P. mexicana and P. caerulescens) used in velada healing rituals
Synthetic psilocybin with psychological support, trialled for treatment-resistant depression, end-of-life distress and addiction

medicinal.cautions: Can trigger psychosis in people with a personal or family history of psychotic disorders. Dangerous with lithium (seizures reported) and with some other drugs. Clinical trials use measured synthetic psilocybin in supervised settings. Possession is illegal in most jurisdictions.

seed.description: Spore print dark purple-brown to purple-black; spores ellipsoid to subellipsoid, thick-walled with a germ pore, about 11–17 × 7–12 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind; also passes through grazing animals and lands in dung

lore: R. Gordon Wasson's 1957 Life magazine article 'Seeking the Magic Mushroom', about the Mazatec curandera María Sabina, introduced psilocybin mushrooms to the West. Albert Hofmann isolated psilocybin in 1958. P. cubensis itself was first described from Cuba in 1906, as Stropharia cubensis.
funFact: 'Teonanácatl', the Nahuatl name recorded by 16th-century Spanish friars, is often translated 'flesh of the gods'.

wiki.extract: Psilocybe cubensis, commonly known as the magic mushroom, shroom, golden halo, cube, gold cap, or bluestain smoothcap, is a species of psilocybin mushroom of moderate potency whose principal active compounds are psilocybin and psilocin. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis. It is the best-known psilocybin mushroom due to its wide distribution and ease of cultivation.

plates.desc: Botanical illustration of Agaricus procerus (Parasol Mushroom) showing two specimens at different stages of growth.
plates.long: Two specimens of the Parasol Mushroom, Agaricus procerus, are depicted against a plain background. The larger mushroom features a broad, scaly cap with a dark central umbo and a tall, patterned stem with a prominent ring. A smaller specimen is shown from a lower angle, revealing the crowded white gills beneath the cap and the characteristic snakeskin-like markings on the stalk.
