summary: A white football (or larger) in a summer meadow, made of a brainless, gill-less sphere of spore-making tissue. One puffball can produce trillions of spores. Sliced while pure white inside, it fries like a mushroom steak.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Europe and North America, also parts of Asia
abilities: Can reach 20–80 cm across, and occasionally more
A single large fruiting body produces several trillion spores
Its outer skin cracks away when mature, letting wind and rain release the olive-brown spore powder
Grows in rich, nitrogen-heavy soil such as pasture and hedgerows
edibleParts: young fruiting body, pure white throughout (cooked)
edibilityNote: Edible only when young, with firm, pure-white interior like marshmallow, and cooked. Discard any with yellow, olive or brown flesh. Deadly lookalikes: the egg-stage buttons of Amanita species, including the death cap and destroying angels. Always slice top to bottom: any outline of a cap, gills or stem means it is not a puffball. Also avoid earthballs (Scleroderma), which have a thick rind and purple-black interior and are poisonous.

uses.tradition: European and North American Indigenous folk medicine
uses.use: Dried spore mass or slices placed on wounds and nosebleeds to stop bleeding

compounds: calvacin (an antitumour protein studied in the 1960s)
medicinal.cautions: Inhaling large amounts of spores can cause lycoperdonosis, a serious lung inflammation. Calvacin research stopped because of toxicity.

seed.description: Spore mass olive-brown; spores globose, minutely warty, about 3.5–5.5 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind and rain as the outer skin cracks open

lore: European herdsmen and North American Indigenous peoples used dried puffballs as tinder, as wound dressings and to stupefy bees when collecting honey.
funFact: Lycoperdon, the old genus name for puffballs, means 'wolf fart', after the dusty puff of spores.

summary: A honeycomb-capped spring mushroom, hollow from cap tip to stem base. It is so prized that wild gucchi from Kashmir and Himachal are among the most expensive foods in South Asia. It is an ascomycete, more closely related to truffles than to gilled mushrooms.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Europe, Asia (incl. Himalaya) and North America (the latter partly as cryptic sister species)
abilities: Fruits in a short spring window, often after soil temperatures reach about 10–12 °C
Produces sclerotia, hardened stores of hyphae that help it survive and fruit
Some morels fruit in huge numbers on the ground the year after forest fires
Shoots ascospores from pits on the cap in visible puffs
edibilityNote: Choice edible, but always cook thoroughly. Raw or undercooked morels cause gastric upset, and some people react even to cooked ones, especially with alcohol. Deadly lookalike: the false morel (Gyromitra esculenta), which has a brain-like, lobed cap and a chambered or cottony interior and contains gyromitrin. Also beware Verpa bohemica, whose cap hangs free like a thimble over a cotton-stuffed stem. A true morel is hollow from tip to base, with the cap attached directly to the stem. Morels from old orchards may contain lead and arsenic from historic pesticides.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds), 8 per ascus, ellipsoid, smooth, about 20–24 × 12–14 µm; spore print cream to pale yellow-orange
seed.dispersal: Ascospores forcibly discharged from the pitted cap and carried by wind

grow.propagation: Spawn on grain; outdoor beds with nutrient bags (method developed commercially in China for M. importuna and related species)
grow.timeToHarvest: Sow spawn in late autumn; harvest the following spring
steps: Prepare a shaded outdoor bed of loose loam, ideally with wood ash or lime mixed in
Broadcast morel grain spawn in autumn and cover lightly with soil
After the mycelium spreads, lay 'exogenous nutrient bags' of moist sterilised grain over the bed
Keep the soil damp through winter; fruiting starts when spring soil reaches about 8–15 °C
Results are unreliable outside specialised farms, so treat it as an experiment

lore: Gucchi gathered in the Himalayan foothills is dried on strings and sold at high prices, and gucchi pulao is a Kashmiri feast dish. In Europe, Carolus Clusius described morels in his 1601 account of the fungi of Pannonia (Hungary), the first book devoted to fungi.
funFact: When a morel releases spores you can sometimes see the puff of 'smoke' rise from the cap.

summary: A tiny, pale bonnet mushroom of subtropical forests whose cap and gills glow eerie green in the dark. On Japan's Hachijō-jima it lights the forest floor after summer rain.
nativeRange: Subtropical and tropical Asia (Japan, Taiwan, Indonesia, Malaysia), Pacific islands, Australia, and Brazil
abilities: Bioluminescent: the oxygen-dependent luciferin–luciferase reaction (fungal luciferin is 3-hydroxyhispidin) gives off green light near 520 nm
Glows most strongly at about 27 °C and stops glowing in cold or dry conditions
Decomposes fallen twigs, bark and palm debris
The caps are only about 1–3 cm across
edibilityNote: Not eaten; too small and its edibility is unknown. Many small Mycena species contain toxins.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores ellipsoid, smooth, amyloid, about 7–9 × 5–6 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores; glowing may attract insects that spread spores

lore: Hachijō-jima, south of Tokyo, has made its glowing yakōtake a tourist attraction. Researchers there cultivate them to study the fungal light reaction.
funFact: The fungal luciferin pathway was mapped in 2018. Its genes have since been used to make plants that glow on their own.

wiki.extract: Mycena chlorophos is a species of agaric fungus in the family Mycenaceae. First described in 1860, the fungus is found in subtropical Asia, including India, Japan, Taiwan, Polynesia, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka, in Australia, and Brazil. Fruit bodies (mushrooms) have pale brownish-grey sticky caps up to 30 mm (1.2 in) in diameter atop stems 6–30 mm (0.2–1.2 in) long and up to a millimeter thick. The mushrooms are bioluminescent and emit a pale green light. Fruiting occurs in forests on fallen woody debris such as dead twigs, branches, and logs. The fungus can be made to grow and fruit in laboratory conditions, and the growth conditions affecting bioluminescence have been investigated.

summary: One of the world's most widely grown mushrooms, making up roughly a quarter of cultivated mushroom production. It has been cultivated on logs in China for about a thousand years. It is rich in the savoury compound guanylate and the sulphur-containing flavour precursor lentinic acid.
nativeRange: East and Southeast Asia (China, Japan, Korea, Indochina); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Decomposes the dead wood of shii, oak, chestnut and other hardwoods (white rot)
Produces lentinan, a β-glucan approved in Japan as an injectable adjunct for gastric cancer
Its sulphur flavour compound lenthionine forms when the mushroom is dried and rehydrated
Contains eritadenine, which lowers cholesterol in animal studies
edibleParts: cap and stem (cooked; stems are tough)
edibilityNote: Choice edible when cooked. Raw or undercooked shiitake can cause 'shiitake dermatitis', a whip-like itchy rash linked to lentinan that appears a day or two later. Wild collection on wood carries the risk of picking deadly Galerina marginata (funeral bell), a small brown wood-rotting mushroom with amatoxins and a rusty-brown spore print. Shiitake has a white spore print. Buy cultivated.

uses.use: Recorded by Wu Rui in the Ri Yong Ben Cao (Yuan dynasty) as a food that strengthens qi and the body
Purified lentinan given by injection alongside chemotherapy for gastric cancer

medicinal.cautions: Shiitake dermatitis from raw or undercooked mushrooms. Allergic lung disease in growers who inhale spores. Medicinal lentinan is a prescribed drug, not equal to eating shiitake.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores ellipsoid, smooth, about 5–6.5 × 3–3.5 µm

grow.sun: Full shade outdoors; indirect light indoors
grow.water: Keep logs moist; soak to trigger fruiting
grow.soil: Fresh-cut oak or other hardwood logs (10–15 cm diameter), or supplemented hardwood sawdust blocks
grow.timeToHarvest: Logs: 6–18 months, then fruit for 3–6 years. Sawdust blocks: about 2–3 months
steps: Cut healthy hardwood logs in late winter and inoculate within a few weeks
Drill holes about every 15 cm in a diamond pattern, tap in spawn plugs and seal with wax
Stack logs in full shade and keep damp while the mycelium colonises (6–18 months)
Force a flush by soaking a log in cold water for 12–24 hours; mushrooms appear in about a week at 10–25 °C
Pick when caps are 70–90% open; rest the log 6–8 weeks between soakings

lore: Chinese tradition credits Wu Sangong of Zhejiang (Song dynasty, around 1000 CE) with discovering that striking logs made them fruit. Longquan and Qingyuan still honour him at temples. The technique spread to Japan, where thick-capped, cool-season 'donko' became a prized grade.
funFact: Drying shiitake in sunlight, gills up, sharply raises its vitamin D content.

summary: A parasite of carpenter ants that takes over its host's behaviour. The infected ant leaves the colony, climbs a plant and bites into the underside of a leaf vein in a 'death grip'. A stalk then grows from the back of its head and rains spores onto the ant trail below.
nativeRange: Tropical forests worldwide (a complex of many host-specific species), especially Thailand, Brazil, Ghana, Australia
abilities: Manipulates Camponotus ants to climb to about 25 cm above the forest floor, where humidity and temperature suit fungal growth
Infected ants bite leaf veins in a synchronised way, often around solar noon
Each cryptic species in the complex specialises on one ant species
Bite-mark scars on 48-million-year-old fossil leaves from Messel, Germany, suggest the behaviour is ancient
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds) long and multiseptate, produced in perithecia on a cushion partway up the stalk; they can germinate into secondary 'capilliconidia' on hair-like stalks that stick to passing ants
seed.dispersal: Spores shot or dropped from the dead ant onto the forest floor, where foraging ants pick them up

lore: The Tulasne brothers described it in 1865 as Torrubia unilateralis. The fungus inspired the infection in the video game and TV series 'The Last of Us'.
funFact: A 2017 study found that fungal cells form a connected network through the ant's body and jaw muscles but leave its brain largely untouched. The fungus works the body like a puppet.

wiki.extract: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, commonly known as zombie-ant fungus, is an insect-pathogenic fungus, discovered by the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859. Zombie ants, infected by the Ophiocordyceps unilateralis fungus, are predominantly found in tropical rainforests.

summary: It bursts from a jelly-filled 'witch's egg' into an unmistakably phallic white stalk capped with olive-green slime that smells of carrion. Flies carry off its spores, and the stalk can grow about 10–15 cm in a few hours.
nativeRange: Europe and parts of Asia and North America; mainly in woodland and gardens
abilities: Grows one of the fastest of any fungal structures, inflating its spongy stalk by water pressure
Its foul smell can be detected from many metres away and attracts flies
Flies eat the spore slime (gleba) and spread the spores in their droppings
Decomposes buried wood and leaf litter
edibleParts: inner layer of the 'egg' stage (raw or cooked)
edibilityNote: The immature 'egg' is eaten in parts of Europe (e.g. Germany and France), sliced raw or fried. Deadly lookalike: the egg-like buttons of Amanita species, including the death cap. Always cut eggs vertically: a stinkhorn shows jelly and a coiled white stalk, an Amanita shows gills and a cap outline. The mature stinkhorn is not eaten.

seed.description: Spores (not seeds) in a slimy olive-green gleba; spores ellipsoid, smooth, about 3–5 × 1.5–2 µm
seed.dispersal: Flies attracted by the carrion smell eat the slime and spread the spores

lore: Gwen Raverat's memoir 'Period Piece' (1952) recalls her aunt Etty, Charles Darwin's daughter, hunting stinkhorns in the woods. She burned them in secret 'for the sake of the maids' morals'.
funFact: Its genus name Phallus and species name 'impudicus' ('shameless') were given by Linnaeus in 1753.

wiki.extract: Phallus impudicus, known colloquially as the common stinkhorn, is a widespread species of fungus in the Phallaceae (stinkhorn) family. It is recognizable for its foul odor and its phallic shape when mature, the latter feature giving rise to several names in 17th-century England.

summary: A single individual of this root-rotting fungus in Oregon's Blue Mountains spreads underground across about 965 hectares, making it one of the largest organisms on Earth. Its estimated age runs from about 2,400 to 8,650 years. Above ground it sends up clusters of brown, ring-stemmed honey mushrooms in autumn.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere conifer forests: Europe, North America, Asia
abilities: Spreads through soil via black, bootlace-like rhizomorphs that can extend metres per year
Kills living conifers by colonising roots and the cambium beneath the bark
Its mycelium in rotting wood glows faintly green ('foxfire')
Feeds the Chinese medicinal orchid Gastrodia elata (tianma), which has no chlorophyll and digests Armillaria
Oregon's 'humongous fungus' (Malheur National Forest) is a single genetic individual covering about 965 ha
edibilityNote: Eaten widely in Eastern Europe, but only well cooked; raw or undercooked it causes stomach upset, and some people react even to cooked ones. Deadly lookalike: Galerina marginata (funeral bell), a smaller brown wood-rotting mushroom with amatoxins and a rusty-brown spore print, which can grow among honey fungus. Also confused with Pholiota and toxic Hypholoma fasciculare (sulphur tuft, greenish gills, purple-black spores). Honey fungus has a white spore print. Take a spore print of every cap in doubtful collections.

seed.description: Spore print white to cream; spores ellipsoid, smooth, about 8–11 × 5–7 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores; it mainly spreads vegetatively by rhizomorphs and root contact

lore: Foxfire, the glow of fungus-infested wood (often Armillaria), was noted by Aristotle. It is said to have lit the depth gauge of David Bushnell's 1775 submarine 'Turtle'. Russians pickle 'opyata' honey mushrooms by the barrel.
funFact: Researchers mapped the Oregon giant by genetically matching fungal samples from hundreds of dying trees across the forest.

wiki.extract: Armillaria ostoyae is a pathogenic species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae. It has decurrent gills and the stipe has a ring. The mycelium invades the sapwood of trees, and is able to disseminate over great distances under the bark or between trees in the form of black rhizomorphs ("shoestrings"). In most areas of North America, it can be distinguished from other Armillaria species by its cream-brown colors, prominent cap scales, and a well-developed ring.

Beside it, immature specimens appear as rounded, egg-like structures, including one shown in cross-section to reveal its internal green layer. This illustration depicts the life cycle and unique structure of the Clathrus cancellatus, commonly known as the Red Cage fungus.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a stylized tree, illustrating the source of 'Agaricus' (larch fungus), a substance highly valued in early modern medicine for its purgative properties. Featured in the 1532 Dutch edition of 'Den groten herbarius', it represents the transition from medieval tradition to more observational botanical study, where the host plant was often depicted to aid identification.

summary: In the wild, this winter mushroom has sticky orange-brown caps on velvety dark stems and survives being frozen solid. Grown in the dark under high CO₂, the same fungus becomes enoki: long, pale noodle-like stems sold in Asian markets.
nativeRange: Temperate Northern Hemisphere: Europe, Asia and North America; cultivated mainly in East Asia
abilities: Fruits through winter and resumes growth after being frozen and thawed
A white-rot decomposer of dead and dying hardwood (elm, willow, ash, gorse)
Cultivated forms have long white stems because darkness and high CO₂ stretch the stalk
Contains flammutoxin, a pore-forming protein that is destroyed by cooking
edibilityNote: Edible but always cook enoki well. It contains heat-sensitive flammutoxin, and packaged enoki has caused deadly Listeria outbreaks (e.g. US 2016–2020) when eaten raw. Deadly wild lookalike: Galerina marginata (funeral bell), a brown wood-rotting mushroom with amatoxins that grows in the same habitats in autumn and early winter. Galerina has a rusty-brown spore print and often a ring; velvet shank has a white spore print, a velvety dark stem base and no ring. Sulphur tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) is also confused with it.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores ellipsoid to cylindrical, smooth, about 6.5–9 × 3–4 µm

grow.sun: Darkness (for white enoki) or low light
grow.soil: Supplemented hardwood sawdust or corncob with rice bran, in bottles
steps: Pack sterilised sawdust-bran mix into wide-mouthed bottles and inoculate with spawn
Incubate at 18–22 °C for 3–4 weeks until fully colonised
Scrape the surface and chill to 10–14 °C to induce pinning
Wrap a paper or plastic collar around the bottle neck and keep in darkness with high CO₂ so stems grow long and pale
Harvest the bundle when stems are 12–15 cm and cook before eating

lore: Enokitake is named after the enoki tree (Celtis sinensis) on whose stumps it grows wild in Japan. Bottle cultivation of white enoki began in Nagano Prefecture, still Japan's main producer.
funFact: The Chinese name jin zhen gu means 'golden needle mushroom', after its thin stems.

wiki.extract: Flammulina velutipes, the velvet foot, velvet stem, velvet shank or wild enoki, is a species of gilled mushroom in the family Physalacriaceae. The species occurs in Europe and North America.

plates.long: This plate from James Sowerby's 'Coloured Figures of English Fungi' (1797) illustrates Agaricus velutipes, now known as Flammulina velutipes or the Velvet Shank. The detailed engraving captures the mushroom's characteristic clustered growth and its distinctive dark, velvety stipe, which is a key identifying feature of the species.

summary: Shelf-like, oyster-shaped clusters on dead hardwood. It is one of the easiest mushrooms to grow and will fruit on straw, coffee grounds or cardboard. It is also a secret predator: its hyphae paralyse and digest nematode worms.
nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical forests worldwide (Northern Hemisphere especially); cultivated globally
abilities: Releases a volatile toxin (3-octanone) from tiny hyphal knobs that paralyses nematodes within minutes, then digests them for nitrogen
Breaks down lignin and cellulose, and can degrade some petroleum hydrocarbons and pesticides (mycoremediation)
Naturally contains lovastatin, a cholesterol-lowering statin drug
Grows on almost any lignocellulose waste, from straw to spent coffee grounds
edibilityNote: Good edible when cooked. Dangerous lookalikes: angel's wings (Pleurocybella porrigens), a thin white conifer-wood species linked to fatal brain disease in Japan (2004), mainly in people with kidney disease; the jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus species), which is orange and causes violent vomiting; and bitter Lentinellus species with saw-toothed gills. Oysters grow on hardwood, have white to lilac-grey spore prints and smell mild and anise-like. Growers indoors can develop spore allergy.

seed.description: Spore print white to lilac-grey; spores cylindrical, smooth, about 7–11 × 3–4 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind; dense clusters release clouds of spores

grow.soil: Pasteurised wheat/rice straw, spent coffee grounds, hardwood sawdust or cardboard
steps: Chop straw and pasteurise it in water at 65–80 °C for about an hour; drain and cool
Mix with grain spawn and pack into perforated bags or buckets
Incubate at 20–24 °C in the dark for 2–3 weeks until white throughout
Fruit at 15–21 °C with fresh air, indirect light and high humidity; mist the walls, not the mushrooms
Harvest whole clusters when cap edges are still slightly curled under

lore: Germany first cultivated oyster mushrooms experimentally on logs and stumps around World War I, as a food-security measure. Today India's dhingri farms and China's ping gu industry grow them on rice and wheat straw.
funFact: It is one of the few mushrooms known to hunt animals. Nematodes that touch its hyphae can be paralysed within minutes.

summary: A glossy, lacquer-red bracket on a side stalk. For two thousand years it has stood in East Asian art for longevity and immortality. DNA studies show most commercial 'reishi' is this East Asian species, not the European Ganoderma lucidum whose name it long carried.
nativeRange: East Asia (China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan); widely cultivated
abilities: Causes white rot in hardwood stumps and roots
Produces more than 150 triterpenoids (ganoderic acids), which make it intensely bitter
Its varnished surface comes from a resinous crust that forms as the bracket grows
Grows into antler shapes instead of caps when kept in high carbon dioxide
edibilityNote: Too woody to eat. It is simmered as a bitter tea or taken as an extract. There are case reports of liver toxicity linked to powdered reishi products. Many products contain other Ganoderma species, and some contain only mycelium grown on grain.

uses.use: A 'superior' tonic in the Shennong Bencao Jing, for calming the spirit, longevity and vitality
Tea for fatigue, sleep problems and general resilience
Studied as an adjunct to cancer treatment for immune markers and quality of life

medicinal.cautions: A Cochrane review (2016) found insufficient evidence to support it as first-line cancer treatment. Case reports describe liver toxicity with powders. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. May lower blood pressure and blood sugar. Avoid before surgery and in pregnancy.

seed.description: Spore print brown; spores ovoid with a truncated tip, double-walled with an ornamented inner wall, about 9–12 × 6–8 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind; mature brackets dust nearby surfaces with cocoa-brown spores

grow.soil: Hardwood logs (oak, maple) or supplemented hardwood sawdust
grow.timeToHarvest: 2–4 months on sawdust; logs fruit in the first or second summer
steps: Inoculate sterilised hardwood sawdust (or fresh-cut short logs) with spawn
Incubate at 24–29 °C until fully colonised
Fruit at 24–28 °C with high humidity; keep the air still and CO₂ high for antlers, or ventilate for caps
Harvest when the white growing edge turns red-brown and spores begin to drop; dry and slice for tea

lore: The Shennong Bencao Jing (c. 1st–2nd century CE) lists lingzhi among the highest grade of herbs. Han dynasty courts recorded its appearance as an auspicious omen. The cloud-shaped ruyi sceptre of Chinese art is modelled on its form.
funFact: The scientific name is a 2012 description; before that, East Asian reishi was misfiled for over a century under the name of a European mushroom.

It portrays a scene where a youth offers a lingzhi mushroom—a potent symbol of immortality—to a scholar, reflecting the period's interest in Daoist longevity practices and natural history.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1596 edition of the Bencao Gangmu depicts various types of Lingzhi (medicinal fungi). These fungi were highly valued in traditional Chinese medicine for their purported health benefits and association with longevity and immortality. The clear, stylized lines are characteristic of Ming Dynasty scientific illustration, designed to aid practitioners in identifying s

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts the Zhicao (芝草), or lingzhi mushroom. Renowned in Chinese culture as the 'mushroom of immortality,' it is shown here with its characteristic tiered caps and surrounding foliage, reflecting its importance in both botanical study and Daoist symbolism.

The woodcut depicts different varieties of Lingzhi, a fungus valued in traditional Chinese medicine for its health-promoting properties. Labels in Chinese characters identify the red, black, and purple types of the specimen.

summary: Thin, velvety brackets banded in browns, blues and creams, fanned out like a turkey's tail across dead logs. It is one of the most common fungi on Earth. It is also the source of PSK (Krestin), a protein-bound polysaccharide used alongside cancer therapy in Japan since the 1970s.
nativeRange: Cosmopolitan on dead hardwood in temperate and tropical forests
abilities: A white-rot decomposer that breaks down lignin in dead hardwood
Its laccase enzymes can degrade dyes, PCBs and other pollutants (studied for bioremediation)
Has a pore surface underneath with 3–5 tiny pores per millimetre, which separates it from gill-less lookalikes
Velvety, concentrically banded caps vary greatly in colour, hence 'versicolor'
edibilityNote: Too leathery to eat; it is simmered as a tea or taken as an extract. Lookalikes such as false turkey tail (Stereum ostrea, smooth underside without pores) and Trichaptum species are not known to be dangerous but have no medicinal value.

uses.use: Yun zhi decoction to clear damp-heat and support the spleen and lungs
PSK (Krestin) given orally as an adjunct to chemotherapy for gastric and colorectal cancer
PSP (polysaccharopeptide) extracts used in cancer supportive care

medicinal.cautions: PSK is an approved drug in Japan, and its trials used that standardised extract, not home tea. May cause digestive upset or darkened stools. Talk to an oncologist before combining it with chemotherapy.

seed.description: Spore print white to pale cream; spores cylindrical to slightly curved (allantoid), smooth, about 5–6 × 1.5–2 µm
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne basidiospores from the pore surface

grow.soil: Fresh-cut hardwood logs or stumps (oak, maple, birch)
steps: Drill and plug fresh hardwood logs with turkey tail plug spawn, then seal with wax
Stack or partly bury logs in a shaded, damp spot
Keep moist; brackets appear along the bark after colonisation
Harvest firm, fresh brackets and dry them for tea

lore: Kureha Chemical's Japanese researchers isolated PSK in the 1960s after a chemical engineer reportedly noticed a neighbour treating his own cancer with kawaratake tea. Japan's health ministry approved Krestin in 1977.
funFact: One fallen log can carry hundreds of turkey tail brackets, each possibly a genetically different individual competing for the wood.

wiki.extract: Trametes versicolor – also known as Coriolus versicolor and Polyporus versicolor – is a common polypore mushroom found throughout the world. Owing to its shape being similar to that of a wild turkey's tail feathers, T. versicolor is most commonly referred to as turkey tail.

summary: A single-celled fungus behind bread, beer and wine for at least 5,000 years. It was the first eukaryote to have its genome fully sequenced (1996), and it is still one of biology's most important model organisms.
nativeRange: Wild ancestors in East Asia (oak bark and fruit); now cosmopolitan through domestication
abilities: Ferments sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide even when oxygen is present (the Crabtree effect)
Reproduces by budding, about every 90 minutes in rich medium
Shares thousands of genes with humans; many human genes can replace their missing yeast counterparts
Under starvation, forms four hardy spores in an ascus (a tetrad)
edibleParts: whole cells (in bread, beer; inactivated as nutritional yeast)
edibilityNote: Safe and eaten worldwide. Live yeast can cause bloating. The probiotic variety S. cerevisiae var. boulardii has very rarely caused bloodstream infections in seriously ill patients with central lines.

uses.use: S. cerevisiae var. boulardii (Saccharomyces boulardii) probiotic for antibiotic-associated and infectious diarrhoea
Engineered strains produce insulin, hepatitis B vaccine antigen and artemisinic acid
Brewer's yeast taken as a B-vitamin and chromium supplement

medicinal.cautions: Avoid probiotic yeast in immunocompromised people and patients with central venous catheters (risk of fungaemia). Brewer's yeast can interact with MAO inhibitors (tyramine).

seed.description: Ascospores, four per ascus (a tetrad), round, about 3–5 µm; cells ovoid, about 5–10 µm. No mushroom or spore print
seed.dispersal: Carried by insects (wasps and fruit flies) between fruits and trees, and by people through fermentation

grow.propagation: A pinch of dried yeast or a portion of active starter
steps: Dissolve yeast in lukewarm water (about 30–35 °C; above about 50 °C kills it)
Mix into flour or sugary liquid; for wild leaven, keep a flour-and-water starter and feed it daily
Keep at about 24–30 °C for bread, or 15–22 °C for most ales and wines
Bubbles and rising show active fermentation; bake, or bottle when fermentation ends

lore: Residue in pottery from Jiahu, China (about 7000 BCE) shows fermented rice-honey-fruit drinks. Ancient Egyptian bakers and brewers worked side by side. Louis Pasteur proved in 1857–60 that living yeast cells cause fermentation.
funFact: Leland Hartwell's 'cell division cycle' (cdc) mutants in this yeast helped win the 2001 Nobel Prize for discovering how cells control division, a mechanism shared with human cells.

wiki.extract: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, also called brewer's yeast or baker's yeast, is a species of yeast. The species has been instrumental in winemaking, baking, and brewing since ancient times. It is believed to have been originally isolated from the skin of grapes. It is one of the most intensively studied eukaryotic model organisms in molecular and cell biology, much like Escherichia coli as the model bacterium. It is the microorganism which causes many common types of fermentation. S. cerevisiae cells are round to ovoid, 5–10 μm in diameter. It reproduces by budding.

summary: Bright yellow-orange rosettes on walls, roofs and tree bark from the sea to the city. It is a partnership of a fungus and a green alga (Trebouxia), coloured by the sunscreen pigment parietin. It thrives where nitrogen pollution kills more sensitive lichens.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, West Asia; introduced or spreading in North America, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: A symbiosis of the fungus with the green alga Trebouxia
Makes parietin, an orange anthraquinone that shields its algae from UV light; in shade it turns greyish-green
Tolerates and even favours nitrogen-rich air (ammonia from farms and bird droppings), making it a pollution indicator
Can survive months of drought and revive within minutes of rain
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

uses.tradition: Early modern European herbalism (doctrine of signatures)
uses.use: Its yellow colour led to its use against jaundice

medicinal.cautions: No proven medicinal value. Lichens accumulate heavy metals from the air.

seed.description: Ascospores (not seeds) colourless, two-celled with a thick central wall (polarilocular), about 12–16 × 6–9 µm, from orange cup-shaped apothecia
seed.dispersal: Ascospores shot from apothecia must meet a compatible alga to form a new lichen; fragments also spread it

lore: Following the doctrine of signatures, 17th-century herbalists prescribed this yellow lichen for jaundice. Lichenologists since have used its spread on twigs to map farm ammonia pollution.
funFact: A drop of potassium hydroxide turns it deep crimson, a standard field test for lichens containing parietin.

wiki.extract: Xanthoria parietina is a common and widespread lichen-forming fungus in the family Teloschistaceae. Commonly known as the yellow wall lichen, common orange lichen, or maritime sunburst lichen, this leafy lichen is known for its vibrant yellow to orange coloration and environmental adaptability. First described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, it has become one of the most thoroughly studied lichens, contributing significantly to scientific understanding of lichen biology. Unlike many lichens that are sensitive to pollution, X. parietina grows in diverse habitats—including coastal rocks, urban walls, and tree bark—even in areas with high levels of air pollution and excess nitrogen. Its structure consists of small, overlapping lobes that typically measure less than 8 cm across, with coloration that varies from bright orange in sun-exposed locations to greenish-yellow in shaded environments.

plates.long: A male Cuvier's Bee-eater is shown in profile, perched on a textured, lichen-covered branch. The bird features a long, curved black beak, a white throat, and distinctive green and blue plumage with long, bifurcated tail feathers. This scientific illustration is a hand-colored engraving from the early nineteenth century.

It is a plate from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 1802 masterpiece 'Histoire naturelle des colibris', which was celebrated for its innovative use of metallic inks and gold leaf to capture the unique brilliance of these birds.

plates.author: François Le Vaillant
plates.desc: A detailed natural history engraving of a male Promerops promerup bird perched on a lichen-covered tree stump, featuring iridescent blue and green plumage and a long curved beak.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a male Promerops promerup, showcasing the iridescent plumage and specialized curved beak characteristic of the species. Produced for François Le Vaillant's 'Histoire naturelle des promerops et des guêpiers' (1807), it represents the peak of early 19th-century French ornithological publication, combining scientific observation with artistic precision.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1486 'Herbarius latinus' depicts Usnea, commonly known as tree moss or lichen. In the late medieval period, such herbals were essential medical texts, and Usnea was documented for its astringent and cooling properties in treating various ailments.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a plant identified in the text as Lichen, likely referring to Lungwort (Pulmonaria). The illustration emphasizes the plant's distinctive leaf patterns, which were historically believed to indicate its medicinal use for lung ailments according to the Doctrine of Signatures.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates 'Lichen Marinus', characterized by its unique chain of rounded, leaf-like segments. It serves as an early taxonomic record of marine flora, demonstrating the precision of Renaissance-era botanical woodcuts.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates 'Usnea', a type of lichen described in the text for its medicinal properties. As an early example of botanical printing, the image was designed to be functional for identification, while the hand-applied green pigment reflects the transition from manuscript traditions to printed books.

summary: A thick-stemmed, scaly brown mushroom that grows under red pine. It has a spicy, cinnamon-and-pine aroma that Japan treasures as the scent of autumn. Top grades sell for hundreds of dollars a kilo. It is listed as Vulnerable because its pine forests are declining.
nativeRange: East Asia (Japan, Korea, China incl. Yunnan and Tibet), and northern Europe (Scandinavia, Baltic) and Siberia
abilities: Ectomycorrhizal mainly with red pine (Pinus densiflora) and other pines; never cultivated
Forms a dense white mycelial mat called a 'shiro' that spreads outward in a ring
Its aroma comes mainly from 1-octen-3-ol and methyl cinnamate
Thrives on poor, disturbed mineral soils, which humans maintained in old Japanese satoyama woodland
edibilityNote: Choice edible. Dangerous lookalikes: buttons of deadly white Amanitas (A. phalloides, destroying angels), which have a volva at the base and white, not spicy, odour; and, in North America, Amanita smithiana, which grows with the related T. murrillianum and causes delayed kidney failure. Check the base, the spicy smell and the absence of a volva.

seed.description: Spore print white; spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, about 6–7.5 × 4.5–6 µm

lore: Matsutake appears in the 8th-century Man'yōshū poetry anthology, where its fragrance is praised. Anna Tsing's 'The Mushroom at the End of the World' (2015) follows the global trade in matsutake gathered by foragers in Oregon, Yunnan and Finland.
funFact: Pine wilt nematode has killed vast areas of Japan's red pine, and Japan's matsutake harvest has fallen by over 90% since the 1940s.

wiki.extract: Matsutake , Tricholoma matsutake, is a species of mushroom, with a cap that can reach up to 40 centimetres (16 in) wide. It resembles at least one poisonous species.

plates.desc: Botanical illustration of Matsutake mushrooms (Tricholoma matsutake) showing different growth stages.
plates.long: A detailed woodblock illustration of Matsutake mushrooms from Sakamoto Kōnen's 1835 mycological treatise, 'Kinpu'. This work is a prime example of Edo-period natural history documentation, blending meticulous observation with the refined aesthetics of Japanese woodblock printing.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut illustration of Matsutake mushrooms comes from the 1835 Japanese mycological treatise 'Kinpu' by Sakamoto Kōnen. The work exemplifies the precision and aesthetic beauty of Edo-period natural history documentation, capturing the specific form and texture of the fungi with scientific care.

summary: An underground, warty black fruiting body of an oak and hazel partner fungus. Its marbled flesh has an intense aroma that can sell for well over €1,000 a kilo. Since its spores cannot travel on the wind, it relies on its smell to lure mammals that dig it up and spread them.
nativeRange: Mediterranean Europe on calcareous soils: southern France, northern and central Spain, Italy; cultivated in Australia, New Zealand, Chile, USA
abilities: Forms ectomycorrhizae with oak (Quercus ilex, Q. pubescens) and hazel
Creates 'brûlés', bare patches around host trees where it suppresses competing plants
Releases volatile compounds including dimethyl sulphide that animals can smell through soil
Has two mating types and needs both to fruit, a finding (2011) now used in managing plantations
edibleParts: whole fruiting body (raw shaved or lightly heated)
edibilityNote: Prized edible. Lookalikes: earthballs (Scleroderma), toxic and hard, with dark purplish-black spore masses but no marbling; and underground Elaphomyces. Cheaper Chinese truffles (Tuber indicum) are sold fraudulently as Périgord truffles. Cut to check the fine white marbling and strong aroma.

seed.description: Spores (not seeds) dark brown, ellipsoid, densely spiny (echinulate), about 25–45 × 20–35 µm, held 1–6 in sac-like asci inside the marbled flesh; no spore print, since it fruits underground
seed.dispersal: Eaten and dispersed by wild boar, rodents and other mammals drawn by its scent

grow.sun: Full sun on the orchard floor
grow.propagation: Oak or hazel seedlings inoculated with truffle in a nursery
grow.timeToHarvest: First truffles typically 5–10 years after planting
steps: Lime the soil to pH 7.5–8.3 and ensure excellent drainage
Plant certified inoculated oak or hazel seedlings at about 4–6 m spacing
Keep the ground weed-free and irrigate during summer drought
From about year 5, hunt mature truffles in winter (December–March) with a trained dog

lore: Brillat-Savarin called the truffle 'the diamond of the kitchen' in 'Physiologie du goût' (1825). The first truffle plantations began in Vaucluse in the early 1800s, when Joseph Talon planted acorns from truffle-producing oaks.
funFact: Truffle pigs were traditionally used because truffle aroma includes androstenol, a pig sex pheromone. Dogs are now preferred because they don't eat the find.

wiki.extract: Tuber melanosporum, commonly called black truffle, Périgord truffle or French black truffle, is a species of truffle native to Southern Europe. It is one of the most expensive edible fungi in the world. In 2013, the truffle cost between 1,000 and 2,000 euros per kilogram.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from Hieronymus Bock’s 1546 'Kreuter Buch' depicts the Stendelwurtz Mennlin, characterized by its broad green leaves and distinct bulbous root system. The illustration reflects the 16th-century transition toward botanical realism, where plants were increasingly drawn from direct observation rather than stylized medieval copies. As one of the earliest European botanical records of New World and tropical flora, this illustration reflects the era's scientific effort to categorize global species through precise line work and morphological detail. The print

plates.title: The Ambonese Herbal, Vol. 4
plates.author: Georg Eberhard Rumphius
plates.desc: Botanical engraving showing a leafy branch and two gnarled root or tuber structures, labeled as Plate IV.
plates.long: This detailed engraving from Georg Eberhard Rumphius's 'Herbarium Amboinense' depicts a plant specimen with its characteristic leaves and unusual, gnarled root structures. Rumphius's work was a monumental contribution to the study of Southeast Asian botany, combining meticulous observation with fine artistic execution to document the natural history of the region.

plates.author: Pierre Bulliard
plates.desc: Scientific illustration of black truffles (Tuber nigrum) showing various sizes and cross-sections.
plates.long: This detailed botanical engraving from Pierre Bulliard's 1791 work 'Histoire des Champignons de la France' illustrates the black truffle, then identified as Tuber nigrum. The plate presents the fungus in several stages of growth and provides cross-sectional views that highlight the characteristic marbled interior, essential for scientific identification in the late 18th century.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of three truffle specimens (Tuber cibarium), showing both the exterior texture and an internal cross-section.
plates.long: This plate from James Sowerby's 'Coloured Figures of English Fungi or Mushrooms' (1797) illustrates Tuber cibarium, the edible black truffle. The engraving captures the characteristic warty exterior and the complex, marbled interior of the fungus, serving as both a scientific record and a work of art.

The work is a prime example of Honzōgaku (natural history) studies in late Edo-period Japan, combining scientific observation with traditional artistic techniques.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from Wu Qijun's 1848 botanical treatise, 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao', depicts a potato plant, identified by the Chinese characters 'Yangyu' (陽芋). The image provides a detailed anatomical view of the plant, including its foliage and the essential tuber, serving as an important record of agricultural knowledge and botanical art in mid-19th century China.

plates.desc: Botanical illustration of a climbing plant with heart-shaped leaves and a hairy fruit or tuber.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from Wu Qijun's 1848 botanical treatise, 'Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao,' depicts a climbing plant with prominent heart-shaped leaves and a textured fruit or root. The work is a significant example of 19th-century Chinese scientific documentation, combining artistic precision with empirical observation to categorize and identify plant species.

plates.desc: Botanical woodcut of Tutuaner (Apios fortunei) showing climbing stem, leaves, and tuber.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the Tutuaner plant (Apios fortunei), showing its characteristic climbing stem and underground tuber. Such illustrations were vital components of the Nongzheng Quanshu, providing visual aids for famine relief and agricultural knowledge.

summary: One of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth, adding up to about half a metre a day and reaching lengths of 45 m or more. Giant kelp is a brown alga, not a plant, and forms underwater forests that shelter fish, sea otters and countless invertebrates.
nativeRange: Cool coastal waters of the eastern Pacific (Alaska to Baja California; Peru and Chile), the southern Atlantic and sub-Antarctic coasts, southern Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Grows up to about 50 cm a day in good conditions
Floats its fronds to the surface with gas-filled bladders (pneumatocysts) at each blade
Grips rock with a root-like holdfast that is not used for feeding
Builds forest habitats that support hundreds of species, kept in balance by sea otters that eat kelp-grazing urchins
edibilityNote: Edible, but very high in iodine; frequent large servings can upset thyroid function. Can concentrate heavy metals such as arsenic from polluted water.

seed.description: Reproduces by microscopic zoospores released from special blades (sporophylls) near the base
seed.dispersal: Water currents, mostly over short distances
seed.germination: Spores grow into tiny male and female gametophytes whose offspring become new kelp

lore: The 'kelp highway' hypothesis proposes that early people followed productive kelp-forest coasts around the Pacific Rim into the Americas. Darwin, on the Beagle, compared southern kelp forests to land forests and said their loss would destroy many animals.
funFact: For much of the 20th century, giant kelp harvested off California was a major source of alginate, the thickener in ice cream, toothpaste and wound dressings.

wiki.extract: Macrocystis is a monospecific genus of kelp with all species now synonymous with Macrocystis pyrifera. It is commonly known as giant kelp or bladder kelp. This genus contains the largest of all the Phaeophyceae or brown algae. Macrocystis has pneumatocysts at the base of its blades. Sporophytes, the macroscopic forms, are perennial and the individual may live for up to three years; stipes/fronds within a whole individual undergo senescence, where each frond may persist for approximately 100 days. The genus is found widely in subtropical, temperate, and sub-Antarctic oceans of the Southern Hemisphere and in the northeast Pacific. Macrocystis is often a major component of temperate kelp forests.

summary: A large, many-armed starfish covered in venomous spines that eats living coral. In population outbreaks it can strip whole reefs, and it is one of the main causes of coral loss on the Great Barrier Reef.
nativeRange: Tropical Pacific Ocean, from Japan and the Philippines through the Great Barrier Reef, Melanesia and Micronesia to Polynesia; other Acanthaster species replace it in the Indian Ocean and Red Sea
abilities: Eats coral by turning its stomach out over the colony and digesting the tissue
A large female can release tens of millions of eggs in a season
Spines contain saponins that cause painful, swelling wounds
Outbreak densities can reach many thousands per square kilometre

animal.diet: Living hard corals, preferring fast-growing table and branching Acropora
animal.habitat: Coral reefs, mostly at depths of a few metres to about 30 m
animal.size: Usually 25–35 cm across, sometimes over 50 cm
animal.behaviour: It feeds mostly at night and hides under coral during the day; feeding leaves bright white patches of dead coral skeleton.
fieldMarks: Large starfish with 7–23 arms
Upper surface covered with long, sharp spines
Colour grey-green, purple, red or blue
White feeding scars on nearby coral
animal.lookalikes: Other crown-of-thorns species (A. planci in the northern Indian Ocean, A. mauritiensis in the southern Indian Ocean, A. benziei in the Red Sea) are separated by range and genetics. No other reef starfish is as spiny.
animal.whereToSee: Reefs of the Great Barrier Reef, Okinawa, Guam and Fiji, particularly during outbreaks.
animal.season: Year-round; spawning in the warm season (about Dec–Feb on the Great Barrier Reef)

lore: A major outbreak was first reported at Green Island near Cairns in the early 1960s; reef managers now cull starfish by injecting them with vinegar or bile salts.
funFact: Its natural predators include the giant triton snail (Charonia tritonis), the humphead wrasse and the starry pufferfish, all reduced by fishing and shell collecting.

summary: A royal-blue surgeonfish with a black 'palette' marking and lemon-yellow tail, famous as Dory in Finding Nemo. Like all surgeonfishes it carries a scalpel-sharp spine at the base of its tail.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Kiribati, Samoa, southern Japan and the Great Barrier Reef
abilities: A sharp, folding spine on each side of the tail base can slash predators or careless hands
Wedges itself into branching coral and erects its spines when threatened, making it hard to dislodge
Spawning is not yet routine in captivity; most aquarium fish are wild-caught, though captive breeding succeeded in 2016

animal.diet: Zooplankton; also algae
animal.habitat: Clear outer reef terraces with strong current, often around Pocillopora coral heads, 2–40 m
animal.behaviour: Groups hover in the water column feeding on plankton and dive together into branching coral when alarmed.
fieldMarks: Vivid royal-blue oval body
Black band running from the eye to the tail that forms a loop resembling an artist's palette
Bright yellow tail and yellow pectoral fins
Tail spine on the caudal peduncle

animal.season: Year-round

lore: The University of Florida's Tropical Aquaculture Laboratory announced the first successful captive rearing of Paracanthurus hepatus in 2016, shortly after Finding Dory raised aquarium demand.
funFact: Surgeonfish are named for the scalpel-like blades on the tail; in a blue tang they fold into a groove until the fish feels threatened.

summary: A short-winged, long-tailed hawk built for ambush, flashing along hedgerows to snatch small birds by surprise. Females are much larger than males, nearly twice their weight.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia across Siberia to Japan; northern birds winter south to Africa and South Asia
abilities: Hunts by surprise, using hedges and buildings as cover to ambush songbirds
Females take prey up to woodpigeon size; males mostly hunt tits and finches
Long legs and toes snatch birds from the air or from inside bushes
Recovered across Europe after organochlorine pesticides such as DDT were banned

animal.diet: Almost entirely small and medium birds
animal.habitat: Woodland, farmland with hedges, towns and gardens
animal.size: 28–41 cm; wingspan 59–80 cm; males ~150 g, females ~260 g
animal.behaviour: Often seen in a brief, dashing attack on a garden bird feeder before vanishing over a hedge.

Male slate-blue above with orange-barred underparts and cheeks
Female grey-brown above, finely barred grey below, with a white eyebrow
Yellow eyes and thin, long yellow legs

animal.lookalikes: Northern goshawk is much larger with a bulging rear body and bold white eyebrow. Common kestrel has pointed wings and hovers. Levant sparrowhawk (southeast Europe, Middle East) has dark wingtips and is pale below.
animal.whereToSee: Widespread over European farmland and gardens; huge autumn passages over Falsterbo, the Bosphorus and Batumi (Georgia).

lore: In medieval falconry the sparrowhawk was the hawk assigned to priests in the 'Book of St Albans' (1486), and its small male was called a 'musket', a word later given to a firearm.
funFact: Ian Newton's decades-long study in southern Scotland made the sparrowhawk one of the best-studied raptors in the world.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian sparrowhawk, also known as the northern sparrowhawk or simply the sparrowhawk, is a small bird of prey in the family Accipitridae. Adult male Eurasian sparrowhawks have bluish grey upperparts and orange-barred underparts; females and juveniles are brown above with brown barring below. The female is up to 25% larger than the male – one of the greatest size differences between the sexes in any bird species. Though it is a predator which specialises in catching woodland birds, the Eurasian sparrowhawk can be found in any habitat and often hunts garden birds in towns and cities. Males tend to take smaller birds, including tits, finches and sparrows; females catch primarily thrushes and starlings but are capable of killing birds weighing 500 g (18 oz) or more.

summary: A dark, powerful eagle with brilliant white shoulder patches, found only in the Iberian Peninsula. Rescued from near-extinction in the 1970s, it has become one of Europe's great conservation recoveries, though it remains Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Iberian Peninsula (central and southwestern Spain, southern Portugal); has occasionally bred in Morocco
abilities: Specialises on rabbits, and its breeding success tracks rabbit numbers
Builds large stick nests in cork oaks and pines
Adults hold territories year-round
Young birds wander widely across Iberia before settling

animal.diet: Mainly European rabbits; also hares, partridges, pigeons, ducks and carrion
animal.habitat: Open oak woodland (dehesa), Mediterranean scrub, pine forest near marshes
animal.behaviour: Pairs soar together over their territory with undulating display flights in late winter.

Bold white patches on the shoulders and the leading edge of the wing
Grey tail with a broad dark terminal band
Juveniles pale tawny-buff with dark flight feathers
animal.voice: A deep, barking 'owk-owk-owk'.
animal.lookalikes: Eastern imperial eagle (eastern Europe, Central Asia) has smaller white shoulder patches and no white leading edge. Golden eagle has a longer tail and lacks white shoulders. Juveniles resemble young eastern imperial eagles but are unstreaked.
animal.whereToSee: Doñana National Park, Monfragüe, Sierra de Andújar and Montes de Toledo in Spain; Alentejo in Portugal.
animal.season: Resident

lore: It was named in 1861 by the German ornithologist Christian Ludwig Brehm in honour of Prince Adalbert of Bavaria, and it became a symbol of Spanish conservation through the protection of Doñana.
funFact: Electrocution on power lines and illegal poison baits were its main killers; retrofitting dangerous pylons has been central to its recovery from a few dozen pairs.

summary: Australia's largest bird of prey, with a distinctive diamond-shaped tail. It soars on thermals for hours and is revered in Aboriginal cultures.
nativeRange: Australia, southern New Guinea
abilities: Soars on thermals to great heights
Hunts cooperatively to take prey like kangaroos and goats
Builds huge stick nests up to 2 m across

animal.diet: Rabbits, wallabies, kangaroos, birds, reptiles, carrion
animal.habitat: Woodland, savanna and open country
animal.behaviour: Pairs soar together, performing undulating flights and talon-grappling displays.
fieldMarks: Very large, dark brown to black plumage
Long, wedge-shaped tail

Pale bill with dark tip
animal.voice: Mostly silent; gives whistling yelps.
animal.lookalikes: Little eagle is much smaller with a square-cut tail and pale underwing band. Black kite has a shallow forked tail and slender build. animal.season: Resident

lore: To the Kulin nations of Victoria, Bunjil the wedge-tailed eagle is the creator ancestor. The Tasmanian subspecies is listed as Endangered.
funFact: Wedge-tailed eagles have been known to attack hang-gliders and drones.

wiki.extract: The wedge-tailed eagle is the largest bird of prey in the continent of Australia. It is also found in southern New Guinea to the north and is distributed as far south as the state of Tasmania. Adults of the species have long, broad wings, fully feathered legs, an unmistakable, wedge-shaped tail, an elongated upper mandible, a strong beak, and powerful feet. The wedge-tailed eagle is one of 12 species of large, predominantly dark-coloured booted eagles in the genus Aquila found worldwide. Genetic research clearly has indicated that the wedge-tailed eagle is fairly closely related to other, generally large members of the Aquila genus. A large, brown-to-black bird of prey, it has a maximum reported wingspan of 2.84 m and a length up to 1.06 m.

abilities: Takes prey as large as young deer and foxes
Can dive at around 240 km/h
Eyesight several times sharper than humans'
Territories can span over 100 km²

animal.habitat: Open mountains, steppe and moorland
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform undulating 'sky-dance' flights, rising and plunging over their territory.

Legs feathered to the toes

Soars with wings in a shallow V

wiki.extract: The golden eagle is a bird of prey living in the Northern Hemisphere. It is the most widely distributed species of eagle. Like all eagles, it belongs to the family Accipitridae. They are one of the best-known birds of prey in the Northern Hemisphere. These birds are dark brown, with lighter golden-brown plumage on their napes. Immature eagles of this species typically have white on the tail and often have white markings on the wings. Golden eagles use their agility and speed combined with powerful feet and large, sharp talons to hunt a variety of prey, mainly hares, rabbits, marmots, and other ground squirrels.

summary: A large, dark eagle that nests on the ground or on low bushes across the open steppes of Russia, Kazakhstan and Mongolia. Once common, it has crashed due to electrocution on power lines, poisoning and habitat loss.
nativeRange: Breeds from southern Russia and Kazakhstan across Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters in East Africa, Arabia, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Nests on the open ground, low shrubs or pylons where no trees exist
Preys heavily on ground squirrels (sousliks)
Migrates thousands of kilometres around the Caspian and through the Middle East to Africa
Gathers in large numbers at rubbish dumps and locust swarms in winter

animal.diet: Ground squirrels, marmots, pikas, hares; carrion; termites and locusts in winter
animal.habitat: Dry steppe and semi-desert; savanna and farmland in winter
animal.behaviour: Thousands funnel through narrow migration bottlenecks, including Eilat in Israel and Bab-el-Mandeb between Yemen and Djibouti.
fieldMarks: Large, uniformly dark brown eagle
Long gape line reaching back below the eye
Juveniles show a broad white band across the underwing and pale trailing edge
Fingered wingtips; adults often have a rufous nape patch
animal.voice: Generally silent; a barking call near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Greater spotted eagle is darker with a shorter gape and a more compact shape. Tawny eagle (Africa, India) is paler with a shorter gape. Golden eagle has a longer tail and golden nape.
animal.whereToSee: Kalmykia and Kazakh steppe in summer; spring passage at Eilat (Israel); winter in Oman's Raysut dump and East African savanna.
animal.season: Summer visitor to breeding steppes Apr–Sep; passage Feb–Apr and Sep–Nov

lore: Its scientific name records the first specimen described from Nepal by Brian Houghton Hodgson in 1833, and for decades it was lumped with the tawny eagle of Africa and India.
funFact: It was uplisted from Least Concern to Endangered in 2015 after evidence of rapid declines across its breeding range.

wiki.extract: The steppe eagle is a large bird of prey. Like all eagles, it belongs to the family Accipitridae. The steppe eagle's well-feathered legs illustrate it to be a member of the subfamily Aquilinae, also known as the "Booted eagles". This species was once considered to be closely related to the sedentary tawny eagle and the two forms have previously been treated as conspecific. They were split based on pronounced differences in morphology and anatomy; two molecular studies, each based on a very small number of genes, indicate that the species are distinct but disagree over how closely related they are.

summary: North America's most familiar large hawk, often seen perched on roadside poles or soaring over fields. Its hoarse scream is the sound film-makers dub in for almost any bird of prey, including Bald Eagles.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada through the US, Mexico and Central America to Panama; the West Indies
abilities: Hunts by watching from a high perch or 'kiting' motionless into the wind
Plumage varies from very pale to almost black across many regional forms and morphs
Has adapted to cities, nesting on building ledges
Pairs often stay together for years and reuse nests

animal.diet: Rodents, rabbits, squirrels; also birds, snakes and carrion
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered perches, from deserts to farmland and city parks
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform high soaring courtship flights, with the male diving and climbing and sometimes dangling his legs.
fieldMarks: Adult tail brick-red above, pale pinkish below
Dark band of streaks across the pale belly
Dark bar (patagial mark) on the leading edge of the underwing
Broad, rounded wings and short wide tail; dark and rufous morphs occur, especially in the West
animal.voice: A hoarse, rasping, descending scream 'kee-eeee-arrr', 2–3 seconds long.
animal.lookalikes: Red-shouldered Hawk has a banded black-and-white tail and pale wing 'windows'. Rough-legged Hawk has black wrist patches and a white tail base. Swainson's Hawk has dark flight feathers below and a brown bib. Juvenile Red-tails have brown banded tails.
animal.whereToSee: Highway edges and fields almost anywhere in North America; hawk-watch sites such as Hawk Mountain (Pennsylvania) and Duluth's Hawk Ridge in autumn.
animal.season: Resident in most of the US; northern birds migrate Sep–Nov

lore: A red-tailed hawk nicknamed Pale Male nested on a Fifth Avenue apartment building in New York City from the early 1990s, becoming one of the most famous wild birds in the world.
funFact: It was first scientifically described from a specimen collected in Jamaica, hence jamaicensis.

wiki.extract: The red-tailed hawk is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America. In the United States, it is one of three species colloquially known as the "chickenhawk". The red-tailed hawk breeds throughout most of the continent, from western Alaska and northern Canada to as far south as Panama and the West Indies. The red-tailed hawk occupies a wide range of habitats and altitudes, including deserts, grasslands, coniferous and deciduous forests, agricultural fields, and urban areas. It is absent in areas of unbroken forest and in the high arctic. It is legally protected in Canada, Mexico, and the United States by the Migratory Bird Treaty.

summary: A huge mountain vulture that lives mostly on bone. It drops large bones from height onto rock slabs to shatter them, and paints its own white plumage rust-orange by bathing in iron-rich mud.
nativeRange: Mountains of southern Europe (Pyrenees, Alps, Corsica, Crete), North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus, the Middle East, Central Asia, the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, and East and southern Africa
abilities: Bone makes up most of its diet; stomach acid with a pH near 1 dissolves bone
Drops bones from height onto rock 'ossuaries' to split them
Swallows bones as large as a lamb's femur whole
Stains its plumage orange with iron oxide-rich mud, a cosmetic behaviour

animal.diet: Bones and marrow from carcasses; occasionally tortoises and live prey
animal.habitat: High mountains with cliffs, alpine pastures and gorges
animal.lifespan: 20–30 years in the wild; over 40 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Patrols ridges on long, narrow wings and may make repeated drops of the same bone until it breaks.
fieldMarks: Very long, narrow, pointed wings and long, diamond-shaped tail
Dark slate upperparts; head and underparts creamy to rusty orange
Black mask and bristly black 'beard' below the bill
Red ring around a pale eye; juveniles all dark
animal.voice: Usually silent; occasional high whistles and shrill calls during display.
animal.lookalikes: Griffon vulture is broad-winged and short-tailed with a pale ruff. Golden eagle has a shorter, squared tail and broader wings. Juveniles can be confused with Egyptian vulture juveniles, which are much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Ordesa and the Pyrenees, the Swiss and French Alps (reintroduced), Crete, the Caucasus, Ethiopia's Simien Mountains and the Himalaya.
animal.season: Resident; nests in midwinter

lore: The Persian Homa (Huma), a bird whose shadow bestowed kingship, has long been associated with the bearded vulture, and Pliny repeats the legend that the playwright Aeschylus was killed by a tortoise dropped by an eagle onto his bald head.
funFact: It was exterminated from the Alps by the early 20th century; reintroduction since 1986 has re-established a wild breeding population there.

wiki.extract: The bearded vulture, also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus. The bearded vulture is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists of 70–90% bone.

summary: A huge, pale-brown vulture that soars on thermals over mountains, finding carcasses by watching other vultures. Colonies clean up dead livestock and wildlife, reducing disease.
nativeRange: Southern Europe, North Africa, Middle East and Central Asia to India
abilities: Soars for hours on thermals with barely a wingbeat
A group can strip a carcass in under an hour
Extremely acidic stomach kills many pathogens in rotting meat
Spots feeding vultures from kilometres away and follows them

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals
animal.habitat: Open mountainous country with cliffs for nesting
animal.behaviour: Nests in cliff colonies, laying a single egg each year.
fieldMarks: Huge vulture with pale sandy-brown body
White fluffy neck ruff and pale head
Dark flight feathers contrasting with paler wing coverts
Soars on long, broad, 'fingered' wings
animal.voice: Hisses, grunts and cackles at carcasses
animal.lookalikes: Cinereous vulture is darker all over. Rüppell's vulture (Africa) has scaly, pale-edged feathers. Egyptian vulture is smaller and white with black flight feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Monfragüe National Park (Spain), Gorges du Verdon (France), and the Strait of Gibraltar on migration
animal.season: Resident; young birds cross the Strait of Gibraltar in autumn

lore: The 'eagle' (nesher) of the Hebrew Bible is likely the griffon vulture, and Tibetan and Zoroastrian sky burials relied on vultures. It was reintroduced to France's Grands Causses in the 1980s.
funFact: The veterinary drug diclofenac, deadly to Gyps vultures, wiped out over 95% of India's related vultures in the 1990s.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian griffon vulture is a large Old World vulture in the bird of prey family Accipitridae. It is also known as the Eurasian griffon or griffon vulture, although the latter term is sometimes used for the genus Gyps as a whole.

summary: A large cliff-nesting vulture of India and Pakistan that once swarmed over every carcass. From the 1990s its numbers crashed by more than 95%, poisoned by the veterinary drug diclofenac in the cattle carcasses it ate.
nativeRange: Central and peninsular India and SE Pakistan (Sindh, notably Nagarparkar)
abilities: Clears carcasses rapidly, reducing disease and feral dog populations
Soars for hours on thermals, scanning for food
Nests on cliffs and old buildings in colonies

animal.diet: Carrion, especially dead cattle
animal.habitat: Open country near villages and cliffs; dry hilly regions
animal.size: About 80–100 cm long; wingspan about 2 m
animal.behaviour: Groups descend on a carcass and can strip it in under an hour; they nest colonially on cliff ledges.
fieldMarks: Large pale sandy-brown vulture with dark flight feathers
Bare dark grey head and neck; white neck ruff
Pale yellowish bill
Long, broad wings held flat in soaring
animal.voice: Mostly silent; hisses and grunts at carcasses
animal.lookalikes: Slender-billed vulture (north India, Nepal) is darker with a thin dark bill and nests in trees; White-rumped vulture is darker with a white back patch; Eurasian griffon is larger and more rufous.
animal.whereToSee: Cliffs of Ranthambore, Orchha and Panna in India; Nagarparkar's Karoonjhar hills in Sindh
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Its collapse led India, Pakistan and Nepal to ban veterinary diclofenac in 2006, and the Parsi tradition of exposing the dead at Towers of Silence in Mumbai has been disrupted by the loss of vultures.
funFact: Researchers estimate the vulture collapse in India allowed rotting carcasses and feral dogs to increase, with a measurable rise in human deaths.

wiki.extract: The Indian vulture or long-billed vulture is a bird of prey native to the Indian subcontinent. It is an Old World vulture belonging to the family of Accipitridae. It is a medium-sized vulture with a small, semi-bald head with little feathers, long beak, and wide dark colored wings. It breeds mainly on small cliffs and hilly crags in central India and south India.

summary: A large griffon vulture of the Sahel and East Africa and the highest-flying bird on record. Specialist haemoglobin lets it breathe at altitudes where a human would lose consciousness.
nativeRange: Sahel and East Africa, from Senegal to Ethiopia and Tanzania
abilities: Struck an airliner at 11,300 m over Côte d'Ivoire in 1973, the highest-flying bird recorded
Has a haemoglobin variant that binds oxygen well at low pressure
Clears carcasses fast, limiting the spread of disease
Soars on thermals for hours while searching for food

animal.diet: Carrion, especially soft tissue of large mammals
animal.habitat: Open savanna and grassland, nesting on cliffs
animal.behaviour: Colonies breed on high cliffs and forage over vast areas, often travelling 150 km from the nest.
fieldMarks: Dark brown body with every feather edged creamy-white, giving a scaly, mottled look
Yellowish to horn-coloured bill
Pale yellow eye
White neck ruff
In flight, thin white lines across the underwing
animal.voice: Hissing, squealing and grunting at carcasses; otherwise silent.
animal.lookalikes: White-backed vulture has plainer, less scaled brown plumage, a dark bill and dark eye, and a white rump in flight. Lappet-faced vulture is larger with a bare pink head and wrinkled lappets.
animal.whereToSee: Serengeti, Maasai Mara, Simien Mountains (Ethiopia), Gol Mountains (Tanzania) for cliff colonies
animal.season: Resident; moves to follow migratory herds

lore: It is named after the German explorer Eduard Rüppell, who collected in north-east Africa in the 1820s. Vulture parts are used in African traditional medicine and divination, which drives poaching.
funFact: Its population dropped by an estimated 97% in three generations, mostly through poisoning, including poachers lacing elephant carcasses so circling vultures won't reveal them.

wiki.extract: Rüppell's vulture, also called Rüppell's griffon vulture or Rüppell's griffon, a species of vulture named after Eduard Rüppell, is a large, resident bird of prey, mainly native to the Sahel region and East Africa. It is considered to be the highest-flying bird, with confirmed evidence of a flight at an altitude of 11,300 m (37,000 ft), where the average temperature is about −56 °C (−69 °F). The former population of 22,000 individuals has been decreasing due to loss of habitat, incidental poisoning, and other factors. It is therefore listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List.

The plate reflects the 17th-century effort to systematically categorize and illustrate the animal kingdom with both scientific accuracy and artistic flair, often relying on specimens brought back from global expeditions.

Published in 1775 by François Bouchard, this plate exemplifies the detailed and artistic approach to ornithological study during the Enlightenment, combining scientific accuracy with decorative flair.

Gessner's work was one of the first attempts at a comprehensive zoological encyclopedia, combining classical knowledge with contemporary observations and detailed illustrations.

summary: Europe's largest eagle, with broad, plank-like wings, a massive yellow bill and a short white tail. Persecution wiped it out across much of western Europe; reintroductions have returned it to Scotland, Ireland and England.
nativeRange: Coasts and large wetlands of Norway, the Baltic, Iceland, Scotland and eastern Europe, east through Russia, Kazakhstan and Siberia to Japan; also western Greenland; winters south to Turkey, the Middle East and China
abilities: Wingspan up to about 2.5 m, the broadest of any European eagle
Snatches fish from the surface and robs otters, ospreys and gulls of food
Builds huge nests used for decades
Recovered across the Baltic after DDT and PCBs were banned

animal.diet: Fish, waterbirds, carrion and occasionally mammals
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, large lakes, rivers and estuaries
animal.lifespan: Often 20+ years; can exceed 25 in the wild
animal.behaviour: Often sits for hours on a shoreline perch, then glides out low over the water to snatch fish.
fieldMarks: Huge, broad, rectangular wings with deeply fingered tips
Short, wedge-shaped white tail in adults
Massive yellow bill and pale head in adults
Juveniles dark with dark bill and tail
animal.voice: A yelping 'kli-kli-kli' or 'krick-krick', often given in duet by pairs.
animal.lookalikes: Golden eagle has a longer tail, narrower wings held in a shallow V and a golden nape. Osprey is white below with long, angled wings. Pallas's fish eagle (Central Asia) has a dark tail with a white band.
animal.whereToSee: Isle of Mull and Skye (Scotland), the Isle of Wight (England), Lofoten (Norway), Danube Delta, Polish lakes, Hokkaido in winter.
animal.season: Resident in the west; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Neolithic people placed white-tailed eagle bones with human remains in the 'Tomb of the Eagles' on South Ronaldsay, Orkney, around 5,000 years ago, and the eagle's Old English name 'erne' survives in place names.
funFact: The last native British bird was shot in Shetland in 1918; reintroduction began on the Isle of Rùm in 1975 with birds from Norway.

wiki.extract: The white-tailed eagle, sometimes known as the "sea eagle", is a large bird of prey, widely distributed across temperate Eurasia. Like other eagles, it is a member of the family Accipitridae which also includes other diurnal raptors such as hawks, kites, and harriers. One of up to eleven members in the genus Haliaeetus, which are commonly called sea eagles, it is also referred to as the white-tailed sea-eagle. Sometimes, it is known as the ern or erne, gray sea eagle and Eurasian sea eagle.

Its plumage is a combination of brown on the wings and back, with white and brown-mottled feathers on its breast and head. summary: A sea eagle of North America, the national bird of the United States. It builds the largest nests of any North American bird, used and added to for decades.
nativeRange: Most of North America, from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico
abilities: Builds nests up to ~3 m wide and weighing over a tonne
Snatches fish from the water surface with its talons
Steals prey from ospreys and other birds (kleptoparasitism)
Gathers by the thousands along salmon rivers in winter

animal.diet: Mainly fish; also waterbirds and carrion
animal.habitat: Near large water bodies with tall trees
animal.lifespan: Around 20 years in the wild; record about 38
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform cartwheel courtship flights, locking talons and spinning downward together.
fieldMarks: Adult has a white head and tail and dark brown body
Massive yellow hooked bill
Young birds mottled brown and white for 4–5 years
Flat, plank-like wings when soaring
animal.voice: A weak, high-pitched twittering chatter, surprising for its size
animal.lookalikes: Golden eagle (vs young bald eagle) has a golden nape, smaller head and bill, and legs feathered to the toes; young goldens show neat white wing patches and a white tail base, not blotchy mottling.
animal.whereToSee: Chilkat Bald Eagle Preserve near Haines, Alaska; Conowingo Dam, Maryland; locks and dams along the Mississippi River in winter
animal.season: Resident in many areas; large winter gatherings Nov–Feb at open water and salmon runs

lore: Sacred to many Native American nations, its feathers are central to ceremony and regulated under US law for tribal use. It became the national emblem in 1782, and its recovery from DDT led to removal from the Endangered Species list in 2007.
funFact: 'Bald' comes from an old meaning of 'piebald' or white-headed, not hairless.

wiki.extract: The bald eagle is a bird of prey found in North America. A sea eagle, it has two known subspecies and forms a species pair with the white-tailed eagle, which occupies the same niche as the bald eagle in the Palearctic. Its range includes most of Canada and Alaska, all of the contiguous United States, and northern Mexico. It is found near large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply and old-growth trees for nesting.

summary: The most powerful raptor of the Americas, a rainforest eagle that snatches sloths and monkeys from the canopy. Its hind talons are as long as a grizzly bear's claws, and a pair raises a single chick only every two to three years.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico (now very rare) through Central America to eastern Bolivia, Brazil and north-eastern Argentina
abilities: Hind talons can reach about 12–13 cm
Carries prey such as sloths weighing several kilograms
Manoeuvres through dense canopy on short, broad wings rather than soaring high
Nests in giant emergent trees such as kapok (Ceiba) and Brazil nut

animal.diet: Mainly sloths and monkeys; also opossums, porcupines, macaws and iguanas
animal.habitat: Large tracts of undisturbed lowland tropical forest
animal.size: 89–105 cm; wingspan 176–224 cm; females 6–9 kg, males 4–5 kg
animal.behaviour: The single chick depends on its parents for over a year after fledging.
fieldMarks: Pale grey head with a split, double crest
Broad black band across the chest
White underparts with barred thighs and enormous yellow feet
Short, broad wings and long, banded tail
animal.voice: A long, wailing scream 'wheeeee-oo', especially from young birds begging at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Crested Eagle is smaller and slimmer with a single crest and lighter feet. Juvenile Harpies are whitish and can be confused with juvenile Crested Eagles; check size and leg thickness.
animal.whereToSee: Darién (Panama), Tambopata (Peru), Alta Floresta (Brazil) and Iwokrama (Guyana), usually at known nest trees with local guides.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Named after the harpies, the bird-bodied spirits of Greek myth, it is Panama's national bird and appears on Panama's coat of arms.
funFact: Its facial disc of feathers may help funnel sound to its ears, like an owl's.
