wiki.extract: The harpy eagle is a large neotropical species of eagle. It is also called the American harpy eagle to distinguish it from the Papuan eagle, which is sometimes known as the New Guinea harpy eagle or Papuan harpy eagle. It is the largest bird of prey throughout its range, and among the largest extant species of eagles in the world. It usually inhabits tropical lowland rainforests in the upper (emergent) canopy layer. Destruction of its natural habitat has caused it to vanish from many parts of its former range, and it is nearly extirpated from much of Central America. It is the only member of the genus Harpia, which, together with Harpyopsis, Macheiramphus and Morphnus, forms the subfamily Harpiinae.

summary: A white-headed sea eagle of African rivers and lakes whose ringing call is called 'the voice of Africa'. It snatches fish from the surface with a swing of its talons and is the national bird of Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Sudan.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa wherever there is open fresh or coastal water
abilities: Grabs fish from just below the surface; spiny scales on its toes grip slippery prey
Can swim using its wings when a fish is too heavy to lift
Steals prey from herons, storks and other birds
Pairs duet with throws of the head, reinforcing territory along a stretch of shore

animal.diet: Mainly fish; also waterbirds, flamingos, carrion and young monitor lizards
animal.habitat: Large rivers, lakes, dams, swamps and coastal lagoons with tall perches
animal.size: 63–75 cm long; wingspan 2–2.4 m; females larger
animal.behaviour: It watches from a tree, then glides down and swings its feet forward at the last moment to pluck a fish within about 15 cm of the surface.
fieldMarks: Snow-white head, breast, back and short tail
Rich chestnut belly and shoulders
Black wings
Bare yellow face and yellow legs
Juveniles mottled brown and white, taking about five years to reach adult plumage
animal.voice: A loud, ringing, yelping 'weee-ah, hyo-hyo-hyo', given with the head thrown back over the shoulders, often as a pair duet.
animal.lookalikes: Palm-nut vulture is white with black wings but has a white belly, bare reddish face and a black-tipped tail. Madagascar fish eagle (Madagascar only) has a brown head and body. Immatures resemble other large brown eagles but usually show some white on the breast and tail.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Naivasha and Lake Baringo (Kenya), Chobe River, Okavango Delta, Lake Malawi, Lake Kariba, Murchison Falls
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The fish eagle appears on the coats of arms of Zambia, Namibia and South Sudan, and Zambia's flag shows it in flight; the Zulu name Inkwazi was given to the South African presidential aircraft.
funFact: Formerly placed in Haliaeetus with the bald eagle, it was moved by the IOC World Bird List in 2023 to Icthyophaga with the smaller tropical fish eagles, though not every checklist has followed.

wiki.extract: The African fish eagle or the African sea eagle is a large species of eagle found throughout sub-Saharan Africa wherever large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply occur. It is the national bird of Malawi, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. As a result of its large range, it is known in many languages. Examples of names include: visarend in Afrikaans, nkwazi in Chewa, aigle pêcheur in French, idì in Yoruba, hungwe in Shona, inkwazi in isiZulu, and ntšhu in Northern Sotho. Though this species may superficially resemble the bald eagle in appearance they are not closely related and the two species occur on different continents, with the bald eagle being endemic to North America.

summary: One of the world's rarest birds of prey, confined to a few lakes, rivers and mangroves of western Madagascar. Pairs are sometimes helped at the nest by additional adults.
nativeRange: Western Madagascar
abilities: Hunts fish from tall waterside perches
Some pairs breed with help from extra adult birds

animal.diet: Mainly fish, especially native species and introduced tilapia
animal.habitat: Large lakes, rivers, estuaries and mangroves with tall trees
animal.behaviour: Pairs defend a lake shore and call loudly from high perches.
fieldMarks: Brown body with pale brownish-white cheeks and throat
Darker brown crown
White tail in adults
Pale bill
Darker brown wings
animal.voice: A loud, high, yelping call, similar to the African fish eagle's but harsher and more rapid.
animal.lookalikes: No similar large eagle occurs in its range. Madagascar harrier-hawk is smaller, grey and long-legged.
animal.whereToSee: Tsimembo-Manambolomaty lakes complex (western Madagascar), Antsalova region
animal.season: Resident

lore: The Peregrine Fund and local communities have run Madagascar fish eagle projects since the 1990s, combining surveys with community-managed lake protections.
funFact: It is the closest relative of the African fish eagle, from which its ancestors likely arrived on Madagascar.

wiki.extract: The Madagascar fish eagle or Madagascar sea-eagle, is a large bird of prey in the family Accipitridae which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as kites, buzzards and harriers. It is endemic to the coastal strip in the northwest of Madagascar. It is about 63 cm (25 in) long and has a pale brown head, dark brown body and white tail. The Madagascar fish eagle has been suffering from a declining population and is threatened by habitat destruction and persecution, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has rated its conservation status as being "critically endangered".

summary: A medium-sized brown raptor with a forked tail that wheels in hundreds over South Asian cities, scavenging from rubbish dumps, slaughterhouses and markets. It is likely one of the most numerous birds of prey in the world.
nativeRange: Much of Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia; absent from the Americas
abilities: Steers with its long forked tail, twisting it constantly to manoeuvre in crowded city air
Snatches food from the ground, water or even people's hands in flight without landing
Northern populations migrate thousands of kilometres, while South Asian city birds are resident
Gathers at grass fires to catch fleeing insects and small animals

animal.diet: Carrion, refuse, fish, rodents, insects, small birds; opportunistic scavenger
animal.habitat: Cities, villages, river banks, wetlands and open country
animal.size: About 50–60 cm long; wingspan about 130–155 cm
animal.behaviour: Soars and circles over cities for hours, then swoops down to snatch scraps with its feet; on summer days flocks of hundreds may circle together.
fieldMarks: Dark brown raptor with a long, shallowly forked tail (looks square when fully spread)
Long angled wings with a pale panel on the upperwing and paler 'windows' near the wingtips below
Pale head with dark eye-patch; yellow feet
Constant twisting of the tail in flight
animal.voice: A high, quavering whinny 'pee-errrr', often given in flight
animal.lookalikes: Brahminy kite is chestnut with a white head and a rounded tail; Red kite (rare in Asia) is rufous with a deeply forked tail; Marsh harriers have long unforked tails and glide with raised wings.
animal.whereToSee: Over every large South Asian city, especially Delhi, Lahore, Karachi and Dhaka
animal.season: Resident in South Asian cities; the black-eared form is a winter visitor from Central and East Asia

lore: In Delhi's Wazirabad, brothers Nadeem Shehzad and Mohammad Saud have rescued thousands of injured kites, many cut by kite-flying strings; their work is the subject of the 2022 documentary 'All That Breathes'.
funFact: Black kites in northern Australia have been documented picking up burning sticks and dropping them to spread grass fires, flushing prey.

wiki.extract: The black kite or fire kite is a medium-sized bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors. It is thought to be the world's most abundant species of Accipitridae, although some populations have experienced dramatic declines or fluctuations. Current global population estimates run up to 6.7 million individuals.

plates.title: Of the Eggs and Nests of Birds
plates.author: Giuseppe Zinanni (Ginanni) (1692-1753)

summary: An elegant rufous raptor with a deeply forked tail that twists constantly as it steers. Almost lost from Britain by the 20th century, it has become a celebrated reintroduction success over English and Scottish farmland.
nativeRange: Europe, chiefly Germany, France and Spain, plus Britain, Switzerland and Sweden; now only a rare winter visitor to North Africa, where it formerly bred
abilities: Can stay aloft for hours with little flapping, steering with its long, forked tail
A scavenger that cleaned medieval city streets of waste
Decorates its nest with rags, plastic and other debris
Gathers in communal winter roosts of hundreds of birds

animal.diet: Carrion, small mammals, earthworms, birds, waste food
animal.habitat: Farmland and open hills with woodland for nesting
animal.behaviour: Drifts low over fields and roads searching for carrion, often in loose groups around feeding stations.
fieldMarks: Rufous body and long, deeply forked orange-red tail
Pale grey head
Long, angled wings with white patches at the base of black primaries
Constantly twisting tail in flight
animal.voice: A high, wavering, buzzard-like whistle, 'weeoo-weeoo-weeoo'.
animal.lookalikes: Black kite is darker brown with a shallower fork that looks straight-edged when spread. Common buzzard has a short, rounded tail. Marsh harrier glides on raised wings and has no forked tail.
animal.whereToSee: The Chilterns of England, Gigrin Farm in mid-Wales, Argaty in Scotland; Germany, Spain and the Swiss lowlands.
animal.season: Resident in Britain and western Europe; central and northern European birds winter in Iberia

lore: Medieval London protected kites as street scavengers; in Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' Autolycus warns 'when the kite builds, look to lesser linen', because kites stole washing for their nests.
funFact: English reintroduction began in 1989 in the Chilterns, using birds mainly from Spain; the region now holds thousands.

wiki.extract: The red kite is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as eagles, buzzards, and harriers. The species currently breeds only in Europe, though it formerly also bred in West Asia and Northwest Africa. Historically, it was only resident in the milder parts of its range in Western Europe and Northwestern Africa, whereas all or most red kites in Northern mainland Europe wintered to the south and west, some also reaching western Asia, but an increasing number of northern birds now remain in that region year-round. Vagrants have reached north to Finland and south to Israel, Libya and the Gambia.

summary: A small, white vulture with a bare yellow face and a shaggy mane. It is one of the few birds that use tools, throwing stones to crack open ostrich eggs, and it migrates between Europe and Africa.
nativeRange: Southern Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and sub-Saharan Africa; European and Central Asian birds winter in Africa and Arabia
abilities: Throws stones at ostrich eggs to break them, a famous case of bird tool use
Uses twigs to roll up wool for nest lining
Eats the faeces of livestock, possibly for carotenoids that colour its face
Migrants cross the Mediterranean at narrow points such as Gibraltar and the Bosphorus

animal.diet: Carrion, scraps, eggs, small animals, insects and dung
animal.habitat: Mountains and cliffs near open country, villages and rubbish dumps
animal.behaviour: Picks over scraps at carcasses and dumps, waiting its turn after larger vultures.
fieldMarks: Adult dirty-white with black flight feathers
Bare yellow-orange face and thin, hooked bill
Wedge-shaped white tail
Juveniles dark brown, whitening over about five years
animal.voice: Usually silent; occasional mewing and hissing.
animal.lookalikes: White stork is longer-legged with a red bill. Griffon vulture is much larger and brown. Booted eagle pale morph has a square tail and feathered head.
animal.whereToSee: Spanish sierras (Monfragüe, Picos de Europa), the Balkans, Socotra (Yemen) and Oman; migration at Gibraltar, Belen (Turkey) and Eilat.
animal.season: Summer visitor in Europe Mar–Sep; resident in Africa, Arabia and South Asia

lore: The hieroglyph for the sound 'aleph' (Gardiner G1) depicts this vulture, and the bird's habit of following people gave it the nickname 'Pharaoh's chicken'.
funFact: Jane Goodall and Hugo van Lawick first described its stone-throwing in Tanzania in 1966.

wiki.extract: The Egyptian vulture, also called the white scavenger vulture or pharaoh's chicken, is a small Old World vulture in the monotypic genus Neophron. It is widely distributed from the Iberian Peninsula, North Africa, West Asia and India. The contrasting underwing pattern and wedge-shaped tail make it distinctive in flight as it soars in thermals during the warmer parts of the day. Egyptian vultures feed mainly on carrion but are opportunistic and will prey on small mammals, birds, and reptiles. They also feed on the eggs of other birds, breaking larger ones by tossing a large pebble onto them.

summary: One of the largest and most powerful eagles in the world, with a shaggy crest, a huge arched blue-grey bill and pale blue eyes. Found only in the rainforests of the Philippines, it is the national bird and among the rarest raptors on Earth.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Philippines: Mindanao, Luzon, Samar and Leyte
abilities: Hunts flying lemurs (colugos), monkeys, civets and large birds in the forest canopy
Pairs hunt cooperatively, one distracting a monkey troop while the other strikes
Raises a single chick every two years

animal.diet: Colugos (Philippine flying lemurs), macaques, palm civets, flying squirrels, hornbills, snakes
animal.habitat: Primary dipterocarp forest on steep mountain slopes
animal.size: About 86–102 cm long; wingspan about 1.8–2.2 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts by perching in the canopy and moving between trees, then flying fast through the forest to seize prey with its massive talons.
fieldMarks: Very large eagle with a shaggy, spiky crest
Huge, deeply arched blue-grey bill
Dark face, brown upperparts, cream-white underparts
Pale blue-grey eyes; broad, short wings and long tail
animal.voice: High-pitched whistles, rising at the end, especially from young birds begging
animal.lookalikes: Changeable hawk-eagle and Philippine hawk-eagle are much smaller with less massive bills; no other Philippine raptor approaches its size.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine Eagle Center near Davao City; Mount Kitanglad and Mount Apo, Mindanao
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Proclaimed the national bird of the Philippines in 1995, it gave its Filipino name Haribon ('king of birds') to the country's leading conservation society. The first captive-bred chick, Pag-asa ('hope'), hatched in 1992.
funFact: Despite its old name 'monkey-eating eagle', its main prey on Mindanao is the colugo, a gliding mammal.

wiki.extract: The Philippine eagle, also known as the monkey-eating eagle or great Philippine eagle, is a critically endangered species of eagle of the family Accipitridae which is endemic to forests in the Philippines. It has brown and white-coloured plumage, a shaggy crest, and generally measures 86 to 102 cm in length and weighs 4.04 to 8.0 kg.

summary: Africa's largest eagle, a powerful hunter of game birds, monitor lizards and small antelope. It hunts from a high soar, spotting prey from several kilometres away.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, in open and semi-arid country
abilities: Exceptional eyesight; spots prey at a great distance while soaring
Kills prey as large as young antelope, jackals and monitor lizards
Uses enormous stick nests that may be reused for decades

animal.diet: Guineafowl, francolins, bustards, hyraxes, hares, monitor lizards, young antelope
animal.habitat: Savanna, thornbush and semi-desert with tall trees or pylons for nesting
animal.size: 78–96 cm long; wingspan about 1.9–2.6 m; 3–6 kg
animal.behaviour: It hunts mainly from a high, wide-circling soar, then drops in a long, shallow stoop on unsuspecting prey.
fieldMarks: Dark brown head, throat and upper breast forming a hood
White lower breast and belly lightly spotted with dark brown
Short crest; bright yellow eye
Feathered legs
Dark underwings in flight, contrasting with pale belly
animal.voice: Mostly silent; in display a loud, ringing 'klee-klee-klooee'.
animal.lookalikes: Black-chested snake eagle has a similar dark hood but an unspotted white belly, bare pale legs, a large round head with orange-yellow eyes and pale underwings. funFact: Even in large reserves such as Kruger, martial eagle numbers fell by more than half in roughly two decades, prompting uplisting to Endangered in 2020.

wiki.extract: The martial eagle is a large eagle native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is the only member of the genus Polemaetus. A species of the booted eagle subfamily (Aquilinae), it has feathers over its tarsus. One of the largest and most powerful species of booted eagle, it is a fairly opportunistic predator that varies its prey selection between mammals, birds and reptiles. It is one of few eagle species known to hunt primarily from a high soar, by swooping down on its quarry. This species, an inhabitant of wooded belts of otherwise open savanna, has shown a precipitous decline in the last few centuries due to a variety of factors. The martial eagle is one of the most persecuted bird species in the world. Due to its habit of taking livestock and regionally valuable game, local farmers and game wardens frequently seek to eliminate martial eagles, although the effect of eagles on this prey is almost certainly considerably exaggerated. Currently, the martial eagle is classified with the status of Endangered by the IUCN.

summary: A small, pale grey hawk that hunts lizards and birds in gardens and groves across South Asia and Africa. Its name comes from the same root as 'shikar', the hunt, and it was flown by falconers in the subcontinent.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa and from southern Central Asia and Iran through Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka to southern China and Southeast Asia
abilities: Ambushes prey from a hidden perch with a short, fast dash
Takes many lizards and large insects from the ground, as well as small birds
Lives quietly in city parks and gardens, often unnoticed

animal.diet: Lizards, small birds, rodents, large insects and frogs
animal.habitat: Open woodland, groves, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: Sits in a leafy tree and launches a short, rapid attack, flying low and fast; small birds give sharp alarm calls when it appears, and Black drongos imitate its call.
fieldMarks: Small hawk with short rounded wings and a medium tail
Adult pale blue-grey above with fine rufous barring below
Thin dark stripe down the centre of the throat
Red (male) or yellow (female) eye; yellow legs
animal.voice: A loud, shrill 'ti-tui' or 'kik-ki', repeated; often heard before it is seen
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian sparrowhawk (winter in Pakistan and the Himalaya) has a longer tail and darker grey back; Besra is darker with a bold throat stripe and heavier barring; Shikra's pale grey back and fine rufous bars are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: City parks, orchards and canal-side trees across Pakistan and India
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Shikras were trained for small-game hawking in Mughal and later Indian falconry, and the English word 'shikra' was taken directly from Hindustani.
funFact: A 2024 genetic study broke up the old genus Accipiter, and the Shikra was moved into the revived genus Tachyspiza.

wiki.extract: The shikra is a small bird of prey in the family Accipitridae found widely distributed in Asia and Africa where it is also called the little banded goshawk. The African forms may represent a separate species but have usually been considered as subspecies of the shikra. The shikra is very similar in appearance, as well as behavior, at least to some degree, to other species including the Chinese sparrowhawk, Eurasian goshawk and Eurasian sparrowhawk. They have a sharp two-note call and exhibit the flap-and-glide flight style typical of Tachyspiza and Accipiter hawks. Their calls are imitated by drongos and the common hawk-cuckoo resembles it in plumage. This species was formerly placed in the genus Accipiter.

summary: A striking eagle with almost no tail, red face and legs, and a rocking, tightrope-walker flight. It spends much of the day gliding low over the savanna searching for carrion and prey.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa and south-western Arabia
abilities: Glides for hours, tilting from side to side, with little flapping
Spreads its wings in 'heraldic' sunbathing postures
Finds carcasses and is often first at them

animal.diet: Carrion, birds, small mammals, reptiles
animal.habitat: Open savanna and woodland
animal.behaviour: It flies with wings held in a shallow V, rocking side to side, a habit that inspired its French name meaning 'acrobat'.
fieldMarks: Very short tail; feet project past it in flight
Black body with chestnut back (cream in some birds)
Bright red face and legs
Grey shoulder patch
Females have grey secondaries, males black
animal.voice: A loud, barking 'kaw-aw' and a harsh 'schaaaw'.
animal.lookalikes: Black-chested snake eagle has a long tail and white belly. Juvenile bateleurs are brown and may resemble other brown eagles but share the short-tailed silhouette.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger, Kgalagadi, Okavango, Serengeti, Maasai Mara
animal.season: Resident

lore: François Le Vaillant named it 'bateleur' (French for a street acrobat) in the 18th century because of its tilting flight.
funFact: Bateleurs can spend 8–9 hours a day in the air and cover hundreds of kilometres.

wiki.extract: The bateleur, also known as the bateleur eagle, is a medium-sized eagle in the family Accipitridae. It is often considered a relative of the snake eagles and, like them, it is classified within the subfamily Circaetinae. It is the only member of the genus Terathopius and may be the origin of the "Zimbabwe Bird", the national emblem of Zimbabwe. Adult bateleurs are generally black in colour with a chestnut colour on the mantle as well as on the rump and tail. Adults also have gray patches about the leading edges of the wings with bright red on their cere and their feet. Adults also show white greater coverts, contrasting with black remiges in males, gray patches on the underwing primaries and black wingtips. The juvenile bateleur is quite different, being largely drab brown with a bit of paler feather scaling. All bateleurs have extremely large heads for their size, rather small bills, large feet, relatively short legs, long, bow-like wings and uniquely short tails, which are much smaller still on adults compared to juvenile birds.

summary: One species, two worlds: a silvery river tetra, and blind, pink cave-dwelling forms that lost their eyes and pigment in the darkness of Mexican caves. Biologists study the pair to see how evolution rewires genes.
nativeRange: Lower Rio Grande and Pecos (Texas) south through north-eastern and central Mexico; cave forms in about 30 caves of the Sierra de El Abra and Sierra de Guatemala, Tamaulipas and San Luis Potosí
abilities: Cave forms begin to grow eyes as embryos, then the eyes degenerate and are covered by skin
Cavefish sleep far less than surface fish of the same species
Cavefish resist starvation by storing fat and live healthily with high blood sugar and insulin resistance
Compensates for blindness with more taste buds and an enhanced lateral line

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, small crustaceans, algae and detritus; cavefish eat bat guano and organic debris
animal.habitat: Surface: clear streams and rivers; cave forms: pools and streams of limestone caves
animal.lifespan: Up to about 15 years in captivity
animal.behaviour: Surface fish school by day, while cave fish forage alone along the bottom with their heads tilted down.
fieldMarks: Surface form: silvery tetra with a dark spot or stripe at the tail base and reddish fins
Cave form: pink-white, no visible eyes, skin over the eye sockets
Adipose fin present in both
animal.lookalikes: Other Astyanax tetras in Central America (A. aeneus and others) are only told apart in the hand. In the caves of the Sierra de El Abra region, no other eyeless fish looks like it.
animal.whereToSee: Cueva de El Pachón and Sótano de la Tinaja (permits needed); surface fish in the Río Tampaón and Río Guayalejo; aquaria and research labs
animal.season: Resident; cavefish breed opportunistically year-round

lore: Mexican biologist Salvador Coronado collected the first blind cavefish at the Cueva Chica in 1936, and they were described as a new genus, Anoptichthys, before they were found to interbreed with river tetras. Darwin, writing before this discovery, had argued that cave animals lose their eyes through disuse.
funFact: Blind cavefish and sighted surface fish can still interbreed, and some of the hybrids have partial eyes.

wiki.extract: The Mexican tetra, also known as the blind cave fish, blind cave characin or the blind cave tetra, is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins. This fish is found in the lower Rio Grande, and the Nueces and Pecos Rivers in Texas, into the Central Plateau and eastern states of Mexico.

summary: A tiny Amazonian schooling fish whose glowing blue-green stripe made it the most popular aquarium fish of the 20th century. Its iridescent colour comes from microscopic reflecting platelets in its skin, not from pigment.
nativeRange: Western Amazon blackwater and clearwater streams of Peru, Colombia and Brazil (Putumayo and upper Solimões area)
abilities: Its blue stripe works like a living light filter: stacked guanine platelets tilt to shift the colour from green-blue in light to violet-blue in dimness
Schools tightly, so the flashing stripes can confuse predators
Lives in soft, very acidic water with almost no dissolved minerals

animal.diet: Micropredator: small insects, larvae, crustaceans and worms
animal.habitat: Shaded, slow, tannin-stained forest streams with leaf litter and roots
animal.lifespan: Usually 2–3 years in the wild; up to 8–10 in aquaria
animal.behaviour: Moves in schools among roots and leaf litter, and at night fades its colours to rest.
fieldMarks: Tiny, slender body with an iridescent electric blue-green stripe from eye to adipose fin
Red stripe on the rear half of the lower body only
Silvery-white belly in front of the red area
Small adipose fin
animal.lookalikes: Cardinal tetra (P. axelrodi) has red along the whole length of the belly beneath the blue stripe. Green neon (P. simulans) is smaller, with a greener stripe and much less red.
animal.whereToSee: Blackwater creeks of the Peruvian and Colombian Amazon near the Putumayo; aquaria worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds at the start of the rainy season

lore: First collected by Auguste Rabaut in the 1930s and shipped to Europe in 1936, it was named after the American aquarist William T. Innes. Most neons in shops today come from fish farms in Southeast Asia and Florida, not the wild.
funFact: The neon's stripe changes colour without any change in pigment: in the dark the reflecting platelets tilt and the stripe shifts from cyan to deep blue-violet.

wiki.extract: The neon tetra is a species of freshwater fish belonging to the family Acestrorhamphidae, the American characins, of the order Characiformes. The type species of its genus, it is native to blackwater and clearwater streams in the Amazon basin of South America. Its bright colouring makes the fish visible to conspecifics in the dark blackwater streams, and is also the main reason for its popularity among freshwater fish hobbyists, with neon tetras being one of the most widely kept tropical fish in the world.

summary: A fist-sized land snail from East Africa that has spread across the tropics and is listed among the world's worst invasive species. It eats hundreds of plant species, can lay over a thousand eggs a year, and can carry rat lungworm, a parasite that causes meningitis.
nativeRange: Coastal East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique); invasive across South and Southeast Asia, the Pacific, the Caribbean and South America
abilities: Eats more than 500 kinds of plants, as well as plaster and concrete for calcium
Lays clutches of 100–400 eggs several times a year
Survives dry seasons by sealing its shell and becoming dormant for months
Hermaphrodite; can store sperm from a single mating for many months

animal.diet: Crops, garden plants, fallen fruit, decaying matter, and calcium from walls and shells
animal.habitat: Farms, gardens, plantations and disturbed land in warm, humid regions
animal.lifespan: Usually 3–5 years; up to about 9 years
animal.size: Shell typically 7–10 cm long, up to about 20 cm
animal.behaviour: Active at night and after rain; in dry periods it hides in soil or under debris, sealed behind a mucus membrane.
fieldMarks: Large, tall, cone-shaped shell
Brown to reddish-brown with darker vertical streaks
Seven to nine whorls
Grey-brown body with long tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Giant Ghana tiger snail (Achatina achatina) is larger with bold zig-zag stripes. Rosy wolfsnail (Euglandina rosea) is smaller, pinkish, and predatory. Native apple snails (Pomacea) live in water and have a rounder shell.

lore: It was carried from East Africa to Mauritius in the early 1800s and to India by the 1840s, then across Asia and the Pacific; in Florida a boy's three pet snails brought from Hawaii in 1966 led to a decade-long eradication campaign.
funFact: The rosy wolfsnail introduced to Pacific islands to eat it instead wiped out dozens of native Partula tree snails, a famous biological-control disaster.

wiki.extract: Lissachatina fulica is a species of large land snail that belongs in the subfamily Achatininae of the family Achatinidae. It is also known as the giant African land snail. It shares the common name "giant African snail" with other species of snails such as Achatina achatina and Archachatina marginata. This snail species has been considered a significant cause of pest issues around the world. It is a federally prohibited species in the U.S., as it is illegal to sell or possess. Internationally, it is the most frequently occurring invasive species of snail.

summary: The largest of the sturgeons and one of the biggest bony fish ever recorded, a long-lived giant of the Caspian and Black Seas that runs up the Volga, Ural and Danube to spawn. Poaching for beluga caviar has driven it to Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Caspian and Black Sea basins (formerly also the Adriatic and Sea of Azov), with spawning runs up the Volga, Ural, Kura, Danube and other large rivers
abilities: Lives over 100 years and may not first spawn until about 15–20 years old
Anadromous: migrates from the sea hundreds of kilometres up large rivers to spawn on gravel beds
Hunts fish with a huge crescent-shaped mouth, unlike the bottom-sucking smaller sturgeons
Historic females weighed over 1,000 kg, a quarter of it roe
edibilityNote: Beluga caviar is the most expensive caviar. International trade in wild beluga caviar is effectively closed under CITES, and buying it supports poaching, so choose certified farmed caviar only. Long-lived sturgeon accumulate mercury and other contaminants. Raw sturgeon flesh should be avoided.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish (gobies, herring, carp, other sturgeon), crustaceans and molluscs; occasionally seals
animal.habitat: Open waters of the Caspian and Black Seas; large rivers during spawning
animal.size: Commonly 2–3 m and 100–300 kg; historically up to about 6–7 m and 1,500 kg
animal.behaviour: Spring and autumn runs move upriver, and autumn migrants overwinter in deep river pits before spawning the following spring.

animal.lookalikes: Russian sturgeon (Acipenser gueldenstaedtii) and stellate sturgeon (A. stellatus) have much smaller mouths and round barbels, and the stellate sturgeon has a very long, narrow snout. The kaluga (Huso dauricus) of the Amur basin is its only true relative.
animal.whereToSee: The Volga delta near Astrakhan; the lower Danube at the Iron Gates (where dams block the old runs); hatcheries and aquaria
animal.season: Upriver spawning runs in spring (March–May) and autumn (August–November)

lore: Herodotus described the great boneless fish of the Borysthenes (Dnieper), called antacaei, that the Scythians salted. Russian tsars and Persian shahs drew huge revenues from Caspian caviar, and a beluga of about 1,571 kg was reported from the Volga estuary in 1827.
funFact: Isinglass, a gelatin once used to clarify beer and wine, was first made from the dried swim bladders of sturgeons such as the beluga.

wiki.extract: The beluga, also known as the beluga sturgeon or great sturgeon, is a species of sturgeon, which are anadromous fish of the family Acipenseridae of the order Acipenseriformes. It is found primarily in the Caspian and Black Sea basins, and formerly in the Adriatic Sea. Based on maximum size, it is the third-most-massive living species of bony fish. Heavily fished for the female's valuable roe, known as beluga caviar, wild populations have been greatly reduced by overfishing and poaching, leading IUCN to classify the species as critically endangered.

funFact: Solitary and swarming forms looked so different that they were long classified as separate species, until Boris Uvarov showed in 1921 they were phases of one.

wiki.extract: The desert locust is a species of locust in the grasshopper family, Acrididae. A periodically swarming, short-horned bird grasshopper, it is found primarily in the deserts and dry areas of northern and eastern Africa, Arabia, and southwest Asia. During population surge years, its range may extend north into parts of Southern Europe, Eastern Africa, and Northern India. The desert locust shows periodic changes in its body form and can change in response to environmental conditions over several generations. It begins life as a solitary, shorter-winged, highly fecund, non-migratory form, to a gregarious, long-winged, and migratory phase in which it may travel long distances into new areas. Due to this traveling, it may join groups, thus, forming locust plagues. This involves invading new areas where it may consume all vegetation including valuable crops. Although at other times, it may live unnoticed in small numbers in various areas.

wiki.extract: The staghorn coral is a branching, stony coral, within the Order Scleractinia. It is characterized by thick, upright branches which can grow in excess of 2 meters (6.5 ft) in height and resemble the antlers of a stag, hence the name, Staghorn. It grows within various areas of a reef but is most commonly found within shallow fore and back reefs, as well as patch reefs, where water depths rarely exceed 20 meters (65 ft). Staghorn corals can exhibit very fast growth, adding up to 5 cm in new skeleton for every 1 cm of existing skeleton each year, making them one of the fastest growing fringe coral species in the Western Atlantic. Due to this fast growth, Acropora cervicornis, serve as one of the most important reef building corals, functioning as marine nurseries for juvenile fish, buffer zones for erosion and storms, and center points of biodiversity in the Western Atlantic.

wiki.extract: The long-tailed tit or long-tailed bushtit is a common bird species belonging to the bushtit family found throughout Eurasia. An insectivore, it inhabits deciduous and mixed woodlands as well as scrub, heathland, farmland, parks and gardens. The plumage of this small long-tailed bird is predominantly black and white with varying amounts of pink and grey. Northern subspecies are paler and have completely white heads, lacking the large dark eyebrows of southern populations. It is a social bird that forms compact family flocks of six to seventeen individuals outside of the breeding season, when these flocks break up. It has a strong preference for nesting in scrub areas and often builds its nest in thorny bushes less than 3 metres above the ground.

A dark 'bullseye' spot on top of the face in front of the eyes
Patrols ponds on long, steady beats
animal.lookalikes: Comet darner (Anax longipes) has a bright red abdomen in males and no bullseye. Giant darner (A. walsinghami) is larger and longer-bodied. Other darners (Aeshna) have striped thoraxes.
animal.whereToSee: Ponds and lakes across North America; spectacular autumn migration along coasts, e.g. Cape May Point, New Jersey
animal.season: Resident broods breed in summer; migrants arrive in the north in spring and fly south Aug–Oct

lore: It is the state insect of Washington. Hydrogen isotopes in its wings, studied in 2018, revealed a three-generation annual cycle from Canada to Mexico and back.
funFact: Some were fitted with tiny radio transmitters and followed by small aircraft as they migrated.

wiki.extract: The green darner or common green darner, after its resemblance to a darning needle, is a species of dragonfly in the family Aeshnidae. One of the most common and abundant species throughout North America, it also ranges south to Panama. It is well known for its great migration distance from the northern United States south into Texas and Mexico. It also occurs in the Caribbean, Tahiti, and Asia from Japan to mainland China. It is the official insect for the state of Washington in the United States.

summary: A graceful ray with a white-spotted dark back and a duck-billed snout, often seen 'flying' in groups over Atlantic reefs. Its jaws crack clams and conchs with plate-like teeth.
nativeRange: Western and central Atlantic from North Carolina to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean; Indo-Pacific populations are now split into other species
abilities: Crushes hard-shelled molluscs with fused, chevron-shaped tooth plates
Digs prey from sand using its shovel-like snout
Leaps clear of the water, sometimes landing in boats
Carries one to several venomous barbed spines at the base of its long tail

animal.diet: Clams, oysters, conchs, whelks, shrimp, crabs
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, bays, reefs and lagoons to about 80 m
animal.size: Disc width up to about 3 m
animal.behaviour: Often swims in loose groups, sometimes in schools of dozens, cruising near the surface or over sand flats.
fieldMarks: Dark blue-black to grey back densely covered with white spots or rings
Pointed, wing-like pectoral fins
Protruding duck-bill snout with a flat, rounded tip
Very long, whip-like tail, often 2–3 times disc width
animal.lookalikes: Southern stingray lacks spots and has a rhomboid disc with no protruding head; cownose ray has a notched, two-lobed forehead and plain brown back.
animal.whereToSee: Bonaire, Cozumel, Belize, Florida Keys, Bermuda
animal.season: Year-round; Florida's Sarasota coast May–Oct

lore: The species name narinari comes from a Tupi-Guarani name recorded by Georg Marcgrave in his Historia Naturalis Brasiliae (1648).
funFact: In 2008 a leaping spotted eagle ray struck and killed a boater in the Florida Keys, one of very few such deaths ever recorded.

wiki.extract: The spotted eagle ray is a cartilaginous fish of the eagle ray family, Aetobatidae. As traditionally recognized, it is found globally in tropical regions, including the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. Recent authorities have restricted it to the Atlantic with other populations recognized as the ocellated eagle ray and Pacific white-spotted eagle ray. Spotted eagle rays are most commonly seen alone, but occasionally swim in groups. They are ovoviviparous, the female retaining the eggs then releasing the young as miniature versions of the parent.

The illustration exemplifies the 17th-century transition toward empirical observation in science, providing European readers with some of the first accurate visual records of South American marine life.

summary: A tree-dwelling dragon of northern Australia and New Guinea that, when alarmed, opens a huge ruff of skin around its head, gapes a pink-yellow mouth and hisses. If that fails it runs off on its hind legs.
nativeRange: Northern Australia (Kimberley, Top End, Cape York) and southern New Guinea
abilities: Spreads a frill up to ~30 cm across, supported by cartilage rods from its jaw
Runs bipedally at speed on its hind legs
Spends most of its time in trees, coming down to hunt insects after rains

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small lizards and mammals
animal.habitat: Tropical savanna woodland, often in eucalyptus trees
animal.size: Up to ~90 cm including tail; males larger
animal.behaviour: Most active in the wet season, when it comes down to the ground to feed. In the dry season it stays high in trees and is much less active.
fieldMarks: Large, loose frill folded around the neck like a cape
Grey to brown or reddish body, often with darker mottling
Long tail and long hind legs
Mouth lining pink or yellow
animal.lookalikes: Bearded dragons (Pogona) have a spiny throat pouch rather than a free frill and live mostly further south. Water dragons have a crest but no frill.
animal.whereToSee: Kakadu and Litchfield national parks (Northern Territory), the Kimberley, Cape York; most often seen on tree trunks or roads in the wet season
animal.season: Most visible in the wet season (November–April)

lore: It appeared on the reverse of the Australian two-cent coin from decimalisation in 1966 until the coin was discontinued in the early 1990s.
funFact: Its frill is controlled by jaw muscles: when it opens its mouth wide, the frill opens too.

wiki.extract: The frilled lizard, also known commonly as the frilled agama, frillneck lizard, frill-necked lizard or frilled dragon, is a species of lizard in the family Agamidae. The species is native to northern Australia and southern New Guinea and is the only member of the genus Chlamydosaurus. Its common names refer to the large frill around its neck, which usually stays folded against the lizard's body. The frilled lizard grows to 90 cm (35 in) from head to tail tip and can weigh 600 g (1.3 lb). Males are larger and more robust than females. The lizard's body is generally grey, brown, orangish-brown, or black in colour. The frills have red, orange, yellow, or white colours.

summary: An Australian desert lizard covered in conical spines. Grooves between its scales pull water from damp sand or dew across its skin to its mouth, and it eats only ants, thousands at a sitting.
nativeRange: Arid and semi-arid central and western Australia
abilities: Wicks water to its mouth: fine channels between its scales draw dew and damp from sand up to the corners of its jaws, where it swallows it
Eats only small ants, licking them up one at a time
Has a knob on the back of its neck that acts as a 'false head' when it dips its real head
Changes colour between yellow, red and brown with temperature and mood

animal.diet: Small black ants, especially Iridomyrmex and Ochetellus
animal.habitat: Sandy desert, spinifex grassland and mallee scrub
animal.behaviour: It walks with a jerky, rocking gait and freezes when watched. When threatened it tucks its head down so the knob on its neck looks like a head.
fieldMarks: Body covered in large conical spines, including two horns over the eyes
Yellow, red and brown camouflage pattern
Spiny knob on the back of the neck
Slow, swaying walk
animal.lookalikes: Unlike any other Australian lizard. North American horned lizards (Phrynosoma) look similar through convergent evolution but live on another continent.
animal.whereToSee: Red-sand deserts near Uluru and Alice Springs, the Great Victoria Desert, and Western Australia's Wheatbelt and Shark Bay; often seen on sandy roads in the morning
animal.season: Active in spring and autumn; breeds in late winter–spring (August–December)

lore: John Edward Gray named it in 1841 after Moloch, the Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice, a reference to its fearsome look.
funFact: A thorny devil can eat thousands of ants in a single day, licking them up one at a time.

wiki.extract: The thorny devil, also known commonly as the mountain devil, thorny lizard, thorny dragon, and moloch, is a species of lizard in the family Agamidae. The species is endemic to Australia. It is the sole species in the genus Moloch. It grows up to 21 cm (8.3 in) in total length, with females generally larger than males.

plates.title: Jean Baptiste Audebert — Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis (1800)
plates.author: Jean Baptiste Audebert
plates.desc: A detailed natural history engraving of a primate, identified as "Le Moloch" (Simia Moloch). The animal is depicted in profile, standing on its hind legs with a slight crouch, its long arms reaching forward. It has light-colored, dense fur, a dark face with visible teeth in a grimace-like expression, and a ruff of lighter fur around its head.
plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts 'Le Moloch' (Simia Moloch), now known as the silvery gibbon, from Jean Baptiste Audebert's seminal work on monkeys and lemurs. The illustration showcases the meticulous scientific observation and artistic skill characteristic of late Enlightenment natural history publications, aiming to categorize and document the natural world with precision.

summary: A russet, ring-tailed tree-dweller of the eastern Himalaya, the only living member of its family and not a close relative of the giant panda. It was called 'panda' first, decades before the giant panda was known to Western science.
nativeRange: Nepal, Bhutan, northeast India, Myanmar and southwest China
abilities: Has a false thumb (an extended wrist bone) for gripping bamboo, evolved separately from the giant panda's
Climbs down trees head-first by rotating its ankles
Lowers its metabolic rate and curls its thick tail around itself to save energy in the cold
Detects sweetness with taste receptors for artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, unusual among mammals

animal.diet: Mostly bamboo leaves and shoots; also fruit, acorns, eggs and insects
animal.habitat: Temperate forest with bamboo understorey, 2,200–4,800 m
animal.lifespan: 8–10 years wild; up to ~15 in captivity
animal.size: 3–6 kg; body 50–64 cm with a tail of 28–59 cm
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary and active at dawn, dusk and night, it sleeps stretched along branches by day.
fieldMarks: Cat-sized with rusty-red fur
White face markings and tear-like stripes
Long, bushy, ringed tail
Black legs and belly
animal.voice: Twittering whistles and huff-quacks
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable in its range.
animal.whereToSee: Singalila National Park, Darjeeling (India)
animal.season: Resident; easiest about Mar–May and Oct–Dec

lore: Frédéric Cuvier named it Ailurus fulgens, 'shining cat', in 1825. The word 'panda' probably comes from a Nepali name for the animal.
funFact: The Firefox web browser is named after it, from a Chinese name meaning 'fire fox'.

wiki.extract: The red panda, also known as the lesser panda, is a small mammal native to the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China. It has dense reddish-brown fur with a black belly and legs, white-lined ears, a mostly white muzzle and a ringed tail. Its head-to-body length is 51–63.5 cm (20.1–25.0 in) with a 28–48.5 cm (11.0–19.1 in) tail, and it weighs between 3.2 and 15 kg. It is well adapted to climbing due to its flexible joints and curved semi-retractile claws.

summary: A streaky brown bird of open fields that rises almost vertically into the sky, hanging there for minutes on end while pouring out an unbroken torrent of song. It has declined sharply in intensively farmed parts of Europe.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Middle East across Central Asia and Siberia to the Pacific; introduced to New Zealand, Australia and Vancouver Island
abilities: Sings continuously in hovering flight, sometimes for over 10 minutes, at heights that make it hard to see
Nests on the open ground, needing short, sparse vegetation
Song contains hundreds of syllables and varies between local neighbourhoods
Northern populations migrate in large daytime flocks in autumn

animal.diet: Seeds and leaves in winter; insects and spiders in the breeding season
animal.habitat: Arable fields, grassland, steppe, dunes, moorland
animal.behaviour: Climbs on fluttering wings while singing, hangs high in the sky, then parachutes down in steps before dropping silently to the ground.
fieldMarks: Streaked brown upperparts and a streaked breast band
Short crest that can be raised
White outer tail feathers and a narrow white trailing edge to the wing
Stout bill and long hind claw
animal.voice: Song a long, high, rapid and unbroken warbling delivered in flight; call a liquid, rolling 'chirrup'.
animal.lookalikes: Woodlark is shorter-tailed with a bold pale eyebrow meeting on the nape and no white trailing edge, and sings a slow, descending 'lu-lu-lu'. Crested lark has a long spiky crest and no white on the tail sides. Meadow pipit is slimmer with a thinner bill.
animal.whereToSee: Arable land, downs and coastal grassland across Europe; steppes of Kazakhstan; winter fields in North Africa and the Middle East.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east; song Feb–Jul

lore: Shelley's 'To a Skylark' (1820) and George Meredith's poem that inspired Vaughan Williams's 'The Lark Ascending' (1914) made it the voice of the English countryside, and 'Chakavak' is the name of a melodic section (gusheh) in the Homayun mode of Persian classical music.
funFact: Shakespeare's Juliet argues with Romeo over whether they hear the nightingale or the lark, the bird that signals dawn and his departure.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian skylark, commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae. It is a widespread species found across Europe and the Palearctic with introduced populations in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and on the Hawaiian Islands. It is a bird of open farmland and heath, known for the song of the male, which is delivered in hovering flight from heights of 50 to 100 metres. The sexes are alike. It is streaked greyish-brown above and on the breast and has a buff-white belly.

Such plates were central to 18th-century scientific documentation, combining artistic precision with botanical and zoological observation to catalog the flora and fauna of the New World.

Catesby was the first to provide a comprehensive visual record of the flora and fauna of North America, often illustrating birds with the specific plants they frequented.

The plate, engraved by Michael van der Gucht, exemplifies the meticulous scientific documentation of Caribbean fauna during the early 18th century, combining Latin nomenclature with local common names.

summary: A tiny flash of electric blue and orange along quiet rivers. It plunges headfirst for small fish and nests at the end of a tunnel in an earth bank.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, South and East Asia to New Guinea and the Solomon Islands
abilities: Its blue back is structural colour produced by the nanostructure of the feathers, not pigment
Dives with eyes covered by a protective membrane and corrects for refraction when aiming
Its bill entering water with little splash inspired the redesigned nose of the 500 Series Shinkansen
Pairs may raise two or three broods a year to offset heavy winter losses

animal.diet: Small fish such as minnows and sticklebacks; aquatic insects, tadpoles
animal.habitat: Clear, slow rivers, streams, canals and lakes with earth banks; coasts in winter
animal.behaviour: Perches still over water, then plunge-dives and beats the fish against a branch before swallowing it headfirst.
fieldMarks: Brilliant cobalt-to-turquoise upperparts with a pale-blue back stripe
Orange underparts and cheek patch, white throat and neck patch
Long dagger bill; female has an orange base to the lower mandible
Stubby tail and tiny red feet
animal.voice: A shrill, piercing whistle, 'tseee' or 'chee-kee', given in low, fast flight over water.
animal.lookalikes: No other small European bird is this colour. In the Middle East, white-throated kingfisher is much larger with a red bill, and pied kingfisher is black and white and hovers.
animal.whereToSee: Lowland rivers across Europe; the Danube Delta, the Camargue, Turkish and Iraqi marshes; wintering birds on Mediterranean coasts.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Greek myth turned the grieving Alcyone into a kingfisher, and the calm 'halcyon days' around the winter solstice were believed to be granted by the gods so it could nest on the sea.
funFact: Engineer Eiji Nakatsu, a birdwatcher, modelled the 500 Series Shinkansen's nose on the kingfisher's bill to reduce the loud 'tunnel boom' (pressure-wave bang) when trains left tunnels.

wiki.extract: The common kingfisher, also known as the Eurasian kingfisher and river kingfisher, is a small kingfisher with seven subspecies recognized within its wide distribution across Eurasia and North Africa. It is resident in much of its range, but migrates from areas where rivers freeze in winter.

plates.title: Jan Jonston — Naeukeurige beschryving van de natuur der viervoetige dieren (1660)
plates.author: Jan Jonston
plates.desc: A scientific plate (Tab. 31) featuring thirteen hand-colored engravings of various bird species, including water hens, snipes, and a kingfisher.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history compendium illustrates various bird species with remarkable detail. The plate, labeled 'Tab. 31', reflects the early modern scientific endeavor to catalog the natural world, combining meticulous intaglio lines with delicate watercolor washes to distinguish between species like the moorhen and the common snipe.

plates.title: The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands, Vol. 1

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands' depicts a Belted Kingfisher (Ispida) with its prey. Catesby was the first to illustrate North American species in their natural environments, often pairing birds with the specific plants they frequented, such as the Wax Myrtle (Myrtus) shown here.

plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts a Racquet-tailed Kingfisher, a species noted for its extraordinary tail feathers. Alfred Russel Wallace's work was instrumental in documenting the diverse fauna of the Malay Archipelago, and such illustrations provided essential visual records for 19th-century science.

plates.title: Of the Eggs and Nests of Birds

plates.long: This plate from Giuseppe Zinanni's 1737 treatise 'Delle uova e dei nidi degli uccelli' represents one of the earliest systematic attempts to document bird eggs and nests. The engraving illustrates the eggs of the Common Gull, Little Gull, Gambettola, and Kingfisher, utilizing sophisticated shading and stippling to convey volume and surface markings. Zinanni's work is considered a foundational text

This illustration reflects the Renaissance shift towards empirical observation and the systematic categorization of the natural world, serving as a foundational work for modern ornithology.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts a kingfisher (翡翠, fěicuì) perched amongst lotus leaves and flowers. The work exemplifies the Ming dynasty's interest in categorizing and illustrating the natural world, combining artistic elegance with descriptive accuracy.

summary: The world's largest kingfisher, famous for its raucous family chorus of 'laughter' at dawn and dusk. It rarely fishes, instead dropping onto snakes, lizards and insects from a perch.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia; introduced to south-western Western Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand
abilities: Kills snakes and lizards by bashing them against branches or dropping them
Family groups 'laugh' together to proclaim territory
Cooperative breeder: older offspring help raise new chicks

animal.diet: Insects, worms, lizards, snakes, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Dry eucalypt woodland, open forest, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: Groups of related birds call in chorus, one starting with low chuckles before the rest join in a crescendo of laughter.
fieldMarks: Large, stocky kingfisher with a massive bill
Off-white head with a dark brown eye-stripe
Brown wings with a small pale-blue shoulder patch
Rufous tail barred with black
Dark eye
animal.voice: A loud, rollicking 'koo-koo-koo-ka-ka-ka' that rises into raucous laughter, often by several birds at once, especially at dawn and dusk.
animal.lookalikes: Blue-winged kookaburra (northern Australia) has a pale eye, no dark eye-stripe, a blue rump and more extensive blue in the wing, and a harsher, cackling call.
animal.whereToSee: Common in eastern Australian bushland, parks and gardens from Queensland to Victoria; Royal National Park (Sydney), Lamington National Park
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The name comes from the Wiradjuri word guuguubarra, imitating its call. A widely retold Aboriginal story says the kookaburra's laughter is the signal for the sky-people to light the sun each morning.
funFact: Its call has been widely used as a 'jungle' sound effect in films, even those set nowhere near Australia.

wiki.extract: The laughing kookaburra is a bird in the kingfisher subfamily Halcyoninae. It is a large kingfisher with a whitish head and a brown eye-stripe. The upperparts are mostly dark brown but there is a mottled light-blue patch on the wing coverts. The underparts are cream-white and the tail is barred with rufous and black. The plumage of the male and female birds is similar. The territorial call is a distinctive laugh that is often delivered by several birds at the same time, and is widely used as a stock sound effect in situations that involve a jungle setting.

otherNames: Bái xiōng fěicuì 白胸翡翠 (Chinese)
summary: A big-billed kingfisher with a chocolate head, a brilliant turquoise back and a shining white bib, often seen far from water on wires above fields. It eats lizards, crabs, insects and even small snakes as readily as fish.
nativeRange: Turkey, the Levant and Iraq through Iran, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and the Philippines
abilities: Hunts on dry land as well as in water, taking lizards, frogs, mice and large insects
Digs a nest tunnel in earth banks with its bill
Beats large prey against a perch before swallowing

animal.diet: Large insects, lizards, frogs, crabs, fish, small snakes, rodents and occasionally small birds
animal.habitat: Open country, canals, rice fields, gardens, mangroves and forest edge
animal.behaviour: Perches conspicuously on wires and posts, dropping to the ground for prey; displays from treetops with wings spread to show the white patches.
fieldMarks: Large kingfisher with a massive red bill
Chocolate-brown head and belly, sharply defined white throat and breast
Brilliant turquoise-blue back, wings and tail
Large white wing patches visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, shrill, whinnying 'kililili' trill, given from perches and in flight
animal.lookalikes: Stork-billed kingfisher is larger with an ochre head and body; Black-capped kingfisher has a black cap and white collar; Common kingfisher is tiny with orange underparts.
animal.whereToSee: Canals and fields across Punjab and Sindh, Keoladeo, Sri Lankan paddies; Lahore and Delhi gardens
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is the state bird of West Bengal. The species name smyrnensis refers to Smyrna (modern Izmir) in Turkey, from where the first specimen described came.
funFact: Despite being a kingfisher, it often lives far from any water, hunting lizards and insects in dry fields.

wiki.extract: The white-throated kingfisher also known as the white-breasted kingfisher is a tree kingfisher, widely distributed in Asia from the Sinai east through the Indian subcontinent to China and Indonesia. This kingfisher is a resident over much of its range, although some populations may make short distance movements. It can often be found well away from water where it feeds on a wide range of prey that includes small reptiles, amphibians, crabs, small rodents and even birds. During the breeding season they call loudly in the mornings from prominent perches including the tops of buildings in urban areas or on wires.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history compendium illustrates various bird species with remarkable detail. The plate, labeled 'Tab. 31', reflects the early modern scientific endeavor to catalog the natural world, combining meticulous intaglio lines with delicate watercolor washes to distinguish between species like the moorhen and the common snipe.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands' depicts a Belted Kingfisher (Ispida) with its prey. Catesby was the first to illustrate North American species in their natural environments, often pairing birds with the specific plants they frequented, such as the Wax Myrtle (Myrtus) shown here.

plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts a Racquet-tailed Kingfisher, a species noted for its extraordinary tail feathers. Alfred Russel Wallace's work was instrumental in documenting the diverse fauna of the Malay Archipelago, and such illustrations provided essential visual records for 19th-century science.

plates.long: This plate from Giuseppe Zinanni's 1737 treatise 'Delle uova e dei nidi degli uccelli' represents one of the earliest systematic attempts to document bird eggs and nests. The engraving illustrates the eggs of the Common Gull, Little Gull, Gambettola, and Kingfisher, utilizing sophisticated shading and stippling to convey volume and surface markings. Zinanni's work is considered a foundational text

The work exemplifies the Ming dynasty's interest in categorizing and illustrating the natural world, combining artistic elegance with descriptive accuracy.

summary: A small auk with a huge, colourful bill, nesting in burrows on grassy sea cliffs. It 'flies' underwater to catch small fish and brings them back crosswise in its bill.
nativeRange: North Atlantic: breeds from Brittany, Britain and Ireland to Iceland, Norway, the Faroes and Svalbard, and from Maine to Greenland; winters at sea, south to the Canaries and western Mediterranean
abilities: Carries a dozen or more fish at once, held against spines on its tongue and palate
Dives to depths of several tens of metres, propelled by its wings
Digs burrows with bill and feet in cliff-top turf
Its bill sheath fluoresces under ultraviolet light

animal.diet: Sandeels, sprats, capelin and other small fish
animal.habitat: Open sea; breeds on islands and cliffs with soft turf
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite at the same burrow each year and greet each other by tapping bills ('billing').
fieldMarks: Black upperparts and collar, white face and underparts
Large, triangular bill striped red, yellow and blue-grey in summer
Orange legs and feet
Fast, whirring flight low over the sea
animal.voice: A low, growling 'arr-arr' from inside burrows; silent at sea.
animal.lookalikes: Razorbill and guillemots are larger with thinner bills and no coloured beak. Little auk is tiny with a stubby black bill. In winter the puffin's bill and face are duller.
animal.whereToSee: Skomer (Wales), Farne Islands and Isle of May (Britain), Látrabjarg and Westman Islands (Iceland), Runde (Norway), Machias Seal Island (Canada/USA).
animal.season: At colonies late Mar–early Aug; at sea in winter

lore: Lundy Island in the Bristol Channel takes its name from the Norse word 'lundi', puffin, and in medieval England the bird's fishy flesh was sometimes accepted as Lenten food.
funFact: The colourful outer bill plates are shed after the breeding season, leaving a smaller, duller bill in winter.

wiki.extract: The Atlantic puffin, also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family. It is the only puffin native to the Atlantic Ocean; two related species, the tufted puffin and the horned puffin, are found in the northeastern Pacific. The Atlantic puffin breeds in Russia, Iceland, Ireland, Britain, Norway, Greenland, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and the Faroe Islands, and as far south as Maine in the west and France (Brittany). It is most commonly found in the Westman Islands, Iceland. Although it has a large population and a wide range, the species has declined rapidly, at least in parts of its range, resulting in it being rated as vulnerable by the IUCN. On land, it has the typical upright stance of an auk. At sea, it swims on the surface and feeds on zooplankton, small fish, and crabs, which it catches by diving underwater, using its wings for propulsion.

summary: A great conservation success: hunted almost to extinction by the mid-20th century, then protected and recovered. It shapes the wetlands of the southeastern US, digging 'gator holes' that hold water and wildlife through the dry season.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, and up the Mississippi valley into Arkansas and Oklahoma
abilities: Digs 'gator holes' that stay wet in the dry season, keeping alive fish, turtles and birds
Survives freezing weather by keeping only its nostrils above ice ('icing')
Males bellow and send infrasound that makes water 'dance' on their backs
Sex of the young is set by nest temperature

animal.diet: Fish, turtles, snakes, birds, mammals; young eat insects and crayfish
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, rivers, lakes, and some brackish water
animal.behaviour: Females build mound nests of rotting vegetation, guard them and carry hatchlings to water in their mouths. Hatchlings call from inside the eggs when ready to hatch.
fieldMarks: Broad, rounded U-shaped snout
Upper jaw covers the lower teeth when the mouth is closed
Dark grey to black; juveniles with yellow bands
Bony plates on the back
animal.lookalikes: The American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus), found only in southern Florida in the US, has a narrow, tapered V-shaped snout, a paler grey-green colour, and a visible fourth lower tooth when its mouth is closed. Caimans (introduced in Florida) are smaller with a bony ridge between the eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Everglades National Park (Anhinga Trail), Okefenokee Swamp, Louisiana's Atchafalaya Basin, Brazos Bend State Park (Texas)
animal.season: Resident; bellowing and courtship April–May; nesting June–July

lore: The name 'alligator' comes from the Spanish el lagarto, 'the lizard'. Listed as endangered in 1967, it was removed from the US endangered list in 1987.
funFact: The Chinese alligator (Alligator sinensis) is its only living close relative; the two lineages diverged tens of millions of years ago.

wiki.extract: The American alligator, sometimes referred to as a common alligator or just gator, is a large crocodilian reptile native to the Southeastern United States. It is one of the two extant species in the genus Alligator, and is larger than the only other living alligator species, the Chinese alligator.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Tuolong' or Chinese alligator, as identified by the calligraphic characters above the figure. It is a classic example of the illustrations found in the 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica), reflecting the meticulous effort to categorize and visualize the natural world in Ming and Qing dynasty China.

summary: A small shrimp with one huge claw that snaps shut so fast it creates a collapsing bubble hot enough to emit a flash of light. The snap stuns prey and is one of the loudest sounds made by any animal.
nativeRange: Western Atlantic, from lower Chesapeake Bay and North Carolina to the Gulf of Mexico; Caribbean and Brazilian records are uncertain because the species was split into a complex
abilities: Claw snap produces a cavitation bubble that collapses with a sound above 200 dB (re 1 µPa at 1 m)
The collapsing bubble briefly reaches several thousand degrees and emits light ('shrimpoluminescence')
Can regrow a lost snapping claw, often switching which side carries it
Lives in mated pairs in burrows

animal.diet: Small fish, worms and crustaceans stunned by the snap
animal.habitat: Burrows and crevices in oyster reefs, rubble, seagrass and muddy estuaries
animal.behaviour: Rivals threaten each other by opening the snapping claw and firing water jets rather than fighting directly.
fieldMarks: Small, greenish to translucent brown shrimp
One massively enlarged claw, up to half the body length
Eyes hidden under a hood on the carapace
Crackling sound from reefs
animal.voice: A sharp click or pop; massed shrimp make a constant frying or crackling sound underwater.
animal.lookalikes: Other Alpheus and Synalpheus snapping shrimps are separated by claw shape and colour; Synalpheus are usually smaller and live inside sponges.
animal.whereToSee: Oyster reefs and estuaries of the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts; listen with a hydrophone or near docks at low tide.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: During the Second World War, the crackle of snapping shrimp beds interfered with naval sonar, and submarines were able to use the noise as acoustic cover.
funFact: Light flashes from its collapsing bubbles were first recorded in this species in 2001 and nicknamed 'shrimpoluminescence'.

wiki.extract: Alpheus heterochaelis, the bigclaw snapping shrimp, is a snapper or pistol shrimp in the family Alpheidae. It is found in the western Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico.

It presents a systematic visual catalog of twenty-five different crustaceans, ranging from large lobsters to small shrimp, reflecting the early modern effort to categorize and document the natural world through direct observation and woodcut reproduction.

plates.long: This illustration shows the 'Potiquiquiya', a type of spiny lobster or large crustacean found in river mouths. The artist has carefully rendered the segmented body and exceptionally long antennae, typical of the descriptive precision sought in 17th-century natural history prints.

summary: A salamander that never grows up: it keeps its feathery gills and lives its whole life in water. It can regrow lost limbs, parts of its spinal cord, heart and brain, and is a major subject of regeneration research. In the wild it survives only in the canals of Xochimilco in Mexico City.
nativeRange: Lake Xochimilco (and formerly Lake Chalco), Valley of Mexico
abilities: Regrows complete limbs, tail, parts of the heart, spinal cord, eyes and brain without scarring
Keeps juvenile features such as external gills into adulthood and breeds that way (neoteny)
Breathes through gills, skin and simple lungs
Accepts transplanted organs from other axolotls with little rejection

animal.diet: Carnivore: worms, insect larvae, crustaceans, small fish
animal.habitat: Cool, high-altitude lake and canal water with dense vegetation
animal.behaviour: Wild axolotls are dark mottled brown; the pink and white forms common in aquariums come from captive breeding lines.
fieldMarks: Stays aquatic with feathery external gills
Wide head and small eyes
Wild form brown to dark grey with gold speckles
Long tail fin running from the head
animal.lookalikes: Larvae of tiger salamanders and other neotenic mole salamanders look very similar. Mudpuppies (Necturus) are also confused with axolotls.
animal.whereToSee: Wild animals are very rarely seen in the canals of Xochimilco, Mexico City; widely shown in zoos and aquariums
animal.season: Resident

lore: Named for the Aztec god Xolotl, who in legend turned himself into an axolotl to escape being sacrificed. Axolotls were eaten in the Aztec period and the 16th-century Florentine Codex records them as food.
funFact: A 2014 survey found about 36 axolotls per square kilometre in Xochimilco, down from about 6,000 in 1998.

wiki.extract: The axolotl is a species of mole salamander. It is neotenic, reaching sexual maturity without undergoing metamorphosis, and the adults remain fully aquatic with obvious external gills. Axolotls may be difficult to distinguish from the larval stage of other neotenic adult mole salamanders, in particular the tiger salamander, or other species such as mudpuppies.

The artist uses stylized blue waves and detailed spotting to characterize the creature, reflecting the natural history focus of the Florentine Codex and the integration of indigenous and European artistic styles.

summary: A living fossil from the age of dinosaurs and one of only two surviving species in an order otherwise known from Jurassic and Cretaceous fossils. It can gulp air and lie up in swamp mud, and fathers guard their young fiercely.
nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain of the south-eastern United States (since 2022 the northern and inland bowfins are a separate species, A. ocellicauda)
abilities: Breathes air through a lung-like swim bladder, so it survives warm, stagnant swamps
Can survive in burrows in drying mud
Males clear nests, then herd and guard a black ball of fry for weeks
Its order, Amiiformes, dates back to the Jurassic
edibilityNote: Eaten in Louisiana as choupique, often fried, smoked or made into fishcakes; the roe is sold as 'Cajun caviar'. The flesh is soft and is best cooked fresh. Unlike gar, bowfin eggs are not toxic.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crayfish, frogs, insects and other prey
animal.habitat: Swamps, bayous, sloughs and weedy, slow waters
animal.size: Commonly 45–60 cm; up to about 1.1 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts at night among weeds. In spring the male builds a circular nest in vegetation, attracts females, and then guards eggs and the swarm of fry.
fieldMarks: Long, cylindrical body with a very long, wavy dorsal fin running along most of the back
Bony gular plate between the lower jaws
Black eyespot at the upper tail base, ringed in orange in males
Short anal fin; rounded tail; tubular nostrils
Breeding males with bright green fins and belly
animal.lookalikes: Eyetail bowfin (Amia ocellicauda) is almost identical and is separated mainly by range and genetics. Northern snakehead (Channa argus, introduced) has a long anal fin, no gular plate and a scaled head. Burbot has a chin barbel and two dorsal fins.
animal.whereToSee: Okefenokee Swamp (Georgia); Florida's St. Johns River; blackwater rivers of the Carolina and Georgia coastal plain
animal.season: Resident; spawns in spring (March–May in the south)

lore: In Louisiana, bowfins have been sold as choupique (from a Choctaw word) as a cheap food fish for generations. When the Caspian caviar trade collapsed, bowfin roe became a domestic caviar substitute.
funFact: The bowfin's order has fossils on several continents, but today only the two North American bowfin species survive.

wiki.extract: The ruddy bowfin is a ray-finned fish native to North America. Common names include mudfish, mud pike, dogfish, grindle, grinnel, swamp trout, and choupique. It is regarded as a relict, being one of only two surviving species of the Halecomorphi, a group of fish that first appeared during the Early Triassic, around 250 million years ago. The bowfin is often considered a "living fossil" because it has retained some morphological characteristics of its early ancestors. It is one of two species in the genus Amia, along with Amia ocellicauda, the eyespot bowfin. The closest living relatives of bowfins are gars, with the two groups being united in the clade Holostei.

funFact: Its species name testudineus means 'tortoise-like', after its tough, armoured head and scales.

wiki.extract: The climbing perch is a species of amphibious freshwater fish in the family Anabantidae. A labyrinth fish native to Far Eastern Asia, the fish inhabits freshwater systems from India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka in the west, to Southern China in the east, and to Southeast Asia west of the Wallace Line in the south.

summary: A cold-water bottom fish with a craggy face and tusk-like canines that crush crabs, urchins and whelks. Its blood carries antifreeze proteins that let it live in near-freezing water.

Replaces its teeth every year
Fertilisation is internal, and the male guards the egg mass for months

wiki.extract: The Atlantic wolffish, also known as the seawolf, Atlantic catfish, ocean catfish, devil fish, wolf eel, woof or sea cat, is a marine fish of the wolffish family Anarhichadidae, native to the North Atlantic Ocean. The numbers of the Atlantic wolffish in US waters are rapidly being depleted, most likely due to overfishing and bycatch, and it is currently a Species of Concern according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Marine Fisheries Service.

animal.habitat: Wooded ponds, rivers and lakes with overhanging trees

wiki.extract: The mandarin duck is a perching duck species native to East and Northeast Asia. It is sexually dimorphic; the males are elaborately coloured, while the females have more subdued colours. It is a medium-sized duck, at 41–49 cm (16–19 in) long with a 65–75 cm (26–30 in) wingspan. It is closely related to the North American wood duck, the only other member of the genus Aix. 'Aix' is an Ancient Greek word which was used by Aristotle to refer to an unknown diving bird, and 'galericulata' is the Latin for a wig, derived from galerum, a cap or bonnet. Outside of its native range, the mandarin duck has a large introduced population in the British Isles and Western Europe, with additional smaller introductions in North America.

nativeRange: Eastern North America, the Pacific coast from British Columbia to California, and Cuba

Ducklings jump from cavities up to about 15 m high without injury
Claws on its feet let it perch on branches
Females often lay eggs in each other's nests ('egg dumping')

funFact: Linnaeus named it sponsa, Latin for 'betrothed' or 'bride', for the male's 'wedding finery'.

wiki.extract: The Indian spot-billed duck is a species of large dabbling duck that is a non-migratory breeding duck throughout freshwater wetlands in the Indian subcontinent. The name is derived from the red spot at the base of the bill that is found in the mainland Indian population. When in water it can be recognized from a long distance by the white tertials that form a stripe on the side, and in flight it is distinguished by the green speculum with a broad white band at the base. This species and the eastern spot-billed duck were formerly considered conspecific, together called the spot-billed duck.

summary: A sooty-black swan with a scarlet bill and white flight feathers, native to Australia. To Europeans it was proverbial for an impossible thing until Dutch sailors saw it on Western Australia's Swan River in 1697.

abilities: Nomadic: moves long distances, often at night, to reach newly filled wetlands

Moults all its flight feathers at once and is briefly flightless

wiki.extract: The black swan is a large waterbird, a species of swan which breeds mainly in the southeast and southwest regions of Australia. Within Australia, the black swan is nomadic, with erratic migration patterns dependent on climatic conditions. It is a large bird with black plumage and a red bill. It is a monogamous breeder, with both partners sharing incubation and cygnet-rearing duties.

abilities: Among the heaviest flying birds, up to about 15 kg
