wiki.extract: The mute swan is a species of swan and a member of the family Anatidae within the waterfowl order. It is native to much of Europe and parts of Asia and the far north of Africa. It is an introduced species in North America, home to the largest populations outside of its native range, with additional smaller introductions in Australasia and Southern Africa. The name "mute" derives from it being less vocal than other swan species. Typically measuring 140 to 160 cm in length, this large swan is wholly white in plumage, with an orange beak bordered with black. It is recognisable by its pronounced knob atop the beak, which is larger in males.

It features both external morphology—showing adult and young specimens—and internal anatomy, specifically detailing the complex looping of the trachea and a complete articulated skeleton, marking a significant step in early modern biological documentation.

plates.long: This striking illumination from a medieval bestiary depicts a swan (Cygnus) standing over a serpent and a human head, symbolizing the triumph of purity or the soul over earthly sin and mortality. The scene is rendered with vibrant pigments and gold leaf, characteristic of high-quality Gothic manuscript production. The accompanying Latin text moralizes the nature of the swan, drawing parallels betw

plates.title: History of Animals, Book I: On Viviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: A large woodcut of a bird, likely a swan, depicted with its neck curved back and head pointing upwards, clinging to a tree trunk.
plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a large bird, identified in the text as a swan (Cygnus), from Conrad Gessner's landmark work 'Historiae Animalium'. The illustration is notable for its attempt at scientific accuracy in the rendering of plumage and webbed feet, despite the somewhat stylized and unusual vertical posture.

plates.title: Bestiary
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: Illuminated miniature of a swan catching a fish
plates.long: This 13th-century miniature depicts a swan (cygnus), identified by the text as a creature whose white plumage masks its dark skin, serving as a moral allegory for the hypocrite who hides sin behind a virtuous exterior. Set against a shimmering gold leaf background, the illustration showcases the high-status craftsmanship of the Bodley 764 bestiary through its vibrant pigments and intricate geometr

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a swan or large water bird with a curved neck, standing near water with bones on the ground.
plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a swan, characterized by its long, curved neck and webbed feet. The inclusion of bones in the foreground reflects the often symbolic or anecdotal nature of 15th-century scientific illustration.

plates.title: History of the Northern Peoples
plates.author: Olaus Magnus
plates.desc: Woodcut depicting a swan on a lake with a serpent in the water and a man standing on the shore.
plates.long: This 1555 woodcut from Olaus Magnus's 'Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus' depicts a swan swimming in a pond while a hunter on the shore aims a bow and arrow at the bird. The illustration serves to document the cunning methods used by Northern hunters to capture swans, which were valued for their symbolic importance and migratory patterns. Such prints are significant for their blend of Renaiss

plates.title: Theater of Earthly Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: A group of four numbered woodcut illustrations of birds, including a swan, a bird in flight, and two ducks.
plates.long: This plate features four numbered woodcut illustrations of birds, serving as a section title for a study on winged land and water creatures. The central figure is a large swan, accompanied by ducks and a bird in flight, demonstrating the early modern interest in cataloging the natural world.

plates.title: History of the Northern Peoples
plates.author: Olaus Magnus
plates.desc: Woodcut depicting various aquatic birds, including a swan and smaller fowl, in a landscape with water.
plates.long: A detailed woodcut from Olaus Magnus's seminal work on Northern peoples and nature, illustrating various species of aquatic birds. This image reflects the 16th-century interest in cataloging the natural world through both observation and inherited knowledge.

plates.title: Of the Eggs and Nests of Birds
plates.author: Giuseppe Zinanni (Ginanni) (1692-1753)
plates.desc: An ornate rococo title plate for the third section of the book, featuring a large unfurled scroll with text, a scallop shell crest, and a swan at the base.
plates.long: This elaborate engraved title plate introduces the third section of Giuseppe Zinanni’s 1737 treatise on bird eggs and nests, specifically focusing on aquatic birds ('Uccelli Aquatici'). The composition features a swan, a quintessential water bird, resting at the base of a dynamic rococo frame topped with a scallop shell. The fine crosshatching and fluid lines are characteristic of mid-18th-century

summary: A snake-like fish that lives for decades in European rivers and lakes, then swims some 5,000 km to spawn in the Sargasso Sea and die. No one has yet seen European eels spawn in the wild.
nativeRange: Rivers, lakes and coasts of Europe and North Africa, from Iceland and Norway to the Mediterranean and Morocco; spawns in the Sargasso Sea
abilities: Migrates about 5,000–6,000 km across the Atlantic to spawn
Changes form several times: leaf-like larva, transparent glass eel, elver, yellow eel and silver eel
Breathes partly through its skin and can wriggle across wet grass between waters
Adjusts its eyes and body chemistry for the deep ocean before its final migration

animal.diet: Carnivore and scavenger: insect larvae, worms, crustaceans, fish, carrion
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, ponds, estuaries and coastal lagoons
animal.lifespan: Usually 5–20 years in fresh water; can exceed 80 in captivity
animal.size: Females up to ~1.3 m; males usually under 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Larvae drift on the Gulf Stream for about one to three years before arriving at European coasts as see-through glass eels.
fieldMarks: Long, snake-like body
Dorsal fin starts well behind the pectoral fins
Lower jaw slightly longer than the upper
Yellow-brown, turning silver before migration
animal.lookalikes: Conger eel is marine, with the dorsal fin starting just behind the pectoral fins and an upper jaw that projects. Lampreys have no jaws.
animal.whereToSee: Elver runs on the River Severn (England)
animal.season: Glass eels arrive Feb–May; silver eels leave in autumn on dark nights

lore: Aristotle concluded that eels arose spontaneously from mud, and a young Sigmund Freud dissected hundreds in Trieste in 1876 hunting for their testes. The Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt traced ever-smaller larvae to the Sargasso Sea between 1904 and 1922.
funFact: Glass eels arriving in Europe have fallen by over 90% since the 1980s, and illegal trafficking of them to Asia has been called one of the largest wildlife crimes in Europe.

wiki.extract: The European eel is a species of eel. Their life history was a mystery for thousands of years, and mating in the wild has not yet been observed. The five stages of their development were originally thought to be different species. They are critically endangered due to hydroelectric dams, overfishing by fisheries on coasts for human consumption, and parasites.

plates.title: De Piscibus Libri V et De Cetis Liber Unus
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Large woodcut illustration of an eel (Anguilla) curved in a U-shape.
plates.long: This large woodcut depicts an eel (Anguilla), shown in a characteristic curved pose to fit the page layout. It is part of Ulisse Aldrovandi's monumental work on fish, showcasing the 17th-century commitment to detailed empirical observation and the use of woodcut prints to disseminate scientific knowledge.

plates.title: The Secrets of Albertus Magnus on the Nature of Women and the Virtues of Herbs
plates.author: Albertus, Magnus, Heiliger
plates.desc: Small woodcut of an eel (Anguilla) with a coiled body.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts an eel, accompanying a text by Albertus Magnus on the properties and medicinal uses of various animals. Such illustrations were essential in early modern scientific and medical texts to help readers identify the species being discussed.

summary: A giant cricket-like insect from New Zealand and one of the heaviest insects in the world; a pregnant female has been weighed at 71 g. Wiped out on the mainland by introduced rats, it survived on Hauturu-o-Toi (Little Barrier Island).
nativeRange: Formerly Northland and Auckland region, New Zealand; natural population now only on Hauturu-o-Toi / Little Barrier Island, with translocated populations on other predator-free islands
abilities: One of the heaviest insects ever weighed, up to about 70 g
Wingless and slow, it evolved in the absence of land mammals
Kicks spiny hind legs upward in defence

animal.diet: Leaves of native trees and shrubs; also fruit and flowers
animal.habitat: Forest canopy and scrub; hides by day in tree holes and among foliage
animal.size: Body up to about 10 cm; weight to about 70 g in gravid females
animal.behaviour: It is nocturnal and arboreal, climbing down to the ground mainly to lay eggs in soil.
fieldMarks: Very large, heavy, wingless body, brown with darker bands
Long, thick hind legs covered in spines
Long antennae, longer than the body
Females with a long, curved ovipositor
animal.lookalikes: Tree wētā (Hemideina) are much smaller, and males have very large heads and jaws. Other giant wētā (Deinacrida spp.) occupy different regions of New Zealand.
animal.whereToSee: Hauturu-o-Toi has restricted access; captive-bred wētāpunga are bred at Auckland Zoo and released to islands such as Motuora and Tiritiri Matangi.
animal.season: Year-round; nocturnal

lore: In Māori tradition wētāpunga are named for Punga, ancestor of ugly and deformed creatures. The species' decline began after kiore (Pacific rats) and later European rats reached New Zealand.
funFact: The 71 g record female, weighed in 2011, was photographed eating a carrot from the hand of the naturalist who found her.

wiki.extract: Deinacrida heteracantha, also known as the Little Barrier giant wētā or wētāpunga, is a wētā in the order Orthoptera and family Anostostomatidae. It is endemic to New Zealand, where it survived only on Hauturu. This very large flightless wētā mainly feeds at night, when it can be found above ground in vegetation. It has been classified as vulnerable by the IUCN due to ongoing population declines and restricted distribution. Its NZTCS threat classification was changed to "Threatened - Nationally increasing" in 2022 because it has been successfully translocated to seven predator-free islands.

summary: A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands, run by a single egg-laying queen and sterile worker daughters. Its foragers tell nestmates where food lies through a coded dance, and its stored nectar became honey, one of humanity's oldest sweeteners.
nativeRange: Africa, Europe and Western Asia; introduced worldwide by beekeepers
abilities: Waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of food relative to the sun
Workers fan wings and evaporate water to turn nectar into honey of about 18% moisture
Colonies hold brood near 35 °C by shivering flight muscles in winter and evaporative cooling in summer
Swarms choose a new home through a quorum-based scout 'debate'
Can perceive polarised and ultraviolet light to navigate under cloud
Produces honey, beeswax, propolis and royal jelly

uses.use: Medical-grade honey (e.g. Leptospermum/manuka honey dressings) used on burns and wounds
Honey listed as a wound salve in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri
Honey described as 'healing for people' in the Qur'an (Surah An-Nahl 16:69)
Propolis as an antiseptic resin; bee venom therapy for joint pain

medicinal.cautions: Never give honey to infants under 12 months (infant botulism). Stings and bee products can cause severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis; bee venom therapy has caused deaths.

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen; larvae fed brood food and royal jelly
animal.habitat: Tree cavities, rock crevices and managed hives near flowering vegetation
animal.lifespan: Workers 5–7 weeks in summer, up to 5 months in winter; queens 2–5 years
animal.behaviour: A forager returning from a rich patch performs a figure-eight dance on the vertical comb; the angle of its waggle run from vertical equals the angle of the food from the sun.
fieldMarks: Slim, hairy worker about 12–15 mm, amber-brown to dark with paler abdominal bands
Two pairs of wings; hind legs carry flattened pollen baskets, often loaded with coloured pollen
Elbowed antennae; flies straight between flowers and hive
Workers from one colony visit one flower type per trip
animal.voice: A steady hum from the wingbeats; a disturbed colony rises to a higher, sharper buzz
animal.lookalikes: Hoverflies mimic bees but have only one pair of wings, very short antennae, large eyes and hover in place. Wasps (Vespula) are glossy, nearly hairless and bright yellow-and-black. Bumblebees are larger, rounder and much furrier.
animal.whereToSee: Flowering orchards, gardens and meadows almost anywhere people keep bees; colonies also nest wild in tree hollows
animal.season: Temperate regions: foraging from early spring to autumn on warm days, clustered in the hive over winter; active all year in the tropics

lore: Honey hunting is painted on Mesolithic rock at the Cuevas de la Araña in Spain (~8,000 years ago), and Egyptian pharaohs used the bee as the hieroglyph for Lower Egypt. Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for decoding its dance.
funFact: To make one kilogram of honey, foragers collectively fly roughly the distance of several trips around the Earth and visit millions of flowers.

wiki.extract: The western honey bee is the most common of the 7–12 species of honey bees worldwide. The genus name Apis is Latin for 'bee', and mellifera is the Latin for 'honey-bearing' or 'honey-carrying', referring to the species' production of honey.

summary: A large, furry social bee that can fly in cold weather and is reared commercially to pollinate greenhouse tomatoes. It buzzes flowers at a precise frequency to shake out pollen honey bees cannot reach.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western Asia; introduced to Chile, Argentina, Tasmania, New Zealand and Japan
abilities: Sonication ('buzz pollination'): vibrates flight muscles to shake pollen from tomato and blueberry flowers
Warms its thorax above 30 °C by shivering, allowing flight near freezing
Detects the weak electric field of flowers to tell recently visited blooms
Learned to pull strings and roll balls for rewards in laboratory experiments
Leaves scent marks so nestmates skip emptied flowers

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen from a wide range of flowers
animal.habitat: Grassland, heath, gardens and farmland; nests underground in old rodent burrows
animal.lifespan: Workers a few weeks; queens about a year, including hibernation
animal.behaviour: Queens emerge from hibernation in early spring and found a colony alone, incubating their first brood on a wax pot like a bird on eggs.
fieldMarks: Large, furry bumblebee, black with two dark-yellow bands (one on the collar, one on the abdomen)
Queens have a buff to off-white tail
Workers have a white tail, often with a faint buff line where it meets the black
Collar band is darker, more orange-tinged yellow than in similar species
animal.voice: A deep, loud buzz; buzz-pollinates some flowers (e.g. tomatoes) with a higher-pitched vibration
animal.lookalikes: White-tailed bumblebee (Bombus lucorum) has a cleaner, lemon-yellow collar and bright white tail; workers of the two are hard to separate reliably in the field. Garden bumblebee (B. hortorum) has an extra yellow band at the rear of the thorax and a very long face.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and farmland across Europe; common on lavender, comfrey and winter-flowering shrubs
animal.season: Queens emerge Feb–Mar; colonies peak in summer; in southern Britain some colonies stay active through winter on garden flowers

lore: Since the late 1980s Belgian and Dutch breeders have shipped colonies worldwide for greenhouse pollination, replacing hand-vibration of tomato flowers. Its introductions to South America have harmed the native giant bumblebee Bombus dahlbomii.
funFact: The old myth that 'science says bumblebees can't fly' came from applying fixed-wing aerodynamics; their flapping wings generate lift from unsteady vortices.

wiki.extract: Bombus terrestris, the buff-tailed bumblebee or large earth bumblebee, is one of the most numerous bumblebee species in Europe. It is one of the main species used in greenhouse pollination, and so can be found in many countries and areas where it is not native, such as Tasmania. Moreover, it is a eusocial insect with an overlap of generations, a division of labour, and cooperative brood care. The queen is monogamous, which means she mates with only one male. B. terrestris workers learn flower colours and forage efficiently.

summary: Europe's largest bee, glossy black with violet-tinted wings. Females carve nest tunnels into dead wood with their jaws.
nativeRange: Southern and Central Europe, North Africa, West and Central Asia
abilities: Excavates nest tunnels in dead wood using strong mandibles
Buzz-pollinates some flowers
Robs nectar by slitting holes at the base of long flowers
Adults overwinter and can live about a year

animal.diet: Nectar and pollen from many plants, e.g. wisteria, lavender and legumes
animal.habitat: Warm, open areas with dead wood
animal.behaviour: A solitary female builds a row of cells in her tunnel, each sealed with chewed wood pulp and stocked with pollen.
fieldMarks: Large, stout bee, 2–3 cm, glossy black with a blue-violet sheen
Dark wings with a strong violet iridescence
Loud, heavy flight between flowers
Bores round holes in dead wood
animal.voice: A deep, loud drone
animal.lookalikes: Other European carpenter bees (X. valga, X. iris) look similar and need close study to separate. Bumblebees are furrier with coloured bands.
animal.whereToSee: Warm gardens, vineyards and old wooden structures in southern and central Europe
animal.season: Adults overwinter and emerge in spring (usually Apr–May); new adults appear in late summer

lore: In recent decades it has spread north into Britain and the Netherlands with warming climate.
funFact: Despite its size and loud buzz, it is docile, and males have no sting.

wiki.extract: Xylocopa violacea, the violet carpenter bee, is the common European species of carpenter bee, and one of the largest bees in Europe. It is also native to Asia.

summary: A sooty, sickle-winged bird that lives almost entirely in the air, feeding, drinking, mating and sleeping on the wing. Screaming parties race around old buildings on summer evenings before the birds return to Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia to China; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Tracked birds remained airborne for up to 10 months without landing, outside the breeding season
Sleeps in brief glides at altitude during the night
Chicks can survive several days without food in cold weather by entering torpor
Feeds on aerial plankton, gathering balls of hundreds of insects to bring to chicks

animal.diet: Flying insects and airborne spiders
animal.habitat: Open skies; nests in holes under roofs, in walls and in towers, and in old tree holes in northern forests
animal.lifespan: Often 5–10 years; ringed birds have reached about 18
animal.behaviour: Gangs of screaming swifts chase low around rooftops in the evening, then climb high into the sky to roost on the wing.
fieldMarks: Sooty brown-black all over with a small pale throat
Long, narrow, scythe-shaped wings
Short forked tail
Never perches on wires or the ground
animal.voice: A shrill, drawn-out scream, 'sreeeee', usually from groups in fast flight.
animal.lookalikes: Barn swallows and house martins have white or rufous underparts and broader wings, and perch on wires. Pallid swift (Mediterranean) is paler brown with a larger pale throat and blunter wingtips. Alpine swift is larger with a white belly.
animal.whereToSee: Over old towns and cities across Europe and western Asia from May to July; Oxford University Museum tower hosts a colony studied since 1948.
animal.season: Summer visitor late Apr–Aug; among the last to arrive and first to leave

lore: Ted Hughes wrote in 'Swifts' that 'they've made it again, which means the globe's still working', and David Lack's 'Swifts in a Tower' (1956) described the Oxford Museum colony.
funFact: Tagged by Swedish researchers in 2013–2014, some swifts stayed aloft for their entire ten-month non-breeding period.

wiki.extract: The common swift is a medium-sized bird, superficially similar to the barn swallow or house martin but somewhat larger, though not stemming from those passerine species, being in the order Apodiformes. The resemblances between the groups are due to convergent evolution, reflecting similar contextual development. The swifts' nearest relatives are the New World hummingbirds and the Southeast Asian treeswifts.

plates.title: History of Serpents and Dragons
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: A woodcut illustration of a winged dragon or serpent, identified in the text as 'Draco alatus Apus ex Greuino'.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Draco alatus' (winged dragon), showcasing the blend of empirical observation and folklore typical of 17th-century natural history. Published in Ulisse Aldrovandi's 'Serpentum et draconum historiae', the image reflects the era's attempt to systematically categorize all known and rumored creatures of the natural world.

summary: A flightless, nocturnal bird of New Zealand that hunts with nostrils at the tip of its long bill. Females lay an egg about a fifth of their own body weight, one of the largest relative to body size of any bird.
nativeRange: North Island of New Zealand
abilities: Only bird with nostrils at the tip of its bill, smelling prey underground
Bill-tip sensory pits detect vibrations of invertebrates
Egg weighs about 15–20% of the mother's weight
Has a body temperature lower than most birds, around 38 °C
Hair-like feathers and tiny vestigial wings

animal.diet: Earthworms, beetle larvae, cicadas, spiders and fallen fruit
animal.habitat: Native and exotic forest, scrub and farmland edges
animal.behaviour: Pairs defend territories with shrill calls at night, and the male incubates the egg for about three months.
fieldMarks: Pear-shaped, flightless bird with no visible wings or tail
Shaggy, streaky reddish-brown feathers
Long, pale, slightly curved bill with nostrils at the tip
Nocturnal, probing the ground
animal.voice: Male gives a shrill, rising whistle repeated many times; female a lower, hoarse cry
animal.lookalikes: It is the only wild kiwi over most of the North Island; little spotted kiwi (on a few island and fenced sanctuaries) is smaller and pale grey with fine mottling.
animal.whereToSee: Trounson Kauri Park night walks (Northland); nocturnal kiwi houses such as Otorohanga Kiwi House
animal.season: Resident

lore: Kiwi are a taonga (treasure) to Māori, and cloaks of kiwi feathers (kahu kiwi) were worn by high-ranking people. The bird gave New Zealanders their nickname.
funFact: Without predator control, around 95% of kiwi chicks die before breeding age, mostly to stoats and cats.

wiki.extract: The North Island brown kiwi is a nocturnal flightless bird and species of kiwi that is widespread in the northern two-thirds of the North Island of New Zealand and, with about 35,000 remaining, it is the most common kiwi species. The eggs laid by the North Island brown kiwi are among the largest eggs relative to its body size.

summary: A large orb-weaving spider striped like a wasp in yellow, black and white, that decorates its web with a bold zig-zag band of silk. It has spread rapidly northward across Europe in recent decades.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia to Japan; expanding northward
abilities: Builds a zig-zag silk band (stabilimentum) whose function is debated, possibly deterring birds or attracting prey
Spiderlings disperse by 'ballooning' on silk threads carried by the wind
Males often mate with females just after their final moult, when females are least dangerous

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, crickets, flies, bees and other flying or jumping insects
animal.habitat: Tall grass in sunny meadows, heath, dunes and verges
animal.size: Females about 1.4–1.7 cm body length (up to about 2.5 cm); males about 0.5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males are frequently cannibalised by females during mating, and often leave part of their palp in the female as a mating plug.
fieldMarks: Female abdomen striped yellow, black and white like a wasp
Silvery-haired cephalothorax
Banded legs held in an X shape at the hub of the web
Orb web low in grass with a vertical zig-zag silk band
animal.lookalikes: Lobed argiope (Argiope lobata) of southern Europe has a silvery, scalloped abdomen. The North American banded garden spider (A. trifasciata) has thinner stripes. Garden spiders (Araneus) lack the bold stripes.
animal.whereToSee: Rough grassland and coastal meadows across Europe; now common in southern England.
animal.season: Adults Jul–Oct

lore: Giovanni Scopoli named it in 1772 after the Danish zoologist Morten Thrane Brünnich. Its arrival in Britain was first noted in the early 20th century, and its range expansion is now followed as a sign of climate change.
funFact: Its egg sac is a brown, paper-like urn hung among grass stems, in which the young overwinter before emerging in spring.

wiki.extract: Argiope bruennichi, commonly known as the wasp spider, is a species of orb-weaver spider found across Central and Northern Europe, several regions of Asia and Africa and the Azores. Like many other members of the same genus Argiope, this species has distinctive yellow, white and black markings on its abdomen.

summary: One of the largest scaled freshwater fish in the world, a red-tailed giant of Amazonian floodplain lakes that must rise to gulp air every few minutes. Overfishing almost wiped it out, and community-managed lakes have brought it back.
nativeRange: Amazon basin floodplains of Brazil, Peru, Colombia and Ecuador, and the Essequibo (Guyana); introduced to Bolivia and parts of Asia
abilities: Obligate air-breather: it gulps air into a lung-like swim bladder and drowns if kept from the surface
Has layered, mineralised scales that resist piranha bites, a structure studied by materials scientists
The male guards the young, which school around his head, and is thought to release substances from his head that nourish or signal to them
Grows to about 3 m and over 200 kg
edibilityNote: Firm, boneless white flesh, traditionally salted and dried as 'bacalhau da Amazônia'. Buy only legal, managed or farmed fish, since wild catches are restricted. Always cooked.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish (especially catfish and characins), crustaceans, and occasionally birds and small animals at the surface
animal.habitat: Calm floodplain lakes, oxbows and flooded forest of whitewater and clearwater rivers
animal.size: Commonly 2 m and 100 kg; up to about 3 m and 200 kg
animal.behaviour: Surfaces every 5–15 minutes with a loud gulp, which fishermen use to count fish. Pairs dig nests in sandy lake beds at low water, and the male guards the fry for months.
fieldMarks: Huge, elongate cylindrical body with a flattened, bony head
Very large scales; rear body and tail flushed bright red, especially in breeding season
Dorsal and anal fins set far back near the rounded tail
Upturned mouth
animal.lookalikes: Silver arowana (Osteoglossum) is much smaller and flattened, with chin barbels and long dorsal and anal fins. Several other Arapaima species have been described (A. leptosoma, A. mapae and others); most wild fish of the central Amazon are A. gigas.
animal.whereToSee: Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve (Amazonas, Brazil); Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve (Peru); Rupununi wetlands (Guyana)
animal.season: Resident; nests during low and rising water, roughly September–February in the central Amazon

lore: In Mamirauá, Brazil, from 1999 local fishers began counting pirarucu by their breaths at the surface and setting their own quotas. Fish numbers in managed lakes rose several-fold, and the method has spread across the Amazon.
funFact: The arapaima's tongue is bony and toothed. Amazonian people traditionally dried it to use as a rasp for grating guaraná seeds.

summary: A deep-sea squid that can reach about 12–13 m including its long feeding tentacles, almost certainly the source of the kraken legend. It was not photographed alive in its own habitat until 2004.
nativeRange: Deep waters of all oceans; most records from Newfoundland, Norway, New Zealand, South Africa, Japan and the Bay of Biscay
abilities: Has eyes up to ~27 cm across, the largest in the animal kingdom alongside the colossal squid's
Grips prey with hundreds of suckers lined with toothed rings
Stays buoyant using ammonium-rich tissues lighter than seawater
Survives as a staple prey of sperm whales, which bear sucker scars from fighting them

animal.diet: Carnivore: deep-sea fish and other squid
animal.habitat: Mid-depths, roughly 300–1,000 m
animal.size: Females up to ~12–13 m total length, ~275 kg; males smaller
animal.behaviour: Its vast eyes are thought to help it spot the glow that sperm whales stir up in bioluminescent plankton from over 100 m away.
fieldMarks: Huge squid with eight arms and two very long feeding tentacles
Eyes as large as dinner plates
Small fins
Red-brown skin
animal.lookalikes: Colossal squid (Antarctic) is heavier with hooks on its suckers.

lore: Bishop Erik Pontoppidan's Natural History of Norway (1752–53) described the kraken, a sea monster big enough to be mistaken for an island. Japetus Steenstrup named the genus in 1857 from a beak washed ashore in Denmark, and Jules Verne used it in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas.
funFact: Its doughnut-shaped brain surrounds the oesophagus, so swallowing large food could damage it; it cuts food into small pieces with its beak.

wiki.extract: The giant squid is a species of deep-ocean dwelling squid in the family Architeuthidae. It can grow to a tremendous size, offering an example of abyssal gigantism; recent estimates put the maximum body size at around 5 m (16 ft) for females, with males slightly shorter, from the posterior fins to the tip of its long arms. This makes it longer than the colossal squid at an estimated 4.2 m (14 ft), but substantially lighter, as it is less robust and its arms make up much of the length. The mantle of the giant squid is about 2 m long, and the feeding tentacles of the giant squid, concealed in life, are 10 m (33 ft). Claims of specimens measuring 20 m (66 ft) or more have not been scientifically documented.

summary: A tall, grey, dagger-billed hunter that stands motionless at the water's edge for long periods before striking. It nests in noisy treetop colonies called heronries, some occupied for centuries.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central, South and East Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar
abilities: Specialised neck vertebrae let it shoot its bill forward in a lightning strike
Swallows prey as large as eels, rats and ducklings whole
Hunts by day and night, standing still for long periods
Grows powder-down feathers that crumble into a dust used to clean slime from its plumage

animal.diet: Fish, eels, frogs, small mammals, ducklings, large insects
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, marshes, estuaries, ditches and garden ponds
animal.lifespan: Typically about 5 years; ringed birds have exceeded 20
animal.behaviour: Begins nesting in late winter, when heronries fill with bill-clattering and harsh croaks long before the leaves appear.
fieldMarks: Grey back, whitish neck and underparts with black streaks down the front
White head with a black stripe ending in a wispy plume
Dagger-like yellow bill; bright orange in breeding adults
Flies with neck pulled in, on slow, bowed wings with black flight feathers
animal.voice: A loud, harsh 'fraank' in flight; heronries are full of clattering, croaking and bill-snapping.
animal.lookalikes: Purple heron is darker and rufous with a thin snake-like neck. Common crane flies with neck outstretched. White stork is white with a red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any European wetland; large heronries in the Netherlands, the Danube Delta and English parks such as Regent's Park, London.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; northern and eastern birds winter south to Africa

lore: The Egyptian Bennu bird, linked to the sun god and later to the Greek phoenix, is usually depicted as a grey heron, and herons were prized quarry of medieval falconers and served roast at royal feasts.
funFact: Hamlet's line 'I know a hawk from a handsaw' is often read as a corruption of 'hernshaw', an old word for heron.

wiki.extract: The grey heron is a long-legged wading bird of the heron family, Ardeidae, native throughout Europe, Asia, and most of Africa. It is resident in much of its range, but some populations from the more northern parts migrate southwards in autumn. A bird of wetland areas, it can be seen around lakes, rivers, ponds, marshes and on the sea coast. It feeds mostly on aquatic creatures which it catches after standing stationary beside or in the water, or stalking its prey through the shallows.

summary: The largest heron in North America, a patient, statuesque hunter of marshes, lakes and coasts. It strikes fish with a lightning thrust of its dagger bill and swallows them whole.
nativeRange: Alaska and southern Canada through the US and Mexico to Central America, the West Indies and northern South America; also the Galápagos

Hunts by day and night, aided by many rod cells in its eyes
Nests colonially in heronries that can hold hundreds of nests high in trees
Swallows prey up to large fish, rodents and even small birds

animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south in winter

wiki.extract: The great blue heron is a large wading bird in the heron family (Ardeidae), common near shores of open water and wetlands over most of North and Central America, as well as Northwestern South America, the Caribbean, and the Galápagos Islands. It is occasionally found in the Azores and is a rare vagrant to Europe. An all-white population found in South Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean islands, is known as the great white heron. Debate exists about whether these white birds are a color morph of the great blue heron, a subspecies of it, or an entirely separate species.

summary: A secretive, streaky-brown heron of dense reedbeds, almost invisible when it freezes with its bill pointed skyward. In spring the male's booming call carries across the marshes like a distant foghorn.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia to Japan; southern African population; northern birds winter south to Africa and South Asia
abilities: Booming call can be heard up to several kilometres away
Freezes with neck stretched and bill up, swaying with the reeds as camouflage
Its eyes are positioned to see forward even when the bill points straight up
Booming is produced by inflating the oesophagus

funFact: Britain's booming males fell to just 11 in 1997; reedbed restoration raised them to more than 200 by the early 2020s and 283 in 2024.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian bittern or great bittern is a wading bird in the bittern subfamily (Botaurinae) of the heron family Ardeidae. There are two subspecies, the northern race breeding in parts of Europe and across the Palearctic, as well as on the northern coast of Africa, while the southern race is endemic to parts of southern Africa. It is a secretive bird, seldom seen in the open as it prefers to skulk in reed beds and thick vegetation near water bodies. Its presence is apparent in the spring, when the booming call of the male during the breeding season can be heard. It feeds on fish, small mammals, fledgling birds, amphibians, crustaceans and insects.

The bird is shown in a characteristic pose on a branch of an ash tree, demonstrating Catesby's innovative approach of illustrating species within their ecological context.

summary: The only spider that lives almost entirely underwater. It spins a silk 'diving bell' among water plants, fills it with air carried down from the surface, and eats, moults, mates and raises young inside.
nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia, east to Japan
abilities: Carries air down on its hairy abdomen, which looks silver underwater
Its bell works as a physical gill: oxygen diffuses in from the water, so it needs to refill only rarely
Males are larger than females, unusual among spiders
Overwinters in a sealed bell or empty snail shell

animal.diet: Aquatic insects, water lice and other small aquatic animals
animal.habitat: Clean, still or slow water with dense submerged plants
animal.behaviour: It waits in its bell with legs touching silk lines, then darts out to seize passing prey and drags it inside to eat.
fieldMarks: Spider moving underwater with a shining silver air bubble around its abdomen
Dull dark-brown, velvety body
Thimble-sized silvery bell of silk among water plants
Long, fine hairs on legs and abdomen
animal.lookalikes: Raft spiders (Dolomedes) are larger, striped, and hunt on the water surface rather than living below it. Pirate wolf spiders (Pirata) dive briefly but live on land.
animal.whereToSee: Clean, plant-rich ponds and fen ditches in Europe, e.g. the Norfolk Broads and Somerset Levels in England.
animal.season: Year-round; most active spring to autumn

lore: Carl Clerck described it in Svenska Spindlar (1757), the work that is the official starting point for scientific names of spiders.
funFact: Measurements in 2011 showed a diving bell spider can stay in its bell for more than a day without surfacing, because oxygen seeps into the bubble from the surrounding water.

wiki.extract: The diving bell spider or water spider is the only species of spider known to live almost entirely under water. It is the only member of the genus Argyroneta and the type genus of the family Argyronetidae. When out of the water, the spider ranges in colour from mid to dark brown, although the hairs on the abdomen give it a dark grey, velvet-like appearance. It is native to freshwater habitats in Europe and Asia.

plates.desc: A comprehensive scientific plate of various insects, primarily caterpillars in different stages, moths, and a large spider, featuring hand-applied color.
plates.long: This plate from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history compendium illustrates a wide variety of 'tree worms' (caterpillars) and other insects. The meticulous engraving and vibrant hand-coloring reflect the early modern period's intense focus on documenting and classifying the diversity of the natural world with scientific precision.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a crab, identified by the heading 'MAIA', which likely refers to a species of spider crab. Appearing in a 16th-century commentary on Dioscorides, this illustration reflects the era's growing interest in the systematic study and visual documentation of the natural world. The artist has carefully rendered the textured, spiny surface of the carapace and the segmented str

plates.desc: A detailed woodcut of a crab, identified in the text as a Maia (spider crab), showing its spiny carapace and long, jointed legs.
plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a crab, specifically identified in the text as a 'Maia' or spider crab. It is part of Conrad Gessner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium', which aimed to catalog all known animals with both textual descriptions and accurate visual representations, marking a significant step in the development of modern zoology.

plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr
plates.desc: A collection of hand-colored engravings of various seashells, featuring a large central spider conch surrounded by scallops and other gastropods.
plates.long: This plate from Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' (1771) presents a meticulously detailed array of seashells. The central focus is a large spider conch, surrounded by various species of scallops and spiral shells, illustrating the era's dedication to cataloging the diversity of the natural world through fine art and scientific observation.

plates.desc: Woodcut of a spider crab (De Aranea)
plates.long: This 1554 woodcut from Guillaume Rondelet’s 'Libri de Piscibus Marinis' depicts a spider, identified in the text as 'De Aranea'. The illustration reflects the Renaissance transition toward empirical observation in natural history, as scholars began to supplement classical texts with detailed visual records of the natural world.

plates.title: Commentaries on the Six Books of Dioscorides
plates.author: Pietro Andrea Mattioli
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of spiders and a spider web
plates.long: This woodcut from Pietro Andrea Mattioli's 1560 commentary on Dioscorides depicts various species of spiders and the intricate geometry of a spider web. Such illustrations were crucial for early modern naturalists in identifying and categorizing the fauna described in classical texts.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a spider crab, identified in the text as 'Maia' or 'Grancevola'. This illustration from Mattioli's commentary on Dioscorides reflects the 16th-century transition toward empirical observation and accurate representation in natural history.

plates.title: Commentaries on the Six Books of Dioscorides on Medical Matter

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a spider crab, identified by the Italian name 'Grancevola'. It serves as a scientific illustration within a Renaissance commentary on Dioscorides' 'De Materia Medica', showcasing the era's commitment to documenting the natural world with increasing accuracy.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Detailed woodcut of a crab, likely a spider crab, showing its spiny carapace and long legs.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates a crab, identified in the accompanying Latin text as a female 'Maia' from Venice. Featured in Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium', such illustrations were revolutionary for their time, providing a visual record to accompany encyclopedic descriptions of the natural world.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica
plates.author: 李時珍

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1596 edition of Li Shizhen's Bencao Gangmu depicts a spider (zhizhu) at the center of its intricate web. Such illustrations were crucial for identifying natural substances used in traditional Chinese medicine, reflecting the era's commitment to empirical observation and systematic classification.

summary: The second-largest slug in the world, a bright yellow giant of the Pacific Northwest rainforest floor. It recycles leaf litter, dung and fungi into soil and spreads seeds and spores as it goes.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from south-eastern Alaska to California
abilities: Grows to about 25 cm long
Thick slime protects from drying out and deters predators
Smells with tentacles and can follow slime trails to find mates
Hermaphrodite; both partners exchange sperm

animal.diet: Leaf litter, fungi, moss, dead plants and animal droppings
animal.habitat: Moist forest floor of conifer and redwood forests
animal.behaviour: It feeds and moves mostly in cool, wet weather, retreating under logs in dry spells, and acts as a decomposer.
fieldMarks: Very large, smooth slug
Yellow to greenish with black spots, or olive to brown
Saddle-like mantle near the head with a breathing hole on the right side
Two pairs of tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Leopard slug (Limax maximus), an introduced European species, is grey with black spots or stripes and a ridge along the tail. Other Ariolimax species occupy different parts of California.
animal.whereToSee: Damp trails in Olympic National Park, coastal British Columbia and the redwood parks of northern California.
animal.season: Year-round in wet weather; most active in the rainy months

lore: Banana slugs are emblems of the Pacific Northwest forests; a related species, Ariolimax dolichophallus, is the mascot of the University of California, Santa Cruz.
funFact: Its eyes sit at the tips of the upper tentacles, which it pulls back into its head when touched.

wiki.extract: Ariolimax columbianus, the Pacific banana slug, is a species of slug found on the Pacific coast of North America. It is the second-largest species of terrestrial slug in the world, growing up to 25 centimeters (9.8 in) long. An important function of this particular species is the role it plays in seed dispersion.

summary: A black-and-white bird famed as one of Australia's finest songsters. It impales prey on thorns and sings complex duets.
nativeRange: Mainland Australia (except far south-east)
abilities: Sings complex fluty duets and choruses
Impales prey on thorns or wedges it in branches
Mimics other birds

animal.diet: Insects, small reptiles, birds, mice
animal.habitat: Open woodland and farmland
animal.behaviour: It stores food by wedging prey in tree forks or impaling it on thorns.
fieldMarks: Black head and bib
White collar and underparts
Black-and-white wings
Hooked grey bill
animal.voice: Rich, flute-like piping, often in duets.
animal.lookalikes: Grey butcherbird lacks the black bib. Australian magpie is larger and lacks the hook-tipped bill.
animal.whereToSee: Inland Queensland, NSW, Northern Territory
animal.season: Resident

lore: Violinist and zoomusicologist Hollis Taylor spent years transcribing its songs in the outback for her 2017 book 'Is Birdsong Music?'.
funFact: Pied butcherbird songs vary from region to region and change from year to year, with individual birds reworking phrases like improvising musicians.

wiki.extract: The pied butcherbird is a songbird native to Australia. Initially described by John Gould in 1837, it is a black-and-white bird 28 to 32 cm long with a long, hooked bill. Its head and throat are black, making a distinctive hood; the mantle and much of the tail and wings are also black. The neck, underparts, and outer wing feathers are white. The juvenile and immature birds are predominantly brown and white. As they mature, black feathers replace their brown feathers. There are two recognised subspecies of pied butcherbird.

summary: A black-and-white songbird whose rich, carolling song is one of the iconic sounds of Australia. It is notorious for swooping people during nesting season.
nativeRange: Australia and southern New Guinea; introduced to New Zealand
abilities: Complex warbling and carolling song with mimicry
Remembers individual human faces
Groups defend territories year-round
Shows strong cooperation, including helping to remove tracking devices from one another

animal.diet: Insects, grubs, worms and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, parks and farms
animal.behaviour: During nesting, some males swoop pedestrians and cyclists who come near.
fieldMarks: Black-and-white plumage
Black head and underparts
White or grey nape and back (varies regionally)
Pale bluish-grey bill with dark tip
Red-brown eye
animal.voice: A rich, flute-like carolling, often by groups; also complex warbles and mimicry.
animal.lookalikes: Pied currawong is mostly black with a yellow eye and white tail tip. Magpie-lark is smaller, with a thin bill and white eyebrow or throat.
animal.whereToSee: Common in parks and playing fields throughout Australia
animal.season: Resident; swooping season August–October

lore: Noongar stories tell of Koolbardi the magpie and Wardong the crow. The magpie is the emblem of many Australian sports teams.
funFact: In 2022 researchers reported that magpies removed tracking harnesses from one another, an unusual example of cooperative rescue.

wiki.extract: The Australian magpie is a black and white passerine bird native to Australia and southern New Guinea, and introduced to New Zealand, and the Fijian island of Taveuni. Although once considered to be three separate species, it is now considered to be one, with nine recognised subspecies. A member of the Artamidae, the Australian magpie is placed in its own genus Gymnorhina and is most closely related to the black butcherbird. It is not closely related to the Eurasian magpie or any other birds known as magpies, which are corvids.

summary: The sea star that gave ecology the idea of the 'keystone species'. When Robert Paine removed it from rocks in Washington State in the 1960s, mussels took over and the variety of shore life collapsed.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from Alaska to Baja California
abilities: Pulls mussel shells apart with hundreds of tube feet
Pushes its stomach out through its mouth to digest prey inside the shell
Regenerates lost arms
Can survive hours out of water at low tide

animal.diet: Mainly California mussels; also barnacles, limpets, snails and chitons
animal.habitat: Wave-exposed rocky shores and mussel beds, from mid-intertidal to about 90 m
animal.size: Usually 10–25 cm across, up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: At high tide it moves up into mussel beds to feed; at low tide it clusters in crevices to avoid drying out.
fieldMarks: Five thick, stiff arms
Colour purple, orange, ochre or brown
Upper surface covered with small white spines in a net-like or star-shaped pattern
Firm, rough texture
animal.lookalikes: Giant spined star (Pisaster giganteus) has larger, blue-ringed spines. Mottled star (Evasterias troschelii) has slimmer arms and is mottled. Leather star (Dermasterias imbricata) is smooth and slippery.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky shores at low tide from Vancouver Island to California, e.g. Olympic National Park, Monterey Bay and Mukkaw Bay (Washington).
animal.season: Year-round; best seen on low spring tides

lore: Robert Paine's experiments at Mukkaw Bay, published in 1966 and 1969, coined the term 'keystone species', one of the most influential ideas in conservation biology.
funFact: Sea star wasting syndrome killed most ochre stars along parts of the Pacific coast in 2013–2014, turning the animals into melting, disintegrating masses; many populations have since partly recovered.

wiki.extract: Pisaster ochraceus, generally known as the purple sea star, ochre sea star, or ochre starfish, is a common seastar found among the waters of the Pacific Ocean. Identified as a keystone species, P. ochraceus is considered an important indicator for the health of the intertidal zone.

summary: A tall, grey bird of African swamps with a huge clog-shaped bill. It stands motionless for long periods before lunging to seize lungfish.
nativeRange: Swamps of East and Central Africa, from South Sudan to Zambia
abilities: Bill up to ~24 cm long and ~10 cm wide, with a sharp hooked tip
Stands still for very long periods to ambush prey
Collapses forward in a lunge to grab lungfish and catfish
Bill-clatters loudly as a greeting
Pours bills of water over eggs to cool them

animal.diet: Lungfish, catfish, tilapia, frogs, water snakes and young crocodiles
animal.habitat: Extensive papyrus and reed swamps
animal.behaviour: Usually two eggs hatch, but typically only one chick survives, the older outcompeting the younger.
fieldMarks: Very tall, grey stork-like bird
Huge, shoe-shaped bill with a hooked tip
Pale yellow eyes
Stands motionless for long periods
animal.voice: Mostly silent; adults clatter their bills at the nest
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable at close range; at a distance Goliath heron is slimmer with a long thin bill and rufous neck.
animal.whereToSee: Mabamba Swamp near Entebbe and Murchison Falls Delta (Uganda); Bangweulu Swamps (Zambia)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Ancient Egyptian art may depict shoebill-like birds. It was described scientifically in 1850 by John Gould from specimens from the White Nile.
funFact: Despite its stork-like look, its closest relatives are pelicans.

wiki.extract: The shoebill, also known as the whale-headed stork, whalebill, and shoe-billed stork, is a large long-legged wading bird. It is named for its enormous, shoe-shaped bill. It has a somewhat stork-like overall form and was previously classified as a stork in the order Ciconiiformes, but genetic evidence has now placed it along with pelicans, herons, and its closest relative, the hamerkop, all in the order Pelecaniformes. Adults are mainly grey, while juveniles are browner. It lives in tropical East Africa in large swamps from South Sudan down to Zambia.

summary: The only baleen whale that lives in the Arctic year-round, a black giant with a massive bow-shaped skull that can smash through sea ice to breathe. Bowheads are the longest-lived mammals known: harpoon points from the 1800s found in living whales, and eye-lens dating, indicate ages of over 200 years.
nativeRange: Arctic and sub-Arctic seas: Bering–Chukchi–Beaufort, Baffin Bay, Hudson Bay, East Greenland–Svalbard–Barents, Sea of Okhotsk
abilities: Can break through sea ice at least 60 cm thick with its head
Longest-lived mammal: one individual was estimated at about 211 years old
Longest baleen of any whale, up to about 4 m
Thickest blubber of any animal, up to about 50 cm

animal.diet: Copepods, krill and other small zooplankton, skimmed at the surface or near the bottom
animal.habitat: Ice-edge waters, leads and polynyas of the Arctic
animal.lifespan: Often over 100 years; 200+ in some individuals
animal.behaviour: Migrates along leads in the sea ice in spring and back south in autumn. Male bowheads sing diverse, ever-changing songs in winter: nearly 200 distinct song types were recorded off Svalbard over three years.
fieldMarks: Huge, black body with no dorsal fin
Strongly arched, bow-shaped mouthline; head up to a third of body length
White chin patch, often with black spots; pale band near the tail
V-shaped blow from two widely spaced blowholes; two humps (head and back) visible when surfacing
animal.voice: Highly varied songs of whoops, moans and trills, likened to jazz because new songs appear each year.
animal.lookalikes: North Atlantic and North Pacific right whales lack the white chin and have rough white callosities on the head. Gray whale is mottled with barnacles.
animal.whereToSee: Disko Bay (West Greenland, spring); Isabella Bay/Igaliqtuuq (Baffin Island, late summer); Utqiaġvik, Alaska (spring migration); Shantar Islands (Sea of Okhotsk); Svalbard (rare)
animal.season: Spring migration April–June; late-summer feeding in Baffin and Beaufort seas; wintering in the Bering Sea

lore: For Iñupiat whaling communities of northern Alaska, the spring bowhead hunt and the Nalukataq festival that follows are the heart of the year. Basque, Dutch and British whalers hunted 'Greenland whales' at Svalbard from the early 1600s.
funFact: In 2007 a fragment of a harpoon made in New Bedford in the 1880s was found embedded in a bowhead caught off Alaska.

wiki.extract: The bowhead whale, sometimes known as the Greenland right whale, Arctic whale, and polar whale, is a species of baleen whale belonging to the family Balaenidae and is the only living representative of the genus Balaena. It is the only baleen whale endemic to the Arctic and subarctic waters, and is named after its characteristic massive triangular skull, which it uses to break through Arctic ice.

summary: The largest animal known to have ever lived, larger than any dinosaur, reaching about 30 m and well over 150 tonnes. It grows that large almost entirely on krill, shrimp-like animals a few centimetres long.
nativeRange: All oceans except the high Arctic; distinct populations in the North Atlantic, North Pacific, Indian Ocean and Southern Ocean
abilities: Lunge-feeds by engulfing a mouthful of water larger than its own body, then strains it through baleen
Can eat up to around 16 tonnes of krill in a day during the feeding season
Produces low-frequency calls of up to ~188 dB that can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater
Migrates thousands of kilometres between feeding and breeding grounds

animal.diet: Filter feeder: almost entirely krill
animal.habitat: Open ocean and productive upwelling zones along shelf edges
animal.size: Typically 24–27 m; record ~30 m; up to ~150–190 t
animal.behaviour: A lunge takes about ten seconds, the throat pleats ballooning to hold tens of tonnes of water. Calves drink a fat-rich milk and gain around 90 kg a day.
fieldMarks: Enormous, mottled blue-grey whale
Tall, straight blow up to about 9 m
Tiny dorsal fin set far back
Broad, U-shaped head; often raises the tail flukes when diving deep
animal.voice: Very loud, low-frequency moans and pulses, mostly below human hearing
animal.lookalikes: Fin whale is darker grey with a taller dorsal fin and an asymmetric jaw (white on the right side). Sei whale is smaller with a more prominent fin.
animal.whereToSee: Mirissa (Sri Lanka), Monterey Bay and the Santa Barbara Channel (California), Loreto in the Gulf of California
animal.season: Sri Lanka Dec–Apr; California Jun–Oct; Gulf of California Feb–Apr

lore: Robert Sibbald described a blue whale stranded on the Firth of Forth in 1692 in his Phalainologia Nova (1694), and the species was long called 'Sibbald's rorqual'. Twentieth-century whaling killed about 360,000 in the Southern Hemisphere before a 1966 ban.
funFact: Its heart weighs about 180 kg, and its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant.

wiki.extract: The blue whale is a species of baleen whale and the largest marine mammal in the rorqual family Balaenopteridae. Reaching a maximum confirmed length of 29.9–30.5 m (98–100 ft) and weighing up to 190–200 t, it is the largest animal known to have ever existed. The blue whale's long and slender body can be of various shades of greyish-blue on its upper surface and somewhat lighter underneath. Four subspecies are recognized: B. m. musculus in the North Atlantic and North Pacific, B. m. intermedia in the Southern Ocean, B. m. brevicauda in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific Ocean, and B. m. indica in the Northern Indian Ocean. There is a population in the waters off Chile that may constitute a fifth subspecies.

plates.desc: A large marine animal, identified as a whale, with a prominent dorsal fin and water spouting from its blowhole.
plates.long: This illustration represents a whale, referred to as 'Balaena vera' in the accompanying text. The woodcut captures key anatomical features such as the blowhole and a large dorsal fin, illustrating early modern efforts to accurately categorize and depict marine life.

summary: An acrobatic baleen whale with enormous wing-like flippers, known for breaching, bubble-net feeding and some of the most complex songs in the animal kingdom. After commercial whaling ended, most populations have recovered strongly. It migrates thousands of kilometres between cold feeding grounds and tropical breeding grounds every year.
nativeRange: All oceans, from polar feeding grounds to tropical breeding grounds; a non-migratory population lives in the Arabian Sea
abilities: Groups blow spiralling 'bubble nets' to herd fish into a tight ball, then lunge through it
Males sing complex, structured songs that change over seasons and spread between populations across ocean basins
Migrations of up to about 8,000 km one way, among the longest of any mammal
Flippers up to a third of body length, with knobbly leading edges that improve lift

animal.diet: Krill and small schooling fish such as herring, capelin, anchovies and sand lance
animal.habitat: Coastal and continental-shelf waters; tropical shallows for breeding
animal.behaviour: Breaches, slaps flippers and tails, and travels in loose groups. Mothers and calves stay together for about a year.
fieldMarks: Very long white or partly white flippers
Small, stubby dorsal fin on a hump, two-thirds of the way back
Knobbly tubercles on the head and jaw
Raises the tail flukes high before a deep dive; black-and-white underside pattern of each fluke is unique
Bushy blow, 3–4 m tall
animal.voice: Males' songs are long sequences of moans, groans, whoops and squeals arranged in repeated themes, lasting up to half an hour and repeated for hours.
animal.lookalikes: Gray whale lacks a dorsal fin and long flippers and is mottled grey. Fin and minke whales have tall, sickle-shaped dorsal fins and seldom raise their flukes. Right whales lack a dorsal fin and have white callosities.
animal.whereToSee: Hervey Bay (Queensland); Maui (Hawaii); Vava'u (Tonga); Silver Bank (Dominican Republic); Stellwagen Bank (Massachusetts); Monterey Bay (California); Juneau (Alaska); Húsavík (Iceland); Gulf of Masirah and the Dhofar coast (Oman) for Arabian Sea whales
animal.season: Northern breeding grounds January–April; northern feeding grounds May–October; Australia and Tonga July–October

lore: Roger Payne and Scott McVay's 1971 paper and the album 'Songs of the Humpback Whale' (1970) helped spark the 'Save the Whales' movement; a recording flew on the Voyager Golden Records in 1977.
funFact: Its genus name Megaptera means 'big-winged', for flippers that can reach 5 m long.

wiki.extract: The humpback whale is a species of baleen whale. It is a rorqual and is the only species in the genus Megaptera. Adults range in length from 14–17 m (46–56 ft) and weigh up to 40 metric tons. The humpback has a distinctive body shape, with long pectoral fins and tubercles on its head. It is known for breaching and other distinctive surface behaviors, making it popular with whale watchers. Males produce a complex song that typically lasts from 4 to 33 minutes.

summary: The heaviest snake in the world, a swamp-dwelling constrictor of South American rivers and flooded savannas. Females are far larger than males, and in the breeding season they are tangled in mating balls of a dozen males.
nativeRange: Tropical South America east of the Andes: Amazon and Orinoco basins, the Llanos, the Guianas, and Trinidad
abilities: Large females can exceed 5 m and weigh well over 70 kg, more than any other snake
Eyes and nostrils on top of the head let it stay hidden underwater with only these exposed
Kills prey as large as capybaras, caimans and deer by constriction
Gives birth to live young, sometimes 20–40 or more

animal.diet: Fish, birds, capybaras, peccaries, deer, turtles and caimans
animal.habitat: Slow rivers, swamps, oxbow lakes and seasonally flooded grassland
animal.size: Females usually 3–5 m, exceptionally more; males much smaller
animal.behaviour: In the Venezuelan Llanos dry season, a female may be courted by up to a dozen males wrapped around her in a 'breeding ball' that can last weeks. It is not venomous, and attacks on people are extremely rare.
fieldMarks: Olive-green to dark green body with large, paired, round black blotches along the back
Black-ringed, yellow-centred spots along the sides
Orange-yellow and black stripes behind the eye
Very heavy body; eyes and nostrils on top of the narrow head
animal.lookalikes: The yellow anaconda (E. notaeus) of the Pantanal and Paraguay is yellowish with more irregular black blotches and is smaller. Boa constrictors have a brown, saddle-patterned body with a reddish tail and do not live in the water. In 2024 a study proposed splitting off the northern green anaconda as E. akayima, but this is still debated.
animal.whereToSee: Venezuelan Llanos (such as Hato El Cedral), the Brazilian Amazon and Pantanal edges, Peru's Pacaya-Samiria; best seen basking in the dry season
animal.season: Resident; easiest to see in the dry season (January–April in the Llanos)

lore: Amazonian peoples tell of the Yacumama or Boiúna, a giant serpent mother of the rivers. Tales of 20–30 m anacondas led the New York Zoological Society to offer a reward, eventually $50,000, for a live snake over 30 feet (9.1 m). It was never claimed.
funFact: Female anacondas can go seven months without eating while pregnant, and may eat a male after mating.

wiki.extract: The green anaconda is a species of snake in the family Boidae (boas). The species is native to northern South America. It is one of the longest and heaviest known extant snake species. Like all boas, it is a non-venomous constrictor. The green anaconda generally has a life expectancy of ten years in the wild, although some specimens live longer when taken care of in captivity. The green anaconda lives in tropical rainforests and tends to prefer shallow, slow-moving waters, such as streams, rivers, and flooded grasslands. It spends most of its time in the water but is also found on land in thick vegetation.

summary: A moth so thoroughly domesticated over about 5,000 years that it can no longer survive in the wild: adults cannot fly and caterpillars barely search for food. Each cocoon is spun from a single continuous silk thread up to about 900 m long.
nativeRange: Domesticated in China from the wild Bombyx mandarina; now reared in sericulture worldwide
abilities: Spins a cocoon from a single filament of fibroin bound by sericin, up to ~900 m long
Silk is among the strongest natural fibres for its weight
Adults are flightless and do not feed
Male detects the pheromone bombykol, the first insect pheromone ever identified (1959)
Genome engineered to produce spider-silk and medical proteins

uses.use: Braided silk sutures, used for centuries and still common in surgery
Jiāngcán (僵蚕), larvae killed by the fungus Beauveria bassiana, used for convulsions and sore throat
Silk fibroin scaffolds for tissue engineering and drug delivery

medicinal.cautions: Strong evidence applies to silk sutures as a surgical material only; traditional jiangcan use has little clinical evidence. Silkworm pupae and sericin can cause allergies.

animal.diet: Larvae eat mulberry leaves (Morus); adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Exists only in human care
animal.lifespan: About 6–8 weeks, including ~4 weeks as a caterpillar
animal.size: Caterpillar to ~7.5 cm; adult wingspan ~4–5 cm
animal.behaviour: A caterpillar spins its cocoon in a figure-eight motion for two to three days, swinging its head hundreds of thousands of times.
fieldMarks: Creamy-white, furry moth with stubby wings, unable to fly
Feathery antennae
Pale caterpillar with a small horn at the tail, feeding on mulberry leaves
Spins a cocoon of a single continuous silk thread
animal.lookalikes: Its wild ancestor Bombyx mandarina is brown and can fly; the domestic silkmoth exists only in captivity.

lore: Chinese legend credits Leizu, wife of the Yellow Emperor, with discovering silk when a cocoon fell into her tea. China guarded the secret for centuries until, by Procopius's account, monks smuggled eggs to Byzantium in hollow canes around 552 CE.
funFact: The Silk Road takes its name from this insect's thread, coined by Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

wiki.extract: Bombyx mori, commonly known as the domestic silk moth, is a domesticated moth species belonging to the family Bombycidae. It is the closest relative of Bombyx mandarina, the wild silk moth. Silkworms are the larvae of silk moths. The silkworm is of particular economic value, being a primary producer of silk. The silkworm's preferred food are the leaves of white mulberry, though they may eat other species of mulberry, and even leaves of other plants. Domestic silk moths are entirely dependent on humans for reproduction, as a result of millennia of selective breeding. Wild silk moths, which are other species of Bombyx, are not as commercially viable in the production of silk.

As an early example of natural history illustration, the image reflects the Renaissance transition toward documenting the medicinal and economic utility of the natural world. summary: A sleek, crested fruit-eater with a black mask and red wax-like droplets on its wing tips. It roams in tight, whistling flocks wherever berries ripen, and can live on fruit alone for months.
nativeRange: Breeds across southern Canada and the northern US; winters throughout most of the US south to Central America and the Caribbean
abilities: Can survive on fruit alone for months, digesting it rapidly
Disperses seeds of cedar, juniper, serviceberry and many other fruiting plants
Flocks pass berries from bird to bird along a branch
Sallies out over rivers in summer to catch flying insects

animal.diet: Berries and small fruits; flying insects in summer
animal.habitat: Open woodland, forest edges, orchards and suburbs with fruiting trees
animal.behaviour: It nests late in summer, timed to fruit ripening, and can become intoxicated or die from eating fermented berries.
fieldMarks: Silky, warm brown-grey plumage with a pointed crest
Narrow black mask edged with white
Yellow belly and yellow-tipped tail
Red waxy tips on the secondary feathers
animal.voice: No true song; very high, thin, buzzy whistles 'sreee' given constantly by flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Bohemian Waxwing is larger and greyer, with rufous undertail coverts and yellow and white marks on the wings. Northern Cardinal females share the crest but have a thick red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Fruiting trees anywhere in North America, especially junipers, crabapples and mountain-ash in winter; along rivers catching insects in summer.
animal.season: Present year-round in much of the north-central US; nomadic, with numbers changing with fruit crops

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The Chatterer', and its sociable habits earned it the old American names 'cedar-bird' and 'cherry-bird'.
funFact: Since the 1960s, some cedar waxwings have orange instead of yellow tail tips — the result of eating berries of introduced Morrow's honeysuckle while their feathers grow.

wiki.extract: The cedar waxwing is a member of the family Bombycillidae or waxwing family of passerine birds. It is a medium-sized bird that is mainly brown, gray, and yellow. Some of the wing feathers have red tips, which resemble sealing wax, giving the bird its common name. It is a native of North and Central America, breeding in open wooded areas in southern Canada and wintering in the southern half of the United States, Central America, and the far northwest of South America. Its diet includes cedar cones, fruit, holly berries, and insects. The cedar waxwing is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a Cedar Waxwing perched on a flowering Sweetshrub branch.
plates.long: This plate from Mark Catesby's 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands' depicts a Cedar Waxwing, identified by the artist as 'The Chatterer.' Catesby's work was revolutionary for its time, as he was among the first to illustrate birds alongside the specific plants they frequented, providing a more holistic view of the natural world.

summary: One of the fastest land mammals, a slim antelope of the Indian plains whose mature males are glossy black and white with long spiralled horns. Once among the most numerous large mammals of South Asia, it survives in protected grasslands and among communities such as the Bishnoi who refuse to harm it.
nativeRange: India and Nepal; extinct in the wild in Bangladesh and Pakistan (reintroduced to Lal Suhanra, Pakistan); introduced in Texas and Argentina
abilities: Can run at up to about 80 km/h and sustain high speeds over long distances
Leaps high in the air while fleeing ('stotting' or pronking)
Males defend small mating territories (leks) in some populations

animal.diet: Grasses; also pods, flowers and crops
animal.habitat: Open short grassland and plains with little tree cover
animal.size: Shoulder height 74–84 cm; 20–57 kg; horns of males up to about 70 cm
animal.behaviour: Lives in herds of females and young with territorial males. Dominant males hold their heads up and back, horns laid along the neck, in displays to rivals.
fieldMarks: Mature males: dark brown to black upperparts sharply divided from white belly; white eye-ring and chin
Corkscrew horns with 3–5 spiral turns (males only)
Females and young males: tan-yellow above, white below, hornless
Signs: territorial males leave large dung middens on their patch
animal.lookalikes: Chinkara (Indian gazelle) is sandy, both sexes have short, near-straight ridged horns, and it has a dark side-stripe. Nilgai is far larger and grey.
animal.whereToSee: Velavadar Blackbuck National Park (Gujarat); Tal Chhapar Sanctuary and Bishnoi villages around Jodhpur (Rajasthan); Point Calimere (Tamil Nadu); Ranibennur (Karnataka); Lal Suhanra National Park (Pakistan)
animal.season: Resident; displays peak in the rut (roughly March–April and August–October, varying by region)

lore: In Hindu tradition the blackbuck is the mount of Chandra, the moon, and Vayu, and its skin was prescribed in Vedic texts for ritual seats. Its hunting by a Bollywood actor near a Bishnoi village in 1998 led to a celebrated conviction.
funFact: The blackbuck is the only living member of the genus Antilope, the genus that gives the antelope subfamily Antilopinae its name.

wiki.extract: The blackbuck is a medium-sized antelope native to India and Nepal. It inhabits grassy plains and lightly forested areas with perennial water sources.

summary: North America's heaviest land animal, which once roamed the Great Plains in herds of tens of millions. Hunted down to fewer than a thousand by the late 1880s, it has recovered to about half a million, though few are wild herds.
nativeRange: Great Plains and western North America from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico; now mostly in parks, reserves and ranches
abilities: Runs at up to ~55 km/h despite weighing up to a tonne
Swings its massive head to clear deep snow and reach grass
Rolls in dust wallows that become seasonal pools and microhabitats
Grazing patterns create a patchwork of short and tall grass that benefits prairie dogs, birds and plants

animal.diet: Herbivore: mainly grasses and sedges
animal.habitat: Open grassland, prairie and meadow; wood bison in boreal clearings
animal.size: Bulls up to ~1.9 m at the shoulder and ~900–1,000 kg; cows ~450 kg
animal.behaviour: Bulls bellow and butt heads during the summer rut. Herds once followed seasonal grazing across hundreds of kilometres.
fieldMarks: Massive, humped shoulders
Shaggy brown front and short back hair
Short curved horns in both sexes
Low-held head
animal.voice: Bulls bellow during the rut
animal.lookalikes: Domestic cattle lack the hump. Stay at least 25 yards away (US park rule).
animal.whereToSee: Lamar and Hayden valleys (Yellowstone); Custer State Park and Wind Cave National Park (South Dakota)
animal.season: Resident; rut Jul–Aug; calves Apr–May

lore: Lakota tradition tells how White Buffalo Calf Woman brought the sacred pipe, and the birth of a white calf is still seen as a sacred sign. Coronado's 1541 expedition described the 'vacas de Cíbola' covering the plains.
funFact: In 2016 the bison became the national mammal of the United States.

wiki.extract: The American bison, commonly known as the American buffalo, or simply buffalo, is a species of bison that is endemic to North America. It is one of two extant species of bison, along with the European bison. Its historical range circa 9000 BC is referred to as the great bison belt, a tract of rich grassland spanning from Alaska south to the Gulf of Mexico, and east to the Atlantic Seaboard, as far north as New York, south to Georgia, and according to some sources, further south to northern Florida, with sightings in North Carolina near Buffalo Ford on the Catawba River as late as 1750.

summary: The largest and tallest of all wild cattle, a black-brown forest giant with white stockings and a muscular ridge over its shoulders. India holds the great majority of the world's gaur, and in the Western Ghats herds have learned to graze tea estates and village edges.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia and southern China
abilities: Adult bulls are so large that even tigers usually avoid them, taking calves instead
Shoulder ridge formed by tall spines on the vertebrae
Climbs steep forested hills up to about 2,800 m

animal.diet: Grasses, bamboo, shoots, leaves, bark and fruit
animal.habitat: Evergreen and deciduous forest with glades and water, usually hilly
animal.behaviour: Herds of cows and young are led by an old female; bulls display by standing side-on to show their bulk, a broadside stance.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: huge dark bovine with a high shoulder hump falling to the middle of the back
White or yellowish 'stockings' from hooves to knees
Pale grey-buff boss of hair between the horns; horns curve up and inward
Tracks: large cloven hoofprints about 13 cm long; dung like domestic cattle pats
animal.lookalikes: Banteng (Southeast Asia) has a white rump patch and lacks the strong dorsal ridge. Wild water buffalo has flat, enormous swept-back horns and sparse grey coat. Mithun (domestic Bos frontalis of northeast India) is smaller with straighter horns.
animal.whereToSee: Nagarhole, Bandipur (Karnataka); Kanha and Pench (Madhya Pradesh); Tadoba (Maharashtra); Periyar and Eravikulam (Kerala); Taman Negara (Malaysia); Kui Buri (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; herds visit forest meadows and salt licks in the dry season

lore: Gaur was the British 'Indian bison' of colonial hunting literature, and is the state animal of Goa and Bihar. Domesticated gaur, the mithun, are a measure of wealth and a sacrificial animal among Naga, Mizo and Adi communities.
funFact: A bull gaur can stand over 2 m at the shoulder, taller than an average man.
