wiki.extract:
The gaur, also known as the Indian bison, is a large bovine native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, and has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 1986. The global population was estimated at a maximum of 21,000 mature individuals in 2016, with the majority of those existing in India.
It is the largest species among the wild cattle and the Bovidae.

summary: The largest antelope in Asia, a sloping-backed, horse-like animal of dry plains and farmland in northern and central India. Because many Hindus associate it with the cow, it is widely tolerated, and it has become abundant enough to be a notorious crop raider.
nativeRange: India, eastern Pakistan and southern Nepal; extinct in Bangladesh; introduced in Texas, USA
abilities: Can go long periods without drinking, getting moisture from plants
Thrives alongside agriculture, feeding on crops at night
Males spar on their knees, pushing neck-to-neck

animal.diet: Grasses, herbs, leaves, fruits and pods (e.g. of Prosopis and Acacia) and crops
animal.habitat: Open scrub, dry forest and agricultural land; avoids dense forest
animal.size: 1–1.5 m at shoulder; males up to about 280 kg
animal.behaviour: Herds use shared dung heaps, sometimes dozens of piles at a site, which mark ranges. Females and calves form small herds while bulls live alone or in bachelor groups.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: horse-like, with high shoulders sloping down to lower hindquarters
Adult bulls blue-grey with a white throat patch and a tuft of black hair (a 'beard') on the throat
Females and young tawny-brown; white spots on cheeks and white rings above the hooves
Bulls have short, straight conical horns (about 20 cm); signs include large communal dung middens
animal.lookalikes: Sambar deer is darker, has branched antlers (stags) and a bushy tail, and lives in forest. Gaur is a much heavier, black bovine with curved horns and white 'socks'.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore, Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Tal Chhapar (Rajasthan); Gir and Little Rann of Kutch (Gujarat); farmland across Haryana and Uttar Pradesh
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Mughal emperor Jahangir recorded hunting nilgai in his memoir, the Jahangirnama, and his court painter Ustad Mansur painted the animal from life. Its association with the sacred cow has long protected it, though India's environment ministry declared it vermin in Bihar in December 2015 to allow culling.
funFact: The nilgai is the only living species in its genus, and with the four-horned antelope it forms a tribe (Boselaphini) whose relatives once roamed Europe.

wiki.extract: The nilgai is the largest antelope in Asia. It is ubiquitous across the northern Indian subcontinent. It is the sole living member of the genus Boselaphus, which was first scientifically described by Peter Simon Pallas in 1766. It is a sturdy, thin-legged antelope with a sloping back, a deep neck with a white patch on the throat, a short crest of hair along the neck terminating in a tuft, and white facial spots. A column of pendant, coarse hair hangs from the dewlap ridge below the white patch. It stands 100–150 cm (39–59 in) at the shoulder; males weigh 109–288 kg (240–635 lb), and the lighter females 100–213 kg (220–470 lb). Sexual dimorphism is prominent; while females and juveniles are orange to tawny, adult males have a bluish-grey coat. Only males have horns, which are 15–24 cm (5.9–9.4 in) long.

summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic water buffalo, a massive bovine of floodplain grasslands with the longest horn span of any living bovid. Fewer than 4,000 are thought to survive, most of them in Assam, and many are at risk of hybridising with domestic buffalo.
nativeRange: Northeast India (Assam, Arunachal), Chhattisgarh, Nepal (Koshi Tappu), Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia
abilities: Spends hot hours submerged in rivers and wallows with only head and horns showing
Horns can span up to about 2 m tip to tip
Herds defend themselves from tigers by charging together

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, herbs and crops
animal.habitat: Wet grassland, swamps and river valleys with dense vegetation and water
animal.behaviour: Females and calves live in herds of 10–30; bulls form bachelor groups and join herds in the rut, after the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: huge, dark grey-black bovine with very wide, crescent-shaped horns swept out and back
Horns flattened and ridged near the base
Pale chevron on the throat and whitish lower legs ('socks')
Sparse coat; signs include mud wallows and trampled reedbed trails
animal.lookalikes: Domestic and feral water buffalo are smaller, with shorter horns and often a sagging belly; hybrids are hard to separate. Gaur has a high shoulder ridge, white socks and shorter upcurved horns.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga and Manas national parks, Dibru-Saikhowa (Assam); Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve (Nepal); Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve (Chhattisgarh); Huai Kha Khaeng (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; best in Kaziranga's dry season (November–April)

lore: The buffalo is the vahana (mount) of Yama, the Hindu god of death, and the demon Mahishasura took buffalo form before Durga slew him. It is the state animal of Chhattisgarh.
funFact: Domestic water buffalo, descended from this species, now number around 200 million worldwide, while their wild ancestor is endangered.

wiki.extract: The wild water buffalo, also called Asian buffalo, Asiatic buffalo and wild buffalo, is a large bovine native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It was first described in 1792.

summary: A great wild goat of the western Himalaya, Hindu Kush and Karakoram, whose males carry immense corkscrew horns and a flowing ruff. It is Pakistan's national animal and a conservation success story: community-run trophy-hunting programmes helped populations recover enough for the species to move from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2015.
nativeRange: Northern Pakistan, eastern Afghanistan, Kashmir (India), southern Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
abilities: Climbs near-vertical cliffs and even into holm-oak trees to browse
Males' spiralling horns can exceed 1.5 m along the curve
Feeds at high altitude in summer and descends to lower slopes in winter, tracking snowline

animal.diet: Grasses and herbs in spring and summer; browses leaves and twigs of oak, juniper and shrubs in winter
animal.habitat: Steep, rugged terrain with scrub or open woodland, roughly 600–3,600 m
animal.size: Shoulder height 65–115 cm; males up to about 110 kg, females much smaller
animal.behaviour: Males live apart from females and young for most of the year and join them for the winter rut, when they clash horns and rear up in contests on steep ground.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: stocky goat with outward-twisting corkscrew horns (males) — the spiral, not a backward arc, is diagnostic
Adult males have a long ruff of shaggy hair on the throat, chest and shins
Coat greyish-tan, paler in winter; females are reddish, short-horned and lack the ruff
Signs: goat-type pellet piles on ledges and cloven, blunt-tipped hoofprints on cliff paths
animal.lookalikes: Siberian ibex has long, scimitar-shaped horns sweeping back with knobbly ridges, not corkscrews. Urial (wild sheep) have curling horns that circle beside the face and lack a goat beard.
animal.whereToSee: Chitral Gol National Park and Tooshi-Shasha Conservancy, Chitral; Kargah and Gilgit-Baltistan community conservancies; Torghar Hills, Balochistan; Kazinag National Park, Kashmir
animal.season: Resident; males are easiest to see near villages and lower slopes during the winter rut (November–January)

lore: The name is popularly read as Persian 'snake-eater', and in Hindu Kush folklore markhor were said to kill snakes and leave a foam whose dried residue was used to draw out snake venom. The Torghar Conservation Project, begun by Pashtun tribesmen in 1985, is a celebrated model of community-led wildlife recovery.
funFact: A Pakistani markhor trophy-hunting permit has sold for more than US$100,000, with most of the fee going to the local community.

wiki.extract: The markhor is a large wild Capra species native to the mountain regions at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, including the Karakoram and Himalayas. It occurs in parts of Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and India. It has been listed on the IUCN Red List as Near Threatened since 2015.

summary: An Ice Age survivor of the high Arctic, a shaggy, short-legged bovid more closely related to goats than to cattle. Its underwool, qiviut, is among the warmest natural fibres. Facing wolves, herds form a tight circle with calves in the middle and horns outward.
nativeRange: Arctic Canada and Greenland; reintroduced or introduced to Alaska, Norway (Dovrefjell), Sweden, Siberia (Taymyr, Wrangel Island)
abilities: Qiviut underwool is warmer than sheep's wool by weight and is shed each spring
Defensive ring formation repels wolves, though not human hunters
Survives winters of −40 °C on frozen sedges and willows dug from snow

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, Arctic willow, herbs and lichens
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra and river valleys with thin snow cover
animal.behaviour: Bulls charge each other head-on in the late-summer rut, colliding with a crash audible far away. Herds of 10–30 are typical.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, boxy dark-brown animal with long skirt of guard hair reaching near the ground
Horns with a massive central 'boss' across the forehead, curving down then up beside the face
Pale saddle and pale lower legs
Signs: tufts of shed qiviut on willows and rocks in early summer; rounded hoofprints
animal.lookalikes: Bison (not in Arctic) has a tall hump and short upturned horns. Reindeer are slimmer with antlers. Takin (Himalaya) is golden with differently curved horns.
animal.whereToSee: Dovrefjell–Sunndalsfjella National Park (Norway); Kangerlussuaq (Greenland); Nunivak Island and Nome (Alaska); Banks Island, Aulavik National Park (Canada); Wrangel Island (Russia)
animal.season: Resident year-round; summer is best for access

lore: Musk oxen were hunted out of Alaska by the early 1900s; a few dozen animals brought from Greenland and released on Nunivak Island in 1935–36 founded most of today's Alaskan herds. Inuit traditionally used the horns for ladles, bows and fish spears.
funFact: Despite its name, the musk ox is not an ox: it is a goat-antelope, closer to sheep and goats than to cattle, and its nearest living relatives appear to be the gorals of Asia's mountains.

wiki.extract: The muskox is a hoofed mammal of the family Bovidae. Native to the Arctic, it is noted for its thick coat and for the strong odor emitted by males during the seasonal rut, from which its name derives. This musky odor has the effect of attracting females during mating season. Its Inuktitut name umingmak translates to "the bearded one".

summary: The most widespread three-toed sloth, a leaf-eater that saves energy by moving very little and very slowly. Its shaggy fur carries algae, moths and fungi, a small ecosystem of its own.
nativeRange: Honduras south through Central America to northern Argentina, east of the Andes
abilities: Has 8–9 neck vertebrae instead of the usual seven, letting it turn its head about 270°
Slows its heart and can stay underwater for many minutes; a good swimmer
Hangs effortlessly thanks to locking tendons in its curved claws
Grows green algae in grooved hairs that camouflage it among leaves

animal.diet: Folivore: leaves of Cecropia and many other trees
animal.habitat: Lowland and montane rainforest canopy
animal.behaviour: About once a week it climbs to the ground to defecate, its most dangerous trip. Moths living in its fur lay eggs in the dung, and their offspring fly back up to colonise the sloth.
fieldMarks: Shaggy grey-brown fur, often greenish with algae
Brown throat and dark eye stripe
Three long curved claws on each forelimb
Males have an orange-and-black back patch
animal.voice: A high, whistled 'ai-ai'
animal.lookalikes: Two-toed sloths (Choloepus) have two front claws, a pinkish snout and no eye mask.
animal.whereToSee: Manuel Antonio and Cahuita national parks, Costa Rica
animal.season: Resident

lore: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, in his 1526 natural history of the Indies, called the sloth the most useless and ugliest animal he had seen and recorded its local name, perico ligero.
funFact: A meal can take up to a month to pass through a sloth's chambered stomach.

summary: A huge hornbill of South and Southeast Asian forests, with a yellow casque atop its bill. During nesting, the female seals herself inside a tree cavity and depends on the male to feed her through a slit.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Southeast Asia to Sumatra
abilities: Female walls herself into the nest with mud and droppings for months
Male delivers fruit regurgitated one at a time through the slit
Major disperser of large-seeded rainforest trees, especially figs
Its loud wingbeats can be heard from far away

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; also small animals
animal.habitat: Tall old-growth forest
animal.lifespan: Up to about 50 years in captivity
animal.behaviour: Birds rub preen-gland secretions onto the casque and wings, giving them their yellow colour.
fieldMarks: Very large black-and-white hornbill
Huge yellow bill with a broad, concave casque
White tail with a black band
Loud whooshing wingbeats
animal.voice: Pairs duet with a rapid mix of loud roars and barks, starting from a steady 'kok'
animal.lookalikes: Rhinoceros hornbill (Sunda region) has an upturned red-and-orange casque. Wreathed hornbill has no casque and a white tail without a band.
animal.whereToSee: Pakke Tiger Reserve (Arunachal Pradesh) and Valparai in the Anamalai Hills, India; Khao Yai, Thailand
animal.season: Resident; breeds Jan–Apr, when pairs are most vocal

lore: It is the state bird of Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh, and Naga peoples traditionally used its feathers and casques in headdresses; Nagaland's Hornbill Festival is named for it.
funFact: Its casque is mostly hollow and light, unlike the solid ivory-like casque of its relative the helmeted hornbill.

wiki.extract: The great hornbill, also known as the concave-casqued hornbill, great Indian hornbill or great pied hornbill, is one of the larger members of the hornbill family. It occurs in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It is predominantly frugivorous, but also preys on small mammals, reptiles, and birds. It has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2018. It is known to have lived for nearly 50 years in captivity. Due to its large size and colour, and importance in many tribal cultures and rituals, the Government of Kerala declared it as the official Kerala state bird. It is also the state bird of Arunachal Pradesh.

summary: A huge black-and-white hornbill crowned with an extravagant upturned orange-red casque, like a rhinoceros horn. It is the state bird of Sarawak, 'Land of the Hornbills', and a major disperser of rainforest seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java and Borneo; long extinct as a breeder in Singapore, with occasional wild wanderers recorded since 2025
abilities: Disperses the large seeds of figs and other rainforest trees over wide areas
Female seals herself into a tree cavity nest, fed by the male
Wingbeats are so loud they can be heard from a distance as a whooshing roar

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; also insects, lizards and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest with large old trees
animal.behaviour: Pairs fly between fruiting trees with loud, whooshing wingbeats; the sealed-in female relies on the male for months.
fieldMarks: Very large black hornbill with white belly and white tail with a black band
Massive ivory-yellow bill topped by an orange-red casque curving upward like a horn
Red eye in males, white eye in females
Loud wing noise in flight
animal.voice: Deep, resonant 'gronk' calls; pairs duet with the male's lower notes and the female's higher ones
animal.lookalikes: Great hornbill has a flatter, yellow, two-pointed casque and a white neck; Helmeted hornbill has a short red casque and long central tail feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Taman Negara (Malaysia), Kinabatangan River and Danum Valley (Sabah), Lambir Hills (Sarawak), Khao Sok (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Among the Iban of Sarawak, the kenyalang is the messenger of the upper world, and carved hornbill effigies were raised in the Gawai Kenyalang festival. The bird appears on Sarawak's coat of arms.
funFact: Its casque is mostly hollow and light, unlike the solid casque of the Helmeted hornbill.

wiki.extract: The rhinoceros hornbill is a large species of forest hornbill. In captivity, it can live for up to 35 years. It is found in lowland and montane, tropical and subtropical climates and in mountain rain forests up to 1,400 metres in the Malay Peninsula from southern Thailand; and the islands of Singapore, Borneo, Sumatra and Java.

summary: A modest grey hornbill with a black casque on its curved bill, common in groves, temples and city avenues across much of the subcontinent. Like other hornbills, the female walls herself inside a tree-hole nest while the male feeds her through a slit.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent: eastern Pakistan, India and the Nepal terai, south of the Himalaya
abilities: Female seals the nest entrance with mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit
Disperses large seeds of figs and other fruit trees
Survives in city parks and avenues with old fig trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit, especially figs; also insects, lizards and small birds
animal.habitat: Dry open woodland, groves, gardens and large trees in towns
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small parties fly between trees with flaps and glides; the female moults her flight feathers while sealed in the nest.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown overall, paler below
Curved dark bill with a pointed black casque
Long, graduated tail with a dark band and white tip
Pale eyebrow stripe
animal.voice: A shrill, squealing 'kee-kee-kee' and a kite-like scream
animal.lookalikes: Malabar grey hornbill (Western Ghats) lacks a casque and has a yellowish bill; Sri Lanka grey hornbill is endemic to Sri Lanka; larger Oriental pied hornbill is black and white.
animal.whereToSee: Old park and avenue trees in Lahore (e.g. Bagh-e-Jinnah); Delhi's ridge forests; Ranthambore and Keoladeo
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is one of the few hornbills to live in large South Asian cities, and urban birdwatchers in Delhi and Lahore have tracked nesting pairs in old trees for years.
funFact: While she is sealed in, the female moults her flight feathers and depends entirely on the male to bring food.

wiki.extract: The Indian gray hornbill is a common hornbill found on the Indian subcontinent. It is mostly arboreal and is commonly sighted in pairs. It has grey feathers all over the body with a light grey or dull white belly. The horn is black or dark grey with a casque extending to the point of curvature of the horn. It is one of the few hornbill species found in urban areas in many cities where they are able to make use of large trees in avenues.

summary: A massive hornbill with a solid, ivory-like casque on its forehead and two very long central tail feathers, whose accelerating hooting call ends in a burst of maniacal laughter. Hunted for 'red ivory', it was uplisted straight from Near Threatened to Critically Endangered in 2015.
nativeRange: Southern Myanmar and Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: The only hornbill with a solid casque, used in head-butting aerial contests between males
Call is one of the loudest in Asian rainforests
Disperses the seeds of strangler figs

animal.diet: Mainly figs; also small animals
animal.habitat: Tall lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforest
animal.size: About 110–120 cm long, plus central tail feathers up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Males clash in flight, striking their casques together with a loud crack; the female seals herself into a tree hole to nest.
fieldMarks: Very large brown-black hornbill with white belly and white tail with a black band
Short, deep red casque and yellow-and-red bill; casque is solid
Bare wrinkled throat skin, red in males and pale bluish in females
Two very long, white central tail feathers trailing behind
animal.voice: A long series of loud 'took' notes, spaced at first and accelerating, ending in a cackling, laugh-like crescendo
animal.lookalikes: Rhinoceros hornbill has a large upturned orange casque and no long tail plumes; Great hornbill has a flat yellow casque and a white neck.
animal.whereToSee: Danum Valley and Tabin (Sabah), Gunung Leuser (Sumatra), Budo-Sungai Padi (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Its solid casque, 'hornbill ivory' (ho-ting in Chinese), was carved into belt buckles, snuff bottles and ornaments during the Ming and Qing dynasties and traded from Borneo for centuries. In Borneo, the Iban and other Dayak peoples revered the bird and wore its tail feathers.
funFact: Its Malay name 'tebang mentua' comes from a folk tale of a man who chopped down the posts of his mother-in-law's house while she was inside and was turned into the bird: the call's accelerating 'took' notes are his axe blows, and the final cackle is his laughter as the house falls.

wiki.extract: The helmeted hornbill is a very large bird in the hornbill family. It is found on the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, Thailand and Myanmar. The casque accounts for some 11% of its 3 kg weight. Unlike any other hornbill, the casque is almost solid, and is used in head-to-head combat among males. It is a belief among the Punan Bah that a large helmeted hornbill guards the river between life and death.

summary: A turkey-sized black hornbill with scarlet facial wattles that walks the savanna in family groups, hunting everything from beetles to tortoises and snakes. It is among the slowest-breeding birds in the world, with groups raising on average one chick every nine years.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya and Burundi south to South Africa
abilities: Cooperative breeder: a dominant pair is helped by older offspring and other group members
Booming dawn chorus carries several kilometres across the savanna
Kills snakes, hares and tortoises with blows of its massive bill
Can live several decades, matching its very slow reproductive rate

animal.diet: Insects, reptiles including snakes and tortoises, frogs, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Savanna and grassland with large trees for nesting cavities
animal.lifespan: Several decades; captive birds have lived over 40 years
animal.behaviour: A group of 2–10 birds holds a large territory, walking together all day and booming in chorus at dawn to declare ownership.
fieldMarks: Very large all-black bird with white primaries visible in flight
Bright red bare skin on face and inflatable throat wattle
Females have a violet-blue patch on the throat
Heavy, down-curved black bill with low casque
Long eyelashes; walks on the ground like a turkey
animal.voice: A deep, resonant booming duet, 'oomph oomph-oomph', given mostly at dawn and audible several kilometres away.
animal.lookalikes: Abyssinian ground hornbill, north of the equator, has blue and red bare skin and an open-ended tubular casque. Distant birds are sometimes mistaken for turkeys or vultures on the ground, but the red face wattle is distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park, Hluhluwe-iMfolozi, the Okavango and Serengeti; often walking in open grass
animal.season: Resident year-round; breeding in the southern summer rains

lore: Among Zulu and Xhosa peoples the bird is linked to rain and storms and is traditionally protected by taboo; its booming is said to forecast rain, and some communities would only kill one in times of drought.
funFact: Usually only one of the two eggs is raised; the second chick hatches days later and normally starves, which is why conservationists 'harvest' second chicks for captive rearing and reintroduction.

wiki.extract: The southern ground hornbill is one of two species of ground hornbill, both of which are found solely within Africa, and is the largest species in the hornbill order worldwide. It can be found in the southern regions of Africa, ranging from Kenya to South Africa. Within these regions, they inhabit both woodlands and savannas. The other species of the genus Bucorvus is the Abyssinian ground hornbill, B. abyssinicus.

summary: A heavy, warty toad of tropical America that was released in Australia, the Caribbean and the Pacific to control cane beetles. It failed at that and instead spread its poison through native wildlife. Its skin glands produce bufotoxins that can kill dogs, quolls, goannas and snakes that bite it.
nativeRange: Southern Texas and Mexico through Central America to the central Amazon; introduced in Australia, the Caribbean, Hawaii, Florida, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and many islands
abilities: Large glands behind the eyes (parotoids) produce bufadienolide toxins that can stop the heart of predators
Eggs and tadpoles are toxic too
Has spread across northern Australia at up to ~50 km per year
Breeds in almost any still water, laying up to 30,000 eggs at a time

animal.diet: Insects, snails, small vertebrates, pet food and garbage
animal.habitat: Open habitats near water, farmland, gardens and towns
animal.behaviour: When threatened it puffs up and tilts its glands toward the attacker. Pets that mouth a toad may drool, collapse and die: wipe the gums with a damp cloth (do not hose into the throat) and get to a vet at once. People who handle toads should wash their hands. Never lick or eat toads or eggs; people have died from eating them.
fieldMarks: Large, warty, brown toad with dry skin
Huge triangular parotoid glands behind the eyes
Bony ridges above the eyes meeting at the snout
Unwebbed fingers, webbed toes
animal.voice: A long, low trill like a dial tone or a distant idling motor, lasting several seconds
animal.lookalikes: In Australia, native frogs such as giant banjo frogs (Limnodynastes) and burrowing frogs have no large parotoid glands or bony head ridges. In the US the Gulf Coast toad (Incilius nebulifer) is smaller with a light stripe down the back.
animal.whereToSee: Introduced: Queensland and the Northern Territory (Australia), Florida, Hawaii; native: Central and South American lowlands
animal.season: Active year-round in the tropics; breeds mostly in the wet season

edibilityNote: Skin, glands and eggs are deadly poisonous; people have died after eating toads or toad eggs.
lore: In 1935, 102 cane toads were brought from Hawaii to Gordonvale, Queensland, to control cane beetles. Their descendants have spread across more than 1.2 million square kilometres of Australia.
funFact: In parts of Australia, crows and native water rats (rakali) have learned to flip cane toads over and eat them from the belly side, avoiding the poison glands.

wiki.extract: The cane toad, also known as the giant neotropical toad or marine toad, is a large, terrestrial true toad native to South and mainland Central America, but which has been introduced to various islands throughout Oceania and the Caribbean, as well as Northern Australia. It is a member of the genus Rhinella, which includes many true toad species found throughout Central and South America, but it was formerly assigned to the genus Bufo.

summary: A brilliant metallic-green jewel beetle with rainbow stripes, whose colour comes from structure rather than pigment and never fades. Its wing cases decorate a 7th-century Buddhist shrine in Japan.
nativeRange: Japan, Korea, Taiwan and parts of eastern China
abilities: Iridescent colour produced by microscopic layers in the cuticle, so it lasts for centuries
Larvae bore into dead and dying wood
Adults fly in bright sunshine around the tops of tall trees

animal.diet: Adults eat leaves of Zelkova, hackberry (Celtis) and cherry; larvae feed in the dead wood of these and other broadleaves
animal.habitat: Broadleaf woods, shrine and temple groves, and parks with old trees
animal.behaviour: On hot summer days adults circle the crowns of tall zelkova and hackberry trees, flashing green in the sun.
fieldMarks: Elongated, bullet-shaped beetle
Brilliant metallic green body
Two purple-red stripes running the length of the wing cases and thorax
Flight high around tree crowns in sunshine
animal.lookalikes: Other Chrysochroa jewel beetles of Southeast Asia and the Ryukyus (e.g. C. alternans) differ in the colour and pattern of their stripes and in range.
animal.whereToSee: Temple and shrine groves and parks in Japan with old zelkova and hackberry trees.
animal.season: Adults June–August, peaking in late July

lore: The Tamamushi Shrine at Hōryū-ji, Nara, made in the 7th century, was originally decorated with thousands of these beetles' wing cases set under its metal openwork. Wings of jewel beetles also adorned horse harness from 5th-century Silla tombs in Korea.
funFact: Because the colour is made by stacked nanoscale layers rather than pigment, the beetle wings on the 1,300-year-old Tamamushi Shrine can still shimmer where they survive.

summary: A reddish-brown scorpion of rural India and Pakistan, often described as the most lethal scorpion in the world. Its venom triggers a storm in the nervous system that damages the heart and lungs, but cheap treatment with the drug prazosin has made deaths far rarer.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan and eastern Nepal
abilities: Venom causes a massive release of adrenaline-like hormones (autonomic storm)
Stings can cause high blood pressure, heart failure and fluid on the lungs
Thrives around village houses, cattle sheds and stone walls

animal.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Rubble, crevices in mud and stone walls, under stones, and inside village houses
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night and often hides in shoes, clothing and bedding, where most human stings happen.
fieldMarks: Reddish- to orange-brown body
Relatively slender pincers
Thick, segmented tail with prominent ridges
Dark-grey keels on the back of the abdomen
animal.lookalikes: Giant forest scorpions (Heterometrus) are larger, shiny black with massive pincers and much weaker venom. Other Hottentotta and Lychas species are smaller or differently patterned.
animal.whereToSee: Rural areas of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh; most stings occur in the hot season and monsoon.
animal.season: Year-round; most encountered in summer and monsoon

lore: The rural Maharashtra physician Himmatrao Bawaskar showed from the 1980s that prazosin, a blood-pressure drug, counteracts the venom; in his patient series, death rates fell from around 30–40% to under 1%.
funFact: Children are at greatest risk, because the same dose of venom is far more concentrated in a small body.

wiki.extract: Hottentotta tamulus, the Indian red scorpion, also known as the eastern Indian scorpion, is a species of scorpion of the family Buthidae. It occurs in most of India, eastern Pakistan and the eastern lowlands of Nepal, and recently from Sri Lanka.

summary: A slender straw-yellow scorpion of north-east African deserts whose venom is among the most dangerous of any scorpion. The same venom has yielded chlorotoxin, a molecule now used to make brain tumours glow during surgery.
nativeRange: North-eastern Africa, chiefly Egypt and Sudan into the Horn of Africa; related Leiurus species formerly included in it range across Arabia and the Levant
abilities: Venom mixes several neurotoxins that can cause intense pain, convulsions, heart failure and pulmonary oedema
Chlorotoxin from its venom binds selectively to glioma cells and is used in tumour-imaging agents
Glows blue-green under ultraviolet light, like all scorpions
Can survive long periods without food

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, other scorpions and small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry, rocky or sandy desert and scrub; shelters under stones and in burrows
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night, relying on venom rather than its slender pincers to subdue prey.
fieldMarks: Straw-yellow to pale yellow-brown body
Slender, weak-looking pincers
Long, thin tail with a darker last segment and sting
Five keels (ridges) along the back, giving the name quinquestriatus, 'five-striped'
animal.lookalikes: Other Leiurus species (e.g. L. hebraeus in the Levant) are separated by fine details and range. Fat-tailed scorpions (Androctonus) have much thicker tails and are often darker. Buthus species are similar but have different ridge patterns.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky desert in Egypt and Sudan, where it glows under ultraviolet light at night; best seen in zoos. Never handle it, and shake out shoes and bedding in its range.
animal.season: Year-round; most active on warm nights

lore: Scorpions were the emblem of Serqet, the ancient Egyptian goddess who healed stings and venomous bites. A peptide toxin from this scorpion's venom, charybdotoxin, became a standard tool for studying potassium channels.
funFact: An imaging drug derived from chlorotoxin, nicknamed 'Tumor Paint', has been tested in clinical trials to help surgeons see the edges of brain tumours.

wiki.extract: The deathstalker is a species of scorpion, a member of the family Buthidae. It is also known as the Palestine yellow scorpion, Omdurman scorpion, and Naqab desert scorpion, as well as by many other colloquial names, which generally originate from the commercial captive trade of the animal. To eliminate confusion, especially important with potentially dangerous species, the scientific name is normally used to refer to them. The name Leiurus quinquestriatus roughly translates into English as "five-striped smooth-tail". In 2014, the subspecies L. q. hebraeus was separated from it and elevated to its own species Leiurus hebraeus. Other species of the genus Leiurus are also often referred to as "deathstalkers". Leiurus quinquestriatus is yellow, and 30–77 millimetres (1.2–3.0 in) long, with an average of 58 mm (2.3 in).

They can be locally very numerous, leading to them sometimes being considered pests. As highly intelligent birds, they are well known in aviculture, although they can be demanding pets.

wiki.extract: The galah, less commonly known as the pink and grey cockatoo, galah cockatoo, or rose-breasted cockatoo, is an Australian species of cockatoo and the only member of the genus Eolophus. The galah is adapted to a wide variety of modified and unmodified habitats and is one of Australia's most abundant and widespread bird species. The species is endemic to mainland Australia. It was introduced to Tasmania, where it is now widespread, in the mid-20th century and much more recently to New Zealand.

wiki.extract:
The dromedary, also known as the dromedary camel, Arabian camel and one-humped camel, is a large camel of the genus Camelus with one hump on its back. It is the tallest of the three camel species; adult males stand 1.8–2.4 m (5.9–7.9 ft) at the shoulder, while females are 1.7–1.9 m (5.6–6.2 ft) tall. Males typically weigh between 400 and 690 kg, and females weigh between 300 and 540 kg .
The dromedary's distinctive features include its long, curved neck, narrow chest, a single hump, and long hairs on the throat, shoulders, and hump. The coat is generally a shade of brown. The hump is 20 cm (7.9 in) tall or more, and is made of fat bound together by fibrous tissue.

wiki.extract: The golden jackal, also called the common jackal, is a wolf-like canid that is native to Eurasia. The golden jackal's coat varies in color from a pale creamy yellow in summer to a dark tawny beige in winter. It is smaller and has shorter legs, a shorter tail, a more elongated torso, a less-prominent forehead, and a narrower and more pointed muzzle than the Arabian wolf. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List due to its widespread distribution and high density in areas with plenty of available food and optimum shelter.

wiki.extract: The wolf, also known as the grey wolf or gray wolf, is a canine native to Eurasia and North America. More than thirty subspecies of Canis lupus have been recognized, including the dog and dingo, though grey wolves, as popularly understood, include only naturally occurring wild subspecies. The wolf is the largest wild extant member of the family Canidae, and is further distinguished from other Canis species by its less pointed ears and muzzle, as well as a shorter torso and a longer tail. The wolf is nonetheless related closely enough to smaller Canis species, such as the coyote and the golden jackal, to produce fertile hybrids with them. The wolf's fur is usually mottled white, brown, grey, and black, although subspecies in the arctic region may be nearly all white.

summary: A long-legged, blotch-coated hunting dog of African savannas and one of the most successful pack hunters among large carnivores. Packs care for pups and injured members, feeding them by regurgitating meat.
nativeRange: Fragmented populations in eastern and southern Africa (Botswana, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Zambia, Kenya, South Africa, Mozambique) and a few in West Africa
abilities: Runs prey down over several kilometres, at up to ~60 km/h; often succeeds in most chases it starts
Packs 'vote' to start a hunt by sneezing; the more sneezes, the likelier they set off
Shares kills with pups and sick or injured pack members
Its coat pattern of black, yellow and white is unique to each dog

animal.diet: Carnivore: impala, kudu, gazelles, wildebeest calves
animal.habitat: Savanna, open woodland and semi-desert, with very large home ranges
animal.behaviour: Usually only the dominant pair breeds, and the whole pack helps raise the litter of up to 10–20 pups.
fieldMarks: Blotched coat of black, brown, yellow and white
Large round ears
White-tipped tail
Lean, long legs
animal.voice: Twittering, hoo calls and sneezes
animal.lookalikes: Spotted hyena has a sloping back, spots and round ears. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger (South Africa), Moremi (Okavango Delta) and Mana Pools (Zimbabwe)
animal.season: Southern Africa breeding Apr–Jul

lore: Coenraad Temminck described it in 1820 as Hyaena picta, 'painted hyena'; its genus name Lycaon, after the king turned into a wolf in Greek myth, came later. Conservationists have popularised the name 'painted wolf' to counter its old reputation as vermin.
funFact: Unlike other dogs, it has only four toes on each front foot.

wiki.extract: The African wild dog, also called painted dog and Cape hunting dog, is a wild canine native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is the largest wild canine in Africa and the only extant member of the genus Lycaon, which is distinguished from Canis by dentition highly specialised for a hypercarnivorous diet and by a lack of dewclaws.

summary: A small, slender fox of open plains, found only on the Indian subcontinent. It favours short grassland and semi-desert, avoiding dense forest, and hunts insects and rodents mostly at dusk and night.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh, from the Himalayan foothills to Tamil Nadu
abilities: Digs complex dens with several entrances, reused over many years
Eats large numbers of rodents, termites and crop pests
Pairs bond and both parents provision the pups

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, rodents, reptiles, birds' eggs and fruits such as ber and neem
animal.habitat: Open short grassland, scrub and semi-desert; avoids dense forest and steep terrain
animal.size: Body 45–60 cm plus a 25–35 cm tail; 2–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Rests in dens through the heat of day and is most active at dusk and early morning; pups are born in the dry season, around February–March.
fieldMarks: Small, long-legged grey fox with rufous legs
Bushy tail with a distinct black tip
Dark smudge on the muzzle in front of the eyes; ears dark-backed
Signs: dens with several entrances on low mounds in open ground, with scats full of insect parts and seeds
animal.lookalikes: Red fox (desert subspecies in the Thar and Pakistan) is larger, redder above and has a white tail tip. Golden jackal is larger, heavier, and has a less bushy tail without a black tip.
animal.whereToSee: Velavadar Blackbuck National Park and Little Rann of Kutch (Gujarat); Tal Chhapar and Desert National Park (Rajasthan); Rollapadu (Andhra Pradesh); Deccan grasslands around Pune and Bengaluru
animal.season: Resident; pups visible at dens around March–May

lore: Foxes and jackals play the cunning roles in the Panchatantra and Jataka tales. The species was described by George Shaw in 1800, hence the name, though it is now rare there.
funFact: Despite its name, the Bengal fox is now scarce in Bengal itself; its strongholds are the dry grasslands of western and peninsular India.

wiki.extract: The Bengal fox, also known as the Indian fox, is a fox endemic to the Indian subcontinent from the Himalayan foothills and Terai of Nepal through southern India, and from southern and eastern Pakistan to eastern India and southeastern Bangladesh.

summary: A small fox of the high Arctic with the warmest fur of any mammal, turning white in winter and brown-grey in summer (or bluish-grey year-round in the 'blue' morph). Arctic foxes follow polar bears to scavenge, cache lemmings and seabird eggs, and some cross sea ice for thousands of kilometres.
nativeRange: Circumpolar tundra of Eurasia and North America, Greenland, Iceland, Svalbard and the Commander and Pribilof Islands
abilities: Does not begin to shiver until the temperature falls to about −70 °C
A young female walked 3,500 km from Svalbard to Ellesmere Island, Canada, in 76 days across sea ice (2018)
Can have litters of up to about 20 pups in good lemming years

animal.diet: Lemmings and voles, seabirds and eggs, fish, carrion including polar-bear kill leftovers, berries
animal.habitat: Tundra, mountain plateaus, sea-ice margins and coastal cliffs
animal.behaviour: Dens are dug in sandy mounds and some are reused for centuries. Pairs raise pups together.
fieldMarks: Small, compact fox with short legs, short rounded ears and a short muzzle
Winter: pure white (white morph) or slate blue-grey (blue morph); summer: brownish-grey with paler belly
Very bushy tail and furred soles
Signs: dens on mounds with many entrances and lush green vegetation, fertilised by prey remains
animal.lookalikes: Red fox, increasingly moving north, is larger, redder, with larger pointed ears and longer legs. In white, distant snowshoe hare or ptarmigan may be mistaken briefly.
animal.whereToSee: Hornstrandir Nature Reserve (Iceland); Svalbard; Dovrefjell–Sunndalsfjella (Norway); Churchill (Manitoba); Commander Islands (Russia)
animal.season: Resident; white coat October–May

lore: The Arctic fox was Iceland's only native land mammal when the Norse arrived around 870 CE. In Finnish folklore, the aurora is 'revontulet', 'fox fires', said to be sparks from a fox's tail brushing the snow.
funFact: Its species name lagopus means 'hare-foot', for the dense fur that covers the soles of its feet.

wiki.extract: The Arctic fox, also known as the white fox, polar fox, or snow fox, is a small species of fox native to the Arctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere and common throughout the Arctic tundra. It is well adapted to living in cold environments, and is known for its thick, warm fur that can be used as camouflage against snow in the winter. It has a large and fluffy tail. In the wild, most individuals do not live past their first year but some exceptional ones survive up to 11 years. Its body length ranges from 46 to 68 cm, with a generally rounded body shape to minimize the escape of body heat.

summary: The most widely distributed wild carnivore on Earth, from the Arctic to the deserts of Pakistan and the suburbs of London. Its South Asian forms include the pale desert fox of the Thar and Balochistan and the thick-furred Himalayan red fox. Introduced in Australia, it has helped drive many small marsupials to extinction.
nativeRange: Across the Northern Hemisphere (Europe, Asia including northern South Asia, North Africa, North America); introduced to Australia
abilities: Hears rodents moving beneath snow and dives on them in a high arcing pounce
Caches surplus food and relocates it later by memory and smell
Adapts to cities, raising cubs under sheds and in railway embankments

animal.diet: Omnivore: rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, earthworms, fruit and scavenged food
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with cover, from tundra to desert to city centres
animal.lifespan: Usually 2–4 years in the wild; up to about 14
animal.size: Body 45–90 cm, tail 30–55 cm; 3–14 kg; desert forms smallest
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular. Pairs share a territory and may be helped by non-breeding young from previous litters.
fieldMarks: Rusty-orange coat with white throat and black-backed ears
Black 'stockings' on the lower legs
Long, bushy tail usually with a white tip
Tracks: neat oval prints about 5 cm long in a near-straight line; strong musky scent at scent posts and dens
animal.voice: Vixens give an eerie, drawn-out scream in winter; both sexes use a sharp triple bark, 'wow-wow-wow'.
animal.lookalikes: Bengal fox is smaller and greyer with a black (not white) tail tip. Golden jackal is larger, greyer, with a shorter tail and longer legs. Arctic fox is smaller-eared and white or blue-grey.
animal.whereToSee: Cities such as London and Bristol; Deosai and Khunjerab (Pakistan) and Ladakh for Himalayan foxes; Desert National Park and the Rann of Kutch for desert foxes; Hokkaido (Japan)
animal.season: Resident; cubs at dens April–June; vixen screams in mating season, December–February

lore: In Japan the kitsune is the messenger of the rice deity Inari, and fox statues guard thousands of Inari shrines. The medieval European beast-epic of Reynard the Fox satirised courts and clergy.
funFact: The Soviet geneticist Dmitry Belyaev bred tame foxes from 1959; within decades they wagged tails, had floppy ears and piebald coats.

wiki.extract: The red fox is the largest of the true foxes, and the most widely distributed member of the order Carnivora. It is present across the entire Northern Hemisphere, including most of North America, Europe and Asia, as well as parts of North Africa. Its range has expanded alongside human settlement, with the species having been introduced to Australia, where it preys on native small and medium-sized rodents and marsupials. The red fox is listed as of least concern on the IUCN Red List. Because of its impact on native species, it is included on the list of the "world's 100 worst invasive species".

summary: The smallest wild canid, a cream-coloured desert fox whose ears can be 15 cm long. Those huge ears give off body heat and pick up prey moving under the sand.
nativeRange: Sahara and adjoining deserts of North Africa, from Morocco and Mauritania to Egypt and Sudan; Sinai
abilities: Hears insects and rodents moving underground with its enormous ears
Sheds heat through ears full of blood vessels
Can go long periods without drinking, getting water from its food
Walks on hot sand with thickly furred soles
Can dig up to about 6 m of burrow in a single night

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, rodents, lizards, birds' eggs, roots and fruit
animal.habitat: Sandy desert and dune fields
animal.lifespan: ~10 years in the wild; up to 14+ in captivity
animal.size: 1–1.5 kg; body 24–40 cm, ears to 15 cm
animal.behaviour: Fennecs are nocturnal and live in family groups in sprawling burrows. Pairs often stay together for life.
fieldMarks: Smallest fox
Huge ears
Cream fur
Black-tipped tail
animal.lookalikes: Rüppell's fox is larger and greyer with smaller ears.
animal.whereToSee: Erg Chebbi (Morocco) and Douz (Tunisia)
animal.season: Resident; nocturnal

lore: The name comes from Arabic fanak, 'fox'. Algeria's national football team is nicknamed Les Fennecs, and the fox in Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (1943) is thought to have been inspired by fennecs he saw in the Sahara.
funFact: Relative to its body, the fennec has the largest ears of any canid.

wiki.extract: The fennec fox is a small fox native to the deserts of North Africa, ranging from Western Sahara and Mauritania to the Sinai Peninsula. Its most distinctive feature is its unusually large ears, which serve to dissipate heat and listen for underground prey. The fennec is the smallest fox species. Its coat, ears, and kidney functions have adapted to the desert environment with high temperatures and little water.

summary: A small ground beetle that defends itself with a boiling chemical explosion. Two harmless liquids stored in its abdomen are mixed with enzymes in a reaction chamber, firing a hot, caustic spray with an audible pop.
nativeRange: Europe, especially the south and west, east into western Asia
abilities: Mixes hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide with catalase and peroxidase enzymes to produce a spray near 100 °C
Fires the spray in rapid pulses with an audible crack
Can aim the spray by swivelling the tip of its abdomen

animal.diet: Adults are predators and scavengers of small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Warm, dry, sparsely vegetated ground, often on chalk and limestone; shelters under stones
animal.behaviour: When grabbed by an ant, spider or frog, it blasts the attacker with hot benzoquinones.
fieldMarks: Orange-red head, thorax and legs
Dark metallic blue to blue-green wing cases
Small, narrow ground-beetle shape
Often in groups under stones in dry grassland
animal.lookalikes: Brachinus explodens is smaller (5–7.5 mm) and very similar; a hand lens and key are needed. Other red-and-blue ground beetles (e.g. Lebia, Drypta) lack the defensive pop.
animal.whereToSee: Chalk downland and dry coastal grassland in southern England and continental Europe.
animal.season: Adults mainly Apr–Sep

lore: Linnaeus named it crepitans, 'crackling', in 1758 for its explosive defence. In the late 20th century it became a famous example in debates between creationists and evolutionary biologists over how complex traits evolve.
funFact: High-speed X-ray imaging of bombardier beetles in 2015 showed that each spray is a rapid series of pulses, with an inlet valve to the reaction chamber closing at each blast.

summary: A slender, long-finned shark of brilliant indigo that roams entire ocean basins. It is the most heavily fished shark in the world, with tens of millions taken each year, many for fins.
nativeRange: Temperate and tropical oceans worldwide
abilities: Makes trans-oceanic migrations, crossing the North Atlantic in a clockwise loop with the Gulf Stream
Females have skin up to three times thicker than males, protecting them from mating bites
Gives birth to large litters, sometimes over 100 pups
Dives repeatedly to more than 1,000 m in eddies to hunt squid
edibilityNote: Flesh needs bleeding and soaking to remove urea; contains elevated mercury. The fin trade drives its large catch.

animal.diet: Squid, small fish, also seabirds and carrion
animal.habitat: Open ocean, from the surface to over 1,000 m
animal.behaviour: Sexes and size classes often segregate geographically; nursery grounds are near the Azores and off Portugal.
fieldMarks: Very slender body with a long, pointed snout
Brilliant metallic indigo-blue back, bright blue sides, white belly
Very long, narrow, sickle-shaped pectoral fins
Large eyes and a low first dorsal fin set back on the body
animal.lookalikes: Shortfin mako is stockier with shorter pectorals and a crescent tail; oceanic whitetip has broad, rounded white-tipped fins.
animal.whereToSee: Offshore snorkel trips from Pico (Azores), Cape Point (South Africa), Cornwall and Rhode Island
animal.season: Azores Jul–Sep; Cornwall Jul–Sep

lore: Its genus name means 'saw' (prion) and its species name 'blue-grey' (glauca); in 2022 it was among the requiem sharks added to CITES Appendix II.
funFact: Blue sharks tagged off New England have been recaptured off Spain, Portugal and Brazil, thousands of kilometres away.

wiki.extract: The blue shark, also known as the great blue shark, is a species of requiem shark in the family Carcharhinidae which inhabits deep waters in the world's temperate and tropical oceans. It is the only living species of genus Prionace. An extinct species, P. clarki, is known from teeth from California of the Late Pliocene. Averaging around 3.1 m (10 ft) and preferring cooler waters, the blue shark migrates long distances, such as from New England to South America. It is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN.

summary: The largest living clam, reaching over 1.3 m long and 200 kg, that farms algae in its own flesh. Sunlight on its colourful mantle feeds the algae, which in turn feed the clam.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific: Great Barrier Reef, the Philippines, Indonesia, Micronesia and Melanesia; extinct in several former parts of its range
abilities: Hosts symbiotic zooxanthellae algae in its mantle, which supply most of its food
Iridescent cells in the mantle spread and shield light for the algae
One of the longest-lived invertebrates, possibly over 100 years
Filters plankton from seawater

animal.diet: Sugars from symbiotic algae, plus filtered plankton
animal.habitat: Sandy patches and reef flats in clear, shallow water, usually less than 20 m deep
animal.size: Shell up to about 1.4 m; weight over 200 kg
animal.behaviour: Adults sit hinge-down on sand, unattached, and spawn by releasing clouds of eggs and sperm into the water.
fieldMarks: Huge, heavy shell with four to six broad, deep folds
Wavy, interlocking shell margin
Golden-brown to olive mantle with iridescent blue-green spots
Lies free on the bottom; large adults cannot close fully
animal.lookalikes: Smooth giant clam (Tridacna derasa) has a smoother shell with lower ribs. Fluted giant clam (T. squamosa) has rows of scale-like flutes. Small giant clams (T. maxima, T. crocea) are much smaller and bore into coral.
animal.whereToSee: Reefs of the northern Great Barrier Reef (e.g. Lizard Island), Palau, and restocking sites in the Philippines (Bolinao, Pangasinan).
animal.season: Year-round

edibilityNote: The adductor muscle is prized in Asian cuisine; overharvesting for meat and shells caused its collapse. Only farmed animals should be eaten.
lore: Giant clam shells serve as holy-water fonts (bénitiers) in European churches, notably the pair in Saint-Sulpice, Paris, said to be a gift from the Republic of Venice to King Francis I.
funFact: The 'man-eating clam' that traps divers is a myth; adults close too slowly to trap anyone, and there is no reliable record of a death.

wiki.extract: Tridacna gigas, the giant clam, is the best-known species of the giant clam genus Tridacna. Giant clams are the largest living bivalve molluscs. Several other species of "giant clam" in the genus Tridacna are often misidentified as Tridacna gigas.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a giant clam shell, known in Chinese as chequ (車渠). It is part of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), a monumental work on natural history and pharmacology by Li Shizhen, illustrating the diverse range of natural substances used in traditional medicine.

plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr; Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch
plates.desc: A natural history plate featuring thirteen detailed watercolor illustrations of bivalve shells (Conchæ bivalviæ). The shells vary in shape, color, and texture, including ribbed cockles, a large fluted giant clam, spiny oysters, and heart-shaped shells. Several specimens are annotated with handwritten German and Latin names.
plates.long: This 1770 plate from 'Schnecken und Muscheln' displays thirteen meticulously rendered bivalve shells, including cockles, clams, and oysters. Each specimen is identified by its Latin and German names, reflecting the era's burgeoning interest in systematic natural history and the aesthetic appreciation of the natural world.

summary: A crested, thick-billed songbird whose scarlet males are the most familiar red bird of eastern North America. Unusually among North American songbirds, females sing too, sometimes from the nest itself, and pairs stay together year-round.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America from southern Canada through the eastern US to Mexico, Belize and northern Guatemala; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Both sexes sing; female song often signals the male to bring food to the nest
Heavy conical bill cracks hard seeds such as sunflower and safflower
Has expanded its range far northward over the past century, helped by bird feeders and suburban shrubbery
Red plumage comes from carotenoid pigments in its diet

animal.diet: Seeds, fruit and insects; nestlings fed mostly insects
animal.habitat: Thickets, woodland edges, hedgerows, suburban gardens and desert washes
animal.lifespan: Usually under 3 years in the wild; banding record about 15 years
animal.behaviour: Territorial males (and sometimes females) attack their own reflections in windows and car mirrors in spring, sometimes for hours.
fieldMarks: Male entirely red with a black face mask around a thick red-orange bill
Prominent pointed crest in both sexes
Female warm buff-brown with reddish tinges on crest, wings and tail
Long tail; juveniles have a dark bill
animal.voice: Loud, clear, slurred whistles repeated in series, often rendered 'cheer-cheer-cheer' or 'birdie-birdie-birdie'; call a sharp metallic 'chip'.
animal.lookalikes: Pyrrhuloxia (south-western US and Mexico) is grey with a red crest and a stubby yellow bill. Summer Tanager males are all red but lack the crest and black face. Scarlet Tanager has black wings.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any eastern US backyard feeder, park or thicket; common through the south-east and Mississippi Valley.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Named after the red robes of Roman Catholic cardinals, it is the official state bird of seven US states — Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, Virginia and West Virginia — more than any other species.
funFact: Linnaeus first named it Loxia cardinalis in 1758, putting it in the same genus as crossbills.

wiki.extract: The northern cardinal, also commonly known as the common cardinal, red cardinal, or simply cardinal, is a bird in the genus Cardinalis. It can be found in southeastern Canada, through the eastern United States from Maine to Minnesota to Texas, New Mexico, southern Arizona, southern California and south through Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala. It is also an introduced species in a few locations such as Bermuda and all major islands of Hawaii since its introduction in 1929. Its habitat includes woodlands, gardens, shrublands, and wetlands. It is the state bird of Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia.

summary: The male is perhaps the most colourful songbird in North America — blue head, red underparts and a lime-green back. Females are the only bright green finch-like bird in their range, and the species was long trapped as a cage bird.
nativeRange: Breeds in two separate populations — the south-eastern Atlantic coast (North Carolina to Florida) and the south-central US and northern Mexico; winters in Florida, the Bahamas, Cuba, Mexico and Central America to Panama
abilities: Western birds pause in the south-western US and north-western Mexico to moult before finishing migration — an unusual 'moult migration'
Males do not reach full colour until their second autumn; first-year males look like females
Males fight fiercely over territories, sometimes drawing blood

animal.diet: Grass and weed seeds; insects in the breeding season
animal.habitat: Brushy thickets, woodland edges, maritime scrub and overgrown fields
animal.behaviour: Despite the male's colours, it is secretive and sings from within cover more often than from open perches.
fieldMarks: Adult male: deep blue head, red eye-ring, red underparts and rump, yellow-green back
Female and immature: bright, uniform yellowish-green with a pale eye-ring
Short conical bill typical of buntings
Small, compact size
animal.voice: A sweet, high, run-on warble of musical notes; call a soft 'chip'.
animal.lookalikes: Female Indigo Bunting is brown, not green. Varied Bunting males are dark purple with a red nape. Green female could suggest a vireo or warbler, but the stubby conical bill identifies it.
animal.whereToSee: Coastal thickets of South Carolina, Georgia and north-east Florida; Texas Hill Country; feeders in south Florida in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor in the US, Apr–Sep; winters in Florida and the tropics

lore: Mark Catesby painted it as 'The Painted Finch' in the 1730s, and it was exported to Europe as a cage bird; in the Caribbean and Mexico trapping for the pet trade continues to threaten it.
funFact: Its French name nonpareil means 'without equal'.

wiki.extract: The painted bunting is a species of bird in the cardinal family, Cardinalidae. It is native to North America. The bright plumage of the male develops beginning in the second year of life; in the first year, they can be distinguished from the female only by close inspection.

The vibrant colors and meticulous detail reflect the 18th-century's growing scientific interest

summary: A blazing red bird with jet-black wings that sings unseen high in the canopy of eastern forests. After breeding the male turns yellow-green, keeping only his black wings, before flying to the Andes for the winter.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters in north-western South America, mainly along the eastern Andean foothills from Colombia to Bolivia
abilities: Undergoes a complete colour change: scarlet in summer, olive-yellow in autumn and winter
Migrates thousands of kilometres between the US and South America
Gleans caterpillars from the high canopy, controlling forest insect pests

animal.diet: Caterpillars, beetles and other canopy insects; fruit in autumn
animal.habitat: Large tracts of mature deciduous and oak–hickory forest
animal.behaviour: It is sensitive to forest fragmentation and is scarce or absent in small woodlots.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: brilliant scarlet body with solid black wings and tail
Female and winter male: olive-green above, yellow below, with dark wings
No wing bars
Stout, pale, rather blunt bill
animal.voice: A hoarse, burry series of phrases, often described as 'a robin with a sore throat'; call a distinctive 'chick-burr'.
animal.lookalikes: Summer Tanager male is entirely rose-red including the wings. Northern Cardinal has a crest and a black face. Western Tanager has wing bars; female orioles have pointed bills and wing bars.
animal.whereToSee: Mature oak forests of the eastern US, e.g. the Appalachians; on migration at sites such as Magee Marsh (Ohio) and Central Park (New York) in May.
animal.season: Summer visitor, May–Sep

funFact: Its species name olivacea ('olive-green') describes the plumage of females and young birds, not the scarlet breeding male.

wiki.extract:
The scarlet tanager is a medium-sized American songbird in the cardinal family (Cardinalidae). It was placed in the tanager family (Thraupidae) until 2009, but was moved to Cardinalidae following several genetic studies indicating the Piranga tanagers are more closely related to cardinals and their allies. Breeding males have bright red plumage with black wings and tails, while females are yellow-olive. Outside the breeding season, males develop plumage similar to that of females, although their wings and tails remain darker. 
The species breeds mainly in large deciduous forests in eastern North America. It migrates through Central America to spend the winter in forests along the Andean foothills of northwestern South America. Scarlet tanagers feed mainly on insects, but they also eat fruit when it is available. Habitat fragmentation can increase nest predation and brood parasitism, and populations are declining in some areas. However, the species is classified as Least Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

summary: North America's largest rodent and one of its most important ecosystem engineers. Beaver dams turn streams into ponds and wetlands that store water, trap sediment and shelter fish, amphibians and birds.
nativeRange: Most of North America from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico; introduced to Tierra del Fuego and Finland
abilities: Fells trees with self-sharpening incisors whose front enamel is strengthened with iron, giving it an orange colour
Builds dams of logs, mud and stone and repairs leaks it hears or feels flowing
Stays underwater for up to ~15 minutes, with ears and nostrils that close and clear membranes over the eyes
Creates wetlands that raise water tables and act as firebreaks during wildfires

animal.diet: Herbivore: bark, cambium, twigs and leaves of willow, aspen and other trees; aquatic plants
animal.habitat: Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes bordered by trees
animal.size: 11–32 kg; 0.9–1.2 m including the flat tail
animal.behaviour: Families live in a domed lodge with underwater entrances and store branches in the pond mud as a winter food cache. A tail slap on the water warns the colony of danger.
fieldMarks: Large brown rodent with a flat, scaly, paddle-shaped tail
Orange front teeth
Swims low with only the head showing
Dams, lodges and gnawed tree stumps nearby
animal.voice: Slaps its tail loudly on the water when alarmed
animal.lookalikes: Muskrat is much smaller with a thin tail. Nutria has white whiskers and a round, rat-like tail. Otters swim with a long tapering tail.
animal.whereToSee: Algonquin Provincial Park (Ontario); Grand Teton and Rocky Mountain national parks
animal.season: Resident; most active at dawn and dusk

uses.use: Castoreum, the scent-gland secretion of beavers, was prescribed for headaches, fevers and 'hysteria'
Castoreum used in remedies for pain and as a scent lure

compounds: salicylic acid derivatives (from willow bark in the diet)
medicinal.cautions: Historical use only; castoreum is not a recognised modern medicine.

lore: Demand for beaver-felt hats drove the fur trade that mapped much of Canada; the Hudson's Bay Company (1670) priced goods in 'made beaver' pelts. In Anishinaabe tradition, Amik is among the animals that dive to bring up mud to make the world.
funFact: A beaver dam in Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada, is about 850 m long and can be seen in satellite images.

wiki.extract: The North American beaver is one of two extant beaver species, along with the Eurasian beaver. It is native to North America and has been introduced in South America (Patagonia) and Europe. The North American beaver is one of the national symbols of Canada and the official state mammal of Oregon and New York. North American beavers are widespread across the continental United States, Canada, southern Alaska, and some parts of northern Mexico.

According to bestiary tradition, when pursued by hunters for its medicinal glands, the beaver would bite off its own testicles and leave them for the hunter to save its life, serving as a moral allegory for man sacrificing his sins to escape the devil.

The illustration serves as a primary visual reference for the accompanying text, which synthesizes classical knowledge from authors like Aristotle and Aelianus to identify and classify amphibious species. summary: A towering, flightless rainforest bird with a bony casque and a dagger-like inner claw. It is a crucial seed disperser for rainforest trees, swallowing fruit whole and depositing seeds far away.
nativeRange: Northern Queensland, New Guinea and nearby islands
abilities: Disperses seeds of more than 200 plant species, some almost entirely dependent on it
Inner toe bears a claw up to about 12 cm long, a formidable weapon
Low-frequency booming calls may be partly below human hearing
Swims well and can run at up to around 50 km/h through forest

animal.diet: Fallen fruit, fungi, invertebrates and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Tropical rainforest, swamp forest, adjacent woodland
animal.lifespan: Up to about 40 years in captivity
animal.size: 1.5–1.8 m tall; females up to about 60–70 kg
animal.behaviour: The male alone incubates the eggs for about 50 days and raises the striped chicks for up to nine months.
fieldMarks: Very large, black, hair-like plumage
Tall, helmet-like brown casque
Bright blue neck with two red wattles
Massive grey legs with three toes
Juveniles brown; chicks striped
animal.voice: Deep, rumbling booms and low hisses; mostly heard at close range.
animal.lookalikes: Emu is grey-brown and lacks the casque and wattles; it lives in open country. In New Guinea, northern and dwarf cassowaries have different wattle patterns (one or none).
animal.whereToSee: Mission Beach and Etty Bay (Queensland), Daintree, Cape York; New Guinea lowlands
animal.season: Resident

lore: A 2021 study of ancient eggshell suggested people in New Guinea may have collected and raised cassowary chicks as long as 18,000 years ago, and cassowary-bone daggers were made there into the 20th century.
funFact: Although listed as Least Concern globally, the Australian population is listed as Endangered under Australian law.

wiki.extract: The southern cassowary, also known as double-wattled cassowary, Australian cassowary, or two-wattled cassowary, is a large, flightless, mostly black bird, found in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and northeastern Australia. It is one of the three living species of cassowary, alongside the dwarf cassowary and the northern cassowary. It is a ratite and therefore related to the emu, ostrich, rhea and kiwi. Southern cassowaries are among the largest birds in the world, only weighing less than ostriches.

summary: Australia's tallest bird and the world's second-tallest, a shaggy-feathered nomad of the outback. It walks long distances following rain, and the male raises the chicks alone.
nativeRange: Mainland Australia
abilities: Can run at about 50 km/h
Makes long nomadic movements following rains
Males incubate eggs for around eight weeks, barely eating or drinking
Females make deep drumming calls via an inflatable throat sac

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds, flowers, green shoots and insects
animal.habitat: Most habitats except dense rainforest and the driest deserts
animal.behaviour: After laying, the female leaves and may mate again, while the male guards the clutch and then the striped chicks for months.
fieldMarks: Very tall, shaggy grey-brown plumage
Bare blue-grey skin on neck
Long, strong legs
Tiny vestigial wings, hidden in the plumage
Chicks have cream-and-brown stripes
animal.voice: Females make a deep, booming drum or thump; males grunt.
animal.lookalikes: Southern cassowary (rainforest, Queensland) is black with a casque and blue-and-red neck. Ostriches (feral, rare) have black-and-white or brown plumage and two-toed feet.
animal.whereToSee: Common in outback NSW, Queensland and Western Australia; Wilsons Promontory, Tower Hill (Victoria), Kalbarri
animal.season: Resident, nomadic

lore: Many Aboriginal peoples see the 'Emu in the Sky', formed by dark dust lanes of the Milky Way. In 1932 Western Australian authorities waged the so-called 'Emu War' with machine guns and largely failed.
funFact: The emu appears on Australia's coat of arms alongside the red kangaroo.

wiki.extract: The emu is a species of flightless bird endemic to Australia, where it is the tallest native bird. It is the only extant member of the genus Dromaius and the third-tallest living bird after its African ratite relatives, the common ostrich and Somali ostrich. The emu's native ranges cover most of the Australian mainland. The Tasmanian, Kangaroo Island and King Island subspecies became extinct after the European settlement of Australia in 1788.

summary: North America's largest flying land bird, with a wingspan near 3 m. It went extinct in the wild in 1987 when the last wild bird was captured, leaving 27 condors, all in captivity; captive breeding and releases have since rebuilt the population to several hundred.
nativeRange: Formerly much of western North America (Pleistocene range continent-wide); reintroduced in California, Arizona–Utah, northern Baja California and, since 2022, the Pacific Northwest
abilities: Soars for hours on thermals and covers well over 200 km in a day
Wingspan up to about 2.9 m
Can live 60 years or more
Lays one egg every one to two years

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals — deer, cattle, marine mammals
animal.habitat: Rugged mountains, canyons and coastal ranges with open foraging country
animal.size: 117–134 cm; wingspan up to about 2.9 m; 8–14 kg
animal.behaviour: Wild-released birds carry numbered wing tags and GPS transmitters so biologists can trap and test them for lead poisoning.
fieldMarks: Very large, black, with white triangular linings on the underwing
Adults have a bare orange-pink head; juveniles a dusky grey head
Black ruff of feathers around the neck
Flat, steady soaring with long, fingered primaries; usually carries numbered wing tags
animal.voice: No song; hisses and grunts at carcasses.
animal.lookalikes: Turkey Vulture is much smaller, rocks in flight and shows silvery flight feathers (not white linings). Golden Eagle has a feathered head and a longer tail with no white underwing triangle in adults.
animal.whereToSee: Vermilion Cliffs National Monument and the South Rim of the Grand Canyon (Arizona), Pinnacles National Park and Big Sur (California), Zion National Park (Utah).
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Yurok people of northern California, who call it prey-go-neesh, regard it as a sacred bird; in 2022 the Yurok Tribe began releasing condors in Redwood National Park.
funFact: By the end of 2025 the US Fish and Wildlife Service counted 607 California condors, 392 of them flying free; lead poisoning from ammunition fragments remains the main cause of death.

wiki.extract: The California condor is a New World vulture and the largest North American land bird. It became extinct in the wild in 1987 when all remaining wild individuals were captured, but has since been reintroduced to northern Arizona and southern Utah, the coastal mountains of California, and northern Baja California in Mexico. It is the only surviving member of the genus Gymnogyps, although four extinct members of the genus are also known. The species is listed by IUCN as critically endangered, and similarly considered Critically Imperiled by NatureServe.

summary: A creamy-white vulture with a bare head painted orange, purple, red and yellow. Other vultures usually find carcasses first, but the king vulture's powerful bill opens tough hides that smaller species cannot.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina
abilities: Tears open large carcasses, giving other scavengers access
Follows smell-guided Turkey and Yellow-headed Vultures to food hidden under forest canopy
Soars for long periods on flat wings over rainforest

animal.diet: Carrion; occasionally weak or newborn animals
animal.habitat: Lowland forest and adjacent savanna, mainly below 1,500 m
animal.behaviour: At carcasses it usually displaces Black and Turkey Vultures.
fieldMarks: Creamy-white body with black flight feathers and tail
Bare, multicoloured head and neck with an orange fleshy caruncle on the bill
Thick grey ruff
White eye with red eye-ring; juveniles all dark
animal.voice: Generally silent; low croaks and bill-snaps.
animal.lookalikes: Wood Stork has long legs and a long neck in flight. Immature king vultures are dark and resemble Black Vultures but are larger with some colour on the head.
animal.whereToSee: Over rainforest in Belize, Costa Rica (Osa Peninsula), Panama and the Amazon; at feeding stations in Brazil and Costa Rica.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Maya depicted the king vulture in their codices, and its Nahuatl name cozcacuauhtli also named the 16th day of the Aztec calendar.
funFact: Spanish 'zopilote rey' reflects an old belief that it was the king the other vultures stood back for.

wiki.extract: The king vulture is a large bird found in Central and South America. It is a member of the New World vulture family Cathartidae. This vulture lives predominantly in tropical lowland forests stretching from southern Mexico to northern Argentina. It is the only surviving member of the genus Sarcoramphus, although fossil members are known.

plates.author: François Bouchard
plates.desc: A hand-colored natural history illustration of a King Vulture (Sarcoramphus papa) perched on a rock. The bird is depicted in profile facing right, featuring a white and tan body with black wing feathers, a white ruff around the neck, and a distinctive fleshy red and orange head with a caruncle over the beak. The rock is situated near a small body of water with reeds and green foliage. The entire scene is enclosed in a yellow rectangular border, with the species names written in Italian, Latin, and French in the bottom margin of the frame.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a King Vulture (Sarcoramphus papa), identified by its distinctive colorful head and caruncle. Perched on a rock within a stylized landscape, the illustration reflects the 18th-century interest in documenting exotic species with scientific accuracy and artistic flair. The labels at the bottom identify the bird in Italian (Avoltoio Indiano), Latin (Vultur Indicus

summary: One of the heaviest flying birds on Earth, with a wingspan of over 3 m, it soars over the Andes and Patagonian coast in search of carcasses. It is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador.
nativeRange: Andes from Venezuela and Colombia to Tierra del Fuego, and adjacent Pacific coasts and Patagonian lowlands
abilities: Wingspan up to about 3.3 m and weight up to about 15 kg
A tracking study found condors flapped only about 1% of their flight time, one bird flying over 170 km in five hours without flapping (Williams et al., PNAS, 2020)
Rides thermals and slope winds to cover over 200 km a day
Lays a single egg, usually every two years

animal.diet: Carrion of large mammals — llamas, guanacos, cattle; marine mammal carcasses on the coast
animal.habitat: Open mountains, high plateaus and coasts with cliffs for roosting and nesting
animal.lifespan: Over 50 years; captive birds have exceeded 70
animal.behaviour: Males are larger than females, unusual among raptors, and carry a fleshy comb on the head.
fieldMarks: Black plumage with a white neck ruff
Large white panels on the upper wing (secondaries)
Bare grey-red head; male with a dark fleshy comb (caruncle)
Long, broad wings with deeply 'fingered' primaries
animal.voice: Almost silent; lacking a syrinx-driven song, it hisses and clucks at carcasses and roosts.
animal.lookalikes: California Condor (no range overlap) has white underwing linings rather than upper-wing panels and lacks the white ruff. Black Vulture and Turkey Vulture are far smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Cruz del Cóndor, Colca Canyon (Peru); Torres del Paine (Chile); Quebrada del Condorito (Argentina); the Antisana reserve (Ecuador).
animal.season: Resident year-round; Colca viewing best in the morning, Jun–Oct

lore: For the Inca, the kuntur was a messenger of the upper world (Hanan Pacha), and in the Peruvian Yawar Fiesta a condor was tied to a bull's back to symbolise the struggle of Andean and Spanish cultures.
funFact: Its species name gryphus refers to the griffin of legend.
