wiki.extract: The Andean condor is a South American New World vulture and is the only extant member of the genus Vultur. It is found in the Andes mountains and adjacent Pacific coasts of western South America. With a maximum wingspan of 3.3 m and weight of 15 kg (33 lb), the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world, and is generally considered to be the largest bird of prey in the world.

In the accompanying text, Kircher attempts to rationalize the creature's existence by suggesting it may be a real, large bird species from Tartary rather than a purely fabled beast. This illustration reflects the 17th-ce

summary: The world's largest rodent, a semi-aquatic grazer of South American wetlands that lives in social groups and seldom strays far from water. With partly webbed feet and eyes, ears and nostrils set high on its head, it can lie almost submerged. Birds, monkeys and other animals often perch on or lounge beside it.
nativeRange: South America east of the Andes, from Colombia and Venezuela to northeastern Argentina and Uruguay; also Panama
abilities: Can stay submerged for about five minutes and sleep in the water with only its nose exposed
Re-ingests its own soft droppings to extract more nutrients from grass
Teeth grow continuously to cope with abrasive grasses

animal.diet: Grasses, aquatic plants, bark and fruit; selective grazer
animal.habitat: Marshes, rivers, lakes and flooded grasslands with nearby dry ground
animal.behaviour: Lives in groups of 10–20 led by a dominant male; groups merge into hundreds in the dry season around remaining water.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: barrel-shaped, tailless, blunt-headed rodent the size of a large dog
Coarse, sparse reddish-brown to grey hair
Dominant males have a large, bare scent gland ('morrillo') on the top of the snout
Tracks: four toes on front feet, three on hind, partly webbed; signs include grazing lawns and droppings near water
animal.voice: Barks sharply in alarm; also whistles, clicks, purrs and grunts within the group.
animal.lookalikes: Lowland paca is smaller with white spotted rows on its flanks. Coypu (nutria) is much smaller with a long rat-like tail and orange incisors.
animal.whereToSee: Esteros del Iberá (Argentina); Pantanal (Brazil); Los Llanos, e.g. Hato El Cedral (Venezuela); Lago Paranoá and city parks in Brasília and Curitiba (Brazil)
animal.season: Resident year-round; dry-season gatherings around shrinking water bodies (roughly July–October in the Pantanal)

lore: Venezuelan Catholics traditionally eat salted capybara (chigüire) during Lent, a custom said to rest on a colonial-era church ruling that the semi-aquatic animal counted as fish. Its name comes from Tupi ka'apiûara, usually translated 'grass-eater'.
funFact: The Brazilian city of Curitiba and the wealthy Nordelta suburb of Buenos Aires both have well-known urban capybara populations.

wiki.extract: The capybara or greater capybara is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile. It is a semiaquatic herbivore that inhabits savannas and dense forests, living near and in bodies of freshwater and feeding mainly on grasses and aquatic plants.

plates.title: Historia naturalis Brasiliae
plates.author: Willem Piso / Georg Marcgraf
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a capybara, shown in profile with detailed fur and facial features.
plates.long: A detailed illustration of a capybara, identified in the accompanying Latin text as a 'water pig' from Brazil. This image serves as a significant early record of South American biodiversity as it was first being categorized by European naturalists.

plates.title: De Indiae utriusque re naturali et medica
plates.author: Willem Piso
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a capybara, shown in profile facing left.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a capybara, the world's largest rodent, as described in a 17th-century natural history text. The illustration captures the animal's distinctive heavy-set body and blunt head, reflecting the era's efforts to document New World fauna for European audiences.

otherNames: Burakku basu ブラックバス (Japanese)
summary: North America's most popular sport fish and the centre of a multibillion-dollar bass-fishing industry. It is a big-mouthed ambush hunter of weedy lakes, and introductions have made it a damaging invader in Japan, southern Africa and Europe.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America: Great Lakes, Mississippi basin and Atlantic and Gulf slope drainages (peninsular Florida fish are now treated as the separate Florida bass); introduced worldwide
abilities: Its jaw opens wide enough to swallow prey nearly half its own length, including frogs, mice and small birds
Males sweep out a nest and guard eggs and fry aggressively for weeks
Hunts by ambush from cover, using vision and lateral-line senses
edibilityNote: Mild white flesh, though most anglers release bass. Large bass from many lakes carry mercury advisories. Always cooked.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crayfish, frogs and insects; occasionally snakes, mice and ducklings
animal.habitat: Warm, clear to slightly turbid lakes, ponds, reservoirs and slow rivers with plants, logs and other cover
animal.lifespan: Up to about 16 years, rarely over 20
animal.size: Commonly 30–55 cm; up to about 75 cm and 10 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring the male fans a saucer-shaped nest in the shallows, drives off intruders, and guards the swarm of fry until they disperse.
fieldMarks: Upper jaw extends behind the rear edge of the eye (in adults)
Dark, ragged horizontal band or row of blotches along each green flank
Spiny and soft dorsal fins almost separated by a deep notch
Greenish-olive back and pale belly
animal.lookalikes: Smallmouth bass (M. dolomieu) is bronze-brown with vertical bars, and its jaw ends below the eye. Spotted bass (M. punctulatus) has rows of small dark spots on the lower flanks and a tooth patch on the tongue. Florida bass (M. floridanus) is told apart mainly by genetics and range.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Okeechobee (Florida bass); Lake Guntersville (Alabama); Lake Biwa (Japan, introduced); reservoirs of the US South
animal.season: Resident; spawns in spring once water reaches about 16–20 °C (Feb in the south to June in the north)

lore: George Perry caught a 22 lb 4 oz (10.1 kg) largemouth in Montgomery Lake, Georgia, in 1932, the most famous record in American angling. Manabu Kurita equalled it at Lake Biwa, Japan, in 2009.
funFact: Most field guides still call it Micropterus salmoides. A recent taxonomic review concluded that the older name M. nigricans belongs to the largemouth, and iNaturalist has adopted it.

wiki.extract: The largemouth bass is a carnivorous, freshwater, ray-finned fish in the Centrarchidae (sunfish) family, native to the eastern and central United States, southeastern Canada and northern Mexico. It is known by a variety of regional names, such as the widemouth bass, bigmouth bass, black bass, largie, potter's fish, Florida bass or Florida largemouth, green bass, bucketmouth bass, green trout, growler, Gilsdorf bass, Oswego bass, southern largemouth, northern largemouth, Alabama bass or Alabama largemouth, marsh bass, and swamp bass.

summary: A small, lime-green frog of Central and South American streamsides whose belly is so transparent that its beating heart can be seen. Males guard egg clutches on the undersides of leaves hanging over the water.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela (some northern South American populations have been split as separate species)
abilities: When sleeping it hides almost 90% of its red blood cells in its liver, becoming two to three times more transparent
Its translucent body helps it blend into leaves by softening its outline
Males guard eggs for weeks, protecting them from wasps and fungus

animal.diet: Small insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Vegetation along streams in lowland and montane rainforest
animal.behaviour: Males call from the underside of leaves over streams on rainy nights and guard the eggs. Hatching tadpoles drop into the stream below.
fieldMarks: Small, flat frog, lime-green with tiny yellow spots
Translucent belly through which the heart and organs can be seen
Large eyes facing forward, with gold irises
Often found on the undersides of leaves over streams
animal.voice: A high-pitched, rising 'peep' or 'wheet', repeated at intervals
animal.lookalikes: Many glass frogs look alike. The reticulated glass frog (H. valerioi) has a net of yellow lines on its back. Emerald glass frogs (Espadarana prosoblepon) have green bones and a white spine on the arm of males. A close view of the underside and the call help with identification.
animal.whereToSee: Streams at La Selva, Monteverde and Arenal (Costa Rica), Panama's Chiriquí highlands; night walks in the rainy season
animal.season: Breeds in the rainy season

lore: Oskar Boettger described it in 1893 from Costa Rican specimens and named it after Carl Fleischmann, who collected them.
funFact: A 2022 study in Science showed that sleeping frogs of this species pack red blood cells into their liver without blood clots forming, which interests researchers studying clotting disorders.

wiki.extract:
Hyalinobatrachium fleischmanni, also known as Fleischmann's glass frog or the northern glass frog, is a species of frog in the family Centrolenidae.
It is found in the tropical Americas from southern Mexico to Ecuador. Specifically, these frogs occur in Mexico, Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama, Colombia, and Ecuador. It has often been confused with related species, and the exact distribution depends on the source. This frog tends to have green skin, pale yellowish spots, yellow fingertips and translucent skin covering its stomach.

summary: The northernmost non-human primate, a red-faced monkey that survives snowy winters in the mountains of Japan. Some troops have learned habits, like bathing in hot springs, that spread from monkey to monkey, an early example of animal culture.
nativeRange: Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and nearby small islands, Japan
abilities: Survives winters at −15 °C with thick fur and by huddling
Troops at Jigokudani soak in volcanic hot springs in winter, which lowers their stress hormones
On Kōshima, a young female named Imo started washing sweet potatoes in the sea in 1953, and the habit spread through the troop
Some troops roll snowballs for play

animal.diet: Omnivore: fruit, seeds, leaves, bark, insects; bark and buds in winter
animal.habitat: Subtropical to subalpine forests
animal.size: Males ~10–14 kg; females ~8–10 kg; short tail
animal.behaviour: Troops are organised around ranked lines of related females. Males leave their birth troop and join others.
fieldMarks: Thick grey-brown fur
Red face and rump
Short tail
Bathes in hot springs
animal.voice: Coos and barks
animal.lookalikes: The only monkey in Japan.
animal.whereToSee: Jigokudani Monkey Park (Nagano)
animal.season: Hot-spring bathing best Dec–Mar

lore: The 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil' monkeys carved at the Tōshō-gū shrine in Nikkō (17th century) are Japanese macaques. Monkeys are messengers of the Sannō deity at Hiyoshi Taisha shrine.
funFact: The hot-spring bathing began in 1963, when a young female at Jigokudani followed soybeans into a pool and others copied her.

wiki.extract: The Japanese macaque, also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan. Colloquially, this macaque is referred to as the "snow monkey", because some live in areas where snow covers the ground for months each year. No other non-human primate lives farther north, nor in a colder climate. It has brownish grey fur, a pinkish-red face, and a short tail. Two subspecies are known.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui (Vol. 92)
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a 'wèi' (a type of long-tailed monkey) sitting on a rock.
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts a 'wèi', a type of long-tailed monkey. The creature is shown in a contemplative pose, seated on a rock beside a leafy plant, showcasing the Ming dynasty's approach to natural history illustration which combined observation with artistic stylization.

plates.title: Valeriano: Hieroglyphica (1575)
plates.author: Pierio Valeriano
plates.desc: Woodcut of a Cynocephalus (dog-headed monkey) lying on the ground, labeled 'LVNA' (Moon).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Cynocephalus, or dog-headed monkey, an animal of great significance in Egyptian hieroglyphics as interpreted during the Renaissance. Positioned under the label 'LVNA' (Moon), it illustrates the belief that these creatures had a mystical, sympathetic connection to the lunar cycles, a central theme in Valeriano's encyclopedic work on symbols.

plates.title: Historia naturalis Brasiliae
plates.author: Willem Piso / Georg Marcgraf
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a monkey, identified in the text as a 'Guariba' (howler monkey), featuring a long prehensile tail.
plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a Guariba, or howler monkey, characterized by its distinctive prehensile tail and robust form. Such illustrations were crucial for disseminating knowledge about the diverse wildlife of the Americas to a European audience during the 17th century.

summary: The familiar temple and street monkey of northern South Asia and China, with the widest range of any non-human primate. It has shaped modern medicine: the Rh blood factor is named after it, and rhesus monkeys were central to polio vaccine development and early spaceflight.
nativeRange: Afghanistan and Pakistan east through northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and Indochina to China; introduced in Florida and Puerto Rico
abilities: Lives from sea-level mangroves to Himalayan forests above 3,000 m and in big cities
Swims well and readily crosses rivers
Stores food in cheek pouches to eat later in safety

animal.diet: Omnivore: fruits, seeds, leaves, roots, insects and human food
animal.habitat: Forests of many kinds, farmland, temples and towns
animal.lifespan: About 25 years; up to 40 in captivity
animal.size: Body 45–64 cm, tail 20–30 cm; males about 7–12 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in multi-male, multi-female troops with strict female dominance hierarchies inherited from mothers to daughters.
fieldMarks: Brown-grey monkey with an orange-red rump and lower back
Bare pink to red face and rump
Medium-length tail (shorter than body)
Signs: bold troops around temples, roadsides and picnic spots
animal.lookalikes: Bonnet macaque (south India) has a cap of hair parted in the middle and a longer tail. Assamese macaque is darker and lacks the orange rump. Langurs have black faces and very long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Temples of Vrindavan and Varanasi; Delhi Ridge; Murree and Margalla Hills (Pakistan); Corbett and Kaziranga national parks; Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico (free-ranging research colony)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Monkeys around Hindu temples are fed as associates of Hanuman, the monkey-god of the Ramayana. India banned the export of rhesus monkeys in 1978 after decades of supplying laboratories worldwide.
funFact: A rhesus monkey named Albert II became the first primate in space in June 1949, aboard a V-2 rocket launched from New Mexico.

wiki.extract: The rhesus macaque, colloquially rhesus monkey, is a species of Old World monkey in the Macaca genus. There are between six and nine recognised subspecies split between two groups, the Chinese-derived and the Indian-derived. Generally brown or grey in colour, it is 47–53 cm (19–21 in) in length with a 20.7–22.9 cm (8.1–9.0 in) tail and weighs 5.3–7.7 kg (12–17 lb). It is native to South, Central, and Southeast Asia and has the widest geographic range of all non-human primates, occupying a great diversity of altitudes and habitats.

plates.title: Jean Baptiste Audebert — Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis (1800)
plates.author: Jean Baptiste Audebert
plates.desc: A detailed color engraving of a monkey, identified as 'Le Maimon' (Southern pig-tailed macaque), shown in profile sitting on its haunches.
plates.long: This detailed color engraving depicts 'Le Maimon,' now known as the Southern pig-tailed macaque (Macaca nemestrina). Created by Jean Baptiste Audebert for his seminal work on primates, it showcases the artist's pioneering use of color printing in natural history, capturing the animal's physical characteristics with scientific accuracy.

plates.title: Jean Baptiste Audebert — Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis (1800)
plates.author: Jean Baptiste Audebert
plates.desc: A detailed natural history illustration of a monkey, identified as a Maimon (Pig-tailed macaque). The animal is depicted in profile, facing left, in a seated position with its long arms extended forward. It has brown fur with a lighter cream-colored underside and throat, a short thin tail, and a visible pinkish ischial callosity.
plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts a 'Maimon' (Pig-tailed macaque) in a characteristic seated profile, showcasing the fine fur texture and anatomical features. It is taken from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 'Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis' (1800), a work celebrated for its innovative use of color printing to achieve scientific accuracy in zoological illustration.

summary: The largest living deer, a long-legged browser of northern forests and lakes. Bulls grow broad, palmate antlers that can span more than 1.5 m and are shed each winter. Moose wade and even dive in lakes to feed on water plants rich in sodium.
nativeRange: Boreal and mixed forests of northern Europe, Russia and Siberia, Mongolia, northeastern China, Canada, Alaska and the northern USA
abilities: Dives to about 5–6 m and stays under for nearly a minute to graze aquatic plants
Can close its nostrils underwater
Long legs let it wade through deep snow and step over fallen trees
Grows a new set of antlers, up to about 30 kg, every spring and summer

animal.diet: Browse: willow, birch, aspen shoots and bark; aquatic plants in summer
animal.habitat: Northern forest with lakes, bogs, rivers and young regrowth
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary. In the autumn rut bulls spar and call, and cows with calves are fiercely protective.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: very tall humped shoulders, long legs, short neck and a long, overhanging muzzle
Dewlap ('bell') of skin hanging from the throat
Bulls' antlers broad and palm-shaped (palmate), less often branching
Tracks: cloven hoofprints 13–15 cm long; signs include stripped bark, browsed tops of young trees and large piles of oval pellets
animal.voice: Cows give a long, nasal, moaning call in the rut; bulls answer with deep grunts or croaks.
animal.lookalikes: Wapiti/elk (Cervus canadensis) is reddish with a pale rump patch and branched (not palmate) antlers. Reindeer are smaller, with white necks and antlers in both sexes.
animal.whereToSee: Algonquin Provincial Park (Ontario); Denali (Alaska); Grand Teton (Wyoming); Baxter State Park (Maine); Biebrza National Park (Poland); forests of central Sweden and Norway
animal.season: Resident; rut in September–October; summer sightings in lakes and ponds at dawn and dusk

lore: Paintings and carvings of moose (elk) appear in Stone Age rock art across Scandinavia and Russia, including the Alta rock carvings in Norway. Julius Caesar's Gallic War records a tale that 'alces' had no knee joints and slept leaning against trees.
funFact: The word 'moose' comes from an Eastern Algonquian name, often glossed as 'twig-eater' or 'he strips off bark'.

wiki.extract: The moose or elk is the world's tallest, largest and heaviest extant species of deer and the only extant species in the genus Alces. It is also the tallest, and the second-largest, land animal in North America, falling short only to the American bison in body mass. Most adult male moose have broad, palmate antlers; most other members of the deer family have pointed antlers with a dendritic ("twig-like") configuration. Moose inhabit the circumpolar boreal forests or temperate broadleaf and mixed forests of the Northern Hemisphere, thriving in cooler, temperate areas as well as subarctic climates.

summary: The only deer in which both sexes grow antlers, adapted to Arctic tundra and boreal forest. Wild caribou herds make some of the longest overland migrations on Earth, while domestic reindeer have been central to Sámi, Nenets and Evenki life for centuries. Many wild herds have declined steeply, and the species is listed as Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Circumpolar: Scandinavia, Russia, Siberia, Greenland, Alaska and Canada; introduced to South Georgia (since removed) and Kerguelen
abilities: Some herds travel over 1,000 km a year between winter range and calving grounds
Eyes see ultraviolet light, helping them spot lichen and predators against snow
Its tapetum changes from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, improving vision in the long dark
Digs through snow ('cratering') with broad hooves to reach lichens

animal.diet: Lichens ('reindeer moss', Cladonia) in winter; grasses, sedges, willow leaves and mushrooms in summer
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra, mountain plateaus and northern taiga
animal.behaviour: Gathers in vast herds on migration and at calving grounds, where most calves are born within a few weeks in late May–June. Calves can follow their mothers within hours of birth.
fieldMarks: Both sexes carry long, sweeping antlers with a forward-projecting 'shovel' brow tine
Greyish-brown body with pale neck and white rump and tail
Large, broad, concave hooves
Signs: lichen grazing craters in snow, trails worn through tundra; tracks crescent-shaped and almost round
animal.lookalikes: Moose is far larger with a long overhanging muzzle and palmate antlers only on bulls. Musk ox is shaggy with horns, not antlers.
animal.whereToSee: Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and Denali (Alaska); Hardangervidda and Snøhetta (Norway, wild reindeer); Finnish and Swedish Lapland (herded reindeer); Western Greenland around Kangerlussuaq
animal.season: Resident or migratory: spring migration April–June; autumn rut September–October

lore: Reindeer herding has defined Sámi culture for centuries, and Nenets herders of the Yamal peninsula still migrate with their herds over 1,000 km a year. A single reindeer first pulled Santa's sleigh in the 1821 poem 'Old Santeclaus with Much Delight'; 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' (1823, attributed to Clement Clarke Moore) raised the team to eight and named them.
funFact: A tendon slipping over a bone in the foot makes walking reindeer give off a clicking sound that helps herds stay together.

wiki.extract: The reindeer or caribou is a species of deer with circumpolar distribution, native to the Arctic, subarctic, tundra, boreal, and mountainous regions of Northern Europe, Siberia, and North America. It is the only representative of the genus Rangifer. More recent studies suggest the splitting of reindeer and caribou. "All caribou and reindeer throughout the world are considered to be the same species, but there are 7 subspecies."

The reindeer is shown with extraordinary antlers that transition into acanthus-like foliage, while the panther is crowned and multi-colored, signifying its status as a 'king of beasts' in heraldic lore. Such

This illustration served to introduce European readers to the unique fauna of the Nordic regions, highlighting the animal's distinctive antlers and its relationship with the local inhabitants.

The image captures the early modern European fascination with Arctic fauna, depicting the animal's distinctive antlers and its interaction with the local inhabitants of the North.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a reindeer, notable for its expansive and complex antler structure. Found within a Renaissance natural history compendium, such illustrations were vital for disseminating knowledge about exotic species to a wider European audience, blending empirical observation with traditional artistic styles.

summary: The second-largest fish, a gentle giant that strains plankton through cavernous jaws. In summer it cruises surface waters off Britain, Ireland and New England with its mouth agape.
nativeRange: Temperate seas worldwide; most often seen in the North Atlantic and North Pacific
abilities: Filters an estimated 2,000 tonnes of water per hour through gill rakers
Passive ram feeder: swims with mouth open rather than sucking water in
Tagging shows it dives deep in winter and crosses ocean basins
Breaches fully clear of the water despite weighing several tonnes

animal.diet: Zooplankton, mainly copepods
animal.habitat: Surface to over 1,000 m; often near tidal fronts where plankton concentrates
animal.behaviour: Gathers in summer groups at plankton-rich fronts and swims slowly in circles; courtship-like 'nose-to-tail' following has been observed.
fieldMarks: Enormous size with a large triangular dorsal fin and tail tip often both visible at surface
Huge gill slits that nearly encircle the head
Cavernous mouth opening wide when feeding; conical pointed snout
Grey-brown mottled body
animal.lookalikes: Whale shark has white spots and a flat, broad head; great white has small gill slits and a dark-edged mouth of teeth. Two fins visible at once often lead to 'sea serpent' or 'two sharks' reports.
animal.whereToSee: Hebrides (Coll, Tiree), Cornwall, west Ireland (Malin Head), Isle of Man, Cape Cod
animal.season: Summer visitor May–Sep in the NE Atlantic

lore: Gavin Maxwell's Harpoon at a Venture (1952) recounts his failed Hebridean basking-shark fishery; the shark's liver oil once lit lamps in Ireland and Scotland.
funFact: Rotting basking shark carcasses lose their lower jaws and gill structure, leaving a long-necked shape mistaken for plesiosaur 'sea monsters' such as the 1977 Zuiyo-maru carcass.

wiki.extract: The basking shark is the second-largest living shark and fish, after the whale shark. It is one of three plankton-eating shark species, along with the whale shark and megamouth shark. Typically, basking sharks reach 7.9 m (26 ft) in length, but large individuals have been known to grow more than 10 m (33 ft) long. It is usually greyish-brown, with mottled skin, with the inside of the mouth being white in colour. The caudal fin has a strong lateral keel and a crescent shape. Other common names include bone shark, elephant shark, sailfish, and sunfish.

otherNames: Rìběn shù yīng 日本树莺 (Chinese)
summary: A drab olive-brown warbler that hides in bamboo thickets but announces spring across Japan with its clear, rising whistle 'hoo-hokekyo'. It is so central to Japanese culture that its name became a byword for a beautiful voice.
nativeRange: Japan and nearby islands including Sakhalin and the Ryukyus; related forms in Korea, eastern China and Taiwan treated as part of this species by some authorities; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Song carries far from deep cover despite the bird's small size
Males sing almost continuously through spring and summer
Introduced population thrives in Hawaiian forests

animal.diet: Insects and spiders; some nectar and fruit
animal.habitat: Dense undergrowth, bamboo thickets, scrub and forest edge from lowland to mountains
animal.size: About 14–16 cm long (males larger than females)
animal.behaviour: Skulks low in dense vegetation and is rarely seen in the open; in winter it moves to lower ground and gives only short 'chat' calls.
fieldMarks: Plain olive-brown upperparts and buffy-grey underparts
Pale eyebrow stripe
Rounded tail and short wings
Lacks the bright eye-ring and yellow-green tones of the Japanese white-eye
animal.voice: A long, rising whistle followed by an explosive flourish, written 'hoo-hokekyo'; also a rapid 'kekyo-kekyo-kekyo' sequence
animal.lookalikes: Japanese white-eye (mejiro) is brighter green with a white eye-ring and is often mistaken for the uguisu; Manchurian bush warbler is larger and browner.
animal.whereToSee: City parks and temple gardens throughout Japan in spring, e.g. Kyoto's Higashiyama and Tokyo's Meiji Jingu forest; also Oahu, Hawaii
animal.season: Resident; sings from late February to summer, in winter heard only as a call

lore: The Kokinshū (905) preface lists the uguisu singing among the blossoms as a voice of poetry, and its song is heard as 'Hokekyō', the Japanese name of the Lotus Sutra. Its droppings (uguisu no fun) were traditionally used in Japanese facial cosmetics.
funFact: The squeaking 'nightingale floors' (uguisubari) of Kyoto's Nijō Castle and Chion-in temple are named after the bird's chirping.

wiki.extract: The Japanese bush warbler, known in Japanese as uguisu (鶯), is an Asian passerine bird more often heard than seen. Its distinctive breeding song can be heard throughout much of Japan from the start of spring.

plates.desc: An engraving of four birds: a lapwing (Kieft), a warbler (Grasmusch), a cuckoo (Koeckoeck), and a quail (Quackel).
plates.long: This detailed engraving from the 1672 work 'Schouw-toneel der aertsche schepselen' depicts four distinct bird species, each numbered for identification. It exemplifies the early modern scientific tradition of cataloging the natural world through precise visual documentation and descriptive text.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby's landmark study depicts a Hooded Warbler, identified here as the 'Hooded Titmous,' perched upon a branch of a Water Tupelo. Catesby was the first to provide a comprehensive illustrated account of the flora and fauna of North America, often depicting birds alongside the plants they frequented in their natural habitats.

Gessner's work was foundational in the transition from medieval bestiaries to modern scientific observation, utilizing detailed woodcuts to document the natural world with unprecedented accuracy for the time.

summary: A big, vividly coloured chameleon of northern and eastern Madagascar. Males of each locality have distinct colour patterns, from turquoise to flame-red, and change colour when they display.
nativeRange: Northern and eastern Madagascar and nearby islands; introduced to Réunion and Mauritius
abilities: Changes colour by adjusting the spacing of guanine nanocrystals in its skin, which shifts how light reflects
Fires its tongue out to more than its body length in a fraction of a second
Moves each eye independently, scanning nearly 360°, then focuses both on prey
Grips branches with pincer-like feet and a prehensile tail

animal.diet: Insectivore: crickets, grasshoppers, flies, other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Bushes and trees in warm, humid lowlands, often near villages
animal.size: Males up to ~50 cm including tail; females about half that
animal.behaviour: When a rival male approaches, a male inflates his body and flashes brilliant colour. A female signals refusal with dark colours and orange patches.
fieldMarks: Large chameleon with a bony crest on the head
Males brightly coloured — green, red, blue or orange depending on locality
Pale stripe along the side
Females smaller, tan or brown
animal.lookalikes: Other Furcifer and Calumma chameleons; colours vary by region.
animal.whereToSee: Nosy Be (Lokobe), Ankarana and Amber Mountain, northern Madagascar
animal.season: Resident; most visible in the warm, wet season

lore: In many Malagasy communities chameleons are fady (taboo), and touching one is unlucky. Georges Cuvier described the species in 1829.
funFact: A 2015 study on panther chameleons showed that their colour change comes from tuning nanocrystals, not just moving pigments.

wiki.extract: The panther chameleon is a species of chameleon found in the eastern and northern parts of Madagascar in a tropical forest biome. Additionally, it has been introduced to Réunion and Mauritius, as well as the state of Florida within the United States.

summary: A green chameleon of the cool East African highlands; males carry three forward-pointing horns like a miniature Triceratops. It gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs, which suits its chilly mountain home.
nativeRange: Highlands of Kenya and northern Tanzania; introduced to Hawaii (1970s) and California
abilities: Bears live young, up to ~30 in a litter, after a pregnancy of about 5–6 months
Eyes move independently and lock together on prey
Shoots out a sticky tongue longer than its body to catch insects
Males use their horns in pushing contests

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, snails
animal.habitat: Moist montane forest, shrubs and gardens at about 1,500–3,000 m
animal.behaviour: Slowly stalks insects among leaves, rocking back and forth like a leaf in the wind. Colour changes reflect mood and temperature.
fieldMarks: Males have three long horns, one on the snout and one above each eye; females have none or small ones
Bright green with yellow, blue or brown patches
Saw-toothed crest along the back
Grasping tail and tong-like feet
animal.lookalikes: Johnston's chameleon (T. johnstoni) also has three horns in males but lives in the Albertine Rift mountains far to the west. Other Kenyan highland chameleons have one horn or none.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and forest of Nairobi and the Aberdare and Mount Kenya foothills; in Hawaii, upland gardens of Maui and the Big Island
animal.season: Resident

lore: George Albert Boulenger named it in 1896 after Frederick John Jackson, a British naturalist and colonial administrator in East Africa.
funFact: Jackson's chameleons were brought to Hawaii in the 1970s for the pet trade and now live wild on several islands, where they eat native snails and insects.

wiki.extract: Jackson's chameleon, also known commonly as Jackson's horned chameleon, the three-horned chameleon, and the Kikuyu three-horned chameleon, is a species of chameleon, a lizard in the family Chamaeleonidae. The species is native to East Africa, and introduced to Hawaii, Florida, and California. There are three recognized subspecies.

summary: A tough air-breathing predator of paddy fields, ponds and swamps across South and Southeast Asia. It can survive in damp mud through the dry season and is a major food fish from Bengal to Vietnam.
nativeRange: Pakistan and India east through Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Indochina and southern China to Malaysia and Indonesia; introduced elsewhere
abilities: Breathes air through a chamber above the gills, so it survives in stagnant, oxygen-poor water
Survives the dry season buried in moist mud
Can wriggle short distances across wet ground between pools
Both parents guard a floating ball of bright orange fry
edibilityNote: Widely eaten and valued as food for people recovering from illness. Never eat it raw or undercooked, for example in fermented or lightly cured dishes: snakeheads carry larvae of the Gnathostoma roundworm, which can migrate through human tissues and cause gnathostomiasis.

uses.use: Haruan fish broth and extract taken after childbirth and surgery to aid wound healing

uses.tradition: Bengali and Southeast Asian folk diet
uses.use: Fish soup given to convalescents

medicinal.cautions: Small clinical studies report faster post-surgical healing with haruan extract, but evidence is limited. Commercial extracts vary in quality. People with fish allergy should avoid it.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, frogs, insects, crustaceans and other small animals
animal.habitat: Swamps, ponds, paddy fields, canals and slow, vegetated rivers
animal.size: Commonly 30–60 cm; up to about 1 m and 3 kg
animal.behaviour: Lies motionless among weeds near the surface, gulping air, then lunges at passing prey. Pairs build a cleared nest in vegetation and fiercely guard their swarm of fry.
fieldMarks: Long, cylindrical body with a flat, snake-like head covered in large scales
Long dorsal and anal fins running almost to the rounded tail
Dark brown to black back with oblique dark bands (stripes) on paler, whitish flanks
Large mouth with sharp teeth
animal.lookalikes: The bullseye snakehead (Channa marulius) grows much larger and has an orange-ringed black eyespot at the base of the tail. Spotted snakehead (Channa punctata) is small, with dark spots and bars. The North American bowfin has a short anal fin and a bony gular plate under the chin.
animal.whereToSee: Paddy fields and beels of Bangladesh and West Bengal; wet markets of Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur and Ho Chi Minh City
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly in the rainy season (May–September in most of its range)

lore: In Malaysia and Indonesia, haruan soup is a traditional confinement food for mothers after childbirth. In Bengal the shol is a favourite curry fish, and it is kept alive in tubs at market because it survives so long out of the water.
funFact: Snakeheads are called 'murrels' in Indian English, and in Thailand grilled salted pla chon (pla chon pao) is a standard street food.

wiki.extract: Channa striata, the striped snakehead, is a species of snakehead fish. It is also known as the common snakehead, chevron snakehead, or snakehead murrel and generally referred simply as mudfish. It is native to South and Southeast Asia, and has been introduced to some Pacific Islands. Reports from Madagascar and Hawaii are misidentifications of C. maculata.

summary: A small, sand-coloured plover that nests on open beaches and lakeshores, where its eggs are almost invisible. Beach development and disturbance made it a flagship of shorebird conservation, with nests now fenced and patrolled across its range.
nativeRange: Breeds on the Atlantic coast from Newfoundland to North Carolina, around the Great Lakes, and on the northern Great Plains; winters on the south Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the Bahamas, the Caribbean and Mexico
abilities: Eggs and chicks are camouflaged against pale sand
Adults perform broken-wing displays to lure predators from nests
Chicks feed themselves within hours of hatching
Foot-trembles on wet sand to startle invertebrates

animal.diet: Marine worms, insects, small crustaceans and molluscs
animal.habitat: Open sandy beaches, sandbars and alkali flats with sparse vegetation
animal.behaviour: It runs in short bursts and stops abruptly, typical of plovers.
fieldMarks: Pale, dry-sand upperparts — paler than any other North American ringed plover
Bright orange legs
Breeding: short orange bill with a black tip, single black breast band and black forehead bar
Winter: bill all dark, breast band faint or partial
animal.voice: A soft, clear, whistled 'peep-lo' or 'peep', like a piped note.
animal.lookalikes: Semipalmated Plover has a dark mud-brown back. Snowy Plover has dark legs and a thin black bill. Wilson's Plover has a heavy black bill and pinkish legs.
animal.whereToSee: Cape Cod and Long Island beaches, Sleeping Bear Dunes (Michigan), Chicago's Montrose Beach, and Gulf coast beaches of Texas and Florida in winter.
animal.season: Breeding grounds Apr–Aug; winter coasts Aug–Apr

lore: Two Great Lakes piping plovers named Monty and Rose nested on Chicago's Montrose Beach from 2019, the first in the city in decades, and became local celebrities.
funFact: The Great Lakes population fell to fewer than 20 pairs in the 1980s before intensive protection helped it grow again.

wiki.extract: The piping plover is a small, sand-colored shorebird that nests and feeds along coastal sand and gravel beaches in North America. The adult has yellow-orange-red legs, a black band across the forehead from eye to eye, and a black stripe running along the breast line. This chest band is usually thicker in males during the breeding season, and it is the only reliable way to tell the sexes apart. The bird is difficult to see when it is standing still, as it blends well with open, sandy beach habitats. It typically runs in short, quick spurts and then stops.

nativeRange: Breeds in the steppes of Kazakhstan and adjacent Russia; winters in Sudan, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Pakistan and northwestern India

Travels in flocks along a long overland migration route
Relies on grazing livestock to keep steppe vegetation short
Uses fallow fields and short grassland on migration

animal.habitat: Dry steppe with short, grazed vegetation; arable land and semi-desert in winter

wiki.extract: The sociable lapwing, referred to as the sociable plover in the UK, is a wader in the plover family. It is a fully migratory bird, breeding in Kazakhstan and wintering in the Middle East, Indian subcontinent, and Sudan with a very small wintering population in Iberia. Historical literature referred to this bird as the black-bellied lapwing.

summary: A tall plover with a black cap, white face patch and a red fleshy wattle in front of each eye, whose frantic 'did-he-do-it' calls raise the alarm across South Asian fields, at all hours. It nests on bare ground and even on flat city rooftops.

animal.habitat: Open ground near water: field edges, riverbanks, dry lake beds, lawns

wiki.extract: The red-wattled lapwing is an Asian lapwing or large plover, a wader in the family Charadriidae. Like other lapwings they are ground birds that are incapable of perching. Their characteristic loud alarm calls are indicators of human or animal movements and the sounds have been variously rendered as did he do it or pity to do it leading to the colloquial name of did-he-do-it bird. Usually seen in pairs or small groups not far from water, they sometimes form large aggregations in the non-breeding season (winter). They nest in a ground scrape laying three to four camouflaged eggs. Adults near the nest fly around, diving at potential predators while calling noisily. The cryptically patterned chicks hatch and immediately follow their parents to feed, hiding by lying low on the ground or in the grass when threatened.

summary: A crested, iridescent plover of fields and wet meadows, named for the 'lapping' sound of its floppy, rounded wings in its tumbling display flight. Breeding numbers have fallen sharply with farming changes across Europe.
nativeRange: Breeds across temperate Europe and Asia from Ireland to the Pacific; winters in western Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, South Asia and China
abilities: Tumbling display flight with wing-throbbing sound and wild calls
Parents mob crows and foxes and perform distraction displays to lure predators away
Chicks feed themselves within hours of hatching
Cold-weather movements can shift huge flocks hundreds of kilometres in a day

animal.diet: Earthworms, beetles, leatherjackets and other soil invertebrates
animal.habitat: Wet grassland, spring-sown fields, marshes; mudflats and pastures in winter
animal.behaviour: Feeds with a 'stop-run-tilt' action and patters its feet on the ground to bring worms up.
fieldMarks: Long, wispy black crest
Dark green upperparts with purple and bronze gloss
Black breast band, white belly, orange undertail
Broad, rounded black-and-white wings in flight

funFact: Its English name comes from Old English 'hleapewince', referring to its leaping, wavering flight.

summary: A big-headed sea turtle whose powerful jaws crush crabs and conchs. Hatchlings from Florida circle the Atlantic, and those from Japan cross the whole Pacific to feed off Mexico, navigating by the Earth's magnetic field.
nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans and the Mediterranean
abilities: Navigates using a magnetic 'map' that reads the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field
Crushes whelks, conchs and crabs with massive jaws
Hatchlings swim continuously for about a day to reach the open sea

animal.diet: Crabs, whelks, conchs, sea urchins, jellyfish
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays and open ocean; nests on sandy beaches
animal.behaviour: Females return to nest on the same region of coast where they hatched, often decades later. Hatchlings head for the brightest horizon, which is the sea, so beachfront lights draw them inland.
fieldMarks: Very large, broad head with heavy jaws
Reddish-brown carapace, yellowish below
Five pairs of plates (costal scutes) along each side of the shell
Barnacles often encrust the shell
animal.lookalikes: Green and hawksbill turtles have four pairs of costal scutes. Kemp's and olive ridleys are smaller and grey, with rounder shells.
animal.whereToSee: Florida's Atlantic beaches (Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge), Masirah Island (Oman), Zakynthos (Greece), Yakushima (Japan), Mon Repos (Australia)
animal.season: Nesting May–August in the northern hemisphere; Nov–Feb in Australia

lore: Archie Carr's studies of sea turtles in Florida and Costa Rica from the 1950s onwards inspired the protection of nesting beaches. Florida's Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge, one of the most important loggerhead beaches in the world, is named after him.
funFact: Laboratory tests by Kenneth Lohmann's team showed that hatchlings change swimming direction when exposed to the magnetic fields of different points on their migration route.

wiki.extract: The loggerhead sea turtle, loggerhead turtle or loggerhead, is a species of sea turtle distributed throughout the world. It is a marine reptile, belonging to the family Cheloniidae. The average loggerhead measures around 90 cm (35 in) in carapace length when fully grown. The adult loggerhead sea turtle weighs approximately 135 kg (298 lb), with the largest specimens weighing about 200 kg (440 lb). The skin ranges from yellow to brown in color, and the shell is typically reddish brown. No external differences in sex are seen until the turtle becomes an adult, the most obvious difference being the adult males have thicker tails and shorter plastrons than the females.

summary: A large sea turtle of tropical and subtropical seas, named for the greenish fat under its shell. Adults are the only sea turtles that graze mainly on seagrass and algae, keeping seagrass meadows healthy.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide; nests on beaches in over 80 countries
abilities: Navigates thousands of kilometres using Earth's magnetic field and returns to nest near the beach where it hatched
Swims about 2,000 km from Brazil to nest on tiny Ascension Island
Mows seagrass beds, which keeps the meadows productive
Can rest underwater for hours by slowing its heart

animal.diet: Juveniles omnivorous; adults herbivorous: seagrass and algae
animal.habitat: Coastal seagrass and reef feeding grounds; open ocean as juveniles; sandy beaches for nesting
animal.behaviour: Females crawl ashore at night every few years to dig nests, laying around 100 eggs several times a season. Nest temperature decides hatchlings' sex: warmer sand produces more females.

Small, rounded head with one pair of scales between the eyes
Shell brown, olive or black
Single claw on each flipper
animal.lookalikes: Hawksbill has a pointed, hawk-like beak and overlapping shell plates. Loggerhead has a large head and reddish-brown shell.

animal.season: Tortuguero nesting Jul–Oct; Ras al Jinz all year, peak Jun–Sep; Heron Island Nov–Mar

lore: In Hawaiian tradition the honu is an ʻaumakua (family guardian), and the turtle Kauila was said to take the form of a girl to watch over children at Punaluʻu. Green turtle soup was a showpiece of London's Lord Mayor's banquets from the 18th century, driving heavy Caribbean harvests.
funFact: In October 2025 the IUCN moved the green turtle from Endangered to Least Concern after decades of protecting nesting beaches, though some regional populations remain threatened.

wiki.extract: The green sea turtle, also known as the green turtle, black sea turtle, and Pacific green turtle, is a species of large sea turtle of the family Cheloniidae. It is the only species in the genus Chelonia. Its range extends throughout tropical and subtropical seas around the world, with two distinct populations in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, but it is also found in the Indian Ocean. The common name refers to the usually green fat found beneath its carapace, due to its diet strictly being seagrass, not to the color of its carapace, which is olive to black.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a land tortoise, characterized by its domed and patterned shell. It appears in Conrad Gessner's seminal work on zoology, representing the 16th-century effort to systematically categorize and illustrate the animal kingdom through empirical observation.

plates.title: Theater of Earthly Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: Woodcut of a tortoise with a detailed, patterned shell.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a tortoise, characterized by its intricately patterned carapace and scaly skin. It appears in a 1672 Dutch work on earthly creatures, reflecting the era's growing interest in documenting the natural world with both scientific curiosity and artistic detail.

summary: A reef-dwelling sea turtle with a narrow, hooked beak and beautifully mottled, overlapping shell plates. For centuries it was killed for 'tortoiseshell', and it is now Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Tropical coral reefs of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans
abilities: Feeds largely on sponges, many of which are full of toxins and glass-like spicules
By eating sponges, it keeps them from overgrowing reef-building corals
Its narrow, bird-like beak can reach into crevices in the reef

animal.diet: Mainly sponges; also soft corals, anemones, jellyfish
animal.habitat: Coral reefs, rocky areas and lagoons; nests on small island beaches
animal.size: Shell up to ~1 m; weight ~45–80 kg
animal.behaviour: Often nests alone and in daylight on remote beaches, sometimes under beach vegetation.
fieldMarks: Narrow head with a sharp, hooked, hawk-like beak
Overlapping shell scutes, giving a saw-toothed back edge
Amber, brown and black 'tortoiseshell' pattern
Two pairs of scales (prefrontals) between the eyes
animal.lookalikes: The green turtle has a blunt rounded snout, one pair of scales between the eyes and non-overlapping shell scutes. Loggerheads have a big head and reddish shell.
animal.whereToSee: Cousin Island (Seychelles), Bahia (Brazil), Mona Island (Puerto Rico), Milman Island (Great Barrier Reef), snorkelling reefs of the Caribbean and Red Sea
animal.season: Resident on reefs; nesting peaks vary by region (e.g. Oct–Jan in the Seychelles)

lore: Tortoiseshell combs and ornaments were traded from ancient Rome to Edo-period Japan, where the craft is known as bekkō. CITES banned the international trade in 1977, and Japan, which had held a reservation, ended imports at the end of 1992 and withdrew its reservation in 1994.
funFact: In 2015 marine biologist David Gruber filmed a hawksbill off the Solomon Islands glowing red and green under blue light. It was the first biofluorescence reported in a reptile.

ancestors.common: Hawksbill, Loggerhead, and Ridley Sea Turtles

wiki.extract: The hawksbill sea turtle is a critically endangered sea turtle belonging to the family Cheloniidae. It is the only extant species in the genus Eretmochelys. The species has a global distribution that is largely limited to tropical and subtropical marine and estuary ecosystems.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica: Illustrated Volume, Middle of the Lower Part

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a hawksbill sea turtle (玳瑁).
plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a hawksbill sea turtle (玳瑁), a species valued in traditional Chinese medicine for its shell. It comes from the 'Bencao Gangmu,' a comprehensive encyclopedia of natural history and medicine compiled by Li Shizhen in the late 16th century. The clear, linear style is characteristic of Ming dynasty scientific illustration, focusing on identifying features of the anima

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts a hawksbill sea turtle (玳瑁) amidst swirling waves. The work reflects the Ming dynasty's interest in categorizing the natural world, blending observational detail with traditional artistic conventions.

summary: North America's heaviest freshwater turtle, with three rows of spiky ridges on its shell and a hooked beak. It lies still on the riverbed with its mouth open, wiggling a pink worm-like lure on its tongue to attract fish.
nativeRange: Rivers draining into the Gulf of Mexico in the southeastern United States, from eastern Texas to the Florida Panhandle and up the Mississippi basin
abilities: Lures fish with a pink, worm-like flap on its tongue
Bites hard enough to sever fingers
Can stay underwater for long periods, surfacing only occasionally to breathe

animal.diet: Fish, other turtles, snakes, crayfish, mussels, carrion, fallen fruit and nuts
animal.habitat: Deep rivers, oxbow lakes, swamps and canals
animal.size: Shell up to ~80 cm; males up to ~80 kg, exceptionally more
animal.behaviour: Rarely leaves the water except for females coming ashore to nest. It is mostly inactive by day.
fieldMarks: Three prominent rows of spiky ridges running along the shell
Massive head with a strongly hooked beak
Eyes on the sides of the head, ringed with fleshy points
Extra row of scutes (supramarginals) along the sides of the shell
animal.lookalikes: The common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) has a smoother shell, eyes visible from above, and a long, saw-crested tail. The Suwannee alligator snapping turtle (M. suwanniensis) of the Suwannee River in Florida and Georgia was split as a separate species in 2014.
animal.whereToSee: Rivers of Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi and Texas; seen basking rarely; best seen at aquariums and zoos
animal.season: Resident; nests in late spring

lore: Commercial trapping for turtle soup in the 20th century took huge numbers from Gulf Coast rivers, and commercial harvest is now banned in most of its range.
funFact: As in many turtles, the sex of the hatchlings is set by the temperature of the nest.

wiki.extract: The alligator snapping turtle is a large species of turtle in the family Chelydridae. They are the largest freshwater turtle in North America. The species is endemic to freshwater habitats in the United States. M. temminckii is one of the heaviest living freshwater turtles in the world. It is often associated with, but not closely related to, the common snapping turtle, which is in the genus Chelydra. The specific epithet temminckii is in honor of Dutch zoologist Coenraad Jacob Temminck.

summary: A plump white scavenger of Antarctic penguin and seal colonies, and the only bird breeding in Antarctica that lacks webbed feet. It lives by stealing, cleaning up and scavenging.
nativeRange: Antarctic Peninsula, South Georgia, South Orkney and South Shetland Islands; winters south to Patagonia and the Falklands
abilities: Steals krill from penguins by startling them while they are feeding chicks
Eats eggs, carcasses, faeces and placentas of seals
Can fly long distances over the sea despite its pigeon-like appearance

animal.diet: Carrion, eggs, krill, seal placentas and faeces, and refuse
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts near penguin, cormorant and seal colonies; research stations
animal.behaviour: It patrols penguin colonies, harassing adults until they spill krill, which it snatches.
fieldMarks: All-white, plump pigeon-like body
Pinkish face with fleshy warts
Horny sheath over base of the yellowish bill
Short pinkish-grey legs and unwebbed feet
animal.voice: Harsh, crow-like 'caw' calls and scolding chatter.
animal.lookalikes: Black-faced sheathbill (southern Indian Ocean islands) has a black bill and face. Pigeons do not occur in Antarctica.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula landings (Port Lockroy, Brown Bluff), South Georgia, Falklands in winter
animal.season: Present in Antarctic summer; many winter in Falklands and Patagonia

lore: Early sealers and explorers called sheathbills 'paddies' and noted their fearlessness around camps.
funFact: Sheathbills are thought to be related to shorebirds such as plovers, despite their pigeon-like look.

wiki.extract: The snowy sheathbill, also known as the greater sheathbill, pale-faced sheathbill, and paddy, is one of two species of sheathbill. It is usually found on the ground. It is the only land bird native to the Antarctic continent.

summary: A red-eyed cicada that spends 17 years underground feeding on tree roots, then emerges in synchronised billions over a few weeks. Each regional 'brood' appears on its own fixed calendar.
nativeRange: Eastern United States, from the Great Plains to the Atlantic and from the Great Lakes to the Gulf states
abilities: Nymphs count years underground and emerge together after 17 years
Emergence is triggered when soil about 20 cm down reaches roughly 18 °C
Sheer numbers, up to around 1.5 million per acre, overwhelm predators (predator satiation)
Males sing in huge choruses that can exceed 90 decibels

animal.diet: Nymphs drink xylem sap from tree roots; adults feed little, piercing twigs for sap
animal.habitat: Deciduous woods and leafy suburbs
animal.lifespan: 17 years, almost all underground; adults 3–6 weeks
animal.behaviour: Females slit thin twigs to lay eggs, which causes 'flagging' of branch tips; hatchlings drop to the ground and burrow.
fieldMarks: Black body with bright red eyes
Orange wing veins and orange legs
Broad orange bands on the underside of the abdomen
An orange patch behind the eye, above the wing base
animal.voice: Males give a low, buzzing, slightly falling 'phaaa-raoh' call lasting a second or two, repeated and blended into a roaring chorus.
animal.lookalikes: Magicicada cassini is smaller with an all-black abdomen underside and a rapid ticking-then-buzz song; M. septendecula has narrow orange abdominal stripes. The 13-year M. tredecim is very similar but has a lower-pitched song, and the 13-year M. neotredecim can be told apart only by its cycle. Annual dog-day cicadas (Neotibicen) are green and brown with dark eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Leafy suburbs and woods within an emerging brood's range (e.g. Brood X in the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, last seen 2021).
animal.season: Mid-May to late June in emergence years only

edibilityNote: Eaten fried or roasted, as several Indigenous nations and modern foragers have done. People with shellfish allergy may react, as cicadas share allergenic proteins with crustaceans.
lore: William Bradford recorded an emergence at Plymouth Colony in 1633, and colonists called them 'locusts', a misnomer that stuck. Pehr Kalm described the 1749 emergence in Pennsylvania for Linnaeus.
funFact: Brood XIII (17-year) and Brood XIX (13-year) emerged together in 2024 for the first time since 1803; they will not coincide again until 2245.

ancestors.common: True Bugs, Hoppers, Aphids, and allies

wiki.extract: Magicicada septendecim, sometimes called the Pharaoh cicada or the 17-year locust, is native to Canada and the United States and is the largest and most northern species of periodical cicada with a 17-year lifecycle.

plates.title: Garden of Health (Hortus Sanitatis)
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Two fish swimming in water, each with a large locust or grasshopper on its back.
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut illustrates a curious interaction between aquatic and terrestrial life, showing locusts riding on the backs of fish. Such depictions were common in early natural history texts like the Hortus Sanitatis, blending empirical observation with traditional folklore.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a lobster or sea locust (Locusta marina)
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1491 'Ortus sanitatis' depicts a 'Locusta marina', or sea locust, which likely refers to a lobster. The illustration serves as a visual guide for the accompanying text describing the creature's medicinal and natural properties in one of the first major printed encyclopedias of the natural world.

plates.title: Ulyssis Aldrovandi ... De animalibus insectis libri septem
plates.author: Aldrovandi, Ulisse
plates.desc: A comprehensive plate of various locust and cricket species, meticulously detailed for scientific study.
plates.long: This detailed plate from Ulisse Aldrovandi's 'De animalibus insectis' (1618) illustrates various species of locusts and crickets, including several specimens of praying mantises. As a pioneer of modern zoology, Aldrovandi's work represents a monumental effort to document the natural world with empirical precision, using woodcuts that remained standard references for generations of naturalists.

plates.author: Dioscorides
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a locust in a landscape
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a locust in its natural habitat, illustrating Chapter 44 of Dioscorides' medicinal treatise. It represents the 16th-century transition toward empirical observation in natural history, providing visual identification for species described in classical texts.

otherNames: Pla nin ปลานิล (Thai)
summary: A hardy African cichlid that has become one of the world's most farmed fish. Females carry their eggs and fry in their mouths. It was a symbol of rebirth in ancient Egypt, and today it feeds millions from Thailand to Brazil.
nativeRange: Nile basin, West African rivers (Niger, Volta, Senegal, Gambia), Lake Chad and Rift Valley lakes such as Turkana and Tanganyika; introduced to over 100 countries
abilities: Females brood eggs and fry in their mouths and let the young dart back in when danger threatens
Filter-feeds on phytoplankton and grazes algae, so it grows on cheap feed
Tolerates warm, low-oxygen, crowded and slightly brackish water
Becomes invasive easily, and has displaced native fish in many tropical lakes
edibilityNote: Mild, lean white fillets; a cheap staple protein. Farm quality varies with water and feed. Always cook it: raw freshwater fish in Southeast Asia have been linked to Streptococcus agalactiae infections, and tilapia can carry trematode larvae.

animal.diet: Omnivore: phytoplankton, algae, detritus and some invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow, warm lakes, rivers, ponds and canals
animal.size: Usually 20–40 cm; up to about 60 cm and 4 kg
animal.behaviour: Males dig pits in the lake floor and defend them, flushing reddish while displaying. Females pick up the fertilised eggs and brood them in their mouths for about two weeks.
fieldMarks: Deep, perch-like body with a long continuous dorsal fin, spiny in front
Regular vertical dark bars on the tail fin (a key mark)
Greyish to olive body with faint vertical bands; breeding males with pinkish-red throat and fins
Single nostril on each side of the snout (typical of cichlids)
animal.lookalikes: Mozambique tilapia (O. mossambicus) has no regular bars on the tail, and breeding males are blackish with white lower jaws. Blue tilapia (O. aureus) has a red-edged tail fin and no regular vertical barring. Redbelly tilapia (Coptodon zillii) has a dark 'tilapia spot' on the soft dorsal fin.
animal.whereToSee: The Nile at Cairo and Aswan; Lake Turkana (Kenya); fish ponds and markets across Egypt, Thailand, the Philippines and Brazil
animal.season: Resident; breeds year-round in warm water

lore: The hieroglyph of a tilapia (Gardiner sign K1) stood for the fish and for rebirth, because the young seemed to be swallowed and reborn from the mother's mouth. Tomb paintings at Thebes, such as Nebamun's, show tilapia ponds in Egyptian gardens. In Thailand the farmed strain was a 1965 gift from Crown Prince Akihito to King Bhumibol.
funFact: The Thai name pla nin was coined by King Bhumibol, from 'Nile', after he bred the 50 fish Akihito sent him at the palace ponds.

wiki.extract: The Nile tilapia is a species of tilapia, a cichlid occurring naturally in parts of Africa and the Levant, though numerous introduced populations exist outside its natural range. This current wide range is caused by its high commercial value as a food fish, where it is marketed as mango fish, nilotica, or boulti, along with many other names, both local and foreign. Due to its value, the Nile tilapia is widely aquacultured across the world due to its hardiness and a mode of reproduction conducive to mass rearing, namely mouthbrooding, and various attempts have been made to increase production yields, including hybridization with other tilapias.

summary: A tall, silver Amazonian cichlid with sweeping fins and black bars, built to hide among reeds and sunken branches. It is one of the best-known aquarium fish, and pairs bond and raise their young together.
nativeRange: Amazon basin in Brazil, Colombia, Peru, French Guiana and Guyana (Amapá, Oyapock and Essequibo rivers)
abilities: Its very compressed body and vertical bars help it blend in among vertical reeds and roots
Pairs clean a leaf or branch, lay rows of eggs on it, and both parents fan and guard them
Parents move wrigglers to fresh pits or leaves in their mouths

animal.diet: Carnivore and omnivore: small fish, insect larvae, crustaceans and worms
animal.habitat: Quiet, vegetated, often tannin-stained water among roots, plants and sunken wood
animal.size: About 15 cm long and up to 25 cm tall including fins
animal.behaviour: Hovers among stems in small groups, then pairs off to breed and become strongly territorial.
fieldMarks: Disc-shaped, extremely compressed body, taller than long with fins
Very long, triangular dorsal and anal fins and threadlike pelvic fins
Silver with three to four bold black vertical bars, one through the eye
animal.lookalikes: Altum angelfish (P. altum) of the Orinoco and Rio Negro is taller, with a notch above the snout. Leopold's angelfish (P. leopoldi) has a dark spot at the dorsal-fin base and a less prominent tail bar. Discus is round, not tall.
animal.whereToSee: Amazonian floodplains near Santarém and Manaus; public aquaria and home aquaria worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds through the rainy season

lore: Imported to Europe in the early 20th century, angelfish were bred in American aquaria by the 1920s and were among the first tropical fish kept as household pets.
funFact: The name Pterophyllum means 'winged leaf' in Greek, after its leaf-like body and wing-like fins.

wiki.extract: Pterophyllum scalare, most commonly referred to as angelfish or freshwater angelfish, is the most common species of Pterophyllum kept in captivity. It is native to the Amazon Basin in Peru, Colombia, and Brazil. Particularly to the Ucayali river in Peru, the Oyapock River in French Guiana, the Essequibo River in Guyana, the Solimões, the Amapá, and the Amazon rivers in Brazil. It is found in swamps or flooded grounds where vegetation is dense and the water is either clear or silty. Its native waters range from a neutral pH of 7.0 down to near 6.0, with a general water hardness (gH) range of 3 to 10 °dH, and water temperature ranging from 26 to 30 °C. This is the species of angelfish most frequently found in the aquarium trade. A similar P. scalare exists in the Rio Orinoco. They are of the same size and shape, the only difference being the stripes; the Orinoco P. scalare has thinner, but dual, stripes.

Its head is brown with a prominent yellow eye and blue markings near the mouth.

This plate, from Mark Catesby's seminal work on the flora and fauna of the Americas, showcases the vibrant colors and distinctive morphology of a tropical species, likely a member of the angelfish family.

summary: A plate-round cichlid of Amazonian floodplain forests and an aquarium icon. Both parents feed their young on a nutrient-rich mucus they secrete from their skin, a strategy compared to mammalian milk.
nativeRange: Central and western Amazon floodplains of Brazil, Peru and Colombia
abilities: Both parents feed fry with secretions from their skin for the first weeks of life
Shoals among sunken branches and roots in flooded forest for protection
Changes colour quickly, darkening with stress and brightening during courtship

animal.diet: Omnivore: small invertebrates, insect larvae, algae, plant matter and detritus
animal.habitat: Warm, soft-water flooded forest and lake margins with fallen trees and roots
animal.behaviour: Gathers in groups among submerged wood at high water. Pairs lay eggs on smooth branches and fan them, and the fry graze mucus from their parents' sides.
fieldMarks: Nearly circular, very compressed body
Nine vertical dark bars, often faint except the first (through the eye) and last (at the tail base)
Brown to bluish base colour with blue wavy lines on head and fins in many populations
Red eyes; long dorsal and anal fins edging the disc
animal.lookalikes: Heckel discus (Symphysodon discus) of the Rio Negro has a bold, wide dark central bar. Angelfish (Pterophyllum) are taller than long, with very elongated fins.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Tefé and the Purus and Solimões floodplains (Brazil); public aquaria; specialist breeders in Germany and Southeast Asia
animal.season: Resident; breeds as waters rise, roughly October–January

lore: Jacob Heckel described the first discus species in 1840 from Johann Natterer's Brazilian collections. Breeders in Germany and later Southeast Asia turned the wild fish into colour strains like turquoise, pigeon-blood and red melon.
funFact: Discus 'milk' contains antibodies and hormones, and in the first days after free-swimming the fry depend on it; aquarists find them very hard to raise without the parents.

wiki.extract: Symphysodon aequifasciatus, the blue discus or brown discus, is a species of cichlid native to rivers of the eastern and central Amazon Basin downriver from the Purus Arch. This discus is found in black-, clear- and whitewater, but its preference for lentic habitats such as floodplains and flooded forests means that the whitewater it inhabits contain little suspended material. It is largely restricted to water with a high temperature of 25–32 °C (77–90 °F) and a pH of 5.2–7.7.

otherNames: Dōngfāng bái guàn 东方白鹳 (Chinese)
summary: A large white stork with black flight feathers and a heavy black bill, breeding in the Amur basin and wintering along the Yangtze. It went extinct in the wild in Japan in 1971 and has been brought back through reintroduction at Toyooka.
nativeRange: Breeds in the Amur and Ussuri basins of the Russian Far East and NE China; winters mainly in the Yangtze basin, with smaller numbers in Korea, Japan and Taiwan
abilities: Migrates between the Russian Far East and the Yangtze floodplain
Nests on tall trees and electricity pylons
Communicates by loud bill-clattering, being almost voiceless

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, snakes, crustaceans and insects
animal.habitat: Wetlands, river floodplains, rice paddies and lake margins
animal.size: About 110–128 cm long; wingspan about 2.1 m
animal.behaviour: Feeds by walking slowly through shallow water; in Japan, reintroduced storks forage in rice paddies managed without pesticides.
fieldMarks: Large white stork with black flight feathers
Heavy, black bill (red in White stork)
Red bare skin around a whitish eye
Red legs
animal.voice: Almost silent; loud bill-clattering at the nest
animal.lookalikes: White stork (Europe, Central Asia) is smaller with a red bill; Black-faced spoonbill and egrets are smaller with different bills.
animal.whereToSee: Poyang Lake and Dongting Lake in China in winter; Toyooka, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan year-round
animal.season: Winter visitor to the Yangtze (Nov–Mar); summer visitor to the breeding grounds; resident in reintroduced Japanese populations

lore: In Japan, as in Europe, the stork came to be linked with bringing babies. Toyooka city began releasing captive-bred storks in 2005, promoting 'stork-friendly' pesticide-reduced rice as part of the recovery.
funFact: Wild storks bred in Japan again in 2007, the first wild-hatched chick in the country in over four decades.

wiki.extract: The Oriental stork is a large, white bird with black-feathered wings in the stork family Ciconiidae.

plates.title: Ulyssis Aldrovandi ... Ornithologiae
plates.author: Aldrovandi, Ulisse
plates.desc: A full-page plate (Tabula XI) featuring a grid of nine ornithological illustrations, including various cranes, flamingos, an ibis, a black stork with a snake, and a detailed crane skeleton.
plates.long: This intricate plate from Ulisse Aldrovandi's 'Ornithologiae' (1610) presents a comparative study of various long-legged birds, including flamingos and cranes. Notably, it includes a detailed anatomical study of a crane skeleton alongside living specimens, reflecting the burgeoning scientific interest in comparative anatomy during the early 17th century.

plates.title: Worksop Bestiary
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: A bird, likely a stork (Ciconia), depicted within a circular blue and red frame.
plates.long: A stork is shown in a circular roundel, illustrating the text's description of the bird's habits. Bestiaries often used such animals to convey moral or religious lessons to the reader through allegorical interpretation.

plates.title: Valeriano: Hieroglyphica (1575)

summary: A tall white wader with black flight feathers and a red bill, which nests on rooftops, church towers and pylons. Its soaring migrations funnel over Gibraltar, the Bosphorus and Israel in hundreds of thousands on the way to Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa, with some in South Asia and increasingly in Iberia
abilities: Soars on thermals to save energy, avoiding long sea crossings
Communicates by bill-clattering, as it is almost voiceless
Reuses enormous stick nests for decades; some nests weigh hundreds of kilograms
Many Iberian storks now winter on rubbish tips instead of crossing to Africa

animal.diet: Frogs, insects (especially locusts and grasshoppers), worms, small mammals, fish and reptiles
animal.habitat: Wet meadows, farmland, river valleys and marshes near villages
animal.behaviour: Mates greet each other at the nest by throwing back their heads and clattering their bills like castanets.
fieldMarks: White body with black flight feathers
Long red bill and red legs
Flies with neck outstretched and legs trailing
Juveniles have dull, dark-tipped bills
animal.voice: Adults are nearly silent except for loud bill-clattering; chicks make hissing and mewing sounds.
animal.lookalikes: Black stork is glossy black above with a white belly. Common crane is grey with a black-and-white head. Great white egret is all white with a yellow or dark bill and flies with its neck folded.
animal.whereToSee: Rooftop colonies in Alsace, Extremadura, Poland (Żywkowo) and Morocco; mass migration at the Strait of Gibraltar, Istanbul's Bosphorus and the Hula Valley, Israel.
animal.season: Summer visitor Feb/Mar–Aug; migration peaks in late August and in March

lore: In 1822 a stork shot in Klütz, Germany, carried a central African spear in its neck; this 'Pfeilstorch' helped prove that birds migrate rather than hibernate. Across the Islamic world storks were revered as pilgrims that travelled towards Mecca each year, and in Turkey the bird is still affectionately called 'hacı leylek', the pilgrim stork.
funFact: The European legend of storks delivering babies is linked to their return each spring and their faithful nesting on houses.

wiki.extract: The white stork is a large bird in the stork family, Ciconiidae. Its plumage is mainly white, with black on the bird's wings. Adults have long red legs and long pointed red beaks, and measure on average 100–115 cm (39–45 in) from beak tip to end of tail, with a 155–215 cm (61–85 in) wingspan. The two subspecies, which differ slightly in size, breed in Europe north to Finland, northwestern Africa, Palearctic east to southern Kazakhstan and southern Africa. The white stork is a long-distance migrant, wintering in Africa from tropical Sub-Saharan Africa to as far south as South Africa, or on the Indian subcontinent. When migrating between Europe and Africa, it avoids crossing the Mediterranean Sea and detours via the Levant in the east or the Strait of Gibraltar in the west, because the air thermals on which it depends for soaring do not form over water.

summary: A tall, striking stork with a glossy black neck that flashes green and purple, a massive black bill and coral-red legs. It is one of the few storks in which males and females can be told apart by eye colour.
nativeRange: India, Nepal and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to New Guinea and northern and eastern Australia
abilities: Hunts large prey including fish, turtles and snakes
Pairs defend large territories in wetlands
Performs a wing-spreading and bill-clattering greeting display at the nest

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, turtles, snakes, crustaceans and occasionally birds
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, river banks, lakes and flooded fields
animal.size: About 130–150 cm tall; wingspan about 2.3 m
animal.behaviour: Stalks slowly through shallow water and stabs prey with its huge bill; pairs nest alone in tall trees rather than in colonies.

Glossy black head and neck with green and purple sheen
Massive, straight black bill
Bright coral-red legs; female has a yellow iris, male dark brown

animal.lookalikes: Lesser adjutant is grey with a bare head; Woolly-necked stork has a white neck; Saddle-billed stork is African.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park and the wetlands of Uttar Pradesh in India; Chitwan and Koshi Tappu in Nepal; Kakadu in Australia
animal.season: Resident

lore: Australians long called it the jabiru, a name borrowed from a quite different South American stork.
funFact: The female's yellow iris is one of the easiest ways to sex any large bird in the field.

wiki.extract: The black-necked stork is a tall, long-necked wading bird in the stork family. It is a resident species across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia with a disjunct population in Australia. It lives in wetland habitats and near fields of certain crops such as rice and wheat where it forages for a wide range of animal prey. Adult birds of both sexes have a heavy bill and are patterned in white and irridescent blacks, but the sexes differ in the colour of the iris with females sporting yellow irises and males having dark-coloured irises. In Australia, it is known as a jabiru, although that name also refers to a stork species found in the Americas. It is one of the few storks that are strongly territorial when feeding and breeding.

summary: A massive, bald-headed stork that scavenges carcasses and rubbish dumps alongside vultures. Its wingspan rivals the largest of any land bird.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Wingspan regularly exceeds 2.5 m and is reported up to 3 m or more
Inflates an air-filled neck sac in display
Has adapted to towns, scavenging dumps and fish markets
Takes live prey including flamingos, frogs and rodents

animal.habitat: Savanna, wetlands, fishing villages and cities
animal.behaviour: In cities like Kampala, marabous nest in trees along streets and patrol rubbish dumps.
fieldMarks: Bald, pinkish head and neck, often with scabby spots
Huge, wedge-shaped pale bill
Pendulous pink throat pouch
Dark grey back and wings, white underparts
Long grey legs often whitened with excreta
animal.voice: Mostly silent; clatters its bill and gives croaks and grunts.

animal.whereToSee: Kampala (Uganda), Lake Naivasha, Serengeti, Maasai Mara, Kruger, Chobe
animal.season: Resident or nomadic

lore: Fluffy marabou undertail feathers were widely traded in the 19th and 20th centuries for hats and trimmings; 'marabou' became a name for any fluffy trim.
funFact: Marabous cool their legs by excreting on them, a habit known as urohidrosis.
