wiki.extract: The marabou stork is a large wading bird in the stork family Ciconiidae native to sub-Saharan Africa. It breeds in both wet and arid habitats, often near human habitation, especially landfill sites. It is sometimes called the "undertaker bird" due to its shape from behind: cloak-like wings and back, skinny white legs, and sometimes a large white mass of "hair". It has often been credited with the largest wingspan of any land bird, with an average of 2.6 metres (8.5 ft) and some recorded examples of up to 3.2 metres (10 ft).

summary: A large white stork with a waxy yellow bill, a bare orange face and rose-pink feathers on its back, nesting in noisy colonies in wetland trees and even village trees. Its numbers have recovered enough that it was moved from Near Threatened to Least Concern in 2023.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Sindh) and India through Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to Southeast Asia and southern China
abilities: Feels for fish by sweeping its half-open bill through water, snapping it shut in milliseconds
Nests in large mixed colonies alongside herons, cormorants and pelicans
Cools itself and its chicks by panting and shading them with spread wings

animal.diet: Mainly fish, also frogs, crustaceans and snakes
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, lakes, rice fields and reservoirs
animal.size: About 93–102 cm long; wingspan about 150–160 cm
animal.behaviour: Wades in shallow water with its bill submerged and partly open, moving it side to side and stirring the water with one foot.
fieldMarks: Large white stork with long, heavy, slightly down-curved yellow bill
Bare orange-red face
Black-and-white wings and black band across the breast
Pink-tinged tertials on the back; pinkish legs
animal.voice: Mostly silent; adults clatter their bills at the nest; chicks give loud begging calls
animal.lookalikes: Asian openbill is smaller, greyish, with a gap in its bill; Woolly-necked stork is dark with a white neck; Black-headed ibis has a black head and curved black bill.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), Kokkare Bellur village in Karnataka and Ranganathittu
animal.season: Resident with local movements; breeds after the monsoon (Aug–Mar)

lore: At Kokkare Bellur in Karnataka, villagers have long protected the painted storks and pelicans that nest in their trees, using the droppings as fertiliser.
funFact: Its bill-sweeping strike is a touch reflex: it can catch fish in muddy water it cannot see through.

wiki.extract: The painted stork is a large wader in the stork family. It is found in the wetlands of the plains of tropical Asia south of the Himalayas in the Indian subcontinent and extending into Southeast Asia. Their distinctive pink tertial feathers of the adults give them their name. They forage in flocks in shallow waters along rivers or lakes. They immerse their half open beaks in water and sweep them from side to side and snap up their prey of small fish that are sensed by touch. As they wade along they also stir the water with their feet to flush hiding fish. They nest colonially in trees, often along with other waterbirds. The only sounds they produce are weak moans or bill clattering at the nest. They are not migratory and only make short-distance movements in some parts of their range in response to changes in weather or food availability or for breeding. Like other storks, they are often seen soaring on thermals.

summary: The only European songbird that swims and walks underwater. This chunky, white-bibbed bird bobs on boulders in fast mountain streams before plunging in to hunt insect larvae on the riverbed.
nativeRange: Fast rivers of Europe, northwest Africa (Atlas), Turkey, the Caucasus, Iran and Central Asia to the Himalaya and western China
abilities: Walks along the stream bed against the current, using its wings to stay down
Has dense plumage and a large preen gland for waterproofing
Can close its nostrils with flaps of skin when submerged
Sings through the winter, even beside frozen torrents

animal.diet: Caddisfly, mayfly and stonefly larvae, freshwater shrimps, small fish
animal.habitat: Clear, fast-flowing upland streams and rivers
animal.behaviour: Bobs constantly on a stone in midstream, blinking its white eyelids, before diving in.
fieldMarks: Plump, short-tailed, wren-like shape
Bright white throat and breast
Dark chocolate-brown head and blackish body; some races have a chestnut belly band
Whirring, low flight over water
animal.voice: A sharp, metallic 'zit' in flight; song a sweet, rambling warble heard even in winter.
animal.lookalikes: Ring ouzel has a white breast crescent but is a thrush of moorland, not water. Brown dipper (Central Asia, Himalaya) is entirely brown with no white bib.
animal.whereToSee: Upland streams in Wales, northern England and Scotland, the Alps, Pyrenees, Norwegian rivers and Atlas Mountains.
animal.season: Resident; northern birds move to ice-free water in winter

lore: Norway made the dipper (fossekall, 'waterfall man') its national bird in 1963, and the Welsh name 'bronwen y dŵr' means 'white breast of the water'.
funFact: Studies in Wales found dipper numbers fell on acidified streams, making it an indicator of river health.

wiki.extract: The white-throated dipper, also known as the European dipper or just dipper, is an aquatic, passerine bird found in Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. The species is divided into several subspecies, based primarily on colour differences, particularly of the pectoral band.

plates.title: Of the Eggs and Nests of Birds
plates.author: Giuseppe Zinanni (Ginanni) (1692-1753)
plates.desc: A scientific plate (Tav. XIX) divided into three horizontal registers illustrating bird eggs. The top panel shows the egg of a wild duck (Anitra salvatica, 94); the middle panel shows the egg of a merganser (Smergo, o Fifolo marino, 95) with marsh grass; the bottom panel shows the eggs of a dipper (Merlo acquatico, 97) and a coot (Folica, 96).
plates.long: This engraving from Giuseppe Zinanni’s 1737 treatise, 'Delle uova e dei nidi degli uccelli', represents one of the earliest systematic scientific studies of bird eggs. The plate utilizes fine intaglio lines and crosshatching to convey the volume, texture, and relative scale of eggs belonging to the wild duck, merganser, dipper, and coot. Such illustrations were critical for the development of oolo

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a cinclus, a bird identified in Conrad Gessner’s 1554 encyclopedic work. The image reflects the Renaissance transition toward empirical observation in natural history, utilizing detailed line work to categorize avian species. Such woodcuts were essential for the early scientific dissemination of zoological knowledge across Europe.

otherNames: Cháng wěi féng yè yīng 长尾缝叶莺 (Chinese)
summary: A tiny green warbler with a rusty cap and a cocked tail that literally sews its nest, piercing the edges of large leaves with its bill and stitching them into a cup with spider silk or plant fibre. Its loud call belies its size.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and Java
abilities: Punches holes along a leaf margin and pulls fibres through, knotting them like rivets
Builds the nest inside one or more living leaves so it stays green and camouflaged
Thrives in city gardens and potted plants

animal.diet: Small insects, larvae and spiders
animal.habitat: Gardens, hedges, scrub, plantations and forest edge
animal.size: About 10–14 cm long; breeding males have longer central tail feathers
animal.behaviour: Restless, moving through low bushes with its tail cocked and flicking; the stitched leaf-cradle holds a soft cup of plant down.
fieldMarks: Tiny bright olive-green warbler with whitish underparts
Rufous forecrown
Long, thin, slightly curved bill
Long tail held upright, sometimes with dark spots near the base of the throat
animal.voice: A loud, repeated 'towit-towit-towit' or 'cheeyup-cheeyup', surprisingly loud for the bird's size
animal.lookalikes: Dark-necked tailorbird (NE India, SE Asia) has a dark throat patch; prinias are browner with long graduated tails and lack the rufous cap.
animal.whereToSee: Garden hedges and shrubs throughout Pakistan and India, e.g. Lahore, Karachi, Delhi and Colombo
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Rudyard Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' features Darzee and his wife, a pair of tailorbirds, named with the Hindustani word for tailor.
funFact: The 'stitches' are not true sewing: the fibres are pushed through each hole and fluffed out on the outside so they hold like a rivet.

wiki.extract: The common tailorbird is a songbird found across tropical and subtropical Asia. Popular for its nest made of leaves "sewn" together and immortalized by Rudyard Kipling as Darzee in his Jungle Book, it is a common resident in urban gardens. Although shy birds that are usually hidden within vegetation, their loud calls are familiar and give away their presence. They are distinctive in having a long upright tail, greenish upper body plumage and rust coloured forehead and crown. This passerine bird is typically found in open farmland, scrub, forest edges and gardens. Tailorbirds get their name from the way their nest is constructed. The edges of a large leaf are pierced and sewn together with plant fibre or spider silk to make a cradle in which the actual nest is built.

summary: One of the most abundant fish in the world, swimming in schools of hundreds of millions. Herring underpinned the Hanseatic League and the Dutch Golden Age and still feeds whales, seabirds, cod and people.
nativeRange: North Atlantic from the Bay of Biscay to Svalbard and from Cape Hatteras to Greenland; Baltic Sea
abilities: Forms some of the largest fish schools on Earth
Filter-feeds and also picks individual zooplankton
Releases bubbles from the anus that produce 'fast repetitive tick' sounds, possibly used to keep schools together at night
Different stocks spawn in almost every season
edibleParts: flesh (pickled, salted, smoked as kippers, fermented as surströmming)
edibilityNote: Low mercury, rich in omega-3 oils. Raw or lightly cured herring can carry Anisakis larvae; freezing before curing (as required for Dutch 'maatjes') kills them. Baltic herring can be high in dioxins, and Nordic food agencies limit consumption advice.

animal.diet: Copepods, krill, fish larvae
animal.habitat: Open shelf waters; spawns on gravel banks and seaweed
animal.behaviour: Migrates between feeding, overwintering and spawning grounds in huge schools; eggs are sticky and laid in carpets on the seabed.
fieldMarks: Slim, silvery body with blue-green back
Single dorsal fin set at the mid-point of the body
Belly keel with scutes that are not sharply serrated
Loose, easily shed scales
Gill cover without radiating ridges
animal.lookalikes: Sprat is smaller with a sharply saw-edged belly keel and pelvic fins starting in front of the dorsal; shads have a notch in the upper jaw and dark shoulder spots.
animal.whereToSee: Northern Norwegian fjords in winter (with feeding orcas and humpbacks), Baltic coasts, Gulf of Maine
animal.season: Year-round; Norwegian spring-spawning herring overwinter in northern fjords and coastal waters in winter

lore: Dutch tradition credits Willem Beukelszoon with 'gibbing' herring in the 14th century, a preservation method that helped make Holland rich; Scandinavians called the shoals 'silver of the sea'.
funFact: The discovery that herring communicate by farting bubbles won an Ig Nobel Prize in Biology in 2004.

wiki.extract: Atlantic herring is a herring in the family Clupeidae. It is one of the most abundant fish species in the world. Atlantic herrings can be found on both sides of the northern Atlantic Ocean, congregating in large schools. They can grow up to 45 centimetres (18 in) in length and weigh up to 1.1 kilograms (2.4 lb). They feed on copepods, krill and small fish, while their natural predators are seals, whales, cod and other larger fish.

The illustration captures the fish's streamlined body and forked tail, reflecting the 17th-century Dutch interest in documenting marine life central to the region's economy and diet. Such prints served as both scientific records and access

summary: A boom-and-bust forage fish of the cool upwelling coasts of the Pacific and southern Africa. Its numbers swing over decades, alternating with anchovies, and its collapse emptied Monterey's Cannery Row.
nativeRange: Temperate upwelling coasts of the Pacific (California, Peru–Chile, Japan, Australia–New Zealand) and southern Africa
abilities: Populations rise and crash over multi-decade cycles linked to ocean temperature regimes
Filter-feeds on phytoplankton and zooplankton
South Africa's winter 'sardine run' draws dolphins, sharks, gannets and Bryde's whales in one of the ocean's great feeding spectacles
edibilityNote: Very low mercury and high omega-3. Like other oily fish, spoils rapidly; poorly handled fish can cause scombroid poisoning.

animal.diet: Phytoplankton and zooplankton
animal.habitat: Coastal pelagic waters, often near upwelling fronts
animal.lifespan: Up to about 13 years; most fewer
animal.size: Up to about 40 cm; commonly 15–25 cm
animal.behaviour: Migrates seasonally along coasts in vast schools; off South Africa's east coast, shoals move north in a tongue of cool water each winter.
fieldMarks: Rounded, silvery body with a blue-green back
One to three rows of dark spots along the upper sides
Radiating bony striae on the gill cover
Single dorsal fin, forked tail
animal.lookalikes: European pilchard (Sardina pilchardus) is very similar but lives in the NE Atlantic and Mediterranean; Pacific herring lacks the dark spots and gill-cover ridges.
animal.whereToSee: Wild Coast and KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa (sardine run); Monterey Bay; California Current upwelling coasts
animal.season: South African sardine run Jun–Jul

lore: Monterey's sardine canneries, immortalised in John Steinbeck's Cannery Row (1945), closed after the stock collapsed in the late 1940s and 1950s.
funFact: Fish scales preserved in Santa Barbara Basin sediments show sardine booms and busts occurred for centuries before industrial fishing.

wiki.extract: Sardinops is a genus of sardines of the family Alosidae. It is found in the Indo-Pacific, East Pacific, Southeastern Atlantic, and southwestern Indian oceans. Its length is up to 40 cm (16 in). It has numerous common or vernacular names, some of which more appropriately refer to subspecies, including blue pilchard, blue-bait, South American pilchard, Chilean sardine, and Pacific sardine.

plates.long: This large woodcut illustrates a sardine, emphasizing its characteristic large scales. It exemplifies the high standard of scientific illustration in Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium', which remained a standard reference for centuries.

The illustration is a significant example of 18th-century natural history art, blending scientific observation with the vibrant, often stylized aesthetic typical of early colonial biological surveys.

summary: The classic red ladybird with seven black spots, a voracious predator of aphids. Gardeners welcome it as one of the oldest natural pest controls.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia and North Africa; introduced to North America
abilities: A single larva can eat hundreds of aphids before pupating
Reflex-bleeds bitter, alkaloid-laden yellow fluid from its leg joints when attacked
Bright warning colours advertise its bad taste
Overwinters in large aggregations

animal.diet: Aphids and other soft-bodied insects; some pollen
animal.habitat: Grassland, crops, gardens and hedgerows
animal.behaviour: Adults cluster in leaf litter or tussocks to hibernate through winter.
fieldMarks: Red domed wing cases with seven black spots (three on each side and one shared at the front)
Black head shield with a whitish patch in each front corner
Black legs
About 7–8 mm long
animal.lookalikes: Harlequin ladybird (Harmonia axyridis) is larger and very variable, often with an M- or W-shaped mark on a white head shield and brown or orange legs. Two-spot ladybird is smaller with only two spots.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, grassland, crops and hedgerows wherever aphids are plentiful
animal.season: Active Mar–Oct; overwinters as an adult in leaf litter and dense vegetation

lore: Its English and German names honour the Virgin Mary ('Our Lady's bird', Marienkäfer), whose red cloak and seven sorrows the colours and spots were said to recall. It was released in the USA repeatedly to control aphids, and wild populations were established there by the 1970s.
funFact: Its seven spots are fixed for life; they do not indicate age, despite the folk belief.

wiki.extract: Coccinella septempunctata, commonly known as the seven-spot ladybird, often abbreviated C-7, is a carnivorous beetle native to Europe, most of Asia, and North Africa. It inhabits many regions with a temperate climate. The beetle has been introduced to several other areas, including North America as a biological pest control agent to combat aphid infestations. It is one of approximately 5,000 species of ladybird worldwide. Tatia Bauer states that C. septempunctata's ability to adapt to many different habitats makes it "one of the most successful aphidophagous insects".

summary: The largest land-living arthropod, a giant hermit crab that abandons its borrowed shell and can weigh 4 kg with legs spanning about a metre. Its claws pinch with a force rivalling the bite of a lion, enough to crack open coconuts.
nativeRange: Islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, from Zanzibar, Aldabra and the Chagos through Christmas Island and Indonesia to Micronesia and Polynesia
abilities: Pinching force measured at over 3,300 newtons, among the strongest of any crustacean
Opens coconuts by stripping the husk and hammering the shell
Breathes air with modified gills ('branchiostegal lungs') and drowns if kept underwater
Climbs trees and can live 60 years or more

animal.diet: Coconuts, fruit, nuts, carrion, other crabs, and occasionally birds and rats
animal.habitat: Coastal forest and rocky areas on islands, sheltering in burrows and crevices by day
animal.size: Up to about 4 kg and a leg span of about 1 m
animal.behaviour: Females release eggs into the sea at high tide; larvae drift for weeks, then young crabs come ashore using snail shells before outgrowing them.
fieldMarks: Enormous land crab with a hard, curled-under abdomen and no shell
Colour varies from violet-blue to orange-red
Very large front claws, the left usually bigger
Long, sturdy antennae
animal.lookalikes: Land hermit crabs (Coenobita) are much smaller and keep living in snail shells as adults. Juvenile coconut crabs also use shells and are told apart by their heavier claws and colour.
animal.whereToSee: Christmas Island (Indian Ocean), Aldabra, the Chagos atolls, Vanuatu and Niue, mostly at night.
animal.season: Year-round; most active at night

edibleParts: meat of legs, claws and abdomen (cooked)
edibilityNote: Prized as a delicacy on Pacific islands, but heavy harvesting threatens it and many places protect it. Crabs that have eaten toxic plants (such as Cerbera) have occasionally poisoned people.
lore: Charles Darwin described coconut crabs on the Keeling Islands in The Voyage of the Beagle, noting how they tear husks fibre by fibre before breaking the shell.
funFact: In 2016 a coconut crab on the Chagos Islands was observed killing and eating a red-footed booby, confirming it can prey on birds.

wiki.extract: The coconut crab is a terrestrial species of giant hermit crab, and is also known as the robber crab or palm thief. It is the largest living terrestrial arthropod, with a weight up to 4.1 kg. The distance from the tip of one leg to the tip of another can be as wide as 90 centimeters. It is found on islands across the Indian and Pacific Oceans, as far east as the Gambier Islands, Pitcairn Islands, and Caroline Island, and as far west as Zanzibar. While its range broadly shadows the distribution of the coconut palm, the coconut crab has been extirpated from most areas with a significant human population such as mainland Australia and Madagascar.

plates.long: A detailed engraving of a large crab, likely the coconut crab (Birgus latro), depicted with its soft abdomen exposed. The illustration includes anatomical labels 'I' and 'H' and uses subtle hand-applied colors to distinguish different textures of the shell and flesh. A heavy cast shadow provides a sense of physical presence and depth.

summary: A tree snake of Southeast Asia that glides between trees. It launches from a branch, flattens its body and undulates through the air. It is mildly venomous to its lizard prey but harmless to people.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia: southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Borneo, Sumatra, Java, the Philippines and nearby islands
abilities: Glides between trees, travelling farther than it drops, steering by undulating
Flattens its body into a concave 'wing' by spreading its ribs
Has rear fangs with mild venom for subduing lizards; harmless to humans

animal.diet: Lizards (especially geckos), frogs, bats, small birds
animal.habitat: Rainforest canopy, mangroves and urban parks
animal.behaviour: It hangs from a branch in a J shape, then jumps and glides. In Jake Socha's experiments, snakes launched from a 10 m tower travelled farther horizontally than they dropped.
fieldMarks: Black body with each scale centred in bright green or yellow-green
Row of red-orange spots along the back
Long thin body, flat head, large eyes
animal.lookalikes: The golden tree snake (C. ornata) is larger, often lacks red spots and has more yellow. The twin-barred tree snake (C. pelias) is banded red, black and white. All are mildly venomous and harmless to people.
animal.whereToSee: Singapore Botanic Gardens and parks, Borneo's lowland forests, Malaysian mangroves
animal.season: Resident; active by day

funFact: Wind-tunnel tests on models of its flattened body showed that its cross-section produces surprisingly high lift, especially when tilted at about 35 degrees.

wiki.extract: Paradise tree snake, paradise flying snake or garden flying snake is a species of colubrid snake found in Southeast Asia. It can, like all species of its genus Chrysopelea, glide by stretching the body into a flattened strip using its ribs. It is mostly found in moist forests and can cover a horizontal distance of 10 meters or more in a glide from the top of a tree. Slow motion photography shows an undulation of the snake's body in flight while the head remains relatively stable, suggesting controlled flight. They are mildly venomous with rear fangs and also can constrict their prey, which consists of mostly lizards and bats.

summary: A slender, huge-eyed tree snake of sub-Saharan Africa. Its fangs sit at the back of the mouth, yet its venom is among the most dangerous of any snake. Bites are rare, but the venom works slowly and can cause fatal internal bleeding a day or more later.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from West Africa to Ethiopia and south to South Africa; absent from the central rainforest and the driest deserts
abilities: Has excellent eyesight for a snake, with very large eyes that help it hunt chameleons by sight
Venom stops blood from clotting, causing bleeding from gums, wounds and internal organs
Inflates its throat to twice its size when threatened, showing the bright skin between its scales

animal.diet: Chameleons and other tree lizards, birds and their eggs and nestlings, frogs
animal.habitat: Trees and shrubs in savanna, woodland, fynbos and Karoo scrub
animal.behaviour: Shy; it flees through the branches and bites only when handled or cornered. Because the symptoms can take hours to appear, anyone bitten must go to hospital at once and be observed for at least 24 hours. A specific monovalent boomslang antivenom is made in South Africa. Keep the limb still; never cut or suck the wound.
fieldMarks: Short, egg-shaped head with enormous eyes, much larger than in most snakes
Colour very variable: males often bright green, or green with black-edged scales; females usually olive or brown
Strongly keeled scales and a slender, whip-like body
Throat inflated into a balloon when alarmed
animal.lookalikes: Harmless green bush snakes (Philothamnus) look very similar but are smaller, with smaller eyes in proportion to the head. They can be hard to tell apart even for experts, so never approach or handle one to check; treat any large-eyed green or brown tree snake as a possible boomslang. Green mambas have a long, narrow head and smaller eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park, KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern and Western Cape, East African savannas; often in thorn trees near weaver nests
animal.season: Resident; active by day, especially in warm months

lore: In 1957 the American herpetologist Karl P. Schmidt was bitten by a juvenile boomslang he was identifying. Thinking a rear-fanged snake could not kill him, he wrote notes on his symptoms as they progressed and died the next day.
funFact: The boomslang has some of the largest eyes relative to head size of any snake.

wiki.extract: The boomslang is a highly venomous snake in the family Colubridae. The species is native to Sub-Saharan Africa.

summary: A harmless water-loving snake with a bright yellow collar, found across central and eastern Europe into Asia. It eats frogs and fish, plays dead when caught, and lays its eggs in compost heaps and manure, which act as natural incubators.
nativeRange: Central and eastern Europe and Scandinavia, east to Lake Baikal and south to the Caucasus and Iran; western populations (Britain, France, western Germany) are now treated as the barred grass snake, Natrix helvetica
abilities: Swims and dives well, hunting frogs, newts and fish
When grabbed, gives off a foul-smelling fluid and may 'play dead', going limp with its mouth open and tongue hanging
Uses the heat of rotting vegetation to incubate its eggs

animal.diet: Frogs, toads, newts, fish, occasionally small mammals
animal.habitat: Ponds, rivers, marshes, damp meadows and gardens
animal.behaviour: Rarely bites. When threatened it hisses and fake-strikes with its mouth closed, then plays dead. Females often lay their eggs together in the same compost heap.
fieldMarks: Yellow, cream or orange collar behind the head, with a black crescent behind it
Olive-grey to green body with small black bars along the sides
Round pupils, rounded head
Chequered black-and-white belly
animal.lookalikes: The adder (Vipera berus) is shorter and stockier, has a dark zigzag down its back, a V or X mark on its head, vertical pupils and no yellow collar. The dice snake (N. tessellata) has no collar and is blotched. In western Europe the barred grass snake (N. helvetica) is very similar but often has bolder side bars and a weaker collar; range is the best guide.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes and wetlands across Poland, the Baltic states, Scandinavia and central Europe; often seen swimming in ponds on sunny days
animal.season: Active April–October; hibernates in winter

lore: In Lithuania the žaltys was a household guardian, fed milk and kept in homes. The folk tale 'Eglė, Queen of Serpents' tells of a girl who marries a žaltys, the Serpent King.
funFact: In 2017 genetic work split the grass snake in two, so the familiar British grass snake is now the barred grass snake, Natrix helvetica.

wiki.extract: The grass snake, sometimes called the ringed snake or water snake, is a Eurasian semi-aquatic non-venomous colubrid snake. It is often found near water and feeds almost exclusively on amphibians.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Natrix torquata' (grass snake), illustrating the creature's sinuous form and scale patterns. It is part of Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium', a foundational work in modern zoology that combined classical knowledge with new empirical observations.

summary: A slender, bright green snake of the eastern US that eats insects and disappears among leaves and vines. It is harmless and rarely bites.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern United States, from New Jersey to Florida, west to Kansas and Texas, and into northeastern Mexico
abilities: Camouflaged in vegetation, it sways in the breeze like a vine
Eats mostly insects and spiders, unusual among snakes
Females sometimes lay their eggs together in tree hollows

animal.diet: Caterpillars, crickets, grasshoppers, dragonflies, spiders
animal.habitat: Shrubs and trees beside lakes, streams and forest edges
animal.behaviour: Sleeps coiled on outer branches over water at night, where it can be found by torchlight.
fieldMarks: Uniform bright green above with a white, yellow or pale green belly
Keeled scales (giving the 'rough' feel)
Very long, thin body and tail
Round pupils and a rounded head
animal.lookalikes: The smooth green snake (Opheodrys vernalis) is smaller, more northern and has smooth scales. Green vine snakes in Mexico and further south have long pointed heads. No venomous snake in its US range is bright green.
animal.whereToSee: Lake and river edges across the southeastern US, e.g. Okefenokee Swamp, Everglades, Ozarks
animal.season: Active April–October; hibernates in winter

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1766 as Coluber aestivus, the 'summer snake'.
funFact: The pigment that colours it green breaks down after death, so preserved specimens and dead snakes on roads turn blue.

wiki.extract: Opheodrys aestivus, commonly known as the rough green snake, is a species of nonvenomous North American snake in the subfamily Colubrinae of the family Colubridae. The species is sometimes called grass snake or green grass snake, but these names are more commonly applied to the smooth green snake. The European colubrid called grass snake is not closely related. The rough green snake is docile, often allowing close approach by humans, and rarely bites. Even when bites occur, they have no venom and are harmless.

summary: A gentle, orange-and-red constrictor of the southeastern US and one of the most widely kept pet snakes. It is a rat-catcher of farms and woodlands, and is often killed because people mistake it for a copperhead.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States, from southern New Jersey to Florida and west to Louisiana and Kentucky
abilities: Climbs trees and walls easily, using the corners of its belly scales as grips
Constricts rodents and is a useful pest controller around barns
Bred in captivity for decades, producing many colour forms

animal.diet: Mice, rats, birds and eggs; juveniles eat lizards and frogs
animal.habitat: Pine forests, overgrown fields, old buildings, rock outcrops
animal.lifespan: ~6–8 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Mostly active at dusk and night in hot weather. When threatened it vibrates its tail in leaf litter and may strike, but it is harmless.
fieldMarks: Orange to brownish-grey body with large red or orange saddles edged in black
Spear-point mark on top of the head extending onto the neck
Black-and-white checkerboard belly
Slender body, round pupils, no heat pits
animal.lookalikes: The venomous copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) has hourglass-shaped tan-to-copper crossbands that are narrow on the back and wide on the sides, a plain unpatterned head, vertical pupils, heat pits and a heavy body. The corn snake has saddles that are widest on the back, a spear-point head pattern, round pupils and a checkered belly.
animal.whereToSee: Pine flatwoods of Florida and the Carolinas, Great Smoky Mountains foothills; often found at night on roads in summer
animal.season: Resident; active April–October in the north, nearly all year in Florida

lore: The name may come from its checkered belly, which resembles kernels of 'Indian corn', or from its habit of hunting rats in corn cribs. Linnaeus named it Coluber guttatus in 1766.
funFact: Captive breeders have produced dozens of colour forms, with names like 'Snow', 'Anery' and 'Bloodred'.

wiki.extract: The corn snake, sometimes called the red rat snake, is a species of North American rat snake in the family Colubridae. The species subdues its small prey by constriction. It is found throughout the southeastern and central United States. Though superficially resembling the venomous copperhead and often killed as a result of this mistaken identity, the corn snake lacks functional venom and is harmless to humans. The corn snake is beneficial to humans because it helps control populations of wild rodent pests that damage crops and spread disease.

summary: A large, fast, non-venomous snake common in fields and towns across South and Southeast Asia, often killed because it is mistaken for a cobra. It eats large numbers of rats and is among the most useful snakes to farmers.
nativeRange: From Iran, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan across Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to southern China, Taiwan, Indochina and Java
abilities: Moves very quickly and climbs trees and walls
When cornered, puffs out its throat and makes a growling sound
Holds prey down with its body rather than constricting it

animal.diet: Rats, frogs, toads, birds, lizards, other snakes
animal.habitat: Rice paddies, scrub, open forest, gardens and suburbs
animal.size: Usually 1.5–2 m; occasionally ~2.5 m or more
animal.behaviour: Active by day. In the breeding season males wrestle in tall, swaying twists, and this is often mistaken for mating between a rat snake and a cobra. It is harmless, but it bites hard if handled.
fieldMarks: Large, prominent eyes with round pupils
Black edges to the lip scales, like vertical bars
Body brownish-olive to black, with dark crossbars or a net pattern towards the rear and tail
Long, slender body tapering into a very long tail; no hood
animal.lookalikes: The spectacled cobra has a hood with markings, a shorter tail, smaller eyes, and rears up and hisses rather than fleeing. The rat snake may inflate its throat but cannot form a broad hood. The banded-tail pattern and large eyes are the key signs of a rat snake.
animal.whereToSee: Rice fields, gardens and city edges across India and Sri Lanka; often seen crossing roads in the day
animal.season: Resident; most active in the monsoon

lore: In rural India the dhaman is falsely said to suck milk from cows, and is thought to be the cobra's mate. Before the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, huge numbers of rat snake skins were exported from India for leather.
funFact: Linnaeus named it Coluber mucosus in 1758, so it was among the first Asian snakes to receive a scientific name.

wiki.extract: Ptyas mucosa, commonly known as the Oriental rat snake, or Indian rat snake, is a common non-venomous species of colubrid snake found in parts of South and Southeast Asia. These are large snakes. Typical mature total length is around 1.5 to 1.95 m though some exceed 2 m. The record length for this species was 3.7 m, second only to their cousin Ptyas carinata among living colubrid snakes. Despite their large size, oriental ratsnakes are usually quite slender with even a specimen of 2 m commonly measuring 4 to 6 cm only around in diameter. Furthermore, the average weight of ratsnakes caught in Java was around 877 to 940 g, though larger males of over 2.3 m may easily weigh over 2.5 kg (5.5 lb). Their color varies from pale browns in dry regions to nearly black in moist forest areas. Rat snakes are diurnal, semi-arboreal, non-venomous, and fast-moving. Rat snakes eat a variety of prey and are frequently found in urban areas where rodents thrive.

summary: The wild ancestor of the domestic and city pigeon, probably the first bird tamed by humans. Homing pigeons can find their way back from hundreds of kilometres away, and carried messages for armies for millennia.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and Western and South Asia; feral populations worldwide
abilities: Homes over 1,000 km using sun compass, magnetic sense and landmarks
Possibly uses low-frequency infrasound for navigation
Both parents feed chicks 'crop milk'
Trained to tell paintings by Monet from Picasso (Watanabe et al. 1995)
Can recognise individual human faces

animal.diet: Seeds and grain; food scraps in cities
animal.habitat: Cliffs and ledges; buildings and bridges
animal.lifespan: 3–5 years in cities; up to 15+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Pairs raise up to six broods a year, breeding in almost any season.
fieldMarks: Blue-grey pigeon with an iridescent green-purple neck
Two broad black bars on each wing
White rump (wild type)
Feral birds come in many colours
animal.voice: Soft, cooing 'oo-roo-coo'
animal.lookalikes: Stock dove has no white rump and only short black wing bars. Woodpigeon is larger with a white neck patch and white wing bands.
animal.whereToSee: Wild-type birds on sea cliffs of western Scotland and Ireland; feral flocks in almost every city
animal.season: Resident

lore: Pigeon posts relayed news for the Persians, Romans and Mughals, and a pigeon named Cher Ami saved nearly 200 American soldiers in 1918. Darwin bred fancy pigeons to illustrate artificial selection in 'On the Origin of Species'.
funFact: Reuters began in 1850 using pigeons to carry stock prices between Aachen and Brussels.

wiki.extract: The rock dove, also known as the common pigeon or rock pigeon, is a member of the bird family Columbidae. In common usage, it is often simply referred to as the "pigeon", although the rock dove is the wild form of the bird; the pigeons familiar to most people are the domesticated forms of the wild rock dove.

summary: A big, iridescent green-and-white pigeon whose wingbeats whoosh through New Zealand forests. With other large fruit-eating birds extinct, it is the only native bird able to swallow the largest forest fruits whole, making it vital for spreading the seeds of trees such as taraire and tawa.
nativeRange: New Zealand
abilities: Swallows fruits up to about 2.5 cm across and disperses their seeds
Main or sole disperser of large-fruited native trees including taraire, tawa, karaka and miro
Performs steep, swooping display flights, stalling at the top before diving

animal.diet: Fruit, leaves, buds and flowers of native and introduced plants
animal.habitat: Native forest, scrub, farmland with trees, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: After gorging on fermenting fruit in summer, kererū are sometimes found too intoxicated to fly properly.
fieldMarks: Large pigeon with iridescent green-bronze head, throat and upperparts
Clean white breast and belly, sharply divided from the green bib
Red bill, eye and feet
Loud whooshing wingbeats in flight
animal.voice: Mostly silent; a soft, low 'ooo' coo. The noisy swish of the wings is usually heard first.
animal.lookalikes: Feral rock pigeons are smaller and grey. On the Chatham Islands the related parea is about a fifth larger, paler on the back, with a pale grey rump and an orange-tipped bill.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia and Otari-Wilton's Bush (Wellington), Tiritiri Matangi, Christchurch Botanic Gardens, native forest throughout New Zealand
animal.season: Resident

lore: Kererū were an important traditional food for Māori, harvested under seasonal restrictions, and their feathers were woven into cloaks; the bird is now fully protected. It was voted New Zealand's Bird of the Year in 2018.
funFact: Because no surviving native bird can swallow fruit as large, the decline of kererū could leave several of New Zealand's biggest-fruited trees with no natural seed disperser.

wiki.extract: The kererū, also known as kūkupa, New Zealand pigeon or wood pigeon, is a species of pigeon native to New Zealand. Johann Friedrich Gmelin described the bird in 1789 as a large, conspicuous pigeon up to 50 cm (20 in) in length and 550–850 g (19–30 oz) in weight, with a white breast and iridescent green–blue plumage. Two subspecies have been recognised; the second—the Norfolk pigeon of Norfolk Island—became extinct in the early 20th century. Kererū pairs are monogamous, breeding over successive seasons and remaining together when not breeding. They construct nests with twigs in trees, with a single egg clutch.

summary: A small, delicately patterned dove whose soft purring song was once a defining sound of European summer. It winters in the Sahel and has declined severely due to habitat loss and hunting on migration.
nativeRange: Breeds in Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western China; winters in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara
abilities: One of the few European doves to make a long-distance migration across the Sahara
Lives largely on small seeds of arable weeds such as fumitory
Produces a soft, purring song rather than cooing
Satellite tracking shows western birds wintering in the Sahel from Senegal to Mali

animal.diet: Seeds of weeds and cereals
animal.habitat: Farmland with tall hedges, scrub, woodland edge and orchards
animal.behaviour: Feeds quietly on the ground and flies off fast and low with a flicking wing action.
fieldMarks: Rufous-orange back with black-centred scalloped feathers
Black-and-white striped patch on each side of the neck
Pinkish breast and blue-grey head
Dark tail with a white border, obvious in flight
animal.voice: A soft, purring, rolling 'turrr-turrr', repeated drowsily.
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian collared dove is larger and plain sandy-grey with a single black half-collar. Oriental turtle dove (Siberia, Central Asia) is larger and darker. Laughing dove (Middle East) is smaller and has a speckled breast band.
animal.whereToSee: Mediterranean farmland in Spain, Morocco and Turkey; Suffolk and Essex hedgerows in England; heavy passage over Malta and Cyprus.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Sep

lore: The Song of Songs (2:12) proclaims 'the voice of the turtle is heard in our land', and in Persian and Urdu poetry the qomri or fakhta sings for the cypress tree; 'turtle' comes from Latin 'turtur', an imitation of its purr.
funFact: The UK population has fallen by over 90% since 1970, and it was listed globally as Vulnerable in 2015.

wiki.extract: The European turtle dove is a threatened or vulnerable member of the bird family Columbidae, the doves and pigeons. It breeds over a wide area of the south western Palearctic including north Africa but migrates to northern sub-Saharan Africa in winter.

summary: A beautifully patterned sea snail responsible for most of the recorded human deaths from cone snails. It hunts fish by engulfing them in a net-like mouth after releasing a cocktail of venoms that includes a fast-acting insulin.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific, from East Africa and the Red Sea to Japan, Australia and Polynesia
abilities: Fires a harpoon-like hollow tooth loaded with venom
Releases weaponised insulin into the water to send nearby fish into hypoglycaemic shock
Venom contains hundreds of different conotoxin peptides
Can kill a human; dozens of deaths are documented

animal.diet: Small fish, engulfed in an expandable mouth (rostrum)
animal.habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and sandy patches between corals
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night, spreading its false mouth over resting fish, which are sedated by venom and insulin before being stung and swallowed whole.
fieldMarks: Thin, light, broad cone shell with a wide aperture
Shoulder of the spire crowned with low knobs
Whitish to pinkish with brown net-like and blotchy bands, like an old map
Buried in sand by day
animal.lookalikes: Tulip cone (Conus tulipa) is smaller with a violet-pink tinge; textile cone (C. textile) has a tent-shaped triangular pattern. All cone snails should be treated as dangerous.
animal.whereToSee: Indo-Pacific reefs at night; often seen in shell collections. Never pick up a live cone.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Georg Rumphius recorded in 1705 that a woman on Ambon died after holding a live cone shell; Japanese call it Anboina-gai, the 'Ambon shell'.
funFact: Fish-hunting cones like this one helped researchers discover very fast-acting insulin forms that are being studied for diabetes treatment.

wiki.extract: Conus geographus, popularly called the geography cone, geographer cone, or geographic cone, is a species of predatory cone snail. It lives in reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific and hunts small fish. While all cone snails hunt and kill prey using venom, the venom of Conus geographus is potent enough to kill humans.

summary: A stocky, big-headed bird that looks dull brown when perched on a roadside wire, then opens its wings in flight to show electric bands of turquoise and deep violet-blue. In the breeding season the male tumbles and rolls through the air in display, the habit that gives rollers their name.
nativeRange: Iraq and the Persian Gulf east through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar
abilities: Hunts by watching from an exposed perch, then dropping onto large insects, lizards and small frogs on the ground
Performs a rolling, diving aerial courtship display with loud harsh calls
Follows tractors, grass fires and grazing cattle to snatch flushed insects

animal.diet: Large insects (grasshoppers, crickets, beetles), also scorpions, small lizards, frogs and rodents
animal.habitat: Open cultivation, grassland, light woodland and roadsides with plenty of perches
animal.behaviour: Sits motionless on wires and dead branches for long spells, then drops to the ground for prey and returns to the same perch; in courtship it climbs steeply and plunges in twisting, rolling dives.
fieldMarks: Thickset bird with large head and strong dark bill
Perched: rufous-brown breast and back, lilac-streaked throat, blue crown
In flight: brilliant bands of pale turquoise and dark violet-blue across the wings
Square blue tail with a dark terminal band
animal.voice: Harsh, crow-like 'chack' and grating 'kak-kak' calls, loudest during the rolling display flight
animal.lookalikes: European roller (a passage migrant in Pakistan and NW India) has a plain pale-blue head and underparts with no brown or lilac breast; Indochinese roller (east of the Brahmaputra) has a dark purplish-brown face and breast without fine streaks.
animal.whereToSee: Common along roadsides and farmland across the Indus plains of Punjab and Sindh and over most of India; easy at Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Ranthambore
animal.season: Resident; some local movements

lore: Its Hindi name Neelkanth ('blue throat') is an epithet of Shiva, and in much of north India seeing the bird on Dussehra is considered auspicious. It is the state bird of several Indian states, including Karnataka and Telangana.
funFact: The dull brown bird on the wire is the same one that flashes vivid blue in flight; the brightest colours are hidden on the wings until it moves.

wiki.extract: The Indian roller is a bird of the family Coraciidae. It is 30–34 cm (12–13 in) long with a wingspan of 65–74 cm (26–29 in) and weighs 166–176 g (5.9–6.2 oz). The face and throat are pinkish, the head and back are brown, with blue on the rump and contrasting light and dark blue on the wings and tail. The bright blue markings on the wing are prominent in flight. The sexes are similar in appearance. Two subspecies are recognised.

summary: One of Africa's most photographed birds: a stocky perch-hunter painted in turquoise, ultramarine, lilac and cinnamon, with two long tail streamers. It sits conspicuously on dead branches and drops onto insects and lizards on the ground.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Ethiopia and Somalia to northern South Africa and Namibia
abilities: Sit-and-wait hunter that spots small prey from exposed perches
Performs a tumbling, rolling display flight that gives rollers their name
Defends nest holes aggressively, diving at raptors and other intruders

animal.diet: Large insects, scorpions, centipedes, small lizards, frogs and occasionally small birds
animal.habitat: Acacia savanna and open woodland with scattered perches
animal.size: About 36 cm including tail streamers; 100–130 g
animal.behaviour: In display a bird climbs steeply and then dives with rocking, side-to-side rolls while calling harshly.
fieldMarks: Lilac throat and breast (blue-breasted in the northern subspecies lorti)
Turquoise belly, crown greenish, back cinnamon-brown
Brilliant ultramarine and turquoise wings, flashing in flight
Two long, thin, dark outer tail streamers
Heavy black bill
animal.voice: Harsh, grating 'rak' or 'kaak' calls, run together into a crackling series during the display flight.
animal.lookalikes: European roller (a winter visitor) has a blue head and breast and no tail streamers. Abyssinian roller has entirely blue underparts and even longer streamers and lives north of the equator. Racket-tailed roller has a blue breast and spatulate tips to its streamers. Purple roller is larger, with streaked purple-brown underparts and a square tail.
animal.whereToSee: Maasai Mara, Serengeti, Kruger, Okavango Delta, Chobe and Etosha; often on roadside dead trees
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Rollers take their common name from the tumbling display flight; the genus name Coracias comes from the Greek korakias, a kind of crow.
funFact: In the subspecies Coracias caudatus lorti of Ethiopia and Somalia the 'lilac' breast is blue, so not every lilac-breasted roller has one.

wiki.extract: The lilac-breasted roller is an African bird of the roller family, Coraciidae. It is widely distributed in Southern and Eastern Africa, and is a vagrant to the southern Arabian Peninsula. It prefers open woodland and savanna, and it is for the most part absent from treeless places. Usually found alone or in pairs, it perches at the tops of trees, poles or other high vantage points from where it can spot insects, amphibians and small birds moving about on the ground. Nesting takes place in a natural hole in a tree where a clutch of 2–4 eggs are laid, and incubated by both parents, who are extremely aggressive in defence of their nest, taking on raptors and other birds. During the breeding season the male will rise to a fair height, descending in swoops and dives, while uttering harsh, discordant cries. The sexes do not differ in coloration, and juveniles lack the long tail streamers of adults. This species is unofficially considered the national bird of Kenya. Alternative names for the lilac-breasted roller include the fork-tailed roller, lilac-throated roller, Mosilikatze's roller, and troupand.

summary: A jay-sized bird of shining turquoise and chestnut that watches for insects from wires and dead trees. It is named for its tumbling, rolling display flight, and it migrates to southern Africa for the winter.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern and eastern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western China and Kashmir; winters in eastern and southern Africa
abilities: Performs a tumbling, rolling display dive in spring
Nestlings vomit a foul-smelling orange fluid to deter predators
Nests in tree holes, banks and nest boxes, often old woodpecker holes
Migrates in loops across East Africa and Arabia

animal.diet: Large insects such as beetles and grasshoppers; lizards and small rodents
animal.habitat: Open country with old trees, steppe, farmland with scattered trees
animal.behaviour: Sits upright on a high perch and drops to the ground to seize prey.
fieldMarks: Bright turquoise head and underparts
Chestnut back
Deep violet-blue and black flight feathers flash in flight
Stout black bill
animal.voice: A harsh, crow-like 'rack-kack' and rattling 'krak-krak-krak' in display.
animal.lookalikes: Indian roller (Middle East, South Asia) has a rufous-pink breast and purple throat. Blue-cheeked bee-eater is green and slimmer. European bee-eater has a long, curved bill and tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura and the Ebro valley (Spain), the Crau and Camargue (France), Hungary, the Balkans, Turkey, Central Asian steppes; passage in East Africa.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr/May–Aug

lore: Its Persian name 'sabzqaba' means 'green robe', and Linnaeus's 'garrulus' (chattering) refers to its harsh calls.
funFact: Studies in Spain showed roller chicks' orange vomit discourages predators and may warn parents of danger.

wiki.extract: The European roller is the only member of the roller family Coraciidae breeding in Europe. Its range extends into the Maghreb, West Asia and Central Asia. It winters in southern Africa, primarily in dry wooded savanna and bushy plains. It occurs in a wide variety of habitats, but avoids treeless plains. It usually nests in tree holes.

summary: The largest songbird, an all-black corvid with problem-solving skills that rival great apes. It lives across the Northern Hemisphere from deserts to the high Arctic.
nativeRange: Northern Hemisphere: North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa
abilities: Plans ahead and saves tools for later use (Kabadayi & Osvath 2017)
Caches food and re-hides it when watched by rivals
Mimics human speech and other sounds
Associates with wolves and human hunters to scavenge their kills
Plays, including sliding down snowy roofs

animal.diet: Omnivore: carrion, small animals, eggs, grain, refuse
animal.habitat: Almost any open or wooded habitat
animal.lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild; over 40 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Young ravens gather in winter roosts and share information about food sources.
fieldMarks: All-black, glossy, crow-like bird, much larger than crows
Heavy, deep bill
Shaggy throat feathers
Wedge-shaped tail in flight; often soars and tumbles
animal.voice: A deep, resonant croak 'prruk', plus a wide range of knocks and gurgles
animal.lookalikes: Carrion and American crows are smaller with thinner bills, square tails and cawing calls; they rarely soar.
animal.whereToSee: Mountain and coastal cliffs (e.g. Snowdonia, Wales); Yellowstone; a captive group at the Tower of London
animal.season: Resident

lore: Odin's ravens Huginn and Muninn ('thought' and 'memory') flew over the world bringing him news, and Raven is the trickster-creator who released the sun in Haida and Tlingit stories. Legend holds that Britain will fall if the Tower of London's ravens leave.
funFact: In Genesis, Noah sends out a raven before the dove.

wiki.extract: The common raven or northern raven is a large all-black passerine bird. It is the most widely distributed of all corvids, found across the Northern Hemisphere. There are 11 accepted subspecies with little variation in appearance, although recent research has demonstrated significant genetic differences among populations from various regions. It is one of the two largest corvids, alongside the thick-billed raven, and is the heaviest passerine bird; at maturity, the common raven averages 63 centimetres in length and 1.47 kilograms in weight, up to 2 kg (4.4 lb) in the heaviest individuals. Although their typical lifespan is considerably shorter, common ravens can live more than 23 years in the wild. Young birds may travel in flocks but later mate for life, with each mated pair defending a territory.

summary: The grey-necked crow of South Asian cities, living almost entirely alongside people and scavenging from markets, rubbish heaps and rooftops. Bold, intelligent and ship-borne, it has spread to ports from East Africa to the Netherlands.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Myanmar; introduced to East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Singapore and elsewhere
abilities: Exploits human settlements so completely that it is rarely found away from people
Spreads by stowing away on ships, founding colonies in distant ports
Mobs predators in noisy groups and is host to the parasitic Asian koel
Gathers in communal roosts numbering thousands

animal.diet: Omnivorous scavenger: food waste, carrion, insects, eggs and nestlings, fruit and grain
animal.habitat: Cities, towns, villages and harbours
animal.behaviour: Highly social and quick to learn; groups gather around a dead crow and call loudly, and they steal food from people and other birds with practised timing.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized crow with glossy black face, crown, throat, wings and tail
Contrasting grey nape, neck and breast forming a collar
Relatively slim black bill and domed forehead
animal.voice: A flat, dry 'kaaw-kaaw', higher-pitched than the Large-billed crow
animal.lookalikes: Large-billed (Jungle) crow is all glossy black with a much heavier arched bill and deeper call.
animal.whereToSee: Every city of the subcontinent, from Karachi and Mumbai harbours to Colombo
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Hindu ritual crows are fed rice balls (pinda) during shraddha and Pitru Paksha as messengers of the ancestors, and a crow cawing on the roof was said in Urdu and Hindi folklore to announce an arriving guest.
funFact: House crows reached Hoek van Holland in the Netherlands by ship and bred there, thousands of kilometres from the nearest native population.

wiki.extract: The house crow, also known as the Indian, greynecked, Ceylon or Colombo crow, is a common bird of the crow family that is of Asian origin but now found in many parts of the world, where they arrived assisted by shipping. It is between the jackdaw and the carrion crow in size but is slimmer than either. The forehead, crown, throat and upper breast are a richly glossed black, whilst the neck and breast are a lighter grey-brown in colour. The wings, tail and legs are black. There are regional variations in the thickness of the bill and the depth of colour in areas of the plumage.

summary: A loud, crested corvid of eastern North America, brilliant blue above and white below. It caches thousands of acorns each autumn, and the ones it forgets are credited with helping oak forests spread north after the Ice Age.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the eastern and central United States, west to the Rockies' foothills
abilities: Carries several acorns at once in an expandable throat pouch and buries them far from the parent tree
Mimics the screams of Red-shouldered and Red-tailed Hawks
Blue colour is structural — feathers scatter light; there is no blue pigment
Mobs owls and hawks in noisy groups

animal.diet: Acorns, beechnuts, seeds, insects; occasionally eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Oak and beech forest, mixed woodland, suburbs and parks
animal.lifespan: Typically about 7 years; banding record over 26 years
animal.behaviour: Some populations migrate in loose daytime flocks along lakeshores and coasts in autumn, but which individuals migrate varies from year to year and is not well understood.
fieldMarks: Bright blue crest, back, wings and tail
Black necklace across whitish throat and face
Bold white wing bars and white tail corners, black barring on wings and tail
Crest raised when excited, flattened when calm
animal.voice: A harsh, screaming 'jay! jay!'; also a musical, squeaky 'queedle-queedle' (the 'pump-handle' call), soft clicks, and convincing hawk imitations.
animal.lookalikes: Steller's Jay (west) has a black front half and no white in the wings or tail. Florida Scrub-Jay lacks a crest and white spots. Belted Kingfisher is blue-grey with a huge bill and a ragged crest.
animal.whereToSee: Oak woods, parks and feeders offering peanuts across the eastern US; migrating flocks along the Great Lakes shores (e.g. Whitefish Point, Michigan) in September.
animal.season: Resident; some northern birds migrate Sep–Oct and Apr–May

lore: Mark Catesby illustrated it as 'The Blew Jay' in his Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands (1731–43); it is now the emblem of Toronto's Major League Baseball team.
funFact: A single blue jay may cache an estimated 3,000–5,000 acorns in one autumn.

wiki.extract: The blue jay is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America. It lives in most of the eastern and central United States; some eastern populations may be migratory. Resident populations are also in Newfoundland, Canada; breeding populations are found across southern Canada. It breeds in both deciduous and coniferous forests, and is common in residential areas. Its coloration is predominantly blue, with a white chest and underparts, and a blue crest; it has a black, U-shaped collar around its neck and a black border behind the crest. Males and females are similar in size and plumage, which does not vary throughout the year. Four subspecies have been recognized.

summary: A colourful, shy woodland crow, pinkish-brown with a white rump and a dazzling blue-barred wing patch. Each autumn it buries thousands of acorns, and the ones it forgets grow into new oak woods.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, the Caucasus and Central Asia, across Asia to Japan and Southeast Asia
abilities: A single jay may cache several thousand acorns in an autumn
Remembers cache locations months later, even under snow
Its forgotten caches are a major means by which oaks spread uphill and into open land
Skilled mimic of other birds, especially buzzards and owls

animal.diet: Acorns, beechmast and other seeds; insects, eggs and nestling birds in summer
animal.habitat: Oak and mixed woodland, parks, large gardens
animal.behaviour: Carries several acorns at once in its throat pouch and bill, pushing each into the ground and covering it with leaves.
fieldMarks: Pinkish-buff body with a bright white rump contrasting with a black tail
Blue-and-black barred patch on the wing
Black moustache stripe and streaked crest
Floppy, rounded wings in flight
animal.voice: A harsh, tearing screech, 'skaaak', the alarm call of the woods; also soft mewing and mimicry.
animal.lookalikes: No other European bird combines the white rump and blue wing patch. Hoopoe also shows a black-and-white pattern in flight but has a long, curved bill and fan crest. Middle Eastern races have a black crown.
animal.whereToSee: Oak woods throughout Europe, most visible in September–October when carrying acorns.
animal.season: Resident; occasional large irruptions in autumn when acorn crops fail

lore: The specific name 'glandarius' means 'of acorns', and the blue wing feathers were sold to Victorian milliners and fly-tyers; jays were persecuted by gamekeepers as egg thieves.
funFact: Studies at Cambridge showed male jays choose food gifts for their mates based on what the female has recently been eating, suggesting they track another bird's desires.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian jay is a species of passerine bird in the family Corvidae. It has pinkish brown plumage with a black stripe on each side of a whitish throat, a bright blue panel on the upper wing and a black tail. The Eurasian jay is a woodland bird that occurs over a vast region from western Europe and north-west Africa to the Indian subcontinent and farther to the eastern seaboard of Asia and down into south-east Asia.

summary: A bold, long-tailed black-and-white crow with iridescent blue and green gloss. Clever and adaptable, it is a familiar bird of farmland and towns, surrounded by centuries of superstition.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to Siberia; birds of North Africa, southwest Arabia and East Asia are now often treated as separate species
abilities: In 2008 it became the first non-mammal shown to recognise itself in a mirror
Builds a large domed nest of sticks with a mud-lined cup
Caches food and recaches it if watched by other magpies
Thrives in cities and farmland across much of Eurasia

animal.diet: Omnivorous: insects, grain, fruit, carrion, small animals, eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees and hedges, parks, suburbs
animal.size: 40–51 cm including tail; wingspan 52–60 cm; 160–250 g
animal.behaviour: Gathers in noisy groups ('parliaments') in late winter and mobs cats, foxes and owls.
fieldMarks: Black head, breast and back with white belly and shoulders
Very long, graduated tail glossed green and purple
Wings glossed blue with white primaries flashing in flight
Strong black bill and legs
animal.voice: A loud, rapid, rattling chatter, 'chak-chak-chak-chak'.
animal.lookalikes: No other European bird has the same shape and pattern. Iberian (azure-winged) magpie is smaller with a black cap and pale-blue wings and tail. Maghreb magpie (North Africa) has bare blue skin behind the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland, parks and suburbs across Europe, Turkey and Central Asia.
animal.season: Resident

lore: The British counting rhyme 'One for sorrow, two for joy' is first recorded in the 18th century, and Rossini's opera 'La gazza ladra' (The Thieving Magpie, 1817) cemented its reputation as a thief.
funFact: A 2014 Exeter study found that wild magpies are actually wary of shiny objects, contradicting the thieving-magpie myth.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian magpie or common magpie is a resident breeding bird throughout the northern part of the Eurasian continent. It is one of several birds in the crow family (corvids) that are designated as magpies, and it belongs to the Holarctic radiation of "monochrome" magpies. In Europe, the term "magpie" is used by English speakers as a synonym for the Eurasian magpie; the only other species of magpie in Europe being the Iberian magpie, which is restricted to the Iberian Peninsula. Despite sharing a name and similar colouration, they are not closely related to the Australian magpie, which is an artamid, only sharing the same clade (Corvides).

summary: A glossy black crow with a curved scarlet bill and red legs, tumbling acrobatically along sea cliffs and mountain gorges. It is an emblem of Cornwall, where it returned naturally in 2001.
nativeRange: Atlantic coasts of Britain, Ireland and Brittany; mountains of Iberia, the Alps, Atlas, Turkey, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Himalaya and China; also Ethiopia
abilities: Probes short turf and dung with its curved bill for soil invertebrates
Performs acrobatic dives and rolls in updrafts along cliffs
Lives at very high altitudes in the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau
Relies on short, grazed grassland maintained by livestock

animal.diet: Ants, beetles, leatherjackets, dung invertebrates; some grain
animal.habitat: Sea cliffs with grazed turf, mountain cliffs and gorges
animal.behaviour: Pairs and flocks play in the wind along cliffs, calling as they swoop and roll.
fieldMarks: Glossy blue-black plumage
Long, decurved red bill
Red legs
Deeply fingered, broad wings in flight
animal.voice: A loud, ringing 'chee-ow' or 'kyaa', more musical than other crows.
animal.lookalikes: Alpine chough has a short yellow bill and longer tail. Jackdaw has a grey nape and a short black bill. Carrion crow is larger with a black bill and legs.
animal.whereToSee: The Lizard (Cornwall), Pembrokeshire and Anglesey (Wales), Islay (Scotland), the Picos de Europa, Atlas Mountains and Himalaya.
animal.season: Resident

lore: Cornish legend says King Arthur's soul passed into a chough, and the bird appears on Cornwall's coat of arms; its name comes from the old jackdaw-like call 'chow'.
funFact: After choughs died out in Cornwall in 1973, a wild pair arrived on the Lizard in 2001 and bred there the following year.

wiki.extract: The red-billed chough, Cornish chough or simply chough is a bird in the crow family, one of only two species in the genus Pyrrhocorax. Its eight subspecies breed on mountains and coastal cliffs from the western coasts of Ireland and Britain east through southern Europe, North Africa and Middle East to Central Asia, India and China.

nativeRange: Western Himalaya (Himachal Pradesh) east through Nepal, Bhutan and NE India to Myanmar, much of eastern China and Indochina
abilities: Raids nests of other birds for eggs and nestlings
Caches food in the ground or crevices
Groups mob predators loudly

wiki.extract: The red-billed blue magpie is a species of bird (magpie) in the crow family, Corvidae. It is about the same size as the Eurasian magpie, but has a much longer tail, one of the longest of any corvid. It is 65–68 cm (25.5–27 in) long and weighs 196–232 g (6.9–8.2 oz).

summary: A vivid magpie of Sri Lanka's wet-zone rainforests with an ultramarine body, chestnut head and wings, and a long white-tipped tail. It lives in family groups that raise young cooperatively.
nativeRange: Endemic to the wet zone and central hills of Sri Lanka
abilities: Breeds cooperatively, with helpers assisting the breeding pair
Joins mixed-species foraging flocks in the rainforest
Hunts large insects, frogs and lizards in the canopy

animal.diet: Insects, frogs, small lizards and fruit
animal.habitat: Undisturbed wet evergreen forest, from lowlands to about 2,100 m
animal.size: About 42–47 cm long including the tail
animal.behaviour: Groups move noisily through the mid-canopy; at Sinharaja they can be approached quite closely along forest trails.
fieldMarks: Bright cobalt-blue body and long blue tail with white tips
Rich chestnut head, wings and neck
Bright red bill, legs and eye-ring
Long, graduated tail
animal.voice: Loud, varied calls including a ringing 'chink-chink' and harsh, rasping notes
animal.lookalikes: No similar bird in Sri Lanka; Red-billed blue magpie of the Himalaya has a black head and does not occur on the island.
animal.whereToSee: Sinharaja Forest Reserve, Horton Plains and Kitulgala, Sri Lanka
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is one of Sri Lanka's most sought-after endemic birds for visiting birdwatchers, and Sinharaja's mixed feeding flocks, often led by its calls, are a classic of tropical ornithology.
funFact: Surveys in 2004–2006 estimated only about 10,000–20,000 individuals left.

wiki.extract: The Sri Lanka blue magpie or Ceylon magpie is a brightly coloured member of the family Corvidae, found exclusively in Sri Lanka. This species is adapted to hunting in the dense canopy, where it is highly active and nimble. Its flight is rather weak, though, and is rarely used to cover great distances. In spite of its ability to adapt to the presence of humans, it is classified as vulnerable to extinction due to the fragmentation and destruction of its habitat of dense primary forest in the wet zone of southern Sri Lanka.

summary: A blazing gold, green and blue surface hunter that grows astonishingly fast, reaching adulthood in months. Bulls develop a tall, square forehead; the colours fade to grey within minutes of death.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide, including the Mediterranean
abilities: One of the fastest-growing fishes, maturing at 4–5 months
Changes colour rapidly, flashing bars and spots while hunting
Gathers under floating sargassum, logs and debris to hunt
Leaps clear of the water chasing flying fish
edibilityNote: Moderate mercury; generally considered a reasonable choice. Prone to scombroid (histamine) poisoning if not iced promptly.

animal.diet: Flying fish, juvenile tunas, squid, crustaceans
animal.habitat: Warm surface waters, often near floating objects and sargassum
animal.size: Commonly 1 m; up to ~2 m and 40 kg
animal.behaviour: Travels in small schools that follow drifting objects across the open ocean; pairs often stay together and a hooked fish is often followed by its mate.
fieldMarks: Long dorsal fin running from the head almost to the tail
Brilliant golden sides, blue-green back and scattered blue spots
Males with a steep, blunt forehead; females rounded
Deeply forked tail
animal.lookalikes: Pompano dolphinfish (C. equiselis) is smaller with a squarer tooth patch on the tongue and fewer dorsal rays (48–55 vs 58–66). Not related to dolphins (mammals).
animal.whereToSee: Sargassum lines off Florida and the Bahamas, Costa Rica, Hawaii, Malta (autumn lampuka fishery)
animal.season: Year-round in tropics; Malta Aug–Dec

lore: Maltese fishers have caught lampuki under floating palm-frond rafts (kannizzati) for centuries, a technique that predates modern fish aggregating devices; 'mahi-mahi' is Hawaiian for 'very strong'.
funFact: Its brilliant colours are produced by chromatophores and iridophores that collapse at death, turning the fish dull grey within minutes.

wiki.extract: The mahi-mahi, common dolphinfish, dolphinfish, dolphin or  dorado is a surface-dwelling ray-finned fish found in off-shore temperate, tropical, and subtropical waters worldwide. It is one of two members of the family Coryphaenidae, the other being the pompano dolphinfish. These fish are most commonly found in the waters around the Gulf of Mexico, Costa Rica, Hawaii, and the Indian Ocean. In Italy it is called corifena, lampuga or pesce capone, and has even given its name to the caponata though eggplant has now taken the place of the fish.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Hippurus', characterized by its long dorsal fin starting from the head. Gessner's work was foundational in zoology, combining visual evidence with philological research into animal names to create a comprehensive encyclopedia of the natural world.

plates.title: De Indiae utriusque re naturali et medica

plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Guaracapema', identified in the accompanying Latin text as the Dorado or dolphin fish (mahi-mahi). It is featured in Willem Piso's seminal work on the natural history of Brazil, representing one of the earliest European efforts to systematically document the diverse marine life of the New World.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a fish, likely a Bonito or Dorado, from Willem Piso's 1658 natural history of the Indies. This illustration exemplifies the early modern practice of scientific documentation, providing visual records of marine species encountered during colonial explorations.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a Dorade-Dauphin (Mahi-mahi), labeled 76.
plates.long: The Dorade-Dauphin is depicted here with its characteristic elongated body and iridescent scales. Renard's text describes the fish's ability to change colors, a phenomenon that fascinated early modern observers.

plates.title: Louis Renard — Poissons, ecrevisses et crabes (1754)
plates.author: Louis Renard
plates.desc: A collection of various tropical fish species, including a large mahi-mahi (dolphinfish) and several smaller reef fish, rendered in a scientific illustrative style.
plates.long: This plate from Louis Renard's 'Poissons, écrevisses et crabes' showcases the vibrant and exotic marine life of the East Indies as understood in the early 18th century. These detailed engravings were instrumental in documenting biodiversity for European naturalists, blending scientific observation with the artistic flair of the Enlightenment era.

summary: A bright green lizard of Central American streams, crowned with tall crests, that escapes predators by running across the surface of water on its hind legs.
nativeRange: Central America, from Honduras to western Panama
abilities: Runs on water for several metres by slapping its feet down and pulling them back before they sink
Fringes of scales on its toes increase the surface area of each step
Swims well and can stay underwater to hide

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small vertebrates, fruit and flowers
animal.habitat: Trees and shrubs overhanging rainforest streams and rivers
animal.size: Up to ~90 cm including long tail
animal.behaviour: Basks on branches over water and drops in to escape. Young basilisks can run farther on water than adults, because they are light.
fieldMarks: Bright green body with blue or white spots
Males have a double head crest and tall sail-like crests on the back and tail
Long hind legs with fringed toes
Yellow-orange eyes
animal.lookalikes: The common basilisk (B. basiliscus) and brown basilisk (B. vittatus) are brown with pale stripes. Young green iguanas are green but have a dewlap and no head crest.
animal.whereToSee: Costa Rica's Caribbean lowlands: Tortuguero, La Selva, Sarapiquí; also Arenal
animal.season: Resident

lore: The name comes from the basilisk of European legend, a serpent-king whose gaze could kill. Its water-running gave it the nickname 'Jesus Christ lizard'.
funFact: Researchers Glasheen and McMahon showed in 1996 that each slap and stroke of a basilisk's foot opens an air pocket in the water that holds it up, and that it pulls the foot out before the pocket collapses.

wiki.extract: The plumed basilisk, also called the green basilisk, double crested basilisk, or Jesus Christ lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Corytophanidae. The species is native to Central America.

plates.author: Pierio Valeriano
plates.desc: Woodcut of a Basilisk, depicted as an upright serpent with a coiled tail.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Basilisk, a legendary reptile reputed to be a king of serpents and said to have the power to cause death with a single glance. In Valeriano's 'Hieroglyphica', it serves as a symbolic representation of royalty and lethal power, often associated with Egyptian motifs and the concept of 'eternity' as discussed in the surrounding text.

plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: A hand-colored woodcut of a basilisk, depicted with the head, comb, and legs of a rooster, and the long, coiled tail of a serpent.
plates.long: A basilisk is shown with the upper body of a rooster and a long, spiraling green serpent tail. It stands in a simplified landscape with a rocky structure, illustrating the medieval belief in this hybrid creature born from a cock's egg.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Woodcut of a basilisk, a mythical creature with a crown and bird-like features.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a basilisk, the legendary 'king of serpents,' shown here with a crown and avian features. In early natural history texts like the Hortus Sanitatis, such creatures were often described alongside real animals, reflecting the era's blend of observation and folklore.

plates.title: The Dialogue of Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: A woodcut illustration depicting a pike, a basilisk, and a snake in a stylized landscape with swirling patterns.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates a scene from a bestiary, featuring a pike, a basilisk, and a snake. The stylized swirls represent the elements of water and air, highlighting the symbolic relationships between these creatures as described in the accompanying Latin text.

plates.title: The Hieroglyphics

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a basilisk and a snake in a rocky landscape.
plates.long: This woodcut from an edition of Horapollo's Hieroglyphica depicts a basilisk, a legendary creature with the head of a rooster and the body of a serpent. In the accompanying text, the basilisk is used as a symbol for a person who has become ill through the slanderous accusations of others, reflecting early modern beliefs about the physical power of words and malevolent intent.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a basilisk, the legendary 'king of serpents' identifiable by its crown. This illustration appears in Sebastian Münster's Cosmographey, reflecting the early modern practice of documenting both real and mythical creatures in geographical texts.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a basilisk, the legendary 'king of serpents,' identified by the small crown upon its head. Featured in Ulisse Aldrovandi's 1640 history of serpents and dragons, it represents the transition from medieval bestiaries to early modern scientific classification, where mythical and real animals were often studied side-by-side.

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates a 'Jenny Haniver', a dried and manipulated ray or skate fashioned to resemble a mythical basilisk. Such specimens were frequently sold to collectors as genuine monsters, reflecting the early modern fascination with the boundaries between the natural and the supernatural.
