The illustration is a significant example of Renaissance natural history, showcasing the era's transition toward empirical observation through detailed renderings of anatomical features like the prominent dorsal fin and mottled scales. Such woodcuts were essentia

summary: A pure white cotinga with a long, fleshy black wattle dangling from its bill, it has the loudest bird call ever measured — about 125 decibels. Males aim the blast directly at females perched close by.
nativeRange: Guiana Shield of Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and northern Brazil, with an isolated population south of the Amazon in Pará
abilities: Produces calls measured at about 125 dB at close range, louder than the Screaming Piha (Podos & Cohn-Haft, Current Biology, 2019)
Swings its head and wattle as it delivers the second note of its call toward a female
Swallows fruits whole and regurgitates seeds, dispersing forest trees

animal.diet: Fruit, especially of trees in the laurel family
animal.habitat: Canopy of humid hill and montane forest
animal.behaviour: Males call from exposed perches high in the canopy for hours each day.
fieldMarks: Male: entirely white, with a single long black fleshy wattle hanging from the forehead over the bill
Female: olive-green above with yellowish, olive-streaked underparts
Large dark eye and broad bill
Stocky, pigeon-like shape
animal.voice: Ear-splitting, bell-like notes — a two-part 'kong-kay' or a single metallic 'boing' that can be heard over long distances.
animal.lookalikes: Bearded Bellbird has a brown head and many short wattles on the throat. Bare-throated Bellbird (Atlantic Forest) has a bare blue-green throat. Three-wattled Bellbird (Central America) is chestnut with a white head and neck and three wattles.
animal.whereToSee: Hill forests of the Guiana Shield, e.g. the tepui foothills of Venezuela, the Iwokrama and Kaieteur areas of Guyana, and Roraima in Brazil.
animal.season: Resident; calling peaks in the breeding season

funFact: Researchers found the loudest calls are the shortest, suggesting a trade-off between volume and duration.

wiki.extract: The white bellbird is a species of bird in the family Cotingidae, the cotingas. It is found in Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, and as a vagrant to Trinidad.

summary: A blazing orange-red cotinga of Andean cloud forest ravines whose males gather at dawn leks, bowing, bobbing and squealing to attract drab females. It is Peru's national bird.
nativeRange: Eastern and western slopes of the Andes from Venezuela and Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to Bolivia, mainly 500–2,400 m
abilities: Males display at communal leks, each defending a small court and performing in front of visiting females
Females build mud-and-plant cup nests glued to rock faces in humid gorges
Important seed disperser for fruiting cloud-forest trees
Takes small vertebrates such as frogs and lizards as well as fruit

animal.diet: Mainly fruit; insects, frogs and small lizards
animal.habitat: Humid montane forest near rocky streams and ravines
animal.behaviour: Females raise the young alone; males spend much of the breeding season at the lek.
fieldMarks: Male: brilliant scarlet or orange body with a disc-shaped crest that hides the bill
Black wings and tail, with pale silvery-grey tertials
Female: dark brownish-orange with a smaller crest
Plump, pigeon-sized shape
animal.voice: At leks, loud nasal squawks, grunts and pig-like squeals; otherwise mostly silent.
animal.lookalikes: Guianan Cock-of-the-rock (Guiana Shield east of the Andes) is orange with a fringed crest and white wing patches; their ranges do not overlap. No other Andean bird has the crest-covered bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lek sites along Peru's Manu Road (Cock-of-the-rock Lodge), near Mindo in Ecuador, and in Colombia's Río Claro and cloud forests.
animal.season: Resident year-round; leks most active at dawn and late afternoon

lore: Known in Quechua as tunki, it was named Peru's national bird and features in Andean folk dances and textiles.
funFact: The genus name Rupicola means 'rock-dweller', from the female's habit of nesting on cliff faces.

wiki.extract: The Andean cock-of-the-rock, also known as tunki (Quechua), is a large passerine bird of the cotinga family native to Andean cloud forests in South America. It is the national bird of Peru. It has four subspecies and its closest relative is the Guianan cock-of-the-rock.

summary: Africa's largest predator in fresh water, famous for ambushing wildebeest and zebra at river crossings. It killed and inspired people throughout history and was worshipped in ancient Egypt as the god Sobek.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, the Nile basin and Madagascar (the West African crocodile, Crocodylus suchus, is now treated as a separate species)
abilities: Ambushes large mammals at the water's edge and drowns them
Can go many months without eating
Females carry hatchlings to the water in their mouths
Groups cooperate to feed on large carcasses, holding and spinning to tear meat

animal.diet: Fish, and mammals up to the size of wildebeest, zebra and buffalo
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, swamps and estuaries
animal.size: Males usually 3.5–5 m, exceptionally ~6 m; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Basks with its mouth open to cool down. Females bury eggs in sandbanks and guard them for about three months. It is thought to be responsible for more attacks on people than any other crocodile species.
fieldMarks: Large, olive-bronze crocodile with dark bands on the tail
Broad, V-shaped snout
Fourth lower tooth visible when the mouth is closed
Basks on sandbanks
animal.lookalikes: The West African crocodile (C. suchus) is smaller and found mainly in West and Central Africa. The slender-snouted crocodile (Mecistops) has a long thin snout. Dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus) are small and dark.
animal.whereToSee: Mara River crossings (Kenya, Tanzania), Kruger National Park, Lake Chamo (Ethiopia), Okavango Delta, Lake Nasser
animal.season: Resident; wildebeest crossings July–October in the Mara

lore: Ancient Egyptians worshipped the crocodile god Sobek at Kom Ombo and Crocodilopolis (Faiyum), where sacred crocodiles were kept, fed and mummified by the thousands. Herodotus wrote that the plover picked its teeth, a story still repeated today.
funFact: DNA from crocodile mummies from ancient Egypt showed that some were West African crocodiles, perhaps chosen because they are less aggressive and easier to keep in temples.

wiki.extract: The Nile crocodile is a large crocodilian native to freshwater habitats in Africa, where it is present in 26 countries. It is widely distributed in sub-Saharan Africa, occurring mostly in the eastern, southern, and central regions of the continent, and lives in different types of aquatic environments such as lakes, rivers, swamps and marshlands. It occasionally inhabits deltas, brackish lakes and rarely also saltwater. Its range once stretched from the Nile Delta throughout the Nile River. Lake Turkana in Kenya has one of the largest undisturbed Nile crocodile populations.

summary: A broad-snouted crocodile of South Asia's rivers, lakes and reservoirs. It is adaptable and digs burrows to survive drought, and it has been seen balancing sticks on its snout to lure nest-building birds.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal and southeastern Iran; extinct in Bhutan and probably Myanmar; possibly surviving in Bangladesh
abilities: Digs burrows into riverbanks to escape heat and drought
Has been seen balancing sticks on its snout near egret colonies during the nesting season, possibly to lure birds collecting nest material
Travels overland between water bodies
Lives in reservoirs, irrigation canals and town lakes

animal.diet: Fish, birds, turtles, deer, monkeys and other mammals
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, marshes, reservoirs, irrigation canals
animal.size: Males up to ~4–5 m; females ~2.5–3 m
animal.behaviour: Basks for long periods, often with its mouth open. Females dig nests in sandbanks and carry hatchlings to the water.
fieldMarks: Broad, heavy snout, the widest of any living Crocodylus
Grey to olive-brown body; juveniles banded
Fourth lower tooth visible when the mouth is closed
Lacks the pair of bony bumps in front of the eyes seen on saltwater crocodiles
animal.lookalikes: The gharial has a very thin snout. The saltwater crocodile, found in coastal areas such as the Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika and Sri Lankan estuaries, has a longer, narrower snout and bony ridges in front of the eyes.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary, Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary (Karnataka), Vishwamitri River (Vadodara), Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka), Bardia (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; nesting February–April

lore: At the shrine of Pir Mangho in Karachi, muggers have been kept in a pool for centuries and are fed by pilgrims, who consider them the saint's disciples. Rudyard Kipling's 'The Undertakers' (1895) features a mugger of a Ganges village.
funFact: In 2013 Vladimir Dinets reported muggers and American alligators balancing sticks on their snouts near bird colonies, probably the first known tool use by reptiles.

wiki.extract: The mugger crocodile is a medium-sized broad-snouted crocodile, also known as mugger and marsh crocodile. It is native to freshwater habitats from south-eastern Iran to the Indian subcontinent, where it inhabits marshes, lakes, rivers and artificial ponds. It rarely reaches a body length of 5 m and is a powerful swimmer, but also walks on land in search of suitable waterbodies during the hot season. Both young and adult mugger crocodiles dig burrows to which they retreat when the ambient temperature drops below 5 °C (41 °F) or exceeds 38 °C (100 °F). Females dig holes in the sand as nesting sites and lay up to 46 eggs during the dry season. The sex of hatchlings depends on temperature during incubation. Both parents protect the young for up to one year. They feed on insects, and adults prey on fish, reptiles, birds and mammals.

summary: The largest living reptile, with old males exceeding 6 m and a tonne. It thrives in fresh and salt water and has crossed open sea to colonise islands from India to the Pacific.
nativeRange: Eastern India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands
abilities: Has the strongest bite measured in any living animal, about 16,000 newtons
Rides ocean currents to travel hundreds of kilometres between coasts
Gets rid of excess salt through glands on its tongue
Can stay submerged for an hour or more while resting
Detects tiny ripples with pressure-sensing pits along its jaws and body

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crabs, turtles, birds, pigs, buffalo; anything it can overpower
animal.habitat: Tidal rivers, mangrove swamps, estuaries and coasts
animal.size: Males usually 4–5 m, exceptionally 6 m+ and 1,000 kg; females ~3 m
animal.behaviour: Mothers guard their nest mounds, dig out the chirping hatchlings and carry them to water in their mouths. Nest temperature sets the hatchlings' sex.
fieldMarks: Largest reptile, heavy-bodied and grey-brown
Broad snout with ridges running from the eyes
Few or no large scales behind the head
Often basks on mudbanks
animal.lookalikes: Freshwater crocodile (Australia) is smaller with a narrow snout. Mugger has a broad snout and large neck scales. Any crocodile here may be a saltie. Never approach on foot; keep well back from the water's edge and obey warning signs.
animal.whereToSee: Yellow Water cruises (Kakadu) and the Adelaide River (Northern Territory); Bhitarkanika (Odisha)
animal.season: Resident; dry season best for viewing

lore: A Timorese legend tells that Timor island is the body of a crocodile who befriended a boy. In Arnhem Land the crocodile is an ancestral being of the Dreaming, painted on bark and rock.
funFact: Lolong, captured in the Philippines in 2011, measured 6.17 m, the largest crocodile ever measured in captivity.

wiki.extract: The saltwater crocodile is a crocodilian native to saltwater habitats, brackish wetlands and freshwater rivers from India's east coast across Southeast Asia and the Sundaland to northern Australia and Micronesia. It has been listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 1996. It was hunted for its skin throughout its range up to the 1970s, and is threatened by illegal killing and habitat loss. It is regarded as dangerous to humans.

summary: Among the largest amphibians alive, recorded at up to 1.8 m. This brown, wrinkled salamander lives in cold mountain streams of China. It is Critically Endangered, mainly because of hunting and farming for meat, and farm-bred animals of mixed origin have been released into wild rivers.
nativeRange: Mountain streams of central and southern China; genetic studies suggest the old 'davidianus' is several species (A. sligoi, A. jiangxiensis and others), with A. davidianus in the narrow sense restricted to part of this range
abilities: Breathes mainly through its wrinkled skin
Detects prey with sensory nodes along its head and body, sensing water movement
Can live for decades; over 50 years in captivity
Males guard eggs in underwater dens

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, crabs, shrimp, worms, insects
animal.habitat: Clear, cold, rocky mountain streams and rivers
animal.size: Usually ~1 m; historically up to ~1.8 m
animal.behaviour: Hides by day in crevices and dens and ambushes prey at night with a fast suction gulp.
fieldMarks: Huge, flattened, brown salamander with wrinkled skin
Broad, flat head with tiny eyes
Fold of skin along the sides of the body
Short limbs
animal.lookalikes: The Japanese giant salamander (A. japonicus) is very similar and lives only in Japan; the two are best told apart by where they are found. The North American hellbender (Cryptobranchus) is much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen in the wild; nature reserves in Zhangjiajie (Hunan), Shaanxi's Qinling Mountains; also in zoos
animal.season: Resident; breeds in late summer

lore: Its Chinese name 'baby fish' refers to its cry, said to sound like a human baby. It was described in 1871 from specimens sent by the French missionary-naturalist Armand David.
funFact: Millions are raised on farms in China for meat, but surveys across its range found few wild animals left.

wiki.extract: The Chinese giant salamander is the largest salamander and the largest amphibian in the world. It is fully aquatic, and is endemic to rocky mountain streams and lakes in the Yangtze river basin of central China. It has also been introduced to Kyoto Prefecture in Japan, and possibly to Taiwan. It is considered critically endangered in the wild due to habitat loss, pollution, and overcollection, as it is considered a delicacy and used in traditional Chinese medicine. On farms in central China, it is extensively farmed and sometimes bred, although many of the salamanders on the farms are caught in the wild. It has been listed as one of the top-10 "focal species" in 2008 by the Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered project.

summary: A large, crow-sized cuckoo with glossy black body, chestnut wings and a ruby-red eye, which clambers through hedges and stalks the ground for snakes and snails. Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest and raises its own young.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through southern China to Southeast Asia and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Hunts snakes, lizards, large insects, eggs and nestlings
Builds a domed nest of grass and leaves in dense cover
Flies weakly, preferring to clamber and run through vegetation

animal.diet: Large insects, snails, lizards, small snakes, frogs, eggs and nestlings; some fruit
animal.habitat: Dense scrub, hedges, reedbeds, gardens and forest edge
animal.behaviour: Walks deliberately through undergrowth and along field edges; suns itself with wings spread on bushes after rain.
fieldMarks: Glossy black head, body and long tail
Rich chestnut wings and back
Deep red eye
Heavy black bill
animal.voice: A deep, resonant, booming 'coop-coop-coop', often in long series and duetting between pairs
animal.lookalikes: Lesser coucal is smaller with buff streaks on the back; male Asian koel is all black with a pale bill; crows lack the chestnut wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and hedgerows across India and Sri Lanka; canal banks and wooded areas of northern Punjab
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: British sportsmen in India called it the 'crow pheasant', a name still found in older Indian bird books.
funFact: Despite being a cuckoo, it is not a brood parasite: both parents build the nest and feed the chicks.

wiki.extract: The greater coucal or crow pheasant, is a large non-parasitic member of the cuckoo order of birds, the Cuculiformes. A widespread resident in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, it is divided into several subspecies, some being treated as full species. They are large, crow-like with a long tail and coppery brown wings and found in a wide range of habitats from jungle to cultivation and urban gardens. They are weak fliers, and are often seen clambering about in vegetation or walking on the ground as they forage for insects, eggs and nestlings of other birds. They have a familiar deep resonant call which is associated with omens in many parts of its range.

summary: A slim, hawk-like grey bird whose two-note call announces spring across Eurasia. It never raises its own young: each female lays her eggs in the nests of a particular host species, often with eggs matched to the host's own.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Asia to Japan; winters in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
abilities: Female lineages (gentes) specialise on hosts such as reed warblers, meadow pipits or dunnocks, often laying mimetic eggs
A female can lay an egg in a host nest within about 10 seconds
The newly hatched chick heaves host eggs and chicks out of the nest on its back
Satellite-tagged British cuckoos fly to the Congo rainforest and cross the Sahara on non-stop flights

animal.diet: Large hairy caterpillars avoided by most birds, plus beetles and other insects
animal.habitat: Woodland edge, reedbeds, moorland, farmland with hedges, steppe
animal.lifespan: Typically a few years; the European ringing record is about 9.5 years
animal.behaviour: Females watch host nests from a perch and slip in to lay while the owners are away, often removing one host egg.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey head, back and breast; barred white belly
Long, graduated tail with white spots; pointed wings
Yellow eye-ring and feet
Rare 'hepatic' females are rufous with black bars
animal.voice: Male gives the famous far-carrying 'cuck-oo', the second note lower; the female makes a bubbling, chuckling trill.
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian sparrowhawk has broad, rounded wings and yellow eyes, and flaps and glides rather than flying with shallow, below-the-body wingbeats. Oriental cuckoo (eastern Russia) gives a hoopoe-like 'poo-poo'.
animal.whereToSee: Reedbeds, heaths and moorland across Europe in May; Wicken Fen and the Norfolk Broads in England; Turkish and Central Asian river valleys.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Aug; adults leave as early as July

lore: Edward Jenner, later famous for vaccination, published in 1788 the first account of the cuckoo chick ejecting its foster siblings, an observation long doubted until photographs confirmed it in the 20th century.
funFact: The medieval English round 'Sumer is icumen in' (c. 1260), one of the oldest surviving songs in English, begins with 'Lhude sing cuccu!'

It is part of Conrad Gesner's monumental encyclopedic work on animals, which laid the foundations for modern zoology by combining classical scholarship with empirical observation.

plates.title: The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors, Vol. 1
plates.author: Max Arthur Macauliffe
plates.desc: Engraving of the head of a Sārang, or pied Indian cuckoo (Cuculus Melanoleukos).
plates.long: This engraving depicts the head of a Sārang, or pied Indian cuckoo, a bird frequently mentioned in Sikh scripture as a symbol of intense longing and devotion. In the context of Guru Nanak's hymns, the bird's legendary thirst for a specific raindrop represents the soul's yearning for divine grace.

plates.title: François Bouchard — Recueil de cent-trente-trois oiseaux des plus belles especes (1775)
plates.author: François Bouchard
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of two cuckoos: a Common Cuckoo in flight and a Great Spotted Cuckoo perched on a stump.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from 1775 depicts two species of cuckoo: the Common Cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) shown in flight and the Great Spotted Cuckoo (Clamator glandarius) perched on a stump. The plate is part of François Bouchard's collection of 133 birds, illustrating the era's dedication to documenting the natural world with both scientific accuracy and aesthetic appeal.

summary: A large cuckoo whose rising, insistent 'ko-EL, ko-EL' is the sound of the South Asian hot season, often heard long before dawn. It lays its eggs in the nests of crows, which raise the koel chicks as their own.
nativeRange: Pakistan and India through Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and southern China to Southeast Asia and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Brood parasite: lays eggs in House crow and Large-billed crow nests in South Asia
Male lures crows away from the nest while the female slips in to lay
Unusually for cuckoos, adults are largely fruit-eaters, dispersing seeds of figs and other trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit and berries (figs, peepal, banyan); also insects and caterpillars
animal.habitat: Leafy gardens, orchards, groves and open woodland
animal.behaviour: Skulks in dense foliage and is heard far more than seen; the male calls repeatedly from cover, each phrase rising in pitch and urgency.
fieldMarks: Male entirely glossy blue-black with a pale greenish bill and crimson eye
Female brown, heavily spotted and barred with white and buff
Long tail and slim, rather crow-like build
Red eye in both sexes
animal.voice: Male: a loud, rising 'ko-el, ko-EL, KO-EL', repeated in crescendo; also a bubbling 'kuil-kuil-kuil'. Female: a shrill 'kik-kik-kik'.
animal.lookalikes: The black male could be mistaken for a crow or drongo, but has a red eye, pale bill and long rounded tail; Greater coucal is larger with rufous wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and avenues across Pakistan and India, from Lahore's Jinnah Garden to Delhi's Lodhi Garden
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; most vocal March–August; in northern Pakistan a summer visitor

lore: As the kokila it is a symbol of spring and longing in Sanskrit poetry, including Kalidasa, and the koyal remains a byword for a sweet voice in Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi songs.
funFact: A koel's voice is sweet only to people: crows recognise the bird as a threat and chase it furiously.

wiki.extract: The Asian koel is a member of the cuckoo family of birds, the Cuculidae. It is found in the Indian subcontinent, China, and Southeast Asia. It forms a superspecies with the closely related black-billed koels, and Pacific koels which are sometimes treated as subspecies. The Asian koel, like many of its related cuckoo kin, is a brood parasite that lays its eggs in the nests of crows and other hosts, who raise its young. They are unusual among the cuckoos in being largely frugivorous as adults. The name koel is echoic in origin with several language variants. The bird is a widely used symbol in Indian, Pakistani and Nepali poetry.

summary: A ground-dwelling cuckoo of the deserts and scrub of the south-western US and Mexico that runs down lizards, snakes and scorpions. It can sprint at about 30 km/h and kills rattlesnakes by beating them against rocks.
nativeRange: South-western and south-central US (expanding into Missouri, Arkansas and Louisiana) and northern and central Mexico
abilities: Runs at around 30 km/h, steering with its long tail
Eats venomous prey including rattlesnakes and scorpions
Sunbathes with back feathers raised to expose black skin, warming up after cold nights
Excretes excess salt through a gland near the eye, conserving water

animal.diet: Lizards, snakes, insects, scorpions, rodents, small birds; some fruit
animal.habitat: Arid scrub, desert, chaparral, open grassland with cover
animal.behaviour: Courting males present food, such as a lizard, to the female before mating.
fieldMarks: Long, white-tipped tail often cocked up
Shaggy dark crest and streaky brown-and-white plumage
Long, heavy bill; bare blue and orange skin behind the eye
Long legs with X-shaped zygodactyl footprints (two toes forward, two back)
animal.voice: A series of slow, descending, dove-like coos 'coo-coo-coo-oo'; also loud bill-clattering.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser Roadrunner (Mexico and Central America) is smaller with a less streaked throat. Ring-necked Pheasant has a short bill and lacks streaks.
animal.whereToSee: Desert parks of Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas — e.g. Big Bend National Park, Sonoran Desert around Tucson, Bosque del Apache.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Pueblo peoples used its X-shaped footprints as a protective symbol, since the tracks do not show which way the bird went; it is New Mexico's state bird.
funFact: Real roadrunners top out around 30 km/h — fast for a bird on foot, but slower than a coyote.

wiki.extract: The greater roadrunner is a long-legged bird in the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, from the Aridoamerica region in the Southwestern United States and Mexico. The scientific name means "Californian earth-cuckoo". Along with the lesser roadrunner, it is one of two species in the genus Geococcyx. This roadrunner is also known as the chaparral cock, ground cuckoo, and snake killer.

summary: A small mosquito that is one of the deadliest animals on Earth because its females transmit the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Malaria still kills around 600,000 people a year, most of them children in sub-Saharan Africa.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Females strongly prefer human blood and bite mainly at night, often indoors
Larvae develop in small, sunlit, temporary pools such as puddles and hoofprints, in about a week
Transmits Plasmodium falciparum, the most lethal malaria parasite
Some populations have evolved resistance to the insecticides on bed nets

animal.diet: Females take blood (mainly human) to develop eggs; both sexes drink nectar and plant juices
animal.habitat: Near people in rural and peri-urban Africa; larvae in shallow, sunny standing water
animal.behaviour: Males gather in dusk swarms over landmarks, and females fly into the swarm to mate once.
fieldMarks: Rests with body angled steeply to the surface, proboscis and body in a straight line
Wings spotted with pale and dark scales
Female palps as long as the proboscis
Larvae lie flat beneath the water surface (no breathing siphon)
animal.lookalikes: Anopheles coluzzii and A. arabiensis are sibling species that look identical and are told apart only by DNA. Culex mosquitoes rest with the body parallel to the surface and have unspotted wings.
animal.whereToSee: Villages and farmland across tropical Africa, especially in the rainy season.
animal.season: Peaks in the rainy season when temporary pools form

lore: Ronald Ross showed in 1897 that Anopheles mosquitoes carry malaria, winning a Nobel Prize in 1902. A member of the A. gambiae complex that invaded north-eastern Brazil in 1930 was eradicated by a campaign led by Fred Soper by 1940.
funFact: In 2018 a gene drive targeting the doublesex gene crashed caged populations of A. gambiae to zero within 7–11 generations.

wiki.extract: The Anopheles gambiae complex consists of at least seven morphologically indistinguishable species of mosquitoes in the genus Anopheles. The complex was recognised in the 1960s and includes the most important vectors of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly of the most dangerous malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. It is one of the most efficient malaria vectors known. The An. gambiae mosquito additionally transmits Wuchereria bancrofti which causes lymphatic filariasis, a symptom of which is elephantiasis.

plates.author: Willem Piso

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Nhatiu', a type of mosquito or biting fly described by Willem Piso in his 1658 work on the natural history of the Indies. The illustration highlights the insect's elongated body and prominent proboscis, reflecting the early modern interest in documenting the flora and fauna of the New World for medical and scientific purposes.

summary: Domesticated in China from a drab olive carp over more than a thousand years, the goldfish was one of the first fish ever kept for beauty. Feral goldfish released into lakes revert to dull colours, grow large and become destructive invaders.
nativeRange: Eastern Asia (China and nearby); ornamental and feral populations worldwide
abilities: Survives months under ice: in oxygen-free water it makes ethanol instead of lactic acid and releases it through its gills
Can be trained to respond to sounds, colours and lights, and remembers the training for months (the 'three-second memory' is a myth)
Breeders have produced dramatic forms such as telescope eyes, bubble eyes, lionheads and double tails

animal.diet: Omnivore: algae, plant matter, insect larvae, crustaceans and detritus
animal.habitat: Still, weedy ponds, lakes and sluggish rivers; aquaria
animal.lifespan: 10–20 years with good care; over 40 recorded
animal.size: Usually 10–20 cm; feral fish to 40 cm and over 2 kg
animal.behaviour: Grazes and sifts the bottom constantly. In spring, males chase females through plants until they scatter sticky eggs.
fieldMarks: Deep carp-like body with no barbels
Orange, red, white, black or calico in ornamental forms; feral fish olive-bronze
Long dorsal fin with a serrated spine
Fancy breeds with paired (twin) tails, long fins or modified eyes
animal.lookalikes: Common carp and koi have two pairs of barbels. Crucian carp (Carassius carassius) has a more rounded, convex dorsal fin and a dark spot at the tail base in young fish. Prussian carp (C. gibelio) is the closest relative and is hard to tell apart without counting gill rakers.
animal.whereToSee: Fancy-goldfish breeders in Hangzhou and Fuzhou (China) and Yatomi, Aichi (Japan); feral populations in Lake Tahoe and many urban ponds
animal.season: Resident; spawns April–July

lore: Red-gold variants of the wild carp were kept in Buddhist monastery 'release ponds' in China by the Song dynasty (10th–13th centuries), and bowl-bred fancy varieties appeared by the Ming. Goldfish reached Japan in the early 16th century and Europe in the 17th, where Samuel Pepys saw them as a novelty in 1665.
funFact: Goldfish and crucian carp are among the very few vertebrates that make alcohol: in airless water their muscles turn sugar into ethanol so they can survive months under ice.

wiki.extract: The goldfish is a freshwater fish in the family Cyprinidae of the order Cypriniformes. It is commonly kept as a pet in indoor aquariums, and is one of the most popular aquarium fish. Goldfish released into the wild have become an invasive pest in parts of North America and Australia.

The accompanying text describes various types of 'goldfish' (jinyu) and 'fire fish' (huoyu), detailing their vibrant colors and patterns. This illustration serves as an early record of ornamental fish varieties in China, reflecting the period's interest in categorizing the natural w

summary: The bottom-feeding member of the Indian major carp trio. It grazes the detritus and algae on the pond floor beneath rohu and catla.
nativeRange: Rivers of northern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal (Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra basins); widely stocked in reservoirs and ponds
abilities: Feeds on decaying organic matter and algae on the bottom, recycling nutrients that other farmed carps cannot use
Tolerates a wide range of temperatures and low water quality
Breeds readily in hatcheries after hormone injection
edibilityNote: Considered a little less tasty than rohu or catla and very bony. Always cooked. Fish from the bottom of polluted water bodies can accumulate contaminants.

animal.diet: Detritus, decaying plant matter, benthic algae and small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Lower layers of rivers, reservoirs and ponds
animal.size: Commonly 40–60 cm; up to about 1 m and 12 kg
animal.behaviour: Moves in schools along the bottom sifting mud; wild fish spawn in flooded river margins during the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Slender, streamlined silvery body with a dark grey back
Pectoral, pelvic and anal fins tipped orange-red, brighter in the breeding season
Blunt snout with thin, unfringed lips and one pair of short barbels
Eyes golden
animal.lookalikes: Rohu has a deeper body, reddish scale centres and thick fringed lips. The white carp (Cirrhinus cirrhosus) of peninsular India is very similar and is told apart by details of scales and fins.
animal.whereToSee: Fish markets and ponds across West Bengal, Bangladesh and Punjab; reservoirs of the Gangetic plain
animal.season: Resident; spawns June–August with the monsoon floods

lore: Buchanan-Hamilton's 1822 account of Ganges fishes recorded mrigal under its local name. Rohu–catla–mrigal 'composite fish culture' was developed by Indian fisheries scientists from the 1960s and spread across South Asia.
funFact: Because each species feeds in a different layer, a pond stocked with catla, rohu and mrigal together gives a bigger harvest than the same pond stocked with only one of them.

wiki.extract: Cirrhinus mrigala is a species of ray-finned fish in the genus Cirrhinus. It is found in northern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal. This species and the Mrigal carp are both considered distinct.

summary: A deep-bodied, barbelled bottom-feeder from the Danube, Black Sea and Caspian basins. The Romans and medieval monks farmed it, and it is now one of the most widespread fish on Earth. It is a cherished food and angling fish, and also one of the world's worst invasive species, even though truly wild river carp in its native range are listed as Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Wild form native to the Danube, Black, Caspian and Aral Sea basins; introduced across Europe and to every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Roots through sediment for food, muddying the water and uprooting aquatic plants, which degrades wetlands where it is introduced
Tolerates warm, low-oxygen, turbid water and a wide temperature range
A large female can lay over a million eggs in a season
Has a sense of taste spread over the lips and barbels, as well as the mouth
edibilityNote: Firm, fatty flesh with many intramuscular Y-bones. Fish from muddy ponds can taste earthy, so they are often kept in clean water for some days before eating. Always cook it: raw or undercooked carp can transmit liver flukes (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) where these occur. Large wild fish from polluted lakes may carry PCBs and mercury, so follow local advisories.

animal.diet: Omnivore: insect larvae, worms, molluscs, crustaceans, seeds and plant matter
animal.habitat: Warm, still or slow water with soft bottoms and vegetation
animal.size: Commonly 40–80 cm; up to about 1.2 m and over 40 kg
animal.behaviour: Spawns noisily in shallow weedy margins in late spring, with males splashing alongside females. Grazes the bottom in groups, leaving clouds of silt and feeding craters.
fieldMarks: Deep, heavy body with large bronze-gold to olive scales (mirror and leather forms have patchy or no scales)
Two pairs of barbels at the corners of the mouth, the rear pair longer
Long dorsal fin with a stout, serrated leading spine
Thick-lipped mouth that protrudes like a tube when feeding
animal.lookalikes: Crucian carp (Carassius carassius) and goldfish or Prussian carp have no barbels. Common bream (Abramis brama) is flatter-sided with no barbels and a long anal fin. Barbel (Barbus barbus) is slender, with a mouth on the underside and four barbels near the lips.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes and gravel pits across Europe; Czech and Polish fishpond districts such as Třeboň (South Bohemia); the Danube Delta; invasive in the Murray–Darling basin (Australia) and the Great Lakes
animal.season: Resident; spawning May–July once water exceeds about 18 °C

lore: Monks raised carp in ponds as Lenten fare across medieval Europe, and in Czechia, Poland and Slovakia a live carp is still bought and kept in the bathtub before Christmas Eve dinner. Izaak Walton in 'The Compleat Angler' (1653) called the carp 'the queen of rivers, a stately, a good, and a very subtil fish'.
funFact: Australia has studied releasing cyprinid herpesvirus 3 (koi herpesvirus) as a biological control to cut carp numbers in the Murray–Darling basin.

wiki.extract: The common carp, also known as European carp, Eurasian carp, or simply carp, is a widespread freshwater fish of eutrophic waters in lakes and large rivers in Europe and Asia. The native wild populations are considered vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), but the species has also been domesticated and introduced into environments worldwide, and is often considered an invasive species, being included in the list of the world's 100 worst invasive species. It gives its name to the carp family, Cyprinidae.

summary: The East Asian carp, wild ancestor of the ornamental koi that Japanese breeders turned into living jewellery. In Chinese and Japanese art it stands for perseverance, because of the carp that leaps the Dragon Gate and becomes a dragon.
nativeRange: East Asia: Amur basin south through China, Korea and Vietnam (wild form); koi now kept in ponds worldwide
abilities: Selective breeding has fixed dozens of named colour varieties, such as kōhaku (red-and-white), taishō sanshoku and shōwa
Learns feeding routines and will take food from people's hands
Survives cold winters by becoming torpid on the pond bottom
edibilityNote: Wild and farmed East Asian carp are an important food fish in China, Vietnam and Korea. Ornamental koi are not normally eaten. Always cook it, because raw carp can carry liver flukes (Clonorchis sinensis).

animal.diet: Omnivore: invertebrates, seeds, algae and plant matter; pellets in ponds
animal.habitat: Slow rivers, lakes and ponds
animal.lifespan: Commonly 25–35 years in good ponds; claims of over a century are unverified
animal.size: Usually 50–90 cm; large koi exceed 1 m
animal.behaviour: Koi crowd to the surface at feeding time and learn individual keepers. Wild Amur carp spawn in flooded vegetation in spring.
fieldMarks: Carp body with two pairs of barbels and a long dorsal fin with a serrated spine
Koi: patterned in red, white, black, yellow, orange or metallic platinum
Wild fish: bronze to olive, slightly more elongate than European common carp
animal.lookalikes: Fancy goldfish (Carassius) have no barbels and are usually smaller, often with double or long fins. European common carp (Cyprinus carpio) is very similar, and the two are best told apart by genetics and origin.
animal.whereToSee: Ojiya and Yamakoshi, Niigata (birthplace of koi breeding); temple and castle ponds across Japan; the All Japan Combined Koi Show in Tokyo (winter)
animal.season: Resident; spawns April–June

lore: Farmers in the mountain villages of Niigata began breeding coloured carp in their rice-terrace ponds in the early 19th century. Japanese families fly carp-shaped koinobori streamers for Children's Day on 5 May, after the Chinese legend of the carp that swims up the Yellow River's Dragon Gate falls and turns into a dragon.
funFact: A famous koi named Hanako was said to be 226 years old when she died in 1977, an age estimated by counting growth rings on her scales. The figure is widely doubted.

wiki.extract: Cyprinus rubrofuscus, or the Amur carp, is a species of freshwater fish belonging to the Cyprinidae family. It is the ancestral form of some domesticated koi fish, which are well known for their striking colors as an ornamental species. Often mistaken for the common carp, the species originated in eastern Asia but has since been widely distributed and cultured across the world. Common names include Amur carp and South China carp.

It appears in Guillaume Rondelet's 1554 treatise, 'Libri de Piscibus Marinis', which was one of the first major works to apply scientific observation to the study of aquatic life.

As one of the first modern zoological encyclopedias, Gessner's work combined classical knowledge with new empirical evidence, setting a standard for scientific illustration in the 16th century.

Published in Ulisse Aldrovandi's posthumous works, these diagrams reflect the 17th-century transition toward empirical observation and comparative anatomy in natural history. summary: The fastest-growing of the Indian major carps, a big-headed fish that feeds at the surface. It takes the top layer of South Asian polyculture ponds, while rohu feeds in mid-water and mrigal on the bottom.
nativeRange: Rivers and lakes of northern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar; introduced widely elsewhere in Asia
abilities: Filters zooplankton and floating algae from surface waters with long, fine gill rakers
Can pass 1 kg in its first year in a fertilised pond
Spawns on monsoon floods; one large female carries hundreds of thousands to millions of eggs
edibilityNote: Coarse, bony flesh, highly valued in Bengal, where the head goes into muri ghonto. Always cooked. The same formalin-adulteration caution as for rohu applies in some markets.

animal.diet: Mainly zooplankton, plus phytoplankton and floating plant matter
animal.habitat: Rivers, reservoirs, floodplain lakes and farm ponds; stays in the warm upper water
animal.size: Commonly 50–80 cm; up to about 1.8 m and 39 kg
animal.behaviour: Cruises close to the surface sieving plankton, and wild fish spawn in shallow flooded river margins during the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Very large, broad head, much bigger than in other carps
Wide, upturned mouth with a prominent lower jaw and no barbels
Deep, short body; greyish back and silvery-white flanks with large scales
Fins dusky grey
animal.lookalikes: Rohu has a smaller head, a mouth on the underside with fringed lips, and reddish scale centres. Bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis), introduced in South Asia, also has a huge head, but its eyes sit low on the head and its scales are tiny.
animal.whereToSee: Kolkata's wholesale fish markets; Bangladesh pond-fish markets; reservoirs of the Gangetic plain; the Indus near Sukkur
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the monsoon (June–August)

lore: Catla was described by Francis Buchanan-Hamilton in 'An Account of the Fishes Found in the River Ganges' (1822), the founding work of Indian ichthyology. In Bengal a catla head cooked with rice or moong dal (muri ghonto) is a classic dish for honoured guests.
funFact: Many references still call it Catla catla. Genetic studies showed it sits inside the genus Labeo, and the iNaturalist name follows them.

wiki.extract: Catla also known as the major South Asian carp, is an economically important South Asian freshwater fish in the carp family Cyprinidae. It is native to rivers and lakes in northern India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, but has also been introduced elsewhere in South Asia and is commonly farmed.

summary: The best known of the 'Indian major carps' and one of the most eaten freshwater fish in South Asia. Rohu, catla and mrigal stocked together in one pond is the classic composite fish farm of India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
nativeRange: Rivers of northern and central India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar (Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra and associated basins); widely introduced
abilities: Feeds in the mid-water column, grazing algae and plant matter, so it shares ponds with surface-feeding catla and bottom-feeding mrigal
Breeds on monsoon floodplains, laying huge numbers of drifting eggs
Spawns in hatcheries after hormone injection, the method that turned Indian carps into a mass-farmed crop
Tolerates warm, turbid, low-oxygen pond water
edibilityNote: Mild, firm flesh with many fine Y-shaped bones. Always eaten cooked. Market fish have sometimes been found treated with formalin. Buy from trusted sellers and prefer clear-eyed fish with red gills.

animal.diet: Herbivore: phytoplankton, algae and soft submerged plants
animal.habitat: Rivers, floodplain lakes, reservoirs and farm ponds
animal.size: Commonly 45–60 cm; recorded up to about 2 m and 45 kg
animal.behaviour: Wild adults spawn in shallow, newly flooded margins after heavy monsoon rains, and the larvae grow up in floodplain waters.
fieldMarks: Moderately deep, silvery body with a bluish back
Each scale with a reddish centre, so the flanks look finely red-chequered, especially in the breeding season
Fins often reddish or orange-tinged
Blunt snout with thick fringed (fimbriated) lips and one small pair of barbels
Mouth on the underside of the head
animal.lookalikes: Catla has a much larger head, a wide upturned mouth and greyer colour. Mrigal is slimmer and silver with orange-tipped fins, and has thin unfringed lips. Kalbasu (Labeo calbasu) is dark grey to black.
animal.whereToSee: Fish markets of Kolkata, Dhaka, Lahore and Karachi; the Ganges and Padma; carp ponds across West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab
animal.season: Resident year-round; spawning in the monsoon, roughly June–August

lore: In Bengali wedding custom, a large rohu decorated with turmeric and vermilion is sent to the bride's family as part of the tattwa gifts. In 1957 Hiralal Chaudhuri bred Indian carps in captivity for the first time by pituitary injection, founding the region's modern fish farming.
funFact: India celebrates National Fish Farmers' Day on 10 July, the anniversary of Hiralal Chaudhuri's first induced breeding of Indian carps.

wiki.extract: The rohu, rui, ruhi, rou or roho labeo is a species of fish of the carp family, found in rivers in South Asia. It is a large omnivore and extensively used in aquaculture.

summary: A huge, golden-scaled barb of fast Himalayan rivers, called the 'tiger of the water' by anglers. It is Pakistan's national fish, and dams and overfishing have pushed it to Endangered.
nativeRange: Himalayan and sub-Himalayan rivers of Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and northern Myanmar (Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra basins)
abilities: Migrates upstream into cool tributaries to spawn during the monsoon and drops back to lower, warmer reaches in winter
Holds station in powerful rapids with a thick, muscular body and large scales
Eats almost anything: algae, fruit that falls into the water, insects, crabs and smaller fish
Grows very large: historical fish reportedly reached over 2 m and about 50 kg
edibilityNote: Traditionally eaten across its range, but it is Endangered and protected or catch-and-release only in many waters. Eating wild mahseer is discouraged. Wild fish from below dams or polluted reaches may carry contaminants.

animal.diet: Omnivore: algae, plant matter, fallen fruit, insects, molluscs, crustaceans and fish
animal.habitat: Clear, fast, rocky rivers and pools in hills and foothills; also some lakes and reservoirs
animal.lifespan: Several decades in large fish (exact maximum not well established)
animal.behaviour: Adults run up snow- and rain-fed tributaries to spawn on gravel during the monsoon. Large fish hunt and feed in the white water at the head of pools.
fieldMarks: Thick, torpedo-shaped body with very large scales
Golden-bronze flanks shading to a dark back; fins often reddish-orange or golden
Two pairs of barbels and thick, fleshy, rubbery lips
Head long, with its length greater than the body depth
animal.lookalikes: Other mahseers, especially the tor mahseer (Tor tor), have a deeper body, so the head is shorter than the body is deep, and they are more silvery. Indian carps such as rohu have much smaller scales and a fringed or small mouth without thick lips.
animal.whereToSee: Temple pools and ghats at Rishikesh and Haridwar on the Ganges; the Ramganga in Corbett National Park; the Poonch and Jhelum rivers (Pakistan/Kashmir); Manas River (Bhutan/Assam)
animal.season: Resident all year; spawning migrations upstream during the monsoon (roughly June–September), with some populations also breeding in spring

lore: Henry Sullivan Thomas's 'The Rod in India' (1873) made mahseer the legendary sport fish of British India. At Hindu temples and ghats, mahseer in sacred pools are fed by pilgrims and protected from fishing, which has kept some of the last large fish alive.
funFact: One explanation for the name is Hindi 'maha-sher', meaning 'great tiger'; another traces it to 'maha-shalka', 'great-scaled'.

wiki.extract: Tor putitora, known as the golden mahseer, putitor mahseer, or Himalayan mahseer, is an endangered species of cyprinid fish that is found in rapid streams, riverine pools, and lakes in the Himalayan region. Its native range is within the basins of the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers.

summary: A small striped minnow of South Asian paddies and streams that became one of biology's most important laboratory animals. Its transparent embryos develop in days, and it can regrow its heart, fins and retina.
nativeRange: India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan (Ganges and Brahmaputra basins), possibly Pakistan and Myanmar
abilities: Regrows damaged heart muscle, fins, spinal cord and retina
Embryos are transparent and develop from egg to swimming larva in about 3 days
About 70% of human genes have a zebrafish counterpart, making it a model for disease research

animal.diet: Omnivore: zooplankton, insects and larvae, algae
animal.habitat: Shallow, still or slow-flowing vegetated water, including rice paddies
animal.behaviour: Forms shoals and spawns at dawn, with females scattering eggs over vegetation and gravel.
fieldMarks: Slender, small minnow body with 5–7 horizontal blue-black stripes running to the tail tip
Silvery-gold to yellow stripes between the dark ones
Two pairs of barbels
Striped anal fin
animal.lookalikes: Pearl danio (Devario/Danio albolineatus) has no stripes but a pinkish iridescent sheen. Giant danio (Devario aequipinnatus) is bigger, with broken stripes and a yellow ground colour.
animal.whereToSee: Paddy fields and streams of West Bengal and Bangladesh during the monsoon; research labs worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds mostly in the monsoon

lore: Buchanan-Hamilton described it from the Ganges in 1822. George Streisinger at the University of Oregon developed it as a lab model in the 1970s, and his 1981 Nature paper on producing clonal, homozygous zebrafish launched zebrafish genetics.
funFact: The zebrafish's stripes self-organise through interactions between three kinds of pigment cells, a textbook living example of the pattern-forming mechanism proposed by Alan Turing.

wiki.extract: The zebrafish is a species of danionin belonging to the genus Danio in the suborder Cyprinoidei. Native to South Asia, it is a popular, hardy aquarium fish, frequently sold under the trade name zebra danio.

summary: A flat, diamond-shaped ray that buries itself in sand with only its eyes showing. In the Cayman Islands' Stingray City, generations of rays have learned to gather around tourist boats for squid.
nativeRange: Western Atlantic from New Jersey to southern Brazil, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean
abilities: Venomous serrated barb on the tail used in defence
Flaps or blows jets of water to excavate buried prey
Electroreceptors detect hidden prey under sand
Followed by jacks and cormorants that snatch prey it flushes

animal.diet: Clams, worms, shrimp, crabs and small fish
animal.habitat: Shallow sand flats, seagrass beds and lagoons, to about 50 m
animal.size: Females disc width up to 1.5 m; males much smaller (~0.7 m)
animal.behaviour: Rests buried in sand by day with only eyes and spiracles exposed; feeds actively at night and at dawn and dusk.
fieldMarks: Rhomboid disc with sharp outer corners
Plain olive-brown to grey upper side, white below
Long whip-like tail with a serrated venomous spine and a low fold below
Eyes and spiracles set high on the head
animal.lookalikes: Atlantic stingray (H. sabinus) is smaller with a rounder disc; roughtail stingray has thorns along the tail; spotted eagle ray has white spots and a protruding head.
animal.whereToSee: Stingray City and Sandbar, Grand Cayman; Bimini; Belize's Hol Chan; Antigua
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Fishermen cleaning their catch on the North Sound sandbar of Grand Cayman in the mid-20th century attracted rays, giving rise to Stingray City, now one of the Caribbean's most visited dive sites.
funFact: It was moved from the genus Dasyatis to Hypanus in 2016 after a genetic revision of whiptail stingrays.

wiki.extract: The southern stingray is a whiptail stingray found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Western Atlantic Ocean from New Jersey to southern Brazil. It has a flat, diamond-shaped disc, with a mud brown, olive, and grey dorsal surface and white underbelly. The barb on its tail is serrated and covered in a venomous mucus, used for self-defense.

plates.author: Willem Piso / Georg Marcgraf
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a spotted stingray with a diamond-shaped body, identified as 'Iabebirete'.
plates.long: This illustration shows a spotted ray, referred to as 'Iabebirete' in the accompanying Latin text. The woodcut captures the characteristic pattern of spots and the elongated tail, reflecting the 17th-century European interest in documenting global biodiversity and the natural world.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a stingray (Pastinaca), illustrating its physical characteristics for medicinal identification. Such images were crucial in early modern pharmacopeias like Dioscorides' work to ensure the correct identification of natural substances used in remedies.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a stingray, illustrating the medicinal and natural history text of Dioscorides. This image exemplifies the 16th-century practice of using woodcuts to provide visual references for scientific descriptions, specifically highlighting the 'mortiferous' sting mentioned in the text.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a stingray, identified as 'Pastinaca Marina'. This illustration from Mattioli's commentary on Dioscorides reflects the 16th-century interest in documenting the natural world with scientific accuracy, focusing on the distinctive flat body and venomous tail spine.

plates.author: Pietro Andrea Mattioli

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a stingray, identified in the text as Pastinaca marina. It appears in a 16th-century commentary on Dioscorides, reflecting the Renaissance effort to categorize and illustrate the natural world based on classical sources and direct observation. The illustration highlights the creature's distinctive diamond shape and long, barbed tail, which the accompanying text discusses in te

plates.title: Commentaries on the Six Books of Pedanius Dioscorides on Medical Matter
plates.author: Pietro Andrea Mattioli
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a stingray (Pastinaca Marina) showing its flat body and long tail with a stinger.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a stingray, identified in the accompanying Latin text as 'Pastinaca Marina'. It serves as a fine example of early modern scientific illustration, where artists sought to provide accurate visual records of marine species for identification and study. The print meticulously renders the creature's distinctive rhomboid shape and its dangerous, serrated tail spine.

plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: A long, whip-like tail of a ray or stingray with a single spine.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the elongated tail of a cartilaginous fish, likely a stingray, emphasizing the sharp defensive spine. It reflects Conrad Gessner's commitment to detailed anatomical observation in early modern natural history.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Woodcut of a stingray or eagle ray (Pastinaca) viewed from above, showing its flattened body and long tail.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a stingray (Pastinaca), as described by the naturalist Guillaume Rondelet. It illustrates the characteristic flattened body and long, serrated tail spine of the species, reflecting the 16th-century drive to categorize and visualize the natural world.

plates.title: Phytognomonica
plates.author: Giambattista della Porta
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration comparing various plants to animal tails, specifically fish and stingray tails.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the concept of 'Phytognomonica', a theory where plants are compared to animal parts based on physical resemblance. The image depicts various grasses and herbs alongside fish tails, suggesting a natural correspondence between the flora and fauna of the world as understood in early modern science.

plates.title: Plant Touchstone (Phytobasanos)
plates.author: Fabio Colonna
plates.desc: Detailed scientific engraving of a stingray, identified as 'Pastinaca marina' and in Greek as 'Τρυγών θαλασσία'.
plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts a stingray, labeled as 'Pastinaca marina,' from Fabio Colonna's 1592 work 'Phytobasanos.' Colonna was a pioneer in using copperplate engraving for scientific illustration, providing a level of anatomical detail that significantly advanced the field of natural history during the late Renaissance.

summary: A bony-shelled digger of the Americas that has spread steadily north through the USA since the 19th century. Females almost always give birth to genetically identical quadruplets, all from one fertilised egg. It is also one of the few animals other than humans that naturally carries leprosy.
nativeRange: South America (to northern Argentina), Central America, Mexico and the southern and central USA (expanding north)
abilities: Gives birth to identical quadruplets from a single egg (polyembryony)
Can hold its breath for about six minutes, walking across stream bottoms or gulping air to float
Leaps about 1 m into the air when startled
Digs dozens of burrows used later by other animals

animal.diet: Insects and other invertebrates (beetles, ants, termites, larvae), small vertebrates, eggs and fruit
animal.habitat: Forest, scrub and grassland with soft soil
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal in summer and active by day in cool weather. Digs for food with its nose to the ground, sniffing out prey.
fieldMarks: Leathery, armoured shell with a shoulder shield, a hip shield and 7–11 (usually 8–9) movable bands in between
Long, armoured, tapering tail
Small, pointed head and large upright ears
Signs: shallow conical feeding holes 'snout-pokes' in lawns and leaf litter; burrows about 20 cm wide
animal.lookalikes: Other Dasypus species in South America are very similar; seven-banded and southern long-nosed armadillos differ in band count and range. Six-banded armadillo is yellowish with fewer, wider bands.
animal.whereToSee: Florida and Texas, e.g. Aransas National Wildlife Refuge and Big Thicket; Pantanal (Brazil); Los Llanos (Venezuela)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Aztecs called it ayotochtli, 'turtle-rabbit', and Andean musicians made the charango, a small lute, from armadillo shells. It is the state small mammal of Texas.
funFact: Its startle leap is so high that it often strikes the undersides of cars, a major cause of roadkill.

wiki.extract: The nine-banded armadillo, also called the nine-banded long-nosed armadillo or common armadillo, is a species of armadillo native to South America. The Mexican long-nosed armadillo of North America was formerly treated as a subspecies of the nine-banded armadillo.

plates.title: Medicinal History of the Things Brought from Our West Indies
plates.author: Nicolás Monardes
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of an armadillo in a landscape with mountains and clouds.
plates.long: This woodcut provides an early European visual record of the armadillo, a creature native to the Americas. It is depicted in a stylized landscape setting, emphasizing its exotic nature to a 16th-century audience as part of Monardes' study of medicinal things from the West Indies.

plates.title: Recherche curieuse d'antiquités, venuës d'Italie, de la Grece, d'Egypte, & trouvées à Nimegue, a Sant...
plates.author: Chevalier, Nicolas
plates.desc: A collection of natural history specimens and mythical creatures, including a crocodile, armadillo, sawfish, and a winged dragon-like beast.
plates.long: This engraving from Nicolas Chevalier's 1714 work depicts a variety of specimens likely found in a 'cabinet of curiosities.' It features a mix of accurately rendered animals, such as an armadillo and a sawfish, alongside fantastical creatures like a winged dragon, reflecting the era's burgeoning interest in the natural world and the exotic.

plates.title: Florentine Codex, Vol. 3 (Books 10-12)
plates.author: Bernardino de Sahagún
plates.desc: Two-panel illustration depicting an armadillo and a lizard in a landscape.
plates.long: This two-panel illustration from the 1577 Florentine Codex depicts an armadillo (aiotochtli) in the upper register and an iguana (quauhcuetspali) in the lower register. The artwork demonstrates the synthesis of Indigenous Nahua observational detail with European artistic conventions, such as the use of landscape horizons and shading. These images served as a vital encyclopedic record of Mesoameric

plates.title: Histoire Naturelle des Indes (The Drake Manuscript)
plates.author: Anonymous (French)
plates.desc: Illustration of a 'Chvpa', an armadillo-like creature with a segmented shell.
plates.long: An early depiction of an armadillo, referred to here as a 'Chvpa'. The artist captures the unique plated armor of the animal, which fascinated early European explorers of the Americas.

plates.title: Ten Books of Exotic Things
plates.author: Carolus Clusius
plates.desc: An armadillo shown in profile, highlighting its armored shell and scaly limbs.
plates.long: This woodcut provides a detailed representation of an armadillo, identified in the text as 'Armadillo, sive Tatou genus alterum'. Illustrations like this were essential for European scholars to visualize the exotic fauna of the Americas, often based on dried specimens or sketches from travelers.

plates.title: Ten Books of Exotic Things
plates.author: Carolus Clusius
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of an armadillo, labeled 'Tatou.'
plates.long: This woodcut depicts an armadillo, identified by the text as a 'Tatou,' an animal from the 'New World.' It appears in Pierre Belon's influential work on natural history, reflecting the 16th-century European fascination with documenting and classifying newly discovered species from distant lands.

plates.title: Historia naturalis Brasiliae
plates.author: Willem Piso / Georg Marcgraf
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of an armadillo, showing its segmented armor and long tail.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts an armadillo, identified in the Latin text as 'Tatu seu Armadillo.' It serves as a prime example of 17th-century scientific illustration, where artists and scholars collaborated to document the diverse species of the Americas for European readers. The meticulous rendering of the animal's protective plates and sharp claws highlights the period's increasing focus on empirical ob

plates.title: Treasury of Medical Matters of New Spain
plates.author: Francisco Hernández
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of an armadillo (Ayotochtli) showing its characteristic armored plates and long tail.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts an armadillo, an animal native to the Americas, which the text identifies by its Nahuatl name, Ayotochtli. It represents the early modern effort to catalog and visualize the exotic species encountered in the Spanish territories of the New World as part of Francisco Hernández's monumental natural history.

plates.title: Theater of Earthly Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: Engraving of an armadillo showing its armored plates and scaly tail.
plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts an armadillo, a creature from the Americas that fascinated European naturalists in the 17th century. The artist meticulously renders the overlapping plates of its protective shell and the scaly texture of its tail and limbs, reflecting the era's growing interest in documenting exotic fauna.

plates.title: Theater of Earthly Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: An engraving of an armadillo in a landscape setting.
plates.long: This 1672 engraving depicts an armadillo, identified in the text as 'Hiatochtly'. It serves as a significant example of early modern European efforts to document and categorize the exotic fauna of the Americas, emphasizing the creature's unique protective plates.

summary: The largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, a stocky, black scavenger with a bone-crushing bite and a spine-tingling screech. Since the 1990s a transmissible cancer, devil facial tumour disease, has killed the majority of wild devils, spread directly by bites. Insurance populations on Maria Island and in mainland sanctuaries now help safeguard the species.
nativeRange: Tasmania; extinct on the Australian mainland for about 3,000 years (small reintroduced populations in New South Wales sanctuaries since 2020)
abilities: Among the strongest bites for its size of any living mammal, crushing bone and eating almost every part of a carcass
Clears carcasses and suppresses feral cats, helping protect small native mammals
Travels up to about 16 km a night foraging

animal.diet: Mainly carrion (wallabies, possums, wombats, livestock); also hunts small animals
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland, coastal heath and farmland across Tasmania
animal.size: Body 52–80 cm, tail 23–30 cm; 6–12 kg (males larger)
animal.behaviour: Solitary but gathers noisily at carcasses, sorting out feeding order with screams, growls and gaping displays. Young spend about 100 days in the pouch.
fieldMarks: Stocky, dog-sized black marsupial with a large head and short legs
White band across the chest and often white patches on the rump
Ears flush pink-red when the animal is stressed
Tracks: five-toed front, four-toed hind; signs include large scats full of bone and fur fragments on tracks
animal.voice: Unearthly screeches, growls and high-pitched screams, especially at shared carcasses at night.
animal.lookalikes: Spotted-tailed quoll is smaller, slimmer and covered in white spots. Feral cats have pointed ears and long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Cradle Mountain–Lake St Clair National Park and Narawntapu National Park (Tasmania); Maria Island (insurance population); Bonorong and Devils@Cradle sanctuaries; Aussie Ark, Barrington Tops (NSW)
animal.season: Resident; breeding in March; juveniles disperse in late summer

lore: Early European settlers in Tasmania named it the 'devil' after its unearthly nocturnal screams. With the extinction of the thylacine in 1936, it became the world's largest surviving carnivorous marsupial.
funFact: Devil facial tumour disease is one of very few known contagious cancers: the tumour cells themselves are transmitted between animals.

wiki.extract: The Tasmanian devil is a carnivorous marsupial of the family Dasyuridae. It was formerly present across mainland Australia, but became extinct there around 3,500 years ago; it is now confined to the island of Tasmania. The size of a small dog, the Tasmanian devil became the largest carnivorous marsupial in the world following the extinction of the thylacine in 1936. It is related to quolls, and distantly related to the thylacine. It is characterised by its stocky and muscular build, black fur, pungent odour, extremely loud screech, keen sense of smell, and ferocity when feeding. The Tasmanian devil's large head and neck allow it to generate among the strongest bites per unit body mass of any extant predatory land mammal. It hunts prey and scavenges on carrion.

summary: A nocturnal lemur of Madagascar with bat-like ears, rodent-like teeth and a strange, skeletal middle finger. It finds grubs by tapping on wood and listening for hollow tunnels.
nativeRange: Madagascar, mainly the eastern rainforests and scattered western and northern forests
abilities: Taps wood with its thin middle finger and listens to find hollow insect tunnels (percussive foraging)
Gnaws into wood with ever-growing incisors, then hooks out larvae with that ball-jointed finger
Has an extra 'pseudothumb' on each wrist
Turns its large ears independently to locate sounds

animal.diet: Omnivore: wood-boring beetle larvae, seeds, nectar, fungi, coconuts and other fruit
animal.habitat: Rainforest, dry forest, mangroves and plantations
animal.lifespan: Poorly known in the wild; 20+ years in captivity
animal.size: 2–2.6 kg; body ~40 cm with a bushy tail of 45–55 cm
animal.behaviour: The world's largest nocturnal primate, it spends the day curled in a ball-shaped nest of leaves high in the canopy.
fieldMarks: Shaggy dark fur
Huge ears
Long, thin middle finger
Bushy tail
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Nosy Mangabe Special Reserve
animal.season: Resident; nocturnal

lore: In parts of Madagascar, local fady (taboos) hold the aye-aye to be a sign of death and it may be killed on sight. Pierre Sonnerat brought the first description to Europe in 1782, and early naturalists classed it as a squirrel.
funFact: It is the only primate known to find food by tapping and listening, a method otherwise used by woodpeckers.

wiki.extract: The aye-aye is a long-fingered lemur, a strepsirrhine primate native to Madagascar with rodent-like teeth that perpetually grow and a special thin middle finger that they can use to catch grubs and larvae out of tree trunks.

summary: The largest dolphin and the ocean's top predator, found in every ocean from the polar ice to the tropics. Orca populations have distinct diets, hunting methods and call dialects passed down through family lines, which biologists describe as culture.
nativeRange: All oceans; most abundant in cold, productive waters of the North Pacific, North Atlantic and Southern Ocean
abilities: Hunts with echolocation and coordinated group tactics
Creates waves in unison to wash seals off Antarctic ice floes
Deliberately beaches itself to snatch sea lion pups, then wriggles back into the sea (Patagonia, Crozet Islands)
Passes learned dialects and hunting traditions from mothers and grandmothers to offspring
Kills great white sharks and blue whales

animal.diet: Carnivore; varies by population: salmon, herring, seals, sea lions, sharks, other whales
animal.habitat: Coastal and open ocean, especially cold waters
animal.size: Males 6–8 m (rarely ~9 m), up to ~6 t; dorsal fin to 1.8 m
animal.behaviour: Resident orcas of the Pacific Northwest stay with their mothers for life. Females live decades past menopause, and these grandmothers lead the family to salmon in lean years.
fieldMarks: Bold black and white pattern with a white eye patch
Grey 'saddle patch' behind the dorsal fin
Males have a very tall, straight dorsal fin
Travels in family pods
animal.voice: Clicks, whistles and pulsed calls; each pod has its own dialect
animal.lookalikes: False killer whale is all-dark and slimmer. Risso's dolphin is grey and scarred. Female orcas have curved fins like large dolphins.
animal.whereToSee: San Juan Islands and Salish Sea (Washington/British Columbia); northern Norway (Skjervøy area) in winter; Península Valdés, Argentina
animal.season: Salish Sea mainly summer; Norway Nov–Jan with the herring; Valdés beach-hunting Mar–Apr

lore: Orcas are crest animals of Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast nations, carved on totem poles. At Eden, New South Wales, a pod led by 'Old Tom' herded baleen whales towards human whalers in exchange for the tongues and lips, a partnership that lasted into the 1920s.
funFact: IUCN lists the orca as Data Deficient because it may comprise several species that have not yet been formally separated.

wiki.extract: The orca, or killer whale, is a toothed whale and the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family. The only extant species in the genus Orcinus, it is recognizable by its distinct pigmentation; being mostly black on top, white on the bottom and having recognizable white eye patches. A cosmopolitan species, it inhabits a wide range of marine environments, from Arctic to Antarctic regions to tropical seas, but is more commonly documented in temperate or cooler coastal waters. Scientists have proposed dividing the global population into races, subspecies, or possibly even species.

summary: A widespread dolphin of warm and temperate seas, one of the most studied animals for intelligence. Each dolphin develops its own signature whistle, which others use to call it, much like a name.
nativeRange: Temperate and tropical oceans worldwide, coastal and offshore
abilities: Echolocates with clicks precise enough to tell objects apart by shape and material
Uses a signature whistle as a personal name and copies others' whistles to address them
Recognises itself in a mirror
Sleeps with one brain hemisphere at a time, keeping one eye open
Some Florida dolphins herd fish with a ring of stirred-up mud and catch them as they leap out

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, squid, crustaceans
animal.habitat: Bays, estuaries, coasts and offshore waters
animal.behaviour: In Laguna, Brazil, bottlenose dolphins drive mullet towards fishermen and give a signal for when to cast their nets, a cooperation passed down through generations of both dolphins and people.

Short, stubby beak and a crease above it
Tall, curved dorsal fin in mid-back
Often bow-rides and leaps

animal.lookalikes: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin is smaller with a longer beak and often belly spots. Common dolphins have an hourglass pattern on the side.
animal.whereToSee: Chanonry Point (Moray Firth) and Cardigan Bay, UK; Sarasota Bay, Florida
animal.season: Resident in many coastal areas; Chanonry best on a rising tide in summer

funFact: Dolphins remember the signature whistles of former companions after more than 20 years apart.

wiki.extract: The common bottlenose dolphin or Atlantic bottlenose dolphin is one of three species of bottlenose dolphin in the genus Tursiops. While formerly known simply as the bottlenose dolphin, this term is now applied to the genus Tursiops as a whole. As considerable genetic variation has been described within this species, even between neighboring populations, many experts think additional species may be recognized and split out.

nativeRange: Guiana Shield: French Guiana, Suriname, Guyana and adjacent northern Brazil
abilities: Stores alkaloid toxins such as pumiliotoxins in its skin, taken from the ants and mites it eats
Warns predators with vivid, highly variable colour patterns (aposematism)
Males carry newly hatched tadpoles on their backs to small pools of water in tree holes or bromeliads
Captive-bred frogs fed on other insects lose their toxicity

animal.habitat: Humid forest floor near streams, boulders and fallen trees
animal.behaviour: Females compete for males and may wrestle rivals. Toxic species like this one are active by day, relying on their warning colours rather than hiding.
fieldMarks: Small frog with bright, highly variable colours
Often black with yellow or white stripes
Bright blue legs
Large finger discs

funFact: The blue 'Okopipi' frogs of Suriname's Sipaliwini savanna were described as their own species in 1969 but are now considered a colour form of this one.

wiki.extract: The cobalt dyeing poison dart frog, also known as the cobalt poison frog or tinc, is a species of poison dart frog. It is among the most variably colored and largest species of poison dart frogs, typically reaching snout–vent lengths of about 50 mm (2.0 in). It is distributed in the eastern portion of the Guiana Shield, including parts of French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, and Brazil. These types of frogs usually tend to stay on the ground as it is easier to catch prey., though in some cases may climb trees as well. They are frequently found in treefall canopy gaps in the Amazon rainforest, as they utilize phytotelmata on the fallen trees for tadpole development.

summary: Probably the most poisonous animal on Earth for its size. This thumb-sized yellow, orange or mint-green frog lives in a few rainforest valleys of Colombia's Pacific coast. Its skin holds batrachotoxin, which Emberá hunters used to poison blowgun darts.
nativeRange: Pacific lowland rainforest of Cauca department, Colombia
abilities: Its skin contains batrachotoxin, which keeps sodium channels in nerves and muscle open and can cause fatal heart failure
A single wild frog is estimated to carry enough toxin to kill about ten people
Has resistant sodium channels so it is not harmed by its own poison
Gets its toxin from its wild diet; captive-bred frogs are harmless

animal.diet: Ants, beetles and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Leaf litter of humid lowland rainforest near streams
animal.behaviour: Active by day and bold because of its toxin. Males carry tadpoles on their backs to water. Wild frogs must never be touched: toxin on the skin can enter through cuts.
fieldMarks: Uniform bright yellow, orange or pale metallic green
Black eyes; often black spots on the toe tips
Larger than most poison frogs
Active in daylight on the forest floor
animal.voice: A long series of rapid trills given by males

animal.season: Resident

funFact: Batrachotoxin is also found in the feathers of some New Guinea birds, the pitohuis and blue-capped ifrit, which probably get it from beetles.

wiki.extract: The golden poison frog, also known as the golden dart frog or golden poison arrow frog, is a poison dart frog endemic to the rainforests of Colombia. The golden poison frog has become endangered due to habitat destruction within its naturally limited range. Despite its small size, this frog is considered to be the most poisonous extant animal species on the planet.

summary: The largest living turtle and the only one without a hard shell. Its back is a leathery skin over a mosaic of small bones. It dives deeper than 1,000 m, crosses whole oceans to feed on jellyfish, and stays warm in cold northern seas.
nativeRange: All tropical and temperate oceans; nests on tropical beaches, forages north to Norway and Alaska and south to Chile and New Zealand
abilities: Dives to over 1,000 m, deeper than any other turtle
Keeps its body warmer than the surrounding water through its size, insulating fat and heat-exchanging blood vessels in its flippers
Migrates thousands of kilometres between nesting beaches and jellyfish feeding grounds
Its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that stop slippery jellyfish escaping

animal.diet: Jellyfish, salps and other soft-bodied animals
animal.habitat: Open ocean; comes ashore only to nest
animal.size: Shell up to ~1.8 m; weight usually 300–600 kg, exceptionally over 900 kg
animal.behaviour: Females haul out at night several times in a season to dig nests and lay about 80 eggs. They return to nest every two to three years. Plastic bags in the sea, which look like jellyfish, are a serious hazard.
fieldMarks: Huge, dark blue-black turtle with white spots and no scutes
Seven ridges running the length of the back
Very long front flippers
Notched upper jaw with two tooth-like points
animal.lookalikes: No other turtle has a ridged, leathery back without plates. Large loggerheads and green turtles have hard shells of plates (scutes).

animal.season: Nesting March–July in the Caribbean and Atlantic; Nov–Feb on some Pacific beaches

funFact: The leatherback's lineage split from other living sea turtles more than 100 million years ago.
