wiki.extract: The leatherback sea turtle, sometimes called the lute turtle, leathery turtle or simply the luth, is a large species of sea turtle. The largest of all living turtles and the heaviest non-crocodilian reptile, it reaches lengths of up to 2.7 metres and weights of 500 kilograms (1,100 lb). It is the only living species in the genus Dermochelys and family Dermochelyidae. It can easily be differentiated from other modern sea turtles by its lack of a bony shell; instead, its carapace is covered by oily flesh and flexible, leather-like skin, for which it is named. Leatherback turtles have a global range, although there are multiple distinct subpopulations. The species as a whole is considered vulnerable, and some of its subpopulations are critically endangered.

summary: South Asia's largest frog. During the first monsoon rains the males turn bright yellow and puff out blue vocal sacs, calling in loud choruses. It was exported in huge numbers for frog legs until India banned the trade in 1987.
nativeRange: Afghanistan and Pakistan through India, Nepal and Bangladesh to Myanmar; introduced to the Andaman Islands and Madagascar
abilities: Males turn bright yellow and show blue vocal sacs in the breeding season
Can leap long distances and skitter across water
Eats almost anything it can fit into its mouth, including other frogs, snakes and small birds

animal.diet: Insects, crabs, fish, frogs, snakes, small birds and rodents
animal.habitat: Ponds, marshes, rice paddies and ditches
animal.behaviour: Comes out in large numbers to breed after the first monsoon rains; males call from shallow water.
fieldMarks: Large olive-green to brown frog with dark spots
Thin yellow line down the middle of the back
Breeding males bright yellow with blue vocal sacs
Pointed snout and strongly webbed toes
animal.voice: A loud, hoarse croak, given in deafening choruses after the monsoon rains
animal.lookalikes: Jerdon's bullfrog (H. crassus) has shorter hind limbs and a shorter snout. Skittering frogs (Euphlyctis) are smaller and more aquatic.
animal.whereToSee: Rice paddies and ponds across the Indian plains; Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Sundarbans; best seen at the onset of the monsoon
animal.season: Breeding with the first monsoon rains (June–July)

edibilityNote: Eaten locally; commercial frog-leg export is banned in India, and catching wild frogs is illegal there. Cook thoroughly.
lore: The Rigveda's frog hymn (Maṇḍūka Sūkta, 7.103) compares frogs croaking at the start of the monsoon to priests chanting; South Asia's monsoon chorus of bullfrogs is the sound it describes.
funFact: Before India banned exports in 1987, tens of millions of frogs were exported every year, and some studies linked the loss of frogs to increases in crop pests and mosquitoes.

wiki.extract: Hoplobatrachus tigerinus, commonly known as the Indian bullfrog, is a large species of fork-tongued frog found in South and Southeast Asia. A relatively large frog, it is normally green in color, although physiological traits vary between populations. Sexual dimorphism exists between males and females. Outside of its native range, H. tigerinus is a rapidly-spreading invasive species. Both adults and tadpoles can severely damage the populations of other frog species. Typically, Indian bullfrogs dwell in wetland environments. Research has been conducted on their ability to control mosquitos.

summary: A glossy black, fork-tailed bird that rides on grazing cattle and fearlessly dive-bombs crows, kites and eagles that come near its nest. Smaller birds often nest close to drongos for protection.
nativeRange: SE Iran and Afghanistan through Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and Java; introduced to the Mariana Islands
abilities: Aggressively attacks much larger birds of prey and crows near its nest
Hawks flying insects stirred up by cattle, tractors and grass fires
Mimics the calls of other species, including the Shikra

animal.diet: Insects caught in the air or on the ground: grasshoppers, moths, termites, bees; occasionally small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open farmland, grassland, roadsides and light woodland
animal.behaviour: Perches on wires, fence posts and the backs of buffalo and cattle, sallying out after insects; during the breeding season it will chase and strike raptors many times its size.

Long, deeply forked tail with the outer tips flaring outward
Small white spot at the gape (corner of the bill) in adults
Upright posture on exposed perches

funFact: Smaller birds such as bulbuls and orioles are known to nest close to drongo nests, apparently gaining protection from its aggressive defence.

wiki.extract: The  black drongo is a small Asian passerine bird of the drongo family Dicruridae. It is a common resident breeder in much of tropical southern Asia from southwest Iran through Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka east to southern China and Indonesia and accidental visitor of Japan. It is an all black bird with a distinctive forked tail and measures 28 cm (11 in) in length. It feeds on insects, and is common in open agricultural areas and light forest throughout its range, perching conspicuously on a bare perch or along power or telephone lines.

summary: The bird with the longest wingspan alive, up to about 3.5 m. It can circle the Southern Ocean and travel thousands of kilometres with barely a wingbeat.
nativeRange: Southern Ocean; breeds on South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen, Prince Edward and Macquarie islands
abilities: Wingspan up to ~3.5 m, the largest of any living bird
Dynamic soaring: harvests energy from wind gradients over waves
A shoulder lock holds wings outstretched with little muscle effort
Can cover over 10,000 km in a single foraging trip
Smells prey and oily slicks from far away with tube nostrils

animal.diet: Squid, fish and carrion taken at the surface
animal.habitat: Open ocean; nests on grassy subantarctic islands
animal.behaviour: Pairs bond for life after years of elaborate dancing with wing-spreading and bill-clapping, and raise one chick every two years.
fieldMarks: Enormous wingspan, often 2.5–3.5 m
Adult males the whitest of the great albatrosses, with black only at the wingtips and trailing edge
Large pink bill
Juveniles chocolate brown with a white face, whitening over many years
animal.voice: At the nest: braying, screams, whistles and loud bill-clapping during courtship dances
animal.lookalikes: Royal albatrosses have a black cutting edge to the upper bill; on adult royals the upperwing whitens from the leading edge back, not from the centre. Several other 'wandering-type' albatrosses (Tristan, Antipodean, Amsterdam) are browner.
animal.whereToSee: Prion Island, South Georgia (boardwalk, cruise landings); at sea in the Drake Passage and Southern Ocean
animal.season: Lays Dec–early Jan; chicks remain at the nest through the austral winter. Prion Island is closed 20 Nov–7 Jan

lore: In Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), killing an albatross brings a curse on a ship. Sailors long believed albatrosses carried the souls of drowned seamen.
funFact: Tens of thousands of albatrosses have drowned on longline fishing hooks, the main threat to the species.

wiki.extract: The snowy albatross, also known as the wandering albatross, white-winged albatross, or goonie, is a large seabird from the family Diomedeidae; they have a circumpolar range in the Southern Ocean. It is the largest species of albatross and was long considered to be the same species as the Tristan albatross and the Antipodean albatross. Together with the Amsterdam albatross, it forms the wandering albatross species complex, which some began referring to more recently as "snowy".

plates.title: Museum of the Royal Society
plates.author: Nehemiah Grew
plates.desc: Scientific plate featuring an albatross skull, a double egg, and two pendulous bird nests.
plates.long: This plate, labeled 'Tab. 6' from Nehemiah Grew's 1681 catalogue of the Royal Society's museum, depicts various ornithological specimens. It features a detailed anatomical study of an albatross skull alongside a rare 'egg within an egg' anomaly and intricate pendulous nests, illustrating the early modern transition toward empirical observation in biology.

summary: The most widespread and numerous albatross, with a dark 'eyebrow' giving it a stern expression. About two-thirds of the world population breeds in the Falkland Islands.
nativeRange: Breeds on sub-Antarctic islands (Falklands, South Georgia, Chile); ranges over the Southern Ocean
abilities: Dynamic soaring lets it travel thousands of kilometres with little flapping
Locks its wings in place with a shoulder tendon
Nests in vast colonies on cliffs and slopes

animal.diet: Fish, squid, crustaceans and fishery discards
animal.habitat: Open ocean; nests on sub-Antarctic islands
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite every year with elaborate dances of bill-fencing and sky-pointing.
fieldMarks: Dark eyebrow stripe
Bright orange-yellow bill with reddish tip
Dark upperwings and back, white body
Broad dark margins to the white underwing
animal.voice: Braying and groaning calls at colonies; silent at sea.
animal.lookalikes: Campbell albatross (New Zealand) has a pale yellow eye. Shy albatross has a pale grey-green bill and narrow underwing margins.
animal.whereToSee: Steeple Jason, Saunders and New Islands (Falklands); off Cape Horn
animal.season: Breeds Sept–April; disperses north in winter

lore: The species was downlisted from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2013 and to Least Concern in 2017, following reductions in seabird bycatch.
funFact: Steeple Jason Island in the Falklands holds well over 100,000 breeding pairs, among the largest albatross colonies anywhere.

wiki.extract: The black-browed albatross, also known as the black-browed mollymawk, is a large seabird of the albatross family Diomedeidae; it is the most widespread and common member of its family.

plates.author: Nehemiah Grew

It features a detailed anatomical study of an albatross skull alongside a rare 'egg within an egg' anomaly and intricate pendulous nests, illustrating the early modern transition toward empirical observation in biology.

summary: A silver shad of the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea that pushes up the Padma, Meghna, Hooghly, Godavari and Indus to spawn with the monsoon floods. Bengalis treat it as the finest fish there is, and it is Bangladesh's national fish.
nativeRange: Northern Indian Ocean coasts from the Persian Gulf and Pakistan to Myanmar, and the large rivers that drain into them
abilities: Anadromous: grows at sea and in estuaries, then migrates hundreds of kilometres upriver to spawn in fresh water
Filter-feeds on plankton with fine gill rakers
Spawns in huge numbers around the full and new moons of the monsoon season, releasing free-floating eggs that drift downstream
Fat content of the flesh rises with the upriver run, which is why river-caught hilsa is prized above sea-caught fish
edibilityNote: Rich, oily and full of fine intramuscular bones, so eat it slowly. Always eaten cooked in South Asia (bhapa, shorshe ilish, smoked palla). Bangladesh bans hilsa fishing for about three weeks around the October spawning peak and bans catching juveniles (jatka) for months each year. Avoid buying jatka.

animal.diet: Plankton: diatoms, algae, copepods and other small crustaceans
animal.habitat: Coastal seas and estuaries; large turbid rivers during the spawning run
animal.size: Usually 30–45 cm; up to about 60 cm and 2.5 kg
animal.behaviour: Shoals move upriver on the monsoon floods and spawn in the main channels. The young (jatka) drift back down to the estuaries and sea to grow.
fieldMarks: Deep, laterally compressed silver body with a bluish-green back
No visible lateral line, and a sharp saw-edged keel of scutes along the belly
A dark blotch just behind the gill cover, often followed by a row of fainter spots in young fish
A distinct notch in the middle of the upper jaw
Deeply forked tail
animal.lookalikes: The Indian river shad (Gudusia chapra) is similar but rarely over 20 cm. The kelee shad (Hilsa kelee) is mostly marine and has a row of dark spots along the flank in adults as well as young. Large mature hilsa is unmistakable in South Asian markets.
animal.whereToSee: The Padma–Meghna confluence at Chandpur and the Meghna estuary (Bangladesh); fish markets of Kolkata and Dhaka during the monsoon; the lower Indus below Kotri Barrage near Hyderabad, Sindh
animal.season: Main upriver spawning run July–October, peaking at the full moon of Bengali Ashwin (usually October); a smaller run January–March

lore: In Sindh the palla is linked to the shrine of Khwaja Khizr on Bukkur island near Sukkur: folklore says the fish swim upriver to pay homage and turn back facing the shrine. Bengali Hindus offer a pair of hilsa at Saraswati Puja and in weddings, and the fish is a long-running theme of Bengali cooking and poetry.
funFact: Bangladesh lands most of the world's hilsa catch. Its seasonal fishing bans, together with food aid for fishing families during the bans, are credited with more than doubling the national catch since the early 2000s.

ancestors.name: Dorosomatidae
ancestors.common: Thread Herrings, Gizzard Shads, and Sardinellas

wiki.extract: The ilish, also known as the ilishi, hilsa, pulasa, hilsa herring or hilsa shad, is a species of fish related to the herring, in the family Clupeidae. It is a very popular and sought-after food in the Bengal region and area and is the national fish of Bangladesh. It is also the state fish of the Indian state of West Bengal.

summary: The only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, a seagrass grazer of warm Indo-Pacific shallows with a whale-like fluked tail. Dugongs plough seagrass meadows like underwater cows, leaving feeding trails across the seabed. Australia holds most of the world's population; in India they survive in tiny numbers in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kutch and Andaman Islands.
nativeRange: Coastal Indo-West Pacific from East Africa and the Red Sea through the Arabian Gulf, South and Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and Vanuatu
abilities: Uproots whole seagrass plants, leaving feeding trails that can promote regrowth of fast-growing, more nutritious seagrasses
Can live over 70 years
Mature males and some old females grow short tusks

animal.diet: Seagrasses, especially roots and rhizomes; occasionally invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow, sheltered, warm coastal waters with seagrass
animal.behaviour: Feeds by rooting through the sediment with its muscular, downturned snout. Mothers nurse a single calf for about 18 months.
fieldMarks: Grey to brown, smooth fusiform body
Whale-like fluked tail with a median notch (not a rounded paddle)
Broad, downturned snout with a bristly upper lip disc
Signs: meandering, sandy 'feeding trails' through seagrass beds; surfaces showing only nostrils
animal.lookalikes: Manatees (Atlantic only) have rounded paddle tails. Sea turtles also graze seagrass but have shells and heads that stay up longer.
animal.whereToSee: Shark Bay and Moreton Bay (Australia); Marsa Alam and Marsa Abu Dabbab (Red Sea, Egypt); Marawah Marine Reserve (Abu Dhabi); Coron, Palawan (Philippines); Bazaruto Archipelago (Mozambique); Palk Bay Dugong Conservation Reserve (Tamil Nadu, India)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Dugongs and manatees, the order Sirenia, are named for the sirens of Greek myth, and seafarers' tales of mermaids are often traced to them. In 2022 Tamil Nadu declared India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay.
funFact: The dugong's closest living relatives on land are elephants.

wiki.extract: The dugong is a marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees. It is the only living representative of the once-diverse family Dugongidae; its closest modern relative, Steller's sea cow, was hunted to extinction in the 18th century.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Large hand-colored woodcut of a river scene with scholars, fish, and a mermaid.
plates.long: Two scholars in academic robes stand on opposite banks of a river filled with various fish, a lobster, and a mermaid. In the background, a river flows between two fortified medieval cities with stone bridges and sailing vessels. The figure on the left bears the inscription 'ANTHI' on his garment, likely referencing the study of aquatic life.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: A hand-colored woodcut depicting a scene with two figures on opposite banks of a waterway filled with various aquatic creatures, including fish, crabs, a mermaid, and a merman. In the background, there are cities, ships, and a bridge.
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1491 edition of Ortus sanitatis depicts a variety of aquatic life, both real and mythical. Two figures, likely scholars or observers, stand on the banks of a waterway teeming with fish, crustaceans, a mermaid, and a merman, illustrating the medieval understanding of the natural world. The inclusion of detailed cityscapes and ships in the background provides a sen

plates.author: Louis Renard
plates.desc: A hand-colored engraving of a mermaid-like creature, described as a 'monster similar to a Siren.'
plates.long: This fantastical illustration depicts a 'Siren' or mermaid, purportedly caught off the coast of Borneo and kept alive in a tub for several days. It reflects the 18th-century fascination with exotic and monstrous sea creatures, where the boundaries between scientific observation and myth were often blurred.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Woodcut of a mermaid and a fish
plates.long: A woodcut depicting a mermaid, a legendary aquatic creature with the upper body of a human and the tail of a fish. In the context of the 'Hortus sanitatis', such figures were often treated as real biological entities within the study of natural history.

plates.title: Athanasii Kircheri Societatis Jesu Magnes sive de arte magnetica opus tripartium quo universa magnetis natura, eiusque in omnibus scientiis & artibus usus, nova medthodo explicatur, ac praeterae e viribus & prodigiosis effectibus magneticarum, aliarumque abditarum naturae motionum in elementis, lapidibus, plantis, animalibus, elucescentium, multa hucusque incognita natureae arcana, per physica, medica, chymica, & mathematica omnis generis experimenta recluduntur
plates.author: Kircher, Athanasius
plates.desc: Woodcut depicting two merfolk (a merman and a mermaid) in the sea.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a pair of 'anthropomorphic fish' or sirens, as described in the accompanying Latin text. In his 1654 work on magnetism, Athanasius Kircher included such cryptozoological figures to explore the 'hidden secrets of nature' and the sympathetic forces he believed governed all living things.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts the egg case of a ray, often referred to as a 'mermaid's purse.' Featured in Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium,' it represents the 16th-century shift toward empirical observation in the study of marine biology and animal reproduction.

summary: A large predatory water beetle that carries its air supply in a bubble beneath its wing cases. Adults and their fearsome larvae, 'water tigers', hunt tadpoles, newts and even small fish.
nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia
abilities: Stores air under the wing cases and refills by poking its abdomen tip through the surface
Larvae inject digestive enzymes through hollow, sickle-shaped jaws and suck out the liquefied prey
Adults fly at night between ponds and can mistake shiny car roofs and glasshouses for water
Remains active under winter ice

animal.diet: Tadpoles, insect larvae, snails, newts, small fish and carrion
animal.habitat: Well-vegetated ponds, lakes, ditches and slow rivers
animal.behaviour: It swims with both hind legs stroking together like oars, unlike scavenger water beetles which move them alternately.
fieldMarks: Smooth, oval, dark olive-black body
Yellow border around the thorax and wing cases
Males have glossy wing cases and suction pads on the front feet; females usually have grooved wing cases
Fringed, flattened hind legs used as oars
animal.lookalikes: Great silver water beetle (Hydrophilus piceus) is larger, all black, has short clubbed antennae and moves its legs alternately. Other Dytiscus species are separated by the shape of the yellow border and underside colour.
animal.whereToSee: Garden ponds and vegetated lakes across Europe; often netted in pond-dipping sessions.
animal.season: Active year-round; most often seen spring to late summer

funFact: The male's front feet bear sucker discs that help him grip the female during mating; the ridges on many females' wing cases are thought to make that grip harder.

wiki.extract:
The great diving beetle is an aquatic diving beetle native to Europe and northern Asia, and in the UK is common in Wales, much of England and southern Scotland but less common on chalk and in the far north.
The great diving beetle, true to its name, is a rather large insect. The larvae can grow up to 60 millimetres (2.4 in) in length, while the adults are generally 27–35 millimetres (1.1–1.4 in).

summary: A glossy, night-hunting member of the Big Four with one of the most potent venoms of any Asian land snake. Many bites happen to people asleep on the floor, often cause little pain, and can lead to paralysis hours later.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka
abilities: Its neurotoxins, including beta-bungarotoxin, stop nerve signals from reaching muscles
Hunts other snakes, including other kraits, at night
Bites often cause almost no pain or swelling, so victims may not realise they have been bitten

animal.diet: Mainly other snakes; also rodents, lizards and frogs
animal.habitat: Fields, scrub, termite mounds, rat holes and houses; often near water
animal.behaviour: By day it is timid and hides its head under its coils, but at night it is active and comes into homes. Signs of envenoming are drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble swallowing and abdominal pain, followed by breathing failure, so anyone who might have been bitten needs hospital care even if they feel fine. In first aid, keep the person still, immobilise the limb and transport them urgently. Breathing support and antivenom save lives. Sleeping on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net prevents many bites.
fieldMarks: Glossy steel-blue to black body with narrow, paired white crossbands, clearest towards the tail and faint or missing on the neck
Row of enlarged hexagonal scales along the spine, giving a slight ridge
Rounded head barely wider than the neck; small black eyes
Plain white belly
animal.lookalikes: Often confused with the harmless common wolf snake (Lycodon aulicus) and barred wolf snake (L. striatus). Wolf snakes are brown and dull rather than glossy blue-black. Their white bands start right behind a flattened head, they have no enlarged ridge scales along the spine, and they often have a pale collar. A banded snake that is black and shiny with bands fading towards the head should be treated as a krait.
animal.whereToSee: Widespread across lowland India and Sri Lanka; most often met at night on paths and in houses during the monsoon
animal.season: Resident; bites peak in the monsoon (June–September), when snakes are flooded out of burrows

lore: The English word 'krait' comes from the Hindi karait. Joseph Fayrer's 'The Thanatophidia of India' (1872), with its hand-coloured plates of the krait and other deadly snakes, first recorded the scale of snakebite deaths across British India.
funFact: Bungarotoxin from the krait's relative, the many-banded krait, became a standard laboratory tool for mapping the receptors through which nerves trigger muscles.

wiki.extract: The common krait is a highly venomous snake species belonging to the genus Bungarus in the family Elapidae. It has a black or bluish-black body with narrow white crossbands, typically reaching a length of 0.91 to 1.22 m. It is widely distributed across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal, inhabiting grasslands, agricultural fields, and human settlements. It is known for its potent neurotoxic venom and responsible for the majority of medically significant snakebites in the Indian subcontinent.

summary: Africa's longest venomous snake, and despite its name grey to olive-brown. The name comes from the inky-black lining of its mouth, which it gapes in threat. Before antivenom, a serious bite was almost always fatal.
nativeRange: Savannas and open woodland of eastern and southern Africa, with scattered populations in West Africa
abilities: One of the fastest snakes on land, able to keep its head and front body off the ground while moving
Venom contains dendrotoxins and other neurotoxins that can cause paralysis and breathing failure within hours
Can strike repeatedly from a raised position
Returns to the same retreat, such as a termite mound or hollow tree, for years

animal.diet: Rodents, hyraxes, bushbabies, birds
animal.habitat: Dry savanna, rocky outcrops, open woodland; takes shelter in termite mounds and hollow trees
animal.size: Usually 2–2.5 m; exceptionally ~3 m or more
animal.behaviour: Shy, and usually escapes if it can. When cornered it rears up, spreads a narrow hood, gapes its black mouth and hisses. A bite needs urgent hospital care with antivenom and breathing support. As first aid, a firm pressure bandage on the bitten limb and a splint may slow the venom while the person is taken to hospital. Do not cut, suck or use tourniquets.
fieldMarks: Long, slender body, grey to olive-brown with a paler belly; never truly black
Long 'coffin-shaped' head with a prominent brow
Black inside of mouth, shown when gaping
Smooth scales; medium-sized round-pupilled eyes
animal.lookalikes: Colour alone is not a reliable guide. The harmless mole snake (Pseudaspis cana) is stockier, with a small head and short tail. The boomslang has a short head and huge eyes. Green mambas are bright green and live in forest canopy. Cobras spread a wider hood. A large, long-headed grey snake moving fast with its head raised should be treated as a mamba.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, Hluhluwe–iMfolozi, the Kenyan and Tanzanian savannas
animal.season: Resident; active by day, often basking in the morning

lore: The name mamba comes from the Zulu imamba. The genus name Dendroaspis means 'tree asp', although the black mamba spends much of its time on the ground.
funFact: Mambalgins, peptides found in black mamba venom, relieved pain in mice about as strongly as morphine and with fewer side effects, which has made them a lead in painkiller research.

wiki.extract: The black mamba is a species of highly venomous snake belonging to the family Elapidae. It is native to parts of sub-Saharan Africa. First formally described by Albert Günther in 1864, it is the second-longest venomous snake after the king cobra; mature specimens generally exceed 2 m and commonly grow to 3 m (9.8 ft). Specimens of 4.3 to 4.5 m have been reported. It varies in colour from grey to dark brown. Juvenile black mambas tend to be more pale in colour than adults, and darken with age. Despite the common name, the black mamba is not black; the colour name describes rather the inside of its mouth, which it displays when feeling threatened.

otherNames: Aomadara-umihebi アオマダラウミヘビ (Japanese)
summary: A banded black-and-silver-blue snake that hunts eels in coral reefs and comes ashore on small islands to digest, shed, mate and lay eggs. It has a powerful neurotoxic venom but is so docile that bites are very rare.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific, from the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea through Southeast Asia to southern Japan, New Guinea, Fiji and Tonga
abilities: Its paddle-shaped tail drives it underwater, while broad belly scales still let it climb on land
Can dive for long periods while hunting eels in crevices
Venom with strong neurotoxins kills eels quickly
Lays eggs on land in rock crevices, unlike true sea snakes, which bear live young at sea

animal.diet: Almost exclusively moray and conger eels
animal.habitat: Shallow coral reefs and their islands, rocky shores, mangroves
animal.size: Usually ~1 m; females larger, up to ~1.5 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts in groups, sometimes alongside trevallies and goatfish that catch prey the snake flushes out. Bites are rare and usually happen only when a snake is grabbed. Envenoming causes paralysis. First aid is a pressure-immobilisation bandage and splint, keeping the person still and getting them urgently to a hospital, where sea snake antivenom and breathing support may be needed.
fieldMarks: Bold black rings on a pale blue-grey body
Bright yellow upper lip and snout
Flattened paddle tail with a yellow-edged black tip
Broad belly scales (unlike most sea snakes)
animal.lookalikes: The blue-lipped sea krait (L. laticaudata) has a dark upper lip. The banded snake eel (Myrichthys colubrinus), which is harmless to people, mimics the sea krait's banding but is a fish: it has a pointed tail with a fin, no scales and no yellow lip, and is never seen out of water.
animal.whereToSee: Common on reefs in the Philippines, Indonesia (Bali, Komodo, Raja Ampat), Fiji, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Okinawa; often seen by divers and resting on islet rocks
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In the Ryukyu Islands its relative the erabu sea snake was smoked and dried to make irabu-jiru, a traditional broth once served to the Ryukyu royal court.
funFact: Sea kraits have to drink fresh water. They cannot get what they need from seawater and seek out rain puddles and freshwater seeps on their island.

wiki.extract: The yellow-lipped sea krait, also known as the banded sea krait or colubrine sea krait, is a species of highly venomous snake found in tropical Indo-Pacific oceanic waters. The snake has distinctive black stripes and a yellow snout, with a paddle-like tail for use in swimming.

summary: A small, secretive snake of the southeastern US, ringed in red, yellow and black, with a strong neurotoxic venom. Harmless kingsnakes and scarlet snakes copy its colours, which has made it the classic example of warning mimicry in snakes.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States: coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana (the Texas coral snake, Micrurus tener, replaces it further west)
abilities: Venom is mainly neurotoxic: it can paralyse breathing hours after a bite that seemed minor
Hunts other snakes, which it swallows whole
When threatened, hides its head and curls up its tail to look like a second head

animal.diet: Mainly other snakes and lizards
animal.habitat: Leaf litter and sandy soil in pine and hardwood forests; also suburban gardens in Florida
animal.behaviour: Spends most of its time underground or under leaf litter, and is seen mainly after rain or in spring. It has small fixed fangs and often hangs on and chews when it bites. Symptoms (drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, weak breathing) can take 12 hours or more to appear, so anyone bitten must go straight to hospital whatever they feel. North American Coral Snake Antivenin is used.
fieldMarks: Wide red and black rings separated by narrow yellow rings; red touches yellow
Black snout, then a broad yellow band across the back of the head
Rings encircle the body including the belly
Small rounded head, no wider than the neck; small black eyes
animal.lookalikes: The harmless scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides) has a red snout and red rings touching black. The scarlet snake (Cemophora coccinea) has red saddles that do not cross a plain white belly, and a pointed red snout. In the US the rule 'red touches yellow, dangerous fellow; red touches black, friend of Jack' works, but it fails for coral snakes in Mexico, Central and South America. Never handle a ringed snake to check.
animal.whereToSee: Pine flatwoods and hammocks of Florida; sandhills of Georgia and the Carolinas; most often seen crossing roads or paths in the morning
animal.season: Resident; most often seen in spring (March–May) and autumn

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1766 as Coluber fulvius. It and its harmless look-alikes became the textbook case of warning coloration and mimicry, and field experiments with plasticine model snakes showed that birds avoid red, yellow and black ringed patterns.
funFact: Wyeth stopped making the US coral snake antivenom in 2003, and for years the FDA extended the expiry dates of the remaining stock to keep some available.

wiki.extract: Micrurus fulvius, commonly known as the eastern coral snake, common coral snake, American cobra, and more, is a species of highly venomous coral snake in the family Elapidae. The species is endemic to the southeastern United States. The family also contains the cobras and sea snakes.

summary: The hooded snake of Indian temples and street performances, and one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebite deaths in South Asia. When alarmed it rears up and spreads a hood marked on the back with a pale spectacle-shaped pattern.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka
abilities: Spreads a hood by swinging its long front ribs outward
Venom is mainly neurotoxic and can paralyse breathing muscles; it also causes painful swelling and tissue death around the bite
Does well in rice fields and villages, where it hunts rats and toads
Females guard their clutch of eggs until hatching

animal.diet: Rodents, toads, frogs, lizards, birds and their eggs, other snakes
animal.habitat: Plains, farmland, scrub, forest edge and human settlements, from sea level into the hills
animal.behaviour: Raises its front third, spreads its hood and hisses loudly when cornered, but would rather escape. A bite is a medical emergency: keep the person still and calm, take off rings and tight items, keep the bitten limb still, and get them quickly to a hospital that has polyvalent antivenom. Do not cut, suck, apply a tourniquet, use ice or rely on traditional healers, because these delays cost lives.
fieldMarks: Hood with a pale 'spectacle' (two linked rings) on the back; some snakes lack the mark
Smooth, glossy scales; colour from yellowish or brown to almost black
Dark band and paired spots across the throat, visible when the hood is up
Medium-sized head barely wider than the neck; round pupils
animal.lookalikes: Most often confused with the harmless Indian rat snake (Ptyas mucosa). The rat snake cannot spread a hood, has very large eyes, and its long thin tail has dark crossbars or a net pattern. When provoked it puffs out its throat, which can look like a narrow hood. The monocled cobra (Naja kaouthia) of eastern India and Bangladesh has a single ring on the hood instead of spectacles. The king cobra (Ophiophagus) is much larger, often banded, and has a narrower hood. If a snake hoods, treat it as a cobra.
animal.whereToSee: Common throughout lowland India and Sri Lanka in farmland and villages; often seen at dusk around rice fields and rat-infested buildings
animal.season: Resident; most active in the hot season and the monsoon, when rats and frogs are plentiful

lore: Cobras are worshipped at Nag Panchami, and the serpent Vasuki coils around Shiva's neck. Rudyard Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' (1894) made the cobra pair Nag and Nagaina famous. India's Wildlife Protection Act (1972) made it illegal to keep cobras for snake charming.
funFact: A cobra cannot hear the snake charmer's pungi as music. It sways because it is following the moving instrument.

wiki.extract: The Indian cobra, also known commonly as the spectacled cobra, Asian cobra, or binocellate cobra, is a species of cobra, a venomous snake in the family Elapidae. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.

otherNames: Yǎnjìng wáng shé 眼镜王蛇 (Chinese)
summary: The world's longest venomous snake, up to about 5.5 m, and a hunter that eats mainly other snakes. Females are the only snakes known to build nests, piling leaves into a mound and guarding the eggs.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia; since a 2024 revision, Ophiophagus hannah in the narrow sense covers eastern Pakistan, northern and eastern India, the Andaman Islands, Myanmar and Indochina south to central Thailand, with the king cobras of the Western Ghats, the Sunda region and Luzon assigned to related species
abilities: Rears up to about a third of its body length and spreads a narrow hood when threatened
Makes a low growl-like hiss with air pushed through its windpipe
Injects large volumes of neurotoxic venom, enough to kill an elephant
Hunts other snakes, including venomous ones, following their scent

animal.diet: Mostly snakes (rat snakes, pythons, cobras, kraits); occasionally lizards
animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and plantations near streams
animal.size: Usually 3–4 m; record about 5.5–5.85 m; 6–12 kg
animal.behaviour: Females stay with their nest of 20–40 eggs for weeks, but leave just before hatching, possibly so they won't eat their young.
fieldMarks: Very long, olive to brown snake with pale bands
Large head with big scales on top
Raises the front part of its body and spreads a narrow hood
Pale yellowish throat
animal.voice: Can give a low growling hiss
animal.lookalikes: Rat snakes and other large non-venomous snakes look similar; never try to tell them apart up close. Spectacled and monocled cobras are smaller with marked hoods. Never approach on foot; back away and alert local snake rescuers.
animal.season: Resident

lore: Cobras, the nāgas of Hindu and Buddhist tradition, are worshipped on Nag Panchami. In Burma and Thailand, snake charmers perform with king cobras, and in some rituals women kiss the snake's head.
funFact: Its genus name Ophiophagus means 'snake-eater'.

wiki.extract: The king cobra is a species complex of snakes endemic to Asia. With an average length of 3.18 to 4 m and a record length of 5.85 m (19.2 ft), it is the world's longest venomous snake and among the heaviest. Under the genus Ophiophagus, it is not phylogenetically a true cobra despite its common name and some resemblance. Spanning from the Indian subcontinent through Southeastern Asia to Southern China, the king cobra is widely distributed albeit not commonly seen.

otherNames: Dandarabilla (Aboriginal name recorded in the Channel Country)
summary: In standard mouse tests it has the most toxic venom of any land snake. It is also shy and lives in the remote cracking-clay floodplains of central Australia, and no human death from it has been recorded.
nativeRange: Channel Country of southwestern Queensland and northeastern South Australia, with outlying records in New South Wales and the Northern Territory
abilities: Its venom, rich in neurotoxins and clotting toxins, is the most lethal of any land snake in mouse LD50 tests
Changes colour with the seasons: dark in winter to absorb heat, paler in summer
Hunts rats in their deep soil cracks and burrows, delivering several quick bites

animal.diet: Almost entirely mammals, especially the long-haired rat (Rattus villosissimus)
animal.habitat: Deep soil cracks and burrows in black-soil floodplains with little vegetation
animal.behaviour: Usually slips away into a crack rather than face a person; almost all known bites have been to people handling the snake. Australian first aid for elapid bites is a firm pressure-immobilisation bandage along the whole bitten limb, a splint, keeping the person still and calling emergency services. Do not wash the bite site, because hospital venom-detection kits use the venom on the skin.
fieldMarks: Glossy, rounded head that is darker than the body, almost black in winter
Body light brown to olive, many scales dark-edged, forming a faint herringbone pattern
Large dark eyes; smooth scales
Slender, medium-large build
animal.lookalikes: Easily confused with brown snakes (Pseudonaja), especially the eastern brown and the western brown or gwardar, which share its range and are also dangerous. Those lack the inland taipan's glossy dark head in cool months. The coastal taipan (O. scutellatus) lives far away in northern and eastern coastal Australia. No harmless species here can be safely told apart in the field; any medium-to-large brown snake in Australia should be treated as dangerous.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; remote Channel Country around Diamantina and Cooper Creek; best seen in reptile parks such as the Australian Reptile Park
animal.season: Resident; most active in the early morning in spring and early summer

lore: Frederick McCoy described it in 1879 from specimens collected near the Murray–Darling junction. It then went almost unrecorded by science for about 90 years until it was rediscovered in 1972.
funFact: Its seasonal colour change is among the strongest of any snake: the same individual can be almost black-headed in winter and pale straw in summer.

wiki.extract: The inland taipan, also commonly known as the western taipan, small-scaled snake, or fierce snake, is a species of extremely venomous snake in the family Elapidae. It is endemic to semiarid regions of central‑eastern Australia. Aboriginal Australians living in areas where Karnic languages are spoken refer to this species as dandarabilla.

summary: The largest land animal in Asia, a forest elephant that has worked, fought and worshipped alongside people for more than 4,000 years. Fewer than about 50,000 remain in 13 countries, the largest share in India, increasingly squeezed into fragmented forest where conflict with farmers kills both people and elephants.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, southern China, Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Trunk contains tens of thousands of muscle fascicles and ends in one finger-like tip that can pick up a single fruit
Communicates with low-frequency rumbles partly below human hearing
Opens forest, digs waterholes in dry riverbeds and disperses large seeds
Females lead herds using decades of remembered routes and water sources

animal.diet: Grasses, bark, roots, leaves, bamboo and fruit; also crops such as paddy, sugarcane and banana
animal.habitat: Forest, grassland and scrub with access to water
animal.size: Shoulder height 2–3.2 m; males up to about 5,000 kg
animal.behaviour: Herds of related females and young are led by a matriarch; adult males roam alone or in loose groups and enter musth, a period of high testosterone and aggression marked by fluid from the temple glands.
fieldMarks: Smaller, rounded ears than African elephants; head with twin domes on top
Back level or arched (convex), highest in the middle
Single finger-like projection on the trunk tip
Only some males have tusks; many males (makhnas) and all females have none or tiny tushes
Signs: large round footprints 40–50 cm across, fibrous dung boli, debarked and broken trees
animal.voice: Trumpets when excited or alarmed; also deep rumbles, roars, and high squeaks and chirps.
animal.lookalikes: African savanna and forest elephants have huge ears, a saddle-backed profile and two finger tips on the trunk. Only captive animals could be confused.
animal.whereToSee: Nagarhole–Kabini and Bandipur (Karnataka); Corbett (Uttarakhand); Kaziranga (Assam); Periyar (Kerala); Minneriya and Kaudulla 'Gathering' (Sri Lanka, July–September); Udawalawe (Sri Lanka); Kui Buri (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident; dry-season gatherings near reservoirs and rivers

lore: Ganesha, the elephant-headed Hindu god of beginnings, and Airavata, the white elephant of Indra, make it a sacred animal across India. Elephants appear on Indus Valley seals, and an elephant is carved from the rock above Ashoka's edicts at Dhauli in Odisha.
funFact: In Sri Lanka fewer than one in ten male elephants carries tusks.

wiki.extract: The Asian elephant, also known as the Asiatic elephant, is the only living species in the genus Elephas. It is the largest living land animal in Asia and the second largest living elephantid in the world. It is characterised by its long trunk with a single finger-like process; large tusks in males; laterally folded large ears and wrinkled grey skin that is partly depigmented on the trunk, ears or neck. Adult males average 4 t in weight and females 2.7 t. It has a large and well developed neocortex of the brain, is highly intelligent and self-aware, being able to display behaviours associated with grief, learning and greeting. Three subspecies are recognised—E. m. maximus, E. m. indicus and E. m. sumatranus.

plates.long: This intricate engraving serves as the visual introduction to a 1672 Dutch work on 'earthly creatures.' It depicts a global menagerie including an elephant and rhinoceros in a lush landscape, reflecting the era's intense interest in cataloging the natural world and the exotic peoples encountered through maritime trade.

plates.long: This woodcut from Gregorius Reisch's 'Margarita philosophica' (1504) illustrates a chapter on the diversity of the natural world. The illustration reflects the early modern European fascination with exotic wildlife and the documentation of animal-human interactions in distant lands.

summary: The largest living land animal, a bull can stand nearly 4 m at the shoulder and weigh over 6 tonnes. Herds are led by old matriarchs whose memory of distant water and danger can decide whether a family survives a drought.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from the Sahel to South Africa, in fragmented populations
abilities: Communicates with infrasonic rumbles below human hearing that can travel several kilometres
Senses ground-borne vibrations through sensitive feet and trunk tip
Uses a boneless, muscular trunk to pluck single leaves, lift heavy logs, suck up water and snorkel
Digs wells in dry riverbeds that other animals later drink from
Clears woodland and opens grassland, shaping whole savanna landscapes

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit; may eat 150 kg or more per day
animal.habitat: Savanna, woodland, semi-desert and river valleys
animal.size: Bulls up to ~4 m at shoulder and 6–7 t; cows ~2.5–3 m and 2.5–3.5 t
animal.behaviour: Families gather around the bones of dead elephants, touching and turning them with their trunks. Matriarchs lead herds along routes remembered over decades.
fieldMarks: Largest land animal, grey and wrinkled
Very large ears shaped roughly like the map of Africa
Back dips in the middle; two finger-like tips on the trunk
Tusks curve outward and forward in both sexes
animal.voice: Trumpeting blasts, and deep rumbles, much of it too low for people to hear, that carry several kilometres
animal.lookalikes: African forest elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) is smaller with rounder ears and straighter, downward-pointing tusks. Asian elephant has small ears and a domed head. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Amboseli (Kenya), Chobe (Botswana), Kruger (South Africa) and Addo Elephant National Park
animal.season: Resident; dry-season gatherings at rivers and waterholes

lore: Pliny the Elder's Natural History (Book 8) called the elephant the animal nearest to humans in understanding. Ptolemaic Egypt captured African elephants for war, fielding them at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE.
funFact: Elephant pregnancy lasts about 22 months, the longest of any living land mammal.

wiki.extract: The African bush elephant, also known as the African savanna elephant, is a species of elephant native to sub-Saharan Africa and the largest living terrestrial animal, with fully grown bulls reaching an average shoulder height of 3.04–3.36 m (10.0–11.0 ft) and a body mass of 5.2–6.9 t ; the largest recorded specimen had a shoulder height of 3.96 m (13.0 ft) and an estimated body mass of 10.4 t. It is characterised by its long prehensile trunk with two finger-like processes; a concave back; large ears which help reduce body heat; and sturdy tusks that are noticeably curved. Its skin is grey with scanty hairs, and bending cracks which support thermoregulation by retaining water.

plates.title: Georg Wolfgang Knorr — Deliciae naturae selectae (1771)
plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr
plates.desc: A natural history plate featuring five distinct specimens of arthropods and invertebrates, labeled with small numerals 1 through 5. Centrally located is a large, detailed spiny lobster (Palinurus elephas). To its left is a smaller shrimp, and to its right is a large centipede (Scolopendra). In the upper left is a whip scorpion (Thelyphonida), and in the upper right is a coiled millipede or worm.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' (1771) presents a meticulously detailed study of five invertebrate specimens. The central figure is a spiny lobster, surrounded by a shrimp, a centipede, a whip scorpion, and a coiled millipede, showcasing the diversity of the natural world as documented in Enlightenment-era cabinets of curiosities.

summary: A tiny frog whose two-note 'ko-KEE' call fills Puerto Rico's nights and has become a national symbol. Its eggs hatch directly into froglets with no tadpole stage. In Hawaii, where it was introduced, it is an invasive pest whose loud choruses cause complaints.
nativeRange: Puerto Rico; introduced to Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Florida and elsewhere
abilities: Eggs hatch directly into tiny froglets, with no tadpole or need for standing water
Males guard eggs and keep them moist
Its call can reach about 90 decibels at half a metre
Climbs using toe pads, with no webbing between its toes

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, snails
animal.habitat: Forest, gardens and towns, from sea level to mountains
animal.behaviour: Males call from leaves and tree trunks at dusk to attract females and defend their territory.
fieldMarks: Small brown or grey frog, often with a pale stripe or W-shaped mark
Large toe pads, no webbing
Large eyes
Loud two-note call
animal.voice: A loud, two-note 'ko-KEE', the first note lower, repeated through the night
animal.lookalikes: Puerto Rico has around 16 other Eleutherodactylus species, many of them small and brown, so the common coquí's two-note call is the best way to identify it.
animal.whereToSee: El Yunque National Forest and almost anywhere in Puerto Rico at night; Hawaii's Big Island
animal.season: Calls year-round, loudest in the wet season

lore: In Puerto Rico people say 'Soy de aquí como el coquí' ('I'm from here, like the coquí'), and the frog appears in Taíno petroglyphs.
funFact: Coquís at higher altitudes in Puerto Rico are larger and have deeper calls than those in the lowlands.

wiki.extract: The common coquí, widely known as the coquí, is a species of frog native to Puerto Rico belonging to the family Eleutherodactylidae. The species is named for the loud call the males make at night, which serves two purposes; the "co" serves to repel other males and establish territory while the "quí" serves to attract females. The auditory systems of males and females respond preferentially to different notes of the male call, displaying sex difference in a sensory system. The common coquí is a very important aspect of Puerto Rican culture, and it has become an unofficial territorial symbol of Puerto Rico.

summary: A finger-length schooling fish whose salted fillets flavour pizza, pasta and Caesar salad. It transfers plankton energy to tuna, dolphins and seabirds across the Mediterranean and Black Sea.
nativeRange: Eastern Atlantic from Norway to South Africa; Mediterranean, Black and Azov seas
abilities: Filter-feeds by swimming with its huge mouth agape
Matures in its first year and spawns repeatedly through summer
Black Sea stocks migrate seasonally to overwinter off Turkey and Georgia
edibilityNote: Low mercury. Marinated raw anchovies (boquerones en vinagre) are a known source of anisakiasis unless frozen first.

animal.diet: Zooplankton: copepods, fish eggs and larvae
animal.habitat: Coastal and shelf waters, often near river plumes
animal.behaviour: Forms dense schools that move inshore in summer and to deeper water in winter.
fieldMarks: Slender, rounded body with a blue-green back and silver stripe
Projecting, pointed snout overhanging an enormous mouth
Jaw extends far behind the eye
Single short dorsal fin mid-body
animal.lookalikes: Sprat and young sardine have a short terminal mouth and no overhanging snout.

It lives off the coasts of Europe and Africa, including in the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov. It is fished by humans throughout much of its range.

summary: The largest octopus in the world, with an arm span that can reach about 4 m. Clever and curious, it lives only 3–5 years, and a female dies after guarding her eggs for half a year without eating.
nativeRange: Temperate North Pacific, from Japan and Korea through the Russian Far East and Aleutians to Alaska, British Columbia and California
abilities: Largest octopus species; adults commonly 10–50 kg
Changes skin colour and texture in a fraction of a second
Captive individuals recognise and respond differently to particular people
Can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak
Each sucker can taste and grip independently

animal.habitat: Rocky dens from the intertidal zone down to around 2,000 m
animal.size: Typically 10–50 kg with an arm span of up to about 4 m; verified records reach about 70 kg
animal.behaviour: A brooding female hangs strings of up to tens of thousands of eggs from her den roof and cleans and aerates them for about six months before dying soon after they hatch.

Wrinkled, folded skin with small flap-like papillae

lore: It is named after Franz Doflein, a German zoologist who studied the marine life of Japan around 1904–05. In Hokkaido it has long been caught in traditional octopus pots.
funFact: About two-thirds of its nerve cells lie in its arms rather than its brain, so each arm can taste, grip and react partly on its own.

Juveniles spend years in mangrove estuaries before moving offshore
Gathers at the same wreck spawning sites each year in late summer
Swallows prey, including small sharks and sea turtles, by powerful suction

wiki.extract: The Atlantic goliath grouper, the jewfish or itajara, is a saltwater fish of the grouper family and one of the largest species of bony fish. The species can be found in the West Atlantic ranging from northeastern Florida, south throughout the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea, and along South America to Brazil. In the East Pacific it ranges from Mexico to Peru. In the East Atlantic, the species ranges in West Africa from Senegal to Cabinda. The species has been observed at depths ranging from 1 to 100 meters.

wiki.extract: The European hedgehog, also known as the West European hedgehog or common hedgehog, is a hedgehog species native to Europe from Iberia and Italy northwards into Scandinavia and westwards into Ireland. It is a generally common and widely distributed species that can survive across a wide range of habitat types. It is a well-known species, and a favourite in European gardens, both for its endearing appearance and its preference for eating a range of garden pests. While populations are currently stable across much of its range, it is declining severely in Great Britain, where it is now Red Listed, meaning that it is considered to be at risk of local extinction. Outside its native range the species was introduced to New Zealand during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

summary: A mottled, barnacle-encrusted baleen whale that feeds on the seafloor by sucking up mud and straining out tiny crustaceans. Eastern Pacific gray whales migrate some 15,000–20,000 km a year between the Arctic and the lagoons of Baja California, where mothers famously approach small boats. The Atlantic population was hunted to extinction by the 18th century.

wiki.extract: The gray whale, also known as the grey whale, is a baleen whale that migrates between feeding and breeding grounds yearly. It reaches a length of 14.9–15.2 m (49–50 ft), a weight of up to 41 to 45 tonnes and lives between 55 and 70 years, although one female was estimated to be 75–80 years of age. One of the longest-living gray whales currently is a female, first sighted in 1977, and estimated to be 53–55 years old as of 2024. The common name of the whale comes from the gray patches and white mottling on its dark skin. Gray whales were once called "devil fish" because of their fighting behavior when hunted, with mothers accompanied by their calves fighting viciously to protect their young if they are attacked. The gray whale is the sole living species in the genus Eschrichtius. It is the sole living genus in the family Eschrichtiidae; however, some recent studies classify it as a member of the family Balaenopteridae. This mammal is descended from filter-feeding whales that appeared during the Neogene.

summary: A long ambush predator of weedy northern lakes, with a duck-bill jaw full of backward-pointing teeth. It is one of the few freshwater fish native around the whole Northern Hemisphere.
nativeRange: Circumpolar in fresh and brackish waters of North America, Europe and northern Asia; introduced to Spain, Ireland (disputed) and parts of western North America
abilities: Launches from a standstill with extreme acceleration, driven by dorsal and anal fins set far back near the tail
Swallows prey up to about half its own length, including ducklings, frogs and other pike

Lives in the brackish Baltic Sea as well as fresh water
edibilityNote: Lean white flesh, a classic of quenelles de brochet and Central European cooking, but full of Y-bones. Pike is a key host of the broad fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum), so never eat flesh or roe raw or undercooked. Large pike accumulate mercury and are under fish-consumption advisories in many regions; children and pregnant women should limit intake.

animal.lifespan: Usually 10–15 years; over 25 in cold northern waters
animal.size: Commonly 40–90 cm; females to about 1.5 m and over 25 kg
animal.behaviour: Hovers motionless among weeds, then strikes sideways in a split second. It spawns very early in spring, often right after ice-out, scattering eggs over flooded grass.
fieldMarks: Long, torpedo-shaped body with dorsal and anal fins set far back near the forked tail
Flattened, duck-billed snout and a mouth lined with sharp teeth
Olive-green to brown with rows of pale, bean-shaped spots (light markings on a dark background)
Cheek fully scaled, gill cover scaled only on the upper half
animal.lookalikes: Muskellunge (E. masquinongy) has dark bars or spots on a light background, pointed tail lobes and no scales on the lower cheek. Chain pickerel (E. niger) is smaller, with a dark chain-like net pattern and a dark bar under the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes of Finland, Sweden and Ireland; the Baltic archipelagos of Stockholm and Åland; Canadian Shield lakes of Manitoba, Ontario and Saskatchewan
animal.season: Resident; spawns March–May just after ice-out

lore: In the Russian folktale 'By the Pike's Command' (Po shchuchyemu veleniyu), the lazy Emelya catches a magic pike that grants his wishes. The 'Emperor's Pike', supposedly ringed by Frederick II in 1230 and caught 267 years later, is a well-known medieval hoax; its skeleton in Mannheim turned out to be assembled from several fish.
funFact: The Finnish national epic Kalevala tells how the hero Väinämöinen made the first kantele, a harp-like instrument, from the jawbone of a giant pike.

wiki.extract: The northern pike, also known as jack, northern or simply pike, is a species of carnivorous fish of the genus Esox (pikes). It is commonly found in fresh waters of the Northern Hemisphere.

summary: A ground-dwelling gecko of the rocky deserts of Pakistan and Afghanistan, with movable eyelids and no sticky toe pads. It stores fat in its tail and is one of the most widely kept pet lizards.
nativeRange: Afghanistan, Pakistan and northwestern India; possibly eastern Iran
abilities: Has movable eyelids, unlike most geckos
Stores fat in its thick tail to survive lean months
Can drop its tail and regrow it
Sex of the hatchlings is set by the incubation temperature

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, scorpions
animal.habitat: Rocky semi-desert, dry grassland and scrub
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal: it hides under stones by day and hunts insects on the ground at night. It waves its tail before pouncing.
fieldMarks: Yellow body with black spots in adults; juveniles boldly banded
Movable eyelids
Thick, fat tail
Slender toes without adhesive pads
animal.lookalikes: Closely related leopard geckos of western India (E. fuscus) and eastern India (E. hardwickii) look similar; range is the best guide. The African fat-tailed gecko (Hemitheconyx) is brown-banded and lives in West Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky slopes of Balochistan and Sindh, Pakistan, and dry hills of Afghanistan
animal.season: Active March–October; dormant in winter

lore: Edward Blyth described it in 1854 from the Salt Range of Punjab.
funFact: Leopard geckos can shed their tails when grabbed and regrow them, but the new tail is shorter and fatter and lacks bones.

wiki.extract: The leopard gecko or common leopard gecko is a ground-dwelling gecko native primarily to the rocky dry grassland and desert regions of Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, and Nepal. The leopard gecko is a popular pet, and due to extensive captive breeding it is sometimes considered as the first domesticated species of lizard.

summary: A shrimp-like crustacean only about 6 cm long whose total weight, hundreds of millions of tonnes, may be the largest of any wild animal species. Almost everything in the Southern Ocean depends on it, from penguins to blue whales.
nativeRange: Southern Ocean around Antarctica, densest in the Scotia Sea and Antarctic Peninsula
abilities: Forms swarms with tens of thousands of individuals per cubic metre
Grazes algae from the underside of sea ice in winter
Can shrink by moulting when food is short
Has light-producing organs (photophores)
Moves carbon to the deep sea in its faeces and moults

animal.diet: Phytoplankton, especially diatoms, and ice algae; some small zooplankton
animal.habitat: Cold open ocean and the sea-ice zone of the Southern Ocean
animal.size: Up to about 6 cm and 2 g
animal.behaviour: Swarms rise towards the surface at night and sink by day, possibly to avoid visual predators.
fieldMarks: Transparent to pinkish shrimp-like body
Large, black, light-sensitive eyes
Feathery legs forming a 'feeding basket'
Green-coloured gut when feeding on algae
animal.lookalikes: Ice krill (Euphausia crystallorophias) is smaller and lives closer to the continent. Thysanoessa species are smaller and more slender.
animal.whereToSee: Surface swarms seen from expedition ships around South Georgia and the Antarctic Peninsula, often signalled by feeding whales and seabirds.
animal.season: Year-round; most visible near the surface in the austral summer (Nov–Mar)

edibilityNote: Fished mainly for aquaculture feed and omega-3 krill-oil supplements; also processed into human food in Japan. Fresh krill spoils quickly and has high fluoride in its shell.
lore: The word 'krill' comes from Norwegian whalers, meaning the small fry of fish. Britain's Discovery Investigations of the 1920s–30s first mapped its role in the whaling grounds.
funFact: Estimates of its global biomass are around 300–500 million tonnes, comparable to the total weight of all humans.

wiki.extract: Antarctic krill is a species of krill found in the Antarctic waters of the Southern Ocean. It is a small, swimming crustacean that lives in large schools, called swarms, sometimes reaching densities of 10,000–30,000 animals per cubic metre. It feeds directly on minute phytoplankton, thereby using the primary production energy that phytoplankton originally derive from the sun in order to sustain its pelagic life cycle. It grows to a length of 6 centimetres (2.4 in), weighs up to 2 grams (0.071 oz), and can live for up to six years. A key species in the Antarctic ecosystem and in terms of biomass, E. superba is one of the most abundant animal species on the planet, with a cumulative biomass of approximately 500 million metric tons ; however, the species is suffering from overfishing.

summary: A blue-backed ocean fish that escapes predators by bursting from the sea and gliding on enlarged pectoral fins. A single glide can carry it tens of metres, and it can extend a flight by sculling its tail in the water.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide
abilities: Glides on wing-like pectoral fins at speeds above 50 km/h
Taxis by beating the elongated lower tail lobe on the surface to relaunch without re-entering the water
Flights of 50 m are common; flyingfish have been filmed in the air for 45 seconds
Two-winged: unlike four-winged species, its pelvic fins are small
edibilityNote: Low mercury, small pelagic fish.

animal.diet: Zooplankton
animal.habitat: Surface waters of the open ocean, away from coasts
animal.behaviour: When chased by mahi-mahi, tuna or billfish, it accelerates under water and launches into the air; it also leaps at night onto the lit decks of ships.
fieldMarks: Very long pectoral fins reaching the tail base
Small pelvic fins (two-winged)
Deeply forked tail with a longer lower lobe
Iridescent blue back, silvery belly
Clear, unmarked pectoral fins in adults
animal.lookalikes: Four-winged flyingfish (Cheilopogon, Hirundichthys) have large pelvic fins too; Exocoetus obtusirostris has a more blunt snout and fewer predorsal scales.
animal.whereToSee: From ships' bows in the tropical Atlantic and Pacific; Barbados (where related flyingfish are a national symbol)
animal.season: Year-round in warm seas

lore: The French Exocet missile is named after flyingfish; Barbados, 'the land of the flying fish', depicts them on coins, though its fishery targets Hirundichthys affinis.
funFact: The name Exocoetus means 'sleeping outside' in Greek, from the old belief that flyingfish came ashore to sleep.

summary: A long-legged, eagle-like falcon with a bare red face that walks the ground scavenging and hunting. It is as likely to be found at a roadkill or behind a plough as on the wing.
nativeRange: Florida, Texas and Arizona south through Mexico, Central America and South America to Tierra del Fuego
abilities: Hunts on foot, turning over debris and dung for insects and small animals
Robs vultures and other birds of food
Follows tractors, fires and cattle to catch flushed prey
Throws its head back over its back while calling

animal.diet: Carrion, insects, small mammals, reptiles, fish and eggs
animal.habitat: Open country — prairies, pastures, savanna, desert scrub
animal.behaviour: Unlike most falcons, it builds its own stick nest, often in palms or cacti.
fieldMarks: Black cap and shaggy crest above bare red-orange to yellow facial skin
Heavy, pale bluish hooked bill
White throat and neck; barred breast; black belly
In flight: white patches near the wingtips and white tail with a black terminal band; long yellow legs
animal.voice: A dry, harsh rattle, given with the head thrown back; the name 'caracara' imitates it.
animal.lookalikes: Black Vulture has a bare grey head and lacks the white neck. Bald Eagle immature lacks the black cap and orange face.
animal.whereToSee: Ranchland of central Florida (Kissimmee Prairie), south Texas, the Pantanal and the Argentine Pampas.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Some historians argue that the bird in the Aztec founding legend of Tenochtitlan — an eagle on a cactus devouring a snake — was a caracara, though Mexico's coat of arms shows a Golden Eagle; in Brazil, João do Vale's 1964 song 'Carcará' made it a symbol of the drought-hardened north-east.
funFact: The Florida population is federally listed as threatened in the US because of the loss of native prairie.

wiki.extract: The crested caracara is a bird of prey (raptor) in the falcon family, Falconidae. It was formerly placed in the genus Polyborus before being given in its own genus, Caracara. It is native to and found in the southern and southeastern United States, Mexico and the majority of mainland Latin America, as well as some Caribbean islands. The crested caracara is quite adaptable and hardy, for a species found predominantly in the neotropics; it can be found in a range of environments and ecosystems, including semi-arid and desert climates, maritime or coastal areas, subtropical and tropical forests, temperate regions, plains, swamps, and even in urban areas. Documented, albeit rare, sightings have occurred as far north as Minnesota and the Canadian provinces of Alberta, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island. The southern extent of the crested caracara's distribution can reach as far as Tierra del Fuego and Magallanes Region, Chile.

summary: A large, powerful falcon of steppe and semi-desert, prized for millennia by falconers from Arabia to Mongolia. Electrocution on power lines and capture for the falconry trade have pushed it to Endangered.
nativeRange: Breeds from central Europe (Hungary, Slovakia, Austria) through Ukraine, Turkey, Russia, Kazakhstan and Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters south to the Middle East, northeast Africa and South Asia
abilities: Hunts ground squirrels (sousliks) close to the ground with fast, low pursuit flights
Can take prey as large as houbara bustards when trained
Uses nests built by other birds, including on power pylons
Readily breeds in artificial nest boxes on pylons, a key conservation tool in Hungary and Mongolia

animal.diet: Ground squirrels, voles, pikas, hamsters; birds such as pigeons and partridges
animal.habitat: Open steppe, wooded steppe, semi-desert, farmland with pylons
animal.lifespan: Typically under 10 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.size: 47–57 cm; wingspan 97–126 cm; males 730–990 g, females 970–1,300 g
animal.behaviour: Hunts by fast, contour-hugging flight, surprising mammals before they can reach their burrows.
fieldMarks: Large, brown falcon with a pale, often whitish, streaked head
Thin, faint moustache stripe
Brown upperparts with rufous edges; heavily streaked underparts
Long tail and broad-based wings; dark underwing coverts contrast with paler flight feathers
animal.voice: A harsh, scolding 'kyak-kyak-kyak' near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Peregrine is darker slate above with a bold moustache and barred underparts. Lanner falcon (Mediterranean, Africa) is smaller with a rufous crown. Gyrfalcon (Arctic) is heavier and barred above.
animal.whereToSee: Hortobágy and Kiskunság plains (Hungary), Kazakh steppe, Mongolian steppe; on migration at Batumi and in the Middle East.
animal.season: Resident in central Europe; migratory from northern and eastern populations, wintering Oct–Mar

lore: Mongolia declared the saker its national bird in 2012, and in Hungary it is widely identified with the Turul, the mythical bird of the founding legend of the Magyars.
funFact: A Mongolian project installing thousands of artificial nests on the open steppe created a large new breeding population of sakers.

wiki.extract: The saker falcon is a large falcon species. It breeds from Central Europe eastwards across the Palearctic to Manchuria. It is a partial migrant, which means that some part of the population is migratory, some part is not. In Europe, for example, a part of the juveniles are migrating, while adults are mostly resident. The European and West Asian migratory sakers spend the winter in the Sahel region. On migration, they cross the Middle East, the Arabian Peninsula, and Pakistan, where they are exposed to illegal trapping. The migratory birds to the east from Altai Mountains spend the winter in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

The work is signed by the engraver, Mag. Bouchard.

summary: The fastest animal on Earth, reaching more than 320 km/h when stooping on prey. Wiped out from much of its range by DDT in the 1960s, it has recovered and now nests on city skyscrapers.
nativeRange: Every continent except Antarctica
abilities: Stoops at speeds recorded up to about 389 km/h
Bony tubercles in its nostrils deflect air so it can breathe in high-speed dives
Arctic-breeding populations migrate up to ~25,000 km a year
Has a third eyelid to protect its eyes in dives

animal.diet: Mainly birds caught in flight, such as pigeons, ducks and shorebirds
animal.habitat: Cliffs, coasts, open country, and tall buildings in cities
animal.behaviour: It climbs high above prey, folds its wings and drops in a steep stoop, striking with clenched talons.
fieldMarks: Powerful falcon with long pointed wings and a medium tail
Adult blue-grey above with a dark 'helmet' and broad moustache stripe
Pale underparts finely barred
Young birds brown above with streaked underparts
animal.voice: A harsh, rasping 'kak-kak-kak' near the nest
animal.lookalikes: Prairie falcon is pale brown with dark 'armpits'. Lanner falcon has a rufous crown and thinner moustache. Gyrfalcon is bulkier with broader wings. Hobby is smaller with rufous 'trousers'.
animal.whereToSee: Sea cliffs and city buildings; many urban nests carry public webcams (e.g. Derby Cathedral, UK); migrants at Cape May and Falsterbo
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; Arctic breeders migrate long distances

lore: Prized in falconry from Mongolia to the Arab world; the 15th-century Boke of St Albans assigned it to earls. Its crash from DDT-thinned eggshells helped drive the US ban of DDT in 1972.
funFact: Its name means 'wanderer', because falconers caught young birds on migration rather than taking them from nests.

wiki.extract: The peregrine falcon, sometimes referred to simply as the peregrine, is a bird of prey (raptor) in the family Falconidae known for its speed. A large, crow-sized falcon, it has a blue-grey back, barred white underparts and a black head. As is typical for bird-eating (avivore) raptors, peregrine falcons are sexually dimorphic, with females being considerably larger than males. Historically, the bird has also been known as the "black-cheeked falcon" in Australia and the "duck hawk" in North America.

summary: A small falcon famous for hovering motionless over roadside verges, head perfectly still while its wings and tail work against the wind. It is the most familiar bird of prey across much of Europe.
nativeRange: Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and Asia to China and Japan
abilities: Hovers into the wind while keeping its head almost perfectly still
Sees ultraviolet light and can detect the UV-reflective urine trails of voles
Nests in cliffs, old crow nests, buildings and nest boxes
Populations rise and fall with vole cycles

animal.diet: Voles and mice; also lizards, large insects and small birds
animal.habitat: Open country, farmland, moorland, roadsides, cities
animal.behaviour: Hangs in the air, then drops in stages before a final plunge onto prey in the grass.
fieldMarks: Male: blue-grey head and tail with a black tail band, spotted chestnut back
Female: brown above with barring, barred tail
Long, pointed wings; long tail
Black moustache mark
animal.voice: A shrill, rapid 'kee-kee-kee' near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser kestrel (Mediterranean, steppes) males have an unspotted back and grey wing panel, and it is colonial. Merlin is smaller, darker and rarely hovers. Sparrowhawk has rounded wings.
animal.whereToSee: Motorway verges and farmland across Europe; city buildings from Madrid to Istanbul.
animal.season: Resident in western and southern Europe; northern and eastern birds migrate south

lore: Gerard Manley Hopkins's 1877 sonnet 'The Windhover' celebrated its hovering, and Barry Hines's 1968 novel 'A Kestrel for a Knave', filmed as 'Kes', took its title from the hawk assigned to the lowest rank in medieval falconry.
funFact: Experiments in Finland in 1995 showed kestrels can see vole scent marks because urine and faeces reflect ultraviolet light.

wiki.extract: The common kestrel, also known as the European kestrel, Eurasian kestrel, Old World kestrel, is a species of predatory bird belonging to the kestrel group of the falcon family Falconidae. In the United Kingdom, where no other kestrel species commonly occurs, it is generally just called the "kestrel".

The bird has reddish-brown plumage with dark spots, a barred tail, and yellow talons. The scene is enclosed in a yellow border with identifying text in French, Latin, and Italian at the bottom.

The bird is captured in a lifelike pose on a rocky ledge, reflecting the Enlightenment-era focus on scientific observation and the aesthetic presentation of the natural world.

In the background, a smaller songbird is shown on a leafy branch, illustrating the diversity of avian species. The plate is signed by the engraver, Maddalena Bouchard, highlighting the contribution of female artists to 18th-century s

plates.long: A woodcut depicting two kestrels, identified in the text as a male and a female of the species. The birds are shown in profile to highlight their anatomical features for scientific study.

summary: The fastest land animal, a slender cat built for sprinting down gazelles on open plains. It trades the power of other big cats for speed, and often loses its kills to lions and hyenas.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, scattered Saharan and Sahelian populations; a tiny remnant in Iran; reintroduced to India in 2022
abilities: Sprints at about 93–104 km/h in short bursts
Accelerates from a standstill to about 95 km/h in roughly three seconds
Grips the ground with semi-retractable claws like running spikes
Uses its long tail as a rudder to turn sharply mid-chase
Chirps like a bird and purrs, but cannot roar

animal.diet: Carnivore: gazelles, impala, springbok, hares and young antelope
animal.habitat: Open savanna, grassland and semi-desert
animal.size: 21–72 kg; body 1.1–1.5 m plus a tail of 60–80 cm
animal.behaviour: Females live alone with their cubs, while brothers often stay together for life in male coalitions that hold territories.
fieldMarks: Slim, long-legged cat
Solid black spots
Black tear lines from eyes to mouth
Small round head
animal.voice: Chirps and purrs
animal.lookalikes: Leopard has rosettes, a heavier build and no tear lines. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Maasai Mara (Kenya), Serengeti (Ndutu) and Kgalagadi
animal.season: Resident

lore: Cheetahs were tamed for hunting from ancient Egypt to medieval Persia and India; the Mughal emperor Akbar was said to keep around a thousand. The black 'tear marks' feature in an African folk tale of a mother weeping for her stolen cubs.
funFact: Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity, probably from a population crash around 10,000 years ago.
