wiki.extract: The cheetah is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx. The cheetah is a pursuit predator and the fastest land animal, capable of running at 93–104 km/h (58–65 mph); it has evolved for speed, having powerful hindlimb muscles and a long lumbar spine. The cheetah has a tawny to creamy white or pale buff fur that is marked with evenly spaced, solid black spots. The head is small and rounded, with a short snout and black tear-like facial streaks. It has a height of 67–94 cm (2.20–3.08 ft) at the shoulder, and the head-and-body length is between 1.1 and 1.5 m. Adults weigh between 21 and 65 kg.

plates.title: The Pagan World and the Origin of its Gods
plates.author: Herold, Johann
plates.desc: A woodcut illustration of a leopard or cheetah in profile, walking towards the right, featuring a spotted coat and long tail. The monogram 'RMD' is visible at the bottom.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a leopard or cheetah, characterized by its distinctive spotted pelt and lithe form. It serves as a visual accompaniment to Johann Herold's 1554 text, reflecting the early modern interest in documenting exotic fauna. The monogram 'RMD' identifies the specific craftsman or workshop responsible for the block.

summary: The largest lynx and Europe's third-largest predator, a long-legged, tuft-eared cat of forest and mountain from Scandinavia to the Tibetan Plateau. Reintroductions have returned it to Switzerland, Germany and France, and the pale Himalayan form lives in Ladakh and northern Pakistan.
nativeRange: Northern and central Europe, Russia, Central Asia, the Caucasus, Ladakh, Gilgit-Baltistan, Tibet and northeastern China
abilities: Kills deer such as roe deer and even reindeer, prey several times its weight
Large, fur-padded paws act as snowshoes
Ear tufts and facial ruff help in visual communication

animal.diet: Roe deer, chamois, musk deer, reindeer, hares, marmots and birds
animal.habitat: Dense forest and rocky mountain terrain; in Ladakh, arid rocky slopes and willow scrub
animal.size: 18–30 kg (males larger); body 80–130 cm, short tail 11–25 cm
animal.behaviour: Solitary hunter that ambushes from cover or stalks; returns to large kills for several nights.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: long legs, short body and short bob tail with a black tip
Black ear tufts and a broad facial ruff
Coat greyish to reddish with varying dark spots; Himalayan lynx pale sandy and faintly spotted
Tracks: round, 7–9 cm, no claw marks; in snow very wide due to hairy feet; signs include roe-deer kills covered with snow or leaves
animal.voice: Mostly silent; in the late-winter breeding season gives far-carrying, mournful calls and hisses.
animal.lookalikes: Iberian lynx (Spain and Portugal only) is smaller with bold dark spots. Caracal (Pakistan and India lowlands) is plain tawny with very long ear tufts and no ruff or bob tail. Wildcat has a long, ringed tail.
animal.whereToSee: Bohemian Forest (Czechia–Germany); Swiss Jura and Alps; Carpathians (Slovakia, Romania); Białowieża (Poland); Hemis and Changthang (Ladakh); Finnish taiga hides
animal.season: Resident; winter snow makes tracking easiest (January–March is breeding season)

lore: Greek legend linked the lynx to Lynceus, the Argonaut who could see through walls, and the 'lynx-eyed' ideal named Rome's Accademia dei Lincei (founded 1603). Theophrastus described 'lyngurium', a gem supposedly formed from hardened lynx urine.
funFact: The Accademia dei Lincei, named after the lynx's keen sight, counted Galileo among its early members.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian lynx is one of the four extant species within the medium-sized wild cat genus Lynx. It is widely distributed from Northern, Central and Eastern Europe to Central Asia and Siberia, the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas. It inhabits temperate and boreal forests up to an elevation of 5,500 m (18,000 ft). Despite its wide distribution, it is threatened by habitat loss and fragmentation, poaching and depletion of prey.

plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach

plates.long: This dynamic woodcut depicts a man amidst a variety of wild animals, illustrating the natural origins of certain medicinal substances. The inclusion of the lynx is particularly significant as the accompanying text discusses 'Ligurium', a stone legendary for being formed from lynx urine.

plates.long: A hunter stands armed with a spear amidst a group of wild animals. This scene illustrates the folklore surrounding the 'Ligurium' stone, which was believed to be formed from the solidified urine of the lynx, as discussed in the accompanying Latin text.

plates.author: Unknown

plates.long: A four-legged animal with feline features and pointed ears stands atop a stylized wooden branch. The text identifies this creature as a lynx, noted in the period for its keen eyesight and the belief that its urine hardens into a gemstone.

plates.long: A hand-colored woodcut depicting a lynx, categorized under 'Linx' in the text. This illustration from the 1491 'Ortus sanitatis' reflects the medieval understanding of zoology, blending observation with traditional lore.

plates.long: This miniature depicts a spotted feline, likely a pard or lynx, characterized by its elongated ears and slender form. In the context of Michael Scot's Liber Introductorius, such animals were often used to illustrate natural history or astrological influences on the animal kingdom.

plates.title: Introductory Book
plates.author: Michael Scot
plates.desc: A lynx, a brown feline with dark spots and pointed ears, walking to the right within a green and gold rectangular frame.
plates.long: A stylized depiction of a lynx from Michael Scot's Liber Introductorius. In medieval lore, the lynx was often celebrated for its supernatural eyesight, a quality reflected here in its alert posture and prominent ears.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Panthera Americana' (American Panther), likely an ocelot or jaguar, as described in the accompanying Latin text by Joannes Faber. It represents the early European effort to categorize and illustrate the diverse fauna of the New World within the framework of classical natural history.

summary: The only truly social cat, living in prides of related females with one or a few resident males. Lions once ranged from southern Europe and the Middle East to India and across Africa; today they survive in sub-Saharan Africa and one small Asian outpost, the Gir forest and surrounding lands of Gujarat, India. Asiatic lions (Panthera leo leo, in the current northern subspecies) grew from a few dozen around 1900 to 891 counted in Gujarat's 2025 census.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; in Asia only the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat, India (Gir National Park and surrounding districts)
abilities: Cooperative hunters: lionesses fan out and ambush to bring down buffalo, zebra and even young elephants
Roar audible to people up to about 8 km away, used to advertise territory
Can eat over 30 kg of meat in a single sitting, then rest for most of a day
As apex predators they shape the behaviour and numbers of large grazers

animal.diet: Carnivore: wildebeest, zebra, buffalo, antelope in Africa; in Gir mainly chital, sambar, nilgai, wild boar and livestock
animal.habitat: Open savanna, grassland, dry woodland and scrub with water; in Gir, dry teak forest, scrub and farmland
animal.lifespan: Females about 15–18 years, males often 10–12 in the wild
animal.size: Males 150–250 kg, about 2.5–3.3 m including tail; females 110–180 kg
animal.behaviour: Prides defend territories for generations; incoming males often kill young cubs to bring females back into breeding. In Gir, prides are smaller and males and females usually associate only to mate or share large kills.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: large, plain tawny cat with a tufted black tail-tip — the only cat with a tail tuft
Adult males with a mane; Asiatic males' manes are usually shorter, showing the ears
Asiatic lions typically have a longitudinal fold of skin along the belly, rare in African lions
Tracks: round prints about 11–14 cm across, four toes, no claw marks, a three-lobed rear edge to the heel pad
animal.voice: A deep, rolling series of moaning roars that fade into grunts, given most at dusk and before dawn, often by several pride members together.
animal.lookalikes: Female lions can be confused with pumas in zoos or photos, but the two never overlap in the wild; lionesses are much larger and have the tail tuft. Leopards are spotted with rosettes.
animal.whereToSee: Gir National Park and Devalia Safari Park, Gujarat; Serengeti and Ngorongoro (Tanzania); Maasai Mara (Kenya); Okavango Delta (Botswana); Kruger (South Africa)
animal.season: Resident year-round; Gir is closed to safaris 16 June–15 October for the monsoon, and dry seasons give the best sightings in Africa

lore: The lion capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, four lions back to back, is the national emblem of India. The Nawab of Junagadh protected Gir's last lions in the early 1900s, saving the Asian population from extinction.
funFact: In 2025 about 57% of Gujarat's lions were counted outside Gir's protected core, living among farms and coastal villages.

wiki.extract: The lion is a large cat of the genus Panthera, currently ranging only in Sub-Saharan Africa and India. It has a muscular, broad-chested body; a short, rounded head; round ears; and a dark, hairy tuft at the tip of its tail. It is sexually dimorphic; adult male lions are larger than females and have a prominent mane that extends from the head to the shoulders and chest.

The accompanying text describes the lion's noble characteristics—such as sleeping with its eyes open and facing hunters without fear—as moral lessons for the reader to emulate in their own spiritual and civic life.

Published in 1672, this illustration reflects the early modern tradition of including mythical beasts within natural history compendiums, treating them with the same descriptive rigor as known animals.

Such illustrations in early printed books like 'De Animalibus' served to categorize both real and imagined creatures within a single cosmological framework.

It depicts a group of land animals, including an elephant, a lion, and a bear, alongside a mythical creature, reflecting the transition from medieval bestiaries to early modern scientific observation.

summary: The largest cat of the Americas and the only living Panthera there, a powerfully built hunter of rivers and forests. Its bite is so strong for its size that it kills by piercing the skull or crushing turtle shells. The Brazilian Pantanal holds one of the densest jaguar populations anywhere.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina; occasional wanderers into Arizona and New Mexico
abilities: Bite pierces turtle and caiman skulls; it often kills by biting through the back of the skull
Excellent swimmer that hunts caiman and fish in rivers
Top predator whose presence regulates capybara, peccary and caiman populations

animal.diet: Carnivore: capybara, peccaries, deer, caiman, turtles, armadillos, fish and livestock
animal.habitat: Dense forest, swamps and seasonally flooded wetlands, generally near water
animal.size: 56–96 kg typically; Pantanal males can exceed 120 kg; 1.6–2.7 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary, mostly crepuscular, and hunts both by stalking on land and by ambush from riverbanks.
fieldMarks: Large, deep-chested cat with a broad head and short, thick legs
Rosettes large and angular, often enclosing one or more black spots
Tail relatively short compared with a leopard's
Tracks: broad, round pugmarks 9–12 cm along riverbanks; signs include tree scratching and scrapes
animal.voice: A deep, hoarse series of grunts, often likened to sawing wood; also called 'roncar' in Brazil.
animal.lookalikes: Leopard (Old World only) is lighter-built with smaller rosettes without central spots. Ocelot is much smaller with chain-like stripes. Puma is plain tawny.
animal.whereToSee: Porto Jofre and the Cuiabá, Piquiri and Three Brothers rivers (northern Pantanal, Brazil); Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary (Belize); Iwokrama (Guyana); Calakmul (Mexico); Corcovado (Costa Rica)
animal.season: Resident; Pantanal river sightings peak in the dry season, roughly July–October

lore: The Olmec carved were-jaguar figures over 3,000 years ago, and Maya kings took jaguar names such as Yaxuun Bahlam (Bird Jaguar). Aztec elite warriors were the 'jaguar knights' (ocelomeh).
funFact: Belize's Cockscomb Basin, made a no-hunting forest reserve in 1984 and a wildlife sanctuary in 1986, is widely credited as the world's first protected area set aside for jaguars.

wiki.extract: The jaguar is a large cat species and the only living member of the genus Panthera that is native to the Americas. Its coat features pale yellow to tan colored fur covered with spots that transition to rosettes on the sides; some individuals have a melanistic spotted coat. With a body length of up to 1.85 m and a weight of up to 158 kg (348 lb), it is the biggest cat species in the Americas and the third largest in the world. The jaguar's powerful bite allows it to pierce the carapaces of turtles and tortoises, and to employ an unusual killing method: it bites directly through the skull of mammalian prey between the ears to deliver a fatal blow to the brain.

It includes a detailed study of a sloth's head and claws alongside a full-body depiction of a sloth and a spotted feline, likely a leopard or jaguar. The illustrations reflect the 18th-century fascination with exotic fauna and the transition from cabinet-of-curi

summary: The most adaptable big cat, found from the Cape to the Russian Far East and from rainforest to desert and the edges of Mumbai. A stealthy, solitary hunter, it is strong enough to drag prey heavier than itself up into trees. It has lost much of its historic range, and some subspecies, such as the Amur and Arabian leopards, are critically endangered.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, scattered in North Africa and Arabia, Caucasus and Iran, South Asia, Southeast Asia, China and the Russian Far East
abilities: Hoists carcasses of antelope and young giraffe into trees to keep them from lions and hyenas
Eats prey from dung beetles to eland; one of the broadest diets of any cat
Lives in and around large cities such as Mumbai, hunting dogs and pigs at night

animal.diet: Carnivore: antelope, deer, monkeys, wild pigs, rodents, birds, dogs and livestock
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with cover: forests, savanna, rocky hills, mountains and farmland
animal.size: Males 37–90 kg, females 28–60 kg; 1.6–2.9 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary and mainly nocturnal, stalking to close range before pouncing. Females raise cubs alone, moving them between hidden dens.
fieldMarks: Golden to tawny coat with black rosettes (rings without central spots) on the body, solid spots on head and legs
Long tail, often with white underside of the tip, used as a signal
Compact, low-slung build; relatively large head
Tracks: rounded, about 7–10 cm wide, four toes and no claw marks; signs include kills cached in trees and scratch marks on trunks
animal.voice: A harsh, repeated rasping cough like a saw cutting wood, given to advertise territory.
animal.lookalikes: Cheetah has solid round spots (not rosettes), black 'tear lines' and a slender build. Jaguar (Americas only) is heavier with larger rosettes containing central spots. Snow leopard is grey-white with a very thick tail.
animal.whereToSee: Yala National Park (Sri Lanka); Jhalana Leopard Reserve (Jaipur); Sanjay Gandhi National Park (Mumbai); Bera (Rajasthan); Margalla Hills (Islamabad); Sabi Sands (South Africa); Maasai Mara (Kenya); South Luangwa (Zambia)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Jim Corbett's 'The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag' tells of a leopard that killed over 120 people in Garhwal before he shot it in 1926. The leopard-skin was the regalia of many African kings and chiefs.
funFact: Black panthers are melanistic leopards (or jaguars): in strong light the rosettes still show through the black coat.

wiki.extract: The leopard is one of the five extant cat species in the genus Panthera. It has a pale yellowish to dark golden fur with dark spots grouped in rosettes. Its body is slender and muscular, reaching a length of 92–183 cm (36–72 in) with a 66–102 cm (26–40 in) long tail and a shoulder height of 60–70 cm (24–28 in). Males typically weigh 30.9–72 kg (68–159 lb), and females 20.5–43 kg (45–95 lb).

summary: The largest wild cat, a solitary ambush hunter whose stripes break up its outline in tall grass and forest shade. Fewer than 6,000 remain in the wild, scattered from the Russian Far East to Sumatra.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Southeast Asia, Sumatra, Russian Far East and NE China
abilities: Kills prey several times its own weight, such as gaur and sambar, with a throat or nape bite
Swims strongly and readily hunts in water, as in the Sundarbans mangroves
Roars that can carry about 3 km through forest
Marks territories with scent sprays and scrapes that tell rivals its sex and status

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, wild pigs, gaur, buffalo; occasionally fish and smaller prey
animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and grasslands with dense cover and water
animal.lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild; to ~20 in captivity
animal.size: Males 180–300 kg and up to ~3 m including tail; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Hunts alone by stalking to within a few metres before a short explosive rush. Each tiger's stripe pattern is unique.
fieldMarks: Largest cat, orange with black vertical stripes
White underparts and white spots on the backs of the ears
Stripe pattern unique to each animal
Long, ringed tail
animal.voice: A deep roar; a soft, snorting 'chuff' (prusten) as a friendly greeting
animal.lookalikes: Leopards have rosettes, not stripes. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore, Bandhavgarh, Kanha and Tadoba (India); Chitwan (Nepal) — all by guided safari vehicle
animal.season: Resident; Indian parks are usually open about Oct–Jun, with sightings easiest in the hot months Apr–Jun at waterholes

lore: The Hindu goddess Durga rides a tiger into battle against the demon Mahishasura. In Chinese cosmology the White Tiger (Bai Hu) guards the West, and the tiger is the third animal of the zodiac.
funFact: The stripes are in the skin as well as the fur: a shaved tiger is still striped.

wiki.extract: The tiger is a large cat and a member of the genus Panthera native to Asia. It has a powerful, muscular body with a large head and paws, a long tail and orange fur that fades to white in parts, with black, mostly vertical stripes. It is traditionally classified into nine subspecies, though some recognise only two subspecies, the mainland Asian tiger and the Sunda Islands tiger.

According to the accompanying text from the Sancai Tuhui, it possesses a composite anatomy including an elephant's trunk and tiger's paws, reflecting the traditional Chinese method of describing unfamiliar or legendary animals through familiar parts.

summary: A smoky-grey cat of the high mountains of Central and South Asia, so rarely seen that it is called the 'ghost of the mountains'. Its long, thick tail works as a balance pole on cliffs and a scarf when it sleeps.
nativeRange: Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, Pamir, Tian Shan, Altai and Tibetan Plateau
abilities: Lives and hunts at 3,000–5,500 m, where the air holds about half the oxygen of sea level
Leaps across ravines and down cliffs several times its own body length
Large, fur-soled paws act as snowshoes
Takes down blue sheep and ibex up to three times its own weight on steep slopes

animal.diet: Carnivore: blue sheep (bharal), Siberian ibex, argali, marmots, pikas; sometimes livestock
animal.habitat: Steep, broken alpine terrain and cliffs above the treeline
animal.lifespan: 10–12 years in the wild; to ~20 in captivity
animal.size: 22–55 kg; body 0.9–1.3 m with a tail 0.8–1 m
animal.behaviour: Unlike other big cats it cannot roar; it chuffs, mews and wails instead. It wraps its tail over its nose and face for warmth while sleeping.
fieldMarks: Smoky-grey to cream fur with dark open rosettes
Very long, thick, furry tail
Short muzzle and pale green or grey eyes
Large, fur-padded paws
animal.voice: Cannot roar; makes yowls, moans and a puffing 'chuff'
animal.lookalikes: Common leopard is golden with denser rosettes and a shorter, thinner tail, and lives mostly at lower elevations.
animal.whereToSee: Hemis National Park (Ladakh) and the Spiti Valley around Kibber, India, with local trackers
animal.season: Resident; winter (Jan–Mar) brings cats lower and is the usual tracking season

lore: The winged snow leopard Aq Bars appears on the coat of arms of Tatarstan, and the snow leopard is an emblem of Almaty and of Kyrgyzstan. Peter Matthiessen's 1978 book The Snow Leopard made the cat a Western symbol of the unseen.
funFact: Its tail can be nearly as long as its body, the longest relative to body size of any big cat.

wiki.extract: The snow leopard is a felid species in the genus Panthera. It has a thick whitish to grey fur with black spots on the head and neck, with larger rosettes on the back, flanks and bushy tail. Males are larger than the females, and both sexes have long canine teeth. Its small rounded ears, broad paws, and thick tails are adaptations for living in cold, mountainous environments.

summary: A large, plain-coated cat with the widest range of any wild land mammal in the Americas, from the Yukon to the Strait of Magellan. It cannot roar, but purrs, chirps and screams. Pumas kill deer and guanaco and leave scraps that feed scavengers from condors to beetles.
nativeRange: Western Canada and the western USA (plus Florida), Mexico, Central America and all of South America to Patagonia
abilities: Leaps up to about 5 m vertically and much farther horizontally
Kills prey several times its size with a bite to the neck
Young males disperse hundreds of kilometres; one travelled about 2,900 km from the Black Hills of South Dakota to Connecticut

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, elk, guanaco, peccary, rodents and hares
animal.habitat: Any terrain with cover and prey, from sea level to 5,800 m in the Andes
animal.size: Males 53–100 kg, females 29–64 kg; 1.5–2.75 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Solitary and territorial. Caches kills under leaves and earth and returns to feed over several days.
fieldMarks: Plain tawny-grey to reddish coat, pale underneath
Small rounded head; long, heavy tail with a dark tip
Dark marks on the sides of the muzzle; kittens are spotted
Tracks: round, 7–10 cm, three-lobed heel pad, no claw marks; signs include kills covered with litter and scrapes under trees
animal.voice: Does not roar; gives whistles, chirps, purrs and, in breeding season, piercing screams.
animal.lookalikes: Jaguar is spotted and stockier. Jaguarundi is much smaller with a weasel-like body. Bobcat and lynx have short bobbed tails.
animal.whereToSee: Torres del Paine National Park (Chile, the best place to watch them); Patagonia Park (Chile); Big Bend and the Rocky Mountains (USA, rarely seen); Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge
animal.season: Resident; Torres del Paine tracking tours run most of the year, best in autumn and winter (April–September)

lore: Tradition holds that the Inca city of Cusco was laid out in the shape of a puma, with Sacsayhuamán as its head.
funFact: The puma holds a Guinness World Record for the animal with the most names: over 40 in English alone.

wiki.extract: The cougar, also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas. It inhabits North, Central and South America, making it the most widely distributed wild, terrestrial mammal in the Western Hemisphere, and one of the most widespread in the world. Its range spans Yukon, British Columbia and Alberta in Canada, the Rocky Mountains and areas in the western United States. Further south, its range extends through Mexico to the Amazon rainforest and the southern Andes Mountains in Patagonia. It is an adaptable generalist species, occurring in most American habitat types. It prefers habitats with dense underbrush and rocky areas for stalking but also lives in open areas.

plates.desc: Woodcut of a mythical beast, identified in the text as a Pardalen (panther or leopard).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Pardalen' (panther or leopard), described in the accompanying text as a fierce beast found in Libya. Sebastian Münster's Cosmographia was a seminal 16th-century work that combined geographical knowledge with folklore, often illustrating exotic wildlife with a mix of observation and imagination.

plates.title: Theater of Earthly Creatures
plates.author: Anonymous
plates.desc: A large spotted feline, identified as a panther, depicted in profile walking to the left.
plates.long: This striking woodcut depicts a panther, or 'Indiaenfche Theotochtli,' from a 1672 Dutch natural history compendium. The illustration reflects the early modern period's fascination with exotic wildlife, emphasizing the animal's powerful musculature and distinctive spotted coat.

summary: A neotropical ant that cuts fresh leaves not to eat but to feed an underground fungus garden it farms. A mature colony can hold millions of workers, among the most complex animal societies outside humans.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern South America and Trinidad
abilities: Cultivates the fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus, part of an ant agriculture tens of millions of years old
Secretes antimicrobial compounds and weeds out parasitic fungi such as Escovopsis to protect its gardens
Workers come in sizes from tiny gardeners to large soldiers, each with its own task
Moves enormous volumes of soil, building nests several metres deep
Clears trails across the forest floor for thousands of foragers

animal.diet: Fungus grown on cut leaves and flowers
animal.habitat: Tropical forest and clearings; nests underground
animal.behaviour: Tiny 'minim' workers often ride on cut leaves, guarding carriers from parasitic flies that try to lay eggs on them.
fieldMarks: Reddish-brown spiny ants in long, cleared trails, carrying leaf pieces held above their heads
Workers in a single column range from tiny to large, big-headed soldiers
Three pairs of spines on the thorax
Huge nest mounds of bare, excavated soil with many entrances
animal.lookalikes: Acromyrmex leafcutters also carry leaves but have four pairs of spines on the thorax and lack Atta's giant-headed soldiers. Soldiers bite hard; watch trails without handling the ants.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests and clearings of Central America, e.g. La Selva and Corcovado in Costa Rica, Tikal in Guatemala and Barro Colorado Island in Panama
animal.season: Resident; trails busiest at night and in the early morning; winged queens fly at the start of the rainy season

lore: Leafcutters are a long-standing farm pest in Latin America, and their winged queens are roasted and eaten in Colombia as 'hormigas culonas'. Darwin's contemporaries were amazed by their trails, and Thomas Belt in 1874 first argued they farmed fungus.
funFact: Neither ant nor fungus can live without the other: the fungus no longer grows in the wild apart from its farmers.

wiki.extract: Atta cephalotes, commonly known as the hairy-headed leafcutter ant, is a species of leafcutter ant in the tribe Attini. A colony can contain up to 5 million members, and each colony has a single queen that can live more than 20 years. The colony comprises different castes, known as "task partitioning", and each caste has a different job to do. This caste system includes minims, medias and majors.

otherNames: Marabunta (Latin American Spanish, army ants generally)
summary: A nomadic ant whose colonies of hundreds of thousands sweep the rainforest floor in a raiding front many metres wide, flushing out insects as they go. It builds no nest, but sleeps in a living ball of its own workers.
nativeRange: Neotropics, from southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Swarm raids up to about 15 m wide, carrying off huge numbers of insects and other arthropods
Workers link legs to form a living nest (bivouac), bridges and road plugs
Colony alternates between a nomadic phase (moving every night) and a stationary phase while the queen lays eggs
Supports more than 300 associated species, including antbirds that follow its raids

animal.diet: Mostly other arthropods, especially social insects' brood, plus spiders, cockroaches and occasionally small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest floor and understorey
animal.lifespan: Colonies can persist for years; queens are replaced by budding
animal.size: Workers from about 3 mm to 12 mm; soldiers largest
animal.behaviour: Raids flush fleeing insects that antbirds, woodcreepers and parasitic flies exploit; the bivouac's temperature is regulated by the living ants.
fieldMarks: Dense, broad carpet of reddish-brown to black ants moving across the forest floor
Soldiers with long, pale hook-shaped mandibles
Antbirds calling and flies hovering above the raid front
Columns carrying insect brood back to the bivouac
animal.lookalikes: Eciton hamatum raids in branching columns rather than a broad swarm and preys mostly on other social insects. Labidus army ants raid partly underground and are smaller and darker.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforest reserves such as Barro Colorado Island (Panama), La Selva (Costa Rica) and Amazonian lodges in Peru and Ecuador.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Henry Walter Bates described Eciton army ants in The Naturalist on the River Amazons (1863); the 20th-century studies of T. C. Schneirla on Barro Colorado revealed their nomadic cycle.
funFact: Some antbird species are 'professional' ant-followers that feed almost only at Eciton burchellii raids and check bivouacs each morning to see where the ants will go.

wiki.extract: Eciton burchellii is a species of New World army ant in the genus Eciton. This species performs expansive, organized swarm raids that give it the informal name, Eciton army ant. This species displays a high degree of worker polymorphism.

summary: A large rainforest ant whose sting is rated the most painful of any insect, a throbbing pain said to last up to a day. The Sateré-Mawé people of Brazil use it in a coming-of-age ritual.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests from Honduras and Nicaragua through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Sting rated at the top (4+) of Justin Schmidt's sting pain index
Venom contains poneratoxin, a peptide that keeps nerve sodium channels open
Squeaks (stridulates) and releases a musky odour when disturbed
Workers forage alone up into the canopy

animal.diet: Nectar and other insects, which workers carry back from the canopy
animal.habitat: Nests at the base of rainforest trees; forages on trunks and in the canopy
animal.behaviour: Colonies of a few hundred to a few thousand ants nest among the roots of a single tree and send solitary foragers into its crown.
fieldMarks: Very large reddish-black ant
Large head with strong jaws
Club-shaped tip to the antennae (clavata, 'club-bearing')
Single node between thorax and abdomen with a visible sting
animal.lookalikes: Giant Amazonian ants (Dinoponera) are larger, all black and lack clubbed antennae. Ectatomma and Neoponera species are smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Tree bases along rainforest trails in Costa Rica (La Selva), Panama and Amazonian Peru and Ecuador.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: In the Sateré-Mawé initiation, young men wear woven gloves filled with sedated bullet ants, stingers pointing inward, for several minutes at a time, repeating the ordeal many times over months.
funFact: The Spanish name 'veinticuatro' (twenty-four) refers to the claim that the pain of one sting lasts 24 hours.

wiki.extract: Paraponera clavata, commonly known as the bullet ant, is a species of ant known for its extremely painful sting. It inhabits humid lowland rainforests in Central and South America.

summary: A pirate of tropical seas with a huge red throat pouch in breeding males. It can stay aloft for days and steals fish from other seabirds.
nativeRange: Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts
abilities: Lowest wing-loading of any bird, allowing effortless soaring
Steals fish from boobies and other seabirds
Can stay aloft for days at a time, even sleeping in flight
Males inflate a red throat pouch to attract females

animal.diet: Fish, squid, stolen prey
animal.habitat: Tropical coasts and islands
animal.behaviour: It chases other seabirds until they drop their catch, snatching it in mid-air.
fieldMarks: Long, angular wings
Deeply forked tail
Males black with a red throat pouch
Females with a white breast
animal.voice: Silent at sea; drumming and rattling at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Great frigatebird males have a green rather than purple gloss on the back and a pale wing bar; females have a red eye-ring and a pale grey throat. Lesser frigatebird is smaller, with white 'armpit' spurs. At distance the shape, long forked tail and angular wings separate frigatebirds from all other seabirds.
animal.whereToSee: Codrington Lagoon (Barbuda), North Seymour (Galápagos), Isla Contoy and Isla Isabel (Mexico), Florida Keys
animal.season: Resident

lore: Sailors called it the man-o'-war bird for its piratical habits.
funFact: Its plumage is not fully waterproof, so it avoids landing on the sea and feeds by snatching prey from the surface or from other birds.

wiki.extract: The magnificent frigatebird, frigate petrel or man o' war is a seabird of the frigatebird family Fregatidae. With a length of 89–114 centimetres and wingspan of 2.17–2.44 m, it is the largest species of frigatebird. It occurs over tropical and subtropical waters off America, between northern Mexico and Peru on the Pacific coast and between Florida and southern Brazil along the Atlantic coast. There are also populations on the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific and the Cape Verde islands in the Atlantic. It is one of the fastest birds in the world, flying at speeds of up to 153 kilometres (95 mi) per hour.

summary: A brilliantly patterned finch with a red face, black-and-white head and broad gold wing bars, often seen in tinkling flocks on thistles. Its beauty and song made it one of the most trapped cage birds of the Mediterranean and Middle East.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia to western Siberia and the western Himalaya; introduced to Australia, New Zealand and South America
abilities: Fine, pointed bill extracts seeds from thistles and teasels that other finches cannot reach
Males' slightly longer bills let them feed more easily on teasel heads
Light enough to cling to swaying seedheads
Some populations migrate to the Mediterranean for winter

animal.diet: Seeds of thistles, teasel, dandelion, groundsel and other plants; insects for young
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, orchards, wasteland, gardens
animal.behaviour: Flocks, known as a 'charm', move together from one weedy patch to the next, constantly calling.
fieldMarks: Red face mask surrounded by white and black
Broad yellow band across black wings
Buff-brown back, white rump, black tail with white spots
Juveniles lack the red face but show the gold wing bar
animal.voice: Song a fast, liquid, tinkling twitter; flight call a cheerful 'tickelitt'.
animal.lookalikes: No adult European bird has the same face pattern. Juveniles have a plain grey-brown head but the same golden wing bar, which separates them from young serins and siskins.
animal.whereToSee: Weedy field margins, orchards and gardens across Europe; abundant in Mediterranean and Anatolian farmland in winter.
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; partial migrant from the north

lore: Renaissance painters such as Raphael ('Madonna of the Goldfinch', c. 1505) placed it in the Christ Child's hand as a symbol of the Passion, because it eats among thorns, and Carel Fabritius painted 'The Goldfinch' in 1654, the year he died.
funFact: In North Africa the hassoun is a prized competition singer, and trapping for the cage-bird trade has depleted wild populations there.

wiki.extract: The European goldfinch, or simply goldfinch, is a small passerine bird in the finch family that is native to the Palearctic zone in Europe, northern Africa, and western Asia. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.

plates.long: Three small birds are depicted around a golden cage, with one bird inside and two perched on the domed roof. This illustration accompanies the text for Carduelis, or the goldfinch, a bird often associated with thorns and cages in medieval lore.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a bird, identified as an 'Acanthis', from Conrad Gessner's monumental zoological work 'Historiae Animalium'. This illustration reflects the 16th-century transition toward empirical observation and systematic classification in natural history.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book I: On Viviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a goldfinch (Carduelis) perched on a small branch.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a goldfinch, known in Latin as 'Carduelis', and is part of Conrad Gessner's encyclopedic 'Historiae Animalium'. The illustration serves as a scientific record, emphasizing the bird's distinctive beak and plumage patterns as understood in the mid-16th century.

plates.title: Noah's Ark
plates.author: Athanasius Kircher
plates.desc: Engraving of a goldfinch (Carduelis) perched on a branch.
plates.long: This engraving shows a goldfinch (Carduelis), noted for its colorful plumage. In the context of 'Arca Noë', these illustrations catalog the diversity of avian life preserved during the Deluge as part of Kircher's reconstruction of Noah's Ark.

summary: One of Europe's most abundant birds: a pink-breasted, blue-capped finch with bold white wing bars. Its short song has regional dialects learned by young birds, making it a classic species for studies of how birds learn to sing.
nativeRange: Europe, western Siberia, Turkey, the Caucasus, northern Iran and western Central Asia; North African birds are now often treated as a separate species
abilities: Young males learn their songs in a sensitive period and refine them the next spring, as shown by W. H. Thorpe in the 1950s
Song shows local dialects that differ between valleys and woods
Females and young migrate further south than adult males, so northern winter flocks are largely male
Huge visible migrations pass coastal headlands in autumn

animal.diet: Seeds from the ground in winter; caterpillars and other insects in summer
animal.habitat: All kinds of woodland, hedgerows, parks, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: Feeds on the ground with a shuffling walk, often in mixed winter flocks with bramblings.
fieldMarks: Male: blue-grey crown and nape, pinkish-orange face and breast, chestnut back
Two bold white wing bars and white outer tail feathers in both sexes
Female olive-brown with the same wing pattern
Greenish rump
animal.voice: Song an accelerating descending rattle ending in a flourish, 'chip-chip-chip-tell-tell-cherry-erry-tissi-cheweeo'; call a sharp 'pink' and a rising 'hweet' rain call.
animal.lookalikes: Brambling has an orange breast and shoulder, and a white rump. Female house sparrow lacks the bold white wing bars. Common rosefinch males are red rather than pink-and-blue.
animal.whereToSee: Any European woodland, park or farmland; Falsterbo (Sweden) and the Curonian Spit see vast autumn passage.
animal.season: Resident in the west; summer visitor in the north and east; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: Linnaeus named it 'coelebs', meaning bachelor, because in Sweden only males stay through the winter. Belgian 'vinkenzetting' contests, in which caged males are scored on how many songs they sing in an hour, go back centuries.
funFact: Hand-reared chaffinches that never hear an adult sing develop only a simple, abnormal song, which showed that birdsong is partly learned.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian chaffinch, common chaffinch, or simply the chaffinch is a common and widespread small passerine bird – in the finch family. The male is brightly coloured with a blue-grey cap and rust-red underparts. The female is more subdued in colouring, but both sexes have two contrasting white wing bars and white sides to the tail. The male bird has a strong voice and sings from exposed perches to attract a mate.

Produced during the 18th century, such plates were essential for documenting the biodiversity of the Americas for a European audience. plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a black bird perched on a pink lady's slipper orchid.
plates.long: This 1743 hand-colored engraving depicts a Smooth-billed Ani (Crotophaga ani) perched upon the stem of a pink Lady's Slipper orchid (Cypripedium). Mark Catesby's work is significant for its pioneering approach to natural history, as he was among the first to illustrate birds alongside the specific botanical species found within their native North American habitats.

The image serves as a fascinating example of early scientific illustration, where domestic scenes were used to visualize the practical application of natural substances. The work was engrav

plates.title: Georg Wolfgang Knorr; Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch — Schnecken und Muscheln (1770)
plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr; Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch
plates.desc: A natural history plate featuring various species of sea urchins (Echinites) and their skeletal tests. The specimens are rendered with fine detail, showing different colors (blue, pink, white, green, brown), textures, and patterns. Some are shown with their spines intact, while others are bare tests showing the pentamerous symmetry of the ambulacral plates.
plates.long: This plate from Knorr and Walch's 'Schnecken und Muscheln' (1770) displays a variety of sea urchins, both with and without their spines. The detailed hand-colored engravings illustrate the diverse forms, colors, and pentamerous symmetry characteristic of these marine organisms, serving as an important record of 18th-century biological classification and the aesthetic of natural history collecting.

plates.desc: A hand-colored copperplate engraving of a Salmon-crested Cockatoo (Cacatua moluccensis) perched on a branch, featuring white and light pink plumage and a prominent reddish-orange crest.
plates.long: A finely detailed hand-colored engraving of a Salmon-crested Cockatoo, identified by its distinctive reddish-orange crest. This plate is from François Bouchard's 1775 work 'Recueil de cent-trente-trois oiseaux des plus belles especes', which documented exotic bird species for a European audience fascinated by global biodiversity.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a mountain finch, part of Conrad Gessner's encyclopedic effort to categorize the animal kingdom. Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium' is considered a foundational text of modern zoology, bridging the gap between classical scholarship and empirical observation.

Catesby was a pioneer in North American natural history, and this plate exemplifies his practice of illustrating species within their ecological context, a significant advancement in scientific illustration of the period.

summary: A small finch whose summer males glow lemon-yellow with a black cap. It is among the strictest vegetarians of North American songbirds and waits until late summer to nest, when thistles have gone to seed.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the United States; winters south to northern Mexico
abilities: Feeds its young almost entirely on regurgitated seeds
Lines nests with thistle down so tightly woven they can hold water
Moults its body feathers twice a year, switching between bright breeding and dull winter plumage
Brown-headed Cowbird chicks raised in goldfinch nests rarely survive on the seed diet

animal.diet: Seeds of thistles, sunflowers, asters and other composites; nyjer and sunflower at feeders
animal.habitat: Weedy fields, roadsides, floodplains, orchards and gardens
animal.behaviour: It flies in deep, bouncing undulations, calling on each rise.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: bright yellow with black cap, black wings with white bars, white undertail
Female and winter birds: dull olive-buff with black wings and pale wing bars
Short, conical pink-orange bill in summer
Notched black-and-white tail
animal.voice: A long, canary-like series of twitters and warbles; flight call 'po-ta-to-chip', 'per-chic-o-ree'.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser Goldfinch (west) has a greenish or black back and yellow undertail. Pine Siskin is streaky brown with yellow wing flashes. Yellow Warbler has a thin bill and no black.
animal.whereToSee: Thistle and nyjer feeders across the US; weedy fields with coneflowers and sunflowers in late summer.
animal.season: Resident across much of the US; northern birds move south in winter

lore: It is the state bird of Iowa, New Jersey and Washington, chosen in Washington by a schoolchildren's vote.
funFact: It nests later than almost any other North American songbird, often starting in July.

wiki.extract: The American goldfinch is a small North American bird in the finch family. It is migratory, ranging from mid-Alberta to North Carolina during the breeding season, and from just south of the Canada–United States border to Mexico during the winter.

plates.title: The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands, Vol. 1
plates.author: Mark Catesby
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of an American Goldfinch perched on an Acacia branch with seed pods.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby’s seminal work depicts an American Goldfinch (Carduelis Americanus) perched on a branch of an Acacia plant. Catesby was the first to illustrate North American flora and fauna together in their natural habitats, a revolutionary approach that influenced later naturalists like John James Audubon.

summary: A plain, rufous ovenbird that builds a domed nest of mud and straw shaped like a traditional clay bread oven. Pairs stay together for years and duet loudly, and it is the national bird of Argentina.
nativeRange: Eastern and central South America: Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and northern and central Argentina
abilities: Builds a heavy, oven-shaped nest of mud, dung and plant fibre with a curved inner wall separating the entrance from the egg chamber
Constructs a nest in a few weeks using thousands of beakfuls of wet mud, often after rain
Old nests are reused by other birds such as Saffron Finches, swallows and parakeets
Mated pairs sing synchronised, shrill duets

animal.diet: Insects, worms and other invertebrates gleaned from the ground
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, pastures, roadsides and city parks
animal.behaviour: Nests are placed on posts, branches, utility poles and even street lamps, in full view.
fieldMarks: Rufous-brown upperparts with a brighter rufous tail
Pale buffy underparts with a whitish throat
Slender, slightly decurved bill
Walks deliberately on the ground with a high-stepping gait
animal.voice: Loud, shrill, accelerating series of notes, often given as a duet by the pair, which sing with wings drooped and quivering.
animal.lookalikes: Pale-legged Hornero (north and west) has pale legs and a whitish eyebrow. Crested Hornero has a small crest and is found in Paraguay and Argentina's Chaco. Thrushes have a different bill shape and do not walk.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and farmland around Buenos Aires, Montevideo and southern Brazil; abundant in the Pampas and Pantanal.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Argentina's national bird since 1928, it appears widely in gaucho folklore as a model of the hard-working household.
funFact: Its mud nests can last several years and weigh several kilograms.

wiki.extract: The rufous hornero is a medium-sized ovenbird in the family Furnariidae. It occurs in eastern South America and is the national bird of Argentina. Also known as the red ovenbird, it is common in savannas, second-growth scrub, pastures, and agricultural land and is synanthropic. Its range includes midwestern, southeastern, and southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern and central Argentina, extending as far south as northern Patagonia. The species is most closely related to the crested hornero of Paraguay and Argentina. There are four accepted subspecies.

summary: The fish that fed empires: dried and salted cod carried Viking and Basque sailors across oceans. The collapse of the Grand Banks stock in 1992 became the textbook warning of industrial overfishing.
nativeRange: North Atlantic from Cape Hatteras to Greenland and from the Bay of Biscay to the Barents Sea
abilities: A large female can release several million eggs in a season
Some cold-water populations produce antifreeze glycoproteins
Chin barbel and pelvic fins carry taste buds used to find buried prey
Makes grunting sounds with swim-bladder muscles during spawning
edibilityNote: Low in mercury. Can carry anisakid (cod worm) parasites, killed by thorough cooking or freezing. Cod liver oil is very high in vitamin A, so excess can be harmful.

animal.diet: Crustaceans, sand eels, herring, capelin and smaller cod
animal.habitat: Cold shelf waters from the shore to about 600 m, near the bottom
animal.size: Commonly up to 1 m; historical record ~2 m and 96 kg
animal.behaviour: Northeast Arctic 'skrei' cod migrate from the Barents Sea to spawn off the Lofoten Islands every winter.
fieldMarks: Three dorsal fins and two anal fins
Single long barbel on the chin
Pale, curved lateral line on mottled greenish-brown to reddish sides
Upper jaw overhangs the lower
Square or slightly concave tail
animal.lookalikes: Haddock has a black lateral line and a dark 'thumbprint' blotch above the pectoral; pollock (saithe) has a straight pale lateral line and protruding lower jaw.
animal.whereToSee: Lofoten Islands, Norway (spawning skrei); Gulf of Maine and Newfoundland coasts; North Sea and Baltic
animal.season: Resident; Lofoten spawning aggregations Feb–Apr

lore: Norse stockfish dried on Lofoten racks has been traded to Europe since the Viking Age, and Basque and other European fleets fished Newfoundland for salt cod by the 1500s; Massachusetts hangs a carved 'Sacred Cod' in its State House.
funFact: The IUCN global status (Vulnerable) still rests on a 1996 assessment; European cod was reassessed as Least Concern regionally, while Newfoundland's northern cod has never fully recovered.

summary: A large, striped generalist predator of warm coasts, famous for eating almost anything, from sea turtles to license plates. Its saw-edged teeth can cut through turtle shell.
nativeRange: Tropical and warm temperate seas worldwide
abilities: Cockscomb-shaped, serrated teeth saw through turtle shells and bones
Diet includes sea turtles, seabirds, dolphins, sea snakes and carrion, plus indigestible rubbish
Undertakes migrations of thousands of kilometres between islands and coasts
Its presence keeps dugongs and turtles from overgrazing seagrass in Shark Bay, Australia

animal.diet: Sea turtles, fish, rays, seabirds, marine mammals, sea snakes, carrion
animal.habitat: Coastal and reef waters, river mouths and open ocean to over 350 m
animal.size: Commonly 3–4 m; up to 5.5 m and over 600 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal hunter that arrives at predictable feasts, such as fledgling albatrosses at Hawaii's French Frigate Shoals each summer.
fieldMarks: Dark vertical bars or spots on the back, strongest in young and fading in large adults
Very broad, blunt, nearly square snout
Long upper tail lobe with a pointed tip
Large, serrated cockscomb teeth
Spiracle behind the eye
animal.lookalikes: Sand tiger (Carcharias taurus) has ragged protruding teeth and a pointed snout; bull shark lacks stripes and has a shorter tail lobe.
animal.whereToSee: Tiger Beach, Bahamas; Fuvahmulah, Maldives; Aliwal Shoal, South Africa; Shark Bay, Western Australia
animal.season: Tiger Beach Oct–Jan; Fuvahmulah year-round

lore: In Native Hawaiian tradition some sharks were ʻaumākua, ancestral guardians, while the man-eating niuhi was hunted by chiefs as a test of prowess.
funFact: Tiger shark stomachs have contained license plates, tyres, tin cans and other rubbish.

wiki.extract: The tiger shark is a species of ground shark, and the only extant member of the genus Galeocerdo and family Galeocerdonidae. It is a large predator, with females capable of attaining a length of over 5 m. Populations are found in many tropical and temperate waters, especially around central Pacific islands. Its name derives from the dark stripes down its body, which resemble a tiger's pattern and fade as the shark matures.

summary: A fish-eating crocodilian of the great rivers of northern India and Nepal, with a very long, needle-thin snout. Mature males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip, the ghara ('pot'), that gives the species its name. It is Critically Endangered, surviving mainly in a few protected stretches of river.
nativeRange: Rivers of northern India and Nepal (Chambal, Girwa, Son, Gandak, Rapti–Narayani, Ganges); extinct in Pakistan, Bhutan and Myanmar, and possibly in Bangladesh
abilities: Snaps sideways at fish with its thin snout, which meets little water resistance
Males make a buzzing sound with the ghara, which also helps them blow bubbles
Among the longest of all crocodilians, with males reaching ~5–6 m

animal.diet: Almost entirely fish
animal.habitat: Deep, fast-flowing rivers with high sandbanks for basking and nesting
animal.size: Males up to ~5–6 m; females ~3.5–4.5 m
animal.behaviour: Rarely leaves the water except to bask and nest on sandbanks. Hatchlings stay in groups (crèches) guarded by adults, sometimes riding on a large male's back. Its legs are too weak for it to walk upright on land, so it slides on its belly.
fieldMarks: Very long, narrow snout with many interlocking teeth
Bulbous knob (ghara) on the snout tip of adult males
Olive to grey-brown body
Basks on river sandbanks
animal.lookalikes: The mugger crocodile has a broad, heavy snout. The false gharial (Tomistoma schlegelii) of Southeast Asia has a slightly broader snout tapering from the head and lives far away.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh–Rajasthan–Uttar Pradesh), Katarniaghat on the Girwa River, Chitwan National Park (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; best seen basking in winter (Nov–Mar); nesting Mar–Apr; hatching in June

lore: In the 1970s fewer than 200 gharials were left in the wild, and India's Project Crocodile, started in 1975, reared hatchlings from collected eggs for release. In Hindu art, the makara, vehicle of the river goddess Ganga, is often shown with a long snout like a gharial.
funFact: In 2007–08 more than 100 gharials died on the Chambal River from a disease or toxin, which showed how vulnerable a few small populations can be.

wiki.extract: The gharial, also known as gavial or fish-eating crocodile, is a crocodilian in the family Gavialidae and among the longest of all living crocodilians. Mature females are 2.6 to 4.5 m long, and males 3 to 6 m. Adult males have a distinct boss at the end of the snout, which resembles an earthenware pot known as a ghara, hence the name "gharial". The gharial is well adapted to catching fish because of its long, narrow snout and 110 sharp, interlocking teeth.

summary: A heavy, dagger-billed diving bird of northern lakes whose wailing and yodelling calls are the signature sound of the North Woods. Its legs are set so far back that it can barely walk on land.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the northern US, Greenland and Iceland; winters on Atlantic and Pacific coasts of North America and western Europe
abilities: Dives to about 60 m and stays under for up to a minute or more
Has dense, mostly solid bones that reduce buoyancy
Needs a runway of 30 m to several hundred metres of water to take off
Each male has a distinctive yodel that changes if he moves to a new territory

animal.diet: Fish such as perch and suckers; crayfish and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Clear northern lakes with fish and islands for nesting; ocean bays in winter
animal.behaviour: Chicks ride on their parents' backs for their first weeks.
fieldMarks: Breeding: black head with green gloss, red eye and dagger-like black bill
Breeding: white-striped necklace and checkerboard black-and-white back
Winter: grey-brown above, white throat, pale bill
Sits low in the water; in flight shows hunched back and feet trailing past the tail
animal.voice: A haunting wail, a quavering tremolo ('crazy laughter'), the male's rising yodel, and a soft hoot.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-billed Loon has a pale, upturned bill. Pacific Loon is smaller with a grey nape and rounded head. Double-crested Cormorant has a hooked bill and swims with head tilted up.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes of Minnesota (Boundary Waters), Maine, the Adirondacks, Ontario's Algonquin Park; Atlantic and Pacific coasts in winter.
animal.season: On breeding lakes Apr–Oct; on coasts Nov–Apr

lore: Canada's one-dollar coin, introduced in 1987, carries a loon and is universally called the 'loonie'; in Ojibwe tradition the loon (maang) is a leadership clan, and it is Minnesota's state bird.
funFact: Loons have been shown to change their yodel when they move territories, apparently to sound unlike the previous owner.

wiki.extract: The common loon or great northern diver is a large member of the loon, or diver, family of birds. Breeding adults have a plumage that includes a broad black head and neck with a greenish, purplish, or bluish sheen, blackish or blackish-grey upperparts, and pure white underparts except some black on the undertail coverts and vent. Non-breeding adults are brownish with a dark neck and head marked with dark grey-brown. Their upperparts are dark brownish-grey with an unclear pattern of squares on the shoulders, and the underparts, lower face, chin, and throat are whitish. The sexes look alike, though males are significantly heavier than females. During the breeding season, loons live on lakes and other waterways in Canada, the northern United States, and southern parts of Greenland and Iceland. Small numbers breed on Svalbard and sporadically elsewhere in Arctic Eurasia. Common loons winter on both coasts of North America as far north as Newfoundland and Alaska, and as far south as Mexico, as well as on the Atlantic coast of Europe.

summary: A large, blue-grey and orange-spotted gecko of Asia, named for its loud 'to-kay' call. It runs up walls and glass on toes covered in microscopic hairs, and is one of the most heavily traded reptiles in traditional medicine.
nativeRange: Northeastern India and Bangladesh through southern China and Southeast Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines; introduced in Florida, Hawaii and elsewhere
abilities: Sticks to smooth surfaces using millions of tiny hairs (setae) on its toes, which grip by van der Waals forces
Has a strong bite that can hold on for minutes
Can drop its tail to escape and regrow it

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, other geckos, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Tree trunks, cliffs and buildings
animal.behaviour: Males call loudly at night from walls and trees to defend territories. When threatened it opens its mouth wide, barks and bites hard.
fieldMarks: Large, heavy-headed gecko, blue-grey with orange to red spots
Big eyes with vertical pupils
Wide toe pads
Loud 'to-kay' call at night
animal.voice: A loud, repeated 'to-kay' or 'geck-o', often preceded by a chuckling rattle; carries far at night
animal.lookalikes: Smaller house geckos (Hemidactylus) are pale and plain. The related Gekko smithii has green eyes and pale rather than orange-red spots. No other gecko in its range is as large or as loud.
animal.whereToSee: Buildings and forest throughout Southeast Asia; often heard at night in guesthouses in Thailand, Malaysia, Bali
animal.season: Resident; calls year-round, especially in the wet season

uses.use: Dried, split tokay (gé jiè) used in tonics for cough, asthma and as a 'kidney tonic'

medicinal.cautions: No good clinical evidence. Wild collection for the medicine trade has depleted populations; the species was listed on CITES Appendix II in 2019.

lore: Its call gave it its name in many Southeast Asian languages, such as tokek and tukko. In parts of Thailand and Indonesia, hearing a tokay call seven times in a row is said to bring good luck.
funFact: Gecko feet have inspired adhesives that can be peeled off and reused many times without losing their grip.

wiki.extract: The tokay gecko is a nocturnal arboreal gecko in the genus Gekko, the true geckos. It is native to Asia and some Pacific Islands.

Featured in Li Shizhen's 1596 'Bencao Gangmu', such illustrations were crucial for the accurate identification of natural substances used in pharmacology. The geckos were traditionally used to treat respiratory ailments and to tonify vital energy.

summary: The tallest living animal, browsing acacia leaves up to nearly 6 m above the ground. Its heart and blood vessels are specially adapted to pump blood all the way up that long neck.
nativeRange: Savannas and woodlands of Sub-Saharan Africa, from Niger and Chad to South Africa
abilities: Reaches leaves up to ~5.5–6 m high
Has a heart of over 10 kg that drives blood pressure about twice a human's
Tight skin on its legs works like a compression stocking to stop blood pooling
Strips thorny acacia with a dark, prehensile tongue about 45 cm long
Can kill a lion with a kick

animal.diet: Herbivore: leaves, shoots and flowers, especially of acacia; up to ~30 kg a day
animal.habitat: Savanna and open woodland
animal.size: Males up to ~5.5 m tall and ~1,200 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Males fight by 'necking', swinging their necks to hit each other with their ossicones. Giraffes sleep only briefly, often standing up.
fieldMarks: Tallest animal
Patched coat
Long neck and legs
Ossicones on the head
animal.lookalikes: Patterns vary between giraffe species and subspecies.
animal.whereToSee: Etosha (Namibia), Maasai Mara (Kenya) and Kruger (South Africa)
animal.season: Resident

lore: A giraffe from Malindi reached the Ming court in 1414 with Zheng He's fleets and was hailed as a qilin, an auspicious beast. Lorenzo de' Medici's giraffe caused a sensation in Florence in 1486, as did 'Zarafa', sent by Egypt's ruler to Charles X of France in 1827.
funFact: Despite its length, a giraffe's neck has only seven vertebrae, the same number as a human's.

wiki.extract: Giraffes are large African hoofed mammals. They are the tallest living terrestrial animals and the largest ruminants on Earth. They are classified under the family Giraffidae, along with their closest extant relative, the okapi. Traditionally, giraffes have been thought of as one species, Giraffa camelopardalis, with nine subspecies. Most recently, researchers proposed dividing them into four extant species, with seven subspecies, which can be distinguished morphologically by their fur coat patterns. Six valid extinct species of Giraffa are known from the fossil record.

summary: The only living relative of the giraffe, a shy forest animal with a reddish body and zebra-striped legs, found only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was unknown to Western science until 1901.
nativeRange: Rainforests of northern, central and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially the Ituri Forest
abilities: Strips leaves with a long, dark, prehensile tongue it can also use to clean its eyes and ears
Calls to its calf with infrasound below human hearing
Striped hindquarters break up its outline in the dappled forest light
Eats over a hundred species of plants, including some that are poisonous to people

animal.diet: Herbivore: leaves, buds, shoots, ferns, fruit and fungi; eats clay and charcoal for minerals
animal.habitat: Dense tropical rainforest at 500–1,500 m
animal.behaviour: Newborn calves hide in a nest for weeks and do not defecate for the first month or two, which may help keep predators from finding them.
fieldMarks: Dark velvety body
Zebra-striped legs and rump
Giraffe-like head
Long blue tongue
animal.lookalikes: Its striped legs suggest a zebra, but zebras are striped all over; its only close relative, the giraffe, lives in open savanna.
animal.whereToSee: Okapi Wildlife Reserve (Epulu)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Henry Morton Stanley heard of a forest 'donkey' in the 1890s, and in 1901 Harry Johnston sent skin to London, where it was named for him. The okapi is a national symbol of the DRC and appears on its banknotes.
funFact: It was first named as a horse species, Equus johnstoni, before skulls showed it was a giraffid.

wiki.extract: The okapi, also known as forest giraffe and zebra giraffe, is an artiodactyl mammal that is endemic to the northeast Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is the only species in the genus Okapia. Although the okapi has striped markings reminiscent of zebras, it is most closely related to the giraffe. The okapi and the giraffe are the only living members of the family Giraffidae.

summary: The tallest flying bird in the world, standing about 1.5–1.8 m, grey with a bare red head and upper neck. Pairs are famously faithful and duet with trumpeting calls in the wet farmlands of northern India.
nativeRange: Northern and central India, the Nepal terai, Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos, and northern Australia; extinct in Pakistan, Thailand (reintroduced) and much of Southeast Asia
abilities: Tallest flying bird alive
Pairs perform synchronised unison calls and leaping dances
Breeds in rice paddies and village ponds alongside farmers

animal.diet: Roots, tubers, grain, aquatic plants, insects, frogs, snails and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Marshes, shallow wetlands, flooded fields and wet farmland
animal.size: Height about 1.5–1.8 m; wingspan about 2.2–2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Pairs stay together year-round and build a large mound nest of reeds in shallow water during the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Very tall, pale grey crane with long pink-red legs
Bare red skin on the head and upper neck; grey crown
Dark grey-green bill
White tertial feathers droop over the tail
animal.voice: Loud, far-carrying trumpeting; pairs give a unison call in which the male's long notes and the female's shorter notes interlock
animal.lookalikes: Common crane (winter visitor) is smaller with a black-and-white head and neck; Demoiselle crane is small with a black neck and white ear tufts; Brolga (Australia) has a red band only on the head and a dewlap.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland and wetlands of Uttar Pradesh (Etawah, Mainpuri), Keoladeo National Park and Gujarat's Kheda district; Lumbini in Nepal
animal.season: Resident; breeds during the monsoon

lore: In the Ramayana, the sage Valmiki's first verse was provoked by grief at a hunter killing one of a pair of krauncha birds, often identified with the sarus. The sarus is the state bird of Uttar Pradesh and is widely protected by farmers who regard it as sacred.
funFact: Uttar Pradesh holds the largest population, and most of these cranes nest in farmland rather than protected areas.

wiki.extract: The sarus crane is a large nonmigratory crane found in parts of the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, and northern Australia. The tallest of the flying birds, standing at a height of up to 1.8 m, they are a conspicuous species of open wetlands in South Asia, seasonally flooded Dipterocarpus forests in Southeast Asia, and Eucalyptus-dominated woodlands and grasslands in Australia.

summary: A tall grey crane with a red crown whose rolling, bugling calls carry for kilometres. Each spring hundreds of thousands gather on Nebraska's Platte River, one of North America's great wildlife spectacles.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the northern US and north-eastern Siberia; resident populations in Florida, Mississippi and Cuba; winters in the southern US and northern Mexico
abilities: Its windpipe coils into the breastbone, producing calls audible several kilometres away
Pairs perform leaping, bowing courtship dances and 'unison calls'
Paints its grey feathers rusty-brown by preening with iron-rich mud
Migrates in high, circling flocks riding thermals

animal.diet: Waste grain, tubers, seeds, insects, snails, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Marshes, wet meadows, tundra and farm fields near shallow roosting water
animal.behaviour: Families stay together through the first winter, with colts learning migration routes from their parents.
fieldMarks: Tall grey crane with long neck and legs
Red bare forecrown and white cheeks
Bushy 'bustle' of tertial feathers over the tail
Flies with neck fully outstretched; often stained rusty brown
animal.voice: A loud, rolling, trumpeting rattle 'garoo-oo-oo'; juveniles give high, whistling 'peeps'.
animal.lookalikes: Great Blue Heron flies with its neck folded and lacks the red crown. Whooping Crane is white with black wingtips. Common Crane (rare vagrant) has a black-and-white neck.
animal.whereToSee: Platte River near Kearney, Nebraska (Feb–Apr, Rowe Sanctuary); Bosque del Apache NWR (New Mexico) and Whitewater Draw (Arizona) in winter; Jasper-Pulaski (Indiana) in autumn.
animal.season: Migratory populations: on the Platte mid-Feb–early Apr; on wintering grounds Nov–Feb

lore: Aldo Leopold's essay 'Marshland Elegy' in A Sand County Almanac (1949) made the sandhill crane a symbol of wildness and deep time; in Ojibwe tradition the crane (ajijaak) is a leading clan.
funFact: Its rusty colour is not pigment at all but mud painted on during preening.

wiki.extract: The sandhill crane is a species of large crane of North America and extreme northeastern Siberia. The common name of this bird refers to its habitat, such as the Platte River, on the edge of Nebraska's Sandhills on the American Great Plains. Sandhill cranes are known to frequent the edges of bodies of water. The central Platte River Valley in Nebraska is the most important stopover area for the nominotypical subspecies, the lesser sandhill crane (A. c. canadensis), with up to 450,000 of these birds migrating through annually.

summary: A crane crowned with a halo of stiff golden feathers, famous for exuberant dancing. Uganda's national bird, it is one of only two cranes able to roost in trees.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Uganda and Kenya to South Africa
abilities: Long hind toe lets it grip branches and roost in trees, unlike most cranes
Elaborate dances of bowing, leaping and wing-flapping strengthen pair bonds
Inflates a red throat sac to produce a booming call

animal.diet: Omnivorous: seeds, grasses, insects, frogs, lizards and small fish
animal.habitat: Marshes, wet grassland and farmland near wetlands
animal.size: About 1 m tall; wingspan around 2 m; 3–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs and flocks dance year-round, bobbing, bowing and leaping high into the air while tossing grass.
fieldMarks: Stiff, bristly golden crown
Bare white cheek patch topped with red, and a small red throat wattle
Pale grey neck and body
White wings with golden and chestnut feathers
Black velvet forehead
animal.voice: A honking, two-note 'mu-hem' or 'ya-oo' call; also a deep booming from the inflated throat sac.
animal.lookalikes: Black crowned crane (West and Central Africa, overlapping in Uganda and South Sudan) has a dark grey to black neck and body and a cheek patch that is white above and red below (red more extensive in the eastern subspecies), whereas the grey crowned crane's cheek is mostly white with only a small red patch at the top. Wattled crane is larger, lacks the golden crown and has long white feathered wattles.
animal.whereToSee: Uganda's wetlands (Mabamba, Lake Mburo), Ngorongoro Crater, Amboseli, KwaZulu-Natal Midlands
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly in the rains

lore: The grey crowned crane is the national bird of Uganda and stands on the country's flag and coat of arms. Its Afrikaans name 'mahem' imitates the call.
funFact: Its population fell by more than half in about 45 years, largely through wetland drainage and capture for the live-bird trade.

wiki.extract: The grey crowned crane or gray crowned crane is a large crane species native to Sub-Saharan Africa. It occurs mainly in dry savannah, although it nests in somewhat wetter habitats, and can also be found in marshes, cultivated lands and grassy flatlands near rivers and lakes. Its body plumage is mainly grey and it has white cheeks, a red throat patch, and a stiff golden crown. It is omnivorous, consuming a wide variety of animal and plant matter, including plants, seeds, grain, insects, frogs, worms, snakes, small fish and the eggs of aquatic animals. It is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. It is the national bird of Uganda.

summary: The tallest bird in North America, a white crane whose only migratory flock fell to about 15 birds in 1941. Protection of its only wild migratory flock, which nests in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park and winters on the Texas coast, has brought it back to several hundred.
nativeRange: Wild flock breeds in Wood Buffalo National Park (Alberta/Northwest Territories) and winters at Aransas, Texas; reintroduced non-migratory birds in Louisiana and an eastern migratory flock in Wisconsin
abilities: Migrates about 4,000 km between Canada and the Gulf of Mexico
Windpipe up to about 1.5 m long, coiled in the breastbone, amplifying its bugle
Pairs bond for life and defend large winter territories in salt marsh
Captive-raised cranes have been taught migration routes by following ultralight aircraft (2001–2015)

animal.diet: Blue crabs, clams, wolfberries and acorns in winter; insects, frogs, fish and plants in summer
animal.habitat: Remote boreal marshes for breeding; coastal salt marshes and bays in winter
animal.size: About 1.5 m tall; wingspan 2–2.3 m; 4.5–8.5 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs usually lay two eggs but often raise only one chick.
fieldMarks: Snow-white body and very tall stature
Black primary feathers visible as black wingtips in flight
Red crown and black 'moustache' on the face
Juveniles mottled cinnamon and white
animal.voice: A loud, clear, trumpeting 'whoop-whoop' unison call that carries several kilometres.
animal.lookalikes: American White Pelican has black on the whole outer wing and a huge bill. Wood Stork has a dark bare head and black trailing wing edges. Great Egret flies with neck folded. Sandhill Crane is grey.
animal.whereToSee: Aransas National Wildlife Refuge and boat tours from Rockport–Fulton, Texas (Nov–Mar); Necedah NWR, Wisconsin (eastern flock).
animal.season: Winter at Aransas Nov–Mar; breeding in Wood Buffalo May–Sep

lore: Its nesting grounds were not found until 1954, when a forest-fire crew spotted cranes in Wood Buffalo National Park; it was among the first species listed as endangered in the United States, in 1967.
funFact: The US Fish and Wildlife Service estimated about 540 whooping cranes wintered in and around Aransas in 2025–26, up from roughly 15 in 1941.

wiki.extract: The whooping crane is an endangered crane species, native to North America, named for its "whooping" calls. Along with the sandhill crane, it is one of only two crane species native to North America, and it is also the tallest North American bird species, with an estimated 22–30+ year life expectancy in the wild. After being pushed to the brink of extinction by unregulated hunting and loss of habitat that left just 21 wild cranes by 1941, the whooping crane made a partial recovery through conservation efforts. The total number of cranes in the surviving migratory population, plus three reintroduced flocks and in-captivity, is just over 830 birds as of 2025. This includes about 560 individuals in the remnant population that migrates between coastal Texas, US, and the Northwest Territories, Canada, which is termed the "Aransas-Wood Buffalo Population" after the protected areas that anchor the population's wintering and breeding ranges, respectively. Additionally, there are about 140 individuals in two reintroduced populations breeding in Wisconsin and Louisiana, US, and an additional 130 individuals in captivity.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a Whooping Crane head and a Prunus branch
plates.long: A detailed hand-colored engraving showing the head and neck of a Whooping Crane (Grus Americana Alba) reaching towards a branch of berries from a Prunus species. Mark Catesby's work was revolutionary for its time, as he was one of the first to depict animals within their ecological context, often pairing birds with the specific plants they fed upon.

summary: A tall, grey crane with a black-and-white head and a bushy tail-bustle, whose trumpeting flocks pass over Europe in spring and autumn. Paired birds perform elaborate leaping, bowing dances.
nativeRange: Breeds from Scandinavia and Germany across northern Europe and Asia to eastern Siberia; winters in Iberia, France, North Africa, the Middle East, India and China

Pairs duet in synchronised 'unison calls'
Migrates in V-formations, with major stopovers used by tens of thousands
Stains its plumage brown with mud when nesting, for camouflage

animal.diet: Grain, roots, acorns, shoots; insects, frogs and small animals in summer
animal.habitat: Bogs, forest swamps and marshes for breeding; open farmland and wetlands in winter
animal.behaviour: Dancing cranes bow, leap into the air with wings spread and toss sticks, at any time of year.
fieldMarks: Tall and grey with long black legs
Black head and neck with a white stripe behind the eye; red crown patch
Drooping tail-bustle of curved inner wing feathers
Flies with neck outstretched
animal.voice: A loud, rolling, bugling 'krroo-krroo', audible from kilometres away.
animal.lookalikes: Grey heron flies with neck folded and lacks the black head. Demoiselle crane is smaller with black breast plumes and white ear tufts. White stork is white with a red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Hornborgasjön (Sweden) in April, Rügen-Bock (Germany) and Lac du Der (France) in autumn, Gallocanta (Spain), Hula Valley (Israel) in winter; the Norfolk Broads and Somerset Levels in England.
animal.season: Summer visitor to northern Europe Mar–Oct; passage migrant; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: In Greek legend the cranes of Ibycus witnessed the poet's murder and revealed his killers, and Persian poetry uses the call of the 'kulang' and 'dorna' as an image of exile and longing.
funFact: Cranes returned to England's Norfolk Broads in 1979 and first bred there in 1981, around 400 years after they were lost as a breeding bird.

wiki.extract: The common crane, also known as the Eurasian crane, is a bird of the family Gruidae, the cranes. A medium-sized species, it is the only crane commonly found in Europe besides the demoiselle crane and the Siberian crane that only are regular in the far eastern part of the continent. Along with the sandhill crane, demoiselle crane and the brolga, it is one of only four crane species not currently classified as threatened with extinction or conservation dependent on the species level. Despite the species' large numbers, local extinctions and extirpations have taken place in part of its range, and an ongoing reintroduction project is underway in the United Kingdom.
