summary: One of the rarest cranes, famous for its paired courtship dances in the snow. It symbolises longevity and fidelity in East Asia.
nativeRange: Breeds in south-east Russia and north-east China; winters in Korea and eastern China; resident in Hokkaido, Japan
abilities: Pairs perform synchronised duets and leaping dances
Migrates between Siberian marshes and Korean and Chinese wetlands
Hokkaido population is non-migratory
Can live 30+ years

animal.diet: Fish, crabs, insects, amphibians and rice
animal.habitat: Wetlands with tall reeds and shallow water
animal.size: ~1.5 m tall; wingspan up to 2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Couples bond for life and greet each other with bowing, leaping and loud unison calls.
fieldMarks: Tall white crane with a red crown patch
Black neck and face
Black secondary flight feathers, looking like a black tail when standing
Pure white primary feathers
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting unison calls given by pairs
animal.lookalikes: Siberian crane has a red face and black primaries. White-naped crane is grey-bodied.
animal.whereToSee: Tsurui-Ito Tancho Crane Sanctuary and Akan International Crane Center, Hokkaido; Zhalong Nature Reserve, China
animal.season: Hokkaido cranes are resident, with winter feeding gatherings Nov–Mar

lore: In Japan folding 1,000 paper cranes (senbazuru) grants a wish, made famous by Sadako Sasaki after Hiroshima; it appears on Japan Airlines' logo. In China it is linked with immortals and longevity.
funFact: Hokkaido's population fell to about 20 birds in the 1920s; winter feeding by local farmers helped it recover to over 1,800.

wiki.extract: The red-crowned crane, also called the Japanese crane and the Manchurian crane, is a large Northeast Asian crane among the rarest cranes in the world. In some parts of its range, it is known as a symbol of luck, longevity, and fidelity.

summary: The smallest of the cranes, elegant and grey with a black breast and white plumes trailing behind the eyes. Steppe populations migrate across the Himalaya and the deserts of the Middle East to winter in India and Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds on steppes from Ukraine and southern Russia through Kazakhstan and Central Asia to Mongolia and China; a few in Turkey; formerly bred in the Atlas of Morocco; winters in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Flies over the Himalaya at great altitude on migration to India
Nests on dry steppe, often far from water, unlike most cranes
Gathers in wintering flocks of thousands
Pairs dance with leaps and bows like larger cranes

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, plant shoots; insects, lizards and worms
animal.habitat: Grassy and shrubby steppe and semi-desert near streams; farmland in winter
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform graceful dances, and winter flocks descend on fields with loud bugling.
fieldMarks: Small, slim blue-grey crane
Black head, neck and long, drooping breast plumes
White tufts of plumes behind the eye
Short bill; grey tail without a bushy bustle
animal.voice: A higher-pitched, more wooden trumpeting than the common crane, 'krrro-krrro'.
animal.lookalikes: Common crane is larger, with a white neck stripe, red crown and bushy tail-bustle. Grey heron flies with neck folded.
animal.whereToSee: Kalmykian and Kazakh steppes in summer; Khichan village in Rajasthan and the Indus floodplains of Pakistan in winter; passage through Pakistan and Arabia.
animal.season: Summer visitor to breeding steppes Apr–Sep; winter visitor to South Asia and Africa Oct–Mar

lore: In Punjabi, Sindhi and Rajasthani folk songs the 'koonj' is a messenger and a metaphor for a woman far from home, and the villagers of Khichan, Rajasthan, have fed wintering flocks grain for generations.
funFact: Unlike most cranes it often nests on dry ground far from water, laying its eggs among a few pebbles with almost no nest.

wiki.extract: The demoiselle crane is a species of crane found in central Eurosiberia, ranging from the Black Sea to Mongolia and Northeast China. There is also a small breeding population in Turkey. These cranes are migratory birds. Birds from western Eurasia will spend the winter in Africa while the birds from Asia, Mongolia and China will spend the winter in the Indian subcontinent. The bird is symbolically significant in the culture of India, where it is known as koonj or kurjaa.

summary: A snow-white crane with a red face and black wingtips that migrates from the Arctic tundra to wetlands in China. Its western flock, which wintered in India and Iran, has all but disappeared.
nativeRange: Breeds in Arctic Yakutia and western Siberia; the main population winters at Poyang Lake on the Yangtze in China; former wintering sites in Iran and India (Keoladeo)
abilities: Migrates around 5,000 km between Siberia and China
Digs for roots and tubers of aquatic plants in shallow water
Depends on very specific shallow wetlands, making it highly vulnerable

animal.diet: Roots, tubers and shoots of aquatic plants; also invertebrates and small animals in summer
animal.habitat: Open tundra wetlands in summer; shallow lakes and marshes in winter
animal.size: About 140 cm tall; wingspan about 210–230 cm
animal.behaviour: Feeds in shallow water by probing deep into the mud; more strictly aquatic than any other crane.
fieldMarks: All-white plumage with black primary feathers visible in flight
Bare brick-red skin on the face and forehead
Long reddish-pink legs and a long, slightly serrated bill
Juveniles are rusty-cinnamon
animal.voice: A soft, musical, flute-like 'koonk-koonk', unlike the harsh trumpeting of other cranes
animal.lookalikes: White stork has a red bill and black flight feathers along the whole rear wing; Great white egret and spoonbills are slimmer and lack a red face.
animal.whereToSee: Poyang Lake, Jiangxi, China, in winter; Momoge reserve in Jilin on migration
animal.season: Winter visitor to China (Nov–Mar); breeds in Siberia (May–Aug)

lore: Keoladeo (Bharatpur) in India was the famous wintering site of the western population until the last birds stopped arriving after 2002. The western flock's route passed through Afghanistan and Pakistan, where hunting took a heavy toll.
funFact: Nearly the entire world population, a few thousand birds, spends the winter at a single lake system in China.

wiki.extract: The Siberian crane, also known as the Siberian white crane or the snow crane, is a bird of the family Gruidae, the cranes. They are distinctive among the cranes: adults are nearly all snowy white, except for their black primary feathers that are visible in flight, and with two breeding populations in the Arctic tundra of western and eastern Russia. The eastern populations migrate during winter to China, while the western population winters in Iran and (formerly) in Bharatpur, India.

summary: The cricket of the hearth, a pale-brown chirper that has lived alongside people for thousands of years. Today it is the world's most widely farmed cricket, raised as pet food and increasingly as human food.
nativeRange: Probably south-western Asia; now worldwide in buildings and farms
abilities: Males chirp by rubbing a scraper on one forewing against a file on the other
Hears through ears on its front legs
Completes its life cycle in about two months in warm conditions
Converts feed into protein more efficiently than cattle

animal.diet: Omnivorous: plant matter, grain, scraps and dead insects
animal.habitat: Warm buildings, bakeries, rubbish tips and cricket farms
animal.behaviour: Males call at night to attract females and switch to a softer courtship song once a female is close.
fieldMarks: Light yellowish-brown body
Three dark bands across the top of the head
Long antennae and two long cerci at the tail; females with a long needle-like ovipositor
Wings cover the abdomen
animal.voice: A clear, repeated chirp, 'cree-cree', from males at night; softer ticking courtship song at close range.
animal.lookalikes: Field crickets (Gryllus) are larger and black or dark brown. Tropical house cricket (Gryllodes sigillatus) is smaller with short wings and a banded abdomen.
animal.whereToSee: Pet shops and cricket farms; occasionally in warm buildings and tips.
animal.season: Year-round indoors; outdoors in warm months

edibleParts: whole insect (roasted, fried or ground into powder)
edibilityNote: Sold as whole roasted crickets and cricket flour; approved as a novel food in the EU in 2022. People allergic to shellfish or dust mites may react.
lore: A cricket chirping on the hearth was long thought to bring luck in English homes, the idea behind Charles Dickens's novella The Cricket on the Hearth (1845).
funFact: Crickets' chirp rate rises with temperature, so a calling house cricket is a rough living thermometer.

wiki.extract: Acheta domesticus, commonly called the house cricket, is a species of cricket most likely native to Southwestern Asia, but between 1950 and 2000 it became the standard feeder insect for the pet and research industries and spread worldwide. They can be kept as pets themselves, as this has been the case in China and Japan.

Catesby was a pioneer in illustrating North American flora and fauna in their natural habitats and behaviors, a significant departure from the static poses common in earlier natural history works. His 'Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands' was

As a pioneer of modern zoology, Aldrovandi's work represents a monumental effort to document the natural world with empirical precision, using woodcuts that remained standard references for generations of naturalists.

summary: Not an eel at all but a knifefish, with organs of modified muscle that fill most of its body and can deliver shocks of several hundred volts. It breathes air through its mouth and leaps out of the water to shock threats directly.
nativeRange: Guiana Shield rivers of the Guianas, northern Brazil and southern Venezuela (since 2019 two other electric eel species are recognised elsewhere in the Amazon)
abilities: Generates high-voltage discharges from three electric organs to stun prey and deter predators; the closely related Volta's electric eel reaches about 860 V
Uses weak electric pulses to sense its surroundings and to communicate (electrolocation)
Fires rapid pulse trains that make hidden prey twitch and reveal itself
Gets most of its oxygen by gulping air, through a heavily vascularised mouth lining
Leaps out of the water and presses its chin against a threat to send current straight into it

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crustaceans and amphibians; juveniles eat invertebrates
animal.habitat: Slow, muddy or rocky streams, pools and swamps, often in oxygen-poor water
animal.lifespan: Poorly known in the wild; 15–20+ years in captivity
animal.size: Up to about 2 m and 20 kg
animal.behaviour: Rises to gulp air every few minutes. Males build foam nests from saliva in the dry season and guard the young, and in Volta's electric eel groups have been seen herding and shocking fish together.
fieldMarks: Long, cylindrical, scaleless body; dark grey-brown to olive above, often with an orange or reddish throat
No dorsal, pelvic or tail fins; a long anal fin runs along most of the underside and drives swimming
Flattened head with small eyes; vent far forward, just behind the head
Regularly surfaces to gulp air
animal.lookalikes: Volta's electric eel (E. voltai) of the Brazilian Shield and Vari's electric eel (E. varii) of the Amazon lowlands look nearly identical and are separated mainly by skull shape, DNA and range. True eels (Anguilla) have dorsal and tail fins, and swamp eels (Synbranchidae) lack the long anal fin.
animal.whereToSee: Rivers of the Guiana Shield in Suriname, French Guiana and Guyana; public aquaria worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the dry season

lore: In 1800 Alexander von Humboldt watched fishermen in the Venezuelan Llanos drive horses into a pool so electric eels would exhaust their charge on them before being caught. Michael Faraday used an electric eel in London in 1838 to show that animal electricity is the same as ordinary electricity.
funFact: The electric eel's organs contain thousands of stacked cells called electrocytes. Each makes only about 0.15 V, but connected in series they add up to hundreds of volts.

wiki.extract: Electrophorus electricus is the best-known species of electric eel. It is a South American electric fish. Until the discovery of two additional species in 2019, the genus was classified as the monotypic, with this species the only one in the genus. Despite the name, it is not an eel, but rather a knifefish. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.

summary: Europe's largest land snail and the classic escargot de Bourgogne. It seals itself in for winter behind a chalky door and can live for 20 years.
nativeRange: Central and south-eastern Europe; introduced in Britain (probably in Roman times), Scandinavia and elsewhere
abilities: Seals its shell in winter with a thick, chalky epiphragm
Shoots a calcium 'love dart' into its partner during courtship
Hermaphrodite: each snail both gives and receives sperm
Can live about 20 years or more

animal.diet: Green plants, fallen leaves and fruit
animal.habitat: Lime-rich soils: chalk and limestone grassland, open woods, hedgerows and vineyards
animal.lifespan: Often 6–10 years in the wild; up to about 20 years or more
animal.size: Shell about 4–5 cm high and wide
animal.behaviour: Before winter it buries itself in soil and seals the shell opening, slowing its heartbeat and breathing until spring.
fieldMarks: Large, globular shell, creamy-buff to light brown
Faint, broad, pale brownish bands
Body pale grey-cream with a coarse, net-like texture
Lip of the shell only slightly thickened
animal.lookalikes: Garden snail (Cornu aspersum) is smaller with a glossy brown shell mottled in darker bands. Turkish snail (Helix lucorum) has bold, dark-brown bands.
animal.whereToSee: Chalk downs of southern England (e.g. North Downs, Chilterns) and limestone country across central Europe after rain.
animal.season: Active Apr–Oct; hibernates in winter

edibilityNote: Eaten as escargots after purging and cooking. Wild snails are protected in Britain and several other countries, so commercial supplies are farmed or imported.
lore: Pliny the Elder credited Fulvius Lippinus with founding the first snail parks near Tarquinia in the 1st century BCE, fattening snails for Roman tables.
funFact: Courtship can last hours, the pair circling and caressing each other before one fires its chalky love dart.

wiki.extract: Helix pomatia, known as the Roman snail, Burgundy snail, or escargot, is a species of large, air-breathing stylommatophoran land snail belonging to the family Helicidae and native to Europe. It is characterized by a globular brown shell.

plates.author: Conrad Gessner

plates.long: This prominent woodcut depicts a 'Cochlea rugosa', characterized by its heavy ribbing and spiral structure. It represents the pinnacle of 16th-century scientific illustration, combining artistic skill with observational accuracy.

plates.title: Georg Wolfgang Knorr; Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch — Schnecken und Muscheln (1770)
plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr; Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch

plates.long: A detailed scientific plate from the 18th century depicting various gastropod shells, including specimens labeled as 'Cochlea lunaris major' and 'Gold-Mund.' This illustration reflects the Enlightenment-era interest in cataloging and classifying the natural world with artistic precision and scientific accuracy.

plates.title: Books on Marine Fishes
plates.author: Guillaume Rondelet
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a large spiral snail shell (Cochlea).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a large spiral snail shell, which Guillaume Rondelet identifies as a species historically used in the context of oil (oleario usu). As part of his seminal work on marine life, this illustration exemplifies the 16th-century shift toward empirical observation and the systematic categorization of the natural world.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Woodcut of a slug (Cochlea nuda) showing its body and eye-stalks.
plates.long: This 1586 woodcut from Conrad Gessner’s 'Historiae Animalium' depicts a 'naked snail' or slug, emphasizing its distinct eye-stalks and textured mantle. As a foundational work in Renaissance zoology, Gessner’s illustrations represent a pivotal shift toward empirical observation and the systematic categorization of the natural world.

summary: A slow, beaded black-and-pink venomous lizard of the North American deserts, spending most of its life underground. A hormone from its saliva inspired the diabetes drug exenatide, an early member of the family of drugs that later includes semaglutide.
nativeRange: Southwestern United States (Arizona, southern Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, California) and northwestern Mexico (Sonora, Sinaloa)
abilities: Delivers venom by chewing, from glands in its lower jaw; bites are very painful
Stores fat in its thick tail, letting it survive months without food
Can eat a third of its body weight in one meal
Its saliva contains exendin-4, which led to the drug exenatide (approved 2005)

animal.diet: Bird and reptile eggs, nestling birds and baby rodents
animal.habitat: Rocky desert hillsides, desert washes, scrub
animal.lifespan: ~20 years in the wild; up to ~30 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Spends about 90% of its life in burrows, coming out mainly in spring to raid nests. Bites are rare and come from handling. It clamps on and chews. The bite is very painful and causes swelling and sometimes low blood pressure, but deaths are almost unknown. Remove the lizard, wash the wound and go to hospital. Do not cut or suck the bite.
fieldMarks: Bead-like scales in black with pink, orange or yellow patches or bands
Heavy body with a short, fat tail
Blunt, rounded head and small eyes
Slow, waddling walk
animal.lookalikes: The Mexican beaded lizard (H. horridum) is larger and darker, mostly yellowish and black, and lives further south. Chuckwallas are flat and grey-brown, with no beaded pattern.
animal.whereToSee: Sonoran Desert around Tucson and Phoenix, Arizona (Saguaro National Park); southwestern Utah; Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum
animal.season: Most active April–June; mostly inactive in winter

lore: In 1952 Arizona protected the Gila monster by law, making it among the first venomous animals to receive legal protection in the United States. Its common name refers to the Gila River basin.
funFact: Endocrinologist John Eng discovered exendin-4 in Gila monster venom in 1992.

ancestors.common: Glass, alligator, monitor lizards and allies

wiki.extract: The Gila monster is a species of venomous lizard native to the Southwestern United States and the northwestern Mexican state of Sonora. It is a heavy, slow-moving reptile, up to 22 in (56 cm) long, and it is the only venomous lizard native to the United States. The Gila monster is sluggish in nature, so it is not generally dangerous and very rarely poses a real threat to humans, though the bite is painful. Nonetheless, it has a fearsome reputation and is sometimes killed despite the species being protected by state law in Arizona.

plates.title: History of Monsters
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: A large woodcut of a demon-shaped sea monster with a horned head, human-like torso, and a long fish tail.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Monstrum marinum Daemoniforme,' or demon-shaped sea monster, from Ulisse Aldrovandi's encyclopedic work on monsters. The creature combines human-like musculature with a horned, demonic head and a powerful, scaly fish tail, reflecting the 17th-century fascination with the boundaries between the known and the supernatural in the natural world. Such illustrations served both a

plates.title: History of Monsters
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Woodcut of a 'Sea Bishop' monster with a mitre-like head and scaly body.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Sea Bishop,' a legendary marine creature reported to have been found in the Baltic Sea. Ulisse Aldrovandi's inclusion of such creatures in his 'Monstrorum historia' illustrates the early modern effort to categorize all aspects of nature, including those that blurred the lines between the human, the animal, and the divine.

plates.title: Louis Renard — Poissons, ecrevisses et crabes (1754)
plates.author: Louis Renard
plates.desc: A hand-colored engraving of a mermaid-like creature, described as a 'monster similar to a Siren.'
plates.long: This fantastical illustration depicts a 'Siren' or mermaid, purportedly caught off the coast of Borneo and kept alive in a tub for several days. It reflects the 18th-century fascination with exotic and monstrous sea creatures, where the boundaries between scientific observation and myth were often blurred.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: A dried and manipulated ray or skate, fashioned to look like a winged dragon or sea monster, known as a Jenny Haniver.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Jenny Haniver,' a dried ray or skate that has been cut and manipulated to resemble a winged dragon or humanoid sea creature. Such specimens were often sold to sailors and collectors as curiosities, reflecting the early modern fascination with the monstrous and the marvelous in the natural world.

plates.title: Ulyssis Aldrovandi ... serpentum et draconum historiae libri duo
plates.author: Ambrosini, Bartolommeo
plates.desc: A woodcut of a 'Jenny Haniver,' a dried ray or skate manipulated to resemble a small dragon or sea monster.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Draco ex Raia effictus,' or a dragon fashioned from a ray. Such objects, known as Jenny Hanivers, were created by drying and carving skates or rays to resemble mythical creatures, serving as popular curiosities in early modern cabinets of wonder and natural history collections.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: A woodcut illustration depicting a large sea monster or eel-like creature with a human-like face in the upper right. Below, two spotted fish are shown. In the foreground, a man in medieval dress and a hood sits on a bench or shore, looking toward the water.
plates.long: A compelling woodcut depicting a man observing aquatic life, including a fantastical sea monster with a human-like face. This illustration reflects the transition between medieval folklore and early modern scientific observation in natural history texts.

plates.title: Cosmographey: das ist Beschreibung aller Laender
plates.author: Münster, Sebastian
plates.desc: A large sea monster or whale devouring a human figure.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a formidable sea monster, identified in the text as a whale (Walfisch), shown in the act of swallowing a person. Such illustrations reflect the 16th-century fascination with the wonders and dangers of the northern seas.

plates.title: Garden of Health (Hortus Sanitatis)
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Composite woodcut illustration featuring a bird (Pavo) and a sea monster with a canine head (Pristis).
plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1491 edition of Hortus Sanitatis depicts a bird-like creature and a fish swimming in water, illustrating the era's fascination with aquatic hybrids. As one of the earliest printed encyclopedias of natural history, Jacob Meydenbach's work is significant for its use of visual aids to categorize the natural and mythical worlds. The illustration reflects the transiti

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Woodcut of a scaly sea monster or dragon (Draco marinus).
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Draco marinus' (sea dragon), a creature described in the 'Ortus sanitatis' as a fierce marine monster. The illustration captures the transition from medieval bestiaries to early modern natural history, blending folklore with attempts at biological classification.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Woodcut depicting aquatic life including a sea monster, a waterfowl, and a conger eel.
plates.long: A composite scene shows three aquatic creatures: a large-headed sea monster emerging from waves, a spotted duck floating in the center, and a long conger eel swimming at the bottom. The woodcut illustrates the diversity of marine life as understood in the late 15th century.

summary: A small, spotted reef shark that 'walks' across tide pools on its paired fins and survives hours of near-zero oxygen when the tide falls.
nativeRange: Shallow reefs of northern Australia and southern New Guinea
abilities: Walks on pectoral and pelvic fins between pools, even across exposed reef
Tolerates severe hypoxia for hours by shutting down non-essential brain activity
Is studied as a model for stroke and climate-related low-oxygen tolerance

animal.diet: Worms, crabs, shrimps and small fish
animal.habitat: Shallow reef flats and tide pools, rarely below 10 m
animal.size: Up to about 1 m; usually under 70 cm
animal.behaviour: Hunts at dusk and night by poking its snout into sand and crevices; hides under coral by day.
fieldMarks: Large black spot ringed in white behind each pectoral fin (the 'epaulette')
Slender body with a long tail
Small scattered dark spots on a pale brown background
Short barbels near the nostrils
animal.lookalikes: Other walking sharks (Hemiscyllium spp. of New Guinea and Indonesia) differ in spot pattern; brownbanded bamboo shark lacks the epaulette spot.
animal.whereToSee: Heron Island and Lady Elliot Island (Great Barrier Reef) reef flats at low tide
animal.season: Year-round; best at dusk low tides

lore: Its common name refers to the military shoulder ornament its eyespot resembles.
funFact: Its fin-walking gait resembles that of salamanders, so it is studied for clues to how early vertebrates moved onto land.

wiki.extract: The epaulette shark is a species of longtailed carpet shark of the family Hemiscylliidae, found in shallow, tropical waters off Australia and New Guinea. The common name of this shark comes from the very large, white-margined black spot behind each pectoral fin, which are reminiscent of military epaulettes. A small species, the epaulette shark has a slender body with a short head and broad, paddle-shaped paired fins. The caudal peduncle comprises over half the shark's length. Adults are light brown above, with scattered darker spots and indistinct saddles.

summary: The famous snake-fighting mongoose of South Asia, a grizzled grey hunter of gardens, scrub and fields. Speed, a thick coat and modified acetylcholine receptors that resist cobra neurotoxins let it tackle venomous snakes, though most of its diet is rodents, insects and lizards.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, west through Afghanistan and Iran to the Arabian Gulf
abilities: Partially resistant to snake neurotoxins, owing to altered receptor proteins
Moves so fast it can dodge a striking cobra, then bites the back of the head
Hunts by darting in and out of reach, often seizing prey such as rats and lizards with a single bite to the head

animal.diet: Rodents, insects, snakes, lizards, birds, eggs, carrion and fruit
animal.habitat: Open forest, scrub, cultivated land and edges of villages and towns
animal.lifespan: About 7–8 years in the wild; to 12 in captivity
animal.size: Body 36–45 cm, tail 45 cm; about 0.9–1.7 kg
animal.behaviour: Diurnal, unlike many mongooses; usually alone or in pairs. Fluffs its fur to look larger when facing a snake.
fieldMarks: Low, long-bodied grey animal with a grizzled, salt-and-pepper coat
Tail as long as the body, tapering, with a pale or reddish tip
Reddish legs and face around the eyes
Runs with tail held out or slightly raised; tracks show five toes with claws
animal.lookalikes: Small Indian mongoose (Urva auropunctata) is smaller with golden-flecked fur; ruddy mongoose (Urva smithii) has a black tail tip; stripe-necked mongoose has a black neck stripe. Squirrels have bushy tails and climb.
animal.whereToSee: Common in gardens, farmland and parks across India and Pakistan; Sariska and Ranthambore (Rajasthan); Gir (Gujarat); Margalla Hills (Islamabad)
animal.season: Resident; active in daylight year-round

lore: Kubera, Hindu god of wealth, and the Buddhist Jambhala are depicted holding a mongoose that spits jewels. The Panchatantra tells of a loyal mongoose killed by a Brahmin who mistook the blood of a slain snake for that of his baby; Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is usually taken to be this species.
funFact: The English word 'mongoose' comes from Marathi/Telugu names such as mangūs and mungisa.

wiki.extract: The Indian grey mongoose or Asian grey mongoose is a mongoose species native to the Indian subcontinent and West Asia. It is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List.

plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: An ichneumon attacking a serpent and a hippopotamus standing by water.
plates.long: The upper portion shows a green dragon-like ichneumon biting a spotted serpent, while the lower portion depicts a hippopotamus as a horse-like creature near a body of water. These images represent the medieval understanding of exotic and predatory animals.

plates.author: Unknown

plates.long: A two-part woodcut illustrating the 'Enidros' (likely an ichneumon or mongoose) and the 'Erinacius' (hedgehog). These illustrations served as vital visual aids in the 'Hortus Sanitatis', one of the most influential early printed encyclopedias of the natural world.

plates.author: Conrad Gessner

plates.long: This woodcut depicts an ichneumon, or Egyptian mongoose, a creature famously known in antiquity for its enmity with crocodiles. Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium' was one of the first modern attempts to systematically catalog all known animals, blending observation with classical lore.

plates.title: Ten Books of Exotic Things
plates.author: Carolus Clusius
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of an ichneumon (mongoose)
plates.long: This woodcut depicts an ichneumon, a type of mongoose native to Egypt, as described in Pierre Belon's natural history observations. The illustration captures the animal's elongated body and sharp features, serving as a visual record for early modern scholars studying exotic fauna.

plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Woodcut depicting two small mammals, likely an Enidros (ichneumon) and a rodent.
plates.long: Two small animals are shown stacked vertically within a rectangular frame. The top creature has a pointed snout and short tail, while the bottom creature features a large, bushy tail and rounded ears.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book I: On Viviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Woodcut of an elongated quadruped, likely another representation of an ichneumon or a similar small carnivore.
plates.long: A secondary illustration of an ichneumon, showing the animal in a horizontal profile. Gessner often included multiple depictions of the same animal to capture different accounts or physical characteristics described by various historical sources.

summary: A nearly hairless, buck-toothed rodent that lives underground in East Africa in colonies run like an insect hive, with a single breeding queen. It is also extraordinarily long-lived and resistant to cancer, making it a major subject of ageing research.
nativeRange: Arid grasslands of Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya
abilities: Lives more than 37 years, about ten times longer than a similar-sized mouse
Survives about 18 minutes without oxygen by switching to fructose-based metabolism
Very rarely develops cancer
Feels no pain from acid or from capsaicin, the burning compound in chilli
Digs tunnels with its large front teeth, which sit outside its lips so it can dig without swallowing soil

animal.diet: Herbivore: large underground tubers and roots
animal.habitat: Underground tunnel systems up to several kilometres long in hard, dry soil
animal.behaviour: A colony of up to ~300 has one queen and a few breeding males; the rest are workers and soldiers. Each colony has its own dialect of chirps.
fieldMarks: Almost hairless, wrinkled pink skin
Large protruding front teeth
Tiny eyes
Lives underground in colonies
animal.voice: Chirps and squeaks; a rich vocal repertoire
animal.season: Resident; almost never seen above ground

lore: Eduard Rüppell described the species in 1842. In 1981 Jennifer Jarvis showed that it is eusocial, the first mammal shown to live like social insects.
funFact: Unlike most mammals, it can barely regulate its own body temperature, so colonies huddle together or move to warmer tunnels.

wiki.extract: The naked mole-rat, also known as the sand puppy, is a burrowing rodent native to the Horn of Africa and parts of Kenya, notably in Somali regions. It is the only species in the genus Heterocephalus.

summary: A huge, semi-aquatic grazer that spends its days in rivers and lakes and comes ashore at night to graze. Despite its plant diet it is one of Africa's most dangerous animals to people.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, in rivers, lakes and swamps from Senegal and Sudan to South Africa; feral population in Colombia
abilities: Secretes a red 'blood sweat' (hipposudoric acid) that acts as sunscreen and inhibits bacteria
Holds its breath for about five minutes, walking or bouncing along river bottoms instead of swimming
Moves huge amounts of grass-derived nutrients into rivers in its dung, fuelling fish and other life
Opens its mouth to about 150° to show tusks up to ~50 cm long

animal.diet: Herbivore: grazes up to ~40 kg of grass a night
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes and swamps beside grassland
animal.size: Males usually 1,500–3,200 kg; up to ~1.6 m at the shoulder
animal.behaviour: Males mark territories by spinning their tails to spray dung. Groups of dozens crowd together in the water by day.
fieldMarks: Huge, barrel-shaped body
Grey-brown skin with pink areas
Large head with eyes and nostrils on top
Spends days in water
animal.voice: Loud wheezing honks and grunts
animal.lookalikes: Pygmy hippo is smaller and lives in West African forests. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Chobe River (Botswana), South Luangwa (Zambia) and Murchison Falls (Uganda)
animal.season: Resident

lore: In ancient Egypt the hippo goddess Taweret protected women in childbirth, and blue faience hippos were placed in tombs. Many scholars think the Behemoth of the Book of Job was inspired by the hippopotamus.
funFact: Pablo Escobar's four hippos in Colombia have grown into a wild herd of over 150, now the largest hippo population outside Africa.

wiki.extract: The hippopotamus, often shortened to hippo, further qualified as the common hippopotamus, Nile hippopotamus and river hippopotamus, is a large semiaquatic mammal native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is one of only two extant species in the family Hippopotamidae, the other being the pygmy hippopotamus. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for "river horse" (ἱπποπόταμος).

plates.long: This engraving from Athanasius Kircher's 1667 work depicts a hippopotamus, referred to in the text as a 'Sea Horse' (Equus Marinus). Set against a coastal backdrop featuring a European galleon and palm trees, the image reflects the early modern European fascination with exotic wildlife encountered during global expeditions. The presence of Chinese characters above the animal underscores Kircher's

plates.title: Georg Wolfgang Knorr — Deliciae naturae selectae (1771)
plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a large mammal, likely a tapir or stylized hippopotamus, in a landscape with a pyramid.
plates.long: A large brown mammal with a short snout stands on a sandy bank. The background features a river, a palm tree, and a pyramid, suggesting an exotic or African setting.

plates.title: Garden of Health (Hortus Sanitatis)

plates.desc: Woodcut of a hippopotamus (Ypotamus) in a landscape, hand-colored.
plates.long: This woodcut represents a hippopotamus, referred to as 'Ypotamus' in the text. The artist's interpretation, featuring a horse-like body and tusks, demonstrates how exotic animals were often reconstructed from textual descriptions in early printed herbals.

plates.long: A large quadruped with a thick mane and cloven hooves stands among rocks. Identified in the text as a 'Potamus' or river horse, the creature is depicted based on historical accounts rather than direct observation.

plates.desc: An engraving of a hippopotamus, showing its body and two different views of its head, accompanied by Chinese characters.
plates.long: This engraving from Michał Boym's 'Flora Sinensis' (1656) depicts a hippopotamus, labeled with the Chinese characters '海馬' (Hǎimǎ, literally 'sea horse'). As one of the first European works to document Chinese natural history, Boym's book provided Western audiences with some of their earliest visual and descriptive accounts of East Asian flora and fauna.

plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of a creature identified as a hippopotamus, depicted with horse-like features and cloven hooves.
plates.long: Labeled as an 'Ipotamus' (hippopotamus), this creature is depicted with horse-like features and cloven hooves, illustrating the reliance on classical descriptions over direct observation in early natural history. The hand-applied color adds vibrancy to this imaginative interpretation of African wildlife, typical of 15th-century European encyclopedias.

Featured in Conrad Gessner’s 1586 zoological work, the illustration reflects the Renaissance practice of blending natural history with Egyptian symbolism and classical allegory. summary: A blood-feeding freshwater leech used in medicine for over two thousand years. Once collected in such numbers that it vanished from much of Europe, it is again used in hospitals to rescue reattached fingers and skin flaps.
nativeRange: Europe, from Britain and southern Scandinavia east to the Urals
abilities: Saliva contains hirudin, a powerful anticoagulant, plus anaesthetic and vessel-widening compounds
Three jaws with many tiny teeth leave a Y-shaped bite
Can take several times its own weight in blood in one meal
Can go months between meals

uses.use: Leeches cleared by the US FDA in 2004 as a medical device to relieve venous congestion in reattached digits and skin flaps
Bloodletting by leeches to rebalance the humours, at its peak in 19th-century France
Leech therapy (jalaukavacharana; irsal-e-alaq) for skin disease, abscesses and joint pain, using local leech species

medicinal.cautions: Use only under medical supervision: bites bleed for hours and can transmit Aeromonas bacterial infection, so patients usually receive preventive antibiotics. Wild collection is restricted under CITES and national laws.

animal.diet: Blood of amphibians, fish, birds and mammals; young leeches feed on frogs and tadpoles
animal.habitat: Warm, shallow, weedy ponds and marshes, often trampled by livestock
animal.size: About 10–12 cm when extended, up to about 20 cm
animal.behaviour: It senses ripples and warmth in the water and swims towards potential hosts with an undulating motion.
fieldMarks: Flattened, segmented, olive-green to brown body
Pair of reddish or orange stripes along the back broken by black spots
Spotted, greenish-yellow underside
Sucker at each end
animal.lookalikes: Mediterranean medicinal leech (Hirudo verbana), widely sold for medical use, differs in stripe pattern and has a plainer underside. Horse leech (Haemopis sanguisuga) is dull grey-brown and cannot bite through human skin.
animal.whereToSee: Rare; scattered ponds in Britain (e.g. Romney Marsh, New Forest, Lake District) and eastern Europe.
animal.season: Active in warm water, Jun–Sep

lore: The Old English word 'læce' meant both physician and leech. In the 1830s France imported tens of millions of leeches a year for bloodletting, emptying wetlands across Europe.
funFact: The anticoagulant drugs bivalirudin and lepirudin were developed from hirudin, the protein in leech saliva.

summary: The most widespread swallow in the world, breeding across the Northern Hemisphere and wintering in the south. Its arrival has marked spring for farmers since antiquity.
nativeRange: Breeds across North America, Europe, North Africa and Asia; winters in South America, Africa, South Asia and Australasia
abilities: Migrates up to ~10,000 km, e.g. from Britain to South Africa
Catches insects in fast, low, agile flight
Builds cup nests from hundreds of mud pellets carried in its bill
Females prefer males with longer, more symmetrical tail streamers

animal.diet: Flying insects
animal.habitat: Open country near water, nesting in barns and under eaves
animal.behaviour: Pairs often return to the same barn each year, and earlier-brood young help feed later broods.
fieldMarks: Glossy steel-blue upperparts and breast band
Red forehead and throat
Long, deeply forked tail streamers
Swift, low, twisting flight
animal.voice: A cheerful twittering song with a grating trill; call a sharp 'vit'
animal.lookalikes: House martin has a white rump and short forked tail. Sand martin is brown. Red-rumped swallow has a pale rufous rump.
animal.whereToSee: Farmyards, stables and open country near water
animal.season: Europe and North America: summer visitor Apr–Sep

lore: Aristotle wrote that 'one swallow does not make a spring', and Gilbert White in the 18th century still wondered if swallows hibernated in mud. Sailors' swallow tattoos traditionally marked 5,000 nautical miles travelled.
funFact: It is the national bird of Austria and Estonia.

wiki.extract: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica. It is a distinctive passerine bird with blue upperparts and a long, deeply forked tail. In Anglophone Europe, it is just called the swallow; in northern Europe, it is the only member of family Hirundinidae called a "swallow" rather than a "martin".

Published in Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium', it represents the 16th-century movement toward empirical observation and the systematic visual documentation of the natural world.

summary: The largest living primate, found in two subspecies: Grauer's gorilla of the lowland forests of eastern DR Congo, and the famous mountain gorilla of the Virunga volcanoes and Bwindi. Mountain gorillas, studied since Dian Fossey's work in the 1960s, have increased to just over 1,000 and were downlisted from Critically Endangered to Endangered in 2018, while the species as a whole remains Critically Endangered because Grauer's gorillas have declined sharply.
nativeRange: Virunga Mountains (Rwanda, Uganda, DR Congo), Bwindi Impenetrable Forest (Uganda) and eastern DR Congo lowland and montane forests
abilities: Silverback males can weigh over 200 kg and are several times stronger than people
Builds a fresh nest of leaves and branches to sleep in every night
Disperses seeds and opens gaps in forest through feeding and movement

animal.diet: Mainly leaves, stems, shoots and pith (wild celery, nettles, bamboo shoots); fruit when available; occasional ants
animal.habitat: Montane and bamboo forest (mountain gorillas, up to about 4,000 m) and lowland rainforest (Grauer's)
animal.size: Males 1.5–1.8 m standing, 140–220 kg; females about half as heavy
animal.behaviour: Lives in groups led by one or more silverbacks. Males display by standing upright and beating their chests with cupped hands, a sound carrying over 1 km.
fieldMarks: Very large black ape; mountain gorillas have long, thick, black hair
Adult males with a silver saddle on the back
Massive head with a prominent sagittal crest in males; broad nostrils
Signs: night nests on the ground with dung, trails of trampled vegetation and broken celery stems; knuckle prints
animal.voice: Chest-beating 'pok-pok' drumming, hoots, roars and soft, contented 'belch' grumbles between group members.
animal.lookalikes: Western gorillas (Gorilla gorilla) of West and Central Africa are browner-grey, with a reddish crown and shorter hair. Chimpanzees are much smaller, with large ears and long arms.
animal.whereToSee: Volcanoes National Park (Rwanda); Bwindi Impenetrable and Mgahinga Gorilla national parks (Uganda); Virunga National Park (DR Congo); Kahuzi-Biega National Park (DR Congo, Grauer's gorilla)
animal.season: Resident; trekking runs year-round, drier months June–September and December–February are easiest

lore: Dian Fossey founded the Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda in 1967 and wrote 'Gorillas in the Mist' (1983) before her murder in 1985. Rwanda's annual Kwita Izina ceremony names each newborn mountain gorilla.
funFact: The species is named for German officer Robert von Beringe, who shot two on Mount Sabyinyo in 1902, the first known to science.

wiki.extract: The eastern gorilla is a critically endangered species of the genus Gorilla and the largest living primate. At present, the species is subdivided into two subspecies. There are 6,800 eastern lowland gorillas or Grauer's gorillas and 1,000 mountain gorillas. Illegal hunting threatens the species.

summary: The largest living primate, a mostly gentle, plant-eating ape of the Congo Basin and Nigeria–Cameroon forests. Families centre on a silverback male who leads, mediates and protects the group.
nativeRange: Western equatorial Africa: Cameroon, Gabon, Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Angola (Cabinda); Cross River gorillas on the Nigeria–Cameroon border
abilities: Beats its chest with cupped hands, a sound that can carry about 1 km; in mountain gorillas, the pitch of the beats has been shown to signal the male's body size
Wild western gorillas have been seen testing water depth with a walking stick
Captive gorillas such as Koko learned hundreds of signs
Disperses large seeds of many forest trees

animal.diet: Herbivore: fruit, leaves, stems, pith; also termites and ants
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest and swamp clearings (bais)
animal.size: Males 140–200 kg and up to ~1.7 m standing; females 70–100 kg
animal.behaviour: Each evening every gorilla builds a nest of leaves and branches on the ground or in a tree. Western gorillas travel further each day than mountain gorillas, following fruiting trees.
fieldMarks: Very large ape with dark grey-brown hair
Adult males have a silver back and a crest on the head
Brownish crown, often reddish
Lives in groups led by a silverback
animal.voice: Chest-beating, hoots and grunts
animal.lookalikes: Eastern gorillas (mountain and Grauer's) are darker and longer-haired and live far to the east.
animal.whereToSee: Odzala-Kokoua (Republic of Congo), Dzanga-Sangha (Central African Republic) and Loango (Gabon), with habituated-group permits
animal.season: Resident

lore: The Carthaginian Hanno's Periplus (c. 5th century BCE) tells of hairy wild people on a West African island that interpreters called 'Gorillai'. Thomas Savage and Jeffries Wyman described the gorilla for science in 1847 and borrowed that name.
funFact: Gorillas hum and 'sing' while they eat, especially when the food is good.

wiki.extract: The western gorilla is a great ape found in Africa, one of two species of the hominine genus Gorilla. Large and robust with males weighing around 168 kilograms (370 lb), the species is found in a region of midwest Africa, geographically isolated from the eastern gorilla. The hair of the western species is significantly lighter in colour.

summary: One of humans' two closest living relatives, found only south of the Congo River in DR Congo. Unlike chimpanzees, bonobo societies are led by alliances of females, and they defuse tension with sexual and social contact rather than violence. They will even share food with strangers.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests of the Congo Basin south of the Congo River, DR Congo only
abilities: Shares DNA with humans at roughly the same level (about 98.7%) as chimpanzees
Shows empathy, consolation and sharing with unfamiliar individuals in experiments
Captive bonobo Kanzi learned to communicate with hundreds of lexigram symbols

animal.diet: Fruit, leaves, pith, seeds, insects and occasionally small mammals
animal.habitat: Humid lowland forest and mosaic forest–savanna south of the Congo River
animal.size: 70–83 cm sitting; males about 39 kg, females about 31 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in fission–fusion communities of 30–80. Females form strong bonds and collectively dominate males.
fieldMarks: Slender ape with long legs and a relatively small, round head
Black face from birth and pink lips
Long black hair parted neatly in the middle on the crown
Signs: night nests high in trees; high-pitched calls distinguish them from chimpanzee pant-hoots
animal.voice: Higher-pitched hoots and whistles than chimpanzees, including a sharp, bird-like 'hi-hi' call.
animal.lookalikes: Chimpanzee (north of the Congo River) is more robust, with a paler face in youth, larger ears and no central hair parting. Ranges do not overlap.
animal.whereToSee: Lola ya Bonobo Sanctuary (near Kinshasa); Wamba and the Luo Scientific Reserve; LuiKotale and Salonga National Park; Lomako-Yokokala Faunal Reserve (all DR Congo)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The bonobo was recognised as a distinct species only in 1929, from a skull in a Belgian museum. In the Wamba region, a Mongandu taboo against eating bonobos, who are seen as ancestral kin, helped protect them.
funFact: Bonobos were not recognised as a species until 1929, more than 150 years after chimpanzees, because they look so similar.

wiki.extract: The bonobo, also historically called the pygmy chimpanzee, is the smallest species of great ape and one of the two making up the genus Pan. While bonobos are today recognized as a distinct species, they were initially thought to be a subspecies of Pan troglodytes, because of the physical similarities between the two species. Taxonomically, members of the chimpanzee/bonobo subtribe Panina—composed entirely by the genus Pan—are collectively termed panins.

summary: Along with the bonobo, the chimpanzee is humanity's closest living relative, sharing about 98–99% of our DNA. Different chimp communities have their own traditions of tool use, grooming and hunting, passed on by learning.
nativeRange: Equatorial Africa from Senegal and Guinea to Uganda and western Tanzania
abilities: Strips twigs into probes to fish termites from mounds
Cracks hard nuts with stone or wooden hammers on anvils, a practice dated to at least 4,300 years ago in Côte d'Ivoire
At Fongoli, Senegal, sharpens sticks into spears to stab bushbabies in tree hollows
Hunts colobus monkeys cooperatively and shares the meat
Swallows rough leaves whole and chews bitter pith, behaviours linked to fighting parasites

animal.diet: Omnivore: mainly ripe fruit, plus leaves, seeds, insects, honey and meat
animal.habitat: Rainforest, swamp forest and savanna woodland
animal.lifespan: 40–50 years in the wild; 60+ in captivity
animal.size: Males 40–70 kg, females 27–50 kg; ~1–1.7 m standing
animal.behaviour: Communities split into shifting subgroups by day and patrol their borders. Males form alliances, and violent conflicts between communities have been recorded.
fieldMarks: Ape with black hair and bare face, hands and feet
Prominent ears
Walks on knuckles
Lives in communities
animal.voice: Loud 'pant-hoots' that rise to a scream; drums on tree buttresses
animal.lookalikes: Bonobo is slimmer with a smaller head, pink lips and hair parted in the middle; it lives only south of the Congo River.
animal.whereToSee: Gombe and Mahale (Tanzania), Kibale (Uganda), with permit-led tracking groups
animal.season: Resident

lore: Edward Tyson's 1699 anatomy of a 'Pygmie', titled Orang-Outang, sive Homo Sylvestris, was in fact a young chimpanzee and was the first scientific dissection of an ape. In 1960 Jane Goodall saw the Gombe chimpanzee David Greybeard fish for termites, overturning the idea that only humans make tools.
funFact: Chimpanzees outperform human students on some quick short-term memory tests for numbers flashed on a screen.

wiki.extract: The chimpanzee, commonly abbreviated to chimp, is a medium-sized great ape species found in the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa. It has four confirmed subspecies and a fifth proposed one. The chimpanzee shares the genus Pan with the bonobo. Evidence from fossils and DNA sequencing shows that the two species are humans' closest living relatives. The chimpanzee is bigger and more robust than the bonobo. It is covered in coarse black hair but has a bare face, fingers, toes, palms of the hands, and soles of the feet.

summary: A red-haired great ape of northern Sumatra's rainforests, the most tree-bound of all great apes. Mothers raise each infant for about eight to nine years, and young orangutans learn which plants to eat and which tools to make by watching them.
nativeRange: Northern Sumatra, Indonesia (mainly Aceh and North Sumatra, including the Leuser Ecosystem)
abilities: Uses sticks to pry nutritious seeds from spiny Neesia fruits without touching the irritating hairs
Builds a fresh sleeping nest of folded branches high in the canopy every night
A wild male, Rakus, was observed in 2022 chewing a medicinal liana and applying it to a facial wound, which then healed
Disperses the seeds of many rainforest trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit (especially figs), plus leaves, bark, insects; occasionally slow lorises
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest and peat swamp forest
animal.size: Males 70–90 kg, ~1.4 m tall standing, arm span over 2 m; females ~35–45 kg
animal.behaviour: Adult males develop broad cheek pads and give 'long calls' that carry about a kilometre through the forest. Births come about every 8–9 years, the longest interval of any mammal.
fieldMarks: Large ape with long, pale reddish-orange hair
Very long arms
Adult males develop broad cheek pads and a beard
Builds nests in trees
animal.voice: Flanged males give a loud, booming 'long call'
animal.lookalikes: Bornean orangutans are darker red with shorter hair; Tapanuli orangutans live in a small area of North Sumatra and have frizzier hair.
animal.whereToSee: Bukit Lawang and Ketambe in Gunung Leuser National Park, Sumatra, with licensed guides
animal.season: Resident

lore: The Dutch physician Jacobus Bontius described an 'Orang Outang' from the East Indies in 1658, and Linnaeus drew on such reports for his 'Homo troglodytes'. Sumatran orangutans were recognised as a species separate from Bornean ones in the late 20th century.
funFact: Rakus's wound treatment was the first systematically documented case of a wild animal treating its own wound with a plant known to contain medically active substances.

wiki.extract: The Sumatran orangutan is one of the three species of orangutans. Critically endangered, and found only in the north of the Indonesian island of Sumatra, it is rarer than the Bornean orangutan but more common than the recently identified Tapanuli orangutan, also found in Sumatra.

The figure is shown with characteristic long, feathered hair and carrying a torch, representing a blend of human and animalistic traits common in early modern scientific and mythological discourse. Such illustrations served to categorize the 'monstrous' and the 'other' in the expanding worl

summary: One of India's two apes (with the eastern hoolock), a long-armed gibbon of the forests of northeast India, Bangladesh and western Myanmar that swings through the canopy by its arms. Pairs greet each morning with loud duets that carry kilometres through the hills. Its range has shrunk sharply with forest clearance.
nativeRange: Northeast India south of the Brahmaputra, eastern Bangladesh and western Myanmar (west of the Chindwin River)
abilities: Moves by brachiation, swinging arm-over-arm and leaping gaps of several metres
Duets can be heard about 1–2 km away
Disperses seeds of many forest fruit trees

animal.diet: Mainly ripe fruits, especially figs; also leaves, flowers and insects
animal.habitat: Tall evergreen and semi-evergreen forest with a continuous canopy
animal.size: Head and body about 60–90 cm; 6–9 kg; no tail
animal.behaviour: Lives in small family groups of a pair and their young, defending a territory with song. Almost never comes to the ground.
fieldMarks: Silhouette in canopy: tailless ape with very long arms, swinging under branches
Adult males black with conspicuous white eyebrows
Adult females buff to golden-brown with a darker face ringed paler
Signs: loud morning duets, fruit drop under fig trees
animal.voice: Pairs duet in the early morning with escalating whooping calls, often rendered 'hoo-kau, hoo-kau', the female's notes rising into a climax.
animal.lookalikes: Eastern hoolock gibbon (east of the Chindwin, and in Arunachal Pradesh) is very similar; males have separated white brows and females paler. Monkeys such as capped langurs have long tails.
animal.whereToSee: Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary (Assam); Lawachara National Park (Bangladesh); Nokrek and Balpakram (Meghalaya); Dampa Tiger Reserve (Mizoram)
animal.season: Resident; best heard in early mornings, especially in the dry season

lore: Richard Harlan described the species in 1834 from Assam, using a local name for the animal. In Meghalaya, community-protected sacred groves still shelter some hoolock groups.
funFact: Hoolocks have 38 chromosomes, the fewest of any gibbon (others have 44–52), which is one reason they were placed in their own genus, Hoolock, in 2005.

wiki.extract: The western hoolock gibbon is a primate from the gibbon family, Hylobatidae. The species is found in Assam, Mizoram, and Meghalaya in India, Bangladesh, and Myanmar west of the Chindwin River.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a gibbon (猿) sitting on a rock, reaching out with its long arm towards a flying insect.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts a gibbon (yuan), a creature celebrated in Chinese culture for its agility and long limbs. The illustration captures the animal in a characteristic pose, reaching for an insect, demonstrating the era's commitment to cataloging the known world.

plates.long: A lively depiction of a 'Yuan' (gibbon), known for its exceptionally long arms. The illustration captures the animal in a characteristic reaching pose, a detail emphasized in the accompanying text which describes the unique anatomy of the primate's shoulders and arms.

plates.long: A woodcut illustration of a white gibbon (Baiyuan) from the Sancai Tuhui. The image captures the primate's characteristic long arms and expressive face, reflecting the era's approach to natural history documentation.

It is depicted in a semi-crouched walking posture with its long arms reaching toward the ground.
plates.long: This color engraving depicts a Lar Gibbon (Simia Lar), characterized by its dark fur and distinctive white facial ring and extremities. Created by Jean Baptiste Audebert for his 1800 treatise on monkeys, it represents a milestone in primatology for its anatomical accuracy and artistic quality.

plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a white gibbon with long arms raised.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a white gibbon (白猿), a primate celebrated in traditional Chinese culture for its agility and haunting calls. Featured in the 'Sancai Tuhui', a monumental Ming Dynasty encyclopedia, the illustration highlights the animal's exceptionally long arms, which were believed to allow it to swing effortlessly through the mountain canopy. Such images served as both scientific records and

summary: A pink-and-white mantis with petal-shaped legs that looks like a flower. It does not hide on orchids but sits in the open and lures pollinating insects to itself.
nativeRange: Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and nearby Southeast Asia
abilities: Aggressive mimicry of a generic flower that attracts pollinators
Lured more pollinators than real flowers in field experiments (O'Hanlon et al. 2014)
To bee and fly eyes its colour is hard to distinguish from real flowers
Can shift colour slightly between pink and white

animal.diet: Bees, flies, butterflies and other flower-visiting insects
animal.habitat: Shrubs and flowers in rainforest
animal.behaviour: Females are more than twice the size of males; tiny males avoid being eaten by approaching cautiously.
fieldMarks: White to pink mantis shaped like an orchid petal
Walking legs with broad, petal-like lobes
Females much larger than males
Sits motionless on or near flowers

lore: An 1879 account by the traveller James Hingston described a mantis from Java catching butterflies while posing as an orchid, fuelling Victorian fascination with mimicry.
funFact: Young nymphs are red and black, mimicking a foul-tasting assassin bug before they turn pink.

wiki.extract: Hymenopus coronatus is a mantis from the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. It is known by various common names, including walking flower mantis, orchid-blossom mantis and (pink) orchid mantis. It is one of several species known as flower mantises, a reference to their unique physical form and behaviour, which often involves moving with a "swaying" motion, as if being "blown" in the breeze. The species has evolved to mimic orchid flowers as a hunting and camouflaging strategy, "hiding" themselves in plain view and preying upon pollinating insects that visit the blooms. They then grab their prey with sudden speed.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a mantis shrimp, identified in the text as 'Squilla'. It is part of Guillaume Rondelet's landmark 1554 study of marine life, which combined Aristotelian tradition with direct observation, laying the groundwork for modern zoology.

It reflects the 16th-century effort to categorize and illustrate the natural world, often blending direct observation with traditional nomenclature from classical sources like Pliny.

Featured in Conrad Gessner's encyclopedic work, the illustration serves as a primary example of Renaissance natural history, where scholars combined classical Greek terminology with detailed anatomical observation. plates.author: Conrad Gessner; Thomas Moffet; Edward Wotton

plates.long: This plate from 'Insectorum sive Minimorum Animalium Theatrum' (1634) displays a diverse array of insects, including a prominent mantis and a large, coiled segmented worm. These illustrations represent the transition toward empirical observation in early modern science, documenting the morphology of species with meticulous detail.

The plate includes a spiny crab (Cancer spinosus), a striped spider crab (Cancer Aragnoides), a mantis shrimp (Squilla arenaria marina), and a large, anatomically precise hermit crab (Einsiedlerkrebs) shown outside its shell. Such illustrations were vital for the classificat

summary: A sleek, waxwing-like grey bird with a black mask, the only member of its family. It breeds in the river valleys and deserts of Iraq, Iran and Central Asia and winters in date palm oases around the Persian Gulf.
nativeRange: Breeds in Iraq, Iran, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan; winters in eastern Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, southern Iran and Pakistan, with strays to western India
abilities: Sole living member of the family Hypocoliidae
Feeds largely on dates and berries in winter roosts
Gathers in communal winter roosts in dense palm groves
Breeds in tamarisk and date palm scrub in hot lowland deserts

animal.diet: Fruits including dates, mulberries and berries; some insects
animal.habitat: Date palm groves, gardens and scrub along rivers in arid lands
animal.behaviour: Small parties move together between fruiting trees, often perching hidden in dense foliage and flying out to roosts at dawn.
fieldMarks: Smooth, pale grey plumage with a long tail
Male has a black mask that joins around the nape
Black tips to the primaries and a black tail tip
Female plainer brownish-grey with no mask
animal.voice: A soft, mewing 'whee-oo' and low chattering in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Great grey and southern grey shrikes have hooked bills and black-and-white wings. Bohemian waxwing has a crest and yellow tail tip and does not occur in the Gulf.
animal.whereToSee: Winter roosts in Bahrain, the Al-Ahsa oasis in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE.
animal.season: Winter visitor to Arabia Nov–Mar; summer visitor to breeding grounds

lore: Charles Lucien Bonaparte described it in 1850, and its relationships puzzled ornithologists for over a century until DNA studies placed it near the silky-flycatchers and waxwings.
funFact: It is one of the few bird families found only in the Middle East and southwest Asia.

wiki.extract: The grey hypocolius or simply hypocolius is a small passerine bird species. It is the sole member of the genus Hypocolius and it is placed in a family of its own, the Hypocoliidae. This slender and long tailed bird is found in the dry semi-desert region of northern Africa, Arabia, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and western India. They fly in flocks and forage mainly on fruit but also some insects, migrating south in winter. During migration they are often found feeding on the fruit of Salvadora persica.

summary: A plump, eight-legged micro-animal about a quarter of a millimetre long and the main laboratory model for studying tardigrades. Like many tardigrades it can survive drying out and freezing by shutting its body down almost entirely.
nativeRange: Described in 2018 from a long-running laboratory culture originating in the UK; tardigrades as a group occur worldwide
abilities: Survives slow drying by curling into a 'tun' and entering cryptobiosis, with metabolism nearly stopped
Tolerates freezing and recovers when thawed
Protects its cells while drying with tardigrade-specific disordered proteins that form a glassy state
Reproduces without males (parthenogenesis), so one animal can found a whole culture

animal.diet: Algae such as Chlorococcum, sucked from cells through a stylet-armed mouth
animal.habitat: Freshwater sediment and aquatic plants
animal.lifespan: A few weeks to a few months when active
animal.behaviour: It lumbers on eight stubby clawed legs and moults its cuticle as it grows, often laying eggs in the shed skin.
fieldMarks: Microscopic, ~0.2–0.3 mm
Barrel-shaped body with eight stubby legs
Claws on each leg
Transparent body
animal.lookalikes: Other tardigrades need microscopy to identify.

lore: The pastor Johann Goeze named tardigrades 'kleiner Wasserbär' (little water bear) in 1773, and Lazzaro Spallanzani gave them the name tardigrado, 'slow stepper', in 1776 after reviving them from dust. This species was long misidentified as Hypsibius dujardini until it was described in 2018.
funFact: Its genome, sequenced in the 2010s, sparked debate over claims that tardigrades had borrowed large amounts of foreign DNA; later analyses found that most of it was contamination.

wiki.extract: Hypsibius dujardini sensu lato is a species complex of tardigrade in the class Eutardigrada. A member of this complex, Hypsibius exemplaris, is widely used for various research projects pertaining to evolutionary biology and astrobiology. The species was described by Louis Michel François Doyère in 1840.

summary: A grey shorebird with a crimson, down-curved bill and a black face and breast band, living on the shingle beds of fast mountain rivers across High Asia. It is so distinct that it sits in a family of its own.
nativeRange: Mountains of Central and High Asia: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan through northern Pakistan, Ladakh, Nepal, Bhutan and Tibet to northern and central China
abilities: Probes under stones in fast-flowing glacial rivers for larvae
Camouflaged grey plumage matches river shingle
Breeds at altitudes up to about 4,400 m

animal.diet: Aquatic insects and larvae, small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Shingle and stony braided river beds in mountain valleys, roughly 1,700–4,400 m
animal.behaviour: Wades in rushing water, reaching under stones with its curved bill; very hard to spot until it moves.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown upperparts and grey neck and breast
Long, down-curved crimson bill
Black face and black breast band bordered with white
Red legs (duller outside breeding season)
animal.voice: A ringing, whistled 'klee-klee' and a 'tee-tee-tee' trill, carrying over the noise of rivers
animal.lookalikes: No real lookalike: curlews and whimbrels are brown, streaked and lack the black breast band and red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Hunza and Chitral rivers in northern Pakistan; Indus valley near Leh in Ladakh; Langtang and Mustang in Nepal; mountain rivers near Beijing in winter
animal.season: Resident, moving to lower river valleys in winter

lore: It is a prize sighting for birders visiting the Karakoram and Ladakh, where its grey plumage vanishes against river stones.
funFact: It is the only member of the family Ibidorhynchidae.

wiki.extract: The ibisbill  is a bird related to the waders, but sufficiently distinctive to merit its own family Ibidorhynchidae. It is grey with a white belly, red legs and long down-curved bill, and a black face and black breast band. It occurs on the shingle riverbanks of the high plateaux of central Asia and the Himalayas.

summary: One of the most abundant birds in North America, whose glossy black males flare scarlet shoulder patches from every cattail marsh in spring. Males defend territories that may hold many nesting females.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada south through the US, Mexico and Central America to Costa Rica; also the Bahamas and Cuba
abilities: Highly polygynous: one male's territory can host up to about 15 nesting females
Males can cover their red epaulets to slip through rivals' territories unchallenged
Gathers in winter roosts that can number in the millions together with grackles, cowbirds and starlings
Mobs hawks, crows and people near its nests

animal.diet: Insects in summer; seeds and grain in winter
animal.habitat: Cattail and bulrush marshes, ditches, wet fields, pastures
animal.behaviour: Males return north weeks before females and sing from cattails even in snow.
fieldMarks: Male: glossy black with red shoulder patch bordered by yellow
Female: heavily streaked dark brown, sparrow-like, often with a peachy face
Sharp, conical, pointed bill
Males puff and spread the epaulets while singing
animal.voice: A gurgling 'conk-la-ree!' or 'oak-a-lee!' ending in a trill; calls a sharp 'check' and a whistled alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Tricolored Blackbird (California) has a darker red patch with a white border. Female could be mistaken for a large sparrow, but the long pointed bill differs. 'Bicolored' males in California lack the yellow border.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any marsh, roadside ditch or wet meadow in North America from March onwards.
animal.season: Resident in the south; summer visitor in the north, Mar–Oct

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The Red-wing'd Starling'.
funFact: Its genus name Agelaius means 'belonging to a flock'.

wiki.extract: The red-winged blackbird is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae found in most of North America and much of Central America. It breeds from Alaska and Newfoundland south to Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico, and Guatemala, with isolated populations in western El Salvador, northwestern Honduras, and northwestern Costa Rica. It may winter as far north as Pennsylvania and British Columbia, but northern populations are generally migratory, moving south to Mexico and the Southern United States.

summary: A flame-orange and black blackbird relative that weaves a hanging, sock-like nest high in the outer branches of elms and maples. It winters in the tropics, where it sips nectar and eats fruit.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern and central North America; winters from southern Mexico to Colombia and Venezuela, with some in Florida and the Caribbean
abilities: Weaves a pendant pouch nest from plant fibres, hair and string, hung from slender twig tips
Uses 'gaping' — stabbing the closed bill into fruit and prying it open — to drink juice
Visits flowers for nectar on the wintering grounds, carrying pollen between blooms
Migrates by night between the US and northern South America

animal.diet: Caterpillars and other insects, ripe fruit, nectar
animal.habitat: Open deciduous woodland, riversides, parks with tall shade trees
animal.behaviour: Readily comes to feeders offering orange halves and grape jelly during spring migration.
fieldMarks: Adult male: fiery orange underparts, rump and tail sides; entirely black head and back
Black wings with a single white wing bar
Female and first-year male: yellow-orange below, olive-brown above, two white wing bars
Sharply pointed, straight grey bill
animal.voice: Rich, flute-like whistled phrases, varying from bird to bird; call a dry, chattering rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Bullock's Oriole (west) has an orange face with a black eye-line and a large white wing patch; the two hybridise on the Great Plains. Orchard Oriole males are deep chestnut, not orange. American Redstart is a tiny warbler with orange tail patches.
animal.whereToSee: Shade trees along rivers and in older parks across the eastern US and southern Canada; migration hotspots such as Magee Marsh (Ohio) and Point Pelee (Ontario) in May.
animal.season: Summer visitor, late Apr–Sep

lore: Its orange and black recalled the heraldic colours of the Calverts, the Lords Baltimore who founded colonial Maryland; it is now Maryland's state bird and the namesake of Baltimore's baseball team.
funFact: Before Dutch elm disease, the American elm was its classic nesting tree; orioles have since shifted to maples, cottonwoods and sycamores.

wiki.extract: The Baltimore oriole is a small icterid blackbird common in eastern North America as a migratory breeding bird. It received its common name from the resemblance of the male's colors to those on the coat-of-arms of 17th-century Lord Baltimore. Observations of interbreeding between the Baltimore oriole and the western Bullock's oriole Icterus bullockii, led to both being classified as a single species, called the northern oriole, from 1973 to 1995. Research by James Rising, a professor of zoology at the University of Toronto, and others showed that the two birds actually did not interbreed significantly.

summary: The only lizard in the world that forages in the sea. On the Galápagos Islands it dives into cold surf to graze algae, then warms up on black lava rocks. Charles Darwin recorded that they had been called 'imps of darkness'.
nativeRange: Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
abilities: Dives to over 10 m and grazes algae on rocks with its short blunt snout
Sneezes out excess salt from glands near its nose
Shrinks its body, even its bones, when food is short in El Niño years, then grows again
Digests seaweed with the help of gut microbes

animal.diet: Red and green algae from intertidal and subtidal rocks
animal.habitat: Rocky lava coasts and nearby water
animal.size: Up to ~1.3 m including tail; males larger
animal.behaviour: Large males dive offshore, while females and smaller iguanas graze on algae exposed at low tide. They pile together on rocks at night to keep warm.
fieldMarks: Short, blunt snout and spiny crest along the back
Black or grey body; on some islands males are mottled red and green in the breeding season
Flattened tail for swimming
Often white-crusted head from sneezed salt
animal.lookalikes: Galápagos land iguanas (Conolophus) are yellow-brown with a long rounded tail and live inland. Lava lizards (Microlophus) are much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: All main Galápagos islands; Española (Punta Suárez) for red-green males, Fernandina (Punta Espinoza) for large colonies
animal.season: Resident; breeding coloration and mating December–January on many islands

lore: Darwin wrote in 1835 that marine iguanas were 'hideous-looking' and 'most disgusting, clumsy lizards', and noted that 'somebody calls them imps of darkness', a phrase used earlier by Lord Byron's 1826 voyage account. He threw one into the sea repeatedly to watch it swim back.
funFact: In El Niño years marine iguanas can shrink by up to ~20% in length, and their bones get shorter, then they regrow when food returns.

wiki.extract: The marine iguana, also known as the sea iguana, saltwater iguana, or Galápagos marine iguana, is a species of iguana found only on the Galápagos Islands (Ecuador). Unique among modern lizards, it is a marine reptile that has the ability to forage in the sea for algae, which make up almost all of its diet. Marine iguanas are the only extant lizard that spends time in a marine environment. Large males are able to dive to find this food source, while females and smaller males feed during low tide in the intertidal zone. They mainly live in colonies on rocky shores where they bask after visiting the relatively cold water or intertidal zone, but can also be seen in marshes, mangrove swamps and beaches. Large males defend territories for a short period, but smaller males have other breeding strategies. After mating, the female digs a nest hole in the soil where she lays her eggs, leaving them to hatch on their own a few months later.

summary: A large plant-eating lizard of tropical American riversides, with a dewlap and a spiny crest. It is eaten across Central America. Released pets have made it an invasive pest in Florida, Puerto Rico and elsewhere.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to Paraguay and southern Brazil; parts of the Caribbean
abilities: Can drop from tree branches over 10 m high into water or onto the ground unhurt
Swims well and can stay underwater for long periods
Has a light-sensitive 'third eye' (parietal eye) on top of its head
Digests leaves with the help of gut microbes, like a cow

animal.diet: Leaves, flowers and fruit; juveniles occasionally eat insects
animal.habitat: Trees along rivers and coasts; urban canals in introduced range
animal.lifespan: ~10–15 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.size: Up to ~1.7 m including tail; up to ~5–8 kg
animal.behaviour: Basks high in trees over water and drops into the river to escape. Males bob their heads and show off their dewlaps to rivals. It eats plants and is not venomous, but it bites and lashes its tail if handled. People eat both the meat and the eggs.
fieldMarks: Large round scale (subtympanic shield) on the cheek below the ear
Large dewlap and a spiny crest along the back
Green to grey-brown; adult males can turn orange in the breeding season
Long tail with dark bands
animal.lookalikes: Spiny-tailed iguanas (Ctenosaura) have rings of spiny scales on the tail and no large cheek scale. The Lesser Antillean iguana (I. delicatissima) also lacks the large cheek scale and has an unbanded tail. Basilisks are smaller, with crests on the head.
animal.whereToSee: Riverbanks throughout Central America, e.g. Costa Rica's Tárcoles and Sarapiquí rivers, Tikal, Belize; in Florida, canals in Miami
animal.season: Resident; mating in the dry season, egg-laying a few weeks later

edibilityNote: Eaten traditionally in Central America and the Caribbean; harvest of wild populations is regulated in many countries. Like other reptiles it can carry Salmonella, so meat must be cooked thoroughly.
lore: The word 'iguana' comes from the Taíno iwana. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo described iguana meat in his 1526 'Sumario' of the natural history of the Indies.
funFact: During cold snaps in Florida, iguanas become torpid and fall from trees; they usually recover when they warm up.
