wiki.extract: The green iguana, also known as the American iguana or the common green iguana, is a large, arboreal, mostly herbivorous species of lizard of the genus Iguana. Usually, this animal is simply called the iguana. The green iguana ranges over a large geographic area; it is native from southern Brazil and Paraguay as far north as Mexico. It is highly invasive in many subtropical and tropical environments throughout the world.

summary: A drab woodland bird with an extraordinary partnership: it leads people to wild bees' nests and feeds on the wax left after the honey is taken. It is also a brood parasite whose chicks kill their foster siblings.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa outside the densest rainforest and driest deserts
abilities: Guides humans to bees' nests with a chattering call and short flights
Responds to specific human calls: Yao honey-hunters' 'brrr-hm' trill raises the chance of being guided
Can digest beeswax, a rare ability among vertebrates
Lays eggs in the nests of hole-nesting birds such as bee-eaters and barbets; the hatchling uses a hooked bill tip to kill host chicks

animal.diet: Beeswax, bee larvae and eggs, and insects
animal.habitat: Miombo and acacia woodland and savanna
animal.behaviour: When guiding, it flies ahead in short hops, calling and fanning its white-edged tail, and waits for its human followers to catch up.
fieldMarks: Male: pink bill, black throat and white ear patch
Grey-brown upperparts with a yellow shoulder patch in males
White outer tail feathers flashed in flight
Females and immatures plainer; juveniles have a yellow throat and breast
animal.voice: Male song a repeated, far-carrying 'vic-tor' or 'whit-purrr'; the guiding call is a persistent, dry chattering rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser honeyguide is smaller, olive-tinged, with a stubby dark bill and no black throat. Scaly-throated honeyguide has a scaly-patterned throat. Juvenile greater honeyguides, with yellow throats, can be mistaken for other small yellow-throated birds.
animal.whereToSee: Niassa Special Reserve (Mozambique), where Yao honey-hunters still work with it; Hadza country around Lake Eyasi (Tanzania); miombo woodland in Zambia and Malawi
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Jesuit missionary João dos Santos described honeyguides eating candle wax in a Mozambique church in the 16th century. A 2016 study in Science showed that wild honeyguides learn and answer the Yao people's traditional honey-hunting call.
funFact: A 2023 study found that honeyguides in different regions have learned to respond to different local human calls, a cross-species culture.

wiki.extract: The greater honeyguide is a bird in the paleotropical family Indicatoridae, that is related to the woodpeckers. Its English and scientific names refer to its habit of guiding people to bee colonies. Claims that it also guides non-human animals are disputed.

summary: A billfish with a towering, sail-like dorsal fin that it raises while groups herd sardines into tight balls. Atlantic and Indo-Pacific sailfish are now treated as one species.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans
abilities: Raises its sail and flashes colour bands while hunting in groups
Rapidly changes colour, lighting up with blue bars when excited
Hunters take turns slashing into bait balls with the bill, injuring and knocking loose sardines
Often called the fastest fish, though 100+ km/h claims are disputed and measured bursts are much lower

animal.diet: Sardines, anchovies, mackerel, squid
animal.habitat: Warm surface waters above the thermocline, often near coasts and islands
animal.size: Up to ~3.4 m and 100 kg; most under 2.7 m
animal.behaviour: Groups encircle a school of sardines, raise sails to compress it, then take turns striking with the bill so that each fish's attack is brief.

Long, round, slender bill
Very long, narrow pelvic fins
Dark blue back, silvery sides with rows of pale blue spots or bars

animal.whereToSee: Isla Mujeres, Mexico (sardine bait balls), Stuart, Florida ('Sailfish Capital of the World'), Guatemala's Pacific coast
animal.season: Isla Mujeres Jan–Mar; Florida in winter

lore: Sport anglers in Stuart, Florida made the sailfish a symbol of catch-and-release fishing in the 20th century; it is Florida's state saltwater fish.
funFact: The bill bears tiny tooth-like denticles that wear down from repeated slashing, and injured sardines are rarely impaled.

wiki.extract: The Indo-Pacific sailfish is a sailfish native to the Indian and Pacific Oceans and is naturalized in the Atlantic where it has entered the Mediterranean Sea via the Suez Canal as a Lessepsian migrant. It is dark blue on top, brown-blue laterally, silvery white underbelly; upper jaw elongated in the form of a spear; first dorsal fin greatly enlarged in the form of a sail, with many black cones, its front squared off, highest at its midpoint; pelvic fins very narrow, reaching almost to the anus; body covered with embedded scales, blunt at end; lateral line curved above pectoral fin, then straight to base of tail. They have a large and sharp bill, which they use for hunting. They feed on tuna and mackerel, some of the fastest fish in the ocean. Most authorities only recognise a single species of sailfish, I. platypterus.

summary: An elegant wetland bird that walks across lotus and water-lily leaves on enormously long toes, its breeding plumage chocolate and white with a golden nape and a long, curving pheasant-like tail. Females are polyandrous, mating with several males that each raise a clutch alone.
nativeRange: Pakistan and India through Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Southeast Asia to southern China and Taiwan; northern birds migrate
abilities: Spreads its weight over very long toes to walk on floating leaves
Females lay eggs for several males, which incubate and rear the young
Males can carry eggs or chicks under their wings to move them

animal.diet: Insects, snails and other invertebrates, and seeds of aquatic plants
animal.habitat: Lakes, ponds and marshes with floating vegetation such as lotus and water lilies
animal.size: About 39–58 cm in breeding plumage including tail
animal.behaviour: The female defends a territory containing several males' nests; each male incubates eggs on a floating nest.
fieldMarks: Breeding: chocolate-brown body, white face and neck, golden-yellow hindneck, long dark sickle tail
Mostly white wings, very conspicuous in flight
Non-breeding: brown above, white below, with a dark breast band and no long tail
Very long legs and toes
animal.voice: A nasal, mewing 'me-onp' or 'tewn', often given in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Bronze-winged jacana is dark glossy with a white eyebrow and short tail; non-breeding birds may recall a large wader but the toes and white wings are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park; lotus lakes in Sindh (Haleji) and Bangladesh's haors; Taiwan's Guantian reserve
animal.season: Resident in South Asia; breeding plumage during the monsoon (Jun–Sep)

lore: In Taiwan, a dedicated reserve for this species was created at Guantian after a high-speed rail line threatened its breeding wetlands.
funFact: It is the only jacana that is a long-distance migrant, with northern birds from China moving south for the winter.

wiki.extract: The pheasant-tailed jacana is a jacana in the monotypic genus Hydrophasianus. Like all other jacanas, they have elongated toes and nails that enable them to walk on floating vegetation in shallow lakes, their preferred habitat. They may also swim or wade in water reaching their body while foraging mainly for invertebrate prey. They are found in tropical Asia from Yemen in the west to the Philippines in the east and move seasonally in parts of their range. They are the only jacanas that migrate long distances and have different non-breeding and breeding plumages. The pheasant-tailed jacana forages by swimming or by walking on aquatic vegetation. Females are larger than males and are polyandrous, laying several clutches that are raised by different males in their harem.

summary: The largest living wrasse, a thick-lipped giant with a bulbous forehead and maze-like facial markings. Its value in the live reef-food trade of Hong Kong and southern China has made it endangered.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to the Tuamotus, Japan and New Caledonia
abilities: One of the few predators that eats toxic crown-of-thorns starfish, sea hares and boxfish
Protogynous hermaphrodite: some females change into males
Crushes hard-shelled molluscs and sea urchins with heavy pharyngeal teeth
Can live over 30 years

animal.diet: Molluscs, crustaceans, sea urchins, fish, crown-of-thorns starfish
animal.habitat: Outer reef slopes, channels and lagoon reefs to 100 m; juveniles in seagrass and branching coral
animal.size: Males up to about 2 m and 190 kg
animal.behaviour: Often approaches divers with apparent curiosity; rests in reef caves at night and gathers at predictable spawning sites on outer reefs.
fieldMarks: Massive size with a prominent hump on the forehead of large adults
Thick, fleshy lips
Two black lines behind each eye and maze-like markings on the face
Blue-green to olive body with fine vertical lines on each scale
animal.lookalikes: Bumphead parrotfish (Bolbometopon muricatum) also has a forehead hump but has a beak of fused teeth and moves in grazing schools; humphead wrasse has fleshy lips and usually swims alone.
animal.whereToSee: Cod Hole and Ribbon Reefs (Great Barrier Reef), Red Sea reefs, Palau, Sipadan
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Listed on CITES Appendix II in 2004 because of the live reef-food trade, where it is a banquet fish in Hong Kong and its lips are especially prized.
funFact: Most humphead wrasse begin life as females; only some change sex to become the large dominant males.

summary: A Caribbean parrotfish whose fused beak grazes algae off coral, keeping reefs from being smothered. Like many parrotfishes, it sleeps in a mucus cocoon and can change sex from female to male.
nativeRange: Western Atlantic from Florida and the Bahamas through the Caribbean to Brazil

Grinds ingested rock in a pharyngeal mill; parrotfishes produce much of the white sand on Caribbean beaches
Secretes a mucus 'sleeping bag' at night that may protect against parasites
Protogynous hermaphrodite: some females become brilliant blue-green terminal males

funFact: Female and initial-phase queen parrotfish look so different from terminal males that they were once described as separate species.

wiki.extract: The queen parrotfish, is a species of parrotfish or marine ray-finned fish that belongs to the family Labridae, part of the subfamily Scarinae. It is found on reefs in the tropical West Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. Other common names include blownose, blue chub, blue parrotfish, blueman, joblin crow parrot, moontail, okra peji and slimy head. The initial phase is female, displaying a reddish-brown color, and quite different in appearance from the bluish-green color of the final phase male. This is a common species throughout its range and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has rated its conservation status as "least concern".

summary: The largest predatory fish, a warm-bodied hunter of seals and sea lions in cool coastal seas around the world. Tagging shows these sharks crossing whole ocean basins.
nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical coastal and open waters worldwide; hotspots off South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, California, Guadalupe Island and the north-west Atlantic
abilities: Senses the faint electric fields of living prey with ampullae of Lorenzini on its snout
Keeps its muscles, eyes and brain warmer than the surrounding water with a heat-exchanging circulation
Launches fully out of the water when ambushing seals from below
Migrates across oceans: one female swam from South Africa to Australia and back, about 20,000 km, in nine months

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, rays and other sharks when young; seals, sea lions, dolphins and whale carcasses as adults
animal.habitat: Coastal and offshore waters, usually 12–24 °C, from the surface to over 1,000 m
animal.size: Usually 3.5–5 m; large females to ~6 m and over 2 t
animal.behaviour: California white sharks gather each winter and spring at a mid-Pacific spot nicknamed the 'White Shark Café', between Baja California and Hawaii.
fieldMarks: Large, torpedo-shaped shark
Grey above, white below with a sharp border
Black tips to the underside of the pectoral fins
Conical snout and large triangular teeth
animal.lookalikes: Shortfin mako is slimmer and more blue, with long curved teeth. Basking shark has huge gill slits and a tiny mouth. Avoid swimming where whites are present.
animal.whereToSee: Neptune Islands (South Australia, cage diving), Cape Cod (Massachusetts) and the Farallon Islands (California)
animal.season: Cape Cod Jul–Oct; Farallones Sep–Nov; Neptune Islands all year

lore: Peter Benchley's novel Jaws (1974) and Spielberg's 1975 film made the great white a figure of fear; Benchley later spent years campaigning for shark conservation. Some Māori coastal tribes honour sharks as kaitiaki (guardians).
funFact: Orcas off South Africa have been seen killing great whites to eat their livers, and the sharks then abandon the area for months.

wiki.extract: The great white shark, also known as the white shark, white pointer, or great white, is a large shark. It is closely related to the mako sharks, the porbeagle, and the salmon shark. It is a robustly built species with a grayish upperside and a white underside. The white shark is one of the largest living shark and fish species, though it is still smaller than the whale shark and basking shark. It has about 300 triangular, serrated teeth that are continuously replaced. Its massive, fatty liver can reach over a quarter of its body weight, providing buoyancy and storing energy. The species is partially warm-blooded, an adaptation that allows it to remain active in colder waters.

summary: The fastest shark, capable of bursts often estimated around 70 km/h and spectacular leaps several metres out of the water. Warm-bodied and long-ranging, it has been heavily overfished for its meat and fins.
nativeRange: Tropical and temperate oceans worldwide
abilities: Regional endothermy keeps muscles, brain and eyes warmer than the water
Flexible scales (denticles) on the flanks may reduce drag by controlling flow separation
Leaps up to about 6 m clear of the water
Tagged makos have travelled many thousands of kilometres across ocean basins
edibilityNote: Meat is eaten widely but contains high methylmercury; pregnant women and children should avoid it. Endangered status means it is best not eaten.

animal.diet: Tunas, swordfish, mackerel, squid, other sharks
animal.habitat: Open ocean from the surface to about 500 m
animal.size: Commonly 3 m; up to about 4 m and 500 kg
animal.behaviour: A highly active, wide-ranging hunter that attacks swordfish and tuna from below.
fieldMarks: Slender, torpedo body with a sharply pointed conical snout
Metallic indigo-blue back and white belly
Long, curved, smooth-edged teeth visible even with the mouth closed
Nearly symmetrical crescent tail with a strong keel
Underside of snout white
animal.lookalikes: Longfin mako (I. paucus) has much longer pectoral fins and a dusky snout underside; porbeagle has a secondary keel and white rear dorsal tip; great white is stockier with serrated triangular teeth.
animal.whereToSee: Offshore cage and pelagic dives off San Diego, Cabo San Lucas, Rhode Island and Cape Point, South Africa
animal.season: Southern California summer–autumn; New England Jun–Oct

lore: Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea (1952) features a mako ('dentuso') attacking Santiago's marlin; in 2019 it was listed on CITES Appendix II.
funFact: In 2021 ICCAT agreed to a two-year ban on retaining North Atlantic shortfin makos because the stock was overfished.

wiki.extract: The shortfin mako shark, also known as the shortfin mako, blue pointer, or bonito shark, is a species of large mackerel shark. It is commonly referred to as the mako shark, as is the longfin mako shark. The fastest known shark species, able to reach speeds of 74 km/h (46 mph) in bursts, the shortfin mako can attain sizes of more than 4 m (13 ft) in length and weigh over 570 kg (1,260 lb). The species is classified as Endangered by the IUCN.

summary: North America's most familiar firefly, a beetle that courts with flashes of cold yellow-green light. Males trace a J-shaped 'swoop' as they flash, and females answer from the grass.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, south to northern South America
abilities: Produces light through the luciferin–luciferase reaction with very little heat
Males flash a species-specific timed pattern; females reply after a set delay
Larvae glow too and hunt snails, slugs and worms
Contains defensive lucibufagins that make it distasteful to predators

animal.diet: Larvae eat soft-bodied invertebrates; adults eat little or nothing
animal.habitat: Open fields, lawns, forest edges and moist ground
animal.lifespan: About 1–2 years, mostly as a larva; adults a few weeks
animal.behaviour: At dusk a male rises while flashing, drawing a J in the air; a receptive female answers with a single flash after about two seconds.
fieldMarks: Flat, soft-bodied beetle 1–1.4 cm long, dark wing covers edged yellow
Head shield (pronotum) yellow with a black central spot ringed pink or red
Males have lanterns on the last three abdominal segments; females a small lantern on one segment
Males fly low in a J-shaped swoop, flashing on the upswing
animal.voice: Silent; signals with light. The male's yellow flash comes every 5–7 seconds and the female answers from the grass 1–2 seconds later
animal.lookalikes: Photuris fireflies are longer and leggier, flash later into the night with different patterns, and females mimic Photinus replies to eat the males. Many other Photinus species differ chiefly in flash rhythm.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, meadows and woodland edges across the eastern and central United States, including suburban yards
animal.season: Late spring and summer (mainly Jun–Jul), flashing from dusk for about an hour

lore: The firefly luciferase gene, cloned from this species in 1985, became a standard tool in molecular biology for reporting gene activity and detecting ATP. Predatory Photuris 'femme fatale' fireflies mimic its female's reply to lure and eat males.
funFact: Its light reaction gives off almost no heat, and about 40% of reactions produce a photon (Ando et al. 2008) — far lower than the once-quoted ~90%, but still among the most efficient light-producing reactions in nature.

wiki.extract: Photinus pyralis, also known by the common names the common eastern firefly or big dipper firefly, and sometimes called a "lightning bug", is a species of flying beetle. An organ on its abdomen is responsible for its light production. It is the most common species of firefly in North America and is typically found east of the Rocky Mountains. Photinus fireflies are often confused with fireflies of the similar-sounding genus, Photuris, which are also found in North America.

summary: A predatory songbird with a black bandit mask and a rufous back, which perches on bushes and wires to pounce on insects, lizards and small birds. Like other shrikes it impales surplus prey on thorns as a larder.
nativeRange: Kazakhstan and Iran through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and Nepal to China, Southeast Asia and New Guinea
abilities: Impales prey on thorns and barbed wire for storage and to tear it apart
Mimics the calls of other birds within its song
Takes vertebrate prey as large as small birds and mice

animal.diet: Large insects, lizards, small birds, rodents and frogs
animal.habitat: Open scrub, cultivation, gardens and hedgerows
animal.behaviour: Sits upright on exposed perches, swinging its long tail, then drops on prey; males defend territories with harsh calls and songs full of mimicry.
fieldMarks: Black mask through the eye, grey crown and nape
Rufous back, rump and flanks
Long, graduated black tail with pale edges
Hooked black bill; small white wing patch
animal.voice: Harsh 'chaak' and grating calls; song is a quiet, rambling warble with much mimicry
animal.lookalikes: Bay-backed shrike is smaller with a black forehead and maroon back; Isabelline shrike is sandy-brown; Grey-backed shrike (Himalaya) has an all-grey back.
animal.whereToSee: Hedgerows and farmland across Punjab, Islamabad's sector parks and northern Pakistan valleys in summer; widespread in India and Sri Lanka in winter
animal.season: Resident or partly migratory; northern breeders move south in winter

lore: The shrike habit of impaling prey earned the family the English folk name 'butcher-bird'.

wiki.extract: The long-tailed shrike or rufous-backed shrike is a member of the bird family Laniidae, the shrikes. They are found widely distributed across Asia and there are variations in plumage across the range. The species ranges across much of Asia, both on the mainland and the eastern archipelagos. The eastern or Himalayan subspecies, L. s. tricolor, is sometimes called the black-headed shrike. Although there are considerable differences in plumage among the subspecies, they all have a long and narrow black tail, have a black mask and forehead, rufous rump and flanks and a small white patch on the shoulder. It is considered to form a superspecies with the grey-backed shrike which breeds on the Tibetan Plateau.

The plate illustrates the birds in various states—flight and perched—providing a scientific yet artistic record typical of Enlightenment-era natural history publications.

plates.long: This fine copperplate engraving from François Le Vaillant's 1807 work illustrates the meticulous detail required for early 19th-century ornithological studies. The artist utilizes cross-hatching and stippling to convey the specific textures of the bird's feathers and the rough bark of the gnarled branch, serving both an aesthetic and scientific purpose.

summary: A tern-like bird with a bright orange bill whose lower half is longer than the upper, which it slices through the water surface in flight to snap up fish. It nests on sandbars of big South Asian rivers that are increasingly disturbed by people and dams.
nativeRange: Rivers of India and Bangladesh (notably the Chambal and Ganges systems), with wintering on the Bangladesh coast; formerly the Indus in Pakistan and the Irrawaddy and Mekong
abilities: Skims with its long lower mandible cutting the water, snapping shut on contact with fish
Its pupils are vertical slits, unusual among birds, which may reduce glare from water
Feeds at dusk and at night as well as by day

animal.diet: Small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Large rivers with sandbars; estuaries and coasts in winter
animal.behaviour: Flies low over calm water with the lower bill slicing the surface; nests in colonies in scrapes on exposed sandbars in spring.
fieldMarks: Black cap and upperparts with a white forehead, collar and underparts
Deep orange-red bill with a yellow tip, lower mandible much longer than upper
Long, pointed wings with a white trailing edge
Short, red legs
animal.voice: Nasal, yapping 'kap-kap' calls, especially at colonies
animal.lookalikes: River tern has a yellow, evenly-sized bill and a grey back; Black-bellied tern is smaller with a black belly in breeding plumage.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh/Rajasthan/Uttar Pradesh); Padma and Meghna rivers and the Bangladesh coast in winter
animal.season: Resident with local movements; breeds March–May on river sandbars

lore: It was once recorded on the Indus in Pakistan and on Myanmar's rivers, but damming, sand-mining and disturbance of river islands have left it rare or absent there.
funFact: Skimmers are the only birds with a lower mandible longer than the upper.

wiki.extract: The Indian skimmer or Indian scissors-bill, is one of the three species that belong to the skimmer genus Rynchops in the family Laridae. They are somewhat tern-like but like other skimmers, have a short upper mandible and the longer lower mandible that is ploughed along the surface of water as the bird flies over the water to pick aquatic prey. It is found in southern Asia, where it is patchily distributed and declining in numbers. They are mainly found in rivers or estuaries. They are very brightly marked in black, white and orange, making them difficult to miss.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a Black Skimmer, which Mark Catesby referred to as a 'Cutwater' due to its unique feeding habit. The illustration meticulously details the bird's specialized beak, where the lower mandible is significantly longer than the upper, allowing it to skim the water's surface for fish. Catesby's 'Natural History' was the first major published work to illustrate the bird

summary: The bird with the longest known migration, flying from Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back each year. It probably sees more daylight than any other animal.
nativeRange: Breeds around the Arctic and subarctic; winters in Antarctic waters
abilities: Round-trip migration averaging ~70,000 km a year, up to ~96,000 km
Lifetime travel can equal roughly three trips to the Moon and back
Takes S-shaped routes to ride prevailing winds across oceans
Plunge-dives to catch small fish
Fiercely mobs intruders, including humans, at nests

animal.diet: Small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Coastal tundra, islands and open ocean
animal.behaviour: Experiences two summers each year, following the sun from pole to pole.
fieldMarks: Slender grey-and-white tern with a black cap
All-red bill without a dark tip
Very short red legs
Long tail streamers and translucent flight feathers when seen from below
animal.voice: A harsh, high 'kee-arr' and rattling alarm calls; dive-bombs intruders at colonies
animal.lookalikes: Common tern has a black-tipped orange-red bill, longer legs, a darker wedge on the outer wing and shorter tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Farne Islands, Northumberland (wear a hat — the birds strike heads), Iceland and Shetland
animal.season: Northern colonies May–Aug; winters in Antarctic waters

lore: Tracking by Carsten Egevang and colleagues in 2010 with geolocators weighing 1.4 g first mapped its full migration. In Iceland and Greenland its eggs were traditionally gathered.
funFact: A tern ringed as a chick in Britain was found in Australia, over 22,000 km away, within months.

wiki.extract: The Arctic tern is a tern in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar breeding distribution covering the Arctic and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. The species is strongly migratory, seeing two summers each year as it migrates along a convoluted route from its northern breeding grounds to the Antarctic coast for the southern summer and back again about six months later. Recent studies have shown average annual round-trip lengths of about 70,900 km (38,300 nmi) for birds nesting in Iceland and Greenland, and about 48,700 km (26,300 nmi) for birds nesting in the Netherlands, while an individual from the Farne Islands in Northumberland with a light level geolocator tag covered a staggering 96,000 km (52,000 nmi) in ten months from the end of one breeding season to the start of the next. These are by far the longest migrations known in the animal kingdom.

otherNames: Pla kapong khao ปลากะพงขาว (Thai)
summary: A large silver predator of Indo-Pacific rivers, estuaries and coasts that migrates downriver to spawn at sea. All barramundi are born male and most later change sex to female. In Bengal it is bhetki, the fish of the classic fish fry.
nativeRange: Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea coasts east through South Asia and Southeast Asia to southern China, Taiwan, Papua New Guinea and northern Australia
abilities: Catadromous: grows in rivers and swims to estuaries and coastal seas to spawn
Protandrous hermaphrodite: born male, it usually becomes female at about 3–5 years old and 80–100 cm
Lives in fresh, brackish or salt water
A big female can release tens of millions of eggs in a season
edibilityNote: Firm, mild white fillets; widely farmed. Bengal's bhetki fish fry and paturi are classics. Always cooked. Large wild fish from polluted estuaries may carry mercury.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, prawns, crabs and insects
animal.habitat: Rivers, billabongs, mangrove estuaries and coastal waters
animal.size: Commonly 60–120 cm; up to about 2 m and 60 kg
animal.behaviour: Adults move down to river mouths and coastal flats at the start of the wet season to spawn on spring tides. Juveniles move up into freshwater swamps and creeks to grow.
fieldMarks: Silver body with a concave forehead and a pointed head
Large mouth with the jaw extending behind the eye; red-glowing eye at night
Spiny and soft dorsal fins almost separate; rounded tail
Freshwater fish golden-bronze; estuarine and sea fish silver
animal.lookalikes: Nile perch (L. niloticus) occurs only in Africa. Mangrove jack (Lutjanus argentimaculatus) has a reddish tint and canine teeth. Giant perch (Lates japonicus) of Japan is very similar.
animal.whereToSee: Kakadu and the Northern Territory rivers (Australia); the Sundarbans and Hooghly estuary; Thai fish markets
animal.season: Spawning migrations to estuaries at the start of the wet season (October–February in northern Australia; monsoon in South Asia)

lore: The name barramundi comes from an Aboriginal language of central Queensland and was popularised as a market name in Australia from the 1980s. Rock art in Kakadu and Arnhem Land includes 'X-ray' paintings of barramundi showing their spine and organs.
funFact: Because they change sex as they grow, almost all the very large barramundi are females.

wiki.extract: The barramundi, Asian sea bass, Asian sea lates, giant sea lates, or giant sea perch is a species of catadromous fish in the family Latidae of the order Carangiformes. The species is widely distributed in the Indo-West Pacific, spanning the waters of the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania.

summary: A giant predator of the Nile, Niger, Congo and Lake Chad that can reach 2 m and 200 kg. Its introduction into Lake Victoria in the 1950s caused one of the largest vertebrate extinction events of the 20th century and built a fillet-export industry.
nativeRange: Nile, Niger, Chad, Senegal, Volta and Congo basins and lakes Albert and Turkana; introduced to lakes Victoria, Kyoga and others
abilities: Eats almost any fish, including smaller Nile perch
Grows fast, so it dominates a lake food web within a few decades of arriving
A large female can spawn millions of eggs per season
edibleParts: swim bladder (dried, exported as fish maw)
edibilityNote: Firm, white, mild fillets, exported from Lake Victoria to Europe and beyond. The dried swim bladder is a high-value export to East Asia. Always cooked. Large fish from polluted bays may carry mercury.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish (cichlids, cyprinids, Nile perch), prawns and insects as juveniles
animal.habitat: Open water and deep zones of lakes and large rivers; juveniles in shallow inshore water
animal.size: Commonly 1 m; up to about 2 m and 200 kg
animal.behaviour: Juveniles feed on invertebrates in shallow inshore water, then switch to hunting fish as they grow.
fieldMarks: Robust, perch-like silvery body with blue-grey to greenish back
Two dorsal fins, almost separated: a high spiny first and a soft second
Large mouth with the jaw extending behind the eye; large eye that shines in torchlight
Rounded tail; concave head profile in large fish
animal.lookalikes: Other Lates species of Lake Tanganyika (L. angustifrons, L. mariae) are hard to separate and limited to that lake. Barramundi (L. calcarifer) is Asian and Australian only.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Nasser (Egypt) and Murchison Falls on the Victoria Nile (Uganda) for sport fishing; fish landings at Kisumu and Mwanza on Lake Victoria
animal.season: Resident; breeds through much of the year, with peaks in the rains

lore: Ancient Egyptians mummified Nile perch at Esna, which the Greeks called Latopolis, 'city of the Lates'. Hubert Sauper's documentary 'Darwin's Nightmare' (2004) showed the social cost of the Lake Victoria Nile perch export trade.
funFact: After its introduction, around 200 of Lake Victoria's endemic haplochromine cichlid species are thought to have disappeared or become extremely rare, although a few have since been found again.

wiki.extract: The Nile perch, also known as the African snook, Goliath perch, Nile lates, African lates, Goliath lates, Victoria lates, African barramundi, Goliath barramundi, Giant lates or the Victoria perch, is a species of freshwater fish in the family Latidae of the order Carangiformes. It is widespread throughout much of the Afrotropical realm, being native to the Congo, Nile, Senegal, Niger and Lake Chad, Volta, Lake Turkana, and other river basins. It also occurs in the brackish waters of Lake Maryut in Egypt. The Nile perch is a fish of substantial economic and food-security importance in East Africa. Originally described as Labrus niloticus, among the marine wrasses, the species has also been referred to as Centropomus niloticus. Common names include African snook, Victoria perch, and many local names in various African languages, such as the Luo name mbuta or mputa. In Tanzania, it is called sangara, sankara, or chenku. In Francophone African countries, it is known as capitaine. Its name in the Hausa language is giwan ruwa, meaning "water elephant".

The illustration emphasizes the fish's distinctive vertical banding and spiny dorsal fin, serving as a primary scientific record for 17th-century zoology.

The illustration serves as a scientific record, aiding in the identification of the species for medicinal use.

summary: A lobe-finned 'living fossil' known only from fossils and believed extinct for 66 million years until a fisherman's catch in South Africa in 1938. Its fleshy fins and ancient lineage make it a cousin of the fish that first walked onto land.
nativeRange: Western Indian Ocean: Comoros, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya and Madagascar
abilities: Moves its paired lobed fins in an alternating pattern like the legs of a walking tetrapod
Senses prey's electric fields with a jelly-filled rostral organ in its snout
Drifts head-down in 'headstands' while hunting
Opens its mouth unusually wide thanks to a hinged joint in its skull
Lives about a century and carries its young for around five years

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, squid and cuttlefish
animal.habitat: Steep volcanic slopes at 150–700 m; shelters in caves by day
animal.behaviour: By day small groups share the same lava caves, then drift out alone at night to hunt along the slope.
fieldMarks: Large, deep blue fish with white blotches
Fleshy, limb-like lobed fins
Three-lobed tail
Sluggish, drifting swimmer
animal.season: Resident; hides in caves by day

lore: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted one in a trawler's catch at East London, South Africa, in December 1938 and the ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith named it for her. Comorian fishermen had long known the fish, which they called gombessa.
funFact: A second species, Latimeria menadoensis, was found in an Indonesian fish market in 1997, about 10,000 km away.

wiki.extract: The West Indian Ocean coelacanth, sometimes known as the gombessa, African coelacanth, and simply coelacanth, is a crossopterygian, one of two extant species of coelacanth, a rare order of vertebrates more closely related to lungfish and tetrapods than to the common ray-finned fishes. The other extant species is the Indonesian coelacanth.

summary: A scruffy grey-brown babbler that lives in noisy gangs of about seven to ten, hopping through leaf litter and squabbling constantly. Families defend territories together and help raise each other's young.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Indus plains), India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh
abilities: Cooperative breeder: helpers feed chicks that are not their own
Groups post a sentinel who watches for predators while others feed
Mobs snakes, cats and birds of prey as a group
Hosts brood parasites such as the Jacobin cuckoo and Common hawk-cuckoo

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small lizards, seeds, nectar and fruit
animal.habitat: Woodland, scrub, gardens and cultivation edges
animal.behaviour: Groups move through low cover in a straggling procession, hopping on the ground and flipping leaves; members preen each other and huddle together on branches.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown with faint streaking, rather untidy-looking
Pale creamy-yellow iris and pale yellowish bill
Long, loose tail and short rounded wings
Always in noisy groups
animal.voice: Harsh, continual chattering and mewing 'ke-ke-ke' from the whole group
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-billed babbler (S India, Sri Lanka) has a paler head; Large grey babbler has white outer tail feathers; Common babbler is smaller and more streaked, in drier country.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and wooded gardens across India, e.g. Delhi's Lodhi Garden and Keoladeo; also Koshi Tappu in lowland Nepal
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Across north India and Bengal it is known as 'seven brothers' (or 'seven sisters' in English), after its habit of moving in squabbling family groups.

wiki.extract: The jungle babbler is a member of the family Leiothrichidae found in the Indian subcontinent. Jungle babblers are gregarious birds that forage in small groups of six to ten birds, a habit that has given them the popular name of "seven sisters" in urban Northern India, and in Bengali, with cognates in other regional languages which also mean "seven brothers".

summary: Madagascar's most familiar lemur, a sun-loving primate of dry forests and rocky canyons in the island's south and southwest. Troops are led by females, and males fight 'stink fights' by wiping their tails with scent and waving them at rivals. Although common in zoos, wild numbers have fallen steeply with forest loss and the pet trade.
nativeRange: Southern and southwestern Madagascar
abilities: Sunbathes in a 'yoga' posture, belly and arms open to the morning sun
Males hold 'stink fights', anointing their tails with scent from wrist and chest glands
Spends more time on the ground than any other lemur

animal.diet: Fruit (especially tamarind), leaves, flowers, bark, sap and insects
animal.habitat: Gallery forest along rivers, dry scrub, spiny forest and rocky outcrops
animal.size: Body about 40 cm, tail 55–62 cm; 2.2 kg
animal.behaviour: Lives in troops of up to about 30 with female dominance. Troop members huddle in 'lemur balls' to keep warm on cold nights.
fieldMarks: Long black-and-white ringed tail (about 13 alternating black and white bands) held up like a flag when walking
Grey back and paler underside
White face with black eye-patches and a dark nose
Signs: troops on the ground and rocks; scent marks on saplings
animal.voice: Cat-like mews to keep contact, loud yelps and wails as alarm calls, and a purring 'contented' call.
animal.lookalikes: No other lemur has a ringed tail. Brown and red-fronted lemurs are browner with plain tails.
animal.whereToSee: Anja Community Reserve; Isalo National Park; Berenty Private Reserve; Andringitra National Park; Tsimanampesotse National Park (all Madagascar)
animal.season: Resident; births in September–October, so young are seen clinging to mothers in spring

lore: Many Malagasy communities hold fady (taboos) against harming lemurs, and in Anja the community-run reserve has turned the species into a source of tourism income. Linnaeus described it in 1758 as the type of the genus Lemur, after the Roman spirits of the dead (lemures).
funFact: Surveys published in 2016–2017 counted only about 2,000–2,400 ring-tailed lemurs at the sites studied, raising fears the wild population had crashed; the true total is debated because many sites remain unsurveyed.

wiki.extract: The ring-tailed lemur is a medium- to larger-sized strepsirrhine (wet-nosed) primate and the most internationally recognized lemur species, owing to its long, black-and-white, ringed tail. It belongs to Lemuridae, one of five lemur families, and is the only member of the Lemur genus. Like all lemurs, it is endemic to the island of Madagascar, where it is endangered. Known locally in Malagasy as maky or hira, it ranges from gallery forests to spiny scrub in the southern regions of the island. It is omnivorous, as well as the most adapted to living terrestrially of the extant lemurs.

The illustration exemplifies the Enlightenment-era focus on precise anatomical observation, capturing the species' iconic ringed tail and facial markings while showing it holding a carrot, a detail likely observed from a capt

summary: A giant armoured fish of southern US rivers and bayous with a broad, alligator-like snout and a double row of fangs. It belongs to a lineage that has changed little for about 100 million years, and its eggs are poisonous.
nativeRange: Lower Mississippi basin and Gulf of Mexico coastal drainages from Florida to Veracruz, Mexico
abilities: Breathes air with a vascularised swim bladder, so it survives warm, stagnant backwaters
Its interlocking diamond-shaped ganoid scales form armour that resists most predators
Lies motionless like a log, then sideswipes fish with its toothed snout
Lives for many decades: fish over 50 years old have been aged from their ear stones (otoliths), and ages near 95 have been reported
edibilityNote: The white flesh is eaten in the US South and Mexico (gar balls, fried gar). The eggs are toxic: gar roe contains an ichthyotoxin that causes vomiting, diarrhoea and other illness in humans, and must never be eaten. The skin and scales are extremely hard to cut, and large old fish may carry mercury.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crabs, turtles and water birds; scavenges carcasses
animal.habitat: Slow, large rivers, oxbow lakes, bayous, reservoirs and brackish bays
animal.size: Commonly 1.5–2 m; up to about 3 m and 150 kg
animal.behaviour: Floats near the surface and rolls to gulp air. In spring, groups spawn over flooded vegetation, scattering sticky green eggs that hatch within days.
fieldMarks: Broad, short, alligator-like snout
Two rows of large teeth in the upper jaw on each side (other gars have one)
Long, torpedo-shaped body armoured with diamond-shaped ganoid scales
Dorsal and anal fins set far back near the rounded tail; olive-brown above
animal.lookalikes: Longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) has a very long, needle-thin beak. Spotted and shortnose gars are smaller (under 1 m), with narrower snouts and a single row of large upper teeth. Florida gar has spots all over.
animal.whereToSee: The Trinity River (Texas); Louisiana bayous and the Atchafalaya Basin; the lower Mississippi and its oxbow lakes
animal.season: Resident; spawns April–June when floods inundate vegetation

lore: Native peoples of the lower Mississippi used gar scales as arrowheads and the skin as armour. Early settlers covered wooden ploughshares with gar hide. In the 20th century gars were persecuted as 'trash fish' until research showed their role in river ecosystems.
funFact: Gar roe is toxic to mammals and birds, which may help protect the eggs from egg-eating predators.

wiki.extract: The alligator gar is a euryhaline ray-finned fish in the clade Ginglymodi of the infraclass Holostei, being most closely related to the bowfins. It is the largest species in the gar family (Lepisosteidae), and is among the largest freshwater fishes in North America. The fossil record traces its group's existence back to the Early Cretaceous over 100 million years ago. Gars are often referred to as "primitive fishes" or "living fossils", because they have retained some morphological characteristics of their early ancestors, such as a spiral valve intestine, which is also common to the digestive system of sharks, and the ability to breathe in both air and water. Their common name was derived from their resemblance to the American alligator, particularly their broad snouts and long, sharp teeth. It is suggested that an alligator gar can grow up to 10 ft (3.0 m) in length.

summary: A golden dragonfly found on every continent except Antarctica, holding the record for the longest insect migration. Generations cross the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa, riding monsoon winds.
nativeRange: Tropics and warm temperate zones worldwide
abilities: Multigenerational migration estimated at 14,000–18,000 km round trip across the Indian Ocean
Flies for days with little effort, gliding on broad hindwings
Breeds in temporary rain pools, with larvae developing in ~5 weeks
Genetic studies show near-global gene flow between continents

animal.diet: Small flying insects; aquatic larvae eat mosquito larvae and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Open areas near temporary freshwater pools
animal.behaviour: Swarms gather ahead of rain fronts, following winds to new rains where pools will form.
fieldMarks: Golden-yellow to orange skimmer about 4.5 cm long
Wings clear and very broad at the hindwing base
Large reddish eyes take up most of the head
Flies for hours on end, gliding high over open ground
animal.lookalikes: Spot-winged glider (Pantala hymenaea) has an obvious brown spot at the base of each hindwing and is slightly darker; saddlebags (Tramea) have a dark band at the hindwing base.
animal.whereToSee: Open ground and paddy fields across the tropics; notable on the Maldives during its ocean crossing between India and East Africa
animal.season: Follows the rains; in India swarms arrive with the monsoons, and the return from Africa reaches India's west coast from May

lore: Biologist Charles Anderson noticed swarms arriving in the Maldives every October with no fresh water for breeding, and in 2009 proposed the transoceanic migration. In Japan it is associated with the Obon festival as 'spirit dragonfly'.
funFact: It is the highest-flying dragonfly recorded, seen at about 6,200 m in the Himalaya.

wiki.extract: Pantala flavescens, the globe skimmer, globe wanderer or wandering glider, is a wide-ranging dragonfly of the family Libellulidae. This species and Pantala hymenaea, the "spot-winged glider", are the only members of the genus Pantala. It was first described by Johan Christian Fabricius in 1798. It is considered to be the most widespread dragonfly on the planet, with good populations on every continent except Antarctica, although rare in Europe. Globe skimmers make an annual multigenerational journey of some 18,000 km ; to complete the migration, individual globe skimmers fly more than 6,000 km ; one of the farthest known migrations of all insect species.

plates.title: The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands, Vol. 1
plates.author: Mark Catesby
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger), identified in the text as 'Larus major rostro inaequali' or 'Cutwater'.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a Black Skimmer, which Mark Catesby referred to as a 'Cutwater' due to its unique feeding habit. The illustration meticulously details the bird's specialized beak, where the lower mandible is significantly longer than the upper, allowing it to skim the water's surface for fish. Catesby's 'Natural History' was the first major published work to illustrate the bird

summary: Not a crab at all but a relative of spiders and scorpions, from a lineage whose body plan has changed little for over 400 million years. Its blue blood is used to test vaccines and medical equipment for bacterial contamination.
nativeRange: Atlantic coast of North America from Maine to the Gulf of Mexico and Yucatán; largest spawning in Delaware Bay
abilities: Blood cells (amoebocytes) clot instantly around bacterial endotoxins, the basis of the LAL test
Has ten eyes, including large compound eyes that become a million times more sensitive to light at night
Rights itself with its long tail (telson) when flipped over
Mass spawning on spring high tides gives migrating shorebirds such as red knots a key food source

animal.diet: Clams, worms, small crustaceans and other bottom invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters and estuaries; spawns on sandy beaches
animal.size: Females up to ~60 cm long including tail; males smaller
animal.behaviour: On spring nights near new and full moons, females crawl ashore at high tide to lay thousands of eggs, with males clinging behind.
fieldMarks: Rounded, horseshoe-shaped shell
Long, spike-like tail (telson)
Brown-green colour
Spawns in crowds on beaches
animal.whereToSee: Delaware Bay beaches, e.g. Reeds Beach (New Jersey) and Slaughter Beach (Delaware)
animal.season: Spawning May–Jun, on high tides near new and full moons

uses.use: Limulus amebocyte lysate (LAL) from the blood detects bacterial endotoxins in vaccines, injectable drugs and implants

medicinal.cautions: Bled crabs are returned to the sea, but an estimated 10–30% die. Synthetic recombinant Factor C tests are an approved alternative.

lore: Coastal Indigenous peoples used the shells to bail canoes and the tails as spear tips, and colonial farmers ground millions of horseshoe crabs into fertiliser. Frederik Bang's discovery in the 1950s that its blood clots on contact with bacteria led to the LAL test.
funFact: Studies of its large optic nerves helped H. Keffer Hartline win the 1967 Nobel Prize for discoveries about how eyes process images.

wiki.extract: The Atlantic horseshoe crab, also known as the American horseshoe crab, is a species of horseshoe crab, a kind of marine and brackish chelicerate arthropod. It is found in the Gulf of Mexico and along the Atlantic coast of North America. The main area of annual migration is Delaware Bay along the South Jersey Delaware Bayshore.

plates.long: This hand-colored copperplate engraving from Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' (1771) meticulously depicts marine arthropods. The upper figures provide both dorsal and ventral perspectives of a horseshoe crab, while the lower figure shows a European lobster in profile, showcasing the era's commitment to detailed taxonomic recording and aesthetic presentation of the natural world.

Appearing in Carolus Clusius's 'Exoticorum libri decem' (1605), it represents the era's burgeoning scientific curiosity and the use of print technology to disseminate knowledge of global flora and fauna.

summary: A tiny, pencil-limbed nocturnal primate of Sri Lanka's wet southwest, with enormous forward-facing eyes for hunting insects at night. It moves slowly and silently along branches, then lunges with both hands. The related grey slender loris lives in drier Sri Lanka and southern India.
nativeRange: Endemic to the wet zone of southwestern Sri Lanka, including a highland form in the central hills
abilities: Huge eyes with a reflective tapetum for vision in near darkness
Grasp so strong it can hang for long periods, aided by special blood vessels (retia mirabilia) in its limbs
Eats toxic or bad-tasting insects that other predators avoid

animal.diet: Mostly insects (including ants and beetles), plus other invertebrates, small lizards, eggs and some plant matter
animal.habitat: Wet lowland and submontane forest and nearby gardens with dense vine tangles
animal.size: Body about 17–26 cm, no external tail; 85–170 g
animal.behaviour: Strictly nocturnal and arboreal. Sleeps by day curled up in a ball among dense foliage, often in small groups.
fieldMarks: Very thin limbs and tiny body with no tail
Huge round eyes ringed with dark patches and divided by a white stripe down the nose
Reddish-brown fur (redder than the grey slender loris)
At night, eyes show bright orange-red eyeshine in torchlight; moves hand over hand slowly
animal.lookalikes: Grey slender loris (Loris lydekkerianus) of Sri Lanka's dry zone and southern India is greyer with a paler underside. Slow lorises (northeast India and Southeast Asia) are much stockier.
animal.whereToSee: Masmullah Proposed Forest Reserve; Kottawa Forest and Kanneliya Forest Reserve; Sinharaja Forest Reserve (all Sri Lanka); best with a guided night walk
animal.season: Resident; active at night year-round

lore: In Sri Lankan and South Indian folk belief, loris eyes and body parts were used in charms and remedies, which, with the pet trade, has long contributed to their persecution.
funFact: Its species name tardigradus means 'slow-stepping', the same root as the microscopic tardigrades.

wiki.extract: The red slender loris is a small, nocturnal strephsirrhine primate native to the rainforests of Sri Lanka. This is No. 6 of the 10 focal species and No. 22 of the 100 EDGE mammal species worldwide considered the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered.

Produced for Jean Baptiste Audebert's 'Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis' (1800), it showcases the artist's skill in rendering texture and form using color-printing techniques.

The plate exemplifies the 18th-century tradition of natural history illustration, which sought to document global biodiversity with both scientific accuracy and aesthetic appeal.

The illustration is notable for its scientific accuracy and the delicate use of stipple engraving to capture the texture of the animal's fur and the branch.

summary: The largest slow loris and one of the world's few venomous primates. When threatened it raises its arms over its head, licks a gland on the inner elbow, and mixes the secretion with saliva to deliver a painful, sometimes dangerous bite. It is the only slow loris in India and is heavily hunted for the pet and traditional-medicine trades.
nativeRange: Northeast India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern China, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam
abilities: Brachial (elbow) gland secretion combined with saliva makes a toxic bite that can cause severe swelling and anaphylactic shock in people
Its grip can hold for hours, aided by networks of blood vessels in the limbs
Feeds on tree gum by gouging bark with its tooth-comb, an important dry-season food

animal.diet: Plant gum and sap, nectar, fruit, insects, snails, birds' eggs
animal.habitat: Evergreen and semi-evergreen forest and bamboo groves with continuous canopy
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal and slow-moving, but capable of quick lunges. Sleeps curled in a ball in dense foliage by day.
fieldMarks: Stocky, woolly primate with a round head and almost no tail
Dark brown stripe along the spine reaching the crown
Large eyes encircled by dark rings with a white stripe between
Bright orange eyeshine in torchlight at night; slow, deliberate climbing
animal.lookalikes: Pygmy slow loris (Indochina) is much smaller and redder. Slender lorises are thin-limbed and live only in southern India and Sri Lanka.
animal.whereToSee: Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary (Assam); Lawachara National Park (Bangladesh); Dampa Tiger Reserve (Mizoram); Khao Yai National Park (Thailand); night walks with guides
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Bengali it is called the 'shy monkey' (lajjabati banor) because it covers its face with its hands when caught in light. Its body parts have been sold in markets in Southeast Asia and China for traditional remedies.
funFact: Slow lorises are the only primates confirmed to produce venom.

wiki.extract: The Bengal slow loris or northern slow loris is a strepsirrhine primate and a species of slow loris native to the Bangladesh, Northeast India, Cambodia, Laos, Burma, Vietnam, southern China, and Thailand. Its geographic range is larger than that of any other slow loris species. Considered a subspecies of the Sunda slow loris (N. coucang) until 2001, phylogenetic analysis suggests that the Bengal slow loris is most closely related to the Sunda slow loris. However, some individuals in both species have mitochondrial DNA sequences that resemble those of the other species, due to introgressive hybridization. It is the largest species of slow loris, measuring 26 to 38 cm from head to tail and weighing between 1 and 2.1 kg. Like other slow lorises, it has a wet nose (rhinarium), a round head, flat face, large eyes, small ears, a vestigial tail, and dense, woolly fur. The toxin it secretes from its brachial gland differs chemically from that of other slow loris species and may be used to communicate information about sex, age, health, and social status.

summary: Europe's largest beetle, whose males carry huge antler-like jaws used only for wrestling rivals. It spends most of its life as a grub in rotting wood underground and emerges for just a few summer weeks.
nativeRange: Europe from southern Sweden to Iberia, east to Turkey, the Caucasus and Syria
abilities: Larvae live 3–6 years feeding on decaying wood
Males' enlarged mandibles function like antlers in contests over females
Adults fly on warm summer evenings with a loud, whirring, upright flight

animal.diet: Larvae eat decaying wood of oak and other broadleaves (stumps, roots); adults sip sap and fruit juice
animal.habitat: Old oak woods, parks, hedgerows and suburban gardens with dead wood
animal.lifespan: Up to about 6 years, almost all as a larva; adults a few weeks
animal.size: Males about 3.5–9 cm including mandibles; females 3–5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males grapple on branches and tree trunks, trying to grip and throw opponents off.
fieldMarks: Male with huge, branched, reddish-brown 'antler' mandibles
Chestnut-brown wing cases and black head and thorax
Female smaller with short, strong jaws
Slow, upright, buzzing flight at dusk
animal.lookalikes: Lesser stag beetle (Dorcus parallelipipedus) is smaller (2–3 cm), all dull black, and has small jaws; female stag beetles have reddish-brown wing cases. Rhinoceros beetle (Sinodendron cylindricum) is small, black and cylindrical.
animal.whereToSee: South-east England (south London, Thames valley, Essex, Kent), and oak woodland across central and southern Europe.
animal.season: Adults late May–July, flying on warm evenings

lore: Pliny the Elder reported that children wore stag-beetle jaws as amulets against illness, and Albrecht Dürer painted a lifelike stag beetle in 1505. Old English folklore blamed it for carrying hot coals and setting thatch alight.
funFact: Despite their size, the male's jaws are too weak to give a painful nip; the smaller-jawed female bites much harder.

wiki.extract: Lucanus cervus, known as the European stag beetle, or the greater stag beetle, is one of the best-known species of stag beetle in Western Europe, and is the eponymous example of the genus. L. cervus is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

summary: A large European earthworm that digs deep vertical burrows and drags fallen leaves underground at night. Its burrowing mixes and aerates soil, and Charles Darwin spent decades measuring how much earth worms move.
nativeRange: Europe; introduced to North America, New Zealand and elsewhere, where it is invasive in some previously worm-free northern forests
abilities: Digs permanent vertical burrows up to ~2 m deep that let air and water into the soil
Pulls leaves into its burrow, mixing organic matter deep into the soil
Breathes entirely through its moist skin
Senses light with cells in its skin despite having no eyes
As a hermaphrodite, each worm both gives and receives sperm when mating

animal.diet: Detritivore: dead leaves, decaying plant matter and soil microbes
animal.habitat: Moist, loamy soils of meadows, woods, fields and gardens
animal.lifespan: Several years; up to ~6 in captivity
animal.behaviour: On damp nights it stretches out of its burrow to feed and mate, keeping its tail anchored inside so it can snap back at the slightest vibration.
fieldMarks: Large earthworm, 11–20 cm
Reddish-brown front end fading toward the rear
Flattened, paddle-shaped tail
Surfaces on wet nights
animal.lookalikes: Aporrectodea trapezoides is similar in size and dark colour.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns and fields after rain
animal.season: Active all year in moist soil

lore: Darwin's last book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms (1881), showed how earthworms slowly bury stones and ancient ruins. It was a bestseller in its day.
funFact: In northern North American forests that lost their native worms in the last Ice Age, this introduced species eats away the leaf litter that native wildflowers and salamanders depend on.

wiki.extract: Lumbricus terrestris is a large, reddish worm species thought to be native to Western Europe, now widely distributed around the world. In some areas where it is an introduced species, some people consider it to be a significant pest for out-competing native worms.

summary: The largest crab in the world by leg span, reaching about 3.7 m from claw tip to claw tip. It lives in deep water off Japan's Pacific coast and climbs to shallower depths to breed in spring.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of Japan, especially Sagami Bay, Suruga Bay and Tosa Bay; also reported off Taiwan
abilities: Largest leg span of any arthropod, up to about 3.7 m
Can regenerate lost legs over successive moults
Young crabs camouflage themselves by attaching sponges and other organisms to their shells

animal.diet: Scavenger and opportunist: dead animals, molluscs and other invertebrates, plus algae
animal.habitat: Sandy and rocky bottoms from about 50 to 600 m deep
animal.size: Leg span up to about 3.7 m; carapace up to about 40 cm; weight up to about 19 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring it moves into waters around 50 m deep to mate and spawn, when fishing for it is restricted.
fieldMarks: Enormously long, thin legs
Orange body and legs with white spots
Pear-shaped, bumpy carapace
Long, thin claws in males
animal.lookalikes: King crabs (Paralithodes) are spiny, have shorter legs and appear to have only three pairs of walking legs. Snow crabs (Chionoecetes) have a flat, rounded shell and much shorter legs.
animal.whereToSee: Large public aquariums in Japan (e.g. Osaka Kaiyukan, Numazu Deep Sea Aquarium) and worldwide; divers occasionally see them in Suruga Bay in spring.
animal.season: Moves shallower to breed in spring

edibilityNote: Eaten locally around Suruga Bay (e.g. Heda on the Izu Peninsula); catches have declined and are managed.
lore: It is named after Engelbert Kaempfer, the German physician who worked at the Dutch trading post of Dejima in the 1690s and wrote one of the first European histories of Japan.
funFact: Its long legs are fragile; it often lives with lost or regrowing legs, which it replaces gradually over several moults.

wiki.extract: The Japanese giant spider crab is a species of marine crab and is the largest crab found in the waters around Japan. At around 3.75 metres (12.3 ft), it has the largest leg-span of any arthropod. The Japanese name for this species is taka-ashi-gani,, literally translating to "tall-legged crab". It goes through three main larval stages along with a prezoeal stage to grow to its full size.

summary: The largest living marsupial, a long-legged hopper of Australia's dry interior. Hopping is so efficient at speed that a kangaroo uses little more energy going faster.
nativeRange: Arid and semi-arid mainland Australia
abilities: Bounds at up to ~60 km/h and covers 8 m or more in a single leap
Stores and returns energy in its elastic leg tendons like a spring
Uses its muscular tail as a fifth leg when moving slowly
Can pause the development of an embryo (embryonic diapause) until conditions improve
Can have an embryo, a joey in the pouch and a joey at foot at the same time, producing two kinds of milk from different teats

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses and forbs; can go long periods without drinking
animal.habitat: Open plains, desert and shrubland with scattered shade trees
animal.lifespan: Up to ~20 years; often less in the wild
animal.size: Males up to ~85 kg and ~1.6 m long plus tail; females ~35 kg
animal.behaviour: Rival males 'box', grappling with forearms and kicking with their hind feet while balanced on their tails. Kangaroos lick their forearms to cool off.
fieldMarks: Largest kangaroo
Males usually red-brown, females blue-grey
Black and white marks on the muzzle
Pale underparts
animal.lookalikes: Eastern and western grey kangaroos lack the black and white muzzle marks and have dark tail tips. Large males can kick and box. Keep a respectful distance.
animal.whereToSee: Sturt National Park (NSW), Flinders Ranges (SA) and Mutawintji National Park
animal.season: Resident; active at dawn and dusk

lore: Joseph Banks and James Cook recorded the word 'kangaroo' from Guugu Yimithirr speakers at the Endeavour River in 1770 (their animal was a grey kangaroo). The red kangaroo appears on Australia's coat of arms.
funFact: Females are often blue-grey while males are red, which is why females are nicknamed 'blue fliers'.

wiki.extract: The red kangaroo is the largest of all kangaroos, the largest terrestrial mammal native to Australia, and the largest extant marsupial. It is found across mainland Australia, except for the more fertile areas, such as southern Western Australia, the eastern and southeastern coasts, and the rainforests along the northern coast.

summary: A tiny, cocked-tailed bird whose breeding males glow electric blue. Its family life is famous for cooperative breeding and very high rates of extra-pair mating.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia and Tasmania
abilities: Cooperative breeding, with helpers raising the young
Mothers teach embryos a 'password' call in the egg
Males pluck yellow petals and display them to females

animal.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense shrubs and grassland edges, gardens
animal.behaviour: Mothers call to eggs before hatching, and chicks incorporate a unique 'password' into their begging calls.
fieldMarks: Breeding males: bright blue crown, cheeks and mantle
Black throat and eye-stripe
Long, cocked tail
Females and non-breeding males brown with orange-red around the eye
animal.voice: A high, rapid, reeling trill.
animal.lookalikes: Splendid fairywren males are blue all over. Variegated fairywren has chestnut shoulders. Females of other fairywrens differ in eye patches and tail colour.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and parks in Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney, Hobart; Royal Botanic Gardens
animal.season: Resident

lore: Known to generations of Australians as the 'blue wren', it is a fixture of suburban gardens; a 2012 study showing that mothers teach their embryos a 'password' call drew worldwide attention.
funFact: Despite living in pairs, most chicks in a superb fairywren nest are fathered by males outside the pair.

wiki.extract: The superb fairywren is a passerine bird in the Australasian wren family, Maluridae, and is common and familiar across south-eastern Australia. It is a sedentary and territorial species, also exhibiting a high degree of sexual dimorphism; the male in breeding plumage has a striking bright blue forehead, ear coverts, mantle, and tail, with a black mask and black or dark blue throat. Non-breeding males, females and juveniles are predominantly grey-brown in colour; this gave the early impression that males were polygamous, as all dull-coloured birds were taken for females. Six subspecies groups are recognized: three larger and darker forms from Tasmania, Flinders and King Island respectively, and three smaller and paler forms from mainland Australia and Kangaroo Island.

summary: An armour-plated ant- and termite-eater of the Indian subcontinent, covered in overlapping keratin scales and able to roll into a near-impregnable ball. It is one of the most trafficked mammals in the world, poached for its scales and meat, and is protected under Schedule I of India's Wildlife Protection Act.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and possibly Bangladesh
abilities: Toothless; a sticky tongue about 40 cm long, extending some 25 cm from the mouth, reaches deep into termite galleries
Rolls into a tight ball, protected by sharp-edged scales, when threatened
Digs burrows several metres long with powerful foreclaws
Can close its nostrils and ears against biting ants

animal.diet: Ants and termites, including their eggs and larvae
animal.habitat: Grassland, dry and moist forest, scrub and farmland, including hilly and semi-desert terrain
animal.lifespan: Poorly known; up to about 19 years in captivity
animal.size: Head and body 45–75 cm, tail 33–47 cm; about 9–16 kg
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal and solitary, sleeping by day in burrows or rock crevices. Walks on its knuckles and hind feet, sometimes rearing up on its back legs.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, tapering body like a walking pine cone, with a broad, thick tail
11–13 rows of large, overlapping yellowish-brown scales on the body
Tiny conical head with small eyes and no visible teeth
Signs: burrows with fresh soil at the entrance, dug-open termite mounds and ant nests, a tail-drag line between footprints
animal.lookalikes: Chinese pangolin (in the northeast Himalayan foothills) has smaller scales, prominent external ears and a shorter tail. Sunda pangolin occurs only in Southeast Asia. No other South Asian mammal has scales.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; nocturnal surveys in Kanha and Satpura (central India), Pothohar Plateau (Pakistan), dry zone of Sri Lanka, and Similipal (Odisha)
animal.season: Resident; active at night year-round

lore: A suit of armour made from Indian pangolin scales was presented to King George III in 1820 by the Marquess of Hastings and is now displayed at the Royal Armouries in Leeds. Demand for its scales in traditional Chinese medicine, which have no proven medicinal effect, drives most poaching.
funFact: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, the same protein as human fingernails.

wiki.extract:
The Indian pangolin, also called thick-tailed pangolin and scaly anteater, is a pangolin native to the Indian subcontinent.
Like other pangolins, it has large, overlapping scales on its body which act as armour. The colour of its scales varies depending on the colour of the earth in its surroundings. It can also curl itself into a ball as self-defence against predators such as the tiger. 
It is an insectivore feeding on ants and termites, digging them out of mounds and logs using its long claws, which are as long as its fore limbs. It is nocturnal and rests in deep burrows during the day.

summary: A scaly, toothless ant-eater of Southeast Asian forests and plantations, armoured in overlapping keratin scales. Pangolins are thought to be the most trafficked wild mammals, poached for meat and scales.
nativeRange: Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra, Java, Borneo and nearby islands
abilities: Rolls into a tight, armoured ball that most predators cannot open
Rips into ant and termite nests with powerful foreclaws
Catches insects with a long, sticky tongue anchored deep in the chest
Seals its nostrils and ears against biting ants while feeding
Grinds food with swallowed stones and keratin spines in its stomach instead of teeth

animal.diet: Insectivore: ants and termites, including eggs and larvae
animal.habitat: Primary and secondary forest, plantations, gardens
animal.lifespan: Unknown in the wild; ~20 years recorded in captivity for pangolins
animal.size: Body 40–65 cm plus a similar tail; ~4–10 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal, it climbs well with its prehensile tail and sleeps in tree hollows or burrows. Mothers carry their single young on the base of the tail.
fieldMarks: Covered in overlapping brown scales
Small head and long tail used for gripping
Rolls into a ball when threatened
Nocturnal and rarely seen
animal.lookalikes: Chinese pangolin has larger ears and a shorter tail; Philippine pangolin lives only in Palawan.
animal.season: Resident; nocturnal

lore: The English word comes from Malay pengguling, 'one that rolls up'. Pangolin scales have long been used in traditional Chinese medicine; in 2020 China removed them from its official pharmacopoeia and gave pangolins top legal protection.
funFact: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, the same protein as human fingernails.

wiki.extract: The Sunda pangolin, also known as the Malayan or Javan pangolin, is a species of pangolin. It is a member of the Manidae family. Its English name comes from the Malay name pëngulin, which means "roller".

summary: The original 'praying mantis', an ambush predator that waits with spiked forelegs folded as if in prayer. It hears with a single ear in the middle of its chest, tuned to the ultrasound of hunting bats.
nativeRange: Southern and central Europe, Africa and Asia; introduced to North America in the 1890s
abilities: Strikes prey with spiked raptorial forelegs in a fraction of a second
Single midline ear detects bat ultrasound, triggering evasive dives in flight
Turns its head almost 180° to watch prey
Females sometimes eat males during or after mating

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, flies, butterflies, crickets and other insects
animal.habitat: Sunny, tall grassland, scrub, vineyards and gardens
animal.lifespan: About one year: nymphs hatch in spring and adults die in autumn
animal.behaviour: Females lay eggs in a frothy case (ootheca) on stems or stones that hardens and protects up to a few hundred eggs through winter.
fieldMarks: Green or brown, slender body with long neck-like thorax
Raptorial forelegs held folded in front
Black spot ringed with white (a dark 'eye') on the inner base of each foreleg
Wings reach the tip of the abdomen in both sexes
animal.lookalikes: Chinese mantis (Tenodera sinensis), also introduced in North America, is larger (to about 10 cm), lacks the black foreleg spot and has a green-edged wing. Carolina mantis (Stagmomantis carolina) is smaller and the female's wings stop short of the abdomen tip.
animal.whereToSee: Rough grassland and vineyards in southern Europe; meadows and old fields in north-eastern North America.
animal.season: Adults Aug–Oct

lore: The Greek mantis means 'prophet' or 'seer', and in Provence it is called prega-Diéu, 'pray to God'. The entomologist Jean-Henri Fabre made it famous in his Souvenirs entomologiques (1879–1907).
funFact: Its 'cyclopean ear' was discovered in 1986: a single slit between the legs on the underside of the thorax, which makes the mantis deaf to the direction of sound but very sensitive to bat calls.

wiki.extract: The European mantis is a large hemimetabolic insect in the family Mantidae, which is the largest family of the order Mantodea (mantises). Their common name praying mantis is derived from the distinctive posture of the first pair of legs, which can be observed when the mantis is in repose, resembling a praying position. Both males and females have elongated bodies with two pairs of wings. The most striking features that the species have are a very mobile, triangular head with large compound eyes and their first pair of legs, which is highly modified for the efficient capture and restraint of fast-moving or flying prey.

summary: A bright green barbet with a sky-blue face and throat and a red crown crossed by a black band, whose loud rolling calls echo through Himalayan foothill forests. It is a fig specialist that carves its nest hole in dead wood.
nativeRange: Himalayan foothills from Uttarakhand through Nepal, Bhutan and NE India to Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern China, Thailand and Indochina
abilities: Disperses the seeds of figs and other fruiting trees
Excavates nest cavities in dead branches
Calls persistently from treetops through the breeding season

animal.diet: Figs and other fruit; some insects
animal.habitat: Broadleaf forest, forest edges, orchards and gardens, up to about 2,400 m
animal.behaviour: Sits motionless high in fruiting trees for long periods, so it is easier to hear than to see despite its colours.
fieldMarks: Stocky bright green barbet with a heavy bill, pale at the base with a dark upper mandible and tip
Sky-blue face, cheeks and throat
Red forehead and crown with a black band across the crown
Small red patch at the side of the throat
animal.voice: A loud, rolling 'took-a-rook, took-a-rook' or 'kutroo-kutroo', repeated endlessly
animal.lookalikes: Golden-throated barbet has a yellow throat; Great barbet is larger with a blue-black head and red vent; Coppersmith barbet is smaller with a yellow throat and red breast patch.
animal.whereToSee: Kathmandu valley gardens (Nepal), Corbett and Nainital (Uttarakhand), Darjeeling, Doi Inthanon (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident year-round; most vocal in spring

lore: Its incessant calling makes it one of the signature sounds of Himalayan hill stations such as Darjeeling and Kathmandu in spring.
funFact: Asian barbets were once placed in the same family as African and American barbets, but genetics showed they form a separate family, Megalaimidae.

wiki.extract: The blue-throated barbet is a green Asian barbet native to the foothills of the Himalayas and Southeast Asia. It inhabits lowland and montane forests at elevations of 200–2,000 m (660–6,560 ft), frequenting fruiting trees. Due to its green colour, it is difficult to spot but is easily located by its continual loud calls. Sexes are similar in most respects and share domestic duties.

otherNames: Chì xiōng nǐ zhuómùniǎo 赤胸拟啄木鸟 (Chinese)
summary: A small green barbet with a crimson forehead and breast patch, whose monotonous metallic 'tuk-tuk-tuk' sounds like a coppersmith hammering a pot. It is a familiar fruit-eater of fig trees in towns from Pakistan to the Philippines.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Punjab and northwest), India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through Southeast Asia to the Philippines and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Disperses the seeds of figs and other fruiting trees
Excavates its own nest hole in soft, dead wood
Calls for long periods with the throat puffing out on each note

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; some insects
animal.habitat: Groves, gardens and open woodland with fig and other fruit trees
animal.behaviour: Often sits on a bare branch at the top of a tree in the morning sun, calling and bobbing its head left and right with each note.
fieldMarks: Small, chunky green barbet with a heavy bill
Crimson forehead and crimson patch on the upper breast
Yellow throat and yellow patches above and below the eye, separated by black
Pale underparts streaked with green
animal.voice: A loud, repetitive, metallic 'tuk… tuk… tuk', kept up for minutes, like a hammer on copper
animal.lookalikes: Brown-headed barbet is larger, brown-headed and streaked, with an orange eye-patch; Blue-throated barbet (Himalaya) has a blue face and throat.
animal.whereToSee: Fig and peepal trees in Lahore, Delhi, Kolkata and Colombo; Keoladeo National Park
animal.season: Resident; calls loudly from February to May

lore: Its English and Hindi names both describe the call; in north Indian towns its steady hammering is one of the signature sounds of the hot season.
funFact: When calling, each 'tuk' is accompanied by a visible bulging of the throat skin, while the bird swings its head so the sound seems to come from different directions.
