wiki.extract: The coppersmith barbet, also called crimson-breasted barbet and coppersmith, is an Asian barbet with crimson forehead and throat, known for its metronomic call that sounds similar to a coppersmith striking metal with a hammer. It is a resident bird in the Indian subcontinent and parts of Southeast Asia. It carves out holes inside a tree to build its nest. It is predominantly frugivorous, but has been observed eating insects, especially winged termites.

summary: A fist-sized black predator of the deep sea that dangles a glowing lure in front of a mouth full of needle teeth. The tiny males seek out females by smell and attach only briefly to mate.
nativeRange: Tropical to temperate waters of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans
abilities: The lure (esca) glows with light from symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria
Stomach and jaws stretch to swallow prey longer than itself
Free-living dwarf males use large nostrils to track female pheromones; unlike some ceratioid anglers, males do not fuse permanently
Survives at depths of 100–4,500 m in near-total darkness

animal.diet: Fish, crustaceans and squid attracted to the lure
animal.habitat: Open ocean, mostly 200–1,500 m
animal.size: Females up to about 18 cm; males under 3 cm
animal.behaviour: Hangs nearly motionless, twitching its lure to draw prey within striking distance in the dark.
fieldMarks: Globular, velvety black body
Huge upturned mouth with long, fang-like teeth
Single fishing-rod spine (illicium) on the snout with a bulbous glowing tip
Small eyes and tiny fins
animal.lookalikes: Other Melanocetus species differ in fin-ray counts and lure shape; footballfishes (Himantolophus) have a branched lure and bony plates.
animal.whereToSee: Effectively only via deep-sea ROV footage (e.g. MBARI, Monterey Canyon, which filmed a live female in 2014); specimens in natural-history museums
animal.season: Year-round in the deep sea

lore: Described by Albert Günther in 1864 from a specimen taken off Madeira; MBARI's 2014 video is believed to be the first footage of a living Melanocetus in its habitat.
funFact: Its species name honours James Yate Johnson, the Madeira naturalist who sent the first specimen to the British Museum.

wiki.extract: The humpback anglerfish is a species of black seadevil in the family of Melanocetidae, which means "black sea monster". The species is named after James Yate Johnson, an English naturalist who discovered the first specimen in Madeira in 1863. The common names include anglerfish, viperfish, and fangtoothfish.

summary: A striking black-and-gold honeyeater of south-eastern Australia's box-ironbark woodlands, now so rare that many males never hear an adult of their own species and fail to learn its song. Fewer than about 300 are thought to remain in the wild.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia, mainly inland slopes of the Great Dividing Range in New South Wales and Victoria
abilities: Pollinates flowering eucalypts such as mugga ironbark, yellow box and white box while feeding on nectar
Tracks irregular eucalypt flowering across hundreds of kilometres
Young males learn song from adults, which is why the song is fading as numbers fall

animal.diet: Nectar, especially of eucalypts and mistletoe; also lerp, honeydew and insects
animal.habitat: Dry box-ironbark eucalypt woodland and riparian forest
animal.behaviour: In a 2021 study, around 12% of wild males sang the songs of other species, such as friarbirds and wattlebirds, rather than their own, having had no regent honeyeater tutors.
fieldMarks: Black head, neck and upper breast
Pale yellow scalloping on back and breast
Bright yellow edges to wing and tail feathers
Bare, warty pinkish skin around the eye
Down-curved black bill
animal.voice: A soft, bell-like, metallic warble; males that have not learned it may give mimicked songs of other honeyeaters instead.
animal.lookalikes: Painted honeyeater has a pink bill, plain black upperparts and unscalloped white underparts. New Holland honeyeater has white-streaked underparts, a white eye and yellow wing panels but no bare facial skin.
animal.whereToSee: Capertee Valley and Hunter Valley (NSW), Chiltern-Mt Pilot National Park (Victoria); release sites in north-east Victoria
animal.season: Nomadic resident; movements follow eucalypt flowering

lore: Taronga Zoo has bred regent honeyeaters for release since the 1990s, and captive young are now tutored with recordings of wild song before release.
funFact: It is one of the first wild birds documented losing its song culture because the population became too small and scattered for young males to find tutors.

wiki.extract: The regent honeyeater is a critically endangered bird endemic to southeastern Australia. It is commonly considered a flagship species within its range, with the efforts going into its conservation having positive effects on many other species that share its habitat. Recent genetic research suggests it is closely related to the wattlebirds.

summary: A New Zealand honeyeater with iridescent plumage and a white throat tuft. Its complex song, with clicks, chimes and wheezes, comes from two voice boxes.
nativeRange: New Zealand
abilities: Two-sided syrinx lets it sing two notes at once
Some song elements are reported to be too high-pitched for people to hear
Pollinates flax, kōwhai and other native plants
Accomplished mimic, including human speech

animal.diet: Nectar, fruit, insects
animal.habitat: Native forest, regenerating scrub, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: Tūī are aggressive defenders of nectar trees, chasing off other birds with loud wing whirring.
fieldMarks: Dark iridescent plumage with blue, green and bronze sheen
Two white throat tufts (poi)
Lacy white collar of filamentous feathers
Curved black bill
animal.voice: A rich mix of bell-like notes, clicks, cackles and wheezes.
animal.lookalikes: Korimako (New Zealand bellbird) is smaller, olive-green and lacks the white tufts.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia (Wellington), Tiritiri Matangi, Otari-Wilton's Bush, Auckland parks
animal.season: Resident

lore: Māori trained captive tūī to recite karakia and greetings. 'Parson bird' refers to the white tufts resembling clerical bands.
funFact: Like other songbirds, the tūī has a two-sided voice box (syrinx), but it uses it with unusual virtuosity, producing two independent sounds at once.

wiki.extract: The tūī is a medium-sized bird native to New Zealand. It is blue, green, and bronze coloured with a distinctive white throat tuft (poi). It is an endemic passerine bird of New Zealand, and the only species in the genus Prosthemadera. It is one of the largest species in the diverse Australasian honeyeater family Meliphagidae, and one of two living species of that family found in New Zealand, the other being the New Zealand bellbird. The tūī has a wide distribution in the archipelago, ranging from the subtropical Kermadec Islands to the sub-Antarctic Auckland Islands, as well as the main islands.

summary: A pheasant-sized songbird of south-eastern Australia and one of the greatest vocal mimics on Earth. Males copy the calls of dozens of other species, and occasionally human-made sounds.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia; introduced to Tasmania
abilities: Mimics the calls of many other birds with near-perfect accuracy
Has been recorded imitating camera shutters, chainsaws and car alarms
Males choreograph songs to specific dance movements
Rakes enormous volumes of forest litter, an important ecosystem engineer

animal.diet: Earthworms, insects, spiders and other invertebrates from the forest floor
animal.habitat: Wet forests and gullies
animal.size: Males up to ~1 m including tail
animal.behaviour: Males sing on cleared mounds, spreading the lyre-shaped tail over their heads in a shimmering display.
fieldMarks: Pheasant-sized brown ground bird
Males have a long tail of 16 feathers, including two lyre-shaped outer feathers
Females have a long, plainer tail
Strong legs; scratches leaf litter
animal.voice: Loud, powerful song full of near-perfect imitations of other birds and sometimes mechanical sounds, mixed with its own ringing calls
animal.lookalikes: Albert's lyrebird of the NSW–Queensland border rainforests is more rufous and males lack the lyre-shaped outer tail feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Sherbrooke Forest (Dandenong Ranges) near Melbourne, the Blue Mountains and Royal National Park near Sydney
animal.season: Resident; most song and display in winter (Jun–Aug)

lore: It appears on the reverse of the Australian 10-cent coin. A lyrebird population in New England National Park is said to sing a flute tune taught to captive birds in the 1930s.
funFact: A single lyrebird can move around 155 tonnes of soil and litter per hectare per year.

wiki.extract: The superb lyrebird is an Australian passerine songbird, one of two species from the family Menuridae, with the other being the much rarer Albert's lyrebird. One of the world's largest songbirds, the superb lyrebird is renowned for its elaborate tail and courtship displays, and for its excellent mimicry. The species is endemic to Australia and is found in forest in the southeast of the country. According to David Attenborough, the superb lyrebird displays one of the most sophisticated voice skills within the animal kingdom—"the most elaborate, the most complex, and the most beautiful".

summary: A gloriously coloured aerial hunter in chestnut, gold and turquoise that catches bees and wasps on the wing. It nests colonially in tunnels dug into sandy banks and winters in Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa, with a small resident population in southern Africa
abilities: Removes the sting of a bee by beating and rubbing it against a perch before swallowing
Digs nest tunnels up to a metre or more long in sandbanks with its bill
Helpers, often previous offspring, assist some pairs in feeding chicks
Its range is moving north with warmer summers, with recent breeding in Germany and Britain

animal.diet: Flying insects, chiefly bees, wasps and hornets, also dragonflies and beetles
animal.habitat: Open warm country with sandy or earthen banks, river cliffs, quarries
animal.lifespan: Typically a few years; the European ringing record is 7 years
animal.behaviour: Sallies from wires and dead branches to snap up insects, then returns to bash them on the perch.
fieldMarks: Chestnut crown and back, golden-yellow shoulders and throat
Black eye mask and black necklace
Turquoise-blue underparts
Long pointed central tail feathers and long, decurved black bill
animal.voice: A liquid, rolling 'prruip' or 'krruup', given constantly by flocks overhead and often the first sign of their presence.
animal.lookalikes: Blue-cheeked bee-eater (North Africa, Middle East) is mostly green with a chestnut throat and longer streamers. European roller is stockier and blue with no long tail streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura and the Ebro valley in Spain, the Camargue, Greek and Turkish river valleys; huge passage flocks over Eilat and the Bosphorus.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr/May–Sep; passage migrant across the Mediterranean and Middle East

lore: Aristotle wrote that beekeepers regarded the 'merops' as an enemy of their hives, and its Arabic name 'warwar' imitates its rolling call.
funFact: In 2022 a small colony bred in a quarry at Trimingham, Norfolk, and drew thousands of visitors.

wiki.extract: The European bee-eater is a bird species in the bee-eater family, Meropidae. It has the largest range of any bee-eater species, breeding in southern and central Europe, northern and southern Africa, and western Asia. Except for the resident southern African population, the species is strongly migratory, wintering in tropical Africa. This species occurs as a spring overshoot north of its usual range, with occasional breeding in northern Europe.

summary: A carmine-and-turquoise bee-eater that nests in colonies of hundreds to thousands of burrows dug into riverbanks. It famously hunts insects flushed by grazing animals, sometimes riding on the backs of kori bustards.
nativeRange: Southern Africa from Angola and southern DR Congo to northern South Africa; spreads more widely after breeding
abilities: Excavates burrows usually 1–2 m long, sometimes more, into vertical sand cliffs
Rides on kori bustards, ostriches and large mammals to snatch flushed insects
Gathers at bush fires to catch fleeing insects
Removes the sting from bees and wasps by beating them on a perch

animal.diet: Flying insects: bees, wasps, locusts, grasshoppers, beetles, dragonflies
animal.habitat: River valleys, floodplains and savanna
animal.behaviour: Colonies of thousands of birds swirl above riverbanks, each pair digging its own tunnel side by side with neighbours.
fieldMarks: Carmine pink-red body
Turquoise-blue crown and undertail
Black mask through the eye
Long, pointed central tail streamers
Slender, down-curved black bill
animal.voice: Deep, throaty 'terk' or 'krik-krik' calls, given incessantly by flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Northern carmine bee-eater, north of the equator, has a blue-green throat rather than a carmine one. Other bee-eaters in its range are mostly green and none is carmine all over.
animal.whereToSee: Luangwa Valley (Zambia), Zambezi and Chobe rivers, Okavango Delta, Mana Pools (Zimbabwe)
animal.season: Intra-African migrant; breeds August to December in southern Africa, then disperses north and south

lore: Southern carmine bee-eater colonies on the Zambezi and Luangwa riverbanks are a celebrated attraction of the southern African dry season.
funFact: A breeding colony can number several thousand birds packed into a single sandbank.

summary: A slim grey bird with a big voice, famous for copying the songs of other birds, frogs and even car alarms. Males may learn around 200 different songs, repeating each phrase several times before switching.
nativeRange: Southern Canada and the US south to southern Mexico, the Bahamas and the Greater Antilles; introduced to Hawaii and Bermuda
abilities: Learns new song types throughout life, adding mimicry of birds, frogs, insects and mechanical sounds
Unmated males sing through the night, especially under bright moonlight or streetlights
Recognises individual humans who have approached its nest and scolds them on sight
Flashes white wing patches while foraging, possibly to startle insects

animal.diet: Insects in summer; fruit and berries in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Open ground with shrubs and trees — suburbs, hedgerows, parks, desert edges
animal.behaviour: It aggressively defends nests and winter fruit trees, diving at cats, hawks and people.
fieldMarks: Grey above, paler grey-white below
Large white patches on dark wings, obvious in flight
Long dark tail with white outer feathers
Thin, slightly decurved dark bill; yellow eye in adults
animal.voice: Long, varied runs of phrases, each repeated three or more times in a row, mixing its own song with mimicry; call a harsh 'chack'.
animal.lookalikes: Loggerhead Shrike has a black mask and a hooked bill and flies with fast, low wingbeats. Gray Catbird is dark slate with a black cap and rusty undertail. Townsend's Solitaire (west) has an eye-ring and buffy wing patches.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parking-lot shrubs and fence posts throughout the southern US; abundant in Texas and Florida.
animal.season: Resident; northernmost birds partly withdraw in winter

lore: Thomas Jefferson kept a pet mockingbird named Dick at the President's House, and the species gave Harper Lee the title of To Kill a Mockingbird (1960); it is the state bird of Arkansas, Florida, Mississippi, Tennessee and Texas.
funFact: Its scientific name means 'many-tongued mimic', and its Nahuatl-derived Spanish name cenzontle means 'four hundred voices'.

wiki.extract: The northern mockingbird is a mockingbird commonly found in North America, of the family Mimidae. The species is also found in some parts of the Caribbean, as well as on the Hawaiian Islands. It is typically a permanent resident across much of its range, but northern mockingbirds may move farther south during inclement weather or prior to the onset of winter. The northern mockingbird has gray to brown upper feathers and a paler belly. Its tail and wings have white patches which are visible in flight.

plates.long: This plate from Mark Catesby's 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands' depicts a Northern Mockingbird (labeled as Turdus minor) on a branch of Flowering Dogwood (Cornus mas). Catesby's work was revolutionary for its time, as he was among the first to illustrate species within their ecological context, showing the relationships between flora and fauna.

summary: The largest ray, with a wingspan of up to about 7 m. It glides through the open ocean filtering plankton and visits reef 'cleaning stations' where small fish pick off parasites.
nativeRange: Tropical, subtropical and temperate oceans worldwide, mostly offshore and around oceanic islands
abilities: Has the largest brain relative to body size of any fish
Captive mantas reacted to their reflection in ways that suggest self-awareness
Funnels plankton into its mouth with cephalic fins that unroll like scoops
Leaps clear of the water and somersaults while feeding
Each individual's belly spot pattern is unique and lifelong

animal.diet: Filter feeder: zooplankton, krill, fish larvae
animal.habitat: Open ocean, upwelling zones, seamounts and offshore reefs
animal.size: Wingspan usually 4.5–7 m; up to ~2 t
animal.behaviour: Females give birth to a single pup every two to five years, one of the slowest reproductive rates of any fish.
fieldMarks: Huge, diamond-shaped ray
Two cephalic fins in front of the mouth
Black above with white shoulder patches
White below with dark spots
animal.lookalikes: Reef manta (Mobula alfredi) is smaller with shoulder patches that curve inward. Devil rays are smaller with mouths on the underside.
animal.whereToSee: Revillagigedo Islands (Socorro), Mexico; Isla de la Plata (Ecuador)
animal.season: Socorro about Nov–Jun

lore: Spanish-speaking pearl divers named it manta, 'blanket', and sailors' 'devil-fish' tales told of mantas wrapping and drowning divers, which are untrue. Its gill plates are now traded as a modern health tonic, the main threat to the species.
funFact: Mantas are close relatives of sharks and have no stinging spine, unlike stingrays.

wiki.extract: The giant oceanic manta ray, giant manta ray, oceanic manta ray, or pelagic manta ray is a species of ray in the family Mobulidae and the largest type of ray in the world. It is circumglobal and is typically found in tropical and subtropical waters but can also be found in temperate waters. Until 2017, the species was classified in the genus Manta, along with the smaller reef manta ray. DNA testing revealed that both mantas are closer related to some Mobula species than these are to other Mobula, being claded together. As a result, the two Manta species were absorbed into Mobula to reflect the new classification.

summary: A giant, tail-less disc of a fish that seems to be all head, propelled by flapping its tall dorsal and anal fins. It is among the heaviest bony fishes and the most fecund vertebrate known.
nativeRange: Temperate and tropical oceans worldwide
abilities: A single female was found carrying an estimated 300 million eggs, the highest count for any vertebrate
Grows from a larva a few millimetres long to over a tonne
Lies flat at the surface to warm up after deep, cold dives and lets seabirds pick off its parasites
Replaces the tail with a rudder-like 'clavus' formed from dorsal and anal fin elements

animal.diet: Jellyfish, salps, siphonophores, also small fish, squid and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Open ocean from the surface to several hundred metres
animal.size: Commonly 1.8 m long and up to 1,000 kg; exceptional individuals over 2 t
animal.behaviour: Visits reef and kelp-edge 'cleaning stations' where fish such as bannerfish and wrasses pick parasites off its skin.
fieldMarks: Huge, laterally flattened oval body with no true tail
Tall dorsal and anal fins set far back, the dorsal often flopping above the surface
Wavy-edged clavus in place of a tail fin
Small mouth with beak-like fused teeth
Grey to silvery, rough sandpaper skin
animal.lookalikes: Hoodwinker sunfish (Mola tecta) has a smooth clavus without a central lobe; bump-head sunfish (Mola alexandrini) has a head bump and chin bulge. A surfaced dorsal fin is mistaken for a shark's, but sunfish fins waggle side to side.
animal.whereToSee: Crystal Bay, Nusa Penida (Bali); Galápagos (Punta Vicente Roca); Azores; Monterey Bay
animal.season: Bali Jul–Oct when cold upwelling arrives

lore: In parts of Japan and Taiwan sunfish meat and intestines are eaten as a local delicacy; in German it has been called Schwimmender Kopf, the 'swimming head'.
funFact: The heaviest bony fish ever measured was a bump-head sunfish (Mola alexandrini) of 2,744 kg found off the Azores in 2021, a close relative of Mola mola.

wiki.extract: The ocean sunfish, also known as the common mola, is one of the largest ray-finned fish in the world. It is the type species of the genus Mola, and one of five extant species in the family Molidae. It was formerly misidentified as the heaviest bony fish, which is actually a different and closely related species of sunfish, Mola alexandrini. Adults typically weigh between 247 and 1,000 kg. It is native to tropical and temperate waters around the world. It resembles a fish head without a tail, and its main body is flattened laterally. Sunfish can be as tall as they are long, between 175 and 180 centimetres, when their dorsal and ventral fins are extended.

summary: A colourful motmot with a long tail ending in two bare-shafted 'rackets' that it swings like a pendulum. It is the national bird of both El Salvador and Nicaragua.
nativeRange: South-eastern Mexico (including the Yucatán Peninsula) through Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua to north-western Costa Rica
abilities: Its tail rackets form when weakly attached barbs near the tips fall off during preening and wear
Wags its tail in a pendulum display aimed at predators — a signal that it has seen them
Digs long nesting tunnels in earth banks, quarries, wells and Maya ruins

animal.diet: Large insects, spiders, small lizards and frogs; some fruit
animal.habitat: Open dry forest, edges, gardens, riverbanks and cenotes
animal.behaviour: It often nests colonially in the walls of Yucatán cenotes and limestone sinkholes.
fieldMarks: Long tail with bare shafts ending in blue-and-black rackets
Bright turquoise eyebrow stripe above a black mask
Black throat stripe edged with turquoise
Rufous back and belly; blue-green wings

funFact: It is a 'pursuit-deterrent' signaller: tail-wagging tells predators they have been spotted and a chase is pointless.

wiki.extract: The turquoise-browed motmot is a colourful, medium-sized bird of the motmot family, Momotidae. It is the only species in its genus Eumomota. It inhabits Central America from south-east Mexico, to Costa Rica, where it is common and not considered threatened. It lives in fairly open habitats such as forest edge, gallery forest and scrubland. It has a preference for higher tree diversity and richness, alongside a low open canopy and dense understory. It also appears to prefer dry forest. This is in contrast to the other motmot known to inhabit the Yucatán, Lesson’s motmot, which prefers moist forest. As a result, their respective distributions allow ecologists to map the process of aridification induced by anthropogenic climate change. Some literature thus considers the turquoise-browed motmot to be a bioindicator.

summary: A small flycatcher whose adult male trails two ribbon-like tail feathers several times its body length, in either rufous or white with a glossy black crested head. Watching one float through a shady grove is among the classic sights of the South Asian monsoon.
nativeRange: Breeds from Turkestan and Afghanistan through northern Pakistan, the Himalaya and India to Sri Lanka and Bangladesh; northern birds winter in southern India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Male grows tail streamers that can add more than 20 cm to a body of about 20 cm
Catches insects in agile aerial sallies beneath the canopy
Males exist in two colour morphs, rufous and white

animal.diet: Flying insects: flies, moths, butterflies, beetles
animal.habitat: Shady deciduous woodland, groves, orchards and wooded gardens, often near water
animal.size: Body about 19–22 cm; male's streamers add up to about 24 cm
animal.behaviour: Both parents share incubation, including the long-tailed male, whose streamers hang over the side of the small cup nest.

Adult male: very long central tail streamers, either chestnut-rufous or white
Female and young male: rufous back and tail, grey breast, no streamers
Small blue-grey bill
animal.voice: A harsh, grating 'chè' or 'chwè' call; a short, warbling song in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Amur paradise flycatcher (passage in NE India, SE Asia) has a darker grey throat and less contrasting hood; Blyth's paradise flycatcher (NE India to SE Asia) is very similar; the long tail separates males from all other South Asian flycatchers.
animal.whereToSee: Margalla Hills National Park near Islamabad and the Murree foothills in summer; Corbett, Pench and Kanha in India; widespread in Sri Lanka in winter
animal.season: Summer visitor to Pakistan and northern India (Apr–Sep); resident or winter visitor in the south

lore: It is the state bird of Madhya Pradesh, and the Urdu name shah bulbul ('king bulbul') reflects its regal tail.
funFact: Young males start out rufous like females, and some white males turn white only after several moults.

wiki.extract: The Indian paradise flycatcher is a medium-sized passerine bird in the monarch flycatcher family, Monarchidae. As the global population is considered stable, it has been listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 2004. It is native to the Indian subcontinent, with resident and breeding populations in most of Bangladesh, India and Sri Lanka, as well as parts of Afghanistan, Bhutan, China, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

summary: A pure-white Arctic whale with a bulbous, shape-changing forehead, so talkative that sailors called it the 'sea canary'. Thousands gather each summer in warm river estuaries to calve, feed and moult their skin against the gravel. Some even travel far up rivers.
nativeRange: Arctic and sub-Arctic waters: Hudson Bay, Baffin Bay, Beaufort and Bering seas, White Sea, Svalbard, Sea of Okhotsk; isolated populations in the St Lawrence estuary and Cook Inlet
abilities: Unfused neck vertebrae let it nod and turn its head, unusual among whales
Changes the shape of its fatty melon to focus echolocation and perhaps to signal
Navigates and finds breathing holes in dense pack ice using echolocation
Has entered rivers far inland, e.g. hundreds of kilometres up the Yukon, Amur and Rhine

animal.diet: Fish (cod, salmon, capelin), squid, shrimp, crabs and worms
animal.habitat: Coastal Arctic waters, estuaries and ice edges
animal.lifespan: Typically 35–50 years; some estimated to reach 80
animal.size: 3–5.5 m; up to about 1,600 kg (males larger)
animal.behaviour: Social, travelling in pods that can merge into gatherings of thousands in estuaries. Calves are born grey and whiten over several years.
fieldMarks: All-white adult (grey young) with no dorsal fin — only a low ridge along the back
Rounded, mobile melon and short beak
Broad, paddle-shaped flippers that curl at the tips in older males
Small, low blow; often seen in shallow, muddy estuary water
animal.voice: A wide repertoire of whistles, chirps, squeals, clicks and bell-like trills audible through boat hulls, giving the name 'sea canary'.
animal.lookalikes: Narwhal is mottled grey-black, and males carry a spiral tusk. In poor light, a white wave crest or ice floe can be mistaken for a beluga's back.
animal.whereToSee: Churchill River estuary, Manitoba (Hudson Bay, tens of thousands in July–August); Saguenay–St. Lawrence Marine Park, Tadoussac (Quebec); Cunningham Inlet, Somerset Island (Nunavut); Solovetsky Islands, White Sea (Russia); Turnagain Arm, Alaska
animal.season: Estuary gatherings late June–August; winter at the pack-ice edge

lore: Inuit communities hunt belugas for muktuk (skin and blubber), a key source of vitamin C in the traditional Arctic diet. In the 1980s a US Navy beluga named NOC was recorded imitating human speech patterns.
funFact: Belugas moult each summer, rubbing off old yellowed skin on estuary gravel to reveal fresh white skin beneath.

wiki.extract: The beluga whale or the white whale is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean. It is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae, along with the narwhal, and the only member of the genus Delphinapterus. It is also known as the sea canary, due to its high-pitched calls; and the melonhead, though that more commonly refers to the melon-headed whale, which is an oceanic dolphin.

summary: An Arctic whale whose males grow a spiralled tusk up to about 3 m long, which is actually a tooth that grows through the upper lip. Medieval Europeans sold these tusks as unicorn horns.
nativeRange: Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland, Svalbard and Russia, mainly the Atlantic Arctic and Baffin Bay
abilities: Grows a tusk, usually the left canine, that spirals counter-clockwise and can reach ~3 m
The tusk has nerve-linked channels that may sense changes in the surrounding water
Dives to about 1,500 m or more, repeatedly, to hunt halibut in winter
Hunts and navigates under dense pack ice by echolocation
Has been filmed tapping Arctic cod with its tusk to stun them

animal.habitat: Deep fjords and offshore pack ice
animal.behaviour: Narwhals migrate seasonally between summer fjords and winter feeding grounds under dense pack ice. Males sometimes rub tusks together ('tusking').
fieldMarks: Mottled grey whale
Males have a long, spiral tusk
No dorsal fin
Rounded head
animal.voice: Clicks, whistles and knocks
animal.lookalikes: Beluga is white with no tusk.

animal.season: Floe edge Jun

lore: The Danish kings' coronation throne at Rosenborg Castle (1660s) is made largely of narwhal tusk, then believed to be unicorn horn. An Inuit story tells of a cruel woman dragged into the sea by a harpooned narwhal, her twisted hair becoming its tusk.
funFact: About 1 in 500 males grows two tusks, and a few females grow one.

wiki.extract: The narwhal is a species of toothed whale native to the Arctic. It is the only member of the genus Monodon and one of two living representatives of the family Monodontidae. The narwhal is a stocky cetacean with a relatively blunt snout, a large melon, and a shallow ridge in place of a dorsal fin. Males of this species have a spiralled tusk, which is a protruding left canine, that is 1.5–3.0 m (4.9–9.8 ft) long and thought to function as a secondary sexual characteristic, a weapon, a tool for feeding, or a sensory organ. Specially adapted slow-twitch muscles, along with the jointed neck vertebrae and shallow dorsal ridge allow for easy movement through the Arctic environment, where the narwhal spends extended periods at great depths. The narwhal's geographic range overlaps with that of the similarly built and closely related beluga whale, and the animals are known to interbreed.

summary: A pied black-and-white bird that cocks its tail and sings sweet, varied songs from rooftops and garden trees at dawn. As the doel, it is the national bird of Bangladesh.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar through southern China to Southeast Asia
abilities: Rich, varied song that includes mimicry of other birds
Nests readily in wall holes and nest boxes in villages and towns
Males defend territories fiercely and sing through the hottest months

animal.habitat: Gardens, villages, open woodland and cultivation
animal.behaviour: Hops on the ground with tail cocked and fanned, flicking it up and down; males sing from exposed perches especially at dawn.

lore: The doel is Bangladesh's national bird and gives its name to Doel Chattar, a well-known monument in Dhaka. In Southeast Asia it was long trapped and kept for its song, causing declines in Singapore and parts of Indonesia.

wiki.extract: The Oriental magpie-robin is a small passerine bird that was formerly classed as a member of the thrush family Turdidae, but now considered an Old World flycatcher. The males are distinctive black and white birds with a long tail that is held upright as they forage on the ground or perch conspicuously. Occurring across most of the Indian subcontinent and parts of Southeast Asia, they are common birds in urban gardens as well as forests. They are particularly well known for their songs and are popular as cagebirds.

summary: A small, round, orange-breasted chat. Both sexes sing and defend territories through the winter, so it is one of the few European birds singing in December. In Britain it is famously tame around gardeners, but on the Continent it is a shy woodland bird.
nativeRange: Europe east to western Siberia, North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran; northern birds winter around the Mediterranean and Middle East
abilities: Both males and females hold separate winter territories and sing to defend them
Sings at night under street lighting in towns
Follows large animals, and gardeners, to snatch invertebrates turned up from the soil
Migrants navigate partly with a light-dependent magnetic compass in the eye, a key study system for avian magnetoreception

animal.diet: Insects, worms, spiders; berries and seeds in winter
animal.habitat: Woodland with undergrowth, hedgerows, parks and gardens
animal.lifespan: Usually 1–2 years in the wild; a few live past 10
animal.behaviour: Territorial to the point of violence: robins attack rivals and even a tuft of red feathers placed in their territory, as David Lack showed in his 1940s experiments.
fieldMarks: Orange-red face and breast bordered with blue-grey
Plain olive-brown upperparts and whitish belly
Plump, upright stance on thin legs; large dark eye
Juveniles are speckled brown with no red breast
animal.voice: Song a wistful, liquid warble of short phrases with pauses, thinner and more melancholy in autumn; call a hard, repeated 'tic' and a thin 'tsiih'.
animal.lookalikes: Common redstart males also show orange underparts but have a black face and a constantly quivering orange tail. Juvenile robins resemble young redstarts and nightingales but lack a rufous tail.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any wooded garden, park or hedgerow in Europe; abundant wintering birds in Mediterranean olive groves and Levantine scrub.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east (Apr–Sep); winter visitor to North Africa and the Middle East (Oct–Mar)

lore: A medieval legend holds that the robin's breast was scorched or bloodied while helping Christ on the cross, and Victorian postmen in red tunics were nicknamed 'robins', which is why the bird appears on so many British Christmas cards.
funFact: In 2015 a public poll organised by ornithologist David Lindo chose the robin as Britain's national bird.

wiki.extract: The European robin, known simply as the robin or robin redbreast in the British Isles, is a small insectivorous passerine bird belonging to the Old World flycatcher family Muscicapidae. It is found across Europe, as far east as Western Siberia, and as far south as North Africa. It is sedentary in the west and south of its range, and migratory in the north and east of its range where winters are harsher.

Catesby was among the first to illustrate birds in their natural habitats, often pairing them with the specific plants they frequented, a revolutionary approach for 18th-century natural history that provided a more complete ecological context.

summary: A plain brown skulker with one of the most celebrated voices on Earth. Males sing by day and, before they find a mate, through the night, from deep inside thickets. It winters in sub-Saharan Africa.
nativeRange: Breeds in southern and central Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Middle East east to Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Afghanistan); winters in tropical Africa
abilities: Males command repertoires of roughly 180–260 different song types
Unpaired males sing through the night to attract migrating females; nocturnal song largely stops once they pair
Raises the volume of its song in noisy places (the Lombard effect), shown in Berlin
Migrates by night between Europe and Africa, crossing the Sahara

animal.diet: Ground invertebrates, especially beetles and ants; berries in late summer
animal.habitat: Dense deciduous thickets, coppice, scrub along rivers and woodland edges
animal.behaviour: Feeds on the ground in deep shade, hopping and pausing with its rufous tail cocked, and is far more often heard than seen.
fieldMarks: Uniform warm brown upperparts with a brighter rufous tail
Pale buffy-grey underparts with no streaks
Large dark eye with a thin pale eye-ring
Rather long-legged, robin-like posture
animal.voice: Rich, loud and varied: deep 'chook-chook' notes, liquid whistles, harsh rattles and a famous slow crescendo of pure 'piu piu piu' notes; call a soft 'hweet' and a croaking 'karrr'.
animal.lookalikes: Thrush nightingale (eastern Europe) is darker, greyer-brown with faint mottling on the breast and a less rufous tail, and its song has dry clicking phrases. Garden warbler is smaller with a short bill and no rufous tail.
animal.whereToSee: Mediterranean river valleys and scrub in Spain, Portugal, southern France and Italy; Kent and Sussex coppice in England; Turkey and the Levant in spring.
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Aug; most vocal late April to early June

lore: The bulbul's love for the rose (gol o bolbol) is a central image of Persian poetry from Hafez and Rumi onward, and in Greek myth the nightingale is Philomela or Procne transformed; Keats wrote his 'Ode to a Nightingale' in Hampstead in 1819.
funFact: In 1924 cellist Beatrice Harrison played in her Surrey garden while wild nightingales sang along, a performance broadcast live by the BBC as one of the first outside broadcasts.

wiki.extract: The common nightingale, rufous nightingale or simply nightingale, is a small passerine bird which is known for its powerful and beautiful song, often described as one of the most beautiful sounds in nature. An Old World flycatcher, it belongs to a group of more terrestrial species, often called chats. Its range partly overlaps with that of the more northerly thrush nightingale, a closely related species with which hybrids have occurred.

summary: Probably the most widespread insect in human company, breeding in dung and rotting waste wherever people live. It tastes with its feet, eats by spitting digestive juices onto food, and can carry the germs of typhoid, cholera and dysentery on its body.
nativeRange: Probably originated in the Middle East or Central Asia; now worldwide wherever people live
abilities: Completes egg-to-adult development in about a week in warm weather
Tastes food with sensory hairs on its feet
Females lay roughly 500 eggs in batches over their lives
Mechanically spreads disease-causing bacteria, viruses and parasites
Larvae can convert manure and food waste into protein-rich biomass

animal.diet: Adults liquefy food with saliva and sponge it up: sugars, rotting matter, dung, food scraps; larvae feed in manure and decaying waste
animal.habitat: Homes, farms, markets and anywhere with garbage or manure
animal.behaviour: It cannot bite or chew; instead it regurgitates digestive fluid onto food and laps it up with a sponge-like mouth.
fieldMarks: Grey thorax with four dark lengthwise stripes
Large reddish-brown eyes (closer together in males)
Abdomen grey to yellowish with a dark midline
A sharp upward bend in the fourth long wing vein
animal.lookalikes: Lesser house fly (Fannia canicularis) is smaller and flies in slow circles under lights. Stable fly (Stomoxys calcitrans) has a forward-pointing piercing proboscis and bites. Flesh flies (Sarcophagidae) are larger with three thorax stripes and a chequered abdomen.
animal.whereToSee: Practically anywhere people live, especially near livestock and waste.
animal.season: Year-round in warm places; summer peak in temperate regions

lore: The Philistine god Baal-zebub, 'Lord of the Flies' in 2 Kings, became the Beelzebub of later Jewish and Christian tradition; William Golding borrowed the phrase for his 1954 novel.
funFact: Its maggots are now farmed in some countries to turn manure and food waste into protein feed for poultry and fish.

wiki.extract: The housefly is a fly of the suborder Cyclorrhapha. From its place of origin, perhaps in the Middle East, it has spread around the world as a commensal of humans. Adults are gray to black, with four dark, longitudinal lines on the thorax, slightly hairy bodies, and a single pair of membranous wings. They have red compound eyes, set farther apart in the slightly larger female.

plates.long: This plate from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 'Histoire naturelle des colibris' (1802) depicts 'L'Oiseau Mouche, tout vert' (the all-green hummingbird). The work is renowned for its innovative use of metallic inks to replicate the shimmering, iridescent quality of hummingbird feathers, marking a significant milestone in scientific illustration.

It showcases the meticulous detail and vibrant color characteristic of early 19th-century French natural history engravings, specifically designed to capture the iridescent quality of the bird's feathers.

summary: One of the smallest marine mammals, and unlike most it has no blubber, keeping warm instead with the densest fur of any animal. By eating sea urchins, sea otters protect kelp forests, a textbook case of a keystone species.
nativeRange: Coastal North Pacific, from Hokkaido and the Kuril Islands through Alaska to California
abilities: Floats on its back and cracks shellfish against a stone balanced on its chest
Keeps a favourite stone in a loose pouch of skin under its forearm
Has fur of up to ~150,000 hairs per square centimetre, which traps an insulating layer of air
Controls urchin numbers, allowing kelp forests to grow and support many other species

animal.diet: Carnivore: sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails; eats about a quarter of its body weight daily
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, often within 1–2 km of shore
animal.behaviour: Rafts of resting otters wrap themselves in kelp or hold paws so they don't drift apart. Mothers float their pups on their bellies.
fieldMarks: Large otter floating on its back
Dense brown fur, paler grizzled head
Small ears, blunt face, flipper-like hind feet
Uses rocks as tools on its chest
animal.voice: Squeals and whistles, especially from pups
animal.lookalikes: Harbour seals lie belly-down and lack visible paws. River otters swim on their bellies with long, tapering tails.
animal.whereToSee: Monterey Bay and Elkhorn Slough (California); Kenai Fjords and Prince William Sound (Alaska)
animal.season: Resident

lore: After Vitus Bering's 1741 expedition returned with pelts, Russian and later British and American traders sold sea otter fur to China, nearly wiping the species out. The 1911 Fur Seal Treaty ended the hunt when perhaps 1,000–2,000 remained.
funFact: Sea otters are among the few mammals other than primates known to use stone tools.

wiki.extract: The sea otter is a marine mammal native to the coasts of the northern and eastern North Pacific Ocean. Adult sea otters typically weigh between 14 and 45 kg (30–100 lb), making them the heaviest members of the weasel family, but among the smallest marine mammals. Unlike most marine mammals, the sea otter's primary form of insulation is an exceptionally thick coat of fur, the densest in the animal kingdom. Although it can walk on land, the sea otter is capable of living exclusively in the ocean.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration from a 16th-century edition of Horapollo's Hieroglyphica depicts a 'water cat' (likely an otter) within a meticulously rendered landscape. The image serves as an emblem for a person who cannot be satisfied, greedily consuming what they have previously rejected, reflecting the early modern fascination with finding moral lessons in the natural world.

summary: A bear-like giant weasel of the far north, famous for its endurance and strength. Wolverines travel tens of kilometres a day over mountains, crunch frozen carcasses with powerful jaws and store food in snow and rock crevices.
nativeRange: Circumpolar: Scandinavia, northern Russia, Siberia, Alaska, Canada and the high Rockies and Cascades of the northwestern USA
abilities: Crushes frozen meat and bone with a strong jaw and a molar turned sideways in the upper jaw
Covers huge home ranges, over 1,000 km² for some males
Climbed some 1,500 m up Mount Cleveland, Glacier National Park, in about 90 minutes in winter (a radio-collared male)

animal.diet: Scavenged carcasses of reindeer, moose and other ungulates; also hunts hares, rodents, birds and sometimes reindeer in deep snow
animal.habitat: Remote tundra, taiga and alpine areas with deep spring snow cover for dens
animal.size: Males 11–18 kg, females 7–12 kg; body 65–105 cm
animal.behaviour: Solitary and wide-ranging. Females dig dens in deep snow to give birth in late winter.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: small bear-like body, arched back, short legs and bushy tail
Dark brown coat with a pale buff band along each flank from shoulders to tail
Pale mask across the forehead
Tracks: five-toed, about 10–13 cm, often in a bounding '2–1–2' or '3–4' pattern in snow
animal.lookalikes: Bear cubs lack the pale side-stripe and have smaller tails; badgers are greyer with a striped face; fishers and martens are slimmer and smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Kuhmo and Lieksa wildlife hides, eastern Finland; Norwegian and Swedish mountains (e.g. Dovrefjell); Denali (Alaska); Kluane (Yukon)
animal.season: Resident; hides in Finland give sightings April–September

lore: Olaus Magnus, in his 1555 History of the Northern Peoples, claimed the 'gulo' gorged until it had to squeeze between two trees to empty its belly. Its Latin name means 'glutton'.
funFact: Wolverine fur resists frost, so Inuit and other northern peoples trimmed parka hoods with it.

wiki.extract: The wolverine, also called the carcajou or quickhatch, is the largest land-dwelling member of the family Mustelidae. It is a muscular carnivore and a solitary animal. The wolverine has a reputation for ferocity and strength out of proportion to its size, with the documented ability to kill prey many times larger than itself.

summary: A stocky, fearless mustelid of Africa and southern Asia, famed for raiding beehives and fighting off lions. Thick, loose skin lets it twist round and bite an attacker that has hold of it.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa's edges, Arabia, Iran, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent
abilities: Resists cobra and other snake venom because of a mutation in its nerve receptors, shared with mongooses
Rips open beehives, termite mounds and burrows with long, strong foreclaws
Escapes and solves problems: captive honey badgers have stacked objects to climb out of enclosures
Releases a foul smell from anal glands when threatened

animal.diet: Omnivore: rodents, snakes, lizards, insects, bee larvae and honey, carrion, fruit
animal.habitat: Almost every habitat from desert to forest edge
animal.lifespan: 7–8 years in the wild; to ~24 in captivity
animal.size: Males 9–16 kg, females 5–10 kg; body 55–77 cm
animal.behaviour: Mainly a solitary forager, it may travel 10–30 km in a day of digging for prey. Its partnership with honeyguide birds is widely told but poorly documented.
fieldMarks: Stocky, low-slung badger
Black below with a silver-grey back
Short legs with long front claws
Small eyes and ears
animal.voice: Growls and rattles
animal.lookalikes: Zorilla (striped polecat) is smaller with black-and-white stripes. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (South Africa/Botswana)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Afrikaans-speaking farmers called it the ratel, a name that entered zoology. The 2011 viral video 'The Crazy Nastyass Honey Badger' made its fearlessness an internet legend.
funFact: Bitten by a cobra, a honey badger may collapse, sleep for a couple of hours, then wake up and finish eating the snake.

wiki.extract: The honey badger, also known as the ratel, is a mammal widely distributed across Africa, Southwest Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It is the sole living representative of the Mellivorinae subfamily of the Mustelidae.

summary: A toothless insect-eater with a tubular snout, a tongue about 60 cm long and a huge, flag-like tail. It raids termite mounds and ant nests for just a minute or so each, flicking its tongue up to 150 times a minute, and moves on before the colony's soldiers mount a defence. Fire, roads and habitat loss have made it Vulnerable.
nativeRange: Central America (rare, Honduras southward) and South America east of the Andes to northern Argentina; extinct in Uruguay and much of Central America
abilities: Eats around 30,000 ants and termites a day
Forelimb claws up to 10 cm tear open concrete-hard termite mounds and can disable a jaguar in defence
Has one of the lowest body temperatures of any land mammal, about 33 °C
Walks on its knuckles to protect its long claws

animal.diet: Ants and termites; occasionally beetle larvae and fruit
animal.habitat: Open grassland, savanna, wetlands and forest edges
animal.lifespan: About 15 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity
animal.size: Body about 1–1.2 m plus a 65–90 cm tail; 27–50 kg
animal.behaviour: Solitary. Mothers carry the single young on their back for months, its dark stripe lining up with hers as camouflage.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: long tubular head, low body and enormous bushy tail held level or over the body like a blanket
Bold black diagonal stripe edged with white running from throat over the shoulder
Pale front legs with a black band above huge curved claws
Signs: termite mounds with fresh, fist-sized holes torn in the side; knuckle-walking tracks turned inward
animal.lookalikes: Southern and northern tamanduas are much smaller, climb trees and have a short, naked prehensile tail. No other animal in its range has the long snout and huge tail together.
animal.whereToSee: Serra da Canastra and Emas national parks (Brazilian cerrado); Pantanal (Brazil); Esteros del Iberá (Argentina, reintroduced); Los Llanos (Venezuela, Colombia)
animal.season: Resident; often active in daylight in cool weather, nocturnal in hot weather

lore: In Guaraní the animal is yurumí, and the giant anteater appears in Indigenous stories across the Gran Chaco and cerrado. Since 2007 a rewilding programme in Argentina has reintroduced giant anteaters to the Iberá wetlands, where they had disappeared.
funFact: The anteater's tongue is anchored to its sternum, not its mouth, allowing it to extend so far.

wiki.extract: The giant anteater is a large insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America. It is the largest of the four living species of anteaters, which are classified with sloths in the order Pilosa. The only extant member of the genus Myrmecophaga, the giant anteater is mostly terrestrial, in contrast to other living anteaters and sloths, which are arboreal or semiarboreal. It is recognizable by its elongated snout, bushy tail, long foreclaws, and distinctively colored fur.

plates.title: Georg Wolfgang Knorr — Deliciae naturae selectae (1771)
plates.author: Georg Wolfgang Knorr
plates.desc: A detailed, hand-colored illustration of a Giant Anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) shown in profile facing left. The animal is depicted with its characteristic long snout, small ears, and a bushy tail. Its fur is rendered in shades of brown and tan, featuring a prominent dark diagonal stripe bordered by lighter fur extending from the chest toward the back.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a Giant Anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), showcasing its distinctive long snout and bushy tail. Produced for Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' in 1771, it reflects the 18th-century interest in documenting exotic fauna with scientific precision and artistic flair. The plate is noted as being from the former Besler museum ('Ex Museo quondam Besl

summary: A bloated, purple-grey frog with a pointed pig-like snout that spends most of its life underground in India's Western Ghats, surfacing only for a few days in the monsoon to breed. Its closest relatives live in the Seychelles, a link to the breakup of Gondwana.
nativeRange: Western Ghats of India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka)
abilities: Lives buried up to several metres underground for most of the year
Feeds on termites and ants in their underground tunnels, probing with its pointed snout
Tadpoles cling to rocks in fast monsoon streams with sucker-like mouths
Its lineage split from its Seychelles relatives tens of millions of years ago

animal.diet: Termites, also ants
animal.habitat: Moist forest and plantations near seasonal streams
animal.behaviour: Emerges for a few days in the pre-monsoon or early monsoon to breed in fast-flowing streams. The small male clings to the larger female's back.
fieldMarks: Bloated, purplish-grey body
Small head with a pointed pig-like snout
Short limbs adapted for digging
Small eyes
animal.voice: A soft, chicken-like 'cluck', given from underground or at stream edges in the early monsoon
animal.lookalikes: No other Indian frog looks like it. The Bhupathy's purple frog (N. bhupathi), described in 2017, is similar and lives in the eastern slopes of the southern Western Ghats; it breeds later, during the northeast monsoon.
animal.whereToSee: Monsoon streams in Kerala's Idukki district and the Western Ghats; rarely seen
animal.season: Emerges for a few days in May–June to breed

lore: S. D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt described the purple frog in Nature in 2003, revealing a new family of frogs. In Kerala it has been proposed as the state frog, and local people call it 'Mahabali' after the legendary king who returns from the underworld once a year.
funFact: Local people knew the purple frog long before scientists; its tadpoles are collected and eaten in parts of Kerala.

wiki.extract: The purple frog, also known commonly as the Indian purple frog, the Mahabali frog, and the pignose frog, is a frog species in the family Nasikabatrachidae. The species is endemic to the Western Ghats in India. Although the adult frog was formally described in October 2003, the juvenile form of the species had been described earlier in 1917.

summary: A living relative of the ammonites, carrying a coiled, chambered shell striped with flame-like bands. Its lineage has changed little for hundreds of millions of years, but demand for its shells has driven heavy local declines.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-West Pacific: the Philippines, Indonesia, New Guinea, northern and eastern Australia, and Melanesia
abilities: Controls buoyancy by moving fluid and gas through its shell chambers via a tube called the siphuncle
Has about 90 suckerless tentacles
Pinhole-camera eyes with no lens
Lives far longer than most cephalopods, possibly 15–20 years

animal.diet: Scavenges dead fish, crustaceans, moulted crab shells and carrion
animal.habitat: Steep reef slopes from about 100 m to over 500 m, rising shallower at night
animal.size: Shell usually about 15–20 cm across; exceptionally to about 25 cm
animal.behaviour: It moves by jet propulsion, rising up reef walls at night to feed and sinking deeper by day, possibly to avoid predators and warm water.
fieldMarks: Smooth, coiled, cream-white shell with orange-brown tiger stripes fading towards the opening
Closed centre of the coil (no open navel)
Leathery hood over the head
Many slender tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Crusty nautilus (Allonautilus scrobiculatus) has an open navel and a hairy shell covering. Palau nautilus (N. belauensis) and New Caledonian nautilus (N. macromphalus) differ in shell shape and range.
animal.whereToSee: Deep reef walls in Palau, the Philippines and the Coral Sea (Osprey Reef), usually by baited camera; public aquariums.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Georg Rumphius described the nautilus in D'Amboinsche Rariteitkamer (1705). Renaissance goldsmiths mounted the shells as ornate 'nautilus cups' for European cabinets of curiosities.
funFact: Its shell is a logarithmic spiral, but measurements show it does not follow the golden ratio, despite the popular claim.

wiki.extract: The chambered nautilus, also called the pearly nautilus, is the best-known species of nautilus. The shell, when cut away, reveals a lining of lustrous nacre and displays a nearly perfect equiangular spiral, although it is not a golden spiral. The shell exhibits countershading, being light on the bottom and dark on top. This is to help avoid predators, because when seen from above, it blends in with the darkness of the sea, and when seen from below, it blends in with the light coming from above.

plates.long: This plate displays several views of the Paper Nautilus, including a living Argonaut octopus within its fluted shell at the top. Below the living specimen are four individual shells of varying sizes and colors, labeled with letters and numbers to correspond with the text. The engraving captures the delicate radiating ribs and spiral form characteristic of the Argonauta argo.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut depicting a nautilus, likely an Argonauta or 'paper nautilus', with its tentacles unfurled. This image represents the early modern effort to categorize and visualize marine life, often based on a combination of direct observation and classical descriptions.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Two woodcuts of a cephalopod, identified as Nautilus Aristotelis, shown in prone and supine positions.
plates.long: These two figures illustrate the same marine creature from different perspectives, labeled 'Pronus' (face down) and 'Supinus' (face up). This comparative approach was a hallmark of Gessner's scientific method, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the animal's form for his readers.

plates.long: This plate from Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' (1771) showcases the intricate beauty of cephalopod shells. It features a detailed cross-section of a Nautilus shell, revealing its internal chambers and siphuncle, alongside specimens of the Argonauta, or paper nautilus. The primary figure is a large nautilus shell, meticulously rendered with geometric lines that highlight its logarithmic spiral, reflecting the Enlightenment-era interest in the intersection of nature and mathematics.

At the top is the Chambered Nautilus (*Nautilus pompilius*), known for its striking striped pattern, while the bottom illustrates the fragile, translucent shell of the Paper Nautilus (*Argonauta argo*). summary: A tiny nectar-feeder whose breeding male is glossy purple-black that flashes metallic blue and green in the sun. It fills the ecological role hummingbirds play in the Americas, but usually perches rather than hovers to feed.
nativeRange: The Persian Gulf, Oman and Iran through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar and Indochina
abilities: Pollinates many flowering plants as it feeds on nectar with a long, curved bill and tubular tongue
Can hover briefly at flowers like a hummingbird
Weaves a hanging purse-shaped nest bound with spider silk and decorated with debris
Pierces the base of long tubular flowers to 'rob' nectar

animal.diet: Nectar, small insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Gardens, dry scrub, thorn forest and open woodland
animal.behaviour: Restless and quick, flicking its wings as it moves between flowers; the hanging nest often has a little porch over the side entrance.
fieldMarks: Very small with a long, down-curved black bill
Breeding male: all glossy purple-black, iridescent in sunlight, with yellow and orange tufts under the wing in display
Female: olive-brown above, pale yellow below
Non-breeding male resembles female but with a dark stripe down the centre of the breast
animal.voice: Sharp, metallic 'chwit' or 'zit' calls; male sings a rapid, twittering 'cheewit-cheewit-swee'
animal.lookalikes: Purple-rumped sunbird (peninsular India, Sri Lanka) has a maroon back and yellow belly; Loten's sunbird has a much longer bill and a maroon breast band.
animal.whereToSee: Flowering gardens across Pakistan and India; common on bottlebrush and hibiscus in Karachi, Lahore and Delhi
animal.season: Resident; males in breeding plumage mainly in spring and summer

lore: Its Urdu and Hindi name shakar khora means 'sugar eater'.
funFact: In the Old World, sunbirds evolved to fill the nectar-feeding niche independently of the New World hummingbirds, a classic case of convergent evolution.

wiki.extract: The purple sunbird is a small bird in the sunbird family. It occurs in parts of the Arabian peninsula and South and Southeast Asia. It has a fast and direct flight and can take nectar by hovering like a hummingbird but often perches at the base of flowers. It feeds mainly on nectar and insects, especially when feeding young. The males can appear all black in harsh sunlight but the purple iridescence is visible on closer observation or under good light conditions. Females are olive above and yellowish below.

plates.title: Jean Baptiste Audebert — Histoire naturelle des grimpereaux et des oiseaux de paradis (1802)

plates.desc: A detailed color engraving of a purple sunbird perched on a gnarled branch.
plates.long: This plate depicts 'Le S. pourpre' (The Purple Sunbird), featured in Jean Baptiste Audebert's 1802 masterpiece 'Histoire naturelle des grimpereaux et des oiseaux de paradis'. Audebert's work is celebrated for its technical innovation, utilizing oil-based colors and occasionally gold leaf to replicate the shimmering, metallic quality of bird plumage.

summary: A living link to the fish that first crawled onto land, almost unchanged from fossils about 100 million years old. Unlike other lungfishes it breathes mostly with gills, using its single lung in low-oxygen water.
nativeRange: South-eastern Queensland, Australia: Burnett and Mary rivers (native); translocated to the Brisbane, Albert, Pine and Coomera rivers
abilities: Breathes with gills and a single lung, gulping air when water is warm or oxygen-poor
Has one of the largest animal genomes ever sequenced, at about 43 billion base pairs
Lives for many decades; one in captivity lived over 90 years
Detects prey with electroreceptors on the snout

animal.diet: Omnivore: snails, worms, shrimps, frogs, small fish and plants
animal.habitat: Slow-flowing, deep pools of rivers with aquatic plants and soft beds
animal.size: Up to about 1.5 m and 40 kg
animal.behaviour: Moves slowly along the bottom using its flipper-like fins. It lays eggs singly among water plants in spring, and the eggs rely on the plant beds that dams and weirs destroy.
fieldMarks: Heavy, elongate body covered in very large, overlapping scales
Paddle-shaped, fleshy pectoral and pelvic fins on stalk-like bases
Continuous fin around the rear body forming a pointed tail
Olive-brown to grey above, often with dark spots; pale belly
animal.lookalikes: Introduced and native catfishes have barbels and no large scales. African and South American lungfishes look different and do not occur in Australia: they are eel-like, with threadlike fins and small scales.
animal.whereToSee: Mary River and Burnett River (Queensland); Wivenhoe and Somerset dams; Queensland Museum and public aquaria
animal.season: Resident; spawns August–December

lore: Gerard Krefft described it in 1870 from a fish sent to him by William Forster, a Queensland squatter. The Mary River Traveston Crossing Dam was cancelled in 2009 under Australian environmental law, partly because of its threat to lungfish.
funFact: 'Granddad', an Australian lungfish at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium from 1933 to 2017, was the oldest aquarium fish on record when he died.

wiki.extract: The Australian lungfish, also known as the Queensland lungfish, Burnett salmon and barramunda, is the only surviving member of the family Neoceratodontidae, and endemic to Australia. It is one of only six extant lungfish species in the world.

summary: The heaviest crustacean in the world, with the record animal weighing about 20 kg. It carries two different claws, a heavy crusher and a sharp cutter, and may live for a century.
nativeRange: North-west Atlantic, from Labrador to North Carolina
abilities: Heaviest crustacean on record (about 20 kg)
Two specialised claws: a blunt crusher and a sharp pincer
Regenerates lost legs and claws
Locates food by smell with its antennules and leg hairs

animal.diet: Crabs, molluscs, sea urchins, worms, fish and some plants
animal.habitat: Rocky and sandy bottoms from the shallows to about 480 m, mostly at 4–50 m
animal.lifespan: Estimated to exceed 100 years in large individuals
animal.size: Commonly 25–50 cm long; record about 20 kg
animal.behaviour: Females carry thousands of eggs under the tail for about a year before they hatch.
fieldMarks: Dark greenish-brown to bluish shell, turning red only when cooked
Two large, unequal claws
Long, reddish antennae
Fan-shaped tail
animal.lookalikes: European lobster (Homarus gammarus) is bluer and lacks the spine on the underside of the rostrum. Caribbean spiny lobster (Panulirus argus) has no big claws and a spiny shell.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky coasts of the Gulf of Maine and Maritime Canada; lobster boats and pounds in Maine and Nova Scotia.
animal.season: Year-round; moves inshore and moults in summer

edibleParts: tail, claw and leg meat; tomalley and roe
edibilityNote: Usually boiled or steamed. The tomalley (digestive gland) can concentrate shellfish toxins during red tides, and authorities sometimes advise against eating it. Shellfish allergy is common.
lore: Early colonial accounts describe lobsters so abundant in New England that they were used as fish bait and fertiliser; only from the 19th century did canning and railways turn them into a luxury food.
funFact: About one lobster in a couple of million is bright blue because of a genetic mutation that alters its shell pigment protein.

wiki.extract: The American lobster is a species of lobster found on the Atlantic coast of North America, chiefly from Labrador to New Jersey. It is also known as Atlantic lobster, Canadian lobster, northern lobster, Canadian Reds, or Maine lobster. It is sometimes called the true lobster or common lobster, but those names are ambiguous. It can reach a body length of 64 cm (25 in), and a mass of over 20 kilograms (44 lb), making it not only the heaviest crustacean in the world, but also the heaviest of all living arthropod species. Its closest relative is the European lobster Homarus gammarus, which can be distinguished by its coloration and the lack of spines on the underside of the rostrum. American lobsters are usually bluish green to brown with red spines, but several color variations have been observed.

plates.long: This dramatic woodcut depicts a giant lobster-like creature seizing a swimming man in its claws. Based on descriptions by Olaus Magnus, it illustrates the blend of empirical observation and legendary lore common in early modern natural history.

The illustration serves as a visual guide for the accompanying text describing the creature's medicinal and natural properties in one of the first major printed encyclopedias of the natural world.

The illustration meticulously captures the intricate textures of the carapace, the segmented tail, and the exceptionally long antennae, serving as a vital record in the early modern effort to categorize global biodiversity.

summary: A hump-backed, knife-shaped fish that swims by rippling a single long fin under its body and can move forwards or backwards. It belongs to the bonytongues, an ancient fish lineage, and in Bengal it is a luxury food fish.
nativeRange: Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra and Mahanadi basins of Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh
abilities: Swims forwards or backwards by sending waves along a long anal fin that merges with the tail
Gulps air with a specialised swim bladder, so it survives in warm, oxygen-poor water
Males guard eggs stuck to submerged logs and posts
edibilityNote: Prized but very bony; Bengali cooks scrape the flesh from the bones to make chital macher muitha (fish dumplings). Always cooked.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, prawns, insects and molluscs
animal.habitat: Deep, clear pools of large rivers, floodplain lakes and reservoirs with submerged cover
animal.lifespan: Not well documented; probably over 10 years
animal.size: Commonly 60–80 cm; up to about 1.2 m
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; by day it hovers among submerged roots and timber. Pairs spawn on hard surfaces in the monsoon and the male fans and guards the eggs.
fieldMarks: Strongly humped back behind the head, with a small feather-like dorsal fin
Body tapers to a knife-blade shape; anal fin runs from belly to tail
Silvery with about 15 or more thin silvery bars on the back and sometimes rows of small dark spots near the tail
Large mouth with the jaw extending well past the eye
animal.lookalikes: The clown knifefish (Chitala ornata) of Southeast Asia, common in the aquarium trade, has large white-ringed black eyespots along the rear flank. The bronze featherback (Notopterus notopterus) is smaller (under 60 cm), has no hump, and has a much smaller mouth.
animal.whereToSee: Floodplain beels of Assam and Bangladesh; the Ganges in Bihar and West Bengal; Kolkata fish markets
animal.season: Resident; spawns May–July

lore: Buchanan-Hamilton described it in 1822 under the Bengali name chitala. In Bengal, a chital muitha curry has long been a festive dish for weddings and guests of honour.
funFact: Featherbacks belong to the bonytongues (Osteoglossiformes), a lineage that also includes the arapaima, the arowanas and Africa's elephantfishes and goes back more than 100 million years.

wiki.extract: Chitala chitala is a knifefish from Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan, found in the Brahmaputra, Indus, Ganges and Mahanadi River basins. It is sometimes known as the Indian featherback or Indian knifefish. In the past, it frequently included several related Chitala species, but these are now regarded as separate species. The main species confused with this species is C. ornata ; a Southeast Asian species seen regularly in the aquarium trade. The true C. chitala is very rare in the aquarium trade.

summary: The largest guineafowl, with a vulture-like bare head and long cobalt-and-white hackle feathers. Researchers found that it lives in a multilevel society, a social structure once thought limited to large-brained mammals.
nativeRange: Dry north-eastern Africa: Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania
abilities: Forms stable groups that associate in a structured multilevel society
Can survive with little drinking water, getting moisture from its food
Group decisions about direction are influenced by many members rather than only dominants

animal.diet: Seeds, fruit, leaves and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry bush and grassland, often along riverine woodland
animal.behaviour: Groups of 15–60 birds roost together in trees and merge into larger supergroups at certain times.
fieldMarks: Bare blue-grey head with a chestnut nape patch
Long cobalt-blue, white and black striped hackles over the neck and back
Cobalt-blue breast
Long tail and slender build
Red eye
animal.voice: Harsh, chinking 'chink-chink-chink' alarms and loud scolding chatter.
animal.lookalikes: Helmeted guineafowl is dumpier, with a bony casque and evenly spotted grey plumage, and lacks the striped hackles and blue breast.
animal.whereToSee: Samburu, Buffalo Springs and Shaba (Kenya), Tsavo East, Meru, Awash (Ethiopia)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Research at Mpala Research Centre in Kenya, published in 2019, described the first known multilevel society in a bird, comparing vulturine guineafowl to primates and elephants.
funFact: Its 'vulture' head lacks feathers, a probable adaptation for losing heat in hot dry country.

wiki.extract: The  vulturine guinea fowl  is the largest extant species of guinea fowl. Systematically, it is only distantly related to other guinea fowl genera. Its closest living relative, the white breasted guinea fowl, Agelastes meleagrides inhabit primary forests in Central Africa. It is a member of the bird family Numididae, and is the only member of the genus Acryllium. It is a resident breeder in northeast Africa, from southern Ethiopia and Somalia through Kenya and just into northern Tanzania.

summary: A noisy, polka-dotted gamebird with a bony casque, living in flocks across African savanna. Domesticated in Africa and carried to Europe and the Americas, it is now kept and eaten worldwide.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; introduced and domesticated widely
abilities: Eats ticks and insects, and is kept on farms partly for pest control
Flocks raise loud alarms that warn other animals of predators
Can run fast and roosts in trees at night

animal.diet: Seeds, bulbs, insects, ticks, snails
animal.habitat: Savanna, grassland, farmland and scrub
animal.behaviour: Flocks of dozens or even hundreds walk in long lines, calling raucously; they flee by running rather than flying.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey plumage covered in white spots
Bony, horn-coloured casque on top of the head
Bare blue and red head with wattles
Rounded, humped body
animal.voice: A harsh, grating 'kek-kek-kek-krrrr' alarm and a rhythmic 'buck-wheat' call; flocks are very noisy.
animal.lookalikes: Crested guineafowl has a curly black crest instead of a casque. Vulturine guineafowl has a long, slim body, cobalt breast and a bare head with no casque.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any savanna reserve in East and southern Africa; Kruger, Serengeti, Etosha
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Greek myth said the sisters of the hero Meleager wept for him and were turned into guineafowl, their tears becoming the white spots, hence 'meleagris'. Romans knew it as the Numidian hen.
funFact: The turkey's genus name Meleagris was borrowed from the classical name of the guineafowl, a legacy of early European confusion between the two birds.

wiki.extract: The helmeted guinea fowl is the best known of the guinea fowl bird family, Numididae, and the only member of the genus Numida. It is native to Africa, mainly south of the Sahara, and has been widely introduced, as a domesticated species, into the West Indies, North America, Colombia, Brazil, Australia and Europe.

summary: A nocturnal insect-eater that spends the day perched bolt upright on a broken branch, so perfectly camouflaged it looks like part of the tree. At night its mournful, falling song is one of the most haunting sounds of the Neotropics.
nativeRange: Southern Central America (Nicaragua and Costa Rica) through South America to northern Argentina and Uruguay; Trinidad and Tobago
abilities: Freezes motionless on a stump with bill pointed skyward, mimicking a dead branch
Notches in its eyelids let it watch for predators with eyes apparently closed
Huge gape catches large flying insects in sallies from a perch
Lays a single egg in a shallow depression on top of a broken branch, with no nest

animal.diet: Large flying insects — moths, beetles, katydids
animal.habitat: Open forest, edges, savanna, plantations and mangroves
animal.behaviour: It returns to the same daytime perch for weeks, which makes it findable once located.
fieldMarks: Mottled grey-brown bark-like plumage
Large yellow eyes; tiny bill above an enormous mouth
Long tail; upright posture on stumps
Dark spots on the breast
animal.voice: A series of 5–8 loud, melancholy whistles falling in pitch and volume, like 'poor-me-one, poor-me-one'.
animal.lookalikes: Northern Potoo (Mexico to Costa Rica, and Jamaica and Hispaniola) is nearly identical but gives a harsh, croaking call. Great Potoo is larger and paler with a growling roar. Nightjars perch lengthwise on branches or rest on the ground.
animal.whereToSee: Pantanal (Brazil), Llanos (Venezuela), Asa Wright Nature Centre (Trinidad) and Amazonian lodges where guides know day roosts.
animal.season: Resident; sings most on moonlit nights

lore: A widespread Guaraní legend tells of a young woman whose lover was killed and who was turned into the urutau, forever crying her grief through the night.
funFact: Its Brazilian name 'mother of the moon' comes from its habit of calling on moonlit nights.

wiki.extract: The common potoo, also known as the kakuy or urutaú, is one of seven species of birds within the genus Nyctibius. It is notable for its large, yellow eyes and a wide mouth. Potoos are nocturnal and are related to nightjars and frogmouths. They lack the characteristic bristles around the mouths of true nightjars.

summary: A rust-red butterfly carrying a large peacock-feather eyespot on each wing. It spends winter as an adult in sheds and hollow trees, and if disturbed it flashes its eyes and hisses.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia east to Japan
abilities: Flashes four large eyespots to startle birds; experiments show the eyespots deter blue tits
Rubs its wings together to make a hissing sound with ultrasonic clicks that deters rodents in dark roosts
Survives winter as an adult, hibernating in cool, dark crevices
Closed wings look like a dead leaf or charred bark

animal.diet: Adults feed at buddleia, thistles, willow catkins and ivy; caterpillars eat stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) and occasionally hop
animal.habitat: Woodland rides, gardens, field margins and anywhere with nettle beds and nectar
animal.behaviour: Caterpillars live in communal silk tents on sunny nettle patches; a threatened adult opens its wings in jerks, revealing the eyespots while producing a hiss.
fieldMarks: Deep rust-red upperside with one large blue, black and yellow eyespot on each of the four wings
Underside almost black, finely streaked, like a dead leaf
Ragged wing edge
Caterpillar black and spiny with fine white dots, in groups on nettles
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable with wings open. At rest the dark underside can resemble a small tortoiseshell (Aglais urticae), but that species' underside has a pale band across the forewing.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with buddleia in late summer; woodland edges in early spring when hibernators emerge.
animal.season: Overwintered adults Mar–May; new generation Jul–Sep before entering hibernation

lore: Linnaeus named it after Io of Greek myth, whose guardian Argus had a hundred eyes that Hera later set into the peacock's tail. It was long placed in its own genus, Inachis, after Io's father Inachus.
funFact: In total darkness, where eyespots are useless, the peacock relies on its hiss: its wing sounds alone are enough to make mice back away.

wiki.extract: Aglais io, the European peacock, or the peacock butterfly, is a colourful butterfly, found in Europe and temperate Asia as far east as Japan. The peacock butterfly is resident in much of its range, often wintering in buildings or trees. It therefore often appears quite early in spring.
