plates.long: This woodcut headpiece from a 1576 Giunta edition of Galen's works depicts a gathering of diverse birds, centered around an owl. In the context of Renaissance medical and philosophical texts, these birds often served as allegories for different human temperaments or intellectual virtues such as wisdom and vigilance.

plates.long: A large grey eagle stands on a rocky outcrop above a peacock with a green and blue tail. The image illustrates the transition between the text describing the eagle's medicinal properties and the general study of birds.

plates.long: This finely detailed woodcut depicts a peacock with its magnificent tail fully displayed, appearing in Conrad Gessner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium'. As one of the earliest attempts at a comprehensive scientific encyclopedia of animals, Gessner's work relied on such illustrations to bridge the gap between classical knowledge and direct observation.

plates.long: A detailed engraving of a peacock ('Pavo'), illustrating the bird's distinctive plumage. Kircher's work combines natural history with biblical exegesis, providing a comprehensive view of the animal kingdom as understood in the late 17th century.

plates.long: A detailed study of a white peacock egg (Pavone Bianco), shown in situ on a stylized landscape. Zinanni’s work was pioneering for its focus on oology, providing a visual taxonomy that served both scientific and aesthetic purposes during the Enlightenment.

plates.desc: Scientific engraving of a common peacock egg (Pavone Usuale) resting on a landscape ground.
plates.long: This engraving from Giuseppe Zinanni’s 1737 treatise depicts the egg of a common peacock (Pavone Usuale). It represents one of the earliest systematic attempts to document bird eggs through detailed scientific illustration, utilizing fine stippling to represent the porous texture of the shell.

plates.desc: A peacock with its tail feathers fanned out.
plates.long: A peacock stands on a small grassy mound with its tail feathers fully displayed in a circular fan. The woodcut detail emphasizes the 'eyes' of the plumage.

summary: An orange milkweed butterfly, a close relative of the monarch, that ranges across Africa, Asia and Australia. Its body holds toxins from milkweed, and many other butterflies have evolved to copy its pattern.
nativeRange: Africa, southern Europe (Canary Islands, southern Spain), the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia, and Australia
abilities: Stores cardenolides from milkweed, making it distasteful to birds
Its pattern is copied by mimics such as the female danaid eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus)
Males gather pyrrolizidine alkaloids from withered plants to make courtship pheromones

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from many flowers; caterpillars eat milkweeds such as Calotropis and Asclepias
animal.habitat: Dry open country, wasteland, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: It flies slowly and openly, relying on its toxicity and warning colours rather than speed.
fieldMarks: Tawny orange wings
Forewing tip black with a slanting white band
Black body spotted with white
Males have a black scent pouch on each hindwing with a white centre
animal.lookalikes: Female danaid eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus) is a mimic with a similar pattern but lacks the white-spotted black body. Striped tiger (Danaus genutia) has bold black veins. Monarch (D. plexippus) is larger with black-lined veins.
animal.whereToSee: Dry gardens and Calotropis scrub across India, East Africa, Arabia and the Canary Islands.
animal.season: Year-round in the tropics

lore: Butterflies identified as plain tigers appear in the wall painting from the tomb-chapel of Nebamun at Thebes (about 1350 BCE), now in the British Museum, among the oldest identifiable butterflies in art.
funFact: In East Africa, populations crossbreed in a hybrid zone where a bacterium kills male offspring of some matings, producing all-female broods.

wiki.extract: Danaus chrysippus, also known as the plain tiger, African queen, or African monarch, is a medium-sized butterfly widespread in Asia, Australia and Africa. It belongs to the Danainae subfamily of the brush-footed butterfly family Nymphalidae. Danainae primarily consume plants in the genus Asclepias, more commonly called milkweed. Milkweed contains toxic compounds, cardenolides, which are often consumed and stored by many butterflies. Because of their emetic properties, the plain tiger is unpalatable to most predators. As a result, its colouration is widely mimicked by other species of butterflies. The plain tiger inhabits a wide variety of habitats, although it is less likely to thrive in jungle-like conditions and is most often found in drier, wide-open areas.

plates.long: This page from the Tudor Pattern Book (c. 1525) illustrates a collection of animals used as models for embroidery or decorative arts. It features a tiger distracted by a mirror—a common medieval bestiary myth where hunters used mirrors to trick tigresses—alongside a meticulously rendered ram and various birds. The work reflects the transition from medieval symbolism to the observational naturalism

plates.long: This 1598 woodcut from Sebastian Münster’s 'Cosmographey' depicts a fierce feline-like creature, identified in the accompanying text as a panther or tiger from the region of Hyrcania. The illustration captures the animal in a muscular, stylized form characteristic of Renaissance natural history, which often blended observation with traditional lore. Such images were essential in early modern Europ

plates.author: Pierio Valeriano
plates.desc: A woodcut depicting a hunter on horseback dropping a tiger cub to distract a pursuing tigress.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the classical belief that a hunter could escape a pursuing tigress by dropping her cubs one by one, forcing her to stop and retrieve them. In Valeriano's 'Hieroglyphica', this scene serves as a symbol for 'Ultio' (Vengeance) and the complexities of maternal instinct.

plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of the mythical beast 'Mo' (貘), described as having an elephant's trunk, rhinoceros' eyes, ox's tail, and tiger's feet.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Mo' (貘), a mythical creature from Chinese folklore often associated with eating nightmares. According to the accompanying text from the Sancai Tuhui, it possesses a composite anatomy including an elephant's trunk and tiger's paws, reflecting the traditional Chinese method of describing unfamiliar or legendary animals through familiar parts.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui, Juan 92 — Birds & Beasts (NCL Original)
plates.author: 王圻、王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of the mythical beast 'Bo', a horse-like creature with a horn and tiger claws.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Bo', a mythical horse-like creature with a single horn and tiger-like claws. According to the text, it inhabits the Zhongqu Mountains and possesses the fearsome ability to prey upon tigers and leopards.

plates.title: The Embassy of the Dutch East India Company to the Tartar Cham
plates.author: Johan Nieuhof
plates.desc: A large copperplate engraving depicting a tiger in the foreground, labeled 'TIGER'. In the background to the right, a smaller deer-like animal is labeled 'Muskus-dier'. The scene includes tropical vegetation, birds in a tree, and two indigenous figures sitting on the ground near a bird.
plates.long: A large tiger dominates the foreground of this landscape, while a musk deer stands in the background. To the right, two seated figures observe the scene near a tree filled with birds. This engraving illustrates the exotic fauna encountered during the Dutch East India Company's embassy to China.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: A hunter uses a long pole to extract tiger cubs from a rocky den while a large tiger watches from behind a wall.
plates.long: A hunter in a green hat uses a pole to reach into a den to steal tiger cubs. A large tiger is depicted behind a stone structure on the right, representing the dangers of the hunt described in the text.

plates.title: Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms: Ceremonial Regulations
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tiger in a seated posture.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a tiger, identified by the accompanying Chinese character '虎' (hǔ). It is part of a series of animal illustrations, likely from a natural history or encyclopedic work, showcasing the traditional Chinese style of zoological representation where form and spirit are emphasized over anatomical precision.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica: Illustrated Volume, Middle of the Lower Part
plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a fish, identified by the text as a 'tiger fish' (虎魚) or 'tiger shark' (虎沙).
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from Li Shizhen's 1596 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica) depicts a species of fish, identified by the accompanying text as a 'tiger fish.' Such illustrations were essential for the accurate identification of medicinal substances in early modern China, representing a major advancement in the systematic documentation of natural history and pharmacology.

plates.title: Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms: Birds and Beasts
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tiger in a crouching pose.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia 'Sancai Tuhui' depicts a tiger in a dynamic, crouching posture. The tiger is a significant motif in Chinese culture, often representing power, bravery, and a ward against evil spirits. This illustration exemplifies the style of natural history documentation during the late Ming dynasty.

summary: An orange-and-black butterfly whose eastern North American population flies up to about 4,800 km to winter in a few mountain fir forests in central Mexico. No individual makes the round trip: the journey north is completed over several generations by its descendants.
nativeRange: North, Central and South America; established in Australia, New Zealand, Pacific islands, Iberia and the Canaries
abilities: Navigates with a time-compensated sun compass housed in its antennae and brain
Can sense Earth's magnetic field as a backup compass
Caterpillars sequester toxic cardenolides from milkweed, making adults distasteful to birds
The autumn 'super generation' lives up to ~8 months, versus 2–6 weeks for summer generations
Clusters by the millions on single trees in Mexico's oyamel forests

animal.diet: Larvae eat milkweeds (Asclepias); adults drink nectar
animal.habitat: Open fields and meadows with milkweed; overwinters in high-altitude fir forest or coastal Californian groves
animal.lifespan: 2–6 weeks for summer adults; up to 8 months for migrants
animal.behaviour: Migrants enter reproductive diapause, travel south on thermals and tailwinds, and roost in dense clusters that keep them cool but above freezing all winter.
fieldMarks: Large orange butterfly with heavy black veins
Black wing borders with two rows of white spots
Males have a small black scent spot on a vein of each hindwing
Caterpillar banded yellow, black and white, on milkweed
animal.lookalikes: Viceroy (Limenitis archippus) is smaller and has a black line crossing the hindwing veins. Queen (Danaus gilippus) is darker chestnut with white spots scattered on the forewing and much thinner black veins.
animal.whereToSee: Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in Michoacán, Mexico (El Rosario, Sierra Chincua); Pacific Grove and Pismo Beach groves in California; Point Pelee and Cape May during the autumn migration
animal.season: Mexico roosts Nov–Mar; California groves Nov–Feb; breeding across the US and Canada in summer; southward migration Aug–Oct

lore: The Purépecha and Mazahua people of Michoacán long linked the butterflies' arrival in early November with the Day of the Dead and the returning souls of ancestors. Scientists only located the Mexican wintering grounds in 1975, with help from local residents.
funFact: The migratory North American subspecies was listed as Endangered by the IUCN in 2022, then reassessed as Vulnerable in 2023; the species as a whole is Least Concern.

wiki.extract: The monarch butterfly or simply monarch is a milkweed butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. Other common names, depending on region, include milkweed, common tiger, wanderer, and black-veined brown. It is among the most familiar of North American butterflies and an iconic pollinator, although it is not an especially effective pollinator of milkweeds. Its wings feature an easily recognizable black, orange, and white pattern, with a wingspan of 8.9–10.2 cm (3.5–4.0 in). A Müllerian mimic, the viceroy butterfly, is similar in color and pattern, but is markedly smaller and has an extra black stripe across each hindwing.

summary: A large rainforest butterfly whose electric blue contains no blue pigment at all. The colour comes from nanoscale ridges on its wing scales that interfere with light.
nativeRange: Central America and northern South America, including the Amazon basin
abilities: Structural colour: Christmas-tree-shaped nanostructures reflect blue light through interference
The underside is brown with eyespots, so it flashes and vanishes as it flaps
Scales repel water and are studied for anti-counterfeiting inks and sensors
Adults ferment-feed on rotting fruit

animal.diet: Larvae eat legumes; adults drink juices of rotting fruit, sap and fungi
animal.habitat: Tropical rainforest, especially along streams and clearings
animal.behaviour: Males patrol sunlit river corridors, their flashing wings visible from far away, even from low-flying aircraft.
fieldMarks: Very large butterfly, upperside brilliant iridescent blue edged with black
Underside brown with rows of eyespots, giving a blue flicker in flight
Females duller above
Rises and dips in a slow, flapping flight along streams
animal.season: Seen all year in the tropics; mostly active in mid-morning sun

lore: Morpho wings were used in 19th- and early-20th-century European jewellery and trays. The genus name recalls Morpho, an epithet of Aphrodite.
funFact: Drop alcohol on a morpho wing and it turns green until the liquid evaporates, because the gaps in the nanostructure fill with a different medium.

wiki.extract: The Menelaus blue morpho is one of 30 species of butterfly in the subfamily Morphinae. Its wingspan is about 12 cm (4.7 in), and its dorsal forewings and hindwings are a bright, iridescent blue with black edges, while the ventral surfaces are brown. Its iridescent wings are an area of interest in research due to their unique nanostructure. Due to its characteristic blue color, Morpho menelaus is considered valuable among collectors and was widely hunted in the 20th century.

summary: A black butterfly marked with pale blue, almost glassy streaks, common across tropical Asia. In southern India it joins huge seasonal migrations between the Western and Eastern Ghats.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Myanmar, Thailand, southern China and Indochina
abilities: Migrates in large numbers across peninsular India around the south-west monsoon; migrating swarms are almost all males
Males gather alkaloids from Crotalaria and Heliotropium to make pheromones and boost their chemical defence
Distasteful to predators thanks to compounds sequestered from its milkweed-family host plants

animal.diet: Adults visit flowers and withered plants rich in alkaloids; caterpillars feed on milkweed-family vines such as Dregea (Wattakaka) and Heterostemma
animal.habitat: Open forest, scrub, grassland and gardens from plains to hills
animal.behaviour: Migrating blue tigers often travel with dark blue tigers and crows, and rest in large clusters on shrubs and dry twigs.
fieldMarks: Dark brown-black wings with many pale blue, semi-translucent spots and streaks
Broad pale streaks in the hindwing cell
Slow, gliding flight
Black head and thorax dotted with white
animal.lookalikes: Dark blue tiger (Tirumala septentrionis) has narrower, darker blue streaks. Glassy tiger (Parantica aglea) is smaller, with thinner, whiter streaks and a more delicate look.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and forest edges across India and Sri Lanka; migration corridors in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
animal.season: Year-round; in South India large migrations take place around the south-west monsoon

funFact: The pale blue of its semi-transparent wing spots comes from pterobilin, a blue bile pigment.

wiki.extract: Tirumala limniace, the blue tiger, is a species of butterfly found in South Asia, and Southeast Asia that belongs to the brush-footed butterfly family, Nymphalidae. More specifically it is part of the crows and tigers or danaid group. This butterfly shows gregarious migratory behaviour in southern India. In some places, it may be found in congregations with Danaus genutia, Tirumala septentrionis, Euploea sylvester, Euploea core, Parantica aglea, and at high elevations, with Parantica nilgiriensis, on Crotalaria.

plates.long: This page from the Tudor Pattern Book (c. 1525) illustrates a collection of animals used as models for embroidery or decorative arts. It features a tiger distracted by a mirror—a common medieval bestiary myth where hunters used mirrors to trick tigresses—alongside a meticulously rendered ram and various birds. The work reflects the transition from medieval symbolism to the observational naturalism

plates.title: Cosmographey: das ist Beschreibung aller Laender
plates.author: Münster, Sebastian
plates.desc: Woodcut of a tiger in a landscape, illustrating the myth of the tiger and the mirror.
plates.long: This 1598 woodcut from Sebastian Münster’s 'Cosmographey' depicts a fierce feline-like creature, identified in the accompanying text as a panther or tiger from the region of Hyrcania. The illustration captures the animal in a muscular, stylized form characteristic of Renaissance natural history, which often blended observation with traditional lore. Such images were essential in early modern Europ

plates.title: Valeriano: Hieroglyphica (1575)
plates.author: Pierio Valeriano
plates.desc: A woodcut depicting a hunter on horseback dropping a tiger cub to distract a pursuing tigress.
plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the classical belief that a hunter could escape a pursuing tigress by dropping her cubs one by one, forcing her to stop and retrieve them. In Valeriano's 'Hieroglyphica', this scene serves as a symbol for 'Ultio' (Vengeance) and the complexities of maternal instinct.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui (Vol. 92)
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of the mythical beast 'Mo' (貘), described as having an elephant's trunk, rhinoceros' eyes, ox's tail, and tiger's feet.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Mo' (貘), a mythical creature from Chinese folklore often associated with eating nightmares. According to the accompanying text from the Sancai Tuhui, it possesses a composite anatomy including an elephant's trunk and tiger's paws, reflecting the traditional Chinese method of describing unfamiliar or legendary animals through familiar parts.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui, Juan 92 — Birds & Beasts (NCL Original)
plates.author: 王圻、王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of the mythical beast 'Bo', a horse-like creature with a horn and tiger claws.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts the 'Bo', a mythical horse-like creature with a single horn and tiger-like claws. According to the text, it inhabits the Zhongqu Mountains and possesses the fearsome ability to prey upon tigers and leopards.

plates.title: The Embassy of the Dutch East India Company to the Tartar Cham
plates.author: Johan Nieuhof
plates.desc: A large copperplate engraving depicting a tiger in the foreground, labeled 'TIGER'. In the background to the right, a smaller deer-like animal is labeled 'Muskus-dier'. The scene includes tropical vegetation, birds in a tree, and two indigenous figures sitting on the ground near a bird.
plates.long: A large tiger dominates the foreground of this landscape, while a musk deer stands in the background. To the right, two seated figures observe the scene near a tree filled with birds. This engraving illustrates the exotic fauna encountered during the Dutch East India Company's embassy to China.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: A hunter uses a long pole to extract tiger cubs from a rocky den while a large tiger watches from behind a wall.
plates.long: A hunter in a green hat uses a pole to reach into a den to steal tiger cubs. A large tiger is depicted behind a stone structure on the right, representing the dangers of the hunt described in the text.

plates.title: Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms: Ceremonial Regulations
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tiger in a seated posture.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a tiger, identified by the accompanying Chinese character '虎' (hǔ). It is part of a series of animal illustrations, likely from a natural history or encyclopedic work, showcasing the traditional Chinese style of zoological representation where form and spirit are emphasized over anatomical precision.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica: Illustrated Volume, Middle of the Lower Part
plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a fish, identified by the text as a 'tiger fish' (虎魚) or 'tiger shark' (虎沙).
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from Li Shizhen's 1596 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica) depicts a species of fish, identified by the accompanying text as a 'tiger fish.' Such illustrations were essential for the accurate identification of medicinal substances in early modern China, representing a major advancement in the systematic documentation of natural history and pharmacology.

plates.title: Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms: Birds and Beasts
plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a tiger in a crouching pose.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia 'Sancai Tuhui' depicts a tiger in a dynamic, crouching posture. The tiger is a significant motif in Chinese culture, often representing power, bravery, and a ward against evil spirits. This illustration exemplifies the style of natural history documentation during the late Ming dynasty.

summary: The most widespread butterfly on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica and South America. Successive generations relay a round trip of up to 12,000 km a year between tropical Africa and northern Europe, much of it flown at high altitude out of sight.
nativeRange: Nearly worldwide: Europe, Africa, Asia, North America and Australia (absent as a resident from South America and Antarctica)
abilities: Completes a multigenerational Africa–Europe round trip of up to about 12,000 km, the longest known insect migration cycle
Crosses the Sahara and the Mediterranean, often flying hundreds of metres above the ground on favourable winds
Caterpillars eat hundreds of host plants, especially thistles, mallows and nettles
Breeds continuously with no winter diapause, so it follows the seasons rather than waiting them out

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from thistles, knapweeds, buddleia and many other flowers; caterpillars eat thistles (Cirsium, Carduus), mallows, nettles and legumes
animal.habitat: Open sunny places of almost any kind: meadows, deserts after rain, farmland, gardens, dunes
animal.lifespan: Adults about 2–4 weeks; the full life cycle takes roughly 4–6 weeks in warm weather
animal.behaviour: Spring generations push north from North Africa into Europe and as far as Scandinavia and Iceland; their offspring fly back south in autumn, mostly at altitude, so the return journey went unnoticed until radar and isotope studies revealed it.
fieldMarks: Upperside salmon-orange with black blotches
Forewing tips black with a band of white spots
Hindwing underside marbled grey, buff and olive with a row of four or five small blue-centred eyespots
Strong, fast flight; often basks with wings open on bare ground
animal.lookalikes: American lady (Vanessa virginiensis) has two large eyespots on the hindwing underside instead of a row of four or five small ones. West Coast lady (V. annabella) has an orange, not white, bar near the forewing tip. Red admiral (V. atalanta) is black with red bands.
animal.whereToSee: Thistle-rich meadows, coastal headlands and gardens with buddleia; spectacular mass arrivals occur in irruption years (e.g. Europe 2009, California 2019).
animal.season: Europe: spring immigrants Apr–Jun, local brood and southward return Aug–Oct; in tropical Africa and the Middle East during the northern winter

lore: The English name 'Painted Lady' dates to the naturalist James Petiver around 1699; the German Distelfalter ('thistle butterfly') and Linnaeus's epithet cardui both point to the thistle (Carduus) its caterpillars eat.
funFact: In 2024 researchers showed, using pollen carried on their bodies and isotopes in their wings, that painted ladies found on a beach in French Guiana had crossed the Atlantic from West Africa, a flight of at least 4,200 km.

wiki.extract: Vanessa cardui is the most widespread of all butterfly species. It is commonly called the painted lady, or formerly in North America the cosmopolitan butterfly.

otherNames: Dēngtǎ shuǐmǔ 灯塔水母, 'lighthouse jellyfish' (Chinese)
summary: A tiny hydrozoan jellyfish, a few millimetres across, that can reverse its own life cycle. When injured, starving or aged, the adult medusa can turn back into a polyp and start again, so in principle it never has to die of old age.
nativeRange: Described from the Mediterranean; similar Turritopsis are found in temperate and tropical seas worldwide
abilities: Reverts from adult medusa to an early polyp stage through transdifferentiation, turning specialised cells into other cell types
Can repeat this rejuvenation many times
Buds many genetically identical medusae from a single polyp colony
Catches plankton with stinging tentacles

animal.diet: Zooplankton, fish eggs, small larvae
animal.habitat: Coastal plankton; polyps attached to hard surfaces
animal.lifespan: Potentially unlimited, though most are eaten or die of disease
animal.behaviour: The bell is transparent with a bright red gut and up to about 90 tentacles.
fieldMarks: Tiny bell 4–5 mm across
Bright red stomach
Many fine tentacles around the bell rim
animal.lookalikes: Other Turritopsis species are almost identical; genetics is often needed.

lore: German student Christian Sommer noticed the life-cycle reversal while keeping specimens collected off Rapallo, Italy, in 1988; Ferdinando Boero and Stefano Piraino's team described it in 1996.
funFact: A few other jellyfish, including a moon jelly, have since been found to rejuvenate in a similar way, but Turritopsis dohrnii remains the best-studied case.

wiki.extract: Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly known as the immortal jellyfish, is a species of small, biologically immortal Medusozoa (jellyfish) found worldwide in temperate to tropic waters. It is one of the few known cases of an animal capable of completely reverting to a sexually immature, sedentary polyps colonial stage after having reached sexual maturity as a solitary individual.

The page features forty numbered specimens, including sea anemones, jellyfish, and various 'zoophytes'—organisms then thought to bridge the gap between plants and animals. plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a 'sea lung', a term historically used for certain types of jellyfish or similar soft-bodied marine creatures. Rondelet's work was foundational in the transition from classical natural history to modern empirical zoology, providing some of the first printed images of these species.

The image shows a central disc with radiating patterns and long, textured appendages, reflecting the early modern period's growing inte

It appears in a botanical and medicinal text, likely a commentary on Dioscorides, reflecting the Renaissance interest in categorizing and illustrating the natural world for scientific and medical purposes.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'sea nettle' (Urtica marina), a term used historically to describe various jellyfish and sea anemones. Featured in Conrad Gessner's monumental zoological work, this illustration represents the 16th-century transition toward empirical observation and the systematic documentation of the natural world.

summary: A sparrow-sized seabird that breeds in Antarctica and migrates to the North Atlantic. It is one of the most abundant birds on Earth and appears to 'walk' on water while feeding.
nativeRange: Breeds in Antarctica and sub-Antarctic islands; winters across all oceans
abilities: Pats the water with its feet while hovering, appearing to walk on it
Migrates from Antarctica to the North Atlantic each year
Finds food by smell

animal.diet: Krill, small fish, plankton
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds in rock crevices
animal.behaviour: It dances over the waves with feet pattering the water as it feeds.
fieldMarks: Dark sooty-brown body
White rump band
Long legs that project beyond the square tail
Yellow webs between the toes
animal.voice: Silent at sea; chattering at nests.
animal.lookalikes: Leach's storm petrel has a forked tail. European storm petrel has a white underwing bar.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula; off North Carolina and Massachusetts in summer
animal.season: Breeds Nov–March (Antarctica); Northern Hemisphere May–Sept

lore: Sailors called storm petrels 'Mother Carey's chickens', thought to be from 'Mater Cara', the Virgin Mary.
funFact: The name 'petrel' is said to come from St Peter walking on water.

wiki.extract: Wilson's storm petrel, also known as Wilson's petrel, is a small seabird of the austral storm petrel family Oceanitidae. It is one of the most abundant bird species in the world and has a circumpolar distribution mainly in the seas of the southern hemisphere but extending northwards during the summer of the northern hemisphere. The world population was estimated in 2022 as stable at 8–20 million birds. In 2010 it had been estimated at 12–30 million. A 1998 book had estimated more than 50 million pairs. The name commemorates the Scottish-American ornithologist Alexander Wilson. The genus name Oceanites refers to the mythical Oceanids, the three thousand daughters of Tethys. The species name is from Latin oceanus, "ocean".

The illustration captures the Tropic Bird's distinctive elongated tail feathers and the Petrel's descending posture, reflecting Catesby's efforts to provide accurate anatomical records that corrected previous naturalists' errors. As a pioneering work of No

summary: A golf-ball-sized octopus that flashes vivid blue rings when alarmed. Its saliva carries tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison that can paralyse and kill an adult human within minutes to hours, and there is no antivenom.
nativeRange: Tropical western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean: northern Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, north to southern Japan
abilities: Saliva carries tetrodotoxin produced by symbiotic bacteria
Flashes about 60 blue rings in a fraction of a second, using muscles that expose reflecting layers
Bite is often painless, so victims may not notice it
Can change from drab brown to warning colours instantly

animal.diet: Small crabs, shrimps and fish, subdued by injecting venomous saliva
animal.habitat: Shallow reefs, rubble, tide pools and seagrass, often hiding in shells and crevices
animal.behaviour: Normally camouflaged in brown and yellow, it displays pulsing blue rings when provoked, a warning to predators.
fieldMarks: Tiny octopus, yellowish-brown at rest
Large, iridescent blue rings outlined in black, larger than in other blue-ringed species
Rings flash brightly when the animal is disturbed
Often found in empty shells or bottles
animal.lookalikes: Southern blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena maculosa) of southern Australia is smaller with smaller rings. Blue-lined octopus (H. fasciata) has blue lines on the body rather than rings. Treat any blue-ringed octopus as deadly.
animal.whereToSee: Muck-diving sites such as Lembeh Strait (Indonesia) and Anilao (Philippines); never handle.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Blue-ringed octopus bites killed swimmers in Australia in the 1950s and 1960s, and the animal became a pop-culture emblem in the James Bond film Octopussy (1983).
funFact: Victims stay conscious while paralysed; people have survived when bystanders gave artificial respiration until the toxin wore off.

wiki.extract: The greater blue-ringed octopus is one of four species of extremely venomous blue-ringed octopuses belonging to the family Octopodidae. This particular species of blue-ringed octopus is known as one of the most toxic marine animals in the world.

summary: A clever, short-lived mollusc of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic, with three hearts, blue blood and most of its neurons in its arms. It changes colour and skin texture in an instant to vanish against rock or sand.
nativeRange: Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic; similar species elsewhere were long included under this name
abilities: Changes colour, pattern and skin texture within a fraction of a second using chromatophores and papillae
Arms, holding about two-thirds of its neurons, can taste, touch and act semi-independently
Solves puzzles, unscrews jars and learns by watching another octopus
Squeezes through any gap larger than its hard beak
Squirts ink clouds and jets away by water propulsion

animal.diet: Carnivore: crabs, clams, snails, fish
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, reefs and seagrass from shallows to ~200 m
animal.size: Mantle up to ~25 cm; arm span to ~1 m; usually 3–10 kg
animal.behaviour: A female guards and cleans her eggs in a den for weeks without eating, and dies soon after they hatch.
fieldMarks: Soft body with eight arms
Rapid colour and texture change
Lives in dens with shell piles outside
Large, golden eyes
animal.lookalikes: Several similar octopuses elsewhere were long called 'common octopus'.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky shores of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic
animal.season: Resident

lore: Octopuses sprawl across Minoan 'Marine Style' jars from Crete (c. 1500 BCE), and Aristotle's History of Animals describes their mating and colour change. Pliny tells of an octopus at Carteia in Spain that raided a fish-salting works by night.
funFact: Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.

wiki.extract: The common octopus is a mollusk belonging to the class Cephalopoda. Octopus vulgaris is one of the most studied of all the octopus species, and also one of the most intelligent. It ranges from the eastern Atlantic, extends from the Mediterranean Sea, Black sea and the southern coast of England, to the southern coast of South Africa. It also occurs off the Azores, Canary Islands, and Cape Verde Islands. The species is also common in the Western Atlantic.

summary: A gigantic, tusked pinniped of the Arctic, gathering in haul-outs of thousands on ice floes and beaches. Walruses find clams by touch with hundreds of sensitive whiskers and suck them out of their shells. Loss of summer sea ice now forces enormous crowds onto shore, where stampedes kill calves.
nativeRange: Arctic seas: Pacific walrus in the Bering and Chukchi seas; Atlantic walrus from Canadian Arctic and Greenland to Svalbard and the Kara Sea
abilities: Uses tusks up to about 1 m long as ice picks to haul out — 'Odobenus' means 'tooth-walker'
Hundreds of stiff, sensitive whiskers detect clams in seafloor mud
Produces powerful suction that pulls clam bodies from their shells, and jets water to dig them out
Can slow its heart rate on dives; most feeding dives last under 10 minutes, though dives of about 25 minutes have been recorded

animal.diet: Mainly bivalve molluscs; also worms, snails, crabs; occasionally seals
animal.habitat: Shallow continental-shelf waters with sea ice; land haul-outs when ice is absent
animal.size: Males 2.7–3.6 m and up to about 1,500 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Extremely gregarious, lying in dense heaps. Males sing underwater courtship songs of knocks, taps and bell-like tones for days in winter.
fieldMarks: Huge, wrinkled cinnamon-brown to pinkish body (pinker when warm)
Two long ivory tusks in both sexes (longer in males)
Broad, bristly 'moustache' of whiskers
No external ears; hind flippers can turn forward to walk on land
Signs: haul-out beaches with flattened gravel, shells and tusk-gouged ice
animal.voice: Loud roars, grunts and barks on haul-outs; underwater, males produce knocks, clicks and a ringing bell-like sound.
animal.lookalikes: Bearded seal has long whiskers but no tusks and is far smaller. Elephant seals (not Arctic) have a trunk-like nose and no tusks.
animal.whereToSee: Round Island, Walrus Islands State Game Sanctuary (Alaska); Svalbard (Poolepynten, Torellneset); Point Lay, Alaska; Cape Serdtse-Kamen and Wrangel Island (Chukotka); Igloolik and Foxe Basin (Nunavut)
animal.season: Svalbard and Round Island haul-outs June–September

lore: The 12th-century Lewis chessmen, found in Scotland, were carved mainly from walrus ivory, likely traded from Norway and Greenland. Norse Greenlanders paid tithes and trade in walrus tusks.
funFact: Walruses can sleep while floating vertically, inflating air sacs in their necks like built-in life jackets.

wiki.extract: The walrus is a large pinniped marine mammal with discontinuous distribution about the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean and subarctic seas of the Northern Hemisphere. It is the only extant species in the family Odobenidae and genus Odobenus. This species is subdivided into two subspecies: the Atlantic walrus, which lives in the Atlantic Ocean, and the Pacific walrus, which lives in the Pacific Ocean.

summary: A rainbow-coloured crustacean of Indo-Pacific reefs with one of the fastest punches in the animal kingdom. Its spring-loaded clubs smash snail shells and crab armour, and its eyes see colours and light polarisation in ways no other animal is known to.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Guam, the Philippines and northern Australia
abilities: Strikes with its club at about 23 m/s, with an acceleration comparable to a .22-calibre bullet
Each strike forms collapsing cavitation bubbles that deliver a second shock to prey
Has 12–16 types of photoreceptor and sees ultraviolet and circularly polarised light
Each eye judges depth on its own, using three separate zones
Its club's spiral (helicoidal) structure absorbs impacts and has inspired new composite materials

animal.diet: Carnivore: snails, crabs, clams, worms
animal.habitat: U-shaped burrows in rubble and sand near coral reefs, 3–40 m
animal.behaviour: It lines the entrance of its burrow with rubble and is known to strike at divers' fingers, which is why aquarists call it a 'thumb-splitter'.
fieldMarks: Brightly coloured green, red and blue
Club-like raptorial limbs folded under the head
Large stalked eyes
Lives in burrows
animal.lookalikes: Other mantis shrimps. Its strike can break aquarium glass and cut fingers; do not handle.
animal.whereToSee: Lembeh Strait (Indonesia) and Anilao (Philippines)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1758 as Cancer scyllarus. Hobbyists tell stories of mantis shrimps cracking aquarium glass, and their punch has been studied with high-speed cameras since the 2000s.
funFact: A mantis shrimp's club regrows each time the animal moults.

wiki.extract: Odontodactylus scyllarus, commonly known as the peacock mantis shrimp, harlequin mantis shrimp, painted mantis shrimp, clown mantis shrimp, rainbow mantis shrimp, peacock odontodactyl, thumb splitter, or simply mantis shrimp, is a large odontodactylid stomatopod native to the epipelagic seabed across the Indo-Pacific, ranging from the Marianas to East Africa, and as far South as Northern KwaZulu Natal in South Africa. It is one of roughly 480 species of mantis shrimp, which are well known for their raptorial claws, exceptional vision, and their unique way of interacting with other marine species.

summary: A crested Amazonian bird that digests leaves by fermenting them in its crop, like a cow. Its chicks have claws on their wings and can climb back to the nest after escaping into water.
nativeRange: Amazon and Orinoco basins of South America
abilities: Foregut fermentation of leaves by bacteria in an enlarged crop
Chicks use two wing claws to climb branches
Chicks drop into water to escape predators and swim back
Smells strongly of manure from its fermenting crop
Sole living member of an ancient lineage

animal.diet: Leaves, buds and flowers of marsh plants
animal.habitat: Swamps, riverbanks and oxbow lakes
animal.behaviour: Groups nest communally in branches overhanging water, with helpers from previous broods aiding parents.
fieldMarks: Pheasant-sized bird with a spiky, ragged crest
Bare blue facial skin and red eyes
Brown above, buff breast, chestnut belly and wings
Clumsy flight over water

wiki.extract: The hoatzin is a species of tropical bird found in swamps, riparian forests, and mangroves of the Amazon and Orinoco Basins in South America. It is the only extant species in the genus Opisthocomus which is the only extant genus in the family Opisthocomidae under the order Opisthocomiformes. Despite being the subject of intense debate by specialists, the taxonomic position of this family is still far from clear.

summary: A deep-sea fish with a transparent, fluid-filled head through which its green, tube-shaped eyes can be seen. Long thought to stare only upward, it was shown in 2008 to rotate its eyes forward to watch what it eats.
nativeRange: North Pacific from the Bering Sea to Baja California and Japan
abilities: Tubular eyes rotate inside a transparent shield to look upward or forward
Green lens pigments may filter sunlight to pick out bioluminescent prey
What look like eyes on its face are actually nostrils (olfactory organs)
Hovers motionless using large, flat fins

animal.diet: Small crustaceans and probably prey stolen from siphonophores
animal.habitat: Twilight zone, about 600–800 m
animal.behaviour: Hangs horizontally in the water, scanning upward for silhouettes of prey and siphonophores, then rotates eyes forward and pivots to feed.
fieldMarks: Clear, dome-like shield over the top of the head
Two bright green tubular eyes visible inside the head
Small mouth at the tip of the snout
Dark body with large scales and broad fins
animal.lookalikes: Other barreleyes (Opisthoproctus, Dolichopteryx) lack the transparent head shield; spookfish have tubular eyes but opaque heads.
animal.whereToSee: Only via ROV footage (Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute); not seen by divers
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Described by Chapman in 1939 from damaged trawl specimens that had lost their fragile head shield; Bruce Robison and Kim Reisenbichler of MBARI published the first living observations in 2008.
funFact: For 70 years scientists did not know its head was transparent because trawl nets destroyed the shield.

wiki.extract: The Pacific barreleye fish (Macropinna) is a genus of ray-finned fish belonging to Opisthoproctidae, the barreleye family. It contains one species, M. microstoma. It is recognized for a highly unusual transparent, fluid-filled shield on its head, through which the vivid green lenses of its eyes can be seen. It was originally believed that the tubular eyes of this fish were fixed in place, offering only tunnel vision above its head. However, in 2008, scientists discovered that its eyes were able to rotate both up and forward within its transparent dome. This feature allows for M. microstoma to observe prey while keeping its eyes protected from stinging tentacles of jellyfish-like organisms it feeds on.

summary: A brilliant golden-yellow bird with a black band running through the eye and around the nape, whose liquid fluting calls carry through gardens and woodland from China to Indonesia. Northern birds migrate south to winter in Southeast Asia and India.
nativeRange: Breeds from the Russian Far East, NE China and Korea south through eastern China; resident in Southeast Asia, the Philippines and Indonesia; winters in India (mainly south and northeast) and Southeast Asia
abilities: Weaves a hammock-like cup nest slung in a horizontal fork
Eats caterpillars, including hairy ones that many birds avoid
Long-distance migrant in the north of its range

animal.diet: Insects, caterpillars, fruit and berries, nectar
animal.habitat: Woodland, parks, gardens, plantations and mangroves
animal.behaviour: Stays high in the canopy and is often seen only as a flash of yellow in undulating flight between trees.
fieldMarks: Bright golden-yellow body
Broad black stripe through the eye that meets at the back of the head
Black wings with yellow edgings; black tail with yellow corners
Pinkish-red bill
animal.voice: Rich, liquid, fluty whistles such as 'lwee-wee-wee-leeow', and a harsh nasal 'kyaaa' alarm
animal.lookalikes: Indian golden oriole has a black mask only through the eye that does not join on the nape; Slender-billed oriole has a thinner bill and narrower nape band; females and young are greener with streaked underparts.
animal.whereToSee: Singapore and Kuala Lumpur parks year-round; Beijing and Seoul parks in summer; Andaman Islands year-round (resident race); scarce winter visitor to peninsular India
animal.season: Resident in Southeast Asia; summer visitor in northern China and Korea (May–Sep); winter visitor to India

lore: The huánglí in Du Fu's famous Tang-dynasty quatrain 'Two orioles sing in the green willows' (两个黄鹂鸣翠柳) is this species, and the bird has been a symbol of spring in Chinese poetry ever since.
funFact: Its Japanese name means 'Korean bush warbler', though it is not a warbler at all; in Japan it is only a scarce visitor.

wiki.extract: The black-naped oriole is a passerine bird in the oriole family that is found in many parts of Asia. There are several distinctive populations within the wide distribution range of this species and in the past the slender-billed oriole was included as a subspecies. Unlike the Indian golden oriole which only has a short and narrow eye-stripe, the black-naped oriole has the stripe broadening and joining at the back of the neck. Males and females are very similar although the wing lining of the female is more greenish. The bill is pink and is stouter than in the golden oriole.

summary: A brilliant yellow-and-black bird that is surprisingly hard to see, hidden in the leafy canopy of poplars and oaks. Its loud, fluting whistle betrays it long before a glimpse of gold.
nativeRange: Breeds across Europe, northwest Africa, Turkey, the Middle East and Central Asia to western Siberia; winters in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Builds a hammock-like nest slung between the forks of a high branch
Its bright yellow plumage is remarkably well hidden among sunlit leaves
Migrates by night to wintering grounds in tropical Africa
Can handle hairy caterpillars that many birds avoid

animal.diet: Insects and caterpillars; fruit, cherries and berries in late summer
animal.habitat: Tall deciduous woods, riverine poplar groves, orchards and parks
animal.behaviour: Moves through the canopy in swooping, undulating flights between trees, rarely coming low.
fieldMarks: Male bright golden-yellow with black wings and black centre to the tail
Pink-red bill and black lores
Female and young greenish-yellow with streaked whitish underparts
Thrush-sized with a woodpecker-like undulating flight
animal.voice: A rich, fluting whistle often rendered 'weela-weeoo' or 'dee-dlee-o'; also a harsh, cat-like 'kweeaah'.
animal.lookalikes: Female resembles green woodpecker in flight, but lacks red on the head. Indian golden oriole (South Asia) has black extending behind the eye. Yellow wagtail and yellowhammer are smaller and ground-living.
animal.whereToSee: Poplar plantations and riverine woods in Spain, France, the Danube Delta, Turkey and the Central Asian river valleys; a rare spring migrant to eastern England, where it last bred in 2009.

lore: Pliny the Elder reported the belief that a jaundice sufferer who looked at the 'icterus', a yellow bird usually identified as the oriole, would be cured while the bird died.
funFact: The German name 'Pirol' and Dutch 'wielewaal' are both imitations of its whistled song.

summary: An egg-laying, duck-billed mammal of eastern Australia's rivers and one of only five living monotremes. It hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut, finding prey by the electrical fields of their muscles.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia and Tasmania; introduced to Kangaroo Island
abilities: Detects the electrical fields of moving prey with about 40,000 electroreceptors in its bill
Males deliver a venom from hind-leg spurs that causes intense, lasting pain in humans
Lays leathery eggs and feeds young on milk sweated from patches of skin, as it has no nipples
Its fur glows blue-green under ultraviolet light
Stores food in cheek pouches and grinds it with horny pads instead of teeth

animal.diet: Carnivore: insect larvae, freshwater shrimp, yabbies, worms
animal.habitat: Freshwater streams, rivers and lakes with earth banks for burrows
animal.lifespan: Up to ~21 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Females dig long nesting burrows and plug them with soil to guard their eggs. Platypuses eat around a fifth of their body weight in a day.
fieldMarks: Small brown furry mammal with a soft duck-like bill
Flat, beaver-like tail
Webbed front feet
Dives briefly, leaving rings on the water
animal.lookalikes: Australian water-rat (rakali) has a white-tipped tail and a rat-like head. Males have a venomous spur on each hind ankle; never handle one.
animal.whereToSee: Broken River, Eungella National Park and the Atherton Tablelands (Queensland); Tasmania's rivers
animal.season: Resident; best at dawn and dusk

lore: When a dried specimen reached the British zoologist George Shaw in 1799, he suspected a hoax and looked for stitches joining a duck's bill to a mammal's body. In Aboriginal stories from New South Wales the platypus is the child of a duck and a water-rat.
funFact: The platypus has no stomach: its gullet connects directly to its intestine.

wiki.extract: The platypus, sometimes referred to as the duck-billed platypus, is a semiaquatic, egg-laying mammal endemic to eastern Australia, including Tasmania. The platypus is the sole living representative of the family Ornithorhynchidae and genus Ornithorhynchus, though a number of related species appear in the fossil record. Together with the four species of echidna, it is one of the five extant species of monotremes, mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to live young. Like other monotremes, the platypus has a sense of electrolocation, which it uses to detect prey in water while its eyes, ears and nostrils are closed. It is one of the few species of venomous mammals, as the male platypus has a spur on each hind foot that delivers an extremely painful venom.

otherNames: Pla kat ปลากัด (Thai)
summary: A small air-breathing fish of Thai paddies and marshes, bred over centuries for combat and later for flowing colourful fins. Wild populations are now Vulnerable as their wetlands vanish.
nativeRange: Central Thailand and the Chao Phraya and Mekong basins (Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam); introduced elsewhere
abilities: Breathes air with a labyrinth organ, so it survives in tiny, stagnant puddles
Males build floating bubble nests and guard eggs and fry
Males flare their gill covers and fins in aggressive displays to rivals

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects and their larvae, zooplankton
animal.habitat: Shallow, still, vegetated waters: paddies, marshes and floodplain pools
animal.lifespan: About 2–3 years; up to 5 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Males guard a territory and a bubble nest. After spawning they catch falling eggs in their mouths and place them in the nest.
fieldMarks: Wild males: dull reddish-brown with iridescent blue-green scales and red-tinted fins
Domestic males: very long, flowing fins in reds, blues and whites
Upturned mouth; long anal fin and short dorsal set back
Females smaller and duller, with shorter fins
animal.lookalikes: Other wild Betta species (B. imbellis, B. smaragdina, B. mahachaiensis) are very similar and best told apart by range and fin and colour details. Gouramis have thread-like pelvic fins.
animal.whereToSee: Paddy fields and marshes of central Thailand (wild fish increasingly rare); fish markets of Bangkok's Chatuchak; aquaria worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the rainy season (May–October)

lore: Siamese villagers bred short-finned fighting strains (pla kat) for wagering for centuries, and King Rama III is said to have licensed and taxed the fights. In 2019 Thailand declared the betta its national aquatic animal.
funFact: The genus name Betta may come from the Malay 'ikan bettah', and splendens means 'splendid'.

wiki.extract: The Siamese fighting fish, commonly known as the Siamese fighter, or locally as the betta, is a freshwater fish native to Mainland Southeast Asia, namely Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. It is one of more than 70 species of the genus Betta, but the only one eponymously called "betta", owing to its global popularity as a pet; Betta splendens are among the most popular aquarium fish in the world, due to their diverse and colorful morphology and relatively low maintenance.

summary: A long, silver bonytongue that cruises just under the surface of Amazonian flooded forests and leaps up to 2 m to snatch beetles, spiders, birds and even bats from overhanging branches. Males brood the eggs and young in their mouths.
nativeRange: Amazon basin and the Rupununi and Oyapock rivers (Guyana, French Guiana); introduced to parts of North America and Asia via aquarium releases
abilities: Leaps clear of the water to catch insects, spiders and small birds and bats on branches, which earns it the name 'water monkey'
Males mouth-brood eggs and then shelter the fry in their mouths for weeks
Two chin barbels sense ripples from prey falling onto the surface
edibilityNote: Eaten locally in the Amazon. Fishing for brooding males to supply the aquarium fry trade is a conservation concern in Peru and Colombia, so buy only legally sourced fish.

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects, spiders, crustaceans, fish, and occasionally birds, bats and snakes
animal.habitat: Surface waters of flooded forests, lakes and slow rivers
animal.size: Usually 60–90 cm; up to about 1.2 m
animal.behaviour: Patrols just under the surface with its large upturned mouth. During the flood season it spreads into the forest canopy layer of flooded trees to hunt.
fieldMarks: Long, laterally compressed, tapering silver body with very large scales
Dorsal and anal fins long and set far back, almost meeting the small tail
Steeply upturned mouth with two forward-pointing barbels on the chin tip
Juveniles carry a large yolk sac under the belly
animal.lookalikes: Black arowana (O. ferreirai) of the Rio Negro is very similar but its juveniles are black with a yellow stripe. Asian arowana (Scleropages) is deeper-bodied, with a shorter anal fin and larger, often coloured scales.
animal.whereToSee: Floodplain lakes near Iquitos (Peru) and Manaus (Brazil); Mamirauá Reserve
animal.season: Resident; breeds at the start of the flood season (roughly December–February)

lore: Georges Cuvier described the species in 1829 from Brazilian specimens. Across Amazonian Brazil the aruanã appears in riverside folklore as a guardian of the flooded forest, and the Karajá people of the Araguaia river hold an Aruanã festival with masked dancers.
funFact: Osteoglossum means 'bony tongue' in Greek: like the arapaima, the arowana has a toothed bony tongue that it uses to crush prey against the roof of its mouth.

wiki.extract: The silver arowana is a South American freshwater bony fish of the family Osteoglossidae. Silver arowanas are sometimes kept in aquariums, but they are predatory and require a very large tank.

otherNames: Pla tapad ปลาตะพัด (Thai)
summary: A metallic-scaled bonytongue revered in Chinese culture as a living dragon that brings luck and wealth. Prized red and gold varieties have sold for tens of thousands of dollars, and wild fish are now rare.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia: Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo (Indonesia and Malaysia)
abilities: Males mouth-brood eggs and young for about two months
Leaps from the water to grab insects, spiders and small vertebrates from overhanging vegetation
Different wild populations carry distinct colours: green, silver, golden (Malaysia, Sumatra) and red (Borneo)

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects, spiders, small fish, frogs and other small animals at the surface
animal.habitat: Slow blackwater rivers, swamp forests and flooded forest with overhanging vegetation
animal.lifespan: Around 15–20 years; captive fish reportedly older
animal.behaviour: Hunts at the surface with an upturned mouth. In captivity it is solitary and aggressive toward its own kind.
fieldMarks: Long, laterally compressed body with very large, often metallic scales in five horizontal rows
Upturned mouth with two short chin barbels
Dorsal and anal fins set far back near a rounded tail
Colour variants: green, silver, golden-crossback or red
animal.lookalikes: Silver arowana (Osteoglossum) is slimmer, with a much longer anal fin and smaller scales. The northern (gulf) saratoga (Scleropages jardinii) of northern Australia and New Guinea and the spotted saratoga (S. leichardti) of Queensland have red-spotted scales.
animal.whereToSee: Wild: the Kapuas basin (West Kalimantan, Borneo) and Danau Sentarum; captive-bred fish in aquaria across East and Southeast Asia
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the rainy season

lore: The fish's large coin-like scales and whisker barbels recall the Chinese dragon, and keeping one is believed in feng shui to bring prosperity. It has been on CITES Appendix I since 1975, and only registered captive-bred fish, each with an implanted microchip, may be traded internationally.
funFact: Each legally traded Asian arowana carries a microchip and a certificate so it can be traced back to a registered farm.

wiki.extract: The Asian arowana comprises several phenotypic varieties of freshwater fish distributed geographically across Southeast Asia. While most consider the different varieties to belong to a single species, work by Pouyaud et al. (2003) differentiates these varieties into multiple species. They have several other common names, including Asian bonytongue, dragonfish, and a number of names specific to the different color varieties.

summary: A tall, ostrich-like bustard, among the heaviest flying birds in the world, now reduced to fewer than 200 birds (including those in captivity), almost all in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan. Collision with overhead power lines is one of its biggest killers.
nativeRange: Formerly much of India and eastern Pakistan; now mainly Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, with tiny remnants in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka; possibly occasional in Cholistan, Pakistan
abilities: Males can weigh around 15 kg, among the heaviest flying birds
In display, the male inflates a large throat pouch and cocks his tail, booming
Lays a single egg on bare ground

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, beetles, small lizards and rodents; also seeds, berries and shoots
animal.habitat: Arid and semi-arid grassland with scattered scrub
animal.size: About 1 m tall; males up to about 15 kg
animal.behaviour: Walks slowly through grassland; its forward-facing eyes and poor manoeuvrability in flight make it unable to avoid power lines.
fieldMarks: Very large, long-legged bird with a horizontal body
Black crown and crest on a white head and neck
Brown back and wings; males have a black breast band
Black-and-white wing pattern in flight
animal.voice: A deep, booming 'hoonk' carried a long way, given by displaying males
animal.lookalikes: Macqueen's (houbara) bustard is much smaller and sandy with a black neck stripe; Lesser florican is small with long head plumes in breeding males.
animal.whereToSee: Desert National Park near Jaisalmer, Rajasthan (with permits)
animal.season: Resident; displays mainly during the monsoon

lore: The ornithologist Salim Ali proposed it as India's national bird. It is the state bird of Rajasthan, and India's Supreme Court has heard cases on burying or marking power lines in its habitat.
funFact: A captive breeding centre at Jaisalmer has hatched dozens of chicks since 2019 as insurance against extinction.

wiki.extract: The great Indian bustard or Indian bustard is a bustard occurring on the Indian subcontinent. It is a large bird with a horizontal body, long bare legs and is among the heaviest of the flying birds. Once common on the dry grasslands and shrubland in India, as few as 150 individuals were estimated to survive as of 2018, reduced from an estimated 250 individuals in 2011. It is critically endangered due to hunting and habitat loss. It is protected under the Indian Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

summary: A sandy, cryptic bustard of deserts and semi-deserts that is the classic quarry of Arab falconry. Hunting and trapping along its migration routes have driven it into decline despite large captive-breeding programmes.
nativeRange: Breeds from Sinai, the Middle East and Iran across Central Asia to Mongolia and China; winters in the Arabian Peninsula, Iran, Pakistan and northwestern India
abilities: Plumage blends almost perfectly with sand and gravel desert
Can obtain water largely from food in arid habitats
Migrates thousands of kilometres between Central Asian breeding grounds and South Asian or Arabian wintering grounds
Squirts a jet of faeces at attacking falcons as a defence

animal.diet: Shoots, seeds and fruits of desert plants; beetles, locusts and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Flat or rolling semi-desert with sparse shrubs
animal.behaviour: Displaying males raise their white neck plumes over their heads and run in zigzags, a display visible from far across the desert.
fieldMarks: Sandy buff upperparts finely vermiculated with black
Black stripe running down each side of the neck into a white ruff
Short crest of white and black feathers
Bold black-and-white wing pattern in flight
animal.voice: Mostly silent; a low booming during display.
animal.lookalikes: African houbara (Chlamydotis undulata) of North Africa is very similar but has an all-white crest; ranges barely overlap. Great bustard is much larger, grey-headed and lacks the black neck stripe.
animal.whereToSee: Kyzylkum Desert in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan in spring; Cholistan and Balochistan (Pakistan) and the UAE in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor to Central Asia Mar–Oct; winter visitor to Arabia and South Asia

lore: Hunting houbara with sakers and peregrines is a centuries-old Bedouin tradition, and special permits for Gulf rulers to hunt it in Pakistan have been the subject of court challenges in Pakistan's Supreme Court.
funFact: Captive-breeding centres in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Morocco release large numbers of captive-bred houbara to support wild populations and falconry.

wiki.extract: The Asian houbara, also known as MacQueen's bustard, is a large bird in the bustard family. It is native to the desert and steppe regions of Asia, east from the Sinai Peninsula extending across Iran and further north toward Kazakhstan and Mongolia. In the 19th century, vagrants were found as far west of their range as Great Britain. Populations have decreased by 20–50% between 1984 and 2004 mainly due to hunting and changes in land-use. The Asian houbara is a partial latitudinal migrant while the African houbara is more sedentary. These two species are the only members of the genus Chlamydotis. The Asian houbara used to be regarded as a subspecies of the African houbara.

summary: A rare bustard of tall floodplain grasslands, whose black male leaps above the grass in spectacular display flights showing almost wholly white wings. Fewer than about 1,000 survive in two populations, in the Indian subcontinent and in Cambodia.
nativeRange: Terai and Brahmaputra floodplain grasslands of Nepal and NE India (Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh); a separate subspecies in Cambodia and southern Vietnam
abilities: Males spring high above the grass in display, gliding back down with a whirr of wings
Females raise chicks alone, hidden in tall grass
Depends on grassland maintained by floods and fire

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, beetles, ants and other insects; shoots, seeds and flowers
animal.habitat: Tall, wet alluvial grassland interspersed with shorter grass
animal.behaviour: Males hold display territories in short grass patches in spring, leaping vertically into the air repeatedly at dawn and dusk.
fieldMarks: Male: black head, neck and underparts with a slight crest
Male: wings almost entirely white, conspicuous in flight
Female: buff-brown and heavily patterned, larger than the male
Long legs and neck; walks upright through grass
animal.voice: Usually silent; a metallic 'chik-chik' when flushed
animal.lookalikes: Lesser florican (India) is smaller and males have long head plumes and a white collar; female Lesser florican is smaller and more slender.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga and Manas (Assam), Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh), Shuklaphanta and Koshi Tappu (Nepal), Tonle Sap grasslands (Cambodia)
animal.season: Resident; best seen during displays Mar–May

lore: Colonial-era hunters prized it as a gamebird, and the drainage and ploughing of floodplain grasslands since have reduced it to protected reserves.
funFact: Unlike most bustards, the female is larger than the male.

wiki.extract: The Bengal florican, also called the Bengal bustard, is a bustard species native to the Indian subcontinent, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List because fewer than 1,000 individuals were estimated to be alive as of 2017. It is the only member of the genus Houbaropsis.

summary: One of the heaviest flying birds on Earth. Males transform themselves in spring into billowing white 'foam baths' of feathers to impress females on open steppe and farmland. Most of the world population now lives in Spain.
nativeRange: Iberia, central Europe (Hungary, Austria, Germany), Morocco, Turkey, Russia, Kazakhstan, Central Asia and Mongolia to China; reintroduced to England
abilities: Males weigh up to about 16 kg, contesting the title of heaviest flying animal
Displaying males turn wings and tail inside out to become a mass of white plumes
Males grow long white whisker feathers in the breeding season
Lek-like display grounds are used for generations

animal.diet: Plant shoots, leaves, seeds, legumes; insects such as beetles and grasshoppers, especially for chicks
animal.habitat: Open steppe, extensive cereal farmland and pasture
animal.lifespan: Typically about 10 years; some exceed 15, with a maximum recorded age of 28
animal.size: Males 90–105 cm, 5.8–16 kg; females 75–85 cm, 3.3–5.3 kg; wingspan 1.9–2.6 m
animal.behaviour: Males gather on traditional display grounds in spring, where females visit to choose a mate.
fieldMarks: Very large, stately, goose-sized ground bird with long neck and legs
Upperparts golden-buff barred with black
Grey head and neck; males with chestnut breast band and white whiskers
Huge white wing panels in flight
animal.voice: Generally silent; a low barking or grunting at close quarters.
animal.lookalikes: Little bustard is much smaller (pheasant-sized) with a black-and-white neck in males. Asian houbara is sandy with a black neck plume. Female great bustard is far smaller than the male and can be mistaken for a goose at distance.
animal.whereToSee: Villafáfila and Extremadura in Spain, Castro Verde in Portugal, Hungary's Dévaványa, Salisbury Plain in England (reintroduced).
animal.season: Resident in Iberia; partially migratory in Russia and Central Asia; display Mar–Apr

lore: Bustards were exterminated in Britain by the 1830s; the bird still appears on Wiltshire's county emblem, and a reintroduction using chicks from Russia and Spain began on Salisbury Plain in 2004.
funFact: Its Latin name 'tarda' means 'slow', but despite its weight it is a strong flier.

wiki.extract: The great bustard is a bird in the bustard family, and the only living member of the genus Otis. It breeds in open grasslands and farmland from northern Morocco, South and Central Europe to temperate Central and East Asia. European populations are mainly resident, but Asian populations migrate farther south in winter. Endangered as of 2023, it had been listed as a Vulnerable species on the IUCN Red List since 1996.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a bustard, a large terrestrial bird, as part of Conrad Gessner's encyclopedic effort to catalog the animal kingdom. Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium' is considered the starting point of modern zoology, combining classical knowledge with contemporary observations and detailed illustrations.

plates.long: A dynamic woodcut showing a large bird, identified as a 'Bistarda' (bustard), standing over a captured hare. The hand-coloring enhances the narrative of predation described in the accompanying text.

plates.desc: Woodcut of a Great Bustard (Gustarda Ave Scotica)
plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a Great Bustard, labeled as 'Gustarda Ave Scotica'. This illustration from Conrad Gessner's monumental zoological work reflects the 16th-century effort to catalog the natural world through a combination of direct observation and traditional accounts.

plates.long: This emblem from Pierio Valeriano's 'Hieroglyphica' (1556) depicts a bustard alongside a horse. The accompanying motto, 'IMBECILLVS FOR- tiori assurgens' (The weak rising up for the stronger), uses the observed behaviors of these animals to create a moral or social allegory, a common practice in 16th-century humanism.

summary: A fish-eating hawk found on every continent except Antarctica, diving feet-first to snatch fish from the water. Its recovery after the banning of DDT is one of conservation's great comeback stories.
nativeRange: Nearly worldwide: breeds across the Northern Hemisphere and Australasia; winters in the tropics and southern continents
abilities: Plunges feet-first into water, sometimes submerging fully
Reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads grip slippery fish
Carries fish head-forward to reduce drag
Long-distance migrant: some Scandinavian and Scottish birds winter in West Africa

animal.diet: Almost entirely live fish
animal.habitat: Coasts, lakes, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries
animal.behaviour: It hovers briefly over water, then folds its wings and dives, throwing its feet forward at the last moment.
fieldMarks: Dark brown upperparts, clean white underparts
White head with a bold dark stripe through the yellow eye
Long, narrow wings held in a gull-like crook with dark carpal patches
Brownish breast band, stronger in females
animal.voice: A series of high, clear, whistled 'cheep-cheep-cheep' or 'kyew' calls, often in flight near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Large gulls share the crooked-wing shape but lack the hooked bill and dark eye-stripe. Juvenile bald eagles and white-tailed eagles are much larger and mottled below.
animal.whereToSee: Loch Garten and Rutland Water (UK), Chesapeake Bay and Florida (USA), Baltic coasts, Red Sea and Gulf of California; wintering in West Africa and South America
animal.season: Summer visitor to the Northern Hemisphere (Mar–Sep); winter visitor to the tropics; resident in Australia and some subtropical regions

lore: Ospreys were extinct as breeders in England by 1840 and in Scotland by 1916; their return to Loch Garten in 1954 and translocation to Rutland Water in the 1990s became milestones of British conservation.
funFact: Its family, Pandionidae, contains only the ospreys (one species, or two where the eastern osprey is split), and it is one of the most widely distributed birds in the world.

wiki.extract: The osprey, historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range. It is a large raptor, reaching more than 60 cm (24 in) in length and a wingspan of 180 cm (71 in). It is brown on the upperparts and predominantly greyish on the head and underparts.

plates.title: François Bouchard — Recueil de cent-trente-trois oiseaux des plus belles especes (1775)
plates.author: François Bouchard
plates.desc: A hand-colored natural history engraving of an Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) perched on a rock. The bird is depicted with its head turned sharply back over its left shoulder, revealing its yellow eye and hooked beak. Its plumage is a combination of brown on the wings and back, with white and brown-mottled feathers on its breast and head. One of its powerful grey-scaled talons is lifted in a defensive or stepping posture. The bird stands on a small rocky outcrop with sparse vegetation, including several broad green leaves and a sprig of small red flowers. The illustration is set against a pale blue wash background and is enclosed within a yellow border. At the base of the image, a yellow horizontal band contains names for the bird in French, Latin, and Italian: 'Aigle Marine, o Canardiere', 'Falco Piscator vulgo Aquila Piscatoria', and 'Falco Pescatore volgarmente detto Aquila Pescatrice'.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts an Osprey, also known as a sea hawk, in a dynamic pose with its head turned sharply. The illustration is part of an 18th-century collection of bird species by François Bouchard, showcasing the era's interest in scientific classification and detailed artistic representation of the natural world. The labels provide the bird's name in French, Latin, and Italian, re

plates.desc: A large woodcut of a bird of prey, identified as an Osprey (Halietos), perched on a gnarled tree stump with a small insect at its base.
plates.long: A large bird of prey stands in profile on a weathered tree stump, its talons gripping the wood. A small insect crawls on the ground near the base of the perch. The illustration depicts the physical form of the Osprey as described in Aldrovandi's natural history compendium.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach
plates.desc: Woodcut of a large bird of prey, likely an eagle or osprey, standing on a rocky landscape.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a bird of prey, identified in the accompanying text as 'Halietus' (an osprey or eagle). It illustrates a chapter from a natural history compendium, showing the bird in a stylized landscape with hand-applied pigments that add depth to the graphic print.

plates.title: Ornithology
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: A detailed woodcut illustration of an eagle (Haliaetus) perched on a vertical wooden post, clutching a fish in its talons.
plates.long: A large bird of prey, identified in the text as a sea eagle or Haliaetus, is shown in profile while perched on a wooden plank. It holds a fish firmly in its talons, demonstrating its nature as a marine hunter. The woodcut uses fine hatching to define the texture of the feathers and the grain of the wood.
