plates.author: Mark Catesby
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of an osprey (fishing hawk) clutching a fish in its talons.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts an osprey, or 'fishing hawk,' in the act of capturing a fish. Created by Mark Catesby for his landmark publication 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands,' this plate is a prime example of early scientific illustration that combined artistic skill with empirical observation.

plates.title: Ortus sanitatis
plates.author: Unknown
plates.desc: Hand-colored woodcut of various birds including a bird of paradise and an osprey.
plates.long: A yellow bird, identified in the text as a bird of paradise, perches above a group of smaller grey birds and a larger osprey. The scene depicts the diverse avian life described in the accompanying Latin text.

plates.title: Ornithologiae: de avibus historiae libri XII
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a bird of prey, possibly an osprey, perched on a wooden board and holding a fish in its talons.
plates.long: This woodcut is featured in Ulisse Aldrovandi's 'Ornithologiae' (1599), one of the most comprehensive early modern studies of birds. It depicts a bird of prey, possibly an osprey, demonstrating its predatory nature by clutching a fish, reflecting the era's growing interest in empirical observation and the systematic categorization of the natural world.

plates.title: Compendium of Materia Medica: Illustrated Volume, Middle of the Lower Part
plates.author: 李時珍
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a ray or skate, identified as 'Hai Yao Yu' (Sea Eagle Fish).
plates.long: This woodcut illustration from the 1596 edition of the Bencao Gangmu depicts a 'Sea Eagle Fish' (海鷂魚), which corresponds to a modern ray or skate. The drawing accurately captures the flat, disc-like body and long tail, and is accompanied by text noting that its mouth is located on its underside, demonstrating the observational detail in early Chinese natural history.

plates.title: Ornithologiae: de avibus historiae libri XII
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Faint woodcut illustration of a bird of prey, likely an eagle or osprey.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a bird of prey, identified in the text as a Haliaetus (likely an osprey or sea eagle). It serves as a scientific illustration accompanying the detailed physical description in Ulisse Aldrovandi's monumental work on ornithology, representing the early modern effort to categorize the natural world through observation and print.

otherNames: Pla buek ปลาบึก (Thai)
summary: Among the largest freshwater fish ever weighed, a toothless, algae-eating giant of the Mekong that can top 290 kg. Wild numbers have collapsed with dams and overfishing, and it is Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Mekong basin of Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and possibly Myanmar and China; farmed in Thai reservoirs
abilities: Grows over 2.5 m and nearly 300 kg on a diet mostly of algae and plants
Loses its teeth as it grows
Makes long migrations along the Mekong, apparently between Cambodian rearing areas and upstream spawning grounds
edibilityNote: Traditionally eaten in Thailand and Laos. Wild capture is now banned or restricted across its range, and most pla buek sold in Thailand is reservoir-farmed. Do not eat wild-caught fish.

animal.diet: Herbivore as adults: algae and plant matter grazed from the riverbed; juveniles eat zooplankton
animal.habitat: Deep channels and pools of the main Mekong and large tributaries
animal.size: Up to about 3 m and 300 kg; the record 293 kg fish was 2.7 m long
animal.behaviour: Adults are believed to swim upriver at the end of the dry season to spawn in northern Thailand and Laos as the river rises.
fieldMarks: Huge, shark-like, scaleless grey body with a white belly
Small eyes set low on the head, below the line of the mouth
Adults have no barbels (juveniles have tiny ones) and no teeth
Forked tail and a small adipose fin
animal.lookalikes: Striped catfish (Pangasianodon hypophthalmus), the farmed 'swai' or 'tra', is much smaller, with barbels and stripes in juveniles. Giant pangasius (Pangasius sanitwongsei) has a toothed mouth, long barbels and dark-edged fins.
animal.whereToSee: Bueng Boraphet reservoir and fishing parks in Thailand (farmed fish); Chiang Khong on the Mekong (historical fishery); public aquaria
animal.season: Upstream migration and spawning April–June as Mekong waters rise

lore: Fishers at Chiang Khong, Thailand, held ceremonies to the river spirits before the yearly pla buek hunt, a tradition of the Tai Lue and Lao. In May 2005 they landed a 293 kg female, the heaviest freshwater fish weighed and documented at the time.
funFact: Even at nearly 300 kg, adults feed mostly on algae, making the Mekong giant catfish one of the largest plant-eating fish known.

wiki.extract: The Mekong giant catfish is a large species of catfish in the shark catfish family (Pangasiidae), native to the Mekong basin in Southeast Asia and adjacent China. It is considered critically endangered due to overfishing and habitat loss.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a catfish (Silurus), characterized by its prominent barbels and elongated body. Published in Conrad Gessner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium', it represents the early modern effort to systematically document the natural world through both observation and inherited knowledge.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a Silurus (catfish), characterized by its elongated body and wide mouth. It appears in Guillaume Rondelet's seminal 1554 work on marine and freshwater life, representing the transition toward empirical observation in Renaissance natural history.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Silurus, or catfish, characterized by its elongated body and prominent barbels. It appears in a commentary on Dioscorides' 'De Materia Medica,' reflecting the Renaissance interest in accurately documenting the natural world for medicinal and scientific purposes.

The illustration showcases the transition from medieval bestiaries to Renaissance natural history, emphasizing anatomical observation through fine-line hatching to suggest scale and form. Such prints were essential in the 16th-century effort to

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a yellowhead catfish (Huángsǎng yú), a species documented for its medicinal properties in Li Shizhen's Bencao Gangmu. The illustration serves as a visual guide for identification, reflecting the meticulous observational approach of 16th-century Chinese natural history.

plates.long: This woodcut illustration depicts a catfish (Nianyu), a species documented for its medicinal properties in Li Shizhen's 'Bencao Gangmu' (Compendium of Materia Medica). The artist captures the essential features of the fish, including its prominent barbels and elongated body, serving as a visual guide for identification in traditional Chinese medicine.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of two catfish swimming in water with aquatic plants, accompanied by identifying text.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts two catfish swimming amidst aquatic plants. It reflects the Ming dynasty's systematic approach to documenting the natural world, combining visual representation with identifying text to categorize various species of flora and fauna.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a species of catfish, identified in the Latin text as 'Bagre'. It serves as a fine example of 17th-century natural history illustration, where artists and scientists collaborated to document and classify the natural world with increasing anatomical precision.

summary: A tawny, long-tailed bird of reedbeds whose males sport a black drooping 'moustache'. Despite its old name 'bearded tit', it is the only member of its own family.
nativeRange: Reedbeds patchily from Britain and Spain across Europe, Turkey and the Middle East to Central Asia, Mongolia and northeastern China
abilities: Switches diet from insects in summer to reed seeds in winter
Changes its gizzard structure seasonally and swallows grit to grind seeds
Clings to reed stems with legs straddled between two stalks
Sole member of the family Panuridae

animal.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; reed seeds in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Extensive reedbeds by lakes, rivers and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Flocks erupt from reedbeds in autumn, flying high and calling before moving to new marshes.
fieldMarks: Tawny-orange body and very long, graduated tail
Male: blue-grey head and broad black moustache
Yellow-orange bill and eye
Whirring flight just above the reed tops
animal.voice: A ringing, metallic 'ping' or 'tching', often the first clue to its presence.
animal.lookalikes: Long-tailed tit is smaller with a pink, black and white pattern and lives in woodland. Reed warblers are brown with short tails.
animal.whereToSee: Minsmere and the Norfolk Broads (England), Oostvaardersplassen (Netherlands), the Danube Delta, Lake Neusiedl (Austria/Hungary).
animal.season: Resident; mass movements Sep–Nov

lore: The species name 'biarmicus' refers to Biarmia, an old name for the region around the White Sea, although the bird does not live there.
funFact: Severe winters can wipe out local populations, which then recover in a few years thanks to multiple broods.

wiki.extract: The bearded reedling is a small, long-tailed passerine bird found in reed beds near water in the temperate zone of Eurasia. It is frequently known as the bearded tit or occasionally as bearded parrotbill, as historically it was believed to be closely related to either the tits or parrotbills. Today it is known to lack close relatives and it is the only species in the family Panuridae.

summary: The largest butterfly in the world: females can exceed 25 cm across the wings. It lives only in a small area of lowland rainforest in Oro Province, Papua New Guinea, and is protected by both national law and CITES Appendix I.
nativeRange: Endemic to Oro (Northern) Province, south-eastern Papua New Guinea
abilities: World's largest butterfly by wingspan
Caterpillars depend on a single group of Pararistolochia vines and absorb their toxins
Adults usually fly high in the rainforest canopy, descending to within a few metres of the ground to feed or lay eggs

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from canopy flowers such as Hibiscus; caterpillars feed on Pararistolochia vines (notably P. dielsiana)
animal.habitat: Primary and old secondary lowland rainforest on volcanic soils
animal.size: Female wingspan up to about 25–28 cm; males smaller, around 16–20 cm
animal.behaviour: Females lay eggs on the host vine high in the canopy; caterpillars can ring-bark the vine stem, forcing the plant to put out new growth.
fieldMarks: Male: long, narrow, pointed forewings of black with iridescent blue-green and turquoise bands
Male abdomen bright yellow
Female: enormous, broad brown wings with cream-white markings and a creamy yellow abdomen
Red patch on the thorax
animal.lookalikes: The common green birdwing (Ornithoptera priamus), which shares parts of New Guinea, has broader male forewings with purer green and is far smaller in the female.
animal.whereToSee: Only in the Popondetta plains and nearby forests of Oro Province, PNG; viewing is through local conservation programmes.

lore: The first specimen, a female, was brought down with a small-shot gun by collector Albert Meek in 1906; Walter Rothschild named the species in 1907 after Queen Alexandra, wife of Edward VII. The 1951 eruption of Mount Lamington destroyed a large part of its habitat.
funFact: It is the only birdwing on CITES Appendix I, the treaty's strictest category, which bans international commercial trade in wild-caught specimens.

wiki.extract: Ornithoptera alexandrae, the Queen Alexandra's birdwing, is the largest species of butterfly in the world, with females reaching wingspans slightly in excess of 25 to 28 cm. This birdwing is restricted to the forests of the Oro Province in eastern Papua New Guinea.

otherNames: Cape York birdwing (Australian English, for the local form)
summary: A huge swallowtail of the New Guinea region whose males flash velvety black and iridescent emerald green across the rainforest canopy. Described by Linnaeus in 1758, it is the type species of the birdwing genus Ornithoptera, 'bird-wing'.
nativeRange: Moluccas, New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago, Solomon Islands and Cape York Peninsula, Australia
abilities: One of the largest butterflies in the world, with females far bigger than males
Caterpillars feed on Aristolochia vines and store their aristolochic acids, making larvae and adults distasteful to predators
Males patrol and soar high around flowering trees in the canopy

animal.diet: Adults take nectar from rainforest flowers such as Hibiscus and Lantana; caterpillars eat Aristolochia and Pararistolochia vines
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest, forest edges and village gardens where the host vines grow
animal.size: Wingspan roughly 11–20 cm; females the larger sex
animal.behaviour: Males guard stands of flowering trees and court females by hovering above them; the female's broad, slow wingbeats give her an almost bird-like flight.
fieldMarks: Male: velvet-black forewings with a broad iridescent green band; hindwings green with black spots
Male abdomen yellow
Female: much larger, dark brown with rows of white or cream patches and a yellow-spotted hindwing
Very large size and soaring flight high in the canopy
animal.lookalikes: Several close relatives (Ornithoptera euphorion of north Queensland, O. richmondia further south, and other green birdwings of the region) differ in the shape and extent of the male's green bands; location is the most practical guide. Queen Alexandra's birdwing males have much narrower, more pointed forewings tinted blue-green.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforest edges and gardens in Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands; in Australia, the Iron Range and northern Cape York.

lore: Linnaeus named it Papilio priamus in 1758 after Priam, king of Troy, in his scheme of naming swallowtails after Trojan and Greek heroes. Like all Ornithoptera birdwings it is listed on CITES Appendix II, so trade in wild specimens is regulated.
funFact: Butterfly farms in Papua New Guinea rear birdwings on planted host vines and sell them to collectors, giving villagers an income from keeping forest standing.

wiki.extract: Ornithoptera priamus, the common green birdwing, Cape York birdwing, Priam's birdwing, northern birdwing or New Guinea birdwing is a widespread species of birdwing butterfly found in the central and south Moluccas, New Guinea, Bismarck Archipelago, Solomon Islands, and north-east Australia.

summary: A large yellow-and-black butterfly with tailed hindwings, found right across the northern hemisphere. Its green caterpillar defends itself by shooting out a forked orange organ that reeks of rancid butter.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, temperate and mountain Asia to Japan, and north-western North America (Alaska and Canada)
abilities: Caterpillars evert an osmeterium, a forked scent gland releasing foul-smelling acids, to repel ants and wasps
Males gather on hilltops to find females ('hilltopping')
Ranges from sea-level fens to Himalayan meadows above 4,000 m

animal.diet: Adults take nectar from thistles, red clover, ragged robin and other flowers; caterpillars eat plants of the carrot family (fennel, wild carrot, dill, milk-parsley)
animal.habitat: Flowery open country: meadows, fens, mountain slopes, coastal hills and gardens with fennel or dill
animal.behaviour: In Britain the native subspecies britannicus is a specialist of the Norfolk Broads, laying eggs only on milk-parsley; continental swallowtails use many carrot-family plants.
fieldMarks: Yellow wings with black veins and a broad black outer border
Row of blue scales along the hindwing border, with a red eyespot near the body
Short black hindwing tails
Caterpillar green with black bands dotted with orange
animal.lookalikes: Scarce swallowtail (Iphiclides podalirius) is pale cream with bold black diagonal stripes and much longer tails. Corsican swallowtail (P. hospiton) is confined to Corsica and Sardinia and has shorter tails. In North America, the black swallowtail (P. polyxenes) is mostly black.
animal.whereToSee: Norfolk Broads in England (Hickling Broad, Strumpshaw Fen, How Hill); flowery hillsides throughout southern Europe and the Alps.
animal.season: Europe: two or three broods Apr–Sep; in England mainly late May–June with a partial second brood in August

lore: Linnaeus named it in 1758 after Machaon, the healer son of Asclepius in Homer's Iliad. In 18th-century England it was called the 'Royal William', a name usually linked to William III.
funFact: Its caterpillar starts life black and white, looking like a bird dropping, and only turns green with black bands in later moults.

wiki.extract: Papilio machaon, the Old World swallowtail, is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae. The butterfly is also known as the common yellow swallowtail or simply the swallowtail. It is the type species of the genus Papilio. This widespread species is found in much of the Palearctic and in North America.

summary: A black swallowtail of South and Southeast Asian gardens whose females come in several forms, some imitating poisonous rose swallowtails. It is a textbook case of mimicry controlled by a single gene region.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia from Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka to southern China, Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands, the Philippines and Indonesia
abilities: Females occur in several forms, including male-like 'cyrus', common-rose mimic 'stichius' and crimson-rose mimic 'romulus'
The mimetic forms are switched by variants of the doublesex gene
Caterpillars mimic bird droppings when young and later flash an orange osmeterium

animal.diet: Adults visit Lantana, Ixora and other garden flowers; caterpillars eat citrus and other Rutaceae such as curry leaf (Murraya koenigii)
animal.habitat: Gardens, orchards, forest edges and towns wherever citrus grows
animal.behaviour: The mimetic females fly in the slow, lazy manner of the distasteful roses they imitate, while males fly fast and erratically.
fieldMarks: Male: black with a band of cream-white spots across the hindwing, and a short tail
Female 'stichius': white patch and red marginal spots on the hindwing, like the common rose
Female 'romulus': red and white hindwing spots, like the crimson rose
Body black (rose swallowtails have red bodies)
animal.lookalikes: The common rose (Pachliopta aristolochiae) and crimson rose (P. hector), which mimetic females copy, have red heads and abdomens; the Mormon's body is black.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any garden with citrus or curry-leaf plants across India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
animal.season: Year-round in the tropics

lore: Its English name 'Mormon' is usually explained as a 19th-century joke about polygamy, because one male seemed to be paired with several very different-looking 'wives'.
funFact: A 2014 study in Nature showed that a single inverted stretch of chromosome containing the doublesex gene decides which mimetic form a female becomes.

summary: The national bird of Papua New Guinea, shown on its flag. Males gather at forest leks, clapping their wings and shaking their heads as they raise cascades of orange-red flank plumes to court females.
nativeRange: Southern and north-eastern New Guinea
abilities: Males display communally at leks, raising and shaking plumes
Raises plumes into an erect fan while calling loudly
Disperses seeds of many rainforest trees
Hybridises with other Paradisaea species where ranges meet

animal.diet: Fruit, especially figs; also arthropods
animal.habitat: Rainforest and forest edge
animal.size: About 34 cm, plus male tail wires
animal.behaviour: A dozen or more males display in the same tree, and females visit to choose among them.
fieldMarks: Male: maroon-brown body, yellow crown and collar, dark emerald throat
Long red to orange flank plumes
Two long black tail wires
Female drab maroon-brown with no plumes or wires
animal.lookalikes: Lesser bird-of-paradise has yellow plumes; the two hybridise where they meet. Plume colour varies among Raggiana subspecies from deep red to apricot.
animal.whereToSee: Varirata National Park near Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea
animal.season: Resident; display at morning leks

lore: Plumes have been worn for centuries in New Guinea headdresses, and traded to Asia; in the 16th century legless skins reached Europe, giving rise to the myth that birds-of-paradise never landed. PNG adopted it as its flag emblem in 1971.
funFact: Named after Francesco Raggi, an Italian marquis from Genoa.

This illustration from Conrad Gesner's 'Historiae Animalium' reflects the early modern belief that these birds lived entirely in the air, as trade specimens often arrived in Europe with their feet removed, leading naturalists to conclude they never landed.

summary: A tiny acrobatic tit with an azure cap, yellow underparts and a white face crossed by a dark eye-stripe. It is a dominant garden and woodland bird across Europe, raising some of the largest broods of any songbird.
nativeRange: Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus, northern Iran and the Middle East; the African blue tit of North Africa and the Canaries is now a separate species
abilities: Lays clutches of up to around 12 or more eggs, among the largest of any European songbird
Crown feathers reflect ultraviolet light; females favour males with brighter UV crowns
Hangs upside down to glean aphids and caterpillars from the tips of twigs
Learned to open milk-bottle tops in 20th-century Britain, a classic case of spreading animal innovation

animal.diet: Caterpillars, aphids, spiders; seeds, nuts and nectar in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous woodland, especially oak, parks, gardens, reedbeds in winter
animal.behaviour: Raises a single large brood timed to the oak-caterpillar peak, with parents delivering hundreds of caterpillars a day.
fieldMarks: Bright blue crown, wings and tail
White cheeks with a dark line through the eye and dark collar
Yellow underparts with a small dark belly smudge
Small, short-billed and very active
animal.voice: Song a high 'tsee-tsee-tsirrrr' ending in a trill; scolds with a rapid 'chur-r-r-r'.
animal.lookalikes: Great tit is larger with a black head and a black breast stripe. Azure tit (Russia, Central Asia) is whiter below with a white crown. African blue tit of North Africa has a dark-blue cap and slate back.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and woods across Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus; common at feeders in winter.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The milk-bottle raids reported by James Fisher and Robert Hinde in 1949 became a textbook example of cultural transmission in animals; the habit faded as doorstep milk deliveries declined.
funFact: Blue tits see in ultraviolet, so males and females that look identical to us are clearly different to each other.

summary: The largest European tit, green and yellow with a glossy black head and a black stripe down the belly. It is one of the most studied wild birds in the world, thanks to long-running nest-box projects such as Wytham Woods near Oxford since 1947.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia east to the Amur; eastern Asian populations are now treated as separate species
abilities: Times egg-laying to the spring peak of winter-moth caterpillars, a classic climate-change study
Learns new foraging tricks socially; traditions spread through populations in experiments
In a Hungarian cave, great tits were recorded hunting and eating hibernating pipistrelle bats
Has dozens of song variants and a large vocabulary of calls

animal.diet: Caterpillars and other insects; seeds and nuts, especially beechmast, in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks, gardens, orchards
animal.behaviour: A bold visitor to feeders that forms mixed flocks with other tits in winter and nests readily in boxes.
fieldMarks: Glossy black head with bright white cheeks
Yellow underparts split by a black central stripe, broader in males
Greenish back, blue-grey wings with a white wing bar
Larger than blue tit
animal.voice: Extremely varied; the classic song is a ringing two-note 'teacher-teacher' or 'tee-cha'; also a scolding 'churr' and a ringing 'pink'.
animal.lookalikes: Coal tit is much smaller with a white nape patch and no yellow. Blue tit has a blue crown and lacks the black breast stripe. Sombre tit (Balkans, Turkey) has a dusky cap and no yellow.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and woods throughout Europe and western Asia; Wytham Woods, Oxford, is its research home.
animal.season: Resident year-round; song from late winter

lore: Its two-note song was called the 'saw-sharpener' in English country lore, and the Wytham Woods population, studied since 1947 by the Edward Grey Institute, has shaped modern ideas about natural selection in the wild.
funFact: Great tit eggs have been laid progressively earlier in the Netherlands and Britain as springs have warmed, one of the best documented biological responses to climate change.

wiki.extract: The great tit is a small passerine bird in the tit family Paridae. It is widespread and common throughout Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia and as far east as the Amur River. It also occurs in parts of North Africa where it is generally resident in any sort of woodland. Most great tits do not migrate, except in extremely harsh winters. Until 2005 this species was lumped with numerous other subspecies. However, DNA studies have revealed that these subspecies are distinct from the great tit, and they have now been classified as two distinct species, the cinereous tit of southern Asia, and the Japanese tit of East Asia. The great tit remains the most widespread species in the genus Parus.

summary: A tiny, fearless black-capped tit that survives northern winters in a body weighing about 11 g. Its namesake call works as a code: the more 'dee' notes, the more dangerous the predator.
nativeRange: Alaska, Canada and the northern half of the United States
abilities: Adds extra 'dee' notes to its alarm call for smaller, more dangerous predators such as pygmy-owls
Caches thousands of seeds each autumn and remembers their locations
Its hippocampus — the brain region for spatial memory — gains new neurons in autumn, when caching peaks
Lowers its body temperature by about 10 °C on cold nights to save energy (regulated hypothermia)

animal.diet: Insects, spiders and eggs in summer; seeds and berries in winter
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, willow thickets, parks and gardens
animal.lifespan: Usually 2–3 years; banding record about 11 years
animal.behaviour: In winter it forms the core of mixed-species flocks that nuthatches, kinglets and woodpeckers join for safety.
fieldMarks: Black cap and black bib separated by bright white cheeks
Grey back; buffy flanks
White edges to wing coverts and secondaries form a pale wing panel
Tiny bill; large-headed, round-bodied shape
animal.voice: The familiar 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee'; song a clear, two-note whistle 'fee-bee', the second note lower.
animal.lookalikes: Carolina Chickadee (south-east) is smaller, shows less white in the wing and sings a four-note 'fee-bee-fee-bay'; the two hybridise where ranges meet. Mountain Chickadee has a white eyebrow; Boreal Chickadee has a brown cap.
animal.whereToSee: Any feeder or woodland in the northern US and Canada; very tame birds take seed from the hand at many nature centres.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is the state bird of Maine and Massachusetts and the provincial bird of New Brunswick.
funFact: Chickadees of other species and even nuthatches respond to black-capped chickadee alarm calls, effectively eavesdropping on its predator warnings.

wiki.extract: The black-capped chickadee is a small, nonmigratory, North American passerine bird that lives in deciduous and mixed forests. It is a member of the Paridae family, also known as tits. It has a distinct black cap on its head, a black bib underneath, and white cheeks. It has a white belly, buff sides, and grey wings, back, and tail. The bird is well known for its vocalizations, including its fee-bee song and its chick-a-dee-dee-dee call, from which it derives its name.

summary: A rare, tail-pumping warbler that nests only in young jack pine stands on sandy soils, mostly in northern Michigan, and winters in the Bahamas. It fell to fewer than 200 singing males in the 1970s and recovered through habitat management and cowbird control.
nativeRange: Breeds mainly in northern Lower Michigan, with small numbers in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, Wisconsin and Ontario; winters in the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos
abilities: Depends on jack pine stands roughly 5–20 years old, a habitat historically created by wildfire
Nests on the ground beneath the low living branches of young pines
Constantly bobs its tail while foraging
Migrates about 2,000 km between Michigan and the Bahamas

animal.diet: Insects and larvae; fruit on the wintering grounds
animal.habitat: Dense young jack pine on sandy outwash plains; low scrub in the Bahamas
animal.behaviour: Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism once affected most nests; trapping cowbirds from 1972 was key to recovery.
fieldMarks: Blue-grey upperparts streaked with black
Bright yellow throat and breast, black streaks on the sides
Broken white eye-ring; males have black lores
Constant tail-pumping
animal.voice: A loud, low-pitched, rich chatter rising at the end, e.g. 'chip-chip-che-way-o'.
animal.lookalikes: Magnolia Warbler has a white wing patch and a white tail band. Prairie Warbler also pumps its tail but is smaller with a yellow face and olive back. Canada Warbler has a necklace and no streaks above.
animal.whereToSee: Guided tours from Grayling (Michigan Audubon) and Mio (US Forest Service), Michigan, May–early July; Bahamian islands such as Eleuthera in winter.
animal.season: Breeds in Michigan May–Aug; winters in the Bahamas Oct–Apr

lore: It is named for Jared Potter Kirtland, the Ohio naturalist on whose farm near Cleveland the first specimen was collected in 1851; it was removed from the US endangered species list in 2019 after decades of recovery work.
funFact: Its nesting grounds were not discovered until 1903, when a nest was found in Oscoda County, Michigan.

wiki.extract: Kirtland's warbler, also known in Michigan by the common name jack pine bird, or the jack pine warbler, is a small songbird of the New World warbler family (Parulidae). Nearly extinct just years ago, populations have recovered due to the conservation efforts of the Kirtland's Warbler Conservation Team and its members. The birds require large areas, greater than 160 acres, of dense young jack pine for breeding habitat. This habitat was historically created by wildfire, but today is created through the harvest of mature jack pine, and planting of jack pine seedlings.

summary: A neat, grey-hooded sparrow whose arrival at feeders signals winter across much of the US — hence the nickname 'snowbird'. Its many regional forms evolved strikingly different colours in only the last several thousand years.
nativeRange: Breeds across Canada, Alaska and the mountains of the western and north-eastern US; winters throughout most of the US and northern Mexico
abilities: Flashes white outer tail feathers in flight, a signal used in both courtship and alarm
Has diversified into distinct forms — Slate-colored, Oregon, Pink-sided, White-winged, Gray-headed — since the last glaciation
Has colonised urban habitats; a population in San Diego evolved less white in the tail within a few decades

animal.diet: Seeds of grasses and weeds; insects in summer
animal.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forest when breeding; open woods, fields and gardens in winter
animal.behaviour: Wintering flocks keep a pecking order, and birds of different forms often mix at the same feeder.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey or black hood with a pale pink bill
White belly sharply cut off from the dark breast
Bright white outer tail feathers flashed in flight
Western 'Oregon' form has a black hood and brown back
animal.voice: A musical trill on one pitch, like a Chipping Sparrow but more ringing; calls a sharp 'tack' and twittering in flight.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-eyed Junco (south-eastern Arizona and Mexico) has yellow eyes and a rufous back. Eastern Towhee is larger with rufous sides. Chipping Sparrow's trill is drier and faster.
animal.whereToSee: Winter feeders and woodland edges across the US; breeding in the Appalachians, Rockies, Sierra Nevada and boreal Canada.
animal.season: Winter visitor (Oct–Apr) in most of the US; resident in western and Appalachian mountains

funFact: Its species name hyemalis means 'of winter'.

wiki.extract: The dark-eyed junco is a species of junco, a group of small, grayish New World sparrows. The species is common across much of temperate North America and in summer it ranges far into the Arctic. It is a variable species, much like the related fox sparrow, and its systematics are still not completely resolved.

Catesby was a pioneer in illustrating North American flora and fauna in their natural associations, providing some of the earliest scientific records of these species.

summary: A streaky brown sparrow that sings from shrubs in almost every brushy habitat in North America. It varies so much across its range that dozens of subspecies are recognised, from small pale desert birds to large dark Aleutian ones.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada south through the US to central Mexico
abilities: Each male sings a repertoire of roughly 5–13 song types, learned from neighbours
Neighbouring males 'match' each other's song types during territorial disputes
Varies dramatically in size and colour across its range in step with climate
Breeds from salt marshes and desert streams to subarctic islands

animal.diet: Insects in summer; seeds and fruit in winter
animal.habitat: Brushy fields, streamsides, marsh edges, hedgerows and gardens
animal.behaviour: In flight it pumps its long, rounded tail up and down.
fieldMarks: Brown upperparts and white underparts with heavy streaks merging into a central breast spot
Broad grey eyebrow and brown stripe behind the eye
Dark malar (moustache) stripe
Long, rounded tail pumped in flight
animal.voice: Opens with two or three clear notes, then a buzzy trill and jumble — remembered as 'Maids, maids, maids, put on your tea-kettle-ettle-ettle'; call a nasal 'chimp'.
animal.lookalikes: Savannah Sparrow has a yellowish eyebrow, finer streaks and a short notched tail. Lincoln's Sparrow is finely streaked on a buffy breast. Fox Sparrow is larger with heavier triangular spots.
animal.whereToSee: Shrubby edges and wetlands across North America; one of the first songs of late winter in the eastern US.
animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south for winter

lore: Margaret Morse Nice's years of observation of individually banded song sparrows in her Columbus, Ohio, backyard, published as Studies in the Life History of the Song Sparrow (1937), became a landmark of bird behaviour science.
funFact: The Aleutian Island birds can weigh about four times as much as the smallest desert populations.

wiki.extract: The song sparrow is a medium-sized New World sparrow. Among the native sparrows in North America, it is easily one of the most abundant, variable, and adaptable species.

summary: A big, grey-brown coastal pelican that hunts by spectacular plunge-dives, unlike most other pelicans. It recovered from near disappearance in North America after DDT was banned.
nativeRange: Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific coasts of the Americas, from the USA to northern South America, and the Caribbean
abilities: Plunge-dives from up to about 20 m, folding back its wings before impact
Air sacs under the skin cushion the impact and help it bob back to the surface
Throat pouch holds up to about 10 litres of water and fish
Glides in lines just above wave crests, riding the air cushion

animal.diet: Small schooling fish such as menhaden, anchovies and sardines
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays, estuaries and mangrove islands
animal.behaviour: Laughing gulls often perch on a pelican's head to snatch fish spilling from its pouch.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown body; the smallest and darkest pelican
White head and neck in non-breeders; chestnut hindneck in breeding adults
Yellowish crown in breeding plumage
Long bill with grey pouch (reddish in Pacific breeding birds)
Juveniles all brown with paler belly
animal.voice: Adults are almost silent; nestlings squeal and grunt.
animal.lookalikes: American white pelican is white with black flight feathers and feeds by swimming, not diving. Peruvian pelican (Peru and Chile) is larger, with a white stripe running down the neck.
animal.whereToSee: Florida Gulf Coast, Louisiana marshes, Monterey Bay and San Diego (California), Gulf of California, Caribbean islands
animal.season: Resident; Pacific birds disperse north after breeding

lore: San Francisco's Alcatraz Island takes its name from the Spanish 'alcatraces', for the pelicans that lived there. The brown pelican is the state bird of Louisiana and appears on its flag.
funFact: Removed from the US endangered species list in 2009, it is one of the clearest success stories of the DDT ban.

wiki.extract: The brown pelican is a bird of the pelican family, Pelecanidae, one of three species found in the Americas and one of two that feed by diving into water. It is found on the Atlantic Coast from New Jersey to the mouth of the Amazon River, and along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to Peru, including the Galapagos Islands. The nominate subspecies in its breeding plumage has a white head with a yellowish wash on the crown. The nape and neck are dark maroon–brown. The upper sides of the neck have white lines along the base of the gular pouch, and the lower fore neck has a pale yellowish patch. The male and female are similar, but the female is slightly smaller. The nonbreeding adult has a white head and neck. The pink skin around the eyes becomes dull and gray in the nonbreeding season. It lacks any red hue, and the pouch is strongly olivaceous ochre-tinged and the legs are olivaceous gray to blackish-gray.

The illustration is particularly interesting for its depiction of teeth within the bird's beak, a detail that highlights the blend of observation and interpretation in early colonial natural history.

summary: A golden, barred schooling fish of North American lakes, beloved for ice fishing and Friday-night fish fries around the Great Lakes. Females lay their eggs in strange, accordion-folded gelatinous ribbons that can be over 2 m long.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America: Atlantic, Arctic, Great Lakes, Hudson Bay and Mississippi basins; widely introduced in the west
abilities: Lays eggs in a single long, hollow, accordion-folded gelatinous ribbon draped over plants, unique among North American freshwater fish
Forms large schools that feed actively all winter under ice
Tolerates cool to warm water and slightly brackish estuaries
edibilityNote: Sweet, flaky white fillets; one of the best-tasting freshwater fish. Some lakes carry mercury or PCB advisories. Always cook it, because perch can carry parasites such as yellow grub, which is harmless when cooked.

animal.diet: Carnivore: zooplankton when young; insect larvae, crayfish, small fish and fish eggs as adults
animal.habitat: Clear, weedy lakes and ponds and slow rivers, usually in schools near the bottom
animal.lifespan: Usually under 10 years; maximum reported about 11
animal.size: Usually 15–25 cm; up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Schools move inshore at dawn and dusk to feed. In early spring females drape egg ribbons over weeds or branches in the shallows, and males fertilise them.
fieldMarks: Yellow to golden-green flanks with 6–8 dark, saddle-like vertical bars
Two separate dorsal fins, the first spiny
Lower fins orange to reddish, brighter in breeding males
Humped back and no canine teeth
animal.lookalikes: Walleye and sauger have large glassy eyes, canine teeth and no bold vertical bars, and walleye has a white tip on the lower tail lobe. European perch (Perca fluviatilis) is extremely similar, with a dark spot at the rear of the first dorsal fin, but does not occur naturally in North America.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Erie, Lake Michigan's Green Bay and Lake Simcoe (Ontario), especially through winter ice; Chesapeake Bay tributaries
animal.season: Resident; spawns April–May soon after ice-out; ice-fishing season December–March

lore: Yellow perch fish fries are a Great Lakes institution, and the Lake Erie commercial perch catch has supported Ohio and Ontario fishing towns since the 19th century. Ojibwe and other Great Lakes peoples have long speared and netted perch, including through winter ice.
funFact: A single female can lay over 40,000 eggs in one gelatinous ribbon, and the jelly seems to protect the eggs from predators.

wiki.extract: The yellow perch, commonly referred to as perch, striped perch, American perch or preacher is a freshwater ray-finned fish from the perch family Percidae, native to much of central North America, particularly the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence River basin and the Upper Mississippi River catchment. It was first described in 1814 by Samuel Latham Mitchill from New York, and is closely related and morphologically similar to the European perch, and is sometimes considered a subspecies of its European counterpart.

summary: A soft, velvety creature with stubby legs that hunts by squirting nets of sticky slime. It belongs to the Onychophora, an ancient group related to arthropods whose body plan resembles fossils from the Cambrian seas more than 500 million years ago.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia, notably the cool forests of south-eastern New South Wales (e.g. Tallaganda State Forest)
abilities: Squirts sticky, protein-based slime from glands beside the mouth, entangling prey several centimetres away
Eats its own slime after a hunt to recycle the protein
Lives in social groups led by a dominant female that feeds first
Gives birth to live young

animal.diet: Crickets, spiders, woodlice and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Inside moist rotting logs in cool forest
animal.behaviour: Group members cooperate to subdue large prey; individuals recognise and are aggressive towards velvet worms from other groups.
fieldMarks: Soft, cylindrical body covered in tiny velvety papillae
Fifteen pairs of stubby, unjointed legs ending in small claws
One pair of ringed antennae
Dark blue-grey to brown with fine patterning
animal.lookalikes: Can be mistaken for a caterpillar or slug, but caterpillars have jointed true legs and slugs have none. Many other Australian velvet worm species differ in leg number, colour and range.
animal.whereToSee: Rotting logs in wet forest of south-eastern NSW; rarely seen in the open except on damp nights.
animal.season: Most active in cool, damp weather

lore: The first velvet worm known to science was described from St Vincent in 1826 by Lansdown Guilding, who thought it was a kind of slug.
funFact: Velvet worm slime turns from liquid into strong fibres as it is stretched, and can be dissolved and re-spun, which has inspired research into recyclable materials.

wiki.extract: Euperipatoides rowelli is an ovoviviparous species of velvet worm of the Peripatopsidae family. It is found in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory.

summary: A large, oily-black diving bird found on coasts and inland waters across much of the world. It pursues fish underwater using its feet and has been trained by fishermen in China for centuries.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia, Africa, Australasia and the North Atlantic coast of North America
abilities: Chases fish underwater, propelled by large webbed feet
Partly wettable plumage reduces buoyancy for diving
Dries wings by spreading them in a heraldic pose
Can dive to more than 30 m

animal.diet: Fish
animal.habitat: Coasts, estuaries, lakes and rivers
animal.lifespan: Usually around 11 years, recorded to over 20
animal.behaviour: Groups sometimes hunt together, driving fish into shallows.
fieldMarks: Black with bronze or blue sheen
White cheek and chin patch
White thigh patches in breeding season
Heavy hooked bill with bare yellow skin at base
Swims low in the water with head tilted up
animal.voice: Generally silent away from colonies; deep guttural croaks at nests.
animal.lookalikes: European shag is smaller and slimmer, with a thinner bill, greenish gloss and in spring a tufted crest; it lacks the white cheek patch. Double-crested cormorant (North America) has an orange throat pouch without white surround.
animal.whereToSee: Coastal and inland waters of Europe and Asia; Lake Naivasha (Kenya), the Li River at Guilin (China), Rutland Water (UK)
animal.season: Resident or partial migrant

lore: In China, fishermen have trained great cormorants to fish for centuries, putting a snare around the bird's neck so that it cannot swallow large fish. Milton's Paradise Lost has Satan perch on the Tree of Life 'like a cormorant'.
funFact: The name cormorant comes from the Latin 'corvus marinus', sea-raven.

wiki.extract: The great cormorant, also known as just cormorant in Britain, as black shag or kawau in New Zealand, formerly also known as the great black cormorant across the Northern Hemisphere, the black cormorant in Australia, and the large cormorant in India, is a widespread member of the cormorant family of seabirds. It breeds in much of the Old World, Australasia, and the Atlantic coast of North America.

otherNames: Kǎolā 考拉 / Shùdàixióng 树袋熊 (Chinese)
summary: A tree-dwelling marsupial that lives almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in energy and toxic to most animals. Koalas sleep or rest for up to 20 hours a day to save energy.
nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern Australia (Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia)
abilities: Detoxifies eucalyptus oils with liver enzymes and gut microbes
Ferments leaves in a caecum up to ~2 m long, the longest relative to body size of any mammal
Males bellow at a very low pitch using a pair of extra vocal folds above the larynx
Has fingerprints that closely resemble human ones

animal.diet: Eucalyptus leaves, from a few dozen preferred species; little need to drink
animal.habitat: Eucalyptus forests and woodlands
animal.behaviour: Mothers feed joeys a special soft dropping called 'pap', which passes on the gut microbes needed to digest eucalyptus.
fieldMarks: Stocky grey marsupial with a big black nose
Large furry ears
No visible tail
Sits in eucalyptus forks, often asleep
animal.voice: Males give loud, deep snoring bellows, mostly in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Great Otway National Park (Kennett River) and Phillip Island's Koala Conservation Reserve (Victoria); Magnetic Island (Queensland)
animal.season: Resident; bellowing Sep–Jan

lore: The name is usually traced to Dharug gula. Millions of koalas were killed for fur in the early 20th century; public outrage at Queensland's 1927 open season led the Commonwealth to stop issuing export permits for koala skins, effectively ending the trade.
funFact: The koala is not a bear; its closest living relatives are wombats.

wiki.extract: The koala, sometimes inaccurately called the koala bear, is an arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia. It is the only extant representative of the family Phascolarctidae. Its closest living relatives are the wombats. The koala is found in coastal areas of the continent's eastern and southern regions, inhabiting Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, and South Australia. It is easily recognisable by its stout, tailless body and large head with round, fluffy ears and large, dark nose. The koala has a body length of 60–85 cm (24–33 in) and weighs 4–15 kg (8.8–33.1 lb). Its fur colour ranges from silver grey to chocolate brown. Koalas from the northern populations are typically smaller and lighter in colour than their counterparts further south. These populations are possibly separate subspecies, but not all researchers accept this.

summary: A plump, grey and buff partridge of rocky hillsides, with a black necklace framing a creamy throat and bold black bars on its flanks. It is the national bird of Pakistan and a celebrated figure of Urdu and Punjabi poetry.
nativeRange: SE Europe and Turkey through the Middle East, Central Asia, Afghanistan, Pakistan and the western Himalaya to China and Mongolia; introduced in western North America, Hawaii and New Zealand
abilities: Runs uphill to escape, using wing-flapping to boost traction on steep slopes
Survives arid mountains by obtaining much of its water from green plants and insects
Introduced populations thrive in the dry ranges of the American West

animal.diet: Seeds, grasses, leaves, berries and insects
animal.habitat: Rocky, sparsely vegetated hills and mountain slopes, from near sea level to above 4,000 m
animal.behaviour: Coveys run up slopes rather than fly, then burst into the air and glide downhill on bowed wings; males call loudly from rocks.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown back and blue-grey breast
Creamy white throat and face bordered by a black band through the eye and around the throat
Bold black-and-chestnut bars on pale flanks
Red bill, red legs and red eye-ring
animal.voice: A loud, accelerating 'chuck-chuck-chukar-chukar', from which its name derives
animal.lookalikes: Rock partridge (SE Europe) has a white throat without buff tones; See-see partridge (Pakistan's low hills) is much smaller and sandy with no black necklace; Red-legged partridge (W Europe) has a streaked black necklace.
animal.whereToSee: Salt Range, Margalla Hills, Balochistan uplands and Gilgit-Baltistan in Pakistan; Ladakh and Spiti in India
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Urdu, Punjabi and Hindi poetry the chakor is said to gaze at the moon all night and drink its light, a symbol of the lover's devoted longing. It is Pakistan's national bird, and chukars are traditionally kept and fought in the northwest.
funFact: Introduced to Nevada and other western US states for hunting, the chukar now thrives in rugged country where few native gamebirds live.

wiki.extract: The chukar partridge, or simply chukar, is a Palearctic upland gamebird in the pheasant family Phasianidae. It has been considered to form a superspecies complex along with the rock partridge, Philby's partridge and Przevalski's partridge and treated in the past as conspecific particularly with the first. This partridge has well-marked black and white bars on the flanks and a black band running from the forehead across the eye down the head to form a necklace that encloses a white throat. Native to Asia, the species has been introduced into many other places and feral populations have established themselves in parts of North America, Malta and New Zealand. This bird can be found in parts of Middle East and temperate Asia.

otherNames: Dà yǎn bān zhì 大眼斑雉 (Chinese)
summary: A huge, secretive pheasant of Sundaic rainforest whose male has enormous wing feathers covered with rows of shaded eyespots, which he fans into a great circular screen during display. Charles Darwin wrote at length about the eyespots as evidence for sexual selection.
nativeRange: Malay Peninsula (southern Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia), Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Male clears a 'dancing ground' on the forest floor of leaves and debris
Fans its huge secondary feathers into an upright disc displaying hundreds of eyespots
Eyespots are shaded so they appear three-dimensional, like balls in sockets

animal.diet: Fallen fruit, seeds, leaves, ants and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforest
animal.size: Males up to about 1.6–2 m including the tail; females about 75 cm
animal.behaviour: Males call from their dancing grounds and display there to visiting females; the species is far more often heard than seen.
fieldMarks: Very large pheasant with a small bare blue head
Male: extremely long central tail feathers and broad secondaries with rows of eyespots
Overall brown, finely patterned plumage
Female much smaller with a short tail
animal.voice: Loud, far-carrying 'kwow-wow' calls from males, and a long series of 'wow' notes that accelerate; one of the classic sounds of Malaysian forests
animal.lookalikes: Crested argus (Vietnam, Laos, Malaysia's highlands) has a crest and different eyespot pattern; peacock-pheasants are much smaller with metallic eyespots.
animal.whereToSee: Taman Negara, Malaysia; Danum Valley, Sabah; Khao Sok and Hala-Bala in Thailand
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Named after Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth. In 'The Descent of Man' (1871), Darwin used the gradation of the great argus's eyespots to argue how sexual selection could build complex ornaments step by step.
funFact: The male's display is so rarely witnessed in the wild that much of what is known comes from captive birds and camera traps.

wiki.extract: The great argus or greater argus is a large species of pheasant native to the jungles of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula in southeast Asia. It is known for its impressive plumage and courtship behavior. It is not to be confused with the two species of closely related crested argus, genus Rheinardia.

summary: A pale, long-tailed pheasant of steep grassy Himalayan slopes, buff-grey and heavily barred, with a long backward-pointing crest. Its dependence on scrubby grassland maintained by grazing and fire makes it unusual among Himalayan pheasants.
nativeRange: Western and central Himalaya from northern Pakistan (now very rare) through Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand to central Nepal
abilities: Lives on precipitous grass and scrub slopes most pheasants avoid
Digs for roots and tubers with its bill
Pairs and families call in loud chorus at dawn and dusk

animal.diet: Roots, tubers, seeds, grubs and insects
animal.habitat: Steep grassy slopes with scattered scrub and trees, roughly 1,200–3,000 m
animal.size: Males about 90–118 cm including the long tail
animal.behaviour: Coveys feed quietly in dense grass and are very hard to see; they call loudly at dawn and dusk and fly off downhill when disturbed.
fieldMarks: Pale buff and grey body barred and spotted with black
Very long, broadly barred, pointed tail
Long, wispy crest swept back from the crown
Bare red skin around the eye
animal.voice: A loud, ringing 'chir-a-pir, chir-a-pir, chir chir chirwa', given in duet or chorus at dawn and dusk
animal.lookalikes: Kalij pheasant is dark blue-black with a white rump; Koklass is greyer with a dark head and long ear-tufts; Cheer's pale barred plumage and very long tail are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Majathal Sanctuary and Chail in Himachal Pradesh; Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve in Nepal
animal.season: Resident; most vocal in spring

lore: The scientific name honours Nathaniel Wallich, the Danish botanist who directed the Calcutta Botanic Garden in the early 19th century.
funFact: Unlike most pheasants, it seems to depend on grassland kept open by village grazing, grass-cutting and burning, so changes in traditional land use can harm it.

wiki.extract: The cheer pheasant, also known as Wallich's pheasant and chir pheasant, is a vulnerable species of the pheasant family, Phasianidae. It is the only member in the genus Catreus. The scientific name commemorates Danish botanist Nathaniel Wallich.

plates.desc: A scientific plate (TAB. I) featuring eight numbered illustrations of birds, including various peacocks, turkeys, and a pheasant.
plates.long: This plate from Ulisse Aldrovandi's 'Ornithologiae' (1610) presents a systematic visual catalog of birds, including the Indian peacock and the North American turkey. The detailed engravings reflect the era's growing commitment to empirical natural history and the documentation of exotic species brought to Europe.

On the right is the crane, symbolizing the first rank, and on the left is the golden pheasant, representing the second rank, both shown in their respective naturalistic settings of clouds and foliage.

plates.author: 王圻, 王思義
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a guqin finger technique, comparing a hand gesture to a pheasant on a tree branch.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui illustrates a specific finger technique for the guqin, a traditional Chinese zither. The hand gesture is poetically likened to a 'wild pheasant climbing a tree,' demonstrating the traditional Chinese method of using natural metaphors to teach complex physical skills.

plates.title: Sancai Tuhui (Vol. 86)

plates.desc: A woodcut illustration from the Sancai Tuhui depicting a series of animals (a goat, a goose, and a pheasant) paired with bundles of silk, representing traditional Chinese taxonomic and material classifications.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 'Sancai Tuhui' illustrates the systematic categorization of animals alongside their associated material products, such as silk. It reflects the Ming Dynasty's intellectual pursuit of organizing the natural and human-made world into a comprehensive, visual encyclopedia.

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut depicts the 'Jacupema', a bird native to Brazil, as described by Georg Marcgraf in his pioneering study of South American nature. It represents a significant early effort to scientifically document and categorize the diverse fauna of the New World for a European audience.

plates.desc: A page from a Tudor pattern book featuring a large black hare, a beaver with a fish-like tail, a pheasant, and two smaller rabbits.
plates.long: This page from the Tudor Pattern Book (c. 1525) displays a collection of animal studies used by artists as templates for decorative arts. It features a large black 'Coney' (hare) and a 'Castor' (beaver), the latter depicted with the traditional medieval attribute of a scaly, fish-like tail. These illustrations reflect the transition between medieval bestiary traditions and the emerging Renaissance

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a pheasant, characterized by its exceptionally long and intricately patterned tail feathers. It is an illustration from Conrad Gesner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium', a foundational text in modern zoology that aimed to categorize all known animals with scientific precision during the 16th century.

The illustration serves Kircher's argument that such species were post-diluvian variations resulting from climate and cross-breeding rather than original passengers on the Ark. This work reflects the 17th-century transition from symbolic bestiaries

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'buzi' or rank patch for a Ming dynasty official, specifically featuring the silver pheasant (lianque). Such patches were sewn onto the front and back of official robes to denote the wearer's civil rank, with the silver pheasant typically representing the fifth rank.

otherNames: Hóng fù jǐnjī 红腹锦鸡 (Chinese)
summary: One of the most brilliantly coloured birds in the world: the male has a golden crest, a scarlet body, a cape of orange feathers barred with black and a very long, mottled tail. Despite its colours it is a shy bird of dense mountain thickets in central China.
nativeRange: Mountains of central and western China (Gansu, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Hubei, Guizhou and neighbouring provinces); feral populations in Britain
abilities: Male spreads his golden-and-black cape into a fan around the face during courtship
Lives in dense bamboo and scrub where its colours are surprisingly hard to see
Roosts in trees at night

animal.diet: Seeds, leaves, shoots, berries and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense young forest, bamboo and scrub on mountainsides
animal.size: Males about 90–105 cm including the long tail; females 60–80 cm
animal.behaviour: Very secretive in the wild; males display to females by fanning the cape sideways and showing it from different angles.
fieldMarks: Male: golden-yellow crest and rump, scarlet underparts
Male: orange cape barred with black, green upper back
Very long, cinnamon tail with dark spots
Female: barred buff-brown with a long tail
animal.voice: A harsh, metallic 'cha-chak' call in spring
animal.lookalikes: Lady Amherst's pheasant male is white, black and green with a white cape barred black; hybrids between the two are common in captivity.
animal.whereToSee: Foping and Changqing reserves in the Qinling Mountains, Shaanxi; Wolong in Sichuan
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Ming and Qing China, the golden pheasant was embroidered on the 'mandarin square' badges of second-rank civil officials. It is widely kept in aviaries and has been in European collections since at least the 18th century.
funFact: Linnaeus described it in 1758 in the first edition of Systema Naturae where modern zoological names begin.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a golden pheasant perched on a rock.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a golden pheasant (Jinji), a bird prized for its vibrant plumage, perched atop a scholar's rock. It is an illustration from the 'Sancai Tuhui,' a comprehensive Ming Dynasty encyclopedia, showcasing the era's interest in documenting the natural world through both text and image.

summary: A wild forest pheasant of South and Southeast Asia and the ancestor of the domestic chicken. With over 20 billion alive at any time, chickens are the most numerous bird on Earth.
nativeRange: Wild form from northern India to southern China and Indonesia; domestic chickens worldwide
abilities: Produces over a dozen distinct alarm and food calls, some referential (aerial vs ground predator)
Domestic hens can lay over 300 eggs a year
Roosters perform 'tidbitting', calling hens to food
Can run, roost in trees, and make short bursts of flight

animal.diet: Seeds, insects, fallen fruit and small animals
animal.habitat: Forest edges, scrub and clearings
animal.behaviour: A rooster gives different alarm calls for hawks overhead and for ground predators, and hens respond appropriately.
fieldMarks: Male: orange-gold hackles, red comb and wattles, long dark green arching tail
Female brown with a small comb
Wild males have slate-grey legs
Wild males moult into a dull eclipse plumage after breeding
animal.voice: Crow is like a domestic rooster's but shorter, ending abruptly
animal.lookalikes: Feral and domestic chickens interbreed with it; mixed birds often have yellow or pale legs and lack the eclipse moult. Grey junglefowl of peninsular India has grey, spotted hackles.
animal.whereToSee: Jim Corbett National Park (India), Khao Yai and Kaeng Krachan (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Domesticated in Southeast Asia around 3,500 years ago, chickens were first kept for cockfighting and ritual before food. Roman generals consulted sacred chickens before battle, and Socrates' last words asked that a rooster be offered to Asclepius.
funFact: Most of the world's influenza vaccines are still grown in fertilised chicken eggs.

wiki.extract: The red junglefowl, also known as the Indian red junglefowl, is a species of tropical, galliform bird in the phasianid family, found across much of Southeast Asia and parts of South Asia.

summary: Sri Lanka's national bird, a wild relative of the chicken whose rooster glows orange-red and gold with a red comb marked by a yellow centre. It is endemic to the island and common in its national parks.
nativeRange: Endemic to Sri Lanka
abilities: Hybridises occasionally with domestic chickens
Lives in both the wet and dry zones of Sri Lanka, from sea level to the hills
Forages by scratching leaf litter for seeds and insects

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, berries, insects and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Forest, scrub jungle and plantations
animal.size: Males about 66–73 cm; females about 35 cm
animal.behaviour: Roosters crow at dawn and dusk from perches; birds often feed in the open along park roads in the early morning.
fieldMarks: Male: orange-red body with golden neck hackles
Male: red comb with a central yellow patch; red wattles
Male: dark purple-black wings and arching tail
Female: mottled brown with patterned wings
animal.voice: A distinctive crow 'chuck-chraw-choyik', quite unlike the domestic cockerel's crow
animal.lookalikes: Red junglefowl and domestic chickens have an all-red comb and a different crow; feral chickens near villages can cause confusion.
animal.whereToSee: Sinharaja, Yala, Udawalawe and Horton Plains national parks
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is the national bird of Sri Lanka and appears on Sri Lankan postage stamps.
funFact: It is one of four wild Gallus species; the domestic chicken descends mainly from the Red junglefowl, but genes from the Grey and Sri Lanka junglefowl have been found in some domestic breeds.

wiki.extract: The Sri Lankan junglefowl, also known as the Ceylon junglefowl or Lafayette's junglefowl, is a member of the Galliformes bird order. It is a common endemic bird in Sri Lanka, where it is the national bird. It is closely related to the red junglefowl, the wild junglefowl from which the chicken was domesticated. However, it is even more closely related to the gray junglefowl. Sri Lankan junglefowl and red junglefowl diverged about 2.8 million years ago, whereas time of divergence between the Sri Lankan junglefowl and grey junglefowl was 1.8 million years ago.

otherNames: Zōng wěi hóng zhì 棕尾虹雉 (Chinese)
summary: A pheasant of high Himalayan meadows and forests whose male shimmers in metallic green, copper, purple and blue, crowned by a wiry crest of spatulate plumes. It is the national bird of Nepal.
nativeRange: Himalaya from eastern Afghanistan and northern Pakistan through India, Nepal and Bhutan to southern Tibet and NE India
abilities: Digs vigorously with its strong curved bill for roots, tubers and insect larvae, even through snow
Lives between about 2,100 and 4,500 m, moving downslope in winter
Male's plumage is iridescent structural colour that shifts with the angle of light

animal.diet: Tubers, roots, shoots, seeds, berries and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Oak, rhododendron and conifer forest with open grassy slopes and alpine meadows
animal.size: About 63–72 cm long; males up to about 2.4 kg
animal.behaviour: Feeds in loose groups on open slopes at dawn and dusk; when flushed it hurtles downhill with a ringing whistle.
fieldMarks: Male: iridescent green head, crest of spatula-tipped plumes, copper nape, purple-blue back
Male: conspicuous white rump and cinnamon-rufous tail in flight
Female: mottled brown with a white throat, bare blue skin around the eye and white-tipped tail
Heavy, curved bill used for digging
animal.voice: Loud, plaintive whistles 'kur-leiu' or 'kleeh-wick', often heard at dawn and when flushed
animal.lookalikes: Sclater's monal (eastern Himalaya) has a curly crest and white-tipped tail; Chinese monal (central China, outside its range) has a drooping purple crest rather than spatulate plumes; Koklass pheasant is streaked grey with a long dark ear-tuft.
animal.whereToSee: Kaghan and Neelum valleys and Ayubia in Pakistan; Tungnath-Chopta and Kedarnath in Uttarakhand; Sagarmatha and Langtang national parks in Nepal
animal.season: Resident; descends to lower forests in winter, easiest to see in spring and autumn

lore: As the Danphe it is Nepal's national bird and appears on Nepalese stamps; it is also the state bird of Uttarakhand. Men in Himachal Pradesh once wore the male's crest on their caps, a practice that drove hunting until legal protection.
funFact: The old English name 'Impeyan pheasant' and the species epithet honour Lady Mary Impey, who kept a menagerie in 18th-century Calcutta.

wiki.extract:
The Himalayan monal, also called Impeyan monal, is a landfowl native to Himalayan forests and shrublands at elevations of 2,100–4,500 m (6,900–14,800 ft). It is part of the family Phasianidae and is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
It is the national bird of Nepal, where it is known as the danphe or danfe, and state bird of Uttarakhand, India, where it is known as a monal.
The scientific name commemorates Lady Mary Impey, the wife of the British chief justice of Bengal, Sir Elijah Impey.

summary: A glossy blue-black grouse with a lyre-shaped tail, white undertail puff and red eyebrows. Males gather at dawn leks to bubble and hiss in one of Europe's great wildlife spectacles.
nativeRange: Britain, Scandinavia, the Alps, eastern Europe, Russia and Siberia to northern Mongolia and northeastern China
abilities: Males display communally at leks, with dominant central males getting most matings
Burrows into snow to roost during cold nights
Feeds on birch buds and catkins through hard winters
Chicks depend heavily on insects, especially sawfly larvae

animal.diet: Birch buds and catkins, heather, bilberry, conifer needles; insects for chicks
animal.habitat: Moorland edge, open woodland, forest clearings and bogs
animal.size: Males 49–58 cm, ~1.2 kg; females 40–45 cm, ~0.9 kg
animal.behaviour: At the lek, males crouch with fanned white undertail and spread wings, rushing at rivals and jumping into the air.
fieldMarks: Male glossy blue-black with a lyre-shaped forked tail
White wing bar and white undertail fluffed in display
Red wattles above the eyes
Female ('greyhen') grey-brown, barred, with a slightly forked tail and thin white wing bar
animal.voice: Male makes a dove-like bubbling 'rookooing' and an explosive sneezing 'tchu-shweee'.
animal.lookalikes: Capercaillie is much larger with a rounded tail. Female resembles female red grouse but is larger and greyer with a forked tail. Caucasian grouse (Caucasus) has a longer, more deeply forked tail without white undertail.
animal.whereToSee: Leks in Scottish Highland glens and the Pennines, Finnish and Swedish bogs, the Alps above the treeline.
animal.season: Resident; leks Mar–May at dawn

lore: The curved tail feather of the black cock (Spielhahnfeder) is the traditional hat ornament of Alpine hunters in Bavaria and Tyrol.
funFact: Black grouse occasionally hybridise with capercaillie, producing a bird that German hunters call the 'Rackelhahn'.

wiki.extract: The black grouse, also known as northern black grouse, Eurasian black grouse, blackgame or blackcock, is a large bird in the grouse tribe. It is a sedentary species, spanning across the Palearctic in moorland and steppe habitat when breeding, often near wooded areas. They will spend the winter perched in dense forests, feeding almost exclusively on the needles of conifers. The black grouse is one of two species of grouse in the genus Lyrurus, the other being the lesser-known Caucasian grouse.

summary: North America's largest gamebird and the wild ancestor of the domestic turkey, first domesticated in Mesoamerica over 2,000 years ago. Hunted to near-extinction by the early 1900s, it now numbers in the millions.
nativeRange: Much of the United States, southern Canada and northern Mexico; introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii and New Zealand
abilities: Domesticated independently in Mesoamerica and by Ancestral Puebloans in the American Southwest
Can burst into flight and roosts high in trees at night
Males gobble to attract females; calls carry over a kilometre
Bare head and neck change colour from red to white and blue with excitement

animal.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, berries, insects and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Mixed forest with clearings, oak woods, farm edges, and increasingly suburbs
animal.lifespan: Usually 3–5 years in the wild; records over 13
animal.size: Males 100–125 cm and 5–11 kg; females much smaller
animal.behaviour: Males strut in spring with tails fanned, wings dragged and feathers puffed.
fieldMarks: Very large, dark, iridescent bronze-green plumage
Bare blue-and-red head with a fleshy snood over the bill and wattles at the throat
Males carry a hair-like 'beard' on the breast and leg spurs
Tail tipped rusty or buff (varies by subspecies), fanned in display
animal.voice: Males' rolling gobble; also yelps, clucks, purrs and a sharp 'putt' alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Ocellated Turkey (Yucatán) has a blue head with orange knobs and eyespots on the tail. Domestic turkeys are usually white or patchy and heavier.
animal.whereToSee: Open woods and field edges across the eastern US; often seen in suburbs and along rural roads.
animal.season: Resident year-round; gobbling peaks Mar–May

lore: In a 1784 letter to his daughter, Benjamin Franklin called the Bald Eagle 'a Bird of bad moral Character' and the turkey 'a much more respectable Bird'; for the Aztecs turkeys were important ritual and food animals, associated with the god Tezcatlipoca in the form Chalchiuhtotolin.
funFact: Europeans called it 'turkey' because they confused it with guineafowl imported through Turkish lands.

wiki.extract: The wild turkey is an upland game bird native to North America, one of two extant species of turkey and the heaviest member of the order Galliformes. It is the ancestor to the domestic turkey, which was originally derived from a southern Mexican subspecies of wild turkey.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a turkey from Conrad Gessner's encyclopedic 'Historiae Animalium'. This illustration represents one of the earliest European attempts to scientifically document the appearance of the turkey, a bird recently introduced from the Americas.

summary: A finely barred grey-brown partridge of dry plains whose loud, rhythmic calls ring across the farmlands of Pakistan and India at dawn. It is the 'teetar' of village life, long kept as a caged songbird and fighting bird in Punjab.
nativeRange: SE Iran and the Persian Gulf through Pakistan, India and Nepal's terai to Sri Lanka; introduced to the Andaman Islands, Hawaii and elsewhere
abilities: Thrives in arid scrub and cultivated plains with little cover
Males call in duet with neighbours to proclaim territory
Prefers running to flight, escaping through crop fields

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, shoots and insects such as termites and beetles
animal.habitat: Open dry plains, thorn scrub, farmland edges and semi-desert
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small coveys forage on the ground in early morning and late afternoon and roost in thorny trees and bushes at night.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown upperparts finely barred with buff and chestnut
Pale, densely cross-barred underparts
Rufous-buff throat bordered by a thin dark line
Chestnut outer tail feathers visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, ringing, repeated 'ka-tee-tar, ka-tee-tar' or 'pateela-pateela', often accelerating; one of the defining dawn sounds of the Indus plains
animal.lookalikes: Black francolin male is black with a white cheek and chestnut collar; females of Black francolin have a chestnut patch on the hindneck; Painted francolin (central India) is spotted white on black.
animal.whereToSee: Common in dry farmland and scrub across Punjab and Sindh, Thar Desert fringes and peninsular India
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The calling teetar in a cane cage is a traditional sight in rural Punjab, and sayings about the bird recur in Punjabi and Urdu folk speech; teetar fighting was a widespread village pastime.
funFact: The species name pondicerianus refers to Pondicherry, the French colony in southern India from which early specimens reached Europe.

wiki.extract: The grey francolin is a species of francolin found in the plains and drier parts of the Indian subcontinent and Iran. This species was formerly also called the grey partridge, not to be confused with the European grey partridge. They are mainly ground-living birds and are found in open cultivated lands as well as scrub forest and their local name of teetar is based on their calls, a loud and repeated Ka-tee-tar...tee-tar, which is produced by one or more birds. The term teetar can also refer to other partridges and quails. During the breeding season, calling males attract challengers, and decoys were used to trap these birds especially for fighting.

plates.long: A woodcut illustration of a francolin (鷓鴣) from the 'Sancai Tuhui', a comprehensive Chinese encyclopedia published in 1609. The bird is shown in a naturalistic pose atop a blossoming branch, reflecting the era's interest in documenting the natural world through both text and image.

summary: A large pheasant of South Asia whose males raise and shiver a train of about 200 eye-spotted feathers. It is the national bird of India and has been carried as a royal ornament across the world for three thousand years.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Pakistan and Bangladesh; introduced widely
abilities: Train of elongated upper-tail coverts with iridescent structural-colour eyespots
Males rattle the train to produce low-frequency infrasound during displays
Kills and eats young cobras and other snakes
Loud alarm calls warn other animals of tigers and leopards

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, insects, small reptiles and snakes
animal.habitat: Forest edges, farmland and villages near water
animal.size: Males up to ~2.25 m including train; females ~1 m
animal.behaviour: Peahens choose mates partly on the vigour of the train-rattling display.
fieldMarks: Male: iridescent blue neck and breast, long green train with eyespots
Fan-shaped crest of spatula-tipped feathers
Female brown with a green neck and white belly
Large, often seen on the ground
animal.voice: A loud, wailing 'may-awe', often at dusk and before rain
animal.lookalikes: Green peafowl (Southeast Asia) has a green, scaly neck and a tufted upright crest.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore and Keoladeo (Bharatpur), India; Yala, Sri Lanka
animal.season: Resident; males display most during the pre-monsoon and monsoon breeding season and shed the train afterwards

lore: The peacock is Kartikeya's mount in Hindu tradition and Melek Taus, the Peacock Angel, in Yazidi faith; Mughal emperors sat on the Peacock Throne. Greeks said Hera set the hundred eyes of Argus on its tail.
funFact: Darwin wrote that 'the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail, whenever I gaze at it, makes me sick', because natural selection alone could not explain it.

wiki.extract: The Indian peafowl, also known as the common peafowl, or blue peafowl, is a species of peafowl native to the Indian subcontinent. While it originated in the Indian subcontinent, it has since been introduced to many other parts of the world. Male peafowl are referred to as peacocks, and female peafowl are referred to as peahens, although both sexes are often referred to colloquially as a "peacock".

plates.long: This hand-colored woodcut from the 1491 edition of Hortus Sanitatis depicts a bird-like creature and a fish swimming in water, illustrating the era's fascination with aquatic hybrids. As one of the earliest printed encyclopedias of natural history, Jacob Meydenbach's work is significant for its use of visual aids to categorize the natural and mythical worlds. The plate meticulously captures the intricate patterns of the male's 'eyed' tail feathers both in full display and at rest, serving as a primary scientific record of the era.
