summary: A tall, upright peafowl clad in shimmering green and bronze scales with a narrow tuft-like crest, the Southeast Asian counterpart of the Indian peafowl. Both sexes are brightly coloured, and the male carries a glittering train of eyespot feathers.
nativeRange: Formerly NE India and Bangladesh to Southeast Asia and Java; now in fragmented populations in Yunnan (China), Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and Java
abilities: Males raise a train of over 100 eyespotted feathers in display
Roosts high in trees and calls loudly at dawn and dusk
Can fly strongly despite its size

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit, insects, small reptiles and frogs
animal.habitat: Open forest, riverbanks and forest edges with grassy clearings
animal.size: Males about 1.8–3 m including the train; females about 1–1.1 m
animal.behaviour: Feeds in clearings and on riverbanks in early morning and evening, retreating to dense cover; males display at traditional sites.
fieldMarks: Upright, slim crest of tufts (not fan-shaped as in Indian peafowl)
Green and bronze scaly neck and breast (not blue)
Bare yellow-and-blue facial skin
Females almost as colourful as males, but without the train
animal.voice: Loud, honking 'ki-wao' or 'aow-aaw', less shrill than the Indian peafowl
animal.lookalikes: Indian peafowl male has a blue neck and fan-shaped crest, and the female is drab brown; hybrids ('Spalding' peafowl) occur in captivity.
animal.whereToSee: Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary (Thailand), Baluran National Park (Java), Cat Tien (Vietnam), and parts of Yunnan
animal.season: Resident year-round; breeding display in the dry season

lore: The peacock was the emblem of the Burmese Konbaung kings and remains a national symbol of Myanmar.
funFact: A 2016 survey estimated fewer than 500 wild green peafowl left in China, all in Yunnan.

wiki.extract: The green peafowl is a peafowl species native to the tropical forests of Southeast Asia and Southern China. It is the national bird of Myanmar. Formerly common throughout Southeast Asia, only a few isolated populations survive in Cambodia and adjacent areas of Vietnam. It has been listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2009. This is primarily due to widespread deforestation, agriculture and loss of suitable habitat, severely fragmenting populations and contributing to an overall decline in numbers. The green peafowl is in demand for private and home aviculture and threatened by the pet trade, feather collectors and hunters for meat and targeted.

summary: The world's largest grouse, a turkey-sized black cock of old pine forests that fans its tail and clicks, pops and gurgles at dawn displays. It survives a whole winter largely on pine needles.
nativeRange: Boreal and mountain conifer forests from Scotland, Scandinavia, the Alps, Pyrenees and Cantabrians across Russia to central Siberia
abilities: Survives winter mainly on pine needles, digested with the help of long caeca
Males are roughly twice the size of females
Displaying males are so absorbed in their song that they briefly cannot hear, giving the Russian name 'glukhar' (deaf one)
Aggressive males in display sometimes attack people and vehicles

animal.diet: Pine needles in winter; bilberry leaves and berries, buds, shoots, seeds; insects for chicks
animal.habitat: Old, open conifer forests with a rich bilberry understorey
animal.size: Males 74–90 cm, around 4 kg; females 54–63 cm, around 1.8 kg
animal.behaviour: Males gather at traditional leks at dawn in spring, strutting with fanned tails and raised beards.
fieldMarks: Male huge and dark slate-grey with a glossy green breast
Fanned, rounded black tail and shaggy throat 'beard'
Ivory bill and red wattle above the eye
Female much smaller, barred brown with a rufous breast patch
animal.voice: Male display song is a sequence of accelerating clicks ending in a 'pop' like a cork and a wheezing, scraping phrase.
animal.lookalikes: Black grouse is smaller with a lyre-shaped tail and white undertail. Female capercaillie can be confused with female black grouse but is larger with a plain orange-rufous breast and rounded tail.
animal.whereToSee: Abernethy Forest and Strathspey (Scotland), Finnish and Swedish taiga, the Bavarian Forest, the Alps and the Pyrenees; leks must be watched only on guided visits.
animal.season: Resident; leks Apr–May

lore: Hunted out of Scotland by about 1785, it was reintroduced from Sweden to Taymouth Castle in Perthshire in 1837; the Gaelic name means 'horse of the woods'.
funFact: The Scottish population has fallen to a few hundred birds and is now largely confined to Strathspey.

wiki.extract: The western capercaillie, also known as the Eurasian capercaillie, wood grouse, heather cock, cock-of-the-woods, or simply capercaillie, is a heavy member of the grouse tribe and the largest of all extant grouse species. Found across Europe and the Palearctic, this primarily-ground-dwelling forest grouse is renowned for its courtship display. The bird shows extreme sexual dimorphism, with males nearly twice the size of females. The global population is listed as "least concern" under the IUCN, although the populations of central Europe are declining and fragmented, or possibly extirpated.

summary: Perhaps the rarest pheasant of the western Himalaya, the male is black and crimson, spangled with white spots, and in display inflates a vivid blue-and-pink throat lappet and two fleshy blue horns. It lives in a narrow belt of temperate forest in Pakistan and India.
nativeRange: Western Himalaya: Kohistan and Kashmir in northern Pakistan, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and western Uttarakhand in India
abilities: Male inflates a bib-like lappet of bare skin and erects fleshy 'horns' during courtship display
Survives on leaves, buds and seeds through snowy Himalayan winters
Unusually for a pheasant, often feeds and roosts in trees

animal.diet: Leaves, shoots, buds, seeds, acorns and some invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense temperate and sub-alpine forest of oak, fir and rhododendron with thick undergrowth, about 1,750–3,600 m
animal.size: Males about 55–72 cm long (published figures vary)
animal.behaviour: Extremely shy and seldom seen; males call from steep, forested slopes in spring and display hidden from view.
fieldMarks: Male: black head and breast with crimson neck, the body covered in white, black-edged spots
Male: bare red facial skin, blue throat lappet and fleshy blue horns visible in display
Female: grey-brown, finely vermiculated and spotted with white
Heavy, short-tailed pheasant shape
animal.voice: A loud, wailing, goat-like 'waa-waa-oo-a', given mostly at dawn in spring
animal.lookalikes: Satyr tragopan (central and eastern Himalaya) is overall deep red with white spots and a red breast; the ranges barely meet, and the Western's black-and-grey body and crimson neck separate it.
animal.whereToSee: Great Himalayan National Park and Daranghati Sanctuary in Himachal Pradesh; Palas Valley in Kohistan, Pakistan
animal.season: Resident; males call April–June; moves lower in winter

lore: As the 'jujurana' it is the state bird of Himachal Pradesh, and a captive breeding programme at Sarahan in Himachal has bred the species since the 1990s.
funFact: The fleshy 'horns' that give tragopans their name (Greek for 'goat-Pan') are bare skin that the male erects only during display.

wiki.extract: The western tragopan or western horned tragopan is a medium-sized brightly plumed landfowl found along the range of Western Himalayas from north-eastern districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province in northern Pakistan in the west to Uttarakhand within India to the east. The species is highly endangered and globally threatened.

summary: The apex predator among Antarctic seals, a sleek, reptilian-headed hunter famous for ambushing penguins at the ice edge. It also sieves huge quantities of krill through intricately lobed cheek teeth. It is the only seal that regularly hunts other warm-blooded animals.
nativeRange: Antarctic and sub-Antarctic waters, especially the pack ice; vagrants reach South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Huge gape and long canines for seizing penguins and young seals
Interlocking three-pointed cheek teeth strain krill from water like a sieve
Patrols penguin colonies and catches birds as they enter or leave the water

animal.diet: Krill, penguins, fish, squid and other seals (especially crabeater pups)
animal.habitat: Edge of the Antarctic pack ice and sub-Antarctic islands
animal.size: 2.5–3.5 m; up to about 600 kg; females larger than males
animal.behaviour: Solitary. During the breeding season (November–January) males hang upside-down underwater and sing loud trills and moans.
fieldMarks: Long, slender, serpentine body with a large, reptile-like head
Dark grey back and pale, black-spotted underside and throat
Wide mouth that appears to 'smile'
Long fore-flippers used for swimming; often seen lounging alone on ice floes
animal.voice: Underwater, males produce loud, long trills and low moans during the breeding season, audible to hydrophones far away.
animal.lookalikes: Weddell seal is chubbier with a small rounded head and short muzzle. Crabeater seal is paler, smaller-headed and usually in groups. Southern elephant seal is massive and shorter-flippered.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula: Pléneau Island, Paradise Bay, Cuverville Island and Brown Bluff penguin colonies; South Georgia; occasionally New Zealand coasts in winter
animal.season: Antarctic cruise season November–March; highest at penguin colonies when chicks fledge (January–February)

lore: On Shackleton's Endurance expedition in 1916 a leopard seal chased Thomas Orde-Lees across the sea ice until Frank Wild shot it. In 2003 a leopard seal drowned British marine biologist Kirsty Brown while she was snorkelling at Rothera Station.
funFact: Photographer Paul Nicklen described a female leopard seal repeatedly bringing him penguins, as if teaching him to hunt.

wiki.extract: The leopard seal, also referred to as the sea leopard, is a long and muscular seal native to the Southern Ocean of Antarctica and southern Patagonia. It is the second largest species of seal in the Antarctic. It is the same length as, but half the weight of, a walrus. Its fur coat is countershaded, being silver on the bottom and dark gray on the top, and is distinctive for its leopard-like pattern of dark spots.

summary: The smallest and by far the most numerous flamingo, gathering in pink rafts of hundreds of thousands on Africa's caustic soda lakes. It feeds almost entirely on microscopic cyanobacteria filtered from the surface water.
nativeRange: East and southern Africa's Rift Valley and salt pans; West Africa; north-western India and Pakistan
abilities: Filters cyanobacteria (chiefly Arthrospira, 'spirulina') with a deep-keeled bill held upside down
Breeds on the mudflats of hyperalkaline Lake Natron, where few predators can follow
Its pink colour comes from carotenoid pigments in its food
Flocks move hundreds of kilometres between lakes, mostly at night, following food

animal.diet: Cyanobacteria and benthic diatoms
animal.habitat: Alkaline and saline lakes, lagoons and salt pans
animal.behaviour: Huge flocks perform synchronised 'marching' displays, heads raised and turning in unison, before breeding.
fieldMarks: Deep pink plumage, often more strongly pink than the greater flamingo
Dark carmine-red bill that looks black at a distance
Deep red eye and facial skin
Crimson wing coverts and black flight feathers in flight
Noticeably smaller than greater flamingo
animal.voice: A high, goose-like murmuring 'murr-err' from feeding flocks; flight calls higher-pitched than greater flamingo.
animal.lookalikes: Greater flamingo is taller and paler, with a pale pink bill with a clean black tip, and a yellow eye. Lessers look compact with a uniformly dark bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Bogoria and Lake Nakuru (Kenya), Lake Natron (Tanzania), Etosha and Walvis Bay (Namibia), Kamfers Dam (South Africa), Little Rann of Kutch (India)
animal.season: Present year-round in the Rift Valley, moving between lakes; breeds at Lake Natron mainly from August to November

lore: The lesser flamingo's main breeding site at Lake Natron was threatened by a proposed soda-ash plant in the 2000s, which its developer dropped in 2008 after international campaigns, although the idea has resurfaced since.
funFact: Lake Natron's water can reach a pH above 10 and temperatures over 40 °C, yet it hosts the largest lesser flamingo breeding colonies on Earth.

wiki.extract: The lesser flamingo is a species of flamingo occurring in sub-Saharan Africa and western India. Birds are occasionally reported from farther north, but these are generally considered vagrants.

summary: The largest and most widespread flamingo, gathering in tens of thousands on salt lakes and lagoons. Its pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the algae and crustaceans it eats.
nativeRange: Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Filter-feeds with its head upside down, pumping water through bill lamellae
Tolerates highly saline and alkaline lakes
Turns pink from dietary carotenoids such as canthaxanthin
Rubs pigment from preen-gland oil onto feathers as 'make-up' in breeding season
Both parents feed chicks a crop milk

animal.diet: Brine shrimp, small molluscs, insect larvae and algae
animal.habitat: Shallow saline and alkaline wetlands
animal.lifespan: Over 30 years in the wild; over 80 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Groups perform synchronised 'marching' displays, heads raised and turning, before breeding.
fieldMarks: Very tall, pale pink wading bird with long neck and legs
Pink bill with a black tip, bent sharply downward
Bright red and black wings in flight
Feeds with head upside down
animal.voice: Goose-like honking and grunting in flocks
animal.lookalikes: Lesser flamingo is smaller and deeper pink with a dark carmine bill that looks all-dark at a distance.
animal.whereToSee: Camargue (Pont de Gau), France; Rann of Kutch, India; Walvis Bay, Namibia
animal.season: Present all year at many wetlands; breeding colonies and numbers shift with water levels

lore: Pliny the Elder recorded that the Roman gourmet Apicius prized flamingo tongue as a delicacy. The Great Rann of Kutch in India hosts one of the largest breeding colonies, called 'Flamingo City'.
funFact: A captive greater flamingo at Adelaide Zoo lived to at least 83 years.

wiki.extract: The greater flamingo is the largest and most widespread species of the flamingo family. Common in the Old World, they are found in Northern (coastal) and Sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian subcontinent, Central Asia, the Middle East, the Levant, the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Aden, the Red Sea, and the Mediterranean countries of Southern Europe.

summary: The most vividly coloured flamingo, a deep coral-pink bird that filters shrimp and algae from salty lagoons with its head upside-down. It is the national bird of the Bahamas.
nativeRange: The Caribbean (Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, Bonaire), Yucatán Peninsula, northern coast of South America and the Galápagos; increasingly seen in Florida
abilities: Filter-feeds with a bent bill held upside-down, pumping water through comb-like lamellae with its tongue
Gets its colour from carotenoid pigments in brine shrimp and algae
Stands on one leg with little or no muscular effort, using passive locking of the joints
Builds mud-mound nests in dense colonies

animal.diet: Brine shrimp, small molluscs, insect larvae, algae and seeds
animal.habitat: Shallow saline and brackish lagoons, salt pans and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Flocks perform synchronised 'marching' displays — head-flagging and wing salutes — that stimulate breeding.
fieldMarks: Deep pink-orange body, brighter than other flamingos
Pale pink bill with the outer third black, sharply bent downward
Very long pink legs and neck
In flight, black flight feathers contrast with pink-red wing coverts
animal.voice: Goose-like honking, given constantly in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Greater Flamingo (Old World) is paler pink with a pink bill with less black. Chilean Flamingo has grey legs with pink 'knees'. Roseate Spoonbill has a flat bill and short neck.
animal.whereToSee: Inagua National Park (Bahamas), Ría Celestún and Ría Lagartos (Yucatán), Bonaire's salt pans, Galápagos lagoons; Florida Bay and the Everglades.
animal.season: Resident year-round; Yucatán flocks largest Nov–Mar at Celestún

lore: John James Audubon's life-size plate of the American Flamingo, bent to fit the page, is one of the best-known images in The Birds of America (1827–38); Mark Catesby painted it a century earlier in the Bahamas.
funFact: After Hurricane Idalia in 2023, dozens of American flamingos were blown north and seen across Florida and as far north as Ohio and Wisconsin.

wiki.extract: The American flamingo is a large species of flamingo native to the West Indies, northern South America and the Yucatán Peninsula. It is closely related to the greater flamingo and Chilean flamingo, and was formerly considered conspecific with the greater flamingo, but that treatment is now widely viewed as incorrect due to a lack of evidence. It is also known as the Caribbean flamingo, although it is also present in the Galápagos Islands. It is the only flamingo that naturally inhabits North America.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a flamingo head and a sea fan coral.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Mark Catesby’s landmark study depicts the head of a Greater Flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) alongside a branched gorgonian coral, then known as Keratophyton. Catesby was a pioneer in North American natural history, and his work is celebrated for its vibrant, often unconventional compositions that brought New World flora and fauna to a European audience.

summary: A flat, spiny lizard of the southern Great Plains and deserts that eats harvester ants. When attacked by coyotes or dogs it can squirt a stream of foul-tasting blood from its eyes.
nativeRange: South-central United States (Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, southeastern Colorado and Arizona) and northern Mexico
abilities: Squirts blood from its eyes up to about 1.5 m to deter dog-family predators
Can puff itself up to look bigger and harder to swallow
Eats harvester ants and tolerates their venom
Collects rain on its back and channels it to its mouth

animal.diet: Mainly harvester ants (Pogonomyrmex); also other insects
animal.habitat: Open, arid and semi-arid land with sparse plants and sandy soil
animal.behaviour: Basks in the morning and buries itself in sand at night. Its numbers have fallen in Texas due to pesticides, habitat loss and invasive fire ants that displace harvester ants.
fieldMarks: Flat, round body covered in spines
Two long central horns on the back of the head, longer than the others
Two rows of fringe scales along each side
Pale stripe down the middle of the back with dark spots on either side
animal.lookalikes: The round-tailed horned lizard (P. modestum) is smaller, with short horns and no side fringe. Greater short-horned lizards (P. hernandesi) have short horns and live at higher altitudes.
animal.whereToSee: South Texas brushland (e.g. Chaparral Wildlife Management Area), west Texas and New Mexico grasslands, western Oklahoma
animal.season: Active April–September

lore: The Texas horned lizard became the state reptile of Texas in 1993, and is the 'Horned Frog' mascot of Texas Christian University. 'Old Rip', supposedly sealed in a courthouse cornerstone in Eastland, Texas, in 1897 and found alive in 1928, became a national sensation.
funFact: Blood squirted from its eyes contains chemicals that dogs and coyotes find foul-tasting, but it has no effect on hawks.

wiki.extract: The Texas horned lizard is one of about 21 North American species of spikey-bodied reptiles called horned lizards, all belonging the genus Phrynosoma. It occurs in south-central regions of the US and northeastern Mexico, as well as several isolated introduced records and populations from Southern United States. Though some populations are stable, severe population declines have occurred in many areas of Texas and Oklahoma. The Texas spiny lizard may be confused for a Texas horned lizard due to its appearance and overlapping habitat. Texas horned lizard populations show strong genetic structuring across their range, with limited gene flow between regions. Because the Texas horned lizard is listed as a threatened species in the state, it is illegal to pick up, touch, or possess them in Texas.

plates.title: Unterhaltungen aus der Naturgeschichte / 3 Die  Amphibien
plates.author: Wilhelm, Gottlieb Tobias
plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of three amphibians, including a green spotted frog, a blue-grey frog, and a horned toad, presented in two panels.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from Gottlieb Tobias Wilhelm's 'Unterhaltungen aus der Naturgeschichte' (1794) showcases the diversity of amphibians. The plate features detailed renderings of different species, highlighting their unique patterns and physiological features, which served as a vital educational tool in the late Enlightenment period.

summary: A flattened, bright-green stick-insect relative that is almost indistinguishable from a leaf, complete with 'veins' and brown 'bite marks'. It even sways gently as if moved by a breeze.
nativeRange: Philippines
abilities: Body and legs are flattened into leaf-like lobes with vein patterns
Rocks from side to side while walking, imitating a leaf in wind
Females can reproduce without males (parthenogenesis)
Eggs look like plant seeds

animal.diet: Leaves of tropical trees and shrubs; in captivity bramble, oak and guava
animal.habitat: Leafy forest canopy and understorey
animal.lifespan: Adults several months; about a year in total
animal.size: Females about 8–9 cm; males smaller (about 5–6 cm) and slimmer
animal.behaviour: Females are flightless and rely on stillness and disguise; slimmer males have full wings and fly to find females.
fieldMarks: Broad, flat, leaf-shaped green body, sometimes with brown or yellow patches
Leaf-like flaps on the legs
Female forewings marked with a pattern resembling a leaf's midrib and veins
Males narrower, with long antennae and functional hindwings
animal.lookalikes: Many Phyllium species are near-identical and are separated by egg shape, the leg lobes and range. In the wild its main 'lookalike' is a leaf.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine forests; one of the most commonly kept leaf insects in captivity.

lore: Leaf insects astonished early European naturalists; Linnaeus named the first known species Gryllus siccifolius, the 'dry-leaf cricket', in 1758.
funFact: Newly hatched nymphs are reddish-brown and look like ants or dead leaf fragments; they turn green only after their first meals of leaves.

wiki.extract: Phyllium philippinicum is a species of leaf insect in the family Phylliidae. It is endemic to the Philippines.

Published in Johann Franz Griendel's 'Micrographia nova', the work reflects the 17th-century fascination with the 'invisible world' made accessible through early microscopy. The inclusion of devotional Latin marginalia alongside the scienti

plates.desc: Magnified view of an insect's anatomy, showing the abdomen and jointed, bristled legs.
plates.long: This intricate engraving from Johann Franz Griendel's 'Micrographia nova' (1687) presents a highly magnified view of an insect, likely a spider. Published shortly after Robert Hooke's seminal work, Griendel's book utilized his own improved microscopes to reveal the 'wonderful magnitude' and hidden complexities of minute creatures to the early modern scientific community.

plates.long: A large bird of prey stands in profile on a weathered tree stump, its talons gripping the wood. A small insect crawls on the ground near the base of the perch. The illustration depicts the physical form of the Osprey as described in Aldrovandi's natural history compendium.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a gibbon (猿) sitting on a rock, reaching out with its long arm towards a flying insect.
plates.long: This woodcut from the 1609 encyclopedia Sancai Tuhui depicts a gibbon (yuan), a creature celebrated in Chinese culture for its agility and long limbs. The illustration captures the animal in a characteristic pose, reaching for an insect, demonstrating the era's commitment to cataloging the known world.

plates.long: This plate from Antony van Leeuwenhoek's seminal work 'Arcana Naturae Detecta' (1695) illustrates his groundbreaking microscopic discoveries. The twenty figures provide a detailed look at insect anatomy, including larvae, eggs, and specialized limbs like the powerful jumping leg of a flea, rendered with the precision of fine-line engraving to convey findings made through Leeuwenhoek's own high-pow

plates.title: Secrets of Nature Discovered
plates.author: Antony van Leeuwenhoek
plates.desc: Scientific plate showing various views and life stages of an insect, with anatomical labels.
plates.long: This intricate engraving serves as a scientific plate, meticulously documenting the anatomy and life cycle of a small insect, possibly an aphid. Through the use of lettered labels and varying scales of magnification, the artist captures the minute details of the creature's body, legs, and eggs, exemplifying the rigorous observational standards of early modern natural history.

plates.title: Garden of Health
plates.author: Jacob Meydenbach

plates.long: This woodcut illustrates the 'Multipes', a creature described in the text as building a nest of twigs. The hand-coloring adds significant detail to this early attempt at scientific illustration from the 1491 Ortus Sanitatis.

plates.title: Ornithologiae: de avibus historiae libri XII
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a bird, identified as a Pyrrhocorax (chough), perched on a branch and holding an insect in its beak.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a Pyrrhocorax, or chough, a member of the crow family, shown here with a large insect in its beak. It is part of a 16th-century ornithological treatise, reflecting the era's growing interest in the systematic study and visual documentation of the natural world. The illustration combines scientific observation with the artistic conventions of early modern relief printing.

summary: A leaf-green tree frog of Central American rainforests with scarlet eyes, blue-and-yellow flanks and orange feet. Its unborn tadpoles can hatch early when they sense the vibrations of a snake attacking their eggs.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests from southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern Colombia
abilities: Embryos hatch up to several days early to escape snakes or wasps, telling attack vibrations from rain
Startles predators by suddenly opening its bright red eyes and flashing its coloured flanks
Lays eggs on leaves over water, so hatching tadpoles drop straight in

animal.diet: Crickets, moths, flies and other insects
animal.habitat: Rainforest trees near ponds and swamps
animal.behaviour: By day it sleeps on the underside of a leaf with eyes closed and bright colours tucked away, appearing all green. Males call from branches over ponds on rainy nights.
fieldMarks: Bright green with large red eyes and vertical pupils
Blue to purple flanks with pale vertical bars
Orange or red toes with suction-cup pads
Slender body and long limbs
animal.voice: A short 'chack' or 'chack-chack', repeated at intervals from vegetation above water
animal.lookalikes: Morelet's tree frog (A. moreletii) has dark red eyes and no bars on its flanks. The gliding leaf frog (A. spurrelli) has large webbed hands and spots on the back.
animal.whereToSee: La Selva, Tortuguero and Sarapiquí (Costa Rica), Panama's Soberanía National Park, Belize; ponds on rainy-season nights
animal.season: Breeds in the rainy season (May–November)

lore: Its picture has become a symbol of rainforest conservation, appearing on countless posters and stamps since the 1980s.
funFact: Karen Warkentin's research showed that red-eyed tree frog embryos can tell the vibration pattern of a snake attack from rain and hatch in seconds.

wiki.extract: The red-eyed tree frog or red-eyed leaf frog is a species of tree frog in the subfamily Phyllomedusinae native to forests of Central America and northwestern South America. One of the most recognizable frog species, A. callidryas is known for its vibrant coloration, having a bright green body with blue and yellow stripes on the side, a white underside, bright red- to orange-colored feet, and its namesake bright red eyes. Despite these bright colors, the red-eyed tree frog is not poisonous like many other brightly colored amphibians; rather, the colors likely provide camouflage against the greenery of the surrounding jungle, and may also serve to provoke the startle reflex to dissuade predators and allow the frog time to escape.

summary: The only mammals that feed exclusively on blood, vampire bats make a tiny cut in sleeping livestock or wild mammals and lap the flowing blood. Heat-sensing pits on the nose guide them to blood vessels near the skin, and their saliva contains anticoagulants studied for stroke drugs. Roostmates famously share regurgitated blood with those who failed to feed.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to northern Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; Trinidad and Margarita islands
abilities: Senses infrared heat with nose pits, using a specially modified TRPV1 receptor
Saliva anticoagulant (draculin and plasminogen activators) keeps blood flowing; a derivative, desmoteplase, was trialled as a stroke drug
Runs and leaps on the ground on its forelimbs, unusual for a bat
Shares blood with hungry roostmates, preferring those who shared with them before

animal.diet: Blood of mammals, mainly cattle, horses and pigs; also wild mammals
animal.habitat: Caves, hollow trees, mines and buildings within reach of mammal prey
animal.lifespan: Up to about 29 years in captivity; about 9 in the wild
animal.size: Body 7–9 cm, wingspan about 35–40 cm; 25–40 g
animal.behaviour: Leaves the roost after full darkness, often avoiding bright moonlight. Drinks about half its own body weight in blood in a 20–30 minute feed.
fieldMarks: Short, flat, pug-like snout with a small U-shaped nose-leaf
Long, strong thumbs used for walking
No tail; grey-brown fur
Sharp, blade-like upper incisors; signs include small cuts and blood trickles on livestock, and roosts that smell of ammonia with dark, tarry droppings
animal.lookalikes: White-winged and hairy-legged vampire bats (Diaemus, Diphylla) feed mainly on birds and have white wing-tips or furry legs. Fruit-eating leaf-nosed bats have tall spear-shaped nose leaves.
animal.whereToSee: Lamanai Archaeological Reserve (Belize, night bat tours); caves of Mexico's Yucatán; Pantanal and Amazon cattle ranches (Brazil)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: European naturalists named it after the vampire of Slavic folklore; in turn, Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) gave the bat a central place in vampire fiction. Rabies spread by vampire bats is a major veterinary problem across Latin America.
funFact: A vampire bat that misses two nights of blood meals can starve, which is why sharing among roostmates matters so much.

wiki.extract: The common vampire bat is a small, leaf-nosed bat native to the Americas. It is one of three extant species of vampire bats, the other two being the hairy-legged and the white-winged vampire bats.

summary: Not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised animals (zooids) that function as one organism, drifting on a gas-filled sail. Its tentacles, often around 10 m and sometimes far longer, deliver an extremely painful sting.
nativeRange: Warm and temperate waters of the Atlantic, drifting widely; Indo-Pacific 'bluebottles' are now generally treated as separate Physalia species
abilities: Colony of zooids specialised for floating, catching prey, digestion and reproduction
Inflates its float with gas including carbon monoxide
Sails can be angled left or right, so wind drives different individuals in different directions
Stinging cells remain active on stranded or dead specimens

animal.diet: Small fish and fish larvae, shrimp and other plankton caught on the tentacles
animal.habitat: Surface of the open ocean; washed ashore by onshore winds
animal.size: Float up to about 30 cm; tentacles commonly about 10 m, recorded to 30 m
animal.behaviour: Tentacles contract to pull paralysed prey up to digestive zooids beneath the float.
fieldMarks: Translucent, blue-violet, gas-filled float with a pink-edged crest
Long blue tentacles trailing below
Often stranded in rows along beaches after storms
No bell or pulsing swimming
animal.lookalikes: By-the-wind sailor (Velella velella) is a small, flat blue disc with a rigid diagonal sail and only short tentacles. Blue button (Porpita porpita) is a flat, round disc. Pacific bluebottles (Physalia utriculus) are smaller with a single main tentacle.
animal.whereToSee: Atlantic beaches of Florida, the Caribbean, the Canary Islands and occasionally Britain and Ireland after strong westerlies. Do not touch stranded ones: their tentacles still sting.
animal.season: Strandings follow onshore winds; Florida mostly winter, Europe often late summer–autumn

lore: Sailors named it after the Portuguese caravel or man-of-war, whose rounded sail its float resembles.
funFact: The blue sea slug (Glaucus atlanticus) eats man o' war tentacles and stores their unfired stinging cells in its own body for defence.

wiki.extract: The Portuguese man o' war, also known as the man-of-war, bluebottle, or sometimes called Caravela Portuguesa, is a marine hydrozoan found in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans. While it is typically considered the only species in its genus, Physalia, and family, Physaliidae, genetic evidence suggests there may be more.

plates.author: Willem Piso
plates.desc: Woodcut of a marine organism, identified in the text as Moucicu, likely a Portuguese man o' war or similar siphonophore.
plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a 'Moucicu', an early modern identification of a venomous marine organism, possibly a Portuguese man o' war. This illustration appears in Willem Piso's seminal 1658 work on the natural history and medicine of the East and West Indies, showcasing the era's descriptive zoology and the study of toxic species.

summary: The largest toothed predator and owner of the largest brain of any animal, which dives into the deep ocean to hunt squid. Its huge, square head holds the spermaceti organ, which focuses the loudest sounds made by any animal.
nativeRange: Deep waters of all oceans; females and young in tropical and subtropical seas, adult males ranging to polar waters
abilities: Makes echolocation clicks of up to ~230 dB, the loudest sounds known from any animal
Dives to over 2,000 m and stays down for an hour or more
Has a brain of up to ~8–9 kg, the largest known
Families share 'codas', click patterns that identify vocal clans and are now studied for structure
Produces ambergris, a waxy gut secretion formed around indigestible squid beaks

animal.diet: Carnivore: mainly deep-sea squid, including giant squid; also fish
animal.habitat: Deep open ocean, especially over canyons and slopes
animal.size: Males 16–20 m and up to ~45–57 t; females ~11 m and ~15 t
animal.behaviour: Groups sleep for short periods hanging vertically just below the surface. Females form lifelong family units that babysit each other's calves while mothers dive.
fieldMarks: Huge, square head
Angled, bushy blow to the left
Wrinkled skin
Low hump instead of a dorsal fin
animal.voice: Loud clicks
animal.lookalikes: Humpback whales have long flippers and a different blow.
animal.whereToSee: Kaikōura (New Zealand), Andenes (Norway) and Dominica
animal.season: Kaikōura year-round; Andenes May–Sep

lore: In 1820 a sperm whale rammed and sank the Nantucket whaleship Essex, the event that inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851). Ambergris, called ʿanbar in Arabic, was prized in medieval Islamic and European perfumery and medicine.
funFact: Whalers named it after the waxy spermaceti in its head, which they mistook for sperm.

wiki.extract: The sperm whale or cachalot is the largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator. It is the only living member of the genus Physeter and one of three extant species in the sperm whale superfamily Physeteroidea, along with the pygmy sperm whale and dwarf sperm whale of the genus Kogia.

plates.long: This woodcut from Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium' depicts a 'Physeter', a term used historically for large whales. The image reflects the Renaissance effort to systematically document the natural world, combining direct observation with traditional accounts of sea monsters.

plates.title: De Piscibus Libri V et De Cetis Liber Unus
plates.author: Ulisse Aldrovandi
plates.desc: Woodcut of a Physeter, a large spouting sea creature or whale
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Physeter', a term used by early modern naturalists to describe large spouting whales. Featured in Ulisse Aldrovandi's 1661 treatise on fish and cetaceans, the illustration captures the transition between medieval sea monster lore and the emerging empirical study of marine biology, evidenced by the detailed rendering of the blowhole and fins.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Physeter', a type of whale or sea monster described by Conrad Gessner in his encyclopedic work on animals. The illustration highlights the creature's massive size and its characteristic ability to spout water, reflecting the 16th-century effort to document the natural world through both eyewitness accounts and classical lore.

summary: A large brown woodpecker that feeds mostly on the ground, licking up ants. In flight it flashes golden-yellow or salmon-red under its wings and a bold white rump.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada through the US and Mexico to Nicaragua; also Cuba and Grand Cayman
abilities: Ants and their larvae make up nearly half its diet, more than any other North American woodpecker
Has a long tongue coated in sticky saliva for collecting ants from the soil
Two forms — eastern Yellow-shafted and western Red-shafted — hybridise across a broad zone on the Great Plains

animal.diet: Ants and beetles; fruit and seeds in winter
animal.habitat: Open woods, parks, edges and burned forest
animal.behaviour: It often drums on metal chimney caps and gutters, which amplify the sound.
fieldMarks: Brown, black-barred back; buff breast with black spots
Black crescent bib
White rump in flight
Yellow (east) or salmon-red (west) wing and tail shafts; males have a black or red moustache
animal.voice: A long, loud 'wik-wik-wik-wik'; also a piercing 'kleer' and a soft 'wicka-wicka' in courtship.
animal.lookalikes: Gilded Flicker (Sonoran Desert) has yellow underwings with a cinnamon crown. Red-bellied Woodpecker has a barred back without a bib. In flight the white rump can recall Red-headed Woodpecker, which has white wing patches instead.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parks and open woods across North America; often seen feeding on the ground.
animal.season: Resident in much of the US; northern birds migrate south in autumn

lore: It is Alabama's state bird; Confederate soldiers from Alabama were nicknamed 'yellowhammers' after the yellow trim on their uniforms.
funFact: It is one of the few North American woodpeckers that regularly migrates.

wiki.extract: The northern flicker or common flicker is a medium-sized bird of the woodpecker family. It is native to most of North America, parts of Central America, Cuba, and the Cayman Islands, and is one of the few woodpecker species that migrate. Over 100 common names for the northern flicker are known, including yellowhammer, clape, gaffer woodpecker, harry-wicket, heigh-ho, wake-up, walk-up, wick-up, yarrup, and gawker bird. Many of these names derive from attempts to imitate some of its calls.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a Northern Flicker, identified by Catesby as the 'golden Wing'd Woodpecker,' perched upon a branch of a Chestnut Oak. Mark Catesby's work was pioneering for its time, as he was one of the first naturalists to illustrate birds within their ecological context, alongside the specific plants they inhabited. This plate exemplifies the meticulous detail and artistic f

summary: Europe's largest woodpecker, crow-sized and all black with a red crown. The large oval holes it carves in old trees become homes for owls, stock doves, bats and pine martens.
nativeRange: Forests from Spain and France across Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus, through Russia and Siberia to Japan and northern China
abilities: Excavates large, oval nest holes that many other species later use
Rips into rotten stumps and trunks to reach carpenter ants
Drums loudly on resonant trunks to advertise territory
Its old holes are key nest sites for Tengmalm's owl, stock dove and goldeneye

animal.diet: Carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae; some berries
animal.habitat: Mature conifer, beech and mixed forests with large old trees
animal.behaviour: Leaves large rectangular excavations at the base of ant-infested trees and stumps.
fieldMarks: All-black plumage, crow-sized
Male has a red crown from bill to nape; female only a red rear crown
Pale ivory bill and pale eye
Flies with a straight, flappy flight, not deeply undulating
animal.voice: A loud, whistling 'kree-kree-kree' in flight, a plaintive 'kleee-a' when perched; long, powerful drumming.
animal.lookalikes: Carrion crow and jackdaw lack the red crown and pale bill and do not climb trunks. Green woodpecker is green with a red cap. Grey-headed woodpecker is much smaller and green.
animal.whereToSee: Białowieża Forest (Poland/Belarus), the Bavarian Forest, Pyrenees, Alpine forests, Finnish taiga.
animal.season: Resident; drumming and calling most frequent Feb–Apr

lore: The species name 'martius' links it to Mars, the Roman god whose sacred bird was the woodpecker, and early naturalists called it the 'great black woodpecker'.
funFact: A single black woodpecker nest hole can be reused by other cavity-nesting animals for decades after the woodpecker leaves.

wiki.extract: The black woodpecker is a large woodpecker that lives in mature forests across the northern Palearctic. It is the sole representative of its genus in that region, and its range is expanding. The black woodpecker is easily the largest woodpecker species in Europe as well as in the portion of Asia where it lives and is one of the largest species worldwide. This non-migratory species tends to make its home in old-growth forest or large forest stands and excavates a large tree hole to reside in. In turn, several species rely on black woodpeckers to secondarily reside in the holes made in trees by them. This woodpecker's diet consists mostly of carpenter ants. This species is closely related to, and fills the same ecological niche in Europe as, the pileated woodpecker of North America and the lineated woodpecker of South America, also being similar to the white-bellied woodpecker which is distributed to the south somewhat of the black woodpecker in Asia.

summary: A crow-sized black woodpecker with a flaming red crest that chisels large rectangular holes into trees in search of carpenter ants. Its old cavities become homes for owls, ducks, bats and martens.
nativeRange: Much of Canada, the eastern United States and the Pacific Northwest
abilities: Excavates rectangular holes up to tens of centimetres long to reach carpenter ant galleries
Its abandoned nest holes are used by Wood Ducks, owls, flying squirrels and bats
Uses a long, barbed tongue to extract ants
Drums slowly and loudly on resonant trunks to claim territory

animal.diet: Carpenter ants, beetle larvae, other insects; fruit and nuts
animal.habitat: Mature forest with large trees and dead wood; increasingly suburban woodlots
animal.behaviour: Pairs hold territories year-round and excavate a new nest cavity each spring.
fieldMarks: Mostly black body with a bright red, pointed crest
Bold white stripes on the face and neck
Large white underwing linings flashing in flight
Male has a red moustache stripe; female's is black
animal.voice: A loud, wild, ringing 'wuk-wuk-wuk-wuk', rising and falling; drumming deep and slow, trailing off.
animal.lookalikes: Ivory-billed Woodpecker, if it survives, has an ivory bill and white trailing edges to the upper wing. Red-headed Woodpecker is much smaller with an all-red head and white wing patches.
animal.whereToSee: Large tracts of mature forest across the eastern US and Pacific Northwest; listen for its call in places like the Great Smoky Mountains or Congaree National Park.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Mark Catesby painted it in the 1730s as 'The larger red-crested Wood-pecker'; its rectangular excavations were used by early naturalists as a sign of its presence.
funFact: Woody Woodpecker's look is often linked to this species, though the cartoon's creator, Walter Lantz, was said to be inspired by an Acorn Woodpecker.

wiki.extract: The pileated woodpecker is a large, crow-sized woodpecker with a prominent red crest, white neck stripe, and a mostly black body. This woodpecker is native to North America, where it is the largest confirmed extant woodpecker species and the third-largest extant species of woodpecker in the world, after the great slaty woodpecker and the black woodpecker. It inhabits deciduous forests in eastern North America, the Great Lakes, the boreal forests of Canada, and parts of the Pacific Coast. This woodpecker is primarily an insectivore, eating insects that live in trees; it is famous for making large, nearly rectangular carvings into trees, which are used to extract prey inside the tree or to make a nest. The species has a large range and an increasing population, causing it to be categorized as a species of "least concern" by the IUCN.

Catesby was one of the first to illustrate North American species in their natural habitats, providing a vital record of the continent's biodiversity for an Enlightenment-era audience.

summary: A tiny Andean manakin whose males 'sing' with their wings. Specialised, club-shaped feathers rub together like a bow on a violin string, producing a sustained high note.
nativeRange: Western slope of the Andes in Colombia and Ecuador (the Chocó region)
abilities: Males produce a tonal note near 1,500 Hz by rubbing modified secondary feathers together over 100 times a second (Bostwick & Prum, Science, 2005)
One wing feather bears a row of ridges and another a stiff tip, like a comb and pick
Unlike almost all other birds, it has solid rather than hollow wing bones, which help support the vibrating feathers

animal.diet: Small fruits and insects
animal.habitat: Understorey and mid-levels of humid foothill and subtropical forest
animal.behaviour: Males display on perches within earshot of each other, flicking their wings above the back to make the sound.
fieldMarks: Male: rich chestnut body with a bright red crown
Black and white in the wings; white on the inner wing visible in display
Female: olive-green with a cinnamon-tinged face
Tiny, short-tailed manakin shape
animal.voice: A mechanical 'tik-tik-ting': two sharp clicks followed by a ringing, violin-like whine made by the wings.
animal.lookalikes: Striped Manakin has a red crown but a red-streaked belly and no chestnut body. Other manakins in its range lack the chestnut-and-red male plumage.
animal.whereToSee: Mindo and Milpe Bird Sanctuary in north-western Ecuador; Chocó foothill reserves in Colombia.
animal.season: Resident year-round

funFact: Its wing sound was first analysed with high-speed video, which showed the feathers vibrating faster than the bird can beat its wings.

summary: A plump, short-tailed ground bird painted green, sky-blue, buff, black and scarlet, which hops on the forest floor turning over leaves. It migrates within the subcontinent, arriving in northern forests with the monsoon to breed.
nativeRange: Breeds in the Himalayan foothills (from NE Pakistan to Nepal), central and western India; winters in peninsular India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Migrates at night within South Asia and is sometimes found exhausted in towns
Flicks dead leaves aside with its bill to expose insects and worms
Builds a large domed nest of twigs and leaves on or near the ground

animal.diet: Insects, earthworms, snails and other ground invertebrates
animal.habitat: Deciduous and evergreen forest undergrowth, scrub jungle, well-vegetated gardens
animal.behaviour: Mostly silent and secretive, but calls loudly at dawn and dusk, often from a tree perch in the breeding season.
fieldMarks: Stocky, almost tailless bird with long legs
Bright green back, shining blue patch on the wing and rump
Buff underparts with a scarlet-crimson belly and vent
Bold black eye-stripe with white above, and a buff crown stripe
animal.voice: A loud, clear, two-note whistle 'wheet-tew', given mostly at dawn and dusk
animal.lookalikes: Hooded pitta (NE India, Southeast Asia) has a black head with a chestnut crown and no white supercilium; Blue-winged pitta has a darker head and more blue in the wing.
animal.whereToSee: Breeding forests of Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra; wintering in Sri Lanka's dry zone and the Western Ghats; occasionally Margalla Hills, Pakistan
animal.season: Summer (monsoon) breeder in the north (May–Sep); winter visitor in the south and Sri Lanka (Oct–Apr)

lore: Its folk name navrang, 'nine colours', is used across north India for a bird whose plumage seems to hold every colour of the forest.
funFact: Migrating Indian pittas regularly turn up in cities in southern India and Sri Lanka after striking buildings during their night flights.

wiki.extract: The Indian pitta also known as Navrang, is a passerine bird native to the Indian subcontinent. It inhabits scrub jungle, deciduous and dense evergreen forest. It breeds in the forests of the Himalayas, hills of central and western India, and migrates to other parts of the peninsula in winter. Although very colourful, it is usually shy and hidden in the undergrowth where it picks insects on the forest floor. It has a distinctive two note whistling call which is heard at dawn and dusk. It is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List as the population is considered large.

summary: A nearly blind river dolphin that navigates the silt-thick Indus entirely by echolocation, swimming on its side and trailing a flipper along the riverbed. Once spread through the whole Indus system, it is now trapped between irrigation barrages in a few stretches of the Indus in Pakistan, with a tiny remnant in India's Beas River. It was recognised as a separate species from the Ganges dolphin in 2021.
nativeRange: Indus River, Pakistan (mainly between Chashma and Kotri barrages); a remnant population in the Beas River, Punjab, India
abilities: Its eyes have no crystalline lens; it can probably sense only light and its direction, and relies on near-continuous echolocation clicks
Swims on its side, sweeping its head and a pectoral flipper across the bottom to find prey in near-zero visibility
Long, narrow beak with interlocking needle teeth that remain visible when the mouth is closed
Unfused neck vertebrae let it turn its head sharply, unlike most dolphins

animal.diet: Fish and freshwater prawns, taken from the riverbed and mid-water
animal.habitat: Deep channels, confluences and eddies of the turbid main Indus; needs water depth through the dry season
animal.size: About 1.5–2.5 m long; females larger than males; roughly 70–110 kg
animal.behaviour: Surfaces every minute or two with a brief, low roll and a sneeze-like blow, then vanishes; it rarely leaps or bow-rides. Usually seen singly or in loose groups at channel junctions.
fieldMarks: Silhouette at the surface: a brief low arc showing a long, thin beak, rounded melon and only a low triangular hump instead of a true dorsal fin
Grey-brown body, often pinkish on the belly; broad, paddle-like flippers
Blow is a short, audible puff with little visible spray
Usually seen in muddy main channels below or between barrages, often near confluences
animal.lookalikes: The Ganges river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) looks almost identical but lives in the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna and Karnaphuli systems; range alone separates them. No other dolphin occurs in the Indus.
animal.whereToSee: Indus Dolphin Reserve between Guddu and Sukkur barrages, Sindh, Pakistan; the Taunsa Barrage Wildlife Sanctuary, Punjab; Beas Conservation Reserve near Harike, Punjab, India
animal.season: Resident year-round; easiest to see in the low-water months of winter and early spring, when dolphins concentrate in deeper channels

lore: In Sindhi folklore the bhulan was once a woman, turned into a blind dolphin after she was cursed by a holy man. Since 1992 the Sindh Wildlife Department and WWF-Pakistan have run a programme rescuing dolphins stranded in irrigation canals.
funFact: Surveys counted around 1,800–2,000 Indus dolphins in recent years, almost all in a stretch of river shorter than 1,000 km.

wiki.extract: The Indus river dolphin is a freshwater dolphin in the family Platanistidae. It is endemic to the rivers of the Indus basin in Pakistan and northwestern India. It was the first discovered side-swimming cetacean. In Pakistan, it occurs in the Indus River, where five small sub-populations are separated by irrigation barrages. In India, a very small isolated population at a very high risk of extinction lives in the Beas River. It is the national mammal of Pakistan and the state aquatic animal of Punjab, India.

summary: The world's largest flatfish, a right-eyed giant that can grow longer than a person. It starts life as a normal symmetrical larva, then one eye migrates across its head as it settles to the seabed.
nativeRange: North Atlantic from Virginia to Greenland and from the Bay of Biscay to the Barents Sea
abilities: During metamorphosis the left eye migrates over the head to the right side
Swims actively in midwater to chase fish, unlike most flatfish
Females can reach 50 years and produce millions of eggs
edibilityNote: Lean white flesh; large individuals contain moderate mercury.

animal.diet: Cod, haddock, herring, sand eels, crabs
animal.habitat: Sand, gravel and clay bottoms at 50–2,000 m
animal.size: Up to about 2.5–3 m and 320 kg
animal.behaviour: Migrates to deep, warm slope waters to spawn in winter and spring.
fieldMarks: Diamond-shaped, thick flatfish with both eyes on the right side
Large mouth reaching to below the eye
Uniform dark olive-brown upper side, white underside
Concave (crescent) tail
Lateral line arches strongly over the pectoral fin
animal.lookalikes: Greenland halibut (Reinhardtius hippoglossoides) has one eye on the edge of the head and a dark underside; Pacific halibut (H. stenolepis) lives in the Pacific.
animal.whereToSee: Norwegian coast (Lofoten, Saltstraumen), Iceland, Gulf of Maine, Nova Scotia
animal.season: Resident; nearshore in summer

lore: Its English name comes from 'haly butte', the 'holy flatfish' eaten on Christian holy days in medieval England.
funFact: Halibut was so overfished that the IUCN listed it Endangered in 1996; its 2021 reassessment improved to Near Threatened.

wiki.extract: The Atlantic halibut is a flatfish of the family Pleuronectidae. They are demersal fish living on or near sand, gravel or clay bottoms at depths of between 50 and 2,000 m. The halibut is among the largest teleost (bony) fish in the world, and is a threatened species owing to a slow rate of growth and overfishing. Halibut are strong swimmers and are able to migrate long distances. Halibut size is not age-specific, but rather tends to follow a cycle related to halibut abundance.

summary: The classic orange-spotted flatfish of the North Sea. It lies buried in sand with only its eyes showing and can change its colour to match the seabed.
nativeRange: Northeast Atlantic from the Barents Sea to Morocco, North Sea, Baltic and western Mediterranean
abilities: Adjusts skin colour and pattern to match the background
Buries itself with a flick of its fins
Young migrate into shallow sandy nurseries like the Wadden Sea
Bites off siphons of buried clams
edibilityNote: Low mercury; mild white flesh. A staple of British fish and chips and Danish open sandwiches.

animal.diet: Bivalves, polychaete worms, crustaceans
animal.habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms from the shore to 200 m
animal.size: Usually 25–40 cm; up to ~1 m and 7 kg
animal.behaviour: Feeds mainly at night and rests buried in sand by day; North Sea plaice migrate to spawning grounds in the Southern Bight in winter.
fieldMarks: Oval flatfish with both eyes on the right side
Brown upper side with conspicuous bright orange-red spots
Row of 4–7 bony knobs on the head behind the eyes
Smooth skin and white underside
animal.lookalikes: Flounder (Platichthys flesus) has rough prickles along the fin bases and dull spots; dab has a strongly curved lateral line over the pectoral fin and rough skin.
animal.whereToSee: Sandy shallows of the North Sea, Danish and Dutch coasts, Irish Sea
animal.season: Resident; inshore in summer, spawning Jan–Mar

lore: Plaice studies by Walter Garstang and the North Sea 'plaice box' were foundational for fisheries science, and plaice catches dropped sharply then rebounded during and after both World Wars when fishing stopped.
funFact: North Sea plaice stocks reached record highs in the 2010s after fishing pressure was cut.

summary: A sparrow-sized bird that builds the largest nests of any bird: colossal communal haystacks in camelthorn trees, housing hundreds of birds in separate chambers. The nest buffers temperatures in the Kalahari's searing days and freezing nights.
nativeRange: Southern Africa: Namibia, Botswana and South Africa (Kalahari and Karoo)
abilities: Builds nests weighing up to around a tonne, with up to 100 or more separate chambers
Nest interiors stay much warmer at night and cooler by day than outside
Colonies may be used for many decades, some for over a century
Provides homes for pygmy falcons, lovebirds, finches and reptiles

animal.diet: Insects, especially termites, plus seeds
animal.habitat: Arid savanna with large trees such as camelthorn (Vachellia erioloba), also telephone poles
animal.behaviour: Members of a colony continually add straw to the roof and maintain individual chambers; helpers feed young.
fieldMarks: Black chin and throat patch
Scalloped back pattern with dark feathers edged pale
Black-and-white scaly flanks
Pale, heavy conical bill
Brownish crown
animal.voice: Chattering, twittering contact calls around the colony; a 'chip-chip' in flight.
animal.lookalikes: Scaly-feathered weaver (scaly-feathered finch) is smaller with a white moustache and black stripes, and lacks the black throat. House sparrows lack the scaly flanks and black chin.
animal.whereToSee: Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, Augrabies Falls, Kalahari roads in Namibia (nests on telephone poles), Etosha
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The French naturalist François Le Vaillant described the giant nests in the 1780s; the bird's French name, républicain, likens a colony to a republic.
funFact: Large nests can collapse the trees that hold them, especially after rain soaks the straw.

wiki.extract: The sociable weaver is a species of bird in the weaver family, endemic to Southern Africa. It is the only species in its genus Philetairus. It is found in South Africa, Namibia, and Botswana, but its range is centered within the Northern Cape Province of South Africa. The species builds large, compound, community nests, a rarity among birds. These nests are perhaps the most spectacular structure built by any bird.

summary: A sparrow-sized weaver whose breeding males stitch long, retort-shaped hanging nests from strips of green grass and palm leaf, often over water. Females inspect the half-built nests and choose a mate by the quality of his work.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through Myanmar and Thailand to Sumatra and Java
abilities: Weaves nests with knots and loops from strips of grass torn from living leaves
Builds a long entrance tube that deters snakes and other predators
Males build several nests in a season and court females at each
Presses blobs of mud inside the nest chamber, possibly to balance it in wind

animal.diet: Seeds and grain, especially rice; insects for nestlings
animal.habitat: Cultivation, grassland and scrub with palms, acacias or trees near water
animal.behaviour: Colonies of nests hang from date and palmyra palms, thorny acacias and telephone wires; males flutter their wings and call at nests to attract females.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: bright yellow crown and breast patch, dark brown face mask and throat
Female and non-breeding male: streaked brown, sparrow-like, with a buff eyebrow
Heavy conical bill
Hanging retort-shaped nest is the easiest sign of the species
animal.voice: Chattering 'chit-chit' calls and a wheezy, sizzling song from males at the nest
animal.lookalikes: Black-breasted weaver has a black breast band; Streaked weaver has a heavily streaked breast; female resembles a House sparrow but has a heavier bill and streaked crown.
animal.whereToSee: Rice and sugarcane country across Punjab, Sindh and India; nests easily seen at Keoladeo and in Kerala and Sri Lankan paddy-lands
animal.season: Resident; colonies active during the monsoon (May–Sep)

lore: The Bengali poet Rajanikanta Sen's poem 'Swadhinatar Sukh' contrasts the babui weaver in its handmade nest with a sparrow sheltering in a borrowed house, a poem learned by schoolchildren in Bangladesh and West Bengal.
funFact: A folk belief holds that the bird sticks fireflies into the mud inside its nest to light it; the mud blobs are real, but the fireflies are not.

wiki.extract: The baya weaver is a weaverbird found across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Flocks are found in grasslands, cultivated areas, scrub and secondary growth. They are known for their hanging retort shaped nests woven from leaves, usually found on thorny trees or palm fronds, near or hanging over water where predators cannot easily reach. They are widespread and common within their range and are prone to local, seasonal movements in response to rain and food availability.

summary: Probably the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with a post-breeding population estimated at around 1.5 billion. Its vast flocks, darkening the sky, can strip a grain field in hours, earning it the name 'feathered locust'.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa outside rainforest and true desert
abilities: Forms flocks of millions that move with seasonal rains to follow ripening grass seed
Breeding colonies can contain millions of nests across many hectares
Chicks can leave the nest about two weeks after hatching

animal.diet: Grass seeds, cultivated grains and insects
animal.habitat: Dry savanna, grassland and cultivated land
animal.behaviour: Feeding flocks 'roll' across the ground as birds at the back leapfrog over those in front.
fieldMarks: Thick, conical red bill (yellowish in breeding females)
Breeding males: black (or pale) face mask framed by pink or buff
Streaky brown sparrow-like body
Red eye-ring
animal.voice: Constant chattering twitter from flocks; male song a jumbled, harsh warble.
animal.lookalikes: Red-headed and cardinal queleas are smaller-billed, with red heads in breeding males. Non-breeding bishops and widowbirds look similar but have dark or horn-coloured bills, not red.
animal.whereToSee: Large flocks across Kalahari, Etosha, Serengeti, the Sahel, especially near water in the dry season
animal.season: Present year-round, moving nomadically with rains; breeds in the wet season

lore: Quelea control, using aerial spraying and explosives at roosts, has been a major agricultural programme across Africa since the mid-20th century.
funFact: Despite control operations killing many millions of birds each year, the quelea's overall population has not noticeably declined.

wiki.extract: The red-billed quelea, also known as the red-billed weaver or red-billed dioch, is a small, seasonally nomadic, sparrow-like bird of the weaver family, Ploceidae, native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is approximately 12 cm (4.7 in) long and weighs 15 to 26 g.

summary: A nocturnal bird often mistaken for an owl, famous for its broken-branch camouflage. It has a wide, frog-like bill and hunts insects at night.
nativeRange: Throughout Australia and Tasmania
abilities: Mimics a broken branch when threatened
Night hunter catching insects with its wide bill
Mated pairs roost together for years

animal.diet: Insects, worms, spiders, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Woodland, forest, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: By day it perches motionless, closing its eyes to slits and stretching its body to blend with branches.
fieldMarks: Silver-grey or brownish streaked plumage
Wide, frog-like bill
Yellow eyes
Bristle tufts around bill
animal.voice: A low, repetitive 'oom-oom-oom'.
animal.lookalikes: Owls have hooked bills and strong talons; papuan frogmouth is larger with red eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and gardens across Australia
animal.season: Resident

funFact: Despite its look, the tawny frogmouth is more closely related to nightjars than to owls.

summary: A tiny, live-bearing fish of Trinidad and northern South America whose wildly patterned males made it a star of evolution research and the world's best-known aquarium fish. It has been released worldwide to eat mosquito larvae.
nativeRange: North-eastern South America (Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, northern Brazil) and Trinidad, Tobago and Barbados; introduced across the tropics
abilities: Gives birth to live young; females store sperm and can have several broods from one mating
Wild populations evolve duller or brighter males within a few generations depending on predators, as shown by experiments in Trinidad
Tolerates polluted, warm and brackish water

animal.diet: Omnivore: algae, mosquito and other insect larvae, small invertebrates and detritus
animal.habitat: Shallow streams, pools, ditches and ponds, including disturbed and polluted waters
animal.size: Males about 2–3 cm; females to about 5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males constantly court females with sigmoid displays or attempt sneaky matings. Females prefer males with more orange.
fieldMarks: Males tiny with mosaic patterns of orange, black, blue and iridescent spots, and often a large tail
Females larger, drab olive-grey, with a dark 'gravid spot' near the vent
Male anal fin modified into a tube-like gonopodium
Upturned mouth
animal.lookalikes: Mosquitofish (Gambusia) are similar livebearers but males are plain grey, sometimes with black spots. Endler's guppy (Poecilia wingei) from Venezuela has smaller, more metallic males.
animal.whereToSee: Streams of Trinidad's Northern Range (Aripo and Yarra rivers); drains and canals across the tropics where introduced
animal.season: Resident; breeds year-round

lore: Named after Robert John Lechmere Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad to the British Museum in 1866. John Endler's experiments in Trinidad in the late 1970s, moving guppies above waterfalls, became a classic demonstration of natural selection in the wild.
funFact: Female guppies can store sperm for months, so a single female introduced to new water can found a whole population.

wiki.extract: The guppy, also known as the peacock fish, millionfish or rainbow fish, is a member of the family Poeciliidae and, akin to most New World members of the family, is classified as a livebearer. Male guppies, which are smaller than females, have ornamental caudal and dorsal fins. Wild guppies generally feed on a variety of food sources, including benthic algae and the larvae of aquatic insects.

summary: A big, shark-like filter feeder of the Mississippi basin with a long, flat paddle for a snout. The paddle is covered in electroreceptors that detect swarms of plankton. Its only recent relative, the Chinese paddlefish, was declared extinct in 2022.
nativeRange: Mississippi River basin and nearby Gulf Coast drainages of the United States; extirpated from Canada and the Great Lakes
abilities: Its paddle-shaped rostrum carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that sense the weak electric fields of zooplankton
Swims with its mouth agape, sieving plankton through comb-like gill rakers
Makes long upstream spawning migrations, sometimes hundreds of kilometres
Belongs to a lineage that goes back over 100 million years; very similar fossils occur in Montana
edibilityNote: Firm white flesh; the roe is sold as American caviar and is a major target of poaching. Commercial and sport harvest is limited to strict seasons. Long-lived fish can accumulate mercury, PCBs and chlordane in some rivers, so follow local advisories.

animal.diet: Filter-feeder: zooplankton (water fleas, copepods) and insect larvae
animal.habitat: Slow, deep, open water of large rivers, oxbows and reservoirs
animal.size: Commonly 1–1.5 m; up to about 2.2 m and 90 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring, adults migrate upriver during floods to spawn over gravel bars. The sticky eggs hatch within days and the larvae drift downstream.
fieldMarks: Long, flat, paddle-shaped snout (about a third of body length in adults)
Smooth, scaleless grey to bluish skin
Huge mouth and a long, pointed, flap-like gill cover
Shark-like tail with a longer upper lobe
animal.lookalikes: Shovelnose sturgeon (Scaphirhynchus platorynchus) has bony scutes, a shovel-shaped snout and barbels in front of a small mouth on the underside. No other fish in its range has a long paddle snout.
animal.whereToSee: Osage River and Lake of the Ozarks (Missouri); Grand Lake o' the Cherokees (Oklahoma); Gavins Point Dam on the Missouri (South Dakota/Nebraska) during spring snagging season
animal.season: Spawning migrations March–May when rivers rise; snagging seasons in spring

lore: Native peoples of the Mississippi basin fished paddlefish long before European contact. Johann Walbaum described it in 1792 as a kind of shark, Squalus spathula.
funFact: Paddlefish with their paddle removed can still feed normally, because electroreceptors on the head and gill covers take over, but the paddle greatly extends their detection range.

wiki.extract: The American paddlefish, also known as a Mississippi paddlefish, spoon-billed cat, or spoonbill, is a species of ray-finned fish. It is the last living species of paddlefish (Polyodontidae). This family is most closely related to the sturgeons; together they make up the order Acipenseriformes, which are one of the most basal living groups of ray-finned fish. Fossil records of other paddlefish species date back 125 million years to the Early Cretaceous, with records of Polyodon extending back 65 million years to the early Paleocene. The American paddlefish is a smooth-skinned freshwater fish with an almost entirely cartilaginous skeleton and a paddle-shaped rostrum (snout), which extends nearly one-third its body length. It has been referred to as a freshwater shark because of its heterocercal tail or caudal fin resembling that of sharks, though it is not closely related. The American paddlefish is a highly derived fish because it has evolved specialised adaptations, such as filter feeding. Its rostrum and cranium are covered with tens of thousands of sensory receptors for locating swarms of zooplankton, its primary food source. The only other species of paddlefish that survived to modern times was the Chinese paddlefish, last sighted in 2003 in the Yangtze River in China and considered to have gone extinct no later than 2010.

summary: An orange-and-white reef fish that lives unharmed among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. All clownfish hatch male, and the largest fish in a group becomes the breeding female.
nativeRange: Eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific: Andaman Sea, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, northern Australia, Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands

Changes sex from male to female if the group's female dies
Defends its anemone, removes parasites and feeds it with scraps and nitrogen from its waste
Larvae find their way home to reefs by following smell and sound

animal.diet: Omnivore: zooplankton, algae, small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow lagoons and reefs, in host anemones such as Heteractis magnifica and Stichodactyla gigantea
animal.lifespan: 6–10 years in the wild; 20+ in aquariums

Thin black edging around the bands and fins
Rounded tail
Lives inside sea anemones

animal.whereToSee: Coral reefs of Bali (Tulamben and Amed) and the Similan Islands (Thailand)

wiki.extract: The ocellaris clownfish, also known as the false percula clownfish or common clownfish, is a marine fish belonging to the family Pomacentridae, which includes clownfishes and damselfishes. A. ocellaris are found in different colors, depending on where they are located. For example, black A. ocellaris with white bands can be found near northern Hawaii, USA, North America, Australia, Southeast Asia, and Japan. Orange or red-brown A. ocellaris also exist with three similar white bands on the body and head. A. ocellaris can be distinguished from other Amphiprion species based on the number of pectoral rays and dorsal spines. A. ocellaris are known to grow about 11 cm long. Females are larger than males. The life cycle of A. ocellaris varies in whether they reside at the surface or bottom of the ocean. When they initially hatch, they reside near the surface. However, when A. ocellaris enter into the juvenile stage of life, they travel down to the bottom to find shelter in a host anemone. Once they find their anemone, they form a symbiotic relationship with them.

summary: A ray with a shark-like body and a long, toothed 'saw' that it uses to sense and slash prey. Born in rivers and estuaries, it can travel hundreds of kilometres upstream, but it has vanished from much of its former range.
nativeRange: Tropical coasts, estuaries and rivers of the Atlantic, eastern Pacific and Indo-West Pacific; now largely confined to northern Australia, parts of West Africa and Central/South America
abilities: The rostrum (saw) is covered in electroreceptors that detect prey in murky water
Swipes the saw side to side to stun and impale fish
Pups are born with their saw teeth sheathed to protect the mother
Moves between seawater and freshwater, travelling hundreds of kilometres up rivers such as the Amazon

animal.diet: Fish, crustaceans, molluscs
animal.habitat: Turbid estuaries, river mouths and freshwater rivers; adults in coastal seas
animal.behaviour: Juveniles spend their early years in rivers, sometimes far inland in isolated pools such as the Fitzroy River of Western Australia, before moving to sea as adults.
fieldMarks: Long, flat, blade-like rostrum with large widely spaced teeth (14–24 pairs)
First dorsal fin starts in front of the pelvic fins
Distinct lower lobe on the tail fin
Grey to yellowish-brown, shark-like body with flattened head
animal.lookalikes: Smalltooth sawfish (P. pectinata) has more, closer-set teeth (20–34 pairs) and no tail lower lobe; sawsharks are true sharks with barbels on the saw and gill slits on the side of the head.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely; Fitzroy and Daly rivers in northern Australia; a few public aquariums in North America, Europe, Australia and Asia
animal.season: Year-round; juveniles move with wet-season floods

lore: Sawfish rostra were sold as curios worldwide; in West African Bijagós culture and among Aboriginal Australians the sawfish is an important spirit figure.
funFact: Three formerly separate species (P. microdon, P. perotteti and P. pristis) were merged into one in 2013 after genetic study.

summary: A chocolate-brown seabird that makes one of the longest migrations of any animal, a figure-of-eight loop of the Pacific of some 64,000 km a year.
nativeRange: Breeds on islands around New Zealand, southern Chile and the Falklands; ranges throughout Pacific and Atlantic
abilities: Migrates up to 64,000 km a year
Dives to nearly 70 m
Shears low over waves on stiff wings
Uses burrows up to a metre or more deep, returning at night to avoid predators

animal.diet: Fish, squid and krill
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds in burrows on islands
animal.behaviour: Rafts of thousands gather off coasts during migration.
fieldMarks: Dark sooty-brown body
Silvery underwing linings
Long, narrow wings
Slender dark bill
animal.voice: Silent at sea; moaning calls at burrows.
animal.lookalikes: Short-tailed shearwater is smaller with less silvery underwings. Flesh-footed shearwater has a pale bill and dark underwings.
animal.whereToSee: Monterey Bay (California), off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, New Zealand coasts and the Tītī (Muttonbird) Islands off Stewart Island / Rakiura
animal.season: Breeds Nov–Apr (Southern Hemisphere); in North Pacific and Atlantic May–Sep

lore: Rakiura Māori harvest tītī chicks on the Tītī Islands under customary rights.
funFact: Satellite tracking published in 2006 showed birds from New Zealand flying a figure-of-eight loop to feeding grounds off Japan, Alaska or California and back, about 64,000 km in a year.

wiki.extract: The sooty shearwater is a medium-large shearwater in the seabird family Procellariidae. In New Zealand, it is also known by its Māori name tītī, and is harvested by Māori people for muttonbird, like its relatives the wedge-tailed shearwater and the Australian short-tailed shearwater.

summary: A fynbos endemic whose males trail tails nearly twice their body length. It is a key pollinator of proteas, pushing its long bill deep into the flowerheads for nectar.
nativeRange: Fynbos of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa
abilities: Pollinates many proteas and other fynbos plants while feeding on nectar
Males perform display flights with their tails flicked over their backs and wings rattling
Lines its nest with downy protea seed fluff

animal.diet: Nectar, especially of Protea, plus insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Mature fynbos with flowering proteas; gardens
animal.size: Males up to ~44 cm including tail; females ~29 cm
animal.behaviour: Males guard flowering protea patches from high perches and chase away rivals and sunbirds.
fieldMarks: Very long tail in males (shorter in females)
Brown upperparts with a brown-streaked white breast
Bright yellow undertail coverts
White moustache and dark malar stripe
Long, down-curved bill
animal.voice: A jumble of harsh, grating and metallic notes; displaying males make a 'frrrt' wing rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Gurney's sugarbird, found further east in the eastern escarpment, has a rufous crown and breast and a shorter tail. Malachite sunbird males are green, not brown.
animal.whereToSee: Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, Harold Porter Garden (Betty's Bay), Helderberg Nature Reserve, Cape Point
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly in the winter rains (April–August)

lore: The sugarbirds form their own family found only in southern Africa, and the Cape sugarbird is an emblem of the Cape Floristic Region, one of the world's richest plant kingdoms.
funFact: Because fire periodically burns the fynbos and proteas take years to regrow and flower, sugarbirds move locally to follow mature, flowering protea stands.

wiki.extract: The Cape sugarbird is one of the eight bird species endemic to the Fynbos biome of the Western Cape and Eastern Cape provinces of South Africa.
