plates.long: This plate depicts a male 'Promerops moqueur' (Green Wood Hoopoe), characterized by its striking iridescent plumage and decurved red bill. Produced for François Le Vaillant's 'Histoire naturelle des promerops et des guêpiers' (1807), the work reflects the early 19th-century obsession with documenting global biodiversity through luxurious, scientifically accurate engravings.

plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a 'Variété du Promerops moqueur' (Green Wood Hoopoe), as documented by François Le Vaillant in 1807. The illustration showcases the bird's characteristic decurved bill and iridescent plumage, reflecting the era's dedication to precise taxonomic recording and the aesthetic beauty of natural history publications.

It is Plate 9 from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 1802 work 'Histoire naturelle des colibris,' illustrating the meticulous detail and scientific observation characteristic of early 19th-century ornithological studies.

The bird, identified as 'Le Promerops rayé,' features a long, slender, downward-curving beak and a very long, graduated tail. Its plumage is primarily brown on the upper parts and wings, with distinct white horizontal barring or 'rayé' patterns on the breast and underparts. The head is a solid reddish-brown.

This plate, from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 1802 work 'Histoire naturelle des colibris', exemplifies the precision and artistry of early 19th-century ornithological illustration, capturing the specific textures of the bird's barred plumage and curved beak.

summary: A blind, pale-pink salamander that spends its whole life in the dark underground waters of the Dinaric Karst. It keeps its feathery larval gills for life, can live for more than a century and may go years without eating. A 2026 study split the olm into nine species, and iNaturalist now restricts Proteus anguinus to one of these lineages; the account here covers the olm group as a whole.
nativeRange: Underground waters of the Dinaric Karst from northeastern Italy and Slovenia through Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina (the olm group as a whole)
abilities: Can live for 100 years or more
Survives years without food
Senses light through its skin and detects electric and magnetic fields
Keeps external gills as an adult (neoteny)

animal.diet: Small crustaceans, snails and insect larvae
animal.habitat: Cold, clean underground streams and lakes in limestone caves
animal.behaviour: Extremely inactive: one olm in a Bosnian cave was recorded in the same spot for more than seven years.
fieldMarks: Long, eel-like, pale pink-white body
Bright red feathery external gills
Tiny skin-covered eyes
Three toes on the front feet and two on the back
animal.lookalikes: The black olm (P. parkelj) of Bela Krajina in Slovenia is dark-skinned, with eyes. No other European amphibian lives permanently in caves.
animal.whereToSee: Postojna Cave (Slovenia), which has a viewing aquarium; Tular Cave Laboratory in Kranj
animal.season: Resident

lore: In 1689 Johann Weikhard von Valvasor wrote in 'The Glory of the Duchy of Carniola' that locals believed olms washed out of caves after floods were the young of dragons living underground.
funFact: In 2016 a female olm in Postojna Cave laid eggs that hatched under the care of the cave's biologists, a very rare breeding record for the species.

photos.attribution: Yerpo (CC BY-SA 3.0), Wikimedia Commons

wiki.extract: Olms are the nine species in the genus Proteus. They are aquatic salamanders, and the only exclusively cave-dwelling chordate genus found in Europe. The genus is assigned to the family Proteidae, along with Necturus. In contrast to most amphibians, this genus is entirely aquatic; eating, sleeping, and breeding underwater. Living in caves found in the Dinaric Alps, the genus is endemic to the waters that flow underground through the extensive limestone bedrock of the karst of Central and Southeastern Europe in the basin of the Soča River near Trieste, Italy, southern Slovenia, southwestern Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Introduced populations are found near Vicenza, Italy, and Kranj, Slovenia. It was first mentioned in 1689 by the local naturalist Valvasor in his Glory of the Duchy of Carniola, who reported that, after heavy rains, the olms were washed up from the underground waters and were believed by local people to be a cave dragon's offspring.

summary: An eel-like air-breather of West African floodplains that survives the dry season sealed in a mucus cocoon in baked mud for months, sometimes years. It walks along the bottom on thin, thread-like fins, a hint of how the first vertebrates moved onto land.
nativeRange: West and Central Africa: from Senegal and Gambia through the Niger, Volta and Lake Chad basins, with populations also in parts of the Congo basin
abilities: Aestivates: it burrows into mud, secretes a mucus cocoon that hardens, and breathes air through a tube to the surface while its metabolism slows
Obligate air-breather that drowns if kept from the surface
Walks and bounds along the bottom with its slender pelvic fins, a gait studied as a model for the origin of tetrapod walking
Males guard the nest and aerate the eggs
edibilityNote: Eaten in West Africa, often dug out of dry-season mud. Always cooked. As a bottom dweller in floodplains it can carry parasites and accumulate contaminants.

animal.diet: Omnivore: snails, crustaceans, insect larvae, fish, frogs and plant matter
animal.habitat: Seasonal swamps, floodplains, marshes and river margins that may dry out
animal.size: Usually 50–70 cm; up to about 1 m
animal.behaviour: As waters recede it wriggles into the mud and curls up in a cocoon, and it emerges when the rains return. Males dig nests and guard eggs and larvae.
fieldMarks: Eel-like body with a continuous fin around the rear
Long, thin, thread-like pectoral and pelvic fins with a fringe on the pectorals
Olive-brown to grey with dark spots, pale belly
Small eyes and a short, rounded snout
animal.lookalikes: Marbled lungfish (Protopterus aethiopicus) of East Africa is larger, with marbled patterning. True eels and spiny eels have no thread-like paired fins.
animal.whereToSee: Gambia River floodplains; the Inner Niger Delta (Mali); rice-growing wetlands of Senegal and Guinea-Bissau
animal.season: Active in the rainy season (roughly June–October); aestivates in the dry season

lore: Richard Owen described it in 1839 as Lepidosiren annectens, 'the connecting one', because it seemed to link fish and amphibians. Lungfish cocoons dug from Gambian mud were shipped alive to Europe, where they 'woke' in aquaria.
funFact: In 2011 researchers filmed this species lifting its body and walking on its pelvic fins along the bottom, a gait once thought to have arisen only in tetrapods.

wiki.extract: The West African lungfish, also known as the Tana lungfish or simply African lungfish, is a species of African lungfish. It is found in a wide range of freshwater habitats in West and Central Africa, as well as the northern half of Southern Africa.

summary: Puerto Rico's only surviving native parrot, a green amazon with a red forehead that fell to just 13 wild birds in 1975. Captive breeding and releases have kept it alive, though hurricanes repeatedly set back the wild flocks.
nativeRange: Endemic to Puerto Rico (formerly also Culebra and Vieques); wild populations now in El Yunque, Río Abajo and Maricao
abilities: Nests in deep natural tree cavities, especially in old palo colorado trees
Gives loud flight calls that keep pairs and flocks in contact over forest
Feeds on more than 50 kinds of native fruits, seeds and flowers

animal.diet: Fruits, seeds, flowers and leaves of native forest trees
animal.habitat: Humid upland forest and limestone karst forest
animal.behaviour: Pairs stay together year-round and fly side by side, wings almost touching.
fieldMarks: Bright green plumage with darker scaling
Narrow red band across the forehead
Broad white eye-ring
Vivid blue primaries visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, bugling squawk; its Taíno name iguaca imitates the call.
animal.lookalikes: Hispaniolan Amazon (introduced and established in Puerto Rico) is larger, with a white forehead and a maroon belly patch. Escaped pet parrots also occur in San Juan.
animal.whereToSee: Río Abajo State Forest near Arecibo and El Yunque National Forest; the Iguaca Aviary and Río Abajo aviary run breeding programmes.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Columbus's expeditions found abundant parrots on Puerto Rico, where the Taíno called them iguaca; deforestation reduced a population once estimated at around a million to a handful by the 1970s.
funFact: Hurricane Maria in 2017 wiped out most of the wild El Yunque flock, but birds in the Río Abajo population largely survived.

wiki.extract: The Puerto Rican amazon, also known as the Puerto Rican parrot or iguaca (Taíno), is the only extant parrot endemic to Puerto Rico. Measuring 28–30 cm (11.0–11.8 in), the bird is a predominantly green parrot with a red forehead and white rings around the eyes. Belonging to the Neotropical genus Amazona, its closest relatives are believed to be the Cuban amazon and the Hispaniolan amazon.

summary: The largest flying parrot by length, about a metre from bill to tail, in deep cobalt blue. Its bill cracks palm nuts too hard for almost any other animal, and it was trapped heavily for the pet trade in the 1980s.
nativeRange: Pantanal of Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay; the Cerrado of interior Brazil; and parts of eastern Amazonia (Pará)
abilities: Cracks extremely hard palm nuts, chiefly acuri (Attalea phalerata) and bocaiúva (Acrocomia aculeata)
Picks palm nuts out of cattle dung, after the cattle have digested the pulp
Uses a 'file' — ridges inside the upper bill — to grip nuts while cracking
Depends on large tree cavities, especially in the manduvi tree (Sterculia apetala), for nesting

animal.diet: Palm nuts almost exclusively; some fruit
animal.habitat: Open palm savanna and wooded wetlands with large nesting trees
animal.behaviour: Nest boxes and protected nest trees in the Pantanal, through the Instituto Arara Azul led by Neiva Guedes since 1990, have helped the population recover.
fieldMarks: Entirely cobalt-blue plumage
Bright yellow eye-ring and yellow crescent of bare skin at the base of the lower mandible
Huge, dark grey-black hooked bill
Very long, tapering tail
animal.voice: Deep, rasping, guttural screeches 'graaa-aah', audible from far away.
animal.lookalikes: Lear's Macaw (north-eastern Bahia only) is smaller, with a greenish tinge and a larger, paler yellow facial patch. Glaucous Macaw, paler and greyer, is probably extinct.
animal.whereToSee: The Pantanal of Mato Grosso do Sul and Mato Grosso, e.g. Refúgio Ecológico Caiman and lodges along the Transpantaneira.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In the 1980s an estimated 10,000 hyacinth macaws were taken from the wild for the pet trade; it is now listed on CITES Appendix I.
funFact: In the Pantanal about 90% of its nests are in manduvi trees — and the Toco Toucan, which spreads manduvi seeds, is also one of its main egg predators.

wiki.extract: The hyacinth macaw, or hyacinthine macaw, is a large parrot native to central and eastern South America. With a length of about one meter it is longer than any other species of parrot. It is the largest macaw and the largest flying parrot species. While generally easily recognized, it could be confused with the smaller Lear's macaw. Habitat loss and the trapping of wild birds for the pet trade have taken a heavy toll on their population in the wild, so the species is classified as Vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List, and it is protected by its listing on Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

summary: A large red, yellow and blue parrot of tropical American forests. It gathers on riverbank clay licks in the Amazon to eat soil.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Beak cracks extremely hard nuts and seeds
Eats clay from riverbanks, possibly for sodium and to neutralise plant toxins
Flies at around 55 km/h
Can live for over 40 years and forms lifelong pair bonds

animal.diet: Seeds, nuts, fruit, flowers and nectar
animal.habitat: Humid lowland forest, especially near rivers
animal.behaviour: Pairs fly wingtip to wingtip and gather in noisy flocks at dawn at clay licks.
fieldMarks: Large scarlet parrot with a very long pointed tail
Yellow band across the upperwing, blue flight feathers
Bare white facial skin
Pale upper bill
animal.voice: Loud, harsh, far-carrying screeches, often given in flight
animal.lookalikes: Red-and-green macaw has green wing coverts instead of yellow and lines of tiny red feathers on its white face.
animal.whereToSee: Clay licks of Tambopata, Peru; Carara National Park and the Osa Peninsula, Costa Rica
animal.season: Resident

lore: Live scarlet macaws were traded north from Mexico to the ancestral Puebloans of Chaco Canyon around 900–1150 CE for their feathers. It is the national bird of Honduras.
funFact: Macaw skeletons at Pueblo Bonito suggest the birds were kept far from their native range a thousand years ago.

wiki.extract: The scarlet macaw also called the red-and-yellow macaw, red-and-blue macaw or red-breasted macaw, is a large yellow, green, red and blue Neotropical parrot native to humid evergreen forests of the Americas. Its range extends from southeastern Mexico to Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Bolivia, Venezuela, Honduras, and Brazil in lowlands of 500 m (1,600 ft) up to 1,000 m (3,300 ft), the Caribbean island of Trinidad, as well as the Pacific island of Coiba. Formerly, the northern extent of its range included southern Tamaulipas. In some areas, it has suffered local extinction because of habitat destruction, or capture for the parrot trade, but in other areas, it remains fairly common. It is the national bird of Honduras. Like its relative the blue-and-yellow macaw, the scarlet macaw is a popular bird in aviculture as a result of its striking plumage. It is the third most common macaw species in captivity after the blue-and-yellow and red-and-green macaw respectively. In recent years it has become much rarer in captivity and much more expensive due to stricter laws, its price being higher than even red-and-green macaws.

summary: A grey, red-tailed parrot of West and Central African forests, renowned for its ability to mimic speech and to use words meaningfully. Capture for the pet trade has devastated wild populations.
nativeRange: Equatorial Africa from Côte d'Ivoire to western Kenya and Tanzania
abilities: Exceptional vocal mimic; captive birds learn hundreds of words
Shows abilities in categorisation, number and inference in laboratory studies
Gathers at dusk in communal roosts of hundreds to thousands
Visits forest clearings to eat clay, likely to aid digestion or mineral intake

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds and nuts, especially oil-palm fruits
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest, forest edges, savanna woodland mosaics and mangroves
animal.behaviour: Flocks fly to communal roosts at dusk with loud screeches and whistles, often in pairs within the flock.
fieldMarks: Ash-grey body with paler scalloped head and neck
Bright scarlet tail
Bare white face patch around a pale yellow eye
Heavy black bill
animal.voice: Shrill whistles, screeches and clicks in flight; wild birds rarely mimic.
animal.lookalikes: Timneh parrot (West Africa, from Guinea to Côte d'Ivoire), now a separate species, is darker grey with a maroon tail and a horn-coloured upper mandible.
animal.whereToSee: Lobéké and Dja (Cameroon), Odzala-Kokoua (Republic of Congo), Kibale (Uganda), Príncipe island; forest clearings known as bais
animal.season: Resident

lore: Irene Pepperberg's grey parrot Alex (1976–2007) could label objects, colours, shapes and quantities. The red tail feathers have long been used in Yoruba ritual and royal regalia.
funFact: Over a million wild-caught grey parrots are estimated to have entered international trade in recent decades; the species was moved to CITES Appendix I in 2016.

wiki.extract: The grey parrot, also known as the Congo grey parrot, is an African parrot in the family Psittacidae. Psittacus erithacus was previously also known as the African grey parrot until the Timneh parrot, previously treated as a subspecies, was elevated to a full species. The grey parrot is known for its intelligence, being considered one of the smartest bird species and is regarded for its speaking abilities.

The bird features detailed scalloped plumage and a hooked beak, accompanied by a small sprig of pinnate leaves. This woodcut represents the African Grey parrot as documented in sixteenth-century natural history.

otherNames: Hóng lǐng lǜ yīngwǔ 红领绿鹦鹉 (Chinese)
summary: A bright green, long-tailed parrot whose screeching flocks streak over South Asian cities and farmland. It is among the most successful parrots on Earth, with feral colonies thriving in London, Amsterdam, Istanbul and dozens of other cities.
nativeRange: Sahel belt of Africa and the Indian subcontinent (Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka) to Myanmar; feral populations across Europe, the Middle East, East Asia and the Americas
abilities: Survives freezing European winters in feral colonies by exploiting garden bird feeders
Learns human speech well in captivity
Raids orchards and grain fields in large flocks, cracking seeds with its hooked bill
Nests early in tree holes, competing with native hole-nesters

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit, buds, flowers and nectar
animal.habitat: Open woodland, farmland, orchards, parks and city avenues
animal.size: About 40 cm including the long tail
animal.behaviour: Gathers in large, raucous communal roosts in city trees each evening; pairs nest in natural holes or excavate soft wood.
fieldMarks: Bright green with a very long, pointed blue-green tail
Deep red hooked bill
Male has a black chin stripe and a thin rose-pink and black neck ring; females and young lack the ring
Fast, direct flight with rapid wingbeats
animal.voice: Loud, shrill screeching 'kee-ak' calls, especially in flight
animal.lookalikes: Alexandrine parakeet is much larger with a heavier bill and a maroon shoulder patch; Plum-headed parakeet has a plum-red (male) or grey (female) head; Slaty-headed parakeet (Himalaya) has a grey head.
animal.whereToSee: Abundant in cities and farmland across Pakistan and India, from Lahore and Islamabad to Delhi; also London's parks
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In Indian myth the parrot (shuka) is the mount of Kamadeva, god of love, and the sage Shuka narrates the Bhagavata Purana. On South Asian streets, trained parakeets still pick fortune cards for passers-by.
funFact: Feral rose-ringed parakeets have bred in Britain since at least the late 1960s, and the London population numbers in the tens of thousands.

wiki.extract: The rose-ringed parakeet, also known as the ring-necked parakeet, or colloquially as the Indian Ringneck, is a medium-sized parrot in the genus Psittacula, of the family Psittaculidae. It has a disjunct native range in tropical northern Africa and the Indian subcontinent, and is now introduced into many other parts of the world where populations have established themselves having been bred for the exotic pet trade and then escaped.

plates.long: A detailed woodcut of a long-tailed parrot, referred to as 'Tuy', shown in a characteristic profile view. Such illustrations were vital for European scholars to study species from the Americas, bridging the gap between traveler's tales and empirical observation.

summary: A noisy, rainbow-coloured parrot with a brush-tipped tongue for lapping nectar and pollen. Common in eastern Australian cities, it is an important pollinator of eucalypts and banksias.
nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern Australia; introduced to Perth and New Zealand
abilities: Brush-tipped tongue collects nectar and pollen
Pollinates many eucalypts, banksias and grevilleas
Forms huge, noisy communal roosts in city trees

animal.habitat: Woodland, forest edges, parks and gardens

Orange-red breast barred with yellow
Green back, wings and tail
Deep blue belly
Red bill

animal.season: Resident

lore: At Currumbin on the Gold Coast, public lorikeet feeding has drawn visitors since the 1940s. In Perth, escaped birds became an invasive pest.
funFact: Rainbow lorikeets have been recorded catching and eating meat, which may be linked to diet shortages.

wiki.extract: The rainbow lorikeet is a species of parrot found in Australia. It is common along the eastern seaboard, from northern Queensland to South Australia. Its habitat is rainforest, coastal bush, and woodland areas. Six taxa traditionally listed as subspecies of the rainbow lorikeet are now treated as separate species.

summary: One of the largest bats in the world, with a wingspan up to about 1.5 m. These fruit- and nectar-eating bats fly long distances each night, spreading pollen and seeds across Southeast Asian forests.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia: mainland from southern Myanmar and Vietnam to Malaysia, plus Sumatra, Java, Borneo, the Philippines and Lesser Sundas
abilities: Flies 50 km or more in a night between roosts and feeding trees
Pollinates night-flowering trees and disperses seeds over long distances
Finds food by sight and smell rather than echolocation
Hangs upside down using tendons that lock its claws without effort

animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and orchards; roosts in large colonies in tall trees
animal.lifespan: ~15 years in the wild; longer in captivity

Fox-like face with large eyes
Black wings and reddish or brown mantle
Hangs in large daytime roosts

funFact: Flying foxes like this one are natural hosts of Nipah virus, which they carry without getting sick.

wiki.extract: The large flying fox, also known as the greater flying fox, Malayan flying fox, Malaysian flying fox, large fruit bat, kalang, or kalong, is a southeast Asian species of megabat in the family Pteropodidae. Despite its scientific name, it feeds exclusively on fruits, nectar, and flowers, like the other flying foxes of the genus Pteropus. It is noted for being one of the largest bats. As with nearly all other Old World fruit bats, it lacks the ability to echolocate but compensates for it with well-developed eyesight.

Pale yellowish bill
Males build an avenue bower of sticks decorated with blue objects

wiki.extract: The satin bowerbird is a species of passerine bird in the bowerbird family Ptilonorhynchidae that is endemic to eastern Australia. It is the only species placed in the genus Ptilonorhynchus.

Lives comfortably in gardens and will nest on verandas and in hanging plants
Pairs mob snakes, cats and owls with loud alarm calls

animal.habitat: Gardens, scrub, farmland edges and dry open woodland

Bright crimson undertail (vent) and white rump
Dark tail with white tip

wiki.extract: The red-vented bulbul is a member of the bulbul family of passerines. It is a resident breeder across South Asia extending east to Burma. It has been introduced in many other parts of the world and has established itself in Argentina, Tonga and Fiji, as well as parts of Samoa, USA and Cook Islands. It is included in the list of the world's 100 worst invasive alien species. In New Zealand they were the target of a successful extermination campaign in 1955, however they are still sporadically reported.

summary: The world's longest snake, patterned in a net of black, gold and silver-grey. It is non-venomous and kills by constriction. Large individuals take pigs and deer, and a few well-documented cases of people being killed and swallowed are known from Indonesia.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia, from Bangladesh, northeastern India and the Nicobar Islands through Myanmar, Indochina, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines to Timor

Kills by constriction, stopping blood flow to the prey's heart and brain
Swims well and has colonised many small islands by sea
Lives in big cities such as Bangkok and Singapore, eating rats in the drains

animal.habitat: Rainforest, woodland, swamps, plantations and urban drains near water

Heat-sensing pits in the lip scales

wiki.extract: The reticulated python is a python species native to South and Southeast Asia. It is the world's longest snake, and the third heaviest after the green anaconda and Burmese python. It is a non-venomous constrictor and an excellent swimmer that has been reported far out at sea. It has colonized many small islands within its range. Because of its wide distribution, it is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List. In several countries in its range, it is hunted for its skin, for use in traditional medicine, and for sale as pets. Due to this, it is one of the most economically important reptiles worldwide. Humans, including adults, have occasionally been killed by reticulated pythons, and several well-documented cases involve victims being swallowed wholly or partly. Most recent reported fatal predation cases have occurred in Indonesia, especially on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

Such illustrations were crucial for the accurate identification of medicinal substances derived from animals, plants, and minerals, reflecting the encyclopedic and scientific ambitions of Li Shizhen's seminal work.

The Compendium of Materia Medica is a monumental work in traditional Chinese medicine, and its illustrations served as essential visual guides for identifying natural substances with medicinal value.

The image captures the creature's distinctive patterned skin and coiled posture, serving as a visual record of natural history and mythology in late Ming China.

Feeds on tussock grasses, snipping off tender bases
Recovered from near extinction through intensive conservation

animal.habitat: Alpine grassland, now also predator-free islands and sanctuaries

wiki.extract: The South Island takahē is a flightless swamphen indigenous to New Zealand and the largest living member of the rail family. It is often known by the abbreviated name takahē, which it shares with the recently extinct North Island takahē. The two takahē species are also known as notornis.

summary: A toucan with a huge rainbow-coloured bill — green, blue, orange and red — and a sulphur-yellow bib. It is the national bird of Belize.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northern Colombia and north-western Venezuela
abilities: Its bill is light — keratin over a honeycomb of bone and fibres — despite being about a third of the bird's length
Tosses fruit into the air and catches it in its throat
Disperses large seeds of rainforest trees
Groups sleep in tree holes with tails folded over their backs

animal.diet: Mainly fruit; also insects, lizards, eggs and nestlings
animal.habitat: Canopy of lowland tropical forest and edges, up to about 1,900 m
animal.behaviour: Small flocks travel through the canopy in follow-the-leader flights of a few flaps and a glide.
fieldMarks: Large, multicoloured bill: lime-green, with blue, orange and a red tip
Bright yellow face, throat and chest
Black body with red undertail coverts and white rump
Lime-green bare skin around the eye
animal.voice: A dry, frog-like croaking 'krrrek-krrrek', repeated monotonously.
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-throated Toucan has a two-tone dark-and-yellow bill and a yelping call. Collared Aracari is smaller with a red-banded yellow belly.
animal.whereToSee: Tikal (Guatemala), Cockscomb Basin and Crooked Tree (Belize), Costa Rica's Caribbean lowlands such as Tortuguero.
animal.season: Resident year-round

funFact: It is the cartoon model for Toucan Sam, the Froot Loops mascot.

wiki.extract: The keel-billed toucan, also known as rainbow-billed toucan or sulphur-breasted toucan, is a species of toucan native to southern Mexico, Central America and the far northwest of South America, and is found in tropical forests. It is the national bird of Belize. It is an omnivorous forest bird that feeds on fruit, seeds, insects, invertebrates, lizards, snakes, and small birds and their eggs.

summary: The largest toucan, with an enormous orange bill tipped in black. Unlike most toucans it lives in open savanna and woodland, and uses its bill as a radiator to shed body heat.
nativeRange: Guianas, Brazil (excluding most of the Amazon rainforest interior), eastern Bolivia, Paraguay and northern Argentina
abilities: Regulates blood flow to its bill to dump heat; the bill can account for a large share of total heat loss (Tattersall et al., Science, 2009)
Bill about 19–23 cm long yet very light
Raids nests of other birds for eggs and nestlings
Disperses seeds of Cerrado and Pantanal trees

animal.diet: Fruit, insects, eggs, nestlings and small reptiles
animal.habitat: Savanna, open woodland, palm groves, plantations and towns
animal.behaviour: It tucks its bill under its back feathers while sleeping, which reduces heat loss on cool nights.
fieldMarks: Huge, bright orange bill with a black tip and a black spot at the base
Black body with white throat and bib
Orange bare skin around the eye, with a blue eye-ring
White uppertail and red undertail coverts
animal.voice: A deep, grunting, croaking 'grrr-grrr' or 'groonk', often in series.
animal.lookalikes: White-throated (Red-billed) Toucan has a dark reddish bill with a yellow ridge and lives in rainforest. Channel-billed Toucan has a black bill with a blue base.
animal.whereToSee: The Pantanal (Mato Grosso), Iguaçu Falls, Emas National Park and towns of the Brazilian Cerrado.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The word 'toucan' comes through Portuguese from the Tupi name for the bird; early European naturalists in Brazil, including Georg Marcgrave in the 1640s, described and drew toucans.
funFact: In the Pantanal it is both the main seed disperser of the manduvi tree — the Hyacinth Macaw's main nest tree — and a major predator of Hyacinth Macaw eggs.

wiki.extract: The toco toucan is a species of bird in the toucan family Ramphastidae. It is the largest species of toucan and has a distinctive appearance, with a black body, a white throat, chest and uppertail-coverts, and red undertail-coverts. Its most conspicuous feature is its huge beak, which is yellow-orange with a black base and a large spot on the tip. It is endemic to South America, where it has a wide distribution from the Guianas south to northern Argentina and Uruguay, and its range has recently been expanding southwards. Unlike other toucans, which inhabit continuous forests, toco toucans inhabit a variety of semi-open habitats at altitudes of up to 1,750 m (5,740 ft). They are especially common in the Brazilian cerrado, gallery forests, and the wetlands of the Pantanal.

summary: North America's largest true frog, whose deep, booming call carries across summer ponds. It will eat almost anything it can fit in its mouth. Introduced around the world for frog legs, it has become an invasive species that eats native frogs and spreads disease.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, from southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico; introduced in western North America, South America, Europe and East Asia
abilities: Eats insects, crayfish, fish, other frogs, snakes, birds and small mammals
Tadpoles may take one to three years to turn into frogs
Can jump more than ten times its own body length
Can carry chytrid fungus without becoming ill, spreading it to other amphibians

animal.diet: Almost anything it can swallow
animal.habitat: Permanent ponds, lakes and slow rivers with vegetation
animal.size: Body ~9–15 cm; up to ~20 cm and ~0.5 kg
animal.behaviour: Males defend calling territories in summer and wrestle rivals.
fieldMarks: Large green to olive frog, often with darker mottling
Large round eardrum (tympanum), bigger than the eye in males
A ridge curving around the eardrum but no ridges down the back
Males have a yellow throat
animal.voice: A deep, resonant 'jug-o-rum' or bellowing 'rumm', like a foghorn or bull; heard on summer nights
animal.lookalikes: The green frog (L. clamitans) has a pair of ridges (dorsolateral folds) running down its back and calls a twangy 'gunk', like a loose banjo string. The pig frog (L. grylio) of the Southeast has a grunting call and a more pointed snout.
animal.whereToSee: Ponds, lakes and marshes across the eastern US and southern Canada
animal.season: Calls May–August; hibernates underwater in winter

edibilityNote: Hind legs are eaten and the species is farmed for meat. Cook thoroughly. Wild frogs from polluted water may carry contaminants.
lore: Mark Twain's 1865 story 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' inspired the jumping frog contest held at the Calaveras County Fair since 1928, where bullfrogs are the usual competitors.
funFact: Bullfrogs released in Japan in 1918 for food spread across the islands, and they are now listed in Japan as an invasive alien species.

wiki.extract: The American bullfrog, often simply known as the bullfrog in Canada and the United States, is a species of large frog in the family Ranidae. The species is native to eastern North America. It typically inhabits large permanent water bodies such as swamps, ponds, and lakes. The bullfrog can also be found in manmade habitats such as pools, koi ponds, canals, ditches, reservoirs and culverts. The bullfrog gets its common name from the sound the male makes during the breeding season, which sounds similar to a bull bellowing. It is a generalist carnivore, consuming a wide variety of prey. In turn, it is eaten by predators such as alligators, snakes, and birds.

summary: A brown, masked frog of northern forests that freezes solid in winter. Its heart stops and much of its body water turns to ice, and it thaws back to life in spring. It ranges farther north than any other North American amphibian, beyond the Arctic Circle.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada to the Arctic treeline, south to the Appalachians and northeastern US
abilities: Survives being frozen, with up to about two-thirds of its body water turned to ice
Floods its cells with glucose and urea, which act as antifreeze
Alaskan wood frogs survive temperatures as low as −16 °C
Breeds in temporary pools free of fish

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, slugs, snails and worms
animal.habitat: Moist woodland, breeding in vernal pools and ponds
animal.behaviour: In early spring, sometimes while ice still covers part of the pond, wood frogs gather for a breeding frenzy that lasts only a few days, laying large egg masses together.
fieldMarks: Brown, tan or rust frog with a dark mask through the eye
White line along the upper lip
Ridges (dorsolateral folds) running down the back
Often a pale stripe down the middle of the back
animal.voice: A chorus of short, rasping clucks, like quacking ducks
animal.lookalikes: Leopard frogs (L. pipiens) are green or brown with large dark spots. Pickerel frogs have squarish spots. The spring peeper is tiny with an X on its back. The wood frog's dark mask is distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Vernal pools in New England, the Great Lakes region, Ontario, Quebec, Alaska; listen in early spring
animal.season: Breeds March–May (as soon as ice melts); hibernates frozen in leaf litter in winter

funFact: A frozen wood frog shows no heartbeat or breathing. Within hours of thawing its heart starts again.

wiki.extract: Lithobates sylvaticus or Rana sylvatica, commonly known as the wood frog, is a frog species that has a broad distribution over North America, extending from the boreal forest of the north to the southern Appalachians, with several notable disjunct populations including lowland eastern North Carolina. The wood frog has garnered attention from biologists because of its freeze tolerance, relatively great degree of terrestrialism, interesting habitat associations, and relatively long-range movements. It is the only North American frog that occurs north of the Arctic Circle.

summary: Northern Europe's familiar brown frog, found from Mediterranean mountains to beyond the Arctic Circle. Each spring it is one of the first amphibians to breed, filling ponds with clumps of spawn.
nativeRange: Most of Europe from northern Spain and Britain to the Urals and western Siberia, north beyond the Arctic Circle; absent from much of the Mediterranean lowland
abilities: Breeds in water as cold as just above freezing
Lives at altitudes up to ~2,500 m in the Alps
Can change skin tone to match its surroundings over hours or days

animal.diet: Insects, slugs, snails, worms, spiders; tadpoles graze algae
animal.habitat: Ponds, ditches, marshes, damp grassland, woodland and gardens
animal.behaviour: Large numbers gather in ponds in early spring for a few days of 'explosive' breeding, often in the same pond each year.
fieldMarks: Brown, olive or yellow-brown with variable dark spots
Dark 'mask' patch behind the eye over the eardrum
Dark bars on the hind legs
Smooth, moist skin; hops rather than crawls
animal.voice: A low, soft, purring croak, like a distant motorbike, often from many frogs together
animal.lookalikes: The common toad (Bufo bufo) has warty skin, crawls and lays spawn in strings, not clumps. The moor frog (R. arvalis) has a more pointed snout and males can turn blue when breeding. The agile frog (R. dalmatina) has very long hind legs and a paler body.
animal.whereToSee: Garden ponds and wetlands across Britain, Ireland, Scandinavia and the Alps
animal.season: Spawns February–April (later in the north and mountains); hibernates in winter, males often in pond mud

funFact: In Ireland it is the only native frog; whether it arrived naturally or with medieval monks has long been debated.

wiki.extract: The common frog or grass frog, also known as the European common frog, European common brown frog, European grass frog, European Holarctic true frog, European pond frog, European brown frog, or simply the frog, is a semi-aquatic amphibian of the family Ranidae, found throughout much of Europe as far north as Scandinavia and as far east as the Urals, except for most of the Iberian Peninsula, southern Italy, and the southern Balkans. The farthest west it can be found is Ireland. It is also found in Asia, and eastward to Japan. The nominative, and most common, subspecies Rana temporaria temporaria is a largely terrestrial frog native to Europe. It is distributed throughout northern Europe and can be found from Ireland to as far east as Japan.

otherNames: Ryūgū-no-tsukai ('messenger from the sea god's palace', Japanese)
summary: The longest bony fish in the world, a silver ribbon with a crimson crest that can exceed 8 m. Rarely seen alive, it probably inspired many sea-serpent legends.
nativeRange: Tropical to temperate oceans worldwide
abilities: Longest bony fish known, with reliable records around 8 m and reports to 11 m
Swims by undulating its long dorsal fin while holding the body vertical
Can shed (autotomise) the rear part of its body; the wound heals but does not regrow
Has no teeth, filtering krill with gill rakers

animal.diet: Krill and other zooplankton, small squid
animal.habitat: Open ocean from the surface to about 1,000 m
animal.behaviour: Hovers vertically in the water column, head up, gliding with rippling dorsal fin.
fieldMarks: Extremely long, compressed, silvery ribbon-like body
Red dorsal fin running the full length, with a tall crest of elongated rays on the head
Long, oar-shaped red pelvic fin rays
Blue-black streaks and spots on the sides
animal.lookalikes: Streamer fish (Agrostichthys parkeri) of southern oceans is shorter and lacks the long oar-like pelvic rays (adults have only low ridges); ribbonfish (Trachipteridae) have a tail fin and shorter body.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely; strandings in California, Japan, Norway and New Zealand; occasional surface sightings in the Gulf of California
animal.season: Strandings most often reported in winter–spring

lore: In Japanese folklore oarfish appearances are said to foretell earthquakes; a 2019 study found no statistical link.
funFact: Norwegian fishermen called it 'king of herrings' because it was seen with shoals of herring and its crest resembled a crown.

wiki.extract: The giant oarfish is a species of oarfish of the family Regalecidae. It is an oceanodromous species with a worldwide distribution, excluding polar regions. Other common names include Pacific oarfish, king of herrings, and ribbonfish.

summary: The largest bird in the Americas, a flightless ratite of the pampas and savannas of South America. Males alone build the nest, incubate eggs laid by several females, and fiercely guard the chicks.
nativeRange: Eastern and central South America: Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina; a feral population in northern Germany descends from escaped birds

One male's nest may hold dozens of eggs laid by several females
Males defend chicks aggressively, charging people and horses
Eats plants toxic or unpalatable to many grazers

animal.diet: Broad-leaved plants, seeds, fruit, insects, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open grassland, savanna and farmland
animal.lifespan: Around 10–15 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: Up to about 1.5 m tall; 20–40 kg
animal.behaviour: Outside the breeding season rheas form flocks of 10–100, often alongside deer, guanacos or cattle.
fieldMarks: Very large, flightless, grey-brown bird with a long neck
Black feathering at the base of the neck and upper back in males
Three forward-pointing toes
Shaggy, drooping wings covering the body
animal.voice: Breeding males give a deep, booming 'nan-doo'.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser (Darwin's) Rhea of Patagonia and the high Andes is smaller and spotted white. There are no other large flightless birds in South America.
animal.whereToSee: The Pampas of Argentina and Uruguay, Emas National Park and the Pantanal (Brazil), the Chaco of Paraguay.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Guaraní and other Indigenous peoples of Brazil see a rhea constellation (Ema) in the sky near the Southern Cross; gauchos hunted it on horseback with boleadoras.
funFact: Its genus name Rhea comes from the mother of the gods in Greek myth.

wiki.extract: The greater rhea is a species of flightless bird native to eastern South America. Other names for the greater rhea include the grey, common, or American rhea; ema (Portuguese); or ñandú. One of two species in the genus Rhea, in the family Rheidae, it inhabits a variety of open areas, such as grasslands, savanna or grassy wetlands. Weighing 20–27 kilograms (44–60 lb), the greater rhea is the largest native bird in the Americas. In the wild, the greater rhea has a life expectancy of 10.5 years. It is also notable for its reproductive habits, and for the fact that a population has established itself in Northern Germany in the 2000s and 2010s. The species is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN.

summary: The largest living fish, a slow-moving filter feeder that can grow longer than a bus. Despite its size it eats plankton, fish eggs and small fish, and it is harmless to divers.
nativeRange: Tropical and warm-temperate seas worldwide; aggregations at Ningaloo (Australia), Yucatán (Mexico), Donsol and Oslob (Philippines), the Maldives and the Gulf of Oman
abilities: Filters plankton through spongy pads across its gills, swallowing by suction as well as by swimming forward
Dives to nearly 2,000 m
Migrates thousands of kilometres to seasonal feeding sites, such as spawning coral and fish
Each shark's spot pattern is unique and is matched using an algorithm built for mapping stars

animal.diet: Filter feeder: plankton, krill, fish and coral eggs, small fish and squid
animal.habitat: Warm open ocean and plankton-rich coasts
animal.size: Usually 5–12 m; largest reliably measured about 18–19 m; up to ~20 t
animal.behaviour: A female caught off Taiwan in 1995 carried about 300 embryos at different stages, showing that the species hatches eggs inside the mother and gives birth to live young.
fieldMarks: Largest fish; flattened head and wide mouth at the front
Dark grey with pale spots and stripes
Ridges along the back
Swims slowly near the surface
animal.lookalikes: Basking shark lacks spots and has huge gill slits.
animal.whereToSee: Ningaloo Reef (Australia), Isla Holbox and Isla Mujeres (Mexico) and Donsol (Philippines)
animal.season: Ningaloo Mar–Jul; Mexico Jun–Sep; Donsol about Dec–May

lore: Japanese fishermen called it Ebisu-zame after the god of fishing and good fortune, because schools of fish gathered around it.
funFact: Its skin can be up to about 10 cm thick, among the thickest of any animal.

wiki.extract: The whale shark is a slow-moving, filter-feeding carpet shark and the largest known extant fish species. An individual with a length of 18.8 m (61.7 ft) has been considered the largest reliably recorded. The whale shark holds many records for size in the animal kingdom, most notably being by far the largest living non-cetacean animal. It is the only living species of the genus Rhincodon and the only extant member of the family Rhincodontidae, which belongs to the subclass Elasmobranchii in the class Chondrichthyes. Before 1984, it was classified as Rhiniodon into Rhinodontidae. An extinct species, Rhincodon ferriolensis, was described in Europe, in the Late Burdigalian stage.

summary: The largest rhinoceros and, after elephants, the heaviest land animal, a grazer with a wide square lip for cropping grass. Southern white rhinos recovered from perhaps fewer than a hundred around 1900 to over 15,000, though poaching for horn remains a constant threat.
nativeRange: Southern Africa (mainly South Africa, plus Namibia, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Botswana and others); the northern form once ranged from Uganda to Chad
abilities: Mows grass with a broad, square lip, creating short 'grazing lawns' used by other grazers
Communicates through shared dung middens, which carry information about sex, age and breeding state
Has a front horn of compacted keratin that can exceed 1 m
Charges at up to ~40 km/h

animal.diet: Herbivore: short grasses
animal.habitat: Open grassland and savanna with water and shade
animal.size: Males up to ~2,300–3,600 kg and ~1.8 m at the shoulder; females ~1,700 kg
animal.behaviour: Calves walk ahead of their mothers, unlike black rhino calves, which follow behind.
fieldMarks: Wide, square lip
Hump on the neck
Two horns
Grazes on grass
animal.lookalikes: Black rhino has a hooked lip, no neck hump and browses; white rhino calves run ahead of their mother, black rhino calves behind. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Hluhluwe–iMfolozi Park and Kruger (South Africa)
animal.season: Resident

lore: Reserves in Zululand, including Hluhluwe-iMfolozi (1895), sheltered the last southern white rhinos, and 'Operation Rhino' in the 1960s moved them to parks across Africa. The name 'white' is often traced, without firm evidence, to Dutch or Afrikaans wijd, 'wide', for its mouth.
funFact: Only two northern white rhinos, both female, survive; scientists are trying to save the subspecies with IVF and surrogate southern white mothers.

wiki.extract: The white rhinoceros, white rhino or square-lipped rhinoceros is the largest extant species of rhinoceros. It has a wide mouth used for grazing and is the most social of all rhino species. The white rhinoceros consists of two subspecies: the southern white rhinoceros, with an estimated 17,464 individuals in the wild as of the end of 2023, and the much rarer northern white rhinoceros. The northern subspecies is critically endangered and on the brink of extinction; it has only two confirmed left as of 2018. Sudan, the world's last known male northern white rhinoceros, died in Kenya in March 2018. White rhinoceros can run up to 40 mph (64 km/h) for very short bursts. They can maintain speeds of around 30–31 mph (48–50 km/h) for a good amount of time, and they have good stamina.

summary: A single-horned rhino with skin folded like riveted armour plates, living in the tall floodplain grasslands of the Brahmaputra and the Nepal terai. From fewer than 200 animals in the early 1900s it has recovered to over 4,000, one of Asia's great conservation comebacks, about two-thirds of them in Kaziranga National Park.
nativeRange: Northeast India (Assam, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh) and lowland Nepal; formerly across the Indus and Ganges plains
abilities: Grazes tall elephant grass, keeping floodplain grasslands open for other species
Strong swimmer that crosses rivers and wallows for hours
Defends itself mainly with sharp lower tusks (incisors) rather than its horn
Uses communal dung heaps (middens) that act as scent noticeboards

animal.diet: Grasses, reeds, aquatic plants, fruit, leaves and crops
animal.habitat: Alluvial floodplain grassland, swamps and adjoining forest
animal.size: 1.7–2 m at shoulder; males about 2,000–2,700 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary, but gathers at wallows and grazing lawns. Feeds mainly in the morning and evening and lies in mud or water through the heat of the day.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: massive grey body with deep skin folds at shoulder, flank and rump giving an 'armour-plated' look
Single horn, usually 20–30 cm, on the nose
Skin covered with wart-like bumps on the shoulders and legs
Signs: large dung middens along trails, three-toed tracks about 25 cm across, wallows in mud
animal.lookalikes: The Javan rhino (also one-horned) survives only in Ujung Kulon, Java, and has finer, mosaic-like skin texture without warts. The African white and black rhinos have two horns.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga, Pobitora and Manas national parks (Assam); Jaldapara and Gorumara (West Bengal); Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh); Chitwan and Bardia (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; Kaziranga is open roughly November–April, closed through the monsoon floods

lore: Rhinos appear on several Indus Valley Civilisation seals from Mohenjo-daro, and the Mughal emperor Babur recorded hunting them near Peshawar in the early 1500s. Albrecht Dürer's famous 1515 woodcut depicts an Indian rhino sent from Gujarat to Lisbon.
funFact: Dürer never saw the animal he drew: his armour-plated rhino, based on a sketch and a letter, remained Europe's standard image of a rhino into the 18th century.

wiki.extract: The Indian rhinoceros, also known as the greater one-horned rhinoceros, great Indian rhinoceros or Indian rhino, is a rhinoceros species native to the Indian subcontinent. It is the second largest living rhinoceros and the largest in Asia, with adult males weighing 2.07–2.2 t and adult females 1.6 t. Its thick skin is grey-brown with pinkish skin folds. It has a single horn on its snout that grows up to 57.2–61.6 cm (22.5–24.3 in) long. Its upper legs and shoulders are covered in wart-like bumps, and it is nearly hairless aside from the eyelashes, ear fringes and tail brush.

summary: A raptor on stilts: an eagle-headed bird that hunts on foot across African grasslands, striding up to 20–30 km a day and killing snakes and rodents with precise, lightning-fast kicks. It is the sole living member of its family.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from Senegal and Sudan south to the Cape
abilities: Kills prey by stamping; a measured kick delivered about five times the bird's body weight in roughly 15 milliseconds
Hunts almost entirely on foot, walking long transects through grass to flush prey
Takes venomous snakes, protected by heavily scaled lower legs and very fast strikes
Flies strongly and soars, despite spending most of the day walking

animal.diet: Grasshoppers and other large insects, rodents, lizards, snakes, small birds and eggs
animal.habitat: Open grassland and lightly wooded savanna; avoids dense woodland
animal.lifespan: Around 10–15 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: About 1.2–1.5 m tall; wingspan about 2 m; 3–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs patrol a territory side by side, stamping at tussocks to flush prey and then pinning it with repeated blows of the feet before swallowing it whole.
fieldMarks: Very long legs with black 'shorts' (feathered thighs) and bare pinkish lower legs
Pale grey body with black flight feathers
Bare orange-red facial skin around the eye
Loose crest of long black-tipped quills at the back of the head
Two very long central tail feathers projecting beyond the tail in flight
animal.voice: Usually silent; gives a deep, frog-like croak or groan, mainly in display or at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: At distance it may be taken for a crane or stork walking in grass, but neither has the hooked raptor bill, orange face, black thigh feathering or quill crest. In flight the long legs and elongated central tail feathers both trail beyond the tail, a combination no eagle shows.
animal.whereToSee: Open grasslands of Serengeti and Maasai Mara, Kruger's southern plains, Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, Etosha and the Karoo
animal.season: Resident year-round; pairs nest on flat-topped acacias in most months

lore: The secretarybird appears on the coat of arms of South Africa adopted in 2000, its rising wings symbolising protection, and on the coat of arms of Sudan. Its English name is often linked to the quill-like crest resembling pens tucked behind a clerk's ear.
funFact: High-speed filming of a captive male showed each kick lasts about 15 milliseconds, shorter than a human blink, so the bird must aim before it strikes.

wiki.extract: The secretarybird or secretary bird is a large bird of prey that is endemic to Africa. It is mostly terrestrial, spending most of its time on the ground, and is usually found in the open grasslands and savanna of the sub-Saharan region. John Frederick Miller described the species in 1779. A member of the order Accipitriformes, which also includes many other diurnal birds of prey such as eagles, hawks, kites, vultures, and harriers, it is placed in its own family, the Sagittariidae.

summary: A glossy black-and-yellow salamander of European forests, out mainly on rainy nights. Its skin secretes toxic alkaloids, and its colours warn predators. It is now threatened by a fungus, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, which has wiped out populations in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany.
nativeRange: Central and southern Europe, from Iberia to the Balkans and the Carpathians
abilities: Secretes samandarin, a neurotoxic alkaloid, from glands in its skin
Can squirt toxic secretions from glands along its spine
Females give birth to live larvae in cool streams; some populations give birth to fully formed young
Can live for decades

animal.diet: Worms, slugs, insects, spiders
animal.habitat: Damp deciduous forests near clean streams, in hilly or mountain country
animal.lifespan: ~20 years in the wild; 50+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Active at night, especially after rain. Its toxin is harmful if swallowed and stings eyes and mouth, so wash your hands after touching one.
fieldMarks: Glossy black with bold yellow (or orange or red) spots or stripes
Large parotoid glands behind the eyes
Rows of glands along the back
Stocky body, short tail
animal.lookalikes: The Alpine salamander (S. atra) is all black and lives high in the Alps. The Corsican and Near Eastern fire salamanders are separate species with their own ranges. North American spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) are dark with yellow spots but live on another continent.
animal.whereToSee: Beech forests of Germany, Switzerland, France, northern Spain and the Balkans; wet nights in spring and autumn
animal.season: Active spring to autumn on rainy nights; larvae born in spring

lore: Pliny the Elder wrote that the salamander was so cold that it could put out fires, and medieval bestiaries and Paracelsus made it the elemental spirit of fire. The belief probably arose from salamanders crawling out of logs thrown on the fire.
funFact: François I of France chose a salamander in flames as his emblem, with the motto 'Nutrisco et extinguo' ('I nourish and extinguish'); it is carved all over the Château de Chambord.

summary: A Pacific salmonid that comes in two lives: a stream trout that stays in fresh water all its life, and the sea-going steelhead that returns from the ocean to spawn. It is one of the most widely farmed and stocked fish on Earth.
nativeRange: Pacific drainages from Alaska to north-west Mexico and the Kamchatka Peninsula; introduced to over 80 countries
abilities: Steelhead migrate to sea and back, and unlike most Pacific salmon can survive spawning and return to spawn again
Leaps waterfalls and rapids on spawning migrations
Feeds on drifting insects by holding station in current, rising to the surface at the right moment
edibilityNote: Farmed rainbow trout is a major food fish. Wild trout can carry parasites, including tapeworms (Diphyllobothrium) and Anisakis in sea-run fish, so cook it or freeze it properly before eating raw. Fish from some stocked lakes have mercury or PCB advisories.

animal.diet: Carnivore: aquatic and terrestrial insects, crustaceans, fish eggs and small fish; steelhead eat squid and fish at sea
animal.habitat: Cool, clear, well-oxygenated streams, rivers and lakes; steelhead in the North Pacific
animal.size: Stream fish 25–50 cm; steelhead and lake fish to over 1 m and 20 kg
animal.behaviour: Females dig gravel nests (redds) with their tails in spring, and dominant males fight for position beside them.
fieldMarks: Pinkish-red to magenta band along each flank, brightest in spawning males
Many small black spots over the back, dorsal fin and the whole tail
Silvery to olive-green back with no red or pale halo spots
Small adipose fin; mouth ends below or just behind the eye
animal.lookalikes: Brown trout has larger black and red spots with pale halos and few spots on the tail. Cutthroat trout has a red-orange slash under the lower jaw. Fresh-run steelhead are bright silver and can be confused with coho salmon, which have spots only on the upper tail lobe and white gums.
animal.whereToSee: The McCloud River, California (source of the original hatchery strains); Kamchatka rivers; the Skeena and Dean rivers, British Columbia (steelhead); trout streams of Kashmir, Chile, Patagonia and New Zealand where introduced
animal.season: Resident trout year-round; spawns roughly February–June; steelhead runs enter rivers in summer or winter depending on the stock

lore: Hatchery eggs from California's McCloud River were shipped around the world from the 1870s, and descendants of that stock now live on six continents. The steelhead is the state fish of Washington.
funFact: Rainbow trout and steelhead are the same species. Steelhead parents can produce stream-resident offspring, and resident parents can produce sea-run ones.

wiki.extract: The rainbow trout is a species of trout native to cold-water tributaries of the Pacific Ocean in North America and Asia. The steelhead is an anadromous (sea-run) form of the coastal rainbow trout (O. m. irideus) or Columbia River redband trout (O. m. gairdneri) that usually returns to freshwater to spawn after living two to three years in the ocean.

summary: A silver ocean salmon that turns scarlet with a green head when it returns to spawn. Its runs in Bristol Bay, Alaska, number in the tens of millions, and the dying salmon carry ocean nutrients deep into lakes and forests.
nativeRange: North Pacific: rivers and lakes from the Columbia (USA) to Alaska and Kamchatka to northern Japan; landlocked kokanee widely
abilities: Navigates thousands of kilometres of ocean back to its natal river, using the Earth's magnetic field and then smell
Young spend 1–3 years in a nursery lake, a stage most Pacific salmon skip
Spawns once and dies, and the carcasses feed bears, eagles, insects and even streamside trees with marine nitrogen
Filter-feeds on plankton with many long gill rakers
edibilityNote: Deep red, rich flesh; a major commercial salmon. Wild Pacific salmon can carry Anisakis roundworms and Diphyllobothrium tapeworm larvae, so freeze it (−20 °C for 7 days) before eating raw or cold-smoked. Mercury is low.

animal.diet: Zooplankton and insect larvae in lakes; at sea, krill, amphipods, copepods and small fish and squid
animal.habitat: North Pacific Ocean; rivers with nursery lakes for spawning
animal.size: Usually 55–70 cm and 2–3 kg; kokanee much smaller
animal.behaviour: Adults stop eating on entering fresh water and live on stored fat for the upstream run. Males grow a hump and hooked jaw and fight over females on the gravel.
fieldMarks: At sea and fresh-run: metallic blue-green back, silver sides, no large black spots on back or tail
Spawning: bright red body, olive-green head, white lower jaw
Spawning males with a hooked jaw (kype) and humped back
Many (about 30–40) long, fine gill rakers on the first gill arch
animal.lookalikes: Spawning coho is red-sided with a dark head but keeps spots on the upper tail lobe and white gums. Chum has calico-like vertical purple and green bars. Chinook is much larger, with black gums and spots on both tail lobes.
animal.whereToSee: Brooks Falls, Katmai National Park, Alaska (with brown bears); Adams River, British Columbia (dominant run every 4 years); Kuril Lake, Kamchatka
animal.season: Spawning runs June–October; peak at Brooks Falls in July and at the Adams River in October

lore: Many Pacific Northwest First Nations hold a First Salmon Ceremony each year, returning the first fish's bones to the river so the salmon will come back. The English name 'sockeye' is an anglicisation of the Halkomelem name used along the Fraser River.
funFact: Nitrogen from sockeye carcasses has been traced in streamside spruce trees, and studies found trees along salmon streams grow faster than those along streams without salmon.

wiki.extract: The sockeye salmon, also called red salmon, kokanee salmon, blueback salmon, or simply sockeye, is an anadromous species of salmon found in the Northern Pacific Ocean and rivers discharging into it. This species is a Pacific salmon that is primarily red in hue during spawning. They can grow up to 84 cm in length and weigh 2.3 to 7 kg (5–15 lb). Juveniles remain in freshwater until they are ready to migrate to the ocean, over distances of up to 1,600 km (1,000 mi). Their diet consists primarily of zooplankton. Sockeye salmon are semelparous, dying after they spawn. Some populations, referred to as kokanee, do not migrate to the ocean and live their entire lives in fresh water.

summary: The largest Pacific salmon. Yukon River fish swim some 3,000 km upstream to their spawning grounds, and southern resident orcas depend on Chinook for most of their diet.
nativeRange: North Pacific: rivers from central California to Alaska and from Kamchatka to the Anadyr; introduced to New Zealand, Chile and the Great Lakes
abilities: Makes one of the longest freshwater migrations of any salmon, up the Yukon to headwaters in Canada
Separate spring, summer and fall runs use the same river at different times
Can exceed 45 kg, making it the largest of all Pacific salmon
edibilityNote: Rich, fatty flesh; the most prized Pacific salmon. Freeze before eating raw (Anisakis and tapeworm risk). Many runs are depleted or protected, so follow local regulations.

animal.diet: Insects and crustaceans in rivers; at sea, herring, anchovies, sand lance, squid and krill
animal.habitat: North Pacific Ocean; large, cold rivers with deep pools and gravel for spawning
animal.size: Commonly 75–90 cm and 9–20 kg; up to about 1.5 m and 60 kg
animal.behaviour: Adults stop feeding when they enter fresh water. Females dig deep redds in large gravel in main-stem rivers, and the dying fish feed bears, eagles and the river itself.
fieldMarks: Black gums along the lower jaw (hence 'blackmouth')
Irregular black spots on the back, dorsal fin and both lobes of the tail
Silvery sides and blue-green to purplish back; spawners darken to olive, maroon or blackish
Large size and a thick tail stalk
animal.lookalikes: Coho salmon has white gums and spots only on the upper lobe of the tail. Steelhead has a smaller mouth, white mouth lining, and the jaw does not reach far past the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Kenai River, Alaska; Yukon River at Whitehorse fishway; Columbia River at Bonneville Dam fish ladder; Rakaia and Waimakariri rivers, New Zealand (introduced)
animal.season: Runs vary by stock: spring (Mar–Jun), summer (Jun–Aug) and fall (Aug–Nov)

lore: The Columbia River Chinook fishery at Celilo Falls was a gathering place for Native peoples for thousands of years until The Dalles Dam flooded the falls in 1957. The scientific name tshawytscha comes from the Kamchatkan name, recorded by Johann Walbaum in 1792.
funFact: The sport-caught record is a 44 kg (97 lb 4 oz) Chinook taken from Alaska's Kenai River in 1985.

wiki.extract: The Chinook salmon is the largest and most valuable species of Pacific salmon. Its common name is derived from the Chinookan peoples. Other vernacular names for the species include king salmon, quinnat salmon, tsumen, spring salmon, blackmouth, and tyee salmon. The scientific species name is based on the Russian common name chavycha (чавыча).

summary: A silver ocean-going fish that is born in cold rivers, feeds in the North Atlantic and returns by smell to spawn in the stream where it hatched. Wild numbers have fallen sharply, even as farmed Atlantic salmon fill supermarkets worldwide.
nativeRange: Rivers and seas of the North Atlantic, from Portugal to the Barents Sea, Iceland, Greenland and north-eastern North America
abilities: Navigates thousands of kilometres back to its home river using the magnetic field and smell
Leaps waterfalls and weirs over 3 m high
Switches its body chemistry between fresh and salt water during smoltification
Unlike Pacific salmon, some survive spawning and return to spawn again
Carries marine nutrients upstream, feeding river and riverside ecosystems when it dies

animal.diet: Young eat aquatic insects; adults at sea eat fish such as capelin, herring and sand eels, and krill
animal.habitat: Clean, cold gravel-bedded rivers for breeding; North Atlantic feeding grounds
animal.size: Usually 60–110 cm and 2–10 kg; record ~1.5 m and ~46 kg
animal.behaviour: Young salmon (parr) stay in fresh water for one to eight years, then turn silver and head out to sea as smolts.
fieldMarks: Streamlined silver fish with small black spots
Slim tail base and forked tail
Upper jaw ends below the eye
Spawning males turn bronze-red with a hooked jaw
animal.lookalikes: Sea trout (brown trout) has a thicker tail base, a squarer tail and an upper jaw reaching past the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Falls of Shin (Scotland) and the River Spey
animal.season: Rivers year-round; leaping at Falls of Shin Jun–Sep; spawning Nov–Dec

lore: In Irish legend the young Fionn mac Cumhaill burned his thumb cooking the Salmon of Knowledge (Bradán Feasa) and gained all the world's wisdom. A salmon carved about 25,000 years ago in the rock shelter of Abri du Poisson, France, is one of the oldest fish images known.
funFact: IUCN moved the Atlantic salmon to Near Threatened in 2023 after its global population fell by about 23% between 2006 and 2020.

wiki.extract: The Atlantic salmon is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Salmonidae. It is the third largest of the Salmonidae, behind Siberian taimen and Pacific Chinook salmon, growing up to 1 m (3.3 ft) in length. Atlantic salmon are found in the northern Atlantic Ocean and in rivers that flow into it. Most populations are anadromous, hatching in streams and rivers but moving out to sea as they grow where they mature, after which the adults seasonally move upstream again to spawn.

summary: The classic fly-fishing trout of Europe, spotted in black and red. Some stay in their home stream for life, others run to sea as silver sea trout. Introduced from Europe, it now lives from Kashmir and the Himalaya to Patagonia and New Zealand.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa (Atlas Mountains) and western Asia east to Afghanistan and the Aral basin; introduced to every continent but Antarctica
abilities: One species, three life histories: river-resident brownies, lake trout and sea trout that migrate to the ocean
Strongly territorial; each fish defends a feeding lie in the current
Large lake and sea fish become fish-eaters and can exceed 15 kg
edibilityNote: Excellent eating. Cook or properly freeze wild fish, which can carry tapeworm larvae. Many wild populations are now catch-and-release only.

animal.diet: Carnivore: insect larvae and adults, crustaceans, snails and fish; sea trout eat sand eels and sprats
animal.habitat: Cold, clean streams, rivers and lakes; coastal waters for sea trout
animal.lifespan: Usually 5–8 years; some lake fish over 20
animal.size: Stream fish 20–40 cm; sea and lake trout to over 1 m
animal.behaviour: Sea trout return to their home river in summer and run upstream at night. Females cut redds in the gravel of headwaters in autumn and early winter.
fieldMarks: Golden-brown to olive body with large black spots and red or orange spots, often ringed with pale halos
Adipose fin often tipped orange-red
Tail square-cut with few or no spots
Sea trout: silvery with X-shaped black spots, like an Atlantic salmon
animal.lookalikes: Atlantic salmon has a slimmer tail stalk, a forked tail and a smaller mouth whose jaw ends level with the eye (in trout it reaches behind the eye). Rainbow trout has a pink band and small black spots all over the tail. Brook trout has worm-like markings on the back and white-edged lower fins.
animal.whereToSee: Chalk streams of southern England (Test and Itchen); Irish loughs; Lidder and Sind valleys, Kashmir; Tasmanian Central Highlands; Taupō and Mataura, New Zealand
animal.season: Resident; spawns October–January; sea trout runs June–September

lore: Aelian, writing around AD 200, described Macedonian anglers on the river Astraeus catching 'speckled fish' with flies of red wool and cock's feathers, the earliest known account of fly fishing. Trout were brought to Kashmir from Britain in 1899, and the trout streams there are still a famous fishery.
funFact: Sea trout and stream-resident brown trout can be siblings: whether a young fish goes to sea depends mostly on its growth and condition, not on separate genes alone.

wiki.extract: The brown trout is a species of carnivorous ray-finned fish and the most widely distributed species of the salmonid genus Salmo, endemic to most of Europe, West Asia and parts of North Africa, and has been widely introduced globally as a game fish, even becoming one of the world's worst invasive species outside of its native range.

summary: The most northerly freshwater fish on Earth, found in High Arctic lakes and rivers around the pole and as Ice Age relics in deep mountain lakes farther south. Spawning males turn a startling fiery red.
nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic and subarctic: Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Iceland, Scandinavia and Arctic Russia; relict lake populations in the Alps, Britain and Ireland
abilities: Lives in lakes that stay ice-covered for most of the year and stay close to 0 °C
Anadromous populations feed at sea in the brief Arctic summer and return to fresh water for winter
A single lake can hold several distinct forms (dwarf, plankton-eating, fish-eating), as in Iceland's Thingvallavatn
edibilityNote: Fine pink flesh, widely farmed in Iceland and Canada and a staple Inuit food (eaten raw, frozen, dried or fermented). Freeze wild fish before eating raw to kill tapeworm larvae (Diphyllobothrium). Some High Arctic lakes have elevated mercury in large char.

animal.diet: Carnivore: zooplankton, insect larvae, snails, crustaceans and fish, including other char
animal.habitat: Cold, deep, clear lakes and rivers; coastal waters near river mouths
animal.lifespan: Often 10–20 years; some High Arctic fish over 40
animal.size: Commonly 30–60 cm; sea-run fish to about 1 m and 15 kg
animal.behaviour: Sea-run char move downriver after ice-out to feed in coastal waters, then swim back up in late summer to winter and spawn in lakes.
fieldMarks: Dark green-grey to blue back with pale pink, cream or red spots (no black spots)
Spawning males: belly and lower flanks bright red or orange
Pectoral, pelvic and anal fins with a crisp white leading edge
Slightly forked tail; small scales
animal.lookalikes: Brook trout (S. fontinalis) has pale worm-like markings on the back and red spots with blue halos. Lake trout (S. namaycush) is grey with pale spots, a deeply forked tail and no red belly. Dolly Varden (S. malma) is very similar and is separated by gill-raker counts and range.
animal.whereToSee: Nunavut rivers (Cambridge Bay, Kugluktuk); Iceland's Thingvallavatn; Windermere (England); Swiss and Austrian alpine lakes
animal.season: Anadromous runs to sea after ice-out (June–July) and back upriver in August–September; spawns September–October

lore: Char from Windermere were potted in butter and sent to London as a delicacy in the 17th and 18th centuries, served in painted 'char dishes'. Inuit communities fish char with leisters (three-pronged spears) at stone weirs, called saputit, that are still used today.
funFact: Lake Hazen on Ellesmere Island, at about 82° N, holds char and is one of the most northerly lakes in the world with fish.

wiki.extract: The Arctic char or Arctic charr is a cold-water fish in the family Salmonidae, native to alpine lakes, as well as Arctic and subarctic coastal waters in the Holarctic. It is the world's most northerly freshwater fish. Some populations are anadromous.

Catesby's illustrations were pioneering for their time, often based on direct observation in the field, and served as a primary reference for European naturalists studying the fauna of the New World.

summary: A jumping spider about 5 mm long whose males raise a brilliantly coloured flap on the abdomen like a peacock's fan and dance for females. If the female is not impressed she may eat him.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia, mainly coastal New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland
abilities: Males unfold and raise iridescent abdominal flaps during courtship
Combines visual display with vibrations drummed through the ground
Excellent vision, including colour vision, typical of jumping spiders

animal.diet: Small insects and other arthropods, stalked and pounced on
animal.habitat: Leaf litter and low vegetation in heath, scrub and woodland
animal.behaviour: The male lifts his third pair of legs, raises his patterned flap, and sidesteps and shimmies in front of the female.
fieldMarks: Tiny jumping spider with large front eyes
Male abdomen patterned in red, orange, blue and green, with fold-out side flaps
Male third legs black with white tips, raised in display
Females mottled brown and grey
animal.lookalikes: Dozens of other Maratus species, most described since 2010, differ in the pattern and colours of the male's fan; females are very hard to tell apart.
animal.whereToSee: Heath and bushland around Sydney (e.g. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park) and in south-east Queensland.
animal.season: Mature males Aug–Dec, displaying in the austral spring

lore: Octavius Pickard-Cambridge described it in 1874 and named it volans, 'flying', after a collector's report that the flaps helped it glide. The photographs and films of Jürgen Otto made peacock spiders internet-famous from the 2010s.
funFact: Its flaps cannot be used for gliding at all; they are purely for courtship.

wiki.extract: Maratus volans is a species in the jumping spider family (Salticidae), belonging to the genus Maratus. These spiders are native to certain areas in Australia and occupy a wide distribution of habitats. They have a specialized visual system that allows them to see the full visible spectrum as well as in the ultraviolet-range; this helps them detect and pursue prey. Males of this species are characterized by their colourful abdomen flaps, which are used to attract females during courtship.

plates.long: This plate from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history compendium illustrates a wide variety of 'tree worms' (caterpillars) and other insects. The meticulous engraving and vibrant hand-coloring reflect the early modern period's intense focus on documenting and classifying the diversity of the natural world with scientific precision.

plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts a crab, specifically identified in the text as a 'Maia' or spider crab. It is part of Conrad Gessner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium', which aimed to catalog all known animals with both textual descriptions and accurate visual representations, marking a significant step in the development of modern zoology.

plates.long: This plate from Georg Wolfgang Knorr's 'Deliciae naturae selectae' (1771) presents a meticulously detailed array of seashells. The central focus is a large spider conch, surrounded by various species of scallops and spiral shells, illustrating the era's dedication to cataloging the diversity of the natural world through fine art and scientific observation.

plates.long: This 1554 woodcut from Guillaume Rondelet’s 'Libri de Piscibus Marinis' depicts a spider, identified in the text as 'De Aranea'. The illustration reflects the Renaissance transition toward empirical observation in natural history, as scholars began to supplement classical texts with detailed visual records of the natural world.

plates.long: This woodcut from Pietro Andrea Mattioli's 1560 commentary on Dioscorides depicts various species of spiders and the intricate geometry of a spider web. Such illustrations were crucial for early modern naturalists in identifying and categorizing the fauna described in classical texts.

Such illustrations were crucial for identifying natural substances used in traditional Chinese medicine, reflecting the era's commitment to empirical observation and systematic classification.

summary: A pale lime-green silk moth with long, sweeping hindwing tails, found in the deciduous forests of eastern North America. Adults have no working mouthparts and live only about a week, just long enough to mate.
nativeRange: Eastern North America, from southern Canada to Florida and eastern Texas
abilities: Spinning hindwing tails create a false echo target that diverts attacking bats away from the body
Females release a pheromone that males detect with feathery antennae over long distances
Adults never feed; they live off fat stored by the caterpillar

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat leaves of walnut, hickory, sweetgum, persimmon and birch; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed hardwood forests
animal.behaviour: Mostly active late at night; caterpillars click their mandibles and regurgitate when disturbed.
fieldMarks: Pale lime-green wings with long, twisted hindwing tails
A transparent eyespot ringed in yellow, black and blue on each wing
Purplish-brown leading edge of the forewing
White, furry body
animal.lookalikes: No similar moth in its range. The Indian moon moth (Actias selene), sometimes reared in captivity, is larger with longer tails.
animal.whereToSee: Around porch lights near hardwood forests across the eastern United States and southern Ontario/Quebec.
animal.season: One generation in the north (late May–July); two or three in the south (Mar–Sep)

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1758 as Phalaena luna, after the Roman goddess of the Moon, from specimens sent from colonial America.
funFact: In experiments where the tails were clipped off, bats caught far more luna moths, showing that the spinning tails act as decoys.
