summary: A huge yellow silk moth from Madagascar's rainforests whose male trails hindwing tails up to about 15 cm long. Adults cannot feed and live only a few days.
nativeRange: Endemic to the rainforests of Madagascar
abilities: Male has one of the longest tails of any moth, about 15 cm
Spins a silver cocoon pierced with holes that let rainwater drain away
Adults lack working mouthparts and survive on caterpillar reserves

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat leaves of native trees such as Eugenia and Weinmannia (and Eucalyptus in captivity); adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Humid evergreen rainforest
animal.size: Wingspan up to about 20 cm; male tails up to about 15 cm
fieldMarks: Bright yellow wings
One brown eyespot on each wing
Very long hindwing tails tipped with red-brown in males (shorter, broader in females)
Reddish-brown leading edge of the forewing
animal.lookalikes: The African moon moth (Argema mimosae) of mainland Africa is greener with shorter tails.
animal.whereToSee: Eastern rainforests such as Andasibe-Mantadia and Ranomafana; often displayed at butterfly houses from captive stock.

lore: Félix Édouard Guérin-Méneville described it in 1847 from Madagascar, originally as Bombyx mittrei.
funFact: Captive breeding means comet moths are regularly displayed in butterfly houses in Europe and North America, far from their Madagascan rainforests.

wiki.extract: The comet moth or Madagascan moon moth is a moth native to the rain forests of Madagascar. The species was first described by Félix Édouard Guérin-Méneville in 1847. The adult moth cannot feed and only lives for 4 to 5 days. Although endangered in the wild due to habitat loss, the comet moth has been bred in captivity. The genus name Argema is Greek for "speckled eye" referencing the abundance of eyespots on their wings, warding off predators.

summary: One of the largest moths on Earth, with a wing area of up to about 400 cm². The adult has no working mouth and lives only on fat stored as a caterpillar, dying within one to two weeks.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia, from India to southern China and Indonesia
abilities: Forewing tips resemble a cobra's head, possibly deterring predators when the moth drops and flaps
Males detect female pheromone with large feathery antennae from far away
Adults survive entirely on larval fat reserves, with vestigial mouthparts
Caterpillars spray a pungent defensive fluid
Cocoons are spun from a coarse brown silk

animal.diet: Larvae eat leaves of citrus, cinnamon, guava, soursop and other trees; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Lowland tropical and secondary forests
animal.size: Wingspan up to ~25 cm; females larger
animal.behaviour: When disturbed, the moth falls to the ground and slowly flaps, displaying its snake-head wingtips.
fieldMarks: Huge moth with reddish-brown wings banded in white, pink and purple
A triangular, scale-less translucent 'window' in each wing
Forewing tips hooked and patterned like a snake's head
Males have broad feathery antennae; females are larger with thinner antennae
animal.lookalikes: Attacus taprobanis of southern India and Sri Lanka is very similar and was once treated as a subspecies; other Attacus species are also called 'Atlas moths'. The New World Rothschildia moths look alike but live only in the Americas.
animal.season: Adults can appear all year but are most numerous Nov–Jan; each adult lives only one to two weeks

lore: In Taiwan the empty cocoons have been used as small purses, and its coarse silk has been spun experimentally. Its name may refer to the Titan Atlas or to the map-like patterns on its wings.
funFact: Its Cantonese name means 'snake's head moth', after the wingtip pattern.

wiki.extract: Attacus atlas, the Atlas moth, is a large saturniid moth endemic to the forests of Asia. The species was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.

plates.long: A detailed botanical study of Tanacetum Africanum, showing the plant's characteristic yellow flower heads and finely divided, feathery leaves. This illustration is part of the Moninckx Atlas, a monumental work documenting the exotic plants grown in the Amsterdam Hortus Medicus during the late 17th century.

plates.long: This illustration shows several birds perched in and flying around a stylized tree. It accompanies a chapter on 'Attacus', illustrating the diversity of avian life as understood in the late Middle Ages.

plates.author: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx
plates.desc: Botanical illustration of Cupressus virginiana (Taxodium distichum), showing the tree's trunk and feathery foliage.
plates.long: This detailed botanical study from the Moninckx Atlas depicts the 'Cupressus virginiana,' known today as the bald cypress. The illustration captures the delicate, needle-like foliage and characteristic structure of the tree, reflecting the era's intense interest in documenting exotic flora from the New World for the Amsterdam Botanical Garden.

plates.long: This exquisite botanical study from the Moninckx Atlas depicts the 'Cassida orientalis' with remarkable precision. Such illustrations were central to the scientific documentation of rare plants in the 17th-century Netherlands, blending artistic beauty with rigorous taxonomic observation.

plates.title: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx — Moninckx Atlas, vol. 3 (1686)
plates.author: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx
plates.desc: A detailed botanical illustration of the plant 'Aster platycarpos' (labeled as 'Afteroplatycarpos'), showing its woody stem, feathery foliage, and yellow daisy-like flowers.
plates.long: This exquisite botanical study from the Moninckx Atlas captures the delicate structure of the 'Aster platycarpos' with remarkable precision. Such illustrations were central to the scientific documentation of exotic flora in the 17th-century Netherlands, serving both as aesthetic objects and vital records for the Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam.

plates.title: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx — Moninckx Atlas, vol. 8 (1686)
plates.author: Jan Moninckx; Maria Moninckx
plates.desc: Detailed botanical illustration of a flowering plant with umbels and feathery leaves, including seeds.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving from the Moninckx Atlas depicts a member of the Apiaceae family, characterized by its distinctive umbel-shaped flower clusters and feathery foliage. Produced in 1686, this plate exemplifies the intersection of art and science in the late 17th century, serving as a permanent record of the exotic and local plants cultivated in the Amsterdam botanical garden.

summary: A small, woolly silk moth coloured like strawberry-lemonade sherbet in pink and yellow. Its caterpillar, the green-striped mapleworm, feeds on maples across eastern North America.
nativeRange: Eastern North America, from southern Canada to Florida and eastern Texas
abilities: Adults do not feed; they mate and lay eggs within days
Caterpillars can partly defoliate maples in outbreak years without usually killing the tree

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat maple leaves (especially red, silver and sugar maple) and sometimes oak; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Deciduous forests and suburbs with maples
animal.behaviour: Adults come to lights at night; young caterpillars feed in groups before dispersing.
fieldMarks: Yellow forewings with a broad pink band across the middle and pink edges
Fluffy yellow body and legs
Pink, feathery antennae (larger in males)
Caterpillar pale green with darker stripes and two black horns behind the head
animal.lookalikes: Pink-striped oakworm moth (Anisota virginiensis) is orange-brown and purplish with a translucent patch on the forewing. Spiny oakworm and other Anisota species are browner.
animal.whereToSee: Porch lights near maple woods across the eastern US and southern Canada.
animal.season: One generation in the north (May–Aug); two or three in the south (Apr–Sep)

funFact: A pale form in Missouri and Kansas, sometimes called var. alba, is almost entirely white with little or no pink.

wiki.extract: Dryocampa rubicunda, the rosy maple moth, is a small North American moth in the family Saturniidae, also known as the great silk moths. It was first described by Johan Christian Fabricius in 1793. The species is known for its wooly body and pink and yellow coloration, which varies from cream or white to bright pink or yellow. Males have bushier antennae than females, which allow them to sense female pheromones for mating.

summary: The longest of all beetles: horned males can reach about 17 cm, more than half of it horn. It ranges from southern Mexico to Bolivia and the Lesser Antilles; some recent studies split the mainland forms into separate species, leaving D. hercules in the strict sense on the Lesser Antilles.
nativeRange: Lesser Antilles (notably Guadeloupe and Dominica) in the strict sense; the wider Dynastes hercules complex ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to the Andes and Amazonia
abilities: Longest beetle in the world, males up to about 17 cm including the horn
Wing cases change from olive-yellow to black as humidity rises, through changes in a porous layer in the cuticle
Males use their pincer-like horns to lift and throw rivals

animal.diet: Adults eat rotting fruit; larvae feed on decaying wood
animal.habitat: Moist rainforest, where larvae develop inside rotting logs
animal.lifespan: Larval stage up to about 2 years; adults about 3–6 months in captivity
animal.size: Males about 5–17 cm including horn; females about 5–8 cm
animal.behaviour: Rival males lock horns, lift one another and slam the loser down or off the branch.
fieldMarks: Male: very long, forward-curving thoracic horn with a brush of golden hairs underneath, opposed by a shorter upcurved head horn
Wing cases olive-green to yellowish with scattered black spots (black when humid)
Head, thorax and horns glossy black
Females hornless, dark and often hairy
animal.lookalikes: Mainland Hercules beetles (D. h. lichyi, septentrionalis, occidentalis and others), treated by some authors as separate species, differ subtly in horn and colour and by range. Neptune beetle (D. neptunus) is all black with extra short horns. Elephant beetles (Megasoma) lack the long thoracic horn.
animal.whereToSee: Montane rainforest of Guadeloupe and Dominica; widely exhibited in insect zoos.

lore: Linnaeus named it Scarabaeus hercules in 1758 after the Greek hero. In Japan, rearing Hercules beetles bought from breeders is a popular hobby.
funFact: The yellow colour comes from a spongy layer in the wing case; when it soaks up water it turns transparent and the black layer beneath shows through.

wiki.extract: The Hercules beetle is a species of rhinoceros beetle native to the tropical forests of southern Mexico, Central America, South America, and the Lesser Antilles. It is the longest extant species of beetle in the world, and is also one of the largest flying insects in the world.

plates.title: Jan Jonston — Naeukeurige beschryving van de natuur der viervoetige dieren (1660)
plates.author: Jan Jonston
plates.desc: A comprehensive plate of various insects, including large horned beetles, smaller beetles, and winged insects, many with hand-applied color.
plates.long: This plate, labeled 'Tab. XV', displays a diverse array of insects from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history compendium. The meticulous engravings, enhanced by contemporary hand-coloring, illustrate the early modern scientific effort to categorize and document the natural world, featuring prominent specimens like the Hercules beetle alongside smaller, local varieties.

summary: One of the heaviest insects on Earth, a flower chafer of the African rainforest whose larvae can weigh around 100 g. Adults are boldly patterned in black and white and fly noisily through the canopy in search of sap and fruit.
nativeRange: Tropical forests of West and Central Africa, from Nigeria and Cameroon to the Congo basin and Uganda
abilities: Larvae can reach about 100 g, among the heaviest insect larvae known
Adult males reach about 11 cm long
Strong fliers despite their bulk, with wings folded under hard wing cases
Larvae need a high-protein diet, unusual among beetle grubs

animal.diet: Adults feed on tree sap and ripe fruit; larvae feed on decaying plant matter in the soil
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest canopy and forest edges
animal.behaviour: Males use a Y-shaped horn on the head to wrestle rivals off feeding sites on tree trunks.
fieldMarks: Very large, broad, flattened scarab
Pronotum white or cream with bold black stripes
Velvety wing cases, black-brown to chestnut with variable white markings
Males with a short forked (Y-shaped) horn; females hornless with a wedge-shaped head for digging
animal.lookalikes: Other Goliathus species differ in pattern: G. regius has mostly white wing cases netted with black; G. orientalis and G. cacicus have their own patterns and ranges. Location and wing-case pattern separate them.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests of Cameroon, Gabon and the Congo basin; captive-bred adults are shown in insect zoos.

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1771 as Scarabaeus goliatus, after the biblical giant Goliath; such beetles were prized centrepieces in European cabinets of curiosities.
funFact: Captive breeders often raise Goliath grubs on dog or cat food mixed into their substrate, because the larvae need far more protein than other scarab larvae.

wiki.extract: Goliathus goliatus is a very large species of beetle of the family Scarabaeidae, native to tropical Africa.

summary: A nocturnal African dung beetle that shapes dung into a ball and rolls it away in a straight line. It is the first animal known to orient by the band of the Milky Way.
nativeRange: Southern Africa
abilities: Holds a straight course using the light gradient of the Milky Way on moonless nights
Climbs onto its ball and 'dances' to take a celestial snapshot before rolling
Buries dung, recycling nutrients and aerating soil
Reduces fly breeding and parasite loads in grazing land

animal.diet: Dung of herbivores
animal.habitat: Open savanna and grassland with large grazing mammals
animal.behaviour: Each beetle races away from the competitive dung pile in a straight line, the quickest way to escape ball thieves.
fieldMarks: Matte black beetle about 2–3 cm long
Broad, shovel-like head edged with teeth
Front legs flattened and toothed for digging and shaping dung
Rolls a dung ball backwards with its hind legs
animal.lookalikes: Southern Africa has many similar ball-rolling Scarabaeus species; telling them apart needs close examination of the head, legs and body sculpture.
animal.season: Active in the southern summer and rainy season, when fresh dung is plentiful

lore: Ancient Egyptians saw the ball-rolling scarab as Khepri pushing the sun across the sky, and carved scarab amulets by the thousands. In 2013 Marie Dacke and colleagues showed this species navigates by the Milky Way, testing it in the Johannesburg planetarium.
funFact: Researchers fitted beetles with tiny cardboard caps to block their view of the sky; capped beetles wandered in circles.

wiki.extract: Scarabaeus satyrus is an African species of dung beetle. These beetles roll a ball of dung for some distance from where it was deposited, and bury it, excavating an underground chamber to house it. An egg is then laid in the ball, the growing larva feeding on the dung, pupating, and eventually emerging as an adult.

Such illustrations were vital for the development of natural history, blending indigenous kno

summary: A wader whose breeding males grow huge, colourful ruffs and ear tufts and battle at leks. Males come in three genetically fixed types, including a rare female-mimic that sneaks matings.
nativeRange: Breeds across northern Europe and Siberia; winters in Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Three male types: territorial 'independents', satellite males with white ruffs, and 'faeders' that look like females
The male types are controlled by a supergene formed by a chromosome inversion about 3.8 million years ago
Males are much larger than females
Huge winter flocks gather in the inland delta of the Niger and other African wetlands

animal.diet: Insects and larvae, worms; seeds and rice in winter
animal.habitat: Wet meadows, marshes and tundra; flooded fields and lake shores in winter
animal.size: Males 29–32 cm, ~180 g; females 22–26 cm, ~110 g
animal.behaviour: On the lek, males posture with ruffs spread, jumping and sparring while females (reeves) choose.
fieldMarks: Breeding males have a variable ruff and ear tufts in black, chestnut, white or mixed
Scaly upperparts with pale feather fringes outside breeding
Small head, medium bill and long orange or greenish legs
White oval patches at the sides of the tail in flight
animal.voice: Largely silent; occasional low grunts.
animal.lookalikes: Redshank has red legs and a white trailing edge to the wing. Common greenshank is grey with a long upturned bill. Juveniles can suggest buff-breasted sandpiper (a rare vagrant from America).
animal.whereToSee: Breeding in Dutch, Swedish and Norwegian meadows; passage at the Wadden Sea; winter flocks in the Senegal and Niger deltas and Indian wetlands.
animal.season: Summer visitor to the north Apr–Jul; passage migrant; winter visitor to Africa and Asia

lore: Ruffs were netted and fattened for the table in 17th–18th-century England, and the bird's name echoes the starched lace ruffs of Elizabethan dress.
funFact: The faeder males, about 1% of males, were only identified in 2006.

wiki.extract: The ruff is a medium-sized wading bird that breeds in marshes and wet meadows across northern Eurasia. This highly gregarious sandpiper is migratory and sometimes forms huge flocks in its winter grounds, which include southern and western Europe, Africa, southern Asia and Australia.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving plate (Tab. 52) depicting various birds, including the Ruff (Avis pugnax) in different plumages, stilts, and a heron.
plates.long: This plate, 'Tab. 52' from Jan Jonston's 1660 natural history, presents a detailed study of various birds. The central focus is on the Ruff (Avis pugnax), known for its elaborate breeding plumage, alongside other species like the Black-winged Stilt and the Grey Heron, all rendered with meticulous detail and vibrant hand-coloring.

plates.long: This 1672 woodcut plate from 'Schouw-toneel der aertsche schepselen' illustrates four distinct bird species: a gull (Meeuw), a partridge (Patrijs), a ruff (Kemphaentje), and a starling (Spreeuw). The illustrations utilize dense cross-hatching to suggest texture and plumage, reflecting the 17th-century Dutch interest in cataloging the natural world through accessible print media. Such works served

plates.title: Introductory Book
plates.author: Michael Scot
plates.desc: A square miniature depicting a black animal with a lion-like ruff and long tail, identified as Leancyo or Leucrocuta, walking to the left against a yellow background.
plates.long: The illustration shows the Leucrocuta, a mythical beast often described as having the body of a stag, the neck of a lion, and the head of a badger. This depiction emphasizes its hybrid nature and predatory stance, serving as a visual aid for the encyclopedic text of the Liber Introductorius.

plates.title: François Bouchard — Recueil de cent-trente-trois oiseaux des plus belles especes (1775)
plates.author: François Bouchard
plates.desc: A hand-colored copperplate engraving of a large bird of prey, identified as a Cinereous Vulture or similar species. The bird is depicted in profile facing right, standing on a rocky outcrop. It has dark brown plumage, a ruff of feathers around the neck, a pale neck, and a dark head with a prominent hooked beak and a reddish eye. To the left is a slender tree branch with green leaves, and to the right are tall blades of grass. The entire scene is enclosed in a yellow rectangular border against a light blue sky background.
plates.long: This hand-colored copperplate engraving depicts a vulture, identified by the inscription as a 'Vautour chasseur des Lievres' (Hare-hunting Vulture). Produced for François Bouchard's 1775 collection of birds and engraved by Maddalena Bouchard, it reflects the 18th-century interest in natural history and the meticulous artistic effort to document avian species with both scientific accuracy and aesth

plates.title: François Bouchard — Recueil de cent-trente-trois oiseaux des plus belles especes (1775)
plates.author: François Bouchard
plates.desc: A hand-colored natural history illustration of a King Vulture (Sarcoramphus papa) perched on a rock. The bird is depicted in profile facing right, featuring a white and tan body with black wing feathers, a white ruff around the neck, and a distinctive fleshy red and orange head with a caruncle over the beak. The rock is situated near a small body of water with reeds and green foliage. The entire scene is enclosed in a yellow rectangular border, with the species names written in Italian, Latin, and French in the bottom margin of the frame.
plates.long: This hand-colored engraving depicts a King Vulture (Sarcoramphus papa), identified by its distinctive colorful head and caruncle. Perched on a rock within a stylized landscape, the illustration reflects the 18th-century interest in documenting exotic species with scientific accuracy and artistic flair. The labels at the bottom identify the bird in Italian (Avoltoio Indiano), Latin (Vultur Indicus

plates.title: Jean Baptiste Audebert — Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis (1800)
plates.author: Jean Baptiste Audebert
plates.desc: A detailed natural history engraving of a primate, identified as "Le Moloch" (Simia Moloch). The animal is depicted in profile, standing on its hind legs with a slight crouch, its long arms reaching forward. It has light-colored, dense fur, a dark face with visible teeth in a grimace-like expression, and a ruff of lighter fur around its head.
plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts 'Le Moloch' (Simia Moloch), now known as the silvery gibbon, from Jean Baptiste Audebert's seminal work on monkeys and lemurs. The illustration showcases the meticulous scientific observation and artistic skill characteristic of late Enlightenment natural history publications, aiming to categorize and document the natural world with precision.

summary: A sparrow-sized sandpiper with a unique spatula-shaped bill tip, breeding only on coastal tundra in Chukotka and northern Kamchatka and migrating around 8,000 km down the East Asian–Australasian Flyway to winter mainly in Bangladesh and Myanmar. Only around 400–450 adult birds survive.
nativeRange: Breeds in Chukotka and northern Kamchatka, Russia; migrates via the coasts of Japan, Korea and China (especially the Yellow Sea); winters mainly in Myanmar (Gulf of Mottama) and Bangladesh
abilities: Spoon-shaped bill tip used to sweep through soft mud for tiny invertebrates
Migrates about 8,000 km each way along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway
Depends on a few critical tidal mudflats as staging sites, especially in the Yellow Sea

animal.diet: Small invertebrates: worms, crustaceans, insect larvae; seeds on the breeding grounds
animal.habitat: Lagoon spits and coastal tundra when breeding; tidal mudflats on migration and in winter
animal.behaviour: Feeds with a sweeping side-to-side motion of the bill, like a tiny spoonbill, in shallow water and soft mud.
fieldMarks: Small, stint-sized sandpiper
Black bill broadening into a flat spatula at the tip (best seen head-on or in profile at close range)
Breeding: rufous head, neck and breast
Winter: pale grey above, white below, with a white forehead
animal.voice: A soft, rasping 'preep' in flight; males give a buzzing, trilling song in display flight on the breeding grounds
animal.lookalikes: Red-necked stint is almost identical in size and plumage but has a fine, pointed bill; check the bill tip carefully and watch for the sweeping feeding action.
animal.whereToSee: Gulf of Mottama (Martaban), Myanmar, and Sonadia Island, Bangladesh, in winter; Rudong and Tiaozini mudflats, Jiangsu, China, on migration
animal.season: Winter visitor to Bangladesh and Myanmar (Nov–Mar); passage migrant in China (Apr–May, Sep–Oct); breeds Jun–Aug in Chukotka

lore: Since 2012 a 'head-starting' project in Meinypilgyno, Chukotka, has collected eggs, hatched them in incubators and released fledglings to raise breeding success. The Tiaozini mudflats where it stages became part of China's Yellow Sea World Heritage site in 2019.
funFact: Its spoon-shaped bill is already present when the chick hatches.

wiki.extract: The spoon-billed sandpiper is a small wader which breeds on the coasts of the Bering Sea and winters in Southeast Asia. This species is highly threatened, and it is said that since the 1970s the breeding population has decreased significantly. By 2000, the estimated breeding population of the species was 350–500.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a water bird, identified in the text as a species of 'Ochropus' (likely a Green Sandpiper). It is a prime example of Conrad Gessner's pioneering work in zoological illustration, which sought to provide accurate visual records of the natural world during the mid-16th century.

plates.long: A precise woodcut of a wading bird, illustrating anatomical features such as its long beak and legs. This image is part of Conrad Gessner's monumental effort to catalog all known animals in the 16th century.

summary: A long-billed shorebird holding the record for the longest nonstop flight of any bird. Godwits fly from Alaska to New Zealand and Australia across the Pacific without feeding, drinking or resting.
nativeRange: Breeds in Arctic Eurasia and Alaska; winters on coasts of Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Recorded nonstop flight of 13,560 km in about 11 days (Alaska to Tasmania, 2022)
Shrinks digestive organs before migration to carry more fat
Fat can make up over half its body weight at departure
Times departure to ride favourable winds from storm systems
Probes deep into mud for worms with a sensitive bill

animal.diet: Marine worms, molluscs and crustaceans; insects on breeding grounds
animal.habitat: Arctic tundra in summer; tidal mudflats in winter
animal.behaviour: Flocks leave Alaska in autumn on north winds and fly over the open Pacific for over a week.
fieldMarks: Large wader with a long, slightly upturned bill
Breeding male brick-red below
Winter birds grey-brown, streaked
Barred tail and no wing bar in flight
animal.voice: A nasal 'kirruk' or 'kew-kew'
animal.lookalikes: Black-tailed godwit has a straighter bill, longer legs, a bold white wing bar and a black tail band.
animal.whereToSee: Miranda (Firth of Thames) and Farewell Spit, New Zealand; the Wash and Morecambe Bay, England
animal.season: Breeds in the Arctic Jun–Jul; New Zealand Sep–Mar; Europe mainly in winter

lore: Māori knew kuaka as birds that flew to Hawaiki and beyond, and their departure marked seasons. Their epic flights were proven by satellite tags in 2007, when a female called E7 flew 11,680 km nonstop.
funFact: The record bird, tagged '234684', was only five months old when it made its flight.

wiki.extract: The bar-tailed godwit is a large and strongly migratory wader in the family Scolopacidae, which feeds on bristle-worms and shellfish on coastal mudflats and estuaries. It has distinctive red breeding plumage, long legs, and a long upturned bill. Bar-tailed godwits breed on Arctic coasts and tundra from Scandinavia to Alaska, and overwinter on coasts in temperate and tropical regions of Australia and New Zealand. The migration of the subspecies Limosa lapponica baueri across the Pacific Ocean from Alaska to New Zealand is the longest known non-stop flight of any bird, and also the longest journey without pausing to feed by any animal. The round-trip migration for this subspecies is over 29,000 km (18,020 mi).

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Limosa', likely a species of godwit, showing the bird's characteristic long bill and legs. It is a prime example of the descriptive natural history illustrations found in Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium', which sought to provide a comprehensive visual and textual record of the animal kingdom.

This illustration is from Conrad Gesner's 'Historiae Animalium', a seminal work that marked the beginning of modern zoology through its emphasis on empirical observation and detailed visual documentation.

summary: Europe's largest wader, with a very long, down-curved bill and a bubbling, haunting call that carries over moors and estuaries. It has declined steeply in Britain and Ireland, which hold a large share of the world's breeding birds.
nativeRange: Breeds from Britain and Ireland across northern and central Europe and Central Asia to Siberia; winters on coasts of western Europe, Africa, the Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Probes deep into mud for lugworms and ragworms with a bill up to about 15 cm long in females
The bill tip is flexible and sensitive, letting it feel for prey underground
Females have longer bills than males, so the sexes feed differently
Gathers in large flocks at estuary high-tide roosts

animal.diet: Worms, crabs, molluscs and insects; leatherjackets and earthworms inland
animal.habitat: Moorland, rough pasture and wet meadows for breeding; estuaries and mudflats in winter
animal.behaviour: On breeding grounds it rises on fluttering wings and glides down giving its bubbling song.
fieldMarks: Very long, down-curved bill
Grey-brown streaked plumage
White wedge up the rump and back in flight
Large size; long, blue-grey legs
animal.voice: A rising, mournful 'cur-lee' and a long, accelerating bubbling trill in display.
animal.lookalikes: Whimbrel is smaller with a shorter bill, a striped crown and a rapid seven-note 'tititititi' call. Bar-tailed godwit has a slightly upturned bill.
animal.whereToSee: Pennine and Scottish moors in spring; the Wash, Morecambe Bay, the Wadden Sea and Banc d'Arguin (Mauritania) in winter.
animal.season: Present on coasts all year; on moorland breeding grounds Mar–Jul

lore: W. B. Yeats used its cry as an image of grief in 'He Reproves the Curlew' (1899), and Benjamin Britten's church parable 'Curlew River' (1964) takes its title from the bird.
funFact: Its smaller relative the slender-billed curlew was last confirmed in Morocco in 1995, and a 2024 study concluded it is very likely extinct.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian curlew or common curlew is a very large wader in the family Scolopacidae. It is one of the most widespread of the curlews, breeding across temperate Europe and Asia. In Europe, this species is often referred to just as the "curlew", and in Scotland known as the "whaup" in Scots.

The bird is shown in profile against a large, vibrant green leaf and a textured plant stalk, a common convention in early natural history books to provide context for the species. Such illustrations were crucial for the scientific documentation and classification of flora and fauna during the E

plates.author: Carolus Clusius
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a long-billed bird, identified as Numenius Indicus.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Numenius Indicus,' likely a species of ibis or curlew, characterized by its long, curved beak and slender legs. It appears in a natural history text by Nicolas Monardes, reflecting the era's growing interest in documenting exotic fauna from distant lands. The illustration serves as a scientific record, emphasizing the bird's physical proportions and plumage patterns.

It is part of Mark Catesby's seminal work, 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands,' which was the first published account of the flora and fauna of North America.

summary: A small, inexpensive mackerel that feeds millions along the coasts of the Indian Ocean. It swims with its mouth open, filtering plankton through long, feathery gill rakers.
nativeRange: Indo-West Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to Indonesia, Australia, Samoa and Japan; entered the eastern Mediterranean via the Suez Canal
abilities: Filter-feeds by ram ventilation with long, dense gill rakers
Forms large schools near upwelling coasts during monsoon seasons
Matures in under a year
edibleParts: whole fish (fried, curried, grilled, salted and dried)
edibilityNote: Low mercury, rich in omega-3. Spoils quickly; poorly chilled fish can cause scombroid poisoning.

animal.diet: Phytoplankton, copepods, larval fish
animal.habitat: Coastal waters and bays with temperatures above 17 °C
animal.behaviour: Schools travel inshore along the Malabar and Konkan coasts with post-monsoon plankton blooms.
fieldMarks: Deep, compressed mackerel body with a pointed head
Narrow dark longitudinal stripes on the upper back
Black spot near the lower margin of the pectoral fin
Golden lateral stripe in fresh fish
Five finlets behind dorsal and anal fins
animal.lookalikes: Short mackerel (R. brachysoma) is deeper-bodied without back stripes; island mackerel (R. faughni) has dark spots instead of lines.
animal.whereToSee: Fish markets of Kerala, Goa, Mangalore, Karachi and Colombo; reef dives in the Maldives and Red Sea where schools filter-feed open-mouthed
animal.season: Peak fishery Sep–Mar on India's west coast

lore: Ayala and bangda fry and curry are staples of Kerala, Goa and Mangalorean cooking, and the fish has been salted and sun-dried on Indian beaches for centuries.
funFact: The species name comes from 'kanagurta', a Telugu name recorded by Patrick Russell in his 1803 account of the fishes of Vizagapatam on the Coromandel coast.

wiki.extract:
The Indian mackerel or bigmouth mackerel is a species of mackerel in the family Scombridae. It is commonly found in the Indian and West
Pacific oceans, and their surrounding seas. It is an important food fish and is commonly used in South and South-East Asian cuisine.

plates.title: History of Animals, Book II: On Oviparous Quadrupeds
plates.author: Conrad Gessner
plates.desc: Large vertical woodcut of a mackerel-like fish (Scomber) showing detailed scale patterns.
plates.long: This large-scale woodcut depicts a fish, likely a mackerel (Scomber), oriented vertically to fit the page layout. The fine lines used to represent scales and fin rays highlight the technical skill of Renaissance printmakers in service of early modern scientific documentation.

plates.title: Books on Marine Fishes
plates.author: Guillaume Rondelet
plates.desc: A detailed woodcut of a fish, identified as Trachurus (horse mackerel).

summary: A fast, striped schooling fish of the North Atlantic that lacks a swim bladder and must swim constantly. Its oily flesh is grilled, smoked and canned throughout Europe.
nativeRange: North Atlantic on both sides; Mediterranean and Black seas
abilities: Has no swim bladder, so it can change depth rapidly
Migrates in huge schools between spawning and feeding grounds
A northward shift of its summer feeding range into Icelandic and Faroese waters triggered the 'mackerel war' over quotas from 2010
edibilityNote: Low in mercury, unlike king mackerel. Spoils quickly and can cause scombroid poisoning if not kept cold.

animal.diet: Zooplankton, krill, small fish
animal.habitat: Shelf waters in the upper 200 m
animal.behaviour: Overwinters in deeper water and moves inshore in summer, where schools drive baitfish to the surface.
fieldMarks: Iridescent green-blue back with 20–30 wavy black bars
Silvery-white belly without spots
Two well-separated dorsal fins and 5 finlets above and below the tail
Torpedo body with small keels on the tail base
animal.lookalikes: Atlantic chub mackerel (Scomber colias) has dusky spots on the belly and a swim bladder; horse mackerel has a row of bony scutes along the lateral line.
animal.whereToSee: Cornwall, Brittany and Norwegian coasts in summer; Gulf of Maine
animal.season: Inshore summer visitor in northern Europe, roughly May–Sep

lore: In 17th-century London mackerel was allowed to be sold on Sundays because it spoils so fast; Cornish handline fishing for mackerel is centuries old.
funFact: The phrase 'mackerel sky' for rippled cirrocumulus clouds comes from the fish's barred back.

wiki.extract: The Atlantic mackerel, also known as Boston mackerel, Norwegian mackerel, Scottish mackerel or just mackerel, is a species of mackerel found in the temperate waters of the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea, and the northern Atlantic Ocean, where it is extremely common and occurs in huge shoals in the epipelagic zone down to about 200 m (660 ft). It spends the warmer months close to shore and near the ocean surface, appearing along the coast in spring and departing with the arrival of colder weather in the fall and winter months. During the fall and winter, it migrates out into deeper and more southern water, seeking warmer temperatures.

summary: A fast, sleek tropical tuna named for its sickle-shaped golden fins. It is one of the most heavily fished tunas, filling much of the world's canned and sashimi-grade 'ahi'.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide except the Mediterranean
abilities: Capable of fast bursts of speed in pursuit of prey
Partially warm-bodied, though less so than bluefin
Schools with dolphins in the eastern tropical Pacific, a link once exploited by purse-seiners
Gathers in huge numbers under floating objects and fish aggregating devices
edibilityNote: Contains moderate methylmercury, more than skipjack but generally less than bluefin or bigeye; pregnant women should moderate intake. Poor chilling causes scombroid poisoning.

animal.diet: Flying fish, squid, small tunas, crustaceans
animal.habitat: Warm surface waters above the thermocline, mostly in the upper 100 m
animal.size: Commonly 1.5 m; up to ~2.4 m and 200 kg
animal.behaviour: Forms large schools mixed by size with skipjack and dolphins, and drives baitfish to the surface in feeding frenzies.
fieldMarks: Very long, scythe-like second dorsal and anal fins in large adults
Bright yellow finlets and a golden lateral stripe
Long pectoral fins reaching the second dorsal
Belly with alternating broken vertical lines and dots
animal.lookalikes: Bigeye tuna has a larger eye, plumper body and shorter second dorsal and anal fins; bluefin has short pectorals. Young yellowfin and bigeye are very hard to separate.
animal.whereToSee: Offshore sportfishing from Hawaii, Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands, the Maldives and Gulf of Mexico oil rigs
animal.season: Year-round in the tropics

lore: In Hawaii 'ahi' has long been eaten raw in poke; the US 'dolphin-safe' label of 1990 was born from yellowfin purse-seine fisheries that netted dolphins.
funFact: Its species name comes from Portuguese albacora; the same word gave English 'albacore', now the name of a different tuna.

summary: The largest tuna, a warm-bodied torpedo that can exceed 600 kg and cross the Atlantic in a matter of months. Its heat-conserving circulation lets it hunt in cold northern waters, and its fatty belly meat has made it one of the most valuable fish on Earth.
nativeRange: North Atlantic from the Gulf of Mexico and Canary Islands to Newfoundland and Norway; Mediterranean Sea
abilities: Regional endothermy: a countercurrent heat exchanger (rete mirabile) keeps muscles, eyes and brain well above water temperature
Crosses the Atlantic between western and eastern feeding grounds, a journey electronic tags show can take only a few months
Dives below 1,000 m and tolerates water from about 3 °C to 30 °C
Retracts its fins into grooves to reduce drag at high speed
edibilityNote: Highly prized raw. As a large, long-lived predator it accumulates methylmercury; pregnant women and young children are advised to limit or avoid it. Improperly chilled tuna can cause scombroid (histamine) poisoning.

animal.diet: Herring, mackerel, sardines, squid, sand lance and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Epipelagic open ocean and shelf waters; spawns in warm, stratified water in the Gulf of Mexico and Mediterranean
animal.size: Commonly 2 m and 250 kg; record ~3.3 m and 680 kg
animal.behaviour: Schools by size and makes seasonal migrations of thousands of kilometres between cold feeding grounds and warm spawning seas, returning faithfully to the sea where it was spawned.
fieldMarks: Massive, deep, spindle-shaped body, deepest near the first dorsal fin
Short pectoral fins that do not reach the second dorsal fin
Dark blue-black back, silvery-white belly with pale spots and bars
Row of yellow finlets edged in black behind the dorsal and anal fins
Strong lateral keel on the caudal peduncle
animal.lookalikes: Pacific bluefin (T. orientalis) is nearly identical but lives in the Pacific. Yellowfin has long yellow second dorsal and anal fins and a slimmer body; bigeye has longer pectorals reaching the second dorsal.
animal.whereToSee: Strait of Gibraltar (historic almadraba traps), Gulf of St. Lawrence and Prince Edward Island, Norway and Scotland in late summer, Balearic Islands
animal.season: North Atlantic feeding grounds Jul–Oct; Mediterranean spawning May–Jul

lore: Phoenicians and Romans worked tuna traps at Gibraltar and Sicily; the Andalusian almadraba of Cádiz still operates, and Aristotle described the fish's seasonal passage through the Bosporus.
funFact: Heavy overfishing in the 1990s and 2000s, especially in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean, was followed by a strict ICCAT recovery plan from 2007; the eastern stock rebounded, and in 2021 the IUCN moved the species from Endangered to Least Concern, although the smaller western (Gulf of Mexico) stock remains depleted.

summary: A plain brown wading bird with a hammer-shaped head and the most extravagant nest of any bird its size: a domed stick mound more than a metre across. It is the only member of its family.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar and south-western Arabia
abilities: Builds a domed nest of thousands of sticks, plastered with mud, with a side entrance and inner chamber
Pairs may build several such nests a year even when not breeding
Abandoned nests are taken over by owls, genets, snakes, bees and other animals

animal.diet: Mainly frogs and tadpoles, also small fish, shrimps and insects
animal.habitat: Shallow water edges of rivers, dams, pools and marshes with trees nearby
animal.behaviour: Groups perform 'false mounting' rituals, climbing on each other's backs, a behaviour not tied to mating.
fieldMarks: Uniform dull brown plumage
Backward-pointing crest balancing a heavy bill, giving a hammer-head profile
Flattened, slightly hooked black bill
Fairly short black legs for a wader
Flies with neck slightly extended, often with a buoyant, soaring flight
animal.voice: A high, nasal 'yip' or 'kek' in flight; groups give excited, rising 'yip-purrr' chorus calls.
animal.lookalikes: Shape is unique. Distant birds may suggest a small heron or immature night heron, but no heron has the thick crest-and-bill hammer silhouette or uniform brown plumage.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any African wetland with trees: Kruger, Okavango Delta, Lake Naivasha, Murchison Falls; also western Madagascar
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In much of Africa the hamerkop is a bird of omen: a Zulu and Xhosa belief warns that harming it or its nest brings lightning or misfortune, and in Madagascar it is associated with bad luck.
funFact: A single hamerkop nest can take months to build, contain thousands of sticks, and is reputedly strong enough to bear the weight of a person.

wiki.extract: The hamerkop, also called the umbrette, is a medium-sized water bird with brown plumage. It is found in mainland Africa, Madagascar and Arabia, living in a wide variety of wetlands, including estuaries, lakesides, fish ponds, riverbanks, and rocky coasts. The shape of its head, with its long bill and crest at the back, gives this species its name, hamerkop being the Afrikaans word for hammerhead. Long considered to sit with the Ciconiiformes, the species and its family is now placed with the Pelecaniformes, its closest relatives thought to be the pelicans and the shoebill. It is the only living species in the genus Scopus and the family Scopidae.

summary: A flamboyant, zebra-striped reef predator with venomous fin spines. Released from aquaria in Florida, it became one of the fastest and most damaging marine invasions known, spreading across the Caribbean in two decades.
nativeRange: Western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean; invasive in the western Atlantic, Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico
abilities: Dorsal, pelvic and anal spines deliver a painful venom
Herds small fish into corners with fanned pectoral fins
Blows jets of water at prey to disorient it before striking
Females can release egg masses every few days year-round in warm waters
edibilityNote: The flesh is not venomous; venom lies only in the spines, which must be removed carefully. Eating lionfish is promoted to control the invasion. Large lionfish from some Caribbean areas can carry ciguatoxin.

animal.diet: Small reef fish and shrimp
animal.habitat: Reefs, wrecks, mangroves and hard-bottom down to 300 m
animal.behaviour: Hovers motionless with fins spread, then lunges with a rapid suction strike; often hunts at dawn and dusk.
fieldMarks: Bold red-brown and white vertical stripes
Long, feathery separated dorsal spines
Huge fan-like pectoral fins
Fleshy tentacles above the eyes
Spotted second dorsal, anal and tail fins
animal.lookalikes: Devil firefish (P. miles) is nearly identical, with usually 10 vs 11 dorsal soft rays and 6 vs 7 anal soft rays, and is the invader in the Mediterranean; both are invasive in the Atlantic. Clearfin lionfish (P. radiata) has white stripes on clear fins.
animal.whereToSee: Native: Indonesia, Philippines, Great Barrier Reef. Invasive: Florida Keys, Bahamas, Belize, Honduras reefs
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Florida and Caribbean islands hold lionfish derbies where divers spear thousands in a day; the first Atlantic sighting was off Dania Beach, Florida in 1985.
funFact: Early mitochondrial DNA studies suggested the Atlantic invasion began with as few as about ten fish, although later modelling (Selwyn et al. 2017) put the most likely number of founders at around a hundred or more.

wiki.extract: The red lionfish is a venomous coral reef fish in the family Scorpaenidae, order Scorpaeniformes. It is mainly native to the Indo-Pacific region, but has become an invasive species in the Caribbean Sea, as well as along the East Coast of the United States and East Mediterranean and also found in Brazil at Fernando de Noronha.

summary: A master of disguise that can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in under a second, despite being colour-blind. Its ink gave artists the pigment sepia, and its internal shell, the cuttlebone, washes up on European beaches.
nativeRange: Eastern Atlantic from the North Sea and Baltic approaches south to north-west Africa; Mediterranean Sea
abilities: Millions of chromatophores give rapid, patterned colour change
Raises skin papillae to mimic rocks and seaweed
Sees polarised light and uses it in signalling
Adjusts buoyancy by pumping fluid in and out of its chambered cuttlebone
Ejects clouds of melanin ink

animal.diet: Shrimps, crabs and small fish, caught with two shooting tentacles
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, seagrass and sandy bottoms, down to about 200 m
animal.size: Mantle up to about 45 cm; weight up to about 4 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring, adults move inshore to spawn; small males have been reported to mimic females to slip past large rival males and mate, a tactic better known in the giant Australian cuttlefish.
fieldMarks: Broad, oval, flattened body with a narrow fin running around the entire edge
W-shaped pupils
Eight short arms plus two long feeding tentacles
Breeding males show bold black-and-white 'zebra' stripes
animal.lookalikes: Elegant cuttlefish (Sepia elegans) and pink cuttlefish (S. orbignyana) are smaller and pinkish, with a sharp spine at the rear of the cuttlebone. Squid have fins only at the tail end, and octopuses have no fins.
animal.whereToSee: Seagrass and sandy bays in the Mediterranean and along the English Channel and Biscay coasts; cuttlebones on beaches in summer.
animal.season: Inshore spawning Apr–Jul

edibilityNote: Eaten grilled, fried and stewed across the Mediterranean; the ink colours black rice and pasta dishes.
lore: Aristotle described its ink, mating and egg-laying in his History of Animals. Brown 'sepia' ink made from it was used for writing and drawing, and the name of the genus became a word for the colour.
funFact: Its cuttlebone is sold as a calcium supplement for caged birds.

wiki.extract: The common cuttlefish or European common cuttlefish is one of the largest and best-known cuttlefish species. They are a migratory species that spend the summer and spring inshore for spawning and then move to depths of 100–200 metres (330–660 ft) during autumn and winter. They grow to 49 centimetres (19 in) in mantle length and 4 kilograms (8.8 lb) in weight. Animals from subtropical seas are smaller and rarely exceed 30 centimetres (12 in) in mantle length.

summary: The most famous piranha, with razor-edged interlocking teeth and a bright red belly. It mostly schools for safety and scavenges or nips fins, and has a far milder nature than its film reputation.
nativeRange: Amazon, Paraguay–Paraná and Essequibo basins and coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil
abilities: Has a single row of triangular, interlocking teeth in each jaw that shear flesh like scissors
Has one of the strongest bites relative to body size of any bony fish
Schools mainly to protect itself from cormorants, dolphins and caimans
Makes barking and drumming sounds with muscles on its swim bladder when threatened or competing
edibilityNote: Eaten across the Amazon and Pantanal, notably as caldo de piranha (piranha soup). Bony. Handle catches with care: the bite cuts deeply.

animal.diet: Omnivore and predator: fish, fins and scales, insects, crustaceans, carrion and some seeds and plants
animal.habitat: Slow, warm rivers, floodplain lakes and flooded forest, often among vegetation
animal.size: Usually 20–30 cm; up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Schools of 20 or more hunt mainly at dawn and dusk. Feeding frenzies are rare and usually happen in drought-stranded pools or around injured or dead animals. Pairs spawn among plants, and the male guards the eggs.
fieldMarks: Deep, compressed disc-shaped body with a blunt head and protruding lower jaw
Silvery-grey to olive back with glittery scales and a red to orange throat and belly
Dark spot near the gill cover in juveniles; large fish darker
Small adipose fin and a black-edged tail
animal.lookalikes: Pacu (Colossoma, Piaractus) are much larger, with square, human-like molar teeth. Black piranha (Serrasalmus rhombeus) is darker, with red eyes and no red belly. Silver dollars (Metynnis) are flat, rounded, toothless-looking and plant-eating.
animal.whereToSee: The Pantanal (Mato Grosso, Brazil); floodplain lakes near Manaus; Llanos of Venezuela
animal.season: Resident; spawning peaks in the rainy season as waters rise (roughly December–April in the Pantanal)

lore: Theodore Roosevelt's 'Through the Brazilian Wilderness' (1914) fixed the man-eating image after he watched starved piranhas strip a cow, a scene staged for him by locals. The name is usually traced to Tupi pirá, 'fish', and sainha or anha, 'tooth'.
funFact: Piranhas shed and replace their teeth in batches, a whole quadrant of the jaw at a time, so they are never left with gaps in their bite.

wiki.extract: The red-bellied piranha, also known as the red piranha, is a species of freshwater ray-finned fish belonging to the family Serrasalmidae, which includes the pacus, piranhas and related fishes. The red-bellied piranha occurs in South America, found in the Amazon, Paraguay, Paraná and Essequibo basins, as well as coastal rivers of northeastern Brazil. This fish is locally abundant in its freshwater habitat.

plates.title: De Indiae utriusque re naturali et medica
plates.author: Willem Piso
plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a piranha labeled 'PIRA'NHA'.
plates.long: This illustration provides an early European view of a piranha, emphasizing its formidable, triangular teeth. The accompanying text describes its predatory nature and habitat, reflecting the era's intense interest in documenting the exotic and often dangerous fauna of the New World.

summary: Europe's largest freshwater fish, a scaleless giant catfish with a cavernous mouth and whiskers like a walrus. Introduced wels in France have learned to lunge onto riverbanks to grab pigeons.
nativeRange: Central and Eastern Europe east to the Black, Caspian and Aral Sea basins; introduced to Spain, Italy, France, Britain and elsewhere
biomes: Brackish Black and Caspian Sea margins
abilities: Hunts in darkness with two long upper barbels and four shorter chin barbels
Beaches itself on riverbanks to seize pigeons, then wriggles back into the water (documented on the Tarn at Albi, France)
Grows to about 2.8 m, the largest verified freshwater fish in Europe
Males guard and fan the nest of eggs for days
edibilityNote: Fatty, nearly boneless flesh, popular in Hungary (harcsapaprikás) and Central Europe. Smaller fish taste better. Very large old wels from industrial rivers can carry high mercury and PCBs, so check local advisories. Always cooked.

animal.diet: Carnivore and scavenger: fish, crayfish, frogs, water birds, rodents and carrion
animal.habitat: Deep, slow lowland rivers, lakes, reservoirs and backwaters with soft beds
animal.lifespan: Up to 30 years or more; some estimates suggest around 50
animal.size: Commonly 1–1.6 m; verified fish to about 2.8 m and over 130 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; by day it rests in holes under banks or sunken trees. It spawns in late spring in shallow vegetation, and the male guards the nest.
fieldMarks: Long, scaleless, slimy body; broad flat head and very wide mouth
One pair of very long barbels on the upper jaw and two pairs of short barbels under the chin
Tiny dorsal fin and a very long anal fin joined almost to the tail
Mottled dark olive-black back, paler marbled flanks and a whitish belly
animal.lookalikes: Aristotle's catfish (Silurus aristotelis) of Greece has only four barbels. Introduced North American channel and blue catfish have scaleless bodies but a forked tail, an adipose fin and eight barbels.
animal.whereToSee: The Ebro at Mequinenza and Caspe (Spain); the Po delta (Italy); the Danube delta; the Volga delta
animal.season: Resident; spawns May–July; active through the warm months

lore: Aristotle described the male catfish guarding its nest in 'History of Animals' (4th century BC). The observation was dismissed until Louis Agassiz confirmed it in 1857 in the related Greek catfish he named Glanis aristotelis (now Silurus aristotelis) in Aristotle's honour.
funFact: About 28% of the wels catfish's beaching attacks on pigeons at Albi succeeded, which the researchers compared with orcas surging onto beaches to catch seals.

wiki.extract: The wels catfish, also called sheatfish or just wels, is a large species of catfish native to wide areas of central, southern, and eastern Europe, in the basins of the Baltic, Black and Caspian Seas. It has been introduced to several countries in Western Europe, Mediterranean and Asia as a prized sport fish. Its modern day range spans from the United Kingdom in the west to western China in the east.

Featured in Ulisse Aldrovandi's 1661 treatise on fish, the image showcases the meticulous detail early modern naturalists used to document aquatic life, from the long sensory barbels to the specific arrangement of fins.

Accompanying the main figure are smaller anatomical studies of internal organs, reflecting the era's growing interest in empirical observation and comparative anatomy. The illustration showcases the transition from medieval bestiaries to Renaissance natural history, emphasizing anatomical observation through fine-line hatching to suggest scale and form. Such prints were essential in the 16th-century effort to

plates.long: Depicting a Silurus, or catfish, this woodcut illustrates the species' elongated body and distinctive barbels. Such images were essential components of early modern scientific texts, aiming to categorize and describe the natural world with increasing precision.

otherNames: Pla khao ปลาเค้า (Thai)
summary: A long, fast-swimming freshwater 'shark' catfish with an enormous mouth, the top predator of South and Southeast Asian rivers. It is now Vulnerable after heavy fishing and river damage.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Indochina, Malaysia and Indonesia
abilities: Its mouth gape reaches well behind the eye, so it can swallow large fish whole
Hunts mostly at night using long barbels and a well-developed lateral-line sense
Swims fast in open water, chasing prey instead of only waiting in ambush
Grows to over 2 m
edibilityNote: Boneless, rich white flesh, popular in Bengali and Thai cooking. Always cooked. As a large, long-lived predator it can carry high mercury and other contaminants in polluted rivers. Avoid very large fish and eat it only in moderation.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, prawns, frogs and occasionally water birds
animal.habitat: Large rivers, lakes, reservoirs and floodplain beels
animal.size: Commonly 1 m; up to about 2.4 m and 45 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; it rests in deep water by day and hunts schools of small fish at dusk. It breeds in flooded areas during the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Long, scaleless, laterally compressed body tapering to a forked tail
Huge mouth with the gape extending behind the eye, and bands of sharp teeth
Tiny dorsal fin and a very long anal fin running almost to the tail
Two pairs of barbels, the upper jaw pair very long
Silvery-grey to olive with a pinkish sheen
animal.lookalikes: The pabda catfishes (Ompok) look similar but are much smaller (under 30 cm), and their mouth does not reach behind the eye. The goonch (Bagarius) is mottled brown, bottom-dwelling and has a flattened head.
animal.whereToSee: Bengal and Assam floodplain beels; the Ganges and Brahmaputra; Thai and Cambodian fish markets
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the monsoon (June–August)

lore: The boal is a stock figure in Bengali proverbs as the greedy big fish that swallows the small. It was described from India by Bloch and Schneider in 1801.
funFact: Anglers in India and Pakistan nicknamed it the 'freshwater shark' because it attacks lures fast in open water and has a slim, shark-like build.

wiki.extract: Wallago attu, boal, or helicopter catfish, is a species of freshwater catfish of the family Siluridae, native to South and Southeast Asia. W. attu is found in large rivers and lakes in two geographically disconnected regions, with one population living over much of the Indian subcontinent and the other in parts of Southeast Asia. This species can reach a length up to 1.1 m.

summary: A nocturnal, shrew-like insectivore of Hispaniola that injects venom through grooves in its lower incisors, one of very few venomous mammals. Its lineage split from other insectivores around 70–78 million years ago, before the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs, making it a living link to the Cretaceous mammal fauna.
nativeRange: Hispaniola (Dominican Republic and Haiti)
abilities: Delivers toxic saliva through a deep groove in each second lower incisor ('solenodon' means 'grooved tooth')
Lineage survived the end-Cretaceous mass extinction
Long, flexible snout supported by a ball-and-socket joint probes crevices

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, millipedes, worms, small vertebrates and some fruit
animal.habitat: Forest and scrub with limestone crevices, caves and hollow logs for shelter
animal.lifespan: Several years; up to about 11 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal. Females have teats far back near the hips, and young may be dragged along clinging to them.
fieldMarks: Large, rat-sized shrew-like animal with a very long, naked, flexible snout
Small eyes and coarse brown fur with reddish sides of the head
Long, naked, scaly tail
Signs: conical 'nose-pokes' in leaf litter and soil where it has probed for invertebrates
animal.lookalikes: Cuban solenodon (Atopogale cubana) lives only in eastern Cuba. Introduced rats and mongooses lack the long probing snout and odd, waddling gait.
animal.whereToSee: Very hard to see; nocturnal surveys in Sierra de Bahoruco and Jaragua national parks, Los Haitises and Pedernales (Dominican Republic); Massif de la Hotte (Haiti)
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Hispaniolan solenodon was described by Johann Friedrich Brandt in 1833 from a specimen sent from Haiti, and was so unusual it was named 'paradoxus'. Long listed as Endangered, it was downlisted to Least Concern by the IUCN in 2020 as surveys showed it to be more widespread than feared.
funFact: Introduced dogs, cats and small Indian mongooses are its main predators: the solenodon evolved without fast-moving carnivores.

wiki.extract: The Hispaniolan solenodon, also known as the agouta, is a small, furry, shrew-like mammal endemic to the Caribbean island of Hispaniola. Like other solenodons, it is a venomous, insect-eating animal that lives in burrows and is active at night. It is an elusive animal and was only first described in 1833; its numbers are stable in protected forests but it remains the focus of conservation efforts.

summary: The longest-lived vertebrate known: radiocarbon dating of eye lenses suggests some individuals are around 400 years old. It cruises the cold Arctic depths at about walking pace.
nativeRange: North Atlantic and Arctic oceans, from the Gulf of Maine and North Sea to Svalbard and the Canadian Arctic
abilities: Estimated lifespan of at least 272 years, possibly ~400 (Nielsen et al., Science 2016)
Reaches sexual maturity at roughly 150 years
Cruises at about 1 km/h, one of the slowest fish swimming speeds relative to size
Tissue contains high levels of trimethylamine oxide (TMAO), which stabilises proteins in cold deep water
edibleParts: flesh only after fermentation and drying (hákarl)
edibilityNote: Fresh flesh is poisonous because of TMAO, which breaks down into trimethylamine and causes 'shark drunk' symptoms in people and sled dogs. Iceland's hákarl is made by fermenting and air-drying for months; it has an intense ammonia smell.

animal.diet: Fish, seals, squid, carrion including drowned reindeer and polar bear remains
animal.habitat: Cold continental shelf and slope waters, 0–2,200 m; nearer the surface in Arctic winters
animal.behaviour: Many adults carry a parasitic copepod (Ommatokoita elongata) attached to the eye, which damages the cornea, yet they still hunt successfully.
fieldMarks: Massive, cylindrical grey-brown body
Small, rounded dorsal fins with no spines
Short, rounded snout and small eyes, often with a dangling copepod
Nearly symmetrical tail with a weak lower lobe
animal.lookalikes: Pacific sleeper shark (S. pacificus) is very similar but lives in the North Pacific; basking shark has huge gill slits and a tall triangular dorsal.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen alive; Arctic Bay and Baffin Island (Canada) under-ice dives, the St. Lawrence estuary at Baie-Comeau, Bjarnarhöfn shark museum in Iceland
animal.season: Year-round; nearer the surface in winter

lore: An Inuit legend tells that the shark arose from the urine-soaked cloth of the sea goddess Sedna's hair, explaining the smell of its flesh.
funFact: A Greenland shark that may have been born before the Mayflower sailed was still swimming when scientists sampled it in the 2010s.

wiki.extract: The Greenland shark, also known as the grey shark or gurry shark, is a large shark of the family Somniosidae, closely related to the Pacific and southern sleeper sharks. Inhabiting the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, they are notable for their exceptional longevity, although they are poorly studied because of the depth and remoteness of their natural habitat.

summary: The largest penguin, and the only animal that breeds on Antarctic sea ice through the polar winter. Males incubate a single egg on their feet for about two months without eating.
nativeRange: Coast and sea ice of Antarctica
abilities: Dives to over 500 m (record 564 m) and holds its breath over 27 minutes
Males fast for up to ~115 days during courtship and incubation
Huddles of thousands rotate so each bird takes turns in the warm centre
Survives temperatures below −40 °C and winds over 140 km/h

animal.diet: Fish, krill and squid
animal.habitat: Fast sea ice around Antarctica; forages in open water
animal.behaviour: In the dark of winter, males huddle in tight masses, shuffling so that no bird stays on the cold edge for long.
fieldMarks: Largest penguin, up to about 1.2 m tall
Black head and back, white belly
Pale yellow ear patches fading into a whitish upper breast
Pinkish-orange stripe on the lower bill
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting contact calls; each bird's call is individually recognisable
animal.lookalikes: King penguin is smaller and slimmer with bright orange, comma-shaped ear patches that are enclosed in black.
animal.whereToSee: Snow Hill Island colony in the Weddell Sea (by icebreaker and helicopter) and Atka Bay; rarely reached by tourists
animal.season: Breeds through the Antarctic winter; chicks visible Oct–Dec

lore: In 1911 Edward Wilson, Apsley Cherry-Garrard and Henry Bowers made 'the worst journey in the world' in Antarctic winter to collect emperor eggs at Cape Crozier.
funFact: Satellite images of the brown guano stains on ice have revealed previously unknown colonies.

wiki.extract: The emperor penguin is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species and is endemic to Antarctica. The male and female are similar in plumage and size, reaching 100 cm (39 in) in length and weighing from 22 to 45 kg. Feathers of the head and back are black and sharply delineated from the white belly, pale-yellow breast and bright-yellow ear patches.

summary: The second-largest penguin, standing nearly a metre tall, with brilliant orange ear patches. Its breeding cycle is so long that pairs can raise at most two chicks every three years.
nativeRange: Sub-Antarctic islands: South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen, Marion, Macquarie, Falklands; Tierra del Fuego
abilities: Dives to over 300 m deep in search of lanternfish
Incubates its egg on its feet beneath a fold of skin
Chicks are fed through winter by parents who may be away for weeks

animal.diet: Lanternfish and squid
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds on flat beaches and valleys on sub-Antarctic islands
animal.lifespan: Up to about 25 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Brown, woolly chicks gather in creches through the winter while parents feed far at sea.
fieldMarks: Bright orange comma-shaped ear patches
Orange-yellow upper breast fading to white
Long, slender bill with orange-pink stripe
Silver-grey back
animal.voice: A loud, trumpeting call, used to find mates and chicks in colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Emperor penguin is larger and stockier, with paler yellow neck patches that are not enclosed by black, and breeds on Antarctic ice rather than sub-Antarctic beaches.
animal.whereToSee: Salisbury Plain, St Andrews Bay and Gold Harbour (South Georgia), Volunteer Point (Falklands), Crozet, Bahía Inútil (Chile)
animal.season: Present year-round at colonies; breeding cycle 14–16 months

lore: In the 19th and early 20th centuries king penguins were rendered for oil in great numbers on Macquarie Island and elsewhere.
funFact: Brown chicks were once thought to be a separate species, nicknamed 'woolly penguins'.

summary: The classic tuxedoed penguin of the Antarctic coast, breeding in vast colonies on ice-free ground. Each winter it follows the pack ice on migrations of thousands of kilometres.
nativeRange: Coasts of Antarctica
abilities: Undertakes winter migrations averaging about 13,000 km in the Ross Sea, following the sun and sea ice
Builds nests of pebbles that lift eggs above meltwater; stones are frequently stolen from neighbours
Dives to around 175 m, though most feeding dives are much shallower
Can toboggan on its belly across snow and ice

animal.diet: Krill, fish and squid
animal.habitat: Antarctic coasts and pack ice
animal.behaviour: Birds return to the same colony and often the same nest each October, walking up to tens of kilometres across sea ice to reach it.
fieldMarks: Entirely black head and throat
Bold white ring around the dark eye
Short bill largely covered by black feathers
Black back, white belly; short tail that often drags on the snow
Pink feet
animal.voice: A loud, rhythmic, throbbing bray given with the head pointed skyward in the 'ecstatic display'; growls and gargles when squabbling.
animal.lookalikes: Chinstrap penguin has a white face and throat crossed by a thin black chin strap. Gentoo penguin has an orange-red bill and a white stripe across the crown. Juvenile Adélies have a white throat but lack the chinstrap line and have a dark eye without the full white ring.
animal.whereToSee: Cape Royds and Cape Adare (Ross Sea), Paulet Island and Hope Bay (Antarctic Peninsula)
animal.season: Breeds at colonies October–February; winters at sea in the pack ice

lore: Jules Dumont d'Urville named it in 1840 after his wife Adèle. George Murray Levick's notes on its sexual behaviour from Scott's 1910–13 expedition were considered too shocking to publish and appeared only in 2012.
funFact: Subfossil remains show that Adélie penguins have used some Ross Sea colony sites for thousands of years, letting scientists track past climate through their bones and eggshell.

wiki.extract: The Adélie penguin is a species of penguin common along the entire coast of the Antarctic continent. It is the most widespread penguin species in the Antarctic, and, along with the emperor penguin, is the most southerly distributed of all penguins. It is named after Adélie Land, in turn, named for Adèle Dumont d'Urville, who was married to French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, who first discovered this penguin in 1840. Adélie penguins obtain their food by both predation and foraging, with a diet of mainly krill and fish.

summary: The fastest-swimming penguin, with a white bonnet stripe and a bright orange bill. Its population has grown and spread south on the Antarctic Peninsula as sea ice declines.
nativeRange: Antarctic Peninsula and sub-Antarctic islands
abilities: Swims at up to about 36 km/h, the fastest of any penguin
Dives to around 200 m
Builds nests from stones and moss

animal.diet: Krill, fish and squid
animal.habitat: Coastal ice-free plains and beaches
animal.behaviour: Pairs build stone nests and may give pebbles as gifts.
fieldMarks: Bright orange-red bill
Broad white stripe over the head
Long, stiff tail
Orange feet
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting braying.
animal.lookalikes: Adélie has an all-black head and short bill. Chinstrap has a black chin strap.
animal.whereToSee: Port Lockroy (Antarctic Peninsula), Falklands, South Georgia
animal.season: Present year-round at most colonies

lore: The name 'gentoo' may come from an Anglo-Indian word for Hindu, but its origin is uncertain.
funFact: A 2020 genetic study proposed splitting the gentoo into four species across its range; most checklists still treat it as one.

wiki.extract: The gentoo penguin is a penguin species in the genus Pygoscelis, most closely related to the Adélie penguin and the chinstrap penguin. The earliest scientific description was made in 1781 by Johann Reinhold Forster with a type locality in the Falkland Islands. The species calls in a variety of ways, but the most frequently heard is a loud, trumpeting call, emitted with the head thrown back.

summary: The only penguin that breeds in Africa, nesting on islands and beaches from Namibia to Algoa Bay. In 2024 it became the first penguin species classified as Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Coasts and islands of Namibia and South Africa
abilities: Dives to around 130 m and swims at up to about 20 km/h
Has bare pink skin above the eye that helps shed heat
Nests in burrows dug into guano or under bushes

animal.diet: Sardines, anchovies and other small shoaling fish
animal.habitat: Rocky islands, sheltered beaches and the Benguela current
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite at the same burrow each season and greet each other with loud braying.
fieldMarks: Black back and white front
Single black band across the chest
Bare pink skin patch above the eye
White stripe curving from above the eye to the breast
Unique black spots on the chest
animal.voice: A loud, donkey-like braying, given with the head thrown back.
animal.lookalikes: Magellanic penguin (South America) has two chest bands; Humboldt penguin has a broader pink face and one band. No other penguin breeds in Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Boulders Beach (Simon's Town), Stony Point (Betty's Bay), Robben Island, Bird Island in Algoa Bay
animal.season: Present year-round; breeds in most months, with peaks varying by colony

lore: Its nests were destroyed by 19th- and 20th-century guano harvesting and its eggs collected for food; millions of eggs were taken from Dassen Island alone.
funFact: The breeding population has fallen below 10,000 pairs, down from perhaps over a million birds a century ago.

wiki.extract: The African penguin, also known as the Cape penguin or the South African penguin, is a species of penguin confined to southern African waters. It is the only penguin found in the Old World. Like all penguins, it is flightless, with a streamlined body and wings stiffened and flattened into flippers for a marine habitat. Adults weigh an average of 2.2–3.5 kg (4.9–7.7 lb) and are 60–70 cm (24–28 in) tall. The species has distinctive pink patches of skin above the eyes and a black facial mask. The body's upper parts are black and sharply delineated from the white underparts, which are spotted and marked with a black band.

summary: A medium-sized penguin of the desert coasts of Peru and Chile, living on the cold, fish-rich Humboldt Current. It once nested in burrows dug into guano deposits metres deep, until 19th-century guano mining stripped them away.
nativeRange: Pacific coasts and offshore islands of Peru and Chile
abilities: Thrives on a hot desert coast thanks to bare facial skin that sheds heat
Dives repeatedly to catch anchovies and sardines in cold upwelling water
Nests in burrows, caves and crevices to protect eggs from sun

animal.diet: Anchoveta, sardines, other small fish and squid
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts and islands near the Humboldt Current
animal.lifespan: About 15–20 years in the wild; over 30 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Breeding often fails in strong El Niño years, when warm water drives fish away.
fieldMarks: Black back and white front with a single broad black band across the breast
White C-shaped band from the eye around the cheeks to the throat
Pink bare skin at the base of the black bill
Black spots scattered on the white belly
animal.voice: Loud, donkey-like braying calls at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Magellanic Penguin (overlaps in central Chile) has two black breast bands. Galápagos Penguin is smaller with a thinner face stripe and lives only on the Galápagos.
animal.whereToSee: Islas Ballestas (Paracas, Peru), Punta San Juan (Peru), and the Humboldt Penguin National Reserve with Isla Damas and Isla Choros (Chile).
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It is named after Alexander von Humboldt, whose name also labels the cold ocean current on which it depends; the guano it nests in was exported as fertiliser in the Peruvian 'Guano Age' of the mid-1800s.
funFact: Its Spanish nickname 'pájaro niño', 'child bird', comes from its upright, toddling walk.

wiki.extract: The Humboldt penguin is a medium-sized penguin. It resides in South America, along the Pacific coast of Peru and Chile. Its nearest relatives are the African penguin, the Magellanic penguin and the Galápagos penguin. The Humboldt penguin and the cold water current it swims in are both named after the explorer Alexander von Humboldt. The species is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN with no population recovery plan in place. The current wild population is composed of roughly 23,800 mature individuals and is declining. It is a migrant species.

summary: Not a lizard but the sole survivor of an order of reptiles, the Rhynchocephalia, which flourished in the age of the dinosaurs. It lives on cool islands off New Zealand, grows slowly, breeds rarely and can live for more than a century.
nativeRange: Offshore islands of New Zealand; reintroduced to fenced sanctuaries on the mainland
abilities: The only living member of the reptile order Rhynchocephalia
Has a 'third eye' (parietal eye) with a lens and retina on top of its head, visible in hatchlings
Active at temperatures as low as ~5 °C, colder than most reptiles tolerate
Sex of hatchlings depends on nest temperature; warmer nests produce more males

animal.diet: Beetles, wētā, spiders, worms, seabird eggs and chicks, lizards
animal.habitat: Coastal forest and scrub on islands, often sharing burrows with seabirds such as petrels
animal.size: Males up to ~60 cm and 1 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal. It shares burrows with nesting seabirds. Females breed only every 2–5 years, and eggs take 11–16 months to hatch.
fieldMarks: Lizard-like body, olive-green to grey or reddish
Spiny crest along the neck and back, larger in males
No external ear openings
Saw-like teeth fused to the jaw bone
animal.lookalikes: Superficially like a large lizard, but no lizard in New Zealand has a spiny crest like this. It has no external ear opening and a beak-like upper jaw.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia Ecosanctuary (Wellington), Orokonui (Dunedin), Tiritiri Matangi Island; Stephens Island (Takapourewa) has the largest population but is closed to the public
animal.season: Resident; most active on warm, humid nights

lore: To many Māori tuatara are taonga (treasures) and kaitiaki (guardians) of knowledge. Albert Günther showed in 1867 that it was not a lizard but the last of an ancient reptile lineage.
funFact: 'Henry', a tuatara at the Southland Museum in Invercargill, became a father in 2009 at the age of about 111.
