wiki.extract: The tuatara is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand. Despite its close resemblance to lizards, it is the only extant member of a distinct lineage, the previously highly diverse order Rhynchocephalia. The name tuatara is derived from the Māori language and means "peaks on the back".

summary: A large, heavy hawkmoth with a skull-like pattern on its thorax that squeaks loudly when disturbed. It raids beehives for honey, slipping past guard bees by smelling like them.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan and North Africa and the Middle East; migrates north into Europe
abilities: Squeaks by sucking air in and pushing it out past a flap in its throat
Mimics the chemical scent of honeybees to enter hives and drink honey
Short, stout proboscis can pierce honeycomb
Migrates from Africa as far as Britain and Scandinavia

animal.diet: Adults drink honey from hives, tree sap and rotting fruit; caterpillars eat potato and other nightshade-family plants, as well as jasmine and buddleia
animal.habitat: Open country, potato fields, gardens and orchards
animal.size: Wingspan about 9–13 cm; one of Europe's largest moths
animal.behaviour: If disturbed it squeaks and flashes its yellow-banded abdomen; the caterpillar also makes a clicking noise.
fieldMarks: Pale yellow skull-shaped mark on the dark thorax
Dark brown, mottled forewings
Yellow hindwings with two dark bands
Abdomen banded yellow and black, like a giant wasp
animal.voice: A sharp, mouse-like squeak, repeated when the moth is disturbed or alarmed.
animal.lookalikes: In Asia, Acherontia styx and A. lachesis are very similar but have different abdomen markings and do not occur in Europe or Africa. No other European moth has the skull pattern.
animal.whereToSee: Potato fields and gardens in southern Europe and North Africa; caterpillars are sometimes found in autumn potato harvests in Britain.
animal.season: Europe: migrants May–Oct, with a local autumn generation

lore: Long treated in European folklore as an omen of death, it is named after Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Death's-head hawkmoths are the killer's calling card in The Silence of the Lambs (1991); the moth on the film's poster is often identified as its Asian relative A. styx.
funFact: Migrants occasionally travel far beyond Britain: one was recorded above the Arctic Circle in northern Sweden in 2019, after an unusually warm summer.

wiki.extract: Acherontia atropos, the African death's-head hawkmoth, is the most widely recognized of three species within the genus Acherontia. It is most commonly identified by the vaguely skull-shaped pattern adorning the thorax, the characteristic from which its common and scientific names are derived. The species was first given its scientific name by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.

summary: A pink-and-olive hawk-moth that hovers at flowers at dusk. It was the first animal shown to see colour in dim starlight, when humans see only grey.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia to Japan
abilities: Colour vision under starlight using highly sensitive superposition eyes (Kelber et al. 2002)
Hovers while drinking nectar through a long proboscis
Caterpillar inflates its eyespots to mimic a small snake

animal.diet: Larvae eat willowherb (Chamaenerion) and bedstraw (Galium); adults drink nectar from honeysuckle and similar flowers
animal.habitat: Gardens, rough ground, heaths and woodland edges
animal.behaviour: When disturbed, the caterpillar pulls its head in and swells its front segments, flashing four eyespots like a snake.
fieldMarks: Olive-green and pink moth with a streamlined body
Pink bands across the olive forewing and a pink body
Caterpillar grey-brown with two pairs of eyespots behind a trunk-like head
Visits flowers at dusk
animal.lookalikes: Small elephant hawk-moth (Deilephila porcellus) is smaller and mainly pink and yellowish-brown, without the olive-green bands.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with honeysuckle, rough ground with rosebay willowherb, heaths and woodland edges across Europe
animal.season: Adults May–Jul; caterpillars Jul–Sep on willowherbs, bedstraws and fuchsia

lore: The common name refers to the trunk-like caterpillar. Linnaeus named it after Elpenor, Odysseus's companion who fell from Circe's roof.
funFact: It is a common garden visitor in Britain, yet its night colour vision was only discovered in 2002.

wiki.extract: Deilephila elpenor, the elephant hawk moth or large elephant hawk moth, is a moth in the family Sphingidae. Its common name is derived from the caterpillar's resemblance to an elephant's trunk. It is most common in Central Europe and is distributed throughout the Palearctic region. It has also been introduced in British Columbia, Canada. Its distinct olive and pink colouring makes it one of the most recognisable moths in its range, but confusing the elephant hawk moth with the small elephant hawk moth, a closely related species that also shares the characteristic colours, is quite common.

summary: A day-flying moth that hovers in front of flowers with a soft hum, uncurling a long tongue to drink, so convincingly that people in Europe often report seeing hummingbirds. It migrates north from southern Europe and North Africa each summer.
nativeRange: Southern Europe and North Africa east across temperate Asia to Japan; summer migrant to northern Europe
abilities: Hovers motionless while feeding, adjusting position as flowers sway
Learns and remembers flower colours, and has colour vision
Proboscis about as long as its body
Migrates hundreds of kilometres north each year

animal.diet: Adults drink nectar from tubular flowers such as red valerian, jasmine, honeysuckle, buddleia and petunias; caterpillars eat bedstraws (Galium) and wild madder
animal.habitat: Sunny gardens, flowery meadows, rocky slopes and coasts
animal.behaviour: It flies in full sunshine and even in rain, moving rapidly from flower to flower and returning to the same flower beds at the same time each day.
fieldMarks: Hovering flight in daylight with a faint audible hum
Grey-brown forewings with fine dark wavy lines
Orange-brown hindwings visible as a blur in flight
Black-and-white chequered sides to the abdomen and a fan-like tail tuft
animal.lookalikes: Often mistaken for a hummingbird, but there are no wild hummingbirds in Europe, Africa or Asia. Bee hawk-moths (Hemaris) also hover by day but have clear, glassy wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with red valerian or jasmine around the Mediterranean; increasingly in southern England and northern Europe in warm summers.
animal.season: Northern Europe: migrants May–Oct, peaking Jul–Sep; adults overwinter in the Mediterranean

lore: In Japan its name hōjaku (蜂雀) means 'bee-sparrow', likening the hovering moth to a tiny bird as Europeans do with hummingbirds; Linnaeus's epithet stellatarum refers to its larval food, the 'stellate' bedstraws with star-shaped whorls of leaves.
funFact: Experiments show it has true colour vision: trained moths pick the rewarded colour even when its brightness is changed.

wiki.extract: The hummingbird hawk-moth is a species of hawk moth found across temperate regions of Eurasia. The species is named for its similarity to hummingbirds, as they feed on the nectar of tube-shaped flowers using their long proboscis while hovering in the air; this resemblance is an example of convergent evolution.

summary: The largest hammerhead, with a tall sickle dorsal fin and a near-straight 'hammer' packed with electroreceptors. It specialises in stingrays, pinning them to the seabed with its head.
nativeRange: Tropical and warm temperate coastal waters worldwide
abilities: The cephalofoil spreads ampullae of Lorenzini wide, helping detect buried prey's electric fields
Uses the head to pin stingrays to the seabed while biting
Swims rolled on its side, using its tall dorsal fin as a 'wing' to cut drag by about 10%
Seemingly immune to stingray barbs; individuals have been found with dozens embedded in the mouth

animal.diet: Stingrays, other rays, groupers, catfish, smaller sharks
animal.habitat: Coastal reefs, lagoons and continental shelves to 80 m
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary nomad that makes seasonal migrations along coasts; extremely vulnerable to capture stress and often dies on lines.
fieldMarks: Broad hammer-shaped head with a nearly straight front edge and a central notch in adults
Very tall, sickle-shaped first dorsal fin
Tall pelvic fins with a curved rear margin
Grey-brown above, white below
animal.lookalikes: Scalloped hammerhead (S. lewini) has a curved front edge with a strong central notch and a lower dorsal fin; smooth hammerhead (S. zygaena) lacks the central notch.
animal.whereToSee: Bimini, Bahamas (Dec–Mar); Jupiter, Florida; Rangiroa, French Polynesia
animal.season: Bimini Dec–Mar; Rangiroa Dec–Mar

lore: Its fins are highly prized in the shark-fin trade; hammerheads were listed on CITES Appendix II in 2013.
funFact: A pregnant female can carry up to about 55 pups, which are born with their hammers bent back to ease birth.

wiki.extract: The great hammerhead is the largest species of hammerhead shark, belonging to the family Sphyrnidae, attaining an average length of 4.6 m (15 ft) and reaching a maximum length of 6.2 m (20 ft). It is found around the globe in all the warmer parts of the oceans. The great hammerhead can be distinguished from other hammerheads by the shape of its "hammer", which is wide with an almost straight front margin, its tall, sickle-shaped first dorsal fin, and its strongly falcated pelvic fins. A solitary, strong-swimming apex predator, the great hammerhead feeds on a wide variety of prey ranging from crustaceans and cephalopods, to bony fish, to smaller sharks. Observations of this species in the wild suggest that the cephalofoil functions to immobilize stingrays, a favored prey. This species has a viviparous mode of reproduction, bearing litters of up to 2-49 pups every two years.

summary: The world's only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird, it roosts and nests in pitch-dark caves and navigates by echolocation using audible clicks. Its fat-laden chicks were once boiled down for lamp and cooking oil.
nativeRange: Northern and western South America — Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Guyana — and Trinidad
abilities: Echolocates in total darkness with clicks around 2 kHz, audible to humans
Finds fruit at night partly by smell and with large, light-sensitive eyes
Disperses seeds of palms and laurels over long distances
Chicks grow much heavier than adults on a fatty fruit diet before slimming down to fledge

animal.diet: Oily fruits of palms, laurels and incense trees, plucked in flight
animal.habitat: Caves and gorges near forest, from sea level to about 3,400 m
animal.behaviour: Colonies of thousands leave caves at dusk and may forage over 100 km away in a night.
fieldMarks: Rich rufous-brown plumage with white spots on wings and head
Strongly hooked bill fringed with long rictal bristles
Long, broad wings and long tail
Large dark eyes
animal.voice: Deafening screams, snarls and clicks inside roost caves; the screams inspired the Spanish name guácharo, 'one who wails'.
animal.lookalikes: Potoos and nightjars are greyer, have tiny bills, and do not roost in caves; no other cave-dwelling bird in its range is as large.
animal.whereToSee: Cueva del Guácharo National Park (Caripe, Venezuela), Dunston Cave at Asa Wright Nature Centre (Trinidad), and the Cueva de los Tayos region (Ecuador).
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Alexander von Humboldt visited the Cueva del Guácharo near Caripe in 1799 and described how the local Chaima people harvested chicks for their fat; the species' name caripensis honours the site.
funFact: Fat oilbird chicks can weigh about 50% more than their parents.

wiki.extract: The oilbird, locally known as the guácharo, is a bird species found in the northern areas of South America including the Caribbean island of Trinidad. It is the only living species in the genus Steatornis, the family Steatornithidae, and the order Steatornithiformes. Nesting in colonies in caves, oilbirds are nocturnal feeders on the fruits of the oil palm and tropical laurels. They are the only nocturnal flying fruit-eating birds in the world. They forage at night, with specially adapted eyesight. However, they navigate by echolocation in the same way as bats, one of the few birds to do so. They produce a high-pitched clicking sound of around 2 kHz that is audible to humans.

Lure on the first dorsal ray may attract prey

wiki.extract: The Pacific viperfish (Chauliodus macouni), is a predatory deep-sea fish found in the North Pacific. It is reported as being either mesopelagic or bathypelagic, with diel vertical migration to shallower waters. The Pacific viperfish is one of the nine different species that belong to the genus Chauliodus, the viperfish. The Pacific viperfish tend to be the largest of the species, typically reaching lengths of up to 1 foot and are considered an example of deep-sea gigantism. The length-weight relationship of the pacific viperfish varies with sex with females tending to be longer and heavier than males.

wiki.extract: The spotted owlet is a small owl which breeds in tropical Asia from North Pakistan to Southeast Asia. A common resident of open habitats including farmland and human habitation, it has adapted to living in cities. They roost in small groups in the hollows of trees or in cavities in rocks and buildings. It nests in a hole in a tree or building, laying 3–5 eggs. The species shows great variation including clinal variation in size and forms a superspecies with the very similar little owl.

wiki.extract: The burrowing owl is a small, long-legged, primarily terrestrial—though not flightless—species of owl native to the open landscapes of North and South America. They are typically found in grasslands, rangelands, agricultural areas, deserts, or any other open, dry area with low vegetation. They nest and roost in burrows, and, despite their common name, do not often construct these dwellings themselves, rather repurposing disused burrows or tunnels previously excavated and inhabited by other species, such as American badgers, foxes, ground squirrels or prairie dogs, among others.

wiki.extract: The snowy owl, also known as the polar owl, the white owl and the Arctic owl, is a large, white owl of the true owl family. Snowy owls are native to the Arctic regions of both North America and the Palearctic, breeding mostly on the tundra. It has a number of unique adaptations to its habitat and lifestyle, which are quite distinct from other extant owls. One of the largest species of owl, it is the only owl with mainly white plumage. Males tend to be a purer white overall while females tend to have more extensive flecks of dark brown. Juvenile male snowy owls have dark markings and may appear similar to females until maturity, at which point they typically turn whiter. The composition of brown markings about the wing, although not foolproof, is the most reliable technique for aging and sexing individual snowy owls.

wiki.extract: The great horned owl, also known as the tiger owl or the hoot owl, is a large owl native to the Americas. It is an extremely adaptable bird with a vast range and is the most widely distributed true owl in the Americas. Its diet consists primarily of rabbits and hares, rats and mice, and voles; it remains one of the few regular predators of skunk. Hunting also includes rodents, larger mid-sized mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and invertebrates.

This plate is part of François Bouchard's 1775 collection, reflecting the 18th-century fascination with cataloging the natural world.

summary: A round-headed, dark-eyed woodland owl whose hooting is the classic night sound of European parks and woods. It is strictly territorial, with pairs occupying the same patch for life.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Levant, northern Iran and western Central Asia; Himalayan birds are now treated as a separate species
abilities: Knows its territory so well it can hunt in near-total darkness
Hears prey moving under leaf litter and pinpoints it with asymmetrically placed ears
Fringed flight feathers make its flight almost silent
Defends its nest fiercely, striking intruders at the head

animal.diet: Woodmice, voles and shrews; also birds, frogs and earthworms
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed woodland, parks, large gardens and churchyards
animal.behaviour: Young owlets leave the nest before they can fly and clamber about branches as 'branchers', calling to be fed.
fieldMarks: Rounded head with no ear tufts
Large dark eyes in a pale-edged facial disc
Mottled plumage in rufous-brown or grey morphs
Stocky, broad-winged and short-tailed
animal.voice: Male gives a long, quavering 'hooo... hu-hu-hu-hooooo'; female and young give a sharp 'ke-wick'. The 'twit-twoo' of legend is a female 'ke-wick' answered by a male hoot.
animal.lookalikes: Ural owl (Scandinavia, eastern Europe) is larger and paler with a long tail and small dark eyes. Barn owl is white below with a heart-shaped face. Long-eared owl has ear tufts and orange eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Mature woods and city parks throughout Europe; often found by listening at dusk in autumn when young disperse.
animal.season: Resident; most vocal in autumn and late winter

lore: Bird photographer Eric Hosking lost his left eye to a tawny owl defending its nest in 1937 and titled his autobiography 'An Eye for a Bird'.
funFact: A tawny owl pair will often stay in one territory for life and rarely leave it, so many young starve if they fail to find a vacant patch.

wiki.extract: The tawny owl, also called the brown owl, is a stocky, medium-sized owl in the family Strigidae. It is commonly found in woodlands across Europe, as well as western Siberia, and has seven recognized subspecies. The tawny owl's underparts are pale with dark streaks, whilst its upper body may be either brown or grey. The tawny owl typically makes its nest in a tree hole where it can protect its eggs and young against potential predators. It is non-migratory and highly territorial: as a result, when young birds grow up and leave the parental nest, if they cannot find a vacant territory to claim as their own, they will often starve.

summary: A large, round-headed owl of eastern swamps and forests with soulful dark eyes and a call that asks 'Who cooks for you?'. In the last century it spread across Canada into the Pacific Northwest, where it now outcompetes the threatened Spotted Owl.
nativeRange: Eastern North America and central Mexico; expanded across boreal Canada into British Columbia, Washington, Oregon and northern California during the 20th century
abilities: Calls frequently by day as well as night
Takes a wide range of prey including crayfish, fish and frogs
Its westward range expansion is one of the largest documented for a North American bird

animal.diet: Small mammals, birds, amphibians, crayfish, fish, insects
animal.habitat: Mature forest near water — swamps, river bottoms, old woodlots
animal.behaviour: Pairs perform raucous 'caterwauling' duets of hoots, cackles and screams.
fieldMarks: Large, round head without ear tufts
Dark brown eyes
Horizontal barring on upper breast, vertical streaks on the belly
Grey-brown plumage with a yellow bill
animal.voice: A rhythmic hooting 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all', ending in a drawl; also monkey-like cackles.
animal.lookalikes: Spotted Owl (West) is darker with white spots instead of bars and streaks. Great Gray Owl is larger with yellow eyes. Great Horned Owl has ear tufts and yellow eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Southern swamps such as Corkscrew Swamp and the Okefenokee, river bottomlands across the east, and forests of the Pacific Northwest.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Its spread into the range of the Northern Spotted Owl led the US Fish and Wildlife Service to adopt a 2024 management plan that includes culling Barred Owls in parts of the Pacific Northwest.
funFact: Barred Owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish and crayfish.

wiki.extract: The barred owl, also known as the northern barred owl, striped owl, or more informally, hoot owl or eight hooter, is a North American large species of owl. A member of the true owl family, Strigidae, they belong to the genus Strix, which is also the origin of the family's name under Linnaean taxonomy. Barred owls are largely native to eastern North America, but have expanded their range to the West Coast of North America, where they are considered invasive. Mature forests are their preferred habitat, but they can also acclimate to various gradients of open woodlands. Their diet consists mainly of small mammals, but this species is an opportunistic predator and is known to prey upon other small vertebrates such as birds, reptiles, and amphibians, as well as a variety of invertebrates.

summary: The world's only alpine parrot, an olive-green clown of New Zealand's Southern Alps. Famously curious and clever, kea solve puzzles, use tools and even have a 'play' call that sets other kea romping.
nativeRange: South Island, New Zealand
abilities: Solves multi-step puzzles and uses tools in experiments
Its 'warble' call triggers play in other kea, an emotional contagion
Understands statistical probabilities in choice tasks
Survives in cold, snowy mountain habitats

animal.habitat: Alpine and subalpine forest, scrub, grassland

Long, narrow, hooked grey bill
Blue-green flight feathers

animal.season: Resident

funFact: Kea are one of the few non-primate animals shown to make statistical inferences.

wiki.extract: The kea is a species of large parrot in the family Strigopidae that is endemic to the forested and alpine regions of the South Island of New Zealand. About 48 cm (19 in) long, it is mostly olive-green, with brilliant orange under its wings, and has a large, narrow, curved, grey-brown upper beak. Its omnivorous diet consists mainly of roots, leaves, berries, nectar, and insects, but also includes carrion. It was once killed for bounty due to concern by sheep farmers that it attacked livestock, especially sheep. The kea is now uncommon, and received absolute protection under the Wildlife Act in 1986.

abilities: Heaviest parrot, up to ~4 kg
Males 'boom' with a call that can carry several kilometres
Breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily
Can live 60–90 years, among the longest-lived birds
Climbs trees and parachutes down on short wings

animal.habitat: Native forest and scrub on predator-free islands

Heavy grey bill
Nocturnal; climbs trees and walks

animal.lookalikes: Kea and kākā are flying parrots; kea is olive-green with orange underwings and lives in the mountains.

animal.season: Breeds only in years when rimu trees fruit heavily; males boom in summer (about Dec–Mar) of those years

lore: Māori hunted kākāpō for food and made feather cloaks (kahu kākāpō). By 1995 only 51 birds remained; a national recovery programme has since more than quadrupled the population.
funFact: A male named Sirocco became famous for trying to mate with a zoologist's head on television in 2009.

summary: A flat, diamond-shaped silvery fish beloved across Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and the Gulf, where whole fried or curried pomfret is a classic. Heavy demand has driven sharp declines in parts of its range.
nativeRange: Indo-West Pacific: Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal to the South China Sea and Japan
abilities: Highly compressed, deep body for manoeuvring in turbid coastal water
Feeds on jellyfish and ctenophores as well as plankton
Lacks pelvic fins entirely as an adult
edibilityNote: Low mercury. A premium market fish in Karachi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Kuwait. No particular toxicity concerns.

Long, sickle-shaped dorsal and anal fins

animal.whereToSee: Karachi Fish Harbour, Sassoon Dock (Mumbai), Kuwait's Sharq fish market
animal.season: Year-round; catches rise after the southwest monsoon closes

lore: Known as 'zubaidi' in Kuwait, where it is considered the national fish; in Bengali its name 'rupchanda' evokes a silver moon.
funFact: The Persian Gulf population has been assessed by IUCN as Vulnerable due to overfishing.

wiki.extract: Pampus argenteus, the silver pomfret or white pomfret is a species of butterfish that lives in the Indo-West Pacific, spanning the coastal waters of the Middle East, Eastern Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and East Asia. The species has been reported only twice, one hundred years apart, from the central Mediterranean Sea.

summary: A spiny purple urchin of North America's Pacific coast that, when its predators decline, can mow down kelp forests and leave bare 'urchin barrens'. It is also a classic laboratory animal for studying fertilisation and embryo development.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from British Columbia (and parts of Alaska) to Baja California
abilities: Grinds algae and kelp with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern
Bores pits into solid rock with its teeth and spines
Senses light with its tube feet, using its whole body as an eye
Can survive years of starvation in barrens in a dormant-like state
Some individuals live 50 years or more

animal.diet: Kelp and other algae, especially drift kelp
animal.habitat: Rocky shores and reefs from the low intertidal to about 160 m
animal.behaviour: When drift kelp is plentiful urchins hide in crevices; when it runs short they emerge and graze living kelp, sometimes creating barrens.

Juveniles may be greenish
Often packed into rock pits it has bored itself
Tube feet extend between the spines
animal.lookalikes: Red sea urchin (Mesocentrotus franciscanus) is larger (to about 18 cm) with long red to maroon spines. Green urchin (S. droebachiensis) has greenish spines and lives mainly further north.
animal.whereToSee: Tide pools and kelp reefs from Oregon to southern California; dense barrens off Mendocino and Sonoma counties since 2014.
animal.season: Year-round

edibilityNote: The gonads are eaten raw as uni. Barrens urchins are often thin, so some ventures collect and 'ranch' them to fatten them for market while restoring kelp.
funFact: Its genome, sequenced in 2006, was the first of any echinoderm and revealed genes for vision-related proteins despite it having no eyes.

summary: The largest living bird, up to about 2.7 m tall, and the fastest runner on two legs. It lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; formerly North Africa and the Middle East
abilities: Runs at about 70 km/h, with strides up to 5 m
Lays eggs about 15 cm long and 1.4 kg
Has the largest eyes of any land vertebrate, around 5 cm across
Has only two toes, an adaptation for running
A forward kick can kill a lion

animal.diet: Plants, seeds and roots; also insects and small animals
animal.habitat: Open savanna, semi-desert and grassland
animal.behaviour: Several females lay in one shared nest; the dominant female and the male take turns incubating, he at night, she by day.
fieldMarks: Tallest bird, flightless, with long bare neck and legs
Males black with white wings and tail; females greyish-brown
Male's neck and legs pinkish, turning red on the shins when breeding
Two toes on each foot
animal.voice: Breeding males give a deep, booming roar
animal.lookalikes: Somali ostrich (a separate species in the Horn of Africa) has blue-grey neck and thigh skin. Ostriches kick hard; watch from a vehicle or at a distance.
animal.whereToSee: Etosha (Namibia), Maasai Mara and Serengeti, and the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park
animal.season: Resident

lore: Ostrich eggshells were engraved by people at Diepkloof Rock Shelter in South Africa about 60,000 years ago, and used as water flasks and beads by San peoples. Ostrich plumes were a fashion craze in Edwardian Europe.
funFact: The story that ostriches bury their heads in sand is a myth, perhaps from seeing them turn eggs in ground nests.

wiki.extract: The common ostrich, or simply ostrich, is a species of flightless bird native to certain areas of Africa and is the largest living species of bird. The common ostrich is one of two extant species of ostriches, the only living members of the genus Struthio in the ratite group of birds. The other is the Somali ostrich, which has been recognised as a distinct species by BirdLife International since 2014, having been previously considered a distinctive subspecies of ostrich.

summary: A swaggering brown starling with a black hood and a bare yellow patch of skin behind each eye, at home on every South Asian lawn, market and railway platform. Taken around the world to eat crop pests, it has become one of the most widespread and controversial birds on Earth.
nativeRange: Iran and Central Asia through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar; introduced to Australia, South Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Hawaii, Florida and many islands
abilities: Thrives in cities, nesting in wall cavities, street lights and buildings
Imitates other birds and, in captivity, human speech
Gathers in communal roosts of hundreds to thousands of birds at dusk
Aggressively evicts other hole-nesting birds from nest sites

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects (especially grasshoppers), fruit, grain, food scraps
animal.habitat: Towns, villages, farmland and open country near people
animal.behaviour: Walks rather than hops, striding across lawns; pairs bob their heads and fluff their plumage at each other in noisy displays, and flocks converge on huge evening roosts with deafening chatter.
fieldMarks: Warm brown body with glossy black head and breast
Bare yellow skin around and behind the eye; yellow bill and legs
Large white wing patch obvious in flight
White under-tail and white tail tip
animal.voice: Very varied: gurgles, chattering 'kok-kok-kok', squawks and liquid whistles; alarm a harsh 'chake-chake'
animal.lookalikes: Bank myna is greyer with a brick-red (not yellow) bare face patch; Jungle myna is slate-grey with a tuft of feathers at the bill base and no bare face patch; Asian pied starling is black-and-white.
animal.whereToSee: Every town and village in Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka, e.g. Lahore, Karachi, Delhi and Colombo parks
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Long kept as a talking cage-bird across the subcontinent. Introduced to Mauritius in the 1760s to control locusts and later to Australia and Hawaii, it is now listed among the IUCN Invasive Species Specialist Group's '100 of the World's Worst Invasive Alien Species'.
funFact: It is one of only three birds on the IUCN '100 worst invasive species' list; the Red-vented bulbul and the Common starling are the other two.

wiki.extract: The common myna or Indian myna, sometimes spelled mynah, is a bird in the family Sturnidae, native to Asia. An omnivorous open woodland bird with a strong territorial instinct, the common myna has adapted extremely well to urban environments.

summary: A glossy East African starling whose iridescent blue-green upperparts and orange belly are divided by a neat white band. Bold and sociable, it lives in cooperatively breeding groups and is a fixture of safari lodges.
nativeRange: East Africa: Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania
abilities: Cooperative breeder in which helpers, often relatives, feed the chicks
Iridescence is structural, produced by arrays of melanin granules in the feathers
Groups in unpredictable dry climates rely more on helpers, a link studied as a driver of cooperative breeding

animal.diet: Insects, especially termites and beetles, plus fruit and seeds
animal.habitat: Dry acacia savanna, thornbush, villages and lodge grounds
animal.behaviour: Groups forage on the ground in loose parties and build bulky domed nests of grass in thorny acacias.
fieldMarks: Metallic blue-green upperparts and breast
Narrow white band across the breast
Rich orange-chestnut belly
Creamy-white eye
White undertail coverts
animal.voice: A long, rambling warble of chattering and whistled phrases, often including mimicry; harsh 'chee-er' alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Hildebrandt's starling lacks the white breast band and has a red-orange eye. Shelley's starling has a darker chestnut belly, no white breast band and an orange eye. Golden-breasted starling has golden-yellow underparts and a long tail.
animal.whereToSee: Samburu, Tsavo, Amboseli and Maasai Mara (Kenya), Serengeti and Tarangire (Tanzania), Ethiopian Rift Valley
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: It was described by Eduard Rüppell in 1845 from specimens collected in Ethiopia, and its tameness around camps and lodges has made it one of the most photographed birds in East Africa.
funFact: Long-term studies in Kenya found that superb starlings in good years and bad years shift between more and fewer helpers, a hedge against an unpredictable climate.

summary: A snow-white starling with black wingtips, a drooping crest and a patch of bare sky-blue skin around each eye, found wild only on Bali. Trapping for the cagebird trade pushed it to a handful of wild birds around 2000; releases have since rebuilt small populations.

abilities: Raises its long, lacy crest in display
Nests in tree holes, including old woodpecker and barbet holes
Survives in a strongly seasonal dry forest

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds, insects and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry deciduous monsoon forest, acacia savanna and village edges
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small groups move through the canopy and forest edge, raising their crests and calling loudly.
fieldMarks: Almost entirely white starling
Black tips to the wings and tail
Bare bright blue skin around the eye
Long, drooping white crest; yellowish bill and blue-grey legs
animal.voice: Loud, varied chattering, harsh calls and whistles typical of starlings
animal.lookalikes: Black-winged myna (Java, Bali) has extensive black wings and a black tail and a yellow face patch; Javan white-eyes are tiny and green.

animal.season: Resident

lore: It is the official faunal symbol of Bali province. On Nusa Penida, Balinese villages agreed under traditional law (awig-awig) to protect released birds, a model for community-based conservation.
funFact: It was only described to science in 1912, and named after Walter Rothschild, the zoologist who owned the famous private museum at Tring.

wiki.extract: The Bali myna, also known as Rothschild's mynah, Bali starling, or Bali mynah, locally known as jalak Bali, is a medium-sized, stocky myna native to northwest Bali in Indonesia. It is almost wholly white with a long, drooping crest, and black tips on the wings and tail. The bird has blue bare skin around the eyes, greyish legs and a brown and yellow bill. Both sexes are similar. It is critically endangered and in 2020, fewer than 50 adults were assumed to exist in the wild.

summary: A glossy, speckled songbird whose winter flocks wheel at dusk in murmurations of hundreds of thousands. Introduced to North America in 1890, it now numbers in the tens of millions there.
nativeRange: Europe, Western Asia and North Africa; introduced to North America, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa
abilities: Murmurations: each bird tracks about seven neighbours, letting waves pass across the flock
Skilled mimic of other birds, phones and human speech
Navigates using a sun compass and magnetic sense
Opens its bill inside the soil to pry prey ('open-bill probing')

animal.diet: Insects, larvae, fruit and seeds
animal.habitat: Open fields, farmland, towns and cities
animal.lifespan: About 2–3 years on average; record over 22
animal.behaviour: Males decorate nests with aromatic green herbs, which may deter parasites.
fieldMarks: Short-tailed, glossy black bird with purple-green sheen
Pale-spotted in fresh winter plumage
Yellow bill in breeding season
Pointed, triangular wings in flight
animal.voice: Varied song of whistles, clicks, rattles and accurate mimicry

animal.season: Resident in much of Europe; murmurations Nov–Feb

lore: Mozart bought a pet starling in 1784 that could sing a theme from his Piano Concerto K.453, and buried it with a poem. Eugene Schieffelin released about 100 in New York's Central Park in 1890–91.
funFact: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1, Hotspur plans to teach a starling to say 'Mortimer' to annoy the king.

wiki.extract: The common starling, also known simply as the starling in Great Britain and Ireland, and as the European starling in North America, is a medium-sized passerine bird in the starling family, Sturnidae. It is about 20 cm (8 in) long and has glossy black plumage with a metallic sheen, which is speckled with white at some times of the year. The legs are pink and the bill is black in winter and yellow in summer; young birds have browner plumage than the adults. Its gift for mimicry has been noted in literature including the Mabinogion and the works of Pliny the Elder and William Shakespeare.

summary: The largest seabird of the North Atlantic, a dazzling white diver with black wingtips and a buttery head. It plunges from height into the sea for fish and breeds in vast, crowded colonies on cliffs and stacks.
nativeRange: North Atlantic: breeds in Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, France, Canada; winters south to West Africa and the Gulf of Mexico, and into the Mediterranean
abilities: Plunge-dives from up to about 30 m, hitting the water at high speed
Air sacs under the skin of the face and chest cushion the impact
Has no external nostrils, which stops water entering on impact
Forward-facing eyes give binocular vision for judging the strike

animal.habitat: Continental-shelf seas; breeds on islands and sea cliffs
animal.behaviour: Pairs greet each other at the nest by 'sky-pointing' and fencing with their bills, and defend a tiny nest site fiercely.

Black wingtips
Yellow-buff head and nape in adults
Dagger bill; juveniles dark brown with white speckles, whitening over four or five years

animal.lookalikes: Great black-backed and other large gulls have rounded wings and lack the pointed tail. Cory's shearwater is brown above. Distant juveniles can suggest brown boobies, which are only rare vagrants in European waters.
animal.whereToSee: Bass Rock (Scotland), Bempton Cliffs (England), Grassholm (Wales), St Kilda, Little Skellig (Ireland), Bonaventure Island (Quebec); offshore passage along Atlantic coasts.

funFact: After the 2022 avian influenza outbreak, many surviving gannets on Bass Rock had irises turned from pale blue to black.

wiki.extract: The northern gannet is a seabird, the largest species of the gannet family, Sulidae. It is native to the coasts of the North Atlantic Ocean, breeding in Western Europe and Northeastern North America. It is the largest seabird in the northern Atlantic. The sexes are similar in appearance. The adult northern gannet has a mainly white streamlined body with a long neck, and long and slender wings. It is 87–100 cm long with a 170–180 cm (67–71 in) wingspan. The head and nape have a buff tinge that is more prominent in breeding season, and the wings are edged with dark brown-black feathers. The long, pointed bill is blue-grey, contrasting with black, bare skin around the mouth and eyes. Juveniles are mostly grey-brown, becoming increasingly white in the five years it takes them to reach maturity.

nativeRange: Tropical islands of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic Oceans and the Caribbean

Catches flying fish in the air as they leap from the water
Forages hundreds of kilometres from the colony and often feeds at night or dusk
Occurs in several colour morphs, from white to all-brown

animal.diet: Flying fish and squid
animal.habitat: Pelagic tropical waters; nests in trees and bushes on remote islands
animal.behaviour: It often follows ships, catching flying fish flushed by the bow.
fieldMarks: Bright red feet and legs (adults)
Pale blue-grey bill with pink facial skin at the base
Variable plumage: all-white with black flight feathers, brown, or white-tailed brown morph
Slender, long-tailed booby shape
animal.voice: Mostly silent at sea; harsh, rattling squawks at the colony.

lore: The name 'booby' is usually traced to the Spanish 'bobo' (fool), from the birds' tameness when sailors landed on their islands.
funFact: The colony on Little Cayman, of several thousand pairs, is one of the largest in the Caribbean.

wiki.extract: The red-footed booby is a large seabird of the booby family, Sulidae. Adults always have red feet, but the colour of the plumage varies. They are powerful and agile fliers, harnessing the wind to fly efficiently, but they are clumsy in takeoffs and landings. They forage by catching flying fish from above the ocean's surface and by performing shallow dives. They are found widely in the tropics, and breed colonially in coastal regions, especially isolated islands such as St. Brandon, Mauritius, and the Chagos Archipelago. Although its population is declining, it is considered to be a least-concern species by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). It faces threats from climate change, competition with fisheries, human disturbance, and invasive species.

summary: The most venomous fish known, a lump of 'rock' that is invisible until stepped on. Thirteen dorsal spines inject a venom causing excruciating pain, and envenomations have been fatal.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to French Polynesia, Japan and Queensland
abilities: Thirteen grooved dorsal spines with venom glands inject verrucotoxin when pressed
Camouflage so complete that algae and hydroids may grow on its skin
Survives out of water on exposed reef flats for up to a day
Strikes and swallows prey in a fraction of a second
Can raise a lachrymal 'sabre' spine on each cheek in defence
edibleParts: flesh (sashimi, soup in Japan, China and Hong Kong)
edibilityNote: The flesh is eaten in Japan (especially Okinawa) and in Chinese cuisine after the venomous spines are removed by skilled preparers; the venom is a protein destroyed by cooking. Handling live fish is dangerous.

animal.diet: Small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Shallow reef flats, rubble, lagoons and tide pools
animal.behaviour: An ambush predator that sits motionless, sometimes half-buried, and gulps passing prey; venom is purely defensive.
fieldMarks: Lumpy, warty, rock-like body, usually mottled brown, grey or red
Upturned, almost vertical mouth with eyes high on the head
Large fleshy pectoral fins
No visible scales; skin often coated with algae or silt
animal.lookalikes: Estuarine stonefish (S. horrida) has bony ridges and a deep pit below each eye; scorpionfishes have a more fish-like shape and visible fin rays.
animal.whereToSee: Red Sea reef flats (Egypt), Great Barrier Reef, Indonesia, Maldives
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Queensland and Pacific Islanders have long feared it; Australia's Commonwealth Serum Laboratories produced the first stonefish antivenom in 1959, still the only one available.
funFact: Immersing the wound in hot water (about 45 °C) eases the pain because the venom proteins are heat-labile; antivenom is needed for severe cases.

wiki.extract: Synanceia verrucosa, the reef stonefish, is a species of venomous, marine ray-finned fish, belonging to the subfamily Synanceiinae, which is classified as being within the family Scorpaenidae, the scorpionfishes and their relatives. It is the most widespread species of stonefish, mostly found in shallow waters of the Red Sea and the Indo-Pacific. It possesses highly effective venom that can kill humans. It is the type species of Synanceia.

summary: A small, upright-swimming fish of Indo-Pacific estuaries and seagrass beds in which the male, not the female, becomes pregnant. Its species name comes from the Malay word for horse.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from India and the Persian Gulf to Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines and Hawaii
abilities: Males carry fertilised eggs in a brood pouch, supply them with oxygen and give birth to live young
Anchors itself with a prehensile tail
Moves each eye independently
Sucks prey into its tube-like snout in a few milliseconds
Changes colour to match its surroundings

animal.diet: Carnivore: copepods, small shrimp and other tiny crustaceans
animal.habitat: Shallow seagrass, estuaries, mangroves and harbours, often in murky water
animal.behaviour: Paired seahorses often greet each other each morning with a 'dance' of changing colour and linked tails.
fieldMarks: Upright seahorse with a curled tail
Yellow, black or brown with fine spots
Low crown and smooth body
Long snout
animal.lookalikes: Other Indo-Pacific seahorses are very similar; experts check spines, crown and ring counts.
animal.season: Resident

lore: Its form recalls the hippocampus, the sea-horse that pulled Poseidon's chariot in Greek myth, and Conrad Gessner illustrated seahorses in his Historiae animalium (1558). Dried seahorses (hǎimǎ) are a long-standing ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, which drives much of the trade in wild seahorses.
funFact: A male can give birth to hundreds of babies at once.

wiki.extract: Hippocampus kuda is a species of seahorse, also known as the common seahorse, estuary seahorse, yellow seahorse or spotted seahorse. The common name sea pony has been used for populations formerly treated as the separate species Hippocampus fuscus, now a synonym of H. kuda.

summary: A relative of the seahorse draped in leaf-like skin flaps, drifting through southern Australian kelp like a fragment of seaweed. As in seahorses, the male carries the eggs.
nativeRange: Southern and western coasts of Australia, from Jurien Bay (WA) to Wilsons Promontory (Vic)
abilities: Leaf-like appendages are purely for camouflage, not propulsion
Males incubate up to ~250 eggs on a brood patch under the tail
Moves using nearly transparent pectoral and dorsal fins
Sucks tiny mysid shrimp through its tubular snout

animal.diet: Mysid shrimp and other small crustaceans
animal.habitat: Rocky reefs, kelp and seagrass beds, 4–50 m
animal.behaviour: Sways gently in time with surrounding seaweed; males carry eggs for about 4–6 weeks before they hatch.
fieldMarks: Yellow-brown to olive body with leaf-like lobed appendages on head and body
Long tubular snout
Thin pale bars on the body
Unlike seahorses, the tail is not prehensile
animal.lookalikes: Weedy seadragon (Phyllopteryx taeniolatus) is red with yellow spots and has few, simple appendages; ruby seadragon is red with no appendages.
animal.whereToSee: Rapid Bay and Edithburgh jetties (South Australia), Kangaroo Island, Esperance (WA)
animal.season: Year-round; males carry eggs in summer (Nov–Mar)

lore: It is the marine emblem of South Australia and has been fully protected there since 1987.
funFact: Leafy seadragons cannot curl their tails to anchor like seahorses, so storms often wash them ashore.

wiki.extract: The leafy seadragon or Glauert's seadragon, is a marine fish. It is the only member of the genus Phycodurus in the family Syngnathidae, which includes seadragons, pipefish, and seahorses.

summary: A soft, almost jelly-like lizardfish with needle teeth that is no duck at all. Sun-dried on bamboo racks along the Mumbai coast, its pungent fillets became a famous condiment of the British Raj.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal to the South China Sea and Indonesia
abilities: Body is about 90% water, making it gelatinous and translucent
Mouth bristles with backward-pointing, barbed teeth
Gathers in huge numbers off river mouths during the monsoon
edibilityNote: Eaten fresh (fried bombil) or dried. Dried Bombay duck has a strong smell. No particular toxicity concerns.

animal.diet: Small fish, prawns and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Turbid, muddy coastal waters near river mouths
animal.size: Usually 20–25 cm; up to about 40 cm
animal.behaviour: Feeds near the surface at night and moves inshore in large shoals with monsoon floodwater.
fieldMarks: Soft, semi-transparent pale body
Large mouth with many fine, curved needle teeth
Tail fin three-lobed, with a middle lobe extended by the lateral line
Pectoral and pelvic fins long and dusky
animal.lookalikes: Other lizardfishes (Saurida) are firmer, scaled and cylindrical; Harpadon translucens has a more transparent body.
animal.whereToSee: Fish markets of Mumbai (Sassoon Dock), Karachi, Chittagong; drying racks along the Konkan coast
animal.season: Year-round; largest catches after the monsoon

lore: One theory traces 'Bombay duck' to the mail trains of the Bombay Daak, whose carriages smelled of the dried fish; another to an English corruption of 'bombil'. An EU ban on imports in 1997 over processing rules prompted a 'Save the Bombay duck' campaign in Britain.
funFact: Its genus name Harpadon means 'hook-toothed'.

wiki.extract: Harpadon nehereus, commonly known as the Bombay duck or bummalo, is a species of lizardfish. Adults may reach a maximum length of 40 cm (16 in), but the usual size is around 25 cm (10 in).

summary: One of only five living monotremes, the egg-laying mammals. A spine-covered ant- and termite-eater with a sticky tongue, it is found across almost all of Australia and in New Guinea. Females lay a single leathery egg into a temporary pouch and suckle the hatchling from milk patches, without nipples.
nativeRange: Australia (all states including Tasmania and Kangaroo Island) and lowland southern New Guinea
abilities: Lays eggs; the young ('puggle') hatches in the pouch after about 10 days
Snout carries electroreceptors that may detect insects in moist soil
Digs straight down into soil within minutes to escape predators, leaving only spines exposed
Enters torpor and hibernation, dropping its body temperature to a few degrees above the surroundings

animal.diet: Ants, termites, beetle larvae and earthworms
animal.habitat: Almost every terrestrial habitat in Australia, from snowfields to deserts
animal.lifespan: Up to about 45 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Solitary. In winter, 'echidna trains' form, with up to 10 or more males following a female nose-to-tail for days.
fieldMarks: Round, spine-covered body with cream, black-tipped spines among brown fur
Slim, tube-like hairless snout (beak)
Short legs with powerful digging claws; hind feet point backwards
Signs: snout-sized holes in soil, torn open termite mounds and ant nests, scats full of ant remains and soil; tracks show backward-pointing hind claws
animal.lookalikes: No other Australian mammal has spines. Introduced hedgehogs do not occur in Australia. Long-beaked echidnas (New Guinea highlands) are larger with longer, downcurved snouts.
animal.whereToSee: Kangaroo Island (South Australia); Tasmania, e.g. Freycinet and Cradle Mountain; Wilsons Promontory (Victoria); Royal National Park (New South Wales); widespread in bushland
animal.season: Resident; most active on mild days in spring; echidna trains June–September

lore: An echidna appears on the Australian five-cent coin. In many Aboriginal traditions stories explain how the echidna got its spines, often through a fight or punishment involving spears.
funFact: When first described in 1792 it was thought to be a type of anteater; its egg-laying was confirmed only in 1884.

wiki.extract: The short-beaked echidna, also known as the common echidna, or short-nosed echidna, is one of four living species of echidna, and the only member of the genus Tachyglossus, from Ancient Greek ταχύς, meaning "fast", and γλῶσσα, meaning "tongue". It is covered in fur and spines and has a distinctive snout and a specialised tongue, which it uses to catch its insect prey at a great speed. Like the other extant monotremes, the short-beaked echidna lays eggs; the monotremes are the only living group of mammals to do so.

summary: A wetland mole whose nose is ringed by 22 pink, fleshy tentacles, the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal. It touches its surroundings about 10 times a second and can identify and eat a prey item in a fraction of a second. It also swims and forages underwater.
nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern USA, south along the Appalachians to Georgia; also coastal Carolinas
abilities: Its star carries about 25,000 touch receptors (Eimer's organs) served by over 100,000 nerve fibres
Identifies and eats prey in as little as about 120 milliseconds, among the fastest foragers known
Smells underwater by blowing out air bubbles and re-inhaling them
Swims well and tunnels into stream banks and under ice

animal.diet: Aquatic insects, worms, small crustaceans, molluscs and small fish
animal.habitat: Poorly drained wet soils of marshes, bogs, wet meadows and stream banks
animal.behaviour: Active day and night year-round, foraging in tunnels, on the surface and underwater, even under winter ice.
fieldMarks: Unmistakable ring of 22 pink fleshy rays around the nostrils
Dark, dense, water-repellent fur
Long hairy tail (thickens in winter as fat is stored)
Broad digging forefeet; signs include molehills in wet soil and tunnels leading into water
animal.lookalikes: Eastern and hairy-tailed moles lack the star and live in drier soils; shrews are smaller with pointed snouts.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; wet meadows and bog edges in Nova Scotia and Quebec; Great Smoky Mountains National Park; Adirondacks (New York); often found by cats or in pitfall surveys
animal.season: Resident; active year-round

lore: It was described by Linnaeus in 1758 as Sorex cristatus; neuroscientist Kenneth Catania's studies since the 1990s made the star a model for how brains map touch.
funFact: Despite its appearance, the star is not used to grab food; it is purely a touch organ, while the mole's teeth do the eating.

wiki.extract: The star-nosed mole is a small semiaquatic mole found in moist, low elevation areas in the northeastern parts of North America. It is the only extant member of the tribe Condylurini and genus Condylura. It has more than 25,000 minute sensory receptors in touch organs, known as Eimer's organs, with which this hamster-sized mole feels its way around. With the help of its Eimer's organs, it may be perfectly poised to detect seismic wave vibrations.

otherNames: Fēilǜbīn yǎnjìnghóu 菲律宾眼镜猴 (Chinese)
summary: A palm-sized nocturnal primate of the southern Philippines, with each eye about as large as its brain. It is entirely carnivorous, leaping onto insects in the dark.
nativeRange: Southern and eastern Philippines: Bohol, Samar, Leyte, Mindanao and nearby islands
abilities: Turns its head nearly 180° in each direction, since its huge eyes cannot move in their sockets
Communicates with calls of up to about 70 kHz, in pure ultrasound that predators and people cannot hear
Leaps several metres between trunks with long hind legs and elongated ankle bones
Catches insects in mid-air with its hands

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects, spiders, small lizards and birds
animal.habitat: Dense lowland forest and scrub, clinging to vertical trunks
animal.lifespan: ~12 years in the wild; up to ~20 in captivity
animal.behaviour: By day it sleeps clinging upright to a stem in dense cover. It stresses easily, which is why it does poorly in captivity and under heavy tourism.
fieldMarks: Tiny primate
Huge eyes
Long, thin tail
Clings to vertical trunks
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine Tarsier Sanctuary, Corella (Bohol)
animal.season: Resident; nocturnal

lore: The Jesuit naturalist Georg Joseph Kamel described it from the Philippines around 1700, and Linnaeus named it Simia syrichta in 1758 from that account. It is now a symbol of Bohol and its tourism.
funFact: Relative to body size, tarsiers have the largest eyes of any mammal.

wiki.extract: The Philippine tarsier is a species of tarsier endemic to the Philippines. It is found in the southeastern part of the archipelago, particularly on the islands of Bohol, Samar and Leyte. It is a member of the approximately 45-million-year-old family Tarsiidae, whose name is derived from its elongated "tarsus" or ankle bone. Formerly a member of the genus Tarsius, it has since been listed as the only member of the genus Carlito, a new genus named after the conservationist Carlito Pizarras.

plates.author: Jean Baptiste Audebert

plates.long: This plate from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 'Histoire naturelle des singes et des makis' (1800) depicts a tarsier (Tarsius daubentonii) in its naturalistic pose, clinging to a branch. Audebert was a pioneer in using color printing from a single plate, a technique that allowed for great detail and lifelike representation in scientific works.

summary: A southern African termite whose colonies raise mounds several metres high above an underground nest. The mound acts like a lung, exchanging gases with the outside air while the colony farms fungus inside.
nativeRange: Southern and East Africa, including Namibia, Botswana and Kenya
abilities: Builds tall mounds with tunnel networks that use daily temperature swings to drive airflow
Farms Termitomyces fungus to digest wood and grass
Creates nutrient-rich islands that support distinct plants and animals
Workers sense and repair breaches in the mound wall within hours

animal.diet: Dead grass, wood and leaf litter, digested via fungus gardens
animal.habitat: Savanna and dry grassland
animal.size: Workers ~5 mm; queen several cm when swollen
animal.behaviour: The queen can lay many thousands of eggs a day, attended by workers in a sealed royal chamber.
fieldMarks: Tall earthen mounds with a central chimney, often several metres high
Small pale workers and larger soldiers with dark heads and strong jaws
Mounds built of reddish or pale soil matching the local ground
animal.whereToSee: Savanna of northern and central Namibia, where the mounds have been studied near Otjiwarongo
animal.season: Mounds visible all year; winged reproductives swarm after the first heavy summer rains

lore: J. Scott Turner's studies of this species' mounds in Namibia reshaped ideas of how termite mounds ventilate, and inspired 'biomimetic' building designs. Termitomyces mushrooms that sprout from mounds are a prized food across Africa.
funFact: The mound itself is not where termites live; it is an air-conditioning structure over the nest below.

wiki.extract: Macrotermes michaelseni is a species of termite in the family Termitidae, found in sub-Saharan Africa. It is associated with the fungus Termitomyces schimperi.

otherNames: Jiālāpàgēsī xiàngguī 加拉帕戈斯象龟 (Chinese)
summary: The largest living tortoise, gave the Galápagos Islands their name. Different islands have different forms, with domed shells in wet highlands and raised 'saddleback' shells on dry islands, which helped shape Darwin's thinking. The IUCN assesses each island species separately, from Vulnerable to Critically Endangered; strictly, the name Chelonoidis niger now belongs to the Floreana tortoise, which is extinct.
nativeRange: Galápagos Islands, Ecuador (Isabela, Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal, Española, Pinzón, Santiago and others)
abilities: Lives well over 100 years
Survives up to a year without food or water by storing water and fat
Saddleback forms raise their necks high to reach cactus pads
Spreads seeds and tramples paths, shaping Galápagos plant communities

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, cactus pads, fruit and lichens
animal.habitat: Dry lowlands to humid highlands of volcanic islands
animal.size: Up to ~1.5 m shell length and over 400 kg
animal.behaviour: Tortoises migrate seasonally between lowlands and highlands, wearing paths used for centuries. Small finches hop in front of them, and tortoises stretch up their necks so the birds can pick off ticks.
fieldMarks: Huge dark grey tortoise
Shell domed or saddle-backed depending on island
Long neck and heavy, elephant-like legs
Wallows in pools in the highlands
animal.voice: Males make loud, rhythmic groans during mating
animal.lookalikes: The different islands' tortoises are now treated as several species; shell shape and island tell them apart.
animal.whereToSee: El Chato and Rancho Primicias reserves on Santa Cruz island; the Charles Darwin Research Station
animal.season: Resident

lore: Spanish sailors named the islands for the galápago, an old word for tortoise. In 1835 the vice-governor told Darwin he could tell which island a tortoise came from by its shell; whalers took more than 100,000 tortoises (some estimates say 200,000) as live food for their voyages.
funFact: IUCN assesses each island form separately, from Vulnerable to Critically Endangered; the Floreana and Pinta forms were wiped out, and Pinta's last tortoise, Lonesome George, died in 2012.

wiki.extract: The Galápagos tortoise, also called the Galápagos giant tortoise, is a very large species of tortoise in the genus Chelonoidis. The species comprises 15 subspecies. It is the largest living species of tortoise, and can weigh up to 417 kg (919 lb). They are also the largest extant terrestrial cold-blooded animals (ectotherms).

summary: A tortoise of the dry scrub of India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, with bold yellow star patterns radiating across black, domed shell plates. It is one of the most smuggled tortoises in the world.
nativeRange: Northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan; southeastern India; Sri Lanka
abilities: Its star pattern breaks up its outline among grass and shadows
Its high-domed shell is hard for predators to crack or swallow
Survives hot dry seasons by eating succulent plants and being active after rain

animal.diet: Grasses, fallen fruit, flowers, succulent leaves
animal.habitat: Dry grassland, scrub forest and semi-desert
animal.behaviour: Most active in the early morning and late afternoon, and after monsoon rains.
fieldMarks: High-domed shell with raised, pyramid-like plates
Yellow or tan star pattern on each black plate
Yellow head and limbs
animal.lookalikes: The Burmese star tortoise (G. platynota) of Myanmar has fewer rays and flatter scutes and is found only in Myanmar.
animal.whereToSee: Dry scrub of Gujarat (Kutch, Saurashtra) and Rajasthan; Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh; Sri Lanka's dry zone (Yala, Wilpattu)
animal.season: Most active in the monsoon

lore: Despite being protected under Indian law, thousands are smuggled abroad as pets every year. In 2019 CITES moved it to Appendix I, banning all international commercial trade.

wiki.extract: The Indian star tortoise is a threatened tortoise species native to India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka where it inhabits dry areas and scrub forest. It has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2016, as the population is thought to comprise more than 10,000 individuals, but with a declining trend. It is threatened by habitat loss and poaching for the illegal wildlife trade. It was upgraded to CITES Appendix I in 2019 by full consensus among all member states, giving it the highest level of international protection from commercial trade. Conservation group TRAFFIC found 6,040 were seized globally that were intended to be sold in the pet trade. Currently they are commonly bred in many countries to be sold as pets.

summary: The most prized fugu, served as translucent sashimi by chefs licensed to cut away its lethal organs. Its compact genome made it a model organism for vertebrate genetics.
nativeRange: Northwest Pacific: Sea of Japan, East China Sea and Yellow Sea
abilities: Inflates with water into a spiny ball to deter predators
Liver and ovaries concentrate tetrodotoxin, a sodium-channel blocker over a thousand times deadlier than cyanide by weight
Has one of the smallest vertebrate genomes (~400 million base pairs), sequenced in 2002
Tetrodotoxin is made by bacteria and builds up through the food chain; farm-raised fish kept on a toxin-free diet are generally non-toxic
edibilityNote: Liver, ovaries and intestines can contain lethal tetrodotoxin, and toxin levels vary unpredictably between individual fish and between related species. There is no antidote, only respiratory support in hospital. In Japan only licensed chefs may prepare it, and serving the liver is banned. Never prepare or eat home-caught or uninspected pufferfish.

animal.diet: Crustaceans, molluscs, small fish
animal.habitat: Inshore sandy and muddy bottoms; juveniles in bays and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Spawns in spring on gravelly shores; adults migrate between coastal spawning grounds and deeper offshore waters.
fieldMarks: Plump, scaleless body with tiny prickles
Large black blotch with a white ring behind each pectoral fin
Dark grey-brown back with small spots, white belly
Beak of four fused teeth
White anal fin (the very similar karasu, T. chinensis, usually has a black one)
animal.lookalikes: Other Takifugu (e.g. T. poecilonotus, T. niphobles) are smaller and lack the single large ringed shoulder spot; some are more toxic in muscle tissue.
animal.whereToSee: Shimonoseki fish market, Yamaguchi (Japan's fugu capital); Seto Inland Sea
animal.season: Eaten in winter Oct–Mar; spawns Mar–May

lore: Toyotomi Hideyoshi banned fugu eating in the 1590s after soldiers died; Itō Hirobumi lifted the ban in Yamaguchi Prefecture in 1888 after tasting it in Shimonoseki.
funFact: Kabuki actor Bandō Mitsugorō VIII died in 1975 after insisting on eating four servings of fugu liver.

wiki.extract: Takifugu rubripes, commonly known as the Japanese puffer, Japanese pufferfish, tiger puffer, or torafugu, is a pufferfish in the genus Takifugu. It is distinguished by a very small genome that has been fully sequenced because of its use as a model species and is in widespread use as a reference in genomics.

summary: The heaviest spider in the world, a tarantula of northern South American rainforests that can weigh over 150 g with a leg span near 30 cm. Despite its name it seldom eats birds, feeding mostly on earthworms, insects and frogs.
nativeRange: Northern South America: Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and northern Brazil
abilities: Heaviest spider known, recorded at over 170 g
Flicks clouds of barbed, irritating hairs from its abdomen at attackers
Makes a loud hissing sound by rubbing bristles on its legs
Fangs about 2–4 cm long

animal.diet: Earthworms, large insects, frogs, lizards and small rodents; birds only rarely
animal.habitat: Deep burrows in moist soil of swampy or upland rainforest
animal.lifespan: Females 15–25 years; males only a few years
animal.size: Leg span up to about 28–30 cm; body up to about 12 cm
animal.behaviour: It sits at its burrow entrance at night and ambushes passing prey, detecting vibrations through silk threads laid around the opening.
fieldMarks: Enormous, heavy-bodied, hairy brown tarantula
Uniform brown with faint pale rings on the legs
Large, rounded abdomen with a bald patch where irritating hairs have been flicked
Mature males lack the tibial hooks found in similar Theraphosa
animal.lookalikes: Pinkfoot goliath (Theraphosa apophysis) has pinkish feet and males with tibial hooks. Burgundy goliath (T. stirmi) is darker with reddish hairs. Giant huntsman (Heteropoda maxima) of Laos has a wider leg span but is flat and lightweight.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests of Guyana, Suriname and southern Venezuela; often kept in zoos and by tarantula hobbyists.
animal.season: Year-round; nocturnal

edibilityNote: Eaten roasted by Indigenous peoples of Venezuela and Guyana, who first singe off the irritating hairs; the hairs can injure eyes and skin.
lore: The name 'bird-eater' traces back to Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium, which showed a large tarantula eating a hummingbird in Suriname.
funFact: Its venom is weak to humans, roughly comparable to a wasp sting; the hairs it flicks are usually the bigger nuisance.

wiki.extract: The Goliath birdeater is a large spider that belongs to the tarantula family Theraphosidae. Found in northern South America, it is the largest spider in the world by mass and body length, and second to the giant huntsman spider by leg span. It is also considerably longer than the largest known prehistoric spider, Mongolarachne, that had a body length of 2.46 centimeters (0.97 in). It is also called the Goliath tarantula or Goliath bird-eating spider; the practice of calling theraphosids "bird-eating" derives from an early 18th-century copper engraving by Maria Sibylla Merian that shows one eating a hummingbird. Despite the spider's name, it rarely preys on birds.

summary: A glossy black spider with a red hourglass on its belly, carrying one of the most potent spider venoms in North America. Its neurotoxin, α-latrotoxin, causes intense muscle pain and cramps, although deaths are now very rare.
nativeRange: South-eastern United States, from Florida north to about New York and west to Texas and Oklahoma
abilities: Venom contains α-latrotoxin, which makes nerve endings release neurotransmitter in a flood
Builds strong, irregular cobwebs with sticky gumfoot lines that snare walking prey
Silk is exceptionally strong and fine

animal.diet: Insects and other arthropods such as beetles, crickets and other spiders
animal.habitat: Dark, sheltered spots: woodpiles, rock walls, sheds, outhouses and under ledges
animal.lifespan: Females 1–3 years; males a few months
animal.size: Female body about 8–13 mm; male much smaller
animal.behaviour: Females hang upside down in their webs and display the red hourglass; cannibalism of males after mating happens but is less common in the wild than its reputation suggests.
fieldMarks: Female shiny jet-black with a round abdomen
Complete red hourglass on the underside of the abdomen
Often a red spot just above the spinnerets on the back
Messy, tangled web near the ground
animal.lookalikes: Northern black widow (Latrodectus variolus) has its hourglass split into two separate marks and a row of red spots on the back. Western black widow (L. hesperus) lives further west. False widows (Steatoda) are brownish and lack the red hourglass.
animal.whereToSee: Woodpiles, stone walls and outbuildings in the south-eastern US; look with a torch at night, but never touch or handle.
animal.season: Year-round in the south; most noticed late summer and autumn

lore: The genus name Latrodectus means roughly 'robber-biter' and mactans 'murderous'. During the Second World War, black widow silk was used for the crosshairs of gun and bomb sights.
funFact: Bites cause latrodectism: severe cramping abdominal pain that has been mistaken for appendicitis; an antivenom exists for serious cases.

wiki.extract: Latrodectus mactans, known as southern black widow or simply black widow, and the shoe-button spider, is a venomous species of spider in the genus Latrodectus. The females are well known for their distinctive black and red coloring and for the fact that they will occasionally eat their mates after reproduction. The species is native to North America. The venom can cause pain and other symptoms, but is rarely fatal to healthy humans.

plates.desc: Woodcut illustration of a black dove in a landscape, representing a widow.
plates.long: This woodcut depicts a black dove in a rocky landscape, a symbol used in Renaissance hieroglyphic tradition to represent a widow. The accompanying text explains that the black dove was chosen for its perceived lifelong fidelity, as it was believed never to take another mate after the death of its first.

summary: A small Amazonian canopy tanager painted in lime-green, black, scarlet, turquoise and violet. Despite its scientific name, it has never lived in Chile.
nativeRange: Amazon Basin and eastern Andean foothills, from Colombia and Venezuela through Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, the Guianas and Amazonian Brazil
abilities: Travels in noisy groups at the core of mixed-species canopy flocks
Searches undersides of leaves and twigs for insects while hanging acrobatically
Disperses small seeds of fruiting trees and epiphytes

animal.diet: Small fruits and berries; insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Canopy and edges of humid lowland and foothill forest, up to about 1,600 m
animal.behaviour: Groups of 5–10 often lead the mixed flocks that sweep through the Amazon canopy each morning.
fieldMarks: Shining apple-green head contrasting with velvety black back
Scarlet (or, in some populations, red-and-yellow) rump
Turquoise-blue underparts and violet-blue throat
Black wings and tail
animal.voice: High, thin 'tsit' and 'zeet' notes given constantly by flocks; no well-developed song.
animal.lookalikes: Seven-colored Tanager (Atlantic Forest of Brazil) has a turquoise-green head, black throat and orange rump; ranges do not overlap. Green-and-gold Tanager is largely green-gold without the black back.
animal.whereToSee: Canopy towers and forest edges in Amazonian Ecuador (Sacha, Yasuní), Peru (Tambopata, Manu) and Brazil (Cristalino).
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Nicholas Vigors named it chilensis in 1832, apparently because the specimens reached Europe from a dealer who mislabelled them as Chilean.
funFact: Its Brazilian name sete-cores means 'seven colours'.

wiki.extract: The paradise tanager is a brilliantly multicolored, medium-sized songbird whose length varies between 13.5 and 15 cm. It has a light green head, sky blue underparts and black upper body plumage.The vivid colours of the paradise tanager have been linked to underlying achromatic feather layers that enhance the brilliance of structural colours. Depending on subspecies, the behind is yellow and red or all red. The beak is black and the legs are grey. It is native to the Amazon rainforest.

summary: An intensely scarlet ibis of South American mangroves and mudflats whose colour comes from carotenoids in its crab and shrimp diet. At dusk, flocks returning to roost in Trinidad's Caroni Swamp turn the mangroves red.
nativeRange: Northern coasts of South America from Colombia and Venezuela through the Guianas to north-eastern Brazil; Trinidad and Tobago
abilities: Probes mud with a long decurved bill to find crabs and molluscs by touch
Gathers in roosts of thousands in mangrove islands
Hybridises with the American White Ibis where they meet in Venezuela

animal.diet: Crabs, shrimp, molluscs, insects and small fish
animal.habitat: Mangroves, tidal mudflats, estuaries and flooded savanna
animal.behaviour: Young birds are grey-brown and white and gradually turn scarlet over their first two years.
fieldMarks: Entirely scarlet plumage
Black tips to the outer primaries
Long, decurved, dark-reddish bill
Flies with neck outstretched in lines or V-formations
animal.voice: Generally quiet; hoarse, nasal honks and grunts in flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Roseate Spoonbill is pink with a flat spoon bill. American Flamingo is far larger with a long neck. White Ibis is white with black wingtips.
animal.whereToSee: Caroni Swamp, Trinidad (dusk boat tours); the Venezuelan Llanos; coastal Amapá and Maranhão, Brazil.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: The Tupinambá of coastal Brazil made ceremonial feather mantles from guará plumes; one held in Copenhagen's National Museum since the 17th century was returned to Brazil in 2024. It is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago.
funFact: Captive scarlet ibises fade to pink unless their food contains carotenoids.

wiki.extract: The scarlet ibis, sometimes called red ibis, is a species of ibis in the bird family Threskiornithidae. It inhabits tropical South America and part of the Caribbean. In form, it resembles most of the other twenty-seven extant species of ibis, but its remarkably brilliant scarlet coloration makes it unmistakable. It is one of the two national birds of Trinidad and Tobago, and its Tupi–Guarani name, guará, is part of the name of several municipalities along the coast of Brazil.

plates.long: This illustration shows the Guara, or Scarlet Ibis, known for its vibrant plumage and long, decurved bill. Such woodcuts were essential for disseminating knowledge about exotic species to European audiences during the Age of Discovery.

It is part of Mark Catesby's seminal work, 'The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands,' which was the first published account of the flora and fauna of North America.

summary: A glossy black ibis with a bare red face, a ragged ruff and a curved red bill. Once widespread in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, it survives in the wild mainly on Morocco's Atlantic coast, with reintroduced populations in Europe.
nativeRange: Wild colonies in Souss-Massa (Morocco); semi-wild colony at Birecik (Turkey); reintroduced in Austria, Germany, Italy and Spain; formerly Syria, central Europe and North Africa
abilities: Nests on cliff ledges in colonies
Probes soil for insects and small reptiles in dry grassland
Reintroduced European birds have learned a migration route by following ultralight aircraft
Formation flying saves energy, as studied in this species

animal.diet: Beetles, larvae, worms, lizards and other small animals
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, cliffs and semi-arid steppe and farmland
animal.behaviour: Feeds in loose flocks, probing the ground with its curved bill while walking.
fieldMarks: Black plumage glossed with green and purple
Bare red face and head
Long, curved red bill
Shaggy ruff of feathers on the nape
animal.voice: A guttural 'hyoh' or 'chrup' and various croaks at the colony.
animal.lookalikes: Glossy ibis is slimmer with a feathered head and darker bill. Cormorants fly with straight bills. Southern bald ibis lives only in southern Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Souss-Massa National Park and Tamri (Morocco), Birecik (Turkey), and reintroduced birds in Austria and Tuscany.
animal.season: Resident in Morocco; reintroduced European birds migrate to Tuscany for winter

lore: The ancient Egyptian hieroglyph 'akh', meaning spirit or shining one, depicts this ibis, and in Birecik it was traditionally believed to guide pilgrims to Mecca.
funFact: Conrad Gessner described it in Switzerland in 1555, but after it vanished from Europe it was dismissed as a mythical bird until it was rediscovered in the Middle East.

wiki.extract: The northern bald ibis, hermit ibis, or Waldrapp is a migratory Old World ibis found in open areas such as grasslands, rocky mountains, and semi-deserts, often close to running water. This 70–80 cm (28–31 in) glossy black ibis, which, unlike many members of the ibis family, is non-wading, has an unfeathered red face and head, and a long, curved red bill. It breeds colonially on coastal or mountain cliff ledges, where it typically lays two to three eggs in a stick nest, and feeds on lizards, insects, and other small animals.
