plates.long: This detailed woodcut depicts the 'Corvus sylvaticus', now known as the Northern Bald Ibis, from Conrad Gessner's 'Historiae Animalium'. Gessner's work was a landmark in natural history, combining classical knowledge with contemporary observation; this specific illustration is a rare record of a bird that would soon disappear from the European landscape.

summary: A white ibis blushed with salmon-pink, with a shaggy nape crest and a bare red face, that came within seven birds of extinction. From a handful found in Shaanxi in 1981, careful protection has rebuilt a population of thousands.
nativeRange: Formerly Japan, Korea, eastern China and the Russian Far East; now wild mainly in Shaanxi province, China, with reintroduced populations on Sado Island (Japan) and in South Korea
abilities: Probes rice paddies and streams for loaches, frogs and invertebrates
Smears a dark secretion from its neck onto its plumage, turning it grey in the breeding season
Recovered from a wild population of seven birds

animal.diet: Small fish, loaches, frogs, crabs, snails and insects
animal.habitat: Rice paddies, streams and wetlands near tall trees used for nesting and roosting
animal.behaviour: Feeds by probing its long curved bill into mud and water; nests in tall trees on wooded slopes near paddies.
fieldMarks: White plumage with a salmon-pink flush to the wings and tail, strongest underneath in flight
Bare red face and red legs
Long, down-curved black bill with red tip
Shaggy crest at the back of the head; grey head and back in breeding season
animal.voice: A harsh, crow-like 'aaa' call
animal.lookalikes: Black-headed ibis has a black head and neck and lacks the pink; spoonbills have a flat, spoon-shaped bill; egrets have straight bills.
animal.whereToSee: Yangxian County, Shaanxi, China; Sado Island, Niigata Prefecture, Japan
animal.season: Resident

lore: The toki gave its colour name 'toki-iro' (a soft pink) to Japanese, and it is the symbol of Niigata Prefecture. Japan's last native-born crested ibis, Kin, died in 2003, and the species was reintroduced to Sado from Chinese stock in 2008.
funFact: Its genus name Nipponia and species name nippon both mean 'Japan', making it one of the most emphatically Japanese names in zoology.

wiki.extract: The crested ibis, also called the Japanese crested ibis, Asian crested ibis or toki (トキ), is a species of bird in the ibis family, Threskiornithidae. It is the only species in the genus Nipponia.

summary: A bright pink wader with a flat, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps side to side through shallow water to feel for prey. Its colour comes from carotenoid pigments in the crustaceans it eats.
nativeRange: Gulf coasts of the US (Florida, Louisiana, Texas), the Caribbean, and Central and South America to Argentina
abilities: Catches prey by touch: nerve endings in the bill snap it shut on contact
Turns pink from canthaxanthin and other carotenoids in shrimp and crabs
Nests colonially in mangroves and trees with herons and ibises

animal.diet: Small fish, shrimp, crayfish, aquatic insects
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal and freshwater wetlands, mangroves and mudflats
animal.behaviour: Feeding groups wade in lines, sweeping their bills in unison.
fieldMarks: Pink body, deeper red on the shoulders and rump
Long, flat bill widening into a spatulate 'spoon'
Bare greenish head in adults
Orange tail and red legs; flies with neck outstretched
animal.voice: Mostly silent; low grunts and croaks at nesting colonies.
animal.lookalikes: American Flamingo has a very long neck and a bent, downturned bill. Scarlet Ibis is uniformly scarlet with a decurved bill.
animal.whereToSee: J. N. 'Ding' Darling NWR (Sanibel, Florida), the Everglades, the Texas coast, the Pantanal and the Venezuelan Llanos.
animal.season: Resident in Florida and the tropics; post-breeding wanderers move north in summer

lore: In the 19th century spoonbill wings were sold in Florida as fans, and plume hunting nearly wiped out the US population before protections such as the 1918 Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
funFact: The name ajaja is from a Tupi–Guaraní name for the bird, recorded by early naturalists in Brazil.

wiki.extract: The roseate spoonbill is a social wading bird of the ibis and spoonbill family, Threskiornithidae. It is a resident breeder in both South and North America. The roseate spoonbill's pink color is diet-derived, consisting of the carotenoid pigment canthaxanthin, like the American flamingo.

The work is a significant example of the hybrid

summary: A white wader with a long, flat bill that widens into a spoon at the tip. It feeds by sweeping the bill from side to side through shallow water, snapping it shut on anything it touches.
nativeRange: Breeds patchily from the Netherlands, Spain and the Danube across the Middle East and Central Asia to China and India; also on the Banc d'Arguin and Red Sea; winters in West Africa, the Mediterranean, Middle East and South Asia
abilities: Detects prey by touch with sensory receptors in its spatulate bill
Feeds day and night by sweeping through water and mud
Chicks hatch with straight, short bills that develop the spoon as they grow
Has recolonised Britain, breeding at Holkham, Norfolk, since 2010

animal.diet: Small fish, shrimps, aquatic insects, tadpoles and molluscs
animal.habitat: Shallow marshes, lagoons, reedbeds and estuaries
animal.behaviour: Feeding birds wade in lines, swinging their heads side to side in a sweeping arc.
fieldMarks: All-white plumage
Long black bill with a yellow spoon-shaped tip
Breeding adults have a bushy crest and yellow-ochre breast patch
Flies with neck outstretched, unlike egrets
animal.voice: Mostly silent; low grunting at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Little egret and great white egret have pointed bills and fly with necks folded. African spoonbill (Africa) has a red face and red legs.
animal.whereToSee: Texel and the Wadden Sea (Netherlands), Doñana (Spain), the Danube Delta, Lake Kerkini (Greece), Banc d'Arguin (Mauritania), Holkham (England).
animal.season: Summer visitor in northern Europe; resident or winter visitor in the south and Middle East

lore: Spoonbills bred in England until the 17th century and are recorded in medieval accounts as 'shovelars' served at feasts; their return in the 21st century followed recovery in the Netherlands.
funFact: The Dutch population fell to roughly 150 pairs in the late 1960s and has since grown to several thousand pairs.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian spoonbill, or common spoonbill, is a wading bird of the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae, native to Europe, Africa and Asia. The species is partially migratory with the more northerly breeding populations mostly migrating south for the winter.

summary: A small grey cliff-dweller that flicks open its wings to flash crimson patches like a butterfly while it creeps up sheer rock faces. It is the only member of its family and one of the most sought-after birds in Europe.
nativeRange: High mountains from the Cantabrians, Pyrenees and Alps through the Balkans, Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran to Central Asia, the Himalaya and western China
abilities: Climbs vertical rock faces using long claws and constant wing-flicking
Probes cracks for spiders and insects with a long, fine, down-curved bill
Descends to lower cliffs, quarries and even old buildings in winter
Sole living species of the family Tichodromidae

animal.diet: Spiders, insects and their larvae from rock crevices
animal.habitat: Damp cliffs and gorges, often near waterfalls, from about 1,000 m to over 3,000 m
animal.behaviour: Moves up a cliff in jerky hops with wings half-open, then drops back down in fluttering flight to start again.
fieldMarks: Ash-grey body and short black tail
Broad, rounded wings with large crimson patches and white spots
Long, thin, down-curved black bill
Breeding male has a black throat; white in winter
animal.voice: Song a series of thin, rising whistles, 'tu-tu-tueee'; mostly silent otherwise.
animal.lookalikes: No other bird looks the same. In flight at distance it can suggest a large butterfly or a hoopoe, but the hoopoe is much larger and has a crest.
animal.whereToSee: Gorges in the Pyrenees (Ordesa), Swiss and Italian Alps, Picos de Europa, the Taurus Mountains and the Caucasus; winter at castles and quarries in southern Europe.
animal.season: Resident at altitude; moves lower in winter (Oct–Mar)

lore: Its scientific name, coined by Johann Illiger in 1811, combines Greek 'teichos' (wall) and 'dromos' (runner), and Linnaeus had placed it among the treecreepers as Certhia muraria.
funFact: Unlike treecreepers and nuthatches, it does not use its tail as a prop when climbing.

wiki.extract: The wallcreeper is a small passerine bird found throughout the high mountains of the Palearctic from southern Europe to central China. It is the only extant member of both the genus Tichodroma and the family Tichodromidae.

summary: A round, marbled ray that stuns prey with shocks of up to about 200 volts from paired electric organs. The ancient Greeks and Romans used it to numb pain, and its electric organs later helped scientists discover how nerves signal.
nativeRange: Eastern Atlantic from the North Sea to South Africa, and the Mediterranean
abilities: Kidney-shaped electric organs in the disc generate shocks of about 70–200 V
Wraps its disc around prey and shocks it into paralysis
Buries itself in sand by day to ambush fish at night
Electric organs are rich in acetylcholine receptors, which made them a key source for neuroscience research

animal.diet: Small bottom fishes, such as gobies, hake and mullets
animal.habitat: Soft sandy or muddy bottoms, seagrass meadows and reefs, 10–100 m
animal.size: Up to about 1 m; usually under 60 cm
animal.behaviour: Lies motionless and buried; when a fish passes overhead it lunges upward and releases a burst of electric pulses.
fieldMarks: Nearly circular, soft disc with a short thick tail
Brown, mottled or marbled upper side
Two small dorsal fins near the tail and a broad tail fin
Spiracles behind the eyes with small finger-like papillae on the rim
animal.lookalikes: Common torpedo (T. torpedo) has five blue-black eyespots; black torpedo (Tetronarce nobiliana) is uniformly dark and much larger.
animal.whereToSee: Mediterranean seagrass dives (Croatia, Greece, Balearics), Canary Islands, Portuguese coast
animal.season: Year-round

lore: The Roman physician Scribonius Largus (1st century CE) prescribed shocks from a live torpedo for headaches and gout; Plato's Meno compares Socrates to the numbing narke.
funFact: The word 'narcotic' traces to the Greek narke, 'numbness', the same root as the Greek name for electric rays.

wiki.extract: The marbled electric ray is a species of electric ray in the family Torpedinidae found in the coastal waters of the eastern Atlantic Ocean from the North Sea to South Africa. This benthic fish inhabits rocky reefs, seagrass beds, and sandy and muddy flats in shallow to moderately deep waters. It can survive in environments with very little dissolved oxygen, such as tidal pools. The marbled electric ray has a nearly circular pectoral fin disc and a muscular tail that bears two dorsal fins of nearly equal size and a large caudal fin. It can be identified by the long, finger-like projections on the rims of its spiracles, as well as by its dark brown mottled color pattern, though some individuals are plain-colored. Males and females typically reach 36–38 cm (14–15 in) and 55–61 cm (22–24 in) long respectively.

summary: A mangrove fish that shoots down insects with a jet of water fired from its mouth, correcting for the bending of light at the surface. Experiments show it can learn to recognise human faces.
nativeRange: Coasts and estuaries from India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and the western Pacific islands
abilities: Spits jets of water up to about 2 m, pressing its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth to form a barrel
Shapes the jet so the water's tail catches up with its head and lands as a heavier blob
Corrects for light refraction at the water surface when aiming
Can learn to tell a familiar human face from dozens of others

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects and spiders shot from overhanging leaves; also crustaceans and small fish in the water
animal.habitat: Brackish mangrove creeks and estuaries; sometimes coastal reefs and freshwater streams
animal.lifespan: Up to around 10 years in captivity
animal.behaviour: It cruises near the surface, often in small groups, and leaps to snatch prey within reach. Group members race to the fallen prey, so shooters predict where it will land.
fieldMarks: Deep, compressed silvery-white body with a flat back from snout to dorsal fin
Four or five bold, black, wedge-shaped bars along the upper side
Large eyes and a sharply upturned mouth
Dorsal fin set far back above the anal fin
animal.lookalikes: Seven-spot archerfish (T. chatareus) has more numerous, smaller black spots and lives more often in fresh water. Spotted scat (Scatophagus argus) is rounder, with many dark spots and no flat back.
animal.whereToSee: Mangroves of the Sundarbans; Kinabatangan River (Sabah); Kakadu (Australia); public aquaria
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Western naturalists heard reports of the shooting fish from the Dutch East Indies in the 1760s. The genus name Toxotes means 'archer' and jaculatrix 'thrower of darts'.
funFact: In 2016 Oxford researchers trained archerfish to spit at one human face out of 44, which they did with over 80% accuracy.

wiki.extract: The banded archerfish is a perciform fish of the archerfish genus Toxotes. Found in brackish water, it is silvery in colour and has a dorsal fin towards the posterior end. It has distinctive, semi-triangular markings along its sides. It is best known for its ability to spit a jet of water to "shoot down" prey. Larger specimens may be able to hit prey 2 to 3 metres away. The banded archerfish may reach the displaced prey within 50 milliseconds of its hitting the water.

summary: A slow, gentle aquatic grazer of warm coasts and rivers from Florida to Brazil, related more closely to elephants than to seals. Manatees cannot tolerate cold water, so Florida's population crowds into warm springs and power-plant outflows each winter. Boat strikes and seagrass loss are its main threats.
nativeRange: Southeastern USA (Florida, occasionally north to Virginia and the Gulf coast), Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, Central America and northeastern South America to Brazil
abilities: Molars are replaced continuously from the back, moving forward like a conveyor belt as worn teeth fall out
Eats about 10% of its body weight in plants each day
Moves freely between fresh and salt water
Prehensile split upper lip grasps vegetation

animal.diet: Seagrasses, freshwater plants, algae and mangrove leaves
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, rivers, estuaries and springs warmer than about 20 °C
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary or in mother–calf pairs, but aggregates in warm-water refuges. Surfaces every few minutes to breathe, more often when active.
fieldMarks: Large, grey-brown, wrinkled body, often scarred by boat propellers and coated with algae
Broad, rounded, paddle-shaped tail
Flippers with three or four fingernails
Signs: 'footprints' (smooth circles of water) on the surface as the tail pushes down, and a nose-only breath
animal.lookalikes: Dugong (Indo-Pacific only) has a whale-like fluked tail. Amazonian manatee (fresh water only) lacks nails and usually has a white chest patch. West African manatee is very similar but lives only off West Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Crystal River and Three Sisters Springs, Blue Spring State Park and Manatee Lagoon (Florida); Swallow Caye (Belize); Puerto Rico; Laguna de Términos (Mexico)
animal.season: Florida springs November–March (cold fronts bring the biggest gatherings); year-round in the Caribbean

lore: In January 1493 Columbus recorded seeing three 'sirens' off Hispaniola that were 'not as pretty as they are painted'. Taíno peoples carved manatee bone into ritual objects such as vomiting spatulas.
funFact: A manatee's lungs lie along its back and help it control buoyancy, letting it hang motionless in the water.

wiki.extract: The West Indian manatee, also known as the North American manatee, is a large, aquatic mammal native to warm coastal areas of the Caribbean, from the Eastern United States to northern Brazil. Living alone or in herds, it feeds on underwater plants and uses its whiskers to navigate. It is divided into two subspecies, the Florida manatee in the United States and the Antillean manatee in the Caribbean, both of which are endangered and face pressure from habitat loss, pollution, and other human activity. The West Indian manatee is the largest living member of the sirenians, a group of large aquatic mammals that includes the dugong, other manatees, and the extinct Steller's sea cow.

summary: The only hummingbird that breeds widely in eastern North America. Weighing about 3 g, many cross the Gulf of Mexico nonstop, roughly 800 km, each spring and autumn.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters in Mexico and Central America
abilities: Flies nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, nearly doubling its weight in fat beforehand
Beats wings around 50–80 times per second and can hover and fly backwards
Enters nightly torpor, dropping body temperature to save energy
Pollinates tubular red flowers such as trumpet creeper and cardinal flower

animal.habitat: Open woodland, forest edges, gardens
animal.behaviour: Males perform U-shaped pendulum display dives in front of perched females.
fieldMarks: Tiny hummingbird with bright emerald back
Male has a glowing ruby-red throat that can look black in poor light
Female has a white throat and white-tipped tail feathers
Forked dark tail in males
animal.voice: Soft, rapid 'chew' chips and squeaky chatter; male wings make a high hum
animal.lookalikes: Black-chinned hummingbird (mainly western) male has a black chin with a narrow violet band; females of the two are very hard to separate. Rufous hummingbird is orange.
animal.whereToSee: Garden feeders across eastern North America; spring migrants on the Texas coast, e.g. High Island
animal.season: Summer visitor Apr–Sep in the east; winters in Mexico and Central America

lore: To the Aztecs, hummingbirds were linked with Huitzilopochtli, whose name means 'hummingbird of the south', and fallen warriors were thought to return as hummingbirds.
funFact: Its heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute in flight.

wiki.extract: The ruby-throated hummingbird is a species of hummingbird that generally spends the winter in Central America, Mexico, and Florida, and migrates to Canada and other parts of Eastern North America for the summer to breed. It is the most common hummingbird in eastern North America, having population estimates of about 35 million in 2021.

This plate comes from Jean Baptiste Audebert's 'Histoire naturelle des colibris', notable for its innovative use of metallic inks to replicate the shimmering feathers of hummingbirds.

Audebert was renowned for his innovative use of gold and oil-based colors in printing to capture the iridescent quality of hummingbird feathers, marking a significant advancement in scientific illustration.

summary: A rose-headed hummingbird of the Pacific coast whose courtship dive is, relative to body length, among the fastest known movements of any vertebrate. At the bottom of the dive its tail feathers sing.
nativeRange: Western North America from British Columbia to Baja California and Arizona
abilities: Display dive reaches ~385 body lengths per second (Clark 2009)
Outer tail feathers flutter to make a loud chirp at the bottom of the dive
Withstands around 9 g of acceleration pulling out of the dive
Stays through winter in the north, aided by garden feeders and exotic plants

animal.diet: Nectar, insects and tree sap from sapsucker wells
animal.habitat: Gardens, parks, chaparral and open woodland
animal.behaviour: A male climbs up to 40 m and plunges in a J-shaped dive past a female, ending in a sharp tail-feather chirp.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized hummingbird, green above, greyish below
Male has an iridescent rose-pink crown and throat
Female often shows a small central patch of pink on the throat
Short straight bill
animal.voice: Male gives a scratchy, buzzy song from a perch; display dive ends in a loud chirp made by the tail feathers
animal.lookalikes: Costa's hummingbird is smaller with a purple crown and a throat patch that flares down the sides. Rufous and Allen's are orange.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and chaparral along the Pacific Coast from Vancouver to Baja California
animal.season: Resident; breeds in winter and spring

lore: It is named after Anna Masséna, Duchess of Rivoli, a 19th-century French collector of hummingbird specimens.

summary: The only bird whose bill is longer than its body, excluding the tail. It reaches nectar at the bottom of long-tubed Andean flowers that no other hummingbird can use.
nativeRange: Andes from western Venezuela and Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to Bolivia, mostly 1,700–3,500 m
abilities: Bill about 9–11 cm long, longer than the bird's head and body
Main pollinator of long-tubed flowers such as Passiflora mixta and angel's trumpets (Brugmansia)
Perches with its bill pointed steeply upward to balance the weight
Grooms with its feet because it cannot reach its feathers with its bill

animal.diet: Nectar from long tubular flowers; small insects caught in flight
animal.habitat: Humid montane forest edge and shrubby clearings
animal.behaviour: It catches insects on the wing with its mouth open wide, keeping the long bill out of the way.
fieldMarks: Extremely long, straight, slightly upturned bill
Bronze-green body; male with coppery head
Forked, greenish-bronze tail
Small white spot behind the eye
animal.voice: A low, rattling 'trrr' and buzzy chips; no complex song.
animal.lookalikes: No other hummingbird has a bill nearly as long. Great Sapphirewing and incas share its habitat but have short or medium bills.
animal.whereToSee: Feeders and flowering edges at Yanacocha Reserve and Guango Lodge (Ecuador), Abra Málaga and Wayqecha (Peru).
animal.season: Resident year-round

funFact: It co-evolved with Passiflora mixta, whose floral tube is long enough that only the sword-bill can reach its nectar.

wiki.extract: The sword-billed hummingbird, also known as the swordbill, is a neotropical species of hummingbird from the Andean regions of South America. It is the only member in the genus Ensifera. Among the largest species of hummingbird, it is characterized by its unusually long bill, being the only bird to have a beak longer than the rest of its body, excluding the tail. It uses its bill to drink nectar from flowers with long corollas and has coevolved with the species Passiflora mixta. While most hummingbirds preen using their bills, the sword-billed hummingbird uses its feet to scratch and preen due to its bill being so long.

summary: The smallest bird in the world, about 5–6 cm long and under 2 g, found only in Cuba. Its eggs are the size of coffee beans.
nativeRange: Endemic to Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud
abilities: World's smallest bird, weighing about 1.6–2 g
Has one of the highest metabolic rates of any warm-blooded animal
Visits up to 1,500 flowers in a day

animal.diet: Nectar and small insects
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland edges and gardens with flowering plants
animal.behaviour: Females build a cup nest about 2.5 cm across, woven from cobwebs, lichen and bark.
fieldMarks: World's smallest bird, about 5–6 cm
Breeding male has an iridescent fiery red-pink head and throat with long lateral plumes
Upperparts bluish; female green above, pale below with white-tipped tail
Very short tail and tiny body
animal.voice: A high-pitched, jumbled twitter, often sung from a treetop
animal.lookalikes: Cuban emerald is much larger, all green with a forked tail.
animal.whereToSee: Zapata Swamp, Cuba (e.g. around Bermejas and Playa Larga); also Alejandro de Humboldt National Park
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly Mar–Jun

lore: It was described in the 1840s from Cuba and appears on Cuban postage stamps; Cubans call it zunzuncito after its buzzing.
funFact: It is smaller than some of the moths that share its flowers.

summary: A fiery orange hummingbird that makes one of the longest migrations of any bird relative to body size, travelling about 6,000 km between Alaska and Mexico. It is famously aggressive at flowers and feeders.
nativeRange: Breeds from Oregon to southern Alaska; winters mainly in Mexico, increasingly along the US Gulf Coast
abilities: Migrates about 6,000 km one way, roughly 78 million body lengths
Takes a clockwise loop route, north along the Pacific coast and south along the Rockies to follow flowering
Breeds farther north than any other hummingbird
Remembers individual flowers and when it last emptied them

animal.diet: Nectar and small insects
animal.habitat: Open coniferous forest, meadows and gardens
animal.behaviour: Males defend flower patches fiercely, chasing off much larger birds and other hummingbirds.
fieldMarks: Small, bright orange-rufous hummingbird
Male has an iridescent orange-red throat and rufous back
Female green above with rufous flanks and tail base
Aggressive at flowers and feeders
animal.voice: Hard 'chewp' chips; adult male wings make a metallic trill
animal.lookalikes: Allen's hummingbird is nearly identical; males usually have a green back, but some rufous males show green too, so many females and young can only be identified by tail-feather shape in the hand.
animal.whereToSee: Pacific Northwest and Alaskan forests and gardens; mountain meadows of the Rockies on autumn passage
animal.season: Breeds Mar–Aug in the Northwest; moves south through the Rockies Jul–Sep

lore: It was described from Nootka Sound, Vancouver Island, during the voyages of James Cook in 1778.
funFact: Its population has fallen by more than half since 1970, and IUCN moved it to Near Threatened in 2018.

Audebert's work is celebrated for its technical brilliance, particularly his pioneering use of gold and metallic pigments to replicate the shimmering, iridescent plumage of these birds in a printed medium.

plates.long: This plate, titled 'L'Eclatant', is from Jean Baptiste Audebert's landmark work on ornithology. It depicts a hummingbird with remarkable detail, utilizing advanced color printing methods of the era to replicate the metallic sheen of its plumage.

plates.long: This engraving depicts a hummingbird, referred to in the text by its Nahuatl name 'Hoitzitzil'. It serves as an early European scientific record of Mexican fauna, highlighting the bird's unique anatomy and its association with the floral nectar of New Spain.

summary: A tiny, round, cocked-tailed mouse of a bird with a voice out of all proportion to its size. It is one of the most widespread birds in Europe, from city gardens to remote sea cliffs.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia and the Himalaya to East Asia; American winter wrens are now separate species
abilities: Song is very loud for a bird weighing about 10 g
Males build several domed nests from moss and leaves, and the female chooses one to line
In hard winters dozens may pack into a single nest box or cavity to keep warm
Isolated island subspecies have evolved on St Kilda, Fair Isle and Shetland

animal.diet: Spiders and small insects gleaned from low vegetation
animal.habitat: Dense undergrowth, hedges, gardens, reedbeds, rocky coasts and moorland
animal.behaviour: Creeps mouse-like through undergrowth and log piles, then bursts out to sing from a low perch with its tail cocked.
fieldMarks: Tiny, round, warm-brown body with fine dark barring
Short tail held cocked upright
Pale eyebrow and thin, slightly curved bill
Whirring, direct flight low across gaps
animal.voice: Song an explosive, rapid outpouring of clear notes and trills lasting about five seconds; calls a hard 'tek-tek' and a dry, rattling churr.
animal.lookalikes: Dunnock is larger with a grey head and does not cock its tail. Treecreeper climbs trunks and is white below. Goldcrest is greener with a striped crown.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, woods and hedgerows anywhere in Europe; the distinct St Kilda wren on the cliffs of Hirta.
animal.season: Resident in most of Europe; northern and eastern birds move south in winter

lore: Aesop's fable tells how the wren became 'king of the birds' by riding on the eagle's back and flying highest, and on St Stephen's Day (26 December) Irish 'wrenboys' traditionally paraded a wren from door to door.
funFact: The wren appeared on the reverse of the British farthing from 1937 until the coin was withdrawn in 1960.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian wren is a very small insectivorous bird and the only member of the wren family found in the Old World, specifically in Eurasia and Africa (Maghreb). In Anglophone Europe, it is commonly known simply as the wren. It has a very short tail which is often held erect, a short neck and a relatively long thin bill. It is russet brown above, paler buff-brown below, overall finely barred darker, and has a cream buff supercilium. The sexes are alike.

It is part of Conrad Gessner's monumental 'Historiae Animalium', a foundational work in modern zoology that combined classical scholarship with direct observation and detailed illustrations.

summary: An iridescent green trogon of Central American cloud forests whose breeding males grow tail-covert streamers up to about 65 cm long, making the bird about 1 m long. It was sacred to the Maya and Aztecs and is Guatemala's national bird.
nativeRange: Cloud forests from southern Mexico to western Panama
abilities: Males grow streaming tail coverts longer than their body
Swallows wild avocados whole and regurgitates the pits, dispersing laurel tree seeds
Its green is structural colour, shifting from gold to blue
Migrates up and down mountains following fruiting trees

animal.diet: Fruit, especially wild avocados (Lauraceae); also insects and small frogs
animal.habitat: Humid montane cloud forest
animal.size: 36–40 cm, plus male tail streamers up to ~65 cm
animal.behaviour: Pairs nest in holes in rotting trees; the male's tail often pokes out of the entrance while he incubates.
fieldMarks: Male shimmering emerald-green with a crimson belly
Male's long green tail streamers up to about 65 cm
Helmet-like crest and yellow bill
Female duller green with grey breast and no streamers
animal.voice: A repeated, mellow 'kyow' and whistled 'kee-oo'
animal.lookalikes: Golden-headed quetzal lives only in South America. Trogons in the same forests are smaller, with no streamers.
animal.whereToSee: Monteverde and San Gerardo de Dota (Costa Rica), and cloud forests of Guatemala's Verapaz
animal.season: Resident; easiest during breeding Mar–Jun, often near wild avocado (Lauraceae) trees

lore: Its feathers were reserved for Maya and Aztec nobility and priests, and the god Quetzalcoatl was the 'feathered serpent'. Guatemala's currency is the quetzal.
funFact: Legend says the quetzal's red breast was stained by the blood of the Kʼicheʼ hero Tecún Umán.

wiki.extract: The resplendent quetzal is a small bird found in Central America and southern Mexico that lives in tropical forests, particularly montane cloud forests. They are part of the family Trogonidae and have two recognized subspecies, P. m. mocinno and P. m. costaricensis. Like other quetzals, the resplendent is mostly omnivorous; its diet mainly consists of fruits of plants in the laurel family, Lauraceae, but it occasionally also preys on insects, lizards, frogs and snails.

plates.title: Tudela Codex
plates.author: Anonymous Nahua tlacuilo
plates.desc: A row of seven painted birds and creatures: a grey hummingbird, a quetzal hummingbird, a small grey dove, a speckled bird, a black crow, a white owl, and a butterfly.
plates.long: This row of seven creatures from the Tudela Codex depicts various birds and a butterfly, likely serving as volátiles (fliers) associated with specific days or deities in the Aztec ritual calendar. The sequence includes the quetzal hummingbird and the owl, rendered in the traditional indigenous style with Spanish annotations.

plates.desc: A blue and green bird, possibly a quetzal, in a framed landscape.
plates.long: This hand-colored illustration from the 1577 Florentine Codex depicts the xiuhquechol bird, characterized by its vibrant green body and blue-tinted wings. The image reflects the encyclopedic efforts of Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua scribes to document the natural history and regional fauna of the Americas. Artistically, the work blends indigenous Nahua observational detail with European-style fr

plates.title: Florentine Codex, Vol. 3 (Books 10-12)
plates.author: Bernardino de Sahagún
plates.desc: Hand-colored illustration of a bird with a crest, likely a quetzal, in a landscape.
plates.long: A detailed depiction of a crested bird, identified in the text as a quetzal, known for its prized feathers. Such illustrations were crucial for documenting the biodiversity of the Americas for a European audience while preserving indigenous knowledge.

plates.title: Tudela Codex
plates.author: Anonymous Nahua tlacuilo
plates.desc: A row of six painted birds including a falcon, a green bird, an owl face, a quetzal, a red bird, and a yellow parrot.
plates.long: A sequence of six birds representing avian auguries or lords of the days. The figures include a brown falcon (totli), an owl (tecolotl), and a quetzal, rendered in the traditional Nahua tlacuilo style with early colonial annotations.

summary: Cuba's national bird, whose red belly, white chest and blue crown echo the colours of the Cuban flag. Its name tocororo imitates its repeated call.
nativeRange: Endemic to Cuba, including Isla de la Juventud
abilities: Sallies from a perch to pluck fruit and insects in hovering flight
Nests in old woodpecker holes and natural cavities
Unusual among trogons for its notched, ragged-edged tail feathers

animal.diet: Flowers, fruit and insects
animal.habitat: Shady forest of all types, from lowlands to mountains
animal.behaviour: Like other trogons it sits motionless for long periods, making it easy to overlook until it calls.
fieldMarks: Blue-violet crown and bright green back
White throat and breast; bright red belly
Long tail with uniquely notched, flared feather tips; white spotting beneath
Wings barred black and white
animal.voice: A repeated, hollow 'to-co-ro, to-co-ro', and a low 'cucuu'.
animal.lookalikes: No other trogon occurs in Cuba; Hispaniolan Trogon lives only on Hispaniola.
animal.whereToSee: Zapata Swamp (Ciénaga de Zapata), Viñales, Topes de Collantes and the Sierra Maestra.
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Cuban tradition holds that the tocororo cannot survive in a cage — a symbol of a people's love of liberty, which helped make it the national bird.
funFact: Its genus name Priotelus comes from Greek for 'saw' and 'end', for the jagged tips of its tail feathers.

wiki.extract: The Cuban trogon or tocororo is a species of bird in the family Trogonidae. It is endemic to Cuba, where it is also the national bird.

plates.desc: Hand-colored engraving of a female Narina Trogon perched on a mossy branch.
plates.long: A female Narina Trogon is depicted in profile, perched on a textured, moss-covered branch. The bird features a vibrant green back and long tail, a greyish throat, and a distinct reddish-pink lower belly. This scientific plate from the early 19th century illustrates the specific plumage characteristics of the female of the species.

plates.title: François Le Vaillant — Histoire naturelle des promerops et des guêpiers (1807)
plates.author: François Le Vaillant
plates.desc: Natural history illustration of a male Trogon (Le Couroucou damoiseau mâle) perched on a branch.
plates.long: A male Trogon is shown in profile, perched on a weathered, broken wooden branch. The bird features iridescent green plumage on its back, a pinkish-red belly, and intricate black and white barring on its wings. This hand-colored engraving is identified by the French caption as 'Le Couroucou damoiseau mâle'.

summary: A shy brown thrush with a rusty tail whose ethereal, echoing song is often called the most beautiful in North America. It is the only spotted thrush that commonly winters in the United States.
nativeRange: Breeds across Alaska, Canada, the north-eastern US and western mountains; winters in the southern US, Mexico and Central America to Guatemala
abilities: Each song begins with a long, clear note at a new pitch, followed by a cascade of flute-like phrases
Song intervals follow simple harmonic ratios similar to those of human musical scales, according to a 2014 study in PNAS
Switches from insects to fruit such as holly and dogwood in winter

animal.diet: Ground insects, spiders and worms; berries in winter
animal.habitat: Conifer and mixed forests when breeding; woodland understorey in winter
animal.behaviour: It habitually raises its tail and lowers it slowly while flicking its wings.
fieldMarks: Warm reddish tail contrasting with olive-brown or greyish back
Spotted breast, spots smaller and smudgier than a Wood Thrush's
Thin, complete whitish eye-ring
Slow tail-raising habit
animal.voice: A clear, sustained opening whistle followed by a spiralling cascade of flute-like notes, each song at a different pitch; call a low 'chuck'.
animal.lookalikes: Swainson's Thrush has buffy 'spectacles' and a uniform brown tail. Veery is tawny with faint spots. Wood Thrush is rufous on the head, with bold round spots. Fox Sparrow has a conical bill.
animal.whereToSee: Northern and mountain conifer forests in summer (e.g. Adirondacks, Green Mountains, Rockies); southern US woodlands in winter.
animal.season: Summer visitor in the north, Apr–Oct; winter visitor in the south, Oct–Apr

lore: In Walt Whitman's elegy for Abraham Lincoln, 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' (1865), a hermit thrush sings from the swamp; it is Vermont's state bird.
funFact: Its genus name Catharus comes from Greek katharos, 'pure' or 'clean'.

Catesby was the first to provide a comprehensive, illustrated account of the flora and fauna of North America, often depicting animals alongside their primary food sources or habitats.

summary: A plump, cinnamon-backed thrush of eastern forests with bold black spots on a white breast. Its flute-like song is one of the most celebrated sounds in North American nature, produced partly by singing two notes at once.
nativeRange: Breeds in eastern North America; winters from southern Mexico to Panama
abilities: Its two-sided syrinx lets it sound two independent notes simultaneously, harmonising with itself
Migrates at night across or around the Gulf of Mexico
Forages by flicking through leaf litter for invertebrates
Relies on calcium-rich prey such as snails when laying eggs

animal.diet: Leaf-litter insects, spiders, snails and earthworms; fruit before migration
animal.habitat: Moist, mature deciduous and mixed forest with a shrubby understorey
animal.behaviour: It often adds white material — paper, plastic or birch bark — to the base of its nest.
fieldMarks: Bright cinnamon-rufous upperparts, brightest on the crown and nape
White underparts with large, round black spots
Bold white eye-ring
Plump, short-tailed thrush shape
animal.voice: A three-part song: soft introductory notes, a liquid flute-like 'ee-oh-lay', then a trilled, buzzy flourish that may contain two notes at once; call a rapid 'pit-pit-pit'.
animal.lookalikes: Hermit Thrush has a rufous tail contrasting with a browner back and smaller spots. Veery has only faint spotting. Brown Thrasher has a long tail, yellow eyes, wing bars and streaks rather than round spots.
animal.whereToSee: Shady deciduous forest across the eastern US — e.g. Great Smoky Mountains, Shenandoah, Rock Creek Park in Washington DC; dusk is the best time to hear it.
animal.season: Summer visitor, late Apr–Sep

lore: Henry David Thoreau praised its song repeatedly in his journals as the finest of any bird, and it has been the official bird of the District of Columbia since 1938.
funFact: Breeding Bird Survey counts show the wood thrush has declined by roughly half since the 1960s, largely through forest fragmentation and wintering-habitat loss.

wiki.extract: The wood thrush is a North American passerine bird in the family Turdidae and is the only species placed in the genus Hylocichla. It is closely related to other thrushes such as the American robin and is widely distributed across North America, wintering in Central America and southern Mexico. The wood thrush is the official bird of the District of Columbia.

summary: A small thrush of open country, sky-blue above and rusty-orange below, that nests in tree holes and nest boxes. Its comeback after mid-20th-century declines is one of the great successes of backyard conservation.
nativeRange: Eastern North America from southern Canada to the Gulf coast, with resident populations in the highlands of Mexico and Central America to Nicaragua
abilities: Spots insects in grass from a perch at up to tens of metres and drops onto them
Raises two or three broods a year, with earlier young sometimes helping feed later ones
Readily adopts nest boxes, which helped it recover after starlings and House Sparrows took natural cavities

animal.diet: Ground insects such as grasshoppers, crickets and beetles; berries in winter
animal.habitat: Meadows, pastures, orchards, golf courses and open pine woods with scattered perches
animal.behaviour: Bluebird 'trails' of nest boxes along roadsides and fences, promoted by the North American Bluebird Society (founded 1978), now support a large share of the population.
fieldMarks: Male: vivid royal-blue upperparts, rusty-orange throat and breast, white belly
Female: greyish above with blue wings and tail, paler orange breast
Upright posture on wires and fence posts
Juveniles grey-brown with spotted breasts and blue in the wings
animal.voice: A soft, low, gurgling warble, often rendered 'tur-a-lee, tur-a-lee'; call a gentle 'tu-a-wee'.
animal.lookalikes: Western Bluebird has a blue (not orange) throat and often a rusty back. Mountain Bluebird lacks orange. Indigo Bunting is blue all over with a conical bill.
animal.whereToSee: Nest-box trails, pastures and golf courses across the eastern US; easy in winter in the south-east.
animal.season: Resident in the southern US; summer visitor in the north, Mar–Oct

lore: Henry David Thoreau wrote in his journal that 'the bluebird carries the sky on his back'; it is the state bird of Missouri and New York.
funFact: Like the blue jay's, its blue is structural: tiny air pockets in the feathers scatter blue light, and a crushed feather looks brown.

wiki.extract: The eastern bluebird is a small North American migratory thrush found in open woodlands, farmlands, and orchards.

Catesby was among the first to illustrate birds in their natural habitats, often pairing them with the specific plants they frequented, a revolutionary approach for 18th-century natural history that provided a more complete ecological context.

summary: A thrush whose males are jet black with a golden-orange bill and eye-ring. Its unhurried, fluty song is one of the defining sounds of European towns at dusk. It moved from forest into cities in the 19th century, and was later introduced to Australia and New Zealand.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, Turkey, the Caucasus, Iran and Central Asia; introduced to Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Urban populations sing at higher pitch, start earlier in the day and are more sedentary than forest birds
Locates earthworms by sight, cocking its head before stabbing into lawns
Spreads seeds of hawthorn, ivy, yew and other berry-bearing plants
Gives distinct alarm calls for ground predators and for hawks

animal.diet: Earthworms, insects, snails; fruit and berries in autumn and winter
animal.habitat: Woodland, hedges, parks, gardens and towns
animal.behaviour: Turns over leaf litter by flicking it aside with its bill, and at dusk 'chinks' loudly while going to roost.
fieldMarks: Adult male all-black with a bright orange-yellow bill and eye-ring
Female dark brown with a faintly mottled throat and breast
Long tail, often raised on landing
First-year males have a dark bill and brownish wings
animal.voice: Song a slow, mellow, fluting warble in relaxed phrases that often trail off into squeaky twitters; alarm a frantic, rattling 'chink-chink-chink' and a thin 'tsee' for aerial predators.
animal.lookalikes: Ring ouzel males have a white crescent on the breast and pale wing panels. Common starling is smaller, short-tailed, glossy and spotted, and walks rather than hops. Females can suggest song thrushes but are much darker and not boldly spotted.
animal.whereToSee: Any European park, garden or woodland; common in Moroccan and Turkish towns and Central Asian orchards.
animal.season: Resident in most of Europe; northern and eastern birds move south and west in winter

lore: The Irish quatrain 'The Blackbird of Belfast Lough', probably composed in the ninth century and preserved in later metrical tracts, is among the best-loved early Irish nature verse; the 'four and twenty blackbirds baked in a pie' of the nursery rhyme echo real Renaissance banquet tricks.
funFact: Blackbirds introduced to Australia in the 1850s–60s became an agricultural pest and help spread invasive blackberry by eating its fruit.

wiki.extract: The common blackbird is a species of true thrush. It is also known as the Eurasian blackbird, or simply the blackbird. It breeds in Europe, western Asia, and North Africa, and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. It has a number of subspecies across its large range; a few former Asian subspecies are now widely treated as separate species. Depending on latitude, the common blackbird may be resident, partially migratory, or fully migratory.

summary: North America's most widespread thrush, a red-breasted lawn hunter whose caroling is often the first song heard before dawn. English colonists named it after the unrelated European robin because of its orange breast.
nativeRange: Breeds from Alaska and Canada to southern Mexico; northern birds winter south to the Gulf coast, Mexico and Guatemala
abilities: Hunts earthworms by running, stopping and cocking its head, locating prey largely by sight
Shifts from a mainly worm and insect diet in summer to fruit and berries in winter
Builds a cup nest with a mud lining, shaped by the female pressing with her breast
Lays the sky-blue eggs that gave the name 'robin's egg blue'

animal.diet: Earthworms, insect larvae, and fruit such as holly, juniper and crabapple
animal.habitat: Lawns, parks, open woodland, farmland and forest to the tree line
animal.lifespan: About 2 years on average; banding record nearly 14 years
animal.behaviour: In winter many robins form large nomadic flocks that follow fruit crops and roost communally, often unnoticed because they stop singing on lawns.
fieldMarks: Brick-orange breast and belly contrasting with grey-brown back
Blackish head with broken white eye-ring
Yellow bill; white lower belly and undertail
Juveniles have heavily spotted breasts, showing the thrush family resemblance
animal.voice: A rich, caroling series of whistled phrases, often rendered 'cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio'; calls include a sharp 'tut-tut' and a high thin 'seee' alarm for hawks.
animal.lookalikes: Varied Thrush (west) has an orange eyebrow, orange wing bars and a black breast band. Eastern Towhee has rufous only on the flanks with a white belly. Spotted juveniles may suggest other thrushes but already show some orange.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns, parks and gardens throughout the US and Canada; winter flocks in fruiting trees across the southern states.
animal.season: Resident across much of the US; summer visitor in Canada and Alaska, Mar–Oct

lore: It is the state bird of Connecticut, Michigan and Wisconsin, and its spring return has long been treated across North America as a sign that winter is ending.
funFact: Many American robins never leave the northern states in winter; they simply switch to fruit and become quiet, so their 'first of spring' sightings are often birds that were there all along.

wiki.extract: The American robin is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family. It is named after the European robin because of its reddish-orange breast, though the two species are not closely related, with the European robin belonging to the Old World flycatcher family. The American robin is widely distributed throughout North America, wintering from southern Canada to central Mexico and along the Pacific coast.

summary: A brown thrush with neat arrow-shaped spots, famous for singing each phrase two to four times over. It breaks snail shells on a favourite stone, leaving a scatter of broken shells around these 'anvils'.
nativeRange: Europe east to central Siberia, Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran; winters around the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Middle East; introduced to New Zealand and Australia
abilities: Smashes snail shells on stone anvils, an unusual tool-like behaviour in a songbird
Repeats song phrases deliberately, building repertoires of over 100 phrases
Sometimes mimics other birds and man-made sounds within its song
Northern and eastern birds migrate at night to wintering grounds as far as Arabia and North Africa

animal.diet: Earthworms, snails, insects; berries and fallen fruit
animal.habitat: Woodland with undergrowth, hedgerows, parks and gardens; winters in olive groves and scrub
animal.behaviour: Grips a snail by the lip of its shell and beats it against a stone until it shatters.
fieldMarks: Warm brown upperparts with no markings
Buff-washed breast with neat dark arrowhead spots
Orange-buff underwing visible in flight
Smaller and shorter-tailed than mistle thrush
animal.voice: Loud, clear and inventive song in which each phrase is repeated 2–4 times ('cherry-dew, cherry-dew, cherry-dew'); call a short, thin 'tsip'.
animal.lookalikes: Mistle thrush is larger and greyer with round spots, white tail corners and white underwings, and gives a dry rattle. Redwing has a bold cream eyebrow and red flanks.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and woods throughout Europe; huge numbers winter in Spanish and Moroccan olive groves.
animal.season: Resident in western Europe; summer visitor in the north and east; winter visitor to the Mediterranean and Middle East Oct–Mar

lore: Robert Browning wrote in 'Home-Thoughts, from Abroad' (1845): 'That's the wise thrush; he sings each song twice over', and Thomas Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush' (1900) uses a winter thrush as a symbol of hope.
funFact: Thrushes are still trapped and eaten illegally in parts of the Mediterranean; the bird was a prized food in ancient Rome, where Varro described aviaries fattening thousands of them.

wiki.extract: The song thrush is a thrush that breeds across the West Palearctic. It has brown upperparts and black-spotted cream or buff underparts and has four recognised subspecies. Its distinctive song, which features repeated musical phrases, has frequently been referenced in poetry.

summary: A ghostly pale owl with a heart-shaped face that can hunt in total darkness by sound alone. It is one of the most studied predators in the world for its hearing.
nativeRange: Europe, Africa, the Middle East and western Asia
abilities: Can locate and catch prey in complete darkness using hearing alone
Asymmetrically placed ears pinpoint sounds in both direction and height
Soft, fringed feathers make its flight almost silent
Facial disc acts as a dish to focus sound

animal.diet: Small mammals, especially voles, mice and shrews
animal.habitat: Open grassland, farmland and marshes with old buildings or hollow trees
animal.lifespan: Usually under 4 years in the wild; record over 15 years
animal.behaviour: It quarters low over fields on silent wings, listening for rustling voles.
fieldMarks: Heart-shaped white facial disc
Black eyes
Golden-buff upperparts finely speckled grey
White to buff underparts
Long, feathered legs
animal.voice: A long, rasping, eerie screech; also hisses and snores at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Short-eared owl has yellow eyes, streaked plumage and a round face. Eastern and American barn owls (now separate species) are very similar but live in other regions.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland and marshes across Europe and Africa; East Anglia (UK), Camargue (France), South African grassland
animal.season: Resident

lore: In European folklore the screeching barn owl was a bird of ill omen, called 'screech owl' or 'church owl'. Farmers in Israel and Jordan now put up nest boxes for barn owls as joint pest control across borders.
funFact: A barn owl pair may eat several thousand rodents in a single year.

wiki.extract: The western barn owl is a species of barn owl native to Europe, southwestern Asia, and Africa. It was formerly considered a subspecies group together with barn owls native to other parts of the world, but this classification was found to be paraphyletic with respect to some other members of the genus.

summary: A translucent, saucer-shaped jellyfish marked with four pale rings, the most familiar jellyfish of European coasts and public aquariums. Its life cycle alternates between a tiny polyp on the sea floor and the drifting medusa.
nativeRange: North-east Atlantic and adjacent seas; very similar moon jellies worldwide are now recognised as separate, cryptic Aurelia species
abilities: Polyps bud off stacks of baby jellyfish (strobilation) when water temperature changes
Blooms can contain millions of individuals and block power-station cooling intakes
Mild sting from short marginal tentacles

animal.diet: Plankton, fish eggs and larvae, caught in mucus on the bell and wiped to the mouth by oral arms
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays and harbours, often in sheltered, nutrient-rich water
animal.lifespan: Medusae usually a few months to a year; polyps can persist for years
animal.behaviour: Medusae drift and gently pulse near the surface; polyps attach to hard surfaces underneath piers and boats.
fieldMarks: Clear, flat, saucer-shaped bell
Four horseshoe-shaped rings (gonads), pale violet, pink or white
Short fringe of fine tentacles around the edge
Four frilly oral arms under the bell
animal.lookalikes: Compass jellyfish (Chrysaora hysoscella) has brown V-shaped markings radiating from the centre. Lion's mane (Cyanea capillata) is reddish-brown with a mass of long tentacles. Blue jellyfish (Cyanea lamarckii) is bluish with long tentacles.
animal.whereToSee: Harbours and bays around Britain, the North Sea and the Baltic in summer; public aquariums worldwide.
animal.season: Medusae mainly May–Sep in European waters

lore: Moon jellyfish polyps were flown into orbit aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1991 to study how gravity-sensing organs develop in microgravity.
funFact: Jellyfish raised in space had trouble swimming normally once back on Earth, apparently because their gravity sensors developed differently.

wiki.extract: Aurelia aurita is a species of true jellyfish in the family Ulmaridae and the type species of its genus, Aurelia. Before the 2020s, the species was considered cosmopolitan, but the taxon has since been split into at least 28 species. The species now identified as A. aurita is only found in the north Atlantic and in Argentina and is not dangerous to humans.

summary: A cinnamon bird with a fan-shaped crest and zebra-striped wings, named for its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call. Nesting females and chicks defend themselves with a foul-smelling secretion produced with help from symbiotic bacteria.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia and Africa; European birds winter in sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Preen-gland secretion hosts Enterococcus bacteria that produce antimicrobials, protecting eggs
Nestlings squirt faeces and hiss like snakes at intruders
Probes soil with a long curved bill for larvae and mole crickets
Raises and fans its crest in alarm and on landing

animal.diet: Insects and larvae, especially beetle grubs and crickets; small reptiles
animal.habitat: Open ground with scattered trees, orchards and vineyards
animal.behaviour: Nests in tree holes or walls, where the female's oily secretion gives the nest a strong stench.
fieldMarks: Pinkish-cinnamon bird with a fan-shaped, black-tipped crest
Black and white barred wings and tail
Long, thin, down-curved bill
Floppy, butterfly-like flight
animal.voice: A soft, hollow 'oop-oop-oop'
animal.lookalikes: Distinctive; no similar bird in its range.
animal.whereToSee: Extremadura (Spain), the Algarve (Portugal) and orchards and villages across southern Europe and South Asia
animal.season: Europe: summer visitor Mar–Sep; resident in southern parts of its range

lore: In the Qur'an (Surah An-Naml) the hoopoe brings King Solomon news of the Queen of Sheba, and in Attar's 'Conference of the Birds' (12th c.) it leads the birds on their spiritual journey. It was named Israel's national bird in 2008.
funFact: Both Leviticus and Deuteronomy list the hoopoe among birds not to be eaten, yet it became Israel's national bird.

wiki.extract: The Eurasian hoopoe or common hoopoe is the most widespread species of hoopoe. It is a distinctive cinnamon coloured bird with black and white wings, a tall erectile crest, a broad white band across a black tail, and a long narrow downcurved bill. Its call is a soft "oop-oop-oop".

summary: A black-and-white bear of the cool bamboo forests of central China that lives almost entirely on bamboo, despite having the gut of a carnivore. Decades of reserve-building helped wild numbers recover to about 1,860 adults.
nativeRange: Mountains of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu provinces, China
abilities: Grips bamboo with a 'pseudo-thumb', an enlarged wrist bone that works like a sixth digit
Eats 12–38 kg of bamboo a day and spends 10–16 hours feeding
Survives on a low-energy diet by keeping its metabolism unusually low for its size
Crushes tough bamboo stems with massive jaw muscles and broad molars

animal.diet: Herbivore in practice (~99% bamboo); occasionally carrion or small animals
animal.habitat: Temperate montane forests with dense bamboo understorey, 1,200–3,400 m
animal.behaviour: Newborns weigh 90–130 g, about 1/900th of their mother, among the smallest newborns relative to the mother of any placental mammal.
fieldMarks: Bear with bold black-and-white pattern
Black eye patches, ears, legs and shoulder band
Round face with heavy cheek muscles
Often seen sitting and eating bamboo
animal.voice: Bleats, huffs, honks and barks
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Wild pandas are very rarely seen; Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding and Wolong reserve's centres in Sichuan
animal.season: Resident

lore: The French missionary-naturalist Armand David sent the first panda skin to Paris in 1869. Since the 1950s China has lent pandas to other nations as diplomatic gifts, a practice called 'panda diplomacy'.
funFact: IUCN downgraded the giant panda from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016 as its wild population grew.

wiki.extract: The giant panda, also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China. It is characterised by its white coat with black patches around the eyes, ears, legs and shoulders. Its body is rotund; adult individuals weigh 100 to 115 kg and are typically 1.2 to 1.9 m long. It is sexually dimorphic, with males being typically 10–20% larger than females. A thumb is visible on its forepaw, which helps in holding bamboo in place for feeding. It has large molar teeth and expanded temporal fossae to meet its dietary requirements. It can digest starch and is mostly herbivorous with a diet consisting almost entirely of bamboo and bamboo shoots.

summary: A shaggy, termite-eating bear of India and Sri Lanka that vacuums insects out of their mounds. It lacks upper front incisors, can close its nostrils, and uses its protrusible lips like a suction tube. Despite its insect diet it is one of the most dangerous animals in India, attacking when surprised at close range.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan; possibly extinct in Bangladesh
abilities: Sucks termites from mounds with a whooshing noise audible 100 m away
Long, curved claws dig out termite mounds and bee nests
Mothers carry cubs on their backs for months, a habit not regularly seen in other bears

animal.diet: Termites, ants and other insects; fruit such as mahua flowers, ber and figs; honey
animal.habitat: Dry and moist forest, scrub and rocky hills with boulder caves, generally below 1,500 m
animal.lifespan: About 20 years in the wild; up to 40 in captivity
animal.size: Males 80–145 kg, females 55–95 kg; about 1.5–1.9 m long
animal.behaviour: Largely nocturnal where disturbed. Does not hibernate. Charges when startled, a defensive reaction that accounts for many human injuries.
fieldMarks: Shaggy, unkempt black coat, longest on the shoulders and neck
Pale, mobile muzzle with a long lower lip
White or yellowish U- or Y-shaped chest mark
Signs: termite mounds torn open with scattered soil; tracks show long claw marks well ahead of the toes; scats packed with termite remains
animal.lookalikes: Asiatic black bear has a neat short coat, a V-shaped crescent on the chest, round ears and lives mainly in the Himalaya and northeast. Wild boar from a distance is smaller-headed with a bristly crest.
animal.whereToSee: Daroji Bear Sanctuary (Karnataka); Satpura, Kanha and Tadoba (central India); Ranthambore (Rajasthan); Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka)
animal.season: Resident; mahua flowering (March–April) draws bears into the open

lore: For centuries the Kalandar community trained sloth bears as 'dancing bears'; through a rehabilitation programme led by Wildlife SOS and partners, the practice ended in India around 2009. Kipling's Baloo in The Jungle Book is a sloth bear.
funFact: European naturalists first classified it as a kind of sloth, naming it Bradypus ursinus in 1791 on the strength of its long curved claws and missing upper incisors; the name 'sloth bear' stuck.

wiki.extract: The sloth bear, also known as the Indian bear, is a myrmecophagous bear species native to the Indian subcontinent. It feeds on fruits, ants and termites. It is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, mainly because of habitat loss and degradation. It is the only species in the genus Melursus.

summary: The most widespread bear, from Spain and Scandinavia across Siberia to Alaska and the Rockies, including the grizzly and the giant Kodiak bear. In South Asia it survives as the pale, rare Himalayan brown bear (U. a. isabellinus) of Deosai, Ladakh and the Karakoram, a lineage genetically distinct from other brown bears.
nativeRange: Northern Eurasia and northwestern North America; isolated populations in the Pyrenees, Apennines, Carpathians, Caucasus, Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush
abilities: Hibernates for up to 7 months without eating, drinking or urinating
Can smell carcasses from several kilometres away
Salmon-eating bears carry marine nitrogen into forests when they drag fish inland

animal.diet: Omnivore: grasses, roots, berries, nuts, insects, salmon, rodents and large mammals; Himalayan bears dig marmots and graze alpine plants
animal.habitat: Forest, tundra, alpine meadows and high plateaus
animal.size: Highly variable: about 80–600 kg; coastal Alaskan and Kodiak males are largest
animal.behaviour: Solitary except mothers with cubs and gatherings at food sources such as salmon falls. Excavates its own winter den on slopes.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: prominent shoulder hump (digging muscle) and a dished face in profile
Coat ranges from near-black to blond; Himalayan bears are sandy-reddish or pale
Short, round ears
Tracks: hind print up to ~30 cm with long claw marks 5 cm or more ahead of toes, toes in a fairly straight row; signs include dug-out marmot burrows and overturned rocks
animal.lookalikes: American black bear and Asiatic black bear lack the shoulder hump, have a straighter face profile, larger ears and short curved claws. In the Himalaya, the Asiatic black bear has a white chest crescent.
animal.whereToSee: Deosai National Park (Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan); Katmai and Denali (Alaska); Yellowstone (USA); Kamchatka (Russia); Shiretoko (Hokkaido); Cantabrian Mountains (Spain); Finnish–Russian border hides
animal.season: Active roughly April–November; best viewed at salmon runs (July–September) and on Deosai in July–August

lore: The Ainu of Hokkaido held the iyomante ceremony to send a bear's spirit back to the gods. The Greek name Arktos for the bear gave us 'Arctic', the land beneath the Great Bear constellation.
funFact: Deosai National Park was created in 1993 largely to protect Pakistan's Himalayan brown bears, which numbered only around 20 there at the time.

wiki.extract: The brown bear is a large bear native to Eurasia and North America. Of the land carnivorans, it is rivaled in size only by its closest relative, the polar bear, which is much less variable in size and slightly bigger on average. The brown bear is a sexually dimorphic species, as adult males are larger and more compactly built than females. The fur ranges in color from cream to reddish to dark brown. It has evolved large hump muscles, unique among bears, and paws up to 21 cm (8.3 in) wide and 36 cm (14 in) long, to effectively dig through dirt. Its teeth are similar to those of other bears and reflect its dietary plasticity.

summary: The largest land carnivore, a bear that lives on Arctic sea ice and hunts seals. It is classed as a marine mammal, and the loss of summer sea ice is its greatest threat.
nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic: Canada, Alaska (USA), Greenland, Norway (Svalbard) and Russia
abilities: Smells seals through snow and ice from about a kilometre away
Swims for days; one female swam 687 km over nine days without rest
Survives Arctic cold with up to 11 cm of fat, black skin and hollow, colourless guard hairs
Fasts for months during ice-free summers, slowing its metabolism

animal.habitat: Sea ice over continental shelves; coasts in summer
animal.size: Males 350–700 kg and up to ~2.5–3 m; females 150–300 kg
animal.behaviour: Pregnant females dig snow dens and give birth in midwinter, nursing cubs for months without eating before leading them out to the ice in spring.
fieldMarks: Large white bear
Long neck and small head
Black nose and skin
Huge furry paws
animal.lookalikes: Brown bears have a shoulder hump and brown fur. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Churchill (Manitoba) by tundra vehicle; Svalbard by boat
animal.season: Churchill Oct–Nov

lore: Inuit hunters treat nanuq with great respect in story and ritual; one Inuit name, Pihoqahiak, means 'the ever-wandering one'. In 1252 King Henry III kept a polar bear, a gift from Norway, at the Tower of London, where it fished in the Thames on a long chain.
funFact: Eating polar bear liver can kill a person, because it holds a toxic concentration of vitamin A.

wiki.extract: The polar bear is a large bear native to the Arctic and nearby areas. It is closely related to the brown bear, and the two species can interbreed. The polar bear is the largest extant species of bear and land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300–800 kg (660–1,760 lb). The species is sexually dimorphic, as adult females are much smaller. The polar bear is white or yellowish-furred with black skin and a thick layer of fat. It is more slender than the brown bear, with a narrower skull, longer neck and lower shoulder hump. Its teeth are sharper and more adapted to cutting meat. The paws are large and allow the bear to walk on ice and paddle in the water.

summary: A rainforest bird of north-eastern Madagascar carrying a huge, arched, bright blue bill. Vangas are a spectacular radiation of birds found only on Madagascar.
nativeRange: Lowland and mid-altitude rainforest of north-eastern Madagascar
abilities: Uses its massive bill to seize large insects, lizards and frogs
Part of the vanga radiation, whose bill shapes span the range of many bird families

animal.diet: Large insects, chameleons, geckos and frogs
animal.habitat: Undisturbed lowland and mid-elevation rainforest
animal.behaviour: Sits still in the mid-canopy for long periods before sallying for prey.
fieldMarks: Enormous arched, bright blue bill
Black head and underparts
Rufous back and tail centre
Pale yellow eye
animal.voice: A long, accelerating, whistled trill descending toward the end.
animal.lookalikes: No other bird has this bill. Rufous vanga is smaller, with a white breast and pale blue-grey bill.
animal.whereToSee: Masoala National Park and Marojejy National Park
animal.season: Resident

lore: It was named in honour of the French artist Florent Prévost; it remains a prized bird for birders visiting Masoala.
funFact: It is the only member of the genus Euryceros, one of the vangas, a family that radiated into many bill shapes on Madagascar.

wiki.extract: The helmet vanga is a distinctive-looking bird of the vanga family, Vangidae, and is classified in its own genus, Euryceros. It is mainly blue-black, with rufous wings and a huge arched blue bill. It is restricted to lowland and lower montane rainforests of northeastern Madagascar. Its diet is composed of invertebrates, predominantly insects. The species is threatened by habitat loss.

The plate is part of a natural history collection by François Bouchard, reflecting the 18th-century drive to document and categorize global biodiversity through detailed artistic representation and multilingual nomenclature.

summary: A large, ground-dwelling monitor of South Asia's plains and forests. It digs out insects, scorpions and eggs with its claws and tracks food with its forked tongue. It is hunted for meat, skins and a fake 'magical root'.
nativeRange: Iran and Afghanistan through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar
abilities: Digs out prey with strong claws and can climb trees
Can run fast on land and swim
Tracks food with its forked tongue
Lives close to farms and villages without depending on water

animal.diet: Beetles, scorpions, snails, frogs, eggs, small mammals, carrion
animal.habitat: Forest, farmland, scrub and semi-desert; often in burrows or tree hollows
animal.behaviour: Active by day, digging for prey in leaf litter and termite mounds. Males wrestle while standing on their hind legs during the breeding season.
fieldMarks: Large monitor, grey-brown to yellowish with dark speckles; juveniles banded
Slit-like nostrils placed midway between the eye and snout tip
Long neck and forked tongue
Laterally flattened tail
animal.lookalikes: The water monitor (V. salvator) is darker with yellow spots or bands and has round nostrils near the snout tip; it lives near water. The yellow monitor (V. flavescens) of the Gangetic plain has bold yellow bands and a short snout.
animal.whereToSee: Common in Ranthambore, Keoladeo, Kanha, Bandipur (India) and Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka)
animal.season: Resident; inactive in cold winters in the north

lore: Legend says the Maratha general Tanaji Malusare used a monitor, Yashwanti, to scale the walls of Kondhana (Sinhagad) fort in 1670. Dried monitor hemipenes are sold illegally as 'hatha jodi', a supposedly lucky root.
funFact: Most 'hatha jodi' seized in Indian markets have turned out to be the dried genitals of male monitor lizards.

wiki.extract: The Bengal monitor, also called the common Indian monitor, is a species of monitor lizard distributed widely in the Indian subcontinent and parts of Southeast Asia and West Asia.

The plate showcases the meticulous detail and artistic quality used in 18th-century scientific documentation to categorize and present the natural world.

summary: The world's largest living lizard, found on only a handful of Indonesian islands. It ambushes deer, pigs and water buffalo, and its bite delivers a venom that stops blood clotting.
nativeRange: Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Motang and Nusa Kode (Gili Dasami), Lesser Sunda Islands, Indonesia
abilities: Has venom glands in its lower jaw that release anticoagulant toxins and cause shock
Picks up the scent of carrion from several kilometres away with its forked tongue
Females can reproduce without males (parthenogenesis), as two zoo dragons did in 2006
Can eat up to 80% of its body weight in one meal
Its serrated teeth have iron-rich orange tips that resist wear

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, pigs, water buffalo, carrion; young eat insects and geckos
animal.habitat: Hot, dry lowland savanna and monsoon forest
animal.size: Males up to ~3 m and 70–90 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Young dragons live in trees to avoid being eaten by adults and roll in dung to make themselves less appealing.
fieldMarks: Largest lizard, up to 3 m
Grey-brown with a long tail
Long forked yellow tongue
Young are greenish with yellow-black bands and live in trees
animal.lookalikes: Water monitors are smaller with yellow patterned skin; any large monitor here may be a Komodo. Never approach on foot; visits require park rangers.
animal.whereToSee: Loh Liang (Komodo Island) and Loh Buaya (Rinca), Komodo National Park — ranger-led walks only
animal.season: Resident; dry season (about Apr–Dec) is the usual visiting season

lore: On Komodo, villagers tell of a princess who gave birth to twins, a human boy and a dragon, Ora, so people and dragons are kin. Western science learned of it in 1910 through Dutch officer J.K.H. van Steyn van Hensbroek, and Peter Ouwens named it in 1912.
funFact: IUCN moved the Komodo dragon to Endangered in 2021, partly because rising seas are expected to shrink its small island habitat.

wiki.extract: The Komodo dragon, also known as the Komodo monitor, is a large reptile of the monitor lizard family Varanidae that is endemic to the Indonesian islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami, and Gili Motang. The largest extant population lives within the Komodo National Park in Eastern Indonesia. It is the largest extant species of lizard, with the males growing to a maximum length of 3 m (10 ft) and weighing up to 150 kg (330 lb).

The illustration is part of Francisco Hernández's monumental work on the flora and fauna of Mexico, reflecting the era's blend of empirical observation and inherited myth.

In alchemical tradition, this scene symbolizes the union or conflict of opposing elements, often associated with the extraction of a potent substance through the mutual destruction of the combatants. The image reflects the early modern fasci

plates.long: This detailed engraving depicts a 'prodigious winged dragon' from the museum of Cardinal Barberini. It serves as a prime example of Athanasius Kircher's efforts to document and categorize the wonders of the natural world, blending empirical observation with folklore.

The dragon is shown coiling around the elephant's legs and neck, symbolizing the natural and spiritual adversaries described in the accompanying Latin text 'De naturis serpentum'.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Monstrum capite asinino' (monster with a donkey's head), a hybrid creature combining human, avian, and reptilian features. Such illustrations were central to the works of Ulisse Aldrovandi, reflecting the early modern fascination with anomalies of nature and the blurred lines between myth and science.

Originating from Ulisse Aldrovandi's encyclopedic work 'Monstrorum Historia' (1642), such images reflect the early modern fascination with biological anomalies and the blending of natural history with mythological tradition. plates.desc: A dried and manipulated ray or skate, fashioned to look like a winged dragon or sea monster, known as a Jenny Haniver.

Such specimens were often sold to sailors and collectors as curiosities, reflecting the early modern fascination with the monstrous and the marvelous in the natural world.

plates.long: This woodcut depicts a 'Draco ex Raia effictus,' or a dragon fashioned from a ray. Such objects, known as Jenny Hanivers, were created by drying and carving skates or rays to resemble mythical creatures, serving as popular curiosities in early modern cabinets of wonder and natural history collections.

In the foreground, a winged dragon-like creature rests on the ground while a hunter with a feathered headdress aims a bow. The background shows elephants near a river, jagged mountains, and a sailing ship on the horizon.

summary: A small woodland bat with ears almost as long as its body, which it uses to hear the rustling of insects on leaves. It 'whispers' its echolocation calls and often picks moths and spiders off foliage, hovering in the canopy. It commonly roosts in the roof spaces of old houses, barns and churches.
nativeRange: Europe from Ireland and Iberia to the Urals, the Caucasus and western Siberia
abilities: Ears about three-quarters the length of its head and body
Very quiet, low-intensity echolocation, plus passive listening to prey sounds
Gleans prey off leaves and can hover
Hibernates in caves, cellars and trees, sometimes with ears tucked under the wings

animal.diet: Moths, beetles, earwigs, spiders and other arthropods
animal.habitat: Woodland, wooded gardens and parks; roosts in attics, barns, churches and tree holes
animal.behaviour: Often carries large moths to a favourite perch to eat, leaving discarded wings in piles beneath.
fieldMarks: Enormous ears joined at the base over the forehead
At rest, ears folded back under the wings, leaving the long pointed tragus showing
Fluffy brown fur, pale below; pinkish-brown face
Signs: piles of moth and butterfly wings under porches or barn rafters (feeding perches); droppings in attics
animal.lookalikes: Grey long-eared bat (Plecotus austriacus) is greyer, with a darker face and longer tragus; reliable separation often needs measurements. Other bats have much shorter ears.
animal.whereToSee: Old churches, barns and country houses in Britain and Ireland; woodlands across Scandinavia and central Europe; Bat Conservation Trust and similar guided bat walks
animal.season: Active roughly April–October; hibernates November–March

lore: Long-eared bats in church roofs are a classic part of English rural life; in the UK all bat species and roosts are protected by law. In medieval Europe bats were linked with witchcraft and the night.
funFact: It can hear a ladybird walking on a leaf, using sound alone to find prey.
