wiki.extract: The brown long-eared bat or common long-eared bat is a small Eurasian insectivorous bat. It has distinctive ears, long and with a distinctive fold. It is extremely similar to the much rarer grey long-eared bat, which was only validated as a distinct species in the 1960s. An adult brown long-eared bat has a body length of 4.5–4.8 cm, a tail of 4.1–4.6 cm, and a forearm length of 4–4.2 cm. The ears are 3.3–3.9 cm in length, and readily distinguish the long-eared bats from most other bat species. They are relatively slow flyers compared to other bat species.

summary: The world's largest hornet, with queens up to about 5 cm long and a 6 mm sting. A few dozen workers can wipe out a European honeybee colony in hours, but Japanese honeybees fight back by cooking scouts alive in a ball of vibrating bodies.
nativeRange: East Asia: Japan, Korea, eastern and central China, Taiwan and the Russian Far East; briefly established in British Columbia and Washington State (2019–2021), declared eradicated from the US in 2024
abilities: Largest hornet in the world
Workers mark a beehive with pheromone and attack in groups, decapitating thousands of bees
Venom contains a neurotoxin (mandaratoxin) and compounds that damage tissue; multiple stings can be fatal
Can fly long distances, foraging several kilometres from the nest

animal.diet: Adults drink tree sap and feed larvae with chewed insects, especially bees and other wasps; larvae give adults a nutritious liquid in return
animal.habitat: Low mountains and forest edges; nests underground in old rodent burrows or rotting root cavities
animal.lifespan: Workers a few weeks to months; colonies last one season, with only mated queens overwintering
animal.size: Queens up to about 5 cm; workers about 3.5–4 cm; wingspan around 7 cm
animal.behaviour: In late summer and autumn, workers enter a 'slaughter phase', killing a hive's adult bees and carrying off the brood to feed their own larvae.
fieldMarks: Very large size
Broad, bright orange-yellow head with large jaws
Dark brown thorax
Abdomen banded dark brown and yellow-orange
animal.lookalikes: European hornet (Vespa crabro) is smaller, with a reddish-brown head and a mostly yellow abdomen. Yellow-legged hornet (V. velutina) is dark with yellow legs. Southern giant hornet (V. soror) of southern China and Southeast Asia is very similar but darker. In North America, cicada killer wasps (Sphecius) and European hornets are commonly mistaken for it.
animal.whereToSee: Forested hills and countryside in Japan and Korea; best viewed in museums or from a safe distance.
animal.season: Queens fly in spring; workers abundant Jul–Oct

lore: In Japan, hornet larvae are eaten in some mountain regions, and a sports drink (VAAM) launched in the 1990s was based on amino acids identified in the liquid larvae feed to adult hornets.
funFact: Japanese honeybees engulf a hornet scout in a ball of hundreds of bees and shiver their flight muscles, raising the temperature to about 46 °C, which kills the hornet but not the bees.

wiki.extract: The Asian giant hornet, also known as the northern giant hornet, is the world's largest hornet. It is native to temperate and tropical East Asia, South Asia, mainland Southeast Asia, and parts of the Russian Far East. It was also briefly found in the Pacific Northwest of North America from late 2019 but was eradicated by December 2024.

summary: A heavy, slow-moving viper whose geometric pattern of purple, buff and brown disappears among the dead leaves of the African forest floor. It has the longest fangs of any snake and produces more venom than almost any other.
nativeRange: Central and East Africa, south to Zambia, Mozambique and northeastern South Africa (the West African Gaboon viper is now treated as a separate species, Bitis rhinoceros)
abilities: Fangs can exceed 5 cm, the longest of any snake
Produces some of the largest venom yields of any snake
Its geometric pattern is so effective as camouflage that it can be stepped over without being seen
Strikes and holds on to prey rather than releasing it

animal.diet: Rodents, hares, small antelope, ground birds, frogs
animal.habitat: Rainforest floor, forest edges, cocoa and coffee plantations
animal.behaviour: Famously placid: it lies still, relying on camouflage, and gives a loud warning hiss before biting. Bites are rare but cause massive swelling, tissue death and bleeding. Keep the limb still, do not apply a tight bandage, and get the person to hospital for antivenom.
fieldMarks: Very broad, flat, triangular cream-white head with a thin dark central line and dark triangles behind the eyes
A pair of small horn-like scales between the nostrils
Back patterned with pale rectangles, hourglasses and purple-brown triangles
Hugely thick body and short tail
animal.lookalikes: The rhinoceros viper (Bitis nasicornis) has two or three pairs of large nose horns and a blue, green and crimson pattern. The puff adder (B. arietans) has pale chevrons on a yellowish-brown back. The West African Gaboon viper (B. rhinoceros) has a dark triangle below each eye and larger nose horns. No harmless snake in its range has its build and head shape.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen in the wild; forests of Uganda, Kenya's Kakamega forest, coastal forest in Mozambique and northern KwaZulu-Natal
animal.season: Resident; mostly nocturnal

lore: The species name refers to Gabon, then a French colony, where the specimens used for its 1854 description were said to have been collected. The IUCN now lists it as Vulnerable, with habitat loss and collection for bushmeat and the pet trade among the threats.
funFact: Despite its fearsome armament, bites are rare: it is so reluctant to move or strike that most bites happen when someone steps on one.

wiki.extract: The Gaboon viper, also called the Gaboon adder, is a large and highly venomous species of viper found in the rainforests and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis. Like all other vipers, it is venomous, and it has the longest fangs of any venomous snake – up to 2 inches (5.1 cm) in length – and the highest venom yield of any snake. No subspecies are recognized.

summary: The pit viper behind most serious snakebites in Central America. It is common on farms and plantations, and females bear large litters. Strictly speaking, 'fer-de-lance' is the Martinique species Bothrops lanceolatus, but the name is widely used for this snake.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern South America (Colombia, Ecuador and northwestern Venezuela)
abilities: Venom causes severe swelling, blistering, tissue death and bleeding
Females give birth to large litters, often 20–40 and sometimes many more
Heat-sensing pits find warm prey at night
Thrives in banana and coffee plantations, where its rat prey is common

animal.diet: Rodents and opossums; juveniles eat frogs and lizards, luring them by twitching a pale tail tip
animal.habitat: Lowland wet forest, forest edges, plantations and pastures, often near streams
animal.size: Usually 1.2–1.8 m; females much larger than males, up to ~2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; it can be nervous and quick to strike when stepped near. Bites need hospital treatment with polyvalent antivenom, such as the ICP antivenom from Costa Rica. Keep the limb still and do not apply tourniquets, cut or suck the wound.
fieldMarks: Large, flat, arrowhead-shaped head with a sharp edge along the top of the snout
Back pattern of dark triangles with pale edges, which meet along the spine to form X shapes
Yellow or cream chin and throat (hence 'barba amarilla')
Heat pit between eye and nostril; vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: The harmless false fer-de-lance (Xenodon rabdocephalus) mimics its colours and flattens its head when threatened, but it has round pupils, no heat pits and smooth scales. Cat-eyed snakes (Leptodeira) have vertical pupils but are slender, with small heads and blotches rather than X-marks. In its range, any large, flat-headed snake with triangles along the side should be treated as a terciopelo.
animal.whereToSee: Lowland forests of Costa Rica (La Selva, Tortuguero, Osa Peninsula), Panama, and Chocó in Colombia; often seen on night walks
animal.season: Resident; most active on wet nights; births are common at the start of the rainy season

lore: Costa Rica's Instituto Clodomiro Picado, founded in 1970 and named after the Costa Rican scientist who studied snakebite in the early 20th century, produces antivenom against this species that is used across Central America and beyond.
funFact: Newborn terciopelos already carry fully working venom and fangs.

wiki.extract: The terciopelo is a species of pit viper found from north-east Mexico to northern South America. At low to moderate elevations, its habitat ranges from northeastern Mexico to Colombian and Ecuadorian Andes, as well as Venezuela. With a mass of up to 6 kilograms (13 lb), and a maximal length of 2.5 metres (8.2 ft), the terciopelo is among the largest vipers. It is light to dark brown in color, often with yellowish, zig-zag patterning on either side of its body. Dubbed "the ultimate pit-viper" for its defensiveness, large size, fangs and potent venom yield, it has a fearsome reputation, responsible for the most envenomated snakebites within its range, largely due to its proximity to humans, livestock and pets. Nonetheless, like all venomous snakes, the terciopelo actively avoids contact with humans and other larger animals, with bites generally only occurring when the snake is cornered, pursued, or threatened. No subspecies are currently recognized.

summary: The largest rattlesnake and the heaviest venomous snake in the Americas, marked with a chain of cream-edged dark diamonds. It is a snake of the longleaf pine savannas of the southeastern US, where it often shelters in gopher tortoise burrows.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States coastal plain, from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana
abilities: Heat-sensing pits between eye and nostril let it 'see' warm-blooded prey in the dark
Its rattle, built from interlocking keratin segments added with each shed, gives a loud buzzing warning
Venom destroys tissue and stops blood from clotting
Can go months between meals

animal.diet: Rabbits, rats, squirrels, birds
animal.habitat: Pine flatwoods, longleaf pine and wiregrass, sandhills, coastal dunes and barrier islands
animal.behaviour: An ambush hunter that waits beside rabbit trails for days, then strikes and follows the scent trail of the dying prey. A bite is a hospital emergency. Keep the person calm and the limb still at about heart level, remove rings and watches, and get them to a hospital for CroFab or Anavip antivenom. Do not use tourniquets, ice, cutting, suction or electric shock.
fieldMarks: Dark brown diamonds outlined with cream along the back, on an olive or brown body
Two pale diagonal lines on each side of the face, one running from in front of the eye and one behind it
Rattle at the tip of a tail banded brown and grey
Heavy body, broad triangular head, heat pit and vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: The timber (canebrake) rattlesnake has dark chevron crossbands and an all-black tail. Harmless rat snakes, racers and hognose snakes may vibrate their tails in dry leaves to make a rattling sound, but they have no rattle and their pupils are round. The rattle, diamonds and pale facial lines identify the diamondback.
animal.whereToSee: Longleaf pine forests of Florida and Georgia, such as Ocala National Forest, and coastal islands such as Little St Simons and Sapelo
animal.season: Resident; most active in spring and autumn; mating takes place in late summer

lore: In 1775 Benjamin Franklin, writing as 'An American Guesser', proposed the rattlesnake as a symbol of the colonies because it gives warning before it strikes. The coiled rattler on the Gadsden flag ('Don't Tread on Me') dates from the same period.
funFact: Rattlesnake roundups, where snakes are gassed out of gopher tortoise burrows and killed, have long threatened this species; Georgia's Claxton roundup was converted to a wildlife festival in 2012.

wiki.extract: The eastern diamondback rattlesnake is a species of pit viper in the family Viperidae. The species is endemic to the Southeastern United States. It is the largest rattlesnake species and one of the heaviest venomous snakes in the Americas. No subspecies are recognized.

summary: A thick-bodied viper of South Asia's grasslands and farmland, marked with three chains of dark, pale-edged ovals. It is thought to cause more snakebite deaths in South Asia than any other snake, because it is common in farmland where people work barefoot.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka (the eastern Russell's viper, Daboia siamensis, replaces it from Myanmar eastwards)
abilities: Its venom turns the blood's clotting system against itself, using up clotting factors so the victim bleeds uncontrollably
Hisses so loudly and so long that it is often heard before it is seen
Bears live young, often 20–40 in a litter
Venom can damage the kidneys, and sometimes the pituitary gland

animal.diet: Rodents especially; also lizards, frogs and birds
animal.habitat: Open grassland, scrub, rice and sugarcane fields; avoids dense forest
animal.behaviour: It lies coiled and still, and when disturbed it hisses hard and strikes with great force. Bites cause severe pain and swelling, bleeding from the gums and wounds, and kidney failure. Treatment is antivenom in hospital, and the 20-minute whole-blood clotting test is used to guide it. Keep the limb still and do not use tight bandages or tourniquets on viper bites.
fieldMarks: Tan to brown body with three rows of dark-brown ovals edged in black then white; the middle row runs together along the back
Large flat triangular head with a pale V or X mark and dark stripes behind the eye
Heavy body, short tail, rough keeled scales
Big nostrils and vertical pupils; no heat pits
animal.lookalikes: Confused with the harmless common sand boa (Eryx conicus), which has a short blunt tail, tiny eyes, and irregular blotches rather than neat rows of ringed ovals. Also confused with the Indian rock python (Python molurus), which has a pale arrowhead on its head, heat pits along the lips and smooth scales. The Russell's viper's large triangular head, keeled scales and very loud hiss give it away.
animal.whereToSee: Rice fields, dry grassland and rocky scrub across India and Sri Lanka; for example, the Deccan plateau and the dry zone of Sri Lanka
animal.season: Resident; most bites happen during harvest and planting seasons

lore: The species is named after the Scottish surgeon-naturalist Patrick Russell, who described the snakes of the Coromandel Coast in 'An Account of Indian Serpents' (1796). In Sri Lanka it is the tic polonga, a name long feared in rural folklore.
funFact: A Russell's viper venom test called the dilute Russell's viper venom time (dRVVT) is used in blood laboratories worldwide to test for lupus anticoagulant.

wiki.extract: Russell's viper is a species of highly venomous snake in the family Viperidae. The species is native to South Asia. It was described in 1797 by George Shaw and Frederick Polydore Nodder. It is named after Patrick Russell. Known for its extremely painful bite, it is considered one of the "Big Four" venomous snake species in the region.

summary: The smallest of the Big Four, rarely longer than a forearm, but irritable, common, and armed with a strong venom that stops blood clotting. It warns intruders with a sizzling rasp made by rubbing its saw-edged side scales together.
nativeRange: India and Sri Lanka west through Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran to parts of the Arabian Peninsula
abilities: Makes a hissing rasp (stridulation) by rubbing serrated, keeled flank scales as it loops its body into C-shaped coils
Venom can cause bleeding and clotting failure that lasts for days
Survives in hot, dry places where few other vipers can

animal.diet: Rodents, lizards, frogs, scorpions, centipedes and insects
animal.habitat: Dry rocky or sandy plains, laterite scrub, bunds of fields
animal.behaviour: Coils in a figure of eight and rasps loudly, then strikes quickly and sometimes again. Bites cause local swelling and bleeding problems, which can appear late. Anyone bitten needs hospital observation, clotting tests and antivenom. Keep the limb still, avoid tourniquets and do not cut the wound.
fieldMarks: Small, stout viper with a short tail
Pale wavy white line along each flank, with a row of pale-edged dark saddles above it
Pale cross, trident or bird's-foot mark on top of the pear-shaped head
Very rough, keeled scales; large eyes with vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: In Arabia and Africa, harmless egg-eating snakes (Dasypeltis) copy its coiling, rasping display. Egg-eaters have a small rounded head barely wider than the neck and lack the pale head cross. In India, juvenile Russell's vipers have rows of ringed ovals, not wavy flank lines. A small, rough-scaled snake rasping in dry scrub should be treated as a saw-scaled viper and left alone.
animal.whereToSee: Common in the dry plains of the Deccan and Rajasthan, the Ratnagiri coast and Sri Lanka's dry zone; often found under stones and in field bunds
animal.season: Resident; most active and most often met on warm nights after rain

lore: The Irula Snake Catchers' Industrial Cooperative in Tamil Nadu, founded in 1978 with herpetologist Romulus Whitaker, milks saw-scaled vipers and the rest of the Big Four and supplies much of the venom used to make India's polyvalent antivenom.
funFact: In parts of Africa and Asia, Echis vipers are among the snakes that cause the most snakebite deaths, and some experts think they kill more people than any other group.

wiki.extract: Echis carinatus, known as the Sindh saw-scaled viper, saw-scaled viper, Indian saw-scaled viper, little Indian viper, and by other common names, is a viper species found in parts of the Middle East and Central Asia, and especially the Indian subcontinent. It is the smallest member of the "big four" Indian snakes that are responsible for causing the most snakebite cases and deaths, due to various factors including their frequent occurrence in highly populated regions, and their inconspicuous nature. Like all vipers, the species is venomous. Two subspecies are currently recognized, including the nominate subspecies described here.

summary: A sturdy, burrowing marsupial of southeastern Australia and Tasmania, famous for its cube-shaped droppings. Its backward-facing pouch keeps soil out while digging, and its burrows give shelter to many other animals, notably during bushfires.
nativeRange: Southeastern Australia (New South Wales, Victoria, southeastern South Australia and Queensland border), Tasmania and Flinders Island
abilities: Produces cube-shaped scats, shaped by varying elasticity of the intestinal wall
Backward-facing pouch prevents soil entering when digging
Digs burrow systems up to about 20 m long
Tough cartilage plate on the rump blocks burrow entrances against predators

animal.diet: Grasses, sedges, roots and tubers
animal.habitat: Forest, woodland, heath and grassland with suitable digging soil
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; grazes slowly, but can sprint at about 40 km/h. Leaves scats on rocks and logs as territorial markers.
fieldMarks: Silhouette: low, barrel-shaped, almost tailless animal with a broad head
Coarse fur, grey-brown to sandy or black
Large, hairless, granular nose; short rounded ears
Signs: cube-shaped scats placed on rocks, logs and track edges; large burrow entrances with spoil heaps
animal.lookalikes: Southern hairy-nosed wombat has a furry nose, longer pointed ears and silkier fur, and lives in drier South Australia. Echidnas are spiny.
animal.whereToSee: Maria Island and Cradle Mountain (Tasmania); Wilsons Promontory (Victoria); Bendeela Recreation Area, Kangaroo Valley (New South Wales); Kosciuszko National Park
animal.season: Resident; often active by day in cool winter weather

lore: The word 'wombat' comes from the Dharug language of the Sydney area. The Pre-Raphaelite poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti kept a pet wombat in London in 1869.
funFact: A wombat can produce around 80–100 cube-shaped scats a night.

wiki.extract:
The common wombat, also known as the bare-nosed wombat, is a marsupial, one of three extant species of wombats and the sole extant member of the genus Vombatus. It has three subspecies: Vombatus ursinus hirsutus, found on the Australian mainland;
Vombatus ursinus tasmaniensis, found in Tasmania; and Vombatus ursinus ursinus, found on Flinders Island and Maria Island in the Bass Strait.

summary: A flattened 'sword' bill and a special heater organ that warms its eyes and brain make the swordfish a night hunter of the deep. Adults lose their teeth and scales entirely.
nativeRange: Tropical and temperate oceans worldwide, including the Mediterranean
abilities: A brown heater tissue derived from eye muscle warms the eyes and brain up to 10–15 °C above ambient water
Warmed eyes improve temporal resolution for spotting fast prey in cold, dark water
Dives daily to 500 m or more, hunting at depth by day and nearer the surface at night
Slashes prey with its flat bill rather than spearing it
edibilityNote: Among the highest-mercury commercial fish; the US FDA advises pregnant women and young children not to eat it.

animal.diet: Squid, mackerel, hake and other pelagic and deep-water fish
animal.habitat: Open ocean from the surface to about 550 m and deeper
animal.size: Commonly 3 m; record ~4.5 m and 650 kg
animal.behaviour: Solitary hunters that may bask at the surface with the dorsal fin and upper tail lobe out of the water.
fieldMarks: Long, flat, sword-like bill about one-third of body length
No pelvic fins and, in adults, no scales or teeth
Tall, rigid, crescent-shaped first dorsal fin that does not fold down
Single large keel on each side of the tail base
Dark bronze-purple back, paler below
animal.lookalikes: Marlins and sailfish have a round, spear-like bill, scales, pelvic fins and a long-based dorsal fin; swordfish's bill is flat and broad.
animal.whereToSee: Strait of Messina (traditional harpoon fishery), Florida Straits night fishing, offshore Chile and California
animal.season: Year-round; seasonal feeding migrations into temperate waters in summer

lore: Pliny the Elder described swordfish piercing ships, and the Strait of Messina harpoon hunt from tall-masted 'passerelle' boats continues a tradition dating to antiquity.
funFact: Swordfish bills have been found embedded in the wooden hulls of ships, and one became wedged in the research submersible Alvin in 1967.

wiki.extract: The swordfish, also known as the broadbill in some countries, are large, highly migratory predatory fish characterized by a long, flat, sword-like, pointed bill. They are the sole member of the family Xiphiidae. They are a popular sport fish of the billfish category. Swordfish are elongated, round-bodied, and lose all teeth and scales by adulthood. These fish are found widely in tropical and temperate parts of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, and can typically be found from near the surface to a depth of 550 m (1,800 ft), and exceptionally up to depths of 2,878 m (9,442 ft). They commonly reach 3 m (10 ft) in length, and the maximum reported is 4.55 m in length and 650 kg (1,430 lb) in weight.

summary: The only member of its family, a disc of black, white and yellow trailing a long white dorsal streamer. Despite its fame, it is notoriously difficult to keep in aquaria.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific, from East Africa to Hawaii and the Gulf of California
abilities: Long, tubular snout probes crevices for sponges
Long pelagic larval stage (up to months) lets it reach remote islands
Settles at a large size, up to ~7.5 cm, after drifting in the plankton

animal.diet: Mainly sponges, also algae and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and outer reef slopes to about 180 m
animal.behaviour: Usually seen in pairs or small groups; occasionally gathers in schools of hundreds.
fieldMarks: Tall, compressed disc-shaped body
Two broad black vertical bands on white and yellow
Very long, whip-like white dorsal filament
Protruding tubular snout with an orange saddle
Adults with small bony horns in front of the eyes
animal.lookalikes: Pennant bannerfish (Heniochus spp.) look similar but have a shorter snout, no orange saddle and a yellow rear body and tail; Moorish idol's tail is black.
animal.whereToSee: Hawaii, Red Sea (rare), Maldives, Great Barrier Reef, Raja Ampat
animal.season: Year-round

lore: The name comes from Moors of Africa, who were said to regard the fish as a bringer of happiness; it gained global fame as the character Gill in Finding Nemo (2003).
funFact: Zanclidae has just this single living species; its closest relatives are the surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae).

wiki.extract: The Moorish idol is a species of marine ray-finned fish belonging to the family Zanclidae. It is the only member of the monospecific genus Zanclus and the only extant species within the Zanclidae. This species is found on reefs in the Indo-Pacific region.

otherNames: Rì fēi xiù yǎn niǎo 日菲绣眼鸟 (Chinese)
summary: A small yellow-green bird with a crisp white ring around each eye, a lively flocking visitor to flowering camellias and plum blossom in Japanese winter gardens. It is a major pollinator of camellias in its native range.
nativeRange: Japan (including the Ryukyu and Ogasawara islands) and South Korea; populations in the Philippines and Indonesia formerly called Mountain white-eye; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Pollinates camellias and other winter flowers by feeding on their nectar
Flocks huddle tightly side by side on branches
Brush-tipped tongue laps nectar

animal.diet: Nectar, fruit and small insects
animal.habitat: Broadleaf forest, parks, orchards and gardens
animal.behaviour: Moves in active groups through blossom, hanging upside down to reach flowers; in winter flocks roost pressed close together.
fieldMarks: Small olive-green bird with a bright yellow throat
Bold white eye-ring
Pale greyish-white belly
Thin, slightly curved, pointed bill
animal.voice: A thin, high 'chii' contact call; song is a fast, twittering warble
animal.lookalikes: Swinhoe's white-eye (China, Taiwan, SE Asia) has paler flanks and a smaller yellow throat; Chestnut-flanked white-eye has rufous flanks; Japanese bush warbler is drabber with no eye-ring.
animal.whereToSee: Plum and cherry gardens in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka in winter and spring; Jeju Island in Korea
animal.season: Resident year-round; most conspicuous in winter at flowers

lore: The Japanese expression mejiro-oshi ('white-eye pushing') describes people crowded together, after the way these birds line up shoulder to shoulder on a branch. Mejiro paired with plum blossom is a classic motif in Japanese painting.
funFact: Many Japanese think of the green bird at plum blossom as the uguisu (bush warbler), but the bird most often seen there is the mejiro; the real uguisu is drab and secretive.

wiki.extract: The warbling white-eye is a small passerine bird in the white-eye family. The specific epithet is occasionally written japonica, but this is incorrect due to the gender of the genus. Its native range includes much of East Asia, including the Russian Far East, Japan, Indonesia, Korea, and the Philippines. It has been intentionally introduced to other parts of the world as a pet and as pest control, with mixed results. As one of the native species of the Japanese islands, it has been depicted in Japanese art on numerous occasions, and historically was kept as a cage bird.

summary: A brilliant yellow, brainless single cell that can spread across a square metre with millions of nuclei. It finds the shortest path through a maze, and in a 2010 experiment it rebuilt something close to Tokyo's rail network. It is an amoebozoan, not a fungus.
nativeRange: Cosmopolitan in cool, moist temperate forests
abilities: Solves mazes, finding the shortest route between two food sources (Nakagaki et al., Nature 2000)
Built transport networks linking oat flakes placed like Tokyo-area cities that matched the real rail system in efficiency (Tero et al., Science 2010)
Learns to cross bitter substances it once avoided, and can pass this habituation to another cell by fusing
Its giant single cell (plasmodium) pumps cytoplasm back and forth about every 1–2 minutes
Has over 700 mating types
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

seed.description: Spores (not seeds) black-brown, globose, spiny, about 9–11 µm, from stalked sporangia that form when food runs out
seed.dispersal: Wind-borne spores; it can also survive drought as a dry, hard sclerotium

grow.soil: Damp paper towel or agar in a Petri dish
grow.propagation: A piece of dried sclerotium or living plasmodium
steps: Place a dried sclerotium on damp paper towel or 2% agar in a covered dish
Keep in the dark at about 20–25 °C
Feed a few rolled oat flakes every day or two; remove mouldy oats
To make a maze, place oats at the ends and watch it find the route

lore: Japanese emperor Hirohito was an amateur slime-mould researcher, like the naturalist Minakata Kumagusu. Paris Zoological Park put 'le blob' on show in 2019, and French astronaut Thomas Pesquet took it to the International Space Station in 2021.
funFact: Researchers at Hokkaido University won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2008 and again in 2010 for showing that slime moulds can solve puzzles.

wiki.extract: Physarum polycephalum, an acellular slime mold, or myxomycete, is an amoeba with diverse cellular forms and broad geographic distribution. The "acellular" moniker derives from the plasmodial stage of the life cycle: the plasmodium is a bright yellow macroscopic multinucleate coenocyte shaped in a network of interlaced tubes. This stage of the life cycle, along with its preference for damp shady habitats, likely contributed to the original mischaracterization of the organism as a fungus. P. polycephalum is used as a model organism for research into motility, cellular differentiation, chemotaxis, cellular compatibility, and the cell cycle. It is commonly cultivated.
